title: What the SpaceX IPO Tells Us About China-US Competition
description: Insights from Winston Ma.
text:
Trans-Pacific View author Mercy Kuo regularly engages subject-matter experts, policy practitioners, and strategic thinkers across the globe for their diverse insights into U.S. Asia policy. This conversation with Winston Ma, Esq. — investor, attorney, author, and adjunct professor in the global AI-digital economy; partner of Dragon Global, an AI-focused family office; and adjunct professor and executive director of the Global Public Investment Funds Forum at NYU School of Law — is the 515th in “The Trans-Pacific View Insight Series.”

Describe the reasons behind the exclusion of investors from China and Hong Kong in the SpaceX IPO.

The most striking fact about the SpaceX exclusion is that it came from the American side, not from Beijing. Underwriters led by Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley were instructed in early June to reject all orders from mainland China and Hong Kong, citing ITAR [International Traffic in Arms Regulation] compliance on defense-adjacent aerospace technology. That order came a full week before the offering priced on June 11 at roughly $135 a share, valuing the company near $1.8 trillion and raising about $75 billion, the largest IPO in history.

In our 2020 interview, we discussed my book “The Hunt for Unicorns,” where I documented how CFIUS [the Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States] and FIRRMA [the Foreign Investment Risk Review Modernization Act of 2018] steadily expanded what counts as sensitive technology. Rather than risking a drawn-out, retrospective national security challenge that could complicate the deal after closing, SpaceX voluntarily executed an aggressive jurisdictional pre-clearance – private screening done before any regulator forced it. A U.S. company voluntarily excluding the world’s second-largest pool of investable capital tells you how normalized national-security self-restriction has become for any American firm with dual-use technology and global capital ambitions.

Explain the significance of Beijing’s State Council Decree 837 and Trade Secret Regulation.

Decree 837 was born from the Meta-Manus case – the first time Beijing ordered a completed transaction unwound under its foreign investment security review framework, establishing that re-domiciliation to Singapore does not sever China’s regulatory reach over technology it considers strategically Chinese in origin. Signed June 1 and effective July 1, it now codifies that principle into a formal 34-article structure governing outbound technology transfer. A parallel Trade Secret Regulation, the first major revision since 1998, newly classifies AI model weights, algorithms, and training data as protectable state assets.

As a lawyer admitted in both New York and China, I consider this China’s own “CFIUS moment”: the same substance-over-form logic Washington has long used to block inbound deals, now deployed by Beijing to control outbound ones. The “Singapore washing” strategy – relocate, reincorporate, then sell to a U.S. buyer – is now formally dead. Decree 837 is that conclusion arriving as statute.

Examine the content and impact of Xi Jinping’s January 30 Politburo speech published in Qiushi.

If Decree 837 is the defensive architecture, Xi’s Qiushi directive is the offensive blueprint. Published by the CCP magazine Qiushi on May 31, five months after delivery, his speech names quantum technology, biomanufacturing, hydrogen and fusion energy, brain-computer interfaces, embodied intelligence, and 6G as China’s “new economic growth points” to be cultivated through “extraordinary measures.”

This is not a model-layer speech; it directs state resources at the layers below and beside AI models – energy, human capital, embodied intelligence – the same foundation the National AI Fund’s subsequent DeepSeek investment was built on.

The sequencing tells you that Beijing’s AI strategy is architectural. As I argued in The Diplomat in 2021, it builds the entire stack, layer by layer, with the legal framework and the capital deployment moving in coordinated sequence.

What is the Chinese public perception of the SpaceX IPO?

This is the question Western coverage answers least well, because the framing inside China differs fundamentally. The exclusion has been read domestically less as punishment and more as confirmation – evidence that China’s own frontier companies must build comparable capacity rather than wait for access to American capital markets. That was the same logic behind DeepSeek’s decision to run its V4 model natively on domestic Huawei Ascend silicon rather than restricted Nvidia chips, at roughly one-seventh the price of comparable Western models.

Having spent a decade inside China’s sovereign capital system, I would describe the dominant reaction as muted rather than aggrieved. Domestic capital markets were already pricing frontier technology assets as strategic infrastructure rather than ordinary equity before the exclusion was announced. The SpaceX restriction does not introduce a new grievance; it closes a loop both sides had already started closing from their own side.

Assess the repercussions of the SpaceX IPO on China-U.S. competition for AI sovereignty and dominance.

As I observed in a recent Financial Times op-ed, Trump is taking a page out of China’s sovereign AI playbook. The headline is that both countries are now actively pursuing sovereign AI strategies. In June, China’s National AI Fund secured the only voting-rights stake in DeepSeek’s first outside funding round – a 50 billion yuan raise in which the Fund’s own position carried voting rights and no lock-up, a structure every other investor was denied. The same month, the Trump administration was exploring equity participation in OpenAI, building on the precedent of its $8.9 billion equity stake in Intel last year.

The SpaceX IPO exclusion is the same sovereign logic expressed as restriction rather than acquisition: control over who is allowed inside the stack, not just who owns it. Every institutional investor with cross-border AI or hard tech exposure is now operating under two simultaneously hardening regimes. The competition for AI sovereignty is no longer about who builds the better model — it is about who controls access to the capital, the chips, and now the public markets that fund the future growth.

title: Why Australia Struggles to Foster Asia Experts
description: A new government report looks at Australia’s “Asia capability” and finds the country wanting.
text:
Earlier this month, the Australian government published an inquiry into the development of the country’s Asia capability titled “Security and Prosperity in Asia: Building Asia Capability in Australia through the Education System and Beyond.” The capability this inquiry sought to evaluate includes the teaching and learning of Asian languages and cultures, alongside how best to facilitate the public’s broader regional engagement.

The report argued that Australia’s prosperity, diplomacy, and strategic independence increasingly depend on Australians developing stronger knowledge of the Asian region; yet the institutions responsible for building this capability are weakening. Without a public who have a good ability to understand and engage effectively with Asia, there is a diminished capacity for Australia to advance itself and secure its future.

The report distinguished between general Asia literacy for the broader population and the deeper specialist expertise required for diplomats, researchers, business leaders, defense officials, and policymakers. Yet the former feeds into the latter. Without a high baseline of knowledge within the general public, it is more difficult for the country to produce the critical mass of experts required to do the specialist roles. Schools should provide all students with a strong general knowledge of the region, and then universities can hone this into producing highly skilled experts with advanced knowledge.

The report highlighted that this pipeline is exhibiting serious problems. It presented evidence that fewer Australians are studying Asian languages than in previous decades, particularly in languages deemed to be the priority for the Australian government – Indonesian, Japanese, and Mandarin. These have fallen sharply in secondary schools, and declined dramatically at universities.

The study of Indonesian was singled out as facing a crisis. Indonesia is Australia’s largest near neighbor, so strategically it should be considered a vital subject. Yet the report described study of the Indonesian language as approaching “functional extinction” within the education systems of some states.

This decline risks having a compounding effect. With fewer students studying Asian languages at school, universities will reduce or close language programs due to low demand. This then diminishes the number of future teachers, academics, and researchers required to sustain the system. The report warned that Australia risks losing the institutional capacity to build the Asia expertise it requires.

There are some structural hurdles that Australia faces. The first is that responsibility of building Asia capabilities is fragmented across schools, universities, state governments, federal departments, and businesses. Because no single institution oversees the system as a whole, there is little coordination between school language programs, university pathways, workforce needs, and national strategic priorities.

Despite the report being chaired by a government MP, former Assistant Minister for Foreign Affairs Tim Watts, the report highlighted the absence of national leadership from the federal government.

The other structural hurdles are cultural, and this has two components. First, there is a deep complacency within the Australian psyche that restricts the country from investing in key capacities. It has long been identified that Australia has prospered from luck rather than effort, and this has bred an ingrained lethargic culture that prevents the country from engaging in foresight and preparedness.

The second cultural problem is one of suspicion toward the region. While Australia has become a highly multicultural society and this has created strong diaspora links within Asia, there remains a cohort of people in the country who do not see the merit in developing greater cultural knowledge of the region and often see this as a threat. The current rise of the One Nation party especially can be viewed as a revolt against the country’s geography.

Yet the thing about geography is that it cannot be changed. Mature countries understand their geographic positions and seek to take advantage of them. Australia’s run of extraordinary luck hasn’t ended, as the world’s economic center of gravity has shifted to the Indo-Pacific. That provides the country with a wealth of opportunities should it develop the skills to harness them.

The report argued that advances in AI or translation technology are no solution, that instead these are lazy ways to address the capability deficit. These digital tools are unable to replace deeper cultural understanding, contextual knowledge, and the human relationships necessary for diplomacy, economic opportunity, and broader regional engagement.

For once, Australians may be required to do some actual work. The report offered 34 recommendations that can create a path forward for Australia to enhance its Asia capabilities. These fall short of making priority languages compulsory school subjects, but they do present a blueprint for improvements. Yet these recommendations may still be futile if Australia cannot confront its own cultural resistance and lack of political will.

title: Why Did China Test a Submarine-launched Ballistic Missile?
description: July 6 was the first time that China has launched a submarine-launched ballistic missile into international waters.
text:
On July 6 China tested a submarine-launched intercontinental ballistic missile into the South China Sea. A PLA statement after the test claimed that “the missile test was a routine part of China’s annual military training program, and relevant countries had been notified in advance.”

In this episode of The Diplomat’s Asia Geopolitics Podcast, hosts Ankit Panda and Katie Putz take stock of the test and the reactions across the Pacific. July 6 was the first time that China has launched a submarine-launched ballistic missile into international waters, and only its the second launch of a ballistic missile into international waters since 1980. Also unusual: China provided notice to Australia, Japan, the United States, and others, through in some cases only half an hour.

You can subscribe to The Diplomat’s Asia Geopolitics podcast on Apple Podcasts and Spotify; and watch the episode on YouTube.
tag: China; China ICBM test; China SLBM test; China submarines

title: 12 Asian Countries Subject to Finalized US Visa Bond Program
description: The program, which launched as a pilot in August 2025, is now permanent and at present affects the citizens of 50 countries.
text:
The United States State Department has made permanent its pilot visa bond program, under which citizens of listed foreign countries seeking to obtain business or tourism visas to come to the United States may be required to pay a significant sum – a bond of up to $20,000 – to obtain a visa.

As stated in the Federal Register notice, the program will be limited to those who are applying for business visitor/tourist (B-1/B-2) nonimmigrant visas and are citizens of specific countries identified by the State Department as “failing to meet rigorous standards relating to overstays, information sharing, screening and vetting, civil, criminal and identity records, and document security.”

Among the 50 countries currently listed in the program, 12 are in Asia: Bangladesh, Cambodia, Fiji, Kyrgyzstan, Mongolia, Nepal, Papua New Guinea, Tajikistan, Tonga, Turkmenistan, Tuvalu, and Vanuatu. The State Department explicitly framed the bond as ensuring that the visa-holder will maintain their nonimmigrant status – meaning they will not apply for asylum or refugee status – and that the individual will depart as required by the limits of their visa.

The latest relevant notice, to be published in the Federal Register on August 3, claimed that the pilot program “has provided sufficient data to suggest that a visa bond program is an effective tool for enforcing compliance among bonded visa holders.”

In FY 2024, the notice stated, there were 45,488 overstays from the 50 countries currently listed for the program. In the first 10 months of the pilot, it continued, “the number of overstays was fewer than 50.” Notably, the rates of visa issuances also dropped dramatically, falling by 83 percent compared to the same 10-month period in the prior year. Nearly half of the 20,000 applicants during the pilot period who were mandated to pay bonds in order to secure their visa decided not to. The notice put it like this: “some applicants appear to self-select by not paying a bond.” (Note: That “self-select” is perhaps better read as “self-reject.”)

The State Department understood this decline in overstay rates as the direct result of the bond program. There are, however, other ways to interpret these points of data. Dramatically fewer visas means dramatically fewer overstays.

The American reputation is not all that welcoming these days. According to data from the National Travel and Tourism Office and reporting by CNN, 4 million fewer foreign visitors visited the United States in 2025 compared to 2024. 2025 represented the worst single-year decline in tourism travel to the U.S. in two decades, excluding the 2020 pandemic. People, simply put, are less interested in traveling to the United States. The Trump administration’s widespread crackdown on immigration – of all kinds – has resulted in violence, including the killing of U.S. and foreign citizens by immigration agents.

For those foreigners who still want to visit the United States for tourism or business, the bond program adds yet another hurdle to an already arduous and, in some cases, expensive process. Non-petition-based nonimmigrant visas require a nonrefundable fee of $185, paid when submitting an application and scheduling an interview appointment. During the interview, for citizens of the listed countries, the consular officer decides whether a visa bond will be required – either $10,000, $15,000, or $20,000. The visa will then be denied. The denial can be overcome if the bond is paid; otherwise it stands as denial. The bond can be posted by the applicant or a third party, such as a friend, family member, or business associate. Once the bond is paid, the application will be reviewed again – the consular officer can decide to approve or deny the visa. If the visa is denied, the bond will be canceled; if it is approved, the bond becomes returnable once the visa expires and if the individual is no longer still in the United States.

Of the 12 Asian countries currently listed, three are in Central Asia (Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, and Turkmenistan), one is in East Asia (Mongolia), two are in South Asia (Bangladesh and Nepal), two are in Southeast Asia (Cambodia and Papua New Guinea), and four are in Oceania (Fiji, Tonga, Tuvalu, and Vanuatu).

As I’ve covered previously, the Trump administration’s hyperfocus on overstay rates – that is, the percentage rather than the actual number – draws a target on countries from which relatively few people travel to the U.S. at all. If the goal of the program is reduce the actual number of overstays, Tuvalu may not be country to punish.

In January I dug into the data:

I’ve written previously in depth about Turkmenistan, which does have a relatively high overstay rate – 15.89 percent in 2024 for B-1/B-02 visa holders – and the reasons this measure is deceptive. That 15.89 percent figure represents just 320 people. Tajikistan’s overstay rate in 2024 was 7.57 percent, or 140 individual overstays. Kyrgyzstan’s overstay rate was lower than Turkmenistan’s, at 8.39 percent, but because of the higher number of travelers from Kyrgyzstan represented 643 people.

For other countries, the listing makes even less sense – the numbers are even lower.

Tuvalu had an overstay rate of 11.63 percent in 2024 for B-1/B-02 visa holders. Out of 43 expected departures, five people overstayed their visas. Vanuatu had an overstay rate of 3.05 percent – hardly high – representing only five people as well. Fiji’s overstay rate in 2024 for business and tourism visas was just under 4 percent, or 294 overstays. Tonga’s rate was twice that of Fiji’s – 6.45 percent – but that figure represents just 152 overstays.

Bangladesh’s overstay rate in 2024 was 5.73 percent, representing more than 2,200 overstays. While Nepal saw just over 1,000 overstays in 2024, its rate was just 3.12 percent. And Bhutan? While it had one of the highest overstay rates in the entire world – 21.75 percent – this represented just 92 individual overstays.

Furthermore, the reality is that even the lowest current end of the visa bond – $10,000 – represents an almost impossible sum for many people. The average gross monthly salary in Turkmenistan, according to wage.is, is estimated at around $714. In Tuvalu it’s $551. In Bangladesh, that figure is just $149.
tag: Fiji; Trump administration; Trump administration immigration policy; Tuvalu; US visa bond program; Vanuatu

title: A Golden Chance to Protect the Pacific’s ‘Blue Corridors’
description: If Albanese is serious about a Pacific COP, he must heed the region’s call on oceans.
text:
The next few months will see a flurry of climate diplomacy involving the Pacific Islands. Later this week, regional leaders are heading to Palau for the Pacific Islands Forum, with this year’s meeting expected to put ocean protection at the forefront. In early October, the world will travel to Fiji and Tuvalu for the pre-COP meeting; in November, Australia will preside over COP31 in Antalya, Turkiye.

Between now and then, Australia has a rare opportunity: to use its COP31 presidency and the new High Seas Treaty to help create connected protection across the Pacific and the high seas.

The idea behind this connection are the Blue Corridors, the migratory pathways used by whales, sharks and other marine species as they travel thousands of kilometers across multiple jurisdictions. To better protect these dynamic habitats, governments must connect networks of marine protected areas across borders and the high seas, while reducing the growing risks species face along their journey.

Consider the humpback whale. This month, humpbacks breeding off Queensland migrate toward Antarctic feeding grounds, while those in Tonga travel through the Cook Islands, Niue, and New Zealand to the same destination. To the whale, Australia, the Pacific Islands, and Antarctica are a single living system.

Marine life depends on connectivity; protecting isolated marine parks is not enough. We must protect the pathways species travel.

For years, this was impossible without an international law to protect waters beyond national jurisdiction. That changed in January, when the High Seas Treaty entered into force, enabling governments to protect the two-thirds of the ocean beyond any single nation’s control. Now, COP31 presents an opportunity to put oceans at the heart of the climate agenda, recognizing that the climate and ocean crises are inseparable.

Science, law, and political leadership have aligned. Thirty years of migration tracking, complementing thousands of years of Indigenous knowledge, have revealed these ocean pathways, and governments now have the tools to protect them. Pacific nations are leading ocean conservation, consistently translating ambition into policy, diplomacy, and action.

In May, Papua New Guinea, Fiji, and Vanuatu signed the Melanesian Ocean Corridor of Reserves, the first Pacific-led declaration linking national waters into a shared corridor of protection. Tonga has announced a National Ocean Policy with a vision for 30 percent protection and is signaling a further step: protecting the Pacific Blue Corridor that humpbacks travel, from Tongan breeding waters south through Cook Islands, Niue, and New Zealand toward Antarctic feeding grounds.

This is the leadership nature demands, grounded in the millennia-old Pacific knowledge that the ocean is a pathway, not a barrier. The Blue Corridors concept shows how solutions can be locally led, informed by science and Indigenous knowledge, regionally connected, and globally scalable through the High Seas Treaty. Ancestral knowledge is reinforced by science and formalized in law, forming an essential foundation of ocean governance.

What Pacific nations seek from Australia at COP31 is not endorsement, but enduring partnership, as demonstrated at the negotiating table in Antalya and in the decisions Australia makes before delegates arrive.

Australia has framed COP31 as the Pacific COP, delivered in partnership with the region. Its role is to translate Pacific leadership into concrete outcomes through three key actions.

First, off Australia’s coast, the Lord Howe Rise is a submerged Tasman Sea plateau and biodiversity hotspot, straddling domestic waters and high seas. It’s home to many migratory species and ancient corals. Commitments to strengthen protections are a welcome first step toward securing its future.

Second, Australia must strengthen protection in its own waters. The government has committed to expanding highly protected marine sanctuaries from 24 percent to 30 percent by 2030. Fulfilling this means firstly increasing protection in the Coral Sea, and around Lord Howe and Norfolk Islands, followed by further protections around the country guided by science.

Third, marine sanctuaries alone cannot safeguard a rapidly warming ocean. Australia cannot credibly lead global climate negotiations while approving fossil fuel projects that accelerate ocean tipping points Pacific communities have warned about for years. Nearly 100 civil society organizations have already called on Australia and Turkiye to lead by example and “advance the just, orderly, and equitable transition away from fossil fuels.”

The urgency is real. CSRIO modeling suggests that one of conservation’s great successes, the recovery of humpback whale populations, could be significantly reversed by 2050 as climate change disrupts Antarctic ecosystems. Decades of research have mapped the whales’ migration corridors, but a warming ocean is already reshaping the conditions that sustain these movements.

A humpback breeding off Queensland follows the ocean, guided by forces older than any border. Her migration is based on instinct, but the future of her path will be shaped by human decisions. Protecting Blue Corridors means addressing the drivers of ocean decline, safeguarding critical habitats, and reducing threats along the journey of migratory species.

The science is settled, the legal framework exists, and Pacific leadership is delivering. The decisions Australia takes before COP31, and the ambition it brings, will help determine whether Blue Corridors become this decade’s defining ocean achievement, or another opportunity that governments let slip.
tag: Blue Corridors; marine protected area; Pacific Islands climate change; Treaty on Biodiversity Beyond National Jurisdiction (BBNJ)

title: A New Japanese Drydock and the Limits of Allied Cooperation
description: Japanese shipyards are expanding, but the future space may already be spoken for.
text:
On August 19, Nikkei Asia reported that Namura Shipbuilding was planning to construct a new drydock for large vessel construction by 2035. Japan is already the third-largest shipbuilder in the world, and the expansion carries significant security and economic implications for the region. It follows a renewed commitment by Japan to invest in the shipbuilding sector, amidst growing security concerns around lackluster U.S. capacity and the role allies like Japan can play in filling security gaps.

Yet the announcement highlights a more sobering reality regarding those prospects. Japanese shipyards are expanding because their current capacity is fully maxed out. Consequently, scaling future alliance cooperation may depend far less on reaching formal agreements than on securing available schedule space.

The new drydock would be located in Imari Bay, on the northwestern coast of Kyushu in Saga prefecture, and would be the first new large drydock in Japan since 2017. Upon completion, it will reportedly focus on construction of liquefied natural gas carriers.

The project follows a string of announcements from both the Japanese government and industry aimed at bolstering the sector. In November 2025, Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae designated 17 nationally important sectors – including shipbuilding – as sources of economic growth through public-private investments. The Japanese shipbuilding industry shared this ambition, outlining a roadmap aimed at doubling annual shipbuilding capacity to 18 million gross tons by around 2035. Both Japan’s government and industry are aiming to establish a 1 trillion yen ($6.5 billion) fund aimed at reviving Japanese shipbuilding.

This slew of investments is motivated by multiple factors. For one, the shipbuilding sector was an important driver of Japanese economic growth and industrialization in the post-World War II period. By shoring up the sector, Japan can maintain the industry’s industrial capacity, even though it has gradually lost market share over the past few decades.

Second, the importance of shipbuilding grows in the context of China’s globally dominant shipyards and growing naval presence. This is in marked contrast to the largely inadequate shipbuilding sector of the United States, whose naval shipyards are plagued by delays and maintenance bottlenecks. Meanwhile, supported by protectionist policies, U.S. commercial shipyards remain competitive solely within domestic markets, building ships at roughly quadruple the international price.

U.S. vessels have long conducted maintenance at U.S. bases in Japan. Discussions between Japanese and U.S. officials at the Defense Industrial Cooperation, Acquisition, and Sustainment forum have explored broadening repair operations for U.S. vessels in Japan beyond American bases. Such cooperation offers tangible benefits to both countries.

Utilizing Japanese shipyards for maintenance allows the U.S. to partly sidestep existing naval maintenance backlogs at home. Furthermore, eliminating the need for these vessels to travel to Guam or the U.S. mainland saves up to 17 days in transit.

On the other side, Japanese companies would commercially benefit from attracting the U.S. Navy as a customer. Japan would also enhance the availability of U.S. naval ships and minimize their time away from the operational environment, thereby strengthening regional deterrence in the Pacific.

The difficulty is that Japanese yards do not appear to have the spare capacity this cooperation would need. Namura’s decision to expand followed sustained high utilization at its existing Imari dock, and Tokyo’s own revitalization roadmap identifies capacity shortfall as the principal obstacle to doubling output. The bottleneck in expanding U.S. naval repair work in Japanese yards may be less a matter of interest than of capacity. It will be difficult for the U.S. Navy to schedule space already committed to paying commercial customers.

The new dock won’t relieve that pressure. It is not scheduled for completion until 2035, and its output is already planned: the facility is intended to construct LNG carriers.

Even if space at shipyards were available, major constraints remain. Namura is a commercial builder of bulk carriers and tankers, and conversion from commercial to naval work is not only a matter of scheduling. Yards require cleared workforces, familiarity with U.S. Navy specifications, and qualification processes that take time to establish. A workforce trained on LNG hulls cannot easily redirect to warship repair.

Labor in particular remains a major constraint for Japan. One estimate identified a shortfall of up to 12,000 workers nationwide in shipbuilding-related fields if the industry achieves its goal of doubling orders.

Japan is serious about underwriting shipyard expansion, but that won’t automatically translate into allied cooperation on maintenance. The capacity Japan is now building will not exist for another decade, and even then the dock time has already been claimed by commercial orders.

If both the United States and Japan want Japanese yards to service U.S. ships in a contingency, the arrangement has to be made before spots fill – and not after.

title: After 9 Years, China Is Reopening Its Borders To Recycled Plastic
description: Now Beijing needs to build domestic demand for recycled materials – and global rules for the trade.
text:
In November 2026, the European Union will prohibit exports of potentially recyclable plastic to non-OECD countries. The EU labeled these exports “waste” and described the cross-border flows as “environmental exploitation.”

At the same time that the EU is shutting down the trade, China has reversed course and committed to expanding the movement of recyclable plastic across its border. For most of the past decade, China was closed to imports of plastic waste entirely.

The EU and China seem to be moving in different directions. Europe’s efforts concentrate on boosting demand for recycled plastic at home while taking a hardline position on exports abroad. China’s new approach is centered on supply and weaker on the demand for recycled plastic. Each holds lessons for the other, because a scalable framework for tackling global plastic pollution requires action on both the demand and supply sides.

And yet the recent developments in China have drawn almost no analysis outside China. That’s a mistake, because no country in recent history has shaped the global recycling trade more than China.

China’s Plastic Ban

China’s “National Sword” policy, launched in 2017, abruptly closed the country to imports of plastic waste – a seachange for China, which had absorbed much of the world’s recovered plastic for two decades. There were good reasons for the change. Much of the plastic waste wealthier countries shipped to China was contaminated or unrecyclable, local importers often lacked the capacity to handle it, and China’s monitoring system was underdeveloped at the time. The result was increased plastic pollution inside China. The National Sword program curbed the air and land pollution that earlier shipments had caused and forced a reckoning in countries that had outsourced their waste sorting problem for a generation.

However, National Sword, on its own, could not build a circular economy for plastic. With imported feedstock of plastic waste unavailable and no demand-side policy pulling recycled material through the system, the market simply started making more virgin plastic.

China’s imports of primary plastic rose from 29.7 million tonnes in 2017 to 40.9 million tonnes in 2020, an average annual increase of 12.6 percent, nearly tripling the rate of the preceding five years. China then developed the capacity to make at home what it had been buying abroad, and self-sufficiency in synthetic resins climbed to 90 percent in 2024. China was still using mountains of plastic; the biggest change was that plastic shifted to virgin material sourced within China.

Recycled plastic inside China competes against a domestic petrochemical sector that accounts for roughly 40 percent of global capacity, exports more than 17 million tonnes a year, is structurally oversupplied, and runs on margins thin enough that producers are incentivized to move volume at whatever price they can get. Recycled resin is not only more expensive without economies of scale; it also faces a well-organized petrochemical industry with close ties to political power.

As crude prices spiked this year, the price gap against recycled materials closed. But when the cost of oil slipped back this summer, the cost of virgin plastic followed it down, and some Chinese buyers moved orders back to virgin material.

The central lesson of the National Sword policy has implications reaching well beyond China: supply-side restriction of recycled plastic without demand-side policies encouraging a circular economy can simply entrench the role of virgin plastic. Today, much of China’s waste is currently incinerated for energy, consuming large volumes of plastic that could instead be reprocessed.

Beijing Changes Course – But Work Remains

It has taken time, but China’s circular economy architecture is now taking shape. The Circular Economy Development 15th Five-Year Plan, published in July 2026, commits China to taking in good-quality recycled feedstock from abroad. It calls for reworking the entry mechanism, simplifying the procedures that govern it, and widening the range of categories that can be brought in, so that imported material supplements domestic supply. The Five-Year Plan targets an internationally advanced recycling sector by 2035, with a separate seven-agency action plan setting an annual benchmark of more than 19.5 million tonnes of recycled plastics by 2030.

In 2017, China’s government closed the world’s largest market for recovered materials. Now Beijing is preparing to reopen it, selectively. That is a significant change of direction, but it’s also a work in progress. The ambitious vision for a circular economy as yet exists only on paper.

Increasing imports of recyclable plastic alone will not create a market: imported material with no mandated offtake produces warehouses of pellets that cannot compete. In China’s case, the glut of virgin plastic from the domestic petrochemical industry makes a compelling case for the government to mandate demand for recycled content. Mandated demand would drive more domestic collection and recovery, and strengthen the case for imported feedstock to reach efficient scale.

When governments require a minimum share of recycled resin in packaging or consumer goods, brands and companies redesign their supply chains to comply, pulling investment into collection, sorting technology, and materials innovation. Mandates also shift the burden away from consumers and sidestep the obstacles that have blocked more drastic steps, notably production caps in the U.N. Plastic Treaty negotiations, which have proved too contentious to command consensus.

Mandates of recycled content are the most important tool missing on China’s side. Chinese national standards for recycled plastic are almost all recommended rather than mandatory. That is changing in principle: the Ecological Environment Code, which took effect this month, establishes for the first time in Chinese law that the state can create a mandatory system for the use of recycled materials in key product categories. National and local authorities should now act on this policy signal.

For China, this is not only about environmental stewardship. It is industrial upgrading. China is the world’s largest producer and exporter of plastic goods, and its export markets are moving. The EU’s Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation requires single-use plastic beverage bottles sold in the EU to contain at least 30 percent recycled content by 2030, rising to 65 percent by 2040. In South Korea, a comparable rule has been in force since January: makers of bottled water and soft drinks running more than 5,000 tonnes a year must meet a 10 percent recycled floor, rising to 30 percent by 2030.

So far, China has no comparable law. These mandates will impact Chinese manufacturers operating in the export sector – but China’s plastics demand is overwhelmingly domestic. Setting its own local and national requirements would accelerate innovation at home.

One constraint deserves particular attention: China has not yet approved recycled plastic for food-contact use. This is where the highest-value demand sits, meaning whichever jurisdiction solves scalable food-grade recycling will command a premium position. China is well equipped to compete in food-grade applications, but on its current trajectory it also risks being left behind.

Reframing the Plastic Trade

The indiscriminate character of China’s National Sword policy created a second problem: a lasting fear of trading plastic at all. Recycling capacity worldwide now sits underused due to the lack of access to qualified feedstock, as well as weak domestic collection. The language of plastic “waste” evokes the unchecked, poorly sorted shipments of the past, but that is a concern modern certification and traceability can address.

Trade bans relocate plastic waste; they do not improve how it is handled across the global economy. The alternative is trade conducted on published, enforceable standards.

Countries that treat recovered plastic as waste to be disposed of will keep writing rules designed to stop it moving. This is EU’s position: processing, it believes, should stay in Europe. By contrast, countries that treat plastic waste as feedstock for an advanced manufacturing sector – one built on robotics, AI-enabled sorting, materials science, and chemical engineering – will write rules designed to verify it instead.

China’s circular economy strategy now reflects the view that recovered plastic holds significant economic value. The National Development and Reform Commission framed the plan in terms of resource security under geopolitical pressure – effectively treating recycled plastic as strategic feedstock. Beijing could have used the same argument to justify self-sufficiency; instead, it gave a seal of approval to increased trade.

China is correctly moving beyond blanket restrictions on plastic flows. The question going forward is whether China’s plastic policy can shape regional and global practices, especially in the area of standards. Standards settle the question of what counts as waste. Europe is restricting the movement of all plastic by-products while China is opening to verified material.

China is well positioned to curtail disguised waste by helping to define high global standards for recyclable materials. Inside its borders it has already redrawn the boundary between waste and secondary raw material: in August 2025 the State Administration for Market Regulation and the Standardization Administration of China issued nine national standards for recycled plastics. By extending and internationalizing that work, China has a chance to write the rules for the global plastic trade, with a focus on environmental permits and verified marketplaces.

China’s recent policy announcements made scant reference to the regional landscape, which is a missed opportunity. As different parts of Asia act on plastic pollution, there is considerable scope for governments to learn from each other and harmonize their standards. The building blocks already exist: recycled-content mandates in India and South Korea, the possibility of an ASEAN feedstock benchmark, Japanese and Korean processing technology, and Australian certified exports.

There is an instructive parallel in the Multi-Jurisdiction Common Ground Taxonomy, the green finance classification agreed jointly by China, the EU, and Singapore. That already serves as a key reference point for practitioners in sustainable finance.

Conclusion

The EU is restrictive on the movement of recovered plastic but has progressive recycled content mandates; China has it the other way around. The best outcome is not for one model to prevail over the other, but for both to keep evolving toward a mix of tools directed at both the supply of and the demand for recycled plastic.

For China, a pragmatic pathway to a circular economy at national, regional, and international levels rests on four measures: introducing recycled-content mandates, innovating on food-grade packaging, leading on certification and traceability standards, and making the case that recycling and open trade in recovered material belong to advanced manufacturing.

Global plastic governance remains fragmented and multilateral negotiations have exposed deep political divisions. In that vacuum, policy in the major economies can shape the global circular economy, most powerfully by reconfiguring regional and international supply chains. The rules for the next phase of this trade are being written now, in Brussels, in Beijing, and elsewhere.

China has the industrial base and now the stated policy. China should match its domestic architecture with new programs to generate domestic demand for recycled plastic, and carry the standards it has built within its territory into regional and international arenas.

title: AI Is Lowering the Barriers to China’s Information Warfare Against Japan
description: China-linked influence operators are increasingly using AI to craft more effective disinformation campaigns.
text:
Japan’s Ministry of Defense recently released its 2026 Defense of Japan white paper, once again drawing attention to China’s rapid advances in artificial intelligence and their implications for the regional security environment. Yet the most immediate danger to Japan may not come from AI’s application to conventional military systems. Generative AI is also lowering the barriers for Chinese information operations targeting Japanese society.

In late 2025, Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae made comments in the Diet linking a Taiwan contingency to Japan’s own security. Since then, disinformation targeting Japanese political figures and domestic issues has grown – not only in volume but also in sophistication. Research by organizations including the Sasakawa Peace Foundation and OpenAI suggests that China-linked influence operators are increasingly using AI to adapt their activities to Japan’s online environment and improve the efficiency of their operations.

AI is beginning to erode what was once one of the most obvious weaknesses of Chinese information operations against Japan: the linguistic and cultural barrier. Content that once featured grammatical mistakes, awkward translations and unnatural expressions is becoming harder for ordinary users to identify at a glance.

If these capabilities are deployed to interfere with elections, discredit politicians or amplify social divisions, their effects could extend far beyond any single piece of false information.

A special report by Nikkei in February found that more than 400 China-linked social media accounts spread negative content about Takaichi during Japan’s House of Representatives election. Separately, the Yomiuri Shimbun, citing research by Japan Nexus Intelligence, reported that under a different set of criteria, thousands of coordinated accounts on X were involved in sharing and amplifying related content.

The narratives did not focus solely on attacking Takaichi personally. They also linked Japan’s efforts to strengthen its defense capabilities with concerns over social welfare, seeking to promote the argument that military expansion was coming at the expense of ordinary people.

In the past, such accounts often left obvious clues. Some had been created only recently. Their Japanese reflected Chinese word order and linguistic habits, while others mixed simplified Chinese characters with Japanese usage. AI-generated images also frequently contained visual errors that made them relatively easy to identify.

Those weaknesses, however, are becoming less pronounced.

The Sankei Shimbun has continued to track PAPERWALL, a China-linked information network that includes 15 websites masquerading as Japanese news outlets. The continued operation of these sites, and the broader ecosystem surrounding them, points toward an increasingly localized approach to influence operations. Improvements in language, imagery, and the appearance of fake news sites are making it more difficult for ordinary readers to distinguish legitimate sources from fabricated ones.

A report released by OpenAI in February offered another important clue. The company found that China-linked actors had used ChatGPT to assist in planning an online influence campaign targeting Takaichi. Influence actors appear willing to incorporate different AI systems into their existing workflows whenever those tools make their operations more effective.

What matters is not the nationality of the model. What matters is that generative AI is reducing the cost of cross-language information operations. In the past, producing large volumes of content tailored to a Japanese audience required translators, graphic designers, social media operators and people familiar with Japanese political and cultural contexts.

Large language models can now help operators correct grammar, adjust tone, generate images, and produce multiple versions of the same narrative for different audiences within minutes. In other words, AI is making China’s information warfare more scalable, faster and more localized.

How, then, should Japan respond? Taiwan offers one useful point of reference.

Taiwan has faced Chinese information operations for years and shares a Chinese-language environment with the mainland. Beijing therefore does not face the same linguistic barrier when targeting Taiwanese society that it encounters in Japan. Precisely for that reason, Taiwan was forced to develop social mechanisms for dealing with large-scale disinformation campaigns and networks of suspicious accounts.

Taiwan’s experience does not rely solely on government agencies or third-party fact-checkers. Individual users also identify, report, and block suspicious accounts, while civil society organizations and researchers continuously monitor information networks and patterns of coordinated behavior.

Language and culture themselves can also serve as tools for identifying manipulation. Although Taiwan and China both use Chinese, there are clear differences in vocabulary, grammar, social experience, and political context. Chinese influence operators can use AI to reduce these differences, but they cannot easily reproduce the cultural background and lived experience accumulated within another society.

Japan retains the same kind of advantage. Japanese language and social culture are highly contextual. Even if Chinese operators use AI to improve translation and content generation, that does not mean they can fully understand the linguistic and political differences between generations, regions, and social groups in Japan.

Japan should therefore move beyond a defensive model that waits for false information to appear and then fact-checks it. The more important task is to strengthen society’s ability to recognize coordinated influence operations before they gain traction.

This is also why information-security cooperation between Japan and Taiwan should become more institutionalized. The two sides could deepen exchanges on identifying coordinated accounts, detecting deepfakes, analyzing foreign influence networks and monitoring information environments during major disasters, elections, or political crises.

AI is making Chinese information operations cheaper, faster and easier to deploy across language barriers. But it still cannot fully replicate the cultural knowledge and lived experience embedded in a society.

Japan therefore does not need to build a wall capable of blocking every piece of false information. It needs to build an information environment in which foreign influence operations are less likely to succeed. As Japan and Taiwan confront increasingly similar information-security threats, sharing their experience in identifying and countering Chinese influence operations could become an increasingly important part of regional security cooperation.
tag: AI and disinformation; China disinformation campaigns; China influence operations; China influence operations in Japan; China propaganda

title: AI, Scams, the Law, and Governance: A Conversation With David Tan
description: How are Southeast Asia's governments facing up to the challenges of AI?
text:
Governments across Southeast Asia are struggling with the arrival of artificial intelligence, both its endless possibilities that can improve everyday life and the threats posed by organized crime and the scam industries that have taken hold in the region.

Singapore-based David Tan, co-director of the Centre for Technology, Robotics, Artificial Intelligence & the Law, says the predominant issues evolve around what he calls the three Ps: permanence, proliferation, and perniciousness.

“We only need to regulate what’s truly important – what’s really pernicious, that proliferates, and has that permanent digital memory,” he said, adding: “Intimate sexual images, child abuse images, whether digital or not, that should be a priority.”

Tan, who also heads Intellectual Property at the EW Barker Centre for Law & Business at the National University of Singapore, spoke with The Diplomat’s Luke Hunt about how to combat the negative impact and AI’s reach into financial markets, public health, and pop culture.

Common law and legislation are key, as are online safety commissions. These commissions have been deployed by a core group of eight countries, Singapore and South Korea among them, where national authorities coordinate across borders through the Global Online Safety Regulators Network.

But Tan said the industrialized scam industry is here to stay, with crime syndicates expected to grow and continue taking advantage of AI and in particular, deep fakes.

“I think that one just has to be more vigilant as to the kind of fakes we get,” he said.
tag: AI; Artificial intelligence; Artificial intelligence in Southeast Asia

title: Airstrikes on Civilians in Rakhine State Will Increase, Say Myanmar Military Defectors
description: The military’s intensification of aerial bombing is aimed at defending key townships in the region.
text:
Defectors from the Myanmar military told The Diplomat that the regime will intensify its airstrikes on the civilian population in the country’s Rakhine State.

In an interview in Myanmar’s Arakan region on February 25 this year, two military defectors – Major Myint Zaw Than and Sergeant Kyaw Han Toe – told this correspondent that the military will increase its air raids in the Arakan region.

“There will be more airstrikes on the civilians in Arakan in the coming months because the military has to defend the three townships [Sittwe, Kyaukphyu and Manaung] still under its control,” Myint Zaw Than said.

Despite this, Kyaw Han Toe predicted that the military would eventually be defeated by the Arakan Army (AA) and will lose control of the three townships.

Of all the ethnic armed organizations operating in Myanmar, the AA has wrested control of the largest expanse of territory.

The defectors identified the “support of the people” for the AA as the outfit’s biggest strength, which has enabled it to stage a series of spectacular victories against the military over the past decade.

An annual report issued by the United Nations Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar (IIMM) that covers the period from July 2025 to June 2026 also pointed to a marked escalation in aerial attacks across the country in the months preceding the elections. Aerial attacks have continued unabated since the elections as well.

The IIMM report pointed out the Myanmar military was increasingly using motorized paragliders, gyrocopters, and drones to carry out low-altitude airstrikes with unguided explosives.

An estimated 228 civilian casualties, including 89 deaths and 139 injuries, have been reported as a result of airstrikes in Rakhine State from January 1 to August 13 this year.

On the resistance movement in other regions of Myanmar, Kyaw Han Toe said that “the resistance groups will emerge victorious if they are able to work together.” If they do, “the junta will collapse within three years,” he said.

About the recent success of the military in regaining territories from the resistance groups, he said that lack of coordination among the groups has been a fundamental drawback that has contributed to the military’s success in some zones. This, he added, stands in sharp contrast to the situation in Arakan, where “there is only one organization [opposed to the military] and so only one chain of command.”

The two military defectors clarified that they had received salaries and health care regularly when they were in service, as did other personnel in the military. Echoing accusations made previously by other defectors and some functionaries of resistance groups, Myint Zaw Than alleged that a small section of military personnel is involved in drug trafficking.
tag: Arakan; Arakan Army; Myanmar air strikes; Myanmar ethnic armed groups; Myanmar military; Myanmar military defectors

title: Armistice Regime, Peace Regime, or Time for a Different Mindset on the Korean Peninsula?
description: Adopting a new mindset for peacebuilding on the peninsula requires preserving what works while targeting individual issues that remain unresolved.
text:
On the 73rd anniversary of the Korean Armistice Agreement late last month, South Korea’s Minister of Unification Chung Dong-young declared, “We must end the Armistice regime and move to a peace regime.” His statement echoed a promise from South Korean President Lee Jae-myung, who earlier in July promised South Korea’s Peace Unification Advisory Council that his administration would work to transition the Korean Peninsula away from the Armistice Agreement toward a “peace regime” paradigm.

But what does this actually mean? What is a “peace regime” and is it attainable with North Korea?

These questions matter because they inform the trajectory of South Korea’s policy toward the North and, more fundamentally, how policymakers in Seoul approach peacebuilding on the peninsula.

In short, the “peace regime” is a long-standing South Korean policy design aimed at establishing a new framework for inter-Korean relations. The operative notion is to transition from the Armistice Agreement to an inter-Korean peace arrangement, to reduce foreign interference in the Korean peace process, and to establish interdependencies that would advance the two countries toward eventual reunification.

While at times showing early promise during brief periods of rapprochement, this approach has ultimately been unable to achieve these objectives. This is principally owing to the fundamental mismatch with North Korea’s policy preferences and domestic politics in South Korea. But the treatment of the peace process as discrete phases also runs contrary to the basic principles of peacebuilding, installing arbitrary friction points and creating missed opportunities for shared cooperation.

Effective inter-Korean policy will eventually require a reframing of the peacebuilding efforts on the Korean Peninsula. This not only includes adapting to the Kim Jong Un regime’s decision to abandon unification as a policy objective, but also an evolution of internal South Korean politics that is currently in tension between different stakeholders. In the meantime, the Armistice Agreement will continue to provide a foundation from which peacebuilding efforts can proceed, just as it has for the past seventy-three years.

What the Armistice Actually Does

To understand Seoul’s desire to move beyond the armistice, it is first necessary to understand what the agreement does to support peace and stability on the peninsula.

The Korean Armistice Agreement is an interim agreement meant to maintain a cessation of hostilities and to give space for peacebuilding on the peninsula. It is therefore not incompatible with the peace process; rather, it is integral to it, as it provides a foundation for preserving a cessation of hostilities, institutionalizing the peace process, and creating opportunities for non-violent engagement. It does this through establishment of rights, duties, and obligations for both sides of the peninsula, designation of buffer areas such as the demilitarized zone (DMZ), and the institution of mechanisms for overseeing implementation of ceasefire provisions.

Although there have been notable violations of the armistice over the years, both sides by and large continue to abide by its rules today. On the north side, there is the Korean People’s Army (KPA) Panmunjom Mission, and on the south, there is the United Nations Command Military Armistice Commission (UNCMAC) staffed by countries including the United States, South Korea, Denmark, and New Zealand, among others. Switzerland and Sweden comprise the Neutral Nations Supervisory Commission (NNSC) and provide third party oversight.

The armistice mechanisms also provide an avenue for communication during periods when broader inter-Korean relations have broken down. Although North Korea ceased communication across inter-Korean channels in April 2023, the hotline between the UNCMAC and the KPA Panmunjom Mission has remained operational since September 2019. Moreover, both sides staff neutral ground at the Joint Security Area in Panmunjom, maintaining a constant presence to allow for both routine and crisis communications, as necessary.

The practical importance of these mechanisms is easy to overlook because their most successful efforts are often invisible. It has been a tool for mitigating escalation cycles following the drone incursion incidents of 2022 and 2024, as well as lower level events such as the May 2020 exchange-of-fire between KPA and South Korean military forces inside the demilitarized zone.

There are limitations to the Armistice Agreement, which contribute to criticism among policy audiences in South Korea. The agreement does not establish mutually agreed maritime boundaries, which has been a factor in acute security incidents in the past and could enable grey zone competition in the future. North Korea’s refusal to allow the NNSC to operate in the northern half of the peninsula prevents on-the-ground oversight of its activities. Also, the boundary markers that were installed in the 1950s have faded. This has paved the way for accidental crossings in recent years as KPA forces carry out construction work in the northern half of the DMZ.

These are all notable shortcomings, but they all stem from the fact that the Armistice Agreement was never meant to be a final political resolution of the conflict. The armistice called for the convocation of a political conference within three months of its signing. That event was meant to deliver a political settlement of the war which would address all the outstanding issues necessary to restore a legal state of peace and normalization of relations.

That conference ultimately took place in Geneva in 1954, but the parties could not resolve their fundamental disagreements, particularly over the future political status and unification of the peninsula.

The armistice therefore remained in place.

This history is important because it demonstrates that the absence of a permanent peace agreement did not prevent peacebuilding from happening; rather, the armistice has provided space for it for the past seven decades.

The Pursuit of a “Peace Regime”

The South Korean conception of a “peace regime” came in the early 1990s. The two Koreas had both acceded to the United Nations and negotiated the “Agreement on reconciliation, nonaggression, exchanges and cooperation” — otherwise known as the “Basic Agreement.” This agreement included the following provision: “South and North Korea shall together endeavor to transform the present state of armistice into a firm state of peace between the two sides and shall abide by the present Military Armistice Agreement until such a state of peace is realized.”

It is from this provision that the South Korean government formed its policies around the notion of the peace process existing in discrete phases. In other words, the concept is that there is an “armistice regime,” which is the existing Cold War-era policy paradigm, and a “peace regime” in which there could be a new framework for inter-Korean relations.

Different South Korean administrations have operationalized that idea in different ways. It was a topic of the four-party talks in the mid-1990s with the two Koreas, China, and the United States. During the Sunshine Policy under presidents Kim Dae-jung and Roh Moo-hyun, efforts focused principally on establishing economic interdependence through projects like the Kaesong Industrial Complex and Kumgang Tourist Resort.

The Moon Jae-in administration made perhaps the most ambitious attempt to advance this concept. Its efforts included an End-of-War Declaration, the September 2018 Comprehensive Military Agreement, and attempts to restore economic projects at Kaesong and Kumgang. These policies ultimately failed to take root for myriad reasons.

Problems with the Peace Regime

There are three major obstacles to the traditional South Korean conception of a peace regime.

The first is the transformation of North Korea’s own policy preferences. Economic interdependence initially appeared to offer a promising avenue for engagement as the Kim regime sought financial gains. But Kaesong and Kumgang became leverage for the South Korean government in times of tension; for example, when the Park Geun-hye administration shut down operations at Kaesong Industrial Complex following a DPRK satellite launch.

More importantly, North Korea’s conception of inter-Korean relations has changed fundamentally under Kim Jong Un. The DPRK has now constitutionally recognized separate, sovereign states on the Korean Peninsula and abandoned unification as a policy objective. In doing so, the Kim regime has dismantled all previous inter-Korean-related organizations and disavowed any prior initiatives.

The second obstacle has been South Korean domestic politics. While the government has been consistent in maintaining the principle of the peace regime, the conservative and progressive parties have been far apart on their interpretations of what it means in practice. This has led to inconsistency in approaches, such as with the inter-Korean military agreement, which the Moon administration negotiated and concluded, the Yoon Suk-yeol government scrapped, and the Lee administration is now trying to revive. From Pyongyang’s perspective, these policy reversals reinforce the argument that agreements reached with Seoul may not survive a change of government.

Compounding these challenges is that there are divides even within the progressive party over how to proceed with North Korea. Some believe that unification must be the ultimate objective, while others contend that peaceful coexistence is a necessary prerequisite. These debates create challenges for any conceptions of what an agreement necessary for underwriting a peace regime may look like.

There is also a second domestic complication: not every South Korean interest in moving beyond the armistice is necessarily about peacebuilding. Debates over the armistice often involve questions of sovereignty, access to the DMZ, tourism, economic development, and the role of the United Nations Command. While these may be policy priorities for Seoul, they are not interchangeable with the question of how to reduce the risk of renewed war. The result is that “ending the Armistice regime” can mean different things to different South Korean constituencies.

The third and deeper problem is the treatment of the peace process as discrete phases. This places too much emphasis on achieving a signed agreement that can quickly fall apart rather than addressing the specific issue areas contributing to continued risk of conflict. Further, it locks the South Korean government into a policy paradigm that is easily rejected whether in Pyongyang or among different policy actors in Seoul. Finally, it creates unnecessary friction among the different organizations charged with peacebuilding on the Peninsula; e.g., UNCMAC and the Ministry of Unification.

There are missed opportunities for cooperation when focusing on disputes between conceptions of an armistice regime versus peace regime. The alternative is to treat peacebuilding as a continuous process which ultimately moves towards a comprehensive peace agreement rather than treating it as a prerequisite.

Toward Continuous Peacebuilding

Adopting a new mindset for peacebuilding on the peninsula requires preserving what works while targeting individual issues that remain unresolved. This makes for a different conception of peacebuilding, one that is more agile in dealing with North Korea and collaborative among the different stakeholders in the South. Rather than focusing on binary regimes, the various stakeholders in South Korea can look at what foundational elements already exist, target specific issues that require resolution, and then take coordinated action to move forward on them.

In practical terms, a durable peace on the Korean Peninsula will ultimately require agreement on a range of issues including the following: basic principles governing peace, territory and boundaries, risk reduction, denuclearization/arms control, compliance management mechanisms, protocols governing relations between the parties and humanitarian considerations.

None of these issues needs to be resolved simultaneously, nor does progress on one require movement on every other issue. In the meantime, the armistice can continue to provide utility to help the two sides weather acute incidents, North Korean recalcitrance, and swings in the South Korean political pendulum.

A shift to this new mindset among stakeholders on the peninsula would make meaningful progress more achievable. Such progress may not carry the pomp that a signing ceremony might bring, but it reduces the risk of incidents, creates opportunities for non-violent engagement, and enables resolution of long-standing sources of conflict. Ultimately, durable peace is achieved through consistent effort and incremental gains, and the Korean Peninsula is no different.

title: As World Bank Retreats From Climate Targets, India’s Most Vulnerable Could Pay the Price
description: Most climate finance goes where it is easiest to lend. Embankments, water systems, shade, and shelters that save lives and livelihoods in villages struggle to find funding.
text:
More than 80 percent of India’s population lives in districts highly vulnerable to floods, droughts, and cyclones, according to the Climate Vulnerability Index developed by the Council on Energy, Environment and Water. In states such as Assam, Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra, Karnataka, and Bihar, that vulnerability is already visible in damaged roads, disrupted farming, and recurring displacement. Local officials know what is needed — higher roads, stronger embankments, safer shelters, and simple early-warning systems. However, the problem is not knowledge, but funding.

Just as these districts need more protection from rising heat and encroaching water, the World Bank has ended its 45 percent climate finance target, a change that could weaken accountability for where money goes. This decision will widen the gap between where climate money is easiest to spend and where it is actually needed. For India’s poorest, most climate‑exposed districts, especially marginalized rural communities, dropping a binding target weakens accountability and makes it easier to bury real adaptation needs under vague “outcomes.”

When there is no hard number to meet, money is more likely to flow toward large, easy-to-package projects such as solar parks, grid upgrades, and metro lines. The risk is that large projects are counted as climate work while flood-prone districts wait for funds for embankments, shelters, or early-warning systems.

We write this as researchers and advocates who have worked inside government and policy settings and seen how funding commitments shrink as they move from paper to practice.

At COP28 in Dubai, the World Bank set a simple rule: 45 percent of its annual financing would support projects with climate co-benefits, meaning work that either cuts emissions or helps people cope with floods, heat, and drought. The 45 percent climate co-benefits target asked a simple question: how much of the Bank’s lending was meaningfully climate related?

In June, under pressure from the United States, the Bank said it would retire that 45 percent target. It now says it will stop counting how much of its lending is climate-related and instead focus on broader “outcomes to maximize development impact,” with climate supposedly woven into everything it does.

On paper, that may sound flexible. But without a clear benchmark, it becomes harder for outsiders, including India, to check what is actually being financed or whether the money is reaching the places that need it most.

India needs substantial climate finance each year: about $160 billion to $288 billion annually through 2030 just to keep up with climate change. Flood barriers, drought relief, and heat-resilient homes matter just as much as mitigation projects. But the finance reaching adaptation work on the ground remains far below what is needed, and states are stuck with strained budgets, borrowing limits, and no steady pipeline of support to count on.

Most climate finance still goes where it is easiest to lend: grid upgrades, solar parks, wind farms, transmission lines, and green hydrogen. These usually sit in or near big cities and industrial corridors. Meanwhile, the smaller projects that save lives in villages and districts — embankments, water systems, shade, cooling centers, and shelters — struggle to find funding. Wealthy nations have repeatedly promised to close this gap, but the shortfall remains. For most Indian states, cheap long-term loans and guarantees from major lenders remain the only realistic path to real climate protection. So, when the World Bank weakens firm climate commitments, these states are left wondering how they will cover even the basics.

The neglected districts are home to Dalit, Adivasi, and other marginalized communities, often landless laborers and informal workers. Their voices rarely shape how public money gets spent. It is also hard to track whether adaptation funds ever actually reach them. A hard number in climate lending gave activists, journalists, and local leaders something to point to. Take the number away, and these communities are being asked to trust a system that has often put them last in line.

The World Bank itself argues that projects with climate co-benefits are “smart development” and says it is shifting from measuring climate inputs to measuring outcomes across its broader portfolio. That sounds plausible, but in an unequal system the loss of a floor can quickly become the loss of a priority. For India’s marginalized districts, flexibility without a hard minimum may simply mean more delay for the projects that matter most.

If the World Bank wants to prove that retiring its climate target is not a retreat, India should ask for two concrete commitments in return. First, a public guarantee that a fixed share of climate lending reaches the most exposed districts and communities. Second, transparent, publicly auditable reporting on where every climate rupee goes, so climate finance can be tracked for equity.

From a meeting room in Washington, the new era may look like smart, flexible development. From a flooded panchayat (local government) office in Bihar, it looks like an embankment, shelter, or warning system pushed further out of reach.
tag: climate finance; Climate Vulnerability Index; India climate finance

title: ASEAN Fractures Widen as Thailand Hosts Myanmar’s Min Aung Hlaing
description: A conversation with Mark Cogan of Kansai Gaidai University in Osaka.
text:
As the people of Myanmar recently commemorated the 8888 uprising that demanded political freedom but was brutally put down in August 1988, Thailand was playing host to Min Aung Hlaing, the former general who seized power through a coup in early 2021.

This was Min Aung Hlaing’s second official visit to an ASEAN member state since military-staged elections in December and January ensured his transition to the presidency and one that widened the schisms within ASEAN, which has barred Myanmar from official summits and events amid a bloody civil war.

Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul broke with that line despite ASEAN protocols and potential legal issues given the International Court of Justice will soon deliver its verdict on whether Min Aung Hlaing and Myanmar’s senior generals committed a genocide against the Rohingya.

Min Aung Hlaing’s first official visit as president was to Laos in early July and his trip to Thailand came less than a week after he allowed a representative from the International Committee of the Red Cross to meet with the jailed former leader Aung San Suu Kyi, who had been unsighted for many years amid concerns for her health.

Mark Cogan is an associate professor of Peace and Conflict Studies at Kansai Gaidai University in Osaka and a regular contributor to The Diplomat. He joined Luke Hunt on Beyond the Mekong to discuss the recent developments in regional politics.

That includes the moral and political questions that have divided maritime and mainland Southeast Asia, including the civil war in Myanmar, which has claimed 100,000 lives, the Code of Conduct in the South China Sea, and Thailand’s simmering border conflict with Cambodia.
