title: Assessing KMT Leader Cheng Li-Wun’s Political Narrative
description: Insights from Wayne Tan.
text:
The Diplomat author Mercy Kuo regularly engages subject-matter experts, policy practitioners, and strategic thinkers across the globe for their diverse insights into U.S. Asia policy. This conversation with Dr. Wayne Tan – professor at the Graduate Institute of International Politics, National Chung Hsing University (Taiwan), where he also serves as director of the Center for Indo-Pacific Strategy and Non-Traditional Security – is the 521st in “The Trans-Pacific View Insight Series.”

How would you characterize Kuomintang (KMT) party chair Cheng Li-wun’s political narrative regarding Taiwan’s autonomy and sovereignty?

Political narratives should not be confused with strategic reality. One of the central arguments in my recent work is that Taiwan’s room for strategic maneuver is increasingly constrained by structural forces beyond the control of any Taiwanese political leaders. Whether one belongs to the KMT or the DPP [Democratic Progressive Party], Taiwan operates within an international system shaped by the intensifying strategic competition between the United States and China.

Viewed from this perspective, Cheng Li-wun’s narrative can be understood as a paradoxical attempt to maximize Taiwan’s autonomy through “self-restraint” rather than “strategic proactivity.” Unlike narratives that seek to reinforce sovereignty through greater international visibility, Cheng appears to argue that Taiwan’s de facto autonomy is best preserved by lowering the probability of military conflict and maintaining channels of communication with Beijing.

However, it is important to realize that any genuine risk of military conflict across the Taiwan Strait arises not from Taiwan’s conduct, but from Beijing’s persistent use of gray-zone coercion, which has steadily eroded the stability of the status quo. Taiwan has never been the problem. Rather, it is the current Xi Jinping administration that has repeatedly generated instability through increasingly coercive actions in the region.

For this reason, I would be cautious about attributing excessive importance to Cheng’s political narrative. Taiwan’s leaders possess agency, but it is constrained agency. They can influence tactics, manage crises, and shape domestic political debate. What they cannot do is fundamentally alter the structural forces driving U.S.-China rivalry. As long as China continues to rise and the United States remains committed to preventing the emergence of a regional hegemon in Asia, Taiwan will remain one of the principal arenas of great-power competition. That reality is largely independent of which political party governs Taiwan or how its leaders frame questions of autonomy and sovereignty.

What are the strengths and weaknesses of Cheng’s rhetorical platform?

The strength of Cheng’s rhetoric is that it recognizes an uncomfortable reality often overlooked in Taiwan’s domestic political debate: military conflict would be catastrophic regardless of who prevails politically. In this sense, her discourse appeals to prudence rather than ideology. From an international relations perspective, reducing misperception and preserving diplomatic communication are entirely rational objectives. Thomas Schelling demonstrated decades ago that deterrence and communication are complementary rather than contradictory. Stability depends not only upon military capability but also upon credible signaling.

However, recognizing the reality mentioned above is not the same as overcoming it. The central weakness of Cheng’s platform lies in the implicit assumption that greater self-restraint or expanded dialogue can substantially reduce China’s ambitions toward Taiwan. That assumption is difficult to sustain when viewed through the logic of realism. If Beijing regards Taiwan as indispensable to its long-term regime security, legitimacy, and regional dominance, then changes in Taiwan’s rhetoric are unlikely to alter decision-makers’ fundamental objectives in Beijing.

This is the critical distinction between tactical tension reduction and strategic conflict resolution. Diplomatic engagement may lower the probability of accidental escalation in the short run, but it does not eliminate the underlying security competition. The continued existence of the Republic of China (Taiwan) represents an enduring legitimacy challenge for the government of PRC. As long as two competing political authorities each claim to represent a state legally, Beijing cannot fully consolidate its political legitimacy. This zero-sum rivalry has shaped the strategic calculations of every Chinese Communist Party leader since 1949 and helps explain why the Taiwan issue has remained central to PRC’s grand strategy.

Compare and contrast the notion of Taiwan’s national identity between the KMT and the DPP.

To be sure, the two parties articulate different political narratives. The DPP increasingly defines Taiwan as a distinct democratic country whose legitimacy derives exclusively from the will of the Taiwanese people. The KMT, by contrast, continues to place greater emphasis on the constitutional framework of the ROC and generally advocates maintaining channels of communication with Beijing as a means of preserving stability.

These differences matter for domestic elections and political discourse. But from the standpoint of international politics, they are of secondary importance. Neither party can alter the structural realities that dominate Taiwan’s security. Beijing has made clear that preventing Taiwan’s permanent separation is a core political interest. The United States, meanwhile, views Taiwan as a critical component of its strategy to prevent Beijing from being regional hegemony. Those are the forces that matter. Taiwan’s geographic location, the military balance across the Strait, and the intensity of Sino-American competition define the boundaries within which any Taiwanese government must operate.

Who are the principal audiences of Cheng’s political messaging?

Domestically, Cheng’s message primarily addresses voters who prioritize peace, economic stability, and risk reduction over ideological confrontation. These voters tend to evaluate cross-strait relations through practical rather than symbolic considerations.

A second audience consists of Taiwan’s business community, particularly firms deeply integrated into regional production networks. For these actors, geopolitical uncertainty translates directly into economic costs.

Internationally, Cheng’s messaging also speaks to observers in Washington, Beijing, Tokyo, and Southeast Asia by signaling that Taiwan’s democratic system contains multiple perspectives rather than a single unified position.

How do Beijing, Washington, and Tokyo view Cheng’s agenda?

Beijing, Washington, and Tokyo will judge Cheng not by her rhetoric but by whether her policies advance or hinder their strategic interests. Beijing may welcome dialogue, yet it will not abandon its objective of bringing Taiwan under control. Washington will support any Taiwanese leader who strengthens deterrence and resists Xi’s regime domination, regardless of party affiliation. Tokyo views Taiwan through the logic of balance of power: Beijing’s takeover would fundamentally undermine Japan’s security.

The crucial point is that Taiwan’s domestic politics cannot override geopolitical realities. In an anarchic international system, small states possess agency, but only within limits imposed by great-power competition. Taiwan’s future therefore will be shaped primarily by the evolving balance of power between Washington and Beijing, not by the preferences or personalities of Taiwanese politicians.

title: Australia and Thailand Deepen Ties to Hedge Against Global Uncertainty
description: The building of collaboration with countries like Thailand is central to Australia’s long-term strategic vision.
text:
In recent months, the Australia government has been incredibly active on the diplomatic front, from new security agreements with multiple Pacific Island countries to visits to Australia by the Japanese, Indian, New Zealand, and Vietnamese leaders. This week Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul made his way to Australia.

For both Canberra and Bangkok, there is a desire to build more substantive regional relationships as a hedge against both a more unreliable Washington and a more assertive Beijing – as well as buttress against the rippling effects of the competition between the two superpowers. The Australia-Thailand relationship is therefore less about alliance-building than about building greater resilience through diversifying partnerships, and creating a latticework of cooperation within the Indo-Pacific region.

The two prime ministers signed a series of agreements during Anutin’s visit that sought to give this strategy practical substance. These included deepening cooperation on transnational crime, including online scams, cybercrime, money laundering, human trafficking, and narcotics. The purpose of these agreements is to enable greater information sharing and coordination between the two countries’ law enforcement agencies.

Alongside this, the prime ministers committed to deepening economic engagement. Since the signing of the Thailand-Australia Free Trade Agreement in 2005, trade between the two countries has tripled, with Thailand becoming Australia’s fifth largest source of imports. But both countries believe there is room for expansion. They highlighted that cooperation across agriculture, clean energy, education, healthcare, critical technologies, resources, creative industries, and the digital economy were areas of greater ambition.

The other major announcement was the establishment of a biennial defense ministers’ meeting. The two countries have had a longstanding, but low-key, defense relationship. A bilateral military exercise called Thai Boomerang was established in 1992, and Thailand has participated in major multilateral exercises in Australia like Talisman Sabre. But consultation on defense policies has been limited. The establishment of a regular forum for the defense ministers to meet and coordinate is a positive elevation of the partnership.

It is unlikely that the two countries will become treaty allies anytime soon. Instead the deepening of the partnership is part of a strategy of diversifying partners, as well as an understanding of security in more holistic terms.

Anutin highlighted this in his August 18 address to the Lowy Institute in Sydney, titled “Beyond the Thailand-Australia Bilateral Strategic Partnership: Advancing International Order through Regional and Minilateral Cooperation.” In the speech, he argued that geopolitics, economics, and technology are becoming increasingly intertwined, leaving middle and smaller powers facing far more uncertainty. Rather than choosing sides in great power competition, Anutin argued that countries like Thailand and Australia have an interest in strengthening cooperation with each other and through regional institutions and smaller groupings.

There is also a recognition that the great powers are unavoidable. Thailand maintains strong ties with the United States, while also valuing its relationship with China. But when trust in a great power is low – as it is at present – other multilateral and minilateral institutions and cooperation gives middle and smaller powers greater options, more flexibility and room to maneuver.

This is particularly important as the concept of security becomes broader. Anutin described traditional defense cooperation alongside economic resilience, supply chains, technology, and energy as interrelated elements. He highlighted that this is increasingly a concern in Southeast Asia where there is a confluence of disrupted trade and energy flows, transnational crime, cyber threats, technological competition, and armed conflict. Australia stands as a trusted and low-friction partner able to help navigate this complexity.

For Australia, while the bilateral relationship is important, the more valuable element is further integration into the regional architecture. Australia’s ability to be seen as a trusted and important partner for ASEAN is vital for Canberra’s diplomatic priorities. The creation of the Office of Southeast Asia in 2022 within the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT) was an indication of this priority. Alongside the Office of the Pacific, there is a level of senior coordination and bureaucratic focus that other regions are not afforded within Australian foreign policy.

This may seem odd given Australia’s security ties to the United States, its vast trading relationship with Northeast Asia, and its cultural links to Europe. But it’s a statement of where Canberra wants to be. The building of collaboration with countries like Thailand is central to Australia’s long-term strategic vision. This effort may be piecemeal and focused on practical cooperation, but it builds the relationship brick by brick, rather than through any single grand gesture.
tag: Australia foreign policy; Australia-ASEAN relations; Thailand-Australia relations

title: Breaking Through Infoglut: Australia’s Anger-information Overload Cycle
description: COVID, global warming, conspiracy theorists, natural disasters, financial collapses – and a sham social media ban. It’s no wonder young Australians are glum.
text:
Why are we so angry? The easy, lazy, and entirely wrong explanation is that our technologies are to blame: the internet, smartphones, social media, artificial intelligence, and so on.

That’s the argument behind Australia’s doomed social media ban for young people, which is inspired by the deceptive claims and cherry-picked statistics peddled by pop-psychology influencers like Jonathan Haidt in his roundly debunked book “The Anxious Generation,” and driven by a moral panic that was cynically manufactured by the Murdoch media.

So why are we so anxious, and angry? Take the average 20-year-old in Australia: born into the aftermath of the 2008 Great Financial Crisis, they have seen companies reap record profits while for ordinary Australians the prospect of affordable housing has slipped ever further from their grasp.

They grew up in the shadows of the unresolved conflicts in Iraq and Afghanistan and today encounter a daily dose of death and destruction in the reporting from Ukraine, Gaza, Iran, and other conflict hotspots. They spent their most formative teenage years in COVID lockdowns and Zoom schooling, while conspiracy theorists tried to convince their parents that the pandemic was a hoax perpetuated by some global cabal.

They’ve experienced more than a decade of the hottest years in human memory during their lifetime, most likely lived through one or more natural disasters in their area and yet have seen utter political inaction on the climate crisis. And those of us who are older have simply experienced all that for longer.

So how could they, and we, not be anxious and angry – regardless of whether we use smartphones and social media, or not? As David Weinberger wrote as early as 2004, in his fabulous take-down of the “echo chamber” fallacy, “the problem with an extraterrestrial-conspiracy mailing list isn’t that it’s an echo chamber,” facilitated by the digital platforms of the day: rather, the problem is “that it thinks there’s a conspiracy by extraterrestrials.”

The same goes for climate crisis denialists, anti-vaccination activists, sovereign citizens, far-right extremists, and other anti-social, anti-societal, and anti-democratic groups: it’s their angry, extreme, exclusionary, and uncompromising views that are the problem, rather than the technologies they use to express and spread them; if they didn’t have X as a platform that actively endorses their views, they’d find another.

Wherever that anxiety and anger comes from, whether “the internet” (whatever that means these days) or the other threatening scenarios: together they have highlighted the complex world we live in.

Conspiracy as Comfort

Let’s take one example: the observation that pandemics like COVID-19 simply happen from time to time and that there’s little more we can do than simply to prepare for the next one, is entirely correct, of course, but also deeply unsatisfying. It’s a great deal more convenient to comfort ourselves with fairytales of bioweapon factories, lab leaks, depopulation agendas, or interference by the Illuminati, aliens, or the Antichrist: they provide a concrete target for our anxiety, anger and action.

Where our modern communication technologies do come in is in the fact that they’ve made all that information – “real” as much as “fake” – so much easier to access and circulate, globally and instantly.

This substantially contributes to an information overload: we can readily access WHO reports about the pandemic and its causes, the more or less careful and insightful coverage of those reports by the world’s media, but also the “explainer” writings and videos of conspiracy theorists and influencers that cherry-pick and misrepresent those facts in order to perpetuate their “alternative” worldviews.

We’re overloaded by this infoglut: we, all of us, have neither the time nor the subject matter expertise to be able to reliably distinguish verified facts from made-up stories, or well-supported conclusions from far-fetched conjecture.

Ironically, the problem we are facing – the reason we are so angry – is the very opposite of the claims made by those still peddling the “echo chamber” and “filter bubble” fallacies that see us all in self-insulating bubbles: rather, the hyperconnectivity enabled by our current media environments produces an information overload that we are ill-equipped to process or reduce.

We may not consciously articulate this all the time, but deep down we recognize this, and that makes us anxious, and even angry. For many, the coping mechanism is to reach for easy explanations and ready-made scapegoats (elites, migrants, secret societies, other countries – or generally, others who simply are not like us).

But that story isn’t new; in fact, it is perhaps as old as humanity itself, even if it now plays out across a different media landscape.

It can’t be solved by banning smartphones, or social media, or AI; indeed, conspiracy theories and other disinformation usually only reach a broader audience when they’re also amplified by politicians, celebrities, and mainstream media.

Anxiety Fuels Scapegoating

Uncertainty produces rumors, which generate anxiety, which results in the scapegoating and exclusion of others; the commercial imperatives of mainstream media as well as social media encourage this further, as both seek sustained audience engagement.

Any attempts to deal with these destructive dynamics must focus first and foremost on the underlying causes of our anxiety and anger, of course; to return to where we started, as governments in Australia and elsewhere are beginning to find out, you don’t make young people less anxious by preventing them from communicating about their anxieties, but by paying serious attention to their actual concerns.

At the same time, we must confront the challenges of hyperconnectivity and information overload more directly, and central to this is to improve literacy in all its forms. This includes, of course, news and digital media literacy, to enable citizens better to distinguish quality, reliable information and sources from those that seek to mislead and enrage them; societal and civic literacy, to improve public understanding of the mechanisms of government and governance in Australia and elsewhere.

We must also ensure that citizens understand their individual rights and (just as importantly) obligations towards others within society, and enhance scientific literacy (across both social and natural sciences) to prevent them from falling prey to scientistic cherry-picking, whether on climate change or the effects of social media use.

Together those initiatives aim to save Australia from a trajectory that promotes deeply polarized, winner-takes-all politics as we see it played out in U.S. politics. Instead, they redirect citizens toward an understanding of political debate that is oriented toward workable compromise between legitimate diverging opinions, even if consensus remains unattainable.

To achieve that will not be a quick fix. It will be a generational project. However, Australia can learn from other countries here: from Finland’s successful media literacy strategy, and Germany’s Federal Agency for Civic Education.

Indeed, education at all levels, from primary to tertiary and beyond to lifelong learning, is central to this, and a substantial boost in investment will be required even just to avoid a further decline in media literacy levels across the population in the short term. All the more important that we confront this urgently, then: if we don’t, we’ll only grow more anxious and ever more angry.

title: Can Japan’s Defense Industry Meet its Ambitious Goals?
description: Japan increasingly recognizes the importance of the defense industrial base as a source of strategic capability. But can the industry actually deliver?
text:
On August 4, the Japanese Ministry of Defense published its annual 2026 Defense White Paper, which outlines Japan’s defense policies and activities. While the report extensively covers the increasingly severe security environment surrounding Japan, notable highlights include an emphasis on one of Japan’s core concepts, “new ways of defense,” and its defense production.

Notably, the White Paper follows Japanese Defense Minister Koizumi Shinjiro’s comment at the Farnborough International Airshow: “Defense production is deterrence itself. No matter how advanced a defense system may be, it means little if it cannot be produced.” His statement suggests a fundamental shift in how Japan views deterrence: rather than mere possession of defense materiel, Japan increasingly recognizes the importance of the defense industrial base as a source of strategic capability.

Japan, like other countries around the world, is learning from Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Some of the takeaways include the decisive role played by unmanned assets, renewed appreciation for strong air defense, and the importance of sustaining a defense industrial base that can keep up with a protracted war. Furthermore, recent conflict in the Middle East and concerns about diminishing U.S. stockpiles have sparked concern among U.S. allies about the reliability of the United States as a supplier of advanced munitions for their militaries. These conflicts have served as critical turning points in Japan’s defense posture, prompting the Japanese government to rethink its defense policies to invest more in developing indigenous capabilities and partner with other U.S. allies that share similar concerns.

Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae’s administration is expected to complete the revision of Japan’s three key security documents by the end of 2026. The updates are anticipated to reorient Japan’s national security strategy to better respond to the aggravating regional security environment, integrate new capabilities with strengthened alliances and partnerships, and develop greater self-reliance. Takaichi has already made notable progress in strengthening Japan’s security posture, including the relaxation of the Implementation Guidelines for the Three Principles on Transfer of Defense Equipment and Technology, lifting a long-standing ban on lethal weapons exports.

The revision, which opened the door for Japan to export lethal weapons to 17 countries that have signed the Equipment and Technology Transfer Agreements (ETTAs), was done with the goal of strengthening Japan’s relations with its allies while contributing to the country’s economic growth through a stronger defense industrial base. Japan has already signed a $7 billion contract with Australia to deliver Mogami-class frigates beginning in 2029 and begun discussions with the government of the Philippines to export Type 88 surface-to-ship missiles. While visiting Singapore to attend the Shangri-La Dialogue in May, Koizumi also engaged in the discussion of the potential sale of Mogami-class frigates with his New Zealand counterpart.

With the new guidelines, Japan will be able to export weapons that were developed under joint production to third countries. That includes the Global Combat Air Program (GCAP) – the trilateral six-generation fighter development program that unites Japan, Italy, and the United Kingdom. Now, Canada has joined the GCAP as an observer.

However, as the Defense White Paper points out, there are multiple factors that Japan must improve to build a strong indigenous industrial base. For example, to ensure efficient production of domestic defense capabilities, Japan must shore up its supply chain resilience. Like other countries around the world, Japan is vulnerable to critical material shortages due to global conflicts and restrictions placed by countries. Japan also needs to improve its manufacturing efficiency and strengthen its cybersecurity. Finally, Japan will need to maintain business management and training personnel in the defense industry. This is a significant challenge for Japan, which is experiencing labor shortages due to its aging society.

In addition, Japan faces challenges with companies reducing their defense business or withdrawing from the defense market altogether. The Ministry of Defense and the Japanese government must make defense production more attractive to companies so that they can strengthen production.

With a stronger defense industrial base, Japan can increase its autonomy and also contribute to greater alliance relationship building with the United States and key partners. The ambitious goals that Japan has set require more than just an increase in defense spending, however. Ultimately, without the basic requirement of having enough companies and labor involved in defense production, Tokyo’s long-term goal will be impossible to reach.

As Japan continues to revise its key security documents, it is critical that the Japanese government and Ministry of Defense realistically assess their industrial capabilities and maintain a long-term focus and commitment to strengthening and sustaining its defense industrial base.

title: China’s World AI Cooperation Organization Agenda
description: Insights from Gloria Chen.
text:
The Diplomat author Mercy Kuo regularly engages subject-matter experts, policy practitioners, and strategic thinkers across the globe for their diverse insights into U.S. Asia policy. This conversation with Gloria Chen – head of Asia-Pacific geopolitical strategy and business development at Rocky Road Resilience, a U.K.-based specialist risk advisory – is the 520th in “The Trans-Pacific View Insight Series.”

Analyze China’s agenda behind the World AI Cooperation Organization (WAICO).

The World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO) was founded in Shanghai this July, with founding members including Russia, Brazil, South Africa, Indonesia, Malaysia, and Pakistan, virtually all BRICS members except India, plus a number of other Global South countries, with no major Western democracies among its members. China positions it as an “intergovernmental organization” and claims to aim for the “beneficial, safe, and fair” development of AI.

Just as Christian civilization shaped Western culture and ways of thinking, the deeply rooted Confucian culture of China has similarly shaped the Chinese value system and language system. Confucian culture emphasizes moral correctness and face-saving, and is centered on family culture. From the perspective of the Chinese regime, China is very clear about what kind of “correct” language to use to legitimize its actions. Looking at the 2026 World AI Conference (WAIC), China tells you it wants global cooperation, AI regulation and world prosperity. However, the manifestation of family culture is often: “I tell everyone I’m promoting the common good, but what I really want is to make my family prosperous and for me to become a leader.”

Because of resource monopolies, long-term wars historically, and internal struggles, Chinese leaders have a deep-seated insecurity. Therefore, they believe that only by seizing power and controlling others can they secure their own safety. As a result, this nation finds it difficult to cooperate with others. WAICO’s abbreviation differs from the United Nations’ World AI Organization (WAIO) by only one character. Those familiar with Chinese culture know that names always have special symbolic significance for China. So I think China’s WAICO agenda is to gradually establish a China-led AI hegemonic empire.

What does the composition of the 29 WAICO signatories reveal about China’s agenda?

The WAICO strategy aims to build an organization of non-Western democratic systems led by China and to co-opt specific regimes. One of its strategic objectives is to connect regimes isolated by the international community, such as Russia, Cuba, and Myanmar, and to influence and control their political situations through financial aid and AI technology.

China provides “unconditional aid” through the Belt and Road Initiative, mobilizing vast amounts of national wealth and resources to support partner countries. This model will also appear in WAICO, with the strategic goal of maintaining relations with Global South countries to gain diplomatic leverage and extend China’s sphere of influence. China can exert influence in distant regions through AI technology and infrastructure, potentially even involving destructive activities.

To gain legitimacy for its global expansion, China attempts to package the organization’s purpose as benefiting impoverished countries and the world, portraying Western countermeasures as hegemonic suppression. China then seizes the narrative through social media platforms like TikTok and YouTube, making young people and the middle class in Western democracies believe that the CCP is a victim of suppression and a true peace advocate, thus tearing Western societies apart and weakening democratic countries from within (a strategic tactic that China excels at).

Compare and contrast China-led WAICO to U.S.-led Pax Silica Initiative.

From Xi Jinping’s speech at the World Artificial Intelligence Conference (WAIC), we can analyze the main goal of WAICO’s establishment, anti-monopoly and anti-injustice, is essentially China’s effort to build its own AI hegemony by uniting with Global South countries to break through Western technological blockades. This is China’s core objective. All the other nice-sounding words China utters, such as equality, openness, and mutual benefit, have already been said during China’s Belt and Road Initiative. Instead of listening to what the Chinese say, it’s better to observe their actions.

The United States’ Pax Silica, on the other hand, is a typical democratic capitalist initiative, emphasizing cooperation and supply chain security, and deepening economic partnerships among democratic countries. After all, for democratic countries, mutually beneficial economic cooperation under international free trade creates the greatest national interest.

Although current narratives often equate the U.S. with hegemony, democratic countries are fundamentally different from authoritarian states. Private enterprises and entrepreneurs remain a significant force in democratic societies, and democratic elections give citizens a certain degree of voice. Alliances among democratic countries are still built on trust, technological cooperation, and shared values, which is drastically different from the absolute dominance of authoritarian hegemony and its opposition to free trade.

If we continue to simply portray China and the United States as two superpowers vying for hegemony, we are likely to fall into the linguistic trap set by China. This kind of argument misleads people into portraying China and the United States as similar countries. However, the United States is a democratic country and China is a dictatorship, and they are fundamentally different in nature.

Examine how WAICO advances China’s geopolitical ambitions.

WAICO can be seen as China’s AI version of the Belt and Road Initiative. Both follow similar paths, and one of their strategic objectives is to connect non-democratic regimes like Russia and Cuba that are not integrated into the international community. Their shared goal is to counter U.S. pressure and establish opposing camps in international geopolitics, using WAICO as an organizational tool for China to extend its sphere of influence.

The Belt and Road Initiative’s strategic objective is to build an “axis of evil” against Western democratic values ​​through monetary diplomacy and alliances with authoritarian regimes. This same strategic objective is also reflected in WAICO. The difference lies in the inclusion of China’s advantageous AI capabilities, shifting the competitive landscape beyond the manufacturing and high-tech industries where China has historically struggled against the West.

Assess the role of WAICO in intensifying the China-U.S. AI race and its implications for AI sovereignty and governance.

China possesses advantages in the AI ​​industry that Western countries lack. In the past, China struggled to truly surpass Western technology at the forefront of innovation. However, in the AI ​​industry, which heavily relies on databases and testing personnel, China boasts a much larger pool of testing personnel and unparalleled data compared to the West.

According to the “Statistical Report on Internet Development in China,” as of December 2025, China had 1.125 billion internet users and 602 million generative AI users, representing a 141.7 percent increase in AI users compared to the end of 2024. This has created one of the world’s largest training data pools, providing a powerful impetus for model development and optimization. This massive scale enables Chinese developers to conduct large-scale AI training and inference faster than most other countries, and to further test, improve, and deploy artificial intelligence systems

Furthermore, the Chinese government has the authority to rapidly and centrally invest its highly monopolized resources in the AI ​​industry, devoting all its efforts to strengthening computing power, algorithms, and data infrastructure. This speed and resource allocation model is difficult for Western democratic governments to achieve. A report released by the China Internet Network Information Center (CNNIC) shows that as of the end of December last year, China’s generative AI computing power exceeded 1590 quadrillion calculations per second. Data from the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) shows that China has become the world’s largest holder of AI patents, accounting for as much as 60 percent.

China has placed artificial intelligence at the core of its economic strategy and, through the establishment of WAICO, is actively promoting the creation of an international system to regulate the use of this technology. By leveraging its ever-growing AI capabilities, China seeks to dominate the AI ​​regulatory system, a part of its efforts to reshape the international order. This is not merely about the AI ​​industry; it’s about overthrowing Western liberal values ​​and reshaping a new world order. This is China’s fundamental strategy.

At this year’s WAIC, Xi Jinping stated, “We should formulate laws and regulations, technology monitoring, early warning, and emergency response systems to ensure that artificial intelligence always remains under human control.” Xi also expressed opposition to prioritizing the security of one nation over the security of others in the field of AI.

While these statements are politically correct, their essence is that China wants to seize control of the discourse and leadership in AI regulation. In other words, China wants to decide how AI can be used and how it can answer questions, much like China’s “DeepSeek,” always avoiding sensitive political issues. The Chinese Communist Party (CCP), which rose to power through propaganda, understands that AI will be the search engine and encyclopedia of the new era. Only by controlling the AI ​​regulatory system can the CCP write its desired historical narrative.

Maintaining power and achieving global dominance are China’s core strategic goals in AI. For China, the arrival of the AI ​​era represents its only historical opportunity to defeat the West, what Xi Jinping calls “seizing historical opportunities.”

At the WAIC, Beijing-based startup Moonshot AI launched its powerful new flagship model, Kimi K3. Other highlights included MiniMax’s M3 model and Huawei’s Atlas 950 “super node.” Compared to the closed systems of American giants OpenAI and Anthropic, an increasing number of foreign companies, such as Siemens, and numerous Silicon Valley engineers are adopting Chinese open-source AI models due to their performance, low cost, and the customization features. If Western countries cannot stop this trend, the increasing use of Chinese AI models by Western companies and AI professionals will create another form of supply chain hijacking.

title: Dr. Moses Haregewoyn and the Operational Case for a Different Kind of Global Health Leadership
description: Filling a gap in global health governance
text:
When governments lose the ability to administer healthcare access, they do not announce it. There is no declaration, no visible collapse. What happens instead is quieter and more corrosive: eligible citizens fall through eligibility systems, enrollment backlogs accumulate, coverage lapses at moments of medical need, and the public health framework that policy makers spent years designing begins to fail the people it was built for — not because the policy was wrong, but because no one built the infrastructure to carry it.

This is the governance failure that rarely appears in international health leadership discourse. And it is the failure that Dr. Moses Haregewoyn has spent more than three decades working to prevent.

As President of Automated Health Systems, Dr. Haregewoyn leads an organization that functions as an operational layer of public health access across the United States. AHS does not provide medical treatment; it does something that health systems increasingly depend on but rarely discuss: it ensures that the administrative architecture connecting citizens to coverage actually works. Eligibility determination, enrollment brokerage, managed care coordination, citizen support infrastructure — these are the systems through which healthcare policy either reaches people or fails to. AHS operates in that space, at national scale, in partnership with government agencies across effectively all fifty states.

The Strategic Dimension of Health Administration

The COVID-19 pandemic clarified something that public health analysts had long argued without sufficient audience: health system capacity is not a social welfare metric. It is a component of national resilience. States that could not administer coverage, manage redeterminations at scale, or maintain contact center operations under surge conditions did not merely fail their citizens medically. They experienced fiscal exposure, workforce disruption, and erosion of the institutional trust that stable governance requires.

Dr. Haregewoyn’s organization was among the contractors that sustained operations through that period without service interruption, maintaining accountability to state government partners at the moment those partners were under the greatest pressure they had faced in a generation. That record is not incidental to his broader standing in health governance conversations. It is the foundation of it.

His academic formation — spanning organizational behavior, public health, sociology, and business administration — reflects an understanding of healthcare that goes beyond clinical delivery. He has described the challenge of modern health systems not as a medical problem but as a governance and information management challenge: the organization of data, access, and administrative coordination at a scale that most institutions have never been designed to handle.

What Global Health Governance Is Missing

The WHO and the multilateral bodies that shape international health policy draw their leadership overwhelmingly from clinical medicine, epidemiology, and diplomacy. They draw it far less frequently from people who have spent careers building and operating the administrative infrastructure through which health policy reaches populations. That gap has consequences that the pandemic made visible and that the global health community has been slow to address.

Dr. Haregewoyn has participated in policy forums across Europe, South Asia, the Gulf, and beyond. He has published on the social determinants of health access, taught graduate-level courses in public health administration and organizational leadership, and built an institution that has operated under binding government accountability for nearly five decades. His 2023 book, Leadership: An Incumbent of Faith, extends that institutional philosophy into a framework for ethical stewardship in public systems — the kind of leadership, he argues, that is measured not by visibility but by the sustained improvement of systems that quietly serve millions.

The Argument for Operational Depth

Policy observers studying the AHS model have noted a consistent finding: effective healthcare expansion requires administrative architecture before infrastructure growth. Digitized eligibility systems, citizen support infrastructure, trained administrative staff, and measurable performance frameworks are not implementation details. They are the preconditions for any health policy achieving its stated purpose.

“People are already mentioning your name in connection with the World Health Organization conversation, and even being part of that discussion matters to you” — the framing that Dr. Haregewoyn has accepted reflects something important about where global health leadership is heading. The institutions best positioned to address the next generation of health governance challenges are not those with the most sophisticated clinical research. They are those who understand how to build systems that work reliably, at scale, for populations that have no alternative when they do not.

That is an operational argument. It is also increasingly a strategic one. Dr. Haregewoyn has been making it for thirty years, in the only language that governments ultimately trust: sustained, accountable, verifiable performance.

This is a sponsored article.

title: Flash Flood Devastates China-Nepal Border Region
description: The flood, centered on Nepal's Rasuwa District and China's Gyirong County, killed at least 160 people, with 900 still missing.
text:
A devastating flash flood along the China-Nepal border has killed at least 160 people, with nearly a thousand more missing. The disaster centered on Nepal’s Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts, including the trading hub of Syabrubesi on the border. On the Chinese side, Gyirong County in Tibet was hit.

Via Google Maps. Nepal’s Rasuwa District is marked in red.

According to Nepali officials, the flood began at 8:40 a.m. on August 26, just three minutes after a magnitude 4.4 earthquake hit in Tibet, on China’s side of the border. That apparently caused a landslide involving both rock and ice from a Himalayan glacier. When the material flowed into the Lhende River in Tibet, known in Nepal as the Bhotekoshi, it caused the river to catastrophically overflow its banks.

The Kathmandu Post summarized a Nepali-language explanation offered by Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA):

The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said a preliminary study, based on an analysis of Planet Labs satellite imagery, indicates that a debris-laden flood entered the Lhende river after a glacial-rock slide occurred along the Nepal-China border, about 20 kilometres northeast of the Rasuwagadhi border point. The flood then flowed through Timure and entered the Trishuli river.

What exactly transformed a relatively minor earthquake into a crushing flood remains unclear. The Kathmandu Post reported that both Nepal and China were struggling to get accurate information in the immediate aftermath of the disaster. Citing Nepal’s consul general in Lhasa, the capital of Tibet, the Post said that “neither Nepali nor Chinese authorities had been able to establish contact with security personnel deployed along parts of the Nepal-China border. As a result, there was no authoritative information on what had triggered the massive outburst.”

Speculation centers on a glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF), and for good reason: this particular kind of natural disaster has become more and more common in the Himalayan region in recent years. As glacial melt accelerates on our warming planet, the meltwater can become trapped behind debris, creating a new glacial lake. But if that natural dam breaks – perhaps under strain from a landslide, or shaken loose by an earthquake, or both – it releases a massive flood, along with all the debris that had been trapped.

A GLOF in India’s Sikkim in 2023 killed more than 100 people. The 2021 Uttarakhand flood, also in the Indian Himalayas, killed more than 200. Floods and landslides have become an annual occurrence in India’s Northeast, which borders both Nepal and China.

According to the latest statement from Nepal’s Office of the Prime Minister, 95 bodies have been recovered, many of which have yet to be identified. Hundreds of people are still missing, including 85 security personnel, 60 people “associated with various hydropower projects,” and 484 tourists (391 foreigners and 93 Nepalis). The tourists include 100 visitors from India, many of whom are in Nepal on a religious pilgrimage, 47 from the United States, and 33 from the United Kingdom.

Update: Nepal’s government has now confirmed 158 deaths, with over 400 people still missing.

Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority reported that nearly 200 people had been rescued from the affected area, with search and rescue operations ongoing. Videos posted online by the Nepal Police show a massive wall of water destroying a bridge and a town partially buried under mud.

As of this writing, China’s state-run broadcaster, CCTV, had confirmed only three deaths, but 265 people remain missing. Between China and Nepal, then, nearly 900 people are still unaccounted for, suggesting the death toll could rise sharply as recovery operations continue.

General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party Xi Jinping, who is also China’s president, instructed local authorities “to make every effort to search for and rescue missing persons, relocate and resettle threatened people, and promptly treat the injured to minimize casualties,” according to CCTV. He also called for strengthening “monitoring and early warning systems.” While Xi didn’t mention it specifically, Nepali researchers have said a lack of timely information sharing about conditions on either side of the border may have contributed to the devastating impact.

In a post on Facebook, Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah said that the Nepali Army, Armed Police Force, and Nepal Police had been dispatched to the scene of the disaster “for rescue and relief operations.”

In a follow-up post, Shah extended his “heartfelt” and “deepest condolences to those brothers and sisters who have mourned the loss of their people, their family, and everything.” He also had a message for the flood victims:

The pain you have suffered and the loss you have suffered is not small. But I want to assure you – you are not alone in these difficult times. The kingdom is with you all with its resources. Please be patient. The government will take full responsibility for your rescue, treatment, food, and shelter.

The flood will pose a test for Shah and his relatively new government. Shah took office as prime minister on March 27, 2026; he hadn’t quite reached the five-month mark before the disaster hit. A relative political neophyte, Shah was elected on a wave of anti-establishment sentiment after Gen Z protesters forced the previous government from office. But his lack of experience was already causing some headaches even before the flood.

title: ‘Golden Kamuy’ and Modern Russo-Japanese Relations
description: The manga-turned-anime serves as an important pop cultural piece in understanding Japan’s place in the world, most specifically its historic role with Russia and their Northeast Asian borderlands.
text:
Spoiler Alert: Key plot points in “Golden Kamuy” discussed in detail below.

Modern-day relations between Japan and Russia are complex, with one of the most pivotal turning points in the relationship being the 1904-1905 Russo-Japanese War. While the conflict has been extensively studied in academic literature, a popular manga and anime known as “Golden Kamuy” uses the backdrop of the Russo-Japanese War to reevaluate Russo-Japanese relations more broadly, as well as the status of the Ainu and other indigenous Far Eastern people.

“Golden Kamuy,” created by Noda Satoru, ran as a serialized manga from 2014 to 2022. It then spawned a five-season anime series, with its final segment expected to wrap up in late 2026, and several live-action movies. “Golden Kamuy” focuses on Sugimoto Saichi, a veteran of the Russo-Japanese War, and an Ainu girl named Asirpa. The two team up in search of a hidden treasure trove of gold, but they have to piece together a map tattooed across the backs of 24 prisoners who escaped from Abashiri prison. The duo encounters both allies and enemies in their quest.

Location plays a leading role in “Golden Kamuy”: most of the action takes place in Hokkaido, today the northernmost island of Japan and historically the homeland of the Ainu people. A prominent subplot also brings the main characters to Sakhalin, a Russo-Japanese borderland that is today Russian territory; the area has also long been settled by indigenous Ainu, Nivkh, and Uilta/Orok peoples. The interplay of Japanese, Russian, and Ainu cultures in the show, especially as territorial claims changed hands (most notably in the case of Sakhalin), drives the plot forward and showcases how those interactions continue to shape relations in this part of the world today.

In addition, “Golden Kamuy” inserts itself into pivotal moments of Russian and Japanese history by weaving its narrative into real-life historical events. For example, Wilk, the father of Asirpa, became a revolutionary in his youth after suffering under Russian and Japanese colonial encroachment in his homeland of Karafuto (today’s Southern Sakhalin). He dreamed of establishing a Far Eastern federation in Hokkaido and Sakhalin, governed by the Ainu and other Far Eastern indigenous people, to preserve their linguistic and cultural heritage. To achieve this goal, he joined the People’s Will, a Russian anti-monarchist organization, and assassinated Tsar Alexander II by throwing a bag of bombs into his carriage.

Despite the creative liberties Noda took by reimagining Wilk as the assassin of the tsar, other elements of this plot point reflect historical fact: the People’s Will was an actual revolutionary movement most famous for carrying out a bomb attack against Tsar Alexander II in March 1881, prematurely ending his reign and reversing Russia’s progressive path with the authoritarian turns of his successors Tsar Alexander III and Tsar Nicholas II.

“Golden Kamuy” also touches upon the Meiji Restoration: Hijikata Toshizou, one of the main ensemble characters, is an elderly samurai based on a real-life historical figure of the same name. He represents the old order, having risen to prominence under the Tokugawa shogunate, and openly clashes with Meiji officials seeking to overturn the old system. The real Toshizou fled to Hokkaido and helped create the Republic of Ezo, a short-lived separatist state; he ultimately died during the Battle of Hakodate in 1869 (well before the Russo-Japanese War), accelerating the fall of this Tokugawa holdover state. Meanwhile, his fictional counterpart in “Golden Kamuy” was imprisoned at Abashiri prison; after he escaped, he still strived to reestablish the Republic of Ezo with the hidden gold.

The legacy of two hugely transformative historical events mentioned in the previous section ultimately collided in the 1904-1905 Russo-Japanese War. Although the war’s impact on Russia is less extensively explored in “Golden Kamuy,” the defeat of the Russian Empire exposed the weaknesses of the Romanov monarchy, including incompetent military leadership overconfident in the Tsarist navy’s power. The loss of the war is arguably one of the catalysts for the 1905 Revolution and ultimately paved the way for the Bolsheviks to seize power in 1917. (Side note: for more information about the Russian perspective on this conflict, accounts include the memoirs of General A.N. Kuropatkin and the collection Русско-японская война 1904–1905 гг. в воспоминаниях.)

On the other hand, the Japanese victory is extensively featured in “Golden Kamuy”: the successful war cemented Japan’s status as a major power, seemingly affirming the societal restructuring pursued during the Meiji Restoration.

Perhaps most consequential for the show’s main characters, however, was how the victory in the Russo-Japanese War influenced imperial Japan’s renewed assertiveness for fully integrating Hokkaido into Japan’s sphere of influence- including the assimilation of its Ainu populace into mainstream Japanese society.

Asirpa serves as a bridge between the Ainu and her Japanese and Russian counterparts, teaching them the Ainu language and explaining cultural traditions. As she leaves her kotan (village) during her travels with Sugimoto and her cohort, she witnesses how her fellow Ainu were losing their sense of identity amid colonial Japanese administrative policies. This realization motivates her quest for the lost gold, as she wants to secure the wealth in Ainu hands to protect and preserve their culture and heritage. As much as Asirpa admires the Ainu way of life, however, she is not frozen in time. Throughout the course of the show, she frequently emphasizes that she is “a new kind of Ainu woman, for a new age!” Thus, she sought to engage with her Japanese, Russian, and other counterparts as a cultural ambassador, learning and engaging with them while ensuring that the Ainu were not overly endangered by outside advances into their territories or ways of life.

Efforts by real life Asirpas to preserve the Ainu way of life were not as successful. Discrimination and pressure to assimilate into Japanese society virtually erased numerous aspects of Ainu cultural identity, including the now critically endangered Ainu language. That being said, recent years have signaled a renaissance of renewed pride in Ainu identity. Language revitalization programs, including immersive classes and AI speech synthesis, are helping to combat Ainu linguistic extinction. The Upopoy National Ainu Museum and Park, opened in 2020, serves as an integral center for preserving Ainu history and culture.

“Golden Kamuy” itself has proven instrumental in sparking modern interest in the Ainu by being featured in international artistic and cultural exhibitions and boosting tourism to Hokkaido. Thus, while the Ainu have faced enormous struggles over the past decades, if not centuries, efforts such as “Golden Kamuy” fight to ensure that this culture’s legacy will endure in the future by educating a new generation of manga and anime-loving Japanese (and global fans) about the existence and importance of the Ainu.

The interconnection between pop culture and geopolitics is arguably one of the lesser-known sub-genres of international relations, but there is growing interest in understanding it. A recent essay by the Lowy Institute, for example, discussed how Japanese manga and anime help improve bilateral relations between India and Japan. “Golden Kamuy” serves as an important pop cultural piece that is integral in understanding Japan’s place in the world, most specifically its historic role with Russia and their Northeast Asian borderlands.

As for Russo-Japanese relations today, they are currently at a historic low due to the long-contested Southern Kuril Islands (which Russia calls the Northern Territories) territorial dispute and Japanese support for Ukraine during the seemingly never-ending Russo-Ukrainian War. While there is currently no major sign of a positive breakthrough between Tokyo and Moscow, it is still worthwhile to examine how “Golden Kamuy” serves as a useful medium for attempting to unpack and disentangle the complexity of their relations, especially their numerous territorial disputes (specifically surrounding Sakhalin and the Kuril Islands) and treatment of the Ainu and other indigenous populations.
tag: Ainu; Golden Kamuy; Russia-Japan relations; Russo-Japanese War

title: Has Life in North Korea Changed Since 2013?
description: The author of “Witness to North Korea” reflects on which lessons from his time in the country are still relevant today.
text:
Last month, as I launched my new book “Witness to North Korea,” conversations with Wall Street Beijing Bureau Chief Jonathan Cheng and NK News’ Alannah Hill brought up one important question: is this memoir of my three years living and working as the United Nations Resident Coordinator in the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK) still relevant to the North Korea of today?

I wrote this book for anyone wishing to understand, as Stimson Center Fellow Frank Aum wrote, “what it actually means to engage with the DPRK – not in the abstract language of policy briefs, but through the granular, often maddening, reality of day-to-day diplomacy and humanitarian work.”

This question of continued relevance between what I observed then and the country today is a valid one. After all, I left Pyongyang in 2013 – and yes, things in the country have changed since my departure. Some North Korea experts talk of a rising middle class with cash to spare, of one mobile phone subscriber for every three North Koreans, of ski resorts – all thanks to the phenomena of marketization and monetization changing the up-to-now closed economy and forcing the hand of the North Korean regime to open to international trade.

Another thing has changed: data has become even harder to obtain. In 2020, North Korea used the COVID-19 pandemic to deny entry to several EU-member countries that had kept an embassy in Pyongyang and to most of the international community’s assistance programs. These embassies and resident U.N. agencies, as well as most international NGOs, have not yet returned. The U.N. population census remains, to this day, an essential source of quality data about North Korean society. Sadly, there has not been such an exercise since I left 13 years ago.

My discussions with U.N. officials and humanitarian organizations point, today, to a continuation of the underlying problems that I describe in my book, which continue to shape the lives of ordinary North Koreans. Kim Jong Un’s regime continues to experience a gap between intention and reality in four major areas: food and nutrition; public health and infectious disease; availability of medicines and medical equipment; and, finally, technical cooperation and capacity building. These problems concern both domestic limitations and international constraints.

During my years in Pyongyang, the United Nations and many NGOs worked with North Korean institutions to improve agricultural production, strengthen health services, support maternal and child nutrition, conduct the national population census, and assist vulnerable communities facing chronic shortages. These efforts were based on a simple reality: despite its political isolation, the North Korean population faced genuine needs that could not be solved through sanctions or diplomacy alone.

Kim Jong Un’s unusually candid admission last February that agricultural production remains inadequate and that decades of rural policy have failed echoes many of the concerns that humanitarian agencies encountered during my posting. While today the emphasis has shifted toward livestock production, dairy farming, and regional development, the objective remains the same: providing sufficient and nutritious food to a population that continues to experience chronic shortages.

During my time in North Korea, workplaces and factories would allow their people to leave during the day to forage in the hills, as the government acknowledged the persistence of a “food problem.” Today, the North Korean government’s ambitious rural modernization program reflects an acknowledgement that food security is still a national challenge rather than a problem of the past.

The health sector presents an equally familiar picture. Authors Joon Hee Han and Yo Han Lee, in a deeply researched January 2026 article titled “North Korea’s 2025 Health Revolution,” found that while North Korea is investing heavily in new hospitals and health infrastructure, questions remain about foundational input such as medicines, trained personnel, reliable electricity, and sustainable financing.

Similarly, during my time in Pyongyang, we repeatedly found that physical infrastructure alone could not guarantee improved health outcomes without parallel investments in equipment, pharmaceuticals, professional training, and institutional capacity. All indications suggest that, aside from the usual showy investment centered on Pyongyang, this lesson remains as relevant as it was when I visited health centers around the country from 2009 to 2013.

Many reports point to a shift in international aid from Russia, and away from Europe and the United States. And yet, the issues the country faces remain unchanged. A Russian court ordered more than 30 North Korean nationals to undergo tuberculosis treatment in Moscow in 2024 and 2025, according to court documents, belatedly confirming both North Korean labor flows into Russia and a suspected infection outbreak among overseas workers.

During my assignment to Pyongyang, tuberculosis was already recognized as one of North Korea’s most serious public health challenges, and international cooperation played an essential role in diagnosis, treatment, and prevention. The prevalence of the disease over a decade later highlights the well-known problem of continuing weaknesses in disease detection, treatment and public health capacity in North Korea – and the continuing importance of international health cooperation.

Finally, aside from North Korea’s unwillingness to receive technical assistance from the United Nations, NGOs, and a few bilateral donors, current international restrictions continue to make international engagement difficult. Engagement is neither a concession to the regime nor an endorsement of its policies. It is a practical means of empowering individuals while creating channels of communication in an otherwise isolated country.

The recent debate over sanctions exemptions, NGO licensing, and restrictions on humanitarian operations demonstrates that this question remains unresolved. If anything, international assistance organizations today face even greater operational obstacles than during my tenure.

Yet international technical cooperation continues to matter. International agencies connect North Korea to the world through a variety of interventions such as civil aviation coordination, vaccination programs, or drug control – albeit within limits and constraints due to their reduced ability to implement and monitor their programs on the ground.

These developments reinforce one of the principal conclusions from my time in the country: technical assistance to North Korea should not be viewed as a political reward but as a means to support the North Korean people. Isolation has not eliminated North Korea’s needs. Instead, it has often made it more difficult for international organizations to respond effectively to them.

The regime is not a static monolith. Parts of the leadership, aware of structural weaknesses, attempt significant reforms in agriculture, health care, and regional development. International assistance should support them, not by replacing domestic responsibility but by providing expertise, resources, and technical cooperation where they are most needed.

The dilemmas I described in “Witness to North Korea” – how to balance sanctions with humanitarian principles, how to engage without legitimizing the regime, and how to reach vulnerable populations while respecting international law – will shape the work in Pyongyang and the international community’s posture toward North Korea. The details have evolved, but the fundamental questions remain consistent.

For readers seeking to understand whether international engagement with North Korea still matters, the answer emerging from both my experience and these recent developments is clear. The country’s population continues to face serious challenges, and sustained, principled, smart engagement remains one of the few practical means of improving the lives of ordinary North Koreans while preserving channels for dialogue in one of the world’s most isolated states.

title: Hitting a High Point: The Australia-Indonesia 2+2
description: The significance of the 2+2 is the growing web of cooperation between Canberra and Jakarta.
text:
Last week, Australia and Indonesia held their tenth 2+2 defense and foreign ministers meeting in Melbourne. The two countries signed the landmark Jakarta Treaty on Common Security in 2024, and although the Indonesian parliament has yet to ratify the treaty, the 2+2 meeting proceeded with the assumption that this is simply the pace of Indonesia’s legislative processes, and that discussions can turn to how best to operationalize their cooperation.

The headline claim is that the relationship between the two countries is now “at a high point.” The Albanese government has made the relationship with Indonesia one of the central pillars of Australia’s foreign policy, understanding how vital friendly, cooperative, relations with its giant near neighbor is to the country’s security. Indonesia, for its part, has recognized it has a capable partner in Canberra that can help advance its own security interests, while maintaining its strategic autonomy.

Although the two countries are seeking to broaden their relationship, at present, defense and security cooperation remain the core elements and these areas were naturally a major focus of the discussions last week.

Given the nature of their geographies, this has developed into a focus on maritime security. At the 2+2 meeting it was announced that Australia will provide aerial drones and training to Indonesia’s Coast Guard. Given that illegal fishing is a central concern throughout Indonesia’s vast waters, and that Chinese often use maritime militia disguised as fishing vessels, greater maritime domain awareness is considered essential for Jakarta.

Alongside this, Australia and Indonesia agreed to increase cooperation on cybercrime, critical infrastructure, and artificial intelligence, building on their existing memorandum of understanding on enhanced cybersecurity and critical technology cooperation. This includes incorporating a defensive cybersecurity component into their bilateral defense exercise, Keris Woomera. Here, cybersecurity is not treated as a separate technical issue, but as a central pillar of military preparedness and national defense.

There is a similar thinking around economic security as inseparable from traditional security. The ministers announced a number of initiatives designed to make their economies more resilient to external shocks and any disruption to supply chains. This included new cooperation to jointly analyze critical supply chain issues and new scholarship courses that will be focused on economic security and resilience – hoping to develop a new cohort of analysts and bureaucrats focused on these issues.

The two countries have already demonstrated how economic interdependence can provide security benefits, with Indonesia working with Australian industry to facilitate a 250,000-tonne agricultural-grade supply of urea due to disruptions from the war in Iran. Alongside this, Australian liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) exports to Indonesia have increased threefold over the past year, again in response to supply chain disruptions in the Middle East.

These practical forms of food and energy security are becoming increasingly intertwined with geopolitics. The two countries therefore have an interest in using the resources of one another to address their vulnerabilities. Given both their proximity to each other, and their current distance from global hotspots, there is an opportunity to build resilience together that can withstand any global shocks.

These shocks include the environment. The 2+2 meeting announced the second phase of KINETIK – the Australia-Indonesia Climate and Sustainable Infrastructure Partnership, which will provide US$430 million over ten years to support sustainable infrastructure and climate investment in Indonesia. Its aim is to mobilize public and private capital into clean energy, water, waste management, and sustainable transport, helping Indonesia build climate-resilient infrastructure and accelerate its energy transition. With the hope of the two countries also developing their green technology capabilities.

The 2+2 meeting also demonstrated considered strategic alignment over the regional order – something that hasn’t always been the case. The two countries reaffirmed their commitment to international law, sovereignty and ASEAN centrality, with both expressing concern about rising tensions in the South China Sea and insisting that the Code of Conduct being developed by ASEAN and China must comply with international law.

The significance of the 2+2 is the growing web of cooperation between Canberra and Jakarta. From defense exercises to maritime surveillance to cybersecurity and economic resilience, there has been a noticeable step up in the relationship. This does not amount to a formal alliance, but more a convergence of interests and a recognition that as neighbors there is a natural interconnectedness. The previous distance in outlook and coordination is starting to be overcome.
