title: How an Election in Okinawa Will Impact East Asian Security
description: Incumbent Governor Denny Tamaki is known for his staunch anti-U.S. base sentiment. His re-election bid will ripple through the alliance and beyond.
text:
Okinawa Prefecture will hold its gubernatorial election on September 13. Incumbent Governor Denny Tamaki, in office since 2018, is seeking a third term. His main challenger is Koja Genta, a former deputy mayor of Naha backed by the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP). While local elections in Japan typically center on issues like the local economy and social welfare, Okinawa’s pivotal geographic location means this election could become a critical variable influencing the future security situation of East Asia.

Okinawa sits at the heart of the First Island Chain and is the Japanese territory closest to both Taiwan and mainland China. Consequently, since the end of World War II, Okinawa has served as the U.S. military’s “Keystone of the Pacific,” bearing a heavy military burden. Currently, nearly 70 percent of U.S. military bases in Japan are located in Okinawa.

Beyond the U.S. presence, Japan’s Self-Defense Forces (SDF) are also expanding their deployments in Okinawa as the country accelerates a defense strategy known as the “Southwest Shift.” For instance, the Ground Self-Defense Force’s 15th Brigade, stationed in Okinawa, is set to be reorganized into a division by March 2027, increasing its personnel from 2,300 to 3,900. Furthermore, over the past decade, the Japanese government has deployed SDF units to Yonaguni, Miyako, and Ishigaki, islands located west of Okinawa Island, while bolstering radar, air defense, and rapid-response capabilities to counter the People’s Liberation Army’s (PLA) growing military activity in the East China Sea and the Western Pacific beyond the First Island Chain.

In fact, the PLA and the SDF have frequently engaged in standoffs in the area in recent years. On December 6, 2025, a fighter jet launched from a Chinese aircraft carrier locked radar on an Air Self-Defense Force fighter while flying over the high seas southeast of Okinawa Island, sparking a strong protest from Tokyo. Additionally, Chinese naval fleets and joint Chinese-Russian fleets have frequently transited the waters surrounding these islands. These developments underscore how Okinawa is increasingly becoming a frontline for great power confrontation.

For the people of Okinawa situated at the eye of the storm, the issue of U.S. and Japanese military deployments is not a simple matter of support versus opposition. It involves conflicting inner sentiments.

On one hand, as China increases its activities near Okinawa – particularly with frequent patrols by its coast guard vessels in the waters around the Senkaku Islands (known in China as the Diaoyu Islands) – Okinawan perceptions of the military forces stationed there are shifting. According to public opinion polls, a greater number of Okinawans now view the presence of the SDF and even the U.S. military as necessary compared to the 1970s, shortly after the islands’ return to Japan.

On the other hand, this shift does not alleviate Okinawans’ collective anxiety. For Tokyo, the deployment of missiles, radar systems, and SDF units may signify enhanced deterrence and situational awareness. However, for the local residents, these facilities also imply a higher likelihood that their home could become a frontline in a conflict or a target for attack. This has sparked a contradictory mindset and an enduring debate among the Okinawan people: Do military assets guarantee their safety or bring greater danger?

Since taking office as prefectural governor in 2018, Tamaki has made opposition to the construction of the new U.S. base at Henoko and the reduction of the base burden on Okinawa the core of his political agenda. However, the LDP’s victory in all four of Okinawa’s electoral districts during the February 2026 House of Representatives election clearly served as a warning sign for Tamaki. Furthermore, a capsizing incident in March involving boats participating in protests against the Henoko base, which resulted in two fatalities, including a student on a school trip, triggered criticism directed at Tamaki, a staunch opponent of the base. The upcoming election will serve as a critical test of Tamaki’s stance against the Henoko base, the expansion of SDF deployments in Okinawa, and joint Japan-U.S. military exercises.

This is why the contest between Tamaki and Koja holds significance that extends beyond local politics. If Tamaki is re-elected, Tokyo may continue to face political resistance from the Okinawa prefectural government. While a governor cannot single-handedly halt the Japanese government’s national defense policies, a local government opposed to Tokyo’s military agenda can still raise the political costs of implementation and engage in ongoing bargaining regarding the burden of military bases and local interests. Under these circumstances, although Japan may proceed with the military deployment in the Nansei (Southwestern) Islands, the rift between Tokyo and Okinawan society could widen further.

For Tokyo, another challenge lies in preventing the discord with Okinawa from undermining Japan-U.S. alliance operations in the region. Clearly, the United States expects Japan not only to sustain investment in military deployments on Okinawa, thereby sharing security responsibilities, but also to effectively manage tensions between military forces and Okinawan society.

In September 2025, U.S. forces and the SDF conducted “Resolute Dragon 25,” a large-scale exercise spanning a vast area that included Okinawa. This sparked widespread protests among local residents. Some protesters took to the streets, directly forcing the SDF to alter its operational plans. This underscores that the Japan-U.S. alliance cannot be sustained by military facilities alone: It requires the understanding and support of the communities hosting them. If Tamaki wins re-election, the friction between Okinawan society and the military presence will be difficult to resolve over the ensuing four years.

Conversely, a victory for Koja could present a significant political opportunity for Tokyo. His election might mark a turning point in the relationship between the Okinawan prefectural government and the central government, potentially opening up greater scope for local cooperation on base policies and defense infrastructure in the Nansei Islands.

If Okinawan society increasingly perceives itself as bearing the risks of war solely for the strategic interests of Tokyo and Washington, the expansion of their military capabilities could exacerbate tensions with the local population. However, if Tokyo can convince Okinawa that strengthening defenses serves not only Japan’s national security but also the protection of Okinawa itself, then the military deployment in the Nansei Islands might secure a more stable political foundation. Ultimately, the outcome hinges largely on who leads Okinawa for the next four years.

Furthermore, this election also has implications regarding China. In recent years, Beijing has paid increasing attention to Okinawa, attempting to leverage the Okinawan people’s historical memories and anti-base sentiment to construct political narratives directed against both Japan and the United States. For instance, following Tamaki’s visit to China in July 2023, Chinese state media highlighted the historical ties between China and Okinawa (Ryukyu), as well as the tensions between Okinawan society and the U.S. military.

Furthermore, in recent years, Beijing has increasingly used its state media to question Japan’s sovereignty over Okinawa, which is a stance Tamaki has generally sought to avoid criticizing. Regarding the upcoming election, Beijing likely hopes that Tamaki, who holds a relatively moderate view toward China, will remain in office, thereby allowing for continued propaganda efforts challenging the Japan-U.S. military presence in Okinawa. However, this is clearly an outcome that neither Tokyo nor Washington desires.

In conclusion, this election will shape the relationship between Tokyo and Okinawan society over the next four years. More importantly, it will determine whether the Japan-U.S. alliance can maintain a solid foundation in Okinawa amidst China’s rise and escalating risks in the Taiwan Strait. This is precisely why the election is bound to draw intense scrutiny from Washington, Beijing, and Tokyo alike.
tag: anti-base protests in Okinawa; Denny Tamaki; Nansei Islands; Okinawa governor election; U.S. bases in Okinawa; U.S.-Japan Alliance

title: How Could the Rise of Progressive Democrats Impact US China Policy?
description: A divide over China, although less pronounced than the divide over Israel, has become increasingly visible among Democrats as progressives have risen within the party.
text:
From Analilia Mejia to Abdul El-Sayed to Peggy Flanagan, a progressive winning streak in Democratic primaries has swept across the country in the lead-up to this year’s midterm elections. Unlike most midterm election cycles, where domestic issues dominate the political agenda, foreign policy has been thrust into the spotlight this time, with the Israel-Palestine conflict emerging as the defining litmus test of the Democratic Party. As progressive candidates have rallied behind the Palestinian cause in their battles against AIPAC-backed moderates, the party’s leftward ideological shift could impact not only the decades-long Israel-U.S. alliance, but also Washington’s policy toward its greatest strategic competitor: China.

Progressives perceive the world through the lens of structural inequality. That worldview lies at the heart of their dissatisfaction with the status quo of the U.S. socioeconomic structure: a widening gap between economic elites and ordinary people. As a result, they fight against corporate interests and political corruption, thereby translating their opposition to economic elites into opposition to the political establishment. The same logic applies to foreign affairs – progressives can readily translate their anti-establishment sentiment into opposition to American primacy, which has long been buttressed by bipartisan support for U.S. military dominance.

This helps explain why Palestine has become such a powerful cause on the left. Progressives tend to view U.S.-backed Israel as an extension of American power in the Middle East and Palestinians as victims of U.S. hegemony. Hence, although a parallel anti-Israel sentiment can also be seen among some Republicans, progressive Democrats have a fundamentally different motivation for their opposition to Israel. Whereas growing Republican opposition to unlimited aid to Israel is rooted largely in “America First” nationalism and isolationism, progressives seek to challenge American exceptionalism and the so-called U.S. global leadership that they believe perpetuates inequality.

Today, the rise of China is increasingly portrayed as a challenge to the U.S.-led global order. As a result, neither Republicans nor Democrats can easily depart from the bipartisan consensus that Beijing represents Washington’s greatest strategic competitor. Whoever is perceived as “soft on China” is almost certain to face attacks from the other side of the aisle. Both parties have thus become more inclined to play the “China card” whenever they deem it necessary – either to inoculate themselves against accusations of weakness or to gain a political advantage.

But the divide over China, although less pronounced than the divide over Israel, has become increasingly visible among Democrats with the rise of progressives. One vision, exemplified by establishment figures such as former President Joe Biden, sees a world defined by strategic competition, in which China-U.S. confrontation is unavoidable across a range of domains, from the economy and technology to culture. The other, exemplified by progressives such as Senator Bernie Sanders, rejects the self-fulfilling logic of the Thucydides Trap and champions a China policy centered on restraint and cooperation.

This progressive vision was on display in the remarks on Taiwan made by Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, known widely as AOC, at the Munich Security Conference this year. Despite her stumbles, AOC – arguably the biggest star among the progressive camp – captured an ethos fundamentally different from a competition-based China policy. Rather than stressing how the United States would defend Taiwan and democracy through strength, as many centrist Democrats might, she emphasized the need to work toward ensuring that the United States and China “never get to that point.”

Although it may still take time for AOC to take the national stage as a leading voice on foreign policy, her remarks epitomize a core tenet of progressive policy toward China: diplomacy before militarism.

Yes, progressives condemn China for its human rights abuses, lack of genuine democracy, and unfair trade practices. But they also hold that, instead of beating the drums for a new Cold War with the Asian powerhouse, the United States should press these issues through bilateral dialogue and multilateral institutions such as the World Trade Organization and the U.N. Human Rights Council. They understand that the effectiveness of such diplomacy depends on the moral legitimacy of the American state, both at home and on the global stage. Only in this way can the United States strengthen its ability to marshal diplomatic pressure on China when necessary, not only on its own behalf but also on behalf of its allies around the world.

For all intents and purposes, progressives are trying to build that moral legitimacy by reshaping the ideology of the Democratic Party. Nowhere is this more evident than in their challenge to the conventional U.S. support for Israel. This July, more than half of House Democrats voted to support cutting $3.3 billion in U.S. aid to Israel – a shift that would have been difficult to imagine ten years ago.

House Democrats’ new stance on Israel has a more profound implication: it could allow Congress to reclaim some of its authority over foreign policymaking from an increasingly power-hungry Donald Trump and hold policymakers accountable for poor foreign-policy decisions.

This matters because of the notoriously self-forgiving nature of the U.S. foreign policy establishment. Policymakers who make consequential mistakes can often walk away scot-free, regardless of their partisan affiliation. China policy has become one of the areas most vulnerable to this dynamic. On the Republican side, we have seen Trump’s relentless use of tariffs as a weapon against China. From the 145 percent “Liberation Day” tariffs in 2025 to the most recent 12.5 percent tariffs on Chinese imports, his aggressive use of tariffs has drawn criticism not only from Democrats but increasingly from Republicans as well. Yet Trump has continued to impose tariffs with little meaningful constraint from Congress.

On the Democratic side, then-House Speaker Nancy Pelosi’s visit to Taiwan in 2022, despite opposition from the Biden administration, likewise drew little public criticism from Democrats. The closest thing to a critique came from progressive Democrats such as Elizabeth Warren and Bernie Sanders, who chose simply to remain silent.

But progressives could change that. Instead of being constrained by so-called party unity, they could translate their ideological commitments into concrete policies to check abuses of executive power in foreign policy.

Take trade policy, for example. Progressives can connect it to their broader critique of wealth inequality in the United States. Greg Casar, chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, illustrated this approach by framing tariffs as part of a larger conflict between working-class Americans and concentrated corporate interests. Senator Ron Wyden has taken that argument a step further by introducing the Congressional Trade Powers Reform Act of 2026. If enacted, the bill would curb Trump’s unfettered tariff powers and put Congress back in the driver’s seat on U.S. trade policy, potentially reshaping China-U.S. economic relations in the process.

As the 2028 presidential election nears, the “China card” is very likely to be played with increasing frequency. If the Democratic Party manages to flip the House in the midterm elections, progressives will have the next two years to negotiate and experiment with their foreign policy ideas alongside centrist Democrats. While a major breakthrough on Gaza may take time, given the establishment’s longstanding ties to Israel, Democrats can test progressive ideas on China without facing the same level of backlash they might face by systematically opposing Israel.

If a progressive China policy proves effective, it could inject fresh energy into a bland Democratic foreign-policy agenda that has left many voters frustrated – and potentially push Republicans to rethink their own approach to China.
tag: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez; Democratic Party; Democrats China policy; progressive Democrats; U.S. 2026 elections; U.S. midterm elections

title: How South Korea Can Survive the Unbundling of International Order
description: South Korea’s strategic challenges – and the potential solutions – make the case for democratic multilateralism.
text:
For most of the post-war era, power, legitimacy, and cooperation reinforced one another. American leadership underwrote security, open markets, and freedom of navigation. Democratic partnerships generated political trust. Universal institutions such as the United Nations, the World Trade Organization, and the nuclear nonproliferation regime provided common rules and legal legitimacy. Though imperfect, these three pillars generally worked in concert.

That alignment has broken down. Security, economic governance, political legitimacy, and practical cooperation are no longer occurring in the same institutions or even among the same groups of states. I call this structural transformation the “unbundling of order.” The result is disalignment, a condition in which power, legitimacy, and cooperation no longer reinforce one another.

Analysts today often ask whether the liberal international order is collapsing or which great power will replace the United States. The real question is whether the essential functions of the international order can be reconnected under increasingly fragmented geopolitical conditions.

Russia’s invasion of Ukraine exposed the inability of existing institutions like the United Nations to prevent or halt great power aggression. The ongoing conflict between the United States and Iran demonstrated that military superiority alone cannot ensure regional stability or the credibility of the global nonproliferation regime. Competition – especially, but not exclusively between China and the United States – over semiconductors, artificial intelligence, critical minerals, and maritime supply chains blurs the traditional boundary between economics and security.

Cooperation is increasingly necessary, but the most inclusive institutions are often the least capable of collective action. This paradox has driven the rise of minilateralism. Smaller groups of like-minded partners can coordinate quickly, protect sensitive technologies, strengthen supply chain resilience, and respond effectively to shared threats. But while minilateral coalitions can act quickly, they lack broad legitimacy. Meanwhile, universal institutions provide legal authority and political inclusion but often struggle to act.

Neither is sufficient alone. Democratic multilateralism must combine legitimacy with operational capacity.

This is why democracy itself retains strategic importance. Democratic multilateralism is more than cooperation among states with shared political values. It provides a foundation for institutional trust. Intelligence sharing, advanced technology cooperation, defense industrial integration, financial coordination, and resilient supply chains all depend on confidence that partners will safeguard sensitive information, uphold long-term commitments, and remain accountable despite changes in government. Democratic governments may disagree, yet transparent institutions and political accountability make sustained strategic cooperation more credible.

South Korea stands at the intersection of today’s defining strategic challenges: nuclear deterrence, China-U.S. competition, technological rivalry, supply chain resilience, and democratic cooperation. Its security depends on the alliance with the United States, its prosperity on an open global economy, and its future competitiveness on reliable technology networks. Few countries are therefore more exposed to the unbundling of order or better positioned to shape what follows.

Seoul must continue to diversify its partnerships, but diversification alone is not a strategy. It needs an organizing logic that connects its alliances, partnerships, markets, and institutions. It must determine which functions remain anchored in the U.S. alliance, which require broader networks, and how smaller, function-specific coalitions can be linked to or nested within broader regional and global institutions.

For South Korea, deterrence will continue to depend primarily on the U.S. alliance. Technological resilience requires secure networks for protecting sensitive knowledge and coordinating investment. Economic security depends on diversified markets, suppliers, and production chains. Wider institutions remain essential for common rules, political inclusion, and international acceptance. The task is to make these different frameworks, each built for different purposes, mutually reinforcing.

South Korea should therefore seek not simply to balance among great powers, but to develop connective power: the capacity to align security commitments, economic partnerships, technological networks, and multilateral institutions around compatible purposes. This is a distinctive source of middle power influence. It rests not only on institutional access, but on a reputation for reliability, effective brokerage, and contributions to regional and global public goods. States with that standing can bridge alliances, functional coalitions, and wider institutions, and thereby shape the terms of cooperation.

The post-war order cannot simply be restored because the architecture that sustained it has already changed. But that doesn’t mean the world is doomed to a fate of closed and competing blocs. Instead, the more plausible alternative is not a singular order but several layered and overlapping ones. States will pursue national interests through different arrangements while cooperating where regional stability and global public goods require collective action. The most indispensable states will not necessarily dominate every arena, but will make cooperation across arenas possible.

For South Korea, bridging these system is a national imperative. Its security, prosperity, technological competitiveness, and diplomatic autonomy depend on its ability to operate across multiple institutional systems.

This essay is one of four to emerge from discussions at an international conference jointly organized by the Seoul Forum for International Affairs and the Hairan Series of Korea University’s Institute for Interdisciplinary Unification Studies, “Democratic Multilateralism at the Edge,” held in Seoul on April 20, 2026.

title: India Has a Complex Youth Unemployment Problem, And There Isn’t a Quick Fix
description: Education and skills don't match available jobs. The economy isn’t creating good-quality employment for an expanding and increasingly educated workforce.
text:
India has been struggling with a multi-faceted employment problem, which is triggering deep frustration among its youth, especially those who are educated.

This frustration was on display recently, when tens of thousands of young women and men protested at New Delhi’s Jantar Mantar, demanding the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan. While the immediate trigger for the protests was leaked question papers for medical entrance examinations, the underlying cause is frustration with an education system that doesn’t lead to meaningful employment.

The Indian economy is among the world’s fastest-growing large economies. Yet, it is producing an ever-increasing number of educated unemployed youth.

The problems are multifold. First, India is struggling to connect education and skills with available jobs. Second, its economy is not creating good-quality employment for a rapidly expanding and increasingly educated workforce. And third, poor government recruitment has rendered generic university degrees largely useless.

The warnings have been there for quite some time. A 2018 article by Indrajit Bairagya in the Economic and Political Weekly noted that the unemployment rate among the educated is not only higher than that among the uneducated, but it also increases with higher levels of education. Youth, both educated and uneducated, are more likely to be unemployed than older people. One reason is that the educated are unwilling to take low-grade informal jobs, while sufficient regular salaried jobs are also not available.

Developments over the last few years reveal a deeply worrying situation. A recent report titled “Reimagining Skilling for Viksit Bharat@2047,” published by NITI Aayog, the top policy advisor to the government of India, in August this year, said only 8.25 percent of graduates are employed in roles aligned with their qualifications. The remaining 91.75 percent are not working in roles that use the qualifications they acquired. They either acquired additional skills or are working below their skill level, the report said, blaming the poor education-to-job transition rate for India’s growing youth unemployment.

The report says that 80 percent of higher education students identify inadequate practical experience and industry exposure as a major problem. Degrees, diplomas and certificates do not consistently translate into employability when curricula remain disconnected from evolving workplace requirements. As a result, the unemployment rate among graduates stood at 13 percent, compared with the national unemployment rate of 3.2 percent; among women graduates, it was 20.4 percent.

The NITI report reveals that generic degrees don’t provide a direct pathway to employment. When a student with a graduate degree fails to land a job, she either turns to additional degrees or invests in coaching classes that she hopes will lead to a job. All these enhance the overall education costs for improving employability. The cost burden adds salt to the wounds of unemployment.

Some, including the NITI report, have suggested linking education to skills that will make youth more employable, but it cannot by itself create demand for their labor. India, therefore, also needs faster creation of productive, reasonably secure jobs capable of absorbing a large and increasingly educated workforce.

There is another problem—the informal sector is massive. Another paper published by NITI in March estimates that only 23 percent of India’s workforce are regular wage/salaried employees, while 19 percent are casual workers. The rest—about 58 percent—are self-employed/micro-entrepreneurs. Here, ‘self-employment’ often masks underemployment rather than genuine entrepreneurship.

Besides, the credibility of government data on unemployment has been called into question. A 2025 Reuters poll revealed that most of the independent economists who participated in the survey believed the Indian government’s unemployment data masks the severity of joblessness and underemployment. Official surveys use outdated definitions — counting anyone who works for as little as one hour per week as employed, they pointed out.

This means that India’s unemployment crisis is bigger than what it appears to be.

Economists have proposed various solutions. Raising concerns about the impact of automation and AI on future employment, development economist Santosh Mehrotra has called for a stronger manufacturing strategy. Former Reserve Bank of India chief Raghuram Rajan said India needed “structural economic pivots toward labor-intensive white-collar and specialized job creation.” Many have urged shifting focus away from purely capital-heavy incentives toward sectors like textiles, leather, and light engineering that can absorb the millions moving away from agriculture.

Such proposals would require policy reversals by the Narendra Modi government. Whether the government aims for such changes to earn the confidence of the youth remains to be seen.

title: India’s Climate Stress and the Solar Power Paradox
description: Rising demand will keep coal the backbone of India’s power grid in the coming years. This buys time for executing an energy transition, if India can see through its plans.
text:
In April and May 2026, all of the 50 hottest cities in the world were located in India, an ominous distinction for the country, which is witnessing deep, systemic climate stress. This trend has continued unabated into subsequent months, with high temperatures and humidity levels driving increased use of cooling appliances such as air conditioners across many states in India.

In July 2026, India’s electrical energy consumption grew 10.93 percent year-on-year to 170.70 billion units (BU). In comparison, the country’s total power consumption was 153.88 BU in July 2025. The peak power demand also jumped to 270.20 GW in July 2026. It was 220.74 GW in July 2025. The all-time record high was set in May this year with demand of 270.82 GW.

The steep rise in temperature and heat waves may be a problem for people, but for the leading air conditioner manufacturers, it is a buoyant market. Companies like Voltas and LG Electronics have reported high sales. Each had already sold over 1 million units in the first three months of the year. Panasonic India said its residential AC sales increased by 50 percent year-on-year in the summer season of 2026, representing its highest-ever level.

These are very high figures for a developing country, where 60 percent of the population depends on food subsidies and power bills are on a constant rise. It also demonstrates the fact that the rising middle class, not just in metros, but also in tier-two towns and beyond, is responding to the threat and discomfort of a warming climate with significant uptake of household cooling options. Access to air conditioning, seen increasingly as a significant health issue globally, also contributes to the global warming and climate crisis.

According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), global electricity demand is expected to grow by 3.6 percent in 2026 and 3.8 percent in 2027, driven by industry, cooling, electric vehicles (EVs), and data centers. In India, one of the world’s fastest-growing major electricity markets, it is projected to grow at 7 percent, twice the global average. In comparison, it will grow at 5.5 percent in China, 1.8 percent in the U.S., and 2.1 percent in Europe.

El Niño, a climate pattern in which surface waters in the central and eastern Pacific Ocean become significantly warmer than average, is projected to turbocharge extreme weather across the planet this year. India is already witnessing a deficient monsoon in 2026, attributable to the El Niño underway. According to the India Meteorological Department (IMD) and government vulnerability assessments, the country’s central, eastern, and northeastern regions face the highest drought risks. Reports have already indicated its possible impact on electricity generation. States like Odisha are considering a halt in hydropower generation to prioritize drinking water and irrigation. The southern states of Karnataka is prioritizing drinking water over irrigation for agriculture.

However, even with the ongoing war in Iran – which has created enormous hurdles for energy imports for India – the country has managed to generate enough power to meet this rise in demand. While international energy prices have risen during the first half of the year, India’s wholesale electricity spot prices declined by around 10 percent. This would not have been possible without India’s perennial and increasing reliance on coal, which provides 74 percent of the total power generation.

There has been a steady growth in solar energy generation as well, under the government’s Solar Parks Scheme. Official data by India’s Ministry of New and Renewable Energy indicated that solar energy generation has surged nearly 138 percent over a four-year period, rising from 73.48 BU in 2021- 22 to 174.76 BU in 2025- 26. Currently, solar energy supplies more than 60 GW, around 22 percent of India’s daytime peak electricity demand, highlighting its growing role in meeting rising consumption.

At the same time, however, the initiative has faced major challenges turning such massive solar capacity into stable power. Billions of units of electricity continue to be wasted because the grid cannot absorb massive surges during peak sunshine hours. Transmission lines lag behind solar park construction, leaving tens of gigawatts of capacity underutilized or on temporary connections. Moreover, coal generators struggle to reduce output quickly during peak solar production without incurring costly and lengthy shutdowns, leading to wasted solar energy on the grid.

India’s chronic pollution problem poses additional challenges. A recent study indicated that in India, aerosols in the air have reduced the amount of solar power generated by 9.6 percent in 2023, equivalent to around 15 terawatt-hours (TWh). The global average loss due to the same cause in 2023 was 5.8 percent. Between 2017 and 2023, pollution-related electricity generation losses from existing installations averaged 74 TWh a year, which is roughly one third of the electricity generated every year by new solar capacity. India’s loss is one of the world’s highest.

The core challenge facing the country is no longer just building solar panels, but managing grid integration, storage shortages, and transmission bottlenecks that force widespread power curtailment. India’s current operational energy storage capacity includes roughly 6 GW to 7.5 GW of pumped storage hydro projects (PSPs) and over 1 GWh to 7.5 GWh of operational battery energy storage systems (BESS), which are grossly inadequate. In comparison, China’s operational non-conventional energy storage capacity reached roughly 153 GW in mid-2026. All this explains India’s continued reliance on coal-driven thermal power generation.

At one level, these can be considered expected transition problems. China, the world’s largest producer of solar energy, for example, went through a similar transition problem between 2011 and 2016, when it built wind and solar capacity far faster than it built the grid infrastructure to move that power around. India could have stood to benefit if it had learned from China’s experience and adjusted its plan accordingly.

To address grid flexibility issues, India plans to move away from standalone solar farms toward integrated systems, making a commitment of nearly $50 billion as a share of solar investment from both the government and private players to establish substantial multi-hour storage infrastructure. But those will not happen in the near term.

India’s energy landscape in 2026 shows that the country is outpacing its infrastructure while also trying to rebuild it. Rising demand will keep coal as the backbone of the power grid in the coming years, which will create more global warming while also providing the short-term means to mitigate the effects. Aligning storage and transmission with growing renewable energy should be a top priority for energy planning. Meanwhile, heat waves and demand spikes will arise regardless of infrastructure readiness. The key challenge is ensuring that coal is not the default option in the future if India genuinely wants to achieve its newly committed climate goals of 47 percent emissions intensity reduction and 60 percent non-fossil power by 2035 alongside a long-term net-zero target by 2070.

title: Is Islamic Extremism Taking Over Bangladesh?
description: Two years after Sheikh Hasina's ouster, what is the role of Islamist movements in Bangladesh?
text:
For 15 years, Bangladesh’s government was viewed as a firm bulwark against religious extremism. Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina had cracked down heavily on the country’s largest Islamist party, Jamaat-e-Islami, as well as various radical and jihadist outfits.

Really, Hasina cracked down on everyone – but to some, her authoritarian bent was an acceptable price to pay to keep religious extremism under wraps.

So when Hasina’s Awami League government was ousted from power on August 5, 2024, it triggered a wave of deep anxiety. Many feared that Islamists in Bangladesh would now have free rein. India, especially, was horrified by the prospect of its eastern neighbor becoming a safe haven for Islamist extremist groups – some of which might dream of carrying out terrorist attacks on Indian soil.

Now, two years after the collapse of Hasina’s government, Jamaat-e-Islami has made a spectacular return to parliamentary politics. Radical groups are mobilizing, and there are escalating attacks against religious minorities.

Does that mean fears about Bangladesh’s Islamist explosion have come true? Not exactly.

title: Is Japan Decoupling From China?
description: The new generation of Japanese policymakers is far less willing to accommodate China than its predecessors.
text:
Japan’s relationship with the People’s Republic of China (PRC) began before formal diplomatic relations were established. Although diplomatic relations were not normalized until 1972, the two countries had already created an unofficial trade mechanism in 1962 that enabled bilateral trade despite the absence of mutual diplomatic recognition.

In a famous article published in Foreign Affairs in 1967, former U.S. Vice President Richard Nixon argued that “we simply cannot afford to leave China forever outside the family of nations.” At the time, Japan’s China policy had already been moving in that direction, going beyond even the policy imagination of its closest ally, the United States.

This was despite intense diplomatic pressure from the United States, which remained firmly anti-communist. Throughout the 1960s, Washington publicly opposed Japan’s efforts to normalize relations with one of its closest neighbors and discouraged any move toward diplomatic recognition of the PRC. The “shock” caused by Nixon’s announcement of his planned visit to mainland China in 1971 stemmed, in part, from Japanese frustration that this policy framework toward China – shaped and constrained by U.S. diplomatic pressure against Japan’s preference – was abruptly reversed without prior consultation with Tokyo.

After normalization, Japan and China entered a honeymoon period in which their relationship resembled a quasi-alliance, rooted in their shared distrust of the Soviet Union as a common adversary. This perception was also shared by the United States, which intensified its pressure against Moscow as Cold War tensions began to rise. From the late 1970s through the 1980s, Japan expanded its industrial assistance to China, while the United States strengthened military cooperation with Beijing, including transfers of military technology. These developments highlight the strategic importance that both Japan and the United States placed on their relationship with China.

A turning point in China-Japan relations came on June 4, 1989, when the People’s Liberation Army moved into Tiananmen Square to suppress student protesters. Images of the violence were broadcast around the world, prompting the U.S.-led Western bloc to impose sanctions in response to China’s violent crackdown.

Although Japan suspended its aid program to China, it was reluctant to fully participate in broader sanctions. It was Japan, at the critical G7 summit in Paris, that took the lead in preventing China’s complete isolation from the international community. Its efforts resulted in the inclusion of the following sentence in the summit declaration: “We look to the Chinese authorities to create conditions which will avoid their isolation and provide for a return to cooperation based upon the resumption of movement towards political and economic reform, and openness.” At that critical juncture, Japan was prepared to break with the emerging Western consensus in order to prevent China from being pushed back into international isolation.

The history reviewed above is essential for understanding the current state of China-Japan relations. Since the 1960s, the two nations have consistently maintained some level of economic exchange despite the political circumstances of each period. The characterization of their relationship as “hot economics and cold politics” has been a defining feature of bilateral ties, particularly over the past several decades. During the 1980s, and especially in the aftermath of the Tiananmen Incident, a strategic dimension also helped sustain the partnership, as both countries continued to view their relationship through the lens of shared geopolitical interests.

However, when examining the China-Japan relationship today, it may be more accurately described as one of “cooling economics and colder politics” – a trajectory that relations had not previously taken.

The turn of events can be traced back to Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae’s controversial statements in late 2025 hinting at the possible deployment of Japan’s Self-Defense Forces in the event of a crisis surrounding Taiwan. Some have argued that Takaichi’s remarks were bold and resolute, while others have criticized them as insensitive to China’s red lines and emblematic of her tendency toward gaffes. Regardless of the interpretation, what is clear is that Beijing was provoked by Takaichi’s statements and has sought to apply maximum pressure on Japan in response.

Even after Takaichi’s electoral victory in early 2026, China has continued to exert pressure on critical mineral supply chains and impose targeted export controls not only on Japanese defense firms but also on companies involved in dual-use technologies. The effects of China’s export controls on rare earths – a sector in which China possesses nearly 90 percent of global refining capacity – have already been felt by Japanese companies. Furthermore, the arrest of Japanese company employees in mainland China on allegations of illegally exporting rare earth magnets has further unsettled Japanese businesses that remain heavily reliant on the Chinese market.

At the same time, diplomatic relations remain stagnant, with a bilateral summit between Xi Jinping and Takaichi appearing unlikely in the near future.

While Japan remains open to a reset in its relationship with China, it appears to be gradually but decisively preparing for a future with reduced dependence on Beijing, reversing a decades-long trend of courting and nurturing its neighbor. This shift was represented in Takaichi’s “updated free and open Indo-Pacific” speech, in which she upheld the core principles inherited from her predecessors while also highlighting the importance of economic security and resilient supply chains with like-minded nations.

Although the country driving this necessity was not explicitly named, China’s ongoing economic pressure makes it difficult not to identify Beijing as the force behind this policy shift. This development may ultimately place limits on how broadly Japan’s strategic concept of a “free and open” Indo-Pacific can continue to accommodate China. However, at present, Japan appears to prioritize responding to geopolitical realities rather than attempting to sugarcoat them.

One theory explaining Japan’s shift in its approach toward China is generational change. The old China hands in Japan held a special sentiment toward mainland China. They were deeply aware that their generation, as well as that of their parents, had been connected to a period in which Japan inflicted immense suffering and destruction across China, as the Empire of Japan fully mobilized its military power from the late 1930s until the end of World War II. While they viewed investment in China as a commercial opportunity, they also regarded it as a means of addressing the wrongs committed by their nation and expressing gratitude for the PRC government’s decision to forgo war reparations.

However, the China hands who once held influential positions within the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) are now aging and gradually exiting the political scene. They are being replaced by a younger generation of more hawkish conservatives who seek to hedge against China and deepen ties with Taiwan. It is striking that both Takaichi and Ishiba Shigeru visited Taiwan before becoming prime ministers – as if doing so had become a rite of passage for aspiring Japanese political leaders.

The reason why younger generations of politicians do not share the same perception of China as their predecessors may be attributed, in part, to their understanding of history. From their perspective, the historical debt has already been repaid, and their generation should not be expected to bear responsibility for the wrongdoings of the past, which occurred before they were born. The statements of prominent conservative politicians such as former Prime Minister Abe Shinzo and Takaichi are emblematic of this changing understanding of history. In a 2015 official government statement, Abe declared that “we must not leave our children, grandchildren, and generations to come, who bear no responsibility for that war, with the obligation to continue apologizing indefinitely.”

Similarly, back in 1994, the then up-and-coming Takaichi criticized Prime Minister Murayama Tomiichi, who would acknowledge and apologize for Japan’s wartime aggression against its neighbors the next year, arguing that “I do not think it is acceptable for someone to offer an apology on my behalf without my consent.” Whether this generational shift reflects a lack of historical awareness or a different interpretation of Japan’s wartime is unclear. Nevertheless, it is notable that both Abe and Takaichi have drawn particularly strong support from younger generations.

At certain points in history, Japan was among the few nations willing to engage with China despite international opposition, investing heavily without fully considering how such efforts might later be used against it. Today, with a fundamentally different relationship and balance of power between the two nations, Japan appears to be preparing for a new era. Today, the obligation to keep China integrated into the international community and maintain extensive economic ties regardless of the cost is no longer viewed as an imperative.
