title: Japan’s Billions Are the Wildcard in Southeast Asia’s Aid Race
description: Few development actors in the region can currently match Tokyo’s combination of credibility and quality.
text:
For the last two decades, the contest for influence in Southeast Asia has almost always been conceptualized as a two-horse race: China floods the region with infrastructure loans and the United States counters with democracy programs and health assistance. This binary framing obscures the presence of a third player, one whose role may prove more decisive than either Washington or Beijing: Japan.

For decades, Tokyo has without fanfare underwritten much of Southeast Asia’s development. According to the Lowy Institute’s 2025 Southeast Asia Aid Map, Japan disbursed around $35 billion in development finance to the region between 2015 and 2023. This is less than China’s $50 billion in actual disbursements, but far more than the United States’ $9 billion. More critically, Japan’s assistance arrives as grants and concessional loans governed by transparent standards, governance principles, and environmental safeguards. In official development finance share for 2022, Japan (30 percent) and the Western bloc combined (31 percent) still outpaced China (24 percent) across Southeast Asia, a fact routinely drowned out by headlines announcing each new Belt and Road mega-project.

Japan’s dominance in the region’s development landscape is not new. For much of the post-war era, Tokyo has treated its overseas development assistance (ODA) as a strategic instrument linking infrastructure to trade expansion and the cultivation of stable bilateral ties. The Fukuda Doctrine of 1977 institutionalized this commitment, resulting in decades of accumulated trust.

That trust is now being tested. Since 2013, China’s Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) has dramatically reshuffled regional development finance. Beijing has committed approximately $149 billion to Southeast Asia, concentrating flows overwhelmingly in transport and energy infrastructure. The competition came into sharpest relief during the bidding war for Indonesia’s Jakarta-Bandung high-speed railway, a contest Japan ultimately lost to China. China’s financing proposal was distinguished by shorter projected delivery timelines and a comparatively limited set of conditionalities, while Japan’s competing offer emphasized more stringent technical benchmarks and governance requirements as preconditions for engagement. Indonesia’s selection of China’s bid reflected a preference for speed and cost over structural prudence.

The subsequent trajectory of the project, which was marked by protracted delays, significant cost overruns, and contentious contractual renegotiations, provides an instructive case study of the governance risks associated with infrastructure financing arrangements. It demonstrates, in particular, the financial vulnerabilities that can emerge when recipient governments prioritize short-term fiscal attractiveness over rigorous due diligence and careful assessment of life-cycle costs.

This episode reflects a structural limitation in China’s development model. Approximately 71 percent of China’s official development finance in Southeast Asia consists of non-concessional, commercially-oriented lending rather than genuine aid. Beijing’s infrastructure support functions more like club goods, which benefit specific bilateral partners and Chinese state-owned contractors, rather than universal public goods. Health, education, and governance each receive less than 1 percent of China’s regional disbursements. These are precisely the domains in which the United States has historically focused its aid efforts in the region.

The visualization below depicts the composition of official development finance (ODF) inflows to Southeast Asia from 2015 to 2023, covering both traditional ODA – i.e. grants and concessional loans – and other official flows (OOFs) of a more commercial character. China’s total ODF reached $211.88 billion over this period, approaching the $248.36 billion from all other bilateral donors combined and the $268.42 billion from multilateral institutions.

Yet the composition of China’s ODF says a lot. Roughly 71 percent of China’s regional portfolio ($150.91 billion) consists of OOF-type transactions, confirming that most Chinese finance is non-concessional and commercially oriented rather than genuine aid. At the structural level, China’s loan-heavy profile ($204.66 billion) contrasts sharply with the grant-led contributions of traditional partners ($117.68 billion), reinforcing the scholarly consensus that Chinese development finance is driven by commercial value extraction and export relations rather than humanitarian capacity-building.

Meanwhile, the United States’ long-standing role as a development actor in Southeast Asia is now being steadily weakened. Recent USAID cuts under the current Trump administration have removed nearly $440 million in development assistance across the region. Indonesia and the Philippines absorbed reductions of 98 percent and 95 percent of their prior allocations, respectively, while Timor-Leste and Thailand face complete program terminations. The United States is withdrawing from governance, health, and civil society – and these are precisely the areas in which China’s infrastructure-heavy aid model has historically been weakest.

Japan is now stepping into this vacuum. Tokyo already leads the region in humanitarian assistance and disaster relief, accounting alongside the World Bank for roughly two-thirds of recorded disaster response finance in Southeast Asia. Japan’s Partnership for Quality Infrastructure, launched in 2015 explicitly as a counterpart to the BRI, foregrounds technical standards, lifecycle costs, environmental sustainability, and fiscal transparency. In renewable energy alone, Japan leads with approximately $1.3 billion deployed in solar investment and $142 million in geothermal technologies between 2013 and 2023.

The elevation of ASEAN-Japan relations to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership in 2023 signaled a long-term regional commitment, though questions are already surfacing about whether Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae’s more security-centric foreign policy risks diluting the development identity that earned Japan its regional standing in the first place.

In any event, there’s more to the picture than Japan substituting for diminished U.S. engagement or serving as a direct counterweight to Chinese influence. Rather, Tokyo’s sustained presence as a standards-based development financier expands recipient governments’ bargaining space vis-à-vis Beijing. This has important geopolitical implications. As the cases of Vietnam and Indonesia illustrate, Southeast Asian governments have demonstrated considerable sophistication in leveraging competing donor offers to extract more favorable financing conditions. Japan’s consistent participation in regional development finance preserves and reinforces this competitive dynamic, thereby buttressing the strategic autonomy that Southeast Asian states regard as a core foreign policy objective.

The broader lesson is that the development finance landscape in Southeast Asia has never been bipolar. Even as China has expanded its material footprint dramatically and the United States is retreating, Japan’s steady, quality-focused engagement continues to shape the regional order in ways that transcend project announcements and ribbon-cutting ceremonies. As Washington’s credibility erodes and Beijing’s ambitions outpace its institutional capacity, Tokyo’s role as a consistent, transparent provider of quality development finance may prove the most consequential force shaping the region’s future. Governments of ASEAN countries should recognize this, and Japan, for its part, should say so more loudly and with considerably greater ambition.

This article was previously presented at the 6th SEASIA Biennial Conference: Forging Southeast Asia’s Futures, organized by the School of Social Sciences, Nanyang Technological University, Singapore on July 8–10, 2026.
tag: Japan development aid; Japan in Southeast Asia; Japan ODA Southeast Asia; Japan ODA strategy

title: Japan’s Nuclear Taboo Is Starting to Crack
description: Whether or not Japan’s nuclear policy is actually revised, the very fact that such a revision is being openly debated is a striking development.
text:
August has been a solemn month in Japan for more than 80 years. Although Japan formally signed the Instrument of Surrender on September 2, 1945, the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki on August 6 and 9, respectively, and Emperor Hirohito’s radio announcement on August 15 accepting the terms of surrender have made August a month from which the Japanese psyche cannot escape. Every year since the Pacific War ended in Japan’s defeat, during August the nation has mourned its war dead and reflected on the horrors of a conflict that inflicted immense suffering and destruction upon the country. The resolve that Japan must never again endure such an ordeal lingers in the air of the sweltering Japanese summer.

But this year, another issue besides the memory of war has been generating heated debate in the Japanese media: will the Takaichi administration revise the government’s Three Non-Nuclear Principles in the upcoming revision of Japan’s national security documents?

Japanese media outlets have been closely scrutinizing Takaichi’s remarks on Japan’s Three Non-Nuclear Principles, under which Japan pledges not to possess, produce, or allow the introduction of nuclear weapons into its territory. This attention stems from Takaichi’s previous position that at least the principle concerning the non-introduction of nuclear weapons should be reconsidered in the interests of Japan’s national security. In an edited volume she published in 2024, Takaichi even argued that Japan’s current nuclear policy was not “realistic” when it came to ensuring the credibility of the U.S. extended nuclear deterrent.

The fact that she has not categorically ruled out revising the principles since becoming prime minister has fueled speculation that she could embark on a major shift in Japan’s decades-old nuclear policy – essentially distancing the country from its longstanding commitment to refrain from assuming any role in the deployment of nuclear weapons, even for defensive purposes.

Questioned about her current stance on Japan’s nuclear policy, Takaichi has maintained that her government “remains committed to the Three Non-Nuclear Principles as a matter of policy.” At the same time, she has declined to “say definitively what their final wording will look like” in the revised security documents. In other words, Takaichi has reiterated – even on the anniversaries of the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki – that the existing nuclear policy remains in place for now, while leaving open the question of how nuclear weapons will be addressed in the future.

Defense Minister Koizumi Shinjiro, Takaichi’s point man for drafting the new national security policies, has also hinted that a revision of Japan’s nuclear policy may be on the table. Appearing on a conservative online program, Koizumi acknowledged that nuclear weapons are “a difficult issue for Japan to discuss,” but argued that it is one that cannot be avoided.

He went further, saying that “we must recognize the sense of crisis we face and discuss and pursue every possible policy option without treating anything as taboo.” He also referred to the efforts of Finland and France to strengthen their nuclear deterrence. For Koizumi, preserving existing policies should not take priority over the fundamental responsibility of protecting Japan.

Whether or not Japan’s nuclear policy is actually revised in the immediate future, the very fact that such a revision is being openly debated is a striking development in Japanese policy discourse. For decades, any positive discussion of the role nuclear weapons might play in Japan’s security policy could be a career breaker for Japanese politicians. In 1999, Parliamentary Vice-Minister of Defense Nishimura Shingo was forced to resign after a Japanese magazine quoted him as saying that Japan should consider becoming a nuclear power. And although he did not meet the same fate as Nishimura, LDP policy chief Nakagawa Shoichi came under intense scrutiny in 2006 after suggesting that Japan should debate nuclear policy in depth.

Even discussing the memory and legacy of nuclear weapons has been a tightrope for Japanese politicians. In 2007, then-Defense Minister Kyuma Fumio came under fierce criticism after saying that, although “countless people suffered terribly,” he viewed the atomic bombings as having brought the war to an end and that he had “no intention of holding a grudge against the United States over it.” He resigned less than two weeks after making the remarks.

However, based on the remarks by Takaichi and Koizumi, which appear to have generated little public backlash, statements about putting nuclear weapons on the table no longer seem to be regarded as political gaffes.

Japan’s Three Non-Nuclear Principles are among the few remaining national security taboos for a country that was once deeply committed to pacifism. Since entering the 21st century, Japan has crossed one security taboo after another: deploying the Self-Defense Forces to active conflict zones, legitimizing the exercise of the right of collective self-defense, establishing a National Security Council and centralized intelligence capabilities, opening a military base overseas, and greenlighting the export of lethal weapons. All of these would have been difficult to imagine in the previous century; today, they are established facts of Japanese security policy.

While Takaichi has not altered the Three Non-Nuclear Principles – yet – she has indicated that she would follow a precedent set by the Democratic Party of Japan government. In 2010, then-Foreign Minister Okada Katsuya stated that, in an extreme emergency threatening Japan’s national security, “the government of the day must make the decision with the nation’s fate at stake and explain its decision to the public.” This interpretation effectively creates a potential exception to the principle prohibiting the introduction of nuclear weapons into Japan, without formally abandoning the Three Non-Nuclear Principles themselves.

However, even if an existing exception has effectively rendered one of the Three Non-Nuclear Principles moot in practice, formally revising it would carry enormous symbolic significance. If the Takaichi administration embarks on an official revision of Japan’s nuclear policy, it would mark yet another postwar taboo overturned. Such a move would have been astonishing in 20th century Japan, but it would also fit the broader trajectory of Japan’s increasingly assertive security policy.
tag: Japan National Defense Strategy; Japan nuclear allergy; Japan nuclear weapons; Takaichi security policy; Three Non-nuclear Principles

title: Japan’s So-Called ‘Rising Militarism’ and Japan-US Relations
description: Insights from Kuni Miyake.
text:
The Diplomat author Mercy Kuo regularly engages subject-matter experts, policy practitioners, and strategic thinkers across the globe for their diverse insights into U.S. Asia policy. This conversation with Kuni Miyake — special adviser and board member of The Canon Institute for Global Studies in Tokyo, president of the Foreign Policy Institute, visiting professor at Ritsumeikan University, and former senior diplomat in the Japanese Ministry of Foreign Affairs — is the 522nd in “The Trans-Pacific View Insight Series.”

Identify the key factors fueling Japan’s so-called “rising militarism.”

With the exception of a few pundits both in Japan and abroad – whom I refer to as “post-World War II utopian pacifists” – almost no one believes that Japan is “becoming militaristic.” At the recent Shangri-La Dialogue in Singapore, only one participant, whose government is non-democratic, spending almost five times more on military than Japan, and continuously threatening its neighbors, engaged in such “propaganda.” Japan’s Minister of Defense thoroughly refuted in response.

The vast majority of the Japanese public, who have supported democratic civilian control over the armed forces for more than 80 years, would likely be perplexed by this kind of question itself.

Analyze Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae’s calculus in strengthening Japan’s Self-Defense Forces as a way to fortify the Japan-U.S. security alliance.

Fortifying the Japan-U.S. security alliance is not the “purpose” of Japan’s efforts to enhance its deterrence, but merely the “result” of it. Since World War II, and particularly after the Vietnam War, power balance among major countries in the Indo-Pacific region had relatively been well maintained. It was not until the 2010s that this regional balance of power began to break down. Since then, the military buildup by our huge neighbor, especially in maritime domains, including the East China Sea and the South China Sea, has heightened concerns among nations in the Indo-Pacific region – including Japan and Southeast Asia – that seek to maintain the status quo.

It is only natural that recent Japanese administrations, including Ms. Takaichi’s, have worked to expand necessary deterrence capabilities of Japan in cooperation not only with the United States or Australia, our “allies,” but also with these neighboring countries, and this approach has garnered understanding from the majority of nations in the region.

Examine Tokyo’s position and pronouncements on Taiwan vis-à-vis Beijing’s retaliation.

Japan’s position on Taiwan has remained unchanged since the normalization of bilateral relations with China in 1972. What is changing is the military policy toward Taiwan adopted by some countries, and Japan, the United States, and neighboring nations are growing increasingly concerned about this. Japan’s stance remains unchanged: it opposes any attempt by any country to “alter the status quo by force” and seeks to maintain the status quo in the surrounding region, including the Taiwan Strait.

Explain Tokyo’s threat perception of North Korea’s cooperation with Russia and dependence on China.

Japan’s policy toward North Korea has consistently been based on the 2002 Japan-North Korea Pyongyang Declaration, which aims to “comprehensively resolve outstanding issues such as abductions, nuclear weapons, and missiles, settle the unfortunate past, and work toward the normalization of bilateral relations between Japan and North Korea.” However, recent changes in North Korea’s military and economic ties with China and Russia must be viewed as negative developments that could heighten regional tensions and increase threats to Japan, the United States, and South Korea. Going forward, Japan will continue to work closely with the international community – including the United States and South Korea – under the principles of “dialogue and pressure” and “action for action” vis-á-vis North Korea.

Assess Tokyo’s ability to fund growing militarism amid an aging population, declining birth rate, and slow-growth economy, while aiming to maintain its regional leadership and partnership with the United States.

To reiterate, condemning Japan’s coordination with the United States – an ally working jointly to expand regional deterrence – as “militarism” is missing the point and nothing more than a propaganda campaign by elements seeking to alter the regional status quo, which fail to face history and reality head-on.

Although Japan faces challenges amid a declining population and a maturing economy, in terms of security, it will continue to maintain a highest degree of civilian control under its parliamentary democracy while sustaining cooperation and coordination with regional allies and friends, including the United States.
tag: Japan militarization; Japan military; Japan military buildup; Japan Taiwan policy; U.S.-Japan Alliance

title: Japan’s Underground Lab Wants to Solve the World’s Nuclear Waste Problem
description: A rare visit to the Horonobe Underground Research Laboratory, where Japanese researchers are testing options for storing radioactive waste.
text:
Reindeer pastures and dairy farms stretch across the flat, windswept plain of Japan’s northernmost prefecture, giving little hint of what lies roughly 300 meters below. Inside the Horonobe Underground Research Laboratory, teams of engineers are trying to answer a question no country has fully solved: how to keep highly radioactive waste isolated from the environment for periods measured not in decades, but in tens of thousands of years.

In May, I gained special access to the facility through the Japan Atomic Energy Agency (JAEA), touring the underground galleries and observing several of the experiments currently underway.

Horonobe Underground Research Laboratory. Photo ©Piergiorgio Pescali.

A Rare Laboratory in Sedimentary Rock

Horonobe is one of only two underground research laboratories Japan has built to study geological disposal of high-level radioactive waste, and the only one still operating. Its counterpart, the Mizunami Underground Research Laboratory in Gifu Prefecture, was built in crystalline rock and was decommissioned in 2022 after its land lease expired. Horonobe, by contrast, sits in Neogene-era sedimentary rock, giving the JAEA a very different and, officials argue, complementary geological environment to study.

The project traces back to November 2000, when the governor of Hokkaido, the mayor of Horonobe town, and the president of the JAEA signed an agreement to permit research on the deep geological environment at the site. Construction and excavation followed over the next two decades, and the laboratory now includes shafts and galleries used to test how engineered barriers, groundwater, and surrounding rock interact over time – the same combination of natural and artificial safeguards that would, in theory, protect a real repository.

Two of the central experiments underway involve what the JAEA calls the “full-scale engineered barrier system performance experiment” and a “solute transport experiment,” both designed to test, at real scale, how bentonite buffers, canisters, and cement-based materials behave once water and pressure are introduced over years rather than months. The JAEA has also been testing how the surrounding sedimentary rock buffers natural disturbances, earthquakes, and groundwater shifts that could compromise a repository’s isolation over the long term.

Researchers conducting tests at Horonobe Underground Research Laboratory. Photo ©Piergiorgio Pescali.

Don’t Call It a Dump

The JAEA is emphatic on one point, repeated in nearly every briefing given to visitors: Horonobe is a research facility, not a candidate site for Japan’s eventual high-level waste repository. Japanese law formally separates the two functions, and the agency overseeing the actual site-selection process, the Nuclear Waste Management Organization of Japan, operates independently of the JAEA’s research program.

That legal separation has not entirely dissolved local unease. Horonobe is a farming town of roughly 2,000 residents, many of whom have lived for two decades with an underground laboratory in their backyard and, despite official assurances, the lingering question of what happens to the facility once the research concludes.

Japan’s broader search for a permanent repository has proven difficult everywhere it has been raised. Only two municipalities, Suttsu and Kamoenai in Hokkaido, have so far agreed even to preliminary literature-based surveys, and neither has committed to hosting a final site.

The outside view of Horonobe Underground Research Laboratory. Photo ©Piergiorgio Pescali.

An International Proving Ground

What distinguishes Horonobe today is its growing international role. In February 2023, the JAEA and the OECD’s Nuclear Energy Agency (NEA) launched the Horonobe International Project, bringing foreign research organizations into the underground laboratory to work on shared technical problems. The first phase ran through March 2025 with 11 participating organizations from countries including Australia, Bulgaria, Germany, South Korea, Romania, Taiwan, and the United Kingdom, alongside Japan.

A second phase, running from April 2025 through March 2029, has continued with roughly 10 member organizations pursuing three joint technical tasks: modeling how dissolved substances move through fractured sedimentary rock, integrating different repository design options, and dismantling a full-scale engineered barrier system to see how it performed after years underground.

For countries such as Australia and South Korea – both still in the early stages of building their own waste-management institutions – Horonobe offers something they cannot yet replicate at home: a working underground facility where design assumptions can be tested in real-world conditions. South Korea’s state nuclear research institute has said it is benchmarking its own disposal-performance models against Horonobe data as it prepares to build an underground laboratory of its own in Taebaek.

NEA officials have described the site as an important international platform for developing and demonstrating repository technology, with plans to eventually extend the laboratory to 500 meters below sea level.

Soil extracted from the galleries at Horonobe Underground Research Laboratory. Photo ©Piergiorgio Pescali.

The Finland Comparison

It is difficult to walk through Horonobe without thinking of Onkalo, the repository under construction on the island of Olkiluoto in western Finland, which is set to become the world’s first operational deep geological disposal site for spent nuclear fuel. Having visited Onkalo myself, the contrast with Horonobe is immediately clear. Onkalo is being excavated roughly 400 meters into Precambrian granite bedrock nearly 1.9 billion years old – rock that geologists consider to have remained structurally stable through repeated glacial cycles. Horonobe, by design, tests young, still-consolidating Neogene sedimentary rock, chosen precisely because it represents a geological setting Japan cannot avoid when it eventually has to site a real repository. Much of the country lacks Finland’s kind of ancient crystalline bedrock.

The difference between the two sides is as much political as geological. Posiva Oy, the utility consortium that owns and operates Onkalo, spent roughly two decades developing its technical solution and benefited from a Finnish system in which nuclear waste responsibility stays under public oversight even where the industry itself is privately run, with the national regulator STUK maintaining permanent inspectors on site. That framework was paired with sustained public consultation and a compensation system for the host municipality, Eurajoki, that turned three decades of engagement into local acceptance rather than opposition. Waste is due to begin arriving at Onkalo in 2026, sealed in copper-and-bentonite canisters designed to maintain their integrity for roughly 100,000 years.

Japan, by contrast, has yet to find a single municipality willing to host a final repository, and Horonobe’s own officials go out of their way to stress that the laboratory is not a step toward designating the town as one.

Finland’s example has not gone unnoticed in Tokyo: Japanese institutions are already among the countries cooperating with Posiva on adapting Finnish containment technology to different geological and regulatory contexts, a channel that runs alongside, but separately from, the JAEA’s own international partnerships through the Horonobe International Project.

That gap helps explain why Horonobe matters beyond Japan’s borders. It is not a repository and, officially, will never become one. But it is one of a small number of places on Earth where engineers can watch, in real time and at full scale, whether the technology underpinning every country’s nuclear waste strategy actually behaves the way computer models predict over years of exposure to rock, water, and pressure.

The elevator to the galleries at Horonobe Underground Research Laboratory. Photo ©Piergiorgio Pescali.
tag: Horonobe Underground Research Laboratory; Japan Atomic Energy Agency; Japan nuclear power sector; Japan nuclear waste

title: Kim Min-seok Wins Democratic Party Chair in Ranked-Choice Runoff
description: The former prime minister defeated incumbent chair Jung Chung-rae 54.1 percent to 45.9 percent in the party’s chairmanship election.
text:
Former Prime Minister Kim Min-seok was elected as the leader of the ruling Democratic Party (DP), closing out a six-week race that exposed deep rifts between rival camps aligned with South Korean President Lee Jae-myung and outgoing party chair Jung Chung-rae.

Kim, a four-term lawmaker, won 54.08 percent of the final vote announced at the party’s national convention in Daejeon, defeating Jung, who took 45.92 percent. Kim fell short of a first-round majority under the combined count of member, delegate, and opinion-poll votes, triggering the party’s ranked-choice runoff for the first time in its history. Under that process, second-choice votes from backers of third-place finisher Rep. Song Young-gil were redistributed between Kim and Jung, producing Kim’s final voting margin.

The new DP leader will oversee candidate nominations for the general elections in April 2028. More than that, the race was widely seen as a test of how firmly Lee has consolidated control over the DP since assuming presidency in 2025. The contest has widely been described as a proxy fight between the pro-Lee camp and a harder-line faction associated with Jung, who has at times pushed back against the presidential office on the pace of judicial overhaul and other issues. Kim’s campaign speech in July framed the race as a referendum on whether the party would fully back Lee’s agenda,

Kim’s strongest results came in Gwangju and the Jeolla provinces and the greater Seoul area after Lee announced an 800 trillion won ($564 billion) semiconductor investment package for the Gwangju region. Overall, however, Lee’s approval rating slipped to 44 percent in recent days, the lowest since he took office, according to local media reports.

How the Election Unfolded

This was the DP’s first party chair race under the new one-member, one-vote system. Dues-paying members and delegates account for 70 percent of the weight, and a national opinion survey makes up the remaining 30 percent.

The public opinion poll was conducted over two days by two polling firms among a combined 4,000 respondents reached by automated phone survey, with participation limited to Democratic Party supporters and independents to screen out backers of the conservative opposition.

Because no rule guarantees a majority winner, the party adopted ranked-choice voting: if no candidate clears 50 percent on first-preference ballots, the last-place finisher is eliminated and votes are reallocated by second choice.

The voting took place in waves, with results announced region by region. Voting opened August 1 in Chungcheong, where Kim narrowly outpolled Jung, 45.05 percent to 44.61 percent, with Song a distant third at 10.34 percent. Jung answered the next day in Busan, Ulsan, and South Gyeongsang Province, beating Kim 46.65 percent to 43.85 percent. Kim then won Jeju and Incheon on August 8 with 47.75 percent to Jung’s 42.08 percent, and a fourth round spanning Gangwon Province, Daegu and North Gyeongsang Province followed on August 9, with Kim ahead 48.54 percent to 44.40 percent and the cumulative gap narrowing to 1.48 points.

The race turned decisively in Kim’s favor on August 15 in Gwangju and the Jeolla provinces, the party’s largest single bloc of members at roughly a third of the total. Kim won 57.54 percent there to Jung’s 32.65 percent, pushing his cumulative share past 50 percent for the first time. The final regional round, in Seoul and Gyeonggi Province on August 16, went to Kim by a far tighter margin, 46.66 percent to 46.28 percent, pulling his majority back below 50 percent and leaving him with an overall cumulative lead of 49.91 percent to 41.51 percent heading into August 17 and the party’s national convention.

Supreme Council Race

Alongside the chair, on August 17 the DP seated five Supreme Council members from an eight-candidate field. Voters picked two of the eight names and the five candidates with the highest combined vote share won seats, with the top finisher becoming senior Supreme Council member. Five of the eight candidates were aligned with the pro-Lee camp – Rep. Park Sun-won, Rep. Kim Yong, Rep. Seo Mi-hwa, Rep. Kim Young-ho, and Rep. Im Mi-ae – while three were aligned with Jung’s camp – Rep. Choi Min-hee, Rep. Han Min-soo, and Rep. Lee Sung-yoon.

Late on August 16, two lower-ranked pro-Lee candidates, Im Mi-ae and Kim Young-ho, dropped out of the race and threw their support behind Kim Yong, in an effort to consolidate pro-Lee votes and prevent Jung’s camp from taking three of the five seats.

The final results confirmed a split verdict. Choi finished first by vote share and will serve as senior Supreme Council member, followed in order by Park Sun-won, Seo Mi-hwa, Lee Sung-yoon and Han Min-soo. Three of the five seats went to lawmakers aligned with Jung while only two went to pro-Lee lawmakers. Kim Yong, the candidate whom Im and Kim Young-ho withdrew to support, fell short of a seat despite their last-minute endorsement.

The outcome leaves incoming DP chair Kim Min-seok with a Supreme Council in which lawmakers aligned with his defeated rival hold a majority of the elected seats. The divide is likely to complicate Kim’s efforts to consolidate the party behind President Lee heading into the 2028 general elections.

Who Is Kim Min-seok?

Kim, the new leader of the DP, belongs to South Korea’s so-called 86 generation, student activists who led the pro-democracy movement of the 1980s and later entered mainstream politics. As Seoul National University’s student council president, he was recruited into politics in 1990 by the late President Kim Dae-jung and joined the merger of Kim’s party with the New Democratic Alliance Party, earning him the nickname “first son of democratic unification.” Elected to the National Assembly in 1996 at age 32, he was the youngest lawmaker of his time and won a second term in 2000.

His rise stalled in October 2002, when he left the party during a dispute over unifying the presidential candidacies of Roh Moo-hyun and Chung Mong-joon, a decision that resurfaced repeatedly as a line of attack from Jung during the campaign. Kim lost his Assembly seat in 2004 and spent several years outside elected politics, including periods of study in the United States and China. He returned to the party’s leadership as a Supreme Council member in 2008 but was later barred from running for office for five years over a political funding case. He founded a small breakaway party in 2014 before it merged back into the DP in 2016 under then-chair Choo Mi-ae.

Kim won back a National Assembly seat in 2020 and secured a fourth term in 2024. His alignment with Lee Jae-myung deepened during the 2022 presidential race, when he headed strategy for Lee’s campaign. Kim went on to serve as the DP’s policy chief and, from 2024, as senior Supreme Council member under Lee’s own chairmanship. After Lee’s election as president following the impeachment of Yoon Suk-yeol, Kim was named the first prime minister of the Lee administration in mid-2025, a post in which he oversaw the APEC summit in Gyeongju and met with U.S. President Donald Trump and Vice President J.D. Vance in Washington before stepping down at the end of June 2026 to run for party chair. He is now regarded within the DP as a potential future presidential contender.
tag: Democratic Party of Korea; DP chair election 2026; Jung Chung-rae; Kim Min-seok; Lee Jae-myung; South Korea politics

title: Mongolia Hosts COP17, Urging Global Partners to Action on Climate Issues
description: Mongolia wanted to see “a shift from talk to action” at COP17. The results were mixed.
text:
The 17th Conference of the Parties to the U.N Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD COP17) was convened in Ulaanbaatar from August 17-28, bringing together 196 country representatives plus the European Union to negotiate action-based measures on several climate challenges facing the world today. This year’s COP17 included segments on finance, water, land and people, and food systems. Parties agreed on a new initiative that includes $1.3 billion in financing, but failed to approve a new financial mechanism to combat drought.

On August 17, the opening ceremony was attended by Mongolian President Khurelsukh Ukhnaa, U.N. Deputy Secretary-General Amina J. Mohammed, Executive Secretary of the UNCCD Dr. Yasmin Fouad, Saudi Arabia’s Deputy Minister of Environment, Water and Agriculture (and president of UNCCD COP16) Dr. Osama Ibrahim Fakiha, and Mongolia’s Minister of Foreign Affairs Battsetseg Batmunkh. The global climate gathering also included a visit by South Korea’s former president, Moon Jae-in, and business leaders from Rio Tinto, Trade Development, Oyu Tolgoi, Asian Development Bank, Global Green Growth Institute, and more.

Welcoming the guests and opening the COP17 gathering, Mongolian Prime Minister Uchral Nyam-Osor stated: “The greatest change we want to see from COP17 is a shift from talk to action, from targets to implementation, and from commitments to measurable results.”

As Fouad, the UNCCD executive secretary, put it in an interview with The Diplomat before the gathering: “COP17 comes at a pivotal moment for global action on land… I believe countries will come to Mongolia with a shared understanding that the challenge is no longer understanding the problem – we know what is at stake. The priority now is implementation.”

In the last two weeks, the Mongolian government, civil society, and environmental organizations cooperated with global financial institutions, policymakers, businesses, and environmental scientists to advance solutions to emerging issues facing not just Mongolia but the globe, including desertification, drought, and land degradation. Building on the progress made at COP16 in Riyadh, governments at COP17 aimed to negotiate practical tools, partnerships, and financing mechanisms needed to help countries turn existing plans into action.

According to the UNCCD, more than 70 countries have now developed national drought plans, compared with only three in 2013 – reflecting growing recognition that drought must be managed proactively rather than only once it becomes a humanitarian and economic crisis.

Desertification, land degradation, and climate change are all interconnected and demand integrated solutions. In Mongolia, the challenge includes extreme climate fluctuations, such as dzud and drought, as well as loss of water, water pollution due to mining activities, as well as mismanagement of rangelands and pastoralism. The combination of these issues in turn becomes additional hindrance to the country’s development.

The last two days of COP17 were designated for all 197 parties to come to some sort of an agreement on a mechanism to combat drought. The Asian Development Bank Partnership estimated $355 billion is needed every year to combat land degradation and drought, yet current investment stands at only around $77 billion, leaving an annual financing gap of $278 billion.

Unfortunately, on August 28, last day of the COP17, parties failed to come to an agreement and passed the issue to the next COP gathering.

One of the main disagreements was whether to establish a new drought protocol initiated by the African Group. The bloc of developed countries – including the European Union, Australia, and the United Kingdom – opposed the establishment of a new drought protocol, preferring to utilize previously agreed multilateral frameworks such as Global Environment Facility and to avoid overlapping agreements.

While drought – and a financial mechanism to combat drought – posed a challenge for the 197 parties to negotiate, rangeland, pastoralism, and water deserve equal attention.

One of the most important segments of COP17 was the High-Level Ministerial Meeting and Finance Day, where delegates, multilateral banks, and participating organizations announce strategic commitments and financial mechanisms focusing on specific issues such as land restoration, rangeland preservation, and invigorating environmentally friendly, green growth.

At the High-Level Ministerial Meeting, Mongolia officially launched the global “Rangelands Flagship Initiative,” which focus on sustainable management and restoration of global pasture lands. The initiative was viewed as one of the most important outcomes of the climate gathering. It will bring together 45 projects across 23 countries, amounting to $1.3 billion in funding, making it the largest investment in the rangelands sector in the history of the UNCCD Convention.

The financial commitments will be assessed by the implementation of individual projects. Participating governments are expected to consider a new policy framework on rangelands and pastoralists designed to increase long-term investment in sustainable rangeland management and strengthen pastoral livelihoods. The initiative also mentioned the establishment of an Eurasian Center for Climate-Resilient Rangelands in Mongolia.

On August 24, Business for Land Forum and Finance Day brought together government, businesses, and investors looking to invest in regenerative landscapes. The Business Council of Mongolia and the UNCCD signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to establish a Business4Land (B4L) platform and Mongolia Hub. The MoU “aims to link consumption, production, and finance through environmental and social standards, as well as financial products focused on preserving natural capital.”

Moreover, Mongolia also signed a Host Country Agreement (HCA) with Global Green Growth Institute to strengthen the legal and institutional framework for climate financing and augmenting investment environments for green projects.

The director of the Protected Areas Policy Department at Mongolia’s Ministry of Environment and Climate Change, Uranchimeg Tserendorj, stated that for the last 32 years, Mongolia’s Law on Protected Areas has protected land all around the country. The legal framework has allowed the country to protect “20.8 percent of land,” Uranchimeg said.

Mongolia is also seeking a deeper action-based cooperation with both UNCCD and the Ramsar Convention on Wetlands. Mongolia’s Environment and Climate Change Minister Sandag-Ochir Tsend met Ramsar Convention Secretary General Dr. Musonda Mumba, “proposing closer cooperation between the Ramsar Convention and U.N. Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD) during Mongolia’s COP17 presidency.”

At COP17, mining giants such as Rio Tinto announced their strategy to contribute to Mongolia’s fight against desertification, water pollution, and restoration of forestry by planting 5,000 hectares of forest, investing in renewable energy for company usage, as well as introducing new technology to replenish groundwater. According to the environmental manager of Oyu Tolgoi, one of Mongolia’s largest mining companies, the firm began paying water pollution fees in 2026, a regular quarterly payment of 150-200 million Mongolian tugrik (roughly $42,000 to $55,000). These practices meant to set an example for other mining giants operating in the country.

In the last two weeks, global partners gathered in Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia to discuss and negotiate an issue that has long been a focus for climate advocates. Mongolia’s hosting of the UNCCD COP17 is viewed as a step up in its global engagement and contribution and commitment to climate change. Considering the country’s own struggle with wetland loss, drought, rangeland and pastoral management, the platform urged global businesses, government, and civil society to take actions to help contribute solve these challenges.

Although the convention did not reach an agreement on solving drought, it has made progress in promoting and implementing global partnership in climate issues.
tag: Mongolia climate change; Mongolia COP17; Mongolia desertification; Mongolia diplomacy; UNCCD

title: Myanmar Nationals Face Deportation From US After Court Ruling
description: The ruling follows a Supreme Court decision in June that limited courts' ability to challenge TPS designations.
text:
A U.S. federal judge has cleared the way for President Donald Trump’s administration to end temporary protected status (TPS) for nearly 4,000 people from Myanmar, presaging their possible arrest and deportation.

In a ruling on Friday, U.S. District Judge Matthew Kennelly of the Northern District of Illinois rejected last-minute efforts by immigrant rights advocates to maintain the TPS designations. The ruling came just hours after a federal judge in Boston handed down a similar ruling rejecting a challenge from an immigrant-advocacy organization against the removal of TPS status from around 232 South Sudanese nationals.

Both rulings referenced a U.S. Supreme Court decision from June, which ruled that the administration had the authority to end similar protections for thousands of people from Haiti and Syria. The Supreme Court ruling limited lower courts’ ability to block DHS’ efforts to end TPS for people from roughly a dozen countries, arguing that federal judges had no authority to weigh in on a challenge to TPS terminations.

TPS was created by the U.S. Congress in 1990, and protects non-U.S. citizens from deportation to countries facing armed conflict or other crises posing a threat to their safety. It also grants them authorization to work in the U.S.

The TPS designation for Myanmar was granted for the first time after the 2021 military coup, which was followed by a nationwide uprising against military rule. The ongoing civil war and military repression have wrecked Myanmar’s economy, displaced more than 3.5 million people, and pushed tens of thousands more to flee the country. There are around 4,000 Myanmar nationals currently in the U.S. under the TPS program.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) revoked TPS status for Myanmar in November of last year, citing the military junta’s upcoming elections as evidence that the country had “made notable progress in governance and stability.” The TPS designation for Myanmar was originally set to expire in January, but court orders kept the protections in place while a class-action lawsuit challenged the DHS decision.

While the Trump administration said that the revocation of TPS status was justified by improvements in Myanmar’s political situation, plaintiffs argued in their lawsuit that the decision failed to account for the real conditions in Myanmar, where conflict and military repression continue unabated, and was just one aspect of a broader campaign to end TPS designations.

During Trump’s second term, the DHS has revoked TPS protections for hundreds of thousands of migrants from countries including Afghanistan, Cameroon, Haiti, Honduras, Nepal, Nicaragua, Syria, South Sudan, and Venezuela.

In addition to losing their ability to work in the U.S., the 4,000 Myanmar nationals now face possible arrest and deportation. According to one report, many of these Myanmar nationals have lived and worked in the United States since fleeing the country; some have even raised U.S. citizen children.

In a statement issued after the ruling, the International Refugee Assistance Project described the decision as “devastating” for these individuals.

“The court’s decision to allow TPS protections to lapse puts thousands of Burmese TPS holders in grave danger,” said Dinesh McCoy, a staff attorney at the Asian American Legal Defense and Education Fund who was lead counsel in the case. “It is unconscionable for the Trump administration to gamble with their lives as part of its larger campaign to use immigration policy as a tool for racial exclusion.”

Thura Doe, a plaintiff in the lawsuit, said that he was “devastated” by the court’s ruling and “terrified of what will happen if I’m forced to return to Burma.”

McCoy said that his organization was “continuing to explore all available legal options.”
tag: Department of Homeland Security; Myanmar conflict; Myanmar refugees; Myanmar refugees in the U.S.; Temporary Protected Status (TPS); U.S.-Myanmar relations

title: Nepal’s ‘Himalayan Tsunami’ Is a Warning for the Whole Region
description: Melting ice, unstable terrain, landslides, river blockages, sudden lake releases, and extreme weather can all combine in unpredictable ways.
text:
For Nepali people, August 26 started like any other day, just another routine morning for the communities in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Gorkha, and Chitwan. But there is a saying in Nepal: “Disaster won’t come by making noise.” On Wednesday, people experienced that reality ruthlessly.

By midday, that ordinary morning had turned into a nightmare. A sudden flood that crashed down from the northern side of the border devastated multiple districts of Nepal. The customs office of the Nepal-China border, Syaphrubeshi, Betrawati, Timure, and Trisuli area in Rasuwa district all suffered extensive damage. Entire villages were swept away. The floodwaters then rushed toward the Trishuli River, threatening more settlements in the areas of Nuwakot and Dhading.

Over 30 bridges collapsed, 42 kilometers of roads were damaged or simply washed away, and communications were disrupted. Thousands of homes were swept away. More than 359 bodies have been recovered so far, and there are still thousands of locals missing. In addition, more than 644 tourists from 33 countries were reported missing. Security personnel themselves were reported missing.

In China also, at least three people were killed and more than 500 people were reported missing. In both countries, rescue and recovery operations are ongoing.

Bahrabise Bazar, Nepal, before and after the Aug. 26, 2026 flood. Photo via Wikimedia Commons.

What exactly caused the disaster is still unclear, but experts believe a massive avalanche or landslide may have blocked the river, creating a temporary dam that eventually burst. It could have been a glacial lake outburst flood – if confirmed, that would be a warning for the entire Hindu Kush Himalayan region about the growing threat of climate crises.

By 3:30 p.m. on Wednesday, the Bhotekoshi River had receded and returned to its original size. But that only made clear the devastation it had wreaked throughout the morning. There was not a trace left of the villages, market towns, bridges, or hydroelectric projects that had once stood along the riverbanks. It is estimated that in one morning the Bhotekoshi washed away over 200 billion rupees worth of investment: roads and bridges were devastated, and neither the hydropower projects nor the transmission lines survived. This is worrisome for a small economy like Nepal.

The Nepal government has declared Rasuwa, Nuwakot, and Dhading districts as disaster crisis zones for the next three months.

While the initial flood has passed, there are still worrying signs coming from China. China’s Ministry of Water Resources warned that a 2 million cubic meter lake near the Chhochen Khola-Purepu Tsangpo confluence is already overflowing, with another 3 million cubic meters expected to flow in, posing a high risk of breach. That could cause a second flood at any time.

Wednesday’s disaster marked the second time in just over a year that Nepal’s Rasuwa district has been devastated by a catastrophic flood, and once again, the disaster didn’t start within its borders. In July 2025, a similar flood in the same region wiped out the Rasuwagadhi border corridor. Satellite images later showed that a glacial lake in Tibet had drained suddenly. At least 11 people were killed in the 2025 flood, which also destroyed bridges, damaged energy infrastructure, and disrupted cross-border trade with China.

Now, just 13 months later, history has repeated itself. That’s not a coincidence.

Professor Ranjan Kumar Dahal of Tribhuvan University said that this is the largest ice tsunami in the last 50 years – not just in Nepal, but across the entire Himalayan region. Whether this turns out to be a glacial lake outburst flood, a landslide-triggered flood, or a mix of both, one thing is clear: the danger is growing, and the damage won’t be limited to any one country.

The devastating flood on Nepal’s Bhotekoshi River was the result of a “massive geological event” in the Himalayas. As per Goran Ekstrom, a geophysicist at Columbia University’s Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory, the event was triggered by a catastrophic chain of occurrences in the Himalayan region.

Nepal’s area of the Himalayas holds an estimated 2,069 to 2,174 glacial lakes. According to the International Center for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD), 47 of these are classified as potentially dangerous glacial lakes, capable of triggering catastrophic outburst floods. Among these 47 glacial lakes, 21 lie within Nepal, while 25 are transboundary lakes in Tibet, sitting right at the headwaters of rivers that flow south into Nepal. If any of the lakes, whether in Tibet or Nepal, cause an outburst flood, this will harm the people and infrastructure of Nepal living downstream.

Across the Hindu Kush Himalaya, rising temperatures are reshaping the frozen landscape. Glaciers are shrinking, lakes are swelling, and mountain slopes are growing more unstable. The ICIMOD has repeatedly warned that glacier-related disasters are becoming more frequent and more complex.

Experts can’t yet say with perfect confidence that climate change directly caused this week’s flood. But it is changing the rules of the game. The new reality isn’t just about more floods, but about cascading threats. Melting ice, unstable terrain, landslides, river blockages, sudden lake releases, and extreme weather can all combine in unpredictable ways. Conventional weather monitoring downstream just isn’t enough anymore.

This can’t be seen as a matter of the environment but also a matter of national security. The affected corridor is at once a lifeline for communities, a trade artery, an energy source, and a strategic border zone.

There is growing hope for positive change in Nepal’s disaster response. Both Prime Minister Balendra Shah and Physical Infrastructure Minister Sunil Lamsal have backgrounds in structural engineering, and Home Minister Sudan Gurung has experience in relief work. The country can’t stop every Himalayan disaster, but the government can make sure fewer people are caught standing by the river when the mountain unleashes its fury. The real challenge is anticipating these events before they strike.

This is not a problem Nepal can solve on its own. The Bhotekoshi River begins in Tibet and flows into Nepal. A hazard born on the Chinese side can become a national emergency in Nepal within hours. Nepal’s ability to prepare depends almost entirely on getting timely information from across the border.

Likewise, there are millions of people living downstream on the same rivers in both Nepal and India. If a glacial lake bursts in Tibet or Nepal, it will also impact and cause severe harm in India too. So this has also become an urgent cross-border problem. The countries from the Hindu Kush Himalayan region must work together to combat this kind of disaster in a timely manner before it becomes too late. Climate diplomacy in the Himalayas can’t just be about emissions and funding anymore. It has to include real-time data sharing, satellite surveillance of risky glacial and landslide-dammed lakes, joint risk assessments, and rapid cross-border early warning systems.

For Nepal, this is the worst natural disaster since the 2015 earthquake. Despite contributing less than 0.1 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions, Nepal is facing disproportionate environmental and economic consequences. Big neighbors like India and China and partner countries must help Nepal in every possible way. The 2025 flood was a wake-up call. The 2026 flood is a blunt reminder that it wasn’t a one-off.

The message is becoming painfully clear: resilience cannot simply mean rebuilding what the river takes away. It means knowing what is happening upstream before the water arrives. Climate change is real and not a hoax, and Nepal cannot face these growing risks alone. Stronger regional cooperation, shared technology, and global support are important and necessary parts of the response to this tragedy.
tag: Bhotekoshi flood 2026; China-Nepal border; China-Nepal flood; China-Nepal information sharing; glacial lake outburst flood; glacial lakes in Nepal; Nepal flooding; Nepal natural disasters; Tibet flooding

title: No Wonderland: Alice’s Shameful Australian Aboriginal Camps
description: The conditions in and around Australia’s Aboriginal camps, such as the one where a 5-year-old girl was murdered in April, are shameful for one of the world’s wealthiest countries.
text:
Alice Springs, or “Alice” as it is commonly known here in Australia, is situated in the country’s Red Center. For over 30,000 years, the Arrernte Aboriginal people have been custodians of this remote land – a land of red earth, awe-inspiring rock formations and ethereal skies.

Alice, or Mparntwe in the Arrernte language, has profound, unhealed wounds, both ancient and recent. The most recent, and still painfully raw, is the murder in late April of a 5-year-old girl. An Aboriginal man by the name of Jefferson Lewis has been charged with her murder.

In accordance with Aboriginal custom, under which the names of the dead are avoided out of respect, the family requested she be called Kumanjayi Little Baby. She was found dead after disappearing from the Aboriginal Old Timers Camp, one of the 18 Aboriginal camps on the fringes of Alice Springs.

Kumanjayi Little Baby’s family were staying in a dilapidated house at the Old Timers Camp after traveling from their remote community in the Tanami Desert to Alice Springs to access medical care. Photos taken at the Old Timers Camp during the search for the girl showed a mattress on the floor where she had been put to bed before her disappearance.

Police said Jefferson Lewis, the alleged killer of Kumanjayi Little Baby, was staying at the Old Timers Camp too. A May editorial in The Sydney Morning Herald hit the nail on the head about the tragedy, describing the camps as “gathering places for the powerless and the outcast, where the most vulnerable are easy prey, and protections are minimal.”

Senator Jacinta Nampijinpa Price, who is also the aunt of Kumanjayi Little Baby, said, “Too many [camps] have become environments where safety is not guaranteed, particularly for children.” She added that “for too long, there has been a reluctance to speak plainly about the conditions in and around town camps.”

The conditions in and around the Aboriginal camps, not only in Alice Springs but all over Australia, are shameful for one of the world’s wealthiest countries. After all, it is, as Australian writer and academic Donald Horne called it, the “Lucky Country.”

In this “Lucky Country,” Aboriginal people remain Australia’s unlucky first inhabitants. In remote regions, especially, they face hardships more often associated with poorer nations: poverty, health inequities, high incarceration rates, inadequate housing, violence – the dreadful list goes on. If there’s a place in Australia where the struggles faced by Aboriginal communities are most vividly felt, it must be the camps.

In the bureaucratic banal parlance, the camps are called: “Alice Springs Community Living Areas.” In the camps, there is nothing that resembles community living; let’s be fair dinkum – using a traditional Aussie expression.

According to a 2025 report by the Menzies School of Health Research, there are approximately 4,000 residents across the Alice Springs camps. Conditions at many camps are poor, with limited services and shared residences among extended family members. Overcrowding is chronic. The number of residents can almost double during major events like the football carnival and the Alice Springs Show, straining already stretched housing stock.

“Overcrowding and poor-quality housing are associated with poor health, educational and employment outcomes, and increased family violence,” concluded a 2022 report by the Australian National Audit Office. “The highest levels of overcrowding occur in remote areas of the Northern Territory.”

Residents report delays regarding repairs and maintenance. When infrastructure breaks down – bore water lines, roofing, essential utilities – residents often struggle to get timely fixes because it is genuinely unclear which agency is responsible.

The governance of the camps is fragmented. Tangentyere Council Aboriginal Corporation, comprising 15 housing associations, manages the town camps and is responsible for their social and infrastructure services.

Residents say the flow of money and the division of responsibilities are opaque and frustrating. “Current governance arrangements in the Indigenous housing system are complex and poorly coordinated,” said a 2026 study by the Australian Housing and Urban Research Institute.

Ken Marchingo, chief executive of Community Housing Central Australia (CHCA), stated that there were too many points of intersection in camp management and that a single responsible organization could clarify accountability.

Many residents and advocates argue that the 2007 “Intervention” has worsened conditions. The 2007 Northern Territory Intervention, officially known as the Northern Territory National Emergency Response, has been criticized for overriding self-determination and for imposing discriminatory, top-down control.

Local organizations, including Tangentyere Council and Community Housing Central Australia, have spent more than a decade developing a proposal to return management of the town camps to the community. They argued that community control would provide clearer accountability and more responsive services.

Many of the camps rely heavily on one-off government grants to get by, and changes to their governance were recommended as far back as 2017. Executive director of township leasing, Pennie Weadon, said her team had repeatedly recommended to the Northern Territory government ways to improve economic opportunities in the camps.

The camps were established in the 1880s, with the arrival of Europeans in Central Australia. Located across the plains and on the outskirts of Alice Springs, they were set up in response to racist policies that banned Aboriginal people, displaced from their lands, from entering the town itself. Between 1928 and 1964, the whole of Alice Springs was a prohibited area for Aboriginal people between sunset and sunrise.

“The town campers, or fringe dwellers as these people were called, were regarded as a problem for the township and much time,” wrote researchers Michael Heppell and Julian J. Wigley in their 1981 monograph about the establishment and development of Alice’s camps. “For decades, Aborigines in Alice Springs were little more than creatures of the authorities, being pushed here and there to suit the whims of some particular administrator or petty official.”

“Welcome to rainy Alice,” the receptionist at my hotel in Alice Springs greeted me. After a steady and unexpected spell of rain, the red earth of Australia’s Red Center is now covered by green grass. It is not the welcome green grass, though. It is buffelgrass, one of the gravest environmental threats to Australia’s arid rangelands.

The flowers at the entrance to the Old Timers Camp – where Kumanjayi Little Baby was abducted last April – have withered. The scars of her murder remain fresh, though. Her solitude on a floor sleeping mattress in the Old Timers Camp and her subsequent murder have once again awakened Australians’ consciousness. No wonderland in the Aboriginal town camps of Alice Springs – just sorrow. And intolerable shame.
tag: Aboriginal people; Alice Springs; Australia Aboriginals; Australian Aborigines; Kumanjayi Little Baby

title: North Korea Dismisses Trump’s Recent Overtures to Kim Jong Un
description: Days after U.S. President Donald Trump showed his interest in meeting with the leader of North Korea, Pyongyang responded by launching short-range ballistic missiles and publishing a harsh statement.
text:
Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, said there was no communication between the leaders of the United States and North Korea, according to a statement published by the North’s state-controlled Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) on August 19.

“As for the news from Washington that shortly ago, there was a communication between the leaders of the DPRK and the U.S., I am not aware of it at all, and perhaps it may be the only thing I do not know as regards the foreign policy of our supreme leadership,” Kim said. (DPRK is an acronym of North Korea’s official name, Democratic People’s Republic of Korea.)

It was the first response of Pyongyang to U.S. President Donald Trump’s claim that Kim Jong Un responded to his overtures. According to the Wall Street Journal, Trump has discussed setting up a meeting with Kim Jong Un on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, which will be held in November in Shenzhen, China.

In the past few days, Trump has made friendly gestures to Kim Jong Un. He posted a photo of him and Kim taking a stroll during the Hanoi Summit in 2019 and a meme of Kim making a phone call, with text suggesting he was calling Trump. On August 17, Trump said on his Truth Social account that he had ordered Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to “substantially reduce” the joint military exercises with South Korea, which began on the same day. The Ulchi Freedom Shield joint military exercises were supposed to last until August 27 but, according to local media reports, they will end on August 21.

South Korea’s Foreign Affairs and Defense Ministries said on August 19 that Washington had not explained or given advance notice regarding Trump’s decision to scale down the joint military exercises. However, South Korean President Lee Jae-myung showed a positive attitude, saying that he will remain fully dedicated to serving as “a peacemaker” to facilitate and contribute to Trump’s peacemaking endeavors.

As North Korea has long deemed the South Korea-U.S. joint military exercises as an invasion rehearsal, some expected that Pyongyang would at least make a reciprocal gesture. However, Kim Yo Jong clearly downplayed Trump’s decision to scale back the ongoing joint military exercises between the U.S. and South Korea.

“As for the reduction of the U.S.-ROK joint military drill abruptly announced by the U.S. president a few days ago, we regard it as the one unworthy of comment and have no interest in it at all,” Kim said. (ROK is an acronym of South Korea’s official name, Republic of Korea.) “The reduction of the scale and duration of the drill does not mean the change of the nature of the military drill with a provocative and offensive feature.”

In a separate statement published by KCNA a day later, also attributed to Kim Yo Jong, she mocked South Korea’s “poor plight” over the cancellation. “The ROK cannot let out a single word of protest at the GIs leaving without any mutual coordination at the U.S. chief executive’s unilateral order,” Kim said. “This is the inevitable fate of the puppet army.” She also compared the South Korea-U.S. alliance to “the relation between master and servant.” However, Kim still refrained from indicating any positive response on Pyongyang’s part to the reduction of the exercises.

Also on August 20, North Korea fired around 10 short-range ballistic missiles toward the ocean off its east coast, according to the South’s Joint Chiefs of Staff. The missiles, which flew around 300 km, were launched from the Pyongyang area around 5 p.m. KST. The South Korean National Security Council convened an emergency meeting and condemned the North’s missile launches.

Despite her explicit accusation that the United States was maintaining its hostile policy against North Korea, Kim Yo Jong confirmed again that the relationship between Trump and Kim Jong Un is “still excellent,” which is the only confirmation of Pyongyang that matches what Trump has said in the past days.

Following Kim Yo Jong’s statement, Trump said North Korea possesses “57 very powerful nuclear weapons” and emphasized that he gets along with Kim Jong Un well. With that, Trump also said that he expects to meet with the North Korean leader later this year.

However, Ahn Gyu-back, the defense minister of South Korea, told lawmakers at the South’s National Assembly on August 21 that North Korea may have around 80 to 120 nuclear weapons. Ahn said that he could not share Seoul’s estimate of the exact number of the North’s nuclear weapons.

Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi happened to be visiting Seoul amid the furor over a potential Trump-Kim summit. In the meeting with his counterpart, South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun, on August 19, Wang said China will play a constructive role for peace on the Korean Peninsula. Regarding China’s role in a potential summit between Trump and Kim, Wang declined to comment, saying it is a matter for the U.S. and North Korea.

title: One Nation’s Dual Assault on Australia’s Structural Realities
description: With a below replacement-level birth rate and a booming elder population, One Nation’s anti-immigration stance, combined with its critique of superannuation, is a toxic combo.
text:
A major structural issue facing most Western and East Asian countries at present is their below replacement-level birth rates. This has the potential to create an unfavorable dependency ratio – the problem of aging societies with a large cohort of retirees, but not enough workers to pay for pensions, healthcare, and other essential services.

Yet simultaneously, many Western countries are experiencing an insurgence of populist, and often extremist, parties hostile to the one mechanism available to alleviate this problem: immigration. In Australia, this year has seen the rise of One Nation – previously a small fringe anti-immigrant party – now consistently polling in the mid-high 20 percent range. One Nation often matches the governing Labor Party’s poll numbers, and is polling far ahead of Australia’s other traditional major political force, the permanent coalition between the Liberal and National parties.

One Nation’s reason for existence is to undermine Australia’s migration program – which it sees as a threat to their idea of the Australian nation. Yet as the party has ascended in the polls it has needed to branch out into other populist causes and conspiratorial theories to promote. One issue the party has landed on is Australia’s retirement savings scheme – known as superannuation.

Australia’s superannuation scheme was made compulsory in its modern form by the Keating government in 1992, requiring employers to contribute a portion of workers’ wages into privately managed retirement funds. The contribution rate has gradually risen to 12 percent – paid on top of wages – and has created one of the world’s largest pools of retirement savings. It is accessible at 60 years old. The basic idea is simple: Australians build up their own nest egg during their working lives, reducing their reliance on the government-funded Age Pension in retirement. Superannuation is ranked one of the world’s leading retirement schemes.

However, there’s always been a strain of suspicion toward superannuation within the Liberal Party. This stems in part from politics – the scheme was introduced by the Labor Party, after all – and in part from the perception of the scheme as paternalistic and undermining the personal responsibility to save for yourself.

But within a consumerist culture, turbo-charged by the ease of online shopping and the relentless product promotion of online influencers, it is arguable that the scheme has saved a great many Australians from difficult retirements. Personal responsibility is important, but there also needs to be a recognition that we are an easily tempted species and sometimes we need some guardrails for our own good.

One Nation’s opposition to superannuation appeals directly to these critiques. As a populist party, it simply says: “You can have more money in your pocket today and the government is keeping it from you.” It may appeal to those suffering current cost of living pressures and who are distrustful of government initiatives, but it plays a dangerous game with Australia’s structural realities. Alongside the party’s suspicion of immigration, is a dual assault on the future sustainability of the Australian state.

Given Australia’s birth rate of 1.48 births per woman, the Treasury estimates that a migration intake of at least 235,000 people a year is required to off-set the worst effects of an aging society. This, of course, isn’t perfect, as the median age of a migrant to Australia is 37. This is around 20 less years paying tax than someone who enters the workforce in their mid-to-late teens. But, given the realities of low birth rates, it is the best solution available.

Despite some internal confusion, the figure One Nation has consistently cited as their policy is 130,000 people per year – although they channel forces that even find this number unacceptably high. This combination with a populace who had greater access to their retirement savings prior to retirement would create an enormous government pension outlay without the tax base to cover it.

Rather than seek ways to off-set a poor dependency ratio, One Nation’s policies are now trying to accelerate it. This is, of course, the nature of the party. Populist parties don’t have a long-term comprehension of the economic sustainability of the country. They fixate on immediate grievances and emotional responses. The implications and consequences of their ideas are not well thought out.

This should present an opportunity for the Liberal Party to regain the ground they’ve lost to One Nation this year. Although there are elements within the party likewise suspicious of superannuation, the Liberals’ traditional selling point has been responsible economic stewardship of the country. The problem the party faces, however, is that administrative sobriety isn’t very attractive at the moment. The people want more and they want it now, even if it may lead to them having far less as they age.
