title: Principled Caution: Navigating AI in Asian Newsrooms
description: In many Asian countries, letting an AI-generated error slip through could mean not only reputational harm but legal and political persecution
text:
Across Asia, public interest media are turning to artificial intelligence (AI) to optimize under-resourced newsrooms. However, these outlets face a high-stakes reality: publishing AI-generated errors, factual inaccuracies, or “AI slop” risks undermining the public trust and credibility central to their legitimacy. At the same time, these media are also aware that they are operating in authoritarian contexts where AI-induced mistakes can lead to legal and political persecution.

Hence, independent outlets in the Asia-Pacific – the media that produce journalism essential to democratic accountability – exercise “principled caution” when deploying AI. They exercise this caution not just because of a desire to maintain their reputation for accuracy. They also do so because there is a real risk of forced state closure, the freezing of assets, or the imprisonment of staff.

This is the core finding of Asia Centre’s latest report, “Principled caution: How AI is used in public-interest media in Asia,” published in partnership with DW Akademie and supported by the German Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development.

Evaluating media ecosystems across eight Asian countries – Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, Cambodia, Indonesia, Myanmar, Pakistan, and Uzbekistan – the study reveals how journalists are managing AI adoption. Rather than blind adoption, Asia’s independent public interest media are approaching AI through a careful and highly selective strategy. In structurally precarious environments where reporting errors can invite censorship, legal action, or operational shutdown, outlets consistently prioritize human editorial oversight over full-scale automation.

The report identifies several key findings:

First, AI usage in newsrooms remains assistive rather than transformative. Outlets primarily use generative AI tools at the preliminary and final stages of editorial workflows, for tasks such as ideation, document summarization, social media adaptation, and headline polishing. The central stages of journalistic work – including original field reporting, investigative narrative drafting, and editorial judgment – remain strictly human-driven.

Second, severe language constraints mean that major global Large Language Models underperform in low-resource Asian languages, including Bahasa Indonesia, Bangla, Burmese, Chittagonian, Dzongkha, Farsi, Jingpo, Khmer, Pashto, and Urdu. These platforms frequently mistranslate context-sensitive terms, flatten cultural nuances, and generate wrong outputs. While translation is the most widely adopted AI task, outputs require labor-intensive human correction.

Third, exiled media from countries like Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Myanmar, and Pakistan face distinct operational threats including digital surveillance, internet blackouts, cross-border security risks, and severe financial instability. These pressures leave little mental or institutional bandwidth to experiment with new technologies. Yet, securely tailored automated tools for transcription, translation, and media-monitoring offer an unrealized opportunity to engage diaspora networks and report on repressed homelands without compromising journalists’ digital safety.

Fourth, a sharp institutional deficit persists across newsrooms. Over 60 percent of surveyed newsrooms report that AI adoption occurs via ad-hoc, individual staff experimentation rather than cohesive organizational strategies. Structural gaps, such as the absence of formal editorial guidelines, missing data protection protocols, and a heavy reliance on Big Tech platforms, leave independent media vulnerable to algorithmic bias, privacy violations, copyright risks, and state surveillance.

Fifth, restrictive political and legal environments across Asia impede responsible AI adoption. While state authorities deploy automated systems for online monitoring, surveillance, and synthetic media campaigns, regulatory ambiguity is routinely weaponized to clamp down on media freedoms. Public interest newsrooms face a stark structural asymmetry; political actors deploy AI at scale to amplify state narratives and disinformation, while underfunded independent outlets lack affordable verification tools to counter these attacks effectively.

Looking ahead, AI integration in Asian newsrooms cannot rely solely on off-the-shelf tools built by Western tech monopolies. Long-term media sustainability requires localized AI infrastructure, enforceable newsroom governance frameworks, and open-source language models tailored to the region’s complex political and linguistic contexts. Without this shift toward technological sovereignty, regional media risk becoming mere data points for foreign algorithmic models that operate without local democratic stakes. We must move beyond being passive consumers of black-box solutions and start architecting a digital future that respects our region’s unique socio-political boundaries.

To achieve this, international donors and media development actors must pivot away from short-term, surface-level training sessions. Instead, capital must be redirected toward regional and local entities to lead core technological infrastructure, secure data storage systems, and create collaborative AI hubs specifically designed to serve independent and exiled media. This requires reimagining “capacity building” as the construction of resilient, shared digital architectures that treat cybersecurity as a foundational reporting tool. By financing regional and local based collective defense, we can turn isolated public interest newsrooms into fortified digital outposts capable of weathering persistent state-sponsored surveillance.

Ultimately, the future of journalism in Asia will not be determined by the speed of algorithmic tools, but by whether newsrooms can harness AI without compromising the trust, accuracy, and independence that underpin public interest reporting. In an era of synthetic media floods, human-centric rigor is not a hurdle to innovation – it is our ultimate competitive advantage. Those who prioritize ethical safeguards now will be the only ones to retain audience loyalty when the inevitable global backlash against AI-generated misinformation arrives.

This op-ed is based on Asia Centre’s new report, “Principled caution: How AI is used in public-interest media in Asia”. Download the full report here. For more information about the Asia Centre, visit asiacentre.org.
tag: AI in Asia; AI in journalism; Media Freedom; public interest journalism

title: Remembering a Genocide: The View From the Rohingya Camps
description: Nine years on, Rohingya refugees still wait for justice and home. But they haven't given up hope.
text:
Every year on August 25, the Rohingya community around the world gather to commemorate Rohingya Genocide Remembrance Day. It is a day of mourning, expression, reflection, and hope. On this day, Rohingya people living abroad and in refugee camps hold banners, join together for mass prayers, recite poems, share their history, organize refugee exhibitions, and participate in social activities.

All of these activities aim to remember their homeland and memories, and to honor their loved ones who were killed by the Myanmar authorities on August 25, 2017.

For the Rohingya, August 25 is not just a black day. It is a day that has buried countless innocent Rohingya, that has mixed the tears of the Rohingya with blood, and that has forced more than a million Rohingya to flee to Bangladesh. On this day, the Myanmar military put into motion its plan to wipe out the Rohingya community from Myanmar’s Rakhine State under the pretext of responding to an attack on a police station.

According to international human rights groups and Rohingya civil society organizations, more than 300 Rohingya villages were partially or completely destroyed following the Myanmar military’s attacks beginning on August 25, 2017. Rohingya women and girls were raped in front of their parents, husbands, and brothers. Children were thrown into fires, and people were burned to death inside their homes. Many were arrested and sent to jail; many family members still don’t know the whereabouts of their jailed family members. Property was looted, and mosques were destroyed. Many died after their trawlers were capsized or broken in the Naf River while fleeing to Bangladesh.

Doctors Without Borders concluded that “[a]t least 9,000 members of the ethnic Rohingya minority died – most of them from violence – in Rakhine State, Myanmar” in the month after the violence began on August 25, 2017.

“I witnessed the brutal massacre of my Rohingya community by the Myanmar military in 2017. The bullets that flew over my head were like raindrops,” Rohingya teacher Wai Yan recounted during a Rohingya Genocide Remembrance Day event. “All I saw were dead bodies with no one to bury them.”

This year, August 25 marked the ninth anniversary of the violence, but the pain has not yet subsided. The Rohingya who fled are still trapped in overcrowded camps in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh, waiting for justice from the world, while the remaining Rohingya in Myanmar continue to suffer from an ongoing genocide by the Arakan Army.

The suffering never ended for the Rohingya. The Arakan Army is fighting Myanmar’s military for control of Rakhine State, and both groups have been attacking Rohingya villages – killing, looting, and burning. Many Rohingya have been killed, women have been raped, homes looted and burned to the ground, often with the occupants inside.

After the military genocide against the Rohingya earlier, they are now facing similar treatment from the Arakan Army. According to a report by Human Rights Watch, the Arakan Army has targeted Rohingya civilians through killings, unlawful detention, forced recruitment of Rohingya youths, and other abuses that may amount to war crimes. Many Rohingya believe that the brutality carried out by the Arakan Army is aimed at driving the Rohingya out of the country, just like the Myanmar military’s campaign in 2017.

Nine years have passed since the Rohingya were driven from their homeland, but the possibility for return remains fragile; not a single Rohingya has returned through the repatriation process since 2017. Bangladesh – a small and densely populated country – continues to shoulder the responsibility of hosting refugees.

Bangladesh had previously tried to repatriate Rohingya, but their efforts failed. The refugees will not return as long as their safety, rights, and dignity are uncertain. Humanitarian assistance has helped the Rohingya endure their displacement, but the root causes of the crisis can only be addressed through political action. Myanmar must recognize the Rohingya as native people of Myanmar and create the conditions for their safe, voluntary, and dignified return with citizenship and rights.

August 25 is not only about remembering what happened to the Rohingya in 2017. It is also about recognizing the challenges that continue today. Rohingya families remain trapped in the refugee camps, uncertain about their future. Children are growing up in the camps far from their homeland, learning about their homeland through the memories of their parents and grandparents.

“If we don’t preserve our stories, others will forget what happened to us,” said Abdo Rohim, a highly experienced Rohingya teacher, writer, and humanitarian worker. “It is our responsibility to observe this important day, not only to remember our lost loved ones, but also to remind the world of what happened to us.”

Despite years of endless suffering in exile, the Rohingya refugees remain hopeful. They continue to fight for justice for the genocide committed against them, for recognition of their rights, and for a future where they can live in peace in their homeland like everyone else. Each year, as the Rohingya mark Rohingya Genocide Remembrance Day, they remember those who were lost, honor those who survived, and support those who continue to struggle for a better future.

The history of the Rohingya must not be erased, and their voices must not be silenced. The Rohingya story is one of immense suffering, but it is also a story of courage, resilience, and hope. Every year, on August 25, the community comes together to ensure that the victims are remembered, the survivors are heard, and the world is reminded that justice remains unfinished.

Sirajul Islam, a Rohingya poet, writer, and human rights activist, said, “Every year, we commemorate this day with the only hope to return home before the next anniversary comes. Today, we are marking the ninth anniversary but this time with both desolation and hope and with the searing question: Will our hope ever come true?”

Rohingya leaders say that remembering is not only about the past. It is about protecting the truth, preserving memories, and strengthening the community that one day they will return home with freedom, safety, citizenship, dignity, and rights.

The United Nations and human rights organizations are calling for an end to the killings, persecution, and impunity, and for justice, accountability, and the restoration of the Rohingya’s rights and citizenship. But despite years of warnings and appeals, their calls seem to be ignored, and the suffering of the Rohingya continues to increase.
tag: Rohingya genocide; Rohingya Genocide Remembrance Day; Rohingya in Myanmar; Rohingya refugees; Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh; Rohingya repatriation

title: Russia’s Fake Missile Test Warning to New Zealand
description: With the warning of a yet-to-materialize missile test in the Southern Ocean, is Russia playing an old joke on New Zealand?
text:
In 2010, at an APEC meeting in Japan, New Zealand Prime Minister John Key, in an awkward attempt to break the ice, asked Russian President Dmitry Medvedev how long it would take a Russian missile to reach New Zealand. Medvedev immediately asked a staffer to calculate it. He turned back to Key and said, “22 minutes,” then added with a smirk, “I will call you in advance.”

The exchange became a New Zealand urban legend. This week, the Russians seem to have replayed the joke – for real this time.

On August 18, the Russian Air Traffic Management Corporation gave the New Zealand Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) an alarming warning of planned “space activity” in an area of the Southern Ocean managed by New Zealand authorities. The CAA’s follow-up Notice to Airmen (NOTAM) identified the activity as a missile launch.

New Zealand has experienced the landing of Russian space debris in its territory before, but never a missile launch.

New Zealand’s Starboard says there are no Russian vessels in the area of the supposed launch. When China launched a long-range nuclear-capable ballistic missile into the South Pacific in June, it sent three space-tracking vessels to observe the trajectory and collect the debris.

So it appears that Russia’s warning is a dummy warning of a dummy missile – an information operation and another example of Russia’s reckless hybrid warfare. The New Zealand government has asked for more information about the launch. Foreign Minister Winston Peters said the information Russia provided was unclear.

NOTAM NZZO B3996/26 reported a foreign agency missile launch and returning space debris until August 27, imposing flight restrictions from 58 and 68 degrees south. The area is approximately 1, 900 km southwest of New Zealand’s South Island, in the Southern Ocean-Antarctic flight region, near the Ross Sea.

There is no international law specifically regulating submarines conducting missile launches in international waters, let alone fake missile launches. Russia, like China, appears to be using international rules – and the gaps in those rules – as a shield for an act of intimidation and show of force.

The only flights that travel in the Ross Sea are U.S., New Zealand, and Australian military planes. They form an international Antarctic flight pool carrying scientists to bases in the Ross Sea area: the U.S. McMurdo and South Pole stations; New Zealand’s Scott Base; South Korea’s Jang Bogo Station and Italy’s Mario Zucchelli Station. Personnel from China’s two Ross Sea bases, one of them only 30 kilometers from South Korea’s base, are not included in this logistics pool. This is likely no accident, but a response to China’s aggressive acts elsewhere including military support for Russia’s war against Ukraine.

After Russia issued its warning, a U.S. Air Force C-17 Antarctic flight was turned back from Christchurch a few hours into its journey on the afternoon of August 18. The Antarctic C-17s are flown by active-duty and Air Force Reserve crews from the 62nd and 446th Airlift Wings at Joint Base Lewis-McChord in the U.S. state of Washington. The international Antarctic programs based in Christchurch had only just begun their Antarctic season and regular flights to the ice; the C-17 flight on August 18 was to be the first.

Antarctic analysts have often speculated that the bases there could be an early target in a global conflict. The U.S., Russian, and Chinese Antarctic programs all host global navigation satellite system (GNSS) ground stations – GPS, GLONASS and BeiDou – which are used for nuclear missile timing and positioning, as well as other facilities with dual civil-military capabilities. Polar ground stations are an essential part of C4ISR – Command, Control, Communications, Computers, Intelligence, Surveillance, and Reconnaissance – the nerve centers of modern defense.

Last week, Russian military forces engaged in a major naval exercise in the Kuril Islands, off the Pacific coast. President Vladimir Putin watched on the final day of the exercises. But Putin had something else on his mind. Addressing naval personnel he said:

We can see that the officials of some countries are attempting to restrict the movement of our economic operators’ vessels by peaceful means in violation of International Maritime Law, but recently it occurred to them that they can seize our vessels and sell our looted property. This is nothing short of piracy and plunder. If this happens, we will have to reciprocate – not necessarily in the waters where they plan to raid our own ships but anywhere we consider necessary or reasonable, including in the Pacific Fleet’s area of responsibility.

Only days earlier, the Italian navy led an EU-team boarding a tanker belonging to Russia’s “shadow fleet,” which helps Moscow circumvent sanctions. New Zealand has also participated in sanctions, through maritime restrictions.

Russia’s Pacific Fleet is responsible for more than near-seas border protection. It provides Russia’s nuclear and non-nuclear deterrence in the Asia-Pacific and protects sea lines of communication. Russia has also strengthened its position in the Blue Pacific through recently announced joint patrols with the People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN), as well as cooperation with India and North Korea.

Since the Cold War, the U.S.-led strategic architecture in the Pacific has sought to limit Russian and Chinese strategic access through a network of hub-and-spoke defense pacts and installations along the three island chains. Antarctica represents the southernmost reach of the Third Island Chain.

That architecture appeared somewhat frayed this week, with the last U.S. aircraft carrier stationed in the Pacific departing for duties in the Middle East. Last year after launching military exercises in the Tasman Sea, China boasted of the “normalization of the deployment” of PLA forces in the South Pacific. The removal of the U.S. aircraft carrier has thus unnerved the U.S. Indo-Pacific allies considerably. Their navies combined are no match for the PLAN’s 234 vessels and six nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarines (SSBNs) plus the Russian Pacific fleet’s 80 major warships and submarines, which include six SSBNs.

TASS coverage of last week’s Russian naval exercises near the Kurils used a picture of a Borei-class (Project 955) ballistic-missile submarine, RFS Vladimir Monomakh (K-551). The submarine is equipped with the very SLBMs that could get to New Zealand in the proverbial 22 minutes. It is not known if the Monomakh participated in the exercise; only Kilo-class submarines were observed departing for its start.

Could Russia’s fake missile-launch warning this week have revived Medvedev’s joke as a lesson for the coalition of states imposing sanctions on the Russian shadow fleet?

A warning about a fake missile launch, apparently from a submarine that may itself have only been pretending to take part in a naval exercise, would be an elaborate – and menacing – Russian prank.

Russia’s missile warning did not make the evening news in New Zealand, nor did it feature on the national radio bulletin. Instead, the news carried the familiar stories of everyday life in our bucolic corner of the world.

Perhaps it is time we stopped assuming that the moat of our vast exclusive economic zone can shield us from a strategic environment unlike any we have faced in living memory. We need to think about how to future-proof New Zealand and protect our interests over the long term.
tag: New Zealand Antarctica; New Zealand security; Russia in Antarctica; Russia in the Indo-Pacific; Russia in the Southern Ocean; Russia Pacific Fleet; Russian military in the Pacific

title: Severe Flooding Bares Garbage and Corruption Problems in the Philippines
description: Lawmakers and contractors used the climate crisis to push forward flood-control projects. But those have turned out to be defective and in some cases even non-existent.
text:
Recent non-stop rains inundated Metro Manila and nearby urban areas in the Philippines, revealing not just the scale and stench of the garbage problem but also the lingering impact of corruption-tainted flood control projects.

For almost two weeks, severe flooding led to the cancellation of classes, stranded thousands of workers, and forced the evacuation of residents in low-lying areas. Fast rising water levels caused dams to overspill, which worsened the flooding in the country’s largest urban center.

As government units scrambled to extend assistance to flooded communities, it also set off a lively debate on who should bear responsibility for the disaster. Many immediately saw a connection between faulty and substandard infrastructure projects and the flooding problem. It revived public outrage against corrupt lawmakers and contractors who used the climate crisis emergency to push forward flood-control projects, which later turned out to be defective and in some cases even non-existent.

Citizens actively documented the flooding in their areas and called out officials for their inaction and involvement in the flood-control scam. They also pointed out the slow pace of prosecution and the selective targeting of politicians implicated in the controversy. Sensing widespread discontent, the office of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. assured the public that irregularities in flood-control projects will continue to be investigated.

Aside from affirming the urgency of addressing corruption, Marcos also highlighted the country’s garbage problem when he inspected pumping stations and coastal areas swamped with a “sea of trash.” In one city alone, three days of “clearing operations” collected 400 tons of garbage in the waters of Manila Bay, enough to fill 72 dump trucks. Later, the government noted the crisis in waste disposal as it enjoined the public to foster a “culture of discipline” in managing trash.

Marcos insisted that flood control will be rendered useless if garbage continues to pollute water systems. He then pushed for the building of waste-to-energy plants as a solution to the problem.

Environmentalists were quick to remind the president that instead of blaming the public for littering, he should focus on the roots of the garbage catastrophe linked to “the relentless, unchecked flood of single-use plastics being pumped into the economy by major corporations.” They also called the plan to build waste-to-energy facilities “a false solution” since “burning waste contributes to greenhouse gas emissions and can release hazardous pollutants.”

The floodwaters have already receded, but debates about what caused the disaster are expected to continue as Congress is set to deliberate the Marcos administration’s proposed 2027 national budget. Despite the unresolved anomalous flood-control contracts, more than a hundred billion pesos have been earmarked for this type of spending in 2027. In the Senate, some lawmakers are looking for a master plan that will guide the government’s flood control projects. Protests could erupt if budget scrutiny uncovers that the corruption-prone pork barrel system remains intact.

Meanwhile, Marcos’ endorsement of waste-to-energy facilities could spotlight ongoing projects in Metro Manila that are being fiercely opposed by residents threatened with displacement and mobility restrictions.

The Marcos government sought to assert its narrative that it is proactive and efficient in responding to the recent flooding disaster. It also offered emergency aid while laying down long-term solutions to the recurring flooding problem. This is intended to counter the arguments of the camp of Vice President Sara Duterte, who seeks to undermine the impeachment process by insisting that people’s everyday concerns like surviving the flooding should be given more attention.

What the supporters of Marcos and Duterte fail to acknowledge is that both leaders are equally liable for their key roles in the rollout of corruption programs. Both are also accountable for the flood control controversy.

As the nation braces for another week of monsoon rains, the recent flooding disaster lead may lead more people to realize that corruption is the biggest trash in society, and the way to remove it is to pursue accountability, good governance, and justice.
tag: Ferdinand Marcos Jr; Philippines corruption; Philippines flood; Philippines politics

title: South Korea’s Nuclear Dilemma
description: The debate over acquiring nuclear weapons continues in Seoul.
text:
The structure of global security has been changing in profound ways. In Europe there is a major conventional war, and the potential for armed conflict seems to be increasing in other parts of the world including East Asia. The United States is no longer seen as a reliable security guarantor by its allies.

One of the puzzling aspects of the global security architecture is that nuclear powers no longer seem to possess a coherent understanding of what their arsenals are for. Strategic capabilities are increasingly developed with conventional weapons, while nuclear deterrence fails to deter major conflict, a phenomenon that Rose Goettemoeller has referred to as “The Strange Defeat of Nuclear Deterrence.” This has the paradoxical consequence that regional powers feel the increasing need to acquire nuclear weapons.

South Korea faces this dilemma very acutely. North Korea is increasing its nuclear arsenal and has developed a significant alliance with Russia even as Pyongyang has renounced unification and designated South Korea as its enemy. At the same time, the preparedness of the United States to defend its allies in the region has come into question. This is exacerbated by the fact that the continental United States is now within reach of North Korean ballistic missiles.

The result has been an intense debate in South Korea about whether the country should acquire nuclear weapons. On July 27, retired Lieutenant General Chun In-bum published an article in the Korea Times that elaborated on a sophisticated proposal for South Korea to acquire a nuclear weapons arsenal, which Seoul would own but which would be imbedded in an integrated network of deterrence with the United States. This would resemble some of the deployments of nuclear weapons in Europe in the early Cold War, with a dual-key system that would require the consent of the host country and the United States for weapons to be launched. Chun admitted that this would raise significant issues with regard to the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT), verification, and decision-making.

Public surveys in South Korea have shown up to 80 percent support for South Korea acquiring a nuclear weapons capability. Among South Korean policy elites, there is less enthusiasm due to the potential consequences for the alliance with the United States, South Korea’s adherence to the NPT, and the economic implications. Policymakers tend to prefer a “threshold capacity” whereby South Korea would have the capability to quickly develop nuclear weapons but would not actually do so while the alliance with the U.S. remains in place.

Strengthening nuclear deterrence on the Korean Peninsula can take several forms. One possibility would be to redeploy U.S. nuclear weapons in South Korea with the purpose of signalling to North Korea, China, and Russia that extended deterrence is serious. In Europe, the deployment of U.S. nuclear weapons was accompanied by the development of independent nuclear deterrents by Britain and France. But these nuclear arsenals were developed in a different environment when the strategic conflict with the Soviet Union was at the core of global security. The United States was unable to prevent the development of these independent arsenals and therefore chose to integrate them into its posture on European security.

All of the proposed variants face the dilemma of “entrapment or abandonment.” Countries hosting U.S. nuclear weapons do not want a nuclear conflict to start without their consent, but they want extended deterrence to be effective. Likewise, the United States does not want to be embroiled in a nuclear conflict initiated by an ally. The fundamental dilemma is how to make nuclear deterrence credible to the adversary while balancing the risks in a manner acceptable to all parties.

The problem with Chun’s proposed scheme is that it does not resolve this fundamental dilemma. If the United States maintains escalation control, this amounts to a veto in a different form. If South Korea had independent launch authority, then the United States could find itself in a nuclear conflict against its will. It is really unclear therefore whether the implementation of Chun’s proposal or anything similar would solve the underlying problem.

South Korea’s negotiations with the United States over the transfer of wartime operational control (OPCON) over ROK forces – a process that has dragged on for two decades – illustrate the practical difficulties of such arrangements. OPCON transition requires highly coordinated intelligence and communication systems, interoperability, training, and finely tuned relations between South Korean and American commanders. Nuclear decision-making would be more complex and would have to include the U.S. president, but given the geography of the battlefield, decision times could be extraordinarily short. It would require substantial reassurance that there would be no unauthorized launch but the threat of retaliation would have to be credible to the adversary.

A South Korean nuclear arsenal, even if embedded in an alliance command structure, could complicate the regional security environment. It could encourage Russia to enhance its support of North Korea and its sharing of technology with respect to nuclear delivery and control systems. Beijing would be likely to consider such a capability as a threat to its own security. The decision to deploy the ballistic missile defense system THAAD in South Korea in 2016 provoked a major reaction from China with the imposition of political and economic costs. Then-South Korean President Moon Jae-in managed to partly assuage China by promising no further deployments of THAAD batteries and no integration into a region-wide U.S. led missile defense network.

A South Korean nuclear arsenal is likely to provoke an even more serious reaction, including economic sanctions, increasing military deployments and potentially the deployment or retargeting of Chinese nuclear forces against South Korea. It could also rekindle the nuclear debate in Japan and lead to further nuclear proliferation.

It is hard to predict how North Korea would react to a South Korean nuclear arsenal. It is true that deterrence of a North Korean nuclear attack would be enhanced. At the same time, it could provoke even more acceleration of North Korea’s efforts to develop a secure nuclear capability that could also strike the United States. It would not necessarily inhibit low-level attacks below the threshold of direct armed conflict.

It would also change the narrative of a democratic South Korea acting in conformity with international law versus a rogue North Korean state if South Korea were to abandon its commitments to the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty. Leaving the NPT is not just a reputational or technical issue. While South Korea would no longer be obliged to forego the manufacture or possession of nuclear weapons, the United States would be constrained under Article I of the NPT not to transfer possession or control over nuclear weapons to South Korea or provide any nuclear assistance. The civil nuclear technology cooperation between the United States and South Korea – the “123 Agreement” of 2015 – would be in jeopardy.

There is little immediate prospect that Chun’s ideas can become policy. But that does not mean that there are no paths forward. The integration of U.S. nuclear weapons and conventional forces into operational planning, nuclear consultation, integration of early warning, intelligence, missile defense, and various signals regarding the commitment to extended deterrence and no tolerance of North Korea aggression could strengthen stability.

If South Korea feels it can no longer rely on the United States, then it could develop its own nuclear deterrent. But it would have to face the consequences, which may include international isolation, severe strains on (or even the collapse of) the South Korea-U.S. alliance, and a more hostile international security environment.

title: Southeast Asia’s Border Disputes: Wars in Waiting?
description: The region's maritime borders are hotly contested, but on land there's the real risk of conflict, too.
text:
You probably have heard of the South China Sea disputes – a major flashpoint involving China, the Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia, and Brunei. But the South China Sea isn’t the only dispute threatening to spark a war in Southeast Asia. There are plenty more contested borders on land as well.

Today, we’re going to talk about three other territorial disputes in the region – the kind of flashpoints that stay below the headlines until it’s too late. Stay tuned, because we’re ranking them in order: from the least likely to spark an actual shooting war to the highest risk of conflict.

In fact, one of these disputes even flared into a full-blown shooting war in 2025 – and it could happen again at any time.

title: Takaichi Is No Abe: Japan’s New Conservative Politics
description: After roughly 10 months in power, the differences between Takaichi and Abe are becoming increasingly difficult to ignore.
text:
For many years, Japan’s current Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae has been portrayed by international media as the heir to Abe Shinzo’s political legacy. Her nationalist views, assertive security posture, and close ties to Japan’s conservative movement have made the comparison seem natural.

There is good reason for the comparison. As Michael Green recently argued in Foreign Affairs, Takaichi has continued an important part of Abe’s strategic legacy: strengthening Japan’s defense capabilities, deepening the Japan-U.S. alliance, and responding more assertively to the challenge posed by China. From this perspective, Takaichi represents the continuation of a strategy that seeks to make Japan a stronger and more indispensable U.S. ally.

But strategic continuity should not be confused with political continuity. After roughly 10 months in power, the differences between Takaichi and Abe are becoming increasingly difficult to ignore. Rather than simply reviving “Abe politics,” Takaichi appears to be developing a new political style of her own: more personalized, more confrontational, and more dependent on emotional mobilization through social media. If Abe represented a conservative politics tempered by strategic pragmatism, Takaichi may represent something closer to a new form of conservative populism.

In other words, Takaichi may be Abe’s heir in grand strategy, but she is not necessarily adopting his tactics. The political methods emerging from Takaichi’s camp suggest a significant change in how Japan’s conservatives seek to mobilize domestic public support.

The controversy over the use of artificial intelligence (AI) during the 2025 Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) leadership election and the 2026 House of Representatives election offers a revealing example. Shukan Bunshun, a Japanese weekly magazine known for exposing political scandals, recently reported that people close to Takaichi’s camp had used AI to produce large numbers of short videos attacking political opponents and circulated them widely online. The revelations triggered a public backlash and created the first serious political challenge of Takaichi’s premiership.

The use of digital technology for political campaigning is hardly unprecedented. What is more significant is how the technology appears to have been used: not simply to communicate policy positions or mobilize supporters, but to amplify political antagonism and shape voters’ emotions. During the Abe era, the prime minister’s office was highly sophisticated in managing the media and political narrative, but Abe generally maintained a clearer distinction between political messaging and outright mobilization through antagonism.

Takaichi’s political operation appears more willing to blur that boundary. This is particularly important because Takaichi has cultivated a direct relationship with voters through social media. Rather than relying primarily on Japan’s established media organizations, she uses X to communicate directly with the public.

According to the Financial Times, Japanese business leaders have become increasingly frustrated with what they see as Takaichi’s unwillingness to listen to views from outside her political circle. They are also concerned that she has become increasingly hostile toward the mainstream media while relying more heavily on social media to maintain her popularity. This approach may be politically effective in the short term. But it also carries potential risks. Social media rewards confrontation, immediacy, and emotional intensity. A political leader who relies heavily on such platforms can easily find herself governing through the logic of mobilization rather than the logic of consensus-building.

A second concern is the uncertainty surrounding Takaichi’s decision-making. In April, the Japanese magazine Sentaku reported that Takaichi had clashed with Imai Nobuya, a senior political adviser during the Abe era, over the possible deployment of the Self-Defense Forces (SDF) to the Middle East. According to the report, Imai opposed Takaichi’s reported intention to send Japanese forces to the Strait of Hormuz to support U.S. military operations against Iran.

The details of the episode remain disputed, and the report should therefore be treated with caution. But the broader question it raises is difficult to dismiss: Does Takaichi have the same capacity for institutional and strategic balancing that characterized Abe’s leadership?

Abe was undoubtedly a committed conservative. Yet he was also an unusually pragmatic political operator. He relied heavily on trusted bureaucrats and political advisers, and he understood the importance of reconciling political ideology with institutional constraints and strategic realities. On major security and foreign policy questions, his administration typically sought to balance competing interests before making consequential decisions.

Takaichi’s approach appears more personal. Her foreign policy positions are often closely associated with her own ideological convictions, and she has shown less evidence of the cautious political calibration that was one of Abe’s defining characteristics.

Nowhere is this difference more consequential than in relations with China. Abe is frequently described outside Japan as a China hawk. That description is not entirely wrong, but it misses an important and delicate part of his diplomacy. Despite his nationalist reputation, Abe repeatedly demonstrated an ability to separate ideological commitments from strategic interests. In April 2018, for example, according to a memoir written by a Taiwanese political figure, Abe declined to meet former Taiwanese President Lee Teng-hui, who was staying at the same hotel in Okinawa, apparently to avoid unnecessarily provoking Beijing.

In 2019, Abe also sent a private letter to Yasukuni Shrine exploring the possibility of removing the enshrined Class-A war criminals, an effort that would have reduced one of the most persistent sources of friction in Japan’s relations with its neighbors. (I learned of this episode in 2025 while interviewing Kitaoka Shinichi, one of Abe’s key foreign policy advisers, at Stanford University.)

Whatever one thinks of Abe’s broader political legacy, these episodes demonstrate that his conservatism was accompanied by a strong instinct for strategic risk management. He understood that nationalist symbolism could generate domestic political benefits while imposing substantial diplomatic costs.

Takaichi has yet to demonstrate the same degree of restraint. Her approach to China appears to be driven more directly by ideological convictions and political instincts than by a broader strategy for managing Japan’s long-term relationship with its most important neighboring power.

This is precisely where the distinction between Takaichi and Abe becomes most important. Abe sought to strengthen Japan’s alliance with the United States while simultaneously maintaining channels for stable relations with China. His foreign policy was not simply “tough” or “soft”; it was fundamentally about strategic management.

If Takaichi is indeed continuing Abe’s grand strategy by strengthening the Japan-U.S. alliance and making Japan more capable of confronting China, that does not necessarily mean that she is reproducing Abe’s broader approach to statecraft. Abe’s strategic vision depended not only on strengthening Japan’s position, but also on managing the risks created by that stronger position.

Even some of the architects of Abe’s foreign policy now appear concerned about the direction of Japanese diplomacy. On July 2, Yachi Shotaro, the former head of Japan’s National Security Secretariat, wrote in his Nikkei series “My Life History” that the most important challenge facing Japanese diplomacy in the 21st century is its relationship with China. Japan, he argued, must think over the medium and long term about how to build a stable and strategic relationship with China while remaining a U.S. ally and recognizing China as an important neighboring country.

Yachi is hardly a dove on China. After Abe returned to power in 2006, he played a central role in efforts to improve China-Japan relations. According to interview records cited in journalist Funabashi Yoichi’s 2024 book on politics during the Abe era, “Children of Destiny,” Yachi also accompanied former Prime Minister Fukuda Yasuo to China in 2014 and helped facilitate the resumption of China-Japan summit diplomacy.

His remarks therefore reveal something important about the Abe-era foreign-policy establishment. Its members may have supported a stronger Japan and a more robust alliance with Washington, but they also understood that strategic competition with China could not substitute for diplomacy. For them, managing the relationship with Beijing was an essential component of Japanese diplomatic statecraft.

Takaichi’s politics appear to place greater emphasis on confrontation. That difference may ultimately determine whether her premiership can endure. A June poll by Jiji Press put Takaichi’s approval rating at roughly 54 percent, down from around 70 percent at the beginning of the year. For a prime minister who has not yet fully consolidated her political authority, this is hardly an unassailable position. A major scandal, economic setback, or diplomatic crisis could quickly weaken her support.

Takaichi may share Abe’s nationalism, his skepticism toward the postwar liberal order, and his determination to strengthen Japan’s security posture. She may also continue many of the strategic policies that Michael Green and other scholars have associated with Abe’s legacy. But political inheritance is about more than policy positions. It is also about governing instincts.

Abe understood that conservative politics could be sustained only by combining ideology with pragmatism, nationalism with diplomacy, and political mobilization with institutional management. Takaichi appears to be experimenting with a different formula – one that places greater emphasis on personal leadership, social media politics, emotional mobilization, and confrontation with perceived political and cultural opponents.

That does not necessarily mean Takaichi will fail. Indeed, such a political style may prove highly effective in an era of fragmented media and growing public distrust of established institutions. Nor does it mean that Takaichi’s foreign policy is fundamentally incompatible with Abe’s. On the contrary, she may succeed in making Japan an even stronger U.S. ally. But a stronger Japan and a more predictable Japan are not necessarily the same thing.

U.S. policymakers should recognize that Japan is entering a new political era. The question of whether Takaichi is Abe’s successor is ultimately a distraction. What matters is whether she can turn her personalized style of conservative politics into an effective governing system. If she can, Japan’s conservatives may have found a new political formula – one that combines strategic nationalism with populist mobilization and direct communication with voters. If she cannot, the same forces that made Takaichi powerful could also make her government increasingly unstable and expose Japan to unnecessary security risks.

title: The Hidden Famine: What I Saw in North Korea’s Darkest Years
description: “With the collapse of the Public Distribution System, which had been the sole source of food, many urban residents, unable to grow anything for themselves, simply wasted away in their homes, starving quietly and out of sight.”
text:
“Miss Kathi: Saving Lives in North Korea” by Kathi Zellweger and Mike Chinoy chronicles the remarkable story of Kathi Zellweger, a native of Switzerland whose history of engagement with a secretive, isolated North Korea over nearly three decades is unprecedented in its scope, access, and humanitarian impact. It is one of the first book-length accounts in English by an aid worker operating on the ground in North Korea – the story of a woman who has lived out her commitment to the poor and most vulnerable undaunted by the tensions and threat of conflict perpetually looming over the Korean peninsula.

For many North Koreans, Kathi was the first foreigner they had ever met or even seen. Playing a central role in the early years of international relief efforts in North Korea was a lonely job, as Kathi addressed the humanitarian needs of a suffering people largely ignored by the world because of their citizenship. She befriended local doctors, nurses, and caregivers; negotiated with suspicious government officials; overcame international doubts about the diversion of relief supplies to the military; and, over a period of years, spearheaded an effort that provided food, medicine, and development aid. Ultimately, her efforts saved the lives of thousands of people – most of them children.

This excerpt from the book describes visits to people struggling to survive the famine in the northern city of Sinuiju.

It was September 1998. I sat on the floor, Korean style, in Mrs. Kim’s apartment in Sinuiju, one of North Korea’s five largest cities. Located on the banks of the Yalu River just across from the Chinese town of Dandong, Sinuiju had been an important industrial center and a key transit point for trade with China before North Korea’s economy collapsed. Yet even though there was more contact with China in Sinuiju now than in other North Korean cities, it remained shabby and dilapidated, especially in contrast to the bright lights and bustling streets visible on the Chinese side of the Yalu in Dandong.

And Sinuiju had not been immune to the devastating impact of the famine. Indeed, earlier in the year, the North Koreans and the World Food Program had asked Caritas, the international charity where I worked, to ship 1,500 metric tons of barley there. As was often the case, providing the aid opened the door for me to visit an area that had previously been off limits to visitors. Along with Mary Healy, a nurse and midwife from the Irish NGO Trócaire (Caritas Ireland), which had become one of our most important international partners, I was making my first trip there. Local officials told us that, for many people, our supplies had been crucial in keeping hunger at bay. But the situation remained bleak.

At the Amnokgang Hotel, a large, square building with damp, smelly rooms and balconies whose doors could not be opened, we were virtually the only guests in the cavernous dining hall. The hotel shop offered an eclectic collection of basic necessities, but most striking to me was the jewelry that was also on sale. It was evident that some desperate citizens had pawned their personal valuables to get money to buy food. I bought a pair of earrings inlaid with small red stones. I still have them today. I keep them in a box. They bring back sad memories.

In a dismal gray Stalinist-style building typical of most North Korean cities, 69-year-old Mrs. Kim shared a tiny flat with her son, daughter-in-law, and six-month-old grandson. The son and his wife both worked in a nearby textile factory. Mrs. Kim and her daughter-in-law kept the apartment spotless. On one wall hung a guitar, which Mrs. Kim’s son apparently liked to play.

As I entered the room, I was startled to hear the gravel-tinged vocals of American country music legend Kenny Rogers coming from a cassette recorder. It made for an incongruous juxtaposition with the obligatory pictures of Kim Il Sung and Kim Jong Il mounted on another wall. I was tempted to ask about the music, but it occurred to me that the tape and the cassette player likely had come from China, that Mrs. Kim might well not be aware that Rogers was an American, and that the “guardian angels” accompanying us were probably equally ignorant. Inquiring as to why the family had popular music from the United States could have caused trouble for everyone, so I stayed silent. Mary and I just looked at each other with slightly puzzled expressions.

Under other circumstances, owning items such as a guitar and a cassette recorder, or the sewing machines and refrigerators I saw in other urban homes, would, in North Korean terms, have been signs of a decent standard of living. But on this visit, they could not mask the family’s grim plight.

“Is this the end of the Great Leader taking care of us?” the daughter-in-law asked plaintively. Her baby was ill. She said she was still breastfeeding and planned to continue to do so as long as possible. She had nothing else to feed her son. Six months had passed since they had received their last rations through the Public Distribution System. Apart from 14 kilos of rice and some bean curd delivered to mark North Korea’s National Day, they had been subsisting on alternative food plus whatever they could obtain by bartering textiles and other items with relatives who lived in the countryside and were able to grow some food for themselves.

Later that day, Mary and I were taken to meet the family of Mr. Lee, a 71-year-old carpenter. We found him sitting on his living room floor designing some furniture. He was surprised to see two unexpected foreign visitors but was gracious and friendly. Mr. Lee lived with his wife and youngest son. Three older sons were married and lived elsewhere. Like Mrs. Kim, Mr. Lee told us he had last received rations from the Public Distribution System in February. He was surviving by making furniture for people in the countryside, which he exchanged for food.

The examples of the Kim and Lee families highlighted two important characteristics of the famine in North Korea. Its epicenter was in urban rather than rural areas. More than two-thirds of the population lived in or near cities and towns. Unlike farmers in the countryside, who had the ability to grow some food on small private plots, which the authorities understood were necessary to survive and thus (perhaps grudgingly) tolerated, urban residents, often stuck in large apartment blocks, had no such option.

The result was unprecedented hunger in what had been a relatively well developed modern industrial society. With the collapse of the Public Distribution System, which had been the sole source of food, many urban residents, unable to grow anything for themselves, simply wasted away in their homes, starving quietly and out of sight. This was one reason I began to describe the situation as a “hidden famine.” In contrast to predominantly rural Somalia or Ethiopia, the worst suffering was not immediately visible. That didn’t make it any less real.

For the families we visited in Sinuiju, and many others, bartering was a crucial survival mechanism. What had begun with urban residents trading items of value, either from their homes or what could be stripped from their places of work, for food grown by farmers in private family garden plots became the foundation for the broader development of markets. As I traveled around the country, I would see people by the side of the road selling everything from buns to cigarettes to vegetables to live fish. As time passed, I also started to see little businesses appearing – people mending shoes, sewing, fixing bicycle tires, transporting wood in simple carts. Almost all of those involved appeared to be women, presumably because men were more likely to have fixed jobs or be serving in the military.

The emergence of these markets was a sensitive political issue. As a de facto privatization of an important part of North Korea’s economy, they posed not only practical challenges to state control but also an ideological one. Initially, when roadside vendors noticed a foreigner like me approaching, they would quickly cover the plastic buckets containing their products and run away. The government officials accompanying me were visibly uncomfortable as well and would often look in the other direction.

But the trend only accelerated with the creation of larger markets, especially in or near urban areas, which took over the role of the largely nonfunctional Public Distribution System. Before long, they became not only a source of food but of many other goods, although as they expanded, prices rose as well, and many people remained too poor or too far away to benefit. Indeed, some people told us they were spending up to 80 percent of their salary just to purchase vegetables.

The availability of cereals was a particularly sensitive issue. The government jealously guarded its monopoly on distributing items such as rice and maize. Occasionally, these products did make their way to the markets but were usually hidden from the public and sold surreptitiously.

In 2002, in an effort to reform the economy, in conjunction with a broader outreach to Tokyo, Washington, and Europe, Kim Jong Il formally sanctioned the existence of some markets in cities and towns. Before then, however, they operated in a kind of gray area. At that time, foreigners were forbidden from visiting them, which made it hard to determine the precise nature, scale, and impact of the phenomenon, but sometimes on my colleagues’ and my travels, we would end up driving right through one, with crowds of people stepping aside to let our vehicle pass. It was yet another of the many paradoxes of North Korea.

title: The Mecca Pact: What Do We Actually Know?
description: There are few concrete details available about the joint defense agreement between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkiye.
text:
In the latest episode of The Diplomat’s Asia Geopolitics podcast, hosts Katie Putz and Ankit Panda discuss the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement – a collective security agreement signed by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkiye in early August. They dive into the motivations for the pact on the part of all three members and the role (or lack thereof) of nuclear deterrence within it. They also compare it to other collective security arrangements like the CSTO.

There are few concrete details available about the pact, but given the tumultuous regions its members span, it’ll be tested soon.

You can subscribe to The Diplomat’s Asia Geopolitics podcast on Apple Podcasts and Spotify; and watch the episode on YouTube.

title: The Reason Japan Cannot Commit to Dialogue with North Korea
description: The Tanaka affair has cast a long shadow.
text:
Only two Japan-North Korea summit meetings have ever been held, both between Japanese Prime Minister Junichiro Koizumi and former North Korean leader Kim Jong Il, in September 2002 and May 2004. Since then, an inter-Korean summit was held in October 2007, followed by three more in 2018. U.S.-North Korea summits were held in June 2018, February 2019, and June 2019. Yet Japan and North Korea have not met at the summit level in over two decades.

What makes summit dialogue uniquely difficult for Japan is the abduction issue. From the 1970s through the 1980s, North Korean agents abducted a large number of Japanese citizens. The abduction of Megumi Yokota, a middle school student at the time, especially shocked Japanese society, and resolving the abduction issue has been declared a “high-priority issue” by every successive administration.

Japanese sanctions on North Korea are the heaviest in the world, yet they have not led to the return of a single abductee to Japan since the five abductees came home in October 2002. Japanese public opinion nonetheless persistently calls for heavier sanctions, driven by anger and distrust. This is despite the fact that it was dialogue, not sanctions, that secured Koizumi’s signal achievement: an apology from North Korean leader Kim Jong Il and the return of five abductees and their family members.

The issue is serious and complex. Even if North Korea were to allow Japanese nationals to return, claiming that “new abduction victims have been identified,” that would not produce unqualified satisfaction on the Japanese side. Distrust toward a country that has long insisted “the abductions have been resolved” would only deepen; and even if ten people were to return, the Japanese public would suspect there may be still more abductees. Japan has struggled for years with the question of what would constitute a “resolution” of the abduction issue, but it proved an impossible task given that human lives were at stake.

The key figure who made Koizumi’s historic visit to North Korea possible was Tanaka Hitoshi, the then Director-General of the Asian and Oceanian Affairs Bureau of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. He conducted nearly thirty secret meetings with the North Korean agent known as “Mr. X,” in China and other third countries. The meetings were so secret that even Shinzo Abe, then Deputy Chief Cabinet Secretary, was not made aware of them.

After Kim Jong Il admitted to and apologized for the abductions and the five abductees were returned to Japan, public anger fell not only on North Korea but also on Tanaka. Not all abductees had returned, and it emerged that Tanaka had accepted a North Korean suggestion for a “temporary return” of roughly two weeks rather than permanent residency for the five abductees.

Tanaka likewise attracted Abe’s ire. Having taken a strong personal interest in the abduction issue, Abe could not forgive Tanaka for advancing negotiations without informing him. Tanaka was ultimately summoned to Diet deliberations, where he broke down in tears under withering criticism of how the negotiations had been handled. Despite having acted on the prime minister’s instructions, Tanaka received no defense from Koizumi, perhaps because public opinion was too hostile. Koizumi’s diplomacy toward North Korea deserves a more positive assessment than it has received, and it is regrettable that this episode cast such a long shadow. Tanaka was so thoroughly pilloried by Japanese conservatives as a “traitor” that this once-promising diplomatic ace never became vice-minister for foreign affairs or ambassador to the United States.

The affair had lasting consequences. It taught subsequent administrations that even if they were to seriously pursue North Korea diplomacy, public support would be hard to secure given widespread skepticism toward dialogue, and that even partial success, short of a “full resolution” of the abduction issue, would expose them to harsh criticism regardless.

Having witnessed the keelhauling of Tanaka, even the most talented Foreign Ministry officials will not actively pursue North Korea diplomacy. Japanese civil servants are divided from the moment of hiring into elite “career” and specialized “non-career” tracks, with the hierarchy between the two tracks never reversed. Career diplomats rotate postings every two to three years and are guaranteed advancement if they handle North Korea safely without taking risks. The perverse result is that the most capable diplomats are the least likely to actively pursue dialogue with Pyongyang.

This structural problem must be addressed before Japan can make progress on any of its outstanding issues with North Korea. Ultimately, overcoming the problem requires strong political leadership from the prime minister.

title: The South China Sea and the Philippines’ Defense Strategies
description: Insights from Su Mon and Tomas Buenaventura.
text:
The Diplomat author Mercy Kuo regularly engages subject-matter experts, policy practitioners, and strategic thinkers across the globe for their diverse insights into U.S. Asia policy. This conversation with Su Mon and Tomas Buenaventura – Asia Pacific senior analyst and senior research assistant, respectively, at ACLED (Armed Conflict Location and Event Data) – is the 523rd in “The Trans-Pacific View Insight Series.”

Examine the South China Sea conflict escalation environment based on ACLED data.

ACLED data reveals the South China Sea security environment is increasingly defined by the normalization of gray zone tactics and rapid militarization. A persistent state of confrontation significantly escalated in the first half of 2026, with a roughly 490 percent increase in Chinese force movements between January and June compared to the previous six months. This activity is concentrated within the Philippines’ Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ), specifically around Scarborough Shoal, Sabina Shoal, and Thitu Island.

This uptick in force movements — including survey vessels, China Coast Guard (CCG) deployments, and maritime militia — is often accompanied by more frequent encounters, ranging from harassment and blocking maneuvers to competing law enforcement operations. These activities are not just about presence, but about altering the status quo on the seas. They represent a coordinated effort to advance territorial claims and consolidate control, keeping tensions high while strategically averting open military conflict.

Essentially, the region has become a primary theater for power projection, where the margin for error is shrinking, and the risks of a miscalculation that could lead to broader instability are becoming more acute.

How are gray zone tactics affecting the chance of escalation in the South China Sea?

The real danger with gray zone operations is not necessarily that they will spark an immediate war; it’s that they gradually normalize coercion. By using persistent, incremental actions — such as the routine deployment of maritime militia and coast guard vessels — Beijing is steadily shifting the status quo, redefining “normal” maritime activity in a way that feels manageable daily but creates significant long-term strategic shifts.

ACLED’s South China Sea Monitor suggests that these gray zone operations are expanding into cyber warfare, intelligence operations, and suspected sabotage against critical infrastructure. This expansion shows the growing imbalance between China and other claimant states, necessitating stronger cooperation among regional partners and allies to respond effectively.

Ultimately, this creates a dangerous environment where the primary risk is not a deliberate decision to go to war, but a miscalculation. As these tactics become more sophisticated, they blur strategic intent and erode the trust needed to manage crises. Regional security and coordination mechanisms, such as the South China Sea Code of Conduct negotiations, have not kept pace with these developments, leaving a widening gap in governance, making the region increasingly vulnerable to unintended escalations.

Identify key developments in the Scarborough Shoal and the Spratly Islands.

The situation at Scarborough Shoal has remained tense since China established de facto control there in 2012, despite the feature falling within the Philippines’ EEZ. Beijing has maintained a constant presence, with the CCG and maritime militia frequently blocking, ramming, and using water cannons against Philippine vessels. Tensions intensified after Beijing designated the shoal a national “nature reserve” in September 2025 — a move China framed as environmental protection, but which Manila viewed as an attempt to consolidate administrative control. Subsequent reports of floating barriers, buoys, and a temporary research platform further heightened tensions, culminating in confrontations on July 23-24, 2026, when the CCG again deployed water cannons against Philippine government vessels.

The Spratly Islands present a more complex, multilayered security environment involving competing claims from Brunei, China, Malaysia, the Philippines, Taiwan, and Vietnam. The challenge here is twofold: immediate flashpoints and gradual, strategic military expansion. Second Thomas Shoal remains one of the most volatile flashpoints. While an informal arrangement since mid-2024 has reduced interference with routine Philippine resupply missions to the BRP Sierra Madre, China continues to block construction materials intended to strengthen the outpost. The recent clash on July 22 at Second Thomas demonstrates that both sides are contending over what constitutes acceptable military presence.

Developments at Scarborough Shoal and the Spratly Islands reflect a broader contest, as China and the Philippines test resolve and respond to perceived encroachments. Each side is enforcing its own red lines, but in doing so is edging closer to crossing the other’s.

Analyze how the United States-Philippines Mutual Defense Treaty (MDT) could draw Washington into a broader regional conflict.

The Mutual Defense Treaty (MDT) signed by Manila and Washington in 1951 obligates both countries to come to each other’s defense in case of an armed attack on either in the Pacific region. As the treaty’s scope explicitly identified armed attacks as the trigger to both sides’ defense obligations, this has given rise to the widespread use of “gray zone” tactics on China’s part in its assertion of its maritime territorial claims against the Philippines. This seemingly hard limit for China’s South China Sea activity allows Beijing to pressure Manila on its claims while keeping the risk of armed conflict with the U.S. at bay. Still, the very nature of gray zone tactics at sea — consisting of close vessel confrontations, tailing and blocking actions, and other delicate maneuvers — means that the risk of a lethal accident is never zero.

Already, this July, a widely publicized confrontation between Chinese and Philippine personnel near Second Thomas Shoal left a Philippine soldier injured after being struck with a wooden baton. Even in this high-profile incident, though, no side has risked employing any sort of actual firepower against each other, as that would be indisputably escalatory and definitely be a notch above the confrontations of recent years — and likely enough reason for the U.S. to consider a heightened presence in the waters.

Assess the current gray zone conditions between the Philippines and China.

Despite the heated rhetoric between Manila and Beijing, the Philippines and China continue to engage each other very closely through diplomatic channels. Nevertheless, the tense environment created by the constant gray zone operations provides a conducive environment for potential triggers to MDT defense obligations, say, a lethal incident that leads both Chinese and Philippine forces to reach for firepower. In such a situation, the Philippines would count on the U.S. to make good on its repeated affirmations of its “ironclad” commitment to the Philippines’ defense.

For the time being, however, neither the Philippines and China seem to have any real desire to engage each other in armed conflict, especially given the otherwise close economic ties between the two countries. Thus, as long as the gray zone activities are managed to a tolerable degree, no matter how feisty the rhetoric gets between Manila and Beijing, they are currently unlikely to draw the U.S. into a conflict in the region.

title: The South Korean Government’s Housing Policy Tanks Its Approval Ratings
description: Even the historic Yongsan Park isn’t safe from the government’s desire for more housing.
text:
Seoulites and tourists primarily associate Yongsan Park with the National Museum of Korea. Located in the middle of the southernmost strip of the park, it attracts the third highest number of annual visitors in the world.

Walking up to the front affords quite a sight. A lone pavilion, with its rooftop faded in jade green, stands in a tree-lined pond. Trace the gaze upward, and there’s the rectangular gap in the museum’s superstructure of concrete covered in granite framing the beautiful expanse of greenery opening up to Namsan Mountain and Namsan Tower. At the back of the premise is a children’s garden, filling the air around the museum with laughter and scampering footsteps.

This break from the city’s noise and visual fatigue is thanks to the fact that it used to be Yongsan Garrison. In 1953, the United States 8th Army moved into what is today Yongsan Park – only a tiny portion is open to the public so far – to deter North Korea. In 1957, the United Nations Command also relocated next to the U.S. base from Tokyo. This 630-acre post, plus Itaewon just outside of the garrison, had become a little America in the heart of Seoul.

It remained untouched until 1989, when then-South Korean President Roh Tae-woo and U.S. President George H. W. Bush got into a chopper and circled over Yongsan Garrison. The view reportedly convinced Bush to agree that “there shouldn’t be foreign troops in the middle of a state’s capital.”

The next year, Washington and Seoul signed an agreement to relocate the U.S. forces somewhere else. Successive South Korean governments then framed the matter of nudging U.S. soldiers out of Seoul as reviving national pride. After much dithering, it was finally decided in 2004 that Camp Humphreys, an hour drive south of Seoul, would absorb Yongsan forces.

What would become of the newly vacated land in Seoul?

The Roh Moo-hyun administration legislated the 2007 Special Act on the Creation of Yongsan Park. The act bound the government to develop the land to be returned from the United States “into a place for leisure and relaxation as well as a natural and ecological space.” It also barred development of the area into anything other than a park.

However, the base territory has changed hands at a painfully slow pace. Although most U.S. personnel and military materiel vacated Yongsan to Camp Humphreys, Washington has coughed up only some 30 percent of the land. The handover of the rest awaits talks on recompensation, environmental inspections, and cleanup.

But its fate is already generating controversy.

In mid-August, the Lee administration kicked up an intense public uproar with its controversial idea to build housing in the Yongsan complex. “Yongsan is so huge … There are places where I think we can build housing,” said the president’s economic development guru in a radio appearance. He then floated the idea of building apartment complexes in the children’s garden section of Yongsan Park.

The land and infrastructure ministry followed up with its announcement that it would survey where to build new housing in the park, particularly those areas already razed to the ground by the U.S. military.

This was all in response to President Lee Jae-myung’s exhortation to his aides on August 13 to “devote all available resources and capabilities to solving housing problems that threaten people’s livelihood and the state’s future.” Indeed, South Korea’s real estate investment and redevelopment frenzy has jacked up housing prices for decades. In a country where owning a flat is a prerequisite for marriage, this has been one of the many factors driving down birthrates. And the increasing inequality in wealth determined by real estate ownership isn’t a tenable social reality.

So, the Lee administration has implemented a slew of policies meant to deter frenetic property purchases. Two of these particularly attracted opprobrium. First, shrinking the proportion of a loan homebuyers can secure out of the total property value has forced them to look to leases. Higher demand for leases led to higher rent and premiums (an upfront lump-sum payment for granting a lease). But now, there’s even a shortage of leases.

Second, the government proposed increasing the cap on the real estate holding tax and the market valuation rates used to assess property value for tax purposes.

Together, these policies had the effect of alienating most Seoul residents, both tenants and homeowners. Polls in mid-August showed that Lee’s approval rating fell below the 50 percentage mark for the first time since his term began. The housing crisis and prosecutorial reform were cited as the two major reasons. Among young residents in Seoul, Lee’s performance was abysmal, at 31 percent.

There is no question that more affordable housing is needed, which is why the government pledged to lay the groundwork for about 1.5 million new publicly funded flats during Lee’s term. That’s also why the Lee administration bucked the liberal regimes’ historical stance against bulldozing greenbelts – and whether Yongsan Park should become part of this plan is now a raging debate.

The government’s urgency is understandable, but the park should be inviolable. Seoul needs a breathing space. The only silver lining in the U.S. Army’s use of the base was that it saved a huge chunk in the heart of Seoul from the city’s unrestrained development and construction before the concept of landscape urbanism – that greenery and ecosystem should inform architectural plans – was even a thing in South Korea. Seoul needs something akin to New York’s Central Park and London’s Hyde Park and Regent’s Park. Yongsan Park, once Washington returns more plots, could be larger and play a vastly positive role. As the lungs of the city, the park could nurture precious ecology, dampen heat waves, and add social value as a shared natural space.

Also, Yongsan Park should be preserved and developed into a full-blown park for symbolic and historical reasons. The location represents the country’s painful history, independence, and modernity.

Empires of old dug in their heels here. In the 13th century, Mongols occupied the area for their war against Korea. In the 17th century, China’s Qing Dynasty quartered their soldiers here, from which they trafficked 5 percent of the Korean population. Throughout the first half of the 20th century, Imperial Japan’s soldiers sojourned here, conscripting and training and sending Koreans to their deaths in Japan’s far-flung wars. And then the United States took over the base in 1945.

It has also been Korea’s gateway to the world. Owing to its centrality and proximity to the Han River and Namsan Mountain, foreign tourists and traders have converged here since medieval times. Goods crisscrossing the country passed through Yongsan’s barter shops and entry routes. Since the late 19th century, it was through here that Koreans introduced modernity, be it steamboats and trams, or multiculturalism and artistic development.

It is time now for South Koreans to savor this space. It should not be turned into apartment complexes.

The Lee administration said that the vast majority of the park will be spared. But apartment complexes mean auxiliary infrastructure. Roads have to be laid down. Malls and schools have to be built. Carving the park this way ruins the last precious chance to rectify Seoul’s cramped landscape and restore biological diversity.

Seoul’s mayor Oh Se-hoon is locking horns with the government over this issue.

“History won’t forgive me for allowing even a small portion of the park to be turned into apartment sites,” Oh said in a video he filmed at the park. “We need to preserve Yongsan’s history and nature for the future generations,” he added.

He’s not alone. The most recent survey released on August 24 found that two out of three Seoulites are against the government proposal. The Seoul Metropolitan Government has been holding a series of talks with the government to persuade the latter of alternatives.

It’s worth remembering that in 2016, the Park Geun-hye administration wanted to build a couple of museums in the park. It was pelted with public outrage for even broaching the idea of pouring concrete in this historical land. The government backed down.

What Seoul needs isn’t traditional housing reconstruction and redevelopment practices, still less marring Yongsan Park for drab, high-rise apartments. It needs a complete regeneration plan that would organically connect residential, commercial, and recreational spaces. Simply put, dilapidated housing in low-density areas should be incorporated into large-scale mixed-use development. Some of the city’s commercial and recreational needs should be moved underground. And all these should be seamlessly accessed through ingenious infrastructure and transportation planning.

In the meantime, the government had better expedite their negotiation with Washington for a quicker transfer of land within Yongsan Garrison, as promised well over three decades ago.
