title: US ICC Sanctions Pose a Test for Japan
description: Japan’s only treaty ally sanctioned the ICC president – who happens to be a Japanese national. That embodies Japan’s rule-of-law conundrum.
text:
When the United States sanctioned International Criminal Court (ICC) President Akane Tomoko on August 18, Tokyo’s response was swift – and carefully calibrated. The next day, Foreign Ministry Press Secretary Kitamura Toshihiro called the move “very unfortunate,” reaffirming Japan’s consistent support for the ICC and the rule of law.

Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae commented publicly on the same day, telling reporters that she considered the sanctions “very unfortunate” and would continue communicating with the United States and other relevant countries. She did not, however, say whether Tokyo would ask Washington to withdraw the sanctions.

It was a statement of principle, but the restraint was noticeable. After all, Akane is a Japanese judge leading an institution that Tokyo has spent nearly two decades championing. Japan became a state party to the Rome Statute in 2007 and has since been one of the ICC’s strongest supporters.

On January 7, Takaichi herself received Akane and International Court of Justice President Iwasawa Yuji separately, describing the two courts as central to the rule of law and pledging Japan’s firm support. Eight months later, Akane has been personally sanctioned by Japan’s only treaty ally.

Washington’s sanctions, which also targeted Senegalese ICC lawyer Abdoulaye Seye, are part of a broader Trump administration campaign against the court. The United States argues that the ICC has overstepped its authority by pursuing nationals of countries, including the United States and Israel, that have not accepted its jurisdiction. In his statement announcing the sanctions, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio called the court “corrupt and fatally politicized” and denounced what he called “its assault on state sovereignty.”

The ICC strongly rejected the latest sanctions, calling them “a flagrant attack” on the independence of an impartial judicial institution. The court warned that threats against judicial officials for applying the law put “the international legal order itself” at risk. The ICC said nine of its 18 judges are now under U.S. sanctions, along with both deputy prosecutors, a former prosecutor, and one staff member.

Akane herself had already expressed a profound sense of crisis over growing pressure on international justice. In an interview with Japanese media, she described the rule of law as “a flickering candle.”

European leaders have rallied behind Akane. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa said they “stand firmly” with the ICC president and officials carrying out its mission, stressing that the court’s judges and officials must be able to act independently and without external pressure. The Netherlands, which hosts the ICC, has likewise rejected the sanctions and reaffirmed its support for the court and Akane.

Pressure on Tokyo to go further is also building at home. A cross-party parliamentary group condemned the sanctions in the “strongest possible terms” and urged Takaichi and Foreign Minister Motegi Toshimitsu to lodge a clear protest and demand their withdrawal.

Tamaki Yuichiro, leader of the Democratic Party for the People, Japan’s second-largest opposition party, made an important distinction: Japan should defend Akane not simply because she is Japanese, but because of the rule of law she represents.

The controversy exposes a wider tension in Japanese diplomacy. What happens when Tokyo’s commitment to the rule of law collides with the policies of its only treaty ally? This is not the first time the Takaichi government has confronted that question.

After U.S. and Israeli attacks against Iran earlier this year, Japan emphasized that Iran must not develop nuclear weapons and called for an early end to the conflict. Yet Tokyo avoided offering a clear judgment on whether the initial use of force was consistent with international law. At a March 3 press conference, Motegi was directly asked about the “legal legitimacy” of the attacks but did not provide such an assessment.

A pattern is emerging wherein Tokyo strongly emphasizes the rule of law as a principle of international order, but becomes more cautious when applying that principle could put it at odds with Washington.

There are understandable reasons for that caution. The Japan-U.S. alliance remains the foundation of Japan’s security strategy amid growing challenges from China, North Korea, and Russia. Tokyo may also calculate that quiet diplomacy is more likely than public confrontation to influence the Trump administration, particularly when Japan has broader security and economic interests to manage with Washington.

But there’s a trade-off: keeping quiet takes a toll on Japan’s credibility. Tokyo has spent years demanding that Beijing and Moscow respect international law and condemning attempts to change the status quo by force or coercion. Such arguments are most persuasive when the same principles are applied not only to competitors and adversaries, but also to allies.

As a middle power rather than a nuclear-armed great power, Japan has a profound interest in an international system in which rules constrain power. If major powers can decide when international institutions deserve respect and when they can be pressured for politically inconvenient decisions, Japan ultimately has much to lose.

Tokyo doesn’t have to choose between the Japan-U.S. alliance and the ICC. A mature alliance should be able to absorb disagreement, and defending judicial independence does not require Japan to endorse every decision made by the ICC.

Tokyo can, however, make clear that judges and court officials must be able to carry out their duties without political coercion. It can ask Washington to withdraw the sanctions, and work with the Netherlands, the EU, and other ICC states parties to ensure that Akane can continue performing her duties.

Such steps would be uncomfortable for Tokyo. But a tepid expression of regret without further action carries its own strategic risk. If Japan allows the rule of law to become a principle applied mainly to rivals, it weakens one of the most important diplomatic tools available to a middle power in an increasingly power-driven international order.

The choice before Tokyo is therefore larger than whether to protect Akane or defer to Trump.

For decades, Japan has said that it stands for a rules-based international order. The sanctions on the ICC president may now force Tokyo to show what that commitment means when the pressure comes not from Beijing or Moscow, but from Washington.
tag: Akane Tomoko; International Criminal Court (ICC); Japan international law; Japan rule of law; U.S. ICC sanctions; U.S.-Japan Alliance

title: US Official Reassures Asia of Commitment, Calls for Greater Burden Sharing
description: Undersecretary of War Elbridge Colby told an audience in Manila that U.S. interests are more engaged than ever in the Indo-Pacific.
text:
The United States remains strongly committed to Asia but wants its partners to bear more of the burden for their own defense, a senior Pentagon official said in the Philippines yesterday.

Seeking to counter concerns about Washington’s reliability, given the capricious character of U.S. foreign policy under the second Trump administration, Undersecretary of War Elbridge Colby said that U.S. interests were “more engaged than ever in the Indo-Pacific.”

“America is definitely not disengaging from Asia,” Colby said in a speech in Manila. “We are not leaving; in fact, we are digging in to ensure a favorable balance of power where it matters most.”

Colby made the remarks at a forum in the Philippines, his first stop on a Southeast Asian tour that will also take him and Assistant Secretary of War John Noh to Indonesia, Thailand, and Cambodia. In a statement, the Department of War said that trip, which will involve meetings with senior officials in each country, “reaffirms the Department’s commitment to build a durable peace in the region through strength.”

During the trip, Colby said in his Manila speech, he intended to “deliver a clear message that is at once both realistic and perhaps bracing but also reassuring: That America’s interests are more engaged than ever in the Indo-Pacific, and that we at the Department of War are concentrated on ensuring those interests are stoutly defended.”

Colby said maintaining a favorable balance of power in the Indo-Pacific required a “posture of deterrence by denial along the First Island Chain,” the barrier of islands that stretches from Japan down to Taiwan, the Philippines, and the northern coast of Borneo.

He pointed to what he said was a growing U.S. military commitment in the region, which has involved the deployment of additional troops, ships, aircraft, and missile systems throughout the First Island Chain. Colby described this as “a formidable, resource-backed posture calibrated to actual structural realities,” contrasting it with the “hollow, merely symbolic engagement of previous decades.”

However, he said that Washington could not manage this itself, and that local partners would need to shoulder more of the burden for their defense.

“When we ask our allies and partners to step up, to invest more in their own defense, and to take responsibility for their own sovereign security, we are not signaling abandonment,” Colby said.

He added, “We are looking for partners, not protectorates.”

The Southeast Asian tour is Colby’s official trip to Southeast Asia as undersecretary of war for policy, and in some ways, it is surprising that it has taken him 18 months to do so. But the intent of yesterday’s speech speaks to an awareness within the Pentagon of the reputational damage that Washington has suffered, in particular due to its indiscriminate tariff policy and misadventure in the Middle East.

Both of these have sent economic reverberations through Asia, and undermined the policy approach preferred by Colby. A hard-nosed realist and advocate of strategic prioritization, he has long advocated a reorientation of U.S. strategic focus from the Middle East toward East Asia, with the goal of preventing China from establishing its hegemony over the region.

While Colby did not explicitly mention China in the speech, his deterrence-focused message is likely to find a receptive audience in parts of the region that face its challenge most acutely. Chief among these is the Philippines, which has recently faced a resumption of China’s maritime pressure campaign in the South China Sea. This culminated in a clash at Second Thomas Shoal in the Spratly Islands on July 20, during which a Philippine sailor sustained a head injury after being struck with a baton by a China Coast Guard member.

Despite its attendant risks, most Southeast Asian governments would prefer the U.S. to maintain a strong presence in Asia, in order to act as a counterweight against China’s growing military power. But security commitments have never been the greatest shortcoming of U.S. policy in Southeast Asia. Indeed, the long-standing complaint is that this is the only thing the U.S. does consistently in the region. This has especially been the case since President Donald Trump’s first electoral victory in 2016, which marked a decisive turn toward economic protectionism and saw the U.S. withdraw from the Trans Pacific Partnership trade pact.

This and the increasingly acrimonious strategic competition with China detracted from the fundamental goals of most governments in the region: trade and economic growth. Despite some stillborn efforts by the Biden administration, such as the Indo-Pacific Economic Framework for Prosperity, these goals have been undermined by much of the agenda of Trump 2.0, in particular the tariffing of close regional partners and allies and the war in Iran, which has led to the blockage of the Strait of Hormuz, through which the region gets a significant proportion of its crude oil.

While the U.S. can help maintain a stable balance of power in Asia, it remains – at least for now – an economically disruptive force on the global stage, to the detriment of its long-term standing in Southeast Asia.
tag: Elbridge Colby; John Noh; U.S.-Philippines relations; U.S.-Southeast Asia relations

title: US Pacific Command Considers Moving Billions in Planned Infrastructure Out of Micronesia
description: The U.S. is threatening to pull a $2 billion infrastructure project in Yap. It's second time recently there have been major problems in U.S. defense negotiations with a COFA partner.
text:
Negotiation failures are leading U.S. Pacific Command (PACOM) to look for alternative locations for the $2 billion Department of Defense investment in infrastructure in Yap, Federated States of Micronesia (FSM).

On June 29, 2026, Admiral Samuel Paparo, the PACOM commander, wrote to President Wesley Simina of FSM that the country’s demand for a “$1.3 billion compensation package is unreasonable, unanchored to demonstrable costs, and divergent from the spirit of our partnership under the Compact of Free Association.” As a result, “U.S. PACOM intends to move forward by assessing alternative locations across the region to meet the needs of Pacific defense.”

Yap state, made up over a hundred islands, is a core part of the Second Island Chain. The main island in Yap state, also called Yap, is just over 500 miles southwest of Guam. The strategic importance of the Yap group of islands was proven toward the end of World War II. After the United States took the region from Japan, one of Yap’s atolls, Ulithi, became the largest and busiest American naval base in the world.

Map by Cleo Paskal and Pavak Patel.

FSM’s Compact of Free Association With the U.S.

In the decades after the war, Yap joined with neighboring island groups to form the independent country of Federated States of Micronesia. FSM then signed a Compact of Free Association (COFA) with the United States that ties the two countries together in profound ways, including the citizens of FSM being allowed to live and work freely in the U.S.

Additionally, according to COFA, the “Government of the United States has full authority and responsibility for security and defense matters in or relating to the Federated States of Micronesia.” This goes far beyond usual U.S. defense agreements as it stipulates that this responsibility includes “the obligation to defend the Federated States of Micronesia and its people from attack or threats thereof as the United States and its citizens are defended.”

However, as seen by the latest negotiations, new U.S. defense site access is not guaranteed and requires agreement on terms. The word “free” in Compact of Free Association has real meaning.

As Howard Hills, former lead counsel and advisor for COFA negotiations under Presidents Ronald Reagan, Joseph Biden, and Donald Trump, explained: “Under COFA the U.S. power to deny military forces of third nations access to the FSM, Palau and Republic of Marshall Islands is absolute and permanent. But to the extent U.S. authority and responsibility for mutual security and defense requires military use and operating rights, that is subject to mutual agreement by the governments concerned, in this case FSM.”

This is at least the second time recently there have been major problems in U.S. defense negotiations with a COFA country. One reason that Washington pursued Yap airport improvements in the first place was that Department of Defense negotiations for increased access in Angaur, in the neighboring Second Island Chain country of Palau, fell apart.

There are at least three interconnected reasons this will keep happening unless efforts are made to course correct.

The Lure of Money

In part because locals see for themselves the comparatively lavish lifestyle of visiting U.S. government officials – often staying the best hotels in town, and eating out every meal – and the relatively astronomical rates given to U.S. consultants and contractors, there is often the perception in FSM that the U.S. government is a bottomless piggy bank. This combines with reporting about the importance of Second Island Chain defenses to give some the feeling they have the U.S. over a barrel.

There is a pool of lawyers, negotiators, environmental experts, and others keen to fan this perception (and, incidentally, few of them seem to be around when Chinese projects are involved). Given human nature, some local leaders and land owners are drawn to hiring these representatives. In this case, Yap’s negotiators and leaders clearly overreached.

The $1.3 billion demand comes out to over $185,000 for each of the 7,000 or so resident of the island of Yap. And that amount, combined with the around $1.4 billion appropriated in the NDAA for the Yap airport makes investments in, for example, the airport on the main island of Palau, cost effective.

The China Factor

Also, at least in the case of FSM, the United States is not necessarily negotiating bilaterally. As made clear in a series of letters written in 2022 and 2023 by then FSM President David Panuelo, the national government of FSM is heavily infiltrated by Chinese political warfare operations – meaning there are some leaders at the national level (at least) with an interest in seeing the negotiations fail.

As Paparo himself said before the Senate in April 2026, in the Pacific “information, influence, cognitive, and cyber operations achieve increasing strategic effects by shaping perceptions and disrupting decision-making.” This dynamic, combined with corruption, is known to be playing out in FSM.

Panuelo’s March 9, 2023 letter stated: “One of the reasons that China’s Political Warfare is successful in so many arenas is that we are bribed to be complicit, and bribed to be silent. That’s a heavy word, but it is an accurate description regardless.… What else do you call it when an elected official receives a check for a public project that our National Treasury has no record of and no means of accounting for?”

This means when the United States is negotiating at the national level in FSM, it is likely China has friends in the room. However, there has been no recent public effort by the United States to help the people of FSM liberate themselves from this elite capture, even though it is also affecting U.S. interests. It is possible to do so.

As a small example, in February, the U.S. Department of State designated some key people in the other two COFA countries, Palau and Marshall Islands. The president of the Senate of Palau, for instance, was called out for “involvement in significant corruption on behalf of China-based actors.”

It’s a good start, with more needed. But not even that much has happened in FSM in spite of a former sitting president of the country calling out his own government for corruption.

As Hills said, “Between scheming PRC agents in the FSM and those who may advise that gouging the U.S. is clever negotiating, let’s hope cooler heads prevail in the national interest of both allies.”

Failure to Understand the Operating Environment

The failure to counter fantasist negotiators with facts or address pervasive Chinese influence is a subset of the more fundamental problem – a U.S. failure to understand local dynamics in FSM.

Yap’s demand for $1.3 billion is unreasonable. However, the fact some on the Yap/FSM side thought they could get away with it – combined with the failure of the Angaur project and myriad other issues – indicates PACOM has a serious problem with understanding the dynamics on the ground in crucial components of the Second Island Chain. These are places where thousands of Americans died in WWII, including on Angaur and the neighboring Palauan island of Peleliu.

The population of Yap island is around 7,000. Angaur’s is under 150. Yet PACOM’s “Micronesia whisperers” (including in Guam) seem to be missing out on developing relationships with, and listening to, locals who truly understand how things work.

It doesn’t help that there are no permanent U.S. government officials in Yap – meaning no one locals can get to know, and talk with on a day-to-day basis. Meanwhile, a Chinese state-owned company has set up shop, seemingly permanently.

Building trust and understanding can’t be done by flying in for a few days, staying in the best available hotels, doing meetings in offices, and relying on AI as well as hamfisted attempts to gain “intel.” On the ground in Yap now, most of the here-today-gone-tomorrow U.S. government officials are thought to be “spies” – a gift to Chinese cognitive warfare operators.

It is possible Paparo’s letter is a negotiating tactic designed to get things back on track. An August 3 letter from President Simina to Yap Governor Francis Itimai acknowledged the “possible setback” and leaves the door open to finding a way forward.

As Hills put it: “I read the FSM president’s letter to be an opening offer, not a final demand at all, importantly based on apparent initial agreement that the proposed military use and operating rights proposal will strengthen the mutual security and defense alliance.”

Regardless, the United States – and the people of Yap – shouldn’t be in this position. The inherent problems with the negotiations were publicly reported on over a year ago, and have not been corrected.

PACOM’s failure to move forward on a project for which NDAA appropriated $1.49 billion – work publicly announced by Hegseth – is possibly the result of not spending a tiny portion of that budget on getting to understand the information, influence, and cognitive environment in one of the United States’ closest allies. The same is true for the failed Angaur plan.

Thinking a change of location without a change of approach will solve things could cost the U.S. – and a free and open Indo-Pacific – years it doesn’t have to waste.
tag: Federated States of Micronesia; PACOM; U.S. military base in Yap; U.S. military bases in the Pacific; U.S.-Micronesia relations; Yap Island

title: Vietnam’s Top Leader Concludes Australia Visit With Trade, Defense in Focus
description: In their updated Joint Vision Statement, Canberra and Hanoi identify a more challenging regional security environment.
text:
Vietnamese President To Lam’s visit to Australia this week highlighted the burgeoning relationship between the two countries. Given that much of Australia’s large Vietnamese diaspora remains suspicious of the Communist Party of Vietnam – and South Vietnam flags are often seen flying in suburbs with a concentration of Vietnamese Australians – there is a domestic balancing act that the Australian government needs to perform. However, the convergence of interests between the two countries is now proving the stronger pull.

The focus of Lam’s visit was on new economic and security agreements. The now dominant lens of Australia’s foreign policy perceives economic security as a central pillar of national security.

The economic angle is where the most movement is already happening. Since 2020, two-way trade has doubled, with Vietnam now approaching Australia’s list of top ten trading partners. The specific measures announced this week were mostly incremental: greater agricultural access (including kangaroo meat), and creating smoother services within e-commerce and banking sectors. The low-cost airline Vietjet confirmed it will fly into the new Western Sydney Airport, due to be opened later this year. These are not transformative arrangements, but things that push the relationship forward in important ways.

The major development was Vietnam approving a license for the Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology (RMIT) to open a campus in Hanoi. The university had already established a campus in Ho Chi Minh City in 2000, and has been keen to establish itself as a major driver of the bilateral relationship, including through the creation of the Australia Vietnam Policy Institute to facilitate building the relationship between the two countries. This is part of a broader push by the Australian university sector to embed itself in Southeast Asia, with four other universities operating in Malaysia and Indonesia.

Although starting from a low base, the two countries’ security relationship has begun to deepen. This is being driven primarily by shared concerns about China’s activity in the South China Sea. Within their updated Joint Vision Statement, Canberra and Hanoi identify a more challenging regional security environment, marked by strategic competition and military build-up in the Indo-Pacific, and express a shared commitment to a rules-based regional order. Although not mentioning China directly, the statement emphasizes a respect for sovereignty and international law, and the importance of peace and stability in the South China Sea, including freedom of navigation and overflight and adherence to UNCLOS.

To facilitate this vision, the countries have been institutionalizing dialogues through regular meetings between defense and foreign ministers. Yet there is now an attempt to create more practical and substantive cooperation through maritime security, defense intelligence and information sharing, cybersecurity, humanitarian assistance and disaster relief, counterterrorism, military medicine, and the defense industry. The two countries also intend to increase bilateral military education and training as well as multilateral exercises, and seek out paths to greater interoperability.

A key element to this is filtering cooperation through regional cooperation. The phrase “ASEAN centrality” has become something of a shibboleth repeated by the Australian government when seeking to enhance relations with Southeast Asian countries. It may have less than solid practical implications, but it is how the region wants to frames its diplomacy and engagement, and so it is necessary for Canberra to respect that.

Due to this, the Joint Vision Statement declared that Australia and Vietnam will work more closely through ASEAN-led mechanisms, particularly the ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting-Plus – the annual platform established in 2010 that enables the 11 ASEAN member states to engage with external dialogue partners for regional defense cooperation. Such dialogues are important confidence building mechanisms for Australia and Southeast Asia.

Australia’s approach to Southeast Asia is based on the idea that no single tool is enough to protect and advance its interests. This means that greater agricultural access, digital economy agreements, and a new university campus in Vietnam are all complementary to securing greater defense cooperation. Each creates a web of intersecting ties that can prove resistant to any potential shocks or attempts at coercion.

In Vietnam, Australia has a receptive partner as its own diplomatic approach has a similar logic – diversify economic and security ties across as many partners as possible so that no single relationship, and no single power, gains leverage over Vietnamese decision-making. While some in the Vietnamese diaspora may be displeased with the To Lam’s visit, the foreign policy objectives of Australia will overwhelm their protests.
tag: Australia; Australia foreign policy; Australia in Southeast Asia; Australia-ASEAN relations; Australia-Vietnam defense cooperation; Australia-Vietnam relations; southeast asia

title: What Does Japan Think of the Sudden Cut to South Korea-US Joint Drills?
description: Although Japanese leaders have been publicly quiet, this incident highlights several points of concern that have existed since the second Trump administration.
text:
On August 16, U.S. President Donald Trump scaled back military drills with South Korea. In a social media post, he cited three different explanations for the move: the cost of the exercises to the United States, his supposedly friendly relations with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, and his displeasure over perceived lack of South Korean support for the U.S. war effort against Iran.

After Trump’s intervention, the annual Ulchi Freedom Shield exercise, which started on August 17, only ran through August 21 instead of the originally scheduled August 27. In practice, the first phase of the exercise – focused on defense – was preserved while the second phase – focused on counterattack – was canceled. In addition, live-training exercises were replaced with simulations.

According to the South Korean new agency Yonhap, South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun told the legislature that “Neither our government nor U.S. officials knew what President Trump wrote on his Truth Social account.” In a meeting with the National Assembly Committee on Foreign Affairs and Unification, Cho said, “We were not notified in advance.”

On August 24, the United States canceled the biennial Ssangyong drills, a large joint amphibious landing exercise, scheduled for September. This time, the justification was constraints on force availability caused by the Iran war. This announcement was not as abrupt, as the U.S. Marine Corps had officially notified Seoul back in June that its force availability would likely be constrained.

On August 28, the United States, South Korea, and Japan announced that they will conduct the annual Freedom Edge drills, joint military drills to test readiness against North Korea’s missiles and nuclear weapons threat, from September 9 to 11.

What is Japan’s perspective on the latest developments in the South Korea-U.S. alliance?

Japan’s initial reaction has been muted. Japanese Defense Minister Koizumi Shinjiro responded to the announcement by saying: “As Japan faces the most severe and complicated security environment in the post-war era, the cooperation among Japan, the United States, and South Korea is critical to the peace and stability of the region.” The statement, however, did not actually criticize the U.S. decision to scale back joint exercises.

Although Japanese leaders have been publicly quiet, this incident highlights several points of concern that have existed since the second Trump administration.

First, it could indicate a more aggressive move by Washington to resume talks with North Korea. Japan would always have been wary of a North Korea-U.S. deal that advanced U.S. security while sidelining Japanese concerns. For example, a hypothetical deal could cut back on Pyongyang’s long-range missiles, which can reach the United States, but do nothing to reduce its stockpile of short-range missiles, which can reach Japan. The threat to Japan remains persistent, as North Korea fired 10 short-range ballistic missiles on August 20; this was the third ballistic missile test in August.

There is also a question of whether the United States will maintain denuclearization as a policy objective, and what Japan will do vis-à-vis North Korea if the United States abandons it. Conservative Japanese leaders also have a vested political interest in the return of abductees, an issue that might get ignored in a North Korea-U.S. deal.

Japanese analysts worry about a more emboldened North Korea, though at the same time they doubt the likelihood of a U.S. overture to Pyongyang succeeding. But experts have failed to predict many aspects of this administration’s foreign policy.

U.S. overtures to North Korea, reciprocated or not, will likely be reflected in the three strategy documents currently being revised in Tokyo: the National Security Strategy, the National Defense Strategy, and the Defense Buildup Program. Japan intends to finish updating these documents by the end of the year. Tokyo could also, much more quietly, consider nuclear weapons for itself if questions about the credibility of the U.S. nuclear deterrent being to mount.

Another worrying aspect of Trump’s social media post is the signal that the United States is prepared to more explicitly make assistance in the Iran War a condition of continued support. Certainly, there are different dynamics between the South Korea-U.S. alliance and that between Japan and the United States. For one, Japan has long relied on its constitutional and legal framework to avoid entanglement in U.S. wars. However, the Trump administration may be less sympathetic to such justifications. If they cannot force Japan to support U.S. military operations in the Strait of Hormuz due to Japan’s constraints, Washington may demand concessions from Japan in other areas, such as reduced joint exercises or increased host nation support.

This administration has shown a tendency to link security and economic issues in a way that previous administrations usually did not (i.e., reducing the benefit of the training exercise to its financial costs). The timing is particularly worrying for Japan as Tokyo begins negotiations with Washington over host nation support. A sudden demand for a large increase is certainly possible.

Trump’s decision – announced on the same day Ulchi Freedom Shield began – makes it clear that U.S. military exercises can be scaled down on a moment’s notice. Japan has its own exercises with the United States, Keen Sword, in October. Though it is expected to be smaller than the 2024 iteration due to U.S. deployments in the Iran war, it could be scaled back even farther. Trump could use the same three-fold justification he used against South Korea to cancel or scale down these exercises.

In a related concern, Trump’s rationale for the decision showed his susceptibility to accepting autocrats’ talking points. Trump appears to have bought Kim’s argument that the training exercises are aggressive, while the U.S. and South Korean governments have long maintained that these exercises are defensive. It’s odd, to say the least, to see a U.S. president describing actions by the South Korea-U.S. alliance as “totally inappropriate and hostile” and North Korea as “unthreatening and respectful.”

Finally, there is real concern about what it would mean for U.S military readiness on the Korean Peninsula and in the Indo-Pacific more broadly if training exercises become scaled back or more erratic.

Alliance readiness is a key concern. While North Korean soldiers are returning to the peninsula after having real world battle experience in the Russia-Ukraine war, the best that the U.S. and South Korean soldiers can do to prepare is live trainings. Yet these live trainings are being replaced by simulations at the same time the enemy is “training” by engaging in real combat.

A U.S. Department of Defense official said in a statement that “These adjustments preserve essential readiness and training objectives,” and “There will be no degradation to U.S. training objectives.” But saying the sky is pink does not make it so.
tag: ROK-US joint military exercises; Trump alliances; U.S.-Japan Alliance; U.S.-South Korea alliance; Ulchi Freedom Shield

title: What Is Life Really Like Under the Taliban? We Asked Afghan Women.
description: Online influencers are framing Afghanistan as a a beautiful, welcoming “hidden gem.” That may be true for tourists – but what about the women who live there?
text:
“Don’t believe what the media tells you about Afghanistan.”

That’s the line turning up on TikTok and Instagram five years after U.S. and NATO forces withdrew and the Afghan Republic collapsed. Travel influencers – even women – are touring bustling Kabul markets and showcasing pristine mountain valleys, telling their audiences that the world has gotten Afghanistan all wrong.

To the Taliban authorities, these foreign tourists are a PR goldmine – a chance to show the world that Afghanistan is safe, stable, and open for business.

What the media reports about Afghanistan is, indeed, bleak. Since September 2021 Afghan girls have not been allowed to attend school beyond the 6th grade. Women have been pushed out of most professional jobs, including in government offices and non-governmental organizations. In December 2022, mere months after thousands of women sat for university entrance exams, the Taliban issued an indefinite ban on women studying at all public and private universities.

And then in August 2024, the Taliban formally enacted a sweeping 114-page “Propagation of Virtue and Prevention of Vice” law. The law introduced strict rules requiring women to completely cover their faces in public and forbidding their voices from being heard singing, reciting, or reading aloud outside the home.

Meanwhile, the U.N. reports that three out of four Afghans — roughly 28 million people — cannot even meet their basic daily needs. Over 64 percent of the population lives in what’s called multidimensional poverty. It’s a fancy term for a dismal reality: it means people are systematically deprived of clean water, adequate food, basic medicine, and housing.

How can the exact same physical space be a beautiful, welcoming “hidden gem” for a travel influencer, and an open-air prison for the women who actually live there?

We wanted to get the answer directly from the people of Afghanistan – not foreigners who parachute in for a vacation. Today, we bring you the voices of Afghanistan’s women, with the invaluable help of Rukhshana Media and other friends in Afghanistan.

These women will be speaking to you directly, though most have asked to hide their faces and alter their names out of fear of retaliation. They see what the world sees of Afghanistan; and they see their own erasure from the Afghan story.

Rukhshana Media is currently fundraising to continue paying their team of 10 brave reporters who work secretly inside Afghanistan. Please support them so they can keep telling the outside world the truth about Taliban rule.
tag: Life in Afghanistan; Taliban restrictions on women; Taliban rule; women in Afghanistan; Women under Taliban rule

title: Where Is Myanmar’s Aung San Suu Kyi?
description: Sean Turnell, an economist and former advisor to the ousted leader, returns to Beyond The Mekong to discuss recent events in Myanmar.
text:
The military-backed government in Myanmar this week released four photos of the country’s jailed former leader Aung San Suu Kyi, who met with Arnaud de Baecque, the resident representative for the International Committee of the Red Cross in Myanmar, on August 3.

“This may be a first step, but it must not be the last,” her son, Kim Aris, said in a statement.

Sean Turnell, an Australian economist who worked with Suu Kyi and then shared a prison with her after the military coup in 2021, agrees, adding that “proof of life” is also required for some 20,000 people who are believed to be held as political prisoners inside Myanmar’s jails.

Turnell returned to Beyond the Mekong and spoke with The Diplomat’s Luke Hunt about the first confirmation of Suu Kyi’s existence in many years and the issues facing the opposition National Unity Government (NUG) and the various armed groups battling the military.

The NUG, its People’s Defense Force (PDF), and the country’s numerous ethnic armed organizations (EAOs) have faced a resurgent military this year and a counter-offensive aimed at retaking territory won by the rebels during 2023 and 2024.

Min Aung Hlaing, the coup leader and now military-backed civilian leader, has also gone on a diplomatic offensive in search of international legitimacy for his administration within ASEAN, which wants the junta to return to its Five-Point Consensus as a roadmap for peace.

Turnell, who spent 650 days behind bars prior to his release in November 2022, says the civil war, which has claimed some 100,000 lives, cannot be won by the military, as the NUG and EAOs continue to formulate a federal framework for a country mired by ethnic differences. But eventually, he says, peace will prevail.
tag: Aung San Suu Kyi; Kim Aris; Myanmar conflict; Myanmar politics; Sean Turnell

title: Why the Pacific Islands Forum Should Watch Taiwan’s East Coast
description: The waters east of Taiwan sit within a strategically integrated maritime space stretching from Northeast Asia, through Micronesia and Melanesia, to Polynesia.
text:
Ahead of the 55th Pacific Islands Forum (PIF), scheduled to take place August 30 to September 4 in Palau, Pacific Island leaders failed to reach consensus on a joint statement criticizing China’s submarine-based ballistic missile testing in the Pacific. The split reflects intensifying great-power competition and divergent threat perceptions between external powers and Pacific governments. Yet China’s growing military activities have clearly heightened concerns among forum members.

Besides missile testing, another less visible source of pressure lies in the growing normalization of Chinese naval and coast guard activity in the waters east of Taiwan, a development the PIF has yet to fully connect to its own maritime interests. This maritime gateway east of Taiwan leads directly into the exclusive economic zones that the forum seeks to protect and deserves greater attention from Pacific Island states.

Rather than a distant flashpoint, the waters east of Taiwan form the northern hinge of the same maritime arc that runs through Micronesia and Melanesia, linked by overlapping sea lines of communication and interconnected ocean current systems. This deep-water gateway to the Blue Pacific is increasingly being trespassed and pressured by Chinese government vessels.

Beijing appears to be using unresolved maritime boundary negotiations involving Japan and the Philippines as justification for expanding coast guard patrols and deploying more research and survey vessels east of Taiwan. Many of these platforms are converted former naval vessels, underscoring the increasingly blurred line between maritime law enforcement and strategic power projection. By increasing the frequency and persistence of deployments along Taiwan’s Pacific coast, Beijing appears to be seeking to normalize a sustained Chinese maritime security presence in the Blue Pacific waters.

This expansion is unfolding alongside a broader rise in Chinese naval activity in the Western Pacific. Since 2025, the Liaoning and Shandong carrier strike groups have conducted operations and flight exercises beyond the first island chain. With China’s third aircraft carrier, the Fujian, reaching full operational capability, Beijing is moving closer to sustaining a regular carrier presence in the Western Pacific.

The growing presence of coast guard, research, survey, and naval vessels east of Taiwan suggests that China is gradually extending its maritime operating space from the Taiwan Strait into Taiwan’s Pacific approaches.

For Pacific Island countries, this expanding presence should not be viewed simply as an extension of cross-strait tensions. It could increase uncertainty along commercial shipping routes, raise maritime insurance premiums, lengthen transit times, and complicate the movement of energy, food, and other essential imports through the corridor linking Northeast Asia with Palau, the Federated States of Micronesia, Papua New Guinea, Solomon Islands, and the wider Pacific.

Even without an armed conflict, heightened tensions or more frequent military exercises could generate delays, rerouting, and higher transportation costs for states that are highly dependent on this maritime corridor. China’s expanding naval reach east of Taiwan therefore has implications well beyond Taiwan, intersecting directly with the maritime trade routes and supply chains on which Pacific Island countries depend.

The PIF’s diplomatic motto of being “friends to all and enemies to none” should not be mistaken for strategic insulation, particularly as the maritime status quo east of Taiwan is being reshaped by China’s growing presence and expanding military activity. In a worst-case Taiwan contingency, Beijing could seek to push through the Taiwan–Philippines–Melanesia corridor and constrain U.S. and allied access to the Western Pacific, regardless of whether any PIF member is involved in the conflict.

For Pacific Island states, preserving free, open, and non-militarized sea lines of communication across the Western Pacific is therefore a vital interest and it should be articulated clearly before shifts in the regional balance of power become more difficult to reverse. The PIF’s “Ocean of Peace” framing should recognize the waters east of Taiwan as part of the same interconnected Pacific maritime space, rather than a separate area.

The Blue Pacific is a Pacific-led regional identity, not a corridor encompassing Taiwan’s east coast, and the argument here is not to redefine that identity. Rather, it is to recognize that the waters east of Taiwan sit within a strategically integrated maritime space stretching from Northeast Asia, through Micronesia and Melanesia, to Polynesia, where developments at one end can directly affect access, connectivity, and security at the other. Recognizing this interdependence is a matter of practical maritime awareness, not a request that Pacific states reframe their own identity or take sides in cross-strait politics.

What is at stake is neither alignment with one great power against another nor a choice between alignment and non-alignment. The more fundamental interest is preserving a maritime space in which all actors can navigate freely and maintain economic and commercial access without coercion, intimidation, or militarization.

Even if PIF members cannot agree on specific issues, such as China’s ballistic missile testing, they should still be able to forge a broader agreement on preserving a free, open, peaceful, and resilient Blue Pacific maritime corridor. That means the Ocean of Peace framework should be able to cover the waters east of Taiwan as a critical component of the broader Blue Pacific maritime domain. The forum could extend information sharing on vessel movements and coast guard activity to this corridor, providing Pacific Island states earlier warning of disruptions to the shipping lanes their economies depend on.

Such an arrangement could provide a common foundation for the PIF to work with willing Pacific partners on maritime domain awareness, infrastructure resilience, and the security of regional sea lines of communication. Rather than requiring consensus on the behavior of any particular major power, this approach would anchor cooperation in a shared interest in an integrated Pacific maritime space that remains open, accessible, and resilient to coercion and disruption.
tag: Blue Pacific; Pacific Island Forum; Pacific island states; PIF; Taiwan and Pacific Island States

title: Ziya Us Salam on the Controversy Over the Taj Mahal
description: The claims of Hindu groups that the Taj Mahal was originally a Hindu temple are “high on prejudice and assumptions, low on evidence.”
text:
The Taj Mahal is caught in a controversy. Some Hindu groups are claiming that the 17th-century white marble mausoleum that Mughal Emperor Shah Jahan built in memory of his favorite wife was originally “Tejo Mahalaya,” a Hindu temple dedicated to the deity Shiva. Both the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) and the courts have dismissed the claims of Hindu groups so far. However, recent developments provide cause for concern. The Allahabad High Court issued directives to the central government and the ASI, asking them to respond to a petition, which, while seeking permission for Hindus to offer prayers in the Taj, sought a survey of the monument. Will the Allahabad court’s directives prove to be the thin end of the wedge, opening the floodgates to political meddling and court rulings to strengthen Hindu claims over the Taj?

In an interview with The Diplomat’s South Asia editor Sudha Ramachandran, journalist and scholar Ziya Us Salam pointed out that in 2017, the ASI was unambiguous in declaring the Taj as a 17th-century tomb. “One expects that the body will maintain its stand and not succumb to political pressure from right-wing bodies.” As for the central government, it is unlikely to go against the ASI report, as “the Taj earns the highest revenue for the exchequer. Any unseemly controversy could keep the tourists away.” Besides, unlike the Babri masjid, the Taj is famous globally. “The stakes are too high to ignore the facts of history in Agra,” Salam said.

What is the dispute over the Taj Mahal?

Mughal Emperor Shah Jahan’s monument of love, the Taj Mahal, has been mired in a controversy for many years. It all started more than 60 years ago when P.N. Oak, a teacher-turned-journalist-turned-lawyer, but never a historian, alleged that the Taj was originally a Rajput palace built more than 1,500 years ago. That allegation was made in 1965. In 1989, under immense scrutiny from historians, Oak revised his claim and this time alleged that the Taj was actually Tejo Mahlaya, a temple dedicated to the Hindu deity Shiva, built in the 11th century.

The Supreme Court has repeatedly dismissed all such contentions, coming down hard on Oak’s claim particularly in 2000.

Last month, though, it all changed when the Allahabad High Court issued notices to the central government and the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI), asking for their response to a plea challenging an Agra trial court order that refused a survey of the Taj Mahal. A Bench of Justice Rohit Ranjan Agarwal passed the order on a petition filed by advocate Harishankar Jain contending that the Taj, a UNESCO World Heritage monument, is actually “Tejo Mahalaya.”

The petitioner had sought permission for Hindus to offer prayers there, and also sought the appointment of an Advocate Commissioner to inspect the monument.

Incidentally, soon after the Allahabad High Court notice, a Hindu body tried to offer Ganga jal (water) at the Taj on the Kanwariya route. Also, there have been periodic attempts by right-wing Hindu bodies to undermine the authenticity of the Taj, with a Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) leader Sangeet Som leading the way in 2019 with fresh allegations of the Taj being a Shiva temple. Interestingly, he got his history lesson mixed up, alleging that the Taj was built by a man who had imprisoned his father!

Is there evidence to prove the claims of either side?

There is no debate in the circle of historians and scholars that the Taj Mahal was built by Mughal Emperor Shah Jahan in memory of his favorite wife Arjumand Bano, popularly known as Mumtaz Mahal. Built over 22 years, its chief architect was Ustad Ahmed Lahori. The land for building it was procured from Mirza Raja Jai Singh of Amber, who had inherited it from Raja Man Singh, a celebrated general of Emperor Akbar, who also happened to be Shah Jahan’s grandfather. Shah Jahan compensated Jai Singh with four havelis from the royal property for the massive haveli. His firman to Jai Singh, the latter’s agreement and the Mughal emperor’s subsequent letter granting him four havelis in lieu of one, are all part of history.

Yet there have been periodic attempts to question the monument’s origin. The first time the Taj Mahal faced a controversy was when many in the West claimed that the architect of the Taj was Geronimo Veroneo, a Venetian jeweler by profession. That was in the 17th century. Then came the claim by Mughal Beg in Tarikh-e-Taj Mahal that the Taj was designed by Muhammad Effendi, an architect supposedly sent by the Sultan of Turkey. Effendi, however, was only as much an architect as Oak was a historian.

Then in the mid-19th century, it was claimed that the monument was the result of the genius of Frenchman Austin de Bordeaux. However, Austin died in 1632, the year the work on the Taj began. With his death, all claims of Austin being the Taj’s architect were buried. And facts began to be raised.

The chief mason of the Taj was Mohammed Hanif from Baghdad, who earned 1,000 rupees a month for his efforts. The pinnacle was built by Qayam Khan of Lahore and its Quranic inscriptions were done by Amanat Khan Shirazi. The mosaic work was done by local Hindu workers. Above all, some 20,000 workmen toiled for 22 years to build the monument to love. Its white marble came from Jaipur, lapis lazuli from Sri Lanka, crystal from China and coral from Arabia. The monument uses the double dome technique, previously seen only in Humayun’s tomb in Delhi, and never seen in the country before the arrival of the Turks.

The Taj Mahal is both Islamic and Indian (two overlapping categories). Quranic verses on the façade visibly mark the monument as Muslim, and the structure incorporates minarets and a mosque. However, like at Fatehpur Sikri, the workers and artisans were largely Hindu. We know this because some workers left mason marks and names on the backs of bricks and stones. Among other things, one takeaway is that the Mughal Empire was built, quite literally, by Hindus and Muslims working together.

What roles have the courts and the Archaeological Survey of India played in the issue?

Beginning in 2000, various courts have dismissed all attempts to question the Mughal origin of the Taj. The Allahabad High Court notice, however, tends to ignore such verdicts in the past, including that of the Supreme Court. In 2000, the Supreme Court rejected Oak’s claims, calling them “a bee in his bonnet.” Half a decade later, another attempt to appropriate the Taj, this time as allegedly built by a Chandela ruler, was dismissed by the Allahabad High Court. The petition was moved on behalf of Amarnath Mishra, now a member of Ayodhya Sadbhavna Samiti. It claimed that the Taj was a temple built by the Chandela rulers in 1189.

There was, however, no let-up in petitions questioning the veracity of the Taj. In 2015, a civil suit filed at the Agra trial court sought to declare the Taj Mahal a Hindu temple. The court, however, didn’t agree with this claim either. After it refused to order a survey of the Taj premises, like the one ordered in Gyanvapi and Bhojshala places of worship, the petitioners went to the Allahabad High Court. The court then sought a response from the central government and the ASI.

Incidentally, back in 2017, the ASI had stated that the Taj was a 17th-century tomb. It stated that the technology used in its construction and design, including pietra dura, did not exist in pre-medieval days. It should have ended any vestiges of controversy. However, a public interest litigation was filed in the Supreme Court by a Bharatiya Janata Party leader in 2022.

What are the implications of the Allahabad High Court’s recent notices to the central government and the ASI?

The Allahabad High Court has sought responses from the ASI as well as the central government. The ASI has already made its point clear in 2017. One expects that the body will maintain its stand and not succumb to political pressure from right-wing bodies. As for the central government, I do not foresee it going against the ASI report. Of all the protected monuments in India, the Taj earns the highest revenue for the exchequer. Any unseemly controversy could keep the tourists away. It is something the government would not like to lose.

Hindu groups have laid claim to other Muslim places of worship or tombs, such as the Babri masjid, the Gyanvapi mosque in Varanasi and the Shahi Eidgah mosque in Mathura. Are there similarities in the Hindu claims and disputes?

There are plenty of similarities, but also crucial differences. While the demand to open the tahkhana (basement) at the Taj is similar to the contention at Varanasi and Dhar (Bhojshala), as indeed the petition to order a survey of its premises, there are stark differences. Unlike Varanasi, Ayodhya and Mathura, the Taj is not a dispute between the places of worship of two religions. It is a case of a monument of love, widely regarded among the Top Ten monuments in the world versus dubious claims based on a book by a person who was not a historian, nor did he provide any evidence to substantiate his claims. Much the same has been the case with subsequent petitions. They seem to be high on prejudice and assumptions, low on evidence.

Hindus have called for Muslims to be forbidden from praying at the Taj Mahal. Do you foresee the Taj suffering the fate of the Babri Masjid in the future?

I am hopeful of history not being repeated. The hope stems from the judiciary foiling repeated attempts by Hindu groups to conduct pooja [Hindu worship rituals] at the Taj. Having said that, the history of Ayodhya, where Hindutva groups destroyed a 16th-century mosque in 1993 and built a Ram temple at that site in 2024, fills one with fear and trepidation. The specter of a Ram idol being smuggled into the Babri masjid at night in connivance with the local administration in 1949 has not been erased from our collective memory. Also not forgotten are the repeated court cases, and the final denouement when the apex court ultimately based its decision on faith rather than hard evidence. One hopes that a similar fate does not befall the Taj. The muted confidence comes from the monument’s international stature as opposed to an obscure mosque in a small town, Ayodhya, in Uttar Pradesh. The stakes are too high to ignore the facts of history in Agra.

title: 3 Ts Will Dominate the Trump-Xi Summit
description: Expect little movement on trade, less on Taiwan, and who knows on tech.
text:
When Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping last sat down in May 2026, talk was centered on three Ts: trade, technology and Taiwan. Their next summit, due to begin in the United States on September 24, looks set to focus on the same set of issues again. The main difference will be that the technology element has been given added urgency by the sudden and rapid shift in developments in artificial intelligence.

What’s less clear is whether the two sides will be able to come to any sort of transformative agreement on that, or any other issue.

The most urgent issue, but also the simplest to solve, will be on trade. Nearly a year ago at Busan in South Korea, Trump and Xi hammered out an agreement whereby the United States agreed to lift some export controls on high-end technology and to reduce the then three-figure tariffs on Chinese goods. For its part, China agreed not to restrict the flow of critical minerals and rare earths to U.S. users.

That pact – only good for one year – is now up for renewal. Both sides are likely to want a continuation of the current arrangement, and while there may be some tweaking on the side, the new deal will probably be similar to the old one.

Each side has proposed in previous meetings that there should be a new instrument, a Board of Trade, that will assess non-sensitive China-U.S. business interests. However, details about the institution remains vague. Some announcements are likely during the summit, but business leaders will want to know how comprehensive and lasting the arrangements for the board will be.

There is still less information on a proposed Board of Investment, which remains on the drawing board. The Chinese side has proposed bringing major Chinese CEOs to the summit to match the likes of Nvidia’s Jensen Huang and Tesla’s Elon Musk – both of whom accompanied Trump on the Beijing trip. But the choice of business leaders is likely to turn on which aspects of trade China thinks are likely to develop most effectively in the short term.

Taiwan is a much harder issue to solve, but it’s unlikely that much that is discussed on Xi’s visit will determine its outcome.

Trump has been less willing than his predecessor to commit the United States to defending the island should Beijing invade, instead reasserting Washington’s long-held position of strategic ambiguity.

And although the U.S. is currently distracted from East Asia by the Iran conflict, China still prefers to find methods short of war to bring the island under Beijing’s control.

The island’s January 2028 presidential election is likely to be a more crucial moment for Taiwan’s future, particularly if the opposition – and more China-friendly – Kuomintang (KMT) wins the presidency, or indeed if an isolationist candidate becomes U.S. president later that year. If the next U.S. president opted to change course by taking a less active involvement in overseas issues – as has been floated by early contenders on both the left and right – that would change things all the more.

For now, Beijing will continue to build the People’s Liberation Army’s naval capacity to have the option of military action against the island. But its preference will be to take advantage of changes within Taiwan’s internal politics while combining economic incentives and coercion, squeezing Taipei’s international footprint and hoping for a slackening of U.S. interest in the western Pacific.

Other international issues are likely to gain less attention. China is expected to make clear its unhappiness about the war on Iran, and the U.S. may remind China that it has passed new legislation allowing sanctions on countries that buy Russian oil – of which, China is the largest purchaser. However, neither issue is likely to lead to any major change in practice.

It’s really in the area of tech, and AI in particular, where both sides will be trying to make diplomacy catch up with reality. The May summit surprised many because the question of mutual agreement on regulation of AI came up in a way that had not been on the agenda for the first year of the Trump administration.

However, both sides agreed that talks in principle about regulation might be possible and even desirable because of the growth in the importance, but also unpredictability, of AI. And on September 20, the United States and China mooted the idea of a “hotline” to notify the other over AI national security risks.

Between the May and September summits, fears about AI in the U.S have created an increasingly unfriendly atmosphere toward unregulated AI.

In China, public sentiment about AI is less openly hostile and some of its major benefits in areas such as health care have softened people’s attitudes. Yet there are still plenty of concerns expressed in private about whether China’s troubled economy will definitively benefit from the AI boom. Although many argue it has created new opportunities for consumers, others point to the relatively few jobs that have been created for a workforce that finds itself buffeted by wide-scale job elimination.

Both the U.S. and China have reasons to talk about AI regulation. The alarming prospect of rogue AI companies causing intense social disruptions through their business choices is clearly one such reason, and in the U.S., voters’ more immediate concerns about data centers are another.

There are also China-specific reasons that Beijing may seek restraint. One of the most common concerns about AI is that it may well run out of control. And “out of control” is a kryptonite phrase for the leadership of the Chinese Communist Party. That’s particularly true of Xi who, as a youth, spent years in rural exile after his father fell to a purge just before the Cultural Revolution – an upheaval during which China’s politics turned to anarchy. It was a formative experience for Xi, which has no doubt influenced his tendencies as a leader toward exercising as much control as possible.

AI that undermines the unchallengeable leadership of the Communist Party would be an unwelcome guest in China’s cyberspace, and regulation that solves that problem would not be rejected out of hand.

However, this recognition of mutual concern about AI – albeit for very different reasons – is still not likely to see much progress in the short term. The competition between the U.S. and China on AI is real, and neither governments nor private sector actors in either country are willing to make concessions that could advantage the other side.

Levels of trust between Washington and Beijing remain very low on the issue. Talks about talks seem the most likely public outcome, though what happens behind the scenes may be pursued more discreetly.

The Trump-Xi summit is less important in terms of any major change in policy on either side, and more because it marks part of a commitment to maintain some form of dialogue between the leaders of the world’s two most powerful countries. The leaders may well meet twice more in the near future, at the APEC and G20 summits, to be hosted by China and the United States, respectively.

To meet four times in just over half a year is a good sign; refusal to meet would be much more worrying. But the underlying difficulties of the three Ts, where the leaders seem to have fundamentally incompatible agendas, remain the thread beneath the ostensibly polite and occasionally amiable conversations.

title: 4 Fault Lines that Could Shape the Trump-Xi Summit
description: The tangible outcomes will be modest, but the stakes are high.
text:
U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping are set to meet next week at the White House in Washington, D.C., provided that the “conditionalities” attached to the summit are met. This will be the second leaders’ summit between Trump and Xi this year, following the U.S. president’s visit to Beijing in May.

This will be Xi’s first visit to the U.S. capital in a decade, after he met then-U.S. President Barack Obama in 2016. Back then, the agenda centered on the much-touted issues of cyberespionage and commercial hacking. Today, there are new concerns.

Both domestically and internationally, this visit is taking place amid considerable friction. On the domestic front, the United States will be holding midterm elections roughly 40 days after the visit. This makes the timing an unusual choice, as noted by Pew Research: many Americans still view the Chinese leader unfavorably, despite a 6-percentage-point rise since last year. Presidents generally avoid such risks to optics as midterms near.

At the international level, the world is still living under the shadow of the Iran-U.S. war. Consequently, Brent crude is trading around $100 per barrel. At the same time, the China-Russia alignment has deepened; a few months ago – just after the last Trump-Xi summit, in fact – Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin reaffirmed their close partnership and signed a joint statement to deepen their strategic partnership. Beijing is underwriting Moscow’s war machine in Ukraine as Washington prepares to welcome Xi.

Meanwhile, Pew Research noted in another survey that Beijing is viewed favorably in more countries than Washington, adding another nuance to the global attention focused on the summit.

However, one must note that Beijing has yet to officially confirm the meeting, even though the United States has given the date of September 24. Some reports even suggested that the meeting will be canceled by Beijing if Washington gives approval for a $14 billion arms sale to Taiwan.

Therefore, the coming week will tell us much about the relationship between China and the United States.

Real Stakes Amid Low Expectations

Even assuming the meeting does go ahead as planned, there are low expectations for what will be achieved. The consensus holds that the tangible outcomes will be modest, possibly just an extension of what was achieved at the last summit held in China. There are four topics of particular interest at the Trump-Xi summit.

First is the tariff question. At the Trump-Xi meeting on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Busan, South Korea, on October 30, 2025, Washington and Beijing agreed to a one-year truce in their trade war. The United States reduced its fentanyl-related tariff on Chinese goods to 10 percent. The U.S. also suspended a 10 percent reciprocal tariff and secured a commitment from Beijing to buy 25 million tons of U.S. soybeans every year through 2028. China also deferred export controls on rare earths. But this truce will expire in November this year.

The upcoming Trump-Xi meeting will build on these arrangements rather than introduce something entirely novel. Already, the rare earth element in the deal is quite fragile. Some reports have suggested that exports of yttrium – a rare earth element used in the aerospace and defense industries – to the United States have declined sharply after April 2025, despite China’s commitment to waive export controls. Some U.S. officials and analysts have discussed imposing new tariffs and charges on certain Chinese goods. This could be used as leverage in negotiations before the meeting.

The second focal point is Iran. The ceasefire in the Middle East has collapsed multiple times, a recurring feature of Trump’s foreign policy. Just over a week ago, Iran retaliated against the U.S. strikes on the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and hit Jordan, Bahrain, Kuwait, and Iraq.

China is currently Iran’s largest trading partner and the top buyer of its oil, and Washington has declared economic war on Iran. In practice, as Iran is already heavily sanctioned, the new U.S. Treasury Department campaign – dubbed “Operation Economic Outcast” – involves pressuring those who “enabled” Iran’s actions.

Trump mentioned speaking directly to Xi over this and asking him not to get involved. In May, both China and the United States agreed that Iran should not have a nuclear weapon, but this small point of agreement is being overshadowed by the heightening tension over other issues.

Third is Taiwan. Taiwan has long remained a thorn in China-U.S. relations. After the summit held in May 2026, Trump called U.S. arms sales to Taiwan a “very good negotiating chip” that he kept in abeyance. This transactional framing alarmed many of the U.S. allies. Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te immediately pushed back against it by declaring that the sovereignty of the island will not be “sacrificed or traded away.”

More recently, reports emerged that China had threatened to cancel the summit if Trump approved the sale. Getting Washington to agree, even temporarily, to halt arms sales to Taiwan has been a major priority for Beijing since the 1980s. Now that Trump has signaled a willingness to view arms sales as a bargaining chip, rather than a routine aspect of the Taiwan-U.S. relationship, Xi will be looking to lock in that mindset.

Even if the sale eventually gets approved, the fact that it is seen as a point of leverage by Trump shows the limits of his interest in Taiwan for its own sake. This problem extends well beyond Taiwan itself. Manila’s ongoing standoff with Beijing over maritime features in the South China Sea, notably Scarborough Shoal, is seen by allies as a test of whether Washington will prioritize optics with Beijing over its interests. If Trump signals that he will, not only Taiwan but Tokyo, Manila, and others can interpret their security guarantees as “negotiable,” especially when they clash with China. This will test the whole alliance architecture in Asia.

The fourth area to watch is AI, which is at the heart of the U.S. strategy on China. Under the Biden administration, export controls effectively banned advanced AI chips from reaching China. Trump also tightened these restrictions in April 2025. However, he sharply reversed that policy between December 2025 and January 2026. The administration changed its approach to Nvidia’s H200 chips from a “presumption of denial” of exports to China to case-by-case approval. Chinese firms placed orders for millions of H200 chips. Trump touted it as a business deal, not as a national security issue. This caused some alarm and pushback within the United States.

On the other hand, even strict export control rules are easy to circumvent. Big Chinese firms like ByteDance, Alibaba, and Tencent have been using Nvidia chips sourced from third countries such as Japan, Thailand, and Malaysia rather than shipping them directly into China.

Amid all these controls, China is still progressing well in AI, though it remains behind the United States. However, their models now account for a much larger share of global AI usage than before, thanks to China’s open-weight strategies and more efficient models. Such contradictions in the U.S. policy will be very visible in the upcoming meetings.

Anyone hoping for a serious discussion on AI safety regulations, meanwhile, is likely to be disappointed. While there have been rumors of upcoming AI talks around the time of the Trump-Xi summit, both states see themselves locked in competition for dominance of AI, and are unlikely to pump the brakes.

Implications for India

India will be closely watching all developments in Washington next week. Last year, Trump left no stone unturned in pressuring India, adding a 50 percent tariff on Indian goods in response to New Delhi’s continued purchases of Russian oil. Trump himself, after seeing Xi, Putin, and India’s Narendra Modi together in a summit last year, posted that the U.S. had “lost India and Russia to deepest, darkest, China.” In February 2026, a framework India-U.S. deal eased the effective tariff rate from 50 percent to 18 percent, but the damage to the trust was already done.

Just days before the upcoming Trump-Xi meeting, Xi was in Delhi for the BRICS summit; both governments said they were committed to working toward the border dispute, resuming direct flights and relaxing investment restrictions. The New Delhi Declaration also voiced opposition to unilateral imposition of tariffs and trade restrictions and called for reform in the multipolar global order. However, genuine issues still prevail between New Delhi and Beijing.

Seen from New Delhi, therefore, the meeting next week will signal to India where it stands in Washington’s priorities and whether Trump’s transactional policy continues to impact India-U.S. ties. Many countries will be watching the summit for similar signs, meaning the ripples will spread far beyond bilateral China-U.S. relations.

title: 5 Years Later, Where Does AUKUS Stand?
description: Over the last five years, as AUKUS has taken shape, the dynamics behind regional security have continued to evolve.
text:
On September 15, 2021, Australia abandoned a $90-billion program to build French-designed conventional diesel-electric submarines. Instead, Australia would embark on a new trilateral security partnership with the U.S. and the U.K. to produce nuclear-powered, but conventionally armed, submarines.

What drove Australia to spurn a good partner and burn an existing project that had been in the works for five years?

Australia’s government decided that it desperately needed the extra stealth and stamina nuclear-fueled submarines provide. And while Canberra didn’t say why, exactly, the reason was clear to anyone who was paying attention.

China is building up its military, especially its navy, at an astonishing speed, and expanding its reach into the Pacific – right up to Australia’s own waters. And Australia decided it needed to respond with its own military build-up.

Over the last five years, as AUKUS has taken shape, the dynamics behind regional security have continued to evolve. With the second-coming of Donald Trump to the U.S. presidency, many of his predecessor’s initiatives have been dismantled. But not AUKUS.

Today on The Diplomat Asia we’ll get to the heart of why AUKUS has survived and why AUKUS matters. But first, what exactly is AUKUS?

title: A Deadly Flood Underscores the CCP-Imposed Information Vacuum in Tibet
description: The disaster exposed a stark contrast: open reporting is emerging from Nepal, while information from Tibet remains almost entirely dependent on China’s tightly controlled state media.
text:
The floods and landslides devastating communities in Tibet and Nepal are a natural disaster. The information vacuum inside Tibet is not.

Hundreds of people remain missing. Families are desperately searching for loved ones. Americans are among the foreign nationals reported unaccounted for. Roads, communications, and power have been cut, while rescue teams race to reach communities across some of the most difficult terrain in the world.

But on the Tibetan side of this disaster, there is another obstacle: the Chinese Communist Party’s longstanding restrictions on access and information.

For years, Beijing has tightly controlled access to Tibet for foreign journalists, diplomats, researchers, and independent organizations. In ordinary times, these restrictions keep the world from seeing Tibet. In a disaster, they can keep the world from understanding what Tibetans need, and potentially from helping them.

That is why Beijing should open affected Tibetan areas to the outside world.

Humanitarian organizations need to be able to safely reach communities and independently assess needs. Journalists need to be able to establish what is happening beyond official accounts. Foreign governments need timely information about their citizens and, where necessary, consular access. Families need to know what has happened to missing loved ones. And Tibetans themselves need to be able to tell the world what has happened to their communities and what they need.

Access is not an abstract human rights principle in an emergency. It is a lifeline.

President Xi Jinping has ordered an “all-out” search for the missing, and China has mobilized hundreds of rescuers in Tibet. But mobilizing the power of the state is not the same as permitting independent scrutiny. If Beijing is confident in its response, it should let the world see for itself.

The stakes also extend beyond Tibet.

The Himalayas may be divided by national borders, but their rivers, glaciers, and climate risks are not. This cross-border disaster has made that reality painfully clear. Not only did the flood devastate communities on both sides of the Nepal-Tibet border, but authorities in Bihar, India moved people from vulnerable areas amid concern that floodwaters could eventually threaten communities farther downstream.

Timely sharing of hydrological, meteorological, glacial, and disaster-risk information is a matter of public safety. China should urgently engage with Nepal, India, and other governments across the Himalayan region to build durable, reliable, and accessible real-time information sharing and cross-border early-warning systems. No community should be left without potentially lifesaving information because a threat originates on the other side of an international border.

The disaster should also change how Washington thinks about access to Tibet. The U.S. Congress has long recognized that restrictions on Tibet have consequences for Americans. The Reciprocal Access to Tibet Act specifically cited the difficulties U.S. consular officials faced assisting Americans trapped in Tibet after the 2015 Nepal earthquake. Today, Americans are again among those reported missing in a disaster affecting the Nepal-Tibet border region.

The administration should press Beijing for timely information about missing Americans and seek whatever consular access may be necessary. It should ask whether independent humanitarian organizations can assess needs inside Tibet and whether affected communities are receiving adequate assistance.

Washington should also examine whether resources Congress has already made available for Tibetan communities can be rapidly mobilized to support the response.

And as the immediate rescue effort gives way to recovery, another question will become increasingly important: Will Tibetans have a meaningful voice in what happens next? Reconstruction should not become an excuse for forced relocation or development decisions imposed without meaningful consultation. Affected Tibetans should participate in decisions about rebuilding their communities, restoring livelihoods, and managing future disaster risks.

The forces of nature that brought devastation to the Himalayas were beyond Beijing’s control. The information vacuum and lack of access in Tibet is not.

Beijing should let the world in.
