title: A Debate Is Raging in China Over English Education
description: Rising youth unemployment, the advent of AI translation, and growing anger against everything foreign are fueling public anger against English education in China.
text:
In the heated public discussions in China over English education, those calling to downgrade or abandon English in Chinese schools and colleges are using an ancient saying: 刻舟求剑 (ke zhou qiu jian), literally “notching the boat to find a sword.” Less literally, the phrase describes a foolish approach to solving problems that fails to account for changing circumstances.

The phrase refers to an ancient fable from the Warring States period (475 BC to 221 BC). In the story, a traveler from the State of Chu was crossing a river in a boat when his precious sword accidentally slipped from his hand and fell into the water. Instead of diving into the water to retrieve it, he calmly took out a small knife and carved a notch on the side of the boat right where the sword fell.

On being asked why he didn’t immediately jump into the river to retrieve his sword, he replied: “There is no need to worry. My sword fell into the river at this marked place. As soon as the boat reaches the dock and pulls into shore, I will jump down from here to retrieve my sword.”

That’s the context needed to understand those using this idiom in order to ridicule the continuation of English being taught in primary, secondary and high schools. Critics point out that the decision to incorporate the English language as a mandatory part of the school curriculum was made 50 years ago. “At the time, the aim was to quickly strengthen education, learn science and technology from abroad, and improve the overall quality of the population. Forcing everyone to learn English, while perhaps a bit of an overreaction, was understandable given the specific circumstances,” Chinese scholar Xiang Ligang commented on WeChat. But, like the position of the boat in the fable, China’s circumstances have changed.

It’s a widely held figure that English learning for a Chinese student – from early schooling to entering a university, in total 12 years of education – requires 3,000 to 5,000 hours of study and at least 100,000 yuan. Many in China are raising the question: is it worth it?

Arguments against the continuation of English as a compulsory subject in schools and colleges were recently further strengthened by a call to “end English’s core status” issued by Tang Jiafeng. Tang is a mathematics professor and online celebrity who has long taught mathematics to candidates taking postgraduate entrance examinations. The latest controversy stemmed from his comments on reforms to the locally administered zhongkao (senior high school entrance examination). Saying that “the history of Chinese people worshiping foreign things and fawning on foreign countries should end,” he advocated for reducing the weight given to English proficiency on the exam.

Currently, English is a required subject starting in third grade. It is weighted on par with Chinese language and mathematics on the entrance exam for secondary schools, the central exam after ninth grade, and the high school graduation exam. Chinese, English, and mathematics (collectively known as CEM) are the three most important subjects on the gaokao, China’s college and university entrance examination. Each subject counts for 150 points out of a total of 750.

Tang Jiafeng called for downgrading the status of English as part of an angry reaction to Chinese history being removed as a scoring subject in exams in several provinces. A large section of China’s nationalist intellectuals – who are also generally labeled as “conservatives” – have come out in support of Tang. Also on their side are parents and students who oppose making English a compulsory subject. English is considered difficult in China, since the Chinese language does not use an alphabetic script. Learning English thus increases the students’ burden and parents’ or guardian’s financial pressure.

Many also ask whether there’s any point to the effort. Given the difficulty involved in mastering a language with an entirely different writing system, rote memorization without real understanding is common. Xiang, in the WeChat commentary cited above, claimed that “95 percent of people who have studied English in primary [school], secondary [school], and university cannot communicate fluently, and 90 percent of those who have studied English will never use it in their lives, except for exams. Learning English without mastering it is a widespread phenomenon.” This argument has gained weight with the advent of AI-enabled translation.

A number of intellectuals, joined by several influential leftist scholars in leading universities, have thus challenged the status of English as a compulsory subject. Other well-known public figures – such as the former Global Times editor Hu Xijin – are defending the primacy of Chinese, English, and mathematics.

Hu in particular rubbished Tang’s claim that English learning was a sign of foreign-worship, saying “only an extreme and narrow-minded group regarded learning English as xenocentric.” Upholding English as the key for modernization and global competitiveness, Hu countered Tang by claiming that English had attained its global status because the West had led modernization for several centuries. “As China rises, the usage of Chinese to describe inventions and innovations is steadily increasing, while the center of gravity in science, technology and the economy is also shifting towards Chinese. But that will be a long process…” Hu said. “Turning this issue into one charged with ‘patriotism’ will only prove counter-productive, leading to unnecessary ideological dispute and confusion.”

Nationalist and leftist scholars dismissed Hu’s argument that English is crucial for China’s science, technology and economy. They cite the example of the outstanding post-World War II industrial and commercial growth of Germany, France, Japan – all of which succeeded without widespread English fluency.

Taking the argument further, these scholars actually blamed English classes for having stymied the growth of STEM (science, technology, engineering, and mathematics) in China in recent years. Last week, a Chinese article, in an apparent appeal to the authorities to break the “English shackles” wrote: “Using an excessively heavy burden of English learning and overly difficult English exams as an important criterion for ‘selecting talent’ has led to the elimination of many science and engineering talents who are not good at English, which has a serious negative impact on the cultivation of STEM professionals and the tackling of technological bottlenecks in my country” (emphasis added).

Liu Qing and Liu Yun, joint authors of the article, cited the specific example of Wang Xingxing, founder and CEO of Unitree Robotics, who almost didn’t test into university due to his poor English. Yet Wang currently enjoys a “rock star” status; he appeared on the cover of Time magazine two months ago with his manned mecha robot GD0, for a story entitled “The Age of Robots is Coming.” A year before that, Wang became a sensation in China after being invited to speak in the presence of Xi Jinping at the Beijing Symposium for private enterprises in February 2025. The other five speakers included Ren Zhengfei of Huawei fame, Lin Jun of Xiaomi, BYD founder Wang Chuanfu, Liu Yonghao of the New Hope Group, and Yu Renrong, popularly known as “China’s semiconductor king.”

Wang’s weak command of English nearly ruined his emergence as what Time called “an atypical prophet of the AI era.” As Liu Qing and Liu Yun pointed out, in spite of achieving outstanding scores in science subjects, due to his poor performance on the English language portion of entrance exams, Wang was forced to go to second-tier universities in Hangzhou and Shanghai for his graduation and postgraduate degrees respectively.

Liu Qing and Liu Yun underscored the fact that many potential scientific talents like Wang are being eliminated in the college entrance examination or postgraduate entrance examination solely because of their poor English skills. They believe that Wang was lucky to avoid this fate. To all those in China who are opposing English as a core subject in schools, this has become a modern-day example of the tragedy of “dying before achieving one’s goal.”

There are several distinct threads to the argument: nationalist (Chinese people shouldn’t be forced to learn a foreign language), utilitarian (mandatory English classes don’t actually achieve the goal of linguistic proficiency), and practical (poor English skills could prematurely end the careers of those gifted in STEM fields). But regardless of the rationale, more and more people are calling for an end to English’s 50-year-old status as a required subject in Chinese schools.

title: A Himalayan Flood Brings Economic Collapse to Nepal’s Border Region
description: The destruction of the Trishuli-Bhotekoshi corridor is a local tragedy with national economic consequences.
text:
On August 26, a massive glacier collapse near Langtang Lirung triggered a chain of flash floods and mudslides along the Trishuli and Bhotekoshi river systems. The event has not only caused damage to what was developed there but also to what was being built in that area, including infrastructure, hydropower projects, and private businesses, primarily small and medium enterprises (SMEs). Losses are estimated at more than $5 billion, which is almost one-third of Nepal’s annual budget.

Settlements, roads, bridges, hydropower plants, trade facilities, farmland, and human lives across Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, and downstream districts were swept away or buried beneath mud and boulders. Early estimates of the damage could be made using the household-level data from these locations and the data from the 2018 economic census. But that could be misleading.

The contribution to the GDP from those areas is going to be minimal when looking at the immediate numbers. However, the share could be far more significant if we factor in indirect benefits from the river systems and economic hubs in that corridor. Especially important is the opportunity cost, as Nepal was attempting to build up a vibrant trade link with China in exactly this region.

The human toll alone is immense. More than 1,300 people are confirmed dead in Nepal, while over 4,000 people are missing. For those who survived, the loss is not limited to houses and belongings. Families have lost relatives, farmland, livestock, food stocks, shops, vehicles, savings, identity documents, and the means to earn an income. Entire local economies in the peripheral areas of the flood-hit districts have been disrupted, which has a direct impact on key sectors such as tourism and agri-businesses.

The Trishuli-Bhotekoshi corridor is more than a river valley. It connects mountain communities to Kathmandu, national markets, tourism destinations, hydropower investments, and cross-border trade with China. Its destruction is therefore a local tragedy with national economic consequences.

The complete destruction of the Gyirong Port border complex is especially serious. The port was Nepal’s primary trade and tourism gateway with China. At the moment, Nepal has no fully functional border crossing point with China, which has a high cost for an economy that relies on imports of raw materials and other goods from China.

When the flood hit, more than 300 vehicles waiting at the border were swept away. About 42 kilometers of road and 41 bridges were damaged, with road and bridge repairs alone estimated to cost 15 billion rupees ($99.4 million).

The estimated cost to repair is one thing; it’s much more difficult to calculate the cost that accumulates when the movement of local people is limited due to the absence of infrastructure, especially in a border region. Sections of the Prithvi Highway are still blocked, delaying relief operations and disrupting the transport of goods, fuel, food, and passengers. The loss of the Gyirong-Rasuwagadhi trade route will affect importers, exporters, freight companies, customs agents, drivers, hotels, warehouses, retailers, and consumers throughout Nepal. Most of the freight companies have been damaged, with their containers being completely wiped out.

China has closed the Tatopani customs point following the complete destruction of the Rasuwagadhi border point linking Rasuwa and Gyirong. With no functional border crossing between Nepal and China at the moment, supply chains have been disrupted. This has a direct impact on customs revenue and will raise prices for consumers due to lack of supply.

People already suffering from the price hikes due to the Iran-U.S. war, among other global events, will have to face more severe economic hardships. Local economic centers, including Syabrubesi, Betrawati, Trishuli, and Rasuwagadhi had been developing through tourism, trade, transport, agriculture, construction, and hydropower investment. Their destruction risks reversing years of local economic progress.

The damage to Nepal’s hydropower system will have consequences beyond the immediate loss. With approximately 431 megawatts removed from the grid and another 470 MW of projects under construction affected, the disruption threatens electricity reliability just as demand is expected to rise during the dry season. In the short term, reduced domestic generation will increase reliance on electricity imports, putting additional pressure on the trade balance and increasing costs for households and businesses.

These losses go way beyond repair costs. Nepal faces lost electricity sales, reduced export potential, lower tax revenue, job losses, increased financing risks, and weakened investor confidence. If climate risks are not incorporated into hydropower planning, lenders and investors may consider Himalayan projects more expensive and less secure.

The estimated direct damage to Nepal’s infrastructure exceeds 200 billion rupees, or about $1.3 billion. Yet the full cost of restoring homes, schools, hospitals, roads, bridges, power systems, farmland, trade facilities, and livelihoods could reach around $8 billion.

The long-term impact is even more worrisome, as the country is again reeling under the burden of long-term rebuilding and rehabilitation. Some of the areas decimated by the flood were still rebuilding from the devastating earthquake of 2015.

Nepal cannot afford to rebuild the same infrastructure in the same vulnerable locations. Reconstruction must be financed through a green, resilient, and climate-informed approach. Roads and bridges should be rebuilt using updated flood-risk projections, with stronger foundations, safer alignments, wider river corridors, and improved drainage. Hydropower projects must account for glacier collapse, permafrost thaw, landslides, sediment flows, and glacial lake hazards – not only historical monsoon floods.

Investment in forests, wetlands, riverbanks, and degraded slopes can reduce erosion, stabilize watersheds, and protect livelihoods. Decentralized solar systems, battery storage, and local microgrids can keep health posts, schools, water systems, and emergency shelters functioning when major hydropower and transmission systems fail.

The government should consider establishing a Himalayan Climate Resilience and Recovery Financing Facility as a permanent platform for post-disaster recovery and long-term climate adaptation. Led by the Ministry of Finance in partnership with sectoral ministries, provincial and local governments, private investors, and development partners, the Facility could mobilize grants, concessional loans, insurance, guarantees, and responsibly structured private investment. It could operate through two windows: a rapid-response window to restore essential infrastructure and services after disasters, and a resilience-investment window.

This second window can operationalize four sub-windows such as public investment, private investment, donors, and other innovative investment solutions to fund climate-resilient hydropower, safer transmission systems, watershed management, glacier monitoring, early-warning systems, and community preparedness. Public and donor resources could reduce risk for private investors through guarantees, first-loss capital, and insurance support.

By pooling domestic and international resources, the Facility could accelerate recovery, protect public finances, and help Nepal shift from recurring emergency response toward sustained Himalayan resilience.

Nepal as a country has contributed very little to global greenhouse gas emissions, but it is suffering some of climate change’s harshest consequences. Rising temperatures are melting glaciers, weakening permafrost – the “cryospheric glue” holding mountain slopes together – and making Himalayan hazards more severe and unpredictable.

Paleo-flood studies suggest that the 2026 Trishuli event may be the largest to affect the valley in approximately 5,000 years. Boulders of this scale may have last moved during the Early Holocene Climate Optimum, about 50 centuries ago. This is a warning that present climatic shifts may be pushing the Himalayas toward prehistoric levels of hydrological instability.

High-emitting countries have benefited from carbon-intensive development for generations. They have a moral and financial responsibility to support Nepal’s recovery through rapid, predictable, and primarily grant-based climate finance. Nepal should not be pushed into deeper debt to recover from a crisis it did little to cause.

The people of Thame, Langtang, Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, and Chitwan cannot bear this burden alone. The people of Nepal need support not only to rebuild what was lost, but to build a safer, greener, and more resilient future.
tag: 2026 Nepal floods; August 26 Nepal floods; Bhotekoshi flood 2026; China-Nepal border; Nepal climate change; Nepal economic losses; Nepal economy

title: A Matter of Trust: Google, Artificial Intelligence, and the Public Sphere
description: Bertha Chan explains how Google seeks to mitigate risk while pushing forward the frontiers of AI.
text:
Singapore-based Bertha Chan heads Trust and Safety Global Engagements across the Asia-Pacific for Google, focusing on the safeguards and considerations needed to prevent AI misuse while keeping pace with the technology.

Her remit covers jurisdictions and partnerships with governments and civil society, as well as combating the ever-evolving online scam industry, which is already adopting the latest advances in AI, especially the production of deepfakes.

Chan says that the foundation of all innovation and technology adoption has to be trust and that Google aims to protect its users at every part of their “entire digital journey,” adding that its email product, Gmail, stops 90 percent of spam, phishing and malware from ever reaching an inbox.

“So that’s what we call all safety by design,” Chan told The Diplomat’s Luke Hunt, adding that Google has deployed research teams that seek to establish policies and frameworks aimed at safeguarding children and families from dangerous and sexual content, and preventing fraud.

“These experts are advisors who specialize in a very wide range of expertise, for example, developmental psychology, cultural anthropology, human development, youth culture [and] youth behavior – when it comes to technology more,” Chan said.

“So with their expertise we collaborate and understand and seek to really fine-tune our products.”

Prior to Google, Chan drove digital transformation and international relations initiatives within the Singapore government. She holds a Master’s degree in sociology from the University of Oxford and a Bachelor’s degree in psychology from University College London.
tag: Artificial intelligence; artificial intelligence Asia; Google

title: A Message to China from Japan’s Takaichi Administration
description: Can Japan ‘normalize’ relations?
text:
The Taiwan Strait came up as an example during a debate on the legal applications of Japan’s right of collective self-defense at the Budget Committee of the Lower House on November 7, 2025, and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi gave her response when asked under what circumstances a “survival-threatening situation” would be legally applicable. China reacted sharply, to say the least: verbally accusing Japan of “neo-militarism” and then moving to normalize activities by the Chinese Navy — especially its aircraft carriers — in the waters between the First Island Chain and the Second Island Chain, while its coast guard began deploying east of Taiwan’s coast. On the economic front, security provisions were applied to Japanese companies, restrictions were imposed on rare earth exports, and measures were taken to curtail tourism and other exchanges with Japan, with economic, local-governmental, and academic ties all affected to a significant degree. China has demanded that Takaichi retract her November 7 statements, but she has refused.

An APEC summit is scheduled in China in November 2026, hosted by Chinese President Xi Jinping, and Takaichi is expected to attend. Significant progress in Japan-China relations has been elusive, however. A Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson made remarks in late June 2026 that appeared to give the green light for private exchanges between Japan and China, and a range of business associations and parliamentary groups are now scheduled to visit China this fall. Whether this supposed “green light” actually came from China’s leadership remains unclear.

So what message is the Takaichi administration sending to China?

First, on the Taiwan Strait. Three days after the original remarks, at a Budget Committee session on November 11, 2025, Takaichi said that “Peace and stability in the Taiwan Strait are important not only for Japanese security but also for the stability of the international community as a whole. Japan has consistently held the expectation that issues surrounding Taiwan will be resolved peacefully through dialogue.” At a plenary session of the House of Representatives on December 3, she added: “Our government’s basic position regarding Taiwan hasn’t changed and is as stated in the 1972 Japan-China Joint Communiqué.” In short, she made clear that the November 7 statement did not represent a change in Japan’s Taiwan policy.

Then, on Japan-China relations broadly. At the Joint Meeting of the Committees of Both Houses on Fundamental National Policies on November 26, 2025, Takaichi said the two sides had “agreed to building constructive and stable Japan-China relations” and that “if there are concerns or challenges between us, they will be resolved through communication, communication between the leaders,” adding that “Japan is always constructive and open to dialogue with China.” Meanwhile, Diet speakers have repeatedly reached for a now-standard phrase: to “closely monitor the situation and respond appropriately, including to the effects of the various measures from China.” At the House of Councillors plenary session on February 25, 2026, Takaichi went somewhat further, saying “Japan is open to different forms of dialogue with China” and citing cooperation with “our allies, the United States and like-minded countries” — remarks likely made with her March visit to Washington in mind. In her post-visit statement at the House of Representatives plenary on March 26, however, Takaichi mentioned “cooperation with the United States” in the context of China policy but otherwise repeated the same formula.

Takaichi’s public statements since November 7, 2025 have largely been repetitions of standard phrases, repeatedly asserting that Japan’s existing Taiwan and China policies are unchanged. She has also signaled that Japan is “open” to dialogue. Chinese protests have escalated regardless, and while dialogue between Japan and China has not disappeared entirely, it remains limited. Ministerial exchanges this year appear confined to APEC-related matters, given China’s role as host. Yet more recently the Takaichi administration appears to be sending a new signal.

First, Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi apparently exchanged a brief greeting with his Chinese counterpart Wang Yi at the ASEAN-related Foreign Ministers’ Meetings. China has denied this, but it appears certain that Motegi made the approach on July 23. The day before, on July 22, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio told Wang in their meeting that he saw a worrying trend of deteriorating Japan-China relations. Whether Motegi’s approach was a direct response to Rubio’s remarks is unclear, but Japan is at minimum signaling a proactive stance toward dialogue with China.

Second, Takaichi’s remarks at a press conference on July 27 are telling. When asked about the November APEC summit, she said simply: “I am looking forward to it.” The likelihood of a formal Japan-China bilateral meeting is low, but as host Xi would be expected to greet all attending leaders, making some form of contact difficult to avoid.

These signals from the Takaichi administration are likely driven by more than just American expectations. Following what may have been a green light from the Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson on June 26, Japanese business associations and parliamentary groups have announced China visits in quick succession. Whether any of this can truly “normalize” Japan-China relations remains to be seen, but the mood on the Japanese side is clearly shifting.
tag: 2026 APEC Summit; China-Japan Relations; China-Japan tensions; Japan Taiwan policy; Sanae Takaichi China policy; Taiwan Strait; Takaichi Taiwan policy

title: Abroad, India’s RSS Speaks of ‘Love.’ At Home, Its Affiliates Attack Christians.
description: From church vandalism to grave desecration, assaults against Christian minorities are increasing in the large state of West Bengal since the BJP, an RSS offshoot, came to power in May.
text:
Sutahata is a rural place in the eastern Indian state of West Bengal, which has been ruled by Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) since the May 2026 state elections. There, on August 26, about 50 people gathered at Goutam Bera’s residence in Ranichak village. It was a house fellowship gathering that involved Bible study and prayer. Many attendees were Hindus, mostly friends and acquaintances of the Bera family.

The news of the gathering reached members of Hindu supremacist organizations. One of them broadcast a live video on Facebook while on his way to Bera’s place. They had heard a Christian priest had gone there to convert Hindus. “Let’s see what they are up to,” he said. By the time the livestreamer reached Bera’s house, some of his fellows were already there. They barged into the house, abused those present and threw people out, before allegedly manhandling the rest of the attendees.

“You are Hindus. You have idols of Hindu deities at home. How could you bring in a Father and practice Christianity?” one can be heard shouting. “They have started this Jesus business now. See, we have recovered a Bible! My God, they have a Bible here!”

One video shows the intruders – carrying saffron flags – ordering the prayer attendees, rather rudely and loudly, to chant “Hare Krishna, Hare Ram” and “Jai Shree Ram.” Another video shows the cops taking the prayer attendees to a police vehicle. At one point, people from the crowd can be heard shouting: “Thrash them, thrash them!”

According to Joy Kumar Ghughu, the pastor who was reading from the Bible, the police first took 17 prayer attendees, including him, to the Sutahata block primary health center for treatment and a medical check-up. They were then taken to the Sutahata police station, where everyone was interrogated about the intention behind the gathering. Their mobile phones were examined. At about 8 p.m., they were told they could go.

“We did not lodge any police complaint against the attackers because Jesus teaches forgiveness. We will pray for their well-being,” Ghughu told The Diplomat.

He, however, asked why propagating Christianity should be objected to, when Article 25 of the Indian Constitution says that all persons are equally entitled to freedom of conscience and the right to profess, practice and propagate their religion freely. “We are not paying anyone to become Christians,” Ghughu said.

The RSS Link

Senior BJP leader Amit Malviya described the incident, along with two others, as “isolated local objections to prayer gatherings… peacefully resolved by the police.” However, videos posted on social media platforms by those involved in the attack tell a different story.

The intruders identified themselves as members of Shree Ram Janmotsab Samity (Lord Ram birthday celebration committee). The Samity does not hide its links to the RSS, the BJP’s ideological and organizational parent. Its Facebook page regularly posts invites to events of the RSS and its affiliates, like the Vishwa Hindu Parishad (VHP).

At Sutahata, a person recording on the spot identified himself and his fellows as belonging to the VHP. Showing videos of the organizers of the prayer gathering and the pastor present there, one of them told the video’s audience: “Beat them up with brooms whenever and wherever you see them. They are worse than terrorists.”

In another video from the incident, uploaded to a Facebook page of Bajrang Dal, the youth wing of the VHP, the intruders said: “We are from VHP Chaitanyapur unit… Sanatan Dharma is the world’s greatest religion. Whenever you spot people we identified in our videos, just inform us.” The Hindu supremacists usually refer to Hinduism as Sanatan Dharma (eternal religion).

A few hours later, in a Facebook post, the Samity said, “Let this serve as a warning to those who spread religious propaganda under the guise of ‘God the Father’: if we catch you, you will face severe consequences.”

Its based on actions like these that a recent database described the RSS family of organizations, popularly called the Sangh Parivar, as “the largest far-right network in history.”

Modi called the RSS the world’s largest NGO (non-governmental organization).

That discrepancy gets to the heart of the RSS’s attempt to paint a very different picture of itself abroad.

Home and Abroad: A Contrasting Approach

Hindu civilizational identity rests on the idea that diversity and unity can coexist, RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat said in London at the beginning of September. “We must never lose sight of the fact that we are one.”

During a September 6 event in London as part of a U.S.-Canada-U.K. tour marking the organization’s centenary, Bhagwat said, “I heard some people say intense hatred is the basis of our work. It is just the reverse. ‘Shuddha Satvik Prem’ (pure and divine love) is the basis of our work.”

Before landing in London, he had visited New York and Toronto. In New York, while addressing a “Universal Oneness Celebration” at Madison Square Garden on August 29, Bhagwat said, “To call oneself Hindu, one must believe that all paths lead to the same destination and that every human has dignity, with no difference between human beings.” He described diversity as a “decoration for our innate unity” that has to be accepted: “It has to be respected. It has to be protected.”

In West Bengal, the next day, activists belonging to different RSS-linked organizations disrupted three separate Christian prayer gatherings and abused and heckled the prayer participants.

Here are some of the incidents, in just one Indian state, that took place during the same weeks Bhagwat was spreading the message of love and oneness abroad:

August 23: A mob broke into a church premises at Uluberia in Howrah district, vandalized the prayer room, and attacked several prayer attendees. Bajrang Dal activists went to close down a Christian house prayer ceremony at Baniberia area in Mograhat of South 24 Parganas district.

August 30: Bajrang Dal activists thrashed a lawyer for hosting Christian prayers at his residence in Baripur, South 24-Parganas. Miscreants stormed the Sunday prayer gathering at Jagatballabhpur, Howrah district. Another prayer venue was vandalized at Hingalganj in North 24 Parganas.

September 1: Hindu Jagran Manch, another RSS affiliate, locked up a school run by Christians at Hasnabad Rupomari bazar in North 24 Parganas district. Protesters told the media: “Their walls are full of Jesus’ photos! No Hindu deities at all! Why should it be so? Why are they teaching kids about Jesus’ life? This school must be closed down.”

September 7: A group of activists claiming to be from the VHP and BD interrupted a prayer gathering at a tiny, makeshift church in Bally of Howrah district and told them that preaching Christianity will not be allowed.

September 9: People identifying themselves as VHP and BD organizers reached a house at Mograhat area in South 24-Parganas district, aggressively quizzed people about who they worship, and objected to praying before Jesus.

September 11: Bajrang Dal activists threatened the organizers of another prayer gathering at Mamudpur in Mograhat, South 24 Parganas.

September 12: VHP activists threatened members of a house prayer gathering at Taldi, Canning, South 24 Parganas, ordered them to tear all of Jesus’ photos apart and sternly told them to stop the gathering for good. “Why Jesus? Why Jesus? Why Jesus?” they kept shouting. “Whoever you may be going to complain to, tell them that we are from VHP and Bajrang Dal. We’ll see who holds how much power.”

The next day, another video went viral on social media that showed a Hindu supremacist mob violently abusing prayer gatherers and publicly tearing apart books on Param-pita (God the Father). “What the hell is ‘God the Father’? Why don’t you read the Gita or chant Hare Krishna?” the attackers shouted as they tore apart books on Christian faith.

Samirul Islam, a parliamentarian of the Trinamool Congress, which lost power to the BJP in the May 2026 election after ruling the state for 15 years, alleged that the constitutional rights of Christians to freely practice, preach, and propagate their religion were being violated. “It’s an affront to India’s constitutional spirit of unity in diversity,” he told The Diplomat.

Hoping Against Hope

Herod Mullick, secretary of the Bangiya Christiya Pariseba (BCP), a Christian community organization in West Bengal, told The Diplomat that they are “deeply moved and encouraged” by the messages Bhagwat spread from the United States and United Kingdom. “He heads the Sangh Parivar, which is the driving force behind the central government and ruling party in the state. So, we are hopeful that the local administration will ensure that the spirit of love, harmony and coexistence will find practical implementation on the ground,” Mullick said.

They plan to meet the state’s minority welfare minister, seeking a prompt and active state response against “systematic attacks and vandalism” during prayer meetings, particularly in house churches, under false allegations of forced conversion.

“Incidents are many, but police complaints have been filed in only a few. In the rest of the cases, the victims were too afraid to take any legal course,” he said. He added that in cases when pastors and worshippers had been beaten up, the police detained and harassed the victims instead of apprehending the miscreants.

Most of these attacks happened during house prayer gatherings, often called independent churches or free churches. In places where few people follow the Christians faith, there are no formal churches and prayer gatherings take place in houses.

Mullick argued that spreading the essence of one’s religion is a natural and sincere urge for believers and pointed out that in ancient times, Hindu and Buddhist missionaries from India traveled across the world to propagate their faiths. Their organization held a protest rally in the state capital, Kolkata, on August 23.

Another pastor who had recently faced harassment told The Diplomat, requesting anonymity, “They are targeting house church gatherings and house fellowship meetings, asking why Hindus are listening to Bible reading. Do people in the U.S. ask why Christians are attending different Hare Krishna chanting events?”

New Trend

Anti-Christian hostility has surged in different Indian states, especially those ruled by the BJP, since Modi, himself an RSS volunteer, came to the helm of India’s affairs in 2014. But they are completely new in West Bengal, where Christians form a minuscule minority and play an important role in running educational and charitable institutions.

“It has become a Sunday horror show. Over the past four months, there have been one or more incidents every Sunday,” said Arpan Rana, a BCP member from East Midnapore district. “If there are specific allegations of forcible or deceptive religious conversion, the government should investigate. But why are mobs taking laws into their hands?”

It all started soon after the change of government. On May 6, two days after results were announced, a group of BJP activists allegedly vandalized the Murshidabad home of Barnali Chatterjee, a Christian widow, and demanded she hand over her property to be converted into a temple. On the same day, in Bankura district, a Protestant prayer meeting was allegedly disrupted, and Bibles were seized.

The list has since kept growing. As a result, Christians have suspended house prayer meetings in several districts — a retreat from religious practice in a state where, per the 2011 Census, Christians make up just 0.72 percent of the population. “The attacks are aimed at destroying West Bengal’s tradition of religious tolerance, coexistence, and syncretic culture,” alleged Subhankar Sarkar, the state unit president of the Congress, India’s main opposition party.

According to Mohammed Salim, secretary of the Communist Party of India (Marxist)’s West Bengal state unit, these low-intensity and localized attacks targeting the smaller, informal prayer set-ups have a dual aim: to terrorize the downtrodden followers of Christianity without creating major news headlines. “They know attacks on prominent churches can become major news abroad,” he told The Diplomat.

That the change of government in West Bengal created the atmosphere for carrying out such offensives against Christianity propagators is understandable from a video of the August 26 incident at Sutahata: “These people were propagating other religions even after the change in the [state] government. Therefore, we have handed them over to the police,” said one of those involved in disrupting the prayer gathering.

The Diplomat has sent questions to the state’s minority affairs minister, Kshudiram Tudu, asking for the government response to such allegations. Biplab Roy, an RSS spokesperson in West Bengal, has also been asked for comment. The story will be updated if responses are received.
tag: anti-Christian sentiment in India; BJP in West Bengal; Christians in India; Hindu nationalists; India attacks on Christians; India communal violence; RSS abroad; RSS activity

title: After a Self-Immolation at the UN, Rethinking What Beijing Fears on Tibet
description: Beijing’s real vulnerability is not international action. It’s rising awareness within the Chinese population.
text:
On July 2, Lobga Rangzen, a Tibetan man who had taken the word meaning “independence and freedom” as his name, set himself on fire outside the United Nations headquarters in New York. His act came one day after China’s Ethnic Unity and Progress Promotion Law took effect. In a video posted before his death, he denounced the law as an erasure of Tibetan identity and called on Tibetans-in-exile to take up their responsibility.

He chose the spot deliberately, too. Tibetans have looked to the U.N. for redress since 1950, when Tibet’s appeal first went to the new global body. The General Assembly passed resolutions on Tibet in 1959, 1961, and 1965. The 1961 resolution explicitly invoked Tibetans’ right to self-determination. Yet after the People’s Republic took China’s U.N. seat in 1971, the issue vanished from the organization’s agenda. Rangzen’s self-immolation was an indictment of six decades of silence.

For weeks after his death, Tibetan communities across the globe marched and demonstrated. CNN, Radio Free Asia, and others covered it; the U.N. secretary-general’s spokesperson offered condolences, and the U.S. State Department reaffirmed its support for Tibetans. Then, within days, the coverage vanished. No government went beyond boilerplate statements of sympathy.

For decades, the Central Tibetan Administration’s envoys and Tibetan human rights organizations have worked in Geneva, Washington, and Brussels with extraordinary persistence, winning legislation like the Resolve Tibet Act. Beijing’s position has never varied: Tibet is an “inalienable part of China.” The one channel that did exist, nine rounds of talks with the Dalai Lama’s envoys between 2002 and 2010, produced nothing, and those talks have been moribund for over 15 years.

The strategy of seeking international support to enact change in Tibet has run its course. The world has heard Tibetans cry out since 1959. Sympathy has calcified into routine: statements, condemnations, calls for dialogue. There is little prospect that external pressure alone will move the Chinese Communist Party on Tibet, and no government has shown any willingness to go beyond words.

But Beijing fears a different kind of pressure, one that comes from inside the Chinese-speaking world.

China’s Real Fear

A year ago, Chinese state security police in Changsha detained Zhang Yadi, a 22-year-old Han Chinese student who had been studying in France, on suspicion of “inciting separatism.” Her offense: writing and editing for Chinese Youth Stand for Tibet (华语青年挺藏会), a bilingual Han-Tibetan exchange platform I founded. Zhang was born and raised in Hunan, Mao’s home province, to Han parents. Nearly all of our members are also ethnically Han.

Many people asked why a Han Chinese person would risk prison for Tibetans. The more useful question is why Beijing treated a small volunteer media project as a state security threat and detained a college student over it.

The CCP understands that its rule in Tibet rests not only on security spending but on the acquiescence of the Han majority – an acquiescence manufactured through decades of disinformation. Since 1959, state propaganda has taught Chinese citizens that old Tibet was a barbaric serf society, that the Dalai Lama was its greatest slaveholder. One particularly enduring myth holds that Tibet’s Buddhist monks made drums out of human skin. A hit 1990s song to that effect, “Sister Drum” (阿姐鼓), was written by a Han composer who knew the story only secondhand, from siblings who had traveled to Tibet. Chinese internet users still cite the song as evidence of Tibetan savagery.

According to the CCP’s preferred narrative, the People’s Liberation Army was Tibet’s savior, and occupation is liberation. Ordinary Chinese people don’t defend the CCP’s Tibet policy out of malice; most sincerely see no case against it.

Han acceptance of this narrative is the foundation for CCP rule in Tibet – but it is more fragile than it looks. In 2025, the Tibet Autonomous Region (TAR) raised just 31.8 billion yuan in local revenue against 310 billion in spending. Central transfers of 253.88 billion yuan, more than 80 percent of the budget according to the TAR’s budget reports, filled the gap, funding both livelihood programs and a vast stability-maintenance apparatus. And that budget excludes spending in the Tibetan areas of Qinghai, Sichuan, Gansu, and Yunnan.

There is already simmering resentment of these policies. On the Chinese internet, a segment of Han nationalists already ask why the government grants ethnic minorities college-entrance bonus points and what it derides as “super-citizen treatment.” As China’s economy slows, complaints about the fiscal burden are growing sharper. That resentment is combustible, as ready to turn on minorities as on the CCP.

The party can ignore foreign condemnation, but not a public at home that calls into question Beijing’s rule in Tibet. Han Chinese who speak fluently to that public, using the Chinese language and Chinese platforms, are the CCP’s nightmare on the ethnic frontier. More and more Han Chinese resent CCP policies in Tibet. Our aim is to redirect the questions they are already asking. Instead of “why are we paying for them?” we ask: “What is this money actually buying, and who does it benefit?”

The Dalai Lama grasped the importance of Han Chinese partnerships decades ago. He appointed Chinese liaison officers at Tibetan offices worldwide and built his Middle Way Approach partly around winning Chinese hearts. But the CTA’s Chinese-language capacity has withered; the Chinese sections of exile institutions have become marginal afterthoughts.

Our group, Chinese Youth for Tibet, formed organically on the Chinese-language internet, among young people fluent in its idiom. Tibetans welcomed us because that gap had gone unfilled for so long.

Falling Between “Two Desks”

Other Han Chinese have taken up the cause before. Grace Wang, a Duke student, was buried in nationalist abuse in 2008 for merely trying to mediate between pro-Tibet and pro-China protesters. The late historian Li Jianglin, born into a Communist family, spent years recording exile Tibetans’ oral histories; her “Tibet in Agony” reconstructed why the Dalai Lama fled in 1959. In July, police in Lhasa detained Zhang Yi, a pro-democracy activist since 1989, for displaying a photograph of the Dalai Lama at Sera Monastery, and formally arrested him on July 28.

One by one, Han Chinese keep arriving at a shared sense of historical responsibility. My moment came in 2018, while teaching at a Tibetan middle school; the government forcibly closed that school two years ago.

Yet groups like Chinese Youth for Tibet fall into an institutional blind spot. When Zhang Yadi was arrested, concern stopped at her as an individual; almost no Tibetan or Western outlet has interviewed our organization to ask what we do, or why Han Chinese would stand up for Tibet at all. Our proposals to foundations disappear without reply. A veteran colleague told me recently: you have fallen into the gap between two desks.

In international media, government bureaucracies, and foundations, the “Tibet desk” and the “China desk” are separate worlds. Most China specialists pay little attention to Tibet. Tibet specialists know little of Chinese administration, law, or society – especially in the Tibetan areas outside the TAR, where most Tibetans live.

This gap explains why Chinese-speaking advocates for Tibet working to raise awareness using Chinese language platforms remain unfunded, uncovered, and unprotected – even as Beijing prosecutes our members as state security threats. The CCP takes our work seriously enough to prosecute it. Western foundations and newsrooms have yet to really register our existence.

Han and Tibetan people have been neighbors for millennia. We drink from the same rivers, and our futures are bound together long after this regime is gone. For that reason, I believe the rise of Han Chinese-driven activism is one of the most strategically significant developments in the Tibet issue.

International advocacy kept Tibet’s cause alive for more than 70 years, and that work must continue. But the diminishing returns were made all too tragically obvious by Lobga Rangzen’s self-immolation. He burned to death on the U.N.’s front steps and the world barely noticed.

The international community is not going to change Tibet’s fate. What could still make a difference is a growing awareness among China’s Chinese-speaking majority. Whoever wants to change Tibet’s future should start funding and covering the people doing this work, and protecting them.

title: After the Flood, Can China, Nepal, and India Move From Earth Observation to Regional Preparedness?
description: A blueprint for building resilience in the Hindu Kush Himalaya.
text:
The recent Bhotekoshi-Trishuli flood near the China-Nepal border, described as a “mountain tsunami,” occurred at a time when glaciers across the Hindu Kush Himalaya (HKH) are already melting rapidly. Extreme events like the catastrophic flood are no longer isolated anomalies but signals of a broader regional climate crisis in the fragile mountain region. Translating Earth observation of the HKH into actionable regional preparedness is therefore an urgent requirement for climate action.

The August 26 flood showed how difficult it is to anticipate some of these risks in advance. Scientific assessments and satellite imagery confirm that a massive rock-ice avalanche collapsed into the Chhochen Khola, triggering a cascading flood of water, mud and debris into the Lhende Khola and further downstream. This disaster was a human tragedy, with more than 1,400 people dead and some 6,000. Fertile Trishuli valley lands were taken away, millions of tonnes of carbon credits were destroyed and economic damages added up to billions of dollars.

Failure zone on Mount Langtang Lirung, source of the August 26, 2026 Bhotekoshi–Trishuli flood. Image from Google Earth.

The impact was not confined to Nepal. The “mountain tsunami” obliterated Gyirong Port, the primary border crossing for both people and trading goods moving from Nepal into China. China has reported over 40 people dead and over 50 missing.

Districts along the India-Nepal border were also put on heightened alert. Indian National Disaster Response Force teams were deployed, and people in lowland areas were requested to move to safer places. And Bihar is currently dealing with a much wider flood situation.

And floods continue to hit the region. As of September 27, at least 56 people had died in monsoon-driven flooding in India, and 14 more perished in Nepal. Several rivers, including the Ganga, Gandak, Koshi, Budhi Gandaki, and Bagmati, are above danger levels at various locations.

Other South Asian countries are experiencing similar extreme climate events – floods and inundation. Pakistan’s disaster agency, the National Disaster Management Authority, has recorded 199 deaths since the rainfall began on June 26 of this year. Nearly 2,000 houses have been damaged. Similarly, in July, more than 1 million people were stranded across seven districts after days of heavy rain in Bangladesh.

The events of 2026 are not an aberration. The flood-risk map in the World Risk Report 2025 places Bangladesh, Pakistan, and India among the highest flood risk countries in the world.

Global flood-risk map showing Bangladesh, Pakistan and India among the four highest-risk countries. Map from the World Risk Report 2025, Bündnis Entwicklung Hilft and IFHV.

It is also worth remembering that these events are happening in a region where per capita greenhouse gas emissions (2.5 for India, 1 for Pakistan, and 0.8 for Bangladesh) are well below the global average of 6.4 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent per person. This raises a wider question of climate inequality, as countries contributing relatively little to global emissions face some of the greatest climate risks.

The effect of these floods – not just those on August 26, but all of them – continues long after the water recedes. As recurring floods damage crops, homes, infrastructure, commerce, and local economies, repeated losses can make it harder for families to recover. This can make farming and other local livelihoods harder to sustain in the long run, forcing the victims to opt for migration in the face of extreme vulnerability. A study conducted by the World Bank estimated that South Asia may see about 40 million internal climate migrants by 2050.

Is it possible to mitigate the damage through information sharing? That’s been a topic of much discussion since the August floods hit Nepal.

What Earth Observations Are Showing Across the Hindu Kush Himalaya

Integrated Earth observations – including visual, thermal, and synthetic aperture radar (SAR) remote sensing – alongside localized field surveys demonstrate widespread cryospheric and geomorphic transformation across the broader HKH. Satellite-based observation and in situ monitoring confirm that Himalayan glaciers are experiencing persistent mass loss averaging around half a meter of ice thickness per year, accompanied by widespread snowline depression and declining snow cover. Generally, river flows are stationary, but some experience a temporary increase of discharge due to glacial ice melt.

According to ICIMOD’s 2026 assessment, glaciers across the HKH region are losing ice at roughly twice the rate seen before 2000. Research in the Everest region shows debris-covered glaciers can experience severe thinning, surface lowering of up to 1.56 m/yr, and flow deceleration. Further, recent research indicates that the human-populated area at the Everest Base Camp has a higher surface warming rate compared to the surrounding unpopulated part of the Khumbu glaciers, a major source of the Koshi River system.

This extensive cryospheric decay destabilizes surrounding slopes, as thawing permafrost and paraglacial moraine degradation increase susceptibility to catastrophic rock–ice avalanches and complex hazard chains. A prime example was the August 26 flood, which began with an ice–rock slope collapse from the northern face of Mount Langtang Lirung into the Chhochen Khola and Lhende Khola. The collapse induced seismic energy equivalent to a 5.2-magnitude earthquake and evolved into a destructive debris flow that rushed downstream across Nepal into China and India.

Bridging the Observation Gap: Connecting Satellites, Sensors, and Communities

Field observations and small-scale studies remain limited in the HKH due to logistical challenges, resource constraints, and field risks. Consequently, monitoring relies heavily on Earth observation and remote sensing, while long-term ground measurements of glacier mass balance, snow, and other cryospheric variables remain sparse. Cloud cover, steep terrain, and limited ground validation further constrain even satellite observations.

One study showed that glacial lakes increased in Nepal (in terms of both numbers and surface area) between 1977 and 2017. However, satellite-based inventories mainly capture such lakes’ extent and change. Gauging lake depth, volume, dam condition, and hydrological behavior often requires field measurements or higher-resolution observations.

Major gaps remain in monitoring remote glaciers, snowfields, glacial lakes, unstable terrain, and headwater rivers. The lack of data limits hazard forecasting, water resource assessments, and long-term mountain planning.

Addressing these gaps will require bringing different forms of observation together. Integrating multi-tiered Earth observations would create a comprehensive framework for monitoring dynamic cryospheric hazards across Nepal and the HKH.

Even though satellite, SAR, and DEM data cover areas well for tracking glacier loss, tools like UAVs, CORS, and automated weather stations give much better detail at specific sites. These tools help to monitor slope instability, ice movement and hydrometeorological conditions.

Complementing these technical solutions, local community observations contribute crucial real-time contextual validation during sudden disaster events. To bridge these diverse inputs, recent scientific assessments emphasize that unifying these streams requires common geodetic reference frames, standardized data protocols, and centralized open-access platforms – such as Mountain GeoPortal – enabling agencies like Nepal’s Department of Hydrology and Meteorology (DHM) to model cascading hazard chains, issue early warnings, and protect downstream river systems.

Downstream authorities and communities across Nepal and the HKH require actionable, localized, and time-sensitive warnings rather than raw scientific data or static maps.

High-priority actionable information includes automated classifications of hazardous glacial lakes, real-time forecasts of peak flood magnitude, expected water and debris arrival times, and dynamic inundation maps highlighting at-risk settlements, roads, and hydropower facilities.

In transboundary river basins like the Koshi and Gandak, saving lives depends on real-time cross-border hydrometeorological data sharing before flood surges cross international borders. Upstream flow warnings allow downstream operators; such as those at the Gandak Barrage-to manage control gates proactively and cushion flood impacts on plains communities.

Ultimately, this data must feed directly into automated multi-language cell alerts and pre-rehearsed local response plans, so communities have enough time to evacuate when necessary.

From Observations to Regional Preparedness

There are already some efforts to build on. Nepal itself is now strengthening monitoring following the recent disaster, and looking for more real-time information from China on glacier movement and upstream water levels. Some of these systems may provide only a few minutes of warning during a very fast event, but even that can matter if information can reach people quickly.

There are also several existing arrangements between countries across the region for sharing flood forecasts, river data and information on mountain hazards. Some of these have been in place for decades.

Afghanistan and Pakistan cooperate through the Flash Flood Guidance System , including flood forecasting tools and technical training supported by the World Meteorological Organization.

Bangladesh and India share real-time flood data through bilateral arrangements and the Joint Rivers Commission to support flood forecasting and early warnings in Bangladesh.

For Bhutan and India, a joint hydrometeorological and flood-forecasting network , established in 1955, supports flood warnings for rivers flowing from Bhutan into Assam and West Bengal.

India and Nepal carry out joint flood forecasting and river management through established bilateral mechanisms, including for the Koshi and Gandak river systems.

China and India have an Expert Level Mechanism on Trans-border Rivers, which provides a channel for technical discussions. Earlier agreements covered flood-season hydrological data sharing for the Brahmaputra and Sutlej, but both have expired, and regular data sharing remains suspended.

China and Nepal cooperate on disaster prevention, emergency management, and information sharing. Nepal and China also exchange hydrological and meteorological information, including information on flood risks and glacial lakes.

China and Pakistan likewise have technical cooperation on hydrological and geological hazards, including glacier risks, monitoring technologies and early-warning systems.

As for India and Pakistan, the Indus Waters Treaty (1960) provides for hydrological data exchange and flood-related notifications. However, India announced that it was holding the treaty in abeyance in 2025. Pakistan maintains that the treaty remains binding and rejects its unilateral suspension.

These mechanisms show that cooperation is happening, but there are still key gaps. Data sharing between some countries has been interrupted, while other mechanisms focus mainly on routine flood forecasting or technical exchanges. There is also limited coordination on how warnings are passed between institutions and used by authorities downstream, particularly when hazards develop quickly and leave little time to respond.

These issues are also getting more attention at the political level. Around the time of Nepal’s devastating floods, parliamentarians from across the HKH met in Bhutan to discuss regional collaboration. Days later, another round of parliamentary dialogue took place in Thimphu, focusing on finding efficient ways to link scientific evidence with policy, budgets and disaster preparedness.

While these arrangements and platforms already exist, there are still gaps in how monitoring information is shared and used operationally, particularly for hazards that can move rapidly across national borders.

Two priorities seem particularly important here. Monitoring systems need to be designed in a way that communities and authorities downstream can easily use. It should include practical information, like where risks may emerge, who could be affected, and how much time they have to prepare.

There is also scope for countries to do more joint planning around shared risks, building on existing arrangements. This could include assessing possible impacts across borders, agreeing on how warnings reach the relevant authorities, and testing these arrangements together. For some Himalayan hazards, there may be very little time to respond, so much of this work needs to happen in advance.

Other regions already have some systems that could offer useful lessons for the region. For example, the Mekong River Commission has formal procedures for countries to share data on water flows, floods, and other basin conditions. It also runs a regional flood and drought center that combines monitoring data with forecasts and shares them with national agencies and the public. This model cannot be directly applied to the Himalaya where geography, politics and types of hazards are different. But there are useful lessons in how countries can make cross-border data sharing more regular and reliable.

Conclusion

The HKH is experiencing rapid glacier loss, bedrock failures, and growing risks from cascading hazards, affecting communities, infrastructure, and economies.

Earth observations and field data can help us understand risk better, but the information must reach people quickly and in a form that people can use. If we strengthen science, monitoring, local efforts, and cross-border cooperation we can boost preparedness for HKH hazards that transcend individual rivers and cut across borders.

title: Ahead of Trump-Xi Summit, North Korea Launches More Missiles
description: On September 20, North Korea fired two short-range ballistic missiles, its second launch in a little over a week.
text:
On September 20, North Korea fired two short-range ballistic missiles from the Wonsan area on its east coast, according to South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff. The first, detected around 3 p.m. KST, flew about 450 kilometers (280 miles). The second, fired about 5:50 p.m. KST, flew more than 600 kilometers (373 miles). Both are presumed to be from the Hwasong-11 series.

It was North Korea’s second missile launch in eight days. On September 12, one day after the Japan-South Korea-U.S. Freedom Edge exercise ended, North Korea fired several short-range ballistic missiles from the same area, which it described as part of a “joint firepower drill.” That launch was its first in 23 days.

The September 20 launches followed a statement two days earlier from Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of Kim Jong Un. She said North Korea must answer U.S.-led drills such as the Pacific Vanguard naval exercise near Guam with measures at least as forceful. Her statement added that North Korea’s nuclear buildup would not change.

A day before that, Kim had rejected renewed calls for denuclearization at an International Atomic Energy Agency conference.

Pyongyang has followed each allied exercise this month with missile fire, and the newest launches follow a warning of a tougher response from Kim Yo Jong.

Beyond that, North Korea’s latest missile launches come at a sensitive time. U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping are scheduled to hold a summit on September 24 in Washington, D.C. It will be Xi’s first trip to the U.S. capital in 10 years, and his first official state visit to the United States since 2015. This week also marks the start of the United Nations General Assembly.

Separately, an explosion during a mine-clearing operation in the Demilitarized Zone injured three South Korean military officers on September 21, according to the South’s Joint Chiefs of Staff. The blast came at about 10:50 a.m. KST south of the Military Demarcation Line (MDL) in the western sector, where soldiers from the Army 25th Division were opening a search route through ground not yet checked for mines and unexploded ordnance. Two of the officers were flown to a military hospital by emergency helicopter and the commander of the reconnaissance battalion reportedly suffered an amputation at the ankle.

The cause of the blast remains unconfirmed, and the JCS said all possibilities remain open. The military is treating a mine as the most likely explanation. It has not said whether the device was one that North Korea planted, an explosive that drifted south in heavy rain, or one that belonged to South Korea. Still, the site lies far from the area in the southern half of the zone where North Korea is believed to have buried mines even as an opposition lawmaker argued that the blast occurred near a North Korean minefield.

It was the first mine explosion to seriously injure South Korean troops south of the MDL line since August 2015 when North Korean wooden-box mines maimed two soldiers. North Korea has been laying mines and building tactical roads near the border since it declared the two Koreas hostile states.

The incident in the DMZ, as well as the missile launches, could increase public skepticism of the Lee administration’s North Korea policy. The Unification Ministry recently devised a plan to support North Korea building hospitals. South Koreans may start to question why Seoul is still making dovish overtures toward Pyongyang, which has repeatedly stressed that it has no intention of renewing the stalled inter-Korean relations.

In a press conference on September 18, before the latest missile launches and the DMZ explosion, Lee said North Korea “is clearly refusing to communicate with South Korea.” He added that Trump wants dialogue with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and that Seoul is coordinating in advance to make talks possible. Lee dismissed concerns that South Korea could be sidelined in North Korea-U.S. diplomacy.

title: Al-Qaida: 25 Years After 9/11
description: The current threat from al-Qaida is diffused. It relies on homegrown, lone-actor terrorists to carry out low-end attacks, such as stabbing and vehicle ramming.
text:
Twenty-five years after the fateful terrorist attacks on the World Trade Center and the Pentagon on September 11, 2001, the fraternity of terrorism scholars and practitioners is divided over al-Qaida’s status. Some believe that al-Qaida still poses a potent threat to global peace and security, albeit of a different nature, while others think it has lost its mojo.

Indeed, al-Qaida failed to create the Sunni global Caliphate it promised its followers. In fact, the global jihadist movement split between al-Qaida and the Islamic State (IS), which weakened the former. IS has superseded al-Qaida as the dominant global jihadist actor. The ideological tussle and inter-group fighting between al-Qaida and IS have helped security and intelligence agencies around the world to cut them to size.

The strategic defeat that al-Qaida desperately wanted to inflict upon the United States has not materialized. Indubitably, the U.S. is struggling to retain its global hegemony in the face of China’s meteoric rise, but it is for a different set of reasons. Attributing power challenges to the U.S.-led unipolar system to al-Qaida would be a gross exaggeration and distortion of facts.

In terrorism, violence is the central benchmark of evaluating the success or failure of a terrorist group. Al-Qaida Core, operating out of Afghanistan, has not carried out an international terrorist attack in more than a decade.

The majority of al-Qaida’s top leaders, barring the current de facto chief Saif al-Adel and his deputy Abd al-Rahman al-Maghrebi, have been eliminated by the U.S. in drone strikes and targeted assassinations. Saif al-Adel likely lives in a safe house in Iran and is dependent on Iranian intelligence for his own security. This has undermined his credibility and capacity to command loyalty and obedience from various al-Qaida affiliates.

Of al-Qaida’s various affiliates, Somalian al-Shabab, al-Qaida in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP) in Yemen, and Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM) in Mali are the strongest, while al-Qaida in the Indian Subcontinent (AQIS), notwithstanding its proximity to the core group, is the weakest.

AQIS has been trying to grow its network in India, especially in Indian-administered Kashmir, Bangladesh, and Pakistan. Barring some nominal successes, it has miserably failed to make an impression since its emergence in September 2014. Nevertheless, it regularly issues a flagship propaganda magazine, “Nawai Ghazwa-e-Hind,” which articulates al-Qaida’s official stance on critical developments. AQIS has been embedding its fighters with various Pakistani jihadist groups to obfuscate its involvement in terrorist attacks, which is consistent with al-Qaida Core’s strategy of focusing on the near-enemy, as discussed below.

Al-Qaida is currently facing a serious leadership crisis, and it will not be surprising if various affiliates still loyal to the mother group adopt the pathway of IS and Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS). The former’s defection made it the most feared jihadist group and leader of the global jihadist movement, while the latter’s rebellion eased its path to victory in Syria and helped it gain international recognition.

Al-Qaida’s Malian affiliate, JNIM, which has made great territorial strides in Mali, is contemplating following HTS’ footsteps and disassociating from al-Qaida to avoid isolation and reprisals ahead of its complete victory.

At its peak, al-Qaida funded and strategically guided different jihadist groups around the world, including the Taliban regime in Afghanistan. Ironically, it is now dependent on the Taliban both for its finances and security. Al-Qaida Core has been reduced to a former shadow of itself; it inspires no confidence in the younger generation of jihadists who self-radicalize online and engage in lone-actor terrorism.

Those who believe al-Qaida continues to be a threat to international peace and security argue that after two decades of the war on terror, the U.S. left Afghanistan by handing back power to the Taliban. Al-Qaida successfully weathered the U.S. strategic pressure and retained its presence in Afghanistan, which constitutes a victory even if it is a pyrrhic one, they claim.

In five years of Taliban rule, al-Qaida has reconstituted itself by embedding with local jihadist movements in Pakistan. It is actively supporting an umbrella militant alliance, Ittehad-ul-Mujahideen Pakistan (IMP). The resurgence of militant violence in Pakistan since August 2021 has increased al-Qaida’s footprint, especially in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan. Likewise, al-Qaida affiliates in Yemen, Somalia, and Mali have made substantive territorial, financial, and organizational gains.

The threat al-Qaida poses today is qualitatively different from the security challenges it posed to international peace in 2001. The absence of an international mass casualty attack does not make al-Qaida less relevant. Rather, there is a need to take a more nuanced view of the threat it poses.

The terror group has not changed its goal of creating a global Sunni Caliphate or carrying out attacks in the West. However, as the international security environment has evolved, al-Qaida has also changed its trajectory and modus operandi. Now, it is focusing on the near-enemy, i.e., Muslim democratic states that it deems apostate, instead of the “far-enemy,” meaning the United States.

Al-Qaida is no longer investing its time and focus in high-profile attacks like 9/11; rather, it is creating space for itself by aligning with local jihadist movements and obscuring its presence to avoid counterterrorism pressure. It is adopting emerging technologies like drones and 3D-printed technology to build weapons, investing in maritime capabilities, and striving to achieve financial self-sufficiency. All these elements make al-Qaida a potent threat in the long run.

Over a period of 25 years, al-Qaida has shown resilience. It has survived by adapting, decentralizing operations to regional franchises, and moving ideological indoctrination to encrypted social and digital media platforms.

The current threat from al-Qaida is diffused. It relies on homegrown, lone-actor terrorists to carry out low-end attacks, such as stabbing, vehicle ramming, and shootings in the West. This threat, due to its low intensity, is more manageable but less detectable and preventable because people are self-radicalizing online. Furthermore, al-Qaida is engaging in hybrid warfare tactics where violence is one of several elements it is using to achieve its objectives.

So, the singular fixation with al-Qaida’s violent credentials is flawed. Al-Qaida engages in information, ideological, and cognitive warfare alongside violent extremism. It has advised its affiliates to focus on governance by moderating their aggressive jihadist postures.

On balance, al-Qaida has survived the war on terror, and it is far from a spent force; however, the threat it poses is now manageable. At the same time, it is facing credibility and leadership crises that are not likely to subside anytime soon.

On the one hand, for the Taliban regime, al-Qaida is a liability. It can neither own the group nor disown it. The former will result in international diplomatic and security pressure, and the latter will dent the Taliban’s ideological legitimacy in the jihadist world. Likewise, for flourishing regional affiliates like Al-Shabab, JNIM, and Al-Qaida in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP), al-Qaida Core is more of a nuisance than an ideological mothership.

Al-Qaida remains relevant, but it has evolved and the threat it poses has also evolved. Putting this fact in perspective will help both practitioners and scholars to develop a better understanding of the terror group.
