title: America’s AI Safety Dilemma and the Trump-Xi Summit
description: Washington will not slow its own AI labs. Slowing China’s instead would look like safety policy, but it could cost the United States the one AI deal within reach this week.
text:
On September 12, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published an essay titled “We Must Pace the Frontier,” arguing that the leading labs should deliberately slow how fast their models gain new capabilities. Within hours, his chief rivals lined up behind him: Sam Altman said OpenAI would match Anthropic’s commitment to host independent evaluators, and Elon Musk replied, “Dario is right.”

Two days later, U.S. President Donald Trump called fears of an AI catastrophe a hoax and claimed that amid the backlash against AI and data centers, “the only one that is happy about it is China.”

That exchange hangs over Xi Jinping’s arrival in Washington this week, the first state visit by a Chinese leader in more than a decade.

The AI pacing debate is a dilemma the Trump administration cannot resolve at home. There is rising pressure from the public to slow down, but the government is convinced that slowing down means losing to China. The easiest way out runs through Beijing. If Washington will not slow American AI, it can try to slow Chinese AI instead, through tighter controls on chips, compute, and access to American models. That option is tempting precisely because it is an area where the safety-minded and the competition-focused, the labs and the White House, already agree.

But Trump should know that choosing this path would also undercut the most promising AI outcome on the summit table.

Public calls to slow the pace of AI development are growing in urgency. In a new Politico poll, 63 percent of respondents saw a real chance that AI could wipe out humanity, and a CBS News/YouGov survey found that most Americans want AI development slowed, though not stopped. With the midterms weeks away, AI risk is becoming an electoral issue, and the labs’ own warnings have lent that anxiety new credibility.

The Trump administration has treated the debate as a threat to American primacy. Trump said he wants to stay ahead of China because “whoever wins AI wins.” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned that there is “no day after tomorrow if China wins” on AI – “nothing [else] would matter.”

Politico’s polling showed that Americans are split, 43 percent to 37 percent, on whether falling behind other countries is acceptable in exchange for safer AI. However, Trump’s supporters have a clear opinion: people who voted for him in 2024 preferred staying in the AI race (50 percent) to prioritizing safety issues (38 percent).

Since Trump is unwilling to slow down AI development and risk falling behind, that leaves the administration searching for a way to look serious about AI risk without constraining American labs. Amodei had a suggestion. The Anthropic CEO’s plan recommended an “attempt to coordinate with authoritarian governments, to the extent this is possible, while taking seriously the challenges of verifying compliance.” Beijing is at the top of the list of authoritarian governments to talk with.

Even while calling for coordination, however, Amodei urged the Trump administration to keep “powerful AI chips or semiconductor manufacturing equipment” out of Chinese hands, close “chip smuggling operations” and remote access to data centers, “crack down on unauthorized distillation,” and harden labs against theft of model weights. Amodei explicitly agreed with Bessent that “a Chinese lead in AI would pose grave danger for the United States and the world.” In his framework, safety at home depends on a durable lead abroad.

That points to a clear area of overlap: the White House can embrace the “slow China” half of the AI industry’s agenda while rejecting the “slow ourselves” half. This is already playing out.

Earlier this month, the NSA, FBI, and CISA jointly accused six Chinese developers, including DeepSeek and Alibaba, of industrial-scale distillation of American frontier models. In July Bessent said Washington could sanction firms found stealing from American models. Trump and Xi are also expected to discuss whether Chinese firms can keep renting top Nvidia compute through Southeast Asian data centers, while the suspension of the Affiliates Rule, which extends export blacklists to affiliates of listed firms, expires with the Busan truce in November.

On semiconductors, restricting Chinese access would be a bigger shift. The Trump administration has cleared roughly 10 Chinese companies to buy Nvidia’s H200 chips, though Chinese customs has kept nearly all the chips out. But a restriction package lets the White House tell anxious voters it is acting on AI risk while asking nothing of American companies. The louder the domestic debate grows, the better that trade looks.

Beijing has already read the room and decided this is the most likely outcome of the United States’ AI pacing debate. China’s Foreign Ministry answered Amodei’s essay by warning that “fearmongering, confrontation and vicious competition” would disrupt global AI governance. The state-run Global Times called the slowdown push a “Cold War playbook” for the sector. China’s Commerce Ministry threatened “resolute countermeasures” if Washington uses the distillation accusations to suppress Chinese firms. Among other options, China could resurrect the rare earth exports controls that were suspended under the Busan truce.

Beijing’s official line is not the whole Chinese conversation, though. This spring, two of China’s most senior AI governance figures – Xue Lan, who chairs China’s national expert committee on AI governance, and Zeng Yi, dean of the Beijing Institute of AI Safety and Governance – joined a Capitol Hill discussion convened by Senator Bernie Sanders. Xue acknowledged the geopolitical rivalry but called for “safe zones” where American and Chinese scientists can build safety standards and protocols together. Zeng, whose institute has catalogued 94 classes of AI safety threats, warned last week that AI’s catastrophic risks, including “the hidden danger of human extinction,” are mounting daily. Both Xue and Zeng helped draft China’s national AI governance principles.

The Trump administration now has a real AI safety deliverable within reach. In New York on September 20, Bessent proposed a standing China-U.S. AI dialogue with a way for each side to flag AI incidents serious enough to threaten national security. A standing channel would be a first for Trump’s second term: the AI consultations he and Xi discussed in Beijing in May were never formalized. Beijing’s response, however, was unclear.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said chip export controls were not part of the AI safety mechanism discussions. That separation is the right instinct, but Beijing is likely to see the two issues as inextricably linked. If China sees “AI safety” as a synonym for containment, voices like Xue’s and Zeng’s lose ground at home. Beijing will worry that every notification through the new channel creates a pretext for new restrictions on Chinese companies.

China-U.S. crisis management mechanisms already have a poor record. After the United States shot down a Chinese high-altitude balloon that had traversed the U.S. mainland in February 2023, Beijing declined a call from the U.S. defense secretary, later explaining that Washington had not created “the proper atmosphere” for dialogue. An AI incident channel that China sees as an extension of the technology war will go quiet exactly when it is needed.

Amodei anticipated this objection and rejected it, arguing that restrictions “increase the leverage held by democracies and make an agreement more likely in the future.” That may hold for a treaty negotiated from a position of strength years from now, but not for an incident channel that runs on day-to-day trust. Amodei himself wrote that sharing information about misaligned models can have value even without formal agreements. That is exactly what a notification channel would do.

Washington can manage this dilemma without breaking the Trump-Xi summit. If the Trump-Xi summit needs a first substantive commitment, Amodei’s essay suggested a modest one: an agreement that neither side will use AI to produce biological weapons.

Beyond that, the leaders should establish the notification mechanism as a standalone safety channel, insulated from trade and technology-control disputes, and pair it with a technical track that brings government evaluators at the Commerce Department’s Center for AI Standards and Innovation together with experts like Xue and Zeng. That track could define what counts as a reportable incident and build shared tests for biological and cyber risks without touching the chips, compute, and model weights where the race is actually run. It would also serve U.S. primacy: if Bessent is right that the real threat to AI safety is “letting any nation other than the United States set the global standard,” Washington should want to be in the room when Chinese experts help write one.

To make cooperation on AI risk more feasible, the United States should call its restrictions what they are. Enforcement against model distillation or chip smuggling may be justified on intellectual property or security grounds, but selling it as the answer to AI risk lets the White House dodge the domestic aspect of AI safety while poisoning the bilateral effort.

The domestic question needs a domestic answer. Bessent has shown an openness to safety concerns. Testifying before the House Financial Services Committee on September 15, he rejected the liability exemption the labs are seeking, arguing that safety is best guaranteed when developers are “liable for what they build and generate.” The independent evaluators that Anthropic and OpenAI have agreed to host do not require the United States to fall behind anyone.

The pacing debate asked Washington to voluntarily slow down AI development. The administration’s answer is that China should be forced to slow down instead. That may play well at home, but it will not make American AI any safer, and it risks scuttling a China-U.S. channel on AI risk before it even begins.

Trump insists the AI race is winner-take-all. This week he can show that staying ahead of China and talking to it about shared risks are not mutually exclusive.

title: Another New Job for Saida Mirziyoyeva: Manager of the Tashkent International Financial Center
description: The daughter of the Uzbek president is head of the presidential administration and now also manager of Tashkent’s ambitious gambit to attract foreign investors.
text:
Saida Mirziyoyeva has another new job. By presidential decree – that is, by order of her own father, President Shavkat Mirziyoyev, whose administration she heads – Mirziyoyeva has been appointed manager of the Tashkent International Financial Center (TIFC).

The TIFC was proposed in a March 2026 presidential decree as part of an effort to bring in long-term foreign direct investment. The financial center aims to attract investors in a range of industries from banking, investment, and insurance services to digital assets, Islamic finance, and green tech, in addition to professional services like auditing, legal counsel, and fintech.

Signed into law in July, the TIFC will operate under a special legal regime, based on English law, with a unique regulatory framework and an independent commercial court. With this arrangement, Uzbekistan seeks to address long-standing concerns foreign investors have had by carving out a legal space that isn’t governed strictly by Uzbek law.

In pursuit of attracting foreign investors, those engaged in the TIFC will reportedly be able to hire foreigners without obtaining the usually required work permits and take advantage of special entry visa options. They will be allowed use foreign currency or cryptocurrency for payments and other monetary obligations and will benefit from tax and customs breaks until 2076.

In announcing the signing of the law in July by Mirziyoyev, Mirziyoyeva said on social media, “This is one of the most important pieces of economic news of the year and the result of reforms that we pursued for almost ten years.” She went on to argue that the TIFC’s special structures “are the mechanisms to which global investors, banks, investment funds and international financial companies are accustomed. This new regulatory ecosystem should make the country more attractive for capital, modern financial services and major international projects.”

According to a Telegram statement posted by presidential press secretary Sherzod Asadov, as manager, Mirziyoyeva will organize the agenda and preside over meetings in the absence of the financial center’s chairman – the chairman is, by law, Mirziyoyev. She will coordinate the TIFC’s launch and represent the financial center in dealings with international organizations, investors and partners – both those abroad and in Uzbekistan. She will have the authority to conclude agreements, establish working groups and “engage experts.”

In June 2025, Mirziyoyeva was appointed head of the presidential administration, effectively becoming her father’s chief of staff. Uzbekistan’s government does not have a vice president post, making Mirziyoyeva the highest-ranking official after her father. In August 2026, Uzbekistan adopted a new law regulating the presidential administration that granted Mirziyoyeva sweeping new powers – everything from judicial reforms to anti-corruption, and an automatic seat on the Security Council – and lifetime immunity to boot. She holds an extraordinarily wide range of power while being subject to no accountability outside of her father’s opinion.

Now she’s also in charge of Tashkent’s ambitious gambit to attract foreign investment.

Uzbekistan is not unique in turning to family to consolidate power. In neighboring Tajikistan, President Emomali Rahmon’s son, Rustam Emomali, holds a variety of important positions – he’s chairman of the National Assembly and also mayor of the capital, both posts he was appointed to by his father, in 2020 and 2017, respectively. As chairman of the Nation Assembly, Emomali is constitutionally next in line for the presidency, should his father resign or otherwise vacate the post. In Turkmenistan, Gurbanguly Berdimuhamedov passed the presidency on to his son Serdar in 2022 before government changed its structure to give the elder Berdimuhamedov a new position technically above that of the president.

Nepotism may be political comforting for those in power, but’s not necessarily comforting for investors.

title: Asia’s Democracy Is Being Rewired: An Early Warning for Global Democracy
description: The emerging contest in the region is between open political systems and “managed” political systems – where citizens are manipulated instead of simply repressed.
text:
Asia’s democratic trajectory is no longer defined by the binary struggle between democracy and authoritarianism. Instead, the real contest is being waged over the frameworks of participation: who controls the technology, the narrative, and the information ecosystem itself.

As we mark International Democracy Day 2026 on September 15, the global conversation on the state of democracy often focuses on the defense of established institutions. Yet, for Asia, this year’s commemoration should serve more as a moment of reckoning. The challenges facing the region are no longer solely about upholding democracy: they are about fundamentally adapting to a new, digitally-manipulated architecture of political control.

The emerging contest in the region is between open political systems and “managed” political systems – rather than explicitly closed ones. In a managed system, the boundaries of institutions and processes – such as parliaments, elections, courts, civil society, media, and free expression – are set by a manipulated information ecosystem that constrains the parameters of its operations. These “managed” systems – once thought to be unique to Asia – are increasingly being adopted by actors in the West, making the regional struggle an early warning for global democracy.

In the old system, the game plan for undemocratic control was to stop people from speaking. In the new model it is to flood the information environment until citizens internalize the boundaries of permissible political articulation and action. The problem isn’t censorship anymore. It is epistemic disinformation – making citizens believe and act based on falsehoods.

AI is accelerating this transition from the explicit repression of citizens to their systemic manipulation. Deepfakes, synthetic political content, microtargeting, automated influence operations, and algorithmic amplification now manipulate political perceptions and actions at scale. Exploited not only by authoritarian governments but also by political parties, commercial actors, foreign networks, and domestic entrepreneurs, this manipulation operates unevenly across borders – fueling distinct regional trajectories.

Rather than a uniform regional slide, Asia’s democratic map is fragmenting into divergent trajectories, characterized by specific, localized struggles over information manipulation. Asia Centre has recorded such trajectories in its reports “State-Sponsored Online Disinformation: Impact On Electoral Integrity In Thailand” and “Youth And Disinformation In Malaysia: Strengthening Electoral Integrity.”

This fragmentation confirms that Asia is not moving uniformly toward authoritarianism. Instead, the region is splitting into distinct manipulated trajectories – a distinction that is critical for anyone trying to navigate the current political landscape. Democracy is being transformed through information manipulation, and how Asian civil society responds to this transformation is critical.

Asia Centre’s 2023 empirical research published in Routledge’s “Fake News and Elections in Southeast Asia: Impact on Democracy and Human Rights” confirms that the manipulation of information, political parties, state actors, social media, and electoral institutions poses a fundamental threat. In Asia Centre’s further evaluations in 2025 assessing whether elections serve as mechanisms for authoritarian consolidation rather than democratic change, the findings were clear: an election does not automatically produce democracy. We published these findings in the Kyoto Review of Southeast Asia, “Eroding Electoral Integrity: Reasons for Democratic Backsliding in Southeast Asia.”

When examining governance, civic participation, inclusivity, legal protection, and resistance, Asia Centre recognizes civil society as essential democratic foundations rather than a mere NGO sector. The evidence demonstrates that democracy exists between elections, not just during them. As we note in our report, “Online Content Regulations in the Asia-Pacific: Limiting Civil Society’s Capacity to Hold Governments Accountable,” a combination of restrictive regulations and funding constraints continues to shrink civic space and hamper civil society operations.

Amid youth-led political movements in the region, in 2025 Asia Centre convened a conference, “Youths, Democracy & Electoral Legitimacy in Asia.” The meeting explored the role of youth participation as a vital buffer against democratic erosion. A key concern that emerged was the urgent need to remove barriers to youth political involvement and transition young people from a passive electoral demographic to active political leaders. In 2026 we see that youth-led reform movements in India, Thailand, and Sri Lanka have struggled to achieve democratic consolidation. The question remains: can Asian democracy renew itself through a new generation?

The emergence of artificial intelligence complicates this challenge further, fundamentally altering the frameworks of political participation and presenting new hurdles for these movements. With the rise of digitalization, AI is intensifying divisions across various fault lines – from ethnicity and religion to economic inequality and political ideology – effectively driving deep societal polarization.

But as AI presents hurdles, it also represents a significant opportunity to expand the democracy agenda by changing the systems through which democracy operates – the relationship between citizens, information, governments, elections and civil society.

Democracy – through pluralism, accountability, and non-violent political engagement – can serve as an antidote to polarization. The question for the region is whether Asia has a democracy movement capable of responding to these changes.

The good news is that there continues to be a proliferation of democracy organizations in Asia. In 2026, when the Centre convened the Global Democracy Coalition (GDC) Asia Regional Forum, members noted that what is needed is greater coordination and better use of resources, including the use of AI for democracy work.

To this end, the Asia Centre has established an AI Hub to support digital transformation of CSOs. In a previous commentary, we outlined our mission to ensure CSOs are not passive observers of the AI revolution but active shapers of it.

Asia doesn’t need another democracy rescue package designed elsewhere. It needs Asian democratic foundations: locally rooted research, civic education, information integrity, AI literacy, youth participation, cross-border civil society cooperation, and stronger connections between political parties and citizens.

In short, Asian democracy is undergoing a profound transformation. The future will not depend solely on whether authoritarian regimes intensify repression or democratic governments defend liberal norms. The question is no longer whether we can defend liberal norms, but whether we can build a new digital-era architecture before the old political ecosystem is fully rewired by those who oppose those norms.

Asia Centre is a member of the Global Democracy Coalition. For more information about Asia Centre and the AI HUB, visit asiacentre.org.

title: Asia’s Economic Integration: A Roadmap for Peacebuilding in the Middle East
description: Economic cooperation in the Asia-Pacific has been the key driver of peace since 1952.
text:
When the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, ASEAN, was formed in 1967, the five founding states intended to produce a front against the spread of communism. The venture has since grown to include a total of 11 countries, producing a remarkable set of unforeseen consequences, from becoming the fifth-largest economy in the world to reinforcing peace across a swath of diverse and developing countries.

Instead of pursuing Cold War initiatives, the bloc has become increasingly integrated, tied together through manufacturing supply chains, trade infrastructure, and shared financial institutions like the Chiang Mai Initiative. ASEAN now produces over $4 trillion in GDP and has a population of 678 million people. The collaboration’s biggest success, however, has not simply been increased commerce. With economic integration comes regional stabilization and peace, a consequence further fostered by the signing of the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) in 2020, which includes Australia, China, Japan, New Zealand, and South Korea. Economic cooperation in the Asia-Pacific has been the key driver of peace in the region ever since 1952 with the Treaty of San Francisco, and it serves today as a key example of how market mechanics can drive peacebuilding. In fact, it was ASEAN that eroded tensions from the Konfrontasi war in the early 1960s, and has solidified the climate of peace between the Southeast Asian members ever since.

Economists and politicians have often considered the question of whether trade contributes to peaceful relations between states. The affirmative answer is not novel; however, in the case of ASEAN and the Asia-Pacific, the specifics begin to clarify the theory. Peacebuilding through economic means is more a matter of building economic capacity and trade interdependence than of simply trading goods between nations. This crucial specification turns the Asia-Pacific from a successful case study into a model for peacebuilding elsewhere, and it is one that has been imitated by the Gulf Cooperation Council or, more recently, by the C5 in Central Asia.

Economic interdependence is a consequence of cooperation, occurring over time by building trust and relying on companies that diversify operations across countries. Daron Acemoglu, a Nobel Prize winner in Economic Sciences, has regularly argued for this by pointing out that both prosperity and stability mutually flow from systems or institutions that offer a broad stake in the economic growth of a nation. Thus, when firms create cross-border commerce, war becomes economically unviable and politically undesirable. The principle is not exclusive to the Asia-Pacific, and despite ASEAN’s success, it is clear that outliers perpetuate risks by building up economic barriers instead of interdependence. Examples include relations between North and South Korea or China and Taiwan. The question, therefore, remains: how can peace be built today through economic interdependence, or in other words, how can rivals begin working together in an economic capacity?

Answers learned in the Asia-Pacific could resound further away. In the Middle East, for example, diplomatic efforts for peace in Afghanistan, Iraq, Syria, and Israel and the Palestinian Territories have worked through a long campaign of advocacy; however, it is only with the additional incentives that economic cooperation brings that peace efforts actually remain sustainable and enduring. For Israel and the Palestinian Territories, economic interdependence and a shared aspiration could enhance the ongoing international effort to ameliorate decades-long tensions. Syria offers an immediate test case as well. When the Assad regime fell in 2025 and the United States and the European Union both lifted sanctions, organizations began to move in, building relationships and supporting the fragile new state’s desire for peace. American companies have established power generation projects, the Gulf states and Turkey have signed dozens of economic memoranda of understanding with the new state, and startups like Behti Betak or nonprofit organizations like the Words of Isa are building grassroots relationships aimed at creating a newly integrated Syria, driving peace across the Middle East. Integration leads to interdependence. Interdependence self-reinforces peace.

Peacebuilding of this sort may be especially critical for Israel and the Palestinian Territories, where conflict and violence have persisted for decades before the Gaza War. Reconstruction and reconciliation efforts require that businesses spread their operations across the divide. Organizations like the Portland Trust, based in the United Kingdom, have focused on the region on the basis that economic co-operation and dialogue between the parties is inseparable from diplomatic peacebuilding efforts. And such economic development (alongside political will) can create hope, ambition, and opportunities for Palestinians. The founding Chief Executive of The Portland Trust, Lord Jonathan Kestenbaum, brings a personal history to the work of reconciliation. His family’s own flight from Nazi persecution ultimately led them to the UK, where he grew up, and whilst a student in London, he was General Secretary (mazkir) of Bnei Akiva UK, a branch of the global youth movement. He then studied at the Hebrew University in Jerusalem in the 1980s completing an MA in education, and thereafter helped to build an international training program for young educators. As a dual national at the time, Kestenbaum was conscripted to military service, with this experience influencing his life-long commitment to reconciliation between Palestinians and Israelis with a particular focus on building bridges through economic co-operation.

Lord Kestenbaum returned home to the U.K. after a few years in Jerusalem and gave up his dual nationality, retaining only British citizenship. He helped found the Portland Trust, and spent many years fostering peace efforts between Israelis and Palestinians. This history gave him a grounding in the region, a commitment to co-existence and a familiarity that exemplifies how peacebuilding through commerce is not abstract policy but is instead built through relationships and real-life experiences. The Portland Trust has to date worked extensively to support Palestinians and Israelis through projects like the Palestinian Agriculture Impact Fund and the building of the city of Rawabi.

Personal experiences bring markets together, and when they come together, they accelerate growth and integration among an increasing number of actors. Each of these actors learns to empathize with their business partners, regardless of historical or political differences. The process reinforces peace, builds harmony, and creates trust. In the case of Israel and the Palestinian Territories, the process is needed alongside reconstruction efforts like Trump’s Board of Peace, which aims to produce lasting peace but has yet to break ground.

Peace is not guaranteed through economics; however, throughout the last century, and in the case of the Asia-Pacific, it has become the most reliable mechanism of sustaining peace, cultivating the types of relationships that grow closer instead of farther apart. Private investment adds a financial tie to the process; however, intentional relationships with an empathetic desire for peace fundamentally secure the process. Southeast Asia’s history, compared to Syria’s cautious reopening or Gaza’s Board of Peace, shows that commerce can lay groundwork that politics otherwise cannot. The region will need institutional support, perhaps even at the level of an ASEAN, but the foundation is growing. More inter-state commerce will bring stronger relationships, paving the way forward to a future of peace, stability, and economic growth.

title: Assam Government Encroaches Into a World Heritage Site in India’s Northeast
description: The encroached area is part of Manas National Park’s core tiger and Bengal florican habitats.
text:
Manas National Park in the northeast Indian state of Assam is in danger. The Assam government, which should be protecting this 1,176-acre World Heritage Site, has encroached on the park for several years.

Originally part of the North Kamrup Reserve Forest, the land under contention, which is spread over 9.3 sq km, was given on a 30-year lease to the Indian government for setting up a seed farm. After the lease expired in 2001, the area became part of the Manas National Park and Tiger Reserve, the Assam forest department said in a letter to the Bodoland Territorial Council (BTC) that governs this region.

In the letter, the Assam forest department pointed out that the BTC had leased the encroached land for cultivation. Sources claimed that local farmers are engaged in farming in the area, which is officially not permitted inside a wildlife sanctuary, national park or World Heritage Site. The letter made a case for its handover to the forest department. The forest department also urged the Assam government to convince the BTC to return the encroached area to the Assam forest department

The area that has been allegedly encroached by local farmers with the BTC’s consent is part of the Manas National Park’s core tiger and Bengal florican habitats. This falls in the Bhuyanpara Range of the park, which is also where the erstwhile government-owned Kokilabari Seed Farm was located.

Concerned about the encroachment and its devastating impact on the park, the National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA) has also been reminding the Assam government to initiate action over the past few years.

In a communique dated July 30, 2026, which was also posted on social media, the NTCA asked the chief secretary of the Assam government to “intervene” and facilitate the “handing over” of the encroached area to the Manas Tiger Reserve authorities. It also reminded the government that a directive on the issue had been sent on June 11, but the authority was “not aware about the progress made in the matter so far.”

Manas National Park was designated as a reserve forest in 1907 and declared a wildlife sanctuary in 1928. In 1973, it became India’s first tiger reserve. Spread across an area of 2,837 sq km, the park was the largest in the country. In 2004, the park secured another feather in its cap when BirdLife International, a global partnership of bird conservation organizations, identified it as an Important Bird Area. UNESCO named it a World Heritage Site in 1985. “Manas has exceptional importance within the Indian sub-continent’s protected areas, as one of the most significant remaining natural areas in the region, where sizeable populations of a large number of threatened species continue to survive,” UNESCO observed.

Manas faced several challenges in the 1980s and 1990s. It was adversely impacted by the powerful insurgency that swept Assam in the late 1980s. With a large area of the park becoming a no-go zone for officials, environmental activists and tourists, conservation efforts suffered a big blow.

Poaching of the one-horned rhino also grew in this period. The number of rhinos reportedly dwindled from around 100 in the late 1980s to zero by the time peace returned to the region in the mid-2000s. Wildlife researcher Anwaruddin Choudhury estimated in 1996 that over 80 percent of the park’s large mammals had also been decimated. In 1992, UNESCO’s World Heritage Convention declared that Manas was “in danger.”

A former official of the forest department told The Diplomat that Assam’s Bharatiya Janata Party-led government was apprehensive of a “backlash” from the BTC if the encroachment is cleared from the park. The Bodoland People’s Front (BPF), which rules the council, is also an ally in the BJP-led coalition government in Assam.

Meanwhile, the Gauhati High Court has issued orders to the Assam government and the BTC to prevent further encroachment in the park after activist Rohit Choudhury filed a Public Interest Litigation (PIL).

The encroachment of national parks lays bare the lackadaisical approach of the Assam government towards the conservation of forests and wildlife in the country. The government evicted illegal settlers from the World Heritage Site of Kaziranga National Park, also in Assam, in 2016, only after the Gauhati High Court intervened and issued orders.

title: At UNGA, Kyrgyz President Japarov Once Again Complains About Sanctions
description: Japarov also thanked Donald Trump for ending funding of NGOs.
text:
Amid his 20-minute remarks before the United Nations General Assembly this week, Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov took time to complain about sanctions and thank U.S. President Donald Trump for ceasing support to NGOs.

“…[T]oday sanctions are, in some cases, used by individual countries as an instrument of interference in the internal affairs of sovereign states,” Japarov said. “The negative consequences of unjustified unilateral sanctions also affect small countries such as ours, which are at the stage of formation and development, and this raises concern among other small states as well.”

Japarov went on to claim that “some major states, in pursuit of their own interests, put pressure on smaller countries such as Kyrgyzstan, attempting to force them to bargain over certain matters and issuing ultimatums.”

At no point did Japarov lay out specifically what countries he believes are pressuring Kyrgyzstan, and to what end.

Then, in the middle of his commentary about sanctions, Japarov pivoted to lauding the U.S. president – although the Trump administration has maintained the prior administration’s sanctions on various Kyrgyz entities.

“In this context, I would like to take this opportunity to note the decision made by the President of the United States His Excellency Mr. Donald Trump after taking office to halt funding of non-governmental organizations around the world,” Japarov said. “As a result, interference by NGOs in the internal affairs and policies of developing states has practically ceased.”

For Japarov, the two issues are inextricably linked. Last year at UNGA, he stated that “sanctions imposed on Kyrgyzstan are based on false information spread by certain non-governmental organizations and malicious citizens.”

Japarov has not specified which NGOs or “malicious citizens” have provided this “false information” that supposedly landed Kyrgyz business and banks on sanctions lists.

In April, Kyrgyzstan’s Bakai Bank won a case in a Belgian commercial court against the Open Dialogue Foundation (ODF) for its publication of reports alleging that the bank was involved in the circumvention of sanctions against Russia. Note that the bank had not been sanctioned. The court classified the NGO as a “commercial enterprise,” opening it to liability as if it were a market competitor.

As the World Liberty Congress, a global alliance of pro-democracy leaders, said in a statement: “The court required published information to meet a commercial verification standard designed for disputes between market operators, a test that is structurally impossible for any organization working in an authoritarian jurisdiction where access to primary banking records is unavailable.”

Meanwhile, also in April 2026, the EU aimed its “anti-circumvention tool” at Kyrgyzstan, the first country so targeted. In the subsequent months, Kyrgyz authorities pantomimed taking action. In June 2026, two state-owned banks claimed to have ended partnerships with more than 130 clients due to sanctions risks. In August, another round of cut connections was announced.

However, Kyrgyz authorities have never specified which companies were affected, making it all but impossible to confirm whether companies that present actual sanctions risks have been cut loose.

According to RFE/RL’s Kyrgyz Service, Azattyk, as of June 2026, 31 companies from Kyrgyzstan were under Western sanctions, including five banks. While three Tajik banks were removed from the EU sanctions list in May, the Kyrgyz banks – such as Keremet Bank, Kapital Bank, Eurasian Savings Bank, and EcoIslamicBank – remain designated by the EU, the U.K., and/or the U.S.

After thanking Trump “for ending the funding of NGOs,” Japarov continued discussing sanctions, arguing that the decision to impose sanctions should “be taken in accordance with the Charter of the United Nations and exclusively within the mandate of the Security Council.”

Kyrgyzstan this year won a non-permanent seat on the U.N. Security Council.

Japarov went on to speak of the U.N. in terms that seem divorced from the body’s current hamstrung reality. “Every decision of the United Nations should be implemented without delay. If a state fails to implement such decision and other countries cease cooperation with it, the effectiveness of sanctions will increase,” he argued.

The permanent members of the UNSC – China, Russia, France, the U.K., and the U.S. – stand on diametrically opposed ends of the global order and this has effectively neutered its possible decisiveness – whether on sanctions or anything else. For example, in September 2022, Russia vetoed a Security Council resolution condemning Moscow’s attempted annexation of parts of Ukraine. The U.S. has repeatedly blocked resolutions targeting Israel. China joined Russia earlier this month to veto an effort to extend the mandate of independent experts monitoring sanctions on Iran.

Suggesting that the UNSC become the central clearinghouse for all sanctions is effectively a call for there to be no sanctions, ever.

title: Australia Launches Bid for a UN Security Council Seat
description: If Australia is successful in returning to the council in 2029, it will be under significantly different circumstances than when it last held a seat.
text:
Last week at the United Nations General Assembly, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese officially launched Australia’s campaign for a 2029-2030 non-permanent Security Council seat. Australia last held one of the non-permanent seats in 2013-2014, a period of geopolitics that now seems an entire era away, not just over a decade.

Given that we have now entered into a new, far more uncertain, period of international affairs, Canberra has decided that it should have a seat at the table to help shape the global environment. In his bid launch, Albanese argued that foreign conflicts – and potential conflicts – will increasingly affect Australia’s security, economy, and way of life. A seat on the Security Council would give Australia a direct role in negotiating resolutions, responding to international crises, and shaping the U.N.’s approach to emerging security challenges. It would also provide an opportunity to strengthen Australia’s diplomatic relationships within and beyond the Indo-Pacific.

Central to Australia’s campaign is its commitment to an international order governed by rules rather than the exercise of power alone. As a middle power, Australia has a strong interest in protecting the sovereignty of smaller states and ensuring that international disputes are resolved through diplomacy rather than coercion. These principles have become pronounced following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and China’s disregard of UNCLOS in the South China Sea. Australia wants to use a Security Council seat to uphold international law, prevent conflict, and strengthen institutions that allow countries to determine their own futures without domination by larger powers.

This worldview may seem quaint. It is clear that three of the five permanent members of the Security Council – Russia, China, and the United States – have a lack of interest in upholding international law at present. A French presidential election in April 2027 may produce a new leader who likewise has a suspicion of the constraining power of international law. The ideals that Australia seeks to uphold may find little support among the Security Council’s most powerful members.

Does this make Australia’s bid for a Security Council seat futile?

It certainly makes what Australia would like to achieve more difficult. But there is now a certain pragmatism within Canberra, rather than an idealism or nostalgia for a previous era of geopolitics. The country will work with the global environment as it is to the advantage of Australia’s interests as best it can.

The most practical response to this new era is to simply be in the rooms where the changes are taking place. Australia wants to be influential in how the world responds to emerging threats that extend beyond traditional military conflict. Cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, and rapidly developing digital technologies are creating new vulnerabilities that require global responses. Many of the U.N. institutions were not designed to address such challenges, and Australia sees a role in helping shape how these institutions evolve.

Alongside this, Australia’s ambition is also to be a voice for Pacific Island countries. A Security Council seat would provide another platform through which to advance the shared concerns of Pacific Islands Forum countries, particularly the relationship between climate change and international security. Australia has already identified ocean and climate security as priorities for its prospective term, recognizing that rising sea levels, environmental degradation, and resource insecurity present serious challenges to countries in its immediate region.

Yet the most important reason for gaining a Security Council seat will be to learn more about how the disruptive members of the Permanent Five think and bargain. For a country whose strategic environment is increasingly shaped by these disruptions, the best path to successful navigation is by knowing as much as possible about how the world is shifting through the interests, attitudes, and ideologies of the great powers.

When Australia last sat on the Security Council over a decade ago its role was simply to help reinforce an order that had broad support, and particularly the support of the United States. If Australia is successful in returning to the council in 2029 it will be under significantly different circumstances. Australia’s position now is that it cannot afford to be a bystander in this period of major geopolitical change. Restoring a world more comfortable to Australia seems unlikely, but making sure Australia can exert some influence as the rules are being rewritten is now vital.

title: Australia Should Work With China, Not Try to Contain It
description: China’s growing power is reshaping the region. Australia should respond with diplomacy and stronger economic ties rather than a military confrontation it cannot hope to win.
text:
Greg Sheridan has always been provocative. The foreign editor of The Australian is well known for his strident view that Australia should fully embrace American military power. One recent sermon focused on the need to support the U.S. Navy base at HMAS Stirling. “Frankly,” he writes, “I’d much rather entrust Australia’s security to the U.S. Navy than to the Albanese government.”

Sheridan then moves to flattery for Labor’s resident Kentucky Colonel, aka the minister for AUKUS, Richard Marles. Marles, he says, has “done quite well on the critical question of U.S. alliance management.” Despite his distaste for most things Labor, Sheridan concludes that Marles is a good fit for the job at hand: kowtowing to the U.S. military and its boss, the belligerent Pete Hegseth. He claims we don’t need to pretend that Stirling is an Australian military base because “we actively and happily shelter under the U.S. extended nuclear umbrella.” Sheridan proposes that the U.S. and Australia should now draw up “common battle plans” to prepare for conflict with “the only candidate for adversary – China”

There is no doubt China has developed its People’s Liberation Army (PLA) land, navy, air force, marines, rocket force, and cyber warfare capabilities to now claim military ascendancy in the South China Sea and beyond. In June, the Lowy Institute in Sydney released a well-researched analysis of the PLA’s military strength entitled “Understanding the Chinese military threat to Australia.”

Authored by Sam Roggeveen and David Vallance, the study is good work. It explains China’s rise and President Xi Jinping’s aim to complete China’s “great rejuvenation” by 2049, the 100th anniversary of Mao’s revolutionary victory. By then, the authors assert, China will be a prosperous, technologically advanced and a global military superpower – “a world class force.” Many would say this has already been achieved.

The Chinese submarine-launched ballistic missile test conducted on July 6 in the Pacific confirmed that the Chinese Navy now has the capability to reach the Australian mainland. Despite the complaints voiced by Penny Wong about “destabilization of the region” and the Prime Minister’s accusation of “a provocative act,” no criticism is ever made by Australia of comparable practices by U.S. forces.

On the day of the Chinese test, The New York Times reported that “the United States routinely carries out test launches of ballistic missiles from land or sea, including one fired from California at a target in the Marshall Islands this March.” They say the U.S. conducts five to 10 tests of its Minuteman and Trident missiles over the Pacific every year. Australia’s hypocrisy is breathtaking.

While analysis of China’s growing military capabilities – as distinct from its threat – is relevant to understanding our legitimate defense needs, it should be understood that China already has the capability to interdict Australia’s trade routes and undersea communications technology – as well as to conduct cyber operations against our critical communications and energy infrastructure. None of this requires missiles to be fired in anger, but there is no reason to conclude that China intends any such interdiction or military threat to Australia.

Contrast this with the fact that China is, by far, Australia’s largest trading partner, taking one-third of our exports, providing 570,000 direct jobs in Australia, and driving two-way trade worth $200 billion per annum. The conclusion is surely that China already has the ability to subdue Australia economically without firing a shot. China also has the ability to continue making Australia rich.

Currently Australia is engaged in what the Canberra press gallery is calling “a diplomatic knife fight” with China over the security preferences of small Pacific nations. There are now calls for a region-wide security network that The Australian says “will further marginalize Beijing.” Former Australian ambassador to China, Dr. Geoff Raby, says the AUKUS deal sends a “very clear signal to the leadership in China that Australia now sees China as an enemy.” Raby and other experienced diplomats have consistently warned us that Australia needs to rely more on diplomacy and statecraft rather than national security rhetoric and military posturing.

Whereas there are good reasons for Australia to invest more in Pacific nations to counter climate change and support infrastructure development, the recent move to convert those relationships into military alliances is wrong-headed and provocative. This policy may also complicate collaborative work with our neighbors in Southeast Asia. Engaging in cooperative regional diplomacy with ASEAN nations and engaging respectfully with China is far preferable to stoking hostility and inciting a conflict that Australia cannot win.

China is asserting its right to exercise power and influence in our region. Some of its actions are open to strong criticism and challenge. But the question we should consider is this: are we more likely to influence China’s behavior as a great power through military containment and confrontation – or by engaging proactively through middle-power statecraft?

A reasonable conclusion is that the rise of China to superpower status is a reality that Australian foreign policy must embrace. The U.S., despite its war-mongering in other theaters, is pulling back from its position as overlord in the Asia-Pacific. Beijing reads this as tacit U.S. recognition of China’s emergence as a strategic and military equal. While Washington prods Japan, South Korea, the Philippines, Taiwan, and Australia to spend more on weapons and develop Sheridan’s relished “battle plans,” Uncle Sam is leaving the front line for its proxies to defend. That is a fool’s errand in any language.

Japan has its own East Asia security preoccupations, South Korea wants détente with North Korea and China, and Taiwan wants the status quo. Only the weak and brash military of the Philippines think a fight with China is advisable. Meanwhile, Australia dithers with AUKUS and a confused diplomacy of “strategic equilibrium” – all while striving to conjure a Pacific alliance of microstates to confront and contain China.

After Suez in 1956, Great Britain, the motherland, finally revealed its impotence as a world power. By then, Australia had already switched horses to pay tribute to Washington. Now, after Vietnam, Iraq, Afghanistan and Iran, the ability of the U.S. to project power across the globe is manifestly waning. Like all empires in decline, America has degenerated into a rogue state engaged in endless conflicts. For Australia, the new geopolitical reality presents a historic opportunity to recalibrate our defense and foreign policy.

Perhaps we should embrace our new ally Papua New Guinea’s dictum: “a friend to all – an enemy to none.” It would surely work better than the current policy of barely concealed hostility toward China. The decline of American power in the Pacific is irreversible because China’s economic, diplomatic, and military rise is inexorable. There is no chance that Australia can resist that power by trying to contain it. It would be, to borrow Paul Keating’s famous metaphor, “like throwing a handful of toothpicks at the mountain.” Our wisest course is to embrace China’s rise and influence it through good neighbor statecraft and the strengthening of existing economic ties.

The irony of our time is that China’s rise, including the military power that Sheridan and Marles so fear, may well prevent war in our region. America’s growing reluctance to confront that power may save us from a toxic alliance that serves only to stimulate endless strife.

title: Australia’s Broken Hill: Where Children Are Sacrificed to Mining Interests
description: A historical mining town in Australia’s outback is confronting severe lead-contamination health threats, disproportionately affecting Aboriginal children.
text:
Broken Hill is an Australian mining town steeped in history. The town’s legacy of union struggles for workers’ rights is chronicled through street plaques, protected heritage buildings, and murals reminiscent of early-20th-century Mexican muralism.

Under the expansive grey sky over Broken Hill, enormous mining wealth has been created – stretching from Australia to northern Chile and further. As with most forms of wealth, it is rooted in human hardship. In Broken Hill, mining wealth has been accumulated at the cost of children’s exposure to lead contamination.

Last July, Australia’s New South Wales (NSW) state government, which includes Broken Hill, announced AU$37.3 million (approximately US$26.74 million) to address lead contamination. The funding, as stated in the announcement, will lead to a “twofold increase in the number of homes remediated annually, including the removal of lead-based paint to eliminate lead contamination, the installation of grass to trap dust, and enhanced monitoring of emissions from existing mines and other localized dust sources.”

In Broken Hill, emissions from mining and smelting are the primary source of exposure. Elevated blood lead levels among local children signal a public health crisis. The announcement “underscored a commitment to protect children and families from the long-term effects of lead exposure.”

The funding announcement follows a January 2026 report on reducing the health and environmental impacts of lead contamination in Broken Hill. The NSW Office of the Chief Scientist & Engineer (OCSE) issued the report. “A long history of lead mining in Broken Hill has left a legacy of widespread contamination and human exposure,” said Professor Hugh Durrant-Whyte, OCSE’s NSW Chief Scientist, in the report.

“While some progress has been made in reducing environmental lead levels and community exposure, improvements have slowed in recent years,” he added. “Delays in effective intervention risk irreversible impairment and potential lifelong complications across successive generations.”

NSW Minister for Health Ryan Park described the AU$37.3 million as an “investment” to “help reduce the risk of harm, particularly for young children and infants.” He added, “To see blood lead levels declining among young children screened in Broken Hill is very pleasing. Still, we know more needs to be done.”

“Underground,” a daily reminder of what lies beneath and around the streets of Broken Hill. Photograph: Antonio Castillo.

Broken Hill is 1,100 kilometers west of Sydney, approximately a two-hour flight. According to 2020 data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS), it has a population of fewer than 20,000, of whom 6 percent are aged 0-4 years. Broken Hill is the birthplace of the mining giant BHP and is built on the world’s largest deposit of lead, silver, and zinc.

Lead mining began in 1885. The first inquiry by the NSW government into Broken Hill’s poisoning dates to the early 1890s. “Lead is a metal that has been mined in Broken Hill for many years,” stated Lead Smart Broken Hill, an NSW public health initiative and community education campaign.

“Lead dust is found in Broken Hill’s dust, soil, dirt, and rainwater tanks, among other places,” according to the Broken Hill Lead Surveillance Program 2023 Annual Report. “It is harmful to people of all ages, but the risk is highest for unborn babies, infants, and young children.”

Cate Faehrmann, an Australian environmentalist and politician, has long been a critic of the NSW government’s lead remediation measures. “Every year we get another report showing Broken Hill children are being poisoned by lead, and every year the government expresses concern,” she said. “It is a national shame that Aboriginal children in Broken Hill are still twice as likely to have dangerous levels of lead in their blood.”

The World Health Organization (WHO) reported that “[l]ead exposure was attributed to more than 3.5 million deaths globally in 2023, primarily due to cardiovascular effects.” It also emphasized that “lead exposure can pose significant health risks for children. When children are exposed to very high levels of lead, it can cause serious damage to their brains and central nervous system, leading to symptoms such as coma, convulsions, and, in extreme cases, death.”

The primary concern is childhood neurodevelopment. Lead affects the central nervous system, kidneys, blood chemistry, and reproductive organs. It impacts children’s cognitive development, and the resulting cognitive impairment can persist into adulthood. The WHO said that lead exposure can also cause irreversible damage to children’s brain development, leading to increased antisocial tendencies and lower educational achievement.

The 2023 Broken Hill Lead Surveillance Program Annual Report found that approximately 35 percent of non-Aboriginal children and a staggering 68 percent of Aboriginal children tested had blood lead levels exceeding the national public health guideline of 5 micrograms per deciliter.

“One in three Broken Hill kids under 5 have blood lead levels higher than the national guidelines,” said Faehrmann.

Aboriginal children and families may face barriers to accessing remediation programs, healthcare, and nutritional interventions, further increasing exposure risks. “No child should have to suffer lifelong health impacts because governments won’t stand up to powerful mining interests,” she said.

Broken Hill is an outback town built on its ore. Photograph: Antonio Castillo.

At the announcement last July of the AU$37.3 million to address lead contamination, Treasurer Daniel Mookhey said: “A long history of lead mining in Broken Hill has left a legacy of contamination that we need to manage better.”

However, the contamination is not merely a matter of better management. It is about neglect or “inaction,” as Richard Weston, chief executive of the Maari Ma Health Aboriginal Corporation, put it. Maari Ma and the Broken Hill Environmental Lead Program monitor lead levels in Broken Hill’s air and soil. They also conduct blood lead tests on children under 5.

“There’s virtually zero interest from the NSW government in the health and well-being of Aboriginal children in Broken Hill,” Weston said. “It’s a waste of time, really.” He added that the funding did not address the inequalities between Indigenous and non-Indigenous children.

Maari Ma withdrew from the Broken Hill Environmental Lead Response Group in November 2025 in protest against “the government’s inaction” and questioned why the NSW government has not adopted a targeted strategy to address Aboriginal contamination and structural injustices.

Weston sad that “structural inequities persist and contribute to lead exposure among Aboriginal children, and that targeted action is required because Aboriginal families have limited access to social housing and rely more on lower-quality private rental housing.” He added, “There’s a strong link between blood lead levels and the quality of housing in Broken Hill.”

Broken Hill faces an acute shortage of affordable housing. This unaffordability forces Aboriginal families to live in uninhabitable, lead-contaminated rental properties. These properties are contaminated by mining activities, exposing children to blood lead levels twice those of the general population.

Weston noted that although lead remediation in homes is ongoing, the housing situation for Aboriginal people remains precarious, citing substandard housing, overcrowding, and unstable tenancies.

He has called for more social housing for Aboriginal people. He said that unless Aboriginal children have secure housing, they will continue to have elevated levels of lead in their bodies. “Aboriginal children in Broken Hill deserve clean homes, safe air, and a future free from the legacy of lead.”

The Broken Hill Miners’ Memorial is a reminder that the town’s mining history has always carried a body count, official and unofficial. Photograph: Antonio Castillo.

title: Ayesha Siddiqa on the Pakistan Army’s Police State
description: Siddiqa argues that Pakistan is not a hybrid regime but a case of constitutional militarism, sanctioned by a parliament that has legislated away its own relevance.
text:
Dr. Ayesha Siddiqa, senior fellow in the Department of War Studies at King’s College London and author of “Military Inc.,” joins host Tushar Shetty to examine the Pakistan Army’s role in the country’s governance.

They discuss the origins of the military’s dominance in the years after 1947, its influence over domestic politics and the economy, its conduct of foreign policy from Ayub Khan to Asim Munir, and its handling of the insurgencies in Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Siddiqa argues that Pakistan is not a hybrid regime but a case of constitutional militarism, sanctioned by a parliament that has legislated away its own relevance.

For more in-depth analysis on South Asia, subscribe to the Beyond the Indus podcast on Spotify or Apple Podcasts, or follow us on YouTube for video episodes.

title: Breaking Down the Philippines’ 2027 Budget
description: The budget, which anticipates a return to strong growth next year, is based on some optimistic assumptions about the direction of the global economy.
text:
Lawmakers in the Philippines are working to pass a proposed PHP 7.2 trillion ($115 billion) budget for 2027. The budget still needs to pass through various legislative committees before a final vote, but so far the process looks less dramatic than last year’s fiscal showdown, when lawmakers slashed funding for the Department of Public Works after a massive scandal involving fictitious infrastructure projects. 2027, by comparison, looks to be pretty calm by budgeting standards.

The 7.2 trillion in expenditures represents a 6 percent increase over last year, with a substantial slice of total spending (17 percent) allocated for education and manpower. A quarter of public spending will go toward economic services such as agriculture, infrastructure and subsidies to local governments, while defense spending is set to get over 6 percent of total outlays. This is all rather unremarkable, but it’s worth digging into some of the underlying assumptions to better understand the Philippines’ spending plans relative to its fiscal position.

The first thing to note is that economic growth is slowing. Budget planners are now expecting GDP growth to come in somewhere between 3.5 and 4.5 percent in 2026. The World Bank agrees, projecting an annual growth rate of 3.7 percent. This is hardly unique to the Philippines. Countries across the region and around the world are facing stiff economic headwinds due to geopolitical instability, trade frictions, and rising energy prices. But in recent years, including 2027, budget planners have adopted very optimistic views about future growth.

Last year, when they were making the 2026 budget, planners assumed GDP growth this year would be between 6 and 7 percent. Actual growth is going to be quite a bit lower than that, potentially below 4 percent. In 2027, planners are forecasting GDP will bounce back to between 5 and 6 percent. This is possible, but right now energy prices, borrowing costs, and foreign exchange rates are going in the opposite direction and make such projections highly uncertain.

The 2027 budget framework assumes the Philippine peso will not pass 62 to the U.S. dollar, and that oil won’t go past $90. Dubai Crude, the benchmark used by planners, is around $115 right now, and the peso is trading at nearly 63 to the dollar. It is not certain these conditions will improve next year, particularly given that Donald Trump will still be loose in the world.

Recent budgets in the Philippines have consistently been anchored by optimistic projections about growth, causing revenue to underperform forecasts in both 2025 and 2026. Tax revenue in particular has been coming up short, as it’s one of the first line items to get squeezed when the economy hits a bump in the road. Revenue shortfalls force the government to either cut spending or seek more non-tax revenue. Indeed, non-tax revenue has been doing a lot to close the gap, which probably helps explain why efforts to privatize state-owned assets like airports and casinos have been gathering steam lately.

As a result, the Philippines has been consistently running budget deficits in excess of 5% of GDP for the last several years. Total government debt is steadily rising, which is not, in and of itself, a problem. But it can be a problem if revenue doesn’t keep up while borrowing costs rise, which is the state of affairs we currently find ourselves in. Budget forecasters are assuming short-term Treasury bills in the Philippines will pay between 5 and 6 percent in 2027. They are currently at nearly 6 percent.

Interest payments on existing debt are beginning to eat up more and more of annual expenditures, rising from 10% of spending in 2021 to 15 percent in the 2027 budget. This leaves less room for spending on priority programs, and infrastructure outlays have borne the brunt of the cuts. Spending on infrastructure is slated to reach PHP 832 billion in 2027, a 35 percent decrease compared to the high point of 2024. A lot of this is from big cuts to the Department of Public Works, which saw its budget slashed by 50 percent in 2026 following a big scandal.

It also means less money for other priority projects, like defense modernization. The Philippines has been at the forefront of territorial disputes with China in the South China Sea and announced a 10-year $35 billion military modernization plan in 2024. While they are making steady progress in procuring new weapons platforms, the 2027 budget allocated just PHP 50 billion ($800 million) to this program, which is well off the pace required to meet the ambitious targets.

Facing the prospect of a prolonged energy shock, a weaker peso, softening growth, rising inflation, persistently high borrowing costs, and a general increase in geopolitical risk and uncertainty, it would seem prudent for fiscal planners to be cautious in their assumptions about the future. But in the Philippines, optimism prevails, which is admirable in some ways but has also caused revenue to underperform forecasts in recent years.

title: BRICS 2026 Reveals Ambition, Contradictions, and Uncertain Futures
description: BRICS’ New Delhi Summit expanded the grouping’s ambitions, but geopolitical divisions and weak institutional clarity continue to challenge its future.
text:
Much fanfare accompanied the two-day (September 12-13) 2026 BRICS Summit in New Delhi. The Indian government shut down the capital through road closures, dignitaries made grand statements – including, notably, one by Russian President Vladimir Putin that the “old leaders” (the G7) are being replaced by “new engines of economic growth” (BRICS countries).

The grouping of an expanded 11 full members (Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Iran, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa, and the United Arab Emirates) issued a 140-point declaration on topics from Bretton Woods to conflict in the Middle East. Indian Member of Parliament Vikramjit Singh Sahney proclaimed that the summit was “historic” and “a major diplomatic achievement for India under Prime Minister Narendra Modi.”

But what did the meeting actually accomplish, and what is the future of BRICS?

The BRICS New Delhi declaration made many pledges. Two of these reaffirmed the “BRICS spirit of mutual respect and understanding, sovereign equality, solidarity, democracy, openness, inclusiveness, collaboration and consensus” as well as a commitment to upholding international law. Though these sounded agreeable, “mutual respect,” “democracy,” “openness,” and “upholding international law” ring particularly hollow in view of ongoing conflicts involving some BRICS members as well as the global tilt toward autocracy in recent years.

Nevertheless, the declaration went on to stress the importance of developing nations’ promoting dialogue for a more just and stable international order. It referenced the BRICS Payment Task Force and the exploration of efficient cross-border payment mechanisms.

That said, BRICS opposes carbon border adjustment mechanisms, deeming them discriminatory toward developing nations. Though this might be true, these nations should account for the carbon output of companies in the Global South via the implementation of their own border adjustment mechanisms, which would capture not only carbon, but also tax revenue.

On the environment, the declaration acknowledged the challenges of urban development, water availability, biodiversity, desertification, deforestation and waste management. This document named a variety of new initiatives to address these problems such as the BRICS Guidelines for Disaster Management Early Warning Data Integration and the Network of BRICS Institutions to Advance Knowledge Sharing, Research and Innovation in Sustainable Lifestyles.

In terms of human rights, it affirmed the importance of intellectual property protection and economic advancement for women. But without proper execution, these statements are just words on paper.

In addition, geopolitical fault lines are hard to ignore. Brazilian economist Paulo Nogueira Batista Jr referred to India as an “outlier,” due to its ties with Israel and the United States (Batista said explicitly that he would not go as far as others in calling India a “Trojan horse” in BRICS, however).

The United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia are currently involved in direct and indirect fighting with Iran, China and India disagree over their shared border, Pakistan and trade, and Egypt and Ethiopia have unresolved issues pertaining to water rights. These are just a few of the geopolitical issues that threaten to dismantle this grouping BRIC by BRIC.

Senior Fellow at the Pune International Centre Ajit Ranade argued convincingly that the greatest achievement of the latest BRICS conference was on the sidelines in the form of bilateral engagement between India and China. With this event being the first time in seven years that Chinese President Xi Jinping has visited India, it enabled leaders of the two countries to make progress within certain compartments of their complex relationship. Any positive developments between China and India – even at the level of increased cultural exchanges and direct flights – benefits humanity.

The idea of advancing humanity by prioritizing the needs of the Global South certainly did not originate from BRICS 2026. The New Delhi Declaration made explicit reference to the 1955 Bandung Conference, where African and Asian countries expressed their commitment to the Ten Principles of Peaceful Coexistence.

Bandung signified an important step in the trajectory of countries then emerging from colonial rule, and BRICS has built upon the idealism enumerated there.

But if BRICS is to succeed, the arrangement needs to have clear membership criteria, take advantage of opportunities made available by the missteps of G7 countries (especially by the United States on climate), build robust, long-lasting supply chains within BRICS, offer attractive investment and trade deals to middle powers, and remain committed to what it favors, rather than merely what it opposes.

As Dean of International Studies at Aligarh Muslim University Aftab Alam observed, although the New Delhi Declaration described the shortcomings of the existing order, BRICS has yet to articulate clearly what a more just and equitable system would look like.

Strict World Trade Organization compliance, additional BRICS members as permanent members of the United Nations Security Council, and a strong BRICS New Development Bank – emblematic of a parallel financial system that gives developing nations more options – might define this new international order.

Originally published under Creative Commons by 360info™.
