title: Burmese Refugees in Thailand Face Fresh Deportation Threat
description: A recently-passed law increases the risk that people fleeing repression will be deported and forcibly recruited into the military’s units of one-way troops.
text:
In April of 2026, 23-year-old Nway became scared of the dark for the first time in her life. She would lie awake at night, jumping at the noise of a car engine humming past the house she shared with her single mother, anxious that she could be dragged from her bed as she slept.

Her fear of the dark was not unfounded. As a Burmese political activist who had spent the last four years of her life in prison until April of this year, she was a high-profile target for forced conscription into the Myanmar military, which seized power in a coup in 2021. The military, which now fully controls only around 20 percent of the country’s territory, has conscripted over 30,000 young people since February 2024 in a bid to strengthen their struggling forces.

Since then, young people have been grabbed from the street, their workplaces, and their homes, after which they are reportedly deployed to the frontlines and used as “cannon fodder and human shields.” Nway said that her cousin was abducted by the authorities while drinking with friends by the river in Yangon one evening in 2024. He returned home earlier this year to share that “everyone except him had died; he was the one and only lucky man.”

Nway’s previous activism meant that when she was released from prison, she was targeted by the police, who would sit outside her home and visit her mother weekly to tell her, “if you don’t give us money, she will be listed.” Concerned for her daughter’s safety, Nway’s mother instead paid the authorities for her to fly safely to Thailand. Nway found a community of Burmese refugees and activists in the northern city of Chiang Mai, many of whom had similarly been targeted for conscription before fleeing the country.

Since the military coup, thousands of young refugees like Nway have started to rebuild their lives in Thailand, following in the footsteps of past generations of refugees and exiles. But harassment and arrests from Thai police and a deportation law approved in August continue to threaten their security. The new legal framework has been developed for “administering deportation issues speedily and effectively” in the absence of pre-existing “concrete guidelines.” According to civil society organizations, the new laws are already a source of concern for refugees in Thailand.

When Nway arrived in northern Thailand, she was reunited with Pho Thar, another activist and photojournalist whom she had known at university. Both had been held in separate facilities in Yangon’s Insein Prison for years, reuniting only once they had left the country. Pho Thar has already secured his migrant worker’s card, known as a “pink card,” which is the most accessible way for Myanmar nationals to gain legal residency, and Nway is in the process of securing her own.

Nway and Pho Thar are comfortable sharing their stories and names because they know they can never return to Myanmar. For Nway, this is because an outstanding legal case ensures she will be arrested and likely conscripted. Pho Thar, who has already been arrested four times by the Burmese authorities, believes he will be killed if he returns. Sitting outside a Burmese-owned restaurant on the edge of the city, he cracks his shoulder, a permanent injury sustained during his last arrest.

When Pho Thar was released from prison in November 2025, he knew he was listed for conscription and left Yangon within five days, travelling to Karen State where friends in the People’s Defense Forces helped him cross the border.

Pho Thar decided to travel straight to Chiang Mai when he entered Thailand because he believed the risk of staying in the border city of Mae Sot without documentation would be too high. Almost half of the nearly 4 million Myanmar nationals living in Thailand are undocumented and they face regular harassment, extortion, and threats of deportation from the Thai authorities. A 2025 report by Human Rights Watch (HRW) identified that police bribes had become so prevalent in Mae Sot that they referred to Myanmar nationals as “walking ATMs.”

Fear of the authorities and deportation has ruled the lives of several young Burmese refugees who agreed to speak to The Diplomat on condition of anonymity.

One 22-year-old Burmese refugee, Aung*, said that as an undocumented migrant, he found work in a garment factory where he is paid only 150 baht a day – the equivalent of around $4.50 and below minimum wage – and receives one day off per month. Despite his exhaustion, he is grateful for the layer of protection this workplace provides from the police. “I’m always afraid of the Thai police so I rarely go out to the town, I always stay in my factory,” he said.

In Myanmar, the parents of young people who have fled the country continue to pay bribes to Burmese authorities so their other children are not conscripted instead. Aung said that until August 2026, his mother continued to pay for him. “If I was deported to Myanmar, I would be taken to the frontlines and I will never go back home,” he said. “I face difficulty in Mae Sot so I always miss my home. I want to go back, but it is not possible.”

Thirty-five-year-old music producer Kyaw* also said that his mother, who recently recovered from breast cancer, continues to pay monthly bribes for her three children who have fled the country. He is still waiting for his documents in Mae Sot, and similarly knows that if he was deported he would be forced to join what he calls the “one-way troops” that are sent to the frontlines. He decided to leave Yangon when he went to the smoking area near his workplace and witnessed several young colleagues being kidnapped by military personnel during a work break.

Having already paid a 14-million-kyat bribe – over $6,600 – after being arbitrarily arrested and threatened with conscription, Kyaw started the long journey to the border. “I didn’t want to serve in the military because it’s just a civil war,” he said. “Since moving to Thailand, I have to start from zero but if I don’t have anything to eat I don’t care; I will sing a song for the revolution.”

Elsa, who fled to Mae Sot in 2023 with her family, said that they had to wait until 2025 for them to receive their migrant worker’s cards. She reported that they did not leave their home for four months between April and August in 2024 due to increased patrols and arrests by the authorities. She now works in an office but said that “it is a difficult life.”

Burmese youth protest the military coup in front of City Hall in downtown Yangon, Myanmar, Feb. 4, 2021. (Photo credit: Pho Thar)

Since Thai immigration laws do not recognize Myanmar nationals as refugees, and Thailand has not signed the 1951 Refugee Convention, the paths to residency are limited and refugees rely on a broker to navigate the application process for a worker’s card. Interviewees in HRW’s report confirmed that it was unclear exactly what the fees they were paying brokers were being used for in the application process.

In late August, new deportation regulations were approved by the Thai government, which facilitate the prompt deportation of “undesirable” foreigners. Civil society organizations have criticized this legislation, calling for it to include safeguards protecting refugees from deportation. As it stands, while the legislation acknowledges decisions around deportation should account for Thailand’s “relevant international obligations” there is no mention of non-refoulement, which would prevent refugees or asylum seekers from being sent back to any country where they could face persecution or serious harm.

Two foreign nationals have already been deported under the new legal framework. Thanida Piyachot, a human rights specialist at the advocacy group Fortify Rights, said that “the Thai government’s enactment of regulations that can directly affect people’s rights without a thorough review is already deeply concerning. Now, with the enforcement of this fast-track deportation process, serious questions remain about how decisions will be made in practice when there are no clear standards of safeguards.”

Tanyakorn Thippayapokin, the policy, advocacy, and communications coordinator at Asylum Access Thailand, added that it’s very likely the law will be used to extort, harass, and deport Burmese nationals because it is written “very broadly to target anyone staying illegally in the country.”

The Coalition for the Rights of Refugees and Stateless Persons, which includes Fortify Rights and Asylum Access, has called for the government to promptly review the regulations with civil society organizations to address gaps that could put refugees at risk of forced returns and have a standard operating procedure that aligns with principles of non-refoulement.

For the undocumented refugees who are waiting for their migrant worker’s card applications to be processed, this law adds to their concerns about being deported to Myanmar and forcibly recruited. Everyone interviewed by The Diplomat believed that deportation would result in them being conscripted against their will and likely dying on the frontlines, a risk that does not appear to have been considered under this new legal framework, according to civil society organizations.

Piyachot argued that the new law is already impacting the security of undocumented Burmese migrants. “It is creating fear among refugee communities. I believe [the authorities] can use this law to threaten them, and worsen the corruption and extortion,” she said.

Meanwhile, Nway is trying to start a new life in Chiang Mai, alongside Pho Thar. Now she is in Thailand, she says she “doesn’t expect a lot. I really want to go back to my country because it’s where my childhood memories are, but it’s impossible.”

Instead, she says she wants a simple life. “I don’t want to worry again about what will happen at night, like in Yangon,” Nway said. “I want to sleep peacefully.”

*Some names have been changed to preserve respondents’ anonymity.

title: Busting the Myths of the US Military’s Presence in Hawai‘i
user_author_name: David Vine; Heidi Peltier; Omar Ocampo
description: As land leases come up for renewal, a new report reveals the facts about the U.S. Armed Forces’ impacts in the Pacific Islands.
text:
In the middle of the Pacific Ocean, the U.S. military’s future in Hawai‘i has become a topic of growing debate given the upcoming expiration of leases for around 46,000 acres of military base land. The armed forces leased the lands from the state of Hawai‘i in the 1960s for 65 years at a token fee of $1. The leases start expiring in 2028.

Some unsurprisingly want to see these territories returned. The U.S. military played a key role in seizing indigenous lands after overthrowing the Hawaiian monarchy in the 19th century. The military still occupies around 25 percent of the most populated island, O‘ahu, and a larger proportion of the state of Hawai‘i – 5.6 percent – compared to any other state.

The state of Hawai’i and the Trump administration have engaged in discussions about the future of these lands. Hawai‘i’s Congress members and the official indigenous-led state agency, the Office of Hawaiian Affairs, have gotten involved in the debates.

With the size of the military’s presence in Hawai‘i hanging in the balance, we helped co-author a major new report earlier this year, “The True Cost of the U.S. Military in Hawai‘i,” to provide a clear assessment of the armed forces’ local impact.

For years, many have made bold claims, in particular, about the economic benefits the U.S. military brings to Hawai‘i. The facts show the military’s contribution is significantly smaller than most people think, while the economic damage and other harms caused by the military’s presence remain hidden or overlooked.

Drawing on what are collectively more than 45 years of experience studying the U.S. military, our calculations show that the Pentagon and others have been exaggerating the military’s impact by billions of dollars. Meanwhile, the military’s presence is driving up rents and fueling the housing crisis, damaging the environment and public health, and limiting the growth of industries that would create more local jobs than the military.

Amid the debates about the expiring leases, here’s what we found to be the military’s true impacts.

Exaggerated Claims

The Pentagon, parts of the state government, media outlets, and boosters often describe the military as part of a “three-legged stool” – with tourism and real estate/construction – that serves as the backbone of the state’s economy. They point to billions of dollars in annual military spending, including $10 billion for FY2023, as evidence of the Pentagon’s contribution to the state’s economic wellbeing.

With the help of a 2025 research trip to Hawai‘i and an examination of government spending data, we identified the fundamental problem with these claims: These sources imply that all Pentagon spending related to Hawaiʻi directly benefits the local economy.

This is untrue.

Significant chunks of Pentagon spending never touch the local economy. Instead, those funds are paid to people and corporations located in other states and countries.

In total, we found that the military’s actual economic impact is closer to $7.2 billion per year. This is $2.8 billion and nearly 30 percent less than the $10 billion spent by the Pentagon.

The military thus represents 6.4 percent of Hawaiʻi’s total gross domestic product (GDP) rather than the 9.2 percent recently claimed by the Pentagon and state government sources. Notably, our 6.4 percent calculation is similar to the most recent estimate of 6.0 percent of GDP made by Hawai’i’s Department of Business, Economic Development & Tourism.

$7.2 billion is still a lot of money, but at least five other industries are larger statewide, including real estate, accommodation and food services, state and local government, retail, and health care and social assistance.

Where the Money Goes

Unlike other industries where the vast majority of employees are residents in the state of Hawaiʻi, the opposite is true for the military. The vast majority of military personnel are not from Hawai‘i.

As a result, significant chunks of military spending going toward salaries and benefits actually leave the local economy when active-duty military personnel from outside Hawai‘i leave the state.

Thousands of military personnel counted as living in Hawaiʻi actually reside on Navy vessels for large parts of the year or are deployed abroad. While some of their salaries end up in the state’s economy, much does not. In total, our calculations show Hawai‘i benefits from $3.7 billion in spending on military personnel, which is around two-thirds less than the $6.2 billion boosters claim.

Large amounts of Pentagon spending also leave the local economy because many military contracts go to corporations that are not based in Hawai‘i. The top recipient of Pentagon contracts performed in Hawai’i in 2023, for example, was a joint venture involving a Spain-based multinational and a Texas-based company partnered with a smaller Hawaiʻi-based firm. Two of the rest of the top five recipients also aren’t locally headquartered.

The state conservatively estimates that 15 percent of contract dollars awarded to non-local companies leaves Hawai‘i in the form of profits and money spent where the companies are based. This suggests that at least $301.5 million in contract dollars claimed to benefit the state in 2023 actually left Hawaiʻi.

Overlooked Costs of the Military’s Presence

Aside from the inflated estimates of economic benefits, the military’s presence costs Hawai‘i in many other ways that are rarely recognized. Because most military personnel and their family members are not legal residents of Hawai‘i, most don’t pay state income taxes, yet they still benefit from the state’s public infrastructure, public services, and other amenities.

The military’s presence also helps fuel the housing affordability crisis. Our report estimated that active duty service members living off base and renting in the private market pushed up rents on the island of O‘ahu by 7.1 percent in 2024 alone. This caused local non-military renters to pay an average of $154 more per month and $1,850 more per year in rent. This upward pressure on rental prices caused by the military helps contribute to housing instability, the homelessness crisis, and the thousands of households forced to move out of the state because they were priced out.

The problem is the generous housing allowances the Pentagon gives its military personnel: a monthly average of $3,679 per service member in Honolulu County. This combined with the military’s occupation of land, which keeps land prices high and the housing supply low, directly harm Hawai‘i’s residents.

Meanwhile, the 46,000 acres of land the military has rented for $1 per lease since the early 1960s represents billions of dollars in lost rental revenue. Based on the fair market value of this land, our report calculates Hawai‘i could claim up to $134 billion in back rent.

This sum does not include the billions of dollars needed to repair the environmental and public health damage caused by military training, testing, and other activities. A 2017 report by ProPublica estimated total past and future environmental clean-up in Hawai‘i to be at $2.77 billion, not including the $400 million spent since 1994 to only partially clean up the island of Kaho‘olawe after decades of Navy bombing.

Some will say that the military creates the jobs needed on Hawai‘i. It is undeniable that military spending creates jobs. However, it’s an inefficient job creator when compared to other industries. Our report followed years of research in showing that military spending creates an average of 5.3 jobs per $1 million invested compared to an average of 12.3 jobs created when the same money is invested in healthcare, education, food production, housing, and energy efficiency.

Put another way, spending in non-military industries creates an average of 134 percent more jobs than military spending, with the vast majority of jobs going to locals. It is simply more efficient to invest in other sectors of the economy rather than rely on military spending.

New Beginnings?

The future of the leased lands remains unclear. Returning most or all of the territory to Hawai‘i would not require any significant change in the military’s overall presence. The leases represent less than 20 percent of the military’s approximately 250,000 acres occupied in the state. Simply put, the U.S. Armed Forces have more than enough space to continue their current operations – although “The True Cost of the U.S. Military in Hawai‘i” report also presented safer alternatives to the military’s current strategy, centered around Hawai‘i, of aggressively confronting China in the Pacific.

The Army already has indicated it will give up nearly 800 acres of a controversial training ground responsible for significant environmental damage. Some locals imagine a university dedicated to learning, cultural preservation, and ecological repair for the space.

As our report showed, hundreds of former bases across the United States and the world have been converted into new spaces benefitting local communities. In Hawai‘i, a former Army fort became a state park and monument, a community college, a state emergency operations center, and a school for children with special needs. Elsewhere, base conversion has produced thousands of jobs and created housing, hospitals, business incubators, solar and wind farms, cultural preservation sites, and much more.

As the people of Hawai‘i consider their future, they deserve an accurate picture of the armed forces’ actual impacts, and the alternatives, rather than billions of dollars in exaggeration.

The co-authored report “The True Cost of the U.S. Military in Hawai‘i” can be found here.

title: Cambodia Confirms Resumption of Joint Military Exercises With US Next Year
description: The move reflects the sea change that has taken place in U.S.-Cambodia relations under the second Trump administration.
text:
Cambodia’s army has confirmed that it will resume joint military exercises with the United States early next year after a decade-long suspension, the latest sign of the improving ties between the two nations.

The Royal Cambodian Army announced on Facebook on Friday that officials from the two nations had concluded an Initial Planning Conference for Exercise Angkor Sentinel 2027, which it said would be held in February of next year.

The exercise has the aim of “strengthening interoperability and disaster-response capabilities, reflecting renewed momentum in Cambodia–U.S. military cooperation and a shared commitment to strengthening defense cooperation.”

The announcement follows several high-level meetings between U.S. and Cambodian officials. These include a meeting last month between Prime Minister Hun Manet and Elbridge A. Colby, undersecretary for policy at the U.S. Department of War, during which the two discussed expanded defense cooperation.

Hun Manet said at the time that he was satisfied with the “positive momentum in Cambodia-U.S. relations” and the ongoing talks about the resumption of Angkor Sentinel, the Associated Press reported. “The joint exercises and training not only build military capability but also serve as a vital bridge to foster close friendship between the armed forces of both countries,” he added.

This was not long after Adm. Steve Koehler, commander of the U.S. Pacific Fleet, traveled to Phnom Penh for meetings with officials including Gen. Vong Pisen, the commander-in-chief of the Royal Cambodian Armed Forces, and Vice Adm. Tea Sokha, the commander of the Royal Cambodian Navy.

The visit “reaffirmed the United States’ long-term commitment to strengthening bilateral relationships and partnerships that advance a shared vision for a free and open Indo-Pacific,” the U.S. Pacific Fleet said in a statement at the time.

Angkor Sentinel was held for the first time in 2010 but was unilaterally canceled by the Cambodian government in early 2017, shortly after Cambodian troops took part for the first time in Golden Dragon, a joint military exercise with the Chinese military. The move reflected the mutually reinforcing deterioration of Phnom Penh’s relations with Washington and its growing proximity to China.

The resumption of the exercise has been anticipated by both sides for some time. It was first publicly discussed in early 2025, just prior to President Trump’s return to the White House, and has been referenced in most high-level diplomatic meetings since then. It reflects the sea change that has taken place in U.S.-Cambodia relations since the midpoint of the Biden administration, as Phnom Penh has sought to diversify its foreign relations and the U.S. has worked to pull the country out of China’s orbit.

However, the rapprochement has gained inexorable momentum since the inauguration of the second Trump administration, whose transactional mode of diplomacy has been much more to Phnom Penh’s liking. In particular, President Donald Trump’s decision to shutter USAID and cut off U.S. funding for democracy promotion efforts and media outlets like Radio Free Asia removed a key impediment to improved relations on the Cambodian side. As I noted in 2025, Cambodia’s government finally has what it has always wanted: “a relationship with the U.S. that strengthens, rather than undermines, the CPP’s hold on power.”

Last June, the U.S. government officially removed Cambodia from its arms sale blacklist, a month after an American ship docked for the first time at Cambodia’s Ream Naval Base. The latter was particularly significant, given the extensive Chinese refurbishment of the base, which U.S. and Western officials feared was intended to host a permanent Chinese military presence. Adm. Samuel Paparo, commander of the United States Indo-Pacific Command, described the port visit as a sign of the “strong upward trajectory” of relations between Phnom Penh and Washington.

These improvements have come even as branches of the U.S. government have come to officially recognize the extent of the Cambodian elite’s involvement in the country’s gigantic online scamming industry. According to U.S. government agencies, online scamming cost U.S. citizens at least $10 billion in 2024.

title: Cambodian Beauty Pageant Acknowledges Mistaken Use of Thai Historical Photograph
description: The unresolved border dispute between Cambodia and Thailand has given rise to a rash of online disputes over cultural ownership.
text:
The organizers of a Cambodian beauty pageant have been forced to acknowledge their use of a historical photograph from Thailand, saying the mistake was unintentional and resulted from “insufficient verification” of the original sources.

The Miss Universe Cambodia pageant came under fire on social media after images of women dressed in traditional attire were displayed on stage during the pageant’s preliminary round last week, along with a description saying they were wearing traditional Khmer clothing.

One of the photographs, which showed seven Thai women in traditional dress, was taken in Kamphaeng Phet province in 1906, during the reign of King Chulalongkorn. According to the Bangkok Post, the photograph is part of a large collection of glass-plate negatives that is preserved at the Phra Vajirayana Royal Library in Bangkok.

The revelation prompted a social media flame-war between Thai and Cambodian nationalists, each of whom accused the other of stealing or appropriating the other’s culture.

Thailand’s Ministry of Culture subsequently sent a letter to the pageant organizers on Monday, demanding an apology and correction for its use of the Thai photograph, which it said “was done intentionally to cause misunderstanding about the picture’s origin,” the Bangkok Post reported. Culture Minister Sabeeda Thaised told reporters that the original photograph contained a watermark, which the Miss Universe Cambodia organizers appeared to have cropped out.

The Miss Universe Cambodia statement, signed by the pageant’s national director Prasat Davin, said that the photograph was intended to highlight the traditional sbai garment, and that its incorrect attribution resulted from “insufficient verification of the original sources of those images.”

“We would like to emphasize that there was no intention to cause misunderstanding, controversy or offend the feelings of any member of the public, whether nationally or internationally,” it said.

Disputes over cultural “ownership” have been a perennial occurrence in relations between Thailand and Cambodia. A long history of cultural cross-pollination between the two nations and their respective premodern civilizations has produced a close overlap in cultural practices, including dance, cuisine, architecture, and sports like kick-boxing, as well as the two countries’ Sanskrit-derived writing systems. In spite of these cultural affinities, or perhaps because of them, the question of ownership is a highly emotive issue – one that can sometimes have real-world impacts.

For instance, in 2003, Khmer-language press reports claimed that a Thai actress said that Cambodia had “stolen” Angkor Wat, and that she would not visit the country until it was “returned” to Thailand. In response, mobs of protesters sacked the Thai Embassy and numerous Thai businesses, causing millions of dollars in damage.

Such cultural disputes have also complicated the resolution of the long-standing frontier dispute between Cambodia and Thailand. The two nations’ land border is dotted with ancient Khmer temples that are shot through with nationalist significance, particularly for the Cambodian side. One of these is Preah Vihear temple, a glorious 11th-century Angkorian temple perched on a cliff on the two nations’ border.

In 1962, the International Court of Justice ruled that Preah Vihear belonged to Cambodia, but Thai nationalists have never accepted the verdict. When UNESCO listed the temple as a World Heritage Site in 2008, royalist protesters heaped pressure on the Thai government and helped precipitate a bilateral crisis that flared into armed conflict on several occasions between 2008 and 2011.

The border dispute again resulted in armed conflict on two occasions last year, embittering relations between Phnom Penh and Bangkok – and between dueling nationalist cohorts online. In the context of the current stand-off, Thai-Cambodian disputes over cultural ownership have become more acute and potentially combustive than ever.

title: Cambodia’s Online Scamming Crackdown Stops at the Top
description: This week's international anti-scam conference is an attempt to distract global attention from Phnom Penh's abetment of criminality on an industrial scale.
text:
On September 23 and 24, Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Manet will preside over an international conference on combating online scams in Phnom Penh that is co-sponsored by Interpol, the U.N. Office on Drugs and Crime, and China’s Lancang Mekong Cooperation mechanism. In the run-up to the conference, Cambodian leaders and state media have been unusually candid that its purpose is to help “restore the country’s international reputation.”

The ruling Cambodian People’s Party (CPP) has spent years denying or minimizing a massive criminal economy operating in plain sight – and repressing those journalists and human rights groups that sought to expose the problem. Now that extraordinary outside pressure compelled it to empty the country’s massive online scamming compounds, the party-state is recasting itself as an anti-scam champion while the politically protected elites who abetted the industry remain largely untouched.

Now comes the harder question: whether the political system that protected this industry will be held accountable – or allowed to write itself a clean bill of health with a global seal of approval.

That question is at the center of a new letter from U.S. House Foreign Affairs Committee Chair Brian Mast and House China Select Committee Chair John Moolenaar. The chairs asked the Trump administration to investigate 26 individuals and two entities and determine within 180 days whether they meet the statutory criteria for sanctions under Global Magnitsky, cyber-related, transnational criminal organization, or other authorities. The letter pointed to what the lawmakers describe as the “financial networks, organizers, and political protection structures” that enabled the industry.

Research I published last week, supported by the National Democratic Institute and Inca Digital, placed Mast and Moolenaar’s letter in its broader context. Our central claim is that Cambodia’s scam compounds were only the visible front end of a deeply entrenched political economy. The scam economy was not a sudden criminal intrusion into an otherwise normal state. Cambodia’s ruling coalition has spent decades converting successive illicit and predatory economies – from land and natural resources to casinos and online gambling – into private wealth and political power. The government’s crackdown, enacted due to external pressure, has reached foreign operators and physical compounds without meaningfully disturbing the domestic political arrangements that enabled the scam economy’s rise and significant durability.

Notably, the chairs’ requested determinations include prominent spokespeople, Cabinet-level officials, personal advisers, and family members of the prime minister.

Consider just one example: Hun To, nephew of former Prime Minister Hun Sen and cousin of Prime Minister Hun Manet. Hun To has acknowledged owning 30 percent of Huione Pay, a vital institution at the core of the Huione network that FinCEN formally deemed a “financial institution of primary money laundering concern” of the United States. Foreign authorities have moved aggressively against Huione-linked infrastructure and executives, while Hun To has faced no publicly verifiable accountability.

At some point, treating relationships like his as cases of merely accidental proximity becomes less an exercise in due process than an excuse not to ask obvious questions.

The Treasury and State departments should conduct the determinations Mast and Moolenaar requested, impose sanctions where the statutory criteria are met, and provide detailed explanations where they are not.

That follow-through has an importance that goes beyond those people named by the U.S. Congress. For years, Cambodian journalists, trafficking responders, survivors, and civil society groups did the dangerous work of documenting compounds, tracing their ownership, and forcing illicit elite connections into public view. This transparency work is not just important in terms of normative values promotion. It directly helps minimize the harms flowing from modern mafia states.

And, if the CPP government wants to clear its name? Washington and its partners should condition that desired reputational rehabilitation on a cessation of harassment of independent reporting and upon evidence that accountability has reached politically protected actors – not merely foreign operators and expendable front-line infrastructure.

The harms of Cambodia’s political economy once fell disproportionately on Cambodians, in the form of predatory extraction, dispossession, and corruption. The scam economy demonstrates what happens when the same governing strategy acquires global digital reach. The victims are now international, the revenues vastly larger, and the security consequences harder to contain.

The broader lesson extends beyond Cambodia. The international community has not eliminated the global narcotics trade, but it has imposed real diplomatic, financial, and legal costs on “narco states” that govern through the protection of large-scale drug trafficking. Cyber-scam economies now require similar treatment. States whose elites turn forced labor, mass fraud, and digital predation into political finance should not be allowed to launder their reputations through conferences, task forces, and scripted cooperation.

Accountability is not about punishment for its own sake. It is about constraining the actors and systems that repeatedly convert illicit opportunity into elite wealth and political power – and protecting those who expose how authoritarian corruption works.

The goal now is to make the next scam state harder to build by making political protection for cybercrime a liability instead of a viable governing model.

title: Can a Network of Miniature Sponge Cities Help Central Asia Curb Climate Change?
description: In lieu of decisive regulatory action and funding, much of the work of adapting to new climate realities falls on individual gardeners and cooperatives.
text:
Can gardens act as a network of miniature sponge cities to have a positive impact on climate change in Central Asia? A preponderance of aesthetic decisions and other barriers hold back the adaptation of Central Asia’s cities, but individuals and local authorities can make a difference.

Kyrgyzstan, and Central Asia more broadly, are experiencing stress on available groundwater reserves. As Dr. Eric Rudenshiold noted in an article for the Caspian Policy Center last year, “Driven by regional temperature increases, the region’s glaciers are melting at a rate four times faster than the global average and far faster than anticipated.”

Central Asia’s glaciers feed rivers and streams throughout the year. One can easily imagine a future in which rivers run dry and entire cities are required to use only water gathered from rain that falls in just a few short months of the year. In a future like this, having the ability to retain water in place could mean the difference between thriving and ceasing to exist. Stronger storms, floods, droughts, deadly heatwaves, and mass migration are putting pressure on policymakers to follow through with plans to update infrastructure.

An empty canal in Bishkek. Water from rain and glacial melt is directed through and away from the city to evaporate downstream. (Photograph by Walt Ohnesorge)

What Can Central Asia Learn from Sponge Cities?

During a public lecture in 2003, architect Kongjian Yu coined the term “sponge cities” while outlining a set of urban planning principles developed to manage water in flood-prone regions of China. Sponge cities have since been enshrined in Chinese public policy by the Chinese Communist Party as a regulatory framework for development in the country.

Kyrgyzstan has been interested in China’s governance model as a way to alleviate poverty, but its development and domestic urban planning initiatives offer other lessons. Time is running out for risk-prone areas of the world to make lasting, meaningful changes in the face of climate change, and some adaptation ideas may have been overlooked in parts of Central Asia.

This oversight is evidenced by the colossal loss of green space in Bishkek since the Soviet era. While Kyrgyzstan’s cities have lost greenery, China has mandated the construction of climate-resilient urban spaces. Adopting a strong approach to state funding and regulation of green spaces is likely to create jobs in the industry and holds potential, where green spaces are fruit-bearing, to reduce food insecurity. Both of these outcomes could reduce poverty in Kyrgyzstan, and Bishkek’s own Green Cities Action Plan acknowledges the need for climate resilience and adequate green spaces.

However, in lieu of decisive regulatory action and funding, much of the work of adapting to new climate realities falls on individual gardeners and cooperatives. Climate change has a disproportionate impact, both geographically on specific regions of Kyrgyzstan, and particularly on marginalized communities. As members of the El-Too foundation point out, “at the municipality and political level, women are not included in the decision-making processes; all issues related to land are discussed with the participation of men mainly… The situation is especially difficult for women that are employed as invisible forces in agriculture and have no other source of income.”

Miniaturizing Sponge Cities

While researching this topic, we were struck by a lack of sources for community-lead gardening initiatives in Kyrgyzstan. We discovered that Bishkek has no immediately identifiable grass roots collectives piloting alternative or sustainable agriculture inside the city. Even a cursory glance at New York City yields several sources and projects, and the same is true for other global cities. It is far easier to identify the challenges, like existing attention to inefficient practices, than attempts at solutions. The scale of new development in Bishkek is profound, dwarfing initiatives to create a greener city, preserve green spaces, and retrofit existing spaces for greater efficiency. With that in mind, we considered what it might look like if individuals in Bishkek took it upon themselves to implement better water preservation systems.

Homemade drip irrigation feeds an area near a condo in Bishkek, where residents improvise to utilize water efficiently during summer months. (Photograph by Walt Ohnesorge)

One dacha owner, Asel, shared that she has never thought of climate change when managing her garden. She planted species that her landscape designer recommended, who was guided by beauty rather than water management or other climate change concerns. The same could be said about the managed gardens of some condominium buildings. Bakyt, a groundskeeper at one such building, said, “We plant roses here and use drinking water to water them.”

Another dacha owner, Zarina, said she’d never seen a list of plants recommended for the local climate, but expressed interest in such a list. This interest leads us to believe that, given a coordinated campaign to make information and tools available, individuals might be easily motivated to shift their habits toward more sustainable gardening practices.

A small container garden near a condo in Bishkek reflects a local desire for more green spaces. (Photograph by Walt Ohnesorge)

As Walt Ohnesorge, an artist and designer (and one of the authors of this piece) observed of many condos in Bishkek, “they could attach a catchment system to the gutter and plant perennial, food bearing plants to save drinking water, supplement tenants’ groceries, and utilize rain water for a more efficient system.”

Nuraiym Syrgak, Kyrgyzstani social researcher and ecologist, and former executive director of the El-Too Public Foundation and a board member of the Association of Legal Entities “Green Alliance of Kyrgyzstan,” shared her ideas and experience implementing ecological projects. There are things people can do, at all levels, to help the land adapt to a changing climate.

She noted that specific patterns of water allocation in villages have consequences. “Water for irrigation is mainly given to large plots. Gardens and zones within the village receive little water,” Syrgak said. “Therefore, we wanted precisely these small areas to become the center of attention.”

Syrgak added that women, in particular, are good agents of change. “Men tend to be skeptical of anything new, especially at first, whereas women try to apply every new thing. In this sense, women are fantastic change agents. That is why we started working with them and later brought the men on board. As a result, we ended up with a family-based approach to agriculture.”

Beyond villages and gardens, parks can also be transformed into miniature sponges within urban landscapes.

“We often see these trees in our parks, which are not adapted to our climate,” Syrgak noted “Of course, they are beautiful. But at the same time they do not give more function. They do not give shade. They require a lot of work. And permaculture is such a philosophy, so that a person works less. And cooperates with nature to minimize work.”

Syrgak stressed that there was no clear list of priority species for cultivation to fight climate change, but the centering of local species is a good place to start.

“If you look at our deserts or abandoned zones, there are always these elms, which is a local type of tree and does not require watering,” Syrgak pointed out. “Then there are a lot of species like local shrubs, which could be useful for changes. We often discussed [these plants] with biologists.”

Syrgak explained that this year, members of El-Too tried to contact construction companies building guesthouses in the Issyk-kul region.

“As soon as construction workers arrive in the area, they clear the entire area of ​​native species. And this is, in fact, very dangerous because there are shrubs there, those roots grow up to 10 meters, and they hold the soil in place. If they are removed, of course, the soil will crumble, and there’s a risk of mudflows and floods. So why are floods increasing in our regions? By removing these roots, we are already destroying the natural environment.”

“We need to think more broadly,” Syrgak said, explaining that attention should be paid to specific conditions when considering what to plant. “For example, you can plant sun-loving plants precisely on the sunny side. Then, those that require more moisture, precisely on the shady side. Before that, you can simply map out and analyze the site to see where there is more shade. Attention should be paid to native species.”

The consequences of not doing so are obvious.

A city-wide abundance of rose gardens contribute to an inefficient use of land, as roses remain one of the most water-demanding options available. (Photograph by Walt Ohnesorge)

“We have plenty of examples – even, I think, these construction companies, wherever you go, they plant very pretty arborvitae, spruces; some of these decorative plants. Well, if maintenance isn’t good, they die off after a year. I think it would be better for construction companies to introduce some deciduous trees so they can provide shade.”

In lieu of clear central government guidelines and enforcement, individuals, urban planners, designers and local authorities could coordinate among themselves implement climate resilient initiatives. These initiatives could include, among other possibilities, planting specific species, implementing tool-sharing programs, providing a grant program for cisterns, catchment, and irrigation systems, and educational campaigns. Cities could even allocate free, otherwise unusable, lands to willing local gardeners for remediation.

New development projects using potable water in automatic sprinkler systems pose inefficiencies at scale. (Photograph by Walt Ohnesorge)

Surviving the scale of global climate change will require strong, coordinated international and state-level interventions to avoid the worst outcomes: mass migration, famine, and war over scarce resources. The state structures that are willing to make unpopular decisions today may be the ones to survive tomorrow. Even sponge cities, after all, were not initially popular with city planners and developers in China. Moreover, while there are specific requirements for labeling a city a sponge city, and Kyrgyzstan faces significantly different climate related challenges from the monsoon rains of Southeast China, importing policies and exogenous knowledge, like sponge city concepts, permaculture, or xeriscaping, from other geographies may be the only way to keep climate-vulnerable states from total collapse.

title: Central Asia’s Energy Transition Depends on Water Security
description: A more integrated and flexible power system could give Central Asian states greater room to manage drought, hydropower volatility, and competing demands for water.
text:
Central Asia is building a new energy system. Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan are rapidly expanding solar and wind generation and battery storage, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan are expanding their hydropower capacity, and governments across the region are investing in stronger cross-border electricity connections. Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan are also both moving ahead with nuclear power.

These projects are usually discussed as separate parts of the region’s energy transition, but they are increasingly connected by single, critical variable: water.

Climate change is making Central Asia’s hydrology less predictable just as electricity demand is growing. Drought can constrain hydropower, extreme heat can increase power demand, irrigation systems consume large amounts of electricity, and new generation assets must be able to operate for decades under water conditions that may look very different from historical averages.

This creates a challenge, but also an opportunity. A more integrated and flexible Central Asian power system could reduce not only the cost of the energy transition, but also the region’s exposure to water shocks.

Five Energy Systems, One Regional Opportunity

Central Asia does not have a single energy model. Kazakhstan remains strongly dependent on thermal and coal-fired generation. Uzbekistan’s system is still largely gas-based, although solar, wind, and battery storage are expanding rapidly. Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan rely heavily on hydropower, while Turkmenistan relies predominantly on natural gas.

These differences are often treated as vulnerabilities, but they can also create complementarity. Hydropower and reservoirs can provide flexibility to systems with growing shares of variable renewable energy. Solar and wind can reduce dependence on hydrological conditions. Thermal generation can provide firm capacity while storage expands. Cross-border electricity trade can allow countries to draw on these different resources rather than each trying to maintain an isolated system capable of meeting every contingency on its own.

The economic case for integration is already substantial. Modeling by Agora Energiewende and the University of Central Asia suggests that deeper integration between Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, and Kyrgyzstan, combined with stronger transmission and greater renewable deployment, could reduce annual system costs by around $3.5 billion, or 18 percent, by 2035 compared with current plans.

The World Bank’s Regional Electricity Market Interconnectivity and Trade (REMIT) program is moving in the same direction. It aims to increase annual regional electricity trade to at least 15,000 GWh, expand transmission capacity to 16 GW, and enable up to 9 GW of clean energy.

But interconnection alone is not resilience. This was demonstrated in dramatic fashion last month when Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan all reported blackouts on August 14. The cause of the regional blackout appears to have been the sudden shutdown of two units at the Toktogul Hydroelectric Station in Kyrgyzstan which disturbed the flow of power through the unified grid. Kyrgyz authorities, however, disputed that the problem at Toktogul was responsible for the cascade of outages in neighboring countries.

Regardless, the lesson stands that interconnection – on its own – does not necessarily result in resilience. Solar peaks can occur at similar times across neighboring countries, while drought can reduce hydropower output just as extreme heat raises electricity demand. Regional integration therefore needs to be accompanied by storage, flexible generation, demand response, stronger grids, and coordinated operating rules. These can also provide countries with greater flexibility when another critical resource becomes constrained: water.

Historical Averages Are Becoming Less Useful

As I argued in a previous article for The Diplomat, “Central Asia’s Water Crisis Is Becoming a Regional Economic Risk,” water scarcity is no longer only an environmental issue. It is increasingly an economic, infrastructure, and regional-cooperation risk. The World Bank reports that Central Asia has lost around 30 percent of its glacier surface area over the past 60 years. For Uzbekistan, it projects water availability to fall by 30-40 percent while irrigation demand will rise by about 25 percent.

Yet describing the problem simply as “less water” misses an important part of what climate change is doing to the region. Research on the Amu Darya Basin indicates that accelerated glacier melt and changing precipitation can temporarily sustain or increase flows in some periods, even as seasonality, year-to-year variability, and extremes change substantially.

For energy planners, that distinction matters. A reservoir, hydropower plant, nuclear facility, transmission system, or irrigation network built today will operate for decades. The relevant question is therefore not simply how much water Central Asia has now, but how reliably that water will arrive, when it will arrive, and what competing demands it will face over the decades-long lifetime of the infrastructure being built today.

Hydropower illustrates the problem particularly clearly. Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan depend heavily on hydropower, and their reservoirs can provide storage and balancing services to a regional system incorporating more solar and wind. But reservoir operation also distributes costs and benefits across borders. Upstream countries may prefer to retain water for winter electricity generation, while downstream agricultural systems depend heavily on summer releases. During droughts, reconciling those priorities becomes more difficult.

Water management is therefore not an external environmental constraint on the energy transition. It is increasingly part of energy security itself.

The Water-Energy Relationship

Water is not just critical to Central Asia’s energy systems, but those systems require energy to operate, too. According to World Bank project documentation, around 2.4 million hectares of Uzbekistan’s irrigated land depend on pumping, and roughly 1,700 pumping stations consume about 7.2 TWh of electricity annually.

Modernizing pumping stations, reducing losses, and improving irrigation efficiency can simultaneously reduce pressure on scarce water resources and electricity demand. In practical terms, water efficiency can itself become an energy-security investment. Put more simply: water efficiency is also energy policy.

But the reverse is equally important: energy flexibility can become a form of water resilience.

Uzbekistan generated 10.5 TWh of electricity from solar and wind in 2025 and is rapidly expanding battery storage, with a further 884 MW of storage scheduled for commissioning in 2026.

Variable renewable generation cannot replace every form of firm capacity on its own. But that is not the relevant comparison. What matters is whether a diversified portfolio of solar, wind, hydropower, storage, flexible generation, efficiency, stronger grids, and electricity trade leaves the system less dependent on any single source of fuel, river regime, or generating facility.

Consider a dry year in which hydropower output falls. In a poorly diversified system, governments have fewer options: increase fossil generation, reduce electricity supply, or place greater pressure on reservoir operations. In a more flexible regional system, imports, solar and wind generation, storage, flexible generation, and demand response can absorb part of the shock.

While none of this creates more water, it does something important all the same: a more flexible electricity system expands the choices available to water managers. Instead of optimizing reservoirs exclusively around immediate electricity shortages, governments have more room to consider irrigation requirements, ecological flows, drought reserves, and downstream needs. Conversely, more efficient irrigation and pumping reduce stress on the power system.

The water-energy nexus is therefore not only a story of two sectors competing for scarce resources. Under the right conditions, investments in one can increase the resilience of the other.

And What About Nuclear?

The same water-aware approach should apply to Central Asia’s emerging nuclear plans. Nuclear power can provide firm low-carbon electricity and diversify generation portfolios. Those characteristics are attractive to countries facing rapidly growing electricity demand while trying to reduce reliance on fossil fuels, descriptions that fit both Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan. Both countries are pursuing the construction of their first modern nuclear power plants.

But nuclear projects are long-lived infrastructure. Their contribution to resilience therefore needs to be assessed against future, rather than historical, conditions. That means considering future water availability and cooling requirements alongside extreme heat, construction timelines, lifecycle costs, safety and waste arrangements, financing exposure, and alternative portfolios capable of providing comparable system services.

Water is not, by itself, an argument for or against nuclear power in Central Asia. It is one of the variables that should determine whether a particular project strengthens the resilience of the wider system. The more useful question is not whether nuclear power is inherently compatible with the region’s energy transition, but under what technical, financial, and environmental conditions it contributes to a system capable of functioning under greater climatic and hydrological uncertainty.

Stop Negotiating Only Over Cubic Meters

A more integrated energy system can create flexibility, but infrastructure alone will not resolve Central Asia’s water tensions. The institutional question is equally important. Regional water negotiations have traditionally focused heavily on allocation: how much water should each country receive? Benefit-sharing offers a different way of looking at the same rivers.

A reservoir does more than hold a particular volume of water. Depending on how it is operated, it can generate electricity, regulate seasonal flows, support irrigation, maintain drought reserves, reduce flood risks, and create economic value through regional electricity trade. The relevant question therefore becomes not only who receives how many cubic meters, but what services coordinated management provides — and how the costs and benefits should be distributed.

There are precedents outside of Central Asia. Under the treaty-based framework of the Organisation pour la Mise en Valeur du fleuve Sénégal (OMVS), Mali, Mauritania, and Senegal jointly own major infrastructure including the Manantali Dam. Its benefits include hydropower, irrigation, navigation, and water regulation. The model cannot simply be transplanted to Central Asia, but Manantali demonstrates an important principle: cooperation can be organized around measurable infrastructure and regulation services rather than around the idea that one country is “selling” another country water or energy.

Central Asia may soon have an opportunity to test that principle. The Kambarata-1 hydropower project in Kyrgyzstan is being developed through a trilateral partnership with Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan. This creates a potential framework for connecting joint investment with agreed reservoir regimes, electricity purchases, drought reserves, and measurable downstream services.

Countries could jointly model how different operating regimes affect electricity generation, irrigation reliability, ecosystem flows, and drought resilience. They could then negotiate co-financing, electricity contracts, or service payments around the additional benefits created by coordinated operation. That would represent a significant change in regional water diplomacy: from negotiating primarily over scarcity toward negotiating over value.

Water Security Is Energy Security

Central Asia does not lack regional institutions or international initiatives. Mechanisms for water allocation and electricity coordination already exist, while programs such as the Central Asia Water and Energy Program and new World Bank-supported regional projects are intended to strengthen infrastructure, data, water management, and cross-border cooperation. The harder task is translating dialogue and modeling into shared drought procedures, coordinated infrastructure decisions, investable projects, and predictable operating rules.

The economic stakes are significant. A July 2026 World Bank regional analysis put the cost of insufficient cooperation among national water systems at more than $4.5 billion annually. Meanwhile, the REMIT program is designed to deepen regional electricity connectivity and trade, creating a platform for larger long-term economic gains from integration.

Central Asia’s energy transition will therefore not succeed simply by adding low-carbon capacity. It will succeed if the resulting system remains reliable during heatwaves and droughts, affordable for consumers, compatible with ecosystem needs, and resilient across shared river basins.

Water security is not an argument against the energy transition; it is a condition for designing it well.

The deeper opportunity is to move beyond negotiating only over cubic meters of water and toward negotiating over the wider benefits that water and energy cooperation can create. If Central Asian states can translate that principle into shared evidence, measurable services, joint investment, and predictable operating arrangements, water may become not only a constraint on the region’s energy transition, but one of the strongest incentives for deeper regional cooperation.

title: China Is Moving Toward a New Form of Coercion at Sea
description: China is pushing patrols into new waters near Taiwan, regularizing its presence, and deploying research vessels that can conduct military reconnaissance.
text:
Since Beijing announced special maritime operations on June 6, its forces have grown more assertive – pushing patrols into new waters, rotating formations to regularize presence, and deploying research vessels that can conduct military reconnaissance. This all points to a new form of coercion taking shape.

On July 4, the Global Times – a mouthpiece for the Chinese Communist Party – declared that China’s maritime patrols had entered “a new phase,” defined by a move towards “a more systematic, institutionalized, and long-term framework” and away from “isolated military exercises or patrols.”

Recent deployments bear this out. Between June 6 and June 10, China’s Ministry of Transport carried out its first special operation in waters east of Taiwan, halting commercial vessels and requesting information on their points of origin and destination.

While China has announced mandatory inspections during past exercises, it has never successfully enforced them. This time was different. Chinese Coast Guard ships conducted inspections en masse through radio communications with all transiting commercial vessels. Even foreign commercial vessels – including three vessels from Singapore, Benin, and Liberia – reported receiving radio messages from Chinese authorities to comply with requests.

According to Chinese state news agency Xinhua, across those four days, Chinese maritime authorities inspected 198 passing vessels, and even “rectified violations involving three ships.” The sheer quantity of reported inspections, followed by a public announcement of the results, demonstrates China’s ability to govern vessel traffic in Taiwan’s waters. Beijing uses that as grounds to assert jurisdiction over the island and to push the narrative that cross-strait dynamics are China’s internal affairs.

These operations may be testing grounds for an eventual quarantine, where China selectively permits commercial vessels to enter or leave, exerting immense pressure on Taiwan’s supply lines. If that is the case, the series of multi-day patrols serve two functions.

First, they test how foreign nations respond to maritime traffic controls. Knowing which nations elect to respond, and to what degree, gives Beijing some sense of what to expect. The United Kingdom, Germany, and France, for instance, issued a joint statement expressing alarm over the maritime activities. Australia raised concerns directly with Chinese officials. How forceful Beijing judges the pushback to be will affect the intensity of operations. In the event of an actual quarantine, though, responses are likely to be more pronounced.

Second, they normalize China’s vessel inspections, shortening the leap to a quarantine. In July, China’s Coast Guard began rotating its formations to regularize its law-enforcement presence. The Global Times has noted the advantages of maintaining a “constant presence” because “a normalized presence itself exerts pressure.” The longer Beijing can keep ships on station, the more quickly it can impose a quarantine.

The location of operations is unusual as well. Until June, China appeared to prioritize the Taiwan Strait, where conditions are most favorable for launching an amphibious invasion. Oddly enough, the maritime operations have been concentrated in waters opposite the strait, to the east of Taiwan. The island’s eastern coast has long been regarded as a low-priority zone as steep mountains make military landings difficult.

But choosing to operate in the east is not random. The move effectively shrinks the space that Taiwan can operate in, aligning with China’s broader boa-constrictor strategy to sever the island from international support. More telling is that these patrols, China claims, were initiated as a response to talks between Japan and the Philippines to delimit maritime boundaries east of Taiwan. Beijing hopes to deter strategic cooperation between two U.S. allies, one located north and the other to the south of the island, that may each play critical roles during a conflict over Taiwan.

A final novelty of the recent operations is the sharp increase in Chinese research vessels operating in waters around Taiwan. While Beijing maintains that these ships only conduct marine scientific research, their missions appear far less benign. Publicly available tracking data shows that these vessels could be systematically mapping the undersea terrain, presaging planning for naval operations. Since June 6, at least seven research vessels have been suspected of conducting research with military applications.

Taken together, these signs indicate that a more intrusive form of coercion is taking form. Regional nations would be unwise to dismiss this as more of the same.

title: China’s Free-Trade Offer to Africa Won’t Solve the Trade Imbalance
description: Beijing has opened its enormous market to African exports. Whether that helps the continent move up global value chains is another question.
text:
In Abuja on August 14, 2026, nearly 500 government officials, diplomats, scholars, and business representatives gathered for a seminar on China’s new zero-tariff policy and what it means for African economic transformation. Nigeria’s minister of state for agriculture, Aliyu Sabi Abdullahi, used the occasion to strike a cautious note. “Zero tariffs alone do not guarantee success,” he told the room. “The question before us, therefore, is not, can Nigeria export more? The question should be, can Nigeria export better?”

Since May 1, China has extended zero-tariff treatment across 100 percent of tariff lines to the 53 African countries with which it holds diplomatic relations. That gives nearly all of Africa (with the lone exception of Eswatini) duty-free access to one of the world’s largest consumer markets. The early results look encouraging: Chinese imports from Africa reached $28.7 billion in May and June, up 23.5 percent from a year earlier. During the seminar in Abuja, China’s ambassador to Nigeria reported that Chinese imports from Nigeria specifically had already grown more than 40 percent year-on-year in both May and June.

African governments have good reason to welcome China’s new zero-tariff policy. The problem is that lower tariffs alone cannot resolve the deeper imbalance that has built up in Africa-China trade.

Africa-China merchandise trade hit a record $348 billion in 2025, but the flows were badly lopsided. China sold Africa $225 billion in goods, Africa sold China $123 billion. For every dollar of goods Africa sold China, it bought back roughly $1.83. The resulting deficit, $102 billion, was 64.5 percent above 2024’s figure. In the same period, Chinese exports to Africa grew 25.8 percent, while African exports to China grew just 5.4 percent.

Market access – like China’s new offer to African countries – can change the volume of trade, but not necessarily the structure of trade. What is actually being exported by each partner matters more than the size of the deficit itself. Research from the Boston University Global Development Policy Center and the African Economic Research Consortium found that from 2000 through 2022, 89 percent of African exports to China came from extractive industries: oil, copper, iron ore, alumina. Over the same period, 94 percent of African imports from China were manufactured goods.

A 2026 update from the same researchers showed that not much had changed. Extracted natural resources still dominate Africa’s exports to China, while agriculture and manufacturing each account for a small share of export value.

Most African countries have clearly stated ambitions to move up the value chain. Lower tariffs alone will do little to accomplish that goal. The rising volume of Africa-China trade is easy to measure and just as easy to celebrate, but the overall numbers are less important than the composition of trade.

The tariff opening still matters, of course. African exports of avocados, apples, and oranges to China have risen sharply since implementation. Market access of this kind can pull real investment toward certification, cold-chain logistics, and packaging, some of the obstacles holding producers back. But that won’t happen automatically.

Take copper as an example. Copper can be exported from Africa as raw ore, or it can be refined and worked into components before it ships. Currently, that work – and the added value – happens almost entirely outside the continent. China’s zero-tariff policy doesn’t care whether the copper is raw or refined; the tariff line is the same either way.

Two recent examples show what greater processing and value capture inside Africa can actually look like. At a processing plant in Kenya’s Athi River Export Processing Zone, locally grown avocados are ripened, sorted, and cold-pressed into extra virgin avocado oil bound for China. In Rwanda, a company that began exporting dried chilies to China in 2022 shipped its first batch of pickled chilies in June – a deliberate move toward a higher-value semi-processed product made only after the tariff change. In both cases, more processing is happening before the goods leave the continent, which means more of the value is captured in Kenya and Rwanda rather than downstream in China.

African countries do have the capability to move up the value chain, and intra-Africa trade proves it. UNCTAD reported that 61 percent of trade happening within the continent consists of processed and semi-processed goods, far above Africa’s share of processed exports to the rest of the world. The opportunity is to pair China’s external market with the regional value chains the African Continental Free Trade Area is meant to build. Cotton grown in Mali or Burkina Faso can be baled and shipped directly to China for processing, or it can move first through mills in Cote d’Ivoire or Ghana and leave as finished cloth.

It’s not tariffs that are holding back African manufacturing. China’s zero-tariff policy won’t solve problems like unreliable electricity, expensive financing, inefficient ports, thin transport links, certification bottlenecks, or customs delays. UNCTAD estimated that road transport alone accounts for about 29 percent of the price of goods traded within Africa, compared with 7 percent for goods traded beyond it. According to UNCTAD, non-tariff barriers constrain intra-African trade roughly three times more than tariffs.

African governments need to treat China’s opening as one input into a larger industrial policy, not as a substitute for having one. Africa-China trade will likely keep setting records, but that alone won’t help African economies climb global value chains. The real test will show up in the breakdown of those trade statistics: whether Africa is still mostly exporting raw materials like crude oil and copper ore or refined metals and finished goods.

title: China’s Global Strategy Under Xi Jinping
description: Insights from Steve Tsang.
text:
The Diplomat author Mercy Kuo regularly engages subject-matter experts, policy practitioners, and strategic thinkers across the globe for their diverse insights into U.S. Asia policy. This conversation with Steve Tsang – professor of China studies and director of the China Institute at SOAS University of London and co-author with Olivia Cheung of “China’s Global Strategy Under Xi Jinping” (Oxford 2026) – is the 524th in “The Trans-Pacific View Insight Series.”

What is China’s global strategy under Xi Jinping and specifically its two primary pivots?

China’s global strategy under Xi Jinping has a double pivot. Its primary pivot is to engage the Global South, in both country and population terms a clear majority in the world, to secure support for China to steadily reshape the existing international order by re-centering the U.N. in global politics. The idea is that under Chinese leadership the Global South can make the U.N. more responsive to them, the majority. Xi calls this the “democratization of international relations.” With the support of the Global South, Beijing seeks to forge “the common destiny for humankind,” implying transforming what remains of the “liberal international order” into the Sino-centric tianxia order.

To signal the advent of Chinese global preeminence or the tianxia order requires a stunning demonstration of China’s might. There is therefore a complementary pivot. This is for China to take Taiwan despite the U.S. committing, under its Taiwan Relations Act (1979), to help Taiwan defend itself against an externally imposed change of its status. Taiwan is geographically in the middle of the strategically vital First Island Chain in the Pacific Ocean and has avoided falling under Chinese control with U.S. protection since 1950. Unlike his predecessors who merely saw Taiwan as a legacy from the Chinese Civil War (1946-9) to be dealt with without a meaningful timeline, Xi has changed the paradigm. While he retains the irredentist language, taking Taiwan is part of his China Dream, to be completed by 2050.

Xi would prefer Taiwan negotiate for a “peaceful re-unification” and thus remove the raison d’être for the U.S. to intervene. Should this not materialize Beijing will use force. By taking Taiwan China will show the U.S. (and its allies) cannot prevent it from seizing the First Island Chain. It will acquire a critical springboard to project power well into the Pacific and make key U.S. allies like Japan and South Korea question if they can rely on their respective defense treaties with the U.S. It will establish dominance in the Western Pacific and mark the advent of Chinese global preeminence.

Examine the concept of “tianxia” as an alternative international order.

Tianxia consists of two Chinese characters, “sky” and “below,” meaning “all under heaven.” As a political concept it was applied when the empire in China was united, rich, powerful, and more advanced than others in organizational, civilizational, and technological terms. China was supposed to be so superior that others looked to it for guidance and inspiration, resulting in pax Sinica without China asserting hegemony. This is the new international order into which Xi would like to steer the existing one to transform. The historical reality of tianxia was different: Chinese empires behaved like other great empires in history and exercised hegemony by force when required.

To Xi, putting tianxia in place implies “restoring” Chinese global preeminence. He does not intend China to replace the U.S. as the global hegemon, not least because American hegemony also included delivering costly public services to the global community. He merely seeks preeminence for China, as it will ensure that the Communist Party system cannot be challenged.

Analyze China’s instrumental approach to global economic engagement.

This is the pragmatic side of China’s global strategy. Xi’s Sino-centrism is not entirely inward looking. He requires China to engage the world to generate an edge. He builds on the Chinese Communist Party’s long-standing concept of comprehensive national power, implying he instrumentally builds up economic power to complement military power to assert Chinese preeminence. Beijing thus seeks to acquire a leadership position in new, particularly strategically important, technologies. It means China uses all means at its disposal to create a situation where acknowledging Chinese preeminence would be less costly than challenging it. China further aims to become a rule maker in the international community and in the global economy. Instrumentalism also applies to how China cultivates support from the Global South, at the U.N. and elsewhere. Xi does not see pragmatism as contradictory to his insistence that all Chinese cadres must ideologically adhere to Xi Thought.

Identify the strengths and weaknesses of China’s global strategy.

The greatest strength of China’s global strategy lies in its capacity to gain traction in the Global South. The reality that most countries in the Global South are not functioning democracies and their leaders are autocrats, and China does not carry a colonial legacy there, makes its rhetoric of the “democratization of international relations” sufficiently credible. In addition, what China asks of them, supporting China to change the U.N. system and securing control of Taiwan, are cost free to them. China being tightly controlled by the Chinese Communist Party and Xi meant China adopts a disciplined approach when it engages Global South leaders, ensuring its message and personal cultivation efforts are effective.

Its greatest weakness is that the distinction between preeminence and hegemony is fundamentally a distinction without a difference. Few leaders in the Global South truly fail to understand its implications. Global South support for Xi’s agenda can only last if it is beneficial to themselves, and if the democracies cannot act in concert to offer a more attractive alternative.

Assess the effectiveness of Washington’s “America First” policy as a credible counterweight to China’s global strategy.

Washington adopting the “America First” policy is a godsend for Beijing, particularly over its engagement of the Global South. It corroborates China’s claim that the world suffers from Western domination centered around the U.S., as “America First” confirms that Washington is first and foremost about advancing American interests. It undermines the moral authority of the liberal international order, which provides a case for China to push for transforming it into the tianxia variant. It also weakens American allies’ solidarity with Washington. As messaging rhetoric “America First” is less appealing than the “democratization of international relations” to the Global South.
