title: China’s Unity Through Erasure Should Worry Central Asia
description: The SCO may serve legitimate Central Asian interests, but it should not become the vehicle through which Beijing’s definitions of security, political loyalty, and ethnic identity become normalized across the Turkic world.
text:
China’s growing efforts to increase control over the Turkic states of Central Asia was the dominant, if little discussed, outcome of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan on September 1.

Beijing wants its relationship with the Central Asian states to be one of vassals thankful for China’s “protection” and economic integration. The recent summit produced the 25th anniversary Bishkek Declaration and 27 other documents, which claimed they would strengthen mechanisms for security, countering terrorism and organized crime, and promised new transport lines and logistics. On its face, the Central Asian states are promised infrastructure, technology and diplomatic engagement. But beneath those promises is guaranteed deeper dependence on Chinese capital, standards, and security concepts.

China successfully got Muslim-majority states (including Iran, Pakistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan) to sign onto documents clearly aimed at China’s own Turkic Muslim populations. The SCO endorsement of combatting “terrorism, separatism, and extremism” was China-sponsored and indisputably about Uyghurs. Under this pretext, the institutional capacity that enables surveillance, intelligence exchange, and political labeling of Uyghurs is being expanded.

Sadly, China’s economic leverage and coercion means the public support that these Muslim-majority states provide to Muslim communities globally is absent when it comes to China.

The Central Asian states should ponder carefully when Beijing uses the security vocabulary noted in the Bishkek Declaration. China’s decade-long ethnic cleansing campaign in Xinjiang, also referred to as East Turkestan, demonstrates what happens when cultural difference is reclassified as a security problem. Religious behavior can be labelled extremism. Cultural autonomy can be called separatism. Overseas relationships of Uyghurs with Turkic states have tended to attract suspicion. Language, memory, and identity become objects of political management.

ASPI’s Xinjiang Data Project has documented mass detention, surveillance, forced labor and political re-education. ASPI’s Cultural Erasure research estimated that around 16,000 of Xinjiang’s 24,000 mosques had been damaged or destroyed, alongside extensive damage to Islamic shrines and other sacred sites central to regional Turkic history. Arguments that Beijing is only concerned about its “ internal affairs” are blind to China’s foreign policy.

Beijing’s formula of combating the “three evils” – terrorism, separatism, and extremism – was incorporated into the SCO establishment document signed in June 2001, and that vocabulary has been institutionalized across Eurasia.

That should matter in the Muslim-majority Turkic states of Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, and Turkiye.

During Xi’s visit to Kyrgyzstan, Bishkek explicitly reaffirmed support for China on Xinjiang-related issues while agreeing to deepen law-enforcement, counterterrorism, and information-security cooperation. China and Uzbekistan have made similar commitments.

Uyghur, Kazakh, Kyrgyz, Uzbek, and other Turkic identities do not end at borders. Families, languages, religious traditions, and diaspora communities extend across the region. When governments repeat Beijing’s anti-separatist language without qualification, they risk allowing legitimate concern for fellow Turkic communities to be recast as interference or subversion.

China’s July 2026 Law on the Promotion of Ethnic Unity and Progress contains a provision on extraterritoriality (Article 63) that authorizes Chinese authorities to pursue organizations and individuals outside of China’s borders.

China’s recent technological advancements increase the risks that might have been assessed in 2001 by the SCO founding nations (Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan) as unlikely to cross borders. Some Chinese tech companies expanding across Central Asia have developed important capabilities within the same security ecosystem used to monitor and suppress Uyghurs and other Turkic peoples in the region.

iFLYTEK worked with China’s Ministry of Public Security on voiceprint systems and supplied voice-recognition technology used by Xinjiang police. It has since established a Central Asian presence in Tashkent offering multilingual AI services.

Technical documentation from Dahua policing systems described functions including “real-time Uyghur warnings” and identification of Uyghur attributes. Dahua disputes allegations that it intentionally designed systems for ethnic targeting. But its technology demonstrates how ostensibly neutral surveillance platforms can be adapted for ethnicity-based policing. Dahua systems are already present in Central Asian security environments.

Genomics raises an equally serious question of sovereignty. BGI has established sequencing capabilities in Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan and has discussed combining AI with large-scale genomic data in Central Asia. Those laboratory platforms are likely to be connected and operate on Beijing’s cyber cloud, in collaboration with companies such as Huawei. But genomic information is permanent, sensitive, and strategically valuable. The Central Asian states should know where samples are processed, where data is stored, who can access it, and whether it can leave national jurisdiction.

The same scrutiny should apply to natural resources.

Chinese entities are expanding into geological exploration, mining, and processing across Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, Tajikistan, and Kyrgyzstan. Joint surveys can give Chinese partners detailed knowledge of strategic mineral deposits long before extraction begins. The China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway will bring genuine commercial benefits, but it will also strengthen Beijing’s overland supply chains and reduce China’s dependence on vulnerable maritime routes.

The answer for the Central Asian SCO members is not decoupling from China as there is a genuine need for infrastructure, capital, technology, and markets to boost living standards. But blindly accepting and complying with Beijing’s demands is also not what a sovereign state should aim for. The Russian invasion of Ukraine has heightened anxiety across the former Soviet republics and encouraged Central Asian states to diversify their external relationships, including by moving closer to Beijing. But that strategic realignment should not proceed without regard to China’s human rights in general and to Xinjiang specifically. The experience of Uyghurs and other Turkic peoples under Chinese rule offers a stark warning about the political costs that can accompany deeper dependence on Beijing.

Turkic governments should distinguish violent terrorism from peaceful political advocacy, religious practice, and diaspora activity. They should scrutinize Chinese surveillance and AI systems, protect biometric and genomic data, retain sovereign control over strategic geological information, and strengthen protections against transnational repression.

The SCO may serve legitimate Central Asian interests, but it should not become the vehicle through which Beijing’s definitions of security, political loyalty, and ethnic identity become normalized across the Turkic world.

title: China’s Visibility Gap Around the Trump-Xi Summit
description: Xi’s U.S. visit was extensively covered by official outlets. It's much harder to gauge public opinion or even interest.
text:
Beijing formally confirmed Chinese President Xi Jinping’s September 23-25 visit to the United States on September 21, just two days before the trip began. The news had barely registered among many of the Chinese people I spoke with the following day. Official coverage began appearing online following the announcement, but visible discussion among ordinary users on platforms such as Weibo, WeChat, and Xiaohongshu (RedNote) remained scarce.

That changed once Xi’s visit was underway. Chinese social media filled with reports about the summit, with much of the visible content coming from official outlets and accounts, emphasizing the diplomatic significance and choreography of the visit, including Trump’s reception of Xi and calls for “constructive strategic stability.” The shift from limited information to abundant official coverage raised a different question: How much did ordinary Chinese people know about the summit before official coverage moved into full gear?

On September 22, the day after Beijing’s formal announcement and one day before Xi’s visit began, I conducted informal interviews with a dozen individuals across China and the diaspora, including overseas students and professionals, domestic public-sector workers, private-sector employees, and an older relative. Awareness varied considerably by location and occupation.

Overseas students and professionals had generally learned of the trip earlier through foreign news outlets or private messaging groups. Some public-sector employees in China learned about it only after the official announcement, noting that senior leaders’ schedules are typically kept confidential until the last minute. Meanwhile, many of the private-sector employees I spoke with in China remained unaware of the visit even after the announcement.

Yet when asked about it, many responded by searching for the news themselves. What they found was a remarkably uniform information environment. On Weibo, Douyin, and Xiaohongshu, searches related to Xi’s U.S. visit were dominated by official and state-media content. On Xiaohongshu, some targeted searches produced either zero visible results or unrelated posts concerning personal travel and visas. Under some official media posts, comment sections were restricted or turned off. The interviews suggested that curiosity could exist even when little of it was publicly visible.

It is tempting to attribute this lack of visible discussion solely to censorship, but the interviews pointed to a more complicated picture. One respondent pointed to self-censorship: “Some of what people might say in private wouldn’t feel appropriate to post publicly.” Others suggested that interest might increase only after the meetings produced concrete outcomes.

The searches themselves could not reveal whether the lack of visible discussion reflected content controls, platform ranking, self-censorship, limited public interest, or some combination of these factors.

The summit itself added another layer to this ambiguity. Once Xi arrived in the United States, information about the visit was no longer difficult to find. Official reports and accounts circulated extensive coverage of the meetings and their diplomatic symbolism. Yet the greater volume of information did not necessarily make public opinion easier to observe: Much of what was readily visible still came from official sources rather than ordinary users.

However, in specialized, interest-driven spaces, discussion was easier to find. On WeChat financial blogs like “Liu Xiaobo Talk Finance” and their commentary threads, retail investors and market watchers debated the summit’s possible implications for tariffs, stock prices, and exchange rates. According to the CGCC-USA 2026 Business Survey Report, 79 percent of surveyed Chinese companies operating in the United States reported negative impacts from tariffs, while 36 percent anticipated a slight improvement in bilateral trade relations, underscoring the concrete economic stakes surrounding the summit.

The Trump-Xi summit thus exposed a broader “visibility gap” in China’s information environment. On September 22, even after the visit had been officially announced, many of the people I interviewed had not heard about it, although they often became curious enough to search once asked. Days later, information about the summit was everywhere, but the most visible narratives remained overwhelmingly official.

For outside observers trying to gauge public sentiment in China, the difficulty is not simply that Chinese people are silent. It is that the Chinese internet makes a lack of discussion unusually difficult to interpret.

title: China’s Young Women Are Rewriting the Rules of Adulthood
description: Modernization has expanded women’s choices and made the traditional sequence of adulthood – marry, have children, settle near family – less inevitable.
text:
In the U.S. state of Hawai‘i, Iris lives far from the pressures of urban China. Growing up in Zhejiang, she spent much of her childhood on what her mother called “self-improvement”: Olympiad math, piano lessons, and daily swimming. After graduating from New York University (NYU), Iris chose a simple, quiet life in Hawai‘i, using geographic distance to protect her personal autonomy from the pressure facing Chinese women in their 20s to settle down, marry, and have children.

Halfway across the world, Jessica is confronting the same expectations from within China. After studying in Shanghai and Europe and working at an international organization in New York, where a mentor once urged her to stop working late and “enjoy the New York night,” Jessica returned to China to finish her master’s thesis and enter the domestic job market. There, she met a second, more intimate pressure: the expectation that she should marry and have children. Rather than quietly accepting it, she confronted the idea directly, over dinner with her mother, asking: “Are you actually happy in your own marriage? What has it genuinely brought you?”

Iris and Jessica belong to a highly educated cohort of young Chinese women whose lives are unfolding alongside a demographic problem the state is eager to solve. Facing an aging population, a shrinking workforce, and historically low fertility rates, Beijing introduced the Three-Child Policy in 2021, allowing Chinese couples to have up to three children. China’s government has since increasingly emphasized marriage and childbearing as social priorities.

Yet China’s demographic crisis gained steam during the same decades of modernization that gave women access to more education, higher incomes, and greater mobility. That means women like Iris and Jessica have more reasons, and more means, to delay or reconsider marriage and motherhood.

Research on China’s education expansion by Jiwei Chen and Jiangying Guo of Nanjing Agricultural University found that increased female education can delay entry into marriage and childbirth and reduce fertility, in part by raising the opportunity costs of childrearing. The modernization that expanded women’s choices has made the traditional sequence of adulthood – marry, have children, settle near family – less inevitable.

Jessica confronts this tension directly, pressing her own mother on whether marriage delivered what it promised and treating parenthood as a choice to question rather than a milestone to check off. Iris resists more obliquely: rather than arguing with the assumption that a good daughter eventually settles down close to home, she puts enough distance (first New York, then Hawai‘i) between herself and the people who would enforce the traditional path, letting their expectations fade into background noise instead of demands she has to answer.

Neither is rejecting family, marriage, or children outright. Both are refusing to treat any of these options as the default for a Chinese woman.

Jessica: Deconstructing the Script

Upon returning to China to finish her thesis, Jessica found the job hunt less a search for a career than a reckoning with what kind of life she was willing to accept. In Europe and New York, she’d grown used to a workplace culture defined by what she calls “松弛感”: ease, dignity, being treated first as a person. One night, working late in New York, her mentor stopped her: “You are in New York. You should go enjoy the night.” The line stuck with her.

The anecdote formed a sharp contrast with Jessica’s internship at a major Chinese internet company, where a hyper-competitive, results-only culture left people passing their anxiety down the hierarchy.

She posted a comparison of the two experiences on Xiaohongshu and it sparked a fight in the comments: some dismissed it as a naive “student mindset”; others agreed with a Chinese woman writing from Europe, who argued that Western employers need their workers enough to treat them decently, while Chinese managers can simply replace anyone who underperforms.

For Jessica, the real question was how much room there was for personal choice to override social norms. That questioning carried over from professional pressures straight into marriage.

Years abroad had sharpened her sense of independence, but her father still pictured a conventional future for her, and relatives kept the pressure alive by mentioning which of her peers had already married. Jessica pushed back on the premise itself, arguing that a mother-daughter bond can matter as much as a marital one. She half-jokingly tells relatives that if marriage is unavoidable, it’s better to get in and out of it quickly than drag out something broken.

The same skepticism shapes how she thinks about children. She’s fond of them but treats parenthood as a serious undertaking that shouldn’t simply follow marriage on a fixed timeline. She has watched enough families to conclude that unhappy marriages, and kids who are under-supported despite material comfort, are more common than the success stories that get celebrated. Teenagers hit adolescence with mental health struggles, some withdrawing from school, often because parents were too consumed by work to be present.

Jessica has also watched women of her mother’s generation absorb the burden of family life, reshaping careers around husbands and children. She has no intention of doing the same by default.

That came to a head at a family dinner, when marriage came up again and Jessica turned the question back on her mother: was she actually happy in her marriage? What had it given her? It was an invitation to examine whether women’s sacrifices for family are as inevitable as they’re made to seem.

“If my pain can never be carried by anyone else,” Jessica told The Diplomat, “then my happiness has to be mine to build, too.” She’s stopped ruling out partners by age, and increasingly by nationality; a good match is rare enough without narrowing the field further. Her mother has softened too, no longer pressing on timelines.

None of this makes her anti-marriage or anti-motherhood. But Jessica insists on the right to decide what place they hold in her life, rather than letting either define her adulthood before she’s had the chance to define it herself.

Iris: Exiting the Room

Growing up in Zhejiang, Iris Liu’s school breaks were a rotation of enrichment classes: Olympiad math, swimming, roller skating, dance, painting, piano. As an only child, she absorbed her mother’s conviction that giving her every possible advantage was simply what good parenting looked like. Before Iris had even reached middle school, her mother was already telling her she needed to learn to swim: American Ivy League universities, she’d heard, liked students who could swim. The plan was always aimed outward, toward a future far from home.

Years later, Iris would indeed leave China. She just wouldn’t use that mobility the way her mother had imagined.

The first crack came early, almost by accident. A two-week middle-school trip to Los Angeles was supposed to preview the life her mother was preparing her for. Instead, Iris came home unimpressed: a suburban campus, cafeteria pizza, none of the excitement she’d expected. Her disappointment rippled into her mother’s plans: the pressure around swimming eased, and the push toward an international high-school track quietly faded. Still, the broader trajectory held.

Iris went on to NYU, and after graduation had the kind of options her education was supposed to produce: interviews for corporate jobs with six-figure salaries. She did not end up in any of these. She chose instead a job in Hawai‘i.

Her parents had a particular idea of success. When Iris told them about interviews with major firms with salaries over $100,000 a year, they barely reacted. Her father countered instead with a story about a colleague’s child who’d quit an investment-banking job after three years, burned out. It was meant to be a cautionary tale about what a prestigious career actually costs. What her parents want for Iris is harder to define than pure career success. They want her to have a manageable life, to be somewhere stable, and eventually to come home.

That expectation rarely arrives as a demand; it shows up in small comments instead. While Iris was in New York, her father compared New York’s infrastructure unfavorably to Shanghai’s. Her mother notes that Hangzhou “isn’t so bad” whenever Iris complains about where she’s living. When Iris mentions a hard week at work, the response is often some version of: why not just come home, find something stable?

Nothing is framed as an ultimatum, and her parents insist the choice is hers, but the suggestions add up to a recognizable idea of what adulthood should eventually look like: stop drifting, settle, put down roots – back in China, of course.

In China, the idea of settling down is hard to separate from marriage. For women in their 20s, stability tends to arrive bundled with questions about where they’ll live, whom they’ll marry, when they’ll start a family. Distance, Iris has found, gives her room to answer those questions on her own schedule.

“In China, there is a pervasive pressure on women in their 20s to quickly find stability, buy an apartment, and marry,” she says. “In Hawai‘i, that marital clock simply vanishes.”

That doesn’t mean the tension disappears, only that it changes shape. Iris is living inside one social world while carrying the expectations of another. The norms around her carry no real urgency about marrying or settling permanently. Her family’s expectations carry plenty. If she followed the culture in her new home, Iris risks feeling like she’s failing her family, but trying to import her family’s values wholesale doesn’t fit the life she’s actually building.

“It’s a little like being caught in the middle,” she said. “The values your family brings with them don’t completely fit the society you’re living in, but you can’t just stop caring about what your family thinks either.”

Iris still sometimes looks at friends her age who are marrying, buying homes, building linear careers, and wonders if she’s falling behind. Her own path has zigzagged instead: an exchange year in Japan, an unplanned application to NYU, offers turned down, a move to Hawai‘i with no five-year plan attached. But the uncertainty isn’t a side effect of her choices – it’s part of what she’s choosing.

Her parents spent years investing in an education meant to expand what was possible for Iris. She did become educated, and mobile. She simply redefined what that mobility was for: not a way of moving closer to the life her family imagined, but a way of gaining enough distance to decide, on her own, whether that life was ever really what she wanted.

Where Jessica confronts the script by questioning it at the dinner table, Iris resists it by leaving the room – going far enough away that she can still hear her family’s expectations without having to obey them.

Choosing to Choose

Jessica and Iris didn’t set out to make a political statement. Jessica wanted a job, and a marriage, that didn’t consume her; Iris wanted a life she’d actually chosen rather than one assembled for her since childhood, class by enrichment class.

They are both ultimately resisting the assumption that a woman’s education and independence are ultimately in service of marriage, children, and “settling down,” rather than choices she gets to make, or decline, on her own terms.

Their parents invested in swimming lessons and Olympiad math and study abroad because those things were supposed to expand what their daughters could become – and they did, just not in the direction their families expected.

Marriage and motherhood remain open questions for both of them. Their parents will keep aging, friends will keep marrying, and the clock Iris describes may eventually start ticking. Neither woman claims to know what they will ultimately decide. But the fact that they see marriage and motherhood as a choice at all – something that can be embraced or refused – is already a small revolution in and of itself.

title: Chinese Data Centers Will Shape ASEAN’s AI Norms
description: Southeast Asian governments' reliance on foreign capital, expertise, and capacity could leave them vulnerable over the longer term.
text:
In June, Alibaba Cloud opened two data centers in Johor, bringing the number of Alibaba facilities in Malaysia to a total of five–its largest data center presence in Southeast Asia. The opening came four months after ASEAN endorsed a Malaysia-led framework governing cross-border cloud computing, which set regional principles for data protection, regulatory access, and cross-border data hosting.

Yet even as Malaysia helps write ASEAN’s cloud rules, the region’s growing reliance on Chinese infrastructure may embed norms shaped by Chinese law and comparatively weak or opaque safeguards against cyber misuse, regardless of the principles expressed in member state policies. It may also favor Chinese models whose developers disclose less about such safeguards, even as Beijing tightly controls politically sensitive content in Chinese-developed models. ASEAN governments should thus treat data center investment as a form of AI governance and norms diffusion, rather than a matter primarily or solely of industrial policy.

Only a few companies can provide data centers, computing capacity, and complete cloud and AI systems at the required scale. Cloud providers can influence technical practices beyond their own facilities. Firms and agencies building on their platforms must make their systems compatible with the providers’ services and meet requirements for access, configuration, and security. Because so many digital services depend on data centers, the technical specifications and operating practices adopted in Chinese-built or Chinese-operated facilities will shape the services that run on them.

These facilities are therefore an early place to examine whether Chinese involvement is translating into broader influence over technical standards and operational norms. Dependency through platform lock-in allows this influence to develop and become durable within systems and creates a risk that the government could lose practical control over its use of those systems. Once government agencies and highly regulated industries build services around one provider, implementing different privacy or security standards would often require redesigning entire ecosystems, retraining workers, and shouldering substantial migration costs.

Chinese cloud providers have expanded their footprint in Malaysia and Indonesia through partnerships with governments and businesses to embed their cloud services into the core infrastructure of the digital economy. Even when operating abroad, Chinese cloud providers must comply with China’s Cybersecurity Law, Data Security Law, and National Intelligence Law. These laws create pathways for the Chinese government to compel access to data deemed relevant to national security, not unlike the USA PATRIOT Act, CLOUD Act, and FISA 702. Those same obligations helped U.S. prosecutors build their case against Chinese intelligence officer Xu Yanjun. Under a warrant issued in December 2017, Apple provided the FBI with his iCloud data, which supported his arrest in Belgium and extradition to the U.S. the following year. ASEAN governments are likely aware that using Chinese infrastructure carries risks to personal data, as does using U.S. infrastructure.

In addition to building AI infrastructure in Malaysia, Alibaba is also beginning to train people in how to use it. In 2025, Selangor state recognized Alibaba Cloud as a provider under its Multi Cloud Services initiative. The company now offers training in its proprietary AI Toolkit and certification courses to government agencies, educators, students, and local communities. It has also partnered with the Malaysia Digital Economy Corporation – the government agency under the Ministry of Digital leading the Malaysian economy’s technological transformation – to train small and medium-sized enterprises in adopting cloud computing and AI.

In Indonesia, Huawei has developed similar relationships, such as partnering with the National Cyber and Crypto Agency and the Institut Teknologi Del, establishing a Huawei Academy, and providing digital literacy and cybersecurity training to the Indonesian Air Force. Huawei describes these programs as a means of sharing cybersecurity “best practices” built on its tools and expertise. Through training and socialization, such practices can become the foundation of professional norms.

Sharing best practices and developing norms is not inherently malicious. But these practices are taking root in a region where digital rules and enforcement remain uneven, while intensifying U.S.-China AI competition is making ASEAN countries an increasing focus of U.S. law enforcement action. In Indonesia, a 2024 study found that vague definitions, limited enforcement, and inadequate provisions for AI or big data weakened implementation of the country’s 2022 data protection law. Although the European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation has influenced regional privacy laws, it has not produced uniform standards or enforcement, leaving room for providers’ practices to become defaults. Malaysia’s proposed safeguards may help, but businesses and agencies dependent on one provider may find switching too costly and accommodate practices at odds with domestic privacy goals.

This Chinese infrastructure buildout may also directly support advanced Chinese AI development. The Financial Times reported in November 2025 that Alibaba and ByteDance were training advanced models in Southeast Asian data centers in order to access Nvidia chips unavailable in China. As these facilities become vital to Chinese AI developers’ ability to train advanced models, Beijing may come to view Chinese-operated data centers in ASEAN as strategic assets rather than ordinary overseas investments. As China’s Data Security Law authorizes countermeasures against countries that restrict Chinese investment or trade involving data technologies, any actions within those bounds by ASEAN governments could become a potential area of friction.

While there is no definitive proof that Beijing directs Chinese data centers abroad, the domestic intelligence and data security laws with which they must comply do complicate the idea that this infrastructure will always remain purely commercial. ASEAN’s focus on faster development and accessing its latent potential as a future digital economic power is understandable, especially when foreign providers offer capital, expertise, and capacity that domestic firms cannot yet match. But a digital economy built on systems governed elsewhere raises a basic question about how much digital sovereignty ASEAN actually retains. Affecting the norms upon which ASEAN’s nascent digital economies and AI ecosystems are built may pose a threat that member country governments may underestimate.

In short, ASEAN need not wholly reject the foreign capital and expertise driving its digital growth. Rather, ASEAN governments should diversify data center providers, clarify foreign data access obligations, focus on creating domestic AI capacity, and require full visibility into the flow of data into and out of the data center. They must also preserve the ability to audit operations and intervene if they uncover unauthorized access or foreign interference. Otherwise, member governments may retain the formal authority to write their own AI and privacy rules, but lose the practical ability to enforce them.

This work was supported by the Fulbright Program.

title: Civil Society Groups File Lawsuit Against Indonesian Government Over Kalimantan Wildfires
description: The suit accuses President Prabowo Subianto and other senior officials of deliberate negligence for failing to prevent and properly handle the ongoing blazes.
text:
A group of ⁠indigenous ⁠and civil society organizations ⁠in Indonesia’s West Kalimantan province has filed a class-action ​lawsuit against the country’s government, accusing it of failing to prevent and handle the wildfires currently raging across the region.

The class action lawsuit was filed on September 17 at the Pontianak District Court by a coalition of civil groups known as Nafas Kalimantan Barat, which translates as “the breath of West Kalimantan,” Tempo reported.

The plaintiffs include the West Kalimantan chapter of the Indigenous Peoples Alliance of the Archipelago, the environmental group Laman Puyung Indonesia, and the leadership of the West Kalimantan Catholic Youth, as well as the citizen-activist Sisilius Rami.

The lawsuit names President Prabowo Subianto, Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka, the national police chief, and the head of the National Disaster Management Agency (BNPB), as well as the governor and police chief of West Kalimantan, and the ministries of health, forestry, and environment.

It accuses them of deliberate negligence for failing to prevent and properly handle the ongoing wildfires, arguing that the disaster has overwhelmed provincial capacity. It also seeks a court order that would force the government to declare a national disaster, which would enable greater financial assistance for affected areas.

For months, Kalimantan has been battling its most intense wildfires since 2015. According to a report in The Guardian, “photos from Kalimantan have shown a thick, sepia-toned haze shrouding streets and obscuring cities, schoolchildren wearing masks at their desks, and even rescuers giving oxygen to smoke-affected orangutans.” Fires are also raging in Sumatra and in parts of Papua.

Since January, nearly 900,000 hectares have been burned across Indonesia, according to data from Nusantara Atlas, which tracks fires and deforestation in Asia. This falls short of the 2.6 million hectares that were destroyed in 2015, and the 1.65 million hectares that were consumed by wildfires in 2019, but Nusantara Atlas stated that burning usually accelerates in August and peaks during September and October, and that as of July 20, cumulative hotspot activity in 2026 “was above every previous year at the same point in the season.”

“Indonesia has not yet entered the period when fire activity has historically accelerated most sharply,” it stated. “The current hotspots signal is therefore an early warning, not yet the peak.” Indonesian Forestry Minister Raja Juli Antoni has warned that with a particularly extreme El Niño climate pattern only now starting to peak, September could be “when the real battle begins.”

Glorio Sanen, the lawyer representing the plaintiffs, told the Jakarta Post that the spillover effects of peatland and forest fires in West Kalimantan – particularly the choking air pollution – continue to threaten public health and damage the environment.

“Meanwhile, our assessment concludes that there has been no sufficient coordination between the central government, ministries and even local administrations to prevent and respond to the disaster in West Kalimantan,” Glorio said.

The haze from the fires in Indonesia has now spread far beyond the country’s borders, including to the Malaysian states of Borneo, peninsular Malaysia, Brunei, Singapore, and the Philippines, affecting the health of millions. As of September 9, more than 113,000 people were reported to have suffered from wildfire-related respiratory illnesses.

Even if this year has been particularly bad for wildfires, the issue is an annual occurrence in Indonesia. As in other parts of Southeast Asia, the blazes are often deliberately lit in order to clear land for oil palm plantations and then spread raging infernos. Indonesia’s environment ministry says that it is investigating 19 companies that it believes may be linked to the wildfires, and has promised to punish any wrongdoers.

The fires have overwhelmed the Indonesian government’s capacity, in part due to the complexity of battling peatland fires. David Gaveau, a landscape ecologist who runs Nusantara Atlas, told The Guardian that fires on dried-out peatland are very difficult to extinguish, because they can burn for weeks underground. He described these fires as “the legacy of 50 years of forest degradation [and] deforestation” in Indonesia.

The initial hearing in the lawsuit is set for October 7.

title: Constitutional Reform as the Lee Jae-myung Administration’s Political Watershed
description: South Koreans have long discussed changing the way the presidency is set up. Should it – and can it – happen now?
text:
On September 18, President Lee Jae-myung convened a press conference. Unlike his other public appearances, this one was devoid of smiles. There were no pleasantries floated. He just trudged to the podium in his crisp dark navy suit, his presence and the ambience made heavier by the royal blue of the presidential office draped in the backdrop.

“I have been lacking fear and humility,” he said. “I shall revive the fear for the people and tackle every task more meticulously and fiercely, from a lower position of service.”

The administration’s poor performance in opinion polls prompted this sense of crisis and humble words. Lee’s approval ratings have been taking a steady dive since the June local elections.

Until late August, the two main factors behind the slide had been the government’s controversial housing policy and the Democratic Party’s much more controversial judicial reform, which entrusts all investigative powers to the police. That change seems premature, or even inappropriate, given the recent barrage of anecdotes of police corruption and incompetence.

In September, Lee’s approval ratings plummeted still more following his ill-fated Cabinet nominations. Back in 2021, Kim Seung-won, Lee’s pick for the justice minister, allegedly streamlined the drug approval process for a pharmaceutical company on behalf of his friend. This allegation resurfaced during nomination hearings.

Meanwhile, Lee picked Yong Hye-in, the only parliamentarian from the Basic Income Party, to lead the gender equality ministry. Yong’s insistence on holding both positions, however, garnered opprobrium.

As opposed to constituency legislators – those who won the most votes from their districts – proportional representatives like Yong owe their positions to their parties. South Korea’s proportional representation ballot, designed to give minor parties a chance at lawmaking, accounts for 46 out of the National Assembly’s 300 total seats. Legislators in these seats are expected to resign when they take up another government job since someone else from their party can replace them without tarnishing the voters’ mandate. It seemed apparent that Yong had no other reason to retain her legislative seat than to enjoy the perks of being a lawmaker.

Kim and Yong both withdrew from their ministerial nominations after much damage to the Lee administration. And now they are both under investigation, the former for alleged sexual harassment of his former staff and the latter for allegedly funneling her political funds to her husband.

The public smarts all the more to questionable behavior by liberal figures. Lee’s approval ratings in major polls hit a nadir in mid-September, dropping to 33.8 percent in a poll by Realmeter and 37 percent in another by Gallup.

So, Lee’s press conference was a revolving door of apology and resolution to do better on all the factors shaving his approval ratings. But the most emphatic point he made – and the one that received the most headlines – was his assertion that “I have no intention whatsoever for a second presidential term.”

The Problematic Presidency

The current South Korean constitution allows the president to serve a single five-year term. In 2025, when Lee was running for the snap presidential election following Yoon Suk-yeol’s impeachment, one of his campaign policies was to amend the constitution so that the president can serve two four-year consecutive terms. At the time, almost two thirds of the voters approved of such reform.

South Korea’s system of a single five-year term for the president has come under much flak. The populace has to wait too long until they can pass judgment on the president through ballots. Besides, without the prospect of another term, the incumbent president has no incentive to behave responsibly when it comes to their government. How frequently the people can make their voices heard through voting and how much accountability with which the president leads the country determine the soundness of democracy. And South Korea has been poor in this aspect.

On top of that, the strong, centralized nature of South Korea’s presidency – often called an “imperial presidency” – has exacerbated the problem. Consider the president’s monopoly on administrative decisions; the government’s monopoly on funding for the rest of the country; the president’s power to appoint some 10,000 top government agency and QUANGO posts; the president’s authority to wield some $400 billion through their budgetary decisions; their decrees overriding local government ordinances; and the National Assembly’s inability to monitor and check the president’s executive arms.

Yoon’s presidency manifested everything that could go wrong, from rampant corruption due to lack of auditory mechanisms to toxic control over law enforcement. South Korea’s presidency depends too much on the good will of that one person at the top.

Naturally, constitutional reform to trim down the imperial presidency and beef up the parliament and local government has been expected to materialize sometime soon. But the speaker of the National Assembly sparked an intense controversy in late July when he said that “the question of allowing the incumbent president to serve consecutively is ultimately up to the public.” The opposition People Power Party (PPP) immediately raised the possibility that Lee could be plotting “treason” by assuming another term.

In fact, the current constitution bars any constitutional reform – whether that’s to prolong the presidential tenure or introduce multiple terms – from applying to the incumbent president. Immediately after, the speaker admitted his error in legal interpretation.

The presidential office also clarified to the press that, when it comes to Lee running for re-election, “our constitution doesn’t allow it, the people won’t condone it, and it’s realistically impossible.” Lee, while visiting France on September 10, mentioned again that “the constitution clearly confines my term.”

Still, the controversy had gained enough traction to drag down his approval ratings ever since. Hence Lee’s forceful, articulate reminder during the September 18 press conference that the notion of him serving consecutive terms “is not only constitutionally impossible but also never have I thought of it.”

Lee then proposed to collaborate with the National Assembly to amend the constitution to allow for consecutive presidential terms – for future presidents, not for himself – and more even distribution of powers among the parliament and the central and local governments. He also didn’t fail to point out that this would require “bipartisan discussion and public opinion and ideas.”

Political Opposition

Despite Lee’s fairly categorical stance, the PPP is deliberately incredulous. “Lee says he has ‘no intention’ of serving another term. Why is it so hard for him to say ‘I will not serve another term?’” wrote Jang Dong-hyuk, the PPP leader, on his social media. To him, Lee didn’t promise anything, therefore “he hasn’t given up the dream of a second consecutive term.”

The PPP floor leader, Jeong Jeom-sig, also made it clear that the PPP wouldn’t partake in any discussion for constitutional reform during the Lee administration. “The PPP is telling you now: There will be no constitutional reform during this administration,” he said to much applause among fellow PPP legislators. Like Jang, Jeong suspects that Lee has an ulterior motive to amend the constitution and run for a second term. (The president is immune from indictment, which is why the trials in various legal cases against Lee are currently on hold.)

But the real reason behind the PPP’s refusal to hash out a constitutional reform could be that it can’t take the lead in remolding the constitution to its taste. Constitutional amendment requires 200 votes in favor. The PPP only commands 109 out of 300 parliamentary seats. Meanwhile, the liberal camp comprises more than 180 seats, with the DP holding the parliamentary majority alone with its 161 seats. The PPP would manage to eke out only a piecemeal compromise at the negotiating table.

Besides, history would only remember the Lee administration, not the PPP, for having reformed the constitution. The PPP is loathe to serve Lee and the DP such an enormous political cachet on a silver platter.

In spite of the PPP’s intransigence, the DP is plowing ahead. On September 20, the DP launched a constitutional amendment committee. “It’s time to stop picking at diction but start discussing constitutional reform,” said Kim Min-seok, the DP’s new leader.

Granted, the timing is convenient for the Lee administration. Public discourse and political haggling over constitutional amendment could overshadow any other agenda. In the process, the government’s sore spots could be covered and even forgotten.

Plus, constitutional reform is not a distant possibility. Although the PPP opposes talk for tweaking the constitution, the conservative bloc is fractious anyways. Quite a sizable pocket despises Jang and the PPP leadership. Breakaway participation and votes are possible for constitutional amendment. Hearsay has it that some in the PPP are already stirring to join the discussion for constitutional amendment.

Notably, Kim Tae-ho, a four-term PPP legislator, sounded the bugle of reason this time after Lee’s press conference. “We should end this war of attrition over this consecutive terms controversy,” he said on his social media, alluding to the PPP’s pathological distrust of Lee. He then underlined the need to reform the constitution “in order to disperse the authority channeled into the president and overcome the political polarization.”

But in the end, it is this “political polarization” that will be hindering the very first step needed to heal this polarization. According to Realmeter’s September 22 survey, 5 out of 10 South Koreans were still dubious about Lee’s true intentions for wanting to introduce a consecutive presidential tenure. No matter how well-meaning and earnest the government may be about reforming the constitution and the polity, if the public isn’t convinced and comforted, no talk of constitutional reform, nor any resulting constitution, would be viable.

title: Delivered to the Wrong Address? F-35 Parts Re-routed to Hong Kong
description: The F-35 is a supremely advanced fighter aircraft with many proprietary components that would be of immense value to several foreign intelligence services. It is also a consumer product.
text:
Last summer a shipment of F-35 parts was reportedly re-routed to Hong Kong from its intended destination in Australia. Australia is a partner in the F-35 program; the People’s Republic of China is not. U.S. authorities are reportedly trying to recover the parts and prevent future breaches. The incident has caused consternation in the United States and Australia, both of which have effectively committed to the F-35 as the foundation of their future airpower. And yet the mis-shipment has made clear a fundamental contradiction at the heart of the F-35 project; high tech proprietary classification does not go well with an aggressive policy of export and offshoring.

In short, it’s hard to keep aspects of the F-35 secret when the United States is aggressively trying to sell the aircraft abroad.

We do not yet fully understand whether this was an innocent (if catastrophic) error, or if it was the result of a complex and successful Chinese espionage operation. If the latter, we don’t know if Chinese intelligence has been able to exploit the shipment, though it appears that Beijing is in possession of the errant parts. But even if the diversion of the shipment to Hong Kong was accidental and not part of an espionage operation, the incident highlights some of the contradictions inherent in the F-35 program.

The F-35 is a supremely advanced fighter aircraft with many proprietary components that would be of immense value to several foreign intelligence services. It is also a consumer product that the United States has been trying to aggressively export over the past two decades to most every country in the Global North and a few in the Global South. Jonathan Caverley has called the F-35 “America’s Belt and Road,” because of both its substantial expense and because of its integrated production over several countries and integrated maintenance over several more. Work in all of these countries is spread among dozens of contractors and subcontractors, each of which offers a potential weak link in terms of keeping the parts of the aircraft secret and secure.

There are a limited number of countries that could usefully exploit the technology in the shipment, and China is one of them. Of particular concern is the canopy, which represents an enormous technological and financial investment and which could conceivably benefit China’s aerospace industry. As with most such cases, the issue here is less that Chinese engineers could copy the equipment and then integrate it into their own aircraft (modern industrial aerospace techniques are remarkably complex) but rather that careful study could reveal vulnerabilities or characteristics that could eventually give Chinese pilots a tactical advantage.

It’s worth noting that the F-35 is no longer a youthful aircraft. It has been in active service for more than a decade, flies for 12 different countries (and often for more than one air force per country), and boasts some 1,200 operational units across the world. It has flown in combat for Israel and the United States in several wars. Given this record, there’s only so much that can be done to keep the details of the aircraft’s manufacture and performance secret from China or Russia. China has its own fifth-generation fighters and has already worked out many of the problems associated with the critical technologies. Indeed, both China and the United States have moved onto sixth-generation programs. Thus, the availability of the canopy of the F-35 may be important, but it’s hardly critical. That said, while entrusting important components of a mainline fighter aircraft to UPS may be unwise, it was also probably inevitable given the nature of the project.
tag: F-35; F-35 Hong Kong; U.S.-China Competition; U.S.-China Relations

title: Drones Offer Central Asia an Escape From Foreign Dependency
description: Central Asian states should jointly develop drone capabilities to prepare for current and future security needs.
text:
Drones are everywhere in the news and on the frontlines of the Iran-U.S. War and the Russia-Ukraine War, but their most recent use on a battlefield in Central Asia represents a long-term issue – continued dependency on foreign suppliers. The Central Asian states may just be replacing their long-term Russian security dependency with a Turkish one.

Central Asian leaders risk deepening this dependency and worsening security vulnerabilities as they announce deals with foreign suppliers that are often headquartered in a single state – Turkiye. However, developments in 2026 show that opportunities for local development and production that would benefit regional economies without offloading security responsibilities exist. Local politicians just need to invest locally.

In the 2022 border conflict between Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan, Turkiye’s Baykar Bayraktar TB2 unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) played a well-publicized role. After that conflict, Bishkek decided to deepen its Turkish dependency, ordering Aksungur and Akinci platforms, both from Turkish manufacturers, TAI and Baykar, respectively. It had already ordered additional TB2s and Anka (from TAI) as well.

Drones are certainly cheaper than manned aircraft, but these imported platforms weren’t without cost. Civil servants took a pay hit to fund the purchase of the new systems. And this doesn’t factor in the cost of operations and maintenance. To keep these aircraft flying with spare parts, ammunition, and sensors will require continual funding. When buying any big-ticket item, that platform is committing the state to long-term sustainment with certain suppliers.

Given Turkiye’s mercurial defense policy in recent years, can Bishkek rely on adequate sustainment in the event of another conflict? Turkiye, a NATO ally, hoped to procure F-35s, but acquired Russian S-400s, and is reportedly trying to resell those air defense system to the UAE, before aiming to rejoin F-35 talks. In addition to the initial procurement, depending on a foreign supplier means worrying about receiving additional parts and frames to replace losses from wear and tear or combat operations.

Russia and Ukraine initially looked to foreign support for their attritive war. Tehran supplied Moscow with propeller-driven one-way attack Shahed-136 drones within the first year of the conflict. Yet, Moscow soon realized that the battlefield demanded the systems evolve. Manufacturing facilities were set up inside Russia and improvements were applied to the platform including jet power, anti-radar materials, and better guidance (the latest Russian-made version is dubbed the Geran-4/5).

A similar learning process happened on Kyiv’s side. Chinese-made DJI Mavics, Turkish TB2s, and American Switchblades provided early inventory for Ukrainian forces. Yet, soon manufacturing was moved in country and development processes brought closer to the frontlines, to incorporate the daily lessons of countermeasures, deception, and the realities of a non-permissive battlespace.

While the support systems needed to keep UAVs aloft are simpler than those required for fighters, the current Iran-U.S. War – a much more permissive environment than that in eastern Ukraine – has shown how vulnerable drones are to anti-air capabilities. The U.S. has lost 45 MQ-9 Reaper tactical UAVs, 25 percent of its fleet, since the start of the campaign. Given the years and cost to replace its vehicles, the Pentagon may just switch over to different systems altogether.

Perhaps as a response to its competition and conflict with Bishkek, Dushanbe turned to its own foreign partner to develop a UAV capability. Around the same time, in 2022, it was reported that a program to produce, likely assemble, Iranian Ababil-2s in Tajikistan, was reached. At the signing were Iranian Major General Mohammad Bagheri and Tajik Defense Minister Sherali Mirzo. Bagheri was killed in Israeli air strikes in 2025 and Mirzo was shuffled out of office the same year.

It is unclear how much progress has been made with this facility, or if this was all just a smoke screen. Yet, even if this project had gotten off the ground, it is hard to see how that would not have resulted in significant risk. Manufacturing drones for Tehran could very quickly bring banking and dollar restrictions from Washington, making such a venture a real security risk and potential big money-loser. Ultimately, this appears to be four years with only minimal progress on UAV capabilities for Tajikistan.

Given the pitfalls of foreign dependency, Central Asia may look to develop its own systems, or at the very least license the full production process for its own domestically manufactured unmanned systems. First off, the costs are not prohibitive, unlike, say, developing an armored vehicle, ship, or manned aircraft. Second, the scale and security needs in the region are sufficient to support domestic UAV production.

Third, regional states already have a start on the research, development, and manufacturing needed to make such cooperation a success. Finally, the opportunities of joint drone research and production could lead to increased security cooperation along borders and against transnational threats. Doing so will help to escape the pitfalls of learned incapacity. What’s key though is that local leaders invest in R&D domestically – not outsource solutions.

Take for example the Kyrgyz company Nanospace that announced in May 2026 plans to open a UAV institute in Tash-Dobo, just outside Bishkek. This plan is still in its infancy, but training operators and developing technologies to network numerous small drones is an important step in developing domestic air defense, research, and surveillance, capabilities that are not dependent on foreign assistance.

Central Asia is already a regional education destination. This will continue, unless domestic actors eliminate academic freedom and quell basic research. Eurasian students have long come to Kyrgyzstan for higher education, whether at the University of Central Asia or the American University of Central Asia. Kazakhstan is a major international academic hub now as well, with some 30,000-plus foreign students attending branch institutions of Cardiff and Woosong, as well as attending homegrown universities like Al Farabi and Eurasian National. So, there are major opportunities to network skills and technologies that could benefit human capital and defense development for the entire region.

Meanwhile, an exhibit in the late summer of 2026 in Uzbekistan highlighted a new Shunqor-8 drone interceptor from the Center for Innovative Technologies that could serve as a cheap alternative to traditional missile defense. Usually, Russian exports have provided most of the region’s air defense. In recent years, for example, even amid a war that is demanding major stocks of air defenses, Kyrgyzstan demonstrated S-300PS and Tor-M2KM (long- and short-range) SAMs and Tajikistan took deliveries from Russia.

The region still connects to legacy CIS Joint Air Defense System (ADS), so this is another important step in terms of Central Asia states providing for their own defense. Boilerplate statements suggested “modernizing” the ADS and advancing cooperation in 2026, though there was a mention of AI being integrated. In addition, the quantities being delivered to the region are likely insufficient for any prolonged conflict. Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan already have experience with joint venture manufacturing lines. There’s no reason for Central Asian states to continue to procure UAVs from abroad rather than building them (even with licenses) at home.

Now, clearly the region won’t replace every imported component with a domestic analogue. Local manufacturers, for example, are unlikely to compete in the international market for electro-optical/infrared sensors. Yet, for smaller first-person view UAVs, and tactical UAVs, there’s plenty of room for choices in terms of cameras for reconnaissance or navigation systems that are mapped to the local environment and do not depend on one satellite network. Anticipating such payload flexibility can help Central Asian states avoid getting “locked in” to one new partner that just supplants the old one.

One-way attack (OWA) drones are another opportunity for Central Asian states to better, more effectively, target security threats. One of the issues in recent combat operations has been an employment of seemingly indiscriminate or inaccurate artillery fire and combat aircraft strikes. OWA drones offer a way to address this and safeguard civilian lives. For example, during the 2022 Tajik-Kyrgyz conflict, indiscriminate artillery shelling and automatic weapons fire contributed to significant civilian casualties in Khistevarz, Ovchi Kalacha, Ak-Sai, and Margun, among other locations.

In much earlier conflicts, manned aircraft with unguided weapons were ineffective, or suffered significant casualties, including in Rasht and the Ferghana Valley region. The cost of manned combat aircraft is such that most states in the region cannot afford such a fleet. And in any case, even if affordable, this still leads to foreign dependency. Training and education, parts and repairs, and operations even depended in large part on Russia. Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan are not unique in this, but surely this is an opportunity to reduce civilian casualties in conflict zones and limit reliance on a foreign power.

Finally, there are a host of interconnected challenges that drones can help the region address. Everything from detecting smuggling and trafficking across remote borders; to monitoring water flow from glaciers and water use downstream; or securing international events like the Nomad Games, there are huge opportunities for cooperative monitoring and security efforts with shared drone capabilities.

Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan, and Tajikistan don’t need Russia or China to address these challenges. They don’t need to depend on a foreign manufacturer for drones or the capabilities to produce many of the UAVs that have wide-ranging applications for the economy, environment, and defense of the region. And, to paraphrase some advice from Kenneth Waltz: they should be considering how to counterbalance new hegemonic threats, not swapping one vulnerability for another. Indeed, Astana is already headed in this direction.

The international order is being remade in real time, so regional governments need to look to their own security. Great powers might “ignore” their smaller neighbors for a time, but who’s to say when that benign neglect will come to an end. Investment in joint education, training, and production today can enable these states to address problems regionally, and sever dependencies at the same time, and make the whole region more secure from external threats over the long run. If they wait until the next regional conflict, it may be too late.

title: East Asia’s Quiet Race to Find the Universe’s Missing Mass
description: China, South Korea, and Japan all run their own programs to detect dark matter, some of them world-leading in sensitivity.
text:
On September 1, 2026, physicists with the LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) experiment, a ten-ton liquid xenon detector buried nearly a mile underground at the Sanford Underground Research Facility in South Dakota, announced they had recorded a single particle interaction that standard background processes struggle to explain. The event, drawn from 220 days of data collected between March 2023 and April 2024, sits at a statistical significance of about 2.6 sigma, far short of the 5-sigma threshold physicists require to claim a discovery, but it’s the strongest hint LZ has produced to date that a weakly interacting massive particle (WIMP) may have grazed its xenon target. It’s potentially a step forward in LZ’s main goal: to detect dark matter.

LZ’s spokesperson, Professor Rick Gaitskell of Brown University, was careful to frame it as intriguing rather than conclusive. “With only one event, we don’t want to get ahead of ourselves,” he said. “We are not claiming to have seen dark matter. But we have seen something interesting that we want to share with the scientific community for their input.” His collaborators similarly stressed that unexpected backgrounds have fooled sensitive detectors before.

Beyond the scientific question itself, it’s notable where the result was unveiled: not in the United States, but at the TeV Particle Astrophysics (TeVPA) 2026 conference in Japan. That is a small but telling sign of how central East Asia has become to the global effort to identify dark matter, the invisible substance thought to make up roughly 25 percent of all matter in the universe. Dark matter’s existence is inferred from galactic rotation and gravitational lensing, but it has never been directly observed.

While LZ, Europe’s XENONnT, and Italy’s DarkSide-20k dominate headlines in the West, China, South Korea, and Japan run their own parallel programs, some of them world-leading in sensitivity, others aimed at settling decades-old controversies that Western experiments cannot resolve alone.

China’s dark matter program is anchored at the China Jinping Underground Laboratory (CJPL) in Sichuan Province, shielded by 2,400 meters of rock, making it the deepest operational underground laboratory in the world, with a cosmic-ray flux roughly two orders of magnitude lower than shallower European sites.

The flagship experiment there is PandaX-4T, a dual-phase liquid xenon time-projection chamber holding 3.7 tons of ultra-pure xenon, run by a consortium including Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Peking University, and the University of Science and Technology of China. Its most recent full-exposure result, published in Physical Review Letters in January 2025 using 1.54 ton-years of data, set the tightest limit yet on spin-independent WIMP-nucleon interactions for dark matter particles above 100 giga-electronvolts (GeV) putting it on a par with or ahead of LZ and XENONnT in that mass range. PandaX has also pushed into more exotic territory, setting the strongest constraints to date on hypothetical dark photons and axion-like particles using low-energy data from the same detector.

A second, complementary Chinese effort, the China Dark Matter Experiment (CDEX), also based at CJPL, uses ultra-sensitive germanium detectors rather than xenon to hunt for lighter dark matter candidates in the 1-10 GeV range. Its CDEX-1B result, published in 2019, excluded the parameter space claimed by two earlier controversial signals (DAMA/LIBRA and CoGeNT) at high confidence for low-mass WIMPs. The collaboration is now building CDEX-50, a 50-kilogram germanium array, at the newly expanded CJPL-II site.

China also pursues dark matter from orbit. The DAMPE satellite (known as Wukong, launched in 2015 from Jiuquan) measures cosmic-ray electrons and positrons up to several tera-electronvolts (TeV), looking for the kind of spectral anomalies that dark matter annihilation might produce. Its first Nature paper in 2017 reported an unexplained break in the electron-positron spectrum around 0.9 TeV, a result the mission continues to refine with larger datasets.

South Korea’s contribution is narrower in scope but scientifically pivotal. Since 1997, Italy’s DAMA/LIBRA experiment at Gran Sasso has claimed to observe an annual modulation in its detector consistent with dark matter, at a very high statistical significance, a result that has never been reproduced by other experiments using different target materials, creating one of the longest-running puzzles in the field.

The COSINE-100 experiment, run at the Yangyang Underground Laboratory by a South Korea-U.S.-U.K.-Brazil collaboration under South Korea’s Institute for Basic Science, was built specifically to test that claim using the same sodium-iodide crystal technology as DAMA/LIBRA. In September 2025, the collaboration published its full 6.4-year dataset in Science Advances: no annual modulation signal was found, disfavoring the DAMA/LIBRA result at more than 3-sigma confidence with the same target material and matched energy calibration. A companion study combining COSINE-100 with Spain’s ANAIS-112 experiment pushed the exclusion of the DAMA/LIBRA claim even further. It is one of the clearest examples of an Asian experiment resolving, rather than merely contributing to, a foundational debate in the field.

Japan’s Kamioka Observatory, run by the University of Tokyo’s Institute for Cosmic Ray Research, has a long pedigree in underground physics, best known internationally for the Super-Kamiokande neutrino detector. Its dedicated dark matter effort, XMASS, operated an 832-kilogram liquid xenon detector from 2013 until it ceased data-taking in 2019; its results, like those of most direct-detection experiments, found no confirmed WIMP signal but helped rule out large regions of parameter space and cross-checked earlier claims of annual modulation.

Since then, Japanese efforts have shifted toward a different technique: directional detection. The NEWAGE experiment, led by Kobe University and also housed at Kamioka, uses a gaseous time-projection chamber designed not just to detect a WIMP interaction but to reconstruct the direction it came from – a capability that could, in principle, distinguish a genuine dark matter signal from background radiation, since dark matter should appear to stream from a consistent direction as the Earth moves through the galactic halo. The collaboration reported in 2025 that it had installed a new, lower-radioactivity detector module at Kamioka and begun final commissioning, with results expected in the coming cycle.

Japan’s more understated role, however, may be as convener. By hosting TeVPA 2026, the conference where LZ chose to unveil its most significant result to date, Japan positioned itself, if only for a week, at the center of the global conversation on dark matter, alongside its own domestic research base.

None of the Asian efforts described here has found a dark matter particle; nor has anyone else. But it is clear that East Asia’s research ecosystem has matured well past a supporting role. China Jinping Underground Laboratory is arguably the best-shielded laboratory on the planet; PandaX and CDEX post limits that rival or beat their American and European counterparts. The South Korea-based COSINE-100 has done something no single Western experiment has managed, closing in on a 25-year-old anomaly. Japan, having pioneered the field with XMASS, is now betting on directional sensing, a technique that could matter enormously if a real signal like LZ’s tentative event is ever confirmed and needs independent verification.

That last point is the crux of why LZ’s cautious announcement is significant for observers of Asian science policy as much as for particle physicists. If a genuine WIMP signal is ever confirmed, no single collaboration’s word will be enough. Physics requires independent replication with different detector materials, different underground sites, and different national teams. China, South Korea, and Japan are no longer just running observatories that look for dark matter; they are building the infrastructure that will be needed to validate any future discovery, no matter where it’s first made.

title: El Niño, Climate Catastrophe, and the Coming Financial Showdown
description: Pablo Berrutti discusses Nepal’s glacial collapse, Indonesia’s wildfires, and why efforts at climate mitigation are falling short.
text:
Pablo Berrutti is founder and managing director of Altiorem, a sustainable finance library, and a strategic advisor with a background in the integration of artificial intelligence, measuring the impact of climate change and its impact on business.

This includes banks and insurance companies and their awkward relationships with factoring in the challenges of climate change and confronting their responsibilities, which have recently been sorely tested by the arrival of a super-charged El Niño weather phenomena.

In recent weeks the glacial collapse in Nepal, wildfires in Indonesia, the haze, droughts, and typhoons across East Asia have taken horrible toll on human life and racked up damage bills that will be measured in the tens of billions of dollars.

Governments and financial institutions were warned. The potential for this year’s El Niño was first raised in May and formally announced on June 16. The World Meteorological Organization says the current conditions are expected to last until February.

But Berrutti told The Diplomat’s Luke Hunt that wealthy countries like Australia had spent very little on preparation and building in resilience into assets. Instead, about 95 percent of disaster funds went to recovery.

“Whereas other countries, sadly, who aren’t as wealthy as Australia, a lot of Southeast Asian countries, clearly aren’t in a position to be able to build that resilience to these types of events,” he said.

He added that it’s not only the big events that made headlines for causing destruction and loss of life that matter, but also the chronic effects of extreme heat. More than 30,000 people had died this year from back-to-back European heatwaves.

“It’s also an economic productivity perspective or a human health perspective, the knock on effects from fires and what that means from a lung disease and heart disease perspective,” Berrutti said.
