title: Europe’s Read of the Trump-Xi Summit
description: Decisions taken in Washington and Beijing increasingly shape European trade, technology, energy, and security.
text:
The summit between U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping achieved one central objective: stabilization. It did not resolve the China-U.S. rivalry but helped contain it, by restoring a more predictable framework for managing tensions over trade, technology, and geopolitics.

Its main concrete outcome was modest: a two-month extension, until January 2027, of the trade truce first agreed after the Trump-Xi meeting in Busan a year ago, when Washington lowered tariffs and Beijing suspended export controls on rare earths and other critical minerals.

The two sides also activated the China-U.S. Boards of Trade and Investment and mutual support for each other’s G20 and APEC presidencies. The message is clear: not genuine rapprochement, but more disciplined management of strategic competition.

Yet the summit’s most consequential exchanges may have taken place behind closed doors over Iran. The public readout was brief, but Trump pressed Xi over Chinese support for Tehran, while both leaders publicly agreed that Iran must not acquire a nuclear weapon.

For the world’s two largest economies, which together account for nearly half of global economic output, de-escalation makes strategic sense, though for different reasons. Both sides would like to use a period of relative stability to buy time to reduce vulnerabilities, strengthen resilience, and recalibrate economic dependencies.

Diplomatically, both leaders are also playing to domestic audiences. Trump is seeking tangible economic gains, from agricultural purchases to aircraft orders, consistent with his long-standing focus on reducing the U.S. trade deficit and addressing structural imbalances that have weakened American manufacturing. Xi, meanwhile, wants to show that Washington is treating China as an equal, while easing the economic pressure Washington has steadily increased toward Chinese companies. For Beijing, stability is economic as well as diplomatic: détente buys time to support a weak domestic economy increasingly reliant on external demand as consumption at home remains subdued.

The European Union was another important audience for the summit. Decisions taken in Washington and Beijing increasingly shape European trade, technology, energy, and security.

First, Brussels and major European capitals have a strong interest in stable China-U.S. relations, particularly at a time when instability in the Middle East is generating mounting economic pressures on Europe through higher energy costs, disrupted trade routes, inflationary pressures, and weaker industrial competitiveness.

Second, Europe fears becoming an adjustment variable in the China-U.S. strategic competition. Washington holds technological leverage; Beijing controls minerals and key manufacturing supply chains. Europe remains exposed to both. The question is whether the EU can turn its own economic weight into strategic agency rather than simply absorb the consequences of decisions taken elsewhere.

Consider trade relations. When China-U.S. trade tensions intensify, Chinese goods shut out of the American market are increasingly redirected toward Europe, raising fears of a deeper China shock. The automotive sector is already reshaping European perceptions of China, but the pressure extend well beyond card. The question is how many other industries will follow.

In 2025, the EU increasingly became China’s primary export destination and trade deficit with China reached nearly 360 billion euro, with Chinese exports to Europe almost double the value of EU exports to China. Additional U.S. restrictions on Chinese imports could deepen this imbalance further.

At the same time, any China-U.S. managed trade arrangement that redirects Chinese purchases toward American goods could come at the expense of European exporters. Europe therefore faces pressure in both directions, from trade diversion when tensions rise and from preferential bilateral deals when they ease. On the other side, if China-U.S. relations stabilize, Beijing has less incentive to make concessions to Brussels. Either way, Europe risks becoming the adjustment variable in China-U.S. competition: absorbing displaced Chinese production while bilateral deals between Washington and Beijing are struck largely over its head.

Third, like the United States, the EU remains heavily dependent on China for rare earths, permanent magnets, and critical minerals, essential for Europe’s green, digital, and defense industries. 98 percent of EU demand for rare earth magnets is met by Chinese imports. The Trump-Xi Busan agreement in October 2025 brought relief also to Europe by easing immediate supply pressures. The recent China-U.S. summit produced no major new breakthrough, only an agreement to keep working on shortages and shipment levels.

For Europe, this may preserve some near-term stability, but it does little to reduce the underlying vulnerability. There is still a risk that a bilateral China-U.S. accommodation could improve supply security for American companies without resolving Europe’s exposure. In response, Brussels is increasingly aligning with U.S.-led initiatives, such as Pax Silica, and its own Critical Raw Materials Act to diversify supply chains, though reducing dependence on China will require years of investment, industrial capacity building, and transatlantic coordination.

Fourth, artificial intelligence. The Trump-Xi meeting produced no binding agreement, although the two sides launched an AI dialogue and a channel to manage serious incidents. Disputes over advanced chip exports remain unresolved. Beijing has an interest in buying time to reduce its dependence on U.S. technology, without the added burden of new tariffs and restrictions on Chinese companies.

For the EU, the risk is that the rules of AI race are increasingly shaped in a China-U.S. channel where Brussels has little influence. In the meantime, Europe remains heavily reliant on American processors and cloud providers and Chinese supply chains. The EU produces less than 10 percent of global semiconductors. Brussels is responding with its Technology Sovereignty Package paired with the Chips Act 2.0 and the Cloud and AI Development Act that aim to triple European data center capacity within five to seven years. Both acts are still proposals, however, with binding law months or possibly years away.

Attention will now turn to the next EU-China Summit, which is slated to take place in Beijing on December 7, as Brussels is seeking tangible results from the EU-China Trade and Investment Council. The European Union has considerable leverage of its own, through its market, regulatory power, trade instruments, and industrial base. The question is whether is prepared and unified to use that leverage with China.

That is also why transatlantic coordination matters. Beijing benefits when U.S. and European positions diverge, while Washington has a clear interest in closer European alignment with its economic security approach. Europe’s strategic challenge is to avoid becoming merely the arena in which China-U.S. competition plays out and instead use its own agency to shape the terms of that competition.

title: Ezra Jin Is Free, But There Are More Pastors in China Behind Bars
description: “I respectfully ask the international community to stand with me – to fight for the freedom of Pastor Gao Quanfu, Pang Yu, and all peaceful Christians imprisoned in China. ”
text:
This July, a miracle took place in China, when Ezra Jin, an imprisoned Christian pastor from an unregistered house church, was suddenly set free. Throughout his 266 days of imprisonment, the international community rallied behind Pastor Jin, culminating in his release.

I write this article in desperate need of one more miracle. My father, Pastor Gao Quanfu of the Light of Zion Church, and my mother, Pang Yu, remain behind bars. My father faces 12 to 13 years in prison on baseless charges of fraud. As their trials approach, I can only hope that the international community will similarly support their cause.

For my parents, faith and service were a calling. My father became a Christian at age 28, at a time when public religious practice was nearly nonexistent in China. He served as a minister for 40 years: mentoring the next generation of religious leaders, carrying out ministry work, and supporting families in his congregation. He was also a talented musician; he played an instrument called the suona horn. My mother had a successful career as an actress, TV anchor, and producer. It was love at first sight for the two of them, and they anticipated a bright future for their family and community.

In 2025, my parents paid a steep price for their faith. On May 16, authorities in Xi’an arrested Pastor Gao and eleven other members of the Light of Zion Church. Initially, my father was charged with “using superstition to undermine the implementation of the law.” The charges were later altered; he is now facing charges of “fraud” for accepting voluntary donations from his congregants. Three weeks after my father’s arrest, my mother was detained, simply because she is married to Pastor Gao.

My parents’ ordeal is reflective of a wider crackdown on unregistered house churches in China. The Light of Zion Church, and other such entities, have drawn Beijing’s ire due to their refusal to submit to state surveillance and restrictions that can include controlling the content of sermons. Although some practitioners have since been released, my parents, Pastor Tang Bingyi of the Light of Zion Church, and eight members of Pastor Jin’s congregation (Zion Church) remain in prison.

My father continues to maintain that Christian churches should respect the governing authorities, but he believes that his church must preserve its autonomy and biblical convictions regarding worship, doctrine, and church governance. Even as his church endured deepening surveillance and pressure, the congregation responded peacefully – with prayer rather than hostility, and faith rather than fear.

What my parents are going through is unimaginable. They languish in overcrowded conditions, with more than a dozen detainees in one cell. They are not allowed to communicate with or visit family members. Authorities closely monitor their visits with legal counsel, adversely impacting their ability to freely communicate with their lawyers.

My parents are almost 70 years old; both have severe health concerns, yet their meals are nutritionally insufficient, and their medical needs are left untreated. I am terrified of what might happen next.

After more than a year in detention, my parents’ cases are underway – and the potential outcome is chilling. At my father’s pretrial hearing on August 10, we learned that he could be sentenced to 12 or 13 years. We await my mother’s pretrial hearing, and potential sentence, with trepidation. Without a groundswell of international support, I fear that my parents will spend the rest of their lives in prison.

I respectfully, but urgently, ask governments and policymakers around the world to stand in solidarity with my parents. To the consulates and embassies in the PRC: please show up at their trials in Xi’an, China. Visible engagement and interest from foreign diplomats will signal that the represented countries protect freedom of belief and religion. It will send a message to Beijing that the world has not forgotten Pastor Gao Quanfu, Pang Yu, and other Christians detained in China.

I cannot be there, so I plead with all those who can to attend. Bear witness and remind my parents that they are not alone.

My mother and father devoted their lives to me and their congregation. Now, they are elderly, sick, and need me, but I cannot do this alone. I respectfully ask the international community to stand with me – to fight for the freedom of Pastor Gao Quanfu, Pang Yu, and all peaceful Christians imprisoned in China.

I am proud to be my parents’ son. One day soon, I hope to be reunited with them, to hear my parents play music and sing together again. Even if it takes a miracle – be it political or preordained – I will not rest until my parents walk free.
tag: China crackdown on religion; Christians in China; Ezra Jin; Gao Quanfu; Pang Yu

title: Filipina Drug Trafficker Walks Free After Receiving Presidential Pardon
description: Mary Jane Veloso has always maintained her innocence, claiming that a relative tricked into carrying a large shipment of drugs.
text:
Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on Friday granted a pardon ​to Mary Jane Veloso, who was serving a ‌prison sentence for drug trafficking in the Philippines after her arrest ​in Indonesia in 2010.

According to PhilStar Global, Gregorio Pio Catapang Jr., the director general of the Bureau of Corrections, “personally handed” Veloso a copy of the pardon and her official release, completing the procedures for her discharge. Earlier on Friday, Marcos confirmed to reporters that he had signed a pardon the day before, without elaborating.

Veloso, a 41-year-old domestic worker and mother of two, was arrested in Yogyakarta in 2010 for trying to bring 2.6 kilograms of heroin into Indonesia. She was subsequently sentenced to death under Indonesia’s severe drug laws, but received a last-minute reprieve from execution in 2015 after Philippine officials asked then Indonesian President Joko “Jokowi” Widodo to let her testify against members of a prominent drug trafficking organization.

In December 2024, Indonesia agreed to repatriate Veloso after years of requests from the Philippines, where Veloso’s relatives and supporters had waged a persistent campaign for her release.

Veloso has always maintained her innocence, claiming that she was tricked into carrying the drugs by her godsister. She smiled as she left her prison cell in the Philippines on Friday, after more than 15 years behind bars. In a press conference with Catapang at the Bureau of Corrections, she held up the “absolute pardon” signed by Marcos, which removes the remaining legal consequences of her conviction, allowing her a fresh start, and offered a tearful thanks to the Philippine leader.

“I just want to tell our beloved President: Thank you so much for clearing my name and allowing me to return to my family,” she said, as per Inquirer.net. She added that she was looking forward to reuniting with her two sons, who have grown nearly to adulthood since her arrest.

“It was really hard being separated from them … I didn’t see my children grow, but I believe it’s not yet too late for me to be their guide,” Veloso said.

Veloso’s release was greeted with joy by family members and advocacy groups that have spent years campaigning for her release.

Veloso’s pardon marks a rare positive development in a story connected to Southeast Asia’s tough anti-drug regime. Indonesia is known particularly for its unforgiving approach to drug crimes, especially large-scale trafficking offenses.

Under the agreement Yusril Ihza Mahendra, then Indonesia’s senior minister for law and human rights affairs, said that the Philippines had agreed to respect the Indonesian court’s sentencing of Veloso and her status as prisoner in Indonesia.

However, Yusril also said that the Indonesian government would also respect any decision made by the Philippines once Veloso is back on Philippine soil, including the possible granting of clemency.

“This only proves that there are really second chances, and we are happy that Veloso can now enjoy her newfound freedom with her family,” Catapang said.

title: Free and Open Indo-Pacific: A Pillar of Deeper Regional Cooperation
description: Japan’s Indo-Pacific vision has outlasted its creator and found new partners. Beijing is not pleased.
text:
In July 2026, the foreign ministers of the Quad countries — Japan, the United States, Australia, and India — met on the sidelines of the ASEAN Foreign Ministers’ Meeting in Manila and issued the “Joint Press Release on Quad Cooperation with ASEAN,” reaffirming their support for ASEAN centrality and unity and the “ASEAN Outlook on the Indo-Pacific (AOIP).” The Quad foreign ministers also reaffirmed their commitment to a “Free and Open Indo-Pacific (FOIP)” and outlined their intention to deepen cooperation with ASEAN, with FOIP as a core pillar.

It has been ten years since former Prime Minister Shinzo Abe proposed the FOIP at the Sixth Tokyo International Conference on African Development (TICAD VI) in Nairobi, Kenya, in August 2016. Abe viewed Asia and Africa, and the Pacific and Indian Oceans, as an inseparable and integrated region, and expressed Japan’s determination to maintain “freedom from coercion,” the “rule of law,” and a “market economy” across it. The FOIP philosophy won broad acceptance across the Indo-Pacific, from advanced Western nations such as the United States and Australia to developing countries including African nations, India, and ASEAN member states. In June 2019, ASEAN adopted the AOIP as its own Indo-Pacific vision, guided by principles including ASEAN centrality, inclusiveness, and respect for international law.

In promoting FOIP, Japan has placed particular emphasis on cooperation with ASEAN. Southeast Asia is a strategically vital region connecting the Pacific and Indian Oceans, and one facing pressure to change the status quo by force or coercion. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi attended the Japan-ASEAN Summit in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, in October 2025. At the meeting, she stated Japan’s commitment to safeguarding the peace, stability, and prosperity of the Indo-Pacific together with ASEAN, by evolving FOIP — a core pillar of Japanese diplomacy — and deepening synergy with the AOIP.

Following the summit, the leaders of Japan and ASEAN issued the “Joint Statement on the Further Promotion and Implementation of the AOIP.” Reaffirming that Japan’s FOIP and the AOIP “share relevant fundamental principles,” the statement affirmed that implementing the AOIP contributes to a rules-based international order and a free and open Indo-Pacific. It also welcomed “Japan’s efforts to promote cooperation rather than division and confrontation through the FOIP.” The statement reflected a shared commitment by Japan and ASEAN to support both frameworks and to cooperate for Indo-Pacific stability and prosperity on the basis of shared principles.

When Takaichi visited Hanoi, Vietnam, in May 2026, she delivered a speech at Vietnam National University outlining the “Updated FOIP.” She asserted that ten years on, the case for FOIP remains as strong as ever, and that Japan will continue working toward an international order based on “freedom,” “openness,” “diversity,” “inclusiveness,” and the “rule of law.” She identified structural changes in the international order — “intensifying geopolitical competition,” “accelerated technological innovation,” and the “rise of the Global South” — and stressed the need to adapt FOIP accordingly. She expressed her determination to drive the updated FOIP with a focus on three priority areas: (1) building economic infrastructure for the AI and data era, (2) co-creating economic growth opportunities and sharing rules, and (3) enhancing cooperation in the security field.

The updated FOIP was also welcomed at the Quad Foreign Ministers’ Meeting held in New Delhi, India, in late May. The Quad foreign ministers reaffirmed their support for a FOIP that enables countries to develop resilience and strengthen autonomy, and announced four concrete initiatives toward its realization: (1) maritime and transnational security, (2) economic prosperity and security, (3) critical and emerging technology, and (4) humanitarian assistance and emergency response. Quad cooperation grounded in FOIP has visibly deepened.

That the Quad Foreign Ministers’ Meeting was held alongside the ASEAN Foreign Ministers’ Meeting in July 2026, and expressed its support for the AOIP, is a clear signal that cooperation among Japan, the United States, Australia, India, and ASEAN — with FOIP as a core pillar — continues to advance. A spokesperson for China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs criticized the updated FOIP as a “sugarcoated scheme that sows division and rivalry” and claimed it “will never win genuine recognition from regional countries.” Ten years after its inception, with broad and deepening support across the Indo-Pacific, the FOIP record speaks for itself.
tag: 2026 Quad Summit; Asia Quad; FOIP 3.0; FOIP and ASEAN; FOIP and the Quad; Free and open Indo-Pacific

title: From 9/11 to the Iran War, Pakistan-US Ties Remain Transactional
description: There’s a reason the nation's relationship with the U.S. has fluctuated while India’s has largely held steady.
text:
Twenty-five years ago, the September 11 attacks transformed Pakistan’s relationship with the United States. Almost overnight, Pakistan went from facing American sanctions and limited diplomatic attention to becoming a frontline partner in the U.S.-led war in Afghanistan.

In its counterterrorism cooperation, Pakistan offered vital ground-and air-based logistical transit to Afghanistan as well as intelligence and military action. In return, the United States provided financial reimbursement and military assistance in the form of subsidized sale of military hardware and technology.

The relationship became increasingly strained as the two sides accused each other of failing to deliver what had been promised. Yet the two sides remained close as long as Washington needed Pakistan for the war in Afghanistan.

When the U.S. military withdrew from Afghanistan in August 2021, much of the urgency behind the relationship disappeared. Washington’s political attention declined, although counterterrorism, trade, health, and other forms of engagement continued at the institutional level.

Twenty-five years after 9/11, Pakistan and the United States appear to have entered another period of warm relations. Pakistan has again presented itself as a useful partner through mediation between Washington and Tehran, alongside cryptocurrency deals, critical mineral investments, and counterterrorism cooperation.

As Pakistan mediates in the Iran-U.S. war, given the difficulties of reaching a truce, there’s a constant fear of Pakistani leaders becoming the eventual fall guys. To avert that outcome, Islamabad has been investing significant time and resources to the success of the mediation efforts. The outcome has been far from assured.

Some see this as another example of Pakistan over-promising and falling short of delivering. But there’s a bigger question behind recent events: Why does every revival of Pakistan-U.S. relations require another geopolitical crisis?

The problem is that Pakistan-U.S. relations lack enough independent commercial, institutional, academic, and professional connections to maintain political engagement when the immediate geopolitical transaction ends.

The contrast with India-U.S. relations helps explain this problem.

During the early 2000s, India-U.S. ties were largely driven from the top. President George W. Bush and Prime Minister Manmohan Singh pushed through the civil nuclear agreement despite serious opposition within both countries. Over the following two decades, the relationship created its own institutional and economic constituencies. Technology companies, universities, defense manufacturers, investors, and the Indian diaspora now have their own reasons for sustaining it. Daniel Markey described this as “a reversal of the motive forces behind U.S.-India ties: from top-down to bottom-up.”

This explains why India-U.S. relations have survived serious political headwinds during current U.S. President Donald Trump’s second term. The two countries disagreed over trade, immigration, Russia, Pakistan, and the war with Iran. Yet their military, economic, and technological engagement has continued.

The clearest evidence is the new ten-year Framework for the U.S.-India Major Defense Partnership signed in October 2025 and the expansion of the Biden-era iCET (initiative on Critical and Emerging Technologies) mechanism into TRUST (Transforming Relations into Utilizing Strategic Technologies) in February 2025, covering artificial intelligence, semiconductors, quantum computing, biotechnology, energy, space, critical minerals, and pharmaceutical supply chains.

When it comes to China, the Trump administration’s narrower focus on denying Beijing control of the First Island Chain arguably reduces India’s direct operational relevance compared with Japan and the Philippines. India’s relevance in the U.S. strategic competition with China will therefore depend on whether Washington continues to see the Indian and Pacific oceans as disjointed theaters and whether India remains restricted to its immediate neighborhood.

Pakistan faces different conditions. For one, it is a close strategic and defense partner of China. Although democratic credentials are not attracting as much U.S. attention under the Trump administration, there are other constraints on the relationship. Pakistan’s security problems discourage tourism, investment, and academic exchange. Its universities and think tanks have fewer sustained partnerships with American institutions. Pakistan also lacks India’s economic scale, technological capacity, and purchasing power.

This does not mean that Pakistan lacks bottom-up ties with the United States. The United States is Pakistan’s largest single export market and one of the largest FDI sources. American companies operate profitably in sectors of Pakistan’s economy – franchising, fast-moving consumer goods, agribusiness and financial services – with growing interest in information technology, renewable energy, and healthcare.

The Karachi-based American Business Council has more than 55 member companies, most of them Fortune 500 firms. The Lahore-based American Business Forum has 23 founding members and 22 associate members. Moreover, thousands of Pakistani healthcare professionals, STEM professionals, and academics actively bridge the economic and educational landscapes of both societies.

Yet these connections remain demonstrably insufficient to determine the overall direction of the relationship. Political leaders, military officials, and regional events continue to provide the ballast for Pakistan-U.S..

Pakistan has apparently sought new ways to demonstrate its utility to Washington. Critical minerals, cryptocurrency, counterterrorism, and mediation with Iran all form part of this effort. While these initiatives can produce real economic and diplomatic gains, they could also reproduce the old transactional cycle if they remain agreements among senior officials or a small number of political- and military-linked businesses.

It is difficult for Pakistan to reproduce India’s bottom-up relationship with the United States, given India’s relative economic scale and its geopolitical position vis-à-vis China.

Still, Islamabad can become less dependent on its temporary geopolitical utility. This would require producing high value-added textile exports and diversifying the overall export supplies. Pakistan can also do more to attract U.S. grassroots engagement by improving domestic security, ensuring constant energy supply, sustaining the current simplified tariff and tax regime to attract investment, protecting contracts and intellectual property, and building stronger links among universities, think tanks, and businesses.

Pakistan should also use its diaspora for professional, technological, and commercial cooperation instead of viewing it mainly as a source of remittances and political support.

Pursuing these policies will ensure Pakistan-U.S. integration beyond just economic diplomacy. Instead of announcing deals and foreign visits to catch ephemeral attention, Islamabad must commit toward building industries and relationships with the U.S. that continue after the leaders leave office or the geopolitical focus shifts. Doing so will give the partnership a stronger foundation.
tag: Pakistan Iran war; Pakistan mediatory role; U.S.-Pakistan Relations; U.S.-Pakistan trade; US-Pakistan counter-terrorism

title: From Idols to KOICA: South Korea’s Disaster Support for Nepal
description: Pop star donations and state aid work together to give Seoul a durable bond with Nepal.
text:
Following the destructive August 26 floods in Nepal, Lee Know of the K-pop boy band Stray Kids donated 100 million won (about $72,600) through World Vision. After Lee Know’s donation, his bandmate Felix donated 50 million won (about $37,000) to the Korean Committee for UNICEF, specifically for Nepal flood relief, on his birthday. Stray Kids’ leader Bang Chan followed with a 200 million won (about $144,000) donation, giving half to the Korean Committee for UNICEF for Nepal flood relief and half to Seoul Rehabilitation Hospital.

The gestures echo acts of support for Nepal by other Korean personalities in the past. For example, figure skater Kim Yuna and actor Lee Min-ho (a different celebrity from Lee Know, whose birth name is also Lee Min-ho) extended aid to Nepal after the devastating earthquake in 2015.

For many Nepalis, this solidarity from Korean public figures has strengthened the goodwill between the two countries. Since diplomatic relations were established in 1974, Nepal-South Korea ties have grown through labor migration and an exchange of culture.

At the time of his donation, Lee Know shared a message through World Vision Korea, which World Vision International Nepal passed on when I reached out to them. “I hope my support can offer some comfort and strength to those going through this difficult time,” Lee Know said. “I sincerely hope that displaced families and everyone working on relief efforts on the ground can return to their peaceful daily lives as soon as possible.”

According to World Vision International Nepal, Lee Know’s donation, along with other contributions, is helping it reach flood-affected communities in Rasuwa and Nuwakot. About 8,600 people have received emergency support so far, including food packages, shelter and hygiene kits, water tanks and pipeline support. Child friendly spaces have been set up for displaced children. Planned next steps include livelihood recovery, temporary learning centers, and restoring community health and water and sanitation facilities.

For Nepalis, the donations from Korean cultural icons have a special resonance.

“I felt really grateful. In Mahottari and Janakpur area we also face heavy floods every year, so when I saw a K-pop idol donated specifically for Nepal flood victims, it felt very personal. It feels like someone far away actually cares about us,” said Priyanshu Kumar Chaudhary, who is from Janakpur, in Nepal’s flood-prone Mahottari district.

Isha Shrestha, from Kathmandu, said her family wasn’t among those who suffered the most direct destruction. But, to her, the disaster still “felt very close” because of how deeply connected the capital is to the affected regions like Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading. When she shared the news of Lee Know’s donation with friends who don’t follow K-pop, she said, “They were genuinely surprised and appreciated that someone from Korea cared enough to support Nepal.” She believes that it’s a sign that such actions shape perceptions of South Korea “beyond K-pop and entertainment.”

But why do idols donate? Dr. Kaushal Kumar, chairperson at the Centre for Korean Studies at Jawaharlal Nehru University, believes that these gestures hold personal weight. Idols like Lee Know, he said, are driven by their humanitarian side. More specifically, they feel a sense of reciprocity toward their fans. In Kumar’s reading, the giving flows from the fandom itself, with the idols showing up for the people who consistently show up for them.

“When I heard that Lee Know had donated 100 million won to help people affected in Nepal, I joined in with a small donation of my own,” a Stray Kids fan told the Korea JoongAng Daily on September 14. The fan said they chose to list the donor’s name as “Stay,” the group’s fandom name, giving as part of the fandom rather than as an individual.

While celebrity giving is personal, emotionally resonant, and reaches Nepalis who might never read a bilateral aid agreement, state aid leaves lasting results as it helps rebuild hospitals and institutional partnerships. Chaeyoon Oh, an economic and development specialist at the Embassy of the Republic of Korea in Nepal, underscored South Korea’s role in the floods’ aftermath. She said that Korea deployed its Disaster Relief Team and sent DNA-identification experts. More recently, South Korea sent emergency equipment through the U.N. Development Program (UNDP) at the request of Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority.

“To me, this goes beyond a government-to-government relationship,” Oh said. “It is an example of how people in one country can see the difficulties faced by people in another country and feel compelled to help.”

Dr. Dhruba Gautam, an expert associated with Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction Center (NDRC Nepal), confirmed that this Nepal-South Korea camaraderie is part of a larger track record. After the 2015 earthquake, South Korea’s aid agency, KOICA, provided $9 million to rebuild Trishuli Hospital and 10 health posts in Nuwakot. Following Nepal’s 2024 floods, South Korea gave $500,000 through UNICEF for medical tents and sanitation support. After this August’s floods, Seoul and the UNDP also supplied Nepal’s disaster authority with camera-equipped drones and portable generators for search and rescue. According to Gautam, South Korea’s clearest contribution has been through practical means such as the provision of equipment and health infrastructure.

Roslyn Hanson Gabriel, national director of World Vision International Nepal, said that help from all sections of society is useful in combating natural disasters. “We are deeply grateful for the generosity and solidarity shown by supporters around the world, including Lee Know and many others who have stood with Nepal during this difficult time,” she said in a written response. “Contributions such as these help us reach children and families affected by the floods with urgent relief assistance while also supporting longer-term recovery efforts. Beyond the financial support, such expressions of global solidarity help shine a light on the needs of vulnerable communities and remind them that they are not facing these challenges alone.”

Diplomacy and culture reinforce the bond between two countries – with the help extended by individual personalities providing an emotional charge that state visits and MOUs find difficult to achieve, even though both work on building the trust between nations.

Both Chaudhary and Shrestha noted that gratitude for the aid is the beginning of a long journey to recovery. Chaudhary pointed to the persisting needs in his district: “We need long-term solutions like better river management, stronger houses, early warning systems. We are a strong community, we just need support to be more prepared.”

Shrestha put it directly when she said, “Thank you for standing with Nepal,” addressing Korean fans and celebrities. “But please remember us beyond the headlines. Long-term support for rebuilding communities and livelihoods can make an even deeper difference.”

This is a partnership that both governments and the general public on both sides seem intent on deepening. It’s the consistency that matters in connecting two nations in times of need.

Comments from officials quoted in this piece were shared in their personal capacity. They do not necessarily represent the official positions of their respective institutions. The statement from World Vision International Nepal was provided by the organization in response to the author’s request for comment.

Donations for Nepal flood relief are being accepted through World Vision and UNICEF.

title: From Nomad Festival to National Showcase: Kyrgyzstan Takes Center Stage
description: In early September, Kyrgyzstan hosted both the World Nomad Games and the SCO summit in a carefully choreographed spectacle of national power and pride.
text:
In early September, the World Nomad Games returned to Kyrgyzstan for the first time in eight years. That same week, a Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit was hosted in Bishkek. The capital went quiet.

Main roads were sealed off for motorcades. Shopping centers along the official routes closed. Residents were told, early and in public: if you can get out of town, get out. By September 1, traffic maps showed more than eighty restrictions. The streets were almost empty.

A few hours east, Kyrchyn gorge came alive. Yurts covered the meadow. Clay forts — built to recall the ancient Silk Road era — rose over the grass. Organizers said 150,000 people came through on day one. Visitors argued over bus seats. Private cars were turned away.

Bishkek was told to clear out and shut down. The summer pasture was told to put on a show.

Bishkek Arena, the 51,000-seat stadium built for the World Nomad Games opening. Aug. 31, 2026. Photo by Aigerim Turgunbaeva.

The Making of the Picture

Eight years ago, when the games were last held beside Issyk-kul, the barricades and the spectacle were centered there. This time the games opened in the new Bishkek Arena, a 51,000-seat stadium, on the same weekend as the SCO summit. In the stands: Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese leader Xi Jinping, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, and Türkiye’s President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

At the opening, Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov said: “Our foundation is independence, and our roots are in nomadic civilization. Our course is international friendship and partnership, and our future lies in building a developed, strong new Kyrgyzstan.”

He also announced that Kazan, in Russia’s Tatarstan, would host the next games in 2028. Moscow had sent a formal request, he said, and he thanked Putin.

Security around the opening ceremony was tight. Snipers stood on the arena roof. A three-kilometer radius was closed for the day. Japarov walked onstage as more than the host of a festival; he was a leader confident in the power he’s consolidated around himself.

In February 2026, Japarov dismissed his longtime ally, then-head of the State Committee for National Security Kamchybek Tashiev, breaking a tandem that had ruled Kyrgyzstan since 2020. In January 2027, he’ll run for president again.

Residents wait at a Bishkek crossing they were not allowed to use. Aug. 31, 2026. Photo by Aigerim Turgunbaeva.

The games were still about horses, yurts, and Kok Boru. The narrative frame around them is not. This was no longer a carnival by the lake, it was a state showcase.

Closer to the SCO summit, the main roads from the airport and through the center of the capital were shut down. Public transport was rerouted. Big malls and markets closed. On September 1, Bishkek really did empty out. Traffic cameras showed almost nothing moving.

A Bishkek street closed for the SCO summit, blocked with trucks. Sept. 1, 2026. Photo by Aigerim Turgunbaeva.

Anyone still on the main streets when the motorcades passed by was taken out of the shot. Pedestrians were told to duck onto side streets. If they were already in the roadway, they were sent down into the underpasses. Tourists who had come for the games stood underground alongside locals and tried to work out what was happening.

“I don’t understand why they treat their own people like this,” a tourist from Germany said. “Why are they hiding them?” She sounded more confused than angry.

Who Gets to Be in the Frame

Kyrchyn was very far from the silenced capital. Yurts covered the meadow. Fortress walls and towers rose above them — not two props at the gate, but the whole outline of a town. Each of Kyrgyzstan’s seven regions, alongside Bishkek and Osh, had its own camp: its yurts, its food, its dancers. It rained. People danced anyway.

Getting to the gorge was a daunting challenge, one many took on. You could not drive in. There were not enough free buses. People waited more than an hour and argued over seats. Those who made it arrived at a crowded, wet, very loud festival. Foreign visitors filmed what they had come to film, and they looked just as happy as the locals. A Brazilian creator with some 300,000 followers said her Issyk-kul videos were “blowing up” at home. An Australian couple looked at the yurts in the mountain meadow and said, “This is exactly how we pictured it.” Social media — and not only in Kyrgyzstan — was filled with dancing in the rain and the opening-night spectacle. The opening ceremony’s dance caught on far beyond Kyrgyzstan. Users in neighboring countries filmed themselves repeating the choreography.

Since 2016, the World Nomad Games sporting program has almost doubled, from 23 sports to 43. Women have entered several of them. In Kyrgyz-style horseback archery this year, 45 women from 32 countries competed. On paper, that looks like a tradition opening up. On the ground, the archery field became one of the most crowded spots for journalists. Women in national dress, galloping, trying to hit a mark against not-so-distant snowy peaks, photographed beautifully.

It was less beautiful up close. Kyrgyzstan’s women’s team was put together in two weeks. One coach ran both the men’s and women’s squads, but the focus stayed on the men. Equestrian sport is still treated as male territory in Kyrgyzstan. A woman, in the old traditions, is decoration — as are the girls in kyz kuumai, the bride-chase game.

Aidana Usenbekova after her last horseback archery run. Kyrchyn gorge, Sept. 3, 2026. Photo by Aigerim Turgunbaeva.

“We ride no worse. We shoot no worse. Sometimes better,” said Aidana Usenbekova, 28, one of three Kyrgyz women on the horseback archery team. “All the horse sports are still seen as men’s sports. For the few girls who even get seen and make the national team, it’s twice as hard. We’re still fighting the stereotypes here. We didn’t even have time to prepare properly. We still put in a strong performance.”

Right before the start of the competition, their mounts were handed to other riders.

“They told us those girls were guests, and we had to take whatever horses were left.”

Aidana cried, then and there, out of sheer frustration at the perceived insult.

“That’s the attitude toward women in this sport. It’s contempt. It happened right before we went out. We all walked into the competition like that.”

The games needed the female archers. They look good in the frame: a woman on a horse, a bow, the mountains behind.

On September 6, at the hippodrome in Cholpon-Ata, Kyrgyzstan beat Kazakhstan 12-0 in Kok Boru, then 7-2 in Kokpar the same day — the two games are similar but the former is Kyrgyzstan’s traditional version and the latter Kazakhstan’s. The stands roared. This was the spectacle the games were invented for. Fans had come from every region for that match.

“I came for Manas,” said Tashtan, 75, who traveled from Uzgen for Kok Boru, referring to the legendary Kyrgyz hero. “I’m a big fan of his.”

There was a mess with tickets. More were sold than there were seats — fraud, people said. Japarov stepped in and ordered the gates be opened to anyone who wanted in. People who had bought tickets and waited in the crowd for the final never made it into the stadium.

The opening ceremony of the World Nomad Games at Bishkek Arena. Aug. 31, 2026. Photo by Aigerim Turgunbaeva.

From Festival to State Showcase

Political analyst Temur Umarov doubts the leaders’ schedules were ever fully in Japarov’s hands. But the dates for the games and the SCO summit luckily lined up. Japarov used the week, Umarov says, to show Kyrgyz voters what he has long promised: order, a Kyrgyzstan visible in Central Asia on political par with Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, something to be proud of. The show had two audiences. The main one was at home.

“The core audience this was aimed at,” Umarov said, “was Kyrgyz citizens.”

On September 9, after the games had closed, Japarov said as much in parliament. The world, he argued, had “seen Kyrgyzstan at a new level and in a new quality.”

Political scientist Asel Doolotkeldieva asks not to reduce the whole week to the coming election. Since Japarov took power, she says, the bet has been on raising the country’s regional standing and widening its foreign ties. His own popularity rises with that but it is not the only point.

“Holding the SCO summit and the Nomad Games together is tied to Independence Day,” she said. “That is a major date for Kyrgyz society. It is meant to scale both the domestic and the external message: Kyrgyzstan now has a stronger state and a sharper identity.”

The spectacle worked, she said. From migrants abroad to ethnic minorities at home, there was “an explosion of pride,” a sense of belonging, support for the current course. “The project hit a very raw nerve, and it hit it on time.”

A clay fortress built for the Games in Kyrchyn gorge. Sept. 3, 2026. Photo by Aigerim Turgunbaeva.

Japarov’s position ahead of the January 2027 election is, in her view, solid. He has never relied on force alone. For many people, a “strong state” means schools, clinics, housing. The scale of the games felt like a summing-up of those efforts. Many citizens attach that record to him.

At the opening ceremony in the Bishkek Arena, the field turned into mountains, a waterfall, a ring of people. Riders circled. For many in the stands — and far beyond them — the games were not a summit and not a campaign. They were a return of what had long been treated as the periphery: the yurt, the horse, Kok Boru, the right to call yourself a nomad at full volume. You could hear that in the arena without any political theory attached.

On the evening of September 6 in Cholpon-Ata, the games closed and the baton passed to Kazan. Kyrgyzstan left its guests the picture it wanted: horses, yurts, a Kok Boru win, a country able to bring the world to its door.

I was at the first World Nomad Games in 2014 as a reporter. Back then, there was no immense grandeur, and nothing like the hordes of journalists or tourists seen this year. There were barely any local spectators at those games. Kyrchyn — now 52 hectares of staged nomadic life, with helipads and good asphalt — was back then just a pasture reached on a dirt road that barely cut through the mountains. The yurts belonged to herders, to people who actually lived that way. Cholpon-Ata had no rebuilt venues, no giant sports grounds, no food courts imported from the capital — only local vendors wrapping up the summer season. Bishkek had not yet been built over. It still had its Soviet texture, old Manas statues on the square, the White House with its black fence.

Japarov did not invent the games, although he commanded them in 2026. The first edition was a project of then-President Almazbek Atambayev.

I was at the games in 2016 and 2018, too, both held in Kyrgyzstan because they had not quite caught on enough for other countries to clamor to host them. In those years I was asked to produce a magazine for visiting delegates, ambassadors, diplomats with bright copy on the main contests, the conferences, ethno-fashion, nomadic heritage.

Coming back in 2026, I could see how far the project had grown: the festival as a tool of national image-making, and the political frame around that image. What I missed from the first games was something that is harder to stage — the spirit of it, people who did not don nomadic culture for a festival but carried it within them always.

The picture in 2026 was not fake. In Kyrchyn, they really did dance in the rain. In the arena, they really did roar, and they were proud of the country. The games put on display the Kyrgyzstan the state wants the world to see. And it demonstrated how tightly Bishkek is prepared to hold that picture in the frame.

Spectators at the Kok Boru venue in Cholpon-Ata. Sept. 3, 2026. Photo by Aigerim Turgunbaeva.

title: From Symbolism to Strategy: The Expanding Operational Role of Women in Baloch Militancy
description: The motivations of individual women who join militant organizations cannot be reduced to a single explanation. The organizational incentives are easier to identify.
text:
On May 22, the Baloch Liberation Army (BLA), one of the principal armed groups in Pakistan’s Baloch insurgency, announced the formation of a dedicated women’s wing and named Shaynaz Baloch as its commander. The announcement was significant not simply because it placed a woman in a more visible position within the organization, but because it appeared to formalize a trend that has been developing since 2022: the expansion of women’s participation in Baloch militancy from largely symbolic and support roles into direct operational activity.

The development raises a broader question: Why are Baloch militant organizations expanding women’s roles now, and what does this mean for an insurgency historically dominated by men?

The shift can be traced most clearly to April 2022, when Shari Baloch carried out a suicide attack at the Confucius Institute at the University of Karachi, killing three Chinese teachers and their Pakistani driver. The BLA claimed responsibility and presented her as its first female suicide operative. Since then, several other women have been linked to suicide operations attributed to BLA factions. In June 2023, Sumaiya Qalandrani Baloch carried out a suicide attack targeting a military convoy in Turbat. In August 2024, a woman identified by the BLA as Mahal Baloch conducted a vehicle-borne attack against a Frontier Corps facility in Bela. In March 2025, Mahikhan Baloch carried out another suicide attack against a paramilitary convoy in Kalat.

In November 2025, the trend extended to another major Baloch armed group, the Baloch Liberation Front (BLF), when Zareena Rafiq carried out a vehicle-borne attack against a Frontier Corps facility in Nokundi. The pattern suggests that the use of women is no longer confined to an isolated form of militant propaganda. It is becoming part of how some Baloch armed groups recruit, operate, and present themselves.

The development became even more visible during the BLA’s January-February 2026 offensive, which the organization called Operation Herof 2.0. The BLA publicized the participation of several women in the coordinated attacks, including female suicide operatives.

Balochistan, Pakistan’s largest province by area and one of its least densely populated, has experienced successive waves of Baloch nationalist insurgency, with the current conflict emerging in the early 2000s. The BLA and BLF are among the principal separatist organizations involved. They frame their campaigns around grievances including political marginalization, resource distribution, and alleged abuses by the Pakistani state. Pakistani authorities classify the groups as terrorist organizations and have attributed aspects of the insurgency to external support. The conflict has also acquired a significant international dimension. Balochistan hosts Gwadar Port and other major infrastructure associated with the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), making Chinese nationals and projects recurring targets for Baloch militants.

For much of the current insurgency, however, women associated with Baloch nationalism were more visible in political activism, advocacy, and community mobilization than in armed operations. Organizations such as the Baloch Students Organization-Azad (BSO-A) and the Baloch Yakjehti Committee have provided platforms for campaigns concerning enforced disappearances, alleged extrajudicial killings, and other grievances involving the Pakistani state. Women such as Mahrang Baloch and Sammi Deen Baloch have subsequently become prominent advocates on these issues. Karima Mehrab Baloch, who became the first woman to chair BSO-A, was another prominent figure in Baloch nationalist activism before she died in Toronto in December 2020.

This established a largely political role for women within the broader Baloch nationalist movement. But the emergence of women in militant operations since 2022 marks a departure from that pattern. The May announcement of a dedicated women’s wing in the BLA represents a potential further step in this evolution, from individual female participation in militant operations toward a more formal organizational role.

The motivations of individual women who join militant organizations cannot be reduced to a single explanation. Political grievances, personal experiences, family or social networks, ideological commitment, trauma, and the search for purpose can all influence recruitment. These factors differ from one individual to another.

The organizational incentives are easier to identify. Women can provide militant groups with additional operational flexibility. Gendered assumptions about who constitutes a security threat can affect how individuals are screened, monitored, or approached by security personnel. This does not make women inherently better operatives. Rather, it gives organizations another category of personnel through which they can attempt to exploit gaps in security practices. Female participation can also broaden the pool from which militant organizations recruit. It allows groups to portray their struggle as extending beyond young male fighters and into families and communities.

The propaganda value may be even more important. A female militant challenges the conventional image of an insurgent as a young man carrying a weapon. Baloch militant groups have used photographs, videos, and biographies of female operatives to portray their participation as evidence that the conflict has reached across gender and social boundaries.

However, reducing female militants to passive victims of manipulation obscures their agency and the possibility that some make deliberate ideological or political choices. At the same time, focusing exclusively on agency can obscure the organizational structures that recruit, train, indoctrinate, and deploy them. The analytical challenge is to account for both.

The Baloch case is part of a much broader history of women’s participation in political violence. Research on female suicide bombers has documented substantial participation by women in conflicts ranging from the Middle East to South Asia and Southeast Asia. Secular separatist organizations such as the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) and the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) were among the groups that developed significant roles for women in their military structures. The LTTE incorporated women into combat units and became particularly associated with female suicide operations. The PKK likewise developed extensive female military and organizational structures.

Later, jihadist organizations including Boko Haram, al-Shabaab, and the Islamic State expanded women’s roles in different ways, including recruitment, propaganda, logistics, and, in some cases, direct participation in attacks. The comparison should not be overstated, however. These organizations differ substantially in ideology, structure, social environment, and strategic objectives. Baloch armed groups are primarily ethno-nationalist and separatist organizations rather than transnational jihadist movements.

The expansion of women’s participation comes amid a broader deterioration in Pakistan’s security environment. The Baloch insurgency is only one component of that deterioration; the resurgence of the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), particularly along the Afghan border, has also contributed substantially to the country’s terrorism burden.

The Global Terrorism Index 2026 ranked Pakistan as the country most affected by terrorism in 2025, recording 1,139 terrorism-related deaths and 1,045 incidents. Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa together accounted for more than 74 percent of terrorist attacks and 67 percent of terrorism-related deaths recorded in Pakistan that year. This wider context matters because the emergence of female militants could tempt security institutions toward an overly broad response.

The answer is not simply increased surveillance of women. A poorly designed response could stigmatize women participating in legitimate political activity and further blur the distinction between peaceful activism and militancy. Instead, intelligence assessments should account for women as potential participants across the spectrum of militant activity, including recruitment, propaganda, financing, logistics, and direct operations. At the same time, investigators must distinguish genuine indicators of militant involvement from political dissent, human rights activism, and ordinary civic activity.

That distinction is particularly important in Balochistan, where a significant political and human rights movement exists alongside an armed insurgency. Conflating the two would not only threaten civil liberties; it could also make counterterrorism less effective by expanding the pool of people who feel alienated from the state. The strategic challenge is therefore twofold: prevent militant organizations from turning women’s visibility into an operational advantage, while ensuring that the state’s response does not itself deepen the alienation that those organizations seek to capitalize on. That means combining intelligence-led counterterrorism with community engagement, strategic communication, and efforts to address the grievances that militant organizations seek to exploit.

The shift from symbolic female participation to a more structured operational role is still developing, but the direction is increasingly difficult to ignore.

title: Goodbye, ‘China Plus One’: The Real Change in US China Policy
description: Beneath the pageantry, here's the change that matters: Washington has stopped talking about leaving China.
text:
U.S. President Donald Trump rolled out the red carpet for President Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington and greeted him in person at Joint Base Andrews on the evening of September 23, a rare gesture for an American president. Critics in both parties warned that the pageantry would reward a rival.

However, the red carpet, the state dinner with its exquisite menu, the cannon salute and the bald eagle sculpture gifted to Xi are just the surface. Beneath them, the bilateral relationship has begun to take a new direction.

At their Beijing summit in May, the two leaders agreed to build a “constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability.” It’s a lengthy phrase, but each word is there for a reason. “Constructive” commits both sides to a positive agenda, not just damage control. “Strategic” places the relationship at the level of leaders and long horizons. “Stability” sets a direction and boundary for the relationship.

This new formula is sharply different from the language used to describe China-U.S. relations since 2018.

Recall Trump’s first term. Washington launched a trade war, imposed tariffs on Chinese goods, and placed Huawei and other Chinese firms under technology sanctions. Washington urged multinational companies to quickly adopt “China Plus One” strategies, moving out of China and building a second supply base in Vietnam, India, or Mexico. It trumpeted decoupling as the goal.

Since 2018, Beijing has gradually diversified its trade across Southeast Asia, Latin America, and Africa. China-U.S. trade fell by around 30 percent in 2025 alone, according to the McKinsey Global Institute’s 2026 update on the geometry of global trade. Meanwhile, China built a complete and strategically critical supply chain, from basic materials to advanced equipment. China now is the only country to make goods in all 41 industrial categories and 666 sub-categories in the United Nations classification.

Today, China sells advanced machinery, components and critical materials to other countries’ factories. McKinsey called it the factory to the world factories, and the Wall Street Journal described the same shift. In many ways, China Plus One did not remove China from the global supply chain. Instead, it has helped China move up the value chain, as India, Vietnam, and Mexico become assembly lines for Chinese products.

These economic shifts have resulted in a telling change in Washington’s vocabulary. In August 2023, then-U.S. Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo said that China was “uninvestable.” This became the preferred talking point of politicians and China hawks across Washington. For years, terms like “de-risking,” “de-coupling,” “friend-shoring” and “China+ Plus One” filled congressional hearings, cable interviews, and opinion pages.

However, references to China Plus One have nearly vanished in Washington. No one among the Trump administration’s senior officials and business executives uses the term anymore.

The change was also symbolized by the guests at the head table during the state dinner for Xi. Beside the two presidents were Tim Cook of Apple, Jensen Huang of Nvidia, Lisa Su of Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) and Elon Musk of Tesla and SpaceX. All of them understand how critical China is to their businesses, both as a market and as the base of their supply chains.

Apple’s first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo, was developed, trial-produced and assembled exclusively in China, according to Apple’s vice president for Asia procurement and operations, not built in India or Vietnam. Tesla previously announced plants to phase Chinese suppliers out of its American-built cars. Now it is seeking multiple suppliers in China for its Optimus humanoid robot, and orders have already been placed. Huang has argued for months that export controls are backfiring on American competitiveness. Su has pledged to deepen AMD’s engagement in China. These executives know China Plus One and decoupling with China are not working.

Smaller firms follow the same logic. EnerVenue, a California battery startup, announced last week that it began mass production in Changzhou after abandoning plans for a $264 million factory in Kentucky. Its chief executive cited China’s skilled workforce and supply chain strength, and called China the “factory of factories.” Chinese business media have also reported cases of American manufacturers that moved orders to India or Southeast Asia to avoid tariffs, struggled with quality and delivery, and returned the work to their original Chinese suppliers.

The toasts at the state dinner on September 24 affirmed the new direction, especially in the people-to-people and business-to-business ties. Both leaders reached back into history. Trump spoke of the foundation of commerce and mutual respect, and of ties between the two peoples that endure.

Xi recalled the trade that began soon after American independence and the Hump airlift over the Himalayas during the war against Japan. He recalled “ping-pong diplomacy,” and the redwoods Richard Nixon gave China that now grow in Zhejiang. He praised Ronald Sakolsky, an American teacher who donated $5,000 to fund a Chinese woman’s desert tree-planting two decades ago and recently returned to China to see a forest in the desert.

Xi’s most strategic move was his remark that Trump’s Make America Great Again and China’s pursuit of national rejuvenation “can surely be mutually reinforcing.” This is a strategic discourse specifically aimed at the idea that dominates Washington’s thinking about the China-U.S. relationship: the Thucydides Trap, which holds that a rising power and an established one are headed for war. Xi’s remark rejected that premise and offered an alternative frame. Two great projects of national renewal need not collide. He called for “a new approach for major countries to get along.”

None of this means rivalry and competition between the two great powers have slowed down. In July the Federal Communications Commission added foreign-made humanoid and industrial robots to its covered list, a move Beijing condemned. Chip export controls remain unchanged. China’s rare earth magnet shipments to the United States fell 21 percent in August to 512 tons, heading toward their lowest level since 2021. Taiwan, Iran, and AI safety will test the newly coined “constructive relationship of strategic stability.” But both leaders have endorsed its guardrails.

While Trump 1.0 started decoupling and China Plus One, Trump 2.0 now regards China as an equal partner in deals, a critical supplier the American economy cannot easily replace, and the other half of a G2.

The festivities at Joint Base Andrews and in the East Room of the White House will soon fade from the headlines. But Washington has stopped talking about leaving China, and corporate America never really left.

title: Hans van de Ven on World War II and the Making of Modern Asia
description: “The Asian theater was never just about defeating Japan – it was also about dismantling European imperialism and creating new national futures.”
text:
In “Blood Dawn: World War II and the Making of Modern Asia,” Hans van de Ven, a professor of modern Chinese history at Cambridge University, provides a much-needed Asia-centric focus on World War II.

While Western histories of the global conflict center the European theater, and typically mark the war’s beginning with with Germany’s invasion of Poland in 1939, van de Ven starts with the reordering of Asia under European colonialism in the 19th century, the awakening of new political movements across the region in response, and Japan’s 1937 invasion of China.

World War II remade Asia, and the consequences thereof linger to this day.

“Many of today’s flashpoints – capable of sparking global conflict – are unresolved hangovers from this war,” van de Ven told The Diplomat’s Managing Editor Catherine Putz. From Kashmir and the India-Pakistan rivalry, to the status of Taiwan and the division of the Korean Peninsula, Asia’s flashpoints have their roots in the legacies of World War II.

“Blood Dawn: World War II and the Making of Modern Asia” will be published on September 8, 2026.

What changes in our understanding of World War II when we shift focus from the European theater to the Pacific?

The Second World War in Asia marked the end of British, French, and Dutch imperial rule and birthed a new Asia structured around the modern nation-state. In that sense, the transformations wrought by the war in Asia were as profound as those caused by the First World War in Europe.

The Asian theater was never just about defeating Japan – it was also about dismantling European imperialism and creating new national futures. Regional independence movements exploited Japan’s attempt to build an empire that rivaled Britain’s. Some built large followings and armies – like the Chinese Communists – while others sought independence by collaborating with the Japanese, as Sukarno did in Indonesia.

Another crucial shift was that the contest between Japan and the United States for control of the Pacific ended decisively in America’s favor. Following the Versailles Peace Treaty [that ended World War I], Japan gained control of the Mariana, Caroline, and Marshall Islands. During the war, the United States expended immense blood and treasure to conquer them. Today’s geopolitical contest between the U.S. and China is, in part, a continuation of this struggle for Pacific dominance. As an emerging superpower, China naturally wants to secure its vulnerable coastline – through which the British invaded in the 19th century and the Japanese in the 20th.

To what extent did the colonization of Asia by European powers set the stage for World War II in the region?

In three distinct ways.

First, prior to Europe’s colonization of Asia, the region was ruled by historic dynasties: the Mughals in India, the Manchus in China, the Tokugawa shogunate in Japan, the Joseon dynasty in Korea, and the Nguyễn dynasty in Vietnam. None survived the colonial regimes the Europeans built in the first part of the 19th century, and their collapses proved deeply destabilizing.

Second, Western military, technical, and scientific dominance created a severe crisis of confidence among Asian elites, who concluded that their own cultural and political traditions were backward. In the late 19th century, nationalist movements emerged that demanded radical political, cultural, and social change. Initially confined to elites, they gained mass followings in the 1920s after the Great Powers at Versailles rejected Asian demands for self-determination. Meanwhile, the 1917 October Revolution in Russia offered an inspiring new model of revolution. Communism provided an organizational framework for anti-imperialism and suggested that a backward country did not need decades of gradual development and industrialization but could through revolution jump to the forefront of history. In orthodox communism, feudalism is followed by capitalism before it finally reaches communism.

Finally, there was Japan. Before World War I, Japanese elites hoped to gain Western acceptance by “leaving” Asia and adopting Western models. However, the Western powers’ refusal to include a racial equality clause in the League of Nations covenant, combined with naval restrictions imposed on Japan at the Washington Conference, convinced Japanese leaders that Japan had to free Asia from European imperialism to achieve equal footing.

Many peg the start of World War II in Asia as the Marco Polo Bridge Incident in July 1937, two years before the war kicked off in Europe. What is most important to understand about that incident?

Chiang Kai-shek transformed a minor military clash near Beijing into an existential crisis involving the survival of China as a nation and civilization. Similar skirmishes had occurred before and were settled locally. However, Chiang insisted that any resolution be approved by China’s central government and demanded a full Japanese withdrawal from northern China.

When Japan refused, Chiang threw his elite troops against Japanese forces in Shanghai, stationed there by virtue of an earlier truce agreement. Chiang’s decision, which lacked unanimous support, ensured that the conflict threatened Western financial interests and received heavy global media coverage. China was quickly framed as a plucky underdog standing up to brutal Japanese militarism.

Equally important was the creation of a United Front between Chiang’s Nationalists and Mao Zedong’s Communists, who had been fighting each other since the mid-1920s. Chiang agreed to take on Japan partly because Joseph Stalin offered massive Soviet military aid and pressured Mao to join the alliance. Chiang hoped this United Front would absorb the Communists into the nationalist political order and end their efforts to overthrow him – a hope that ultimately proved to be a catastrophic miscalculation.

How did the twin forces of nationalism and anti-imperialism interact in World War II in Asia?

A really good question. We often equate Asia’s anti-imperialism with nationalism, but that oversimplifies reality. It was far from guaranteed that the nations of post-war Asia would be unitary states led by secular nationalists. For instance, there was massive support in Indonesia for establishing an Islamic state, which did not come to fruition largely through Sukarno’s personal charisma. Alternative visionaries imagined a Confucian East Asia or a vast federation of Islamic states spanning from Southeast Asia to the Middle East. Gandhi was a nationalist, of course, but he wanted a new Indian polity based on village councils. The Confucian leader Qian Mu wanted the same in China.

One core question driving my research was why China, India, and Indonesia rejected federalism, which, one could argue, would have suited their enormous internal diversity and for which there was support. First, federal structures were strongly associated with European “divide-and-rule” colonial tactics. Second, the war made it starkly obvious that only large, centralized powers possessed the strength to determine their own futures and to matter geopolitically.

“Blood Dawn” emphasizes how contingent these post-war outcomes really were. The 1947 partition of the Indian subcontinent into India and Pakistan is a prime example; neither Jawaharlal Nehru nor Muhammad Ali Jinnah originally desired a hard partition, but they exhausted each other and the British through endless negotiations. Similarly, as Mao Zedong later acknowledged to Japanese visitors in the 1950s, the Chinese Communists might never have emerged out of the hills of northwest Chia without the catalyst of WWII. Their ultimate victory was far from guaranteed until 1947 at the earliest.

Russia – at the time the Soviet Union – bridges all of Eurasia. How did Soviet leaders approach the conflict in East Asia at first and how did their approach evolve?

For Stalin, the ultimate nightmare was a two-front war requiring the USSR to fight Germany and Japan simultaneously across vast distances. To counter the rise of Hitler, Stalin advocated Popular Front alliances starting in 1932, encouraging communists to ally with all anti-fascists. This strategy shaped Léon Blum’s government in France, Manuel Azaña’s in Spain, and China’s United Front.

In 1939, Stalin reversed course. Japanese forces had become bogged down in China, and Soviet forces dealt a decisive blow to Japan’s Kwantung Army at the Battle of Khalkhin Gol. While that battle raged, Stalin negotiated simultaneously with Hitler’s Germany, which stood at the brink of invading Poland, as well as with Britain and France, who had guaranteed Poland’s security. Stalin ultimately chose a pact with Hitler. That and an armistice agreed with Japan meant that the Soviet Union did not have to fight either of its enemies for some time. To explain this awkward change, which left socialists and communists the world over confounded, Stalin declared that the new world war was not against fascism after all, but merely a contest between empires who could be left to slaughter each other.

Only in the summer of 1945, after Germany’s defeat, did Stalin enter the war against Japan by invading occupied Manchuria. Although Soviet troops eventually withdrew, the operation secured the USSR a major voice in post-war Asian affairs.

Finally, why do you think it is important to continue to revisit and reexamine the past – such as World War II writ large and in Asia, specifically?

For Asia, World War II was an axial moment. The modern states of Asia trace their origins directly to this period; the leaders of its independence movements remain central heroic figures, and wartime narratives still dominate national identity.

Furthermore, many of today’s flashpoints – capable of sparking global conflict – are unresolved hangovers from this war. These include Kashmir, the India-Pakistan rivalry, the status of Taiwan, and the standoff on the Korean Peninsula.

In the immediate post-war decades, Western observers often ignored Asia due to its poverty. That luxury is gone. China is now an emergent superpower, and Asia’s economies are driving global growth. Yet Western audiences remain strikingly ignorant of Asian history. While some Americans know a bit about China and some British know about India, very few people pay attention to Indonesia – which features prominently in “Blood Dawn.”
