title: Hindutva Is Slowly Seeping Into Nepal
description: The number of Hindu-Muslim clashes is growing as India’s brand of Hindu majoritarianism gains ground in Nepal.
text:
On the night of July 26, a Hindu procession was on its way back after collecting holy water from the Koshi River. The procession being taken out at Kaptanganj of Sunsari district in eastern Nepal was accompanied by loud music, to which some local Muslims objected. A scuffle broke out. Police got involved.

Hindu-Muslim tensions soon spread across Nepal’s Tarai-Madhesh belt, the east-west strip of land abutting India. In ensuing clashes between protesters and the police, four people died while curfews disrupted life across the region.

Such incidents follow a recognizable pattern. One newspaper investigation identified 17 Hindu-Muslim documented clashes over the past decade – with around two-thirds of them involving religious processions or idol immersions. The number of undocumented cases is undoubtedly higher.

The History

Over the past decade or so the influx of Hindutva ideas from India has been steadily stoking Hindu-Muslim tensions. Before that, these communities had mostly lived in harmony in a country where over 80 percent of people are Hindus. Muslims, by contrast, make up just 5 percent of the national population. But seldom did this small religious minority feel persecuted. After the recent devastating floods, the coming together of people from different faiths to help and pray for victims offered a glimpse of the inter-faith harmony Nepal has long been known for.

For most of its modern history, Nepal has been a de facto Hindu state. Prithvi Narayan Shah, the 18th-century founder of modern Nepal, famously described his kingdom as Asal Hindustan, or the “real Hindustan.” He wanted to build “a true home for Hindus” at a time when much of the Indian subcontinent was under Muslim rule.

The 1962 constitution promulgated by King Mahendra was the first to officially declare Nepal as a Hindu kingdom, with the divine monarch as its protector. After this, the 1990 charter introduced following a popular movement heralded a constitutional monarchy but kept the Hindu state characterization.

Things would drastically change in 2006 following the end of the decade-long Maoist insurgency and the second people’s movement. The interim constitution promulgated a year later held in abeyance the institution of the monarchy – which was later abolished by the first meeting of the Constituent Assembly – and formally declared Nepal a secular state.

Yet with the Maoists losing electoral ground in the second Constituent Assembly election in 2013, conservative forces began to reassert themselves. This is why the new (and currently operative) constitution promulgated in 2015 gave continuity to Nepal’s secular designation but added a rider: Nepali secularism would entail the “protection of religion and culture being practiced since ancient times.”

As the new charter was being finalized, the country’s secularism debate was also being closely watched in India. Hindu nationalist politicians and organizations there were openly lobbying for the restoration of Nepal’s Hindu status.

Narendra Modi’s election as Indian prime minister in 2014 had given the cause an added impetus. But the new Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) establishment in New Delhi wouldn’t get its way.

It was partly because Nepal’s secular status was retained in the 2015 charter that India imposed a crippling, four-and-a-half-month-long blockade on the land-locked country.

As Nepal was struggling to finalize its constitution and consolidate its status as a secular republic, Hindu nationalist politics was becoming dominant across its southern border. Hindutva ideas, symbols, and organizations started making greater inroads into Nepal.

For and Against a Hindu State

Hindutva is a right-wing ideology that seeks to organize all Hindus as a political community. It portrays Hindu civilization as coming under threat from other religions like Islam and Christianity whose origins lie outside India.

There are compelling arguments for why a wholesale import of Hindutva is unlikely in Nepal.

Richard Bownas, a scholar who has been closely following Hindu politics in Nepal, argued that the kind of “actionable package” that makes mass Hindu mobilization for political ends so effective in India is absent in Nepal. For instance, Nepal has only around 250 active shakhas of the Hindu Swayamsevak Sangh (HSS), an offshoot of the Rastriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), the Hindu nationalist volunteer paramilitary organization closely associated with the BJP.

The HSS has made rapid inroads into Nepal. Still, the country has just one shakha for every 120,000 people, in comparison to one for 17,000 people in India. Nepal’s heterogeneous religious landscape as well as the lack of religious zealotry of its political leadership, Bownas argued, also prevent Hindutva from exerting the same kind of influence.

But with ideological politics taking a backseat and populists now running Nepal, there is a distinct possibility of a greater embrace of religion as a political tool by ruling and opposition parties alike. Early signs are that the government of Balendra Shah formed after the 2025 Gen Z uprising and March 2026 elections is partial to Hinduism.

The new prime minister’s inauguration ceremony was steeped in Hindu Vedic rituals, making people of other faiths suspect the credentials of the head of government of a secular state. Even the recent ceremony to mark the first anniversary of the Gen Z protests drew controversy over the presence of certain Hindu religious leaders.

The ruling ideology-lite Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP), it appears, will find the allure of Hinduism as a political weapon hard to resist.

The top leaders of more established political parties, which were trounced in the March 2026 general elections, also see religion as perhaps the only tool that can pave the way for their unlikely comeback.

Sher Bahadur Deuba, five-time prime minister and long-time leader of the Nepali Congress, traditionally the country’s biggest democratic force, has of late been openly flaunting his Hindu identity and emphasizing the country’s Hindu roots. Until now the committed secularist had been resisting the call of a vocal Congress faction to lobby for the restoration of the Hindu state.

K.P. Sharma Oli, the three-time prime minister and current chair of the Communist Party of Nepal-Unified Marxist-Leninist (CPN-UML), the country’s biggest communist outfit, has been courting Nepali Hindus for much longer. Among his infamous anti-India post-blockade pitches was the claim that Ram, a central deity in Hindutva mobilization, was born in Thori of Nepal rather than across the border in Ayodhya of India.

It is becoming clear that as older ideological distinctions like social democracy, communism, monarchy, and regionalism lose their mobilization power, religion is increasingly likely to fill the vacuum.

Two trends make the present moment different: the weakening of Nepal’s older political identities and the ready availability of a Hindu nationalist vocabulary from across the border.

In order to reshape Nepali politics, Hindutva does not have to look exactly the same as it does in India. Local politicians can borrow its symbols, grievances, and methods of mobilization and adapt them to their political circumstances.

That process is especially salient in the Tarai-Madhesh belt.

Saffronization of the Plains

For decades, political mobilization in Nepal’s plains – which constitutes less than 25 percent of the country’s landmass but is home to over 50 percent of its people – revolved around caste, regional exclusion, identity, and demands for representation within the Nepali state. This was especially true of Madhesh Province, the epicenter of Madheshi identity politics.

With the RSP sweeping the last general elections – winning 30 of 32 seats in the province – traditional Madheshi parties have been greatly weakened.

The erosion of ideological and regional loyalties, as has been seen in Madhesh, has prompted local politicians to try to regain their influence by presenting themselves as defenders of the “Hindu community” or “Muslim community.” This was also evident in the aftermath of the Kaptanganj clashes.

More broadly, the rise of the BJP in India, culminating symbolically in the inauguration of the Ram Mandir in Ayodhya in 2024, has coincided with more conspicuous and competitive displays of religious identity in Nepal.

Saffron pennants are increasingly visible on Hindu homes and neighborhoods in the Tarai-Madhesh – thanks in part to sustained activism of the HSS foot soldiers who encourage such displays of Hindu religiosity. Green religious flags are similarly displayed by Muslims. Religious processions are often larger, louder, and more assertive.

Before the July 26 incident, the local Hindu community in Kaptanganj was apparently unhappy because some of the green pennants planted during the Muslim festival of Muharram a month before were not uprooted at the festival’s end. Once a procession or flag is interpreted as demonstrating which community controls a road, neighborhood, or public space, minor disputes can take on existential significance.

The Tarai-Madhesh is vulnerable to the allure of Hindutva also because of geography. Nepal and India share an open border and the neighboring Indian states of Bihar and Uttar Pradesh are the heartlands of Hindu nationalist politics. Communities on the two sides have “roti-beti relations” as they are tied together by marriage, trade, pilgrimage, language, and culture.

Political ideas thus cross the border as easily as people do. This also makes it easy for organizations like the RSS – whose ideology Indian historian Ram Chandra Guha distilled as “We will show Muslims their place” – to operate in the belt.

The Corrosive Effects of Social Media

Social media has dramatically accelerated religious polarization.

Many participants in the Kaptanganj protests had hurried to the incident site after seeing provocative videos and messages on their mobile phones. Instant social media amplification then spread the clashes across the Tarai-Madhesh belt.

In the past, an argument over a flag or procession in one Tarai village would remain confined there. Local party representatives, elders, and community leaders would intervene before an argument acquired a wider communal character. Increasingly, the mediators themselves arrive as representatives of religious constituencies.

This in turn can contribute to polarization along religious lines. Once members of a religion feel politically or physically insecure, they have an incentive to mobilize on the basis of their religion.

Today, audio and video footage of a communal clash can spread across Nepal and among the diaspora communities around the world within minutes.

Videos are often stripped of context and accompanied by inflammatory claims. Hindu and Muslim influencers circulate clips portraying their respective communities as victims. Old footage can be rehashed as evidence of new attacks.

Social media changes the geographical scale of communal tensions. A local dispute between neighbors becomes an event in a much larger Hindu-Muslim struggle. That makes traditional local mediation much more difficult.

Radicalization and Demographic Fear

The emerging Hindu nationalist narrative in the Tarai-Madhesh is anti-Muslim. Yet the larger national narrative is of Hindu demographic and cultural vulnerability.

Christianity is another focus of Hindu mobilization (although this is more of an issue up in the hilly regions than down in the Tarai plains). Royalist and Hindu nationalist groups frequently claim that aggressive Christian proselytization, backed by foreign money, is eroding Nepal’s traditional culture. Opposition to conversion has consequently become intertwined with campaigns to restore Hindu statehood.

Supporters of Hindu political mobilization argue that secularism was surreptitiously introduced during Nepal’s turbulent political transition without a popular mandate. They point to Christian conversion, greater activity of foreign-funded religious organizations, and “Islamist radicalization” as the unwanted consequences. Restoring Nepal’s Hindu identity, they believe, would protect rather than divide society.

The debate over Nepal’s religious identity predates Modi and the recent communal clashes. Even the constitution reflects that unresolved tension by simultaneously declaring Nepal secular and promising protection for religions and cultures practiced since ancient times.

Hindu nationalist narratives also increasingly portray Nepal’s Hindu majority as endangered. Some YouTubers and news channels have attributed recent communal disturbances to Rohingya Muslim refugees allegedly entering Nepal from Bangladesh.

But the vast majority of Nepal’s Muslims are not a recently arrived population – nor has their presence caused any problem for much of Nepal’s modern history. They are established Nepali communities, overwhelmingly concentrated in the Tarai, often speaking the same languages and participating in the same local economies as their Hindu neighbors.

Some of these concerns deserve factual scrutiny. Religious radicalization and illicit foreign financing should not be ignored wherever credible evidence exists. Nepali laws ban forced conversation; the challenge is their judicious implementation.

State Failure and Elite Apathy

The Nepali state has responded poorly to this emerging challenge.

Even as communal tensions simmered across the Tarai-Madhesh during the latest crisis, Shah, the prime minister, remained silent for several days. He addressed the nation only after the unrest had spread and the situation was threatening to get out of control. Security institutions also appear poorly prepared to handle communal violence.

The problem is not just inadequate riot-control capacity. Resolution of communal conflict calls for local knowledge, trusted intermediaries, early intelligence, and officials capable of distinguishing between a normal religious celebration and an organized attempt at provocation. Nepal’s security forces frequently lack those advantages.

Provinces still do not have the degree of independent policing authority envisioned by the constitution, leaving crucial decisions to officials in Kathmandu. There is also an old perception in the Madhesh that Kathmandu’s political and bureaucratic establishment treats violence in the plains as somehow peripheral to the country’s central political life.

The most troubling aspect is that the violence in Kaptanganj was foreseeable.

The Armed Police Force warned the government years ago that organized actors were fanning religious and ethnic tensions in the Tarai and recommended political and administrative intervention. Yet the state continued to see such tensions principally as a law-and-order problem and failed to prepare for the worst.

Crossing a Threshold?

Is Nepal crossing a dangerous threshold whereby every major political force feels the need to employ Hinduism as a political tool? That would be unfortunate. One of the hallmarks of post-1990 Nepali politics has been the ability of Nepali political parties to come together to face moments of national crisis.

This was most clearly visible in 2015. That year, after the devastating earthquakes had brought the country to a standstill, parties from across the political spectrum set aside their ideological differences to promulgate the new constitution and put national politics back on track.

After Kaptanganj too, the parties eventually came together to call for calm. But compromise will become harder when politics is built around sacred identities. The recent clashes are warning signs of a potentially much larger transformation in Nepali politics.

Nepal is not India. Its history, social structure, and religious traditions are different. The syncretic nature of Nepali society and its long record of coexistence protect against wholesale import of India’s communal politics.

But those protections should not be taken for granted.

title: Indonesia Reopens Airports After Suspension Due to Volcanic Eruption
description: The eruption of Anak Krakatau, which is located on a small island in the Sunda Strait, forced the closure of eight airports, including two serving the capital Jakarta.
text:
Indonesia reopened five airports early this morning, after a volcanic eruption over the weekend forced them to suspend operations for two days.

Anak Krakatau, which is located on a small island in the Sunda Strait between the islands of Java and Sumatra, began erupting late on Friday and remained active for around 25 hours.

The eruption threw up black plumes of volcanic ash that were carried by the wind over the skies of the capital, Jakarta, which lies around 150 kilometers to the east, and across Lampung province in the southern part of Sumatra.

This forced the closure of eight airports, including two servicing Jakarta. As the BBC reported, “snaking queues had formed at the departure halls in Jakarta’s Soekarno-Hatta International Airport on Monday as stranded passengers sought refunds and tried to get updates on when they would be able to fly.” Indonesian officials said yesterday that 2,961 flights were disrupted, leaving around 341,000 people stranded.

In a statement today, Transport Minister Dudy Purwagandhi said that Jakarta’s Soekarno-Hatta International Airport, the capital’s primary airport, resumed operations this morning after wind blew the ash away from the ⁠vicinity, Reuters reported. Four other airports, including a smaller one in Jakarta and another in the neighboring city of ​Bandung, also reopened today. Two airports remain closed, while one resumed operations yesterday.

Dudy ​told reporters that authorities would now need to confirm the airworthiness of the 178 aircraft that were at Soekarno-Hatta during ‌the closure. “Perhaps it’ll ⁠take some little extra time to prepare the planes,” he said.

Anak Krakatau, which means “child of Krakatoa,” emerged from the sea in the 1920s in the caldera formed after the 1883 eruption of Mount Krakatoa, which destroyed the island of Krakatau and unleashed a tsunami that killed more than 36,000 people. It has been sporadically active for much of the last decade, and an eruption in 2018 caused a devastating tsunami that killed hundreds of people and displaced tens of thousands.

On Sunday, the Center for Volcanology and Geological Hazard Mitigation said that although the volcanic eruption has come to an apparent end, Anak Krakatau remained on alert, and further eruptions were possible.

Also yesterday, Malaysian authorities lifted a declaration of emergency in Serian, a district in the southwest of Sarawak state, that was imposed due to toxic haze from wildfires across the border in Indonesia. Sarawak, which runs along the north of the island of Borneo, is one of the areas most affected by the resulting air pollution, which has forced the closure of 647 schools across the state.

Malaysia’s king, Sultan Ibrahim, gave his consent to end the state of ‌emergency following reports from government agencies showing that air quality readings in Serian were no ​longer at a ​hazardous level, Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s office said in a statement.

“The Federal government and the Sarawak state government will continue to closely monitor ⁠the ​situation, and residents in affected areas ​are advised to limit outdoor activities and to always comply with instructions from ​the authorities,” it added.

title: How Great Power Rivalry Is Fracturing the Pacific Islands Forum
description: Absences from this year's Leaders' Meeting are raising questions about the group's solidarity amid growing China-U.S. competition.
text:
The 55th Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) Leaders’ Meeting opened on August 31 under a banner of unity, but it can’t escape the reality that outside powers are competing for influence in the Pacific. The question now facing the PIF is whether the forum’s consensus model, once a safeguard for small-state sovereignty, has become the very mechanism through which that influence reshapes regional outcomes.

The official theme of this year’s PIF Leaders’ Meeting, held in Palau, is B.E.L.A.U., or Building Economies, Life, Action, Unity, an acronym that doubles as a tribute to the host nation’s indigenous name. It was meant to signal collective resolve. Instead, the gathering has been defined by conspicuous absences and blocked consensus. Given the return of Taiwan as a development partner after last year’s exclusion, some see this year’s PIF as proof of Beijing’s growing capacity to paralyze the region’s most important multilateral institution from within.

At least five Pacific leaders chose not to attend. The leaders of Kiribati, Samoa, and Vanuatu dispatched deputies, while Fiji’s Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka stayed home to manage domestic affairs. The most dramatic absence was that of Solomon Islands’ Prime Minister Matthew Wale, who landed in Palau only to leave hours later after a no-confidence motion was filed against him back in Honiara. Wale had served as prime minister for barely three months and as outgoing PIF chair, was meant to hand the gavel to Palau’s President Surangel Whipps Jr. Instead, he left Foreign Minister Rick Hou to represent his country at the summit.

Kiribati’s case is particularly revealing. President Taneti Maamau dispatched not a cabinet minister but David Teaabo, his director of foreign service and a former ambassador to China. In an organization where decisions require consensus at the level of heads of state, sending a lower-ranking delegate who cannot commit to communique language with full authority is itself a political statement.

Kiribati’s posture becomes clearer against the backdrop of the missile crisis that preceded the summit. On July 6, China conducted a submarine-launched ballistic missile test in the Pacific, firing what Taiwan identified as a JL-2 from the South China Sea. The missile, carrying a dummy warhead, transited the exclusive economic zones of the Federated States of Micronesia, Naoero (formerly Nauru), and Kiribati before landing near Tuvalu’s maritime boundary. Beijing provided only a few hours’ notice to the affected Pacific Island nations.

The reaction was swift – at least from those countries that did respond. Papua New Guinea’s Prime Minister James Marape invoked the region’s traumatic history of nuclear testing, insisting that Pacific nations “do not want history repeated.” Australia’s Prime Minister Anthony Albanese called the test “provocative” and “destabilizing.” Yet when Pacific foreign ministers gathered in Fiji in early August, Kiribati and Naoero blocked the consensus needed to issue a joint condemnation.

The PIF has historically operated on the principle of unanimity, a practice rooted in what Pacific leaders call the “Pacific Way,” designed to ensure that no island nation, however small, could be overruled by its larger neighbors. But the model assumed that external pressures would remain at the margins of PIF deliberations. When a member state with deep ties to the power responsible for a security event deploys its consensus rights to shield that power from collective criticism, the model risks becoming a means of undermining collective action.

New Zealand’s Foreign Minister Winston Peters made the frustration explicit, noting that two countries “were seeking to use the need for consensus as a veto provision.” Peters said that he had “made it very clear that we didn’t think outsiders should be telling insiders” what positions to take.

Kiribati’s alignment with Beijing extends beyond the blocking of a PIF statement. In late August, its parliament passed the first reading of a constitutional amendment that would restrict diplomatic recognition to states holding U.N. membership or permanent observer status, effectively locking future governments into recognizing Beijing. Graeme Smith of the Australian National University characterized the move as “almost entirely about sending a message to Beijing.”

With that in mind, Taiwan’s return to the PIF may also have contributed to Kiribati’s lack of top-level representation.

Last year, when the Solomon Islands hosted the 54th PIF Leaders’ Meeting, all external partners were excluded. The stated reason was a review of partnership arrangements, but the practical effect was to remove Taiwan from a gathering it had attended as a development partner since 1992. This year, with Palau – which has official diplomatic ties with Taiwan – as host, the dynamics reversed.

Taiwan’s Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung arrived in Koror leading a delegation that included representatives from energy, technology, construction, and agriculture, and he met with Whipps, Palau’s president, to strengthen bilateral ties before participating in the Taiwan/Republic of China-Forum Countries Dialogue.

Only three PIF members still maintain formal ties with Taipei, but Taiwan’s development programs extend well beyond those allies. Just in July 2026, Taiwan donated $2 million to the Forum Secretariat and in 2025 it pledged $3 million to the Pacific Resilience Facility.

Beijing, however, doesn’t take kindly to Taiwan’s inclusion in any form. China’s special envoy Qian Bo confronted Whipps directly at the Forum Troika meeting in Fiji, demanding Taiwan’s exclusion and warning that Beijing would “have to retaliate.” He dismissed Palau as “a small country.” Whipps was unfazed: “It doesn’t matter. We’re a country.” He later characterized Qian’s conduct as inappropriate, remarking that “if you want somebody to love you, usually you come with chocolates and nice cards.”

China made good on Qian’s threat on August 19, when Beijing’s Ministry of Culture and Tourism issued a travel advisory for Palau, warning of alleged theft and dangerous marine conditions and portraying one of the Pacific’s safest destinations as a place to avoid. The U.S. Embassy rejected the advisory, stating that “the United States opposes any attempts by China to weaponize tourism to coerce Palau.”

Tourism accounts for roughly 40 percent of Palau’s gross domestic product, and Beijing has used this lever before. After Palau refused to break ties with Taiwan, China banned package tours in 2017 and visitor numbers collapsed, but the country absorbed the shock and the weapon’s effectiveness has diminished with repeated use.

Whipps has been characteristically blunt about the situation “China continues to try to influence us, whether its threatening us with weaponizing tourism or attacking us personally,” he told reporters. “We’ve made it very clear from the beginning [that] nobody is going to tell us who our friends can be.”

Palau, with a population of roughly 18,000, has held its ground on Taiwan. Other Pacific Island states haven’t. Solomon Islands switched recognition to Beijing in 2019; Kiribati followed within weeks. Naoero switched in January 2024. Taiwan’s Pacific footprint has halved, going from six diplomatic partners in 2019 to just three today: the Marshall Islands, Palau, and Tuvalu.

The PIF Leaders’ Meeting, of course, is about much more than Taiwan, or even China. The summit’s agenda includes a climate declaration ahead of COP31 and a new maritime anti-smuggling initiative called Waqa Moana. The Pacific Resilience Facility, with $173 million in pledges toward a $500 million target, represents a genuine institutional innovation as a Pacific-owned climate finance mechanism.

But the credibility of a regional body rests on its capacity to address threats as well as opportunities. A forum that can mobilize around climate finance but cannot issue a statement when a nuclear-armed power tests a ballistic missile in its own members’ waters with barely any warning faces a fundamental question about what regional solidarity actually means.

The empty chairs in Palau are symptoms of a regional order under pressure, one in which the line between domestic sovereignty and external manipulation grows harder to draw with each passing year.

title: Human Rights Are Essential to Australia’s Interests
description: Governments such as Australia’s need to recognize that defending civil society and a free press throughout the region and beyond are not luxuries but central to a democratic resurgence.
text:
World politics feels like it is in disarray. Rules intended to regulate the behavior of all countries and institutions seem not to matter. International human rights norms now appear decidedly unfashionable, even in Australia, a country that should be one of the staunchest defenders of global human rights, where I have just spent two weeks meeting with government officials and civil society.

Transactional power politics increasingly disregard internationally agreed rules, enabling powerful governments, from China and Russia to the United States and their allies, to accelerate violations of human rights with few consequences.

But the longing for human rights is not going away. Respecting them remains critical for so many people around the world, especially those facing the most severe repression. In recent years, protesters throughout Asia – often led by young people – have fought for rights and equality in Bangladesh, Nepal, Sri Lanka, and India, even at the cost of their lives.

Democracies that remain committed to human rights and a rules-based world order should recognize that. Instead of cowering to this geopolitical moment, they should seize the uncertainty by doubling down and recognizing that rights are central to their long-term national interests. Canberra should be first in line.

Instead, Australia and other democracies have become focused on military security, diminishing the focus on human rights. In the past year, Australia has prioritized signing new regional defense and security agreements while doing little to re-energize a rules-based world order.

To be sure, military and cyber threats pose real dangers in this new world disorder. But coercion from abroad can take many forms. It also works by intimidating exiled dissidents, silencing journalists, corrupting democratic institutions, and exporting surveillance. Defense pacts alone cannot address these tactics.

Governments such as Australia’s need to recognize that defending civil society and a free press throughout the region and beyond are not luxuries but central to a democratic resurgence. Doing so means weaving human rights into domestic and foreign policies.

Australia should establish an Asia Democracy Fund together with other democratic governments to support embattled independent journalists, human rights defenders, and civil society organizations, particularly those already endangered or in exile, and groups that cannot safely access funding otherwise. Australia, like Canada, could also provide a safe haven to threatened rights defenders by establishing a special immigration pathway for them.

Australia should also support independent groups documenting serious abuses, particularly important at a time when the United States and other governments are attacking the international justice system. The country should stand up for the embattled International Criminal Court. It should also advance international justice by taking on some of the world’s worst atrocities in its own court system, a practice known as universal jurisdiction. Unfortunately, few countries in the Asia-Pacific region have been willing to use universal jurisdiction to investigate and prosecute alleged war criminals.

Issue by issue – from international crimes to technology to labor rights – Australia and other governments need to push back against increasing global repression. A comprehensive foreign policy approach in multilateral and bilateral forums is crucial, but so is adopting effective domestic laws and practices. This can include continuing to strengthen laws to prevent importing goods made with forced labor and stronger laws on privacy that regulate technology.

When governments that care about rights come together on the international stage to promote and protect them, and at the same time create laws and policies that demonstrate their own state won’t become a refuge for rights abusers, there is a much greater chance that together they can fend off the pressure being placed on human rights protections.

Rights-respecting democracies and like-minded allies need to find strength in numbers. They should create diplomatic and economic cover, to coalesce around key norms and tools, and international law more generally, while containing – and reversing – the damage done. A global alliance in support of a rules and rights-based international order can act in concert to protect the International Criminal Court or the United Nations’ independent fact-finding mechanisms, or the integrity of human rights treaties under attack. Australia is well positioned to present itself as a reliable leader and partner in this pursuit.

The international system that has been built over decades to protect and promote human rights has never worked perfectly or consistently. It has at times failed, at great cost to many people. But it has constrained abusive governments, given smaller and middle powers like Australia leverage to promote reform, reduced risks to marginalized populations by providing some level of global and regional stability, and offered victims of atrocities an opportunity for justice.

The rules-based order will not be saved by post-Cold War nostalgia, nor by international law that goes unenforced. It will survive and flourish only if democracies make human rights practical, a shared pursuit, and costly for others to violate. Australia, I came away believing, still has the standing to lead that effort.
tag: Asia human rights; Australia; Human Rights; Human Rights Watch

title: In Cambodia, Floating Houses Are Stuck Aground as Climate Change Takes Hold
description: Researchers are seeing a change in Cambodian weather patterns as climate change takes hold across the region.
text:
Siem Reap province, Cambodia — A 63-year-old woman watched her two grandchildren play on dry ground beneath her high-stilted house in mid-July.

By this time of the year, Pou village in Siem Reap province is normally flooded as the nearby Tonle Sap lake rises and expands with the monsoon. Stilted houses would be perched over the water, while floating houses drift on the bloated river.

When Sok Rina was young, the water would begin rising in June, flooding the riverbank and surrounding forests by July. The floodwaters would become rich with fish, supporting the livelihoods of villages on the water.

Recently, however, the Tonle Sap has been low, year after year.

Researchers are seeing a change in Cambodian weather patterns as climate change takes hold across the world. The traditional monsoon season in June and July appears to be weakening, even as intense easterly storms return in September and October.

At the same time as weather patterns are changing, more than 200 large dams are planned, completed, or under construction in the lower Mekong basin. Together, climate change and hydropower dams are restricting the flow of water into the Tonle Sap.

And without water, there’s no fish. In Siem Reap province, residents of Pou, Me Chrey and Chong Khneas villages say they are facing severe challenges to their survival.

Collapsing Fisheries

Cheim Oeurn, 40, caught only about one kilogram of fish one July morning. It was all small climbing perch and moonlight gourami, which have almost no market value.

The Sangkae river is too low for fish to spawn in the flooded forests around Tonle Sap, he said. Rising water temperatures in shallow areas also threaten to destroy fish eggs.

“If there is a lot of water, there will be more fish; as the water rises, fish will breed. Less water means fewer fish,” Cheim Oeurn said.

In the past, fishers in Pou village could earn 50,000 to 100,000 riel ($12.50 to $25) daily with a 50- to 60-kilogram catch. Today, they often return with nothing of value.

In Chong Khneas village, Choum Chreb said her son had caught exactly five fish after fishing from 4 a.m. on July 23.

“He hasn’t caught any in the past three days, and today’s five fish aren’t even enough to cover the cost of gasoline,” Choum Chreb said.

The family has lived and fished on the Tonle Sap for 25 years, and this life is all they have.

“We lack land to move to,” she said. “We just earn enough to survive on the water.”

The Tonle Sap is Southeast Asia’s largest freshwater lake, and vital to millions of livelihoods. It is connected to the Mekong River, and its flow famously reverses direction twice a year.

In the wet season, the Mekong rises and pushes water into the Tonle Sap. The lake expands and floods nearby forests – creating a unique ecosystem around the lake that supports fish spawning and local livelihoods. In the dry season, the lake drains back into a lowered Mekong River.

“The reversal is the key driver of the Mekong’s robust fisheries, making the Tonle Sap the largest inland fishery in the world,” said the Stimson Center’s Mekong Dam Monitor.

Two Factors

The center has observed stark changes to the region’s river systems, and this year is no different: The Tonle Sap’s reversal started about six weeks late, and the flow is much weaker than average for this time of year. The reverse flow was measured at 4 billion cubic meters, below the average of 11 billion.

Both climate change and hydropower developments have combined to disrupt Tonle Sap water levels and livelihoods.

For the past five years, June and July have had less rain than normal, said Stimson Center Southeast Asia program director Brian Eyler.

“It seems like the traditional monsoon pattern that builds at the beginning of the wet season is weakening in strength,” he said.

At the same time, some recent September and October storms had been “extremely intense,” he said, explaining that the Mekong basin’s wet season was made up of two weather patterns: the early monsoon and the later easterly storms that come from the Pacific Ocean.

Floating houses on the Tonle Sap lake in Cambodia. (Wikimedia Commons/LBM1948)

It’s during the early rains, however, that hydropower dams fill up their reservoirs. They produce electricity during the dry season by releasing stored-up water, and by the start of the wet season they are typically near-depleted.

“This all makes the expansion of the Tonle Sap Lake get off to a very weak start,” Eyler said.

This year was a case in point. “The Tonle Sap has hardly expanded and this will have a negative effect on fisheries. Just a few weeks ago, parts of the Mekong were recording all-time lows for that time of year.”

Both climate change and dam impacts play a role, but in the immediate term “there is opportunity to rethink the way upstream dams are operated,” he said, suggesting that dams could wait to fully fill up their reservoirs until late in the wet season when there is plenty of rain.

Data from the Mekong River Commission show that water levels on the Tonle Sap river in Prek Kdam, southeast of the lake, have been largely below the historical average during the early wet season for eight years in a row.

Damaged Livelihoods

In Siem Reap’s Me Chrey village, Pon Niem said her first daughter dropped out of school in grade 12 and has worked at a garment factory in Kampong Speu province since 2025. Her second son dropped out in grade 11 to start working at the same factory this year. They are now 21 and 19.

“They see the family’s hardships,” the 43-year-old said. “They told their two younger sisters to continue their school, not to worry.”

Preap Nakrei, 40, said her eldest daughter left school in grade eight to work in a restaurant in Siem Reap. Now 18, she works at a cigarette factory in Phnom Penh to help repay family debts.

While lower secondary school is available in the village, upper secondary students from ninth grade must relocate to the district center – a financial burden few families can afford.

“If we could earn 30,000 riel a day, we could support our children’s education,” she said, hoping her younger children will complete high school.

Declining catches have pushed many families into severe debt. Preap Nakrei’s family owes 10 million riel (about $2,500) to a private lender for fishing nets and 3 million riel ($750) to the microfinance institution AMK, requiring a monthly interest payment of 45,000 riel ($11.25).

“Under our contract, I was supposed to repay AMK 1.5 million in July, but I could not. I asked them to delay repayment until December, and they agreed,” she said.

Sorn Chavy, 28, a resident of Pou village, faces a similar struggle. Her family owes 2 million riel ($500) to microfinance institution Chamroeun and 3 million riel to AMK, while her husband struggles to catch fish.

In addition to microfinance loans, she owes a private lender approximately 17 million riel ($4,250) for fishing nets and fish-raising expenses. However, she has decided not to start raising fish yet because the water remains too low, which could kill the fish.

“It’s hard for us to move out of this area; I’m three months pregnant and my first son is just six years old,” Sorn Chavy said. “Since birth, we have known only fishing.”

A recent study by researchers from the Cambodia Development Resource Institute and Royal University of Phnom Penh observed wide-ranging impacts on communities around the Tonle Sap. The study highlighted a 50 percent drop in fish production between 2018 and 2020, from 291,260 to 144,635 tons, due to reduced water volumes and shorter flood durations.

“Fishing is no longer reliable, and fishing communities are shifting into farming by clearing the flooded forest areas,” the study said. Meanwhile, more young people are migrating to towns and overseas for employment.

It also noted physical changes in traditional floating villages: “Some floating communities are no longer floating.” Meanwhile, other communities that split their time on land and water “stay on land longer than on water throughout the year.”

Marks of Change

To reach Pou village, one travels down from the Puok district town along a red gravel road pocked with potholes, passing rice fields and dense forests.

The village reveals the changing climate at a glance: Traditional homes stand high on 5-meter wooden stilts marked by faint waterlines from past floods, but in mid-July the ground beneath them remained dry silt.

Along the Sangkae River, floating houses built on bamboo rafts and empty gasoline drums sat grounded on riverbanks, marooned above water levels that continue to arrive later and lower over time.

Sok Rina said her children – the parents of the grandchildren she kept an eye on – had moved away for work.

Her eldest son, 32, married in 2020 and moved with his wife to Sihanoukville last year. His wife works at a garment factory while he works at a plastic factory. Two other children moved to Sihanoukville for work in tourism, and another to Phnom Penh to work as a swiftlet nest cleaner.

“They dropped out of school because they witnessed our impoverished living conditions,” Sok Rina said. “They used to live with us, and fished, but they couldn’t earn a living. So they migrated for work.”

Living in the village was only getting harder. Last year, the area didn’t flood until August, and the floodwaters stayed just a few weeks until September.

“I’m not sure about this year,” she said.

This article was first published by the Mekong Independent and is reprinted under a Creative Commons license.

title: In India, Death Sentences Are Mostly the Result of Arbitrary Exercise of Judicial Power
description: Recently, a district judge awarded 23 death sentences in ten cases over a span of four months.
text:
Earlier this month, a judge in the northern Indian state of Uttar Pradesh hit the headlines for delivering 23 death sentences in just four months. Judge Ravi Kumar Diwakar’s 23rd death sentence involved a dowry death case where the man had burnt his wife over dowry demands. In his order, the judge made a grandiose claim that he would “prefer death than to be called a coward judge.” He alleged he was being targeted by “mafias, gangsters, criminals.”

Incidentally, Uttar Pradesh stands first in the country with regard to the number of death sentences being handed out.

Under Indian jurisprudence, only the “rarest of rare cases” justify the sentencing of a convict to death. However, Diwakar dispensed the death penalty rather freely, awarding 23 death sentences in just 10 cases. Alarmed by his propensity to award capital punishment, the more senior District Judge Virendra Kumar Singh transferred nearly 100 cases dealing with heinous crimes to his own court in August.

Diwakar’s verdicts drew public attention to the larger issue of capital punishment in India. While permitted only in the “rarest of rare” instances, the death penalty, in practice, is being awarded on the discretionary views of the judge.

Capital punishment is controversial and has triggered heated discussion in the past as well. While it is often welcomed by the public, especially in cases of brutal rape and murder, critics argue that the death penalty should not be allowed in a civilized society.

Under Indian law, when the death penalty is handed out by a lower court, it needs to be ratified or adjudicated by the higher court, including the Supreme Court. If the courts uphold the death sentence, the president of India has the power to decide on a mercy petition or clemency plea of the convict. The president can commute the death sentence to rigorous imprisonment, grant remission, or even pardon the convict.

Pranab Mukherjee, who was India’s president between 2012-2017, earned a reputation for being unsympathetic to mercy or clemency pleas. During his tenure, 34 mercy pleas came before him; he rejected 30 of them and commuted four to life imprisonment. Three executions were carried out while he was in office – that of 1993 Mumbai blast accused Yakub Memon, Parliament attack accused Afzal Guru and 26/11 Mumbai terrorist attack accused Ajmal Kasab.

Mukherjee was unlike any of his predecessors. President Pratibha Patil was the most lenient; she commuted 34 death sentences and rejected five mercy petitions. While President K.R. Narayanan, an erudite man, did not decide on any mercy plea, President Abdul Kalam, a missile scientist, decided on only two, commuting the death sentence in one case and rejecting the other. They chose to leave to their successors the difficult decision of sending a man to the gallows.

Statistics reveal a troubling reality. Indian trial courts have been meting out death sentences rather easily. In the majority of these cases, the punishment falls through when examined by higher courts.

According to the legal news portal, Law Beat, “364 wrongful convictions have been recorded in capital cases over the past decade.” Since 2023, the Supreme Court has not confirmed any death sentence, citing procedural errors and wrongful convictions by lower courts.

According to the Death Penalty in India Report 2000- 2015, of the 1,486 prisoners sentenced to death by trial courts, only 73 death sentences (5 percent) of the total were confirmed by higher courts. So, a whopping 95 percent of death sentences were thrown out by the higher courts.

Particularly shocking is the fact that over a quarter of those sentenced to death were actually innocent. Of the 1,486 individuals sentenced to death, as many as 443, i.e., 29 percent, were found by higher courts to be “not just undeserving of the death sentence but actually to be innocent of the crime for which they were being sent to the gallows.”

India’s criminal justice system is notorious for its slow delivery of justice. Those convicted spend years in jail, several on death row, before their appeals are finally decided, commuted, or acquitted. As of December 2025, approximately 574 individuals remained on death row, the highest figure this century.

Proponents of the death penalty have often argued that it deters people from committing brutal crimes. However, global human rights watchdogs like Amnesty International have reiterated that there is no evidence that capital punishment deters crime, including crimes against women like sexual assault.

Yet the clamor for the death penalty increases when heinous crimes, which evoke public outrage, occur. This was the case, for example, when “Nirbhaya,” a young woman, was brutally gang-raped in a moving bus in New Delhi in December 2012. She was thrown out on the streets with her entrails hanging out. When she subsequently died, the clamor for the accused to be hanged increased.

When sexual violence laws were reformed in 2013, the death penalty was included among the penalties for sexual assault. In cases of rape leading to the victim’s death or resulting in her being left in a “persistent vegetative state,” and rape by repeat offenders, the maximum sentence could be death. The rape laws also expanded the definition of rape and criminalized acts including stalking, voyeurism, and acid attacks.

These stringent punishments have not deterred rape. It is not the severity of punishment that deters crime but the certainty of conviction and punishment that could deter it.

Rights activists have argued that rather than knee-jerk reactions like awarding the death penalty, what is required is systemic reform of the criminal justice system, police reforms, better investigations, and access to justice. An analysis of the profile of convicts reveals that capital punishment impacts the poor and marginalized members of society more severely due to a lack of proper legal representation.

In 2019, Justice Kurian Joseph, while commuting a death sentence to life imprisonment, urged that the death penalty in India be reviewed. He noted that trial courts had been awarding it “arbitrarily and freakishly” under the influence of “emotionally charged public and media discourse.”

Under the Bharatiya Nyay Sanhita (formerly the Indian Penal Code), awarding the death penalty is the absolute exception, in the “rarest of rare” cases. Before awarding it, the court needs to ascertain why the alternative option of life imprisonment cannot be handed out instead. Also, as per the law, the judge must actively consider mitigating circumstances (such as the criminal’s age, mental health, and potential for rehabilitation/ reform) along with the aggravating severity of the crime.

Although there is no evidence that capital punishment deters crime, the Indian political class and society at large continue to demand and justify the death penalty.

Globally, countries are working toward abolishing capital punishment, but India refuses to abolish it. It is ironic that India prides itself on having a human rights-based criminal justice system where even the accused are not denied fundamental rights. Yet its judicial system continues to mete out an outdated and “inhumane punishment” of the death penalty.

title: In Taiwan, a Disaster Exercise Prepares for Conflict, Too
description: This year’s natural disaster drill sought to stress-test Taiwan against cascading, multisystem failures – with obvious implications for an invasion scenario as well as an earthquake.
text:
Taiwan’s National Disaster Medical Assistance Team (NDMAT) discuss triage in a tent with Ministry of National Defense field medical response team members in Taitung, Taiwan. Photo by Katie Sizemore.

In the seaside town of Taitung, four hours from Taipei by train, Taiwan’s premier national disaster preparedness exercise simulated a response to a 7.3 magnitude earthquake – layered with variables Taiwan could face in a conflict contingency. This year’s drill marked a critical operational shift, moving past standard disaster response to stress-test Taiwan against cascading, multisystem failures alongside expanded participation from regional and international partners.

The base scenario estimated damage to 43 bridges and nearly 1,800 buildings, along with 63 casualties. Search-and-rescue teams and fire departments from seven cities and counties in Taiwan conducted a full-scale mobilization southward, while everyone on Taiwan’s cellular network received mobile alerts testing the national alert system. What was once a routine annual drill has evolved into a vital benchmark for Taiwan’s ability to manage crises requiring a whole-of-society response and international assistance.

Since 2018, the “921” exercise has commemorated the devastating September 21, 1999, Chi Chi earthquake, but its scale, complexity, and visibility increase each year. The evolution of the 921 exercise reflects Taiwan’s shift toward unscripted, full-scale scenarios modeled on U.S. curriculum. What used to be a photo-ready display of capabilities is now a deliberate effort to integrate civil government officials, military field medical teams, the private sector, and NGOs into a unified command system responsible for coordinating life-saving rescues, medical treatment, sheltering, and long-term recovery.

Turkish and German search and rescue teams participate in a simulated Unified Command Center setup in Taitung, Taiwan during the 2026 921 earthquake exercise. Photo by Katie Sizemore.

Particularly notable is the Taiwanese government’s willingness to test unfamiliar concepts and navigate uncertainties in front of an international audience. The 921 exercise integrates international teams and observers, many of whom face similar natural – and geopolitical – threats. The active international participation marks a key distinction between this drill and Taiwan’s Urban Resilience exercise held in June. During this year’s 921 exercise, 180 international participants brought gear and equipment to the island, working alongside local teams for three days, including the exercise’s first overnight, 24/7 continuous operation.

A Japanese Disaster Medical Assistance Team (DMAT) coordinated with six Taiwanese DMATs, formed by local hospitals and supervised by the Ministry of Health and Welfare. In an adjacent tent, American and Taiwanese medical teams simulated joint field care.

Additionally, 100 international observers traveled to each exercise site to observe the capabilities on display. Beyond Taiwan’s warm hospitality during events like this, international partners get to visualize what a civilian-supported response might look like during conflict – and how they might see themselves in it.

Taiwan and Philippine search and rescue teams conduct drills at the Leji Bridge in Taitung, Taiwan. Photo by Katie Sizemore.

Taiwan’s Ministry of Interior aimed to establish and test a humanitarian assistance and disaster response (HADR) corridor during the 921 exercise, embedding regional allies directly into its civil resilience planning. Taiwan’s emergency responders practiced working together to salvage trapped vehicles from floodwaters in a riverbed and conducted field medical treatment alongside teams from Japan, the Philippines, and Turkiye. The exercise is also of great interest to Nordic partners like Finland, which sent firefighters to bring back lessons as they rebuild their own civil defense plans alongside a volatile neighbor.

Taiwan faces strong typhoons and regular earthquakes, requiring a professional and ready emergency response mechanism. Organizers have now begun to smartly layer these exercises with wartime injects – the scripted crisis events used to test responders. One drill simulated rescuing a downed foreign fighter pilot from the mountains, transporting him to a multinational field hospital, and then airlifting him to a Taiwan Coast Guard vessel. I watched on a livestream, powered by mobile communication units, as a stretcher was lowered onto the ship off the coast.

A Taiwan medevac team simulates transporting a downed foreign fighter pilot to a Taiwan Coast Guard Vessel in Taitung, Taiwan. Photo by Katie Sizemore.

Each September, the 921 exercise grows in scale and complexity as responsibility rotates among cities and counties. Familiarizing jurisdictions with this integration is essential preparation. Taiwan sits between two tectonic plates, the Philippine Sea Plate and the Eurasian Plate, and the train from Taipei to Taitung runs through the East Rift Valley. Taitung could easily be isolated in an extreme disaster caused by an earthquake, so it’s important to test local capability.

Beyond the natural disaster threat, China conducts continuous drills along the coastlines of Yilan County, where 921 took place in 2025, and Taitung County in the southeast. Equally serious for Taiwan’s preparation is practicing the mobilization of its resources and testing the HADR corridor with these potential, aggressive operations in mind.

Taiwan’s government also wants to be ready to assist its neighbors, as reinforced in President Lai Ching-te’s remarks closing the exercise.
tag: Taiwan 921 drill; Taiwan disaster prepardness; Taiwan natural disasters; Taiwan whole-of-society defense strategy

title: In Turkmenistan’s Data Desert, the Golden Age Is a Mirage
description: The IMF says Turkmenistan, in failing to provide key economic data, is in breach of its obligations.
text:
It was a short press release, published on a Friday afternoon and easily missed.

The International Monetary Fund’s executive board had considered a report on “Turkmenistan’s observance of its obligations… which requires member countries to provide data necessary for the IMF’s activities.”

Ashgabat, the board said, “has not provided key required data, including information on international reserve assets, official holdings of gold and foreign exchange, and a complete balance of payments.”

This non-provision, the statement continued, “could not be explained by a lack of capacity and therefore constitutes a breach of Turkmenistan’s obligations.” In six months, the board will consider again Turkmenistan’s progress, the statement said, noting that the provision of data helps the IMF support effective policy formation.

The IMF probably shouldn’t hold its proverbial breath.

“This is not something new,” Aynabat Yaylymova, executive director of the Progres Foundation told The Diplomat. “Concealing information is a key to a regime’s survival.”

The Progres Foundation works with Turkmen experts to monitor, research, and highlight human development in Turkmenistan in absence of reliable government data or adequate government attention.

Keen readers of the regular World Bank Global Economic Prospects reports will have noted that for years, footnotes touch on Turkmenistan’s exclusion from various data sets. In 2021, one such report noted: “Due to lack of reliable data of adequate quality, the World Bank is currently not publishing economic output, income, or growth data for Turkmenistan and República Bolivariana de Venezuela.”

A 2024 World Bank publication titled “Turkmenistan Economic Report” explained via a highlighted box buried at the end of the report that, “Turkmenistan provides limited trade data publications, compounded by concerns about the reliability of Turkmenistan’s official statistics.” The box went on to explain how the analysts triangulated trade statistics for the country via the mirrored data sets of 109 other countries, but noted that this method has its own failings – especially since Russia and Belarus no longer share trade data either.

In March 2018 the IMF issued a declaration of censure against Venezuela, in light of its failure to take action on a November 2017 warning that mirrors the notice issued last week to Turkmenistan. Since Venezuela was not, at the time, actively borrowing from the IMF the censure had little bite.

“I am not sure the IMF has leverage in this case since the government does not use its financial resources,” Yaylymova commented. “The government also does not care about its reputation.”

Ashgabat joined the IMF in 1992 but has engaged only marginally, never taking part in any assistance or borrowing programs. Doing so would undercut the myth the Turkmen government repeats ad nauseum: Turkmen are living in a golden age.

***

“Turkmenistan’s story since independence is the story of the government that operates with impunity and extreme opacity,” Yaylymova explained.

When The Diplomat asked why Turkmenistan is so recalcitrant with its data, Yaylymova said that, “Providing the IMF with a complete, verifiable balance of payments and official reserve data would force the government to expose exactly where the billions from the sales of natural gas are held, how they are managed, and how they are spent. This is in the context where citizens have never seen the state budget.”

Turkmenistan’s state news platform is named “Altyn Asyr” – “Golden Age” – and ostentatiously hopeful language pervades government statements, regardless of the actual reality of life in Turkmenistan.

“If the government provides the data requested by the IMF,” Yaylymova continued, “it will officially dismantle the autocratic regime’s domestic propaganda narrative and expose the true state of the economy to both its citizens, international community, and markets.”

According to the Turkmen government, the growth rate sits at 6.3 percent – around where it has been since 2015. Not even the COVID-19 pandemic dented Turkmenistan’s officially reported growth rate. But, according to Ashgabat, in Turkmenistan there was no COVID-19 pandemic.

“During COVID… Turkmens counted graves to understand the level of infection,” Yaylymova said, noting that there are always indirect ways of understanding reality in the absence of data.

“In economic mismanagement and grand corruption we should look at deeply neglected human potential and increased migration out of the country.”

Earlier this month, RFE/RL’s Turkmen Service, Radio Azatlyk, reported that young people who previously studied abroad were being prevented from leaving the country. This isn’t new either.

“It is crucial to understand the domestic context. Poverty is deepening in Turkmenistan,” Yaylymova told The Diplomat.

The Progres Foundation publishes a unique economic index, the Palaw Index, which tracks inflation via the ingredients of palaw, the national dish of Turkmenistan comprised of beef, oil, onions, carrots, and rice, known elsewhere as plov, osh, or pilaf. According to the April/June 2026 index, the average cost of making the dish in the capital city reached 91.4 Turkmen manat ($26.16), a 29.4 percent jump from the same period in 2025. The increase was driven primarily by a sharp rise in beef prices which the analysis attributes to “substantial livestock losses – particularly in the Ahal region – caused by drought, malnutrition, and disease.”

None of that was reported in Turkmen state media.

On September 14, however, one headline announced that “The National Leader of the Turkmen people, Chairman of the Halk Maslakhaty of Turkmenistan, Hero-Arkadag, got acquainted with the progress of the second stage of the new city and the developed projects,” in reference to Turkmenistan’s top leader, Gurbanguly Berdimehamedov – father of the current president, Serdar Berdimehamedov – and the bespoke smart city being built for an estimated $5 billion that bears his nickname, meaning “protector.”

***

Turkmenistan ranks fourth globally in terms of proven gas reserves, sitting between Qatar and Saudi Arabia. An estimated 90 percent of its gas exports go to China for unknown billions in revenue. But Turkmen citizens and international financial institutions alike don’t know exactly where the money goes.

“The public has no idea where the revenues from natural resources go,” Yaylymova told The Diplomat. “In an authoritarian and kleptocratic regime such as Turkmenistan data means accountability, it means that someone is going to keep you accountable by questioning your data, logic, and assumptions and what you do or you do not do.”

An absence of data is an absence of accountability. It “enables economic mismanagement, arbitrary and opaque rule,” Yaylymova said.

The IMF may lack leverage over Turkmenistan, but censure, Yaylymova said, is nevertheless long overdue.

“The government keeps exaggerating the growth rate while the population is plunging deeper into despair and poverty,” she stressed. It’s important, she concluded, for international organizations and Turkmenistan’s partners to “start naming the structural issues” directly and start “calling on the government publicly to meet its obligations.”

“No investment, no engagement should come without the government’s demonstrated capacity [for] accountability.”
tag: Gurbanguly Berdimuhamedov; Serdar Berdimuhamedov; Turkmenistan; Turkmenistan data; Turkmenistan economy

title: Indian Navy Augments Its Submarine Rescue Capability
description: Commissioned on August 31, INS Nipun significantly augments the Navy’s specialist diving, underwater intervention, salvage, and submarine rescue support capability.
text:
On August 31, India commissioned INS Nipun, the second dedicated Diving Support Vessel (DSV) that serves as the mothership for the two Deep Submergence Rescue Vehicles (DSRVs) in service. With this, the Indian Navy crossed a threshold in a critical operational capability – submarine rescue – that has a bearing not just for India but for the entire region.

Submarines are some of the most complex machines in existence and their operation is highly specialized. Submarine rescue takes that to another level and is a forte of a very small group of countries.

Indian Navy Chief Admiral Krishna Swaminathan’s remarks at the commissioning ceremony in Mumbai aptly encapsulate this. The Nipun significantly enhances the capacity to respond to a distressed submarine, whether of the Indian Navy or that of a partner navy, he said, adding that this capability would also enable India to support submarine rescue and emerge as the “preferred submarine rescue partner” in the region.

The Indian Navy signed a deal worth 193 million British pounds (around $217 million) with U.K.-based James Fischer Defense in 2016 under which it procured two DSRVs, a Launch and Recovery System (LARS), and a LARS-integrated decompression chamber. They were operationalized at Mumbai on India’s western seaboard at the end of 2018 and at Visakhapatnam on the eastern seaboard in early 2019. Concurrently, in September 2018, the navy signed a deal with state-owned Hindustan Shipyard Limited, located at Visakhapatnam, for the construction of the two DSVs, with the first vessel to be delivered in 36 months.

Until the DSVs were completed, INS Sabarmati of the Ship Building Corporation of India acted as the interim ship for both the vessels. This left a major operational void, as it meant more time, which is the most critical factor in the event of a submarine disaster in the ocean depths.

The two vessels were launched into water in September 2022, and the first, INS Nistar, was commissioned on July 18, 2025. The induction of INS Nipun now closes that loop, significantly augmenting the Indian Navy’s specialist diving, underwater intervention, salvage, and submarine rescue support capability.

So far, the Indian Navy operated an older diving support vessel, INS Nireekshak, with limited submarine rescue capabilities. In the backdrop of the capability gaps in the past, India had signed an agreement with the United States for utilizing the U.S. Navy’s global submarine rescue flyaway kit.

The Capability

Displacing 10,000 tons, measuring over 118 meters in length, and with an endurance of 60 days, the Nistar and the Nipun were purpose-built for deep-sea diving and underwater operations for inspection and intervention and to serve as mother ships to the DSRVs. Each DSV can accommodate 25 officers and 225 sailors.

Further, the expansive deep-sea diving systems with specialized diving complex, dynamic positioning capability, and associated life-support and medical facilities enable them to conduct sustained operations at sea, according to the Indian Navy. For this, they carry a 15-ton subsea crane, a diving bell, remotely operated vehicles (ROVs), side-scan sonar, compression chambers, and a self-propelled hyperbaric lifeboat. They can undertake deep-sea diving and salvage operations up to a depth of 300 meters.

The DSRVs, in turn, can go down to a maximum depth of 650 meters and rescue 14 people in one go. They also carry a ROV and, together with the side-scan sonar, can locate a submarine at depths of up to 1,000 meters. Once a submarine is successfully located, a sub-module of the system, the Submarine Rescue Vehicle, mates with the submarine to rescue trapped personnel. The same feature can also be utilized to provide emergency supplies to a submarine.

In 2018, before induction, the DSRV was put to trials, during which it set several “firsts” for the Indian Navy. It dived to a depth of 666 meters, the deepest submergence by a manned vessel in Indian waters, and carried out ROV operations at over 750 meters and side-scan sonar operations at over 650 meters.

Given the nature of its operation, the DSRV is designed for ease of transportation. For this purpose, the entire system has been divided into 24 components, which can be easily transported by road, sea, and air. In addition to being paired with the mothership, the system can also be airlifted by heavy transport aircraft like the IL-76 and C-17 operated by the Indian Air Force, enabling swift deployment across theaters.

The Criticality

Reaching a disaster-struck submarine in the narrow time window is critical and a DSRV offers that lifeline for any submarine-operating Navy. For the Indian Navy, the order of criticality multiplies manifold, given its aging submarine fleet.

The Indian Navy operates 16 conventional submarines – six Russian Kilo-class submarines and four German HDW-class submarines, both aging fleets long awaiting replacement, as well as six newer French Scorpene-class submarines. The newest Kilo-class sub is 26 years old, and the HDW class is over 30 years old. The fleets saw life extensions to keep them going amid delayed procurements. As stated by Captain Vikas Gautam, officer-in-charge of the Submarine Rescue Unit (East), during Exercise Milan in February this year, the true measure of any navy is not only its firepower, but “its resolve and capability to bring its men and women home safely.”

Regional Assistance and Cooperative Arrangements

The maritime domain with its wide expanse is inherently complex, and submarine rescue is a restricted capability both in terms of complexity and economics. In the last few years, India has signed several cooperation agreements with countries in the region for submarine rescue, offering its capabilities, which span bilateral arrangements and multilateral engagements.

The Indian Navy also actively cooperates with the International Submarine Escape and Rescue Liaison Office (ISMERLO), established by the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO), which coordinates international submarine rescue responses.

In a demonstration of India’s capabilities in real time, in April 2021, India dispatched the two DSRVs to locate the missing Indonesian submarine KRI Nanggala, one with the mother ship and another airlifted in a C-17. However, they were recalled midway as the disaster-stricken submarine was located in the ocean depths. All crew onboard were dead.

In January 2021, India and Singapore signed an implementing agreement on submarine rescue support and cooperation between the two navies. In September 2024, India and South Africa signed an implementing agreement that ensures the safety of the South African Navy’s submarine crew in times of distress or accident. In October 2025, during the visit of India’s Defense Minister Rajnath Singh to Canberra, India and Australia, which have transformed their maritime engagement over the last decade, signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) on submarine search and rescue cooperation. A month later, in November 2025, India and Vietnam signed an MoU on mutual submarine search and rescue support.

Submarine rescue has also become a major part of bilateral and multilateral exercises, underscoring its importance. In September 2025, the Indian Navy deployed the Nistar for Exercise Pacific Reach (XPR-25), hosted by the Singapore Navy in the South China Sea, which saw the participation of over 40 nations. During this event, the DSRV Tiger X carried out its maiden dive outside the Indian Ocean Region (IOR) and achieved mating with South Korea’s submarine Shin Dol-Seok.

The Indian Navy also regularly showcases its submarine rescue capabilities at multilateral engagements it hosts, like the Exercise Milan and Goa Maritime Conclave, offering assistance to countries in the region.

As the IOR and beyond see a proliferation of submarines, their search and rescue in times of crisis will be much needed. India is now well positioned to lend immediate assistance, expanding the ambit of humanitarian assistance and disaster relief efforts.

title: Indian, Pakistani Naval Vessels Collide in Arabian Sea, Prompting Diplomatic Tensions
description: This is the first time since the May 2025 military clashes that tension between the two sides has erupted into the open.
text:
On September 15, PNS Hunain, a Pakistan Navy corvette, collided with an Indian Navy warship, INS Kolkata, in the north Arabian Sea, 220 kilometers east of Oman. The following day, India’s Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) summoned Pakistan’s top-most diplomat in New Delhi, Chargé d’Affaires Saad Ahmad Warraich, to the foreign ministry to protest the “unacceptable and unprofessional conduct” of ​Pakistani naval units.

“While the incident, which took place in international waters, did not cause any major damage, the conduct of the Pakistani naval ship was in direct contravention of Article 10 of the Agreement between India and Pakistan on Advance Notice on Military Exercises, Manoeuvres and Troops Movements of April 1991,” the MEA said in a statement.

Article 10 of the 1991 Agreement, which Pakistan reportedly flouted, states that naval ships and submarines belonging to the two countries should not come within three nautical miles of each other while operating in international waters. The agreement was signed as a confidence-building measure to put in place mechanisms for India and Pakistan to inform each other about military exercises or troop movements to prevent a crisis from arising due to the misreading of the other side’s intentions. It came following heightened tension when India conducted Brass Tacks, a massive military exercise in the states of Punjab and Rajasthan along the India-Pakistan border, in January 1987.

Meanwhile, across the border in Pakistan, the response mirrored that of India, with Islamabad blaming India for the incident. “While the Pakistan Navy was undertaking its biennial exercise, SEASPARK-26, the Indian vessel carried out aggressive maneuvers in dangerously close proximity to a Pakistani naval ship, resulting in contact between the two vessels, ” the Pakistan Foreign Office said in a statement.

While the MEA described the incident as a collision, unnamed officials “aware of the matter” said that “it involved a close-in maneuvering by the Pakistani vessel, which approached the Indian warship at high speed and in an unsafe manner,” Hindustan Times reported. Another report in First Post, citing “sources within India’s defense establishment” claimed that “the Pakistani vessel shadowed the Indian ship, ignored multiple warnings and then made a high-speed crossing directly in front of the bow, resulting in the crash.”

A report in The Hindu, which cited sources in the defense ministry, said that INS Godavari was “on a routine surveillance mission,” when PNS Hunain “approached the Indian vessel while attempting to intercept or follow it. The close-range maneuver caused the two vessels to graze each other.” The Pakistani vessel “sustained damage in the collision and returned to the harbor. As for INS Godavari it “suffered minor damage and continued on its mission.”

Indian and Pakistani naval vessels last collided in 2011, when Pakistan’s PNS Babur “brushed past” INS Godavari in the Gulf of Aden, causing minor damage to the Indian warship’s helicopter safety net and triggering diplomatic tension.

Following the latest collision, both India and Pakistan summoned the charge d’affaires of the other side to lodge strong protests and have also asked their own charge d’affaires in the other country to register complaints with the government.

“Pakistan was advised to convey to the concerned Pakistani authorities, the need for all military units to observe due care and respect the provisions of the relevant agreements between the two sides in order to prevent any repeat of such incidents,” the MEA statement said.

Collisions involving naval warships are rare. This is the first instance of military tension between India and Pakistan erupting into the open since the four-day military clashes in May of last year.
