title: India’s Javelin Deal: The Unending Loop of Procurement
description: The deal is one of the earliest defense deals between India and the U.S. It is also the one that dragged on the longest.
text:
“BIG news! India plans to buy the battle-tested Javelin anti-tank system,” U.S. Ambassador to India Sergio Gor announced on X on August 28, as the Indian Army signed the letter of offer and acceptance (LOA) for the purchase of the missile system through the foreign military sales (FMS) route, also adding that it’s opening the door to “co-production possibilities.” For the Indian Army, it marks 16 years of ups and downs and the long lead time to fill a critical capability gap in anti-tank guided missiles (ATGM), even if only piecemeal.

The Javelin is a versatile, one-man-portable and platform-mounted fire-and-forget anti-tank precision weapon system that is capable of defeating all kinds of armor and fortified positions. It is in service with more than 25 countries, including the U.S. Army and the U.S. Marine Corps.

Following this, Lockheed announced a memorandum of understanding (MoU) between Tata Advanced Systems Limited (TASL) and the Javelin Joint Venture (JJV), a partnership between Raytheon and Lockheed Martin, for the “co-production of the Javelin All Up Round (AUR) in India.” The MoU will explore establishing a final assembly and integration facility for the Javelin AUR, along with component production capabilities, in India, Lockheed said in a statement.

While the specifics of the LOA haven’t been released yet, the U.S. Defense Security Cooperation Agency notification of November 2025 said that India would purchase 100 Javelin rounds and 25 launch units at an estimated cost of $45.7 million.

The entire saga can be viewed through two prisms: the deepening India-U.S. defense cooperation, and India’s rickety military modernization epitomized by the Javelin saga.

The Quest for ATGMs

The nearly 1.3 million-strong Indian Army started looking for a new generation fire-and-forget ATGM in the early 2000s to replace the Konkurs and Milan in service. The overall requirement is for over 40,000 missiles to equip the 382 infantry battalions and 44 mechanized regiments. However, as the indigenous effort by the Defense Research and Development Organization (DRDO) was delayed, the Army started looking for import options to partly fill the deficiency.

In August 2010, Defense Minister A. K. Antony informed the Indian parliament that his ministry proposed to issue a letter of request to the U.S. government for procurement of the Javelin ATGM along with transfer of technology under their FMS route. After the issue of the letter of request, further procurement-related necessary action will follow, he added.

The Army’s first experience with the Javelin came in 2009 during the bilateral exercise Yudh Abhyas, where the U.S. Army fielded it and so, was under consideration. While it was extensively tested, the deal didn’t move forward due to U.S. technology transfer limitations. This was when the Army moved to acquire the Spike ATGM manufactured by Rafael Advanced Defense Systems of Israel.

The Spike Journey

The Defense Acquisition Council, the highest decision-making body on procurements in the Ministry of Defense, accorded initial approval for procurement of Spike in 2009 for over 8,000 missiles and 300 launchers with technology transfer for their domestic manufacture, a deal worth $500 million. It was approved in October 2014, but the contract negotiations went into a loop over cost and technology transfer.

In fact, in 2016, in anticipation of the deal and to meet the domestic manufacturing requirement, Rafael set up a joint venture with Kalyani Group to manufacture sub-assemblies, with defense public sector firm Bharat Dynamics Limited (BDL) being the system integrator. The deal was cancelled in January 2018, just ahead of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s visit to India visit, as it was felt that indigenous development was making progress. However, the deal was revived soon after, by the end of 2018, for the purchase of 170 launchers, 4,500 missiles and 15 simulators. This too dragged on for a few years but never came to fruition due to questions being raised over the missile’s performance during the validation trials.

All through this, the Javelin was never fully out of the picture.

After the Balakot air strike in February 2019 in response to the Pulwama terrorist attack and simmering tensions with Pakistan, the Army procured a small number of Spike-LR (long-range) ATGMs under the emergency procurement route sanctioned by the MoD to fill critical deficiencies. The order was for 12 launchers and around 250 missiles. The Army repeated the order for the Spike-LR in 2020 in another round of Emergency Procurement sanctioned after the standoff with China along the disputed border at Ladakh.

Orders were capped at 3 billion Indian rupees, valued at $42 million in 2019. The Spike-LR, a 4th-gen missile with a range of up to 4 kilometers, is a different variant from the one originally tested. This remains the only new generation ATGM inducted by the Indian Army in the whole period.

Given the long and convoluted procurement process, emergency procurement has become the preferred way to fast-track critical procurements.

India-U.S. Defense Industrial Cooperation

The Javelin deal, which emerged out of growing India-U.S. bilateral defense and strategic cooperation, is one of the earliest defense deals between the two countries and the one that dragged on the longest.

Incidentally, the Javelin was also tested in 2024 along with Stryker infantry combat vehicles. However, the performance of the missile was sub-optimal as the lot provided for trials was dated. While the Stryker deal drags on, Operation Sindoor in 2025 reinforced the deficiencies.

The Javelin deal strengthens the U.S.-India Major Defense Partnership and also opens discussions on mutually beneficial co-production and additional opportunities to strengthen the defense industrial bases of both countries, a U.S. Embassy statement said. The local manufacture of assemblies and parts of the Javelin fits into the overall deepening of India’s presence in the supply chains of U.S. companies manufacturing components and sub-assemblies.

TASL itself is now a major player in this segment with a series of tie-ups with U.S. defense majors. For instance, with Boeing, it manufactures fuselages, secondary structures and vertical spar boxes for AH-64 Apache attack helicopters, and vertical fins for 737 aircraft; and fixed wings for Lockheed Martin’s C-130J and F-16 aircraft. Such integration of Indian industry over the last two decades has positioned the U.S. as India’s top defense export destination.

While India has significantly increased its defense procurements from the U.S., the effort for co-development and co-production has had no real success to date. The crown jewel of that effort, the license manufacture of the GE-414 jet engine domestically to power the Light Combat Aircraft-Mk2, has been stuck for several years now.

Though small as a system, the Javelin is high in its battlefield impact and will be a step forward in the joint endeavor. That this was announced amid the current turbulence in the India-U.S. relationship showcases the distance travelled by the two countries on the defense and strategic front.

Acquisition of the Javelin too is through the Emergency Procurement route that limits the numbers that can be purchased. The larger requirement of the Indian Army for ATGMs remains unfulfilled.

An ATGM is a critical battlefield weapon whose importance has grown manifold since its utility was underscored in Ukraine and other conflicts. While the Indian armed forces look at niche and emerging technologies, procurement of several other such basic but critical systems are caught in a loop. This merits immediate attention and action even as India keeps Operation Sindoor rolling and prepares for the next round of confrontation with Pakistan.

While development of the indigenous man-portable ATGM by DRDO has made progress, the timelines are still long. Coupled with evolving threats, this Javelin deal is likely the first of many.

title: India’s New Eye in the Sky: EOS-05 Satellite and What It Means for South Asia
user_author_name: Abdul Moiz Khan; Sher Ali Kakar
description: EOS-05 is a single satellite that is part of a broader initiative of India to strengthen its ISR capabilities.
text:
The Indian Space Research Organization (ISRO) recently launched a new surveillance satellite designated as EOS-05 into geosynchronous earth orbit (GEO). The launch was carried out with the GSLV-F17 rocket.

The satellite – launched on September 4 – is the first earth observation satellite deployed in GEO by India. The satellite will allow New Delhi to continuously observe the subcontinent from an altitude ranging between 34,903 km and 35,884 km. The chairman of ISRO, V. Narayanan, said that “EOS-05 will become India’s first dedicated imaging satellite from the geo orbit providing important strategic data for the country.”

The launch of the satellite is part of India’s long-term plan to strengthen its intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) capabilities. The satellite will provide India with the capability to persistently track military movements in the subcontinent – especially Pakistan’s naval warships, aircraft, strategic assets movements, and force mobilization during crisis time. A new eye in the sky is an important military asset for India and can increase its counterforce capabilities in the age of emerging and disruptive technologies.

India’s current space architecture consists of navigation, communication, ISR, and scientific satellites. For the purpose of communication, India has three dedicated military satellites – two of which are used by the Indian Navy and one by the Indian Air Force. Besides this, India has around 10 satellites that are dual-capable and can be used for military communication. The Indian navigation satellitessystem – known as Navigation with Indian Constellation (NavIC) – has three operational satellites, IRNSS-1B, IRNSS-1I , and NVS-01. However, for basic positioning service four satellites are required in orbit ; the next satellite NVS-03 would be launched soon. The Indian ISR architecture consists of the CROSAT series for Optical purposes, the RISAT and NISAR series for SAR purposes, and the EMISAT satellite for Electronic ISR. The newly launched EOS-05 would be India’s first ISR satellite that would give real-time persistent observation of the subcontinent.

In 2024, India’s Cabinet Committee on Security (CCS) approved the Space Based Surveillance Phase-III (SBS-III) program that aimed to deploy 52 defense satellites into low-earth orbit (LEO) and geostationary orbit for surveillance. Under this project, ISRO will deploy 21 satellites and the private sector will develop 31 satellites.

After the May 2025 crisis, there have been calls within the Indian strategic community to further strengthen Indian military capabilities in the space domain. For example, former Indian Chief of Defense Staff General Anil Chauhan, speaking at the Indian Defense Space Symposium (IDS) 2026, stressed the importance of military space based assets. He said, “If we fail in space, we will be forced to fight blind. However, if we dominate in space, we will fight with foresight.”

The statement reflects a transformation in India’s strategic thinking vis-à-vis the military utility of space. The evolving character of warfare necessitates strengthening ISR architecture for maintaining persistent surveillance of strategically important areas both during peacetime and crisis situations.

The newly launched EOS-05 satellite is particularly important as it adds to the persistent surveillance layer of India’s existing ISR architecture. Currently, India’s satellites are mainly in LEO, where they provide high-resolution imagery but have limitations because of rapid movement across the earth’s surface. EOS-05 being in geosynchronous orbit will provide prolonged observation of the subcontinent. This capability will strengthen India’s precision-strike capacity, as precision-strike missiles not only depend on range and accuracy but also timely information regarding the location of targets. Thus, in the broader sensor-to-shooter chain of network-centric warfare, space-based surveillance would play an important role.

Moreover, persistent eyes in the sky can also strengthen India’s counterforce capabilities for both conventional and strategic purposes. For Pakistan, the implications of India strengthening ISR architecture and enhanced counterforce capabilities are direct. A persistent Indian eye in the sky would give its tri-services a near real-time picture of Pakistani naval deployments in the Arabian Sea, aircraft movements, and the dispersal of mobile missile launchers. As the survivability of mobile systems rests largely on their concealment, continuous wide-area surveillance, combined with high-resolution follow-up, shortens the time between detecting a target and striking it. India’s growing arsenal of long-range precision-strike missiles may become far more threatening with an added eye in space.

Moreover, there are also benefits to India of the new satellite system for defensive purposes. It can also help India be better prepared for a counterstrike by Pakistan, especially with an advanced missile defense system. Having persistent capability to monitor movements of Pakistan’s troops, India can be more prepared to defend itself.

However, this can have implications for South Asian deterrence dynamics. Faster detection, enhanced targeting information, and better precision-strike capabilities would lead to a compression of decision-making timelines during crisis. Because of territorial contiguity between India and Pakistan, decision-making timelines are already very short. Thus, increasing vulnerability of strategic assets to detection can induce Pakistan to early dispersal, mobilization, and further concealment of its military assets. This can also create a “use-it-or-lose-it dilemma” and further increases the risks of miscalculation and inadvertent escalation. Thus, enhanced space-based ISR capabilities can help in increasing situational awareness but would present new challenges for crisis stability and escalation management in South Asia.

In conclusion, EOS-05 is a single satellite that is part of a broader initiative of India to strengthen its ISR capabilities under the SBS-III program. However, its launching points toward an Indian strategic shift from periodic snapshots to persistent watch, and this enhancement of capability can have implications on how the next crisis between India and Pakistan will unfold. Islamabad has to further strengthen survivability of its conventional and strategic assets through concealment, deception, and mobility practices.

title: India’s Semiconductor Journey: Old Designer, New Producer
description: India already has the design talent; what it needs is to turn this talent into Indian-owned companies, and to build the supplier base its fabs lack.
text:
The fifth edition of SEMICON India closed on September 19 in New Delhi, after featuring a massive scale of over 600 exhibitors and 300 international companies across 52 countries. Themed “Silicon to Systems: Building the Ecosystem,” the exhibition-cum-conference served two objectives. For industry, it showcased expansion in India’s indigenous technology, ranging from high-performance computing and domestic processor design to system-on-chip design automation tools. On the policy front, the platform highlighted the evolution of India’s semiconductor ecosystem, stressing its expanding capabilities and role in the global semiconductor landscape.

Semicon 2.0, the second phase of the India Semiconductor Mission (ISM), was approved in July 2026 with an announced outlay of around $13 billion. The mission pitches India as a trusted and reliable partner in the global semiconductor value chain. India’s Electronics and IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw described the new phase as moving “from demonstrating intent to executing projects at scale.” With increasing participation from global stakeholders, India is turning its ambitions into a credible reality.

India, an old designer in the semiconductor ecosystem, is becoming a new producer. ISM 2.0’s progress is to be measured by two key strengths: the intellectual property created by India’s talent, and the inputs its factories consume.

India’s semiconductor journey is not a rags-to-riches developing country story. India was a capable and serious player in the industry early on. Back in the 1980s, it had a considerable semiconductor push, with only a thin gap between India and the latest semiconductor manufacturing technologies available globally. Unfortunately, India’s chip industry lost its momentum after a devastating 1989 fire at the state-run Semiconductor Complex Limited in Mohali. Then, after the 1991 economic liberalization, the zeal for at-home manufacturing diminished. Chips could be imported from abroad for less money, while Indian fabs faced thin subsidies, bureaucratic bottlenecks, and inadequate infrastructure.

Although manufacturing became a lost cause, what India tremendously excelled in was chip design. Design is the most intellectually demanding and value-dense task of the supply chain, and India hosts around 20 percent of the world’s chip design talent working out of its Global Capability Centers (GCCs). The Indian tech cities of Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Noida, and Pune harbor massive engineering talent providing R&D for firms like Intel, Qualcomm, Texas Instruments, and NXP. This part of the supply chain existed and thrived in India even before the ISM policy and rebranding.

No matter how impressive it sounds, domestic capabilities in designing chips for multinational companies and filing patents for foreign parent firms is one thing. Success in domestic manufacturing and design ownership is another.

ISM 2.0 targets the ownership gap by funding full-stack Indian semiconductor IP, startups, and deployment-linked design incentives. To ensure the IP claims, the policy conditions that the strategically important chip designs supported under the scheme will be co-owned by a state agency and remain in the country. However, co-ownership of IP tends to complicate licensing, acquisitions, and the venture funding that fabless startups need to scale. How this debatable condition pans out will determine whether India’s design talent concretizes into Indian companies.

ISM 1.0 was applauded for meeting its objectives early, by approving 12 manufacturing projects, including nine packaging units, with India’s first commercial fab under construction. Despite the achievements, India still imports more than 90 percent of its chipmaking equipment. To fill this gap and develop an ecosystem, ISM 2.0 offers fiscal support to producers of semiconductor equipment, chemicals, gases, and raw materials.

There is also a geoeconomic angle here that weighs as heavily as the domestic ownership argument. With the United States, the European Union, Japan, and South Korea all de-risking by diversifying supply chains away from geographical concentration in Taiwan and exposure to China, global players like Micron and Applied Materials are investing in India. They see India as a politically safe node in the supply chain network. Analysts have argued for strengthening chip cooperation between Japan, South Korea, and India, using complementary strengths in fabrication, market size, and labor power, to balance out the United States’ use of tariffs as geopolitical leverage.

The risk-diversification-minded friend-shoring might benefit India as long as the China-U.S. tensions persist. While this motivation could weaken if the tension eases, that shows no signs of happening in the near future. Plus, India is not in a zero-sum game; every plant and supply facility built today strengthens its domestic base irrespective of the geoeconomic shifts of tomorrow.

The challenge India now faces is beyond the capital-allocation problem, where the government offers subsidies and willing chipmakers strike the deal. The task is to build a domestic base of semiconductor-grade equipment and specialty chemical suppliers, which requires tacit knowledge, iterative supplier relationships, and long-term capital, complemented by sustained state support, not just a single funding cycle. This is how Taiwan, South Korea, and Japan built up their chip industries.

India already has the design talent; what it needs is to turn this talent into Indian-owned companies, and to build the supplier base its fabs lack. Amidst global de-risking and domestic ambitions, the real test of ISM 2.0 lies in India’s success in increasing Indian IP ownership and increasing the share of fabs’ inputs made in India. If both rise, India’s chip story will be the output of its full ownership endeavors, and not a byproduct of other countries’ de-risking.

title: India’s Sheikh Hasina Dilemma
description: New Delhi’s difficult decision serves as a masterclass in how personal diplomacy can trap a major power.
text:
The mass street uprising that overthrew Bangladesh’s long-serving prime minister, Sheikh Hasina, in August 2024 did more than just reset the politics of a nation. It completely broke the security architecture of eastern South Asia. For 15 years, India’s foreign policy in its immediate neighborhood relied on a single, unwavering rule: keep Hasina stable, and India’s eastern border remains secure.

Today, that strategy has brought about a major crisis. Hasina is living in exile on Indian soil, while a newly elected government led by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman and the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) runs Dhaka. A Bangladeshi court has convicted Hasina in absentia for crimes against humanity and sentenced her to death, leading Dhaka to officially demand her extradition.

This situation creates a complex challenge for New Delhi, known as the “Hasina dilemma.” It is a problem that cannot be solved simply by picking a side. Instead, it serves as a masterclass in how personal diplomacy can trap a major power, leaving India with difficult arguments to balance as it navigates this regional crisis.

India’s dilemma is rooted in a fundamental rule of global statecraft: credibility. For over a decade, Hasina risked her own domestic popularity to fulfil India’s core national security demands. Her government cracked down heavily on anti-India insurgent groups that used to hide in Bangladesh, arresting their leaders and handing them over to New Delhi. She opened up crucial transit routes, allowing Indian cargo ships and trucks to cut through Bangladesh to reach India’s landlocked northeastern states.

If India gives in to Dhaka’s demands and extradites Hasina to face a death sentence, it sends a dangerous signal to other neighbors like Bhutan, Nepal, and Sri Lanka: India will abandon its closest partners if the political winds change.

However, keeping Hasina protected inside India comes at an equally high cost. It provides permanent fuel for anti-India sentiment within Bangladesh’s civil society. The longer India acts as her shield, the easier it is for the BNP government to label New Delhi as an enemy of Bangladesh’s democracy. This anger puts India’s vital trade links and transit corridors at immediate risk of being shut down by a hostile public.

The strain on the relationship is no longer just quiet, back-channel friction; it has broken out into visible diplomatic boycotts. Rahman’s recent decision to skip the high-profile BRICS Summit hosted by India in New Delhi served as a clear example of this shift.

Dhaka viewed the invitation to the summit – extended to Rahman as the chair of a regional group (BIMSTEC) rather than as a direct, standalone invite to the premier – as a deliberate diplomatic snub by India. In retaliation, Rahman refused to travel to New Delhi altogether.

Instead, Rahman deliberately focused his diplomatic efforts elsewhere: a high-profile trip to the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), where he held a sideline meeting with the Pakistani leadership. At the same time, Rahman’s administration deepened talks with Beijing over major infrastructure loans.

By refusing a standalone visit to New Delhi, Rahman is sending a clear message: The days of Bangladesh automatically aligning with India’s foreign policy goals are over. Dhaka is demonstrating that it is fully willing to use its strategic geography to balance India’s influence, using closer ties with Islamabad and Beijing as leverage to show that Bangladesh is no longer dependent on New Delhi’s approval.

The Hasina Dilemma serves as a systemic warning to foreign policy planners worldwide: never mistake a single political leader for an entire country.

For 15 years, India’s Ministry of External Affairs operated under the assumption that keeping Hasina happy was equivalent to keeping Bangladesh stable. New Delhi looked the other way during consecutive, highly controversial Bangladeshi elections, prioritizing immediate border security over the growing domestic anger building up against her regime.

By tying its national interests so tightly to one person, India failed to build deep institutional relationships with Bangladesh’s opposition parties, its student movements, and its wider civil society.

Now that Hasina has fallen, India faces a significant penalty for this policy. The new leadership in Dhaka views almost every regular, technical bilateral issue – from regular border management to daily electricity grid sharing – through a lens of deep suspicion. Because India did not engage with the broader political spectrum when it had the chance, it must now build diplomatic capital from scratch with a suspicious administration, all while dealing with the political liability of hosting the former leader.

The relationship between India and Bangladesh cannot remain frozen in this defensive stance forever. Bangladesh relies heavily on India for daily essential food imports, medical tourism, and electricity. Conversely, India requires a cooperative Dhaka to ensure its northeastern states do not become cut off or vulnerable to security threats.

Signs of a realistic compromise are slowly beginning to show. Recognizing the danger of a complete breakdown in relations, India’s diplomats have adopted a quiet, disciplined approach, consistently stating their desire for a “constructive and forward-looking relations” with the new government. This back-channel diplomacy has successfully defused the initial freeze, setting up an official state visit for Rahman to New Delhi in late November or early December 2026.

To make this upcoming visit a success and move past the crisis, both nations must cooperate on a silent, two-part strategy.

First, find a third country willing to provide permanent asylum to Sheikh Hasina. India must quietly work to relocate Hasina to a secure country outside South Asia, such as in the Middle East or parts of Europe. This move would allow Dhaka to claim a political victory to its domestic voters while sparing India the immense loss of face that would come from direct extradition.

Second, India and Bangladesh must shift to transactional institutionalism. Both capitals must agree to treat critical issues – like the upcoming December 2026 Ganga Water Sharing Treaty deadline – as technical, non-negotiable economic necessities rather than emotional political weapons.

The Hasina Dilemma proves that in modern geopolitics, yesterday’s absolute stability can easily become tomorrow’s greatest strategic trap. Bangladesh-India relations will likely never return to the close, personal alliance of the past decade. The relationship has permanently shifted into a cooler, more transactional reality.

Even so, if both New Delhi and Dhaka can successfully separate their internal political speeches from their shared geographic realities, they can prevent the presence of a single deposed leader from turning a temporary diplomatic crisis into a long-term regional disaster.
tag: Bangladesh-India relations; Hasina in India; India and Sheikh Hasina; Sheikh Hasina extradition; Tarique Rahman's India visit

title: Indonesia Finally Has Its Aircraft Carrier. Now Comes the Hard Part.
description: Following a controversial acquisition, the most pressing question is whether and how Indonesia can convert the vessel into a viable military asset.
text:
Last year, reports surfaced that Indonesia was considering acquiring an aircraft carrier for the first time in its history. This prompted a heated debate over whether Indonesia truly needed an aircraft carrier. In an article published in The Diplomat, I argued that Indonesia didn’t need such an acquisition, at least for the time being, for a variety of reasons. The arrival of the KRI Sriwijaya, as the new vessel is known, thus marks the end of one discussion and the start of another. The key question now is whether Indonesia can turn the ship into a sustainable military capability.

On September 18, the aircraft carrier, formerly known as ITS Giuseppe Garibaldi, arrived at Tanjung Priok Port in Jakarta. The ship was personally welcomed to port by the minister of defense, the commander of the Indonesian National Armed Forces, and the chief of naval staff. A formal handover from the Italian Navy to the Indonesian Navy took place on September 24, at which the carrier was reflagged and christened with its new name,

The name chosen by the Indonesian government has important symbolic importance. Sriwijaya was a strong monarchy and a respected naval power in Sumatra from the 7th to the 13th centuries.

However, with the ship’s arrival, the most important question is whether and how Indonesia can convert the ship into a viable military asset?

A Ship Doesn’t Equal Capabilities

Aircraft carriers are often associated with naval superiority. Their ability to carry and operate aircraft or helicopters from the sea provides flexibility in projecting power, extending a navy’s range of operations, while also offering strategic options that do not entirely depend on land-based airfields. Moreover, the possession of an aircraft carrier with its various strategic values also brings prestige.

However, an aircraft carrier is not an arms technology that can produce strategic effects independently. Like other conventional weapon technologies, the effectiveness of an aircraft carrier heavily relies on the supporting ecosystem that enables it to operate sustainably and safely. In general, aircraft carriers never sail independently. In operation, the aircraft carrier will be part of a carrier strike group (CSG), which usually consists of an aircraft carrier, a guided missile cruiser, anti-aircraft warships, and anti-submarine destroyers or frigates. In carrying out its operations, the aircraft carrier is also often escorted by attack submarines.

The ITS Giuseppe Garibaldi was always escorted by other warships while still flying the Italian flag. For example, during the Passing Exercise in the Mediterranean Sea in 2020, Garibaldi was accompanied by at least two multirole frigates and one supply ship.

In a CSG, each element has a complementary function, ranging from air defense, anti-submarine warfare, protection of the aircraft carrier, logistics, to command and control. Therefore, the capabilities produced by the CSG are the result of the integration of various platforms, not merely a consequence of the presence of an aircraft carrier itself.

In the context of Indonesia, the issue of the availability of escort and support fleets for aircraft carrier operations becomes is a very important issue. Indonesia indeed now has its long-awaited carrier, but still lacks surface warships to form a CSG as commonly found in the United States or French navies. Referring to the Laboratorium Indonesia 2045 database, Indonesia still lacks 12 frigates and seven fast missile boats to fulfil the government’s Archipelagic Trident Shield defense posture goals. The same goes for the submarine fleet. Indonesia is recorded to still be short of at least eight submarines.

A Carrier For Disaster Operations

The government and the Indonesian National Armed Forces (TNI) have indeed stated on several occasions that the presence of KRI Sriwijaya is not intended for expeditionary combat missions. They argue that the aircraft carrier will instead be prioritized for military operations other than war, specifically humanitarian assistance and disaster relief (HADR). For instance, once operational, the government stated that KRI Sriwijaya would join other TNI forces to assist in handling the ongoing forest fires in Kalimantan. In addition to HADR missions, the Indonesian Navy chief of staff has said that the carrier will be used for defense diplomacy activities, such as port visits.

At first glance, the government’s and TNI’s statement to prioritize HADR missions and defense diplomacy for KRI Sriwijaya sounds rational. Besides the fact that Indonesia’s military posture does not allow for offensive operations, this statement is also expected to prevent diplomatic tensions with other countries, especially in the region.

However, this again raises the question of whether Indonesia truly requires an aircraft carrier. HADR can be a relevant mission for KRI Sriwijaya, but the relevance of a mission does not automatically prove that the chosen platform is the most effective way to achieve that capability. To ensure that KRI Sriwijaya can fulfill its role, Indonesia must still build the right ecosystem around it. For example, if it is intended for HADR missions on land, then Indonesia must ensure the availability of adequate transport helicopters. If Indonesia does not invest in acquiring a sufficient number of transport helicopters, then the KRI Sriwijaya will only become a sitting duck in the middle of the Nusantara sea when a disaster occurs on land.

In other words, if Sriwijaya is to be used for HADR missions, the measure of its success should not stop at the ship’s ability to carry helicopters to disaster areas. A more important question is whether the entire ecosystem built around the ship produces HADR capabilities that are significantly higher than the simpler and more cost-effective alternatives. At this point, Indonesia needs to realistically define the capabilities that it actually wants to derive from Sriwijaya so that it can then build the appropriate ecosystem around it.

title: Indonesia Replaces Finance Minister Amid Growing Investor Skepticism
description: The appointment of Suahasil Nazara, who has served as deputy finance minister since 2019, is intended to calm investors worried about Jakarta's fiscal profligacy.
text:
Indonesia’s President Prabowo Subianto has fired and replaced his finance minister, Purbaya Yudhi Sadewa, just over a year after his appointment.

Suahasil Nazara, 55, who has served as deputy finance minister since 2019, was yesterday sworn in as Purbaya’s replacement.

The government did not say why Purbaya was removed, but his year in the post has been marked by ructions in the Indonesian economy, including a sharp depreciation of the rupiah and growing investor skepticism.

After being sworn-in yesterday afternoon, Suahasil told the press that he had only learned about his appointment in the morning.

“This is, of course, an expression of the trust placed in me by the president and the country. I am grateful for that trust, and I hope I can carry out the responsibility entrusted to me by the president,” Suahasil said, as per the Jakarta Globe.

He added that Prabowo had instructed him to safeguard “the health and credibility” of the state budget.

The replacement of the finance minister comes after a turbulent year at the top echelons of Indonesia’s major economic institutions. In late July, Perry Warjiyo, the governor of Bank Indonesia, the country’s central bank, stepped down, two years before the expiry of his current term as BI governor.

Purbaya was appointed finance minister last September, after the resignation of Sri Mulyani Indrawati, who had served in the post under three presidents. While Sri Mulyani initially agreed to serve in the role under Prabowo after he took office in October 2024, she eventually was forced out, reportedly due to differences between her conservative economic approach and Prabowo’s fiscally expansive economic agenda. The Indonesian president has set an ambitious goal of 8 percent annual GDP growth for the rest of his term, and he introduced a number of high-spending populist policies, including a multibillion-dollar free meal program, that have widened the fiscal deficit.

The removal of Sri Mulyani unsettled investors who were already unsure about Indonesia’s economic trajectory under Prabowo. The year since her departure has only compounded these concerns. In March, both Moody’s and Fitch announced ratings outlook downgrades for Indonesia, with the latter citing the “increasing ⁠policy uncertainty and erosion of Indonesia’s policy mix consistency and credibility” and the “growing centralization of policymaking authority.”

This came shortly after the global index provider MSCI threatened to downgrade Indonesia to “frontier market” status due to a number of transparency concerns in its stock market, including the high concentration of ownership in certain companies and the limited “free float” of shares. MSCI will announce its verdict in November.

At the same time, the rupiah has fallen to record lows this year, passing the psychological threshold of 18,000 rupiah to the U.S. dollar in June. A spike in ​the fuel subsidy budget following the rise in global crude prices has added to the deficit and pushed it toward its legally mandated ceiling of 3 percent of GDP.

Amid these various challenges, Purbaya’s tendency to veer off script – Channel News Asia described him yesterday as “brash and unfiltered” – has not helped calm investor sentiment. In April, Purbaya courted international controversy when he half-jokingly floated the idea of imposing a levy on ships passing through the Malacca Strait, describing it as a possible way that Indonesia could leverage its proximity to a key artery of global trade. The Foreign Ministry was subsequently forced to walk back his comments.

While the removal of Sri Mulyani was intended to align the Ministry of Finance with Prabowo’s economic goals, the cashiering of Purbaya appears to be aimed more at outside constituencies. According to the Financial Times, Suahasil “is seen as a technocrat and has extensive experience in fiscal policymaking, having previously led the country’s fiscal policy agency for more than three years.”

Reuters described the move as an attempt “to win back investor confidence amid long-festering concerns about policymaking and fiscal profligacy.” Richard Borsuk of Singapore’s S. Rajaratnam School of International ​Studies told the news agency that Suahasil’s appointment was a “good move.” He said, “The market should like it and rating agencies would already know and like Nazara.”

Speaking yesterday, Suahasil said that he would ensure that the country’s fiscal deficit would be kept under the legal ceiling of 3 percent. “This is just a continuation, not a change… We will continue to manage the state’s finances in a better way,” he said.

title: Indonesian Parliamentary Committee Debates Changes to Fiscal Deficit Limit
description: Some lawmakers say that the current administration should have the right to a 3 percent ceiling in order to support its expansive economic agenda.
text:
Indonesian lawmakers have begun debating potential changes to the country’s fiscal deficit ceiling, with several ‌lawmakers arguing yesterday that President Prabowo Subianto’s administration should have the right to exceed the current limit in order to fund its ambitious welfare policies.

During a public hearing in Jakarta yesterday, the House of Representatives’ Commission XI debated a series of revisions of the State Finance Law. Passed in the wake of the Asian financial crisis of 1997-1998, the law sets a maximum budget deficit of 3 percent of gross domestic product and limits government debt to 60 percent of GDP.

Mukhamad Misbakhun, chairman of the House of Representatives’ Commission XI, told the hearing that the deficit limit should not necessarily be treated as a rigid annual threshold if the government needs additional fiscal space to support economic growth.

“Is 3% really ‘sacred’?” said Mukhamad, according to a report in the Jakarta Globe.

Misbakhun, who is also a lawmaker of the Golkar Party, a member of Prabowo’s expansive coalition, proposed that the law be revised to establish clear conditions under which a larger deficit could be permitted, such as when tax revenue is weak, or state energy subsidies rise due to a spike in global energy prices – as happened in Indonesia after the outbreak of the U.S.-Israel-Iran war earlier this year.

“We have the momentum to get out of the middle-income trap, ​take 233 million people out of middle income and head to high income,” Misbakhun said, according to Reuters. “That needs growth expansion. How ‌are ⁠we going to expand growth if we lock ourselves and always talk about 3 percent?”

Mohamad Hekal, deputy head of the committee and a member of Prabowo’s party Gerindra, agreed that changes to the budget deficit ceiling should be discussed.

While a deputy finance minister said yesterday that the government is committed to keeping the 3 percent ceiling in place, the ongoing parliamentary debates are likely to be watched closely by institutional investors.

The State Finance Law was passed in 2003, as Indonesia was pulling itself up from the economic rubble of the Asian financial crisis, the political reverberations of which brought down the three-decade-long reign of President Suharto.

As one scholar noted at the time, the law marked “a major step forward in Indonesia’s drive to establish a sound system of public finance management and realize good governance.” More importantly, perhaps, the law was intended to reassure foreign investors that the country would maintain a disciplined fiscal policy after the chaos and corruption of the late Suharto years.

The fiscal deficit rule has been largely unquestioned by Indonesian governments in the two decades since, but has come under scrutiny since Prabowo took office in October 2024. Shortly before his inauguration, reports emerged that the former general was exploring ways to raise the fiscal deficit and debt-to-GDP ratio ceilings in order to fund his ambitious policy agenda. This included a multibillion-dollar free lunch program, a broad defense modernization plan, and an ambitious target of 8 percent annual GDP growth across his five-year term.

The suggestion that Indonesia was preparing to loosen, or even do away with, these financial safeguards unsettled markets, as did Prabowo’s bull-headed and unilateral approach to economic management. In March, both Moody’s and Fitch announced ratings outlook downgrades for Indonesia, with the latter citing the “increasing ⁠policy uncertainty and erosion of Indonesia’s policy mix consistency and credibility” and the “growing centralization of policymaking authority.”

This has contributed to a high turnover of personnel atop Indonesia’s main economic policymaking institutions. This week, Prabowo fired his finance minister, Purbaya Yudhi Sadewa, just over a year after his appointment, and replaced him with his deputy. Purbaya himself was appointed after the removal of Sri Mulyani Indrawati, who had served as finance minister under three presidents, over disagreements about the direction of economic policymaking under Prabowo. July also saw the resignation of Perry Warjiyo, the governor of Bank Indonesia.

“If the deficit ceiling is indeed raised from the current 3 percent of GDP, a potential positive impact would be greater flexibility in financing government programs,” the local brokerage Phintraco Sekuritas said, according to the Jakarta Globe. At the same time, this could also increase government debt and affect the absorption of government securities and corporate bonds issued by private companies.

“Furthermore, global investors and international rating agencies could perceive Indonesia’s fiscal discipline as weakening, potentially triggering credit rating downgrades, capital outflows and rupiah depreciation,” Phintraco Sekuritas added.

However, not all members of the Commission agreed that the deficit limits should be tampered with. Harris Turino, a lawmaker from the Indonesian Democratic Party of Struggle, the only political party in parliament that is not a member of Prabowo’s coalition, said that it was important to keep the deficit ​ceiling in place.

“If we are unable to ⁠discipline ourselves, including in maintaining the 3 percent deficit limit, the market will eventually discipline us,” he told Reuters.

title: Is BRICS Actually Benefiting India?
description: As India prepares to host the group's summit, what does it want from BRICS? And what is Delhi actually getting from the group?
text:
All eyes are on India right now. From September 12 to 13, presidents and prime ministers from Brazil, China, South Africa, Egypt, Indonesia, Russia, and more will converge on New Delhi for the 18th BRICS summit.

It’s India’s fourth time hosting BRICS, but leading the group today is a diplomatic minefield. Barely two months after Delhi took over as chair, the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran, a BRICS member. Tehran then retaliated against the UAE and Saudi Arabia – also BRICS members. Now, India has to sit all three in the same room.

The U.S.-Iran war made it impossible to ignore the serious conflicts within BRICS. In a major diplomatic fail, the BRICS foreign ministers’ meeting in May, also hosted by India, ended without a joint statement. The group’s members just couldn’t agree on how to approach the crisis in West Asia.

Some worry that the upcoming BRICS summit will also end without a joint statement. That would be a huge embarrassment for the host, India – and something Delhi is keen to avoid.

In 2021, the last time India hosted the annual summit, BRICS was just five countries, the ones that form its name: Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa.

Today, it’s an unwieldy 11-member bloc – or 10, depending on whether Saudi Arabia ever formally confirms it joined. Reaching a consensus was already tough when it was just India and China at odds within the group; now, BRICS includes rivals actively shooting at each other.

What does India get out of BRICS? And are the benefits worth the growing headache?

title: Is Indonesia’s 100 GW Solar Plan Realistic?
description: Whether or not the goal is achievable, it sends a strong signal that Jakarta is serious about putting more resources toward clean energy.
text:
Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto has set an extremely ambitious target of building 100 GW of solar capacity by 2029. Naturally, many people are wondering if this a realistic goal. I’ll spare you the suspense. The answer is no. But it does send a strong signal that the government is serious about putting more resources toward cleaner energy.

People often look at Indonesia’s energy sector, dominated by coal and other fossil fuels, and the extremely slow progress on renewables to date, and conclude that clean energy is a non-starter. I don’t agree. The government has been signaling for some time that it is willing to pivot toward clean energy. The catch is that it wants to do so on its own terms, without simply opening Indonesia up as a market for private developers and investors where the state-owned utility PLN ends up on the hook for expensive purchase agreements. This, in my estimation, was the major flaw with how Indonesia’s Just Energy Transition Partnership was originally designed.

The actually important question is not whether Indonesia can build 100 GW of solar power – obviously, it cannot do so in three years. The question is whether we are getting closer to an approach that can actually be implemented and scaled given the peculiarities of Indonesia’s political economy. I think the answer is a tentative yes. Prabowo recently unveiled the first stage of the 100 GW plan, announcing 5.3 GW of solar power projects under development or which will soon be opened for bidding.

The first thing we need to do is unpack the headline figure. 5.3 GW of new solar capacity would be a very significant step forward in Indonesia’s clean energy ambitions, but only eight of these projects are actually in an advanced stage of development. The bulk of the announced capacity, some 4.5 GW worth of projects, are still in the early stages without financing or confirmed project developers. However the eight projects that are further along tell us a lot about how to build clean energy in Indonesia.

Two of the announced projects are small off-grid solar facilities, designed to replace diesel generators in remoter areas. One of these is being developed by a subsidiary of state-owned oil and gas giant Pertamina, and the other by PLN itself. Together they account for under 2 MW of capacity. The other six projects are larger utility-scale solar and battery storage facilities mainly using floating arrays built on top of reservoirs. They range in size from 46 MW to around 133 MW and, once completed, will add almost 670 MW of solar generating capacity to the grid.

These six projects are in various stages of development, with some quite far along or nearly operational. They feature a range of financial backers including state-owned infrastructure fund PT Sarana Multi Infrastruktur, development banks as well as European lenders. Private sector developers include local firm TBS Energi, as well as Saudi Arabia’s ACWA Renewables, China’s GCL, and Singapore-based Vena Energy. The 92 MW Saguling facility in West Java is one of the few projects to be developed under the JETP framework.

The really important observation is that in all of these projects, state-owned electric utility PLN is not just the off-taker. They are an active equity partner, in most cases holding 51 percent ownership of the project. This is the same model, and equity split, we saw in the Cirata floating solar project in West Java, the first really successful large-scale solar power plant in Indonesia that went into operation in 2023. The new wave of solar power projects is clearly using the Cirata model.

The big puzzle has always been: how do you get PLN to buy-in to a national solar project? PLN operates a large fleet of Indonesia’s coal-fired power plants, and has been reluctant to simply act as a market-maker and off-taker for private renewable energy developers. Involving PLN in these projects as an equity partner provides the utility with an incentive to actually support them. Is it the most efficient design, or the one private developers and financers would ideally want? Probably not. But it is a model that can scale in Indonesia. We are seeing proof of that now.

As projects get bigger, and as more solar power is added and more investment is required, can state-owned energy firms like PLN and Pertamina continue to dominate the clean energy landscape in this way? That we don’t know. The state-directed model may very well need to change as the scale and pace of investment changes. But for now, after many years of false starts, it appears clean energy is actually gaining some traction in Indonesia. The key is that policy efforts stop viewing Indonesia simply as a market to be opened up to private investment, and start giving serious though to the interests and incentives of powerful local stakeholder like PLN.

title: Ismat Ara on India’s Crackdown on Love
description: Ara explains the insidious harm of the “love jihad” myth: “A deeply personal decision, two people deciding to marry, gradually becomes something that others felt entitled to violently police.”
text:
Love and marriage across religious and caste lines have always been frowned upon and forbidden in India. However, Hindu right-wing organizations have taken this to a new extreme by conjuring up a conspiracy theory they term “love jihad.” India is witnessing a systematic strategy being implemented by Hindutva activists to not just prevent Hindu women from marrying Muslim men but to malign the latter by ascribing to them sinister motives of enticing Hindu women with false promises of love and marriage for the sole purpose of converting them to Islam. Bharatiya Janata Party politicians have used the “love jihad” bogey to deepen Hindu anxieties and polarize society. BJP governments in several states have enacted anti-religious conversion laws. Meanwhile, right-wing goons have wreaked enormous havoc in the lives of young couples who dare to love across religious lines.

In her recent book, “Under a Saffron Sky: Inside India’s Crackdown on Love,” author Ismat Ara recounts the enormous stress and suffering that Hindu-Muslim couples experience. She draws attention to how the “love jihad” “myth” has come to “define an entire community.” In an interview with The Diplomat’s South Asia editor, Sudha Ramachandran, Ara pointed out that while an interfaith relationship is a private matter between two people, “within the ‘love jihad’ narrative, the Muslim man is reimagined as part of a larger, organized project to convert Hindu women, increase the Muslim population, and eventually alter the country’s demographic and religious character.”

What is “love jihad”?

“Love jihad” is the idea that Muslim men are deliberately targeting Hindu women for relationships and marriage in order to convert them to Islam, and that this is part of a larger organized conspiracy. It is an elaborate example of political myth-making and what happens when paranoia about “Muslim danger” enters the mass psyche.

While doing fieldwork for my recent book, “Under a Saffron Sky,” what interested me was not only whether individual cases of deception or coercion exist — they can, as they do in any relationship — but how these individual cases are transformed into evidence of a larger, vast conspiracy, one that comes to define an entire community. The leap from “a Muslim man deceiving a woman” to “Muslim men are conducting an organized campaign against Hindu women to take over this country” is the crucial political leap. When it becomes part of a larger conspiracy, the myth then becomes powerful enough to shape families, communities, police action, and even public policy, acquiring a life of its own, with its own set of myths.

There have been cases such as the 2023 Purola episode in Uttarakhand, where an alleged attempt to abduct a 14-year-old girl was quickly branded as “love jihad,” triggering communal protests and the exodus of Muslim families. The case later collapsed in court, with the girl and her uncle contradicting the initial police version. The minor also told the court that police had tutored her to make allegations against the accused, who were subsequently acquitted.

Could you share with us an example of what an interfaith couple undergoes when they are accused of “love jihad”?

Once people believe the myth of “love jihad,” real couples have to live with its consequences. One of the stories I reported from Uttar Pradesh is of a Hindu woman and a Muslim man who got married. After their nikah (wedding), when the couple went to the district magistrate’s office for their marriage registration, the man was shot in the head by two unidentified assailants right outside the government office in broad daylight. The couple wanted to register their marriage, make it official so no harm could touch them. But the woman saw her husband die before her eyes, minutes before that.

What made the story particularly chilling is the context. The couple had received warnings for weeks and months from local right-wing outfits and people opposed to the relationship and believed that once they had an official stamp from the government, no harm could touch their marriage. So, what began as a deeply personal decision, two people deciding to marry, gradually becomes something that others felt entitled to intervene in, threaten, and violently police.

In another example, from Gujarat, a state still scarred by the communal violence of 2002, a stamp vendor who had sold the couple their marriage stamps went on to call the woman’s family to inform them of their daughter’s “misdoings,” escalating the tension further.

In your book, you argue that “love jihad” is all about controlling women. Could you explain how?

One of the book’s main premises is that this is ultimately about controlling women, and that control operates across communities, although in very different ways. When a Hindu woman is told that she cannot choose her own partner because he belongs to another faith, her agency is being taken away. She is often treated as someone who has been deceived or brainwashed rather than as an adult capable of making a decision. But I also looked at Muslim women in the book. There is a case of a Muslim woman whose parents oppose her marriage because the man she has chosen was not just Hindu, but also belonged to a lower caste. The woman was told by her family that they might have considered a Hindu man — but only if he was upper caste. So, the policing of women’s choices isn’t confined to one community.

It’s an old story of women’s choices being made to represent the honor of an entire community, but what is distinctive about the “love jihad” campaign specifically is the way the Hindu woman has increasingly been made into a symbol, used as a tool, almost as the keeper of her entire community’s honor, purity, and demographic future. Her personal choices are seen as a collective threat. She is considered incapable of making her own decision, but in reality, her decision is powerful enough to threaten the demographic future of an entire community.

Article 21 of the Indian Constitution guarantees the right to life and personal liberty, which includes an individual’s freedom to choose whom they wish to marry. In reality, less than 3 percent of marriages in India are actually interfaith, so this has never been an easy choice. It has always meant navigating disapproving parents, nosy neighbors and hostile looks. But increasingly, crossing that boundary can also mean the police coming to your home. These single-digit marriages are framed as “dangerous” or as something that could alter India’s demography.

“Love jihad” is fundamentally a threat-based concept: it brings together anxieties around women, community honor and national security. But what about the real wars being fought by women? The opposite can be opportunity-based concepts, focusing on potential gains, growth, and positive outcomes rather than on “avoiding dangers or risks.” We must look at the basics that affect the majority of our country’s women, from the girl child being killed to girls not getting education or healthcare access.

Could you share with us how right-wing organizations mobilize and prevent interfaith marriages?

The “foot soldiers,” as well as organizations that work around “love jihad” cases, have multiple sources of information and multiple ways of mobilizing. Some maintain strong local networks; others are highly visible on the street, actively watching for such cases. In some places, they don’t even need to go looking. They have become such recognized “authorities” that people from neighboring areas approach them directly to report what they see as suspicious behavior, or word that a Muslim man is trying to “lure” a Hindu woman.

There are also rehabilitation programs aimed specifically at women, meant to remind them of their religious identity and, in the language of these organizations, to “correct” or undo the ideological influence they are believed to have absorbed from Muslim men. It is not one form of mobilization but many: surveillance, family pressure, public intervention, ideological programming, and street action. Together, they create an environment in which an interfaith relationship becomes something the wider community feels entitled to police.

The Special Marriage Act of 1954 was supposed to help interfaith couples marry. Why hasn’t it worked?

A law can create a legal route, but societal adoption of that route is equally important. The Special Marriage Act was meant to allow people of different faiths to marry without requiring either person to convert. But over the years, interfaith marriage has become increasingly politicized, particularly when it involves a Hindu woman and a Muslim man. The problem is that couples aren’t operating in a social vacuum. They have to navigate families, communities, local officials, and, increasingly now, political scrutiny. A legal provision cannot by itself remove the social stigma or the fear surrounding the choice. The Special Marriage Act exists, but the real question is whether people feel genuinely safe to use it. What do couples do when the law gives you a right, but the process through which you exercise that right can expose you to physical, mental, emotional and legal risks?

Allegations of “love jihad” are usually hurled at Muslim men marrying Hindu women. Are such allegations levelled against Muslim women marrying Hindu men?

Yes, there have been cases where Muslim women have faced similar allegations, particularly allegations that they were attempting to convert Hindu men through marriage. In Uttar Pradesh, for instance, there have been cases where criminal complaints under anti-conversion laws were filed against Muslim women and their male relatives, with families alleging that conversions were being orchestrated through the promise of marriage. In some cases, Muslim women have even been sent to custody in connection with such allegations. So, the idea of a Muslim woman being an agent of conversion is certainly present in some cases.

If religious conversions did not happen, would anxieties that fuel “love jihad” allegations reduce?

Conversion sits at the center of the “love jihad” narrative, but I don’t think its absence would make the deeper anxiety disappear. One thing that became clear to me while reporting these stories is that suspicion often exists even where no conversion has taken place at all. A Hindu woman simply being in a relationship with a Muslim man can be enough to trigger the allegation of “love jihad.” There has been no substantial body of cases establishing an organized “love jihad” conspiracy behind forced conversions. Individual cases of coercion or deception can occur, of course, and deserve to be investigated on their own merits, but that is a very different thing from proving a larger, organized conspiracy.

What happens, then, is that the political idea becomes much larger than the evidence behind it. I sometimes think of it like Mary Shelley’s Frankenstein’s monster: something that is created and then acquires a life of its own. The narrative begins to generate its own evidence. An interfaith relationship becomes suspicious because people have already been told what such a relationship means; the absence of conversion does not necessarily dispel the suspicion. So, conversion is important to the mythology, but it is not really the whole story. The deeper anxiety is about the crossing of community boundaries through intimacy and marriage. Who is allowed to love whom? What happens when a woman chooses a partner from another community? What religion will the children follow? Will the family retain its religious identity? And that is why I see “love jihad” as part of a larger politics of controlling women’s choices.

The policing of interfaith marriage exists across communities. Muslim women too can face enormous family and social pressure when they marry outside the community. But “love jihad” has given that anxiety a particularly powerful political vocabulary when the relationship is between a Hindu woman and a Muslim man.

The Christian Church in Kerala has also accused Muslims of “love jihad.” How similar is their campaign against interfaith marriage?

While there are similarities, there are also important differences. The similarity is in the underlying anxiety: the fear that women from one’s own religious community are being targeted by men from another community, and that such relationships could lead to conversion, loss of community identity, or demographic change. But the Christian discourse in Kerala has been more localized and has emerged from a very different social and political context, rooted largely in concerns within the Christian community about young women, interfaith relationships, and conversion.

The “love jihad” narrative in the wider Hindu nationalist discourse, on the other hand, has acquired a much larger political vocabulary. It has been linked not just to conversion and interfaith marriage, but also to concerns about demography, population growth, religious identity and, at times, national security. It has therefore travelled far beyond individual relationships and become part of a broader political narrative. These campaigns may emerge from different contexts, but they draw upon an older anxiety around women, sexuality and community boundaries.

So I would say the resemblance is real, but the scale, impact, context, and political consequences are different.

The Sangh Parivar’s “love jihad” campaign, you write, brings together several strands of its agenda, including national security. Could you explain?

The idea of “love jihad” draws together things that might otherwise seem unrelated: women’s sexuality, interfaith marriage, religious conversion, demography, Muslim identity, and national security. That is precisely what makes “love jihad” such a potent political idea in the larger Hindu nationalist discourse. An interfaith relationship begins as a private matter between two people, but within the “love jihad” narrative, the Muslim man is reimagined as part of a larger, organized project to convert Hindu women, increase the Muslim population, and eventually alter the country’s demographic and religious character.

There is a kind of escalation at work: first, the relationship is framed as a question of conversion; then conversion is linked to demography and Muslim population growth; and from there, the narrative is stretched to a much larger claim, a threat to the nation’s social and national fabric. That is where national security enters. Once an intimate relationship is recast as part of an organized threat, intervention starts to look like protection. Surveillance, police action, restrictions on marriage, mobilization against individual couples, even mob violence, all justified in the name of the larger public interest.

title: Japan and South Korea Face Off Again in the US Navy’s Frigate Search
description: South Korea has an industrial head start, but is Japan’s upgraded Mogami class merely a stalking horse for the Chungnam class?
text:
The U.S. Navy’s reported interest in foreign frigate designs has opened a new front in Japan-South Korea defense industrial competition. USNI News reported on September 1 that the White House and Navy are considering three allied designs: Japan’s upgraded Mogami class, known as the New FFM or 06FFM; South Korea’s Chungnam class; and Turkiye’s Istanbul class. Up to two ships could be built overseas before production shifts to U.S. yards.

The idea did not come from nowhere. As Naval News reported in June, the Pentagon’s fiscal year 2027 budget proposal included $1.85 billion for an effort involving foreign warship designs, with Japan and South Korea at the center of the discussion.

Japan’s top naval officer has now publicly welcomed the reported U.S. interest. Asked by The Diplomat at a September 8 press conference about the New FFM’s reported inclusion in the U.S. review, Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force (MSDF) Chief of Staff Adm. Saito Akira stressed that he was not in a position to comment on individual U.S. Navy shipbuilding plans. But if the United States or other countries were considering adopting platforms used by the MSDF, he said, “We see this as reflecting a high level of trust in and appreciation for equipment that embodies the advanced technologies of our ships.”

“I am frankly pleased,” Saito said, adding that if Japan received requests for cooperation on such matters, “we would respond proactively.”

The reported competition has encouraged a view that Seoul is the real front-runner and Japan’s New FFM merely a stalking horse. Hanwha acquired Philly Shipyard in 2024, giving a South Korean company a direct U.S. shipbuilding foothold. U.S. officials have repeatedly visited South Korean yards, and in December 2025 U.S. President Donald Trump said the Navy would work with Hanwha on a new frigate.

But that conclusion does not necessarily follow.

Trump’s remarks referred to cooperation on the U.S. Navy’s FF(X), a U.S.-designed frigate concept based on the Coast Guard’s National Security Cutter. That was not a decision to adopt South Korea’s Chungnam design. USNI News’ September 1 report described a separate review of foreign designs and identified no favorite.

Moreover, Hanwha is not the company most closely associated with the Chungnam class. The detailed design and lead ship were handled by HD Hyundai Heavy Industries, while Hanwha Ocean and SK Oceanplant are building follow-on ships. Thus, Hanwha’s U.S. shipyard investment does not automatically translate into an advantage for the Chungnam design.

Nor has Washington’s shipbuilding outreach been limited to South Korea. Then-Navy Secretary John Phelan visited Japan in April 2025, meeting Saito and other Japanese defense officials and touring Japan Marine United. The U.S. Navy said Phelan visited JMU to learn about industry best practices and encourage investment in American shipyards.

Asked whether Phelan or other U.S. Navy officials had previously expressed specific interest in or praise for the Mogami class or New FFM, Saito declined to disclose details, saying only that he regularly exchanges views with U.S. Navy counterparts on a broad range of issues, including defense equipment, capability enhancement, and operational cooperation.

South Korea nevertheless has some important advantages in the U.S. competition. Its major shipbuilders have substantial production capacity, while Hanwha already has a direct U.S. shipbuilding presence at a time when Washington faces serious shipbuilding delays and capacity constraints. That U.S. footprint also fits the administration’s “Finland model”: initial construction overseas followed by investment and production in the United States.

Yet Japan’s New FFM should not be dismissed. There is already a precedent for Japanese-South Korean frigate competition. In 2024, Australia identified Japan’s Mogami class and South Korea’s FFX Batch II and III, among other designs, as exemplars for its future general-purpose frigate. Canberra later narrowed the field to Mitsubishi Heavy Industries and Germany’s TKMS before selecting the upgraded Mogami – the New FFM – in August 2025.

Now the two Asian competitors could find themselves facing each other again in the United States, with the New FFM and South Korea’s Chungnam class – the FFX Batch III design – both reportedly under consideration.

Australia’s decision gives Japan a major naval export success with a close U.S. ally. The New FFM is expected to feature a 32-cell vertical launch system, long range, stealth-oriented design features, and reduced manning – attributes relevant to the U.S. Navy as it seeks a frigate that can relieve Arleigh Burke-class destroyers of lower-end missions.

None of this guarantees a Japanese win. Both designs would require adaptation to U.S. Navy combat systems, weapons, communications, cybersecurity, and information-security requirements. Congress also remains wary of building U.S. warships overseas.

The better reading, then, is that South Korea has an industrial head start, not a guaranteed design victory. Hanwha’s U.S. footprint and South Korea’s shipbuilding capacity make it a formidable contender. But those factors do not prove that the Chungnam class is the Navy’s preferred frigate, nor that Japan’s New FFM is merely a stalking horse.

Washington is effectively weighing two questions: which ally can best help rebuild the U.S. shipbuilding industrial base, and which frigate design best fits the fleet. South Korea’s U.S. investments give it important advantages on the first. On the second, the competition remains very much open.

title: Japan Faces Hard Choices in Weaning off Russian Energy
description: Beyond the question of energy security, Tokyo may want to avoid antagonizing Russia further by cutting off LNG purchases.
text:
Japan is one of the most energy-insecure countries in the world relative to the size of its population and economy. Liquified natural gas (LNG) accounts for 30 percent of its electricity generation, and Japan imports more than 97 percent of its total LNG. Japan’s supplies of crude oil and coal are almost 100 percent imported.

Successive energy shocks produced by Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz have raised household costs and depressed growth. The International Energy Agency forecast that Japanese electricity prices for the second half of 2026 will surge 40 percent year-on-year, compared to only 25 percent for the European Union.

This context helps to explain why Japan has continued to resist pressure from the United States to phase out its procurement of Russian LNG from the Sakhalin-II project in the Russian Far East. The Takaichi government justifies its stance by asserting that Russian LNG plays an “extremely important role” in Japan’s energy security.

Domestic gas industry leaders warn that efforts to substitute the 5 million tonnes of LNG Japan buys from Russia annually – amounting to 9 percent of its total LNG imports – would risk supply shortages and increased costs for consumers. Cargoes from Sakhalin Island reach Japan in only two or three days, resulting in significantly lower transport costs compared to the seven days for Australian LNG and 20-40 days from the U.S. Gulf Coast. As Japanese households strain under a continuing cost-of-living crunch, there is little political appetite in Tokyo for measures that could add to that pain.

This June, the U.S. Treasury extended Japan’s sanctions waiver for purchases of Russian LNG until the end of 2026, marking the fifth extension since restrictions were introduced in 2022. However, Tokyo’s lobbying for exemptions is unlikely to succeed indefinitely. Officials must plan for the possibility that sooner or later, patience in Washington will run out.

Does the Takaichi administration have the stomach to make a major break with Russia? A litmus test came in August with Russian President Vladimir Putin’s unprecedented visit to one of the four disputed Kuril Islands controlled by Russia. Japan regards the islands as “illegally occupied” and the dispute remains the main reason both sides have never signed a formal treaty ending World War II. Given the importance of the issue to Japanese foreign policy, Putin’s incendiary move demanded a forceful reply.

Instead, Takaichi’s response – calling the visit “absolutely unacceptable” and saying it had “hurt the public sentiment of the Japanese people” – was panned domestically as weak and inadequate. The government announced it was weighing further economic sanctions and other countermeasures but has yet to follow through. According to government insiders, concerns over energy loomed large and any cessation of imports from Sakhalin-II was ruled out.

Putin’s provocative visit underlined the failure of former Prime Minister Abe Shinzo’s strategy of stepping up engagement with Russia in the hopes of resolving the territorial dispute. This effort, too, has links to Japan’s energy policy. As part of the economic sweeteners Tokyo extended to Moscow, its companies invested in Russian energy and infrastructure, taking equity stakes in Sakhalin-I and -II. These efforts not only failed to pay off but that the needle has now swung sharply in the opposite direction. Rather than inducing positive behavior from Moscow, those Japanese investments created dependencies that constrain Tokyo’s actions.

Japan is not ready to wholly abandon this Abe-era strategy. However, its continuing energy purchases and the sending of business delegations to Moscow risk negatively impacting its reputational standing among G7 allies. Critics can point to the example of the EU, which was far more reliant on Russian energy than Japan but has moved to institute a complete ban on Russian gas imports by September 2027.

Looking ahead, Japan is faced with difficult choices as the bulk of its Sakhalin-II LNG contracts are due to expire between 2028 and 2033. Domestic buyers’ preference for long-term contracts to avoid spot market volatility limits options and requires extensive planning and supplier diplomacy in advance. Simultaneously, Japan will be competing with strong demand from other Asian customers, as the Iran-U.S. war has cut off most of Qatari LNG from the global market and put its liquefaction facilities out of commission for years.

Japan may look to buy more from Australia or the United States. However, Australian gas production is reaching a plateau, while U.S. LNG cargoes loaded in the Gulf of Mexico must either transit the Panama Canal, which is increasingly susceptible to drought-induced closures and fee rises, or take the long, expensive route around the Cape of Good Hope.

Canada is emerging as a major LNG exporter, with significant capacity coming online between 2028–2032. Loaded on the Pacific Coast, Canadian LNG is cost-competitive and reaches Japan in a chokepoint-free journey taking only 10 days.

However, none of these alternative supplies will be as cheap and accessible as buying LNG from Russia. The broader risk is that abandoning energy cooperation will torpedo bilateral relations and close the door to a diplomatic resolution of the disputed Kuril Islands. The costs of further antagonizing Russia, at a time when Japan faces simultaneous security challenges emanating from both China and North Korea, may simply be too high.
