title: Japan-Korea: Working Together as Like-Minded Countries?
description: Japan and South Korea share more than enough to work together on North Korea — but less than is often assumed.
text:
It is frequently argued that “Japan and South Korea are like-minded countries who share values and ought to strengthen their cooperation in dealing with North Korea.” The question worth asking is what the two countries are actually “like-minded” about — and what they are not.

There is no settled definition in international politics of “like-minded countries” — a concept increasingly prominent in Japanese diplomatic discourse as dōshikoku —, but the term generally refers to countries that share objectives or an understanding on specific issues. The two countries are not automatically like-minded simply because they are both democracies, nor do their policies automatically align across diverse fields because they are both U.S. allies. The degree of alignment has to be assessed issue by issue.

Japan-South Korea relations on the North Korean issue do have an evident duality. On the “threat” dimension, the two are quite robustly like-minded: both are concerned about North Korea’s growing nuclear and missile capabilities, and there is considerable room for cooperation in countering cyberattacks and cryptocurrency theft. The importance of Japan-South Korea security cooperation is also growing as the Russia-North Korea military relationship deepens. In managing relations with an unpredictable U.S. president, too, the bilateral Japan-South Korea framework has become if anything more important than the broader trilateral one.

The differences become apparent, however, the moment North Korea is treated not as a “threat” but as a potential “negotiation partner.” In South Korean eyes, North Korea is simultaneously a military threat and one half of a divided nation sharing a common language. Depending on the administration, the emphasis varies, but Seoul can never entirely set aside the questions of peaceful coexistence and eventual reunification.

Japan, by contrast, regards North Korea as a foreign country across the sea. Drones do not fly over from North Korea to Japan as they do to South Korea, and Japan’s North Korea policy is heavily constrained by the abduction issue — a factor absent for every other country in the region. Even if progress were made on nuclear and missile issues, it would be politically impossible for Tokyo to move toward normalization without meaningful progress on abductions.

Even if both Tokyo and Seoul were to support “dialogue” and “diplomacy” with Pyongyang, the underlying expectations would differ. Seoul values dialogue that eases inter-Korean tensions; Tokyo requires dialogue that advances its outstanding issues with Pyongyang. Even on denuclearization, where the ultimate goal may appear aligned, the two sides diverge over whether to treat a freeze of North Korea’s nuclear capabilities as an intermediate milestone, and over when sanctions should be eased — Japan still insisting on CVID (complete, verifiable, irreversible denuclearization).

And then there is the Chinese variable. It is difficult to consider the efficacy of sanctions or future diplomatic negotiations without involving China, North Korea’s foremost economic partner. Yet Japan and South Korea often view China quite differently. Japan perceives China primarily as a long-term security threat, while South Korea sees it as both a concern and an indispensable partner for managing the Korean Peninsula. Even conservative South Korean presidents have at times prioritized ties with Beijing over alignment with Tokyo. The geopolitical weight of sharing a land border with China is not something Seoul can ignore.

These differences, however, hardly make cooperation impossible. On the contrary, the right approach is to treat cooperation as necessary precisely because interests and priorities diverge. If U.S. President Donald Trump were to pursue a summit with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un for legacy purposes, both Japan and South Korea would seek to resume negotiations with Pyongyang in some form, each naturally prioritizing its own interests. History shows repeated failures to act in concert, each time expanding North Korea’s room for maneuver. Pyongyang has always sought to drive a wedge between Tokyo and Seoul, and between the two of them and Washington.

Japan-South Korea cooperation on North Korea need not aim for complete policy alignment. Japan should pursue its own diplomacy with Pyongyang; South Korea should occupy its own space in inter-Korean relations. On that foundation, the two should share information closely and keep each other fully informed of what each prioritizes and where neither can compromise. The same applies to China: a shared understanding of when Beijing should be treated as a partner and when it should be viewed with caution. On issues of this kind, diplomatic channels matter more than defense channels.

Japan and South Korea will never adopt identical policies toward North Korea — nor should they need to. That does not mean they cannot be like-minded countries. The real question is whether they can manage their differences on North Korea and China with sufficient steadiness and dexterity. That capacity, more than any policy alignment, is what will determine whether the “like-minded” label truly fits.

title: Japan, South Korea, and the New Logic of Nuclear Energy Security in Northeast Asia
description: The two neighbors are reshaping the nuclear politics of Northeast Asia – and doing so increasingly in concert with Washington.
text:
After the 2011 accident at the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Plant, Japan stopped all nuclear power production. Today, the country is restarting reactors, rewriting its energy law, and recasting nuclear power as a pillar of national and regional security rather than a liability to be managed. South Korea, its neighbor and rival in reactor exports, is moving along a parallel track, despite a change of government that briefly appeared to threaten the opposite.

Together, the two countries are reshaping the nuclear politics of Northeast Asia and doing so increasingly in concert with Washington, as energy policy folds into the broader architecture of trilateral security cooperation.

The unresolved question behind both countries’ restarts is what to do with the spent fuel piling up at reactor sites. I explored one effort to solve that issue earlier this month in a visit to Japan’s Horonobe Underground Research Laboratory. There, hundreds of meters below the surface, engineers are testing whether the geological disposal methods every nuclear country is counting on actually hold up over time. Horonobe is a research site, however, not a repository, and Japan still has no designated location for permanent waste disposal. That gap has not slowed the political momentum above ground.

Before 2011, nuclear power supplied roughly 30 percent of Japan’s electricity. After the meltdown at Fukushima Daiichi, every commercial reactor in the country was taken offline, and public opinion turned sharply against nuclear power. What followed was over a decade of dependence on imported liquefied natural gas and coal, at a cost Japan, which imports about 90 percent of its primary energy, could not sustain indefinitely, especially as global gas markets tightened after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

The return to nuclear power began in earnest with Prime Minister Kishida Fumio’s Green Transformation (GX) policy, launched in 2022. The GX Basic Policy, approved by the Cabinet in February 2023, explicitly committed the government to restarting reactors already cleared by regulators and to building next-generation designs.

The Seventh Strategic Energy Plan, approved by the Cabinet in February 2025 along with the accompanying GX2040 Vision, cemented nuclear power’s return as government policy rather than a temporary emergency measure. In early 2026, that policy produced its most tangible result yet: the restart of Unit 6 at Tokyo Electric Power Company’s Kashiwazaki-Kariwa plant, the world’s largest nuclear facility by capacity. Perhaps more pointedly, it’s run by the operator directly responsible for Fukushima Daiichi. Such a restart would have been politically unthinkable a decade ago.

The motivation is obvious. New public funding for data center and semiconductor facilities, worth over a trillion yen, requires that the electricity used come entirely from renewable or nuclear sources. That sends an unambiguous signal that Tokyo now considers nuclear energy to be indispensable to industrial policy, not just decarbonization.

South Korea is moving along a similar trajectory, even if it once looked to be headed in a different direction. President Lee Jae-myung took office in June 2025 after having campaigned on skepticism toward nuclear power. Lee argued that the technology was inherently dangerous and that the country’s reactor-heavy generation mix needed re-examining in favor of renewables. Seven months later, confronted with polling showing strong public support for nuclear energy and with surging electricity demand from an AI-driven data center boom, his government reversed course.

Seoul confirmed it would proceed with two new large reactors under the 11th Basic Plan for Electricity Supply and Demand, which targets a nuclear share of nearly 32 percent by 2030 and over 35 percent by 2038. In August 2026, Lee’s government went further, naming small modular reactors and nuclear fusion among seven technologies it wants to establish as future growth engines for the South Korean economy.

Korean reactor technology is already competitive with Western vendors. Around the same time Lee took office, Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power signed a contract to build two APR-1000 reactors in Dukovany, Czechia, a deal worth roughly $18.6 billion. The company has since signed cooperation agreements covering nuclear development in the Philippines, small-reactors studies with Singapore, and full fuel-cycle cooperation with France’s Orano. South Korea, which imports roughly 90 percent of its own energy needs and around 30 percent of its low-enriched uranium from Russia, is treating nuclear exports and domestic energy security as two sides of the same policy.

In July 2026, nuclear energy became an area of interest for trilateral cooperation between the United States and its two East Asian Allies. Japan, South Korea, and the United States agreed to jointly develop and export small modular reactors across the Indo-Pacific, explicitly extending their trilateral security partnership into commercial nuclear cooperation.

With Russia and China as the only realistic nuclear vendors for many developing countries, Washington has a clear interest in ensuring that Japan and South Korea enter the race. It would benefit Washington if its two Northeast Asian allies, rather than Beijing or Moscow, become the default suppliers of reactor technology to the rest of the region.

For Tokyo and Seoul, folding nuclear commerce into the trilateral security relationship also offers insurance against the awkward fact that both countries’ export ambitions still run through Washington’s non-proliferation rules and, in South Korea’s case, the 123 Agreement governing nuclear cooperation with the United States.

Japan’s own export potential remains constrained precisely because its domestic restart is still incomplete. Barely a handful of reactors are back online out of the roughly three dozen that existed before 2011. That leaves South Korea, for now, as the more credible reactor exporter of the two.

What the restart narrative tends to leave out is that neither country has solved the problem I found researchers still puzzling over at Horonobe: Japan has no operating deep geological repository and no site formally designated to host one. That means the used fuel accumulating at reactor sites, including at the restarted Kashiwazaki-Kariwa plant, has nowhere permanent to go. South Korea faces the same problem, with domestic opposition to any proposed storage site consistently more intense than opposition to reactors themselves.

That gap matters for the trilateral SMR push, too. Exporting reactor technology to Southeast Asia or the Pacific Islands without a credible regional answer on waste management invites the same criticism that has dogged nuclear power at home in both countries: that the industry is better at building political consensus for new construction than for dealing with what construction leaves behind.

For now, Northeast Asia’s nuclear revival is a story about energy security, industrial competitiveness, and alignment with Washington against Chinese and Russian reactor diplomacy. But underneath all these developments lurks the unanswered question of what to do with the increasing amounts of nuclear waste. That may end up mattering as much to the region’s energy future as any restart or export deal announced so far.

title: Japan’s Electricity Shock Is a Contract Problem
description: It’s not a matter of counting suppliers.
text:
The International Energy Agency expects Japanese wholesale electricity prices to rise by nearly 40 percent year on year in the second half of 2026, reaching roughly $105 per megawatt-hour. The equivalent increase across the European Union is around 25 percent. Two advanced economies buying from the same global gas market are absorbing the same disruption at very different rates, and the reason has less to do with how much gas Japan imports, than with how the price of that gas is written into contracts.

Each market’s exposure is structural. Natural gas accounted for 32 percent of Japan’s power generation in fiscal year 2024, and almost all of it was imported by ship. When the delivered cost of a cargo moves, it feeds directly into the marginal cost of generation, and there is little in between that can help absorb the increase. The nature of European systems means that these have somewhat more options for substitution available. Europe’s geographic position also means that it has greater interconnectivity with neighboring markets. Japan’s geographic position means that very differently, its grid converts an LNG price shock into an electricity price shock at a significantly faster rate. This of late, has been climbing.

The Japan Korea Marker, the spot benchmark for Northeast Asian LNG deliveries, reached about $24 per million British thermal units (MMBtu) in August, up 13 percent over the month. More telling is the forward curve. Cargoes for October through December are trading above $22 per MMBtu, against an average of just under $17 for 2026 so far. Traders are not pricing a spike that fades before the heating season; rather they are pricing a winter that begins short.

The squeeze began upstream of Asia. Disruptions to Qatari exports and shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a result of the ongoing U.S.-Iran war, have pulled flexible volumes out of a market that was already operating with a thin cushion. LNG is fungible in theory; in practice, it is not. A cargo redirected to a European regasification terminal is a cargo that does not reach its destination in Asia. Such unanticipated redirections come at an increased price. Japanese buyers are now bidding against European utilities rebuilding storage, as well as Chinese, Korean and South Asian buyers who are looking to ensure they are covered for their own winters.

The contest runs through a narrow layer of an already challenging market: portfolio sellers such as Shell and TotalEnergies, alongside independent trading houses including Vitol, Gunvor and BGN Group, hold some of the volumes that have not already been committed to a fixed destination. Their decisions about where a cargo ultimately goes are one of the mechanisms by which a disruption in the Middle East can potentially create a higher generation cost in Japan.

Dubai-based BGN Group is an instructive example of how this part of the market is changing. Having built its business around physical commodity trading and logistics, the company is now expanding its LNG portfolio across the Atlantic and Pacific basins, including through long-term supply arrangements and greater access to flexible FOB volumes. Its recent agreement for long-term LNG supply from Texas LNG is one example of that strategy at work, with BGN Group and Glenfarne Global Commodities agreeing on a framework for 1 million tons per annum and a proposed 20-year sale and purchase agreement. Such a model is important because the value of a portfolio seller is not simply the number of cargoes it controls. Rather, it is the ability to decide where those cargoes have the greatest commercial value as markets move. A Japanese utility competing for those volumes in the dead of winter in December negotiates from the weakest position possible, because the alternative to paying is not being capable of generating power at a time when their market needs it most. Buying less gas is therefore not a near-term option.

Traditional Asian LNG supply is priced against crude oil. The convention dates from an era when gas was sold as a substitute for fuel oil and no liquid gas benchmark existed against which to price it. The impact of this is still being felt in 2026. Utility costs in the Japanese market are thus inextricably tethered to a barrel of oil produced in the Middle East, where ongoing supply uncertainty is defining the market. Whenever the United States and Iran exchange fire, the crude and Asian spot gas benchmarks both respond.

American LNG is priced on a different basis. Volumes lifted from U.S. terminals are typically indexed to Henry Hub, the North American gas benchmark, plus a liquefaction fee and freight. Henry Hub responds to US production, storage levels and North American weather rather than risk in the Gulf. Pricing the spread between the two formulas is what trading desks do on a daily basis. This spread does not mean that Henry Hub-linked gas will always come out cheaper. Rather, a portfolio split between oil-linked and hub-linked supply stops the market from moving as one position.

This is where the increasing prominence of independent portfolio players becomes particularly relevant. A company such as BGN Group is not simply competing with other major players for individual cargoes; its expanding LNG business is built around assembling supply, logistics and market access across regions. Its recent push into long-term US LNG supply is an example of how American production can increasingly be connected to demand outside the traditional US-European trade. For Japanese buyers, that creates another potential route to diversification: not necessarily buying every cargo directly from a US producer, but contracting with counterparties like BGN Group capable of managing supply across multiple basins and pricing structures.

Japanese officials have heard the diversification argument before and are right to be skeptical of oversimplifications that treat American cargoes as a hedge against everything. Henry Hub-linked supply carries its own exposures: U.S. domestic price swings during a cold North American winter, tolling fees agreed years before first delivery, and freight rates that are sensitive to shipping disruption. Splitting the pricing basis reduces correlation but does not eliminate risk entirely.

There is also a question of timing which needs to be fully addressed. U.S. liquefaction capacity under construction will reach the market over the second half of this decade. However, offtake for much of this is being negotiated now, with sellers requiring creditworthy long-term buyers to underwrite final investment decisions. Japanese utilities and trading companies signing into a tight spot market have less leverage than they may appear to have, because sellers can read the same forward curve. And yet, an offtake agreement for volumes arriving in 2030 is negotiated against a different balance of need.

How the required energy supplies finally reach Japan – directly from a U.S. exporter or through a portfolio seller – is a commercial detail that will impact the final electricity bill, but the details of which will not be known to many. For two decades, Japanese LNG security has been measured by counting suppliers. The dynamic energy market however, argues for a different measure. It is the pricing formula, the one variable that can still be negotiated before the next disruption arrives, that Japanese buyers must pay more careful attention to.

title: Japan’s Failed Centrist Experiment
description: The CDP-Komeito alliance is breaking apart. But a return to resistance-oriented politics may not be the answer for Japan's opposition.
text:
The Centrist Reform Alliance (CRA), once thought to pose a significant threat to Takaichi Sanae’s hold on power, came to an unremarkable end. After nearly seven months of negotiations among the CRA and its sister parties, the Constitutional Democratic Party (CDP) and Komeito – both of which had dissolved in the lower house but continued to exist in the upper chamber – the three parties concluded that a complete merger would not proceed. As a result, the CRA is set to split into two groups, with former Komeito members returning to their former party and former CDP-affiliated members launching a new party. One member of the latter group will remain in the CRA to oversee its dissolution.

While the process of ending the CRA is already complicated enough, what makes it even more difficult for voters to grasp is that former CRA members will form a parliamentary group in the lower house. In other words, while the two parties have decided that they cannot be part of the same party, they still believe that they need to act as one, at least within the lower house.

The main cause of the breakdown in negotiations has been said to be the CDP’s reluctance. While Komeito was willing to join the CDP, which essentially shared its policy positions, the CDP ultimately could not reconcile its policies with those of Komeito. Komeito is more right-wing than the CDP’s positions on national security and nuclear energy.

Moreover, with local elections approaching next spring and the CRA having performed poorly at the February 2026 polls, local branches of the CDP have grown concerned that joining the party could put them at a disadvantage electorally. With the CDP having the largest number of local legislators among the opposition parties, second only to the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP), it had much to lose by alienating its local candidates and organizations.

However, confidence may also have factored into the CDP’s calculations. While the CRA had consistently struggled in the polls, the CDP has significantly outperformed the alliance in some polls. According to an August poll by TV Asahi, the CDP recorded 4.7 percent support, compared with just 1.8 percent for the CRA. Similarly, an NHK poll put support for the CDP at 2.8 percent, compared with 1.7 percent for the CRA. These figures may have reinforced the CDP’s belief that it could perform better on its own than as part of a broader alliance.

Nevertheless, the CDP’s record in national elections tells a different story. Since its reorganization in 2020, the CDP has either lost seats or significantly underperformed other opposition parties in terms of changes in its parliamentary strength. In both the 2021 lower house election and the 2022 upper house election, the CDP ended up with fewer seats than it had before the election.

Although the party surged from 98 to 148 seats in the 2024 lower house election, the increase came overwhelmingly from single-member districts, where the CDP benefited from a favorable electoral environment, including the political-funds scandal involving LDP candidates. By contrast, its performance in the proportional ballot barely improved from the previous election: its proportional vote total increased only marginally, despite higher voter turnout.

In the 2025 upper house election, the CDP’s parliamentary representation remained essentially flat, while it fell to third place among the opposition parties in the proportional vote, behind the Democratic Party for the People and Sanseito.

Before the 2026 lower house election, the CDP’s alignment with, and eventual incorporation into, the CRA alongside Komeito was intended to reverse the party’s declining appeal among younger voters. Younger Japanese were thought to favor tangible policy outcomes – from lower costs of living to robust national security measures – over simply opposing the governing party. However, the electoral strategy failed.

This does not mean that so-called “resistance opposition,” a label that some pundits have come to associate with the CDP brand, lacks sufficient appeal to give the party staying power. Especially among older generations, opposing the LDP on normative issues such as the interpretation of Article 9 of the constitution and a zero-tolerance stance on nuclear energy – both core issues on which the CDP has refused to compromise – remains essential to their political orientation. However, as past election results make manifestly clear, those who could be described as “resistance liberals” do not constitute a majority, while parties that have performed well electorally in recent elections are gaining ground among younger voters.

With a weakening yen driving up prices across the board and a deteriorating security environment not only across the region but around the globe leading to abandonment of strict application of pacifism, resistance-oriented politics is increasingly seen as an unrealistic approach to governing a country. The CDP may be playing it safe by relying on tactics that succeeded in a different era, but by going it alone, it risks doing a disservice to its constituents and diminishing the political standing it might otherwise have strengthened through its alignment with the CRA.

title: Japan’s FOIP 3.0: Is Pragmatism That Delivers Resilience Enough?
description: Japan’s updated vision is sharper and more self-interested.
text:
When Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae visited Vietnam in early May this year, she presented an “evolved version” of the Free and Open Indo-Pacific (FOIP), a key plank in Japanese foreign policy, which is being called FOIP 3.0. The “Updated FOIP” specifies as priority areas “Building economic infrastructure for the age of AI and data,” “Co-creation of economic growth opportunities through public-private collaboration and rule sharing,” and “Enhancing cooperation in the field of security to ensure regional peace and stability,” each with its own items for concrete cooperation.

The FOIP was first proposed by the late Prime Minister Abe Shinzo in a speech in Nairobi in 2016. The keyword for FOIP 1.0 was “connectivity,” reflecting the fact that it was launched in the middle of a major shift in the power balance triggered by the rise of China.

International division has only deepened since, following the outbreak of the Russo-Ukrainian war, and with the rise of the Global South, international politics have become more complex still. It was in response to this that then Prime Minister Kishida Fumio proposed the New Plan for a FOIP, or FOIP 2.0, in 2023, along with the keyword “inclusiveness.”

Building on this foundation, the keyword for FOIP 3.0 as proposed by the Takaichi administration is “resilience.” With any improvement of relations with China unlikely in the near time, and with the United States pursuing an exceedingly unpredictable foreign policy under Trump, Japan faces what might be called a double risk. It needs to deepen cooperation with Indo-Pacific countries to mitigate those risks and ensure autonomy and resilience. The new FOIP is thus heavily shaped by the imperative to revitalize the Japanese economy and strengthen economic security through cooperation with the Global South, including the ASEAN countries.

The idea of connecting Japanese growth strategy, economic security, and Global South strategy has been clear enough since the Kishida administration. That administration adopted the New Policy toward Enhanced Cooperation with Global South Countries in June 2024. It also implemented institutional schemes to strengthen cooperation with the Global South, such as launching the Global South Future-Oriented Co-Creation Project and Official Security Assistance (OSA) as well as reforming the Official Development Assistance (ODA). The Asia Zero Emission Community (AZEC) is another scheme launched under that administration. However, whereas FOIP 2.0 emphasized Japan’s ideal international order and its commitment to that order, FOIP 3.0 does not define an order as explicitly; instead it pushes a pragmatism that more clearly emphasizes economic renewal and the restoration of Japan’s vitality.

The three priority areas specified in the FOIP 3.0 each list their own spheres for concrete cooperation. They are the 17 strategic fields identified by the Council for Japan’s Growth Strategy established under the Takaichi administration, areas in particular where Japan wants to promote development, with special emphasis being placed on AI and semiconductors, digital server security, and information and communications, quantum technology, and other fields that are relevant to digital hegemony.

What the times may call for is precisely this kind of pragmatism: an emphasis on revitalizing the Japanese economy and strengthening economic security in the name of “resilience.” Resilience has become an equally important theme for the ASEAN countries as they navigate what one might call the “geoeconomic turn.” Confronted with Trump tariffs, the energy supply disruptions from the Strait of Hormuz crisis, and related pressures, they have become increasingly interested in cooperation to mitigate geoeconomic risks. Key to surviving this uncertainty will be each ASEAN country’s ability to connect its national interests and resilience to broader cooperation across the region. Through FOIP, Japan aims not only to cooperate with individual ASEAN countries but to support ASEAN’s collective efforts to build resilience, contributing to risk mitigation across the region.

Japan can no longer rely on overwhelming economic power and technological advantage as the basis for cooperation with ASEAN countries and other parts of the Global South. There are limits to cooperation built solely on the pragmatism of shared gains. For Japan to earn the trust of ASEAN countries and others in the Global South, it must also clearly demonstrate its commitment to a rules-based international order capable of constraining the arbitrary actions of major powers. Japan is advancing concrete initiatives, but it must also clearly articulate the worldview behind FOIP — the kind of order it is trying to build — in light of today’s upheavals.
tag: FOIP 3.0; Free and open Indo-Pacific; Updated FOIP

title: JASDF Global Hawk Presumed to Have Crashed off Western Japan
description: The incident could strain Japan’s persistent wide-area surveillance capabilities, as the JASDF operates only three of the high-altitude unmanned aircraft.
text:
A Japan Air Self-Defense Force (JASDF) RQ-4B Global Hawk is presumed to have crashed into the Sea of Japan (East Sea) on September 15 after experiencing communication problems and disappearing from radar. It’s the first such incident involving a JASDF Global Hawk, a high-altitude, unmanned surveillance aircraft manufactured by U.S. defense firm Northrop Grumman.

The aircraft, assigned to the 502nd Squadron of the Airborne Warning and Control Wing at Misawa Air Base in Aomori Prefecture, took off from the base at around 10:20 a.m., according to the JASDF.

Problems connecting with the aircraft’s communications equipment began after 12:55 p.m. Three minutes later, at around 12:58 p.m., its radar track disappeared over waters about 50 kilometers north of Tottori Prefecture in western Japan.

Japan immediately mounted a search for the missing UAV. The effort involved two F-15J fighters, a U-125A search-and-rescue aircraft, a UH-60J helicopter, and a KC-46A tanker from the JASDF, as well as the Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force frigate Agano and missile boat Hayabusa.

The Japan Coast Guard discovered floating debris at around 2:19 p.m., and a JASDF F-15J fighter reported a debris sighting six minutes later. The U-125A search-and-rescue aircraft photographed the debris at 3:12 p.m. By 5:20 p.m., the JASDF had determined from the photographs that the debris was likely from the missing Global Hawk.

“Based on the floating objects discovered, the aircraft is presumed to have crashed,” the Air Staff Office said in its second report on the incident.

The cause remains under investigation. No damage outside the Self-Defense Forces had been reported as of 5 p.m.

The incident raises questions not only about what caused the Global Hawk to go down but also about the potential impact on Japan’s intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) capabilities.

At a press conference earlier on September 15, JASDF Chief of Staff General Morita Takehiro said the aircraft “was not on a training flight,” but declined to disclose what it had been doing.

Asked by this author whether the Global Hawk was likely to have crashed, Morita said at the time that the JASDF was considering “all possibilities” as it conducted the search. The subsequent discovery of debris led the service to presume that the aircraft had indeed crashed.

The JASDF operates three RQ-4Bs, all based at Misawa. Morita said this was the first time a JASDF Global Hawk had gone missing.

Japan began acquiring the Global Hawk in fiscal year 2015 to strengthen its persistent wide-area surveillance capabilities. The first aircraft arrived at Misawa in March 2022; the third arrived in June 2023, completing the planned three-aircraft fleet.

The RQ-4B is one of the JASDF’s key intelligence-gathering platforms. With a wingspan of about 40 meters and a length of about 15 meters, the UAV can remain airborne for around 36 hours and operate at altitudes of around 60,000 feet. Its high-altitude endurance allows it to monitor vast areas for extended periods without putting an aircrew at risk.

It is also an expensive asset. Japanese Defense Ministry documents put the unit cost of a Global Hawk at approximately 17.3 billion yen ($111.7 million). If the aircraft is ultimately confirmed lost, it would represent not only a significant financial loss but also the loss of one-third of Japan’s small Global Hawk fleet.

Retired JASDF Lt. Gen. Araki Junichi told NHK that a simple loss of communications would not necessarily explain the presumed crash because the aircraft is programmed to return to base if communications are lost. He suggested that an engine or other mechanical problem may have prevented normal flight, although the cause has yet to be established.

Araki also warned that losing one of the three aircraft could make continuous surveillance operations more difficult, potentially requiring other aircraft to compensate and increasing the burden on operational units.

The immediate priority is to recover as much of the aircraft as possible and determine what happened during the critical three-minute period between the onset of communication problems and the disappearance of its radar track.

Investigators will also need to establish what the aircraft was doing at the time, why communications failed, whether its automatic return-to-base function was activated, and why the aircraft was apparently unable to continue flying or return to base.

The answers will be important not only for preventing a recurrence, but also for assessing the reliability of a strategically important surveillance capability at a time when Japan is seeking to strengthen persistent intelligence-gathering around its increasingly contested neighborhood.
