title: Making the Most Out of Growing US-Uzbekistan Trade and Investment
description: Uzbekistan aims to attract greater U.S. investment, and is making its own investments in the United States. But it can’t forget the people.
text:
The purchase of U.S.-made commercial aircraft and an Uzbek company’s historic opening of a manufacturing facility in Kentucky demonstrate the dynamic and growing economic relations between the United States and Uzbekistan. As U.S. diplomatic engagement with Tashkent increases – new contracts and trade and investment frameworks signed – understanding each country’s priorities and objectives will help explain this new chapter of the partnership. Moreover, stronger trade and investment numbers must translate into employment opportunities and an improved quality of life for the Uzbek population.

Relations between Washington and Tashkent have generally strengthened over the past couple of years. U.S. President Donald Trump and Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev will next meet in December, as Trump has invited the Uzbek leader to be a guest at the G-20 summit in Miami.

Stronger diplomatic links are translating into trade and investment deals. In June, the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR) Ambassador Jamieson Greer visited Tashkent and signed “an early harvest of trade commitments to strengthen the bilateral economic and investment relationship.” Specifically, Tashkent committed “to eliminate or reduce tariffs” on U.S. industrial goods and agricultural products. In contrast, Washington committed “to provide favorable consideration” in tariff actions for Uzbekistan’s industrial goods and agricultural products. The two sides are also working to conclude an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade and Investment.

Also in June, the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation (DFC) launched the U.S.-Uzbekistan Joint Investment Platform, which will “aim to identify strategic investments in Uzbekistan for U.S.” in areas like energy, infrastructure, critical minerals, transportation and logistics infrastructure.

The topic of investment in critical minerals, energy, and transportation was also reportedly discussed during a meeting between Mirziyoyev and Sergio Gor, the U.S. special envoy for South and Central Asian affairs, on the sidelines of the recent Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan.

This activity builds upon the momentum of earlier deals. In 2025, Tashkent announced a $8.5 billion deal to buy as many as 22 Boeing 787 Dreamliner aircraft to modernize the country’s commercial aviation industry. The aircraft will allow direct, long-distance flights with the United States, increasing connectivity and tourism.

Investment now goes both ways, breaking stereotypes and assumptions of the U.S. being the only actor in the Central Asia-U.S. relationships that invests on the other side. The Uzbek company AFKA is building a manufacturing facility in Bowling Green, Kentucky. It will be the first Uzbek manufacturing company to operate in the U.S. The groundbreaking ceremony took place in July, and when complete, the AFKA Aluminum Solutions plant will employ 331 people, supporting the local economy and strengthening bilateral commercial ties.

Stronger economic links between the two governments occur at a time when Tashkent is looking to develop the entire country, not just the capital. For example, the historic city of Khiva is getting a face-lift through the expected construction of a conference hall, a 3-star hotel, and a reception house, which will create jobs and attract tourism. Plans also include building a toll road and a railway to connect the Urgench airport with Khiva. Other plans include modernizing regional airports to improve domestic and international connectivity.

As for Nukus, the capital of the Republic of Karakalpakstan, the goal is to upgrade the city’s public transportation via a loan from the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development.

From Washington’s perspective, there is a new race on to access resources like oil, gas, and especially critical minerals. Central Asia has been blessed with many of the resources that the world’s great powers desire. Central Asian governments like Uzbekistan view this situation not as a game or a race but as an opportunity to build new commercial partnerships and attract investors. While the Trump administration continues to focus on energy, minerals, and transportation infrastructure as vital areas for future investment and trade, Tashkent can hopefully also redirect U.S. interest to other projects and industries.

For example, during the November 2025 summit between Trump and the five Central Asian leaders, Washington pledged to explore “the expansion of a partnership in the upcoming sale and privatization of UzAuto Motors” in addition to a potential $3 billion investment from Air Products for a methanol production facility in Uzbekistan. The Uzbek government aims to generate 54 percent of its power from renewable sources by 2030. Washington and Tashkent hope to encourage U.S. companies to invest in this field.

There are limitations to consider, specifically the Jackson-Vanik Amendment, which denies permanent normal trade relations to Uzbekistan. To be fair, while the amendment irritates political relations, its impact on bilateral trade and investment is negligible. Tashkent has, for decades, received temporary normal trade relations through annual presidential waivers.

Moreover, even if U.S.-Uzbek trade grows considerably, it will still be dwarfed by trade between Uzbekistan and China, which reached between $7.7 and $8.9 billion in the first half of the year. Simply put, stronger U.S.-Uzbek trade and investment ties will not dramatically create a new architecture of priority partners for Uzbekistan.

There is also a domestic component to consider: Uzbekistan has the region’s largest population, with around 39 million (according to a new census), and a vast young workforce who deserve jobs and a future in their homeland. Unfortunately, a significant portion of the population lives below the poverty line, and unemployment is still problematic, more than a million Uzbeks migrate abroad for work every year.

As in many countries, wealth and development concentrate in the capital. While the examples of regional infrastructure development mentioned in this commentary are positive, a 2025 study conducted by the National Statistics Committee of Uzbekistan in collaboration with the World Bank showed that the largest numbers of poor residents were recorded in the Samarkand region (265,000 people), as well as in Fergana (239,000), Kashkadarya (238,000), and Andijan (214,000) regions.

In other words, Uzbekistan must invest more in infrastructure projects and economic growth across its regions, not just the capital.

In a September 3 speech, Mirziyoyev said a new system to reduce poverty and unemployment across the country will be introduced. This new strategy must be monitored to ensure it promotes employment and helps low-income individuals, rather than falling victim to bureaucratic incompetence or corruption.

As interest in Central Asia’s natural resources continues to grow, it is also important to understand the priorities of the five Central Asian governments. In Uzbekistan, the momentum is to diversify the country’s energy production and bring development to areas outside Tashkent. Washington and American industries must keep Tashkent’s priorities and objectives in mind to secure win-win contracts and agreements and ensure this partnership continues as the so-called race for critical minerals heats up.

For Uzbekistan’s population, particularly those living outside Tashkent, this stronger partnership must mean more jobs, economic growth, and a better quality of life.
tag: Boeing; U.S. investment in Central Asia; U.S.-Uzbekistan relations; U.S.-Uzbekistan trade; Uzbekistan investments in the U.S.

title: Micronesian Islands Meet Against Backdrop of Great Power Competition
description: Micronesian governments are elevating unilateral hedging efforts in forums like the MIF, in pursuit of a unified risk-management strategy and regional identity.
text:
From August 17 to 21, leaders and heads of delegation throughout the Micronesian subregion convened for the 28th Micronesian Islands Forum (MIF). Held in Pohnpei – one of four states of the Federated States of Micronesia (FSM) and home to a population of roughly 26,000 people – delegates met to discuss ongoing regional issues and identified areas for strategic collaboration under the theme “Promote Healthy Communities, Open Doors to Learning.”

I attended the MIF as the head of Delegation and Special Representative for the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands (CNMI), a non-sovereign United States territory. As great powers pursue their foreign policy agendas, the event in Pohnpei revealed a continuing trend often overlooked in the Pacific: Micronesian governments are elevating unilateral hedging efforts in forums like the MIF, in pursuit of a unified risk-management strategy and regional identity.

This year, the MIF met weeks before the more prominent Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) Leaders Meeting, which is being held in the neighboring Micronesian country of Palau from August 30 to September 4. Seated in the front row of the forum’s audience were senior members of the diplomatic corps posted in the FSM, including ambassadors representing Australia, China, and Japan, and the United States’ newest Chargé d’Affaires to Palikir, who arrived in the country just a week before the MIF.

The venue itself was striking: the State of Pohnpei Administrative Building and Governor’s Office, built by Beijing in 2007 and renovated last year by the Chinese government and state-owned contractors. The Federated States of Micronesia have had formal diplomatic relations with Beijing since 1989, and is the only U.S. Freely Associated State – all of which are located in Micronesia – that maintains such a relationship.

Chinese Ambassador to FSM Wu Wei speaks at the handover ceremony of the State of Pohnpei Administrative Building, Jan. 10, 2025. Photo courtesy of the Embassy of China in FSM.

China and the United States are not the only development partners competing in Pohnpei. Just two kilometers north of the Governor’s Office off the Dekehtik Causeway, Japan’s government is investing 4.6 billion yen ($30 million) in a project to expand the Pohnpei Port, the FSM’s primary maritime gateway. In the Pohnpeian outer island of Pingelap, Australia has financed a solar mini-grid and battery storage system for a geographically disconnected island community. These recent investments showcase the strategic importance of MIF member states to great powers and are not unique to FSM.

Officials from Japan, the State of Pohnpei, and the National Government of the Federated States of Micronesia break ground on the Pohnpei Port expansion project, Oct. 8, 2025. Photo courtesy of the Embassy of Japan in FSM.

Similar practices can be found elsewhere across Micronesia. Foreign direct investment, infrastructure improvements, and diplomatic engagement have become increasingly visible in a region where small island economies are often balancing relationships with several development partners at once. For Micronesia, these relationships are not necessarily mutually exclusive. The same governments that have maintained a historically close partnership with the United States can pursue infrastructure and development partnerships with Japan, Australia, China, and others, depending on domestic needs and priorities.

The discussions held at the MIF centered around the outcomes of the forum’s several standing committees, including the approval of resolutions focused on U.S. deep sea mining efforts in Micronesia, the development of competitive commercial fisheries in Guam and the CNMI, and the financial stability of the forum itself. The latter action was arguably the most important to the MIF, functioning as a soft call to attending development partners and multilateral institutions for financial support. Member states underscored the need for sustainable funding to support a permanent secretariat, lifting the planning and implementation burden off of any future host government. The emphasis on establishing a more permanent institutional structure comes as Micronesian states continue to navigate their role within the broader Pacific regional infrastructure.

Five years ago, five Micronesian countries initiated the formal process to withdraw from the PIF after their supported candidate for the forum’s secretary-general position – a diplomat from the Marshall Islands – lost the body’s vote. The region instead decided to look inward, pursuing the strengthening of subregional collaboration. After reformation efforts in 2022 and 2023, those Micronesian nations rejoined the PIF, with the forum being held in the subregion for the first time since the 49th PIF in Nauru (now spelled Naoero) in 2018.

The history of that split remains relevant to the MIF today. The forum’s renewed focus on institutional sustainability is not only an administrative concern, but part of a broader effort to ensure that Micronesian governments have a regional mechanism through which they can coordinate their interests. Concurrently, the subregion’s reintegration into the PIF underscores that a robust MIF serves to complement, rather than contradict, expansive Pacific multilateralism.

This year’s PIF meeting further highlights the diplomatic complexity of Micronesia. Palau is hosting the meeting, with the Marshall Islands among the Micronesian states participating in the forum. Both countries maintain official diplomatic ties and a close relationship with Taiwan. Their participation comes as Micronesian governments continue to maintain contrasting relationships with the great powers active across the subregion, even as they pursue greater coordination on issues of common interest.

The timing of this year’s MIF, held two weeks before the PIF Leaders Meeting, provided an opportunity for Micronesian governments to coordinate ahead of the larger regional gathering. The standing committee outcomes raised in Pohnpei can be carried into discussions and actionable lines of effort in Palau. The proximity of the two meetings is particularly relevant this year, as the PIF returns to Micronesia.

For the MIF, member states must work diligently to make the regional forum in its 28th iteration more durable. The return of Micronesian states to the Pacific Islands Forum has restored their participation in the broader Pacific community, while the continued development of the Micronesian Islands Forum provides a concentrated platform for Micronesia’s concerns. How effectively the forum can maintain that balance will largely depend on whether its members and development partners can provide the resources required to sustain it.

The attention surrounding this year’s meetings suggests that the stakes are becoming higher. Micronesia is receiving more development assistance and greater strategic interest from external powers. As ministers, diplomats, and development partners switch gears from Pohnpei to Palau, and as U.S. Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau leads Washington’s delegation to the 55th PIF, one thing remains clear: all eyes are on Micronesia.

title: Mohan Malik on Trump, Asia, and the Legacy of the Global War on Terror
description: The veteran strategist and security analyst joins Beyond The Mekong to discuss the region's ongoing security challenges.
text:
Mohan Malik is a veteran China-Asia analyst and military strategist who has advised senior brass on geopolitics at the U.S. Defense Department’s Asia-Pacific Center for Security Studies and is a former director of Defence Studies at Deakin University in Australia.

Malik spoke with The Diplomat’s Luke Hunt, his former student, about how China, Asia, and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) are shaping up as U.S. President Donald Trump prepares for the mid-term elections and as the world marks 25 years since the 9/11 attacks that spawned the Global War on Terror.

Also known as the 9/11 Wars, the Global War on Terror ended with the withdrawal of U.S.-led forces from Afghanistan five years ago. Left behind was a vastly different geopolitical landscape, whose ramifications have continued to influence diplomacy in China, Asia, and ASEAN to this day.

ASEAN is divided between maritime and mainland countries but also by religion, mainly Buddhism, Christianity, and Islam, and Malik says they are still confronted by major problems. But some nations emerged from the 9/11 Wars stronger than others.

“Thailand, Indonesia, and India in South Asia, to some extent Sri Lanka to Bangladesh have done relatively better, they have been able to manage, contain the threat of domestic terrorism,” he said.

China also emerged in a stronger position and is now facing headwinds from the Trump administration and perhaps ASEAN, which wants to finalize its Code of Conduct in the South China Sea with Beijing by the end of this year.

“Even if Code of Conduct is concluded it’s not going to stop China’s creation of artificial islands and militarization of those artificial islands,” Malik said.

“It’s going to provide greater legitimacy to China’s efforts to subdue Southeast Asian countries and other rival claimants to the South China Sea.”
tag: Code of Conduct for the South China Sea; South China Sea disputes; Southeast Asia security; Southeast Asia war on terror; U.S. Global War on Terror

title: Mongolia’s New Government Set Ambitious Goals. But Are They Realistic?
description: Data centers, the Sovereign Wealth Fund, and a hydropower plant – will any of it better the lives of Mongolian people?
text:
On September 15, Mongolia’s parliament, the State Great Khural, began its autumn session – and it started full throttle. The incumbent government headed by Prime Minister Uchral Nyam-Osor has an ambitious agenda that saw it propose one of the largest state budgets. Among its goals: establishing a sovereign wealth fund, securing energy from China, and building data centers. Parliament will likely scrutinize many of these big initiatives.

The State Great Khural has much to decide, but it is operating within a highly politically divided environment. Mongolia is still wrangling with government instability that began with the ousting of Oyun-Erdene Luvsannamsrai’s administration in June 2025. Uchral’s government only took office on March 31 of this year – less than six months ago.

When parliament convened on September 15, the new government revealed one of the largest state budget proposals in Mongolia’s history, asking for 41.3 trillion tugrik, with a deficit of 2.3 trillion tugrik. Economists and skeptics worry that, with inflation standing at 12.5 percent, such a large deficit will only increase Mongolia’s debt, forcing the government to increase taxes on businesses and individuals. The state budget proposal has already faced massive scrutiny within the parliamentary committees. In a warning sign for Uchral’s government, parliament failed to reach the required quorum last week.

One of the major issues with the 2027 state budget proposal is the 2.3 trillion tugrik deficit. One of the solutions the Uchral government proposed is to utilize the increased Oyu Tolgoi dividend.

On September 11, Mongolia and Rio Tinto agreed to amend the Oyu Tolgoi contract, the Shareholder’s Agreement that was first established 17 years ago. The amendment will allow Mongolia to receive 13 trillion tugrik, approximately $3.6 billion. Uchral also announced that Rio Tinto agreed to reduce operational costs by approximately 30 trillion tugrik, an equivalent of $8.4 billion.

While the Mongolian parliament has to review another state budget amid the constant changes of government, a second issue that will face major scrutiny is the establishment of Mongolia’s Sovereign Wealth Fund. Under the Oyun-Erdene administration, in 2024, the Parliament of Mongolia passed new laws on a Sovereign Wealth Fund. In February 2026, just before it was forced from office, the Zandanshatar Gombojav government signed a preliminary agreement with companies to allocate 60 percent of the benefits from Mongolia’s strategic deposits to the Sovereign Wealth Fund as a new profit-sharing mechanism meant to benefit the public.

The current trajectory and the goal of the Sovereign Wealth Fund, however, may have pivoted from Mongolia’s welfare system, which would have directly benefited the public. The fund is now leaning more toward a corporate governance structure.

The initiative is now part of a larger reform in Mongolia’s state-owned companies. To support this reform, on September 10, Mongolia signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with the U.S.-based BlackRock Financial Markets Advisory. BlackRock and the Mongolian government outlined a general framework that looks to explore selling shares in state-owned enterprises in both domestic and international capital markets.

After the MoU was signed, critics asked whether BlackRock’s corporate model – the restructuring of Mongolia’s state-owned enterprises – aligns with the country’s semi-welfare system. The government will need to have access to those funds to provide public assistance to the elderly, the disabled, children, the poor, and for public education and health. These welfare systems are indeed at the heart of Mongolian society today.

In 2025, Mongolia experienced intermittent protests and strikes from educators and medical workers, demanding a pay raise. If the Uchral government fails to deliver these promises, this wealth fund policy and priority changes will have a great impact on the Mongolian people who depend on these funds.

Beyond the financial wrangling, the issue of energy security looms over Mongolia. The Iran-U.S. war has roiled global energy markets, as have repeated Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy infrastructure. Mongolia is uniquely dependent on Russia for fuel, importing over 95 percent of refined petroleum products from its northern neighbor. When Russian supply dwindled, Mongolia felt the pinch. In the summer and fall of 2026, nationwide fuel shortages highlighted the country’s vulnerability and pushed policymakers to seek an additional source: China. In September, delegates from the Ministry of Industry and Mineral Resources held bilateral meetings with China National Petroleum Corporation (CNPC) to discuss importing 10,000 tonnes of refined petroleum, 4,000 tonnes of jet fuel, and 3,000 tonnes of diesel.

Moreover, China is currently financing one of Mongolia’s first hydropower plants, Erdeneburen Project in Khovd province. With a Chinese soft loan line of approximately $288 million, the construction contract was awarded to Engineering, Procurement, and Construction (EPC) and PowerChina in 2023.

In mid-September, Mongolian President Khurelsukh Ukhnaa and officials inspected the progress on the construction of the Erdeneburen Hydropower Plant. The Office of the President announced that the project is now 40 percent complete. When finished, the plant will have the capacity to supply reliable electricity to five provinces, including Khovd, Bayan-Ulgii, Uvs, Zavkhan, and Govi Altai.

Considering Mongolia’s energy infrastructure, combined with the landlocked challenges, full energy independence may not be in the cards as a short or medium term goal. That said, managing fuel shortages by reaching out to diverse global partners is in the national interest. Even prior to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Mongolia experienced intermittent energy shortages, which motivated the government to seek third-neighbor investments and diversify energy sources.

In August, Mongolia’s Deputy Prime Minister Dorjkhand Togmid announced Mongolia’s interest in building data centers in connection with accelerating Mongolia’s renewable energy sources. While the initiative is an attempt to kill two birds with one stone, even before discussing investment opportunities, Mongolia will need to decide how to handle data centers’ demand not only for energy, but for water.

According to the Brookings Institution, “A typical data center uses 300,000 gallons of water each day… but large data centers can use an estimated 5 million gallons of water each day.” The study warned: “Building a new facility and pledging economic impact mean little without sustainably incorporating water resources into ongoing operations.”

In 2025, an OECD study on water resources highlighted Mongolia’s water scarcity. Mongolia’s geographic disparities as well as surface water distribution make constructing – let alone maintaining – data centers a highly questionable endeavor.

The Uchral government is viewing China’s data centers in Inner Mongolia as a template and following the global trend. However, despite the similarities in wind and solar capacity and the cold climate, the water issue is one of the most important areas that needs to be scrutinized before Mongolia moves forward.

The State Great Khural has entered another highly politicized season with much to resolve. Unfortunately, the internal feud within the Mongolian People’s Party (MPP) will continue to weaken the parliament’s function. The MPP, the nominal ruling party with 68 total seats, is now effectively divided into two blocs of 30 and 38 legislators.

The Uchral government’s proposals are supposed to bring Mongolia economic prosperity and development, but without truly addressing the long-standing challenges of corruption, air pollution, water shortages, and energy security, the people’s confidence in governance remains extremely fragile. What the Mongolian people need is lawmakers and a government that prioritize the well-being of its citizens – not political vendettas.

title: Mongolia’s President at the SCO Summit
description: For Mongolia, the highlights were the bilateral meetings held on the sidelines with Kyrgyzstan, China, and Russia.
text:
Mongolian President Khurelsukh Ukhnaa is attending the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Council of Heads of State in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan as the organization recognizes its 25th anniversary. While the SCO spent much of its existence focused on security and regional cooperation, the Bishkek Declaration demonstrates a much larger global agenda. Mongolia, in the new partner state status, is seeking deeper ties with SCO member states in emerging sectors via robust bilateral links.

For example, Khurelsukh and Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov, the summit’s host, held bilateral talks to accelerate political, economic, and trade relations under the Comprehensive Partnership Agreement that was signed during Khurelsukh’s state visit to Bishkek in 2025.

Mongolia and Kyrgyzstan are aiming to boost regional trade turnover to $100 million. During Khurelsukh’s remarks, he noted the trade volume between the two countries had grown from $2.6 million in 2023 to $19 million as of 2025. The Mongolian side expressed interest in further Kyrgyz investments and joint projects in developing industries, minerals exploration, transport and logistics, and direct flights.

Mongolia’s interim free trade agreement with the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) creates additional trade opportunities for the two countries. Kyrgyzstan will be chairing the EAEU in 2027.

But there were more leaders in Bishkek than just Japarov. For Mongolia, the SCO Summit was a valuable opportunity for face-to-face diplomacy as the world faces major geopolitical and economic challenges.

On August 31, Khurelsukh held bilateral talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping. During their meeting, Xi reiterated Beijing’s long-term support for Mongolia as close neighbors and promised to support “win-win cooperation.”

Mongolia and China discussed opportunities to expand cooperation in emerging sectors such as green minerals, AI, digital economy, and supporting Mongolia’s efforts in combating desertification and climate issues. According to the Mongolian presidential office, Khurelsukh and Xi discussed several projects that are underway, including China’s support for the operation of the Erdeneburen Hydropower Plant, a long-stalled mega-project that received new life in 2022.

Xi and Khurelsukh also discussed the need to make progress on constructing the Shiveekhuren-Sekhee, Bichigt-Zuunkhatavch, Khangi-Mandal railways which are crucial to the countries’ bilateral economic activities.

Moreover, one of the most important discussion points was China’s willingness to continue exporting petroleum product supplies to Mongolia amid fuel shortages triggered by supply disruptions from Russia. The two sides are currently aiming for Mongolia to import 71,000 tons of petroleum product per month from China.

More broadly, Xi promised to support Mongolia’s fuel industry, and cooperate in the exploration of oil and gas, a key priority for Mongolia as it seeks to address its energy dependencies.

While China is a leading investor in Mongolia’s mining sector, it has yet to allocate investments into the renewable energy sector. Considering Mongolia’s push to transition to renewable energy and diversify its energy sources, Beijing’s contribution will be crucial in the coming years.

Khurelsukh also met with Russian President Vladimir Putin while in Bishkek. During the meeting, Putin reiterated the historic links between Mongolia and Russia. He expressed hope that Ulaanbaatar’s interim free trade agreement with the EAEU will provide “preferential treatment for Mongolian traditional exports across the customs territory of our association.”

Moreover, Putin highlighted that Mongolia – previously an observer in the SCO – now will receive “partner state” status. Last year, the SCO streamlined its various levels of participation to just two: full members and partner states. Mongolia thus became a partner state along with other states previously recognized as observer states. The debate on whether Mongolia should join the SCO as a full member has been a hot topic among scholars and policymakers in the last decade.

The Khurelsukh-Putin summit was also attended by the Russian energy minister and president of Rosatom, Russia’s nuclear power corporation. Rosatom’s leader reportedly met with Mongolian partners to discuss small modular nuclear reactors as a way to diversify Mongolia’s energy mix.

According to Russia’s Pivot to Asia official website, “Mongolia is reviewing a proposal from the Russian state nuclear corporation to build a small modular nuclear reactor in the country, which may be built near New Kharkhorum, a planned new capital city located about 230 kilometers west of Ulaanbaatar.”

Following Khurelsukh’s high-level meetings with both Xi and Putin, separately, Xi and Putin resumed high-stakes negotiations on the construction of Power of Siberia 2, a long-discussed gas pipeline that would bring LNG from Russia’s Yamal gas fields to China via Mongolia.

According to Pipeline Technology Journal, “Kremlin foreign policy aide Yury Ushakov confirmed Friday that the flagship energy project will feature prominently during talks in Bishkek.” Ushakov added that discussions will continue at the Eastern Economic Forum currently underway in Vladivostok, where Chinese Vice Premier Ding Xuexiang will meet with Russian officials.

Russia is keen to export more gas to China, and Mongolia has welcomed the construction of the pipeline. However, China has been driving a hard bargain on pricing, especially as it moves away from fossil fuels toward renewable energy.

There was no China-Mongolia-Russia trilateral meeting scheduled in Bishkek. However, Mongolian Prime Minister Uchral Nyam-Osor is in Vladivostok through September 4, so trilateral talks might be resumed there.

The three heads of state gathered last year in Beijing shortly after the 2025 SCO summit in nearby Tianjin. At that meeting, Mongolia emphasized the importance of trilateral cooperation and reaffirmed its commitment to jointly implementing the projects and programs outlined in the Economic Corridor Construction Program.

As evidenced by the Bishkek Declaration, the SCO is setting itself up as a much larger player in global political, economic, and security arenas. As SCO member states encompass approximately 42 percent of the global population, SCO-linked global governance, multipolarity, and economic and trade are set to expand in the organization’s next 25 years.

While Mongolia’s participation in this year’s SCO in Bishkek has been primarily economically motivated, Ulaanbaatar is aware of the shifts in global geopolitics. Mongolia engagement in the SCO is underpinned by its bilateral relationships: comprehensive strategic partnerships with Russia, China, Kyrgyzstan, and Uzbekistan, coupled with strategic partnership frameworks with other SCO members such as India and Kazakhstan. In all of these relationship, Mongolia envisions greater cooperation in emerging critical sectors and seeks to strengthen the country’s political, economic, and cultural capital. Ulaanbaatar can achieve that through robust bilateral links without having to a commit to the SCO as an organization.

title: North Korean Elites and Regime Weakness
description: Insights from Jieun Baek.
text:
The Diplomat author Mercy Kuo regularly engages subject-matter experts, policy practitioners, and strategic thinkers across the globe for their diverse insights into U.S. Asia policy. This conversation with Dr. Jieun Baek – author of “Privileged but Powerless: How North Korean Elite Grievances Reveal the Regime’s Greatest Weakness” (Yale 2026) – is the 525th in “The Trans-Pacific View Insight Series.”

Describe the key characteristics of North Korea’s elites.

North Korea officially rejects the idea that it has an elite class, yet it is one of the world’s most stratified societies. Its elites include Korean Workers’ Party cadres, intellectuals, senior military and security officials, and individuals personally close to Kim Jong Un. The traditional elite largely inherits status through favorable songbun [North Korea’s hierarchical classification system], family history, and proven political loyalty. A newer unofficial elite – the donju, or “masters of money” – derives influence from capital, markets, and connections.

These groups are not monolithic, but they share one defining characteristic: their positions help maintain the regime. In return, they may receive Pyongyang residency, superior housing and education, better food, prestigious employment and education, overseas opportunities, and access to luxury goods – European watches, imported cosmetics, pet poodles.

None of this is discreet. The regime stages elite reward deliberately. When the Kyongru-dong neighborhood opened, officials framed the new housing not as a public good but as the deserved inheritance of those whose loyalty had earned them “the best of civilization.”

Yet every privilege is conditional. Elites must continuously demonstrate political reliability, professional usefulness, and personal loyalty to Kim. And the most privileged are also the most closely watched: privilege and surveillance rise together.

Examine why North Korean elites are “privileged but powerless.”

North Korean elites possess influence, wealth, and access unimaginable to most citizens, but they lack the most basic power over their own lives. They cannot safely criticize policy, organize independently, protect their families from guilt by association, or know whether today’s privilege will survive tomorrow’s purge. Even the most senior officials can be demoted, imprisoned, or executed without due process, like Jang Song Thaek in 2013.

Their proximity to power actually creates additional danger. Elites face intense surveillance, mandatory ideological activity, extractive “loyalty” contributions, workplace rivalries, and constant evaluation. Thae Yong Ho, the most senior North Korean diplomat to defect in years, put it with characteristic economy: “The closer you are to the Sun, the higher the chances you will burn.” Several escapees told me middle-ranking posts felt safer than the apex.

They may supervise institutions or control substantial resources, but they cannot challenge the system that grants those privileges. As one elite escapee told me, they are “disposable slaves to Kim Jong Un.” They are powerful downward, toward those beneath them, but powerless upward, before the Leader.

Analyze the correlation between North Korean elite “feigned fealty” and the erosion of elite loyalty to Kim Jong Un’s regime.

North Korean public life is a carefully directed performance. Elites attend rallies, recite ideological texts, participate in self-criticism sessions, and display intense devotion. But visible obedience should not be mistaken for sincere belief.

One interviewee described this perfectly through an anecdote. Inspectors would arrive at his home in white gloves to check the portraits of the Kim leaders, hunting for a speck of dust that could bring serious consequences down on his family. He cleaned those portraits, he told me, not out of reverence but out of self-preservation.

As depicted in the table below, “Feigned fealty” describes that widening gap between low inward loyalty and high outward loyalty. Many elites perform devotion because doing so protects their careers, families, status, and lives. This is preference falsification under extreme coercion: everyone plays a role, while few can know what others truly believe.

Source: “Privileged but Powerless: How North Korean Elite Grievances Reveal the Regime’s Greatest Weakness,” (Yale University Press 2026), Jieun Baek.

The gap appears to be widening under Kim Jong Un. Elite defections have increased dramatically; younger elites prioritize money, business, foreign study, and opportunities for their children over service to the Party; and many privately favor economic reform and greater access to information. The regime’s elaborate demands for loyalty reveal not confidence, but anxiety. A system sustained by genuine conviction is resilient. One sustained by surveillance, rewards, and fear may look stable until a shock exposes how shallow its support has become.

Identify the five options for North Korean elites with grievances.

Aggrieved elites have five primary options.

First, they can maintain the status quo and do nothing. This is the least immediately dangerous and most rational choice, but it allows resentment and distrust to accumulate beneath the surface.

Second, they can defect and seek asylum abroad. Defection is an unequivocal rejection of the regime, but it carries extraordinary risks for escapees and their families.

Third, they can erode the regime’s monopoly over resources by building alternative power structures. Markets, private food production, solar energy, informal finance, tutoring, communications, housing, and healthcare can gradually reduce dependence on the state.

Fourth, they can engage in dissent – from coded criticism and hidden transcripts, to use James C. Scott’s concept, and subtle defiance to clandestine information sharing or organized resistance.

Fifth, they can push for democratization and systemic reform. This is the most ambitious and dangerous option because it requires trust, coordination, and first movers willing to confront enormous barriers to collective action.

Assess the role of North Korean elite grievances in revealing the regime’s greatest weakness and its implications for U.S., European, and Asian policymakers and geopolitical strategists.

The regime’s greatest strength and greatest weakness are the same: its dependence on elites. Elites are its architects, administrators, financiers, enforcers, and protectors. The broader population can be controlled through isolation and terror, but the regime must continuously manage elites through a delicate combination of privilege, surveillance, and coercion. If elite allegiance fractures, the system’s foundation begins to crack.

Policymakers should therefore look beyond missile tests and leadership imagery to study elite incentives, generational change, defections, market activity, information consumption, and signs of preference falsification. They should avoid assuming that elite dissatisfaction will automatically produce reform; North Korea’s barriers to trust and collective action remain formidable.

They should also avoid inadvertently improving the regime’s capacity to reward loyalty. Hard-currency access, prestige projects, and engagement channels the state can capture are redirected into patronage for insiders. Sanctions design and diplomatic sweeteners deserve to be tested against that standard.

The United States, Europe, South Korea, Japan, and other partners should expand secure access to outside information, combining radio and portable media with technologies that circumvent censorship. North Korean escapees should lead content creation so that it is credible, tailored, and safe for intended audiences. Governments should also protect escapees, strengthen pathways for asylum, document elite testimony, and support decentralized economic and information networks that reduce the state’s monopoly over daily life.

Finally, strategists must prepare for multiple futures, including gradual liberalization, elite-led reform, succession instability, or sudden internal shock. North Korea may appear immovable, but a regime that requires constant performances of loyalty is revealing its fear: that when people are finally free to choose, many of its most privileged citizens may choose something else.

title: North Korea’s Ukraine POWs Are Now in South Korea. What Comes Next?
description: Both the South Korean government and the two former soldiers face an unprecedented resettlement process.
text:
The immediate fate of two North Korean prisoners-of-war captured by Ukrainian forces is no longer in question, but the saga is not yet over.

Ukraine has transferred custody of the pair to South Korea in what was perhaps a predictable outcome given their reported desire not to return to North Korea. However, the circumstances surrounding the disclosure have introduced new political dynamics to the situation. Now, both the South Korean government and the two former soldiers face an unprecedented resettlement process.

Kyiv first announced that it had captured the two North Korean soldiers in January 2025, immediately prompting questions of what would come of the pair. The legal provisions surrounding their eventual disposition were complicated. International rules pointed toward repatriating them with other POWs to Russia. Before the capture happened, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said it was his government’s position that all POWs in Ukrainian custody would receive the same treatment.

The two soldiers, however, reportedly expressed fear of repatriation and a desire to defect to South Korea. Given the Kim Jong Un regime’s publicized insistence that soldiers kill themselves rather than be captured, returning to North Korea could have exposed them to reprisals for allowing themselves to be taken into Ukrainian custody. Under the principle of non-refoulement, the potential risk of persecution, torture, or other serious human rights violations if the soldiers were ultimately repatriated to North Korea was a necessary consideration.

The South Korean government stepped in early with offers to take the POWs into their custody. With advocacy stretching back to the previous Yoon Suk-yeol administration, there was little doubt over Seoul’s desired outcome for the two individuals.

What is now evident is that the two governments came to a confidential agreement to transfer the custody of the POWs. The handover reportedly took place ahead of the U.N. General Assembly debates, and the two former soldiers are now in South Korean government care. Details of this arrangement first came to light via Zelenskyy himself.

During his speech at the U.N. General Assembly, the Ukrainian president captured international attention when he revealed that Ukraine had transferred custody of the two POWs to South Korea. In the speech, he noted that “these guys are not easy to capture alive,” adding that one of the soldiers, “when he realized he was going to be taken prisoner, tried to kill himself.” Zelenskyy’s disclosure came unilaterally and without warning to the South Korean government.

Kyiv’s decision to reveal information despite the confidential arrangement created a diplomatic problem with Seoul, but it also served a clear Ukrainian purpose. Kyiv’s intelligence has repeatedly claimed that the Kremlin is seeking an additional 30,000-50,000 North Korean troops to support a new offensive. Zelenskyy therefore used the U.N. General Assembly debates as a platform to highlight the Kim regime’s continued support for Russia’s war effort and to put North Korea’s military involvement back on the international agenda.

But Zelenskyy’s announcement caused a stir in South Korean domestic politics. Opposition lawmakers immediately chastised the Lee Jae-myung administration for not disclosing the transfer. Some argued that the government was withholding details out of fear of how North Korea may react.

Lee took to social media to push back against this criticism. He said that there was an agreement to keep the transfer confidential, expressing that it was “deeply regrettable” that the Ukraine side released details on the matter. He added that publicly disclosing the successful repatriation could have helped boost approval ratings, but it would not have been right to risk “someone’s life or the national interest” for one’s “own petty benefit.”

There are political reasons why some in the Lee administration may have sought to avoid disclosing information about the POW transfer. The government has been working to rekindle any form of inter-Korean engagement, and some policy groups within Seoul have warned that North Korea could react strongly to the decision.

However, such concerns may be unfounded. North Korean state media has not commented on the POWs since their reported capture, and there are much more significant sticking points between the two Koreas; namely, Pyongyang’s preconditions that Seoul must drop unification and denuclearization as policy objectives. Since Zelenskyy’s announcement, the only reporting from Pyongyang directed toward the South Korean government has been a statement attributed to Foreign Minister Choe Son Hui on a familiar issue: reiterating the Kim regime’s position that denying the reality of North Korea’s nuclear weapon status “is to give up the future.”

Meanwhile, from a security perspective, there are justifiable concerns related to the information disclosure. There have been North Korean assassination attempts against South Korea-based defectors in the past. The most prominent recent example occurred in a 2011 incident in which a North Korean agent attempted to kill prominent defector-turned-activist Park Sang-hak with a poison needle.

The two POWs could therefore present a different security challenge from the average North Korean defector. Their firsthand knowledge of North Korean involvement in the Russia-Ukraine War means that there is a reasonable risk that they could become targets of elimination efforts.

Given the confidential nature of the South Korea-Ukraine agreement, there are few details on what comes next for the two former soldiers. There may have been an understanding that they will remain in custody until the conclusion of the war, or Kyiv may have conceded that South Korea can treat the individuals as they would any other defector. This would affect how long the individuals remain in the government’s custody.

Whatever the length of their initial detention in South Korea, the eventual next step will be resettlement.

Resettlement can be difficult for any defector. New arrivals generally undergo a months-long program at the Hanawon resettlement facility under the Ministry of Unification’s remit, and it includes tasks such as teaching individuals about South Korean customs and courtesies, how to manage bank accounts and finances, and finding employment.

Upon completion of the resettlement process, they are then given relocation assistance to a new residence somewhere in the country. There, they are typically assigned a local officer – either a Ministry of Unification, Korean National Police, or National Intelligence Service (NIS) official – to continue supporting their transition process and to contact in the event of any issues.

The system is different for higher profile or high-risk defectors. They may be former senior North Korean officials like Thae Yong Ho, or figures such as Park Sang-hak who have used their newfound freedom to lead civic movements in protest of the Kim regime. In those cases, the individuals can remain in NIS protective custody until officials determine that it is safe for them to return to public life. Even then, there may be continued protection services.

The two former soldiers transferred from Ukraine will likely fall into that latter category, particularly with the amount of media coverage they have received.

Thus, the arrival of the two North Korean soldiers to South Korea resolves the most immediate question surrounding their fate, but the next steps remain dynamic. The situation has now entered a new phase where South Korean politics will continue to scrutinize the issue as the government works to navigate an unprecedented resettlement process.

title: Okinawa Voted for a New Governor
description: Koja Genta didn't win because of his stance on U.S. bases. He won because of his vision for the economy.
text:
On September 13, Japan’s Okinawa Prefecture held its gubernatorial election. Koja Genta, a 42-year-old former mayor of Naha City, emerged with a convincing victory – 59 percent (423,124 votes) to 38 percent (276,060 votes) – against incumbent Governor Denny Tamaki.

His election can create genuine – and long overdue – momentum to transform the relationship between the Japanese government and Okinawa from the confrontation over U.S. bases in the prefecture into a partnership to move Okinawa forward.

As a home to the U.S. Marines Third Expeditionary Force (III MEF) headquarters, local elections in Okinawa from the governor’s race on down always attract not only national attention but also a great deal of interest from the U.S. defense establishment. With the ongoing plan to realign and consolidate the U.S. Marine Corps’ presence in Okinawa, Sunday’s election was particularly critical.

As a governor, Koja has a profile that is different from any of his predecessors. First and foremost, at the age of 42, he is the youngest governor that Okinawa has ever elected. Born in 1983, he is also the first governor who was born after Okinawa reverted to Japan in 1972.

Furthermore, while he was born and grew up in Okinawa, he spent his formative years as a young adult in Tokyo as a college student, a civil servant at the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications, and a program manager in the private sector.

His profile – born and grew up in Okinawa but left his hometown for mainland Japan for higher education and employment before returning to Okinawa to run for office – crystallizes the economic challenge that the working-age generation in Okinawa has long been facing. Okinawa’s economy lacks diversity; it is heavily dependent on tourism. This makes employment in the prefecture more seasonal and temporary in nature. Furthermore, while its aging population continues to create greater demand for workers in senior living management, medical assistants, and nursing, there are far fewer opportunities for high-skilled and well-paying jobs.

The local economy makes it challenging for the working-age population, especially younger people, to live in Okinawa and raise families. Its unemployment rate is twice as high as the national average, with persistent structural unemployment.

Mindful of this reality, Koja placed vitalization of the Okinawan economy front and center in his election campaign. His landslide victory – he earned the most votes in 40 out of 41 localities in Okinawa – demonstrates that Koja’s message of moving the Okinawan economy forward resonated much more than Tamaki’s message, which attempted to campaign by continuing to tap anti-base sentiment within the prefecture.

This election exposed a clear generational divide. The exit polls showed that over 60 percent of voters younger than 60 years old voted for Koja, while Tamaki continued to retain strong support among older constituents. That said, this split should not be reduced to a simplistic contest between “younger” vs. “older” Okinawans, let alone the stereotypical explanation of the younger generation being “pro-base” because they see a greater threat from China while the older generation remains “anti-base” due to their memories of the Battle of Okinawa and its tragic ending.

Kaja’s victory reflects a much deeper shift in priorities among Okinawans. For many voters in their working and family-raising years, kitchen-table issues – such as stagnant incomes, inflation, lack of well-paying employment and the island’s overall economic prospects – have become much more urgent than repeating political battles over U.S. bases. Those long-running political fights have produced little practical change, let alone improvement in the local economy. Exit polls clearly demonstrated this unmistakable shift, with a greater percentage of the voters identifying “economic growth” as their top issue of concern.

Still, Koja’s position on relocating Marine Corps Air Station Futenma to Henoko – as agreed to by the U.S. and Japanese governments back in 1996 – is significant. Koja argued that his acceptance of the existing relocation plan is not an endorsement of Okinawa’s disproportionate base burden. Rather, he insisted that the fastest, most practical way to eliminate the risk posed by Futenma is to work with the government to ensure the completion of the relocation.

Koja ran on a practical platform of a three-pronged approach: complete the relocation to Henoko, demand that Tokyo establish a credible return date for the land currently occupied by Futenma and additional land south of Kadena Air Force Base, and begin planning for how to utilize the property upon return.

What comes next should be the center of the new administration’s agenda. The eventual return of Futenma and other U.S. facilities south of Kadena Air Base presents Okinawa with a rare development opportunity. Land-use decisions, transportation links, housing, education, research, tourism, and private investment cannot be improvised after the fences come down. Koja should convene municipalities, residents, businesses, universities, and the national government to produce a transparent redevelopment strategy with timelines, financing, and measurable benefits for local communities. If managed well, base consolidation can become not merely a security adjustment but a catalyst for higher productivity and durable growth.

With Koja’s election, Okinawa will have a governor who has the backing not only from the ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) and its coalition partner Nippon Ishin no Kai (the Japan Innovation Party) but also from other conservative and center-right political parties that endorsed Koja during the election. This allows the Takaichi government to attempt a “reset” of Tokyo’s relationship with Naha under Governor Koja as a partner.

However, as tempting as it may be for the Japanese government to intensify its push toward completing the long-stalled Futenma relocation, Tokyo must first understand the drivers behind Koja’s decisive victory. In other words, Tokyo needs to appreciate the reality that Koja’s convincing victory reflects more than a change of administration. It is a reflection of a strong public demand for a new direction for Okinawa, especially in its economy.

Koja’s landslide is therefore not a blank check. It is a mandate for results: reduce the danger at Futenma, complete the relocation without further unnecessary delay, return the land on a dependable schedule, and convert that land into opportunity for Okinawans. The voters have chosen a younger leader who promised to move forward. His success will depend on whether every party to the agreement now does the same.

title: On Taiwan, US ‘Strategic Ambiguity’ Is Not Dead Yet
description: What look like indications of U.S. abandonment of Taiwan are relatively superficial, while substantive investment in capabilities that could deter China continues apace.
text:
Under the longstanding policy of “strategic ambiguity,” the U.S. government has refused to say ahead of time whether or not it would send American forces to help defend Taiwan against an attack from China. Some analysts say the Trump administration has rendered this policy ineffective by generating doubt that U.S. forces would intervene.

To cite just one example, the title of a September 14 analysis by columnist James Crabtree in Foreign Policy proclaimed that “Trump is killing ‘strategic ambiguity’ over Taiwan.” Crabtree argued that based on “signals from Washington,” the United States is “inching more toward a position of nonintervention.” Similarly, geopolitical risk analyst Shahn Louis said “the era” of strategic ambiguity “is over.” Michael Schiffer, a former U.S. deputy assistant secretary of defense for East Asia, argued that “strategic ambiguity is no longer a sustainable or effective policy.”

Multiple opinion polls show the belief among Taiwan’s people that the United States would ride to the rescue has decreased since 2025. The reasons for this loss of credibility are not hard to find.

Trump has repeatedly made four points about Taiwan, all of which call into question a robust U.S. response to military action by Beijing. The first is that Taiwan is vastly smaller and less important than China. Second, he says Taiwan is indefensible – too close to China and far from the United States. Third, Trump thinks Taiwan free-rides on U.S. defense. Finally, he complains about Taiwan allegedly stealing America’s semiconductor industry. Shortly before he took office for the second time, Trump said he would respond to a Chinese invasion of Taiwan with economic sanctions.

On top of this, Trump avoids antagonizing Beijing over the Taiwan issue, presumably to clear the way for a China-U.S. bilateral economic deal. During his keynote speech at the 2026 Shangri-La Dialogue, U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth did not mention Taiwan, a change from his speech the previous year. The unclassified version of the 2026 U.S. National Defense Strategy also does not mention Taiwan by name.

After his May 2026 meeting with Xi Jinping, Trump criticized the Taiwan government for allegedly flirting with independence due to the presumption of U.S. support. “[W]e’re not looking to have somebody say, ‘Let’s go independent because the United States is backing us,’” he told Fox News.

For good measure, Trump announced that he was delaying a large arms sale to Taiwan already approved by Congress, calling such sales a “very good negotiating chip” in talks with China. He also dismissed the Six Assurances, part of U.S. policy toward Taiwan since the Reagan era.

The idea that strategic ambiguity has lost its usefulness, however, is wrong. Despite particular statements by Trump that are adverse to Taiwan, U.S. policy remains broadly supportive of Taipei.

The Pentagon’s 2026 National Defense Strategy said the United States will “erect” and “sustain a strong denial defense along the First Island Chain.” Even a cursory look at a map indicates that aspiration is meaningless without a U.S. intent to prevent China from absorbing Taiwan.

The large arms sale is delayed, but not canceled. This latest package of armaments is all business, not symbolic. It includes weapons systems appropriate for the scenario of an attempted amphibious invasion by the People’s Liberation Army (PLA): HIMARS rockets, ATACMS missiles, ALTIUS loitering munition drones, Javelin and TOW anti-tank missiles, and mobile howitzers.

U.S. military transits through the Taiwan Strait continue, albeit about half as often as during Trump’s first term.

U.S. security cooperation with the Philippines and Japan, highly relevant to deterring China from moving aggressively against Taiwan, has deepened during the second Trump administration.

The United States got access to, and set aside funding to develop infrastructure in, additional base sites in the northern Philippines, close to the Taiwan Strait. The annual Balikatan military exercises were larger than ever before in 2025 and 2026 and brought in Japan and Australia. U.S. forces deployed NMESIS and Typhon missile systems to the Philippines. The stridency of China’s complaints about these deployments indicate they present problems for Chinese planners.

Washington’s plan to upgrade U.S. Forces Japan to a joint force combat headquarters has proceeded under Trump’s second administration. U.S. and Japanese armed forces increased their interoperability in 2025 and 2026 through more integrated command-and-control structures, more complex joint exercises, and more sharing of data. The United States started supplying Tomahawk cruise missiles to Japan. Washington and Tokyo are engaged in serious discussions about Japan producing warships or components for the U.S. Navy to help it close the gap with China’s production.

Strategic ambiguity still holds because what look like indications of U.S. abandonment of Taiwan are relatively superficial, while substantive investment in capabilities that could deter China continues apace.

The stances of the Joe Biden presidency and the second Trump administration are different. Biden said on four occasions that the United States would militarily intervene in a cross-strait war, placing him close to an unambiguous pre-commitment to intervention. Trump is closer to the other end, a pre-commitment to non-intervention.

Both, however, represent forms of strategic ambiguity. One president seemed committed and the other reluctant, but who knows what either of them would actually decide to do at crunch time. Beijing still cannot confidently assume a Trump-led United States would not intervene in a Taiwan scenario despite Trump seemingly indicating reticence to do so.

Chinese analysts consider Trump to be unpredictable. They cannot be sure he will act in a way consistent with his past statements. The Chinese remember how quickly Trump turned on them in 2020. In January, he said “our relationship with China now might be the best it’s been in a long, long time.” Later in the year, largely over the COVID-19 pandemic, Trump regularly berated China with statements such as “I’m very angry at China” and “The world is now suffering as a result of the malfeasance of the Chinese government.”

There are, nevertheless, reasons to doubt the American commitment to defend Taiwan, and these reasons go beyond the current U.S. presidential administration.

First, the demographic trend in the United States is increasingly anti-war. Gen Z Americans, born 1997-2012, are significantly less fearful of China attaining a stronger global position and less likely to see China as an adversary. The succession of unpopular wars against Afghanistan, Iraq and Iran further strengthens the aversion of Americans toward getting embroiled in foreign conflicts.

Second, the costs and risks of maintaining U.S. strategic pre-eminence on the western Pacific Rim against the determination of China to achieve regional supremacy are rising. The United States already dominates the Western Hemisphere. The rationale for dominating the Asia-Pacific, as well, is that doing so makes war less likely and opens the door for U.S. commerce. This rationale is less persuasive, however, if China supports international trade and if opposing China’s aspirations for “rejuvenation” makes war more rather than less likely.

Military analyst Jennifer Kavanaugh’s September 10 proposal for a “Second Island Chain strategy” attracted much attention. Kavanaugh, a member of the “restrainer” camp in U.S. foreign policy, argued that to reduce the risk of war with China while still protecting the most vital U.S. interests, Washington should end its alliances with Japan, South Korea, Australia, and the Philippines, pull most of its military forces out of the region, and announce that it will not intervene to protect Taiwan in a cross-strait war. Expect arguments such as this to grow in volume and frequency.

Finally, the U.S. defense industrial base is currently unable to compete with China’s productivity. This weakness is not easily fixed, even with an increased defense budget. As the modernization of its armed forces have made China a near-peer adversary of the United States, China’s advantage in manufacturing capacity becomes potentially decisive in a theoretical China-U.S. war.

Recent wargaming suggests both China and the U.S. would suffer huge losses in a conflict. Even where the U.S. “wins,” China is better placed to quickly rebuild and rearm its forces, giving Beijing hope that it would prevail in a second round. If American leaders conclude the math leaves them without a path to victory, they will reconsider whether an intervention is feasible.

But for now, Beijing would be reckless not to assume that both the United States and Japan would militarily oppose an attempt to conquer Taiwan. And Xi is not reckless.

title: Options for the Royal Brunei Air Force’s Fast-jet Decision
description: One important mantra for the RBAirF: Don’t try to run before you can walk.
text:
The Royal Brunei Air Force (RBAirF), which turned 60 in June, finds itself in a rapidly changing geostrategic environment, characterized by conflict and instability. Brunei is unlikely to suffer outright military aggression but could face spillover effects of increased super power confrontation in the region.

Brunei’s recent defense white paper identified major power rivalry, regional and global conflicts, radicalization, and rapidly advancing disruptive technologies as sources of concern. It also laid out a path to secure national sovereignty and territorial integrity. The RBAirF is actively looking to expand its means to do so, including with plans to acquire medium-range ground-based air defense systems and fast-jet combat aircraft.

Currently, the RBAirF operates a small fleet of modern turboprop-powered fixed-wing aircraft and helicopters. In May, Brunei took delivery of the last two CASA (Airbus) C295W medium-airlift aircraft, first ordered in 2022. The aircraft replaced older C235 aircraft in the No. 15 Squadron in territorial and maritime surveillance, airlift, and humanitarian assistance and disaster relief missions.

For rotary-wing tactical airlift, search and rescue, and combat air support (CAS), the RBAirF operates a fleet of 12 S-70i Black Hawk helicopters and a handful of ageing BO105 helicopters. The latter is slated to be replaced by six Airbus H145M multirole helicopters.

Finally, for basic flight training, the RBAirF flies four Pilatus PC-7 Mk.II turboprop aircraft. The aircraft were put into service in 1997, which makes them among the oldest aircraft in Bruneian service and in dire need for replacement.

To meet the air force’s mission – “to deliver responsive air power in securing Brunei Darussalam’s territorial integrity and national interests” – amid a changing security environment, more capable combat aircraft are also needed urgently.

As the RBAirF considers the acquisition of a squadron of fast-jet combat aircraft, original equipment manufacturers (OEM) are lining up to offer their fighters to Brunei Darussalam.

Options like the Lockheed Martin’s F-16 Viper offer a leap in capability for the RBAirF and come with closer ties with the U.S. defense industry and Washington D.C. However, the F-16 or an equivalent is not the best solution for the RBAirF as it seeks to enter fast-jet operations. Any decision regarding the RBAirF’s future combat aircraft should go beyond simple fighter comparisons and consider the air force’s broader requirements across its stated roles.

Entering fast-jet operations also poses new training demands for the air force. Brunei will need a revised flight training syllabus and modern training aircraft to ready its future generation of pilots.

Training Jets

Brunei could consider adopting the Singapore model by dispatching pilots to another country for advanced jet training (Phase 3-4), or join international advanced military flight training courses in Italy or Canada, while maintaining the elementary and basic training (Phase 1-2) at home.

Alternatively, the RBAirF could acquire the Embraer A-29 or Textron Aviation T-6 Texan II turboprop trainers to replace the aging PC-7 Mk. II fleet to meet its own advanced training (Phase 3) demands.

Some air forces like Switzerland, for example, employ modern turboprop aircraft to fulfill their pilot training needs entirely (Phase 2-4), enabling pilots to transition from turboprop aircraft directly to jet combat aircraft.

Moreover, both Embraer and Textron offer missionized and armed variants of their aircraft, which would offer Brunei an affordable light combat aircraft capability. The A-29 and AT-6 can be equipped with advanced electro-optical and infrared search and track, and laser track sensors, gun and rocket pods, and a variety of precision-guided munitions.

Critically, this would allow the RBAirF to meet many of its CAS, counterinsurgency (COIN), combat search and rescue, airborne forward air controller, armed reconnaissance, helicopter escort, and border and maritime surveillance patrol missions assigned to it with greater efficiency and capability than is possible today.

Therefore, the two types offer substantial value at low cost. They would help support the Bruneian ground forces and navy, and other government agencies, and offer major savings that come from maintenance, operational, and training synergies of operating a common platform that meets the RBAirF’s basic military flight training requirements while fulfilling many of its lower end combat needs.

To effectively protect Brunei’s airspace against intruders and assist in land and maritime border surveillance, rapid response (i.e., Quick Reaction Alert or QRA) is of essence.

Neither the current turboprop aircraft or helicopters, nor turboprop light combat aircraft, can effectively intercept fast-moving and high-flying intruders near Bruneian sovereign airspace or above the exclusive economic zone. Therefore, the RBAirF requirement for fast jet combat aircraft is understandable.

Multirole Light Combat Aircraft

To meet the requirement, Brunei should consider acquiring modern multirole jet-trainer aircraft and their light combat aircraft variants, which could also fulfill the majority of the air force’s border protection and combat requirements.

Good candidates to fill this role include, for example, the Leonardo M346F Block 20 and the Korean Aerospace Industries (KAI) TA/FA-50 Block 70 advanced jet trainer and light combat aircraft from Italy and South Korea respectively. Like the previously discussed turboprop options, Leonardo and KAI aircraft offer many synergies like in maintenance, training, and operations.

The M346F Block 20 is a missionized advanced jet trainer, which is equipped with a modern active electronically scanned array (AESA) radar, advanced cockpit with large-area display, and a helmet-mounted sight, datalink, targeting pod, short- and medium-range air-to-air missiles and a range of precision-guided air-to-ground and antiship weapons.

Similarly, the latest FA-50 versions, such as the FA-50M and FA-50 Block 70 destined for Malaysia and the Philippines respectively, are fitted with an AESA radar, a targeting pod, a datalink, and a range of air-to-air and air-to-ground weapons.

Critically, the AESA radar, targeting pod, datalink, and the ability to carry both within-visual-range and beyond-visual-range missiles, enable the aircraft to take up the essential QRA and combat air patrol duties and respond to any airspace violations with force, if needed.

The FA-50 holds an important advantage over the M346 in this regard. It can use its afterburning F404 powerplant to accelerate to a supersonic speed and reach the farthest reaches of Brunei’s EEZ faster than what is possible with the subsonic Italian aircraft.

Besides their light combat aircraft attributes, both types were originally designed as advanced jet trainers to meet the common Phase 3 training requirements. The addition of a radar, fire-control computer and associated data bus, hardpoints, and weapons have enabled the use of the aircraft in lead-in fighter training (Phase 4) as well.

In addition, both aircraft are equipped with large-area displays, helmet-mounted sights, and Virtual, Live, and Constructive (VLC) training aids, which promise to transform jet training in the coming years. The use of VLC allows air forces to achieve many previously difficult to resource training, such as large-force operations or weapons deployment at a significantly lower cost.

For example, VLC can emulate a fire-control radar and simulate a beyond-visual-range missile engagement with all associated target and missile-launch symbology and cues projected on the displays and the helmet. Air forces can dispatch a pair of aircraft into air (“live”) while other trainees may join the same mission in simulators (“virtual”), while facing virtual enemy aircraft (“constructive”) – all linked to the same VLC environment.

Moreover, due to the rapid technological change and observations drawn from conflicts around the world, one-way attack drones (OWAD) have become a prominent aerial threat that requires solutions from air forces and the industry.

Understanding this demand, OEMs like Embraer, Textron, and Leonardo market their aircraft as cost-effective counter-OWAD platforms, equipped with AESA radar and/or targeting pods, datalink, gun pods, short-range air-to-air missiles, and semi-active laser-guided rockets to address the threat.

Therefore, light combat aircraft offer the RBAirF a cost-effective solution to stand up fast-jet operations from zero.

Lessons From Brunei’s Neighbors

A good point of reference is the Philippine Air Force (PAF), which made a return to fast jets with the FA-50PH between 2015 and 2017, after a ten-year pause in operating fighter aircraft. The PAF took delivery of 12 aircraft and signed a follow-on order in 2025 consisting of 12 FA-50 Block 70 aircraft.

During the last decade, the PAF has made great strides in training and reacquiring the skills needed to operate fast jets. Today, Manila is not just looking to expand the well-liked FA-50 fleet but also to acquire a higher-end multirole combat aircraft.

The Philippine example shows that it can take a decade or more to develop required operational proficiency and human resources, and capacity to operate fast jets.

The KAI aircraft has become a popular type in Southeast Asia and is operated by four air forces, including the Philippines, Indonesia, Thailand, and Malaysia.

In comparison, the M346 remains a less well-known type in the region, although it is used by Singapore for basic jet training, with its entire fleet based in France due to training area constraints in the island state.

In addition, Indonesia recently placed an order for a total of 48 M346F Block 20 aircraft, which will transform the Indonesian Air Force’s flight training and help replace ageing BAE Hawk aircraft in both jet training and light combat duties.

Modern trainer aircraft, which also come in light combat aircraft versions and are equipped with modern sensors, datalinks, air-to-air missiles, and precision-guided munitions offer significant cost benefits and training, operational, and maintenance synergies for small air forces.

For the RBAirF, these aircraft offer the most cost-effective pathway to fast-jet air power. One must not run before learning to walk.
