title: Pakistan and Terrorism: When the Tables Turn
description: Islamabad cannot use its own people’s suffering to erase its record of supporting forces that have devastated lives in other countries.
text:
In his address to the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly, Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif described Afghanistan as a haven for terrorist groups carrying out attacks against Pakistan. He specifically named Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan, or the TTP, and the Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA), and called on the Afghan Taliban to take decisive action to prevent Afghan soil from being used against Pakistan and other countries.

Coming from a Pakistani official, this demand raises many questions. The first is: since when has Pakistan decided that supporting armed groups in a neighboring country is dangerous? When the Taliban were fighting in Afghanistan against the Republic government and the Afghan people were the victims, where was this concern? Why does the same government that supported the Taliban for years now speak about terrorist sanctuaries as though it had no role in creating this situation?

Pakistan’s support for the Taliban is not merely an allegation made by Afghans out of anger or without grounding. Financial support, the training and recruitment of fighters, the transfer of ammunition and fuel, and cooperation between Pakistani military and intelligence officials and the Taliban have been extensively documented over the years by credible international organizations. For much of the last 25 years, Pakistan helped strengthen a force that imposed war and repression on the people of Afghanistan.

The Haqqani network is a clear example of this conduct. Its sanctuaries in North Waziristan and its ties to Pakistan’s intelligence apparatus have been the subject of reports and official objections for years. In 2011, Mike Mullen, then chairman of the U.S. Joint Chiefs of Staff, described the network as effectively an arm of Pakistani intelligence, an allegation Islamabad denied. Now that Pakistan is complaining about sanctuaries across the border, it must explain why it refused to meet the same demand regarding the Haqqani network more than a decade ago.

Even after the Taliban returned to power in 2021, then-Pakistani Prime Minister Imran Khan spoke of Afghans breaking the “shackles of slavery.” The political meaning of this response was clear: the Taliban’s victory was welcomed in Islamabad. But now that the Taliban are not behaving as Pakistan expected, that same victory has become a threat. Has the Taliban’s nature only just become apparent, or has Pakistan’s calculation that it could control the Taliban’s behavior simply proved wrong?

To me, this reversal shows that the central problem is a selective definition of terrorism. When the Taliban were fighting in Afghanistan and helping expand Pakistan’s influence, justifications could be found for supporting them. Now that groups close to the Taliban are fighting against Pakistan, Islamabad is suddenly concerned about sanctuaries, support, and the responsibility of the host state. Human lives should not suddenly become valuable simply because the place where people are killed has changed.

Of course, the people of Pakistan are, indeed, the victims of terrorism. No disagreement with Islamabad’s policies can justify killing Pakistani citizens. The TTP is a real threat and must be confronted. But the same standard must also apply to victims in Afghanistan and India of groups supported by Pakistan. Pakistan’s government cannot use its own people’s suffering to erase its record of supporting forces that have devastated lives in other countries.

Pakistan’s hostility toward the TTP is not new. It has conducted operations against the TTP and other groups that target Pakistan. The issue, therefore, is not that Islamabad has never fought terrorism; it is why its response to armed groups has varied depending on where their attacks are directed. If opposition to terrorism is a matter of principle, networks that recruit fighters, raise funds and organize attacks against neighboring countries must be viewed as equally unacceptable.

As long as this contradiction remains, Pakistan’s statements about terrorism cannot be taken seriously. That can only change if Pakistan moves beyond general statements and actually fights terrorism, something it appears to have no intention of doing. Lashkar-e-Taiba is one of the clearest examples. The U.N. Security Council’s sanctions committee identifies this Pakistan-based group as responsible for numerous attacks against military and civilian targets, including the 2008 Mumbai attacks. The same records identify Jamaat-ud-Dawa, also based in Pakistan, as a front for financing, training and supporting Lashkar-e-Taiba.

Jaish-e-Mohammed (JeM) is another example. Founded by Masood Azhar after his release from prison in India, the group is on the U.N. sanctions list, too. The Security Council has documented its links with al-Qaida and the Taliban, as well as its role in attacks in Kashmir. In May 2025, JeM was reported to be based in Bahawalpur, in Pakistan’s Punjab province.

Hizbul Mujahideen is another longstanding group active in Kashmir, fighting to end Indian rule and unite the region with Pakistan. According to U.S. State Department reports, the group has carried out numerous attacks against Indian security personnel and politicians and has been involved in abductions and killings. Reports from June 2026 also describe its leader, Syed Salahuddin, as being based in Pakistan.

Harakat-ul-Mujahideen is another example of these cross-border networks. The Security Council’s records identify Muzaffarabad and Rawalpindi as bases for the group and record attacks against military and civilian targets in Kashmir, the training of fighters and cooperation with other groups. The hijacking of an Indian aircraft in 1999 has also been attributed to the group. This history shows that the connection between Pakistan-based groups and violence across the region has not been limited to the Afghan Taliban and stretched across decades.

In April 2025, Pakistani Defense Minister Khawaja Asif was asked in an interview with Sky News about the country’s history of supporting, training and financing terrorist groups. He replied: “We have been doing this dirty work for the United States for about three decades, and the West, including Britain.” He called this policy a mistake and spoke about its costs for Pakistan. But what about the price the people of Afghanistan have paid? How does pointing to the role of the United States and the U.K. remove the responsibility of Pakistani officials?

If Pakistan wants its words to be taken seriously, it must demonstrate at home the same thing it demands of the Taliban: action against international terrorism and measures that can be verified. The fight against terrorism has credibility when past political ties to a group do not stand in the way of action against it. Pakistan’s statements about terrorism can be taken seriously only when it acts to cut off funding, stop recruitment and dismantle the operational structures of known terrorist groups on its own soil.

Until then, these words will remain just words; neither the problem of terrorism in Pakistan nor the threat that has driven it to make these statements will go away. Otherwise, the very danger then U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton warned about in 2011 will persist: “You can’t keep snakes in your backyard and expect them only to bite your neighbors.”

It is the continuation of this same policy that makes Pakistan’s language about terrorism difficult to take seriously in 2026.

Islamabad wants an end to the threat directed at itself, but it must show that it judges its neighbors’ security by the same standard. Terrorism was no less dangerous or criminal when it helped extend Pakistan’s influence. To give its words credibility, Pakistan must demonstrate that its concern is terrorism itself, even when terrorists are fighting against another country.

So far, what we can see is that Pakistan’s current dispute with the Taliban does not, in itself, mean it has abandoned its longstanding policy of using armed groups to further its aims. The test of change is an end to the logic of using such groups. If Islamabad raises its voice only when these groups defy its wishes, what has changed is the relationship between the patron and the group; the value of human life is still judged by the same selective standard.

Before Sharif describes Afghanistan as a haven for terrorism, he must explain what role his own country has played in bringing Afghanistan to this point. The people of Afghanistan never invited Pakistan to support the Taliban, and they should not now have to pay the price for that failed calculation.

title: Pakistan’s Escalating Response to Cross-Border Terrorism
description: The recurring clashes represent the failure of months of diplomacy and external mediation. Where does the Afghanistan-Pakistan relationship go from here?
text:
Tensions are on the rise between Pakistan and Afghanistan once again as both countries have traded fire as well as accusations over the past few days. The current flare-up is a direct consequence of a terrorist attack on a mosque in the north-western Pakistani town of Kohat on September 18, in which at least 31 people, including 16 police personnel, were killed and over 100 injured.

After neutralizing the attackers after an hours-long gun battle, Pakistan launched retaliatory airstrikes against the alleged positions of the Hafiz Gul Bahadur-led Ittehad ul Mujahideen Pakistan (IMP), which had claimed responsibility for the attack, and its ideological ally, the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), in Paktika and Kunar provinces of Afghanistan on September 21. Pakistan claimed to have killed 28 terrorists in those strikes.

Instead of engaging Pakistan’s border posts with machine guns and mortars like in most previous instances, the Taliban government of Afghanistan launched drones against Pakistan from its territory in the early hours of September 23. Eight of the drones were downed by Pakistan’s air defenses, according to Pakistani authorities.

The Afghan drone incursions did not cause any casualties or damage to civilian or military infrastructure in Pakistan; the spokesperson for the Pakistani president dismissed them as unfrightening “flying toys.” Even so, Islamabad conducted fresh air raids in Afghanistan, targeting 10 different locations in the early hours of September 24. Pakistan’s information minister confirmed that the second round of strikes was indeed a response to the Afghan drone incursions.

Quite ironically, the Kohat terrorist attack came a day after Turkiye’s intelligence chief, Ibrahim Kalin, arrived in Islamabad following his trip to Afghanistan. Kalin was continuing Turkiye’s effort to mediate a long-term peace between the two countries. Kabul had already expressed its lack of enthusiasm toward the Turkish mediation when the Taliban’s Supreme Leader Mullah Hibatullah Akhunzada refused to see Kalin in Kandahar, reportedly calling him “Westernized.” Then Islamabad’s identification of one of the suicide bombers as an Afghan national and the subsequent events sealed the fate of the ongoing peace efforts by Turkiye and Qatar.

While Pakistani and Afghan security forces continue to trade fire across the border and accusations in the media, the question on many a mind right now is whether any meaningful mediation between the two countries is possible any time soon. The short answer seems to be “no.” Here is the longer explanation for it.

Looking at Pakistan’s kinetic responses to terrorist attacks that its officials associated with terrorist safe havens across the border in Afghanistan, one can discern a break from the past since October last year. Even though Islamabad has been alleging an Afghan connection to earlier terrorist attacks as well, its kinetic responses were sparse and cautious.

Pakistan’s first reported use of force inside Afghanistan since the Taliban’s return to power in August 2021 occurred in April 2022, following a terrorist attack in the North Waziristan district bordering Afghanistan. At the time, Pakistan’s Foreign Office did not even acknowledge the airstrikes, even though the Taliban government of Afghanistan complained to the United Nations Security Council about them and initiated limited cross-border retaliatory fire against Pakistani border posts.

Two years later, in March 2024, Pakistan once again responded with airstrikes inside Afghanistan after a terrorist attack in North Waziristan. This time, Pakistan’s Foreign Office was quick to acknowledge the attack but its spokesperson hastened to add that Islamabad “respect[ed] the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Afghanistan and look[ed] forward to working together” with Afghanistan. In a subsequent press briefing, the Foreign Office even clarified that its actions were not against the government or the people of Afghanistan.

The response of the Taliban government of Afghanistan was also measured. Even though it claimed that it had conducted cross-border strikes against Pakistani posts, which was corroborated by the local population, the damage to personnel and infrastructure was limited. Like in April 2022, the crisis de-escalated quickly.

In December 2024 Pakistan conducted another round of airstrikes inside Afghanistan in response to a terrorist attack. Even though the airstrikes came at a time when Pakistan’s Special Representative for Afghanistan Ambassador Muhammad Sadiq was on his first visit to Kabul after resuming his responsibilities in the position, the aftermath followed a somewhat similar pattern to April 2022 and March 2024.

In October 2025, however, things changed significantly. Pakistan not only conducted an airstrike in the heart of Kabul targeting the head of the TTP, but responded to Afghanistan’s cross-border retaliatory fire on Pakistani border posts with much more intensity than the previous instances.

This led to a quick escalation of the conflict, forcing Qatar and Turkiye to make frantic efforts toward a ceasefire as well as a longer-term rapprochement. While the ceasefire held for a time, negotiations on the signing of a longer-term peace deal between Afghanistan and Pakistan remained unsuccessful, resulting in a tense diplomatic impasse that has persisted ever since.

Things got even worse in February 2026, when Pakistan initiated a long-term military operation aimed at neutralizing terrorists inside Afghan territory through the sustained use of air power.

Thus October 2025 marked a break from the past and February 2026 made the use of coercive power a norm. The reason for the new normal was the failure of months of bilateral and trilateral diplomacy starting in March 2025, when Sadiq travelled to Kabul again for talks after the December 2024 debacle. His visit paved the way for a visit of Pakistan’s Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar to Kabul in April. Pakistan’s Foreign Office explicitly described Dar’s visit as part of its effort to develop “good, friendly, neighborly relations” with Afghanistan.

From May through August, Islamabad considerably intensified this diplomatic track with the involvement of China. In May, Pakistan, China, and Afghanistan held a trilateral foreign minister meeting in Beijing, where the three sides agreed to strengthen communication, economic cooperation, regional connectivity, and security cooperation. China and Pakistan also supported the extension of the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) to Afghanistan.

This was the time when Pakistan and Afghanistan also agreed to upgrade diplomatic representation from chargé d’affaires to the ambassadorial level. Dar subsequently described the diplomatic interactions as laying the foundations for a “qualitative change” in Pakistan’s bilateral relations with Afghanistan.

On July 7, 2025, the two foreign ministries institutionalized another channel through an additional-secretary-level mechanism covering trade, transit, security, connectivity, and Afghan nationals. Dar made two back-to-back visits to Kabul in July and August to sign the framework agreement for a joint feasibility study of the Uzbekistan-Afghanistan-Pakistan railway and the sixth Pakistan-China-Afghanistan trilateral, respectively. Pakistan even provided Afghanistan with humanitarian assistance after the September 2025 earthquake.

Despite all this intense positive diplomacy, however, terrorist attacks inside Pakistan with purported links to Afghanistan continued. That is what has led Islamabad to treat coercion – not diplomacy with Afghanistan – as the primary option of choice since October 2025, even if the results of that change are highly debatable. As the escalation hurts populations on both sides of the border, there seems to be a perception among Pakistani policy circles that coercion is more likely to persuade the Afghan Taliban to quit supporting the TTP and its affiliated groups than diplomacy. And even if not, perhaps, at least Pakistan would be getting even with the Taliban.

title: Pakistan’s Punitive Gamble in Afghanistan: An Open War With No End in Sight
description: The Afghan Taliban have little incentive to accede to Islamabad’s demands.
text:
In the early hours of September 24, Pakistan carried out air and drone strikes on ten locations inside Afghanistan. Subsequently, Afghan media identified Kandahar – where the Taliban’s supreme leader (Amir-al-Mu’minin) Hibatullah Akhundzada is based – as well as Khost and Paktia as the provinces targeted. A few hours later, Pakistani Information Minister Attaullah Tarar posted on social media that the strikes were “deliberate, precise, calibrated and proportionate” and were “strictly limited to identified military objectives directly linked to the attempted attacks against Pakistan.” “Attempted attacks” was a reference to earlier Pakistani claims that it had shot down ten rudimentary drones launched from inside Afghanistan that entered Pakistani territory with a “soft kill” approach.

Two days earlier, on September 21, Pakistani air strikes on Kunar and Paktika provinces killed three civilians – a man, a woman, and a girl – in Kunar’s Nurgal district. Islamabad claimed to have killed 28 militants in the attack. The civilian casualties, which were confirmed by UNAMA, saw Afghan protesters hitting the streets in Kabul and elsewhere.

This Pakistani strike was in response to an attack on a police compound in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s Kohat, killing at least 16 police officers on September 18. On that day a vehicle-borne explosive device breached the police compound during Friday prayers. This was followed by an armed assault by militants. The attack was claimed by the Ittihadul Mujahideen Pakistan (IMP), an alliance led by the Hafiz Gul Bahadar (HGB) group, which shares close linkages with the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP). Pakistani authorities identified one of the attackers as an Afghan national.

Pakistan has carried out air and drone strikes inside Afghanistan on at least 15 occasions between October 2025 and September 2026. Private estimates suggest that more than 1,100 civilians have been killed or injured by cross-border violence in Afghanistan this year. An attack on a drug rehabilitation center in Kabul in May killed 269 people, leading to calls for the attack to be investigated as a war crime.

Inside Pakistan, the death toll of civilians and security forces in terrorism-related incidents in 2026 so far is close to 1,700. Of these, 545 have taken place in the province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, where the TTP and the IMP operate.

Pakistani claims that Afghan soil is being used by the TTP and the IMP are supported by periodic reports from the U.N. monitoring committee, including one released in August 2026. The report unequivocally said that the Afghan Taliban “continued their support” to the TTP. The Afghan Taliban has responded to such assertions by repeated public denials.

Behind the scenes, however, the Afghan Taliban may have tried to restrain the TTP. The U.N. report mentioned that the Afghan Taliban authorities have “relocated approximately 2,000 TTP fighters and families from the Pakistani border to further inside Afghanistan.” Akhundzada has reportedly “warned the TTP leadership through back‑channel communications to halt attacks targeting Pakistan or risk losing the Taliban’s support,” it added. It is unclear if any attempt was made to reign in the IMP as well.

While efforts to control the TTP may not have worked completely, according to data by ACLED, “HGB and IMP’s activities have less than halved since the latest outbreak of hostilities between Afghanistan and Pakistan in late February, compared with the immediately preceding period.”

On February 27, Pakistan launched Operation Ghazab lil-Haq (Righteous Fury) against the Taliban in Afghanistan, marking the first such attack on its former ally and protégé. On that occasion, “unprovoked firing” from across the border by the Taliban was cited as the reason. Pakistan’s Defense Minister Khawaja Asif declared, “Now it is open war between us.”

Given the levels of violence the TTP and the IMP continued to perpetrate inside Pakistan, the country is facing a classic case of strategic blowback. More importantly, the sense of impunity with which Islamabad has repeatedly carried out its attacks in Afghanistan, despite their low efficacy, indicates serious lacunae in Pakistan’s counterterrorism strategy. Most of these attacks have led to angry statements by Taliban officials, vows of retaliation, and incidents of cross-border firing by Taliban soldiers but little else.

In addition to reining in the TTP and IMP, Pakistan seems to be pursuing a larger strategic objective of finding its lost leverage in Kabul. In Islamabad’s view, its former ally has gone rogue and demonstrating coercive power, along with providing support to the anti-Taliban resistance fronts, is the only path forward. A weak and client state in Afghanistan is the end state Pakistani establishment has pursued for decades.

During the days of the previous Afghan Republic, the HGB largely spared the Pakistani state and instead focused its fight on American and NATO forces in Afghanistan. Post-August 2021, backed by al-Qaida, the HGB has grown to be a prominent face of jihadist insurgency against Islamabad. It is numerically smaller than the TTP, but that hasn’t stopped it from carrying out some of the more complex attacks on security installations in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

Therefore, eliminating the IMP threat, if not the far larger TTP, will potentially address the blowback Islamabad is currently receiving for its past policies. Similarly, repeated attacks including some directed at the Taliban regime itself, could possibly lead to internal ruptures within the faction-ridden Islamic Emirate and embolden the small pro-Pakistan elements within it.

That, however, is much easier said than done. Despite reports of factionalism and internal differences within the Kandahar (Rahbari shura or the leadership council) and Kabul (administrative) shuras of the Taliban, the Rahbari shura functioning under the strict Islamic edicts of the Supreme leader, still retains control and uncontested legitimacy. Moreover, each attack by Pakistan so far has further raised anti-Pakistan sentiment inside Afghanistan. It could embolden the Afghan Taliban as well, who have little incentive to accede to Islamabad’s demands. The ethno-nationalist Taliban regime with strong Pushtun identity across the contested Durand Line could raise its head of Pushtun nationalism once again.

The Taliban seem to have learnt from their former sponsor’s playbook the art of cultivating strategic assets and using them as leverage. Attempting to bomb them into submission could be a myopic and counterproductive strategy if there are any lessons learned from the last two decades of American intervention in Afghanistan.

title: Pax Silica vs WAICO: Will Central Asia Have to Pick a Side?
description: One clue as to how the U.S. plans to proceed might be glimpsed in how Uzbekistan progresses in following Kazakhstan into dual membership.
text:
Kazakhstan presently sits in a unique and potentially precarious spot: It’s the only country in the world to have joined both Washington’s Pax Silica and China’s World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO), competing AI alliances. With a Reuters report last month suggesting that the U.S. may pressure partners to pick a side, Central Asia’s – and Kazakhstan’s – multivector methods may soon be challenged.

Astana joined Pax Silica officially on June 27, with Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development Zhaslan Madiyev signing the relevant declaration and the joint statement on the AI Opportunity Partnership during the second Pax Silica Summit in Washington, D.C.

Less than three weeks later, Madiyev attended the World Artificial Intelligence Conference 2026, in Shanghai and became a founding member of WAICO alongside 28 other countries.

As it stands now, Washington’s Pax Silica counts 24 countries as signatories, with Taiwan listed as a “non-signatory participant.” Beijing, meanwhile, counts 37 countries as members of WAICO, with Bangladesh taking on an “observer” status.

Pax Silica, launched in December 2025, is branded by the U.S. State Department as its “flagship effort on AI and supply chain security, advancing new economic security consensus among allies and trusted partners.” The declaration highlights supply chain resilience, particularly as it applies to the AI supply chain – everything from energy to critical mineral, manufacturing to technology and infrastructure.

Although China is not directly named, the declaration’s references to “reducing excessive dependencies” and “forging new connections with reliable partners and suppliers committed to fair market practices” are clear dog whistles screaming Beijing.

WAICO, meanwhile, was first proposed by China in July 2025 and came into being in July 2026. It frames itself as an international organization focused on AI governance. Notably United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres attended the signing as a guest, providing at least the impression of U.N. endorsement.

Despite the differences in focus – Pax Silica is crafted around physical concerns, while WAICO homes in on governance and norms – the two blocs are being positioned as the combatants in a new cold war. Whether that analogy works or not comes down to whether countries are effectively forced to pick a side.

And that day may be coming.

In mid-August, Reuters reported on an undated draft letter addressed to the 35 signatories of the AI ⁠Opportunity Statement from the State Department. The draft stated: “To be part of everything is to be part of nothing. Signature of the Pax Silica Declaration is not merely a membership subscription, but a commitment.” According to Reuters, the letter urged the countries to “choose deliberately” on AI, and explicitly stated that membership in Pac Silica “cannot be held alongside membership in duplicative initiatives whose expectations conflict with our own.” The letter, apparently, did not directly mention China.

As of writing, it does not appear that the letter has been sent. But the warning stands, and the Central Asian countries might have gotten it first hand. In early August U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for South and Central Asian Affairs Paul Kapur visited several countries, including Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan. In Kazakhstan, among other meetings, he met Madiyev to “discuss digital development.”

One clue as to how the U.S. plans to proceed might be glimpsed in how Uzbekistan progresses in following Kazakhstan into dual membership. Uzbekistan, like Kazakhstan, joined WAICO in July (as did Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan).

In late August, Uzbekistan’s ambassador to the U.S., Furqat Sidikov, told a group of journalists that Tashkent had requested to join Pax Silica. He said a diplomatic note had been sent to the State Department: “Now, the U.S. should confirm. We are ready to sign.”

Sidikov pushed back on the idea of red lines circumscribing participation in this or that initiative, calling it “counterproductive.” He said countries should have a “chance to be part of any kind of international cooperation.”

That is certainly Central Asia’s perspective. Now, what will Washington do? Some of Pax Silica’s core areas – such as critical mineral dependences – are directly addressed by the budding U.S.-Central Asia partnership. But as Edward Lemon and Bradley Jardine argued earlier this year in The Diplomat, the “United States is losing the race for Central Asia’s critical minerals.” Despite various investment announcements, Russia and China remain dominant in the critical minerals mining sector in the region.

Forcing the region to choose a side may not yield the result Washington wants.

title: POGOs and Online Scams, From the Philippines to Myanmar
description: A conversation with award-winning Filipina journalist Eunice Barbara Novio.
text:
Filipina journalist Eunice Barbara Novio. (Photo supplied)

Eunice Barbara Novio is a Thailand-based journalist and an English lecturer at Vongchavalitkul University who has has written extensively on human trafficking in Southeast Asia, particularly focusing on Filipino victims trafficked to Myanmar.

A veteran writer for Inquirer.net, she has reported about how trafficking networks lure Filipinos with false job offers, only to exploit them in scam hubs or forced labor situations.

Novio has also helped victims of organized crime escape from their ordeal, particularly from compounds operating inside Myanmar and close to the Thai border.

She told The Diplomat’s Luke Hunt that the current scam compound phenomenon had its roots in the Philippines dating back to 2016, when Philippine Offshore Gaming Operators, commonly known as POGOs, took hold and flourished in places like Bamban – a small agricultural town north of Manila.

POGOs were banned in late 2024 and a former Bamban mayor, Alice Guo, was sentenced to life in prison in November 2025 after a Philippine court found her guilty of qualified human trafficking, involving hundreds of people who were forced to run scams on pain of mistreatment and torture.

What also sets the Philippines apart is its Department of Migrant Workers, which has a long history of handling its country’s extensive expat working population and has been used to help extract and repatriate victims of organized crime.

Novio, a two-time Plaridel Awardee for Journalism conferred by the Filipino American Press Club, says that the numbers of Filipinos still in Myanmar scam compounds can be measured in the thousands as organized crime restructures its operations further inland, away from the Thai border.

title: Prioritizing Social Stability Over Democratic Reforms: Uzbekistan Announces New Development Programs
description: Uzbekistan’s new national development programs prioritize socio-economic developments over democratic reforms.
text:
As Uzbekistan celebrated its 35th independence anniversary this week, President Shavkat Mirziyoyev announced seven national programs for the years ahead. The programs focus on socio-economic development and conspicuously omit any reform related to political pluralism, press freedom, freedom of conscience, or other democratic elements.

Mirziyoyev has prioritized areas viewed as critical to retaining popular support for his government. The first is improving public education, with a special focus on extending compulsory education to age six, supporting private kindergartens, and having at least ten universities ranked in the top 1,000 higher education institutions in the world. Uzbekistan has one of the highest numbers of schoolchildren in the region, with 6.8 million students and 600,000 teachers in public mandatory schools alone.

The next few national programs announced by Mirziyoyev also concern socio-economic well-being: improving public health and increasing longevity; transitioning to a high technology economy, and ensuring high labor productivity as well as changing public attitudes toward the environment and addressing environmental challenges.

The fifth national program is set to ensure judicial independence and the rule of law. The Diplomat recently reported that one of the country’s new laws allows the president’s daughter, who heads the presidential administration, to be directly involved in shaping the judicial system while having lifetime legal immunity for her actions with no accountability. A few areas – cybercrime, drug trafficking, and human trafficking – are singled out for additional attention but concrete steps in this regard have not been outlined.

The sixth program Mirziyoyev announced identified mahallas as the “‘main customer (or commissioner)’ of development.” This program basically aims to further empower mahallas along with slightly altering the district budgeting system. Mahallas are unique self-governing institutions established at the neighborhood level. Each household is part of a mahalla. As of 2021, there were 9,251 mahallas across the country.

“The mood of our people, the well-being of families, the dreams and aspirations of young people, and the initiative of entrepreneurs are first and foremost reflected in the neighborhood,” Mirziyoyev said in his speech. “Mood” is an odd word to pick – not financial stability, safety, employment or other aspects of socio-economic life. It reflects mahallas’ role as an observer of citizens’ sentiment (and hopefully their needs too).

Historically, mahalla institutions have played a distributing role rather than a commissioning one, carrying government policies down and out to the people rather than gathering and feeding social sentiments upward into the system. Mirziyoyev is now saying that mahallas ought to be “the main customer (commissioner) of social development.” While this is, in one sense, a form of decentralization where citizens might participate in some degree of decision-making, it is not a genuine political decentralization. It appears that mahallas will report upward the social and financial needs on the ground and the budget allocation will be made accordingly. The president’s announcement noted, “District budgets, investment programs, and infrastructure projects are developed based on the needs of neighborhoods.”

But mahallas still will not have a final say in anything. They will not receive full control over their own budgets. Ultimate decisions on budget allocations will remain at the hands of the central government. The proposed change, if implemented, will result in participatory or needs-based local governance, but does not grant fiscal independence.

The last area of development focuses on a peaceful foreign policy and economic diplomacy.

The proposed national development programs place emphasis on socio-economic areas. These are safe areas wherein changes, minor or even radical, will not threaten or challenge the political regime. Instead, increased attention to these spheres will increase Mirziyoyev’s popularity and thus further consolidate power in the existing government.

The programs as outlined do not address areas in which Mirziyoyev initially promised reforms, particularly freedom of expression. His early promises on supporting journalists and allowing the press to become a true watchdog has undergone a clear backslide. The Diplomat has continuously reported on waves of arrests of local bloggers, including popular religious scholar and blogger, Mubashshir Ahmad. Not only journalists or bloggers, but ordinary citizens are also regularly charged with crimes and sentenced to prison for expressing their personal religious views, sharing religious songs online that are not approved by the government or for saying anything negative about the president or his family. The recent law that expanded the authority of the presidential administration, headed by Mirziyoyev’s first daughter, Saida Mirziyoyeva, also prohibits “insulting the honor and dignity” of its officials. The law does not explicitly differentiate between healthy criticism and insult.

The Mirziyoyev administration’s priorities are clear in its announced programs: to keep average people happy by ensuring their basic needs are covered. Anything else, particularly those related to freedom of speech, mobilization, or independent teaching and practice of religion that can eventually challenge the status quo, has been swept under the carpet.

title: Public Scrutiny Really Does Help the Unjustly Detained
description: Concerned citizens and civil society groups working in tandem can help free the unjustly imprisoned. But the work is far from finished.
text:
Every August 30, the international community observes the International Day of the Victims of Enforced Disappearances. Historically, any mention of enforced disappearances has evoked images of clandestine detentions and unacknowledged abductions by shadowy operatives operating with impunity in totalitarian states. In the contemporary era, however, the architecture of erasure has evolved into something far more institutionalized.

Across authoritarian regimes and even democracies, state apparatuses frequently achieve the same outcome through formal legal machinery: weaponizing extraordinary counterterror statutes in the name of national security, imposing endless pre-trial detention, and relying on procedural delays to remove dissenting voices from the public sphere.

Nowhere is this tension between extraordinary security legislation and constitutional safeguards more evident than in India’s handling of civil society advocates exposing the most serious human rights violations. As we speak, a film dedicated to the life of Jaswant Singh Khalra – who exposed enforced disappearances in Punjab in the 1990s and who himself became a victim of enforced disappearance – has been banned by the Indian government.

Notably, the case of Kashmiri human rights defender Khurram Parvez illustrates how thin the line between public witness and administrative oblivion has become. For over two decades, Parvez dedicated his life to documenting human rights violations and unearthing the records of enforced disappearances in Jammu and Kashmir. In an unsettling paradox, the advocate who spent his career ensuring that the vanished were not forgotten has become the target of institutional silencing himself.

Arrested in November 2021 by the National Investigation Agency under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA), Parvez has spent nearly four-and-a-half years in pre-trial incarceration without the commencement of a substantive trial. The evidentiary basis for his detention was deemed so lacking that in 2023, the United Nations Working Group on Arbitrary Detention issued an opinion declaring his imprisonment unlawful and calling for his immediate release.

When an Indian court recently granted Parvez bail in both cases against him – recognizing the fundamental injustice of indefinite pre-trial detention – state authorities moved instantly in the Delhi High Court to challenge his release. This procedural maneuvering reflects a growing structural concern within India’s criminal justice system: when special security statutes curtail judicial discretion on bail, the legal process itself becomes the penalty. Prolonged pre-trial detention strikes at the core of Article 21 of the Indian Constitution, which guarantees that no person shall be deprived of life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law.

This dynamic forms part of a wider global contraction of civic space. According to the latest data from the CIVICUS Monitor, 83 countries are currently classified as having “Closed” or “Repressed” civic space, with a mere 7 percent of the global population residing in open or narrowed environments. Within this landscape, India is currently rated as “Repressed” – reflecting severe restrictions on fundamental freedoms of expression, association, and peaceful assembly. Special counterterrorism laws, national security directives, and procedural roadblocks are increasingly deployed worldwide to treat legitimate civic participation as a national security threat.

When formal multilateral channels stall and domestic legal safeguards are subordinated to executive discretion, what counterweight remains?

The answer lies in organized, sustained citizen solidarity. Solidarity is often dismissed as a purely moral sentiment, but empirical evidence demonstrates that public witness functions as a viable legal and political strategy. Six years ago, CIVICUS launched the “Stand As My Witness” campaign on the premise that naming detained defenders publicly and maintaining consistent scrutiny prevents them from being erased.

One such person is Sudha Bharadwaj, who dedicated a significant chunk of her working life to advocating for the rights of Indigenous communities in Central India. She spent three years in jail awaiting trial before being granted bail in the controversial Bhima Koregaon case while being charged under the draconian UAPA.

Coordinated campaigns in other countries have helped secure the release of journalist Floriane Irangabiye in Burundi, civil society leader Muhammad Ismail in Pakistan, and women’s rights activist Loujain al-Hathloul in Saudi Arabia.

Public scrutiny acts as an indispensable shield. It ensures that detainees receive medical attention, restrains custodial mistreatment, and signals to the judiciary that international eyes remain fixed on procedural fairness. In the case of unjustly imprisoned human rights defenders it also restores faith in our common humanity that people who dedicate their lives to the service of others are not forgotten when they become victims of the same crimes they seek to prevent.

Constitutional democracies derive their international standing and domestic resilience not from the suppression of critical voices, but from their institutional capacity to accommodate dissent and uphold the rule of law. Defending human rights advocates is not an act of charity; it is a moral obligation for public servants and active citizens in any democracy. Thus, addressing the prolonged pre-trial incarceration of human rights defenders and protest leaders like Khurram Parvez, Umar Khalid, and Sharjeel Imam is essential to safeguarding constitutional heritage.

These issues are not limited to India. They persist in countries with political systems as diverse as Belarus, China, Egypt, Israel, Myanmar, Nicaragua, and Russia, which are among the worst jailers of journalists. Yet, electoral democracies are rightly held to a higher standard and must strive to be better custodians of the people’s right to dissent. Repressive laws such as the UAPA, the National Security Act, the Chhattisgarh Public Security Act, and the Jammu and Kashmir Public Safety Act – which allow people to be held for extended periods of time without the right to due process and a fair trial – contribute to an atmosphere of impunity in which crimes such as torture and enforced disappearances thrive.

After another marking of the International Day of the Victims of Enforced Disappearances, the collective mandate for concerned citizens, jurists, and policymakers is clear: learn the names of those unjustly imprisoned, say them out loud, and refuse to allow the machinery of procedural cruelty vanish them into silence.
tag: arbitrary detention; enforced disappearances; India human rights; Khurram Parvez; Sudha Bharadwaj; Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA)

title: Rahul Bajoria, BofA India Chief Economist, on India’s Manufacturing Ambitions
description: Why has India's manufacturing sector has remained stuck at around 15 percent of GDP despite decades of rapid growth?
text:
Rahul Bajoria, head of India and ASEAN Economic Research at Bank of America, joins host Tushar Shetty to examine why India’s manufacturing sector has remained stuck at around 15 percent of GDP despite decades of rapid growth.

They discuss the colonial and planning-era roots of India’s weak industrial base, the regulatory and compliance burdens that keep Indian firms small and push them into informality, why regulatory progress has been driven by a handful of competitive states rather than by the center, India’s limited gains from China Plus One and its growing exports to China, the mixed record of production-linked incentives and the scaling up of the Apple ecosystem, and the electricity, labor and land reforms needed to lift manufacturing to 25 percent of GDP by 2047.

title: Rare Earths at the Trump-Xi Summit: Relief Without a Resolution
description: The Trump-Xi meeting may temporarily ease anxiety over rare earth supplies, but it is unlikely to lower the political and regulatory threshold for access.
text:
Rare earths entered the Trump-Xi summit before the two leaders even sat down. On September 21, two days before President Xi Jinping’s arrival in the United States, China’s Foreign Ministry faced a series of questions on whether Beijing had “fully resumed rare earth deliveries,” whether a “November 10 deadline or expanded restrictions on rare earth exports” could be extended, and whether rare earths controls involving Japan would feature in the Washington talks. The responses were deliberately cautious: Beijing reiterated its commitment to “keeping the global industrial and supply chains of critical minerals safe and stable,” but emphasized that dual-use exports would remain subject to legal and security considerations.

The Foreign Ministry’s responses captured the central paradox of the summit: it may temporarily ease anxiety over rare earth supplies, but it is unlikely to lower the political and regulatory threshold for access.

In April 2025, China’s Ministry of Commerce and General Administration of Customs placed several medium and heavy rare earth elements – including samarium, gadolinium, terbium, dysprosium, lutetium, scandium, and yttrium – under export controls. Exporters of these items are required to apply for licenses, with the stated legal basis including China’s Export Control Law and regulations on dual-use items. This does not amount to a blanket ban on exports, but it does shift rare earth access from a purely commercial transaction to a regulated process shaped by licensing, end-use review, and national security considerations. Once such controls are embedded in a legal and bureaucratic system, they are not easily removed. A summit can improve predictability, but it will not result in the dismantling of China’s carefully built legal framework for export controls.

The same logic applies on the U.S. side. Even if the summit reduces short-term pressure, Washington is unlikely to abandon its effort to diversify away from China-centered critical mineral supply chains. In January 2026, the White House framed U.S. dependence on imports of processed critical minerals and their derivative products as a national security concern, noting that even where the United States has domestic mining capacity, it often lacks sufficient downstream processing capacity. The policy response has therefore gone beyond asking China for more predictable deliveries. The United States is investing in domestic processing, recycling and alternative supply chains, while also working with allies and partners to reduce exposure to single-source dependence. In this sense, any relief produced by the summit may buy some time, but it will not weaken Washington’s broader push for supply-chain diversification.

Rare earths occupy this strategic space because they are not simply another category of traded minerals. Their importance lies less in the raw materials themselves than in the capabilities of the downstream industries they support: high-performance magnets, electric vehicles, wind turbines, advanced electronics and defense systems. This gives rare earths a dual character. They are commercial inputs for global industries, but they are also strategic enablers for military and technological power.

Once a commodity acquires this dual-use profile, access to it is unlikely to be governed by market logic alone. For China, this strengthens the case for licensing and end-use scrutiny. For the United States, it reinforces the argument that dependence on China-centered supply chains is not merely an economic risk, but a strategic vulnerability. Rare earths can be discussed at the summit but the underlying strategic issues are not easily resolved.

This creates an asymmetric form of interdependence. China does not control every part of the global rare earth supply chain, but its position in processing and export licensing gives it a more immediate ability to shape access. The United States is not without options, but its alternatives require time: new processing capacity must be built, recycling systems expanded, and supply arrangements with allies and partners made commercially viable. This mismatch between China’s immediate leverage and the United States’ long-term adjustment capacity creates bargaining space, but not enough for a full reset. The result is a prolonged period of managed vulnerability on rare earths.

Where the summit could still matter lies in the management of risk. Neither side benefits from an uncontrolled shock to the rare earths market. China wants to preserve its right to screen sensitive exports, but it also has an interest in presenting itself as a stable supplier of critical minerals. The United States, meanwhile, wants to reduce dependence on China-centered supply chains, but it also needs time to build alternatives. This creates room for limited accommodation: clearer licensing procedures, smoother civilian trade, and more regular communication over end-use concerns. Yet these would be instruments of crisis management rather than signs of strategic convergence. The summit may reduce uncertainty over how the rules are applied, but it is unlikely to change the rules themselves.

The Trump-Xi summit, therefore, should not be read as a turning point in rare earth politics. Its significance lies less in changing the direction of policy than in clarifying the limits of what diplomacy can achieve. For Beijing, rare earths will remain a strategic resource subject to state control. For Washington, any temporary easing will not remove the underlying concern that dependence on China-centered supply chains creates long-term strategic exposure.

This is the meaning of relief without a resolution. In the emerging logic of China-U.S. geoeconomic competition, critical minerals are instruments of leverage, symbols of vulnerability, and test of strategic resilience.

title: Reciprocal Trade Deal With the US Close to Completion, Vietnamese Media Reports
description: Hanoi's top leader To Lam met yesterday with U.S. Trade Representative Ambassador Jamieson Greer in New York, where he is set to attend the U.N. General Assembly.
text:
Vietnam and the United States are close to finalizing their reciprocal trade and tariff agreement, following positive negotiations between the country’s top leader To Lam and U.S. officials this week.

To Lam, who serves as president and chief of the Communist Party of Vietnam (CPV), met yesterday with U.S. Trade Representative Ambassador Jamieson Greer in New York, where he is scheduled to attend the ​81st Session of the U.N. General Assembly.

According to a state media report, Greer yesterday hailed the “substantial progress” in the trade talks, adding that negotiators from both sides were “very close to reaching the final outcome.”

In turn, Lam expressed his desire “to work with President Donald Trump’s administration to continue advancing bilateral relations in a stable, substantive, effective, and sustainable manner,” the report stated. Lam said that Vietnam has in recent years “made efforts to substantively promote cooperation and purchase goods from the U.S. in order to boost bilateral trade in a more balanced direction.” He also “called on the U.S. to take a comprehensive approach to outstanding trade issues,” including a number of investigations that Washington has initiated under Section 301 of the U.S. Trade Act of 1974.

Vietnam is currently the subject of a number of Section 301 investigations. It was among 60 nations that the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR) threatened in June with tariffs of 10-12.5 percent due to their alleged failures to take action on forced labor. It is also the subject of separate Section 301 probes into alleged excess manufacturing capacity and intellectual property rights.

These investigations have been interpreted as a way of rescuing President Trump’s protectionist trade policy after the U.S. Supreme Court in February struck down the sweeping global tariffs that his administration imposed on allies and adversaries alike last year.

In Vietnam’s case, the investigations have slowed down the trade negotiations that were initiated shortly after President Trump’s “liberation day” tariff announcement in April 2025, when Vietnam was hit with a 46 percent tariff. The two nations signed a framework for a trade agreement in October that lowered the tariff rate by 20 percent, but despite months of negotiations, they have yet to reach a final agreement.

The talks have snagged on U.S. concerns about transshipment – the alleged routing of Chinese goods through Vietnam to avoid U.S. tariffs – and market access for American companies. The Trump administration is also concerned about Vietnam’s yawning trade surplus with the United States, which, despite the imposition of last year’s tariffs, continues to grow. According to the USTR, the U.S. goods trade deficit with Vietnam rose to $178.2 billion in 2025, a 44.3 percent increase over 2024. It remains the third-largest of any country after China and Mexico.

The outstanding trade talks have been a subject of persistent, if minor, friction in the U.S.-Vietnam relationship, and the conclusion of a final reciprocal trade agreement would no doubt deliver a positive fillip for both sides and allow them to capitalize on the opportunities created by the establishment of a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership in 2023.

In a statement issued today, the Vietnamese government argued that “a trade agreement would provide a stable and long-term ‌framework ⁠for economic, trade and investment ties between the two countries.”

title: Rethinking Russia, Re-evaluating Risk: The Changing Face of Kyrgyz Migration
description: The war in Ukraine has produced a much longer-term transformation of the institutional and political environment in which migration takes place.
text:
Labor migration to Russia has traditionally played a central role in Kyrgyzstan’s economy. Between 2012 and 2021, average remittance inflows were the equivalent of 30 percent of Kyrgyzstan’s GDP. Following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the share of remittances in GDP has fluctuated, falling to approximately 17.6 percent in 2024. Despite this instability, remittance inflows have remained historically high in absolute terms. The volatility of recent years nevertheless points to a broader shift in the relationship between remittances and the Kyrgyz economy, suggesting that the country’s long-standing dependence on migration income is becoming more complex and potentially less predictable.

Russia’s war in Ukraine has contributed to changes in migration flows from Kyrgyzstan to Russia. According to estimates based on Kyrgyzstan’s 2022 National Population Census, approximately 854,000 Kyrgyz citizens were working in Russia. By 2026, the Kyrgyz Ministry of Labor reported that around 502,242 Kyrgyz citizens were engaged in labor migration in Russia. While differences in methodology and timing mean that these figures should not be treated as a precise measure of the decline, the overall trend is significant. Russia has not ceased to be the dominant destination for Kyrgyz labor migrants, but the changing scale of migration suggests that the long-standing Russia-centered migration system is undergoing a broader transformation.

Kyrgyzstan’s citizens have benefited from relatively open access to the Russian labor market through membership in the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) since 2015. Problems certainly existed: migrants frequently encountered arbitrary treatment by police, informal payments, document checks, and other forms of everyday insecurity. Yet the basic institutional framework remained relatively stable, and migration continued to be understood primarily as an economic and labor-market issue.

The system has experienced crises before. Since the mass development of labor migration to Russia in the early 2000s, migrants have experienced several major disruptions, including the 2008-2009 global financial crisis and the COVID-19 pandemic. Yet the current crisis is fundamentally different. Earlier shocks were primarily economic or epidemiological and, after a period of disruption, the established migration system largely recovered to its prior state. The war in Ukraine, by contrast, has produced a much longer-term transformation of the institutional and political environment in which migration takes place.

The most important change since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine has been the securitization of migration in Russia. This involves more than simply tightening migration controls; migrants are increasingly treated as objects of national security governance, with migration policy becoming more closely linked to counterterrorism, border control, and internal security.

In addition, Russia has increasingly sought to draw Central Asian migrants into its wartime manpower system, as the prolonged war in Ukraine created sustained demand for military personnel. Since 2022, Russian authorities have offered foreign nationals simplified access to citizenship in exchange for military service, while police raids and other forms of administrative pressure have increasingly been used to identify and recruit migrants and recently naturalized citizens of Central Asian origin.

This has created a striking duality in Russia’s approach to migration: migrants remain economically important because of persistent labor shortages, yet their precarious legal status also makes them a particularly accessible population for military recruitment. In this sense, migration governance has become intertwined not only with border and internal security, but also with the state’s efforts to sustain wartime manpower.

For migrants from Kyrgyzstan the significance of these changes extends beyond the immediate risk of detention or deportation. The rules governing everyday life in Russia have become more complex and restrictive, including requirements relating to registration, documentation, medical examinations, language testing, and other forms of administrative control. Migration is therefore becoming not simply more difficult, but less predictable.

This unpredictability is particularly important because the traditional Russia-Central Asian migration system depended on predictability. Families could plan around seasonal migration, circular movement, and the expectation that migrants would return to Russia after spending time at home. When the rules governing entry, employment, and residence become uncertain, the entire household migration strategy becomes harder to sustain.

A Gendered Transformation of Migration

This ongoing transformation is also likely to change the gender composition of migration. Historically, men dominated migration to Russia, particularly in construction, transport and other physically demanding sectors. The prospect of increasingly restrictive migration controls, detention, military recruitment, and uncertainty over legal status changes the calculation. Women have become a significant part of Kyrgyzstan’s migration system. Kyrgyzstan has historically had a relatively high proportion of female migrants compared with other Central Asian countries and war has accelerated this feminization of migration.

The gender implications of the current transformation require more attention. If young men increasingly avoid Russia while women become more visible in migration corridors, the social organization of migration, and potentially household roles and care responsibilities, will change as well. For women especially, these may include more precarity. Recent research from the International Organization for Migration (IOM) shows that female migrants from Kyrgyzstan continue to experience significant vulnerabilities throughout the migration cycle.

The asymmetric risks facing men in wartime Russia – specifically military mobilization and targeted security sweeps – are accelerating the structural feminization of Kyrgyz migration. This shift changes not only domestic division of labor and remittance flows within households, but also transfers the burden of economic survival onto female workers who navigate highly precarious service sectors.

The Family Implications

One of the most consequential developments is that the new restrictions increasingly affect not only workers but also their families. A particularly important example is education. Since 2024, foreign children seeking admission to Russian schools have been required to demonstrate sufficient knowledge of Russian through testing, alongside requirements concerning their legal status in the country. Children who do not meet the language requirement cannot be enrolled in school. In June 2025, the State Duma approved a bill requiring schools to report information about migrant children and their parents to the Ministry of Internal Affair. In August, a draft amendment to the Law on Education prohibiting free education for migrant children was submitted to the State Duma for discussion.

The significance of this change should not be underestimated. For many migrant families, migration to Russia was not simply an individual labor strategy. It was a family strategy in which children could live with their parents and attend Russian schools. The new rules therefore challenge one of the assumptions on which family migration had been built.

The Kyrgyz government has subsequently had to wrestle with how to provide education and social support to children whose parents work abroad.

In March 2025, the Kyrgyz government established the Tunguch online school as a pilot state institution for 2025–2028. The school provides education for students in grades 5-11 and was explicitly designed to expand access to education for children who cannot attend conventional schools because of geographical distance. By September 2025, the school had 43 classes – 28 in Kyrgyz and 15 in Russian – and children from more than 15 countries were studying through the online school, with Russia housing the largest group.

Tunguch represents an important change in the way the Kyrgyz state approaches migration. For more than two decades, the economic contribution of migrants was treated as a given, while many of the social costs of migrant children left behind, fragmented families, access to education, and reintegration were largely managed by households themselves.

By targeting the educational access and legal standing of migrant dependents, Russian policy has dismantled the “family migration” model. This systemic exclusion has forced the Kyrgyz state to pivot from passive economic beneficiary to active social mediator. Initiatives like the Tunguch online school mark the institutionalization of state-supported transnational living, signaling the state’s growing need to build infrastructure to mitigate its social externalities.

Preparedness for Migrant Reintegration

A potentially more consequential shift in Kyrgyzstan’s migration policy is emerging around the question of what happens when migrants return. On May 14, 2026, the Cabinet of Ministers approved the Program for the Reintegration of Returning Migrants for 2026–2030. This is the first national policy document specifically dedicated to migrant reintegration and signals an important change in how the state is beginning to understand migration: not only as a mechanism for absorbing domestic labor-market pressures and generating remittances, but also as a process that can reshape the country’s labor force, skills base, and economic development.

For much of the post-Soviet period, Kyrgyzstan’s migration policy was largely oriented toward managing outward mobility. Labor migration offered an important pressure valve in an economy with limited employment opportunities, while remittances became a major source of household income and foreign exchange. The policy challenge was therefore primarily how to facilitate migration, protect citizens abroad, and channel its economic benefits home. The new reintegration program suggests a different policy problem is now being centered: how to absorb and make use of the human, professional, and financial capital accumulated through migration when migrants return.

The program includes measures to support employment and self-employment, provide economic assistance, expand vocational retraining, and develop mechanisms for recognizing qualifications acquired abroad. Yet the adoption of the program should not be confused with evidence that Kyrgyzstan is prepared for a large-scale return. A policy framework is a first step; implementation capacity will determine whether reintegration becomes a viable alternative to renewed migration. The more fundamental question is whether the Kyrgyz economy can generate sufficient productive employment, wages, and opportunities for entrepreneurship to make staying economically meaningful for returnees. If these conditions are absent, reintegration programs may end up functioning primarily as short-term assistance schemes while migrants continue to view re-migration as the most viable livelihood strategy.

Diversification Beyond Russia, A Migration Crisis Unlike Any Before

The changing environment in Russia is also pushing Kyrgyzstan to diversify migration destinations. The United Kingdom has become one of the most visible alternatives. Kyrgyzstan began participating in the U.K.’s Seasonal Worker visa program in 2022. The quota available to Kyrgyz citizens increased from around 1,500 places in 2022 to 10,000 in 2025.

South Korea represents another increasingly important destination. Under the Employment Permit System, the quota for Kyrgyz workers increased by approximately 18 percent between 2023 and 2024, reaching more than 3,000 places. At the same time, South Korea has also been accessible through another route: Kyrgyz citizens who acquired Russian citizenship could take advantage of Russia’s visa-free arrangement with South Korea, which allow Russian passport holders to enter the country for short stays without a visa. This created an additional channel of mobility for some Central Asian migrants holding Russian passports, although visa-free entry should not be equated with legal authorization to work. Taken together, these developments illustrate how migration system is becoming more diversified, combining formal labor-migration programs with alternative mobility channels.

The current migration system crisis should therefore not be understood simply as another temporary decline in migration to Russia. The post-2022 crisis is different because it affects the foundations of the system. Russia is not simply becoming a more difficult labor market. It is becoming a more securitized environment in which migrants face greater uncertainty over entry, residence, employment, education for their children and personal security.

This is a profound shift. For more than two decades, Russia occupied a particular place in the social imagination of Kyrgyzstan as the most accessible foreign labor market, a familiar destination connected through networks and post-Soviet institutions, and a place where generations of Kyrgyz citizens had built their livelihoods. That perception is now changing. The significance of this transformation may ultimately extend far beyond migration statistics.

title: Samarkand to Host the Largest Chess Olympiad in History
description: The 46th World Chess Olympiad is being held in Samarkand.
text:
On September 15 this year, the 46th World Chess Olympiad will start at the Silk Road international tourism center in the city of Samarkand. In the history of the prestigious competition, held since 1927, Central Asia will host the chess world’s largest team tournament for the first time.

The Olympiad is expected to set a new record for the number of participants and teams. A total of 398 teams will take part: 208 teams in the men’s (Open) section and 190 teams in the women’s section will compete for victory. This will break the record of 380 teams set in Budapest in 2024. The Olympiad will bring together 1,974 players, including 240 grandmasters. Together with coaches and delegation members, Samarkand will welcome more than 4,000 guests during the competition. The tournament will consist of 11 rounds and will run until 27 September.

From 10 to 18 September, Samarkand will also host the 3rd Chess Paralympiad. A total of 41 teams will take part — the highest figure in the history of the Chess Paralympiad. By comparison, 26 teams competed in Belgrade in 2023 and 34 in Astana in 2024. This year’s event will bring together 196 players, including 150 men and 46 women. It will be held over seven rounds under the Swiss system. The record scale of the Chess Paralympiad is particularly significant for the development of inclusive sport and for raising the standing of chess as an intellectual sport open to all.

Holding the competition in historic Samarkand, a city inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List and one of the key crossroads of the Great Silk Road, combines a sporting contest with a platform for cultural diplomacy and international dialogue.

According to the teams’ average rating, the United States is seeded first in the men’s (Open) section. Its line-up features Fabiano Caruana, Wesley So, Levon Aronian and Hans Niemann, who is making his Olympiad debut. Reigning champion India is seeded second and Uzbekistan third. Germany will be represented by Vincent Keymer and France by Maxime Vachier-Lagrave.

Credit: Michal Walusza / FIDE

According to the teams’ average rating, India starts as the top seed in the women’s section. The Kazakhstan team includes three-time world blitz champion and Norway Chess Women 2026 winner Bibisara Assaubayeva. Ukraine’s first board will be 16-year-old European champion and woman grandmaster Anastasiya Hnatyshyn.

The line-ups of the Uzbekistan national teams reflect the emergence of a new generation of Uzbek chess. For the first time, the men’s and women’s squads will each enter three teams made up of young players. In particular, Nilufarkhon Imomkuziyeva and Khumoyun Begmurodov, both aged 16, will make their Olympiad debut. Gulrukhbegim Tokhirjonova, who played for the United States at the 2024 Olympiad in Budapest, will defend the colours of Uzbekistan this time.

FIDE World Champion Rustam Kasimdzhanov has been brought into the main men’s line-up, and Uzbekistan’s first woman grandmaster, Nafisa Muminova, has joined the women’s team as captain. In the Uzbekistan men’s team, Javokhir Sindarov (4th), Nodirbek Abdusattorov (7th), Nodirbek Yakubboev (39th) and Shamsiddin Vokhidov (61st) are among the 100 strongest players in the world rankings. The fact that Javokhir Sindarov and Nodirbek Abdusattorov are among the world’s ten strongest players clearly demonstrates the competitiveness of the Uzbek chess school. The women’s team also holds high positions in the world rankings. Afruza Khamdamova is 26th and Gulrukhbegim Tokhirjonova 80th.

The rise of Uzbek chess on the international stage is also reflected in the team rankings. Compared with 2025, the Uzbekistan men’s team has climbed 15 places in the FIDE ranking of 204 countries to take sixth place. The women’s team has climbed 17 places to take 21st.

Credit: Michal Walusza / FIDE

Alongside the Olympiad, the 97th FIDE Congress will be held in Samarkand from 19 to 28 September. Leaders of more than 200 chess federations are expected to attend. The Congress will also include the election of the FIDE President.

The 46th World Chess Olympiad will be another important stage for Uzbek player Javokhir Sindarov. Eight weeks after the Olympiad ends, he will take on reigning world champion Gukesh Dommaraju for the world chess crown. Both players will be 20 years old at the start of the match, which is scheduled to be held in Geneva from 22 November to 13 December. It will be the youngest World Championship match in chess history. Notably, before their title clash both players will be defending the colours of their national teams in Samarkand: Sindarov for Uzbekistan and Gukesh for India.

Holding the 46th World Chess Olympiad, the 3rd Chess Paralympiad and the FIDE Congress in Samarkand at the same time demonstrates Uzbekistan’s capacity to organise major international sporting and intellectual events at a high level. These competitions will not only showcase the current strength of Uzbek chess, but will also take the country’s efforts to develop youth sport, support inclusive sport and strengthen international sports diplomacy to a new level.

Full details are available on the official tournament website: chessolympiad2026.fide.com

This is a sponsored article.

title: Schools Close Across Sarawak Due to Toxic Haze From Indonesian Wildfires
description: Wildfires have raged for weeks across swathes of Sumatra and Kalimantan, exacerbated by a particularly severe dry season.
text:
Hundreds of schools across the Malaysian state of Sarawak have closed their doors because of hazardous haze from ongoing wildfires in neighboring Indonesia.

Sarawak, which runs along the north of the island of Borneo, is currently under a pall of air pollution that is among the worst it has seen this decade. On September 3, Malaysian authorities declared an emergency in Serian Division, a region in the southwest of Sarawak bordering Indonesia, after air pollution levels hit critical levels.

King Sultan Ibrahim “has consented to the declaration of emergency throughout Serian Division, Sarawak, following haze conditions that have reached air pollution levels hazardous to public health and safety,” Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s office said in a statement on September 3.

“The government will continue to monitor developments from time to time and ensure that all necessary actions are implemented immediately, including mitigation measures and the dissemination of information and health advice to the public,” it added.

Under the emergency measures, government and private offices in the town of Serian will be closed, as well as plantations, construction sites, and quarries, the AFP news agency reported. The Sarawak Disaster Management Committee also announced a three-day cloud-seeding operation that was subsequently extended to today.

On Friday, authorities also announced that 647 schools across 12 districts, including Serian and the state capital Kuching, will close their doors this week, moving lessons to an online format. A further 54 primary schools and nine secondary schools in Bintulu Division further to the east will also shut their doors due to haze, the Sarawak Education Department announced on Saturday.

The Sarawak Disaster Management Committee formally requested the declaration when the Air Pollutant Index (API) in Serian soared into dangerous territory, peaking at 519 on Friday. The Malaysian government considers API levels above 300 to be “hazardous” to human health, while readings beyond 500 justify the announcement of an emergency declaration. The Malaysia Meteorological Department told Channel News Asia (CNA) that this is Sarawak’s “worst” haze episode since 2019.

The deteriorating air quality has disrupted daily life across Sarawak. According to CNA, “outdoor events, including carnivals, community runs and sporting activities, have been cancelled, while poor visibility has disrupted some flights.”

“Transboundary haze” has become a seasonal crisis in large parts of Southeast Asia, in line with the expansion of agricultural monocultures such as palm oil, maize, paper pulp, and sugar. These are compounded by vehicle and industrial emissions and naturally occurring dry-season forest fires.

This year, the main cause is the wildfires that have raged for weeks across Indonesia’s Sumatra and Kalimantan regions, exacerbated by a particularly severe dry season. The Ministry of Forestry says that wildfires burned at least 202,010 hectares of land from January to July, around half of which took place in the month of July.

The ASEAN Specialized Meteorological Centre reported on Friday that “moderate smoke plumes were … observed to emanate from hotspots in the southern parts of Kalimantan and the southern and central parts of Sumatra.” There have also been reports of fires in South Papua, which has not traditionally seen many dry season fires. One environmentalist told CNA that this was likely “linked to land clearing in food estate and energy project areas.”

While bordering areas of Sarawak have been hardest hit by the poisonous haze, the pollution has also spread to Sabah and peninsular Malaysia, Brunei, and as far as the Philippines. On Friday, Singapore also announced it would start providing daily haze advisories from Friday evening, after the 24-hour air quality readings entered the unhealthy range for the first time since 2023.

Indonesian authorities suspect that most of the fires in Kalimantan and Sumatra were deliberately set by individuals or companies for various purposes, Forestry Minister Raja Juli Antoni said last week.

“It is almost certain that the cause is deliberate burning, not wildfires, whether carried out by individuals, ordinary farmers, or corporations,” Raja told a press conference on September 1, the Jakarta Globe reported.

Rizal Irawan, a senior official at the country’s Environment Ministry, told Reuters that the authorities were investigating 19 companies that it believes may be linked to the wildfires, and would punish any found to be responsible.

“Regardless of the cause, strict liability applies whenever a fire occurs within a concession area,” he said.

While API readings in Serian have dropped since the state of emergency came into effect – the reading as of press time was 162, in the merely “very unhealthy” zone – Indonesian authorities say that there is no immediate relief on the horizon.

Raja said that the month of September is expected to mark a critical period in efforts to contain fires due to intensifying El Niño conditions.

“We must remain extremely vigilant because, for me, September is when the real battle begins,” Raja said, according to the Jakarta Globe. “September is the peak of El Niño, so we have to stay alert.”
