title: SCO Summit Produces Surprising Winners
description: The organization’s smaller members can use a China-India-Russia-dominated forum without becoming subordinate to any single major power.
text:
The Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan August 31-September 1 marked a quarter century since the organization’s founding. Its anniversary motto, “Together for Sustainable Peace, Development and Prosperity,” hinted at ambitions considerably grander than the institution’s record. The SCO now encompasses ten member states, including China, India, Russia, Iran, Pakistan, and four Central Asian republics – Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan – representing nearly half of humanity and a substantial share of global economic activity.

Yet headlines emerging from Bishkek often highlighted the organization’s internal dynamics and differing national priorities. Unlike last year’s summit, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi did not hold a formal bilateral meeting, although their brief interaction during the summit quickly became a meme template among Indian netizens. Modi and Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif traded predictable barbs. Most stunningly, Modi directly urged Russian President Vladimir Putin to end the war in Ukraine “for humanity’s sake.” This comes shortly after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy revealed that China delivered an ultimatum to Russia not to use nuclear weapons in Ukraine, something China has not denied.

This focus on discord is not merely dramatic headline chasing; it reflects a genuine and consistently noted problem with the SCO. The organization brings together several geopolitical rivals. It is therefore difficult to imagine the institution ever evolving into a mirror of NATO. The SCO lacks the degree of institutionalization necessary to impose coherent policy on its members, while its principal powers lack sufficient leverage over one another to establish a common strategic direction.

But these features should not lead observers to dismiss the organization’s practical value for its members, especially the smaller ones.

Institutionalization is a slow process, particularly among states with divergent political systems and strategic interests. The SCO already possesses permanent structures, including its Regional Anti-Terrorist Structure (RATS) in Tashkent, while members continue to debate additional mechanisms for economic and security cooperation.

The summit featured credible proposals for institutional development, including Xi proposing AI hubs, Uzbekistan proposing an industrial cooperation mechanism, Kyrgyzstan pushing its Tamchy Special Financial Investment Territory for joint SCO projects and advocating for Bishkek as the headquarters of a joint development bank, and Tajikistan pushing for a regional digital agro-ecological platform.

Other developments emerged from the forum, especially multilateral initiatives in which the SCO serves not as an institutional organizer but as an exhibition hall for projects that individual governments want to pursue.

This has created an unusual dynamic within the organization. While SCO’s largest powers are often stalemated by competing interests, institution-building initiatives that make the greatest practical progress frequently emerge because smaller member states want them to.

SCO summits have increasingly become venues where host governments promote their own economic and diplomatic priorities. The pattern was particularly visible after the 2017 meeting in Astana. The massive Astana Expo opened the following day, underscoring how the summit could function as a platform for the host country’s broader international ambitions rather than simply as a meeting of an increasingly institutionalized organization.

Kyrgyzstan continued that tradition in Bishkek this year. As the outgoing chair and summit host, Bishkek had an obvious incentive to use the gathering to advance national priorities. The China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway received prominent attention. The project, a flagship Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) corridor running from Kashgar through Kyrgyzstan into Uzbekistan, has the potential to reshape the country’s position within Eurasian transportation networks. Kyrgyzstan also successfully promoted emerging trade routes connecting with India and Pakistan via China and the China Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) and inked a deal to drastically increase trade with Pakistan.

Kyrgyzstan, like many smaller SCO members, appears interested in maximizing the benefits of participation without presenting itself as uncritically aligned with the organization’s largest powers. While Bishkek has been open about its close economic relationship with Beijing, it retains an interest in attracting capital from outside the SCO’s economic orbit. Western capital remains valuable precisely because it provides an alternative source of financing, expertise, and commercial relationships. The establishment of the Tamchy Special Financial and Investment Territory in 2025, a special economic zone which serves as an outpost of Western regulatory codes and law in the region, illustrates this broader effort to create a more attractive investment environment.

This behavior should not be interpreted as contradictory or even unique. For smaller SCO states, strategic ambiguity is an asset. Kyrgyzstan has no interest in choosing between China, Russia, India, and Western investors when it can instead extract advantages from all of them. The same logic explains why Central Asian governments routinely embrace Chinese infrastructure while simultaneously seeking European, American, Turkish, Gulf, Japanese, and South Korean investment. Their objective and chief concern is maintaining their own agency.

That agency may be one of the SCO’s most fascinating unintended characteristics. Multilateral institutions often develop institutional behaviors their founders did not explicitly design. The European Union, NATO, and ASEAN all have political cultures and operating assumptions that went beyond the intentions of their architects. The SCO appears to be developing something different: an environment in which its smaller members possess greater freedom of economic maneuver than the organization’s nominal power structure would suggest.

China, India, and Russia each have substantial reasons to use the SCO for their own strategic purposes. That divergence limits any one major power’s ability to turn the SCO into an instrument of strategic alignment.

China has the largest economy in the organization and increasingly supplies the infrastructure connecting its members. Russia retains military influence and longstanding political relationships. India possesses substantial economic and demographic weight while maintaining relationships with both Russia and the West. Yet, none can herd the others into an arrangement that systematically disadvantages the others or Western involvement.

The result is particularly visible in Central Asia. Governments there have little incentive to surrender their ability to balance among external powers. Chinese railways and investment can expand economic opportunity, while American or European capital can provide diversification. Turkish, Gulf, Indian, Japanese, and Korean partnerships provide additional options. For governments sitting between much larger powers, dependency on any single patron is inherently dangerous.

The SCO therefore produces a paradox. Its smaller members often determine whether any institutionalization actually moves forward. The major powers may act as veto-players or set strategic priorities, but implementation often depends on whether smaller governments see a direct benefit. It seems that the SCO’s largest members increasingly result to multilateral arrangements bypassing the SCO when convenient.

This is why Bishkek may ultimately prove more revealing than dramatic images of Modi, Xi, and Putin standing together. The central question is not whether the three largest powers can appear united, nor is it whether they can identify areas of common interest. The more important question is whether they can convert that shared interest into an institutional structure capable of constraining the strategic choices of the organization’s other members.

The answer so far: no.

The organization’s most surprising winners are the states that were never expected to exercise much influence over it. Kyrgyzstan successfully used the summit and its 2025-2026 chairmanship to promote its economic priorities. Other small SCO states in Central Asia have long done the same, using the organization to attract capital, build connections, and preserve strategic options.

This is a very different outcome from the emergence of a unified Eurasian bloc or some grand anti-Western alliance some have predicted. For Washington, that distinction should matter. The SCO should not be dismissed as an ineffectual talking shop, but neither should it be treated as an embryonic anti-Western alliance with the activities of Beijing or Moscow ascribed to all of its members. Washington too would be better served by watching the multilateral announcements on the sidelines of the organization rather than taking grand declarations at face value.

So long as Beijing, New Delhi, and Moscow remain at loggerheads, they will be unable to impose a common strategic direction, and the organization’s smaller states will retain outsized influence and room to maneuver – particularly in the economic domain.

In Bishkek, that room was on display. The summit produced declarations, initiatives, infrastructure commitments, and political theater. More importantly, it showed that the organization’s smaller members can use a China-India-Russia-dominated forum without becoming subordinate to any single major power. The SCO may eventually become a more coherent institution. Until then, its greatest surprise is that the tail continues to wag the dog, and its smallest states, by converting membership into tangible development gains, are the biggest winners.
tag: 2026 SCO Summit; Shanghai Cooperation Organization; Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO)

title: Security Is the Key to Resolving the Thai-Cambodia Border Conflict
description: “The first step is security: uphold the ceasefire, reduce military risks, clear mines, strengthen law enforcement, and cooperate against criminal networks.”
text:
With UNCLOS conciliation proceedings between Thailand and Cambodia now formally under way, Thailand is preparing to engage constructively. We would have preferred to resolve the matter directly with Cambodia. Direct diplomacy is usually faster, less cumbersome and, when there is sufficient political will, more effective. But Thailand is a State Party to UNCLOS, the U.N. Convention on the Law of the Sea. We accepted the process and will take part in good faith, with the interests of the Thai people and our sovereign rights firmly in view.

That willingness to engage through international law should not be mistaken for a willingness to treat every dispute along the Thailand-Cambodia border as if it existed in a vacuum. They do not.

A boundary is not drawn on a blank sheet of paper. It is surveyed on actual ground, by actual people, in communities that need to be safe enough for technical work to take place.

This is the point that risks being lost in Cambodia’s push to convene the Joint Boundary Commission, because no technical or legal process can be separated from conditions on the ground. Before survey teams can do their work, the border must be sufficiently safe, stable, and properly managed.

That means implementing the commitments already agreed by both sides on ceasefire and de-escalation, joint demining, and cooperation against transnational crime. These measures are what make credible border discussions possible in the first place.

Consider demining. Thai soldiers have repeatedly been injured by landmines along the border, including incidents involving mines that have been identified as newly laid. Just a couple weeks ago, yet another Thai deminer lost a limb. Whatever political narrative one prefers, a mine does not become less dangerous because a meeting has been scheduled. Nor can a Joint Boundary Commission survey team be expected to work in an area potentially littered with mines.

Joint demining is a practical prerequisite to constructive talks. It is also an obligation rooted in the commitments that both Thailand and Cambodia have undertaken bilaterally and internationally, including under the Ottawa Convention. If both sides are genuinely committed to resolving border problems peacefully, making the ground safe for the people expected to do that work should hardly be controversial.

The same logic applies to transnational crime. A border is not secure if criminal syndicates can exploit weak enforcement, traffic people across it, and operate industrial-scale scam networks with impunity.

The scale of the problem is well known. The global online scam industry generates more than $1 trillion a year, while the International Organization for Migration estimates that more than 300,000 people from over 80 countries have been trafficked into illicit call-center networks in Southeast Asia. Reports have identified operational bases in our neighboring countries, but Thailand is not exempt from responsibility. We have a duty to act on our side of the border as well, and we have been doing exactly that.

Thailand has helped tens of thousands of Thai and foreign victims return home. We have expanded intelligence and information sharing with foreign partners, strengthened cooperation on prosecution, and pushed for wider international partnerships. These efforts intensified after last year’s clashes with Cambodia, when Thai authorities uncovered large scam operations along the border, including in areas previously used by Cambodian forces as military positions. The discoveries helped expose the scale of the networks, their methods, and the extraordinary degree of impunity in which they had been operating.

This matters to the border question because lawlessness does not politely stay in its own policy silo. Areas affected by mines, military tensions, or organized criminal activity are also areas where communities cannot return to normal life, while cross-border commerce suffers, and any serious effort to resolve contested claims becomes harder.

The sequence is therefore important. The first step is security: uphold the ceasefire, reduce military risks, clear mines, strengthen law enforcement, and cooperate against criminal networks. Then technical border work can proceed on firmer ground, literally and politically.

These security issues are already reflected in the Joint Statement painstakingly negotiated and signed by both sides on December 27, 2025. What is needed now is implementation.

Thailand will continue to do what it can and what it must. We will engage international mechanisms seriously and uphold our legal obligations. We will continue to advocate for a rules-based international order in which law is not treated as an à la carte menu. States cannot insist on rules they find useful while treating inconvenient obligations as optional.

That principle applies to Thailand as much as to Cambodia. A durable settlement will not come from public posturing, legal theater, or technical talks detached from realities on the ground. It will come from concrete steps that reduce risk, protect communities, and create the conditions in which both countries can address difficult boundary questions peacefully and credibly.

Thailand is ready to turn that page. We hope Cambodia is ready to do the same. But first, we must make sure the proper foundations are in place.

title: Shifting Poles and Power 35 Years After the End of the Soviet Union
description: For many post-Soviet states, multipolarity is nothing new. Navigating between competing powers has been an important part of their security strategy since independence.
text:
Since late August, seven of the 15 republics of the former Soviet Union celebrated the 35th anniversary of the declaration of their independence. Some marked the occasion in spectacular fashion, such as Uzbekistan and others with more sedate celebrations. But all sought to display and embrace the national identities they have developed since attaining sovereignty.

In 1991, the Soviet Union collapsed and the bipolar world of the time came to an end. In the post-Cold War period, widely described as a period of U.S. unipolarity, when there was no power that could seriously challenge U.S. supremacy, the new republics worked hard to strengthen their national identities.

The rise of China, and Russia’s resurgence under President Vladimir Putin, changed the balance of power in the late 2000s.

Today, the dominant narrative – not only in countries of the Global South in general and in the post-Soviet space in particular but increasingly in Western discourse, too – is that the world is shifting toward a different system, a multipolar one.

This multipolarity is on display across the post-Soviet space. The Baltic states, for example, became NATO members in the early 2000s. In Eastern Europe, while Belarus became a close ally of Russia, Ukraine hedged and then inched toward the West. In Russian discourse, Ukraine’s desire to join NATO was a threat to Moscow’s security. Other states in the South Caucasus and Central Asia continue to hedge among the various poles in the emerging multipolar world.

What does security look like for the current post-Soviet states? Has the world indeed become multipolar for these states or has it been multipolar for them all along? There is a plethora of alliances, blocs, and various other groups in the world today, many which border or reach into the post-Soviet space: From the Western-led NATO, to BRICS, the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, and the Collective Security Treaty Organization, each built around the perceived national interests of states, their history and power politics in the region. More recently, one could argue, such groups have formed around religious identity, such as the Mecca Pact involving Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Türkiye. The world is transitioning toward an international system with several centers of power. Whether we call it a multipolar world or something else, the emergence of different poles seems clear.

In the post-Soviet space, over the past three decades, these poles have largely been centered around Russia, China, and the United States. Chinese expansion in the region has reached unprecedented levels in particular. China has replaced Russia as the main trading partner of most of the Central Asian states. While Russia has pursued an alternative Eurasian security order in the post-Soviet space, China’s economic power and the scale of its economic engagement have made it increasingly dominant through its geoeconomic programs, including the Belt and Road Initiative and other credit and assistance schemes.

Until Russia’s war in Ukraine, security and international relations scholars were broadly discussing and researching how interstate war had declined since the Second World War, with more casualties coming from civil wars and domestic unrest.

In my security and international relations classes, we mostly focused on internal conflicts, conflicts involving non-state actors, and terrorism. This thinking changed in 2022, when Russia invaded Ukraine, followed by Israel’s war in Gaza in 2023 and, more recently, the U.S. war in Iran. None of these active wars appears to be ending soon. Multiple conflicts and ongoing Cold War-like rivalries indicate that there are several powers fighting for what they believe is their sphere of influence.

While countries in the Global South have been talking about multipolarity for some time, it was only after U.S. President Donald Trump’s shift towards a more isolationist foreign policy for the U.S., as well as his demands for NATO members to look after their own security, that the topic of multiple poles and spheres of influence has became more serious. This was reinforced by the Canadian prime minister’s reference to the importance of middle powers working together in the new world, presented in a speech to the World Economic Forum in Davos in January. The transition toward multiple spheres of influence is accompanied by a shift toward nationalist and isolationist policies.

More recently, Türkiye has emerged as a new pole for the Central Asian states. Four Central Asian states share a common Turkic identity. Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan ,and Türkiye are members of the Organization of Turkic States (OTS), which brings these countries together around their Turkic identity, while Turkmenistan is an observer. It is perhaps the first organization that unites these states based on their local Turkic languages and culture rather than the prior regional lingua franca, Russian.

It is hard to say if we are now in a fully multipolar world or whether it has always been so for the states in the post-Soviet space. Nationalist tendencies are on the rise in many societies today, for example the rise of Reform U.K. in the United Kingdom, the recent victory of Germany’s far-right AfD, and the growing influence of One Nation in Australia. In this changing global system, we see not only an ideological dimension, reflected in the Western and non-Western divide, but also an identity-driven dimension, as illustrated by the recent Mecca Pact and the OTS. For many states in Central Asia, it remains important to maximize their national interests while coexisting with multiple poles competing for influence in the region – something that has always been the case.
tag: Central Asia; multipolar world; multipolarity; spheres of influence

title: Shipki La and the Battle Over the History of China-India Trade
description: The Chinese narrative attempts to erase the independent agency Tibet exercised before 1951, framing Shipki La as a historical link between China and India (not Tibet and India).
text:
After a six-year hiatus, the China-India border trade via Shipki Pass, a 3,930-meter pass in Himachal Pradesh’s Kinnaur district, resumed on August 1, 2026. After the 2020 Galwan military standoff, the border trade from this pass, often called the “Gateway to Tibet,” was suspended. With limited operations and economic scope but significant political symbolism, the resumption of border trade has also rejuvenated interest in the competing legitimacy narratives over the Tibet question.

According to China’s state-affiliated think tanks and media, border trade via the Shipki L Pass dates to the 7th to 9th centuries when the Tubo Empire reigned over the plateau. China frames trade along this route as a sub-set of the Silk Road. Between the 14th and early 20th centuries, Chinese tellings claim Tibet as a commercial bridge between China and South Asia, while in the late 18th century, the Qing Dynasty of China took measures to standardize trade activities between Tibet and its neighboring countries, for “better management” of Tibet.

As per the Chinese accounts, the “peaceful liberation” of Tibet in 1951 and the signing of the Panchsheel Pact led to the abolishment of India’s trade “privileges” in Tibet and the formalization of a new paradigm for Indo-Tibetan trade.

China claims to have set Sino-Indian border trade free from unequal terms set by colonial rule, ushering in an era of normalized development. Cut to the present: the reopening of Shipki La Pass, despite the minuscule trade volume, is received by Chinese media as a welcome move toward improving China-India strategic ties.

Every aspect of the Chinese reading of history sidelines the Tibetan side of the story. For starters, what the Chinese narrative misses is the independent agency Tibet exercised before 1951.

By contrast, Tibetan scholars characterize Shipki Pass as a major route for trade and cultural exchange between Indian territories and Tibet, independent of Chinese involvement. Consistent with Tibet’s claim to political and commercial autonomy, historical records describe Shipki Pass as a crucial route connecting Tibet with the Kingdom of Bushahar, Ladakh, and Kashmir. The exchange across the regions, involving a variety of products, was governed by gamgya, a traditional informal oath of mutual trust that was respected and maintained across generations.

However, with the development of modern state infrastructure on either side of Shipki Pass and growing geopolitical disputes culminating in the Sino-Indian War in 1962, the centuries-old trade system was fractured.

The Tibetan accounts also challenge the Chinese manipulation of history to appropriate the Shipki Pass trade route into a meta-narrative of the Silk Road. The commentaries consistent with the Tibetan narrative challenge the engulfing of Tibet in Chinese historical narratives as a simple commercial bridge, stripping it of its agency and independent existence.

Tibetan scholars argue that it was the PRC’s administrative and military consolidation post 1951 that led to the dismantling of traditional trade and transit networks, not the British colonial disruption. The PRC’s normalization with India involved the isolation of Tibet and the enforcement of new restrictions on previously autonomous trade practices between India and Tibet

This is not a dispute over mere historical fact-checking. It leads to the question of who holds legitimacy over Tibet, and the framing of the India-China-Tibet relationship since the 1950s.

The re-opening of Shipki Pass – often framed in terms of the overall China-India relationship – is seeing one version of history eclipse the other. Popular media crowds out the complicated, contesting narratives and historical claims by constructing a more attractive narrative around boosting local trade, development, and restoration of ancient ties. Given the meager economic value of this barter-driven border trade, the Chinese media has woven the narrative around regional livelihood, the possibility of infrastructure development, and building mutual trust. The Chinese commentary construes the opening as a “revival” of ancient Sino-Indian border trade, with Tibet as a commercial bridge, and part of efforts to eliminate the colonial inequalities after the “liberation of Tibet.”

Over the last few years, the construction of border village resettlement projects, combining civilian housing with military and surveillance infrastructure, in the Tibet Autonomous Region near the Shipki Pass has gained momentum. These villages help give physical form to China’s version of the story, elevating ancient Sino-Indian trade ties over India-Tibet exchanges. Expanding beyond academic and journalistic narratives, Beijing is consolidating its rendition of Tibet as a commercial bridge through trade resumption and border infrastructure.

The reopening of Shipki Pass matters for reasons beyond trade resumption and China-India diplomacy. It highlights the disputes over sovereignty, history, and measures to consolidate control over the border. As it turns out, the trade diplomacy along the Sino-Indian border is less about trade and more about whose history triumphs.

title: Siddhant Kishore on BRICS and the New Geopolitics of Asia
description: Siddhant Kishore joins host Tushar Shetty to examine the BRICS summit in New Delhi and the strategic realignment underway across Asia.
text:
In this episode of Beyond the Indus, Siddhant Kishore, a New Delhi and Washington D.C.-based national security and foreign policy analyst, and former analyst at the Institute for the Study of War, joins host Tushar Shetty to examine the BRICS summit in New Delhi and the strategic realignment underway across Asia.

They discuss the consensus preserved in the New Delhi Declaration and India’s diplomatic win on Pahalgam, the tactical stabilization between New Delhi and Beijing and why it falls short of realignment, the costly Iran-U.S. stalemate and Washington’s undefined war aim, the Houthi advance on the Bab al-Mandeb and the reconstitution of Iran’s proxy network, the operational hollowness of the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, and the hedging by U.S. allies as Washington’s security commitments turn conditional.

title: ‘Small-Yurt Diplomacy’ Prevails at Kyrgyzstan’s World Nomad Games
description: This year, as Kyrgyzstan was busy showcasing its culture to the world, foreign countries were competing for the attention of locals.
text:
You are walking through an ethno-village in rural Kyrgyzstan. On the right is a string of cultural zones organized by each of the country’s seven regions and two major cities, Bishkek and Osh. In each, traditional music is played, food is cooked, and dances are performed.

You keep walking, beyond a mound where spectators are watching age-old martial arts, past a bazaar where local wares are being bought and sold, before you finally reach the end of the road. You see another cluster of yurts.

As you approach, you get the feeling that you’re truly in a place where custom and culture still reign supreme. And then you almost get hit in the head with a lacrosse ball, flung in your direction from a tent conspicuously featuring an American flag.

Such was the setting in eastern Kyrgyzstan’s Kyrchyn Gorge at the start of September, as the country again hosted the World Nomad Games. The alpine valley was one of seven major locations during the games, featuring an extensive cultural program that included traditional games, music and dance, and sports such as eagle hunting, horseback archery, and tug-of-war.

For foreign governments and international organizations — including the United States, Qatar, South Korea, Turkiye, the European Union, and UNICEF — the occasion offered an enormous opportunity to engage with Kyrgyz visitors and practice a little cultural diplomacy of their own.

A Kyrgyz family poses for a photo at a yurt being operated by Qatar’s Al Gannas falconry society. Photo by Oliver Fisk.

At some level, the strategy of directly appealing to people from across Kyrgyzstan made perfect sense.

Kyrchyn drew more than 150,000 people a day during the weeklong festivities, organizers say, more than four times the average attendance at previous editions of the games. The ethno-village offered foreign governments and organizations something formal diplomacy in Kyrgyzstan rarely provides: thousands of casual, face-to-face interactions with ordinary people.

The U.S. yurt, for example, let visitors try a number of American sports, like lacrosse, corn hole, and American football. It also featured a cardboard version of George Washington, mini tutorials on U.S. history, and a cutout of an American prairie wagon.

The European Union, meanwhile, brought eight European countries together under one canopied roof, allowing visitors to sample German pastries, Norwegian brown goat cheese, Swiss fondue, and Spanish olives while learning about the countries behind them.

The goal, according to yurt organizer Zarina Toichubekova, who works for a Kyrgyz-German organization aimed at helping the needs of the Kyrgyz diaspora in Europe, was to “demonstrate the friendship and cultural connections between Europe and Kyrgyzstan” while building new “people-to-people connections.”

“Many people were genuinely curious to learn about the traditions behind the products,” Toichubekova told me. “So while it was certainly an opportunity to present European culture and traditions, it was [also about] having a genuine two-way cultural exchange.”

Kyrgyz children are taught sustainable water conservation and cleaning habits while sitting inside the UNICEF yurt. (Photo provided by UNICEF Kyrgyzstan.)

That two-way exchange was perhaps most readily apparent at the UNICEF Yurt, where the focus was less on promoting a particular country than on connecting with the next generation. The organization opened its space for children and families to play traditional Kyrgyz games while learning about child rights, nutrition, and other issues.

“That intergenerational interaction was especially valuable. It showed that promoting a healthy lifestyle and preserving cultural heritage can reinforce each other,” UNICEF Kyrgyzstan’s Cholpon Zhanadylova told The Diplomat.

But beyond what was being put on show for local attendees, the fact that foreign countries used the World Nomad Games to appeal to Kyrgyzstan’s domestic audience is another reminder of how the event’s original logic has been turned on its head.

As Dr. Arzuu Sheranova, an independent researcher based in Germany, recently told The Diplomat, the games were initially intended to be “a kind of instrument” to “improve Kyrgyzstan’s national image” to the outside world.

“Especially after the coups in 2005 and 2010, and the looting [that took place] during those periods of time, the trust of foreign businesses and investors had been shattered,” Sheranova said. “So the games were introduced in order to attract foreign investments again, to develop tourism, and to rebrand the country as a stable, safe place.”

But this outward-facing focus seems to have largely dissipated. During this year’s games, despite the authorities’ repeated claims that the games will spur a “significant increase” in international tourism moving forward, attending almost any of the week’s events left you with the impression that the organizers were not measuring their success by the number of foreigners they had attracted.

That apparent shift in priorities is part of a broader change in how the government views the World Nomad Games, Kyrgyz political scientist Emil Juraev told The Diplomat.

“The primary target these days is actually a domestic audience,” Emil Juraev said, noting that the Kyrgyz government seemed to have intentionally arranged for host privileges of the World Nomad Games to cycle back to the country ahead of its elections in 2027.

Several major infrastructure projects completed before the games got underway, he also pointed out, had to be worked on around the clock to finish in time.

“Hosting the [Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit], the World Nomad Games on a whole different level… this is all supposed to be very legitimacy- and approval rating-confirming for the Kyrgyz government,” Juraev said.
tag: Kyrgyzstan; Kyrgyzstan soft power; World Nomad Games; World Nomad Games 2026

title: South Korea and Arctic Shipping: A Game Changer on Thin Ice?
description: South Korea is clearly ambitious about seizing potential economic and strategic opportunities from Arctic shipping. But the Arctic is also a geopolitical minefield.
text:
On September 16, 2025, South Korea’s Lee Jae-myung administration formally adopted Arctic shipping development as a national policy. The Ministry of Ocean and Fisheries has subsequently moved to Busan, aiming to establish the city as South Korea’s maritime hub for Arctic shipping.

South Korea sent its first trial container, the PanStar Acro (under the flag of Panama), via the Northern Sea Route (NSR) to Europe in August 2026, following a few weeks behind the Chinese container ship Dubai Tower (under the flag of Liberia).

On September 11, 2026, Hanwha Ocean, one of Korea’s big three shipbuilders, began constructing the country’s second ice-breaker, which is expected to be more than twice the size and 50 percent better than the existing RV Araon.

South Korea, an Asian middle power, is clearly ambitious about seizing potential economic and strategic opportunities of the development of Arctic shipping. The challenges and prospects for South Korea’s Arctic ambitions hold insights for other interested countries as well.

The Arctic is warming at an alarming rate due to human-induced climate change. According to NASA, in September, when the Arctic sea ice reaches its minimum extent, the ice-covered area is now “shrinking at a rate of 12.2 percent per decade, compared to its average extent during the period from 1981 to 2010.” A decrease in the extent of sea ice and the loss of older, thick ice makes longer navigation seasons possible and generates new access to previously difficult to reach regions of the Arctic.

According to the Arctic Council, the number of ships operating in the Arctic reached a record high in 2025, with 1,812 unique ships entered the Arctic Polar Code area. This is a 40 percent increase compared to 2013. The shipping activities in the Arctic are likely to further increase in years to come, since the Arctic Ocean could possibly have its first ice-free day in summer 2027.

The Arctic shipping routes, especially the NSR along the Russian Arctic coastline, could cut shipping times by 10-20 days between East Asia and Europe, compared to traditional routes via the Strait Suez Canal or the Cape of Good Hope. Moreover, the freedom of navigation in “strategic chokepoints,” such as the Strait of Hormuz, is being shaken by geopolitics. This makes Arctic shipping routes strategically attractive for East Asian economies as an alternative for their foreign trade and energy security. China is so far the most active user of the NSR. And here comes South Korea.

In my view, the development of the NSR must be considered in the context of the China-Russia-U.S. strategic triangle. Both Russia and the United States are Arctic states, but they hold divergent views about the legal status of the NSR. Article 234 (“Ice-Covered Areas”) of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea provides a legal basis for Russia to exert jurisdiction over the NSR. However, Russia actually treats the NSR as its domestic waters. The United States, on the contrary, views the NSR as straits used for international navigation. Under this view, ships should have free transit rather than needing to apply for a permit from Russia’s Northern Sea Route General Administration.

China is in a tense geopolitical rivalry with the U.S., while Russia is now China’s most important partner in international affairs. Nevertheless, Russia and China have profound differences about how the Arctic should be governed. China is not openly challenging Russian regulation of the NSR, but that does not mean China is satisfied with Russia’s position. China wants to be seen as an equal partner with Arctic states and have a bigger say in Arctic governance.

Therefore, when South Korea enters into the scene as an active user of the NSR, there are potential risks and challenges from three aspects.

First, there is geopolitical risk. Russia is interested in increasing the use of the NSR and welcomes foreign investment and technology to develop the Russian Arctic. However, since the Ukraine War, national security concerns now supersede economic development and environmental protection in many parts of the Arctic. The region has sadly become confrontational again. Any future geopolitical incident, such as a Freedom of Navigation Operation (FONOP) by the U.S. against Russia’s “excessive claims” of the NSR, could spark fierce Russian retaliation. South Korea, as a U.S. ally, might be caught in the crossfire.

Second, and related, is the sanctions risk. The U.S. has introduced massive sanctions against Russian entities, both primary sanctions and secondary sanctions. Those sanctions paid special attention to Russia’s oil and gas industry as well as the banking system, to cut the Russian economy off from the West and reduce Russia’s revenue to fund its war. Secondary sanctions are particularly powerful. They are used to maintain or put additional pressure on the sanctions target by penalizing third parties that engage with the primary sanctions target in activities that could undermine or evade the purpose of the primary sanctions.

Therefore, Chinese and Japanese enterprises have become very cautious about doing business with Russia. For example, according to the website of Northern Sea Route General Administration, in 2025,only one Chinese-flagged ship submitted an application for a navigation permit on the NSR. The R/V Tan Suo San Hao is a scientific vessel owned by the Institute of Deep-sea Science and Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences, which was delivered in 2024 with capacity to conduct scientific expedition in the Russian Arctic. China’s state-owned global shipping giant, COSCO, has tempered its enthusiasm about using the NSR. Rather, unknown shipping companies, such as New New Shipping and Sea Legend (which runs Dubai Tower), were established to provide regular container service only between Russian and Chinese ports, using the NSR. The U.S. secondary sanctions are applied universally. South Korea’s status as a U.S. ally does not necessarily shield its companies from future U.S. sanctions.

Third is the competition South Korea will face in Arctic shipping. China is the most active user state of the NSR so far. The Polar Silk Road was officially announced by China’s 2018 Arctic Policy White Paper. Originally, the PSR aimed to cover the whole Arctic as China’s overall strategy in the region. However, due to what I call a “push and pull effect” between the U.S., Russia, and China, the PSR has evolved to focus on collaboration with Russia.

Building upon China’s “unlimited” bilateral cooperation with Russia, the PSR has two dimensions. It reflects China’s strong interest in developing and using Arctic shipping routes, not only connecting the Chinese and Western European markets, but also China and the resource-rich Russian Arctic for China’s energy security. Therefore, South Korean companies will be facing economic and technological competition from Chinese companies in the Russian Arctic.

That being said, I think South Korea’s ambitions for Arctic shipping should be lauded. The NSR has potential to serve South Korea’s national interest as an alternative, strategic shipping route. Moreover, because Russia wants to diversify sources of foreign investment and increase the usage of NSR, South Korea’s interest in the Arctic shipping is likely to be welcomed by Russia. Therefore, South Korea could become a game changer in the Arctic amid geopolitical headwinds.

As a middle power that has been thriving in the epicenter of East Asian geopolitics for decades, South Korea has a proven record for managing great powers relations for national security and prosperity. Now it will try to make use of that experience in the Arctic.
tag: China-Russia in the Arctic; Northern Sea Route; Russian Arctic policy; South Korea Arctic policy; South Korea Arctic shipping; South Korea in the Arctic

title: South Korea Embraces the Silk Road Spirit With Central Asian Leaders
description: In the first Central Asia-South Korea leaders summit, energy and critical minerals were top of the agenda.
text:
Amid their first leader-level summit, South Korea and the five Central Asian states set a course for deeper relations centered on critical minerals, energy, and emerging technology, with a focus on seeking out mutual benefits and climbing the value chain together.

South Korean President Lee Jae-myung called for the forging of a “new Silk Road.”

“If we walk together, I am certain that the road of 1,500 years ago will reopen as a new and beautiful Silk Road,” Lee said. “If the five countries gathered here today and we in the Republic of Korea pool our wisdom and join hands, there is nothing we cannot achieve together.”

On September 16 in Seoul, Lee met with the presidents of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan together for the first time, taking advantage of the C5+1 format that has become an increasingly popular vehicle for external powers to engage with the Central Asian region.

Since 2007, Central Asian and South Korean officials have met at the vice-ministerial level, upgrading to the ministerial level in 2019 and now the presidential level.

South Korea has long been an important partner for the region, though it flies under the geopolitical radar homed in on Russia, China, and the United States. Although the Central Asian states are marginal trade partners for South Korea, whose GDP of approximately $1.93 trillion makes it the 15th largest globally, Seoul is a top-10 trade partner for Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and Uzbekistan. That trade, however, is often heavily weighted in South Korea’s favor, as in the case of Tajikistan – according to the Observatory of Economic Complexity (OEC), in July 2026 South Korea exported $31.6 million in goods to Tajikistan (mostly cars and other vehicles) and imported $0.

For Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, the balance is better and the trade volumes bigger. In July 2026, OEC data stated, South Korea exported $158 million in goods (mostly cars and other vehicles but also beauty products) to Kazakhstan and imported imported $142 million (mostly crude petroleum, coal, and ferroalloys). In regard to Uzbekistan, South Korea exported $182 million in goods (mostly cars and other vehicles, as well as vehicles parts, but also – and I confess I don’t understand – $21.1 million in the “brochures” category); Uzbekistan meanwhile sent $7.06 million in goods (refined petroleum, perfume plants and medical instruments) to South Korea.

In his remarks, Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev highlighted Kazakhstan’s leading place in Central Asia-South Korea trade – representing half of it – and the prevalence of well-known Korean companies in Kazakhstan.

“More than 1,000 joint ventures with Korean capital operate in Kazakhstan,” he said. “Leading companies such as Kia, Hyundai, Doosan, Posco, Samsung, Lotte, and Hanwha have been successfully operating in the Kazakhstani market for many years.”

“There is significant potential in the industrial sector that requires further deepening economic cooperation,” Tokayev added. He made the case for further Korean investment in Central Asia, taking advantage of expanding trade and transit corridor across the Eurasian landmass.

Tokayev proposed launching a Central Asia-Korea industrial and technological development partnership. “Within this framework, our governments could create a portfolio of flagship joint projects with a focus on localization of production, technology transfer, development of regional cooperation, and export of finished products to third-country markets,” he added.

Meanwhile, Uzbekistan’s President Shavkat Mirziyoyev had his own proposals, mirroring those of Tokayev, including for a Central Asia-Korea Industrial and Technological Park

Energy and critical minerals – the former always in vogue and the latter the hottest topic at present – naturally received intense attention.

On the energy front, conditions are not ideal but ambitions remains. “We are prepared to expand cooperation in this area, including resuming energy supplies to Korea,” Tokayev said. Recurring attacks on Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC) infrastructure in recent years (and problems in the Red Sea in past years) have hassled and occasionally halted exports. About 80 percent of Kazakhstan’s oil exports pass through the pipeline system that carries Kazakh crude from the country to Russia’s Novorossiysk port, on the Black Sea.

Critical minerals are the crux of nearly every conversation with Central Asian states these days, with external powers interested in what Central Asian can provide and regional governments keenly aware of both the opportunity at hand and the risks.

Mirziyoyev commented, “Today, Central Asia is no longer just a supplier of raw materials.” That may be putting the cart before the horse, but highlights regional ambitions to move up the value chain when it comes to critical minerals.

“Given the rapidly growing demand for this valuable raw material and its vast reserves in Central Asia, the region is capable of becoming a leading supplier on the global market. Korea’s advanced technology and capital can play a decisive role in this,” Mirziyoyev said. He proposed a “Regional Investment Alliance for Critical Minerals.”

“Remarkably, all 10 minerals classified by Korea as strategic are present in our country’s mineral resource base,” Tokayev said, pitching Kazakhstan’s resource wealth. “The combination of Kazakhstan’s resource potential and Korea’s technological capabilities opens up broad prospects for mutually beneficial cooperation.”

Lee, in his remarks, spoke right to the heart of Central Asian ambitions. If trade at present is dominated by Korean cars and Central Asian oil, both sides are looking to what’s next.

“We now need to move beyond these items and expand the scope of trade into new industries, including consumer goods, biotechnology, and digital sectors,” Lee said. He added, “As global supply chains are being reorganized, Central Asia is emerging as a treasure trove of critical minerals essential for the production of electric vehicles, batteries and semiconductors.”

The summit ended with a declaration – the Seoul Declaration – charting out a 30-year plan to expand ties and to institutionalize relations. As Ji Da-gyum wrote for The Korea Herald, one of the central motivations for the Seoul Declaration is to turn existing political commitment “into a more durable institutional framework.” Under that emerging framework leaders-level summits are expected biennially, with the next envisioned for 2028 in Kazakhstan.
tag: Central Asia-South Korea relations; Kazakhstan-South Korea relations; South Korea-Central Asia leaders summit; Uzbekistan-South Korea relations

title: South Korean Submarines Could Save Australia From the AUKUS Shambles
description: Could the conventionally-powered KSS-III sub offer a more affordable and timely alternative to the planned nuclear-powered fleet?
text:
In July, the Canadian government announced that it has chosen the German-Norwegian bid to build 12 conventionally-powered submarines to replace their obsolete Victoria class fleet. The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation reported the estimated cost of the submarines at CA$24 billion. With 35-year lifetime maintenance and sustainment costs added, the overall program cost is likely to be in the vicinity of CA$100 billion. This compares more than favorably to the A$368 billion (the dollar equivalents are similar) allocated so far to AUKUS.

The Canadians said they had a hard time choosing between two excellent options – the other being the South Korean KSS-III submarine.

Professor Hugh White has long experience with our Collins class submarine project and, more recently, with the details of AUKUS. He says that as an alternative to the AUKUS project “any off-the-shelf submarines Australia could get its hands on, we should take.”

One option is to turn back to the French Naval Group for a new order of 12 submarines. In evidence given to the AUKUS public inquiry in Canberra on 2 September, retired admiral Peter Briggs gave an informed presentation on the capabilities of nuclear-powered submarines. He favors procurement of a low-enriched uranium nuclear-powered submarine, based on the French Suffren class, for the Royal Australian Navy (RAN). He strongly opposes purchase of the US Virginia class and the proposed British-designed SSN AUKUS boats, describing the plan as “flawed and undeliverable”.

His conclusion about the AUKUS submarines is widely supported by the evidence and a strong consensus of military and academic opinion.

During his presentation Admiral Briggs stated his view that conventional diesel-electric submarine technology was not acceptable for the next generation of RAN operations. His argument was that conventionally powered submarines have neither the stealth features nor the endurance needed for effective undersea naval operations. Nonetheless, the example he cited concerned the limitations of the existing Collins class submarine design. As is well known, Collins is an outdated platform that is nearing the end of its operational life.

Given the South Koreans only recently lost the bid for 12 submarines to replace the ageing Canadian fleet, their new submarine should be available for export without delay. The KSS-III proposal had an appealing range of handover deadlines promised for Canada. The expected first boat delivery date was scheduled to be 2032, with the initial batch of four submarines delivered by 2035 and the remaining eight boats at the rate of one per year until 2043, when the entire fleet of 12 would be in service. It has been reported that the South Korean tender may have suffered a disadvantage because Canadian infrastructure and crew capacity to absorb the fleet in that timeframe is underdeveloped. This is much less a problem in Australia.

These delivery timeframes compare to 2032 proposed for the first second-hand AUKUS Virginia; thereafter delivery in 2035 and 2038 respectively. The first British-designed AUKUS SSN boat is not expected to be delivered until the fuzzy “2040s.” Obviously, procurement of an entire one-class fleet of 12 KSS-III submarines by 2043 is an attractive option. It would adequately cover the capability gap of decommissioned Collins class submarines, scheduled to begin in 2040. If the argument about needing more naval capability now has any relevance, early delivery is a must.

KSS-III Capability

Defence Central is the authoritative London-based bureau for published defence intelligence. They produce “deep-dive reports on procurement, weaponry and integrated command structures”.

Defence Central notes that in 2021 South Korea became the first country without nuclear weapons to successfully test a submarine-launched ballistic missile (SLBM). The launch came from the Dosan Anh Changho, the first KSS-III class submarine produced. South Korea’s KSS-III program represents the third phase of the country’s indigenous submarine development strategy. Earlier phases relied heavily on German technology. The KSS-III represents a leap forward to a fully domestic design capable of supporting strategic missions, including nuclear deterrence.

The KSS-III supersedes two earlier models in both size and capability. Measuring 83.5 meters in length with a beam of 9.7 meters, the submarine has a submerged displacement of approximately 3,800 tons. It is powered by a diesel-electric propulsion system with an air-independent propulsion module that allows for greater submerged endurance compared to conventional diesel-electric submarines. The crew complement needed is 50 people – a massive reduction on the 135 sailors required to operate the US Virginia class boats – and the 100 crew required for the 10,000-ton SSN AUKUS boats, should they ever reach naval service.

The design configuration allows the KSS-III to remain submerged for up to 20 days without surfacing, a key feature for survivability in contested waters. The boat has a top submerged speed of 37 kph, or 20 knots, and an operational range of around 19,000 kilometers. These specifications allow for long patrols in both coastal and open sea environments. The latest version boats are also capable of generating electricity underwater to recharge their fuel cell batteries. This enables long underwater voyages and obviates the need for frequent “snorts,” when the submarine has to come to the surface and potentially reveal its position to an enemy satellite.

One of the defining features of the KSS-III is its vertical launch system (VLS). It is the first South Korean submarine equipped with a VLS capable of deploying a battery of underwater-launched missiles. The Korean-designed Hyunmoo-3 cruise missiles offer a credible second-strike capability, especially relevant given the regional missile capabilities of North Korea and China. The Hyunmoo-3 is roughly equivalent to the US Navy’s Tomahawk but is supersonic, with a reported speed of Mach 1.2. In addition to SLBMs, the KSS-III can carry heavyweight torpedoes and anti-ship missiles launched from its standard torpedo tubes.

The newest design KSS-III, known as Batch 2 submarines, will have an increased displacement of approximately 4,000 tons and an expanded VLS capable of carrying up to ten missiles. They will also feature enhanced sonar systems, improved stealth characteristics and a more advanced combat management platform. Batch 2 construction is already under way, with the second unit expected to be launched this year.

The new boats also feature advanced anechoic tiles covering their HY-100 steel hulls to suppress underwater radiated noise and reduce active/passive sonar detectability. The K-111 class submarines are part of South Korea’s three-axis defense system, a strategy aimed at detecting, intercepting and retaliating against missile threats. The inclusion of SLBM capability on a conventional submarine makes the KSS-III unique.

Should the AUKUS public inquiry find that a non-nuclear-powered alternative to the Collins class is a desirable option for Australia’s defense, it is manifest that the KSS-III should be considered as a replacement. The independent publication Naval News describes the KSS-III as “the most potent conventionally powered and armed submarine in the world”. The cost is much more affordable; its performance is outstanding; it has none of the problems associated with nuclear waste disposal and security – and it can be delivered on a much faster schedule than the AUKUS boats.

Perhaps more importantly than all of this, discontinuing the purchase of AUKUS nuclear attack submarines surely removes a powerful incentive for China to attack Australia.

This article was originally published by the website Pearls and Irritations and is reprinted with permission.

title: Taiwan Isn’t Giving Up, It’s Pulling Apart
description: Rising passivity in Taiwan doesn’t mean Taiwanese have given up on resisting. It means the conditions for political action are eroding.
text:
In a recent article for The Diplomat, Mor Sobol offered an even-handed assessment of the debate set off by Simon Shuster’s piece in The Atlantic, which asked whether Taiwan might simply “give up” under growing pressure from China. Sobol argued that both Shuster’s pessimistic answer and his critics’ confident rebuttals rest on thinner evidence than either side recognizes.

Sobol pointed out that telling a pollster “I would defend Taiwan” is very different from making that decision when missiles are falling, and that Taiwan is not a unitary actor. The question worth asking is how the trends in public opinion, military recruitment, defense spending and other metrics move over time, not what any single snapshot shows.

I agree. As a scholar who studies Taiwanese defense attitudes with survey data, I want to add evidence showing why the much-discussed “willingness to fight” has, to some degree, misled outside observers. The problem with polling is not that attitudes can’t be measured. It’s that pollsters keep asking the most superficial question. “Would you fight?” captures a sentiment. What decides whether that sentiment translates into action is whether citizens believe the conditions for sacrifice are in place. Those conditions can be measured, tracked over time, and broken down by group.

When we do that, the picture is more troubling than either the optimists or the pessimists suggest, though for different reasons.

Citizens never accept the risks of war unconditionally. They take part in what I call a Defense Social Contract, which rests on three pillars, all of them vitally important.

The first pillar is trust in the state. People will sacrifice for a government they believe governs competently and fairly, and for a country they believe has a future worth defending. When citizens feel the state has failed them, its claim to extraordinary sacrifice loses legitimacy.

The second pillar is trust in one another. Defense is a public good, and public goods invite free-riding. I will hold the line only if I believe my neighbors will too. That means the burden must be shared, rather than some Taiwanese being expected to serve while others are exempt. Resistance must also be the common cause of all Taiwanese, not the property of one political camp.

The final pillar is trust that resistance can work. Facing a far more powerful adversary, citizens of a small democracy must believe their own military is capable and that allies will arrive in time. Sacrifice that looks futile turns into fatalism.

If any one pillar gives way, professed willingness to fight stays a sentiment and never becomes action.

What the Surveys Show

All three pillars can be measured. To do so, I used two nationally representative waves of the Taiwan National Security Survey (TNSS), fielded in June 2024 and September 2025, with 2,745 respondents in total. This makes it possible to do what Sobol recommends: track change over time and look inside the aggregate. The timing deserves emphasis. The 2024 survey was fielded about a month after President Lai Ching-te took office. The 2025 survey was fielded about a month after the final round of Taiwan’s Great Recall votes, a national effort to recall all legislators from the Kuomintang (KMT) that ultimately failed.

The TNSS directly asks respondents what they would actually do if China invaded. One option is to “let nature take its course” (shun qi zi ran). That answer is not surrender, and it is not a rejection of Taiwan. It is withdrawal: wait and see. I call it fatalistic passivity. Between the two waves, the share of Taiwanese choosing it rose from about 26 percent to nearly 37 percent.

From 2024 to 2025, the TNSS results showed that all three pillars weakened or came under strain.

On trust in the state, the share of respondents who said the national economy had gotten worse rose from 31 to 48 percent. Negative economic evaluations are strongly associated with passivity, although the association weakens once other factors are taken into account.

The share who doubt Taiwan’s military could defend the island on its own rose from 69 to 74 percent. Confidence in the military and the expectation of U.S. intervention are among the strongest and most consistent predictors of lower passivity across every model. Passivity is highest among those pessimistic on both counts.

Finally, there’s trust in fellow Taiwanese. Respondents who believe “most Taiwanese would resist” are much less likely to opt to “let nature take its course.” Predicted passivity falls from about 36 percent among those who think their compatriots definitely would not resist to about 25 percent among those who think they definitely would.

The most important finding, however, is not the numbers themselves. It’s the breakdown of the survey results along political lines. Among respondents who identified with the KMT, expressions of passivity rose from 22 percent in 2024 to 40 percent in 2025, an 18-point jump. That difference holds after controlling for national identity, unification-independence preferences, confidence in the military, expectations of U.S. assistance, economic evaluations, and demographics. Among Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) identifiers, it rose from 26 to 30.5 percent, a change statistically indistinguishable from zero. The 13.6-point gap between the two trajectories is statistically significant.

I want to stress what this does not mean, because the finding is easy to misread. On its face, it might seem to show that KMT supporters love Taiwan less or are less willing to defend it. That’s not accurate. In 2024, KMT identifiers were actually slightly less fatalistic than DPP identifiers. In other words, at the start of Lai’s presidency, KMT supporters showed no sign of giving up on Taiwan’s defense simply because the DPP had won another term.

In neither wave is the partisan gap on its own statistically significant. Both surveys took place under a DPP government, with KMT supporters in opposition throughout. The divergence between June 2024 and September 2025 therefore suggests that something changed over those 15 months in how the opposition camp relates to the DPP government.

Between the two surveys, Taiwan went through more than a year of fierce executive-legislative conflict, ending in the 2025 Great Recall. Advocates framed the campaign to remove 31 KMT legislators as a defense of national security against Chinese infiltration. Opponents saw it as an attempt to overturn an election result. All 31 recall votes failed. The September 2025 survey was fielded weeks later.

The partisan gap was already there. In both waves of the TNSS, KMT identifiers were about 20 points less likely than DPP identifiers to believe most Taiwanese would resist (roughly 61-63 percent versus 80-82 percent). In both the DPP and the KMT, the share who believe “most Taiwanese would resist” barely moved from 2024 to 2025. A substantial share of the electorate had already lost confidence that the burden would be shared.

But people’s own willingness to act did change, and it fell most among supporters of the KMT, whose political opponents had been presenting national security as a partisan cause.

Survey data cannot prove that any single event caused the shift. But when the language of national security becomes a weapon in domestic political combat, this pattern should come as no surprise.

What We Should Be Tracking

My reading is that the problem for Taiwan’s defense is not a lack of will but a lack of unity. It is very hard to ask citizens to risk their lives alongside people they already dislike and distrust in everyday politics, or to sacrifice for a government they see as a political adversary. The TNSS does not directly measure cross-partisan trust, so this interpretation needs further testing. It fits the evidence, though: a society that still sees itself as one nation but is increasingly unsure it can fight as one.

To gauge Taiwan’s willingness to fight, Sobol argued for watching behavior: recruitment, retention, reserve training, and civil defense participation. I strongly agree. I would add three sets of attitudinal indicators that come before this behavior and help explain it.

Do supporters of every party believe that the government asking for sacrifice governs fairly and competently, and that the country has a future?

Do citizens believe the burden is shared? Conscription reform, reserve obligations, and civil defense must be seen as universal, not selective. National security must stop being used against political opponents. Leaders of all parties should stop branding one another as Beijing’s proxies and should negotiate defense budgets and reforms as cross-party agreements.

Are allied signals consistent? Taiwanese must believe they can hold out until help arrives. Mixed messages from Washington or Tokyo damage the very pillar my data identify as most critical. Allies should also engage Taiwan’s major parties evenly, so that outside support is not seen as backing one camp.

These indicators should be broken down by party, age, gender, and region, and tracked across survey waves. If behavior and attitudes move together, across various segments of society, we can trust them more. If the aggregate holds steady while part of society quietly pulls back, we are looking at what I call “fragile resilience.”

So is Taiwan giving up? The evidence says no. Taiwanese still identify with their country, and most still expect their compatriots to resist. What the data show is a society pulling apart. Fatalism rose most sharply among those who identify with the KMT, whose legislators had just been targeted in a campaign that cast national security as a partisan cause.

This polarization is harder to see; the headline number on willingness to fight won’t capture it. It’s also dangerous. Beijing doesn’t need Taiwanese to embrace unification. It only needs enough of them to decide that the war belongs to someone else.

But pulling apart is also easier to fix than giving up. It is a political problem, and political problems have political remedies: a government that earns trust across party lines, a defense burden that everyone shares, and allies whose signals don’t waver. The fate of 23 million people depends on whether Taiwan’s leaders can rebuild a defense contract that citizens across the political spectrum believe in.

No one can save a small democracy that cannot stand together, however many polls say it is willing to fight.

title: Taiwan Should Be Kept Off the Negotiating Table
description: The fact that Trump didn’t give anything new away on Taiwan shouldn’t obscure how much ground he has already conceded to Xi.
text:
The much-heralded China-U.S. summit is now behind us, and the consensus is that it produced nothing of substance. President Donald Trump and Xi Jinping extended their trade truce, talked about artificial intelligence, and agreed on little else.

Many have applied the same measure to Taiwan: Xi pressed Trump to shift American policy on the island, the American leader appears not to have obliged, and so, the reasoning goes, the U.S. position held and nothing happened. That reading is wrong. What looks like nothing is the clearest sign yet of how far the U.S. position on Taiwan has shifted. And Trump is solely responsible for such a change.

Consider how the island came to be on the negotiating table in the first place: Trump placed it there. Back in February he told reporters he was discussing U.S. arms sales to Taiwan with Xi, something no president had done since 1982, when President Ronald Reagan promised Taipei that Washington would not consult Beijing on such matters. In May, in an interview taped just after the Beijing summit, Trump called a $14 billion arms package for Taiwan a “negotiating chip.” Then, on his flight home, he confirmed that he and Xi had again discussed the sales. Reminded of Reagan’s commitment, Trump dismissed it as ancient history. The package, ready for his signature since March, is still unsigned.

Each of these points marked a unilateral concession on Taiwan, made without receiving anything durable in return.

Trump went into the summit last week needing an agreement with Xi even more than he had in the spring. Inflation had risen, the war with Iran had dragged on, and his approval stood at or near the lows of his presidency weeks before the midterms. A meeting that produced a “win” of any kind would have allowed him to claim a much sought after victory. The concern was that he would further sacrifice Taiwan to achieve it.

That he appears not to have taken this route, while not to be overlooked, is almost beside the point. Before the curtains rose on the Trump-Xi summit, Trump had already moved the U.S. position on Taiwan toward China, and as a result Xi arrived in a position where he simply could not lose. Had Trump conceded further, it would have been a ground-changing win for China. When Trump instead lavished praise on his guest and declined to give more, it was still a win, only a quieter one: Beijing banked the new status quo, the one Trump created this year, in which merely holding the line counts as U.S. firmness.

Such a prospect is compounded by two further issues. First, it is not known what Trump said to Xi in private; public silence is reassuring only if it matches what passed behind closed doors. And just after the summit, he did little to quell concerns on this score. Instead, on his way to a college football game, he responded enigmatically to a question about Taiwan: “We didn’t talk about it too much.” He added, “Right now, it’s fine. It’s just moving along,” and then, referring specifically to Xi, Trump said: “He understands very much how I feel.” His comments served to suggest that some private understanding with Xi on Taiwan has been reached but not disclosed.

Second, Trump has confirmed that he and Xi will meet twice more before the year is out, at the APEC summit in Shenzhen in November and the G20 in Miami in December. That will make for an unprecedented four encounters between the Chinese and U.S. presidents in a single year. Each is another occasion for Beijing to test Trump’s resolve, now from the easier starting point of pressing him merely to hold a line he has already let slip, while angling for more.

Such waffling has real costs for the United States and Taiwan. For the U.S., the price is to the country’s reputation. A security commitment held by every administration for nearly 50 years, now treated as a “negotiating chip,” is proof to the world that no U.S. promise is safe from the next bargain. In Japan, and even more in South Korea, security rests on precisely the kind of promise Washington has just shown it will treat as negotiable. Once other governments conclude that U.S. assurances are only as good as the next election cycle, they hedge, and hedging is how the existing U.S.-led international order has already begun to come apart at the seams.

In Taiwan itself, a large majority of Taiwanese – 85 percent in one recent poll – favor the status quo, which in practice means the island’s de facto independence. What they ask of Washington is not a harder line toward Beijing but the assurance that the United States will keep the commitments it has already made. Now simply standing by those commitments is cast as a provocation to China, rather than a continuation of existing policy. This cuts away at Taiwan’s security – a heavy cost to bear indeed.

The needed corrective is not to provoke Beijing or manufacture a confrontation over Taiwan. It is the opposite. The president himself, not an aide and not the secretary of state, should state plainly that Washington’s Taiwan policy has not changed. And he should sign the arms package, because it was never Beijing’s to veto. The Taiwan Relations Act directs that such sales be decided “based solely upon” Taiwan’s needs; on a fair reading of that language, consulting Beijing about them is difficult to square with the law in the first place. This is not about goading China. It is about standing on American law, American interest, and the near-universal wish of the people on Taiwan that the status quo endure.

Taiwan was not bargained away at the Trump-Xi summit. But it was left on the table, within reach, and it will stay there for as long as an American president treats Taiwan as something he might one day be willing to sell.
tag: Trump Taiwan policy; Trump-Xi summit; Trump-Xi summit Taiwan; U.S. arms sales to Taiwan; U.S.-Taiwan Relations

title: Tajikistan Eyes ICC Exit
description: The move comes a year after Tajikistan’s refusal to arrest Russian President Vladimir Putin brought a formal rebuke from The Hague.
text:
On September 16, Tajikistan’s lower house of parliament considered a draft resolution on withdrawing from the International Criminal Court (ICC) at an extraordinary session. The parliamentary press service reported only that “corresponding decisions were taken,” naming neither the sponsor nor the rationale and saying nothing about a plenary vote.

The domestic steps required for the withdrawal under Tajik law have not been made public. Internationally, Article 127 of the Rome Statute requires written notification to the U.N. secretary general, with withdrawal taking effect one year later; the U.N. treaty database still lists Tajikistan as a state party.

Tajikistan’s ICC membership was always a regional outlier. Dushanbe signed the Rome Statute on November 30, 1998 and ratified it on May 5, 2000. It is the only Central Asian country ever to do so. The statute entered into force for Tajikistan on July 1, 2002, five years after a civil war that killed tens of thousands.

The presumed catalyst for Tajikistan’s apparent plan to withdraw from the ICC is Russian President Vladimir Putin. In October 2025 Dushanbe hosted Putin for a Russia-Central Asia summit and a Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) gathering despite an arrest warrant the ICC issued in March 2023 for the Russian president over the deportation of Ukrainian children. Weeks before the visit, Tajik officials told the court they would not execute the warrant, citing head-of-state immunity, Russia’s non-membership in the ICC, and CIS commitments to guarantee the “security and unhindered movement” of visiting leaders. The ICC’s Pre-Trial Chamber II rejected those arguments on March 19, 2026, and the court’s presidency referred the non-compliance finding to the Assembly of States Parties in May.

Dushanbe was never going to arrest Putin. Russia is simply too important of a partner for Tajikistan. Russia’s 201st Guards Military Base sits in Tajikistan under an agreement that runs to at least 2042, which Moscow described at the time as virtually free. Remittances, overwhelmingly from workers in Russia, were worth the equivalent of about 49 percent of GDP in 2024, and the International Organization for Migration counted some 1.2 million Tajiks in Russia in mid-2024.

That said, a non-compliance finding does not mean a country must leave the ICC. Mongolia was found in breach in October 2024 over the same arrest warrant and remains a state party. It’s like that Tajikistan’s reconsideration of ICC membership has to do with something else entirely.

On April 10, 2025, Freedom for Eurasia, the Ukrainian Fund of International Volunteers, and the banned Islamic Renaissance Party (IRPT), represented by French lawyer Nicolas Ligneul, filed an Article 15 communication with the ICC. The filing organizations say it documents killings, torture, sexual violence, enforced disappearances, and forced exile between 2002 and 2024, and asks prosecutors to examine the responsibility of senior officials, including President Emomali Rahmon. Their chosen start date for communication is the day the ICC statute took effect in Tajikistan.

A communication does not mean a case has been opened; the Office of the Prosecutor has not announced an investigation. Even if it did, exiting the ICC wouldn’t be a clean escape for Tajikistan. Withdrawal does not cancel obligations incurred while a party, and it does not automatically strip the court of jurisdiction over alleged crimes committed before the exit date. An exit would mainly limit exposure for conduct after that – which matters to the Tajik leadership given that succession from father to son is widely expected, and rumored to require Putin’s approval.

The international cost of leaving the ICC looks lower than it did even a year ago. Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger notified withdrawal in June, Venezuela and Chad in July; none of those states will be out before mid-2027. Hungary rescinded its notification on May 29, days before it was due to take effect. The EU criticized Tajikistan’s failure to arrest Putin but initialed an Enhanced Partnership and Cooperation Agreement (EPCA) with Dushanbe in July 2025 anyway and aims to sign it this year. Quitting the ICC breaches no trade condition – the Rome Statute is not among the conventions the EU’s preference schemes require – but it is a poor advertisement for an agreement whose selling point is shared values.
