title: Takaichi’s Pre-emptive Diplomacy: What Japan Needs From the Trump-Xi Summit
description: Prime Minister Takaichi made Tokyo’s concerns clear to Trump before Xi Jinping arrived in Washington. Will that actually impact the summit?
text:
When Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae sat down with U.S. President Donald Trump in New York on September 22, the timing itself was the message. Chinese President Xi Jinping would arrive in Washington, D.C. the next day for state visit to Washington and his second summit with Trump this year. Takaichi said afterward that holding the talks at such a moment demonstrated the strength of the Japan-U.S. alliance. But the most important audience may have been Trump himself.

Tokyo’s anxiety is not hard to understand. Trump personally greeted Xi on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews, an unusually warm welcome for a visiting foreign leader. Xi, for his part, struck a conciliatory tone upon arrival, declaring in a written statement that China and the United States “should be partners, not rivals.”

The hospitality will continue at the White House, with an elaborate welcoming ceremony and a state dinner. But expectations for substantive breakthroughs remain low. Washington and Beijing still face deep divisions over trade, artificial intelligence, Taiwan, and other issues.

With U.S. midterm elections about six weeks away, Trump has strong incentives to secure tangible economic results from China. Just before the summit, Washington and Beijing agreed to extend their trade truce by another two months, until January 10, postponing additional tariffs and export restrictions. The agreement reduces the immediate risk of renewed confrontation while giving both sides more time to negotiate.

For Tokyo, however, one concern stands above the economic bargaining: Taiwan.

China strongly opposes U.S. arms sales to Taiwan, while Trump has described such sales as a bargaining chip. Xi could use Trump’s desire for a broader economic deal to press Washington to continue delaying arms sales to the island. That has fueled concern in Tokyo that Taiwan could become part of a wider bargain between Washington and Beijing.

For Japan, Taiwan is a critical security issue. Japan’s southwestern islands lie close to Taiwan, and Takaichi’s remarks in the Diet last November that a Chinese use of force against Taiwan could constitute a “survival-threatening situation” for Japan triggered a sustained Chinese pressure campaign against Tokyo. Any significant weakening of U.S. support for Taiwan could therefore have direct implications for Japan’s security and for deterrence across the Western Pacific.

That made Takaichi’s meeting with Trump more than a routine alliance check-in. According to the Japanese government, the two leaders discussed the economy, issues related to China (including economic security, AI , semiconductors, and critical minerals), and North Korea, and exchanged views on China with the Trump-Xi summit specifically in mind. Takaichi also said Japan hoped stable China-U.S. relations would contribute to international stability.

Foreign Minister Motegi Toshimitsu, who attended the Takaichi-Trump meeting, told NHK ahead of the Trump-Xi summit that he believed Washington’s position on Taiwan remained unchanged from the leaders’ previous summit in May. Motegi said he believed Japan and the United States shared an understanding on this point.

Whether or not that is the case will become clearer only after Trump’s talks with Xi – particularly in how Washington handles Taiwan.

Takaichi’s U.N. General Assembly speech on the same day as her meeting with Trump illustrated the other side of her China diplomacy. She declared that the “stable post-Cold War era” was over and warned that the international order based on the rule of law was facing serious challenges. She explicitly named Russia over its invasion of Ukraine and North Korea over its nuclear and missile programs. Yet she did not mention China by name, saying instead that unilateral attempts to change the status quo by force or coercion must not be tolerated anywhere in the world.

The omission was notable after months of deteriorating China-Japan relations. It suggests that while Takaichi wants Washington to remain firm in the face of Chinese pressure, Tokyo is also seeking to prevent a further deterioration in its own relationship with Beijing.

That approach fits the broader diplomatic environment surrounding the Trump-Xi meeting. Despite fierce competition over trade, technology, and AI, both Washington and Beijing appear interested, at least for now, in managing their rivalry rather than allowing it to spiral into another confrontation. Xi’s message that the two countries should be “partners, not rivals,” and the extension of the trade truce both point in that direction.

For Japan, stable China-U.S. relations are desirable. But stability achieved through a bargain that changes Washington’s approach to Taiwan would present a very different calculation for Tokyo.

Takaichi made Japan’s concerns clear before Xi arrived in Washington. The Trump-Xi summit will show whether those concerns figure in Trump’s calculations – and whether his pursuit of deals with Beijing changes the strategic environment Japan must navigate.
tag: China-Japan-U.S. triangle; Japan Taiwan policy; Takaichi-Trump summit; Trump-Xi summit; Trump-Xi summit Japan; Trump-Xi summit Taiwan; U.S.-Japan Alliance

title: Tashiev and the Letter of 75: Charges Reclassified, Sentences Lessened, Confusion Reigns
description: Both Tashiev’s lawyers and the prosecutors filed appeals after the July verdict, the former seeking complete acquittal and the latter harsher sentencing. Neither has gotten what they asked for.
text:
When the trial of the former head of Kyrgyzstan’s State Committee for National Security, Kamchybek Tashiev, ended in July the judge delivered what appeared to be a damning verdict followed by an absurdist reprieve.

Tashiev – alongside former Speaker of the Zhogorku Kenesh Nurlanbek Turgunbek uulu, former Member of Parliament Kurmankul Zulushev, and five others – was found guilty of a coup attempt under Article 326 (“Violent seizure or retention of power, as well as an attempt to violently change the constitutional order”) of the Kyrgyz criminal code and acquitted of abuse of office charges.

Tashiev and the rest were sentenced to four years in prison – the prosecutors had sought nine. The judge immediately replaced the prison terms with three years of supervised probation.

Tashiev, technically convicted of a coup attempt, served not a single day in detention.

Both Tashiev’s lawyers and the prosecutors filed appeals, the former seeking complete acquittal and the latter harsher sentencing.

In early September, the Bishkek City Court heard the appeal. Like most of the first trial, the proceedings were held behind closed doors, so what happened next doesn’t have a clear explanation. The court apparently reclassified the charges from a coup attempt under Article 326 to “obstruction of the exercise of electoral rights,” Article 195.

According to various lawyers representing the defendants, all eight were sentenced to four year prison terms, converted immediately to two years of probation.

Zhoomart Ashirbaev, the lawyer for Zulushev, told RFE/RL’s Kyrgyz Service, Azattyk, that they intended to file a cassation appeal with the Supreme Court.

“The court’s reclassification of the charge from a serious crime to Article 195 demonstrates that the investigation brought an unfounded and unproven charge. I spoke with Kurmankul Zulushev immediately after the verdict was announced. We will file a cassation appeal to the Supreme Court.”

Latypbek Nuralimov, a lawyer representing Turgunbek uulu, told TASS, “They sentenced him to four years in prison, but they applied probation [for two years] because the crime is less serious.”

Chinara Dzhakupbekova, a lawyer representing Kursan Asanov, a former deputy minister of internal affairs charged in the case, expressed confusion over how Article 195 could even apply to the case. According to 24.kg, she said, “Article 195 can essentially only function when elections are underway. And there weren’t any elections, so this article is irrelevant.”

Kyrgyzstan isn’t due for a presidential election until January 2027.

The original trial, which started in May behind closed doors, before being briefly opened in mid-June and then closed again, centered on what’s become known as the “Letter of 75.”

The letter – an appeal signed by 75 public figures – circulated in early February and precipitated Tashiev’s sudden ejection from the ruling tandem. The letter urged Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov to call for an early presidential election and framed Tashiev favorably, highlighting that many of the Japarov administration’s greatest successes were initiatives spearheaded by the security chief.

During the brief period in which the trial was open, witnesses were questioned about the reception of the letter by members of parliament. The trial was closed again at the request of the defendants after Tashiev engaged in a verbal clash with a witness that included mention of the witness’s father’s 2005 murder.

Precisely how the letter constituted, or indicated, a coup attempt is not an argument the prosecutors have made clearly in public. And now the charge has been changed entirely, from coup plot to electoral obstruction – it’s not clear why or how or who made that change. The ultimate sentences shrunk from three years probation to two.

Tashiev’s lawyer, Ikramidin Aitkulov, was rather direct with his comments to the media after the result of the appeal was announced: “Well, this is a stupid decision, frankly. Completely illegal and unfounded. Of course, we will appeal.”

title: Thailand’s Independent Institutions Have Lost All Credibility
description: The institutions created by the “People’s Constitution” of 1997 have become tools of the country's political and economic elite.
text:
Earlier last week, Thailand’s Election Commission (EC) announced its long-awaited decision on whether to refer allegations of collusion in the manipulation of the 2024 Senate election to the courts. The referrals were the product of a joint investigative panel formed by the EC and the Department of Special Investigation in July 2026. That recommendation produced 229 potential referrals to the Supreme Court. The question of whether the EC would refer all 229 individuals to the authorities for trial was closely watched – and posed a stiff test of political transparency and accountability in Thailand.

However, in investigating whether powerful political interests, including executives of the ruling Bhumjaithai Party, members of parliament, cabinet ministers, and local political officials, conspired in the election, the EC decided to take the middle road and refer just 77, none of whom were political party executives, House MPs, or reserve senators. The rationale, the EC claimed, was based on the evidence against each individual, their direct conduct in the scheme, and verification of paper or financial records.

The Senate collusion case centers on claims of fraud, rigged voting, and coordinated manipulation in the 2024 Senate election. Senators were chosen through a multi-round system where candidates voted among themselves rather than through a public ballot, which arguably strengthened allegations of impropriety and collusion by election observers. Investigations also centered on hotel stays, travel costs, and cash to secure compliance in the scheme, with many involved linked directly to Bhumjaithai, giving rise to the dubious “Blue Senate” moniker.

The EC’s decision was not the least bit surprising, as the body has long been accused of being politically compromised. Narong Klunwarin, the chair of the EC, and other members of the Commission were a key part of the regulatory process that further exacerbated Thailand’s flawed electoral processes. Narong Rakroi, who lost a 4-3 decision to become chair in November of 2025, allegedly had the support of the so-called “blue” bloc of Bhumjaithai politicians, a slate that ended up being caught in the Senate collusion investigation. Under Prime Minister Prayut Chan-o-cha’s administration and since, the EC had ample opportunities to rule in a transparent fashion, but did not. During the 2019 election, it failed to investigate widespread allegations of fraud; it quickly intervened that same year in the eventual dissolution of the Thaksin-backed Thai Raksa Chart party, and also requested the dismissal of the Move Forward Party in 2024 on grounds that it violated Thailand’s lese-majeste laws.

And while this perceived dereliction of duty by the EC currently dominates headlines, the dilemma for a host of independent institutions in Thailand remains the same, as they share the same reputation for malfeasance, the same deficiencies in public trust, and compromised independence due to documented political connections and authoritarian appointments. The “People’s Constitution” of 1997 was supposed to usher in a new era of constitutionalism, with the EC, the National Anti-Corruption Commission (NACC), and the Constitutional Court created by this semi-democratic legislative act.

The current political climate was created by consecutive authoritarian interventions by military and royalist elites, which slowly eroded what remains of institutional independence, beginning with the 2006 coup, which led to the creation of the 2007 Constitution. This was then replaced by the 2014 Interim Constitution after the May 2014 military coup, which in turn was replaced by the 2017 Constitution that was put to a referendum in February 2016. Each intervention saw the mutation of these independent institutions into their current, politically compromised states.

The NACC has also fallen far, rather quickly. During the Yingluck Shinawatra government (2011-2014), the NACC seized on petitions by the opposition to bring charges of political corruption for the government’s rice pledging scheme. While the program had serious flaws, the NACC worked suspiciously quickly, moving to file formal charges within three weeks. Another Pheu Thai Party government was brought down by the same NACC playbook. With Prayut using his Article 44 powers under the old interim Constitution, he stacked the NACC with loyalists, extending then-NACC President Panthep Klanarongran, while Suchart Trakulkasemsuk, the current president of the NACC, was selected by the junta-controlled Senate in 2020. The political connections of junta-era officials have led to prison sentences, as was the case for Supa Piyajitti, the NACC commissioner who was instrumental in the rice pledging investigation.

Last, but certainly not least, is the Constitutional Court. The Court is loathed in democratic circles for its dissolution of both the Future Forward and Move Forward parties, including a 10-year ban from politics on the charismatic Pita Limjaroenrat, the leader of the Move Forward Party. Critics (including myself) have suggested that the unchecked power of the Court goes beyond overreach into a sort of rolling judicial coup. Of course, when it was Prayut’s power that was in question – in particular, the question of how long he was able to remain in power – the Court took the middle ground and allowed him to extend his term beyond eight years.

The worst outcome may still lie ahead. While there has been optimism that this year’s general election greenlit conversations about the prospect of a new Constitution, it was a 2025 ruling by this Constitutional Court that required three separate referenda on a new charter, making a smooth transition less likely. In the forthcoming discussions on potential drafts, there is no guarantee that the institutions of old will be removed and replaced with more transparent, accountable ones.

As Hamlet once said, “Aye, there’s the rub.”
tag: Thailand 2024 Senate election; Thailand Constitutional Court; Thailand corruption; Thailand Election Commission; Thailand elections; Thailand National Anti-Corruption Commission; Thailand politics; Thailand Senate

title: The Battle for Taiwan’s East: Taipei’s Western Pacific Strategy
description: The PLA has stepped up both the scale and intensity of its activities in the airspace and waters east of Taiwan. How can Taipei respond?
text:
Since July, China has begun conducting more regularized coast guard patrols in waters east of Taiwan. These operations are, of course, partly connected to recent maritime developments involving Japan and the Philippines. Yet a broader trend is also becoming increasingly visible: the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) has stepped up both the scale and intensity of its activities in the airspace and waters east of Taiwan.

In addition to continuing its joint combat readiness patrols across the Taiwan Strait median line and into Taiwan’s southwestern airspace, the PLA has noticeably increased reconnaissance and surveillance operations to Taiwan’s east and southeast. On September 5, the PLA deployed J-11 fighters, Su-30s, H-6 bombers, Y-8 electronic warfare aircraft, KJ-500 airborne early warning and control aircraft, and other platforms, with some entering Taiwan’s southeastern airspace. During another joint combat readiness patrol on September 9, PLA aircraft operated in Taiwan’s northern, central, and eastern airspace, further demonstrating that Chinese military activity is no longer concentrated primarily west of the island.

According to data released by Taiwan’s Ministry of National Defense, PLA aircraft repeatedly operated east of Taiwan in September, including on September 5-6, September 9-10, September 14-16, and September 18-19. During the September 9 patrol, the PLA also deployed combat aircraft, support aircraft, and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), with activities extending into Taiwan’s eastern airspace.

Compared with manned aircraft, UAVs offer longer endurance, lower operating costs, and greater suitability for sustained intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance missions. The PLA’s growing use of drones east of Taiwan therefore serves not only as a form of military pressure, but also as a means of systematically collecting battlefield intelligence on Taiwan’s force posture.

Potential targets of such surveillance include air base activities in Hualien and Taitung, aircraft takeoffs, landings, and dispersal patterns, the operation of radar and air defense systems, movements of naval and air forces, and possible external reinforcement routes through waters and airspace east of Taiwan.

Cutting Taiwan’s Sea Lines of Communication

For Taiwan, the strategic importance of its eastern coastline becomes particularly apparent in a wartime scenario. In the event of a PLA attack, airports and ports along Taiwan’s western coast could be subjected to sustained strikes or interdiction by long-range rocket artillery and Dong Feng-series ballistic missiles. Eastern ports would therefore become critical rear-area logistics hubs and potential lifelines for sustaining Taiwan’s war effort.

This concept was reflected in Taiwan’s Han Kuang 42 live-fire exercise earlier this year. On August 13, Taiwan’s navy and coast guard jointly conducted blockade-breaking escort and strategic logistics transfer drills. A combined naval and coast guard formation escorted the ROCS Yushan, which was acting as a simulated merchant vessel, into Hualien Port. Civilian vehicle convoys were then used to transfer supplies inland. The exercise was intended to test Taiwan’s ability to break a maritime blockade and maintain strategic supply lines during wartime.

This is precisely the kind of contingency the PLA is likely seeking to counter.

Since July, China has used maritime law enforcement vessels to increase its presence in waters east of Taiwan. Even before that, PLA Navy warships had regularly conducted patrols and surveillance in the area. In the past, however, such activity was often reactive, particularly when Chinese vessels encountered Taiwanese surveillance ships operating in waters east of the island. Since June, Beijing appears to have increased the intensity of such patrols and begun integrating UAVs more systematically into operations east of Taiwan.

Expanding Intelligence Collection and Close-In Reconnaissance

The deeper significance of the PLA’s expanding presence east of Taiwan lies in its ability to build a more comprehensive intelligence picture of Taiwan’s eastern military infrastructure.

Under Taiwan’s longstanding defense planning, the eastern side of the island could become a critical sanctuary in wartime. Air bases, naval facilities, and other military infrastructure in eastern Taiwan may be used to disperse aircraft and warships, conduct repairs and resupply, regenerate combat power, and support possible external intervention by the United States, Japan, or other partners.

Unmanned systems can do more than conduct reconnaissance or launch direct strikes. They can also provide targeting data for long-range precision weapons, including Dong Feng-series missiles, helping the PLA build a more integrated sensor-to-shooter architecture. This reflects the PLA’s broader emphasis on integrating reconnaissance and strike capabilities into a single operational system.

If the PLA can systematically monitor patterns of military activity during peacetime — including radar activation cycles, force movements, dispersal routes, and the operating rhythms of key bases — it can improve the effectiveness of wartime joint strikes and blockade operations by the PLA Rocket Force, Air Force, and Navy.

Future indicators should therefore include the duration of PLA UAV operations east of Taiwan, the frequency of appearances by Chinese electronic intelligence and reconnaissance aircraft, and the degree of coordination between PLA aircraft and naval vessels operating east of the island.

This trend has become particularly important as Taiwan itself expands military activity in the Western Pacific. Recent developments include testing of the MQ-9B unmanned aerial system, military deployments to Orchid Island during the Han Kuang exercise, and tri-service precision munitions drills conducted in the waters east of Taiwan, including the sinking exercise involving the decommissioned frigate ROCS Lan Yang.

These activities provide the PLA with strong incentives to increase intelligence collection east of Taiwan. Through close-in reconnaissance, Beijing can seek to gather technical and operational data on Taiwan’s emerging capabilities, including new unmanned systems, missile deployments, force movements, and joint operational procedures.

Conclusion: The Battle for Taiwan’s East

For Taiwan, recent PLA activity suggests that the eastern side of the island can no longer be treated simply as a protected rear area.

Taiwan’s deployments during this year’s Han Kuang exercise already indicate a response to the PLA’s growing operational focus on the region. In addition to increasing naval and air patrols east of the island, Taiwan has begun deploying missile units to Orchid Island.

Orchid Island is located relatively close to the Philippines’ Batanes Islands, creating potential space for closer Philippines-Taiwan security cooperation. If combined with Japan’s southwestern islands — particularly Ishigaki and Yonaguni to Taiwan’s northeast — these locations could form important nodes in a broader defensive network along the First Island Chain. Such a network would not necessarily depend on the large-scale forward deployment of naval forces. Instead, it could emphasize an “anti-sea from land” approach, using distributed land-based missiles, sensors, UAVs, and intelligence networks deployed across strategically located islands.

The objective would be to turn geography into an operational advantage. By integrating Taiwan, the Batanes, and Japan’s southwestern islands into a more resilient surveillance and strike architecture, Taiwan and its partners could complicate PLA naval operations in the waters east of the island and partially offset China’s numerical superiority at sea.

The strategic competition over Taiwan is therefore increasingly extending beyond the Taiwan Strait itself. The waters east of Taiwan – linking the First Island Chain to the broader Western Pacific – are becoming an increasingly important operational theater. For Taiwan, the next major challenge may not be defending its western coastline, but ensuring that its eastern flank remains open, survivable, and connected to the wider Western Pacific.

title: The China-Russia Factor in the Iran War
description: Insights from Stephen J. Blank.
text:
The Diplomat author Mercy Kuo regularly engages subject-matter experts, policy practitioners, and strategic thinkers across the globe for their diverse insights into U.S. Asia policy. This conversation with Dr. Stephen J. Blank – non-resident senior fellow in the Foreign Policy Research Institute’s Eurasia Program and author of numerous publications on Soviet/Russian, U.S., Asian, and European military and foreign policies – is the 527th in “The Trans-Pacific View Insight Series.”

How is China-Russia cooperation supporting Iran’s resistance against U.S. military actions?

Sino-Russian cooperation supports Iran in many ways. Russia is transmitting satellite intelligence about the location and movement of American troops, ships, and aircraft. Iran used this intelligence to strike U.S. bases in Jordan and Saudi Arabia and may also have obtained Russian intelligence to strike at secret CIA installations.

Second, Moscow is making good Iranian drone losses, having helped Iran restock about 60 percent of its losses, often with improved versions of drones Iran sent to Russia. Russia also gives Iran tactical guidance on drone use, e.g. how many drones Iran should use and should use and from what altitudes it should shoot. Thus, Iran benefits from Russian lessons in Ukraine.

Third, Russia’s “Caspian Express” has become a major logistical lifeline for Iran. Lastly Russia provides diplomatic support for Iran.

China and possibly Russia are selling Iran shoulder-fired air missile defenses MANPADS. Chinese engines power the Russian drones sent to Iran, which reportedly also incorporate Chinese radio modems and cameras. China also has recently closed a deal to sell Iran supersonic anti-ship missiles with a range up to 290 km to deter or strike U.S. vessels.

Likewise, Chinese entities provide chemical precursors and dual-use items for Iran’s ballistic missile program. Chinese entities are also reportedly loading Iranian vessels with the solid rocket-fuel precursor, sodium perchlorate, and may be preparing to supply spare parts and missile components. Iran also has military-grade access to China’s Beidou satellite navigation system and China has given Iran geospatial intelligence through state-affiliated commercial satellite companies.

What is the strategic calculus for Beijing and Moscow in bolstering Tehran’s position?

Both Russia and China share a common motivation to weaken the U.S. either leading to its defeat or to a protracted war that bleeds U.S. strength, ties it down in the Gulf, and prevents greater military support for Ukraine, Taiwan, and Washington’s Asian and European allies. They also aim to weaken American alliances, damage America’s global standing and economy, and increase its domestic polarization. Moreover, this war validates their ideology about the decline of an American-led world order and the alleged rise of a new multipolar order, thereby lending credence to that ideology.

How is China benefitting from protracted conflict in both the Ukraine and Iran wars?

These wars benefit China in many ways. Since it previously built up its energy reserves the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz does not threaten it. China already gets Turkmen and Russian energy at a discount. Iran’s dependence has grown while Washington’s military-political-economic capabilities and strategy have failed. Meanwhile Russia’s economy gains a reprieve, and a distracted Washington is increasingly unable to support Taiwan or other Asian allies as needed. Trump has proven himself to be strategically incompetent, giving China more freedom to threaten Taiwan, the Philippines, Japan, etc. In Ukraine, the lack of aid to Kyiv and energy windfalls for Russia thanks to Iran divert Western attention from Asia while Russian dependence on China grows. Lastly the war has enabled China to project air and naval power into the Middle East at an unprecedented scale.

Examine the impact of the Strait of Hormuz imbroglio on China-U.S. competition in the Middle East.

The stalemate over the Strait of Hormuz benefits China by showing what can only be described as Trump’s egregious strategic malpractice. When his ravings and utter lack of strategic capability are juxtaposed – or more precisely contraposed – to China’s steadiness, refusal to commit its military but substantial support for Iran and Russia’s war in Ukraine, Beijing looks better and better. Moreover, it diverts Washington, which has done little or nothing to push back on Chinese encroachments against Taiwan, Japan, and the Philippines, or against Russia since the May summit in Beijing.

Assess the effectiveness of U.S. leadership vis-à-vis China-Russia cooperation in advancing U.S. interests in the Iran war.

As I noted above, egregious strategic malpractice and incompetence have characterized Trump’s wartime policies, and arguably almost all of his foreign and defense policies. This war had no strategic planning, its goals change daily, and enormously damaged U.S. interests. Indeed, as of today Iran has arguably won, which benefits Russia and China.

While the Moscow-Beijing axis is tightening in economics, politics, and military affairs; every U.S. alliance system – NATO, our alliances in Asia and in the Middle East – is under pressure or in growing disarray. Although there are some structural causes for this trend, the common denominator is Trump and his team, many of whom are equally strategically incompetent, for their attacks on allies, reckless ignorance of strategic realities, and failure to plan for this war.

Consequently, there is diminished pressure on Russia; indeed there are secret talks with it rather than support for Ukraine, China advances on our Asian allies while the administration is either silent or spouts platitudes as Assistant Secretary Colby’s tour of Southeast Asia and speech there show. There is apparently no effort to strengthen our alliances against this Moscow-Beijing axis or the larger axis including Iran and North Korea, i.e. the CRINK. Instead, leading members of this administration regularly depreciate, devalue, or even threaten our allies, giving them reasons for distrusting America’s commitment.

So, while our alliances are all faltering Russo-Chinese ties, along with ties among the CRINK, e.g. Iran-North Korean ties, are expanding. The contrast with the Trump administration policy is both telling and ominous.

title: The Climate Crisis Is Stretching the Nepali Military Beyond Its Limits
description: The question here is not whether the military should be involved in disaster response, but how the military itself is responding, adapting, and transforming amid the climate crisis.
text:
The footage of the avalanche that triggered devastating floods along Nepal’s Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers near the China-Nepal border on August 26 is deeply sobering. The road, bridges, customs, and immigration office with China, and the entire settlement and traditional bazaar along the riverbank, were wiped out in a moment.

In the wake of the flood, the Nepali government deployed security forces, including the Nepal Army, Nepal Police, and Armed Police Force, as first responders. Nepal has put more than 20,000 security personal into responding to the disaster, possibly the largest such deployment since the aftermath of the 2015 earthquake. The collapse of local and provincial governments and the inaccessibility of flood-affected areas prompted the government to rely on the security forces at a desperate moment.

The use of security forces in disaster response is not new in Nepal. Security forces often get involved, ranging from rescue and relief operations to rehabilitation activities. The Nepali Constitution 2015 (2072 BS) enshrined a provision for deploying the military in national crises arising from disasters and development projects. The National Security Policy (2016) also considers climate change and the environment as part of the national interest.

But the ad hoc stretching of the security forces into disaster response can result in the security forces themselves being increasingly exposed to vulnerabilities and capacity constraints amid the climate crisis in Nepal. As environmental disasters become more frequent and severe in the Himalayan region, the recent flood must be an important case study in the growing complexity of the military’s engagement in disaster governance and preparedness.

The scale and intensity of the recent flood was unimaginable and it is becoming evident that there were significant casualties among security forces. A week since the incident, and a total of 85 security force members – encompassing 45 from the Nepal Army, 28 from the Nepal Police, and 13 from the Armed Police Force – are still unaccounted for.

The police forces went missing while on duty near the border, customs area, and river corridor. Some Nepal police personnel went missing due to a sudden surge in flooding while circulating a notice to downstream communities. Similarly, Nepal army personnel were on duty at Langtang National Park and were stationed at multiple hydropower projects. Armed police forces went missing from a border post. In addition, three police posts in Timure, Rasuwagadhi, and Syafrubesi were damaged or swept away.

The unique circumstances of the flood gave security personnel very little time to respond. The absence of an early warning system and the lack of any cross-border disaster communication made the situation even more complicated.

Rescue operations are still ongoing, particularly in areas with multiple hydropower tunnels, such as Upper Trishuli-1, Rasuwagadhi Hydropower, Chilime Hydropower, Langtang Khola, and Upper Trishuli-3A. Hundreds of workers are believed to be trapped in these tunnels. As the days pass, families of those trapped and even security personnel are increasingly frustrated. Some tunnel rescue operations have been halted due to a lack of progress and the rescue team’s inability to advance. The security forces are exploring their options, including conducting a controlled blast to clear debris blocking the tunnel.

Nepali Prime Minister Balendra Shah, speaking at parliament on September 2, said that “tunnels present a very distinct problem, they are filled with mud, debris, and floodwater. Clearing them requires specialized skills that none of the countries, including Nepal, have had. Though we have mobilized at short notice, and progress depends on weather and drier conditions.” He added that the security forces should be commended for their efforts, made under various constraints.

Footage of Nepal Army personnel laboring and displaying their willingness to risk their own lives in a tunnel operation has drawn attention. The security forces have been widely praised for their courage and bravery. But an emerging consensus has made it clear that the Nepali government, including the Nepal Army, lacks the advanced expertise, technology, and equipment for effective tunnel rescue operations. Bravery is not a substitute for preparedness, equipment, and expertise.

The Nepali government has sought international assistance in specific areas, including tunnel rescues and forensic work, and reached out to countries like India, China, and South Korea for critical equipment and technology. This, however, highlights Nepal’s disaster vulnerabilities and preparedness deficits.

The recent flood reiterates the changing environmental security landscape in the Himalayan region. The International Center for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) has identified dozens of potentially dangerous glacier lakes in the Hindu Kush Himalayan region; the recent floods may be less of an outlier and more of a warning.

The climate crisis, and the use of security forces in response to climate-driven disasters, decisively alters the strategy, function and operating environment of military institutions. The question here is not whether the military should be involved in disaster response, but how the military itself is responding, adapting, and transforming amid the climate crisis. This is particularly important in Nepal, where the military institution is deeply embedded in disaster response and preparedness already.

title: The Future of Shipbuilding in Southeast Asia
description: There are significant opportunities – and risks.
text:
Global shipbuilding demand is likely to remain resilient for the long-term, with increasing geopolitical conflict and uncertainty one of the primary drivers. The 2026 war between Iran, the United States and Israel has caused a spike in demand for alternative suppliers and routes, leading Fitch Rating to revise sectoral outlook to “neutral” from “deteriorating.” According to the non-profit Container Trades Statistics, global container volumes reached 16.2 million 20-foot-equivalent units (mTEUs) in April — the first full month of data since the Strait of Hormuz closures triggered by February’s Persian Gulf crisis — marking a 4 percent year-over-year increase and a 1.6 percent rise over March. Year-to-date volumes are also running 5 percent ahead of 2025 levels.

Shipping sector analysts also predicted that the market had become oversaturated with vessel capacity and fewer orders would be placed to shipbuilders in 2026 and 2027. However, geopolitical disruptions are one major reason why orders have remained strong. Shocks such as Red Sea attacks, the Russia-Ukraine war, the Panama Canal drought, the Baltimore bridge collapse, and now the Iran-Israel-US conflict have demonstrated the importance of excess capacity. Carriers can more easily navigate these conflicts with a large and diverse fleet, resulting in expansive orderbooks that are now treated as insurance rather than oversupply.

These trends are good news to the world’s leading shipbuilding nations, which are highly concentrated in East Asia, particularly China. However, in the current geopolitical climate, there are significant opportunities for Southeast Asian nations to scale up their shipbuilding industries and take advantage of the sustained demand for global trade.

Southeast Asian nations are taking the initiative to capture greater shipbuilding market share through structured international partnerships. At the OECD-Southeast Asia Policy Roundtable on Shipbuilding, Steel, and AI held in Tokyo in February 2026, Indonesia, Vietnam, and Thailand agreed to a regional peer review of their shipbuilding sectors with the OECD, covering priorities such as workforce skills, technical capabilities, supply chain dependencies, energy-efficient ships, and leveling the competitive playing field. The Philippines separately agreed to follow up on implementation pathways for OECD peer review recommendations, while all four countries were invited to join the OECD’s shipbuilding committee meeting in Paris in April.

Continue reading for free at The Diplomat’s new companion publication, The Investor.

title: The Geopolitics of AI in the Asia-Pacific
description: Insights from Jouko Ahvenainen.
text:
The Diplomat author Mercy Kuo regularly engages subject-matter experts, policy practitioners, and strategic thinkers across the globe for their diverse insights into U.S. Asia policy. This conversation with Jouko Ahvenainen – founder and chairman of Mission Grey and serial entrepreneur in data analytics, fintech, and external intelligence – is the 528th in “The Trans-Pacific View Insight Series.”

In what ways is artificial intelligence shaping geopolitical trends in the Asia-Pacific?

AI is increasingly connecting technology policy, national security, industrial policy, and geopolitics. Nowhere is this more visible than in the Asia-Pacific.

It is important, however, not to see the region simply through a China-U.S. lens. Taiwan is critical to advanced semiconductor manufacturing; South Korea and Japan have major positions in semiconductors, materials, and industrial technology; India is building its own AI capabilities; and Singapore and other ASEAN countries are developing their own approaches to AI infrastructure, governance, and investment.

China is particularly important because of its ability to combine technology development with hardware manufacturing, industrial scale, and rapid deployment. We already see this with electric vehicles and many other technologies: Chinese companies are increasingly selling globally, including throughout Europe despite trade frictions. AI will become another layer in this industrial and commercial expansion.

This creates a much more complex geopolitical network. Countries are asking where their compute comes from, whose models they use, where their data resides, what hardware and infrastructure they depend on, and how dependent they want to become on any single technology ecosystem.

I divide my own time between Asia, Europe, and the Americas, and one thing I see clearly is that AI development is happening in all of these regions. The differences are often in emphasis, speed, business culture, and the relationship between government and industry rather than simply in technological capability.

For businesses, these developments are no longer abstract geopolitical questions. They can quickly affect suppliers, market access, regulation, cybersecurity and investment. This is why at Mission Grey we see external intelligence becoming increasingly important: technology signals need to be understood together with political, economic, industrial, and supply chain signals.

Share your perspective on a recent comment from European technology chief Henna Virkkunen that “AI is a geopolitical weapon.”

I understand her point, and the concern behind it is real: Europe’s dependency on foreign models and infrastructure, and the leverage that dependency creates. I share that concern. But I would not describe AI itself as a weapon.

It is a general-purpose technology that is becoming strategically very important. There is a useful comparison with aviation and drone technologies. They can clearly have major military applications, but the technologies themselves are much broader than weapons. They also transform transportation, logistics, agriculture, communications, and many other areas. AI is similar, although potentially even broader in its impact.

AI can certainly be weaponized. It can strengthen military systems, intelligence capabilities, cyber operations, and information influence. Access to advanced chips, computing infrastructure, cloud services, or models can also be restricted and used as geopolitical leverage. This is where Virkkunen’s warning is most relevant, and it is a legitimate one.

But AI’s strategic importance goes much further. It will influence productivity, scientific research, industrial competitiveness, education, healthcare, and the ability to create new companies and services. Its geopolitical significance may ultimately come as much from these economic and societal effects as from direct military applications.

I would say AI is becoming a strategic capability and source of geopolitical power. That is broader, and in my view more important, than simply calling it a weapon.

What is the geopolitical impact of Asia’s AI developments on the United States and Europe?

The first impact is that Asia should no longer be viewed simply as a manufacturing base or market for Western technology. It is increasingly a source of technology, capital, standards, products, and AI ecosystems itself.

China is the most obvious example. Its strength is not only in AI models, but also in combining software with hardware, manufacturing capacity, and the ability to scale products very quickly. Its electric vehicle industry, which I mentioned earlier, shows how rapidly this can become a global commercial force. Similar dynamics can emerge around robotics, autonomous systems, and AI-enabled products.

But the broader Asian picture matters just as much. Japan and South Korea remain major technology powers, Taiwan has an exceptional position in semiconductors, India is building significant AI capabilities, and Singapore has positioned itself as an international technology and AI hub.

For the United States, maintaining leadership therefore increasingly depends not only on domestic innovation but also on partnerships and supply chains throughout Asia.

Europe faces a somewhat different challenge, but I think the common description of Europe as mainly a regulator is too simplistic. There is substantial AI innovation in Europe. France has become an important AI hub, while Sweden has a strong technology startup ecosystem, with companies such as Lovable reaching a multi-billion valuation within about two years and demonstrating how quickly new AI businesses can emerge. Both countries are also significant in defense technology.

Europe also brings another dimension to the discussion: individual control over data and technology. Concerns about data are not simply regulatory bureaucracy. People and companies are genuinely asking who controls their information, how large technology companies or governments may use it, and whether they retain the freedom to choose between different services, models and jurisdictions.

These issues will increasingly become geopolitical as well as commercial.

Examine the geopolitical stakes of pursuing technological sovereignty.

Technological sovereignty is becoming increasingly important, but the concept is often misunderstood. Sovereignty should not mean trying to manufacture everything domestically or disconnecting from global technology networks.

No major economy is genuinely independent across the entire AI stack. Advanced AI depends on an international network of semiconductor design, fabrication, memory, manufacturing equipment, cloud infrastructure, energy, data, software, and talent.

The practical objective should therefore be strategic optionality.

A country, company, or even an individual should understand which dependencies are acceptable, which are strategically critical, and where alternatives are necessary. Government systems, defense applications, and critical infrastructure naturally require particularly strong safeguards.

But sovereignty also has another level that receives less attention: the position of the user.

People and organizations increasingly depend on a small number of technology platforms for data, identity, communication, and AI. The ability to control your own data, move between services, and choose where your information is processed is therefore becoming part of technological sovereignty as well.

This is not only about Europe versus the United States or China. Different jurisdictions will make different choices concerning privacy, data access, national security, and technology governance. Users and businesses may increasingly want the ability to choose between them.

Too little sovereignty creates strategic dependence. Too much isolation can increase costs, fragment markets, and slow innovation. The objective should therefore be resilience and freedom of choice rather than complete technological independence.

Ultimately, sovereignty means maintaining the ability to make your own decisions when circumstances change.

Assess how policymakers and business leaders should understand the China-U.S. AI race and its implications for technological dominance in the global economy.

The biggest mistake is to treat the China-U.S. AI competition as a race on a single track with one finishing line.

The United States has exceptional strengths in frontier AI companies, capital, computing infrastructure, and semiconductor design. China has major strengths in hardware integration, manufacturing, engineering capacity, industrial deployment, and the ability to scale technology rapidly into real-world products.

We should also remember that China increasingly competes globally. Its technology companies are not developing only for the Chinese domestic market. They sell industrial and consumer products throughout Asia, the Middle East, Latin America, Africa, and Europe, and AI-enabled products will follow the same routes.

At the same time, a two-player framing hides much of what actually matters. Europe has significant AI and defense technology capabilities. India is becoming increasingly important. Japan, South Korea, and Taiwan remain critical parts of the technology ecosystem. Smaller countries such as Singapore can have influence far beyond their size.

The global AI landscape therefore contains many gray zones. Countries may use American cloud infrastructure, Asian hardware, European industrial technology, and locally developed models simultaneously. Companies will often make decisions based on capability, price, reliability, data requirements, and market access rather than geopolitical ideology alone.

For policymakers and business leaders, the key is therefore not simply to ask who is ahead.

They need to understand dependencies, emerging capabilities, export restrictions, technology alliances, standards, talent flows, data rules, and changes in global supply chains. Most importantly, they need to recognize early signals showing when those relationships are beginning to change.

That is also central to how we think at Mission Grey. In a world where geopolitics, technology, regulation, business, and supply chains increasingly interact, the challenge is not simply obtaining more information. It is understanding which developments matter, how they connect, and what they could mean for decisions under different scenarios.

title: The Global Data Center Boom Has Arrived in Southeast Asia
description: Will the region's demand for artificial intelligence services justify the enormous outlays of money and resources?
text:
Processing and storing data is now pushing the frontier of economic development around the world, and huge amounts of capital are flowing into building out the infrastructure to support this big bet on cloud computing and Artificial Intelligence. The race to establish an advantageous position on the digital frontier is driving a major capex boom in the United States and elsewhere, and this wave has now fully arrived in Southeast Asia.

Data centers require substantial land and resources, like electricity and water, and they need reliable connectivity such as access to subsea cable networks. Countries that have land, reasonably well-developed energy and telecommunications infrastructure and friendly regulatory environments are attracting investors and developers looking to ride the data center wave. Affordable inputs, like electricity, can sweeten the deal. It just so happens that many countries in Southeast Asia fit this bill.

Malaysia is leading the pack. Clear policy guidance, well-developed infrastructure and close proximity to land-constrained Singapore are helping fuel a boom in data centers. The Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone has seen a flurry of activity, but it is part of a broader phenomenon. In the first quarter of 2023, the Department of Statistics recorded a cumulative $11 billion of foreign investment in the information and communication sector, accounting for 5 percent of total foreign investment. By first quarter of 2026, this figure had risen to $32.5 billion, equal to 12 percent of total inbound investment.

And there is no sign of slowing. According to the Malaysian Investment Development Authority, the body that reviews and approves investment projects, between 2021 and the first quarter of 2026, $96 billion worth of data center and cloud computing projects were approved, including $24 billion in the first half of 2026 alone. These are project approvals rather than realized investment, but it gives a sense of the speed and scale at which the data center boom is unfolding across Malaysia.

Indonesia is also seeing an uptick in data center investment. Like Malaysia, some of this is driven by demand from Singapore, particularly in and around the island of Batam. Nongsa Digital Park is a Special Economic Zone that offers eligible projects tax and other fiscal incentives. Combined with Batam’s strong subsea cable connectivity, this has fueled a wave of new data center construction in the area.

There is also a lot of investment activity in and around Jakarta where a number of large industrial scale data centers are being developed by state-backed players such as Telkom, as well as private sector firms and investors. As reported by Antara News, Indonesia’s current data center capacity sits around 580 MW and the plan is to grow it to 1.3 GW in the near-term. Government data shows that investment in information services jumped from $967 million in 2023 to $3.4 billion in 2025 and it looks set to keep climbing.

Thailand is also now rushing to add more data centers, with several large industrial-scale projects in the pipeline. According to the Board of Investment, in 2025 they received $24 billion worth of applications across 151 projects in the digital industry, mainly data centers. Not all of these projects will be approved and become operational, but it again gives a sense of the speed and scale with which this industry is moving. Vietnam is following suit, with local media reporting that the government plans to reach 870 MW of data center capacity by 2030.

The trend is clear: data centers are beginning to pop up all around Southeast Asia, attracting billions of dollars in investment and uncorking a major construction boom. But a bigger, perhaps more fundamental, question is whether demand for digital services can justify these enormous outlays and the resources they will absorb. Investment is pouring into Southeast Asian digital infrastructure, with the expectation that businesses and consumers will spend billions of dollars on cloud computing, AI and other digital services in the years ahead.

This is not unique to Southeast Asia, of course. The same assumption about future demand has been driving eye-popping capex investment in data centers and cloud computing all around the world, raising similar questions. What we can say for sure is that the data center boom has reached the major economies of Southeast Asia. Whether these massive bets on future demand for digital services pays off is anybody’s guess. But considering the amounts of money involved, how this plays out is something we should all be watching very, very closely in the months and years ahead.

title: The Illusion of Technocratic Transformation in Cambodia
description: The country is hitting a developmental wall because necessary structural reforms clash directly with the needs of an entrenched patronage system.
text:
Over the past 25 years, Cambodia successfully cut its poverty rate from over 50 percent to under 20 percent. However, the model driving this success now faces severe headwinds. Due to ongoing global price shocks and a sharp, year-long slump in remittances prompted by the Cambodian-Thai border dispute, more than a million people risk falling back below the subsistence level, according to the World Bank. This vulnerability underscores the fragility of Cambodia’s growth model. Without structurally transforming the domestic economy, hard-won social progress remains in jeopardy.

In its June 2026 Cambodia Economic Update, the World Bank painted its usual optimistic picture of macroeconomic resilience with projected GDP growth of 3.9 percent in 2026 and 4.9 percent in 2027 amid rising exports and accelerating momentum in new industrial sectors. Yet these signs of progress conceal a deep structural problem: Cambodia remains a dual economy.

On the one hand, the country boasts a highly productive export sector, dominated almost entirely by foreign, primarily Chinese, investment, which manufactures garments and footwear for global companies. This side of the economy operates largely as an enclave, relying on few domestic factors other than cheap labor. On the other hand, a fragmented and technologically deficient domestic economy consists largely of small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) that struggle to compete internationally and remain concentrated in the informal sector. In 2022, 90 percent of all businesses fell into this category, yet they generated only about 40-45 percent of GDP, according to World Bank statistics.

Cambodia Could Fall Into the Middle-Income Trap

All of this points to the exhaustion of Cambodia’s existing growth model. The purely quantitative shift of labor from subsistence farming into textile factories – the classic “reallocation dividend” described by the Lewis model – is no longer generating significant productivity gains. To avoid falling into a middle-income trap, Cambodia must turn FDI into a vehicle for technology and knowledge transfer to the domestic economy. The middle-income trap occurs when countries escape poverty but then stagnate: rising wages erode their advantage in low-cost labor, while they lack the innovation capacity needed to compete with advanced economies.

Should East African nations, particularly Ethiopia and Kenya, boost their competitiveness in the coming years, Cambodia could face intensified pressure in labor-intensive export industries. Domestic pressures are also mounting, driven by what the World Bank anticipates to be the inevitable closure of Cambodia’s demographic window around 2043. Currently, the country benefits from an exceptionally young population and a temporary surplus of working-age people. However, if Cambodia fails over the next two decades to equip this generation with the skills it needs through substantial investment in education and to integrate young workers into higher-value supply chains, the country risks growing old before it becomes prosperous.

In its update, the World Bank recommended a three-stage reform: safeguarding subsistence farms through social protection; boosting SME productivity through better credit access and digitalization; and formalizing high-performing local businesses to help them qualify as suppliers to major foreign investors.

However, this economically sound solution reflects a purely technocratic understanding of Cambodia. It treats the country as a rational institutional landscape while ignoring its political economy. The country’s real obstacle is not a lack of administrative guidelines or digital portals, but the deeply entrenched system of patronage and oligopoly that has developed under the ruling Cambodian People’s Party (CPP) and significantly constrains market efficiency and innovative entrepreneurship.

The Elite Pact and the Limits of Innovation

In Cambodia, economic success depends less on productivity or innovation than on proximity to political power. This system, closely resembling the crony capitalism of Suharto’s Indonesia and Marcos’ Philippines, is institutionalized within the Oknha class – an oligarchic economic elite that secures exclusive market access, state land concessions, and protection from foreign competition through million-dollar donations to the regime.

This elite pact fundamentally distorts entrepreneurial risk. Large domestic conglomerates, such as the Royal Group, Canadia/OCIC, Chip Mong, or the LYP Group, focus heavily on protected, domestic-market-oriented sectors like real estate, financial services, gambling, telecommunications, and trade. While not all of these entrepreneurs lack productivity, the institutional environment rewards political rent-seeking rather than competitive, global industrial value chains. For a Cambodian oligarch, making high-risk, multimillion-dollar investments in R&D or high-precision manufacturing is simply not economically attractive.

Politically safeguarded rent-seeking in a protected domestic market offers a far more lucrative risk-return profile than fierce international competition against regional rivals. Simultaneously, this system stifles the productive middle class. Independent, innovative SMEs find it nearly impossible to scale up. If they break into profitable niches, they risk having their business models appropriated by politically connected actors, as property rights in Cambodia remain poorly protected without political patronage. Under such conditions, qualified Cambodians seek advancement mainly in the civil service or the military, two arenas where power easily translates into personal gain.

Cambodia Lags Behind in Regional Comparisons

When seeking solutions, international analyses frequently point to regional success stories, particularly Malaysia and Vietnam. Yet these comparisons serve only to highlight Cambodia’s severe shortcomings. This institutional gap is vividly reflected in the Bertelsmann Transformation Index (BTI). While Cambodia has scored the absolute lowest mark of 1 out of 10 in anti-corruption policy since 2018, Vietnam (5 points) and Malaysia (6 points) remain on an entirely different institutional trajectory.

According to BTI criteria, Cambodia’s minimum score indicates a total failure to control corruption, with core integrity mechanisms – such as independent public expenditure audits, official accountability mechanisms, or transparent procurement systems – effectively non-existent. While Vietnam and Malaysia also display functional shortcomings, they maintain established core mechanisms that guarantee businesses at least a basic level of institutional predictability. These quantitative discrepancies have fundamentally crippled the country’s economic dynamics.

The prime historical example of overcoming this form of dual economy is Malaysia’s Penang region. In the 1970s, Malaysia faced similar enclave challenges that Cambodia encounters today. Building on a more professional bureaucracy, Malaysia broke this enclave structure through three approaches: a targeted cluster policy; state-run matchmaking agencies like the Penang Development Corporation, which guided local firms toward multinational corporations’ quality standards; and the Penang Skill Development Centre, a state-funded education hub managed directly by foreign tech giants. Cambodia, by contrast, lacks both the institutional capacity for such matchmaking and an education system aligned with real-world market needs.

Conversely, Vietnam, with its socialist-oriented market economy, outperforms Cambodia in strategically coordinating economic actors. Although links between FDI and its local economy remain weak, Hanoi has countered this with an assertive, state-led industrial policy and a relatively effective anti-corruption campaign. Rather than leaving the market to its own devices, Hanoi deliberately cultivates state-affiliated conglomerates like Vingroup or Viettel to act as spearheads of its industrial strategy. In exchange for market access, the government leverages these “national champions” to demand technology transfers from global giants like Samsung or Intel. In contrast, Cambodia’s laissez-faire approach in its Special Economic Zones leaves such matchmaking entirely to a flawed market, where local inefficiencies prevent it from ever taking place.

Political Implications and Necessary Measures

The generational transition from long-serving Prime Minister Hun Sen to his son Hun Manet has done little to alter the existing political dynamics in Cambodia. While the Western-educated, second-generation CPP cadres push for superficial modernization and administrative digitalization, the underlying political deal remains untouched: the Oknhas continue to bankroll the regime’s grip on power in exchange for the protection of their domestic fiefdoms. Hence, dismantling the dual economy requires more than new, technocratic reform packages; it demands a fundamental realignment of economic incentives with measurable conditions that do not fundamentally conflict with the regime’s political interests.

First, the government must stop shielding domestic monopolies. State concessions, loans, and licenses for domestic conglomerates should be strictly contingent on international competitiveness and export revenues. Those who fail in the global market must lose their political protection.

The second priority is to create a genuinely meritocratic civil service. As long as posts in key ministries and regulatory bodies are bought or inherited at exorbitant prices, SME support is doomed to fail. Subsidies and administrative aid must be managed by a professionalized, merit-based civil service, isolated from dysfunctional patronage networks.

Finally, the government must recognize that relying purely on SEZs for diversification is no longer enough. To break the dual economy, the government must offer tax incentives to foreign investors who enter long-term joint ventures with local firms, ensure technology transfers, and promote local talent to management positions. Simultaneously, physical technology clusters must logistically and geographically link local suppliers to anchor multinational corporations.

As long as the systemic logic of elite distribution dominates economic policy, technocratic proposals like those that the World Bank has suggested for years will remain insufficient. The case of Cambodia proves that sustainable economic modernization is inextricably linked to the quality of governance. A political transformation grounded in the rule of law and oriented toward the common good is a mandatory prerequisite to prevent the market order from becoming a mere façade. Without shifting away from a rent-seeking economic model, Cambodia will miss its chance to become a competitive industrial nation, remaining permanently stuck in a stalled transformation.

title: The Islamabad Memorandum Returns to the Spotlight
description: For Pakistan, the coming days will test whether its mediation capacity can keep pace with a conflict that continues to expand in both geography and complexity.
text:
The Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) that Pakistan helped negotiate between Iran and the U.S. in June and which had largely dropped out of public discussion in recent months is back in the news again. The renewed attention on the MoU, however, does not necessarily indicate a clear pathway toward a lasting de-escalation of the conflict. Rather, it signals a new high level of endorsement since its signing in June.

The Pakistan-mediated 14-point interim understanding that Washington and Tehran endorsed was intended to halt the armed hostilities, reopen the Strait of Hormuz and create space for broader talks on nuclear and other issues. Its recent return to high-level conversations during the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) summit in New York suggests that, despite repeated setbacks, the agreement still serves as the primary reference point for those seeking to prevent further escalation.

The latest references to the MoU emerged largely at meetings held on the sidelines of this year’s UNGA. Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, speaking after discussions with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, stated that the entire Pakistani leadership remained united in its resolve to expedite the peace efforts outlined in the Islamabad MoU. Pezeshkian, for his part, reaffirmed that the memorandum remained “totally acceptable” to Iran and that Tehran was ready to take it forward. These remarks, delivered after weeks of relative quiet, signaled that both sides of the original mediation still viewed the document as a viable baseline for de-escalation.

Chinese President Xi Jinping added further weight to the MoU during his state visit to the United States last week. In talks with U.S. President Donald Trump at the White House, Xi expressed support for the U.S. and Iran returning to the June deal that was meant to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz. He also said that both parties should resolve differences through dialogue and negotiation and reach a comprehensive agreement that included the nuclear issue.

Amid this renewed focus on the June agreement, President Xi’s intervention carried particular significance because it came amid broader discussions on global economic stability. The Chinese leader also noted that new economic and trade arrangements between Beijing and Washington represented positive news for the economies and peoples of both countries and for the world economy at large. By linking regional de-escalation to the condition of the global economy, Xi underscored that the prolonged crisis in West Asia carries costs that go far beyond the immediate theater of conflict.

While these high-level statements are important, developments on the ground indicate that negotiations have not gathered significant momentum. For instance, Iranian officials held three hours of talks with U.S. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff on the sidelines of UNGA. This was the first such contact since U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance met an Iranian delegation in Switzerland in June to advance the memorandum. The meeting itself produced no public breakthrough, but its occurrence after months of silence suggested that channels remain open.

Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi injected urgency into these latest conversations by stating that if the necessary conditions were met, the Strait of Hormuz could be reopened and normal maritime passage restored within seven days. He emphasized that the actions required of the U.S. are already contained in the MoU and that the choice now resides with Washington.

Meanwhile, Trump has rejected the Iranian proposal for the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, with some reports indicating that the U.S. is planning another round of attacks on Iran after the upcoming midterm elections. Meanwhile, Iranian officials appear to have ignored Trump’s rhetoric, saying that they are waiting for an official response from mediators on the proposals under discussion within the Islamabad framework.

For Pakistan, the renewed focus on the MoU offers another opportunity to press for de-escalation between Iran and the U.S., especially since the agreement now has Xi’s explicit backing.

However, the stakes for Islamabad have grown considerably since June. Pakistan is no longer focused solely on salvaging the original understanding. The country’s policymakers are simultaneously attempting to help ease tensions between Yemen’s Houthis and Saudi Arabia as well as Iran and the U.S.

Last week, the military leadership from Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, and Pakistan convened under the joint Makkah defense pact to discuss urgent steps in support of the Saudis amid Houthi attacks. The three countries resolved to accelerate military cooperation, with Islamabad and Riyadh separately committing to joint efforts to confront threats to Saudi territory. This expanded mediation portfolio has arguably stretched Pakistan’s diplomatic capacity at a time when the original Iran-U.S. conflict has only broadened in scope.

Moreover, there are additional risks which can complicate the picture. For instance, Trump has reportedly hinted at the possibility of renewed military action against Iran even as de-escalation talks continue. Tehran has responded with warnings of new military surprises should it come under attack. Iranian officials have also cautioned that any future confrontation could extend the conflict into the Arabian Sea.

It is pertinent to mention that Pakistan possesses no enforcement mechanism within the Islamabad MoU. The country’s influence rests solely on the goodwill of the primary parties and the diplomatic capital it has accumulated through mediation efforts. As the war continues to stretch and new fronts are opening, there is a growing risk that the original understanding may be overtaken by events, which could put additional pressure on Islamabad’s carefully cultivated role as a regional mediator.

The Islamabad MoU has arguably returned to the diplomatic conversations not because its implementation is imminent, but because it remains the only structured framework both sides have formally accepted as part of a de-escalation mechanism.

Whether that framework can still function as a roadmap depends less on statements delivered in New York or Washington and more on the willingness of Iran and the U.S. to translate words into actions on the ground.

For Pakistan, the coming days will test whether its mediation capacity can keep pace with a conflict that continues to expand in both geography and complexity.
