title: The Promises the Afghanistan War Left Behind
description: Five years after the U.S. withdrawal from Afghanistan, the relationships built over 20 years of war still matter.
text:
“It felt almost like you were playing God with their life at that moment,” recalled Joe Laude, executive director of the Operation Allies Refuge Foundation (OAR), reflecting on the final days of the U.S. evacuation from Kabul. A Marine machine-gunner with Echo Company, 2nd Battalion, 1st Marines who served at Abbey Gate during the evacuation in August 2021, Laude witnessed firsthand the impossible choices facing Americans as approximately 123,000 people were evacuated and thousands of Afghans sought a way out.

Every decision – to let someone through the gate, to turn someone away – carried life-altering consequences. When the last U.S. aircraft departed Kabul on August 30, 2021, those decisions lingered. For people like Laude, the uncertainties remained: Who could he have helped? Who was left behind? And what did it mean to feel responsible for people he could not protect?

Psychologists describe these experiences as moral injury, the psychological and ethical harm that occurs when individuals witness, participate in, or are unable to prevent actions that violate their deeply held moral beliefs and values. In the aftermath of the United States’ 20-year war in Afghanistan, that injury can take the form of responsibility, helplessness, perceived betrayal, and the painful belief that a promise was left unfulfilled.

For two decades, Americans and Afghans worked shoulder to shoulder in pursuit of a shared mission. Afghan interpreters, journalists, civil society leaders, educators, and security personnel risked their lives alongside American soldiers, diplomats, and aid workers. These relationships were often more than professional. They were built through years of shared danger, trust, friendship, and a belief that those who had stood beside one another would be protected if the situation deteriorated. However, with the Taliban’s return in August 2021, much of that shared progress disappeared almost overnight.

Lida Kharooti Sayeed, who served as a judge on Afghanistan’s Anti-Corruption Serious Crimes Court for 13 years before the Taliban returned to power, remembers with gratitude the Americans who tried to help her and others like her.

“I do not blame the individuals who tried to help us,” she said. “Many of them showed kindness and compassion where people were frightened and uncertain about their future. Their efforts meant a great deal to Afghan people like me.”

Sayeed’s gratitude complicates an easy narrative of American failure. The people who formed these relationships fought on the same side of a war. They were people who trusted one another.

That trust also made the withdrawal so difficult for those who were unable to protect the people they had worked beside. Laude describes the guilt he felt: “I had betrayed the Afghan community, even though it was ultimately our leadership’s decision that led to what happened.”

That distinction did not necessarily ease the burden. Knowing that institutions and leaders made the ultimate decisions did not erase the responsibility he felt toward the Afghans who were calling, asking for help, and waiting for a way out.

Helping Afghan allies became a way to channel that unresolved feeling into action. Through OAR, Laude has turned his experience in Kabul into work supporting veterans struggling with moral injury through peer support, humanitarian service, research, and advocacy.

Laude acknowledged that staying busy also meant putting his own emotions aside. “Part of what I did was try to mask the emotional side of this situation through work. That’s why I started OAR. I tried to take away from my own healing and help other people.”

For some, continuing to serve Afghan partners may be a form of moral repair – not an attempt to pretend the past can be fixed, but a decision to remain accountable to the values and friendships that still matter.

For Afghan partners left behind, the story did not end with the evacuation. Families remain separated, immigration cases stretch on, and careers and lives are disrupted.

Sayeed is still rebuilding the life she lost. She’s now a visiting scholar and researcher at the William & Mary Law School.

“We survived very difficult days, but surviving was only the beginning,” she said. “We are still trying to rebuild our lives, support our families, continue our education, and find meaningful opportunities.”

Five years later, Afghanistan is still often discussed in terms of the political failures surrounding the withdrawal. Those debates are important, but they do not capture everything that remained after the last plane left Kabul. What happens to the relationships built during 20 years of war when the war itself is over? Can there be closure?

For some, the answer has been to keep showing up. “That closure isn’t necessarily going to come through the leadership that betrayed you. Instead, I think it comes through relationships at the grassroots level,” Laude said.

For Laude, those relationships offer more than a path toward closure. They shape how he answers a harder question about the war itself: whether the years of service, sacrifice, and relationships built along the way ultimately mattered.

“One of the most important long-term psychological questions is whether any of it mattered,” Laude said. “I believe it does matter.”

What endures, five years later, is not only the memory of the withdrawal, but the relationships and obligations it could not erase. The war may have ended, but for those who believed they were responsible for one another, the question of what was owed did not end with it.
tag: Afghanistan; moral injury; U.S. War in Afghanistan; U.S. withdrawal from Afghanistan

title: The Space Security Landscape Is Deteriorating Rapidly
description: With the United States announcing that it has deployed “on-orbit space control weapons,” the space arms race now appears to be fully underway.
text:
There is little doubt that great power competition is ramping up. Now, another front has opened, with the United States announcing that it has deployed a space weapon. China, and subsequently Russia, had been pushing the limits in space, testing advanced technologies with possible offensive uses in outer space, including cyber weapons, ground-based lasers, and artificial robotic arms that could be used for repairing satellites but also have obvious military and intelligence uses. Now the U.S. has responded by joining the developing arms race, which is likely to spur further competition.

The space arms race now appears to be fully underway.

The acknowledgement of U.S. space weapons was made by U.S. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink. He revealed that the U.S. Space Force has launched “space control weapons” into orbit. Delivering a keynote address at a recent Air and Space Forces Association (AFA) conference, Meink said that “the United States now has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the joint force against hostile adversary action.”

Not surprisingly, he justified this step with reference to the threats from China and Russia, both of which “continue to demonstrate aggressive maneuvers and are developing – and demonstrating – space weapons of their own.”

Meink is not the only U.S. official who has talked about these new space weapons.

Addressing the “State of the Space Force” at the AFA conference, Chief of Space Operations Gen. Douglas Schiess made an unequivocal claim that the U.S. Space Force “uses active space-based weaponry to support United States national defense.” He noted the “increasingly contested” space domain where adversaries have technologies that are meant to disrupt or destroy satellites in orbit. He also made a mention of hypersonic weapons that pose a threat to the United States and its allies and partners.

While details are scanty and there has been no elaboration of the weapon systems that have been launched, this is clearly a recognition of and a response to what Russia and China have been doing in terms of their own space weapons. In fact, Meink dismissed ideas from journalists that the U.S. announcement of developing space control weapons could give permission to its adversaries pursuing space weapons. The race is already on.

Space is central to U.S. national security and war fighting efforts. The domain represents essential eyes and ears for military operations, which meant that the United States could not afford to ignore China and Russia’s threats and advancements.

Threats to national assets in outer space have grown rapidly and are very diverse today. Just as the world seemed as if it was outgrowing fears about nuclear weapons, it was revealed that Russia was developing and potentially deploying nuclear anti-satellite (ASAT) weapons. If used, such weapons can result in the indiscriminate destruction of entire satellite orbits. These developments were revealed in February 2024 by U.S. intelligence officials.

Kinetic anti-satellite (ASAT) weapons have also made a comeback since the first successful ASAT test by China in January 2007. China in effect broke an unwritten moratorium that had been in place since the 1980s. Since the Chinese ASAT test, others followed: the U.S. (2008), India (2019), and Russia (2021). The Russian ASAT test, using the A-235 / PL-19 Nudol kinetic interceptor missile system, resulted in the creation of “more than 1,500 pieces of trackable orbital debris” according to a statement from U.S. Space Command. The United States saw this as a direct effort to target it.

Gen. James Dickinson, commander of the U.S. Space Command, stated that “Russia is developing and deploying capabilities to actively deny access to and use of space by the United States and its allies and partners.” He added that the test was a clear demonstration of the Russian pursuit of counterspace weapons that “undermine strategic stability and pose a threat to all nations.”

Both the Chinese and Russian ASAT tests were also conducted at a higher altitude – 865 km and 480 km respectively – which would mean that the debris generated as a result would stay afloat in space orbits for decades because the atmosphere drag at that altitude is lower.

In addition, there is an entire range of non-kinetic counterspace weapons that have been deployed in space, causing innumerable incidents of interference, disruptions, and destruction of space assets. Non-kinetic weapons include electromagnetic pulses, high-powered lasers, and high-powered microwaves, in addition to electronic and cyber options including jamming and spoofing as well as data interception and/or corruption and taking full control of data. All of these weapons have been employed and there have been growing incidents of space interference as far back as 2008. Attribution is difficult but many of these threats are thought to be sourced from Russia and China.

Therefore, while the open U.S. claim about deployment of space weapons have made headlines everywhere, with many even suggesting that this will push Russia and China to develop such weapons, the reality is that Beijing and Moscow have been developing and employing these weapons, all while using the rhetoric of non-weaponization and peaceful use of space. Calls for non-weaponization and getting more countries to see the benefits of keeping space safe, secure, and sustainable are important, but this effort is increasingly being overtaken by a space arms race that now appears inevitable.
tag: China space weapons; Space weaponization; Troy Meink; U.S. Space Force; U.S. space weapons

title: The Transitions Shaping Australia’s Future
description: In its latest Intergenerational Report, the Australian Treasury lays out five transitions shaping the coming decades.
text:
Every five years, the Australian Treasury releases its Intergenerational Report (IGR). The report is designed to look at the major structural changes and challenges the country faces to understand how Australia can best navigate the world in the coming decades. This week, the Treasury released its latest report. It argued that despite significant global changes, Australia remains relatively well placed to maintain its prosperity, but its major advantages cannot be taken for granted.

The report highlighted five transitions that will shape the coming decades: artificial intelligence, geopolitical fragmentation, the energy transition, an aging population, and the transformation of Australia’s industrial base. A sixth, overarching, issue is a continuation of intergenerational inequality, with older generations remaining better off than younger Australians. This affects the major structural components of people’s lives – affordable housing, what taxation younger generations will have to pay, and their overall access to opportunity.

The most significant new development to arise since the previous IGR is the ascent of AI. Here, the actual real world outcomes remain unknown, but the Treasury treats AI as a general-purpose technology capable of shifting the economic realities of a wide range of industries. AI is expected to automate some tasks while – hopefully – increasing demand for other forms of work, particularly where human judgment and relationships remain important. The question remains whether Australian businesses and institutions can adjust quickly enough to capture its potential gains, while being aware of and adaptable to any potential negative side effects.

The other major change since the last report has been the acceleration of change in the international environment. Australia’s primary security partner, the United States, is seemingly working hard to dismantle the network of allies that has maintained relative peace and stability over the past 80 years, and it cannot be assumed that this tendency in Washington will subside when President Donald Trump leaves office. China’s massive military build-up and flouting of international law in the South China Sea remains a potential major disruptive force in the Indo-Pacific, while Russia’s invasion of Ukraine has shifted Europe’s focus away from opportunity in the Indo-Pacific to security at home.

The 2026 IGR expects geopolitical fragmentation to make economic relationships increasingly dependent on security considerations, rather than efficiency alone. This creates significant tension for Australia as it has benefited from the openness of international trade, and in particular from trade with China. The report highlighted that Australia is a resource-rich country that has commodities that other countries need, but cannot simply rely on market demand to maintain this advantage in a world where other considerations need to be balanced.

This demand and geopolitical complexity, however, is also affected by the energy transition. Australia may lose advantages in coal and LNG exports, but gain greater energy security through renewables – with Australia currently being heavily dependent on foreign oil. The energy transition requires an enormous investment in generation, storage, and transmission, as well as a shift in consumer habits toward electric vehicles (and the charging infrastructure to support this shift). The growth in data centers – an issue highly controversial in Australia at present – adds another layer of complexity to how the country will manage its energy requirements.

Yet the potentially most consequential issue that the report addressed is Australia’s aging population. Lower fertility combined with an increasing public suspicion of immigration means that the country will grow more slowly, and by the 2060s deaths are projected to exceed births. Longer lives means that the number of Australians over 85 years old will triple in this period, creating increased demand for health care, aged care, and pensions, but with less working-age people to pay for these services.

These demographic changes feed directly into the report’s concerns about productivity. The Treasury projected that average annual economic growth will be about two-thirds of what it has been over the previous four decades. Therefore there is a need to focus on investment, greater skills acquisition, innovation, and regulatory reform to maintain the country’s prosperity. AI may help or hinder this.

It is here where intergenerational inequality becomes more pronounced. House prices have risen faster than incomes for the past two decades, substantially lowering rates of home ownership. Slower economic growth compounds this problem with less opportunity for younger people, less wage growth, and higher tax burdens to pay for government services for older generations. Each of those trends makes it more difficult to have more children.

Taken together, the Intergenerational Report is less a forecast than an account of the pressures Australia will have to manage simultaneously. Australia starts from a strong position as a wealthy, well-educated country, but the test of these assets will be how the population adapts to change.
tag: 2026 Australian Intergenerational Report; AI in Asia; Australia; Australia AI; Australian Politics

title: The Trump-Xi Summit Is Over, But Taiwan Is Still Bracing for the Fallout
description: Given what happened in May, Taiwanese may have been more nervous after the latest Trump-Xi summit ended.
text:
The latest meeting between U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping led to much anxiety in Taiwan, with fears that Trump could potentially throw Taiwan under the bus in the course of negotiations with Xi. The two leaders agreed to dialogue on AI, as well as tariff reductions on $30 billion in “non-sensitive goods” going both ways. Even so, readouts between the two sides differed as to what was agreed to be purchased, and any discussion of semiconductors, chips, and export controls was not mentioned.

Besides trade deals, there have been few concrete outcomes from the meeting to date, and the two leaders initially remained silent when asked by reporters if Taiwan featured in their summit. Trump later denied that Taiwan was discussed at length, then stated that he and Xi “didn’t spend a lot of time talking about Taiwan.”

Other reports suggest that Xi tried press Trump to curtail support for Taiwan, and accept Beijing’s framing on Taiwan. Chinese state-run media quoted Xi as stating during the meeting: “I hope that the United States adheres to the correct position of opposing ‘Taiwan independence’ and handles the Taiwan issue prudently.”

In particular, ahead of the Trump-Xi meeting, international media reporting suggested that Xi would try to convince Trump to cut weapons sales to Taiwan. Although the Trump administration approved $11 billion in arms sales to Taiwan last December, the Trump administration has yet to approve a further $14 billion package.

It was generally understood that Trump would not approve the arms sale ahead of his meeting with Xi, in order to ensure that the talks went smoothly. For its part, the Taiwanese government has attempted to reassure the public that ties with the United States are stable, and reiterated that U.S. policy on Taiwan has not changed after the summit. Nevertheless, the real question will be whether Trump reveals any unexpected curveballs for Taiwan after the meeting itself.

If so, this would follow the precedent set by Trump after his meeting with Xi in May 2026 in Beijing. Little happened during the meeting itself, which was mostly a non-event. In May, as with this latest summit, Trump initially declined to answer questions on Taiwan from reporters. The readouts of the May 2026 meeting differed between the United States and China, with the U.S. denying that Taiwan had come up at all, while China claimed that it had been discussed. As if to forestall a potential shift in position by Trump, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio emphasized during the May trip that U.S. policy on Taiwan was unchanged in an interview with NBC.

During an interview with Fox News shortly after his return from China, however, Trump seemed to hit out at Taiwan, stating that he was “not looking to have somebody go independent,” and that Taiwan needed “cool down a bit.” Trump then moved on to attack Taiwan with accusations that it had stolen the U.S. semiconductor industry, while calling on semiconductor companies to move back to the United States.

Most alarming of all, Trump cast doubt on U.S. commitment to Taiwan as a whole, while suggesting that the Taiwan-U.S. relationship was mostly transactional. In particular, Trump suggested that arms sales to Taiwan were up for negotiation, and that this made for a “good bargaining chip” in talks with China.

Such comments provoked alarm in Taiwan, seeing as this contravenes U.S. commitments to provide weapons to Taiwan dating back to the Reagan-era Three Assurances. Trump also raised questions about whether the United States would intervene in the event of a conflict with China, stating that he did not think it was logical for American troops to “travel 9,500 miles to fight a war.”

Given that recent history, Taiwanese may have been more nervous after the latest Trump-Xi summit ended.

Indeed, indications have since emerged that Trump offered to sell arms to China during his September meeting with Xi. David Perdue, the U.S. ambassador to China, stated that Trump made such comments to Xi in an interview with Fox News on September 27. Although Perdue also stated that U.S. policy remained unchanged on Taiwan, this was an unusual comment by Trump. The offer came only a few days after controversy erupted about F-35 parts that were mistakenly diverted to Hong Kong, raising concerns about sensitive U.S. military technology ending up in Chinese hands.

As such, while Taiwan may have breathed a sigh of relief that the September summit has not resulted in any overt shift in U.S. policy on Taiwan, what remains is to see whether Trump shifts later on. As some analysts have noted, Trump has already echoed Chinese language on Taiwan on numerous occasions in the past. And while some elements of his administration, such as Rubio, may emphasize that policy remains unchanged, this is not reassuring when Trump himself contradicts those statements.

It is still uncertain when further U.S. arms sales to Taiwan will be approved. Trump and Xi are set to meet two more times this year, in November at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, as well as at the G20 summit in December at the Trump National Doral Miami Golf Club in Florida. It is possible that Trump will hold off on arms sales until after these meetings, or until 2027. Trump’s decision whether to approve arms sales or not could also be impacted by the U.S. midterm elections in November.

With the Trump administration holding off on approving arms sales to Taiwan, this may complicate the domestic debate on defense spending. In past years, the United States has sought to pressure Taiwan to increase defense spending to 5 percent or even 10 percent of GDP, with Trump himself suggesting that the U.S. should not defend Taiwan if Taiwan is not serious about its own defense.

But at a time of stark partisanship, the Kuomintang (KMT) delayed for over 200 days on reviewing the central government budget, while enacting widespread cuts to government ministries it views as antagonistic. The delays impacted defense spending, as well as spending on Taiwan’s domestic drone program. Even so, the KMT suddenly reversed course in August to finally approve the budget, though it limited drone spending by passing it as part of the central government budget rather than as a special expenditure.

Efforts by the United States to push Taiwan to increase defense spending are likely to ring hollow in Taiwan if Washington refuses to sell Taiwan arms. Likewise, comments by Trump will increase doubts about U.S. reliability as an ally in wartime – indeed, survey polling shows that skepticism about the U.S. is up across the board in Taiwan. (Such polling also shows an increase in the Taiwanese public’s willingness to fight – even without U.S. intervention.) Certainly, with the United States holding off on arms sales to Taiwan for so long, Trump suddenly offering to sell arms to China is not likely to reaffirm faith in the U.S. in Taiwan.

Increased skepticism about U.S. reliability is likely to lead to efforts to shore up Taiwan’s domestic defense programs, which are not reliant on the mercurial nature of arms sales. Taiwan is especially likely to seek cooperation from non-U.S. partners on drone development, while positioning itself as an alternative to drone supply chains highly reliant on China.

It can be expected that summits between Trump and Xi will fall into this familiar script going forward – even when the meetings themselves may result in little substance, the point is to see what occurs afterward, and how left-field comments or actions by Trump are perceived.

title: The Trump-Xi Summit: Stakes for Australia
description: Trump wants more sales. Xi wants fewer constraints. What does Australia need from the Trump-Xi summit?
text:
Chinese media have confirmed that Xi Jinping will make a state visit to Washington from September 23 to 25 for a much-anticipated summit with U.S. President Donald Trump. The announcement followed talks between their economic chiefs in New York on September 20.

Although the two sides have framed those discussions differently, it is clear that trade and AI will be on the summit agenda. Trump could leave with more orders, Xi with fewer constraints on China’s technological development, and both declare success. For Canberra, the question is what their bargain would mean for Australian investments and security arrangements built around sustained China-U.S. competition.

Allied unease is already visible. On September 21, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio met his Japanese and South Korean counterparts in New York. Their joint statement reiterated the United States’ “ironclad” defence commitments, opposed economic coercion, and stressed peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait. Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae secured a meeting with Trump on September 22, just before the summit, while South Korean President Lee Jae-myung sought contact during the United Nations General Assembly. Tokyo and Seoul want their security and economic concerns heard before Trump meets Xi. Canberra should draw the same lesson.

Like the Trump-Xi summit held in Beijing in May, this one is likely to buy time rather than lasting stability. The deadline that matters for business falls around November 10. Three temporary arrangements approach their expiration date: Washington’s suspension of restrictions on majority-owned affiliates of listed entities, China’s suspension of expanded rare earth and related export controls, and 178 U.S. tariff exclusions for Chinese goods. The practical questions are how long these pauses will be extended and on what terms.

Trump wants commercial wins ahead of the midterms. Xi wants fewer constraints on China’s technological development. Trade concessions can serve both purposes without resolving the contest over power in the digital age.

Trade and technology may therefore move in different directions. Tariff relief and purchase commitments could coexist with tighter restrictions on advanced chips and overseas computing access. Xi cannot assume Trump can trade these restrictions away. They have bipartisan support in Congress and deep backing in the Pentagon and Commerce Department.

Beijing increasingly treats efforts to block its technological advance as a challenge to its right to development, one of the four red lines in Xi’s book. It will resist broader technology restrictions and pressure on third countries to choose sides.

The two leaders have different philosophies of negotiation. Trump assumes that, at the right price, almost any arrangement can be renegotiated. Xi allows for pragmatism and ambiguity within fixed limits. Beijing accepts broadly worded commitments but demands clarity on Taiwan and its political system. Washington insists on verifiable trade commitments while deliberately leaving uncertain whether it would intervene militarily over Taiwan. Both leaders have domestic reasons to compromise, but both may sign the same wording and mean different things.

Australia has to plan for the consequences. Canberra should compare their announcements for differences in scope, duration, and conditions before treating a diplomatic statement as a reliable basis for the future.

The Albanese government has spent years restoring normal trade with China while supporting Washington’s efforts to reduce dependence on it. If Trump and Xi compromise with one another, Australia could be left bearing the costs of reducing dependence on China while Washington negotiates exceptions for itself.

Canberra should seek durable support for mineral projects, cooperation on shared AI risks, and security commitments that survive a bargain with Beijing.

First, critical minerals offer one test. The Australia-U.S. framework envisages price support and financing to develop alternatives to Chinese supply. If Washington and Beijing extend their rare earth arrangements, Canberra should seek assurances that support for Australian alternatives will endure. Australian projects need dependable financing and long-term customers, even when Chinese supplies become easier to obtain.

Second, AI risks extend beyond chips and data centers. Australian businesses use software and digital services shared across borders. Canberra should therefore press for an agreement to warn affected countries and operators of serious AI incidents while there is still time to contain them. Building more local data centers would not, by itself, remove those shared dependencies.

Government hotlines alone cannot do this: the first warning may come from a developer, cloud provider, or independent researcher. Those warnings need to reach Australian authorities and affected businesses without waiting for governments to establish blame. That would give Australia something a bilateral technology deal cannot guarantee: timely notice of a failure that could spread into its own economy. The test is whether warnings reach those who must act, rather than whether the leaders agree to keep talking.

Finally, Australia needs maritime security. Defense-commissioned research reported in 2022 found that a major regional conflict would threaten routes supplying 90 percent of Australia’s refined-fuel imports. With disruption in the Strait of Hormuz already imposing costs, Australia can ill afford another obstructed route in the South China Sea.

Canberra should seek consultation before Washington negotiates any changes affecting its regional military presence or commitments under AUKUS. It should also press for functioning military hotlines and arrangements for reporting incidents at sea and in the air. These mechanisms need procedures both sides will use when tensions rise.

Reaffirming that decisions to use nuclear weapons must remain under human control at the summit would provide another practical safeguard.

Canberra’s test is whether the summit leaves Australia better able to invest, keep essential services running, and protect its trade routes. That requires commitments Washington will honor and crisis arrangements both powers will use. If Trump and Xi buy themselves time while Australia is left carrying the uncertainty, their success will not be ours.

title: The US Arms Bottleneck Is Impacting Its East Asian Allies
description: Taiwan's Patriot missiles, and Japan's Tomahawks are competing in the same queue as Ukraine and the Iran replenishment. But there are solutions.
text:
In May, Taiwan was offered no less than four different explanations for the delays in receiving a $14 billion arms package of Patriot PAC-3 interceptors and NASAMS air defense systems.

Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao testified to senators that the United States was “doing a pause” on the arms sale to Taiwan “in order to make sure we have the munitions we need for Epic Fury,” the U.S. military operation in Iran. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio then claimed that the sale was under review, not “paused.” Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth said it wasn’t about Iran at all: “our stockpiles are more than suited… both there [in Iran] and around the globe.” Meanwhile, U.S. President Donald Trump said the arms sales were “a very good negotiating chip” with China, suggesting a purely political motivation for the delay.

Beyond the problem of conflicting explanations, none of these statements provided the answer Taipei really wants: a delivery date.

Taiwan is not alone in waiting for promised U.S. weapons. The U.S. government informed Japan that delivery of 400 long-awaited Tomahawk cruise missiles would be delayed two years to meet drawdown demands from the current war in Iran.

The problem is obvious: the U.S. has finite supplies of these missiles, and a growing need. Taiwan and Japan are queuing up, in the same line, behind Ukraine and behind resupplies for the Iran war.

Lockheed Martin exceeded their production record with over 500 interceptors in 2024. But the U.S. military itself shot nearly 1,500 Patriot interceptors in the Iran war. In the fiscal budget for next year, the U.S. Army asked for over 2,700 interceptors, a large jump from the 357 it previously funded. Taiwan’s order of 102 interceptors sits somewhere within that request. Japan’s order does too.

The U.S. requirement for 2,700 interceptors merely scratches the surface of the problem. The United States is facing depleted assets of its own while also tasked with supporting vital allies through arms deliveries. If the United States spent 1,500 interceptors in a matter of months on Iran, what will Taiwan require to defend itself? Certainly, more than the 102 systems that currently only exist on paper.

In evaluating the strength of U.S. deterrence, Chinese military and political leaders will consider whether or not they can deplete U.S. and allied stocks more rapidly than they can replenish them. Beijing doesn’t have to guess if the United States can sustain a major war in the Indo-Pacific; the U.S. fiscal budget request, the contracts awarded, and the backlog of arms sales are all public information.

U.S. allies aren’t blind to this. Chen Yi-fan of Tamkang University wrote that even if the deal was opened up for bidding immediately it would take four to five years for a Patriot system to arrive in Taiwan – and that’s the exact timeframe during which American and Taiwan planners believe a crisis could occur.

Meanwhile, the AUKUS initiative was retooled in May due to the realization that the United States would be unable to produce new submarines for Australia. Allies know what that means.

You can’t ramp up factories, suppliers, machine shops, and skilled labor immediately. Even when Congress appropriates budgets, production capacity slotted to come online in 2030 isn’t going to deter Beijing in 2027. Funding the U.S. munitions supply chain is no longer the bottleneck. The challenge is accelerating the construction timeline for new production capacity.

The normal sequence is government demand first, then new capacity being developed. Contracts are awarded before firms invest in facilities, machines, and the people who will do the work. Flipping that model on its head could shorten the time between a shortage and the production to address it by years.

Some private firms are rapidly building capacity and production, before contracts are even awarded. They’re putting their own money where their mouths are and betting on guaranteed future demand. One of the leaders in that race is Hadrian, recently valued at nearly $8 billion in its latest funding round. In March, the private manufacturer opened Factory 4: a 2.2 million square foot machine shop in Cherokee, Alabama making parts for the Virginia- and Columbia-class submarines, the most relevant vessels to a potential war in the western Pacific. Under AUKUS, the United States was supposed to provide Australia with a new Virginia-class submarine before production constraints forced it to settle for in-service subs instead.

Hadrian’s move seeks to directly address one of the largest challenges facing the United States’ Navy and its Indo-Pacific presence. This approach is the one which should be replicated: they invested over $1.5 billion in private capital before receiving a roughly $900 million contract from the Navy.

The same model could expand the capabilities needed by Taiwan and Japan. In December, Lockheed Martin signed an MOU with Hadrian to co-locate a machine shop and inspection facility within Lockheed’s factory that produces the PAC-3 MSE and THAAD interceptors. To be clear: this is an arrangement, not a production deal. The company claims their Opus manufacturing system can have new production facilities operational in less than six months and new technicians operating at full productivity in 30 days.

These are not vetted performance metrics, just internal targets. That said, Hadrian has already been producing parts for Anduril’s autonomous weapons since 2023. Anduril says it has decreased delivery times up to 50 percent. Scaling up machine shops is no longer a pipe dream.

Part of the solution will also come from other countries. Japan currently produces PAC-3 interceptors under license at Mitsubishi Heavy Industries at a rate of about 30 interceptors per year, with the potential to double production. In November, Japan successfully exported its first domestically manufactured PAC-3 interceptors to the United States.

Production is bottlenecked by the Boeing seeker; the new seeker production lines won’t be running until 2027. However, Japan and the United States are negotiating joint production of the PAC-3 MSE. Japan could expand production of its own seekers, avoiding the bottleneck for itself but also for every other Patriot user in the area.

Taiwan cannot manufacture Patriots under license, but it can ramp up manufacturing for drones, naval mines, and shore-based missiles. These conversations might not make headlines, but they would contribute more to Japan and Taiwan’s defense than one more extended deterrence communique.

How quickly a country can replenish its arms is a key question of deterrence. Taken together, there’s a rough blueprint for quickly addressing production constraints. The United States can encourage the private-sector-first, public-sector-later approach Hadrian took to financing production, but only for already-approved suppliers on both sides of the Pacific.

Private firms taking action is the beginning of a solution, but without global engagement with allies, interceptor batteries will stay empty. Second, Washington should develop a surge production roadmap among allied industries: what U.S., Japanese, Australian, South Korean, and Taiwanese industries can ramp up or repurpose in six, twelve, or eighteen months, starting with seekers, rocket motors, and castings/forgings. National export controls are crucial for this, but I am advocating for selective industrial integration, not open and indiscriminate technology sharing.

Finally, Taiwan and Japan should demand to know, officially and on the record, how long their Patriot and other major arms systems will take to deliver once funded, and the Pentagon should provide those numbers. Taiwan’s 102 interceptors are lumped in with the U.S. Army’s 2,798, along with other allied requests, as well as the re-supply for each missile used over Iran. Japan’s Tomahawks are in that same queue. The United States can make a statement immediately, but what Taipei, Tokyo, and just as importantly, Beijing care about is the delivery at the pier.

title: To Succeed in AI, South Korea Is Reinventing Its Developmental State Model
description: South Korea is betting big on universal AI access, using state activism and corporate collaboration to strengthen its position in the global AI race.
text:
South Korea has embarked on an ambitious plan by launching the “AI for All” initiative, which aims to make artificial intelligence (AI) widely accessible to all its citizens. This initiative reflects a broader effort to integrate AI into almost every corner of Korean society. Rather than treating AI simply as another emerging technology, South Korea increasingly views it as a technology that will help realize its domestic economic development plans and geoeconomic objectives, retain its technological advantages in key strategic industries, and gain a strong foothold in emerging technologies amid intensifying technological competition.

The South Korean government plans to provide AI learning opportunities to approximately 5.14 million people in 2026. To support this initiative, it is developing AI services based on South Korea’s sovereign AI models, including a general-purpose AI chatbot that citizens will be able to use without charges or usage limits. More importantly, Seoul’s long-term ambition is to move toward an environment in which its citizens can have access to their own AI agents.

This plan can be understood as part of a broader trend among East Asian countries, particularly South Korea and China, toward emphasizing the rapid implementation and widespread application of AI. This approach reflects the distinction drawn by Kai-Fu Lee in his book “AI Superpowers: China, Silicon Valley, and the New World Order,” in which he contrasted China’s implementation-driven model with the innovation-first strategy associated with the United States. It also differs from the European approach, which places greater emphasis on AI governance, regulation, fundamental rights, and data privacy.

In many parts of the world, especially in liberal democracies, AI remains a subject of debate over safety concerns. In South Korea and other East Asian countries, however, the debate is different: it focuses on how rapidly AI can be deployed. The geoeconomic logic behind this approach is that rapid deployment will not only strengthen their positions in the AI ecosystem but also enable them to become future leaders.

South Korea views AI as one of the most promising next-generation growth engines and a strategic technology that will determine the country’s economic competitiveness. Seoul is learning from its historical experience, as the country’s growth has largely depended on technological upgrading and export-oriented manufacturing. Therefore, South Korea has linked AI to national survival, just as it did with semiconductors, which now form the backbone of the South Korean economy. South Korea’s strength in the semiconductor industry also supports its advancement in AI, as the expansion of AI is closely connected to growing demand in semiconductor-related sectors, including advanced memory, computing infrastructure, and AI chips.

A Shared National Commitment to AI

The continuing legacy of developmental state practices in South Korea has generated a unique level of commitment among the state, businesses, and society to realizing the country’s national ambitions. Historically, South Korea’s rapid technological advancement resulted from the state’s long-term planning, the establishment of national targets and industrial strategies, businesses’ active support and compliance, and, most importantly, society’s largely unopposed embrace of rapid, growth-oriented development. This national consensus prioritizes technological advancement and the fostering of key strategic industries over other considerations. The same pattern can clearly be observed in the case of AI.

In South Korea, political parties across the ideological spectrum support not only the rapid advancement of AI but also the goal of making the country a leading AI superpower. When the conservative government led by Yoon Suk-yeol was in power, South Korea set the ambitious goal of becoming one of the world’s top three AI powers, alongside the United States and China. The progressive government under Lee Jae-myung came to power in 2025 after Yoon was impeached, amid significant political conflict and turmoil involving conservative political forces. Nevertheless, one objective remained unchanged: South Korea’s national ambition to become a world-leading AI power. Therefore, a national consensus exists around realizing this ambition, regardless of changes in government and the high level of bipartisan political conflict within South Korea. That’s a consensus rarely seen in many liberal democracies.

The government’s ambition is also being reinforced by extensive business participation and, more importantly, growing societal demand for AI adoption. Frequent meetings between the government and business leaders are taking place in Seoul, with both sides agreeing that they must cooperate extensively to realize South Korea’s national ambitions.

Even more important is the growing social demand for AI implementation in South Korea. The general view is that rapid deployment will enable society to adopt AI more quickly, ultimately creating new opportunities for both the public and the country. According to a recent survey, almost seven out of ten South Koreans believe that AI services, deployed in collaboration with the government and corporations, will positively impact society.

This contrasts sharply with debates in Western liberal democracies, where AI adoption is often discussed in terms of privacy violations, job displacement, and other risks. Moreover, state-led AI planning is often viewed with greater suspicion in societies where anti-statist attitudes are more widespread. This does not mean that such concerns do not exist in South Korean society. However, many people appear to place these concerns within the broader context of the national priority of technological advancement and the belief that South Korea should not fall behind in the global AI race.

Deploying Developmental State Practices

In implementing its AI strategy, Seoul is deploying the practices of the developmental state, through which it previously achieved rapid technological advancement and built globally competitive strategic industries, including semiconductors and shipbuilding. Under this model, the state acts as a proactive planner, investor, and coordinator while collaborating closely with major domestic conglomerates.

Such practices are less common in neoliberal regulatory states, where proactive state intervention and close state–business collaboration – particularly with large corporations – are often viewed negatively. In South Korea, however, the state is actively fostering AI development in cooperation with major domestic companies. Meanwhile, many other countries, particularly liberal democracies, remain preoccupied with debates concerning AI regulation, oversight, and responsibility.

As a result, South Korea has moved far ahead in terms of large-scale investment in AI. While many parts of the world are waiting for, or heavily dependent on, private-sector investment in AI, the South Korean government is taking the lead in creating and expanding a substantial domestic AI market. One important example is South Korea’s decision to increase its national AI budget from 3.3 trillion won in 2025 to 10.1 trillion won in 2026 – almost three times the previous year’s allocation. This expansion occurred despite concerns about the country’s fiscal health. Such aggressive spending on a particular strategic industry also reflects South Korea’s developmental state philosophy of concentrating substantial resources on selected industries with high growth potential.

In addition to its investment role, the state is acting as a coordinator, which is another characteristic of developmental state practices. Under this model, state agencies play proactive roles as pilot agencies responsible for fostering strategic industries. For example, the Ministry of Science and ICT has been actively working with major conglomerates and other technology companies to establish consortia and accelerate AI development and implementation. This was evident in the ministry’s 2025 selection of five industry-led teams – Naver Cloud, Upstage, SK Telecom, NC AI, and LG AI Research – to develop sovereign foundation models.

More recently, the ministry selected three consortia, led respectively by SK Telecom, KT, and Kakao, to operate the “AI for All” project. In both initiatives, the ministry has acted as a pilot agency coordinating public and private actors around national strategic objectives.

This extensive collaboration is not limited to ministerial-level coordination. The government is also providing financial and material support to foster public–private partnerships. For example, to accelerate the implementation of “AI for All,” the South Korean government will provide the three selected consortia with access to up to 512 Nvidia B200 GPUs. Moreover, the government will subsidize part of the expenses involved in developing and operating these AI services.

The government will also finance public access by supporting the provision of AI chatbots to citizens without subscription fees or usage limits. Above all, participating companies will gain access to public service systems, enabling them to connect their chatbots with public AI agents that provide services related to taxation, healthcare appointments, education, and government support programs. Such access has generally remained restricted for private companies in many other parts of the world.

The Global Implications of South Korea’s AI Strategy

South Korea’s rapid deployment of AI across society offers several insights into the country’s political-economic approach to AI in particular and strategic industries more generally. By encouraging the widespread use of AI at an early stage, the government aims to create a large domestic market in which South Korean companies can develop, test, and improve their AI models, thereby supporting South Korea’s sovereign AI strategy. This approach strongly recalls the developmental state model that South Korea previously adopted to accelerate the growth of its strategic industries.

Indeed, South Korea’s lead in AI deployment is driven by a geoeconomic logic through which it seeks to maintain its technological advantages and become an AI superpower. More importantly, it reflects the deployment of developmental state practices, with the state playing a pivotal role and fostering collaboration with South Korea’s major technology companies to realize its national ambitions. Equally significant is the broad societal support for this state-business nexus in AI development. This is a distinctive feature carried over from South Korea’s developmental state era and is once again visible in its approach to AI deployment.

Nevertheless, a major challenge remains: how South Korea will address its shortage of AI talent. If South Korea is able to overcome this challenge, we may witness the emergence of a new technological power in the global AI race alongside the United States and China.

South Korea’s efforts to become one of the world’s top three AI powers also have global implications. If South Korea continues to compete with the U.S. and China for a leading position in AI, it would not be surprising to see a large number of South Korean AI companies, alongside American and Chinese firms, emerge as dominant players in the global market. As seen in today’s semiconductor industry, where companies from a small number of countries dominate and control key technologies, we may similarly witness the emergence of an AI landscape in which companies from only a few countries exercise extensive control, while the rest of the world remains primarily on the consumer side.

South Korea’s rapid deployment of AI across society is likely to place it among the first group of countries. The actions taken today are likely to produce results for countries actively developing AI, in contrast to the more passive approach currently adopted by many others. It should therefore not be surprising if South Korea emerges as a global AI leader in the near future.

title: Trump and Xi: Strongmen at the Temple of Thymos
description: The ego-driven fragility of a world run by recognition-hungry autocrats.
text:
When U.S. President Donald Trump made his second state visit to China in May 2026, Xi Jinping escorted him through Beijing’s magisterial Temple of Heaven, where the Ming and Qing emperors performed rites that mediated between heaven and the earthly order. But when these two men with autocratic impulses and outsized egos strolled through the complex, it became not a Temple of Heaven but a Temple of Thymos – a stage for distributing recognition rather than cosmic concerns. Now, the neoclassical architecture of the White House provides the set for their September 23–25 encounter. Readers of The Diplomat can find in it many articles on the “Thucydides Trap” popularized by the political scientist Graham Allison. The Thucydides Trap suggests that China and the United States are headed for inevitable conflict. Several scholars dispute Allison’s reading, and yet the ancient historian’s ghost still hovered as Xi and Trump moved through the temple, with the Chinese Communist Party’s general secretary, who has a pattern of citing Allison, even referencing the phrase.

I want to propose a lens for power rivalry that’s equally ancient but different and complementary: a Thymos Trap.

Thymos – also rendered thumos – is an ancient Greek word (θυμός) that expresses the desire for recognition. Both Xi and Trump display an unquenchable thymos and take pains to appear outwardly strong. But in fact, countries led by strongmen who build regimes around their personalities are only outwardly magnificent. Internally, they tend to be precarious. Anyone who assumes that the superficial strength of such regimes and leaders makes them permanently durable may be falling into a Thymos Trap. As popularized by the political philosopher Francis Fukuyama, thymos is “the part of the soul that craves recognition of dignity.” It’s innate to all of us and not a marker of damaged, narcissistic men. But Fukuyama makes distinctions between isothymia (recognition as equal) and megalothymia (recognition as superior). The genius of liberal democracy is that it satisfies the human need for isothymia. But megalothymia can never be extinguished, because its fossil fuel is the trauma of prior humiliation, now powering a yearning for reversal. Nationalism can transfer that dynamic from individual to nation: Xi wears it on his sleeve as China’s “century of humiliation,” ensuing “hurt feelings of the Chinese people,” and his Chinese Dream of rejuvenation. Trump emblazons it on his “Make America Great Again” baseball caps.

This desire for status, as the journalist Will Storr explained in “The Status Game,” is pursued through dominance, virtue, or success. These differing tactics can depend on the cultures in which status-seeking individuals operate.

According to political philosopher Ye Xue, in the United States, where status is relative and must be defended, the cultural tendency is to pursue self-esteem through demands for honor. China, by contrast, is rooted in a stable hierarchy in which status is relational and harmony is sought. Trump and Xi represent these different cultural approaches to recognition perfectly; Trump’s is deeply individualistic and even antagonistic, while Xi’s is more concerned with a collective megalothymia that demands deference to China as a whole.

For all their differences, Xi and Trump share a common insistence on staking their own legitimacy on the nation’s self-esteem, updating French King Louis XIV’s apocryphal line, l’État, c’est moi (“I am the State”). But they do differ in noteworthy ways. Per Ye Xue’s research, Trump demands conspicuous displays of deference to him as an individual, while Xi is more concerned with displays of “face” – something he has fused with gestures toward China as a whole. In that way, Xi is a quintessentially Chinese statesman, in being tactful, understated, and formal.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney reflected after a January 2026 meeting with Xi how the general secretary had said something to him to the effect of “don’t lecture me in public.” Xi wasn’t averse to hearing complaints, Carney implied, but to be seen being criticized was an unacceptable loss of face.

The U.S. president, meanwhile, has a grammar that is distinctly American. The historian Walter Russell Mead identified Trump as following in the line of President Andrew Jackson’s heirs: populist, informal, and quick to respond to insults. Trump must win visibly while Xi must not lose face. They are reflective of their different cultural traditions but are variations on the same substance. And they suffer from the same paradox of outward strength and inward fragility.

Despite the cultural variations, megalothymia is a perennial human temptation, which is why institutional safeguards are needed to prevent the emergence of strongmen. Liberal democracies have flourished through centuries by erecting exactly those guardrails. “Ambition must be made to counteract ambition,” wrote James Madison in “The Federalist Papers.” The particulars vary, but the strongman style has clear commonalities. As the columnist Gideon Rachman outlined in “The Age of the Strongman,” it is defined by four overlapping traits: a cult of personality, contempt for the rule of law, populism, and a politics of fear and nationalism. The style runs along a continuum, ranging from unchallenged autocrats like Xi and North Korea’s Kim Jong Un through strongmen in hybrid regimes – think Russia’s Vladimir Putin – to wannabe dictators operating in democratic systems, such as Trump.

The insatiable need for recognition is the engine of these men who pretend to be (and perhaps wish to be) truly larger than life. But every actor needs a stage. And for strongmen, the summit provides that. All summits are manufactured encounters where protocol and positioning become deeply important displays of honor for both states and their statesmen. Particularly in China, a summit is as closely choreographed as a Broadway play or Peking opera. That’s why in May Trump’s effusive rhetoric – and Xi’s comparatively aloof demeanor – was so significant. The U.S. president described his counterpart as his “good friend” and “a man I admire greatly.” He even waxed poetic about receiving “the most beautiful roses anyone has ever seen.” It was a perfect example of political scientist Todd Hall’s research showing how affective ties – love, affection, attachment, and devotion – shape, constrain and manipulate leaders. China’s officials likely aimed to induce warm feelings from Trump through the summit’s flattery, and they succeeded. Xi’s language didn’t approach Trump’s rhapsodizing. He did, however, oversee the lengthy Chinese readout of the meeting, which consisted of a new four-pillar framework of stability – what the Communist Party calls a tifa – centered on Taiwan. The White House readout, by contrast, was just one paragraph. That’s because, for the CCP, a summit that shows the U.S. president as an equal (or lesser) statesman is a crucial moment in a legitimating narrative of how it is returning China to greatness. That story is bolstered when a powerful foreign leader who is desperate for a sense of superiority feels flattered by the pageantry. What kind of man is most susceptible to this theater, and most addicted to building one? Without direct clinical psychoanalysis, it would be inappropriate to presume any formal diagnosis. But there are psychological constructs that offer an interpretive framing for leaders who spend a lot of time in the public arena. The Dark Triad, fashioned by psychologists Delroy L. Paulhus and Kevin M. Williams, suggests that a combination of Machiavellianism, narcissism and psychopathy forms a unique personality construct. Psychologists have observed that Trump and Xi align well with these traits in some respects.

Long before he ran for the presidency, Trump gave a revealing interview in Playboy magazine in 1990, where he praised China’s leaders for their “strength” in crushing the previous year’s Tiananmen Square protests and conversely called Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev “weak” for his restraint. Similarly, analysts Ursula and Dennis Wilder have noted Xi’s “iron Machiavellian detachment.” Climbing to the apex of the Chinese Communist Party requires calculated ruthlessness. To be sure, this tidy mapping is a metaphor, not a psychological finding. But it pinpoints something very real. These traits really become a lasting problem – a structural issue – once a man fuses himself with a state and a regime stakes its legitimacy on his recognition. That’s because, ironically, the institutionalization of megalothymia is what makes it particularly vulnerable. Eventually, the leaders of all personalist regimes tend to fall prey to the fatal sins of isolating themselves, suppressing bad news, overreaching, and overly centralizing decision-making. The very ego that builds the regime is precisely what hollows it out. The insatiable lust for status that represses critics makes critical feedback impossible. This is the Thymos Trap.

Internationally, it’s equally fragile, because when a regime stakes its legitimacy on delivering ever-more recognition to a lone individual, then foreign humiliation becomes a domestic survival threat. The insistence on recognition is not a personality footnote but essential to national identity, requiring displays of deference. In “The Red Emperor,” Michael Sheridan related an anecdote from 2011: Xi told a visiting U.S. Vice President Joe Biden the lesson he’d drawn from history was that China must never make concessions. But compromises, power-sharing, and diffused power centers are inherent to the nature of the modern state system, which means such perceived humiliations are inevitable.

As political scientist Milan W. Svolik has observed, most deposed dictators fall not to mass uprisings but to regime insiders who scent weakness or failure in their nation’s leader – precisely the type of thing that occurs when an ostensibly indestructible leader faces some sort of defeat abroad. As a keen reader of Josef Stalin, Xi’s response has been a ceaseless struggle against what John Garnaut memorably called the “calcification and putrefaction that inevitably corrodes and degrades every dictatorship.” The perpetual purges that have engulfed China’s military in the past few years illustrate not Xi’s strength but the regime’s brittleness; a succession crisis becomes far more possible and serious when competent rivals are absent. The Thymos Trap is a tendency, not a forecast; a pattern, not a promise. For all that men like Trump, Xi, and Putin follow a script laid down by dictators and would-be dictators before them, each is an actor playing unique parts. Xi’s face-saving culture and lack of electoral cycles enable him to be more patient in service of delayed gains than Trump. Perhaps that explains the type of off-ramps Beijing has taken during trade disputes with Washington.

A trend like the Thymos Trap operates over the long term, and some caveats should be acknowledged. The serious disarray in what used to be called the Western alliance means that autocratic systems in China and Russia look more harmonious and even attractive to some doomsayers than liberal democracies. After the meeting in May between Xi and Trump, the headline on a Hal Brands column lamented that “Xi sets the terms for everyone now.”

The best understandings of the thymotic leaders recognize their recurring, ongoing appeal. The historian Stephen Kotkin, in a Foreign Affairs article aptly titled “The Weakness of the Strongmen,” recognized that such regimes “last far longer than generally anticipated” even as they “remain prone to sudden runs on their political banks.” Another caveat in the Thymos Trap is that not all strongmen perfectly fit the mold. For all his predilections toward amassing power and ego, Trump is operating in a country with a rich democratic tradition. The United States Constitution has so many built-in checks and balances that most presidents have been frustrated by their inability to bend the country to their will. The U.S. has a vibrant civil society and a powerful opposition party. All of that constrains Trump’s Thymotic urges.

He has “autocrat envy,” as Fiona Hill, one of his former National Security Council officials, put it: praising all sorts of dictators and strongmen while insulting democratic leaders for their adherence to liberal democratic norms. But his palpable desire for the powers of autocrats is precisely what indicates that Trump cannot be one of them, much as he might want to be. Xi can be satisfied with modest gestures of face precisely because he actually is in the position that Trump wishes he was, with near-absolute control over the population over which he rules. Conversely, “Trump would love to have the situation that Viktor Orban has, but he doesn’t,” as his former ambassador to Hungary put it – not long before fed-up Hungarians decisively ejected that deeply thymotic and illiberal prime minister from office. When Trump was escorted by Xi through the Temple of Heaven in May 2026, it is fair to assume that the U.S. president didn’t know the history of the structure before his host extolled it. But there was irony for Xi, too. According to Chinese cosmology, the emperor performed the Temple of Heaven rites because the Mandate of Heaven could be withdrawn. Magnificence and precarity are always linked in this tradition. So it is in reality. As Rachman put it, strongman rule is “an inherently flawed and unstable form of government” that “will ultimately collapse.” But he hastened to add, “there may be a lot of turmoil and suffering” before that happens.

The Communist Party leader radiates the confidence and gravitas of a man who appears to have mastered his thymos. But the Thymos Trap ensnares leaders because the fragility it engenders is structural, not peculiar to their individual pathology. Their regimes have the same architectural drawbacks, regardless of their national flavors. The same impulses that propel a one-man cult become the forces that bedevil it. The trap is that strongmen must keep appearing strong – and whether their opiate of choice is honor or face, the performance eventually consumes the substance. The counter-model to the thymos-doomed leader would be Marcus Aurelius, the Roman Emperor who interrogated his own status-hunger by wielding near-absolute power with a brake on it in the form of Stoicism. Xi styles himself as this sort of contemplative, omnipotent philosopher-king, and yet his heavily propagandized “Xi Jinping Thought” is most likely the ghost-written output of a CCP committee. Marcus is the inversion, the vanishingly rare leader who distrusts and even resists his own urges for recognition, challenging his own thymos in a private notebook. Leaders like that are few and far between, a tragic reality that only highlights the ever-present danger of the Thymos Trap.

title: Trump Doesn’t Need to Be a Prop in Xi’s Political Show
description: Whether he means to or not, the U.S. president is feeding China’s active disinformation campaigns – especially on Taiwan.
text:
This September, I came across a post claiming that Hillary Clinton, the former U.S. senator and secretary of state, had urged Taiwan to surrender. With tens of thousands of likes and thousands of shares, the clip was spreading fast through Taiwan’s Chinese-language social media. Something felt off, so I checked. The truth was revealing.

On September 10, the former U.S. secretary of state had appeared on “Morning Joe,” the MS NOW program’s September 11 anniversary special, to discuss U.S. President Donald Trump’s national security strategy. Iran, she said, backed by China and Russia, was deftly draining the United States’ capacity to defend its allies.

Here’s what Clinton actually said (starting about 15 minutes into the interview): “We have to look at our potential dangers, especially what Xi is thinking, that they can’t defend anybody anymore, because they don’t have the capacity to defend. Maybe we can coerce Taiwan into just giving up because there’s not going to be any support.”

She was describing what she believed Xi Jinping might now be calculating – not making a call of her own. By the time it reached Taiwan, her words had been mistranslated and spliced into something else entirely: “Hillary Clinton urges Taiwan to abandon resistance to China.”

I know this playbook well. For years, as a spokesperson for Taiwan’s Cabinet and the Presidential Office, intercepting disinformation like this consumed most of my working hours. It is not a footnote to how Taiwan defends itself; it is the front line. We have learned, often the hard way, that 21st-century warfare runs on two tracks at once: the physical battlefield, where force is threatened or used, and the cognitive one, where information is weaponized to reshape how an adversary thinks, what it values, and what it believes to be true. Ideally for the attacker, cognitive warfare undermines the target from within before a kinetic attack is even contemplated.

In May, U.S. President Donald Trump suggested publicly that arms sales to Taiwan could be treated as a bargaining chip in negotiations with Beijing. Whatever his intent, the remark landed squarely inside a narrative Beijing has spent years constructing: that Taiwan is China’s internal affair, and that outside powers – namely, the United States – have no legitimate role to play. Since then, Trump’s words have been recycled as raw material for Chinese cognitive warfare, feeding a relentless undertow of narratives that “America will abandon Taiwan,” “American troops are pulling out,” and “resistance is futile.”

As this happened, the U.S. government remained silent. The State Department’s Chinese-language spokesperson, asked directly about the arms package, declined to comment and referred reporters to the Department of Defense. White House officials, pressed by reporters, would only say that Trump would decide on the arms sale “soon.”

Beijing has spent years trying to push the United States out of the Indo-Pacific, and especially the Taiwan Strait. China has now effectively shifted the burden of keeping the peace onto Washington’s shoulders. What alarms me is that the Trump administration appears willing to accept that framing, treating Taiwan’s defense as something to be traded away. I believe this is a serious miscalculation.

Some will say Trump’s remark was just tactical posturing, not a genuine concession, and they may be right. But intent matters less than how Beijing hears it: ambiguity is interpreted as weakness. China’s playbook over the past decade shows that such statements are seized upon, amplified, and repeated until they harden into a settled narrative. Whether he meant it or not, Trump’s comment on arms sales compresses Taiwan’s room for defense while enlarging the stage for Beijing’s cognitive warfare, adding pressure across the Western Pacific.

China’s cognitive warfare tied to Trump-Xi summits is a well-established fact. During Trump and Xi’s meeting in Beijing this past May, Taiwan’s National Security Bureau traced roughly 100 suspicious accounts spreading more than 9,000 coordinated messages across social media platforms, most of them dressed up as pleas for peace. “Taiwan is part of China,” one read. “Taiwan is the real provocateur,” read another. Timed to launch in lockstep with Beijing’s own messaging, they were built to do two things at once: sow doubt about the United States’ commitment, and paint Taiwan as the aggressor.

In September, as the next Trump-Xi summit approached, the same pattern surfaced again, almost move for move. Xi is using the meeting to restage Beijing’s long-running “peace” narrative for three audiences at once: at home, to shore up his own standing; globally, to sell the line that Taiwan is part of China; and inside Taiwan itself, as a direct cognitive assault. Trump’s hesitation on arms sales, whether he intends it or not, has bolstered those propaganda campaigns..

To Beijing, the United States has never been a friend, only an adversary to be defeated. Watching the once mighty Soviet Union collapse in 1991 badly rattled the Communist Party. Party leaders are convinced that Moscow did not simply fail economically or politically; it was worn down by a deliberate U.S. ideological campaign that hollowed out Soviet identity until there was nothing left to hold the union together.

Whether or not that account is correct, it is what Chinese strategists believe. That is why Beijing has spent the decades since the Cold War studying U.S. information warfare and folding cognitive operations into its own military doctrine as a weapon to be used at home to secure the party’s grip, and abroad to advance its interests.

Xi is contending with mounting challenges to his authority at home. He needed a show that put him on equal footing with the president of the United States to rally support domestically and help secure his continued leadership at the Communist Party’s 21st National Congress in 2027. Trump just handed him exactly that.

Chinese state media have spent this week hailing the summit as “the first head-of-state reception of its kind in 60 years,” a “milestone” that cast Xi as the anchor of stability in China-U.S. relations. A CCTV program portrayed him as a great power leader steering the relationship “onto the right course.”

Quietly, Beijing has also dispatched scholars and researchers to place op-eds in major American outlets, repeating to American policy circles a new narrative of “constructive strategic stability.” This messaging also subtly recasts Taiwan not as a democracy under threat, but as the problem that could drag China and the United States into war.

All this is happening at a pivotal moment for Taiwan’s own domestic politics. As Taiwan heads into local elections, Beijing and its local collaborators have intensified efforts to undermine confidence in Taiwan’s government, targeting both its domestic governance and its relationship with Washington. The goal is to manufacture a specific kind of anxiety: that Taipei cannot protect its own people, and that Washington will not help. China’s goal is not simply to sway one election. It is to paralyze Taiwan’s democratic system and lower the future cost of trying to invade the country.

Trump does not have to play the prop in Xi’s political show. He could be the lead in his own narrative. That would mean delivering the arms already promised to Taiwan without further delay and resisting the temptation to treat Taiwan’s defense as a bargaining chip in any deal with Beijing. It would mean recognizing that every ambiguous remark about Taiwan’s status is heard in Taipei or Beijing, where it translates as an opening that China will exploit.

Maintaining the balance of power in the Indo-Pacific is not a favor to Taiwan. It is the thing standing between a fragile peace and a war that would have unimaginable consequences, not only for the Taiwanese people.

title: Trump-Xi Meet Again: A Summit Without Substance?
user_author_name: Ankit Panda; Catherine Putz; Shannon Tiezzi
description: The visit's outcomes are thin: a small extension of the trade truce and two pandas.
text:
In the latest episode of the Asia Geopolitics podcast, hosts Katie Putz and Ankit Panda are joined by Shannon Tiezzi, The Diplomat’s editor-in-chief, to discuss the outcomes – as we know them so far – from the latest Trump-Xi meeting, this time in Washington, DC. Xi’s state visit was heavy on vibes, as Tiezzi wrote in the aftermath, but light on substance. All the same, the meeting has implications for trade, tech, Taiwan, and more.
