title: Trump-Xi Summit: Heavy of Vibes, Light on Substance
description: Good feelings were on display, but there was no real movement on the many areas of friction.
text:
When Chinese President Xi Jinping held a summit with U.S. President Donald Trump on September 24, Trump made sure Xi knew how he felt. The U.S. leader expressed no fewer than three times in the first minute of their joint remarks that it was his “honor” – or even “great honor” – to host Xi.

The “honor,” apparently was all Trump’s. Xi made no similar expression of feeling “honored” to be hosted by the U.S. president, simply saying he was “glad” to be in Washington.

That set the tone for a meeting that was long on symbolism but short on substance. Trump was eager to impress; Xi was all business.

Trump was reportedly keen to match the lavish hosting he received during his visit to Beijing in May. As Xi pointed out at the state dinner in Washington, it’s “unprecedented” for the Chinese and American presidents to exchange state visits in such a short period of time.

“Today, President Trump and I had sincere and in-depth exchanges and reached common understanding on many issues,” Xi said. “This has added new substance to the constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability, and provided new strategic guidance for China-U.S. relations.”

“The constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability” is Beijing’s new mantra for the relationship – and the first that China has successfully gotten Washington to buy into. The basic gist is that China and the United States will continue to compete – something Beijing has finally admitted is happening, after years of studiously denying any rivalry – but keep their competition “within bounds.”

Other than agreeing, in principle, not to let their competition spill into conflict, though, it wasn’t immediately clear what “common understandings” were reached at the summit. No major breakthroughs were expected, and that turned out to be accurate.

The biggest deliverable was an agreement – actually reached before the summit, during China-U.S. economic talks on September 20 – to extend their trade truce through January 10. The original deal, reached at the first Trump-Xi summit in Busan, South Korea in October 2025, saw the U.S. lower tariffs on Chinese goods, while Chinese agreed to pause enforcement of export controls on certain critical minerals. The deal was only good for a year initially, and was set to expire in November.

Many experts had predicted an extension was in the offing – if that hadn’t been the case, it was suggested that there wouldn’t have been much reason for Trump and Xi to meet at all. But the short length of the extension – just two extra months – was a bit of a surprise. Bessent mentioned that China needed to make good on its promises, suggesting that the deal could be extended again if Washington is satisfied with what it sees. Or it could be eventually scrapped.

China, meanwhile, hasn’t confirmed even that limited extension. The official readout from the Chinese Foreign Ministry said a “new joint arrangement” had been reached in economic and trade discussions, but did not elaborate on what that deal was.

To recap: the biggest practical impact of the Trump-Xi summit was a possible agreement to slightly extend a pause – not a cancellation – on the worst of the trade war. Oh, and two more pandas for the Atlanta Zoo. That about sums up the fruits of the fragile truce currently in place between China and the United States.

If the outcome on trade was a mixed bag, other areas were even murkier. There was much focus on artificial intelligence (AI) prior to the summit, especially as U.S. AI companies themselves have begun raising safety concerns. There had been suggestions that the U.S. and China could unveil an “AI safety mechanism” that would see both sides notify the other of concerning incidents.

Trump, however, has consistently rejected any calls for additional oversight of AI – precisely because he wants the United States to go full speed ahead in the race against China. In a Truth Social post, prior to the summit, Trump stated that AI (which he has started referring to as “super intelligence”) “will be a big topic of discussion, but I want to leave it exactly where it is. That is China’s position also.”

Xi, however, was more cautious on AI, referencing the need to “jointly prevented the misuse and abuse of AI,” and emphasizing that “AI must be kept under human control.” But, like Trump, his primary concern was the AI race and preventing the U.S. from “guarding against” China’s AI development through export controls and other restrictions. As James Wang noted in a recent analysis for The Diplomat, Beijing is well aware of Washington’s tendency to frame restrictions on Chinese technology as safety measures.

As expected, Xi also brought up Taiwan. He explicitly asked “the U.S. side” to “adhere to the correct position of opposing ‘Taiwan independence.’” Much reporting ahead of the summit held that Xi was hoping to get Trump to explicitly say that the U.S. “opposes Taiwan independence.” The usual phrasing is that the U.S. “does not support Taiwan independence.” For China, an outright expression of opposition would be a key win – especially because Beijing purposefully conflates Taiwan’s ruling party and president with “Taiwan independence forces.”

Beijing is also hoping to extend the current “pause” on U.S. arms sales to Taiwan to a de facto moratorium – something it’s tried to do in the past, but without success. Whenever a U.S. administration signals openness to scaling back arms sales to please China, Beijing ups the pressure.

Rupert Hammond-Chambers, president of the U.S.-Taiwan Business Council, called the current period the “fourth Taiwan arms sale freeze,” following “two under former President George W. Bush from 2005-2007 and 2007-2008, and one under former President Barack Obama from 2011-2015.” In all these cases, Hammond-Chambers argued, the “freeze” did nothing more than embolden Beijing.

“The Trump Administration has let the fox in the henhouse. Telegraphing sensitivity to the Chinese position on Taiwan this past spring, Trump has empowered China to affect his decisions [on arms sales],” Hammond-Chambers wrote in a media release.

There’s been no movement on the arms sale, which has been on hold since before the May summit.

As with the Trump-Xi summit in May, this time there was another brief reference to an exchange of views “on major international and regional issues including the situation in the Middle East, the Ukraine crisis and the Korean Peninsula.” There was, however, no suggestion of any agreement or alignment on those issues – unlike after the May summit, when Trump got Xi to say that China opposes Iran’s development of nuclear weapons and supports “the free flow of energy” through the Strait of Hormuz.

If the actual substance showed little sign of convergence, you’d never know it from the optics. Trump lauded his “truly great friendship” with Xi and showed special deference to the Chinese president, including personally meeting him on the tarmac upon Xi’s arrival in the United States. Trump and First Lady Melania Trump also arranged an opulent welcome ceremony, featuring musical performances and drills by 479 military personnel and ending with a flyover by a B-2 stealth bomber and four F-22 fighter jets.

After the summit proper came the state dinner attended by a who’s who list of top American businesspeople: OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, Apple’s Tim Cook, Amazon’s Jeff Bezos, Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, Google’s Sundar Pichai, and Elon Musk of Tesla, X, and SpaceX.

Notably, though, Xi did not bring his own entourage of business leaders – a marked contrast with Trump’s visit to Beijing, when he included top CEOs in his delegation. Speaking to the New York Times, Emily Kilcrease of the Center for a New American Security called the absence of Chinese business leaders “a rather depressing marks of how bad the relationship has gotten.”

Overall, the summit left the impression of a stable, positive relationship, but there was little to back up that sentiment. Trump claimed that he and Xi had “made tremendous strides on the issues facing our two countries” – including the “unbelievably successful” Board of Trade, which hasn’t actually even launched yet – but as always, there were no specifics.

Xi’s positive comments, meanwhile, were mostly forward-looking. “[T]hrough candid, in-depth, and continued dialogue, our two countries can understand each other better, seek common ground while shelving differences, and build up mutual trust,” he said – an aspiration, not an accomplishment.

Xi also emphasize the parallels between the “great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation” and Trump’s “make America great again” slogan, which he argued can “be mutually reinforcing.” Xi continued: “Our competition should be a healthy one and should be kept within bounds. It should be a race of catching up with one another, not a wrestle in which one either wins or loses.”

It was a somewhat odd way of trying to cast competition as “win-win.” I don’t know what races Xi has been watching, but generally those have a winner as well – and multiple losers.

Given the shallow nature of the current era of good feelings in China-U.S. relations, it’s telling that the trade truce was extended only until January 10 – just long enough to keep relations steady through the APEC summit (to be held in Shenzhen, China from November 18-19) and the G20 summit (Miami, the United States, December 14-15). Assuming Trump and Xi attend both events, that could set up two additional summits, for a total of four in 2026 alone.

After that, all bets are off.
tag: Trump-Xi summit; Trump-Xi summit AI; Trump-Xi summit Taiwan

title: Turkish, Kazakh, and Malaysian Companies Hit With New US Sanctions Over Iran
description: In addition to sanctioning 27 Iranian airlines, the U.S. designated Turkish, Kazakh, and Malaysian companies for serving as general sales agents for long-sanctioned Iranian airline Mahan Air.
text:
On September 8, the U.S. Treasury Department announced new sanctions aimed at grounding Iranian airlines, as part of the Trump administration’s “Operation Economic Outcast.” The sanctions hit 36 entities, including cargo service providers and general sales agents based in Turkiye, Kazakhstan, and Malaysia.

The Trump administration’s war against Iran has stretched into its seventh month. Although the U.S. government claims to be in control of the vital Strait of Hormuz, traffic remains low. Reuters reported that six ​commodity vessels passed through the strait on September 8, “down from ‌nine a day earlier and below the 10-day average of about 12.” In 2025, before the U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran, more than 100 commodity vessels passed through the strait each day on average.

In late August the Treasury Department announced an “economic D-Day.” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent explained: “In the Second World War, D-Day marked the historic beginning of a campaign with our allies to target and drive the enemy from its positions, including those in third countries. Today, in that same spirit, we are launching an economic onslaught against Iran’s financial connections around the globe. Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone.”

The Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) on September 8 designated 27 Iranian commercial airlines “for operating in the aviation sector of the Iranian economy.”

In addition, OFAC took aim at a number of companies tied to Mahan Air, a privately owned Iranian airline. It was first sanctioned back in 2011 for providing “financial, material, and technological support to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps-Qods Force (IRGC-QF).” The Treasury Department at the time alleged that Mahan Air secretly ferried IRGC operatives, weapons, and funds.

In 2020, OFAC designated two UAE-based companies, Parthia Cargo and Delta Parts Supply FZC, “for their material support of Iranian airline Mahan Air.” At the time, the Treasury Department outlined how the sanctioned companies helped Mahan Air “sustain its fleet of Western-manufactured aircraft.” The Treasury Department alleged that Mahan Air transported “terrorists and lethal cargo to Syria” and also “ Iranian technicians and technical equipment to Venezuela…”

In its latest round of sanctions, the Treasury Department designated several UAE-based companies it claims were involved in the transfer of three B-777 aircraft to Mahan Air.

The sanctions also designated a pair of Turkiye-based companies – S Sistem Lojistik Hizmetler Anonim Sirketi and Mes Cargo Transportation Tourism and Foreign Trade Limited Company – for coordinating shipments and serving as a general sales agent for Mahan Air. Similarly, Malaysia-based Icargo SDN BHD and Kazakhstan-based Tour Invest LLC were designated for acting as general sales agents for Mahan Air.

title: Underwater Autonomy in the China-US Naval Race
description: Insights from Verineia Codrean.
text:
The Diplomat author Mercy Kuo regularly engages subject-matter experts, policy practitioners, and strategic thinkers across the globe for their diverse insights into U.S. Asia policy. This conversation with Verineia Codrean – chief strategy and partnerships officer at EUROATLAS, the Bremen-based company building the world’s longest-endurance autonomous underwater vehicle (AUV), GREYSHARK – is the 526th in “The Trans-Pacific View Insight Series.”

Explain why the China-U.S. naval race may increasingly depend on who controls the underwater operating landscape.

I would use the word “understands” rather than “controls.” No country can fully control such a vast and difficult environment. But the side that can map it, monitor activity persistently, communicate underwater, and turn sensor data into decisions faster will gain a significant operational advantage. The underwater landscape affects submarine movement, anti-submarine warfare, mine warfare, and the security of critical infrastructure, so situational awareness below the surface is becoming central to maritime power.

How might China’s expanding underwater reach undermine U.S. maritime dominance?

Greater underwater reach can complicate U.S. and allied operations by making submarines, ports, sea lanes, and critical infrastructure harder to protect. Persistent sensing and autonomous systems could extend surveillance over much larger areas and increase uncertainty for an opponent. But reach alone does not equal dominance: effectiveness depends on sensor quality, communications, data fusion, logistics, and the ability to operate reliably in complex environments.

In what ways is Taiwan a preview of deniable, below-threshold disruption in the China-U.S. naval race?

Taiwan illustrates the difficulty of distinguishing accidents, commercial activity and deliberate coercion at sea. Cable damage, vessels operating under flags of convenience, ambiguous ownership, and activity near sensitive infrastructure can create disruption without producing immediate, conclusive attribution. That ambiguity is strategically useful because it delays both political and operational responses. However, individual incidents should not be presented as deliberate state action unless the evidence supports that conclusion.

Analyze why underwater autonomy is becoming crucial for detecting, monitoring, and attributing threats below the surface.

The central problem underwater is persistence. Ships and crewed aircraft can only monitor limited areas for limited periods, while fixed sensors cannot cover every route or depth. Autonomous systems can extend presence, revisit anomalies, and collect data over time. That helps distinguish a one-off event from a pattern of behavior and can strengthen attribution. But autonomy does not solve attribution by itself: evidence still has to be combined with vessel tracking, acoustic data, intelligence and legal assessment.

Assess the top three trends in underwater intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance and their implications for risk management in maritime chokepoints, such as the Taiwan Strait, Strait of Malacca, and Strait of Hormuz, among others.

Persistence: navies are moving from occasional patrols toward continuous coverage using autonomous vehicles and distributed sensors. For chokepoints, that improves early warning but also increases the number of contacts and false alarms that operators must manage.

Sensor fusion: Underwater acoustic data is increasingly combined with satellite imagery, vessel tracking, airborne surveillance, and intelligence sources. This can improve attribution, but poor-quality or incomplete data can also produce false confidence.

Faster sensor-to-decision cycles through onboard processing and AI. Systems will increasingly identify anomalies and prioritize what humans need to examine. That can shorten response times, but governments must establish clear thresholds for escalation because rapid detection is not the same as reliable attribution.

One important geographic distinction I want to highlight is that the risk is not identical across all chokepoints. The Taiwan Strait is primarily shaped by military and grey-zone competition; Malacca combines strategic rivalry with extreme commercial density; Hormuz combines state confrontation, energy security, and asymmetric threats. The technology may be similar, but the rules for interpreting and responding to an underwater contact must differ.

Underwater advantage will not belong simply to the country with the most platforms. It will belong to the side that can maintain persistent awareness, interpret ambiguous activity, and turn reliable data into proportionate decisions fastest.

title: US Drugmakers Are Dependent on Chinese Supply Chains
description: Analysts warn a disruption in Chinese sources of common antibiotics or blood thinners could leave American patients with no reliable alternative.
text:
China controls the upstream production chemistry for many of the most widely used generic drugs in the United States, leaving few backup suppliers if that access were disrupted, according to a recent report by former U.S. government officials. The vulnerability is drawing fresh attention as Chinese leader Xi Jinping is expected to travel to Washington, D.C. for a state visit on September 24, the first trip by a Chinese leader to the U.S. capital in more than a decade.

American and Chinese officials have spent recent weeks preparing for the visit, and artificial intelligence and trade friction are expected to dominate the agenda. Still, pharmaceutical dependence carries the same kind of coercive potential Beijing has shown in other sectors, and it touches medicines that tens of millions of Americans take every week.

Beijing has used that kind of leverage before. It restricted rare-earth exports to Japan during a 2010 territorial dispute, imposed trade barriers on Australian barley and wine after Canberra called for a COVID-19 origins inquiry, and curtailed trade with Lithuania after Vilnius opened a Taiwanese representative office. In none of those cases did Chinese officials announce the move or explain the reasoning beforehand.

According to the recent report published on September 2 by Scalare Advisors, a consultancy based in Washington, D.C., China supplied more than 70 percent of the antibiotic active ingredients by volume imported into the United States in 2024, and three of the most commonly used outpatient antibiotic drugs – amoxicillin, azithromycin, and ciprofloxacin – all depend on Chinese-made ingredients. A simultaneous disruption in all three would leave doctors with no reliable outpatient antibiotic option that could be obtained at the necessary scale and speed.

One Chinese conglomerate, CSPC Pharmaceutical Group, produces both amoxicillin and azithromycin for the U.S. market, meaning a single company controls the fermentation-to-tablet chain for two of the three dominant outpatient antibiotic drugs. No equivalent domestic or allied producer exists for either drug.

Bristol-Myers Squibb announced the closure of its last U.S. penicillin fermentation plant in 2004 and ended production there the following year, eliminating domestic manufacturing of 6-aminopenicillanic acid, the building block for the penicillin-class drugs used to treat strep throat, ear infections, pneumonia, and Lyme disease. Today, no U.S. plant produces penicillin from scratch. This decision conceded penicillin production to China, which now makes about 90 percent of that ingredient worldwide.

Heparin – one of the most commonly used blood thinners – illustrates the same pattern. Pfizer has one heparin injection product on an active shortage list maintained by the Food and Drug Administration. The two remaining U.S.-based producers of the raw ingredient used to make it – Scientific Protein Laboratories in Wisconsin and Smithfield BioScience in Ohio – are both now owned by Chinese parent companies. The broader supply of crude heparin traces back to China, leaving roughly 550,000 Americans who rely on the anticoagulant for dialysis with no clinical substitute if that supply were interrupted.

Hydrocortisone, a prescription drug essential for treating inflammation, is manufactured by Pfizer in Michigan but still depends on a Chinese supplier – a state-owned enterprise named Tianjin Tianyao Pharmaceuticals – for the drug’s active ingredients, according to the same review of federal drug-safety programs. The FDA detected hydrogen cyanide contamination in active ingredient shipments from Tianjin Tianyao Pharmaceuticals in December 2015, following a chemical warehouse explosion in August of that same year. If the FDA had not caught the tainted ingredients, it would have triggered a public health crisis in the United States.

This has happened before. Back in 2008, contaminated heparin traced to a supplier in China killed at least 149 Americans. At the time, Chinese officials denied that the contamination originated there and refused U.S. federal investigators access to conduct a criminal inquiry.

Industrial policy in Beijing adds a different type of risk. The 15th Five-Year Plan, issued in March, named biomanufacturing as one of the sectors targeted for “decisive breakthroughs.” An industry analysis published in May found that the number of product categories in which China held a dominant market position rose from 192 in 2021 to 315 in 2024.

Analysts increasingly view China’s dominance in supply chains as a national security threat, rather than a purely economic one. The concentration of drug manufacturing in China means that decisions made in Beijing shape whether American hospitals can fill a prescription.

Experts also point to the drug manufacturers’ lack of transparency about their supply chain exposures to potentially hostile markets like China. Currently, there is little U.S. federal regulation that requires these companies to publicly disclose the origins of active pharmaceutical ingredients or key starting materials of their products. Experts agree that both relevant agencies and the pharmaceutical industry should be held more accountable to make this information more transparent, especially as these market exposures increasingly become national security concerns.

Washington has confirmed the September 24 date for Xi’s state visit, and U.S. and Chinese trade officials held a video call in July to prepare for the visit. Neither government has signaled that pharmaceutical supply chains will be part of the formal agenda, yet the medicines Americans use every day are intrinsically linked to the broader China-U.S. relationship, whether or not they are named in a joint statement.

title: US Republicans Weren’t Happy With Trump’s Hosting of Xi
description: A spate of Republican senators took umbrage at Trump's reception of “a brutal, unelected, and oppressive dictator.”
text:
Surrounding Chinese President Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington, D.C. – capped by a summit at the White House with U.S. President Donald Trump – was a spate of commentary from both sides of the political aisle. Clearly, not everyone was convinced of the need for Xi to visit in the first place.

Even Trump loyalists such as Louisiana Senator John Kennedy spoke out against having Xi at the White House. One of the Senate’s most colorfully spoken members, Kennedy made his point of view known in no uncertain terms, speaking on the Will Cain show.

Kennedy opined: “All four of them are the same. It’s like the same hooker in different dresses. They all lie like time share salesmen. You can’t trust ‘em. You can’t turn your back on any of ‘em, even if I thought, I knew they were two days dead.”

Kennedy was referring to the leaders of China, Iran, North Korea, and Russia – Xi Jinping, Masoud Pezeshkian, Kim Jong Un, and Vladimir Putin, respectively.

Kennedy went on to dub the quartet “a colony of reptiles,” giving Xi pride of place as the “chief reptile” and “quarterback.”

Taking a more serious approach from his powerful perch as chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, Mississippi Senator Roger Wicker, also a strong Trump supporter, forcefully stated his opposition to the state visit and summit. From the Senate floor, Wicker said, “Quite frankly, had the White House asked me for advice, I would have suggested the president not invite Xi Jinping to Washington for such a lavish welcome here in the United States of America based on all of the troubling issues we have with President Xi and the Chinese Communist Party.”

The Senate Armed Services Committee carries enormous influence and prestige in Washington and beyond, and Wicker used that platform to call out Trump’s decision to bring Xi to Washington, and roll out the red carpet for him.

Key among the core functions of the committee itself is responsibility for aeronautical and space activities associated with the development of weapons systems, and for the Departments of Defense, Army, Navy, and Air Force. It also oversees military research and development.

With that authority behind him, Wicker said, “I want to take a moment to suggest a list of topics that the president might mention during the summit.”

“This summer,” he continued, “it was all over the press that China gave Iran satellite imagery intelligence, and that intelligence led to the death of American troops. So I would certainly suggest that the president try to get an answer to that.”

Wicker’s list continued. He wanted answers on the plight of the Uyghur people, along with Tibetan Buddhists, Christians, and Falun Gong practitioners. “Why not suggest,” Wicker reflected, “releasing all imprisoned Christians and allowing all people of whatever faith to worship freely?”

Finally, Wicker listed the abuses by China of its neighbors, of Taiwan, of Hong Kong, of African nations, of dissidents, and of Jimmy Lai, the 78-year old former Hong Kong newspaper publisher who ran afoul of security laws pushed through by Beijing and who is now serving a 20-year sentence for sedition and collusion with foreign forces.

Wicker continued, “During every minute of dialogue, our commander in chief should keep in mind that his guest is a brutal, unelected, and oppressive dictator who seeks to dominate his neighbors and whose massive military arsenal is aimed directly at the United States of America.”

Joining the chorus, North Carolina Republican Senator Thom Tillis told CBS News on September 24 – the day of the summit and state dinner – that Trump’s hosting of Xi was “bad timing.”

Calling the meeting a “WTF moment,” Tillis questioned why Xi had received a red-carpet welcome that surpassed those given to traditional U.S. allies.

Axios reported that Tillis was “worried about the trend of spending more time with despots and less time with democratic leaders of nations.”

“It’s not that Xi Jinping is coming here to learn how to become a democratic, capitalist nation,” Tillis said. “Xi Jinping is trying to understand how his opposition will ultimately embrace their worldview.”

Tillis went on to question what prompted the “sea change” he sees in Trump’s posture toward China after years of pledging to take a hard line against Beijing.

The White House downplayed the criticism from the Republican senators, with spokeswoman Anna Kelly pointing out that Trump was “reciprocating” the “hospitality” Xi showed when Trump visited China in May.

It could be argued that it is less hypocritical to honor Xi with a state dinner than not. The reasons are myriad. From 1990 through 2020, the United States invested $284 billion into Xi’s country, not including venture capital. And, according to the Global Times, there are over 84,000 U.S.-invested companies in China.

Notably, the United States has educated over 3 million Chinese students since visas became available in the late 1970s.

And, as strong as the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) is, its belief and behavioral systems have had to radically alter in order to build an economy that serves the people well enough to keep the CCP in power.

The CCP has had to abandon the command economy that is central to communist countries in favor of a fusion economy that blends state-owned enterprises, private domestically owned enterprises, and importantly, foreign-owned enterprises. It is the latter, the foreign-owned enterprises, that have brought about profound changes to the mindset and living standards of much of the Chinese population. By manufacturing in China products never seen before in the country, whether for domestic use or export, or both, China experienced a rapid modernization by exposure to the products themselves, the processes and standards of quality required to manufacture them, and the labor standards and management styles that make those businesses profitable.

Perhaps, then, instead of focusing on a state dinner for a Chinese leader little trusted in the United States, it is more fitting to view that dinner and the pomp and ceremony that surrounded it as a state dinner in honor of the Chinese people. They have had to put up with a lot, and still do. They may not have had a seat at the table in the White House, but they will have viewed with pride the American treatment of a Chinese leader. Diplomatically, and historically, that goes a long way.
tag: Republicans China policy; Trump China policy; Trump-Xi summit; U.S.-China Relations

title: Uzbekistan’s Death Penalty Debate Returns After Child Abuse Case
description: The debate over the death penalty is back in Uzbekistan, this time involving the country’s most senior officials.
text:
For the second time in the span of a year a brutal child abuse case has sparked heated public discussion in Uzbekistan. Reportedly, a five-year-old girl was repeatedly raped in a public kindergarten by a facilities manager who worked at the school in the Uchkurgan district of Namangan. According to the mother of the survivor, the alleged perpetrator is their neighbor and she became suspicious after she saw him smiling at her five-year-old daughter. She gently asked the girl questions only to find out that the facilities manager would buy sweets for the girl, tell her he loved her, and promised to buy more presents and sweets if she didn’t expose him. The mother suspects the man had threatened her daughter.

Last year a similar case, which also occurred in Namangan, where a previously imprisoned convict raped a seven-year-old girl, caused a wave of demands by the public to restore the death penalty for serious crimes such as the sexual assault of minors. Public discussions over the death penalty typically emerge in Uzbekistan after news of an especially brutal crime against children breaks. An earlier wave of loud discussions took place in 2024 after a three-year-old was stabbed 12 times.

What’s new this time is that high-ranking political figures are getting involved.

Saida Mirziyoyeva, the head of the presidential administration and a deputy chair of the Security Council (and also the president’s daughter) chimed in. “In my opinion, the death penalty should be used for such heinous crimes. Unfortunately, the current legislation does not provide for the death penalty,” she wrote on her Telegram channel on September 27.

“We are preparing a proposal to amend the legislation to maximize liability for this type of crime,” she added.

Echoing Mirziyoyeva’s words, Alisher Qodirov, leader of the Milliy Tiklanish (National Revival) Democratic Party and deputy speaker of the Uzbek parliament, called death penalty a “necessity.” Qodirov is famous for making nationalist, sometimes controversial statements.

“The continued existence of those who intentionally kill innocent people, especially child murderers and pedophiles, is a motivation for further crimes of this kind!” Qodirov wrote on his Telegram, reposting Mirziyoyeva’s earlier statement.

This is not the first time Qodirov has voiced his position on the death penalty. Previously, in 2024, after news reports about a three-year-old girl being murdered, Qodirov suggested “cleansing” society. “It’s illogical to use our taxes to support a criminal who’s become an animal, keep him healthy, feed him, and then wait for someone else to die! Society needs to be cleansed of such people!” he wrote.

Both Mirziyoyeva and Qodirov know that Uzbekistan abolished capital punishment in 2008 and acceded to the Second Optional Protocol to the ICCPR aimed at abolition. Uzbekistan has no mechanism to reinstate the death penalty without a much larger legal overhaul, and no such overhaul is presently underway.

In a rather unusual course of developments for Uzbekistan, the discussion over the death penalty divided the country’s political parties. As a new bill to increase liability for violence against children was introduced to the Legislative Chamber on September 29, Qodirov announced a neutral position on the proposed bill and doubled down on his stance regarding the need to resurrect the death penalty. Qodirov referred to Norwegian neo-Nazi and mass murderer Anders Behring Breivik, stating that he had complained “about the lack of facilities for writing a book, and those conditions were subsequently provided for him.”

Qodirov’s interpretation isn’t quite accurate. While Breivik did complain about the “stab-resistant” pen he was made to write with and was reportedly provided with an electronic typewriter, Breivik’s communications continue to be censored by prison authorities and he has not published a book.

Nevertheless, using Breivik as a point of reference, Qodirov questioned the compatibility of Uzbek values and international law.

“Whose footsteps are we following!?” he asked. “We will also be forced to create conditions for our pedophile if he asks, because the international law we follow sees him as a human being, not as a dead person.”

Bobur Bekmurodov, a member of the Legislative Chamber of the Oliy Majlis and leader of the Yuksalish movement, opposed Qodirov’s statements openly. His arguments are clear: the constitution prohibits the death penalty, bringing the death penalty back could put child victims in greater danger, break Uzbekistan’s international obligations and raise the possibility of errors in judicial practices.

“If child rape is punishable by death, there is nothing to stop the perpetrator from destroying the only witness, the child himself,” wrote Bekmurodov.

While the grief over the case is genuine, the debate over the death penalty is a populist, opportunistic response. In a country where no other important questions are debated by high (or low) profile politicians, children and women’s abuse is a risk-free topic. Not only does it attract empathy from millions of citizens, but it also gains praise from international organizations. Siding with an innocent child is always a winning move.

As outrage grows, officials do their best to appease the public. The investigation over the case is now under the prosecutor general’s control. Shakhnoza Mirziyoyeva, another daughter of President Shavkat Mirziyoyev and the first deputy director of the National Agency for Social Protection, reported that her agency is also involved in the case and the survivor’s family will be moved to another city and provided with housing. The agency also suggested changing the girl’s surname to ensure her privacy as she rehabilitates. The Ministry of Preschool and School Education formed a working group to address the situation.

Right now, all attention is being given to maximizing punishment for one perpetrator and not letting another incident happen. What is left out of these debates is the failure of the systems that should have protected this girl. The mother of the survivor told local media that the cameras in the kindergarten did not record anything that day. And more absurdly, she had been told that the perpetrator was responsible for the cameras. The perpetrator’s wife allegedly offered her a bribe to close the case, too.

The staff of the kindergarten who are supposed to protect the children in their care, are hiding behind paperwork instead of showing compassion. The director of the kindergarten said she was on a holiday when the alleged incident occurred and she had already provided explanatory letters to the police. She also added that children are never left unsupervised. The girl’s teacher also swore the girl was never left alone – “Not an hour, not a minute, would [she] be left unattended.”

Local media outlets and the authorities have not disclosed the perpetrator’s name or released a mugshot. Netizens, however, have found his photos and full name and doxed his identity on social media pages.

Yesterday, Shakhnoza Mirziyoyeva noted that her agency, together with other relevant bodies, had been working on a draft law that would introduce life imprisonment for crimes involving child sexual abuse.

“We also propose to strengthen the responsibility of parents for neglecting children and of educators for allowing violence and discrimination, and to provide legal assistance and protection to child victims at every stage of the investigation and trial,” the agency’s Telegram post stated.

From 2022 to 2026 445 cases of rape involving minors under 14 years old were formally registered in Uzbekistan. Not all cases make headlines. Journalist and economist Bakhodir Abdullayev noted that the legislation on lifetime imprisonment for sexual abuse of minors was supposed to be passed by April 2026. But it wasn’t until the current furor, when it became politically expedient to take action, that the legislature actually moved.

The Legislative Chamber of the Oliy Majlis passed the bill on September 29.

title: Warming Himalayas: Nepal’s Climate Justice Test
description: Nepal’s devastating Himalayan floods have exposed the human and economic cost of a warming region, reviving demand for climate justice.
text:
The recent floods in Nepal exposed the growing vulnerability of Himalayan communities and the widening gap between the scale of climate losses and international support. The devastating Himalayan disaster of August 26, 2026, has left Nepal facing enormous reconstruction costs. The critical question for the global community is whether climate finance will be treated as a matter of justice, instead of charity.

The high-altitude glacier collapse in the northern part of Langtang/Lirung Mountain caused a Himalayan tsunami that killed more than 1,451 people as of September 19, 2026, left 5,786 missing, and affected about 1.6 million people in five districts of Nepal, according to the government’s situation report.

The Nepali government has rescued 13,784 people and mobilized security forces for rescue operations. It assessed damage to 41 motorable bridges, 3,702 private houses, roads, and 12 hydropower projects.

The recently released Rapid Damage and Need Assessment (RDNA) estimates total damage and losses at more than $2.66 billion. About $4.72 billion is required for reconstruction and rehabilitation, while $5.7 million is needed for immediate relief and short-term rehabilitation over the next six months.

The flood damaged 7,570 private houses, 48 public buildings, 18 schools, seven health facilities, and 30 cultural heritage sites. About $685 million will be required to rehabilitate the social sector.

But the cost of physical damage does not capture the full social impact. Children, women, and senior citizens have suffered severe psychosocial impact, while marginalized communities have become further marginalized. These “costs” have been undermined or overlooked in the assessment report.

Scientists working with World Weather Attribution (WWA) described the disaster as a “catastrophic rock-ice avalanche that transitioned into a debris flood in the Himalayas along the Nepal-China border.” They said climate change and rising temperatures in the Himalayan region contributed significantly to the disaster. Floods in the Himalayan region have become more frequent and more devastating in recent years.

The government of Nepal has written to the Loss and Damage Fund, seeking reparation for the impacts of climate change and calling on polluters to provide compensation and justice. The Loss and Damage Fund said Nepal should provide sufficient evidence about the causes of the flood. Its board will consider providing up to $20 million in compensation. Compared with the estimated losses, the proposed support is small.

The World Bank has also offered concessional loans to Nepal. Members of the civil society and youth are demanding grants as reparation rather than loans. They have been demanding climate justice, focusing on the causes of glacier melt in the Himalayas, known as the “Third Pole” and a source of water for large numbers of people in the region.

Campaigners argue that the climate crisis is a fundamental human rights issue linked to the right to life and a sustainable environment. They are also calling for climate finance to be treated as justice rather than charity and for a regional framework across the Hindu Kush Himalaya region to share information, establish early-warning systems and develop institutional mechanisms.

Ten young people began a hunger strike on September 18, 2026, at the base camp of Mount Manaslu. They are demanding assessments of future glacial lake outburst flood risks, regular joint monitoring of lakes along the China-Nepal border, and climate compensation and justice for Nepal, which has to bear the costs of climate-related impacts to which it has not contributed.

Nepali Prime Minister Balendra Shah is attending the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York, where he will raise the issue of climate crisis impacting Nepal. It is an opportunity for Nepal to present the context and causes of the recent disaster internationally. Foreign Minister Sisir Khanal has already left for the UNGA and is due to attend side events in New York. He is also expected to appeal for international support to overcome the crisis.

Civil society and the public have raised concerns about delays in rescuing people trapped in a hydropower tunnel, saying the government did not allow international experts to assist during the early phase of the rescue. They have also raised concerns about delays in search operations.

Nepal will need to amplify its demands for climate justice, including through the Loss and Damage Fund, while ensuring accountability and transparency in the use of funds. The federal government’s initial hesitation to collaborate with local governments also created tensions between federal and provincial governments.

The internally displaced are being housed in 27 holding centers in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, and Dhading, where 1,743 people are living. The government has offered $98 (15,000 Nepali rupees) per family member to stay outside the holding centers for four months.

The disaster gives Nepal an opportunity to raise concerns about climate change at the global and regional levels. Communities living in river basins and near glacier lakes remain at high risk. Nepal should seek timely information-sharing from the international community to reduce those risks, while international partners can provide technology for faster warnings.

Existing early-warning technology and knowledge may not be sufficient to predict disasters of this kind. Investment is, therefore, needed not only for recovery but also for research and knowledge exchange. Digital technology and empowered communities could help reduce vulnerabilities.

Nepal also needs people-centered development to cope with such disasters, including the exchange of knowledge on infrastructure capable of withstanding harsh Himalayan conditions. Nepal, China, and India need to minimize human activities that directly or indirectly affect the ecology and environment of the Himalayas.

Community-led initiatives, respect for indigenous knowledge and participation in development could help sustain the region’s ecology and reduce degradation.

Small states such as Nepal need global support to rebuild after large-scale disasters. The Government of Nepal also needs to prioritize community rebuilding in future interventions rather than focusing on the business community.

title: Was Abe Shinzo an Idealist?
description: A new biography of Japan's longest-serving prime minister reevaluates his realist legacy.
text:
In Japan, books written about Abe Shinzo, the country’s longest-serving prime minister, have become an industry unto themselves. However, most of them tend to reflect a partisan bias – perhaps fitting for such a controversial political figure, who once described himself as a “fighting politician.” At worst, his detractors have portrayed him as a would-be dictator, while his devotees have cast him as a messianic figure. More analytical assessments, meanwhile, have earned his foreign policy a strong reputation as pragmatic and realistic.

Yet, until recently, no full-length biography of Abe had been published, partly for the obvious reason that his death came so suddenly. The closest thing to a biographical study was Tobias Harris’ “The Iconoclast,” published in 2020. That has now changed. A more comprehensive biography on Abe by Hattori Ryuji, professor of Chuo University, was just released by Chuo Koron Shinsha.

Hattori’s short but detailed biography of Abe Shinzo could be regarded as a revisionist work in its own right, challenging the conventional wisdom – one that has also gained international currency – that Abe can be strictly characterized as a realist foreign policy thinker. Written by a diplomatic historian, the book focuses extensively on the foreign policy decisions made during Abe’s tenure as prime minister, drawing on newly declassified diplomatic documents that the author was able to access. Hattori’s conclusion is that, while Abe possessed a “remarkable strategic vision,” he was ultimately “an imperfect realist.”

Abe’s visionary thinking was an outlier in a country whose postwar prime ministers – almost all of them from the Liberal Democratic Party – were generally known for their conciliatory approach and skill in building intraparty coalitions. They were politicians more accustomed to working behind the scenes than articulating bold visions in public.

Among Abe’s many foreign policy conceptions, the most famous was the “Free and Open Indo-Pacific,” a strategic vision that not only articulated Japan’s broader interests in the world but also encouraged other governments to adapt to a new century in which the influence and potential of the Indo-Pacific region had become greater than ever before.

One of the clearest examples of the practical implementation of this vision was Abe’s promotion of free trade. His administration played a crucial role in bringing the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP) to fruition after the United States withdrew from the original TPP, while also advancing the Japan-EU Economic Partnership Agreement and the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) negotiations.

However, while Abe’s vision of maintaining a liberal international order fostered a strong affinity with the West, his misconceptions and even biases may have constrained his ability to pursue constructive diplomacy in East Asia. This, in turn, highlights the imperfect side of Abe’s realism. According to Hattori’s account, Abe’s eagerness to reach deals with Russia and China may have led him to surrender valuable leverage – and, perhaps more importantly, some of the legitimacy underpinning Japan’s position on the disputed Senkaku Islands, which China claims as the Diaoyu. In negotiations with Beijing, this resulted in a memorandum that could be interpreted as acknowledging that a territorial dispute existed, even though Japan’s official position has long been that no such dispute exists.

Abe also failed to achieve a breakthrough in his foreign policy toward the Korean Peninsula. He built a reputation as a champion of the Japanese citizens who had been abducted by North Korea. Yet he was ultimately unable to translate his hardline stance into a successful diplomatic strategy, nor was he willing to resort to inducements – the road not taken.

Also, vis-à-vis South Korea, Abe never developed a genuine rapport with any of his counterparts, unlike some of his successors. His determination not to give an inch on historical controversies constrained his ability to compromise, plunging bilateral relations into their worst state since the normalization of diplomatic ties. Nevertheless, when Abe did in fact cede ground – as in the agreement with South Korea that acknowledged Japan’s remorse over the “comfort women” while framing the settlement of the issue as “final and irreversible” – his failure to follow through on the resulting rapprochement allowed the issue to resurface once there was a change in government in Seoul.

The apparent failure of Abe’s East Asian diplomacy is all the more remarkable given the influence of his grandfather, Kishi Nobusuke. Kishi instilled in his grandson a mission to right the wrongs of the U.S. occupation – most notably, by revising the pacifist Constitution – as well as a commitment to a strong alliance with the United States, which Kishi himself helped lay the foundation for by revising the security treaty on more equal terms.

Although Kishi was said to have been influenced by Pan-Asianism and understood the importance of maintaining good relations with Japan’s neighboring countries, the premium he placed on Asian diplomacy was not inherited by his grandson. In fact, Abe seemed emotionally incapable of identifying Japan with the East rather than the West. This sentiment was manifested in a book he co-authored in 1996, when he was still a rising young conservative. The book warned: “Such an excessive attachment to the idea that ‘we are a part of Asia’ can become a dangerous spark that, from a policy perspective, risks triggering fatal mistakes.”

To understand the limits of Abe’s realism, it is necessary to identify the factors that prevented him from fully realizing the realist ideal. These included his historical perceptions, his strong concern with his political legacy, and his sense of duty and personal sentiment. Taken together, these characteristics suggest that Abe may be better understood as an idealist in the broader sense: a political actor who sought to translate deeply held beliefs and principles into political reality, regardless of the distance between his ideals and the circumstances he faced.

Hattori himself does not characterize Abe as an idealist. Nevertheless, his contribution in questioning the realist label so often attached to Abe as a foreign policy strategist represents a meaningful starting point for a more clear-eyed and constructive discussion of a politician who continues to evoke considerable passion and controversy.

More pages will be written about Abe, both domestically and abroad, in the years ahead. And with every page turned, the present will see how much of a mark he left on Japan.

title: What Did Chinese Analysts Think of the Trump-Xi Summit?
description: To some, Trump's hospitality was “historic.” To others, it was an attempt to “lull China into a false sense of security.”
text:
Both in China’s official media and in the world press, the summit between Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump last week – their second so far this year – generated usual, predictable descriptions: “ambiguous,” “highly symbolic,” “historic summit,” and so on. However, a section of China’s strategic affairs community – definitely not the pro-U.S. faction – has taken exception to Trump’s “dramatic,” “personal diplomacy” hospitality in welcoming Xi. Cautioning Chinese Communist Party (CCP) leadership to tread carefully with the untrustworthy, capricious, and unpredictable Trump, a skeptic in China’s “leftist” media even observed, “It’s possible they’re [the U.S.] trying to lull China into a false sense of security.”

U.S. watchers in mainland China are split into two factions: pro-U.S. (qin-Mei) and anti-U.S. (fan-Mei). The qin-Mei faction among the Chinese intelligentsia, as expected, celebrated Trump personally greeting the Chinese leader at the airport, as well as the grand welcoming ceremony and the meticulously arranged state banquet at the White House.

“The U.S. side welcomed the Chinese leader with a level of courtesy rarely seen in recent years,” a qin-Mei-leaning Chinese language media outlet reported as Xi returned home.

Some scholars in China highlighted the “historic” and “diplomatic” significance that Trump served Xi the same wine that former U.S. President Richard Nixon used during his visit to China in 1972. In an interview with a popular digital e-paper published from Shanghai, Professor Wu Xinbo, the director of the Center for American Studies at the city’s Fudan University, noted, “The serving of the same wine Nixon used during his China visit in the early 1970s indicates that the current China-U.S. relationship is at an important and historically significant juncture, and President Xi’s visit is historic and a milestone.”

Further, it was widely reported in China that following a tea reception held at the White House for Xi and his wife Peng Liyuan, Trump remarked: “The United States was very pleased with this visit, and that the visit has been very productive.” Asked why Trump placed such importance on Xi’s visit, Wu said: “Interactions outside of formal talks, whether it’s taking a walk, having tea, or visiting culturally and historically significant sites, can create a relaxed and informal atmosphere for the leaders of both countries.”

Notably, Wu was invited to attend the state banquet welcoming Trump in Beijing earlier in May this year. Hence, it is understandable that he attaches great importance to opportunities leaders create beyond formal meetings.

At another level, some scholars in China, especially economists, see the current friction in China-U.S. relations arising out of “imbalance” in the economies of the world’s two largest powers. Addressing the issue of the need for “balance” and “equilibrium” between China and the United States at a recent economists’ forum on the eve of Xi’s Washington visit, Professor Ju Jiandong of Tsinghua University in Beijing said: “The currently existing extreme pattern of China doing manufacturing and the United States doing finance is inherently unstable, which is the root cause of the competition between China and the United States.” The Tsinghua professor recently published a controversial book, “The Great Power Competition and the Restructuring of World Order,” in which he argued that the “only way for China and the U.S. to avoid a lose-lose situation is to move from hegemonic iterations to competitive coexistence.”

In sharp contrast, scholars belonging to the fan-Mei faction in China have become more suspicious of the United States given Trump’s “rare, dramatic” personal touch in welcoming the Chinese leader. Scholars in this camp pointed out two examples of Trump going out of his way to impress. One, Trump made a great show of personally greeting Xi at the airport, at Joint Base Andrews outside Washington, D.C. The last time a U.S. president personally welcomed a foreign leader in this manner was 11 years ago, when Barack Obama met Pope Francis at the airport in 2015. Earlier, in 1962, John F. Kennedy had similarly welcomed British Prime Minister Harold Macmillan.

The other dramatic event that particularly drew attention from the Chinese skeptics was Trump making some startling remarks at the banquet welcoming the Chinese head of state. Citing reports widely circulated in Chinese media, one commentary noted Trump “shamelessly” declaring that the relationship between the two countries has never been as harmonious as it is now. Reacting adversely to the word “harmonious,” the commentary called it “a remarkable attempt by U.S. President Trump to whitewash the current state of the relationship.”

Three factors explain this skepticism targeting Trump and his theatrics while hosting Xi. First, as mentioned, China’s skeptics are apprehensive of China being lulled into a false sense of security. Characterizing Trump as a leader who is “two-faced and hypocritical,” these scholars assert that Trump cannot be trusted. They want CCP leaders to always be vigilant of “untrustworthy” Trump. As the commentary cited above put it: “Trump acted this way towards Russia, and he did the same toward Iran, North Korea, Cuba, and Venezuela. Regarding China, he has repeatedly attacked over the years, displaying the same ugly nature of a two-faced and hypocritical person.”

Second, some in China suspect Trump’s lavish reception of Xi was a tactic to sow discord between China and Russia. It is argued that Trump has always been outspoken about breaking up the close relationship between China and Russia, seeking to isolate them. These Chinese scholars further argue that before his “dramatic” hospitality toward Xi, Trump was on record in making efforts to cultivate the most “harmonious” Russia-U.S. relationship possible. However, that attempt backfired, resulting in domestic criticism and accusations of collusion with Russia. Now, he’s elevating the China-U.S. relationship to an unprecedented level.

Some in China are even drawing parallels between Trump’s statement praising unprecedented harmony in China-U.S. relations at present with the historic scenario of the United States and China joining forces against the Soviet Union.

“This baseless accusation is not without purpose; its direct effect is to place China-U.S. relations above China-Russia relations, while still maintaining a strong intention to dismantle them,” scholar Zhang Zhikun argued.

Third, some Chinese skeptics are putting forward what appears to be bizarre logic: Trump’s attempt to “whitewash” China-U.S. relations are aimed to stabilize ties so that the United States can act without restraint. Scholars advancing this argument acknowledge that a section of the media and political elite in the United States is highly critical of Trump’s “subservient” approach toward Xi. However, given Trump’s capricious and ambitious nature, it is extremely difficult to fathom the U.S. leader’s true intentions. The fan-Mei faction vehemently argues that “he [Trump] is using appeasement to stabilize [relations with] China, allowing the U.S. to act with greater impunity and wage war around the world.”

To sum up, it is quite clear Trump has succeeded in further deepening the divide between rival qin-Mei and fan-Mei factions among Chinese foreign policy experts, especially the U.S. watchers in China. They interpret the summit – and its implications for China – quite differently.

The two Chinese factions do have one thing in common: they share the viewpoint that changes in Sino-U.S. relations will inevitably lead to corresponding changes in relations among countries around the world. Many Chinese scholars agree that any change in the highly complex China-U.S. relations will not affect Taiwan and Japan, as the two have “secured” their respective interests vis-a-vis the United States. However, some Chinese scholars are of the opinion that changes in China-U.S. relations will lead North Korea to gravitate toward Russia and India toward the United States.

title: What Do Taiwan’s People Think About Its Annual Military Exercises?
description: Taiwan’s Han Kuang exercises are winning public approval, despite the growing impact on civilians. Understanding is another matter.
text:
Taiwan’s annual Han Kuang military exercises were difficult for ordinary citizens to ignore this year. Mobile internet was deliberately slowed for 30 minutes to simulate wartime communications disruptions. Troops barricaded Guangfu Bridge, a key route connecting New Taipei City with the capital, setting up metal barriers and barbed wire as they rehearsed stopping enemy forces from advancing into Taipei. Hospitals also practiced moving medical operations underground as part of exercises designed to keep essential services running during a conflict. These scenes showed how Taiwan’s preparations for a possible war are moving beyond conventional military exercises and increasingly into the spaces of everyday civilian life.

The shift reflects a broader change in Taiwan’s approach to defense. This year’s Han Kuang exercises placed greater emphasis on realistic wartime scenarios while more closely integrating military training with urban resilience exercises. Preparing for a potential conflict is increasingly not only a task for the armed forces, but also a challenge involving civilian infrastructure, local governments, reservists, and ordinary citizens. But as Taiwan brings society more directly into its defense preparations, a basic question becomes more important: What do Taiwanese themselves make of the country’s most important annual military exercise?

To answer this question, the Institute for National Defense and Security Research (INDSR) commissioned a nationwide telephone survey shortly after this year’s exercises. Conducted by National Chengchi University’s Election Study Center from August 20 to 24, the survey interviewed 1,215 adults across Taiwan. Public satisfaction with the Han Kuang exercises reached its highest level in our survey series, yet most respondents said they knew relatively little about what the exercises actually involved. The findings suggest that as Taiwan expands whole-of-society defense, public approval and public understanding should not be treated as the same thing.

Public satisfaction with the Han Kuang exercises reached 60 percent this year, the highest level in our survey series. As shown in the chart below, satisfaction had generally hovered around 50 percent in previous surveys. It stood at 51.9 percent in 2021 and 53.6 percent in 2022, before falling to 45.5 percent in 2023. Satisfaction recovered to 51.3 percent in 2025 (there was no comparable survey in 2024) and rose further this year. The longer-term pattern has therefore fluctuated rather than followed a steady upward trend, but the 2026 result is noticeably higher than the levels recorded in previous surveys.

The figure also shows another shift. The share of respondents who did not offer a clear evaluation of the exercises – whether they chose now to answer or were unaware of the exercises at all – fell from 36.7 percent in 2021 to 25.3 percent in 2026, the lowest level in our survey series, although the decline was not consistent across years. Among those who reached the satisfaction question this year, about three-quarters expressed either a positive or negative view of the exercises.

These comparisons require some caution because the screening questions and skip patterns were not identical across survey waves. More importantly, being able to evaluate the exercises does not necessarily mean understanding them better. When we asked respondents directly how well they understood the Han Kuang exercises, the results told a different story.

Only 2.3 percent of respondents said they understood them very well and 22.6 percent somewhat well. By comparison, 46.1 percent said they did not understand the exercises very well, while another 26.4 percent said they did not understand them at all. In other words, nearly three-quarters of respondents described their understanding of the exercises as limited.

These findings do not necessarily contradict the relatively high level of satisfaction with this year’s exercises. People can form an overall impression of Han Kuang through news coverage, social media, or the activities they encounter in daily life without knowing in detail what individual drills are designed to test. Satisfaction captures how people evaluate the exercises, but it tells us less about how well they understand their purpose.

As Taiwan places greater emphasis on whole-of-society defense, the distance between approval and understanding becomes harder to ignore. Citizens are no longer simply an audience observing how well the military performs. They are increasingly expected to understand how society would function under crisis conditions and how civilian preparedness connects to national defense. That makes public understanding more consequential than it was when military exercises were viewed mainly as the work of the armed forces.

Satisfaction, understanding, and preparedness are therefore related but distinct. A citizen can support the Han Kuang exercises without knowing what they are intended to test or how they fit into Taiwan’s broader defense planning. Such support is still valuable. It gives the exercises public legitimacy and suggests that many people see value in continued preparation. But support alone does not tell us whether citizens are better prepared to interpret official instructions, understand disruptions during a crisis, or recognize their own responsibilities.

Of course, not every citizen needs detailed knowledge of military operations. What is needed is a more basic level of understanding. People should know what the exercises are trying to prepare for, why civilian participation is necessary, and how individual drills connect to the wider goal of national resilience. Public communication should therefore do more than make Han Kuang visible. It should help citizens make sense of what they are seeing.

For Taiwan, the next challenge is not simply getting citizens to watch Han Kuang, but helping them understand what they are watching and why it matters.

title: What Has AUKUS Pillar II Achieved Over 5 Years?
description: Pillar II’s progress has proven difficult to judge – not due to a lack of activity, but because there’s no agreed metric for what success should look like.
text:
It’s been five years since the leaders of Australia, the United Kingdom, and the United States announced AUKUS, a security partnership designed to deepen technology and capability-sharing among the three countries.

While its much-publicized Pillar I component – centered on Australia’s acquisition of conventionally-armed, nuclear-powered submarines – is reported to be “on track,” the lesser-known Pillar II component has come under mounting criticism for “failing” to deliver fast enough.

As a framework for the joint development and fielding of advanced military capabilities, Pillar II was initially pegged by some analysts to be the “more consequential” arm of the AUKUS partnership – not only for delivering on a shorter timeline than Pillar I, but also for leveraging the latest technologies known to be reshaping how modern conflicts are fought.

In the years that have passed since its announcement, Pillar II’s progress has proven difficult to judge – not due to a lack of activity, but because there’s no agreed metric for what success should look like. For some, its incrementalism is indicative of its failure, while to others, the breadth of its objectives warrants a slow and steady approach.

Five years on, it’s time to take stock of Pillar II’s objectives and efforts to better understand this evolving debate, and consider what lies ahead.

What Is Pillar II Trying To Do?

Pillar II, known as Advanced Capabilities, involves the collaborative development, fielding and production of advanced military capabilities in six key areas: artificial intelligence (AI) and autonomy, cyber, electronic warfare, hypersonics and counter-hypersonics, quantum, and undersea warfare.

Developments in each of these technology areas are reshaping how conflicts are fought. The wars in Ukraine and Iran reveal how AI, unmanned systems, hypersonics, cyber, and electronic warfare have been leveraged in new ways by actors on all sides of these conflicts.

It’s also no coincidence that these are technology areas where China is reported to be outperforming the United States, the United Kingdom, and Australia in research and innovation. China is leading in 69 of 74 technologies deemed critical to strategic competition by the Australian Strategic Policy Institute. AUKUS Pillar II is intended to close this gap by combining each country’s strengths in innovation, technology, and industry to create advanced military capabilities at a faster speed than any one of them could achieve individually.

More specifically, the three AUKUS partners seek to achieve greater interoperability and industrial integration between participating countries. Part of this is achieved through co-developing new capabilities that are designed, from the outset, to integrate into each countries’ existing military platforms and processes. Similarly, significant changes to the policy landscape – or “enabling environment” – in each country intend to make it easier for them to share information and technology with each other.

It’s due to these reasons that some analysts believe Pillar II will generate “greater long-term value” than the Pillar I nuclear-powered submarines – not just for the advanced capabilities Pillar II would produce, but because of its long-term role in reducing barriers to collaboration between the three countries.

Where Has There Been Progress?

Over the last five years, cooperation has taken place across the different workstreams. The most notable activities have primarily focused on the collaborative research, development, and testing of capabilities, and the achievement of regulatory alignment between AUKUS countries. One early example of this collaboration is a jointly developed AI algorithm for reconnaissance aircraft that was unveiled in December 2023 and used operationally in August 2025.

The table below summarizes the publicly reported Pillar II activities to date.

Since the announcement of Pillar II wasn’t accompanied by a signature project, like the nuclear-powered submarines for Pillar I, judging the extent to which these activities count as progress depends on how success is measured.

AUKUS countries have established defense trade exemptions for around 80 percent of U.S. defense exports to Australia and the U.K. that were previously subject to the International Traffic in Arms Regulations (ITAR). Experts agree that the regulatory reforms are necessary to facilitate technology and industrial collaboration between the three countries.

That said, some argue that too much emphasis has been placed on these reforms as evidence that things are on track – especially since they haven’t completely resolved the issues created by tough U.S. defense export controls. If Pillar II’s success is measured against the delivery of an operational capability, the picture looks different. The testing and demonstration of new technologies, while evidence of successful collaboration, have not fulfilled Pillar II’s intention to deliver capability.

Others contend that Pillar II should be seen as more of a crawl-walk-run process. In this view, regulatory alignment and capability testing are legitimate outputs in their own right, since they have established the groundwork needed before genuine trilateral collaboration can happen.

These contrasting metrics speak to a broader PR problem that has long plagued Pillar II. Since it was initially framed as a way of delivering a tangible product faster than Pillar I, the expectation of an AUKUS-branded output has loomed over Pillar II.

Hence the most recent milestone: the announcement of the first Pillar II signature project in May 2026, which would see AUKUS countries jointly produce shared payloads and systems for uncrewed underwater vehicles (UUVs) by 2027. This comes after years of analysts calling for a signature project to demonstrate proof of concept and for Pillar II’s priorities to be narrowed.

On paper, the logic is evident– the delivery of a UUV capability aligns with Pillar I’s focus on undersea warfare and complements surface vessel maritime operations. It also fulfils a stop-gap maritime capability for each country. Australia is expecting its first Virginia-class submarine from the United States in 2032. The U.S. is working to increase its submarine production from the current rate of 1.2-1.3 boats per year to 2.33 per year. The United Kingdom is focused on the sustainment of its Astute-class fleet, which are all currently in maintenance.

What’s Next for Pillar II?

Moving forward, Pillar II has several enduring structural challenges to overcome if it is to translate its ambitions into tangible capabilities.

First, as of September 2026, roughly 20 percent of intra-AUKUS defense trade was not captured by licensing exemptions – and these sectors are directly relevant to Pillar II capability requirements. This includes technology areas like undersea acoustics, missile technology controlled under the Missile Technology Control Regime (MTCR), and sensitive technical data and source code associated with advanced weapons and fire-control systems. Addressing this will require mitigating U.S. concerns about protecting sensitive technologies, maintaining competition within the U.S. defense industrial base, complying with domestic and international non-proliferation obligations, and preventing the compromise of critical technologies by strategic competitors.

Second, unlike Pillar I, which has clear national funding architectures centered on the acquisition and construction of SSNs, Pillar II spans a much broader set of technologies and workstreams that cut across existing national capability programs. As a result, Pillar II lines of effort have had to pull resources from existing national capability priorities. This does not necessarily require AUKUS members to establish dedicated funding streams to realize Pillar II’s potential. But the three countries must ensure that they can reliably access the resources needed to deliver Pillar II technologies, even as they compete with other national defense priorities across their broader defense industrial ecosystems.

Third, AUKUS policymakers face the question of whether Pillar II should narrow its technological scope to enable more targeted funding, senior-level attention, and industrial capacity. Doing so would involve concentrating resources toward operational requirements, including long-range strike and targeting, multidomain missile defense, command, and control, and enhanced logistical networks.

The U.K. Parliament’s Defense Committee concluded in its April 2026 AUKUS report that the breadth of Pillar II had become an impediment to delivery. This sentiment has also been reflected by the Pentagon’s scaling back in late 2025 of its initial list of 14 critical technologies – expected by the Joe Biden administration to maintain the U.S. military’s future superiority – to six: applied AI, biomanufacturing, contested logistics technologies, quantum and battlefield information dominance, scaled directed energy, and scaled hypersonics. AUKUS leaders are yet to offer clarity as to whether Pillar II is formally defining its future collaboration against operational challenges rather than its original technology categories.
