title: What Kazakhstan’s New Unicameral Parliament Means for Its Foreign Policy
description: Although Kazakhstan’s Senate rarely exercised its influence over the country’s foreign policy, its abolishment has left the country without the diplomatic expertise and sequential vetting that the upper chamber once provided.
text:
In early June, Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev signed enabling laws, putting into effect the new constitution passed via referendum in March 2026. Among the most significant changes was the abolishment of the bicameral parliament and its replacement with a new unicameral body, the Kurultai, whose 145 deputies were subsequently elected through party lists on August 23.

While the domestic consequences of the changes to the legislature have been debated widely, the question of how they will affect Kazakhstan’s foreign policymaking remains underexamined.

With the abolishment of the bicameral parliament – comprising an upper house, the Senate, and a lower house, the Mazhilis – the number of committees under the new legislature was reduced to eight, down from 13 (seven in the former Mazhilis and six in the Senate).

Under Article 61 of the prior constitution, the dual-committee structure provided checks and balances within the legislative branch. The Mazhilis’s Committee on Foreign Affairs, Defense, and Security served as the primary chamber for drafting, amending, and holding preliminary readings for security and international agreements, while the Senate’s Committee on International Relations, Defense, and Security acted as a second layer of technical and diplomatic vetting. Treaties and defense pacts moved sequentially through both chambers and both committees. The Senate could approve, return for revisions, or reject a bill passed by the Mazhilis.

Another structural change lies in how deputies are selected. In the previous bicameral parliament, the president could appoint a certain number of deputies, and often appointed seasoned diplomats such as former ambassadors, ex-ministers, and career officials. The most prominent example is the current president, Tokayev, who was twice appointed as Senate speaker. Under the previous constitution, the Senate speaker was designated to become acting president if a sitting president stepped down or could not perform their duties – that’s what happened in 2019 when Nursultan Nazarbayev resigned. When Nazarbayev resigned, that arrangement delivered the presidency to an experienced diplomat, an outcome read at the time as a signal that Nazarbayev considered foreign policy the greatest challenge of the transition.

Although the previous Senate could reject the Mazhilis’ bills, it rarely rejected one outright. A strong presidency in Kazakhstan mostly sets direction of foreign policy, and the upper and lower chambers were typically aligned with the president’s objectives and policies. There was a case in 2011 when the Senate rejected a Mazhilis bill on the planned deployment of military personnel to Afghanistan. Most of the time, however, the two chambers did not come into conflict, and international agreements and treaties passed smoothly.

Under the new Kurultai, all foreign policy affairs fall to the Committee on International Relations, now chaired by Marat Kozhayev. The committee will be responsible for legislative review and preliminary scrutiny of international treaties, security pacts, and bilateral agreements. Given how much further the presidency has been consolidated under the new constitution, the Kurultai’s foreign policy outlook is likely to align closely with Tokayev’s. And with all deputies now elected through party lists, the Kurultai may lack experience in international law and negotiation that the previous Senate held via presidential appointments, as mentioned above.

Tokayev has framed these constitutional and structural reforms as a modernization, an answer to the turbulence in world politics. The changes are supposed to push the agenda of creating an “effective, transparent and responsive” system. Ambitious as it is, this path poses several risks to foreign policy. First, with no second layer of review, the risk of ratifying rushed or flawed agreements increases.

Second, the new system further consolidates executive power. The president holds the right to dissolve the Kurultai if it repeatedly rejects the presidentially nominated parliamentary chairman, further weakening the legislature. Moreover, according to Article 42 of the new constitution, the president, as the head of state, holds the authority to determine the primary directions of foreign policy, as well as negotiate and sign treaties. A newly created advisory institution, the People’s Council (Halyk Kenesi), will also “possess the right of legislative initiative and will be empowered to introduce bills to parliament,” as well as “the power to prepare legislation for the Kurultai and, on the same basis as parliament, to propose nationwide referendums.” Notably, the People’s Council consists of 126 members drawn from three categories – ethnocultural organizations, local governments (Maslikhats), and civil society – but all approved by the president.

To minimize the risks to Kazakhstan’s foreign policy now that the Senate, its chamber of sober second thought, has been abolished, the country should consider introducing minimum review windows to avoid rushed decisions, empowering the Kurultai’s Committee on International Relations, and ensuring that the newly created People’s Council remains strictly an advisory, consultative forum.

title: What Lies Behind the Rise in Anti-Israel Sentiment in Thailand?
description: Nationalist rabble-rousers have accused Israelis of trying to seize Thai territory, and Israeli tourists of misbehaving or disrespecting the country's culture.
text:
For three years, small-scale pro-Palestine protests, centered around Israel’s human rights abuses in Gaza, have become common in Thailand. A few dozen left-wing activists would turn out to chant slogans more commonly associated with the massive street demonstrations in the West, to little interest from the general public or international media.

But on September 10, something changed.

A few hundred protesters showed up at the Israeli embassy in Bangkok, with another 500 at the Chabad House in Phuket. These protests featured some explicitly anti-Semitic signs, like “Jews out,” and the protest in Phuket forced the cancellation of a small, private gathering for the Jewish New Year, due to security concerns.

“We are monitoring the situation surrounding the Jewish New Year event in the Patong area. These Jews are staying inside their mansions,” one protest organizer was quoted as saying by local media outlet Bangkok Post. The Chabad House did not respond to The Diplomat’s request for comment.

Left-wing activist groups said that these protests don’t represent them. Rather, the pro-Palestine cause has been hijacked by xenophobic far-right groups that also regularly target vulnerable migrant workers from neighboring countries.

The previous left-wing protesters had largely focused on Israel’s well-documented atrocity crimes against Palestinian civilians.

A Hamas-led attack on October 7, 2023 left over 1,000 people dead in Israel, including 39 Thai migrant workers. Israel responded with a massive air and ground assault on the besieged Gaza strip, killing over 70,000 people, including over 20,000 under the age of 18. The International Criminal Court has issued arrest warrants for crimes against humanity for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and then-Defense Minister Yoav Gallant.

“At that time, the Israeli military began carrying out increasingly severe measures that went far beyond what could reasonably be described as mere ‘retaliation,’ as the Israeli government claimed. We saw these actions as part of a deliberate process of colonization,” said Nai, a protester who first became active in the pro-Palestine movement in late 2023, as a 19-year-old university student.

The Boycott, Divest, Sanctions (BDS) Movement in Thailand calls for the Thai government to stop sending Thai migrant workers to Israel, screen Israeli tourists and arrest those suspected of war crimes, end all arms trade and military agreements with Israel, and ultimately sanction Israel and sever diplomatic relations.

“BDS Thailand abides by the same values as the international BDS movement: freedom, justice, and equality. Thus, we oppose the bigoted, anti-Semitic, racist/xenophobic, and nationalist rhetoric that such right-wing opportunists espouse. BDS Thailand is NOT affiliated with and does NOT approve of right-wing demonstrations or their signage,” added the BDS Movement’s Thailand chapter.

The right-wing protesters have focused more on domestic issues, accusing Israel of trying to seize Thai territory, and Israeli tourists of misbehaving or disrespecting Thai people, allegations that have little empirical evidence to support them.

The land seizure allegation is rooted in an extremely common business practice in Thailand. Foreigners are prohibited from owning land, but many skirt this law by buying property through a company started with a Thai frontman – known locally as a “nominee.” This is done both to purchase private residences and launch small businesses, or at times for more large-scale real estate developments.

The government is cracking down on this practice, and some Israeli companies have been targeted. But Israelis are far from unique in this, and are unlikely to rank among the highest offenders.

The Ministry of Commerce released data on land owned by businesses with foreign investors, finding Chinese nationals held by far the most land, at around 35,000 acres, more than double the next nationality – Japanese. The United Kingdom, Singapore, and Hong Kong rounded out the top five, while the ministry said 147 nationalities own shares in companies that own land in Thailand.

(Not all of these companies would be illegal. The legitimacy of a business can be very hard to determine, because the main factor is whether the Thai business partner is a legitimate partner or just a frontman. The government says it is in the midst of a close review of suspicious businesses).

Accusations of Israelis misbehaving or disrespecting locals are harder to quantify. To be sure, there have been some viral incidents on social media, such as a young Israeli woman arrogantly claiming that “my money builds your country.” In another shocking episode, four Israeli men caused property damage and allegedly threatened staff at a hospital where a friend was receiving treatment following a motorbike accident.

Still, the vast majority of the 400,000 Israeli tourists who visited Thailand last year came and went without incident. Out of context social media clips hardly prove a statistical trend, but they have contributed to rising xenophobic sentiment the world over. Thai media outlets have seemingly realized that articles about Israelis generate high engagement, providing a steady churn of social media posts about even minor disputes or arrests.

An Australian national’s recent murder of a 17-year-old sex worker, meanwhile, did not provoke protests outside the Australian embassy. A massive influx of Russians to Phuket since the invasion of Ukraine has similarly not sparked protests, despite a rise in organized crime, including multiple high-profile incidents of kidnapping, extortion, and murder.

The anti-Israeli protests can be contextualized as part of a broader, growing anti-foreigner sentiment, that has targeted both unruly Westerners and vulnerable migrant workers.

When a group of Italian students insulted a Thai woman on a train in Bangkok, for example, a mob of protesters descended on their hotel, while the Italian embassy was flooded with angry comments on social media, though faced no in-person demonstrations.

The protester Nai said focusing on personal dislike of Israelis is a distraction from the issue at hand.

“From my perspective, although nationalist and right-wing groups have succeeded in turning opposition to Israel into a national-level issue and have brought some sections of the pro-Palestine movement into their demonstrations, this does not necessarily make the Palestinian cause itself a central political issue,” he said.

“If this movement were eventually to lead to a boycott of Israel, for example, the message communicated to both the international community and Thai society could simply become that ‘Israelis are bad,’ which is essentially a form of generalized racial prejudice,” he added. “What would be missing is the argument that a boycott of Israel should serve as a political statement to the international community: that Israel, which we see as a fascistic colonial state responsible for genocide, should face international pressure and consequences until genuine justice is achieved.”

Amid a floundering economy, others have directed this same xenophobic anger towards vulnerable migrant workers. Some 900,000 Cambodians were pressured to leave the country following border clashes last year, which also helped sweep the conservative, pro-military Bhumjaithai party to power at a general election earlier this year. With the Cambodians gone, migrants from Myanmar seem to be the next target, having sought refuge in Thailand by the millions amid a massive civil war back home.

Royalist activist Akkarawut Kraisrisombat, who organized the Chabad protest in Phuket, previously launched a 2024 campaign to deport pregnant migrant workers, though this failed to gain parliamentary support. He has since started a vigilante group called “Thais Won’t Tolerate” mainly focused on monitoring and reporting suspected illegal migrants, and has accompanied police on immigration raids.

Influencer Siranudh “Psi” Scott was present at the more recent, nationalist anti-Israel protests in Bangkok. He previously made waves when he accused foreign migrant workers who are unable to speak Thai of “taking advantage of our home.” In a social media post, he said if he goes to a restaurant and the staff speak to him in English, he will only speak Thai and request a new server. Many Burmese migrant workers in particular work in the service industry in Bangkok, and are often more proficient in English than Thai.

The Bangkok protest was led by Sondhi Limthongkul, an infamous conservative firebrand. Sondhi played a key role in destabilizing successive, democratically elected governments in 2006 and 2008, accusing them of undermining the monarchy, among other alleged malpractice. In 2008, Sondhi’s followers created a political crisis by occupying government buildings and an airport, giving an opening for the conservative establishment to wrest back control. While unproven, many have suspected Sondhi of colluding with the military to this end.

BDS Thailand said it is not affiliated with these right-wing activists or the ruling party, and accused “warmongering opportunists” of co-opting the pro-Palestine cause to “spread bigotry.” It added that the protests by Sondhi were “largely performative” and “unconnected to Palestinian liberation.”

While the recent anti-Israel protests were relatively small, the ruling Bhumjaithai party has ensured that the issue doesn’t remain on the fringes. The party seems happy to capitalize on rising anti-foreigner sentiment, having benefited enormously from the surge in nationalism during the war with Cambodia. Party leader and Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul, also showed a degree of disdain for Westerners as health minister during the COVID-19 pandemic.

While historically an ally to the conservative establishment, the activist Sondhi has more recently also set his sights on the ruling party, accusing Bhumjaithai of corruption, rigging the 2024 Senate election and selling out the country. Anutin may therefore feel even more pressure to take strong action, lest this issue become a liability rather than a strength for his government.

In comments on September 17, Anutin slammed reports of an illegal cemetery and foreigners using a restaurant as a religious site – clear references to Israelis, though he didn’t name them explicitly. But then he set his scope more broadly, saying Thailand is happy to welcome foreigners only if it’s mutually beneficial and they don’t take advantage, which he said applies to people from all over the world.

title: What Malaysia’s Recent State Election Results Say About the Country’s Political Direction
description: Oh Ei Sun of the Singapore Institute of International Affairs discusses the outcome of the recent elections in Johor and Negeri Sembilan.
text:
The Malaysian states Johor and Negeri Sembilan recently held state elections that produced disappointing results for Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s coalition.

During the July 11 polls in Johor, an economically important state at the tip of peninsular Malaysia, Barisan Nasional (BN), ​secured a commanding victory, winning 48 of 56 state assembly seats, up from 40 at the last election in 2022. Anwar’s Pakatan Harapan (PH) coalition won the remaining eight seats, down from 12 previously.

This result was largely replicated in Negeri Sembilan on August 1. Here BN won 18 of the 36 seats in the state’s legislative assembly and was set to form government with the pan-Malay Perikatan Nasional (PN) coalition, which won seven seats. PH, which had ruled the state in coalition with BN prior to the election, saw its share of seats drop from 17 to 11.

In both contests, the losses were particularly marked for the Democratic Action Party (DAP), a key member of the PH coalition that is traditionally associated with Malaysia’s ethnic Chinese community. In Negeri Sembilan, the election was also marked by close cooperation between the United Malays National Organization (UMNO) and the Islamist party PAS, the primary components of the BN and PN coalitions, respectively. This has raised suggestions that a new “Malay wave” could be set to wash away Anwar’s coalition at the next general election.

The twist is that BN and PH remain in coalition at the federal level, following the close-run general election of 2022. The growing competition between the two nominal partners has even raised the possibility that Anwar may choose to call a snap election.

Dr. Oh Ei Sun, a senior fellow at the Singapore Institute of International Affairs, spoke to The Diplomat’s Southeast Asia Editor Sebastian Strangio recently about what the results might mean for Anwar’s leadership and federal politics as Malaysia moves toward its next general election.

Let’s start with the most obvious question: How do you interpret the collapse of PH’s position in Johor and Negeri Sembilan?

I think there are similarities and differences in some of the major factors that led to PH’s collapse in these two states. The similarities lie primarily in the voters’ seeming conflation of PH’s perceived performance (or non-performance) at the federal level with their political solicitation at the state level.

To be more specific, we may look closer into PKR [the People’s Justice Party] and DAP – PH’s two largest component parties – respectively but also relatedly. PKR’s core supporters are those seeking social and political reforms, ranging from those advocating revamp of parliamentary and electoral systems to those who are fervently against corruption and power abuses. Many of them have become increasingly impatient with what they perceived as PKR’s feet-dragging since coming to federal power at fulfilling its reform promises that were loudly proclaimed during its opposition years. Worse still, some of them saw regressive measures that were unashamedly touted, such as those controlling freedom of expression online, that were reminiscent of pre-2018 BN days.

At the same time, PKR at the government’s driver seat was also perceived to be at best lackluster in its microeconomic performance, with many members of lower- and even middle-income groups finding it hard to carry on with livelihood, a scenario that was perceived to be worse than the BN days. So these core PKR supporters carried this rather disgruntled attitude toward PKR from the federal to the state level, and did not come out in droves to support PKR. Yet PKR, with its same, reformist image, remained inept in competing with UMNO and PAS in attracting an increasingly conservative Malay voters cohort to make up or surpass the difference.

DAP shared many of these misgivings and thus non-votes by its core supporters as PKR, plus disillusion from its non-Malay core supporters who had even higher expectations of DAP championing their long-held dream of attaining political and social equality. When they perceived DAP as having been non-enthusiastic in advancing this dear cause of theirs since coming to federal power, and furthermore remained silent when their rights were perceived to have been trampled upon, they wanted to “punish” DAP by not voting for it.

But these conflated or “transferred” disfavors against PH aside, there were also respective distinct factors that favor BN in these two states. The Johor chief minister, Onn Hafiz, turned out to be both charismatic and pragmatic, having brought in large amounts of foreign investment into the state that were transforming the state’s economic outlook. So the voters were comfortable with his helmsmanship and would like to see him continue in his leading role. In Negeri Sembilan, UMNO and PAS non-contest arrangements prevented vote splitting and handed easy wins to UMNO and participation by PAS for the first time in the state administration. This was a win-win situation for both parties. How long the state ruling coalition could hold is quite another question, if past disastrous collaboration history between UMNO and PAS provides any lesson.

Do you anticipate a similar result in Melaka, the next state to hold an election?

The conflated or “transferred” disfavors against PH by its core supporters would most likely remain quite intact in Melaka, as nothing much is likely to take place within a space of at most a few months to dissuade them otherwise. On the other hand, the Onn Hafiz favorite-son factor is certainly missing in Melaka, which saw at best average socioeconomic performance over the last half decade. And it would appear that BN and the PAS-led PN could still not reach a no-contest agreement in Melaka. As such, PH could aspire to holding on to its present state seats in Melaka. Anything more would be a distinct bonus.

The Negeri Sembilan election in particular was marked by close cooperation between BN and PN (particularly between UMNO and PAS), which have recently been at loggerheads. This has prompted some to suggest that a “Malay wave” could wash away Anwar and PH at the next general election. Do you think this is likely, and if so, why?

I think a Malay-Muslim wave that would be swept to power remains a very viable political scenario, as it almost did in the last general election. This is due not so much to PAS’ or UMNO’s revitalized political or electoral prowess. Rather, it is an electoral manifestation of an increasingly vibrant Malay-Muslim desire to attain a much more conservative and religiously oriented social and political outlook for the country. This is in line with yet another wave of religious revivalism that is sweeping across many Muslim-majority countries, ranging from Turkey to Indonesia. So the majority of Malay voters see PAS as a most conducive political vehicle for the soonest realization of this earnest desire, with UMNO as perhaps second best in realizing so. Therefore, a PAS-UMNO electoral alliance is likely to trump PH hands down.

But ironically, Anwar may remain prime minister after the next general election. This is due to the power struggles that are taking place within UMNO and PAS, which are usually more intense than their confrontations with PH. UMNO’s internecine fights are mainly factional in nature, with different warlords and their power bases rallying against one another. So Zahid the party president may ultimately not be touted as a viable prime ministerial candidate, with his many unresolved legal cases as the pretext. The fights in PAS, on the other hand, are usually ideological in nature, pitching the conservative ulamas against the more moderate professionals. The ulamas would loath to see a moderate such as the much-mentioned Terengganu chief minister Shamsuri to become prime minister. So Anwar, with his sizable religious and communal credentials in the past, may actually emerge as a compromise figurehead prime minister with PAS and to a lesser extent UMNO pulling the string behind the scene.

PH and BN insist their federal ​partnership can co-exist with rivalries at the state level, but how sustainable is the current situation? Do you anticipate Anwar calling a GE any time soon?

Malaysia has entered a very fragmented political landscape, with perhaps no single party being able to command an outright parliamentary majority, thus necessitating the forming of ruling coalitions. So the main calculation for alliance or split is not so much an ideological one as a politically convenient one. Therefore, the answer to the sustainability of any political coalitions really depends on the electoral viability and the thirst for power of its potential component parties.

It really does not matter when Anwar would call for a general election. The Malay-Muslim wave will sweep aside a large portion of its PH, but he may remain politically useful as prime minister.

How do you interpret the collapse of the DAP vote in the two recent elections, and also the state election in Sabah in November? What does this say about the dynamics of ethnic Chinese politics in peninsular Malaysia? If the party decides to leave the PH coalition, what impact could that have on Anwar’s political chances at the next GE?

See particularly the answer to the first question above. But there is a bit of a nuance to DAP in Sabah. DAP was trounced in Sabah mainly because it aligned itself too closely to the state ruling coalition there that was evidently disfavored by DAP’s core Sabah supporters, who decided to pitch their tent with Warisan instead, which they thought would come back to power. Nationally, the non-Malays continue to aspire to a fairer and more equal Malaysia. DAP’s decision to remain in cabinet is likely to come back to haunt it in the general election, as it would have to continue to collectively shoulder the kind of decisions which non-Malays may perceive to be unfair and unequal.

title: What Will Indonesia Do With Its New Aircraft Carrier?
description: The KRI Sriwijaya is a small aircraft carrier and may be better understood as an amphibious support ship.
text:
Febry Triantama has asked difficult questions in these pages about the strategic reasoning behind Indonesia’s acquisition of KRI Sriwijaya, a small aircraft carrier formerly owned and operated as the Giuseppe Garibaldi by the Italian Navy. Much regarding the future of the carrier (and the future of the Indonesian Navy) depends on how much Indonesia invests in maintaining and optimizing the vessel and its air wing.

The acquisition of the warship puts Indonesia into a growing club of navies in the Western Pacific to operate aircraft carriers. In recent years Australia, India, China, and Japan have all built or acquired flat-decked aircraft carrying warships. Most of these are considerably larger than the new Indonesian warship and can accordingly carry more and more varied aircraft and operate at greater distances from base. Thailand joined the aircraft carrier club in the 1990s with the Spanish-designed Chakri Naruebet, similar in size to KRI Sriwijaya.

Two decades ago vessels like the Thai and Indonesian carriers might be expected to operate V/STOL (vertical or short take off and landing) fighters. But it does not appear that Indonesia will go this route. The world’s only operational V/STOL fighters are the AV-8B Harrier and the F-35B Lightning II; the former are old and expensive to operate, while the latter have yet to be offered to Jakarta, and in any case are extremely expensive. The Sriwijaya is better understood as an amphibious support ship than as an aircraft carrier, a warship with substantial aviation capabilities but without an airwing capable of offensive or defense air superiority operations. This would place the ship in the same category as Australia’s Canberra-class landing helicopter docks (LHDs).

The best model for the Indonesia Navy may be the TCG Anadolu, a Turkish amphibious warship built along the same lines as vessels operating for Spain and Australia. While Anadolu was originally expected to fly the F-35B, disputes with Washington have put those plans on ice, perhaps permanently. Instead, the Turkish Navy has used Anadolu as a platform for experimenting with a variety of uncrewed aircraft, including the Bayraktar TB3 and the Bayraktar Kimilelma, both of which have multimission capabilities. Following the Turkish lead would allow Indonesia to avoid the expense of acquiring F-35Bs and, perhaps more importantly, the difficulties of maintaining trained pilots and aircrew for a very small combat wing. Indonesia has already signed a deal with Turkiye for the transfer of a number of drones, and may be able to take advantage of Turkiye’s experience operating advanced UAVs from a maritime platform.

If Anadolu represents the best case, the Thai Chakri Naruebet represents the worst. The Thai carrier was initially expected to operate AV-8B Harriers, but the notoriously difficult fighter proved too much of a hassle and the small force was retired in the early 2000s. Since the Chakri Naruebet has become known as a “harbor queen,” barely operational beyond a few high profile humanitarian assistance/disaster relief (HADR) operations. Thailand had expected more from its carrier but serial financial crises de-emphasized the navy and the navy’s most expensive ship.

Of course, Indonesia is considerably larger than Thailand and its navy has far greater responsibilities. The Sriwijaya is an older vessel and will require considerable modification before service, but Indonesia has already engaged with Italian shipbuilder Fincantieri to modernize the warship, an arrangement that should also improve Indonesia’s capacity for keeping the ship at sea.

An aircraft carrier of any size is a huge opportunity, but also a huge responsibility. Indonesia is rolling the dice on its capacity to keep the ship in service, as well as on the durability of a very old vessel. It could pay off with a much enhanced HADR capability, as well as a platform capable of taking advantage of the latest in drone technology. Or Indonesia could end up with its own harbor queen.

title: What’s Behind Australia’s New $42 Million in Assistance to Ukraine?
description: Canberra’s desire to learn from Kyiv is a sign of enormous respect and its pledge to ongoing support an expression of Australia's support for the Ukrainian cause.
text:
Australia’s Prime Minister Anthony Albanese met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York this week. Out of that meeting came a new bilateral security agreement, unlocking a further US$42 million in Australian assistance to Ukraine – split between Australian Defense Force (ADF) equipment, Ukraine’s Energy Support Fund, and humanitarian assistance. This brings Australia’s total contribution to almost US$1.4 billion.

Ukraine is obviously far away from Australia’s immediate security concerns in the Indo-Pacific, but Canberra’s support for the country is driven principally by its interest in preventing territorial conquest from becoming an accepted instrument of international relations. As a geographically isolated country with considerable economic interests beyond its immediate region, Australia depends on international rules that constrain the use of force. Canberra understands that allowing this principle to be undermined in Europe would weaken its application elsewhere, including in the Indo-Pacific. Alongside this is the position that smaller and middle-sized countries should retain the freedom to make their own security and diplomatic decisions.

Alongside its assistance package, Australia will also join the United Kingdom and Norway-led Maritime Capability Coalition which is helping Ukraine develop its naval capabilities. Yet what is most interesting about the new security agreement with Ukraine is not so much the assistance that Australia can provide Ukraine, but what Australia can learn from Ukraine.

Over the past four years, Ukraine has been forced into one of the more consequential live experiments in modern warfare. It has had to develop systems and capabilities that can counter a larger and more well-equipped military force with cunning and creativity. The most visible product of this has been in unmanned systems. Ukraine’s naval drone program, epitomized by the Magura platform, has proved to be a relatively inexpensive, but high impact weapons program adaptable to multiple roles, from attacking warships and aircraft, to striking the industrial infrastructure inside Russia that funds its invading force.

What makes this experience important and valuable to Australia is not just the technology itself, but what it can learn from how quickly Ukraine has been able to develop and adapt its capabilities. Ukraine has significantly shortened the gap between identifying a battlefield need, developing a solution, and putting it into action. Its defense-tech sector operates more like a startup than a traditional defense industry, as it is constantly adapting and replacing systems as Russia responds. The key lesson is that in a rapidly changing battlefield, the ability to adapt faster than the enemy can be more important than having the most advanced individual systems.

Australia still relies heavily on a small number of highly capable and expensive defense platforms. Yet it is coming to the realization that in a modern warfare scenario, these may not be as impactful as necessary. It is this realization that has driven an element of the new security agreement with Ukraine to deepen cooperation on uncrewed systems. Albanese and Zelenskyy committed the two countries to explore joint production of drones and similar defense technologies.

Of course, Australia’s own desire to develop autonomous systems predates this week’s agreement. Australia’s flagship Ghost Shark autonomous undersea vehicle is considered one of the more advanced technologies in the maritime space. Australia is not a novice here, but what it is trying to do is fuse the systems it has been working on with the capabilities that Ukraine has developed within an ever-evolving combat zone. The technology has to match the real world practicalities to be useful.

The Indo-Pacific relevance is what concerns Australia the most. China has been closely observing how Russia’s invasion of Ukraine has unfolded and how Ukraine’s defense of itself could be replicated by Taiwan. The potential for conflict over Taiwan remains the most pressing concern in Australia’s defense planning. Australia is heavily reliant on the sea lines of communication to northeast Asia, making deterrence a vital national interest. Ukraine’s innovative resistance may prove to be a powerful deterrence to any Chinese invasion plans.

Yet it would be wrong to read this new security agreement with Ukraine purely as one of Australia’s strategic self-interest. Canberra’s support for Ukraine also comes from a straightforward belief that Russia’s invasion is wrong, and helping Ukraine is the right thing to do. Australia’s desire to learn from Ukraine is a sign of enormous respect, and that cooperation in advancing peace is central to any good friendship.

title: What’s Behind One Nation’s Attacks on Andrew Hastie?
description: In its relentless attacks on Liberal Party MP, the One Nation party’s contempt for the rule of law is on full display.
text:
What populist nationalists find most offensive about liberal democracy is the rule of law. The idea that there should be an equal and impartial exercise of laws is an affront to both their belief in social hierarchies, and also their desire to exercise power in an arbitrary manner. To them, the law should be used to advance their concept of the nation, and privilege or discriminate based on who represents or challenges their beliefs. This hostility toward the rule of law intensifies when they find a prominent symbolic vehicle for their political ambitions.

This attempt to bend the country to their will is now being demonstrated in Australia through the One Nation party and its relentless attacks on Liberal Party MP Andrew Hastie. The party has commissioned cartoons that refer to Hastie as a “traitor” and a “gutless maggot.” The social media swamp that One Nation swims in and facilitates has become so aggressive and threatening that Hastie has had to employ security at both his electorate office and his home – something incredibly rare in Australia.

Hastie’s crime, in One Nation’s eyes, is that he testified in the defamation case that Ben Roberts-Smith, a former corporal in the Special Air Service (SAS) Regiment, launched against the publishers of The Sydney Morning Herald, The Age, and The Canberra Times, after they reported on allegations that he had committed war crimes in Afghanistan.

Hastie, a former SAS captain himself, and 20 other SAS veterans were subpoenaed to provide evidence in the case. A Federal Court judge found that on the balance of probabilities, Roberts-Smith was responsible for, or complicit in, unlawful killings in Afghanistan. The full bench of the Federal Court subsequently unanimously dismissed Roberts-Smith’s appeal. A criminal trial for Roberts-Smith remains pending.

For One Nation, the question of Roberts-Smith’s guilt is irrelevant because they believe the law itself to be fraudulent. The idea that there should be rules of engagement that the Australian Defense Force (ADF) is held to is something One Nation rejects. The military is considered an institution that sits above both domestic and international law.

For the ADF to investigate itself – as it did over allegations of war crimes committed in Afghanistan – is evidence to One Nation that it has been captured by a weak and “woke” series of ideas that have no place on a battlefield. Roberts-Smith has therefore become a symbol of the unrestrained manhood that the military should be a demonstration of. Those SAS soldiers – and especially Hastie – who testified in the defamation case therefore are guilty of betrayal.

It is here that “patriotism” in One Nation’s view has shifted from loyalty to the country’s institutions and principles toward loyalty to an individual who is deemed to embody what they see as a national virtue. This has also become bound to an immense sense of victimhood that One Nation cultivates. The rule of law is victimizing not just Roberts-Smith, but the nation itself. And if this is the case, then the rule of law must go. What is being challenged is whether Australian institutions have the authority to determine what conduct in war actually means.

Hastie has also become a perfect target for One Nation because he is a Liberal Party MP. One Nation may be mired in dystopian fantasies about global left-wing conspiracies, but the electoral threat they pose is actually to the Liberal Party. This is the party they want to replace, and it is the Liberal Party’s traditional voters from which One Nation are drawing most support. Bringing down Hastie therefore also has an electorally symbolic value. One Nation just won a by-election in a Western Australian state seat that overlaps with Hastie’s federal seat. It was another shot over Hastie’s bow.

One Nation’s attempt to replace the Liberal Party has further symbolic value because as the party that claims to be the holder of the classical liberal tradition in Australian politics, belief in the rule of law should be central to the Liberals political project. Theoretically, it should make the Liberals the party most resolutely opposed to One Nation and its radical objectives. Bizarrely, however, the Liberal Party seems to be a willing participant in its own decline. The party’s psychology is bound to its opposition to the Labor Party; it can’t comprehend threats from anywhere else.

Yet the threat here is not just against the electoral fortunes of the Liberal Party, or the reputation and physical personhood of Andrew Hastie. There is a wider battle taking place over what “patriotism” actually means. One Nation’s political strategy is to wrap itself in the flag and present its politics as an expression of national loyalty, while directing its hostility toward the institutions and principles that actually constitute the nation’s liberal democracy.
tag: Andrew Hastie; Australian Liberal Party; Ben Roberts-Smith; One Nation; One Nation Party

title: What’s Wrong With US Pacific Islands Policy?
description: It’s the relationships, stupid.
text:
There is currently an active debate about U.S. policy in the Pacific Islands. Some are saying the U.S. is AWOL in the region. Others have said this is one of the most active times for U.S. engagement, including the Heritage Foundation, which just published a detailed “policy inventory” of announced U.S. activities in the region.

What do I think? Let me start in a Pacific Islands way, with a story.

In May 2025, I took a China-donated cargo ship from Yap to Woleai atoll, in the Federated States of Micronesia (FSM). Several hundred Micronesians (from babies to grandmothers), five Chinese construction workers, and I slept on the deck, used communal bathrooms, and ate the food we brought along for the days-long trip down the island chain.

By the time I got back to Yap weeks later, I had lice, parasites, and a leg wound that took U.S. military-grade salve to heal. I also had friends for life.

Onboard the China-donated ship that is the only regular transport along the Yap island chain. Families eat and sleep on deck for up to weeks at a time. Photo by Cleo Paskal.

Why did I go? The U.S. Department of Defense (DoD) had announced around $2 billion in infrastructure investments on the main island of Yap State, an island also called Yap. Meanwhile, I had heard from Micronesian friends that the Chinese were working on something in Woleai, in a different part of Yap State.

There was also a Dolly Parton angle – but that’s for later.

People in DoD assured me (and their superiors) that everything was fine. Knowing how the U.S. government operates in other parts of the Pacific, I wondered if they had the full picture. So, I packed a bag full of tins of Chef Boyardee, bottles of water, and Dramamine and went to take a look.

Soon after I arrived on Woleai, the president of FSM, Wesley Simina, arrived on his own boat. After the traditional beach greeting, he and his entourage disappeared on one of the island’s few pick-up trucks. His wife rode on the truck’s bed.

Local kids told me he had gone to the groundbreaking for the runway. The runway? I wanted to see, so they led me on a dash through a shortcut in the jungle, past overgrown machinery left behind from the years Woleai spent under the control of Imperial Japan.

Then the woods opened up, exposing the cracked runway first built by the Japanese, rows of Chinese heavy machinery, and a stage announcing the imminent groundbreaking.

While the president’s official schedule may have said he came to Woleai for the high school graduation, it wasn’t a coincidence that he was also on the island when a Chinese state-owned company began work to rebuild an Imperial Japanese runway just over 640 kilometers from Guam.

The groundbreaking ceremony for the runway reconstruction on Woleai, Yap, on May 26, 2025. Photo provided by Cleo Paskal.

That’s me, just behind the Chinese flag.

Based on reactions, key people in the U.S. government were caught by surprise. Their “Micronesia whisperers” had failed them.

A few days later, on a School of War podcast – an interview I conducted via Starlink, while I was a ten-minute walk from the Chinese workers’ barracks on Woleai – I commented the United States wasn’t listening to the right people, and there were going to be problems moving forward with the $2 billion investment in infrastructure in Yap, unless something changed.

Nothing changed.

On June 29, 2026, just over a year later, Admiral Samuel Paparo, the commander of U.S. Pacific Command (PACOM), wrote to FSM’s President Simina that, due to a breakdown in the negotiations, “U.S. PACOM intends to move forward by assessing alternative locations across the region to meet the needs of Pacific defense.”

That may just be a negotiation tactic. But the fact the situation has deteriorated to the point that a threat was deemed necessary is one indication that, in spite of the serious attempt by the Trump administration to work more – and better – with the Pacific Islands, it is not necessarily achieving the desired outcomes.

They should have asked Dolly Parton, the late country star and all-around American icon, for advice.

Dolly Parton, Habele, and More Untapped Wisdom

Tasur with his books from Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library on Woleai Atoll, Yap. Photo by Cleo Paskal.

While on Woleai, I took an hour-long outboard motor boat trip to an island across the lagoon for an elementary school graduation. I had heard that Parton’s Imagination Library delivers free books to kids out there. It does, which was how I met Tasur.

Think about the social, political, bureaucratic and practical logistics involved in getting “The Little Engine That Could” from the U.S. state of Tennessee, where the Imagination Library is headquartered, into the hands of Tasur on Woleai. Someone helping Parton’s non-profit knows Yap well enough to do not just that, but to ensure hundreds of kids across Yap get a free book every month from Tennessee.

That “someone” is Neil Mellen and the team at Habele, an educational NGO that, for years, has provided not just free books, but scholarships and more to kids across FSM. Founded and funded by former Peace Corps volunteers and other Americans, its sister organization, Habele Research Institute, runs a comprehensive Wiki on Yap, which includes one of the largest online collections of historical material on the region.

If those involved in negotiating the U.S. military’s runway and port development didn’t read the Habele page on the topic – and then ask to talk to the people who put it together – they might want to consider another line of work. I’m pretty sure they didn’t.

Father Francis X. Hezel at work in his office in Guam. Photo by Cleo Paskal.

I do know they didn’t spend time talking to Father Francis X. Hezel – I asked him. Father Fran, as he’s called, now lives in Guam. He has been in region since the early 1960s and literally wrote the book(s) on Micronesia. U.S. policymakers used to go out of their way to meet with him regularly.

Not anymore, even though PACOM’s Joint Task Force – Micronesia is also based in Guam.

Father Fran, an American Jesuit, set up Micronesia Seminar Library, a physical, comprehensive collection of books, video, articles, periodical, photos, and more covering the sweep of Micronesian history, culture, politics, etc.

Father Rich McAuliff, another American Jesuit, has also been in Micronesia for years, and is on Yap taking care of the Library.

Given the changes to the local economy that $2 billion in investment might bring – Yap Island has a population of around 7,000 – it would also be helpful to talk to Americans in the business community, like Mark Hartman, about complexities around access to financing, human resources, logistics, land rights, the regulatory environment, etc. Hartman wrote a brief for Habele to try to inform the U.S.-Pacific Investment Summit. It is, as he says, the basics, but even that is usually overlooked.

The DoD negotiators (and any others, including from the State Department, Interior Department, etc.) also would benefit from extensive conversations with the fine folks at Pacific Mission Aviation (PMA), a missionary airline that has been proving free medical evacuations, search and rescues, and more in Yap for over 50 years.

Pacific Mission Aviation pilot Amos Collins at Ulithi Airport, getting ready to load the plane. Photo by Cleo Paskal.

PMA pilots, almost all American, are the only ones regularly using the Woleai airfield. They know every runway, rock, and reef in the region. Almost every family in Yap has a story about good done by the PMA. At the Ulithi high school graduation last year, Simina, the FSM president, was the opening act; it was Amos Collins, a PMA pilot, who gave the keynote.

As Brock Welge, the PMA’s director of maintenance, said in a recent interview: “Probably the biggest misconception people have is how long it takes to build relationships out here… I’ve been out here since 2019 and I’m just now starting to feel accepted and integrated into the community. Which is amazing – but it takes a long time to build those relationships, sometimes lifetimes.”

It’s the Relationships, Stupid

Yes, the U.S. government is paying much more attention to the Pacific Islands region than it has in years. There is also a desire for a new approach, which is needed. That new attention and new money is attracting new “experts.” There are myriad reports being commissioned by various parts of the U.S. government on how to understand the region, and what to do about it.

Few of these reports are written by people who have lived and worked in the region (or in some cases even visited), or who have spoken directly with Americans on the ground. For those “reporting on” Yap, the smartest of them will steal liberally from Habele Institute – if they (or their AI) can find it. That will ensure their contracts are renewed, but won’t help keep Habele and its relationships going.

I used the example of Yap and the wide range of Americans to learn from – note that I haven’t even started with the locals, another obvious point of engagement – because this should be one of the locations with the most focus. Yap is the site of the potential $2 billion investment, with close to $1.4 billion of that location-specified by the National Defense Authorization Act. And yet there is no permanent U.S. government presence in Yap, outreach to Americans on the ground is limited, there is little effective attempt to develop understanding and trust with locals. This can’t be done by AI. The same applies to other locations across the region.

There are some attempts to have “presence.” For example, the Army’s Oceania Engagement Team has two people on Yap, though there have been frequent personnel changes to the team. However, unlike in some other locations, the deployment has not resulted in building meaningful relationships. Especially given the lack of comparative streams of knowledge, this particular presence may give a false sense of understanding about Yap.

That gets to the heart of the problem. And it’s why, unlike the usual pieces about the area that focus on geography, this article is about people. Any successful U.S. policy in the region needs to be about relationships, and trust.

And this isn’t a benign environment.

That Chinese state-owned company that rebuilt the Imperial Japanese runway on Woleai? It’s now rebuilding a bridge on the main island of Yap, and is working on secondary roads. Its people are settling in for the long run, establishing their own relationship networks, ones designed to cut off ties to the United States and other democracies.

It’s not an accident a Chinese operator tried to take over the PMA’s routes from Yap to Palau. Washington may not have identified who is important in providing human security in Yap, but Beijing has. And they are working to undermine the Americans doing just that.

While the new money, approach, and attention from Washington are promising, and needed, we’ll know things have really changed when someone from the U.S. government rides on that transport ship through the outer islands of Yap – alongside locals, at least some of whom will likely be U.S. military veterans – and starts to see for themselves what’s really going on.

That may not happen, because the U.S. embassy has likely heard just enough to know that the ship isn’t safe. Someone thousands of miles away may even be writing a report on it. But if Washington wants to know why, left on their own, the FSM and Yap governments won’t replace it with something seaworthy, how China fits in, and what Japan can do to help, they’ll need to talk to a new set of people.

In the meantime, just like much in the rest of the region, that ship will sail on, shrouded by a cloud of potential, imminent disaster that could easily be blown away by asking the right people the right questions.

title: When Xi Visits Washington, Trump Must Raise China’s ‘Ethnic Unity’ Law
description: Trump should raise the ethnic unity law directly with Xi and make clear that attempts to enforce it against people in the United States will not be tolerated.
text:
When Chinese President Xi Jinping arrives in Washington on September 24, the agenda will be crowded: trade, technology, fentanyl, Taiwan, and global security. But there is another issue that the United States cannot afford to leave out: China’s newly adopted Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress.

U.S. President Donald Trump should raise a question that goes to the heart of American sovereignty: Why are Uyghur Americans being forced to choose between exercising their freedoms here and protecting their relatives from retaliation in China?

The Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress was passed by China’s National People’s Congress in March and took effect July 1. Beijing presents it as a measure to promote harmony among China’s ethnic groups. Uyghurs, Tibetans, Southern Mongolians, and others know better. The law does not protect unity; it codifies the forced assimilation campaigns our communities have long experienced.

Since 2017, the Chinese government has waged a systematic campaign to extinguish Uyghur national identity, religion, and cultural life. With the ethnic unity law, Beijing has codified and expanded this assault.

Americans must pay particular attention to the law’s reach beyond China’s borders. Article 63 of the law says organizations and individuals outside China can be held legally responsible for actions deemed to “undermine ethnic unity and progress or create ethnic division.” China’s vice justice minister openly defended this overseas provision as “legitimate, lawful, necessary, and feasible.”

Article 10 asserts that foreign entities “using excuses such as ethnicity, religion, or human rights to insult and disparage, contain and suppress, or infiltrate and undermine the PRC are to be resolutely opposed.”

That is an unmistakable message to Uyghurs, Tibetans, Hong Kongers, and other communities: Beijing claims the right to police our identities even outside its borders.

But it is also a threat to all Americans, even those without family ties in China. Any person who expresses a view China deems as contrary to ethnic unity can be targeted under the new law.

These risks are not hypothetical. As I wrote last month, Uyghurs abroad already feel its impact. Since the law went into effect, families have stopped sending their children to Uyghur language schools out of fear of retaliation by Chinese authorities. People who live thousands of miles from China are asking whether a speech, a social media post, a cultural event, or even a private act of faith could put family members back home in danger.

This is how transnational repression works. The Chinese government does not need to arrest every Uyghur activist living in the United States or Europe. It only needs to create an atmosphere of fear. It only needs people to believe that what they do abroad may have consequences for themselves or their loved ones.

That is why this law is not only a human rights issue, it is an immediate challenge to U.S. sovereignty.

Other governments have spoken out. Australia reportedly raised concerns with Beijing. Members of the European Parliament called for the law’s repeal. U.N. experts warned that it risks entrenching forced assimilation and expanding transnational repression. But the United States, which formally recognized China’s treatment of Uyghurs as genocide and is home to several prominent Uyghur civil society organizations, has not clearly condemned the law.

Trump should raise the ethnic unity law directly with Xi and make clear that attempts to enforce it against people in the United States will not be tolerated.

No foreign government has the right to determine what people living in America or in any democratic societies say, believe, teach their children, or advocate for. Washington should say clearly that China’s “ethnic unity” law stops at America’s borders.

title: Where Does North Korea’s Nuclear Program Stand in 2026?
description: Here’s what satellite imagery and the IAEA are telling us.
text:
Nearly two decades after international inspectors were expelled from North Korea, satellite imagery and open-source analysis remain the only windows the outside world has into Pyongyang’s nuclear program. What that window shows in late 2026 is a program that is visibly expanding, on multiple fronts at once.

On August 28, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) issued a report to its Board of Governors documenting the construction of a second uranium enrichment facility at North Korea’s main Yongbyon nuclear complex. The new facility could house up to 28 centrifuge cascades, alongside an already-operating expanded annex at the Kangson enrichment site. The agency identified the new two-story building by comparing satellite images taken during its construction with state media photographs of a June 2026 visit by Kim Jong Un, during which centrifuges and cascades resembling those at known enrichment sites were visible.

IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi told the Board that the continued operation of the Kangson and Yongbyon facilities, together with the reported further expansion of weapons-grade nuclear material production, was “a cause for serious concern.” The IAEA has not had inspectors on the ground in North Korea since 2009 and now builds its assessments entirely from commercial satellite imagery and open-source material, including North Korean state media itself.

The picture built up over 2026 by independent monitors is consistent with the IAEA’s findings. Analysts tracking Yongbyon have documented near-continuous water discharge from the 5-megawatt-electric (MWe) reactor, North Korea’s original plutonium producer, consistent with it running through what is now believed to be its seventh irradiation cycle since October 2024, alongside periodic steam activity at the Radiochemical Laboratory suggesting reprocessing campaigns. A separate site review by Daily NK reached similar conclusions, also noting that the long-delayed Experimental Light Water Reactor (ELWR) is showing renewed discharge activity after a shutdown period, and that demolition of the old, unfinished 50 MWe reactor at Yongbyon continues in parallel with the new construction.

A review by 38 North covering 2025 activity framed this as a direct response to political direction: Kim Jong Un had described that year as decisive for “bolstering up the nuclear forces,” and the satellite record showed the 5 MWe reactor running steadily since January 2025. 38 North also flagged pre-operational testing of the ELWR, a probable summer reprocessing campaign, and construction of what are assessed to be new enrichment and waste-storage buildings.

North Korea’s declared and suspected enrichment infrastructure now spans at least two locations at Yongbyon (the original uranium enrichment plant and the new building identified in August) plus the Kangson facility outside Pyongyang, whose 2024 annex expansion appears to have become operational around January 2026. Because clandestine centrifuge halls are comparatively easy to conceal, nonproliferation researchers have long argued that the more reliable way to bound North Korea’s enrichment capacity is to track its uranium supply rather than guess at hidden buildings. In 2021, an academic study using satellite-based land-use analysis around the Pyongsan uranium mill concluded that North Korea’s tailings output implies it could produce substantially more milled uranium than it is believed to currently be enriching, meaning supply is not the constraint on how fast the program could grow.

Unlike uranium enrichment, North Korea’s plutonium supply chain runs through a small number of well-mapped facilities. It starts at the Pyongsan Uranium Concentrate Plant, roughly 45 kilometers from the DMZ, which remains the country’s only confirmed source of yellowcake. Uranium ore is processed there into oxide concentrate before being shipped to Yongbyon for conversion into reactor fuel. That fuel feeds the 5 MWe reactor, whose spent fuel rods are then reprocessed at Yongbyon’s Radiochemical Laboratory to extract weapons-grade plutonium. This lab is believed to be responsible for the totality of North Korea’s plutonium stockpile to date, estimated by outside experts to support somewhere in the range of dozens of warheads.

The ELWR adds a second, more ambiguous track. Rated at 100 megawatts-thermal, it began sustained operation in late 2023 after a decade of delay. The ELWR has since gone through at least one documented shutdown-and-restart cycle, with Grossi telling the IAEA board of direction in November 2025 that it had “likely been shut down” in early August of that year, after months of stable running. As noted above, the ELWR is believed to have restarted once again.

A light-water reactor of this design is not optimized for weapons-grade plutonium production the way the graphite-moderated 5 MWe unit is, and North Korea has publicly framed it as an electricity source. Even so, should it reach stable, full-power operation, outside analysts assess it would function as a supplementary plutonium source layered on top of the existing reactor, meaningfully increasing Yongbyon’s total fissile material output.

The reactor most often described in older reporting as North Korea’s “second 200-megawatt reactor” is not at Yongbyon at all, but roughly 20 kilometers away at Taechon. Construction of this larger, 200 MWe graphite-moderated, gas-cooled unit began in the late 1980s as the planned full-scale successor to the 5 MWe design but was frozen under the 1994 U.S.-North Korea Agreed Framework, at which point North Korea had manufactured none of the reactor’s required graphite blocks). The most recent detailed satellite review of the site, by 38 North in 2019, found administrative and support-building upgrades but no changes to the derelict reactor structure itself or its generator hall. The analysts concluded that renewed construction was less likely than signaling or preparation for eventual inspections. No subsequent commercial satellite analysis has documented a resumption of reactor construction at Taechon; as of 2026 it remains, by all available open-source evidence, an abandoned shell.

The reason Taechon still draws attention despite decades of dormancy is the scale of what it was designed to do. At full design output, a 200 MWe graphite-gas reactor of this type could produce on the order of 220 kilograms of weapons-grade plutonium per year – enough, by some open-source estimates, for 25 to 40 additional nuclear weapons annually, dwarfing the output of the 5 MWe reactor that has anchored North Korea’s plutonium stockpile for four decades.

In practice, most nonproliferation analysts consider a Taechon restart unlikely in the near term: the design is nearly 40 years old, the site has been exposed to the elements for three decades, and North Korea’s more recent investment has gone into the ELWR and centrifuge halls rather than graphite-gas technology. But the reactor’s unfinished shell, still standing, is a reminder that North Korea’s ambition for plutonium production was never defined by its current 5 MWe reactor.

There are three main takeaways from open source analysis of North Korea’s nuclear program in 2026. First, North Korea is continuing a steady, uninterrupted plutonium cycle at the original 5 MWe reactor. Second, its light-water reactor has started on-again, off-again operation, which could add a second plutonium stream if it stabilizes. Finally, its uranium enrichment complex has now visibly doubled its footprint at Yongbyon while continuing to expand at Kangson.

The fact that North Korea did all this without meaningfully touching the Taechon project tells us that Pyongyang has found it more efficient to build new capacity rather than revive old designs. That may be the most consequential inference to be drawn from Taechon.
tag: Kangson Enrichment Site; North Korea enrichment; North Korea Experimental Light Water Reactor; North Korea nuclear program; North Korea plutonium; North Korea uranium; Pyongsan Uranium Concentrate Plant; Taechon; Yongbyon nuclear reactor

title: Who Is Indigenous? The Politics of Tribal Identity Terminology in India and Bangladesh
description: Tribal people in South Asia prefer being called adivasi or original inhabitants, but nationalist forces in India and Bangladesh oppose it for different reasons.
text:
On August 9, the government in the eastern Indian state of West Bengal did not host events marking the International Day of the World’s Indigenous Peoples. Last year, the day was celebrated with events across the state over four days. The new Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) government that came to power in May issued a notice on August 5, stating that this year’s celebration was cancelled. No reason was given for the decision.

West Bengal’s indigenous people’s organizations protested the move, as did the opposition parties. “This is an assault on the indigenous people’s identity and pride,” Mayukh Biswas, a leader of the West Bengal unit of the Communist Party of India-Marxists, said, alleging that the decision stemmed from the BJP’s ideological project of denying the adivasi (indigenous/aboriginal) identity of the tribal population.

Peeved by the government’s neglect, several indigenous peoples’ organizations in West Bengal took out processions to celebrate the day on August 9.

In Bangladesh on the same day, tribal groups pressed for their long-standing demand that they be called adivasi/indigenous people. As the Bangladesh government does not officially celebrate the International Day for the World’s Indigenous Peoples, tribal groups celebrated on their own.

West Bengal’s BJP government’s decision does not come as a surprise. In 2021, it formally institutionalized November 15 as “Janjatiya Gaurav Divas” (Tribal Pride Day). Since 2022, neither President Droupadi Murmu, who comes from a tribal community, nor Prime Minister Narendra Modi has shared any celebratory message on August 9. In contrast, November 15 receives extensive state patronage.

In fact, in 2024, one of the BJP’s crucial ideological partners alleged that “external forces and Christian missionaries” were seeking to divide society using Indigenous People’s Day.

The August 9 event has “indigenous people” in the name of the day. In the Indo-Aryan group of languages like Sanskrit, Hindi, Bengali, Nepali, and Sinhalese, this is best expressed by the word adivasi. The name of the November 15 event includes janajati, which translates to “tribal” in English.

The argument over what to call the tribal peoples — adivasi, janajati or upajati — may look like a dispute over vocabulary. But it is not. It is actually an argument over history, nationhood, and political rights, especially in India and Bangladesh.

The term “adivasi” literally means original inhabitants and stands closer to globally popular terms like indigenous people and aboriginal. It carries a claim of original or prior inhabitation. When linked to land, historical continuity, and collective rights, this can acquire political significance. Terms such as janajati (tribe), upajati (sub-tribe) or vanvasi (forest dwellers) do not make that claim in the same way.

This is why the term “adivasi” is also popular in Nepal and Sri Lanka. Nepali society has gone through phases of intense debate over using adivasi or janajati. However, the debate faded somewhat as Nepal legally termed them Indigenous Nationalities or Adivasi Janajati — combining adivasi and janajati, calling the two terms complementary. In Sri Lanka, the usage of adivasi is rather new, gaining popularity since the 1990s, without much of a conflict over the term.

While organizations of the tribal people prefer the term adivasi/Mulbasi/mulnibasi (indigenous/aboriginal), Hindu religious nationalists in India and different nationalist groups in Bangladesh oppose this.

In India, the Hindu nationalists, which include Modi’s BJP and its ideological-organizational parent, the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), argue that “original inhabitants” would imply that other Indians are outsiders. The Sangh therefore prefers terms such as vanvasi and janajati to describe the adivasis.

In contrast, Rahul Gandhi, India’s main opposition leader, issues celebratory messages and calls adivasis the “original owners” of the land.

In Bangladesh, successive governments and sections of the political establishment have resisted recognizing the country’s tribal peoples through the term “adivasi” or Indigenous Peoples. The arguments and political positions have varied, but the stance has not changed. Officials have been formally instructed not to use adivasi in communications. The government uses upajati or Khudra Nrigoshthi (minor ethnic races). Even this year, tribal groups demanded to be called adivasi.

In contemporary international usage, Indigenous Peoples are associated with collective rights, cultural continuity, self-identification, and relationships with ancestral territories. The U.N. Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP), adopted in 2007, establishes a framework for such rights, including rights relating to cultural identity, lands, and resources.

India’s Congress-led government voted for the Declaration; Bangladesh abstained, pointing to ambiguities in the Declaration, particularly the absence of an explicit definition of “indigenous people.”

The U.N. does not provide a single universal legal definition of who constitutes an Indigenous People, as it believes identifying them is more important than defining.

In Bangladesh, the arguments against calling them adivasi include: a) the Bengali-speaking people are the original inhabitants of the deltaic plains, which form the overwhelming majority of the country’s territory; b) the tribals of the hills had originally migrated from other neighboring hills that now fall in India or Myanmar; and c) granting indigenous status could create legal avenues for claims regarding autonomy, self-determination, or specialized territorial rights, which could endanger national security at the trijunction of India, Bangladesh and Myanmar.

Another intriguing argument is that as there has been a large influx of Bengali people on these lands, demands for relocating these non-tribal settlers will create further complexities and social tension. The irony is that the settler influx happened with state backing in the first place.

The Indian scenario is different. Here, the legal/constitutional term is Scheduled Tribe (ST) (anusuchit janjati). Adivasi has long been used in Indian public discourse and by official institutions alongside the constitutionally specified category of ST. People falling under the ST category enjoy certain protections, including reservations in education and jobs. There are tribal autonomous districts where non-tribals cannot purchase or own land or business.

The BJP and the wider Sangh Parivar, however, have explicitly objected to the term on ideological grounds. Since the launch of the RSS-backed Vanvasi Kalyan Ashram (VKA) in 1952, the Hindu nationalist camp has used and promoted the term vanvasi. RSS leader Ram Madhav stated that the Sangh believes that “we all are original inhabitants of this continent.”

Later, they also incorporated the term janajati and helped launch an outfit named Janjati Suraksha Manch (tribal protection committee). The VKA’s Nepal chapter calls itself Janajati Kalyan Ashram, perhaps because tribal people in Nepal live more in the hills than the forests.

Opposition parties often argue that terms like vanvasi and janajati reduce indigenous peoples to a subset of a larger Hindu civilization. In Nepal, tribal people oppose the use of janajati, arguing that jati comes from the Hindu varna (caste) system.

Therefore, in India, it is mostly the Hindu nationalist force that opposes the adivasi term. And that, too, primarily from an ideological perspective: They claim the Aryans are as much the original inhabitants of India as different tribes are — a claim scientifically unproven but essential for the Hindu nationalist pride in Vedic Aryan supremacy over world cultures.

Gandhi, however, warned that what now appears to be a war on identity can also transform into one on their traditional and historical ownership of natural resources.
