title: Will Taiwan Fight? We Need Better Evidence.
description: Both those making pessimistic predictions and those confidently rejecting them often rely on thin evidence.
text:
Simon Shuster’s recent article in The Atlantic, asking whether Taiwan might simply “give up” in the face of growing pressure from China, attracted considerable attention in Taiwan and among the broader community of China and Taiwan watchers. Some praised the piece for its candid analysis and for asking uncomfortable questions that are too often avoided in discussions about Taiwan’s security. Others were somewhat less impressed.

The article quickly came under fire from Taiwanese and (mostly) Taiwan-based foreign analysts, who pointed to factual errors, questionable interpretations of domestic politics, and what they saw as a selective and misleading portrayal of Taiwanese society. Legislator Puma Shen, one of those interviewed for the article, issued a public statement accusing Shuster of taking his comments out of context. The Taipei Times devoted an editorial to rebutting the article, and even Taiwan’s National Security Council weighed in, with Secretary General Joseph Wu publicly rejecting its central premise.

Essentially, there are rather good reasons to take these criticisms seriously. Some concern basic facts and context, which are obviously important when making such a sweeping argument about Taiwan. That said, the reaction also exposed another problem. A significant part of the response has questioned what a foreign journalist who spent limited time in Taiwan and has no evident prior expertise on Taiwan or the region can really know about Taiwanese society. Critics pointed to a lack of understanding of Taiwanese politics, insufficient engagement with Taiwanese voices and opinion polls showing considerable willingness to defend Taiwan, and Taiwan’s own experience – from democratization and the Sunflower Movement to its remarkable response to COVID-19 – as evidence of a society capable of mobilizing when necessary.

As compelling as these arguments are, none of them give us a particularly convincing answer either.

Predicting what Taiwan and its people would actually do if China decided to use force is extraordinarily difficult. Both those making pessimistic predictions and those confidently rejecting them often seem to rely on evidence that tells us much less than we think.

Opinion polls are perhaps the clearest example. As argued previously in The Diplomat, they are useful for understanding attitudes, but telling a pollster that you would defend Taiwan is very different from making that decision when missiles are falling, casualties are mounting, electricity and communications are disrupted, and nobody knows whether outside help is coming. That does not make polls useless. Questions involving actual costs, such as longer military service, higher taxes, or greater personal obligations, can tell us more. But saying that you are willing to sacrifice something and actually sacrificing it are not the same thing.

Historical examples have only limited relevance. Taiwan’s democratization, the Sunflower Movement, and its response to COVID-19 have all been cited as evidence of a society capable of mobilizing when necessary. Comparisons can also be drawn with Finland’s resistance to the Soviet Union during the Winter War, Ukraine’s response to Russia’s invasion, or other societies that proved far more willing to resist than outsiders expected. These are indeed powerful examples. But what exactly do they tell us about how Taiwanese society would respond to a Chinese attack today?

Israel offers a useful example of why we should be careful in making predictions. Israeli society has repeatedly shown an extraordinary ability to mobilize against military threats. Following the October 7 attacks, more than 300,000 reservists were mobilized in a very short period, including Israelis who returned from abroad to report for duty. Nonetheless, during COVID-19, Israel struggled to sustain public compliance with government restrictions. Trust and willingness to follow regulations declined as the crisis continued. The same society generated two very different responses to calls for public action.

The type of threat, its perceived seriousness, public trust, political divisions, and personal costs can all shape how societies respond. Historical experience and comparisons can give us useful clues. But they cannot tell us what Taiwanese will do when confronted by the People’s Liberation Army (PLA).

So perhaps we need to look elsewhere. Instead of endlessly asking whether Taiwanese will fight or give up, we should look more closely at what Taiwanese society, its politicians, and its military are actually doing as the threat from China grows.

And here the picture remains concerning.

Taiwan has struggled with military recruitment and retention, personnel shortages, and a reserve force in which too few receive regular and meaningful training. Political polarization has repeatedly turned defense into another battlefield between the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) and Kuomintang (KMT), most visibly in the continuing fights over defense spending. Institutional cooperation and coordination remain problematic, while deeply rooted institutional and military cultures can slow necessary reforms and adaptation. Taiwan also faces serious constraints in expanding its defense-industrial capacity quickly enough to meet its growing needs. All of these problems tell us something about how much Taiwanese citizens, politicians, and institutions are actually willing, and able, to change as the threat grows.

There are, however, signs that some things are moving in the right direction. After years of decline, military recruitment and retention have recently improved, although it is too early to know whether this represents a lasting reversal. Organizations such as Kuma Academy and Forward Alliance have attracted thousands of people who are willing to spend their own time on civil-defense training, and defense spending has increased substantially. Taiwan’s annual Han Kuang exercises have also become significantly more realistic and comprehensive, with this year’s iteration, Han Kuang 42, featuring longer and less scripted training, involving a broader range of military, government, and civilian actors, and placing much greater emphasis on whole-of-society defense.

This still isn’t definitive proof that Taiwanese will fight, nor does it negate the more troubling signs. But these are precisely the kinds of developments we should be watching. Are more people joining the military, and are they staying? Are reservists receiving more serious training? Are citizens willing to give their time to civil defense? Are Taiwanese willing to accept longer service, higher defense spending, or other personal costs? Are political leaders willing to put defense above partisan interests? Are government institutions actually cooperating and changing the way they operate? And is the military becoming more serious about preparing for the kind of war it may actually have to fight?

More importantly, we should follow these indicators over time. One bad year of military recruitment could be an aberration. A decline continuing for five or ten years as the threat grows tells us considerably more. The same is true of retention, reserve training, civil defense participation, defense spending, and military reform.

We should also look at whether these indicators move in the same direction. If what Taiwanese tell pollsters corresponds with what citizens, politicians, and institutions are actually willing to do, we can have greater confidence in those attitudes.

There is another complication. Talking about “Taiwan’s resilience” or “Taiwan’s will to fight” often treats Taiwan as a unitary actor when it clearly is not. The differences go well beyond the DPP-KMT divide. The military, government agencies, local authorities, civil society, businesses, and different parts of the public may have very different levels of preparedness, commitment, and willingness to bear costs. Reducing all of this to a single national characteristic risks obscuring more than it reveals.

To muddy the waters even more, resistance itself is not binary. “Will Taiwan fight?” or “Will Taiwan give up?” sounds straightforward, but what exactly are we imagining? A Chinese quarantine? A prolonged blockade? The seizure of an offshore island? Missile strikes? A full-scale invasion? Taiwanese might react very differently to each.

Even after fighting begins, attitudes may change. A population initially determined to resist might think differently after weeks of casualties, shortages, and destruction. An attack could also have the opposite effect and produce much stronger determination. The military, political leaders, and broader public may respond differently, while much could depend on whether Taiwanese believe the United States or Japan will eventually intervene.

Ultimately, there is no fixed amount of “will to fight” sitting somewhere inside Taiwanese society waiting for the right journalist, pollster, or academic to discover it. That brings us back to Shuster. His article deserves criticism where its facts, evidence, and interpretations are wrong. But the same analytical standard should apply to those challenging his conclusions.

Nobody can confidently tell us exactly what Taiwan and its people will do if China uses force. We can, however, do a much better job of examining what they are doing now and how that changes over time. Indeed, it will not tell us for certain whether Taiwan will fight. But it does give us a much better place to start.

title: Will the World Ever Take Action on Myanmar?
description: The evidence of atrocities is there. What are governments prepared to do with that knowledge?
text:
We came to Geneva for the 63rd Human Rights Council from different points in our advocacy journeys and different parts of the world, but with a shared commitment to the people of Myanmar. One of us has spent years walking the corridors of the United Nations, meeting diplomats, and pressing governments to act on the crisis in Myanmar. The other was attending the Human Rights Council for the first time, after years of documenting human rights violations in the country.

We were there for the same reason: to ask governments what they are prepared to do about Myanmar. After years of documenting atrocities, we left Geneva with a question that is becoming increasingly difficult to avoid: what happens when the evidence is already there?

Inside the Human Rights Council chamber, the scale of the crisis was once again laid bare.

The United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Türk, described a deepening crisis marked by attacks by the military junta, including airstrikes, forced conscription, arbitrary detention, sexual violence, displacement, and the weaponization of humanitarian assistance. He urged United Nations member states to refer the situation in Myanmar to the International Criminal Court through the Security Council and halt transfers of arms, ammunition, jet fuel, and dual-use items that risk facilitating violations of international law.

The head of the Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar, Nicholas Koumjian, reported that serious international crimes are being committed with greater frequency and intensity. The mechanism is continuing to collect and preserve evidence for future accountability.

At HRC63, we heard a wide range of approaches to the crisis in Myanmar.

Of the 39 governments and entities that took the floor, fewer than half – just 14 – explicitly raised accountability, justice, impunity, or international accountability mechanisms. While 20 speakers expressed broad support for stronger action, the rest of the room fragmented: eight, including Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, India, and Vietnam, appeared supportive but cautious, favoring regional engagement, dialogue, and a “Myanmar-owned or Myanmar-led” process.

Five governments – Laos, Belarus, Russia, China, and Venezuela – actively shielded the regime, emphasizing sovereignty, non-interference, and engagement with Myanmar’s authorities, while opposing international pressure.

After the session, we met with several diplomatic missions in Geneva. For us, these meetings created space for conversations about what more can be done. What we heard in the Council and in those meetings was not a lack of awareness. Myanmar is simply not a sufficiently high political priority for many governments to generate sustained action.

There are real diplomatic complications. Myanmar’s political representation remains contested, including at the United Nations, where the question of who represents the country remains unresolved. Governments also have different relationships with the military junta, the National Unity Government, ethnic resistance organizations, and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN). But these complications cannot be grounds for indefinite inaction and impunity.

In our view, a Myanmar-led or ASEAN-led process should have a major role. Humanitarian assistance is essential. But none of these should mean putting accountability or the protection of civilians on hold.

Dialogue with a brutal regime cannot become a substitute for accountability, and sovereignty cannot serve as a shield against international scrutiny.

Human rights defenders, within Myanmar and outside, are still doing their part. We continue to document violations, speak with survivors, share evidence with the Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar, and engage with the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights. Other Myanmar and regional organizations are doing the same.

Fortify Rights has documented the military’s aerial attacks on civilians, including the chain of command behind attacks in Kachin and Karenni states, and has continued to record new methods of aerial warfare.

Although more documentation is needed, what is missing is a comparable machinery of political action.

Some governments are already using some of the tools available to them. Canada maintains an arms embargo and aviation-fuel prohibition and has continued imposing targeted sanctions on Myanmar military officials and entities. The United Kingdom and the European Union have also imposed sanctions targeting aviation fuel suppliers and other entities linked to the military.

At the same time, accountability efforts are moving forward. Myanmar and Rohingya organizations have pursued universal-jurisdiction cases in Argentina, Germany, Indonesia, the Philippines, Timor-Leste, and Turkiye. In November 2024, the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Court requested an arrest warrant for Min Aung Hlaing, while in January 2026, the International Court of Justice held merits hearings in The Gambia’s genocide case against Myanmar.

And yet, from where we sit, there is still a striking gap between the evidence being gathered and meaningful accountability for crimes committed since the 2021 coup. No international court is currently prosecuting the full range of those crimes. National cases and international proceedings offer important pathways, but they do not yet amount to a comprehensive accountability process.

What stayed with us from the 63rd Human Rights Council was not a lack of information or evidence. The evidence is being collected, and governments should continue to fund human rights documentation. Cases are being pursued. Some governments are taking action. But the pieces are still not coming together at the scale needed to match the crisis.

We can continue to document, share evidence, and engage governments. But documentation can only go so far without political action. The people of Myanmar have been waiting for years, and the evidence is there. What happens next depends on what governments do with it.
tag: Myanmar crimes against humanity; Myanmar crisis; U.N. Myanmar coup response; UN Human Rights Council; United Nations

title: Xi Jinping Is Coming to the US. Why Is He Skipping the UNGA?
description: Xi’s coming to the U.S. East Coast while the United Nations’ biggest event is going on. That makes his absence all the more striking.
text:
If you read The Diplomat, you probably follow Asia-Pacific affairs – and thus you probably already know that Chinese President Xi Jinping is due to arrive in Washington, D.C. today for a much-anticipated summit with U.S. President Donald Trump.

According to the White House’s itinerary, Xi will land at Andrews Air Force Base on September 23, where he will be personally received by Trump himself. The next day, he’ll receive a formal welcome ceremony at the White House, followed by the actual summit and a state dinner. On September 25, Trump and First Lady Melania Trump will host Xi and his wife for tea; both couples will then visit the National Archives, “where they will view a variety of important records and documents significant to the American and Chinese relationship throughout history.” Then Xi and his delegation will fly home.

What’s most remarkable about this itinerary is what it doesn’t include: a stop in New York, where the United Nations’ General Assembly is currently holding its 81st session. Heads of state and government from around the world are making the trip to New York just for the UNGA, including top leaders from Bangladesh, Japan, Indonesia, Kyrgyzstan, Nepal, Mongolia, South Korea, and Vietnam, just to name a few from The Diplomat’s coverage region.

Meanwhile, Xi is making a trip across the Pacific Ocean and the entire continental U.S. and not bothering to take an extra jaunt up the coast to attend the United Nations’ most important annual event.

Instead, Vice President Han Zheng will be in New York from September 24 to 26 to represent China at the UNGA. According to China’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun, “On the sidelines of the general debate, Vice President Han will attend the High-Level Dialogue on the Fifth Anniversary of the Global Development Initiative hosted by China, and meet with [the] U.N. secretary-general, president of the 81st UNGA session, and leaders of relevant countries.”

Apparently, these are meetings Xi couldn’t be bothered to attend himself, despite being just an hour’s plane ride away.

Xi’s absence from the UNGA would seem to undermine China’s consistent rhetorical emphasis on the United Nations’ importance. China’s white paper on global governance, released in June 2026, repeatedly emphasized the U.N. as the “core” of the international order. “The United Nations is the primary platform for practicing multilateralism and advancing global governance,” the white paper declared. “Its leading position must be upheld and remain rock solid; its role can only be reinforced, not weakened.”

In the same press conference where Guo announced Han’s trip, the spokesperson repeated a similar line: “The United Nations is the core platform for global governance, and the general debate of UNGA is a vital opportunity for countries to build political consensus and coordinate multilateral actions.” But if the United Nations, and the UNGA, are so important, why can’t Xi be bothered to attend?

Xi has gone to the UNGA just once since becoming China’s top leader in late 2012. He went in 2015, to commemorate the United Nations’ 70th anniversary, and addressed the UNGA in person for the first and only time.

Notably, this coincided with Xi’s last state visit to the United States, when he included attendance at the UNGA within a broader itinerary that saw him also hold a summit with then-U.S. President Barack Obama. That makes the decision not to do the same thing in 2026 all the more notable.

In 2021, Xi gave a video address to the UNGA, in which he announced China’s Global Development Initiative. He has not delivered a speech before the UNGA since.

Perhaps most notably, Xi chose to skip last year’s UNGA – the 80th session. China puts much stock in these round-number anniversaries, pegging trips abroad and major upgrades in bilateral relations to special dates. Remember that Xi took the time to attend the United Nations’ 70th anniversary in person. That wasn’t an aberration – China’s top leader had attended every decennial anniversary of the U.N. since Jiang Zemin in 1995. That made Xi’s absence from the 80th anniversary in 2025 all the more conspicuous.

As I wrote at the time:

Instead [of attending the UNGA], Xi stayed in China, where he “extended festive greetings” for the farmers’ harvest celebration and visited Urumqi to mark the 70th anniversary of the founding of the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region.

Those events were duly splashed across the front-page headlines of People’s Daily, the official newspaper of the Chinese Communist Party. Premier Li Qiang’s presence at UNGA received just a one-line mention on the front page for September 24.

Xi has also stopped announcing China’s major global initiatives at the United Nations. He unveiled the Global Development Initiative at the UNGA back in 2021, albeit in a virtual speech. But in 2025, Xi chose to announce the new Global Governance Initiative – even more directly related to the United Nations’ mission – at the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit held in China a month before the UNGA.

Similarly, China founded its own World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO) – “an independent intergovernmental international organization that… aims to promote international cooperation and global governance on artificial intelligence” – rather than working within the United Nations to legitimize its efforts toward the same ends. China announced WAICO at its own AI conference, rather than at the U.N. Global Dialogue on AI Governance held a month earlier.

Meanwhile, as Trump reduces U.S. funding for the United Nations, China hasn’t stepped up to fill the gap. Its own U.N.-assessed contributions have been chronically late and remain a mere fraction of what the United States was contributing prior to Trump taking office.

No matter the lip service China pays to the United Nations’ “core role” in global governance, Beijing clearly prefers to give attention, money, and prestige to settings where it exerts more control. That includes China-led groups like the SCO, but also purely bilateral meetings like the summit with Trump.

Nikkei Asia theorized that Xi’s decision to skip the UNGA was an attempt to position China as a true equal to the United States – a message that apparently would have been diluted by Xi rubbing elbows with leaders from smaller states in New York. That in itself is telling. For all China’s rhetoric about a multipolar world where all states have equal representation – and equal say – in global governance, when push comes to shove Beijing defaults to a different perspective.

As China’s top diplomat put it, fairly undiplomatically, in a heated ASEAN meeting back in 2010: “China is a big country and other countries are small countries, and that’s just a fact.” One of the perks of being a “big country,” as Trump has repeatedly shown, is the privilege of ignoring the United Nations to pursue national interests in other settings.

title: ‘Xi, You’re Not Welcome’: As Trump Hosts China’s Leader, Thousands Protest in Washington
description: Over 3,000 Tibetans, Chinese dissidents, Uyghurs, Hong Kongers, and other groups joined protests during Xi’s state visit, calling for human rights and political freedom.
text:
On September 24, more than 3,000 Tibetans gathered in Washington to protest Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to the White House, in what organizers described as the largest-ever Tibetan rally in North America. The rally was organized by Tibetan Youth Congress (TYC) and supported by other Tibetan activist organizations.

The protesters came with demands that they said should be part of the China-U.S. relationship: that Trump raise human rights with Xi, that China release political and religious prisoners, and that Tibetans be allowed to preserve their language and culture. The group also demanded the repeal of China’s new Ethnic Unity and Progress Promotion Law, which took effect in July and promotes what Beijing calls a shared sense of identity among China’s 56 ethnic groups. Tibetan activists say the law further advances Beijing’s efforts to assimilate Tibetans into Chinese identity. Chinese authorities say the law protects minority rights while promoting ethnic unity.

“Human rights should not be left outside of their talks,” said Tencho Gyatso, president of the International Campaign for Tibet. “The Tibetans, the Uyghurs, the Hong Kongers, the Taiwanese, we want to make sure our voices are also heard there.”

The demonstration unfolded as Xi made his first state visit to Washington in more than a decade. U.S. President Donald Trump welcomed him to the White House for talks that touched on AI, trade, and other issues, while the two governments were also dealing with disputes over Taiwan, Iran and rare earths. Trump hosted Xi at a state dinner on the evening of September 24.

Outside, Tibetan protesters marched through the capital carrying Tibetan flags and signs reading “Xi Jinping is guilty of genocide” and “Tibet was never a part of China.” By the end of the day, the demonstration had expanded into a coalition that included Uyghur, Southern Mongolian, Chinese democracy, Taiwanese, Burmese, Falun Gong, and Chinese Christian groups, all people that have suffered under the Chinese Communist Party.

Protesters holds signs criticizing Chinese President Xi Jinping during a demonstration in Washington, D.C., on September 24, 2026. Photo by Tsering Dolka Gurung

The rally began at about 9 a.m. outside the Chinese Embassy, where protesters gathered before marching toward the U.S. Capitol. Police were deployed around the demonstration as the crowd assembled. The protesters then moved through Washington, with Connecticut Avenue closed to accommodate the march. The crowd passed through Dupont Circle before arriving at the Capitol, where several speakers addressed the demonstrators.

Former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi and Rep. Jim McGovern, a Massachusetts Democrat, joined the rally. McGovern called for human rights to be included in Trump’s discussions with Xi.

“No Xi in D.C. without human rights,” McGovern told the crowd.

He also criticized Republican lawmakers, who he said had declined to join efforts urging the administration to press China on human rights. “Are they afraid of Donald Trump? Are they afraid he’ll be offended if they ask him to ask Xi to release prisoners of conscience?” McGovern said.

U.S. Rep. Jim McGovern speaks at a rally outside the U.S. Capitol during a demonstration against Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington, D.C., on September 24, 2026. Photo by Tsering Dolka Gurung.

Pelosi also spoke in support of the protesters, calling attention to human rights in Tibet and urging the release of prisoners of conscience.

For many Tibetan protesters, Thursday’s demonstration was also shaped by the death of Lobga Rangzen, a longtime Tibetan independence activist who died after self-immolating outside the United Nations in New York on July 2. Rangzen, 52, had called for Tibetan independence and unity in a final message before setting himself on fire.

Jigme Ugen, president of the Tibetan National Congress, said the size of the demonstration showed that the Tibetan independence movement remained active.

“This is the biggest gathering, as such, to not just protest Xi Jinping, but also to tell the world and the U.S. government that the Tibetan movement, and the call for Tibetan independence, is still very much alive,” Ugen said.

Tsering Chomphel, president of the Tibetan Youth Congress, who traveled from India for the protest, said people had come from New York, New Jersey, Connecticut, Philadelphia, Boston, Chicago, Vermont, and Toronto. “This is the first-ever mass gathering in North America. Whenever Xi Jinping or a Chinese delegation visits, TYC will be there to make sure our voices are heard.”

Tibetan protesters hold flags outside the U.S. Capitol during a demonstration against Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington, D.C., on September 24, 2026.Photo by Tsering Dolka Gurung.

Seventeen Tibetans had set off on foot from the United Nations headquarters in New York on September 17, walking through Philadelphia before reaching Washington on the evening of September 23 – the same day Xi arrived. Rangzen Dolkar, one of the walkers, said the journey was meant to raise awareness about Tibet and Pawo Lobga Rangzen’s death.

Pawo is an honorary title given to any individual who has sacrificed their lives through self-immolation to bring attention to Tibet’s situation.

“I am a mother of two kids, and I left my kids home. We all took off from work and left on this journey,” she said. “People stop us on the way and ask us what we’re doing because they see the flag. It gives us an opportunity to speak about Tibet and what Pawo Lobga Rangzen sacrificed his life for.”

After the rally at the Capitol, the protestors marched to Franklin Park, half a mile from the White House, where speakers from the Uyghur, Taiwanese, Burmese, and Hong Kong communities addressed the crowd.

Misran Dolan, president of the Uyghur American Association, framed the gathering as a common demand for political and religious freedom. “Free the Uyghurs. Free the Tibetans. Keep Taiwan free. Keep Hong Kong free. Keep China free,” Dolan told the crowd.

“All of us here have moved away from our homelands,” he said. “And now we’re here in the United States … to exercise those rights – freedom of speech, freedom of expression, freedom of religion.” About 200 members of the Uyghur community attended, according to Dolan.

Protesters hold Taiwanese, Tibetan, and Uyghur flags and signs during a demonstration against Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington, D.C., on September 24, 2026. Photo by Tsering Dolka Gurung.

The gathering also included Chinese democracy activists. About 50 members of the Democratic Party of China traveled from Los Angeles, according to Zheng Zhou, a member of the group.

“We want Xi Jinping to stop persecuting people. We want him to free Jimmy Lai, Ding Jiaxi,” said Zhou. Lai, the billionaire founder of Apple Daily, Hong Kong’s most prominent pro-democracy newspaper, and a vocal critic of the Chinese Communist Party was sentenced to 20 years in prison earlier this February after being convicted of conspiracy to commit sedition and collusion with foreign forces. Marco Rubio, the U.S. secretary of state, had urged the CCP to grant him humanitarian parole calling the sentence unjust and tragic,

Daniel Zhao, a Chinese Christian affiliated with an underground church – churches that operate outside China’s state-controlled religious system and whose members can face detention and other restrictions from authorities – spoke about the persecution of Christians in China.

“Our church leaders have to stay in Chinese jails, leaving their families praying and crying at home, just because they wanted to practice their religion peacefully in China,” Zhao said.

Cynthia Sun, a senior researcher at the Falun Dafa Information Center, said her friends from the United States had family members killed in Chinese prison through forced organ harvesting. “When they went to see their dead parents at the mortuary, their bodies were split open, there were stitches, and they were missing a heart or a kidney,” she said.

Falun Gong is a spiritual practice that emerged in China in the 1990s and was banned by Chinese authorities in 1999. The Chinese government has been accused of forcibly harvesting organs from imprisoned Falun Gong practitioners. In 2019, the China Tribunal, an independent people’s tribunal, concluded that forced organ harvesting has occurred in China on a significant scale and that Falun Gong practitioners were likely the main source of organs.

Sun described the persecution of Falun Gong practitioners as something that had followed her throughout her life.

“I was born in July 1999, the month and year that the persecution began,” she said. “When I graduated high school, I thought the persecution would end by the time I got to college. But now I’m in grad school. I’m engaged, I’m getting married, and the persecution is still going on.”

“I don’t want this to be the burden of my children, my grandchildren,” she said.

For the Tibetan organizers, the rally was not simply a call for another statement from Washington.

“Tibetans are not looking for a statement at this point,” Ugen said. “The U.S. government already has enough laws that have been passed by Congress, and all they need to do is to actually stand on those.” In 2020, Trump signed the Tibetan Policy and Support Act of 2020 into law, which strengthened U.S. policy on Tibet.

Later in the evening, protesters marched toward the White House.

Police had erected barricades near 14th Street and Pennsylvania Avenue, separating the demonstrators from another group of people carrying Chinese flags and supporting Xi. The two groups shouted at each other from opposite sides of the barricades. Tibetan protesters waved Tibetan flags and chanted as the other group shouted back across the street. The confrontation grew increasingly loud, but there was no physical altercation.

Xi Jinping supporters gather behind police barricades during demonstrations surrounding Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington, D.C., on September 24, 2026. Metropolitan Police Officers stand between the groups. Photo by Tsering Dolka Gurung.

Inside the White House, Xi was attending the state dinner hosted by Trump. Outside, the opposing groups remained separated by police barricades.

For Ugen, the demonstration was ultimately about making sure Tibet was not left out of the China-U.S. conversation.

“The basics of the conversation is beyond Taiwan, AI, trade,” Ugen said. “We are telling the world that if there’s justice in the world, it should come through Tibet.”

This article originally misspelled a name as Daniel Zhou instead of Daniel Zhao.
tag: China Human Rights; Tibetans in the U.S.; Trump-Xi summit; U.S. anti-China protests; Xi U.S. state visit protests

title: A Raid on a Gay Bar Risks Taiwan’s LGBTQ-Friendly Reputation
description: An attorney says authorities overstepped legal bounds, and activists warn of discrimination ahead of Asia's largest Pride event.
text:
A patron at a well-known gay bar in Taipei recalls being “extremely shocked and confused” when around 30 police staged a dramatic raid on October 3 and took dozens of people away for questioning.

The raid occurred just four weeks before Taipei’s annual Pride celebration. Footage of officers using demeaning language and what attorneys have described as unlawful treatment spurred an estimated 100 protesters to march on precinct headquarters the next day.

While several officers have been disciplined, LGBTQ+ advocates say the issue goes beyond the actions of a few. They are calling for structural changes to protect the rights of sexual minorities in a city that has come to be known for tolerance.

“This incident exposes a serious gap. A city can celebrate LGBTQ+ communities publicly but still not ensure everyone is treated equally by institutions like the police,” Sean Du, secretary-general of the Taiwan Tongzhi Hotline Association, Taiwan’s largest LGBTQ+ advocacy group, said.

Taiwan has built a reputation as one of Asia’s most LGBTQ+-friendly societies in the decades since the police crackdowns and harassment of the martial law era that ended in 1987.

Taiwan became the first in Asia to legalize same-sex marriage in 2019. For queer travelers from countries in the region where same-sex relations are stigmatized or even criminalized, Taipei has become something of a liberal bastion. The island also boasts Asia’s largest Pride parade, held annually on the last Saturday of October, with an estimated 150,000 attending last year.

The Raid

The raid targeted Commander D, a 14-year-old BDSM-themed club in Wanhua District’s Ximending area. Wanhua Precinct police said they had received 13 complaints about Commander D from members of the public between January 1 and Saturday, October 3.

Police visits are not unusual at Taipei clubs; officers typically check IDs before heading on their way. But this time officers came armed with a search warrant approved by the Taipei District Court.

Lin, 34, a clinical psychologist and founder of the independent Threads publication Taipei Rainbow Party Weekly, said he had witnessed numerous nightclub inspections before but that Saturday’s was a “fundamentally different” encounter, one that left some of his friends traumatized.

More than 30 police, including uniformed and plainclothes officers, flooded Commander D at around 4:30 p.m., stopping the music and turning on the lights, Lin said. Videos shared on social media by others showed officers ordering customers to squat down and put away their phones.

Police told the media they had found used condoms and that some customers were nude. Those not wearing clothes were not allowed to put them back on, while those who had hastily gotten dressed were made to remove their clothes to preserve evidence, Lin recounted.

Of the 58 customers police say were inside, around two-thirds were shirtless and most of the rest in their underwear. Only a few were completely naked, Lin said.

Police did not initially display the warrant to those gathered, witnesses said. A video shared on social media shows police repeatedly ordering customers to stop talking, telling them to challenge the operation in court.

Officers also mocked a man for being in a wheelchair, questioning whether he was able to have sex. When a manager came to the man’s defense, he was handcuffed and made to kneel on the floor, local media cited eyewitnesses as saying.

Patrons had their belongings searched and were subjected to a urine test for drugs. After several hours, 51 people were loaded into police vehicles and taken to the precinct for further questioning as “witnesses.”

Commander D did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Did Police Overstep Their Authority?

Several police actions that day were legally problematic, according to Lingwei Li, founder and managing lawyer at Zenkuan Law Firm and founder of the Taiwan Nonbinary Queer Sluts, Taiwan’s first support group for nonbinary people.

A warrant to search the premises does not automatically entitle police to search every customer’s property, and individual searches require separate criteria or consent, Li said.

Compulsory drug tests, meanwhile, should be limited to persons placed under arrest, not witnesses. Li told The Diplomat they were not aware of any legal basis for barring witnesses from using their phones.

Police also blurred the line between a witness and a suspect, Li said. A witness cannot simply be detained unless they fail to appear without good reason after being formally summoned to testify and a warrant has then been issued.

Addressing the question of nudity, Li said the Social Order Maintenance Act requires more than mere nudity to qualify as an offense, including conduct that offends public decency and continues despite a warning. “This case involves an abuse of police authority,” Li said. “Evidence indicates that the police prohibited the nude individual from putting on clothes, which also contradicts the requirement of ‘failing to heed warnings.’”

“Ordering people who were already dressed to undress is not preserving evidence. It’s humiliation.”

Officers Disciplined

Wanhua Precinct’s investigation found four officers had used inappropriate language. “They have been dealt with strictly,” the precinct told The Diplomat. Each received two reprimands. The official who supervised the operation received a demerit, while the precinct chief himself was issued two reprimands after voluntarily requesting disciplinary action.

“The precinct respects diverse communities and will undertake a thorough review of officers’ on-site enforcement procedures,” the statement said. “It will comprehensively strengthen education and training and require officers, when carrying out their duties in the future, to continue to respect the cultures of a diverse society, in order to safeguard residents’ rights and interests and prevent similar controversies from occurring again.”

No charges have been filed yet in connection with the raid. In a separate statement, police said Commander D’s owner, surnamed Zhong, 44, was referred to the Taipei District Prosecutors’ Office on suspicion of violating public decency, according to a press statement viewed by the Central News Agency.

Commander D had been in the news before. During a September 11 session at the Taipei City Council, Councilor Hung Chien-yi repeated a parent’s claim that minors were entering bars and displayed photos of a venue media identified as Commander D.

The club denied these claims and insisted its staff check IDs before allowing patrons to enter. It’s not clear if those allegations were related to the raid last week.

On October 7, a civil society group filed a criminal complaint with the Taipei District Prosecutors’ Office over alleged police misconduct during the raid, the precinct told the Diplomat. The police said the matter was now subject to investigative confidentiality.

In remarks to the press on October 4, Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an said an investigation should follow any suspected misconduct but stopped short of criticizing the Commander D search. After more footage of the operation emerged, Chiang issued an apology and said all Taipei residents are entitled to equal rights. He said he had instructed the police department to improve force discipline to prevent discrimination in the future.

Chiang’s office had not responded to a request for comment by publication time.

Discrimination

Du, the secretary general of Taiwan Tongzhi Hotline Association, believes there was “concrete discrimination” on display on October 3. “And there are sufficient grounds to investigate whether an LGBTQ+ venue was subjected to differential policing,” he told The Diplomat.

The precinct’s acknowledgment is just one step, he said. “We need to look at whether the venue’s gay and BDSM character contributed to it being presumed criminal. Would a comparable non-LGBTQ+ venue face police action with the same frequency and scale? Was it necessary to take dozens of patrons away?”

Du called for an independent investigation, arguing discrimination often goes beyond individual officers’ conduct. “We aren’t claiming every officer had an anti-LGBTQ+ motive. Discrimination also involves assumptions and unequal standards and treatment.”

The Commander D episode recalls a police investigation into Body Fresh, an LGBTQ+ venue in the city of Taichung, that subsequently closed following allegations that it was facilitating commercial sex. Advocates argued authorities had singled out the business while heterosexual-oriented venues avoided similar scrutiny.

“The similarities are frustratingly striking, and traumatizing to many in the community,” said Li, the Zenkuan Law Firm attorney. “In both cases, morality charges were applied to consensual adult conduct in a space serving LGBTQ+ people. Complaints and political pressure, not an identifiable victim, led to enforcement,” they added.

Lin, one of the eyewitnesses, believes the raid has injected energy into the upcoming Pride. “Taipei is, in fact, still friendly and still inclusive. Although society still needs some time to digest what happened in this incident, the social mobilization that followed was faster and more diverse than before,” he said.
tag: Taiwan gay bar raid; Taiwan gay rights; Taiwan LGBT; Taiwan Pride

title: A Tajik Bank Shuts Side Door for Russian Cardholders
description: Humo Bank's ultimatum to its Russian clients shows how Western sanctions can shape Tajikistan's banking sector.
text:
Tajikistan’s Humo Bank has warned its Russian clients that their cards will be blocked on October 1 unless they visit one of its offices in Tajikistan by September 30 to undergo biometric identification. “If you can’t come to Tajikistan in person and complete the identification, unfortunately, your card will be closed,” the bank told Russian news site Lenta.ru, advising clients to move their remaining balances to ruble cards before the deadline.

The bank cited the need to protect clients from fraud. A Russian client, however, told the Telegram channel Ostorozhno Novosti that the bank’s support staff explained it had decided to restrict services for “certain categories of non-resident individuals” whose cards were opened online. She said a transfer of about 300 euros had been stuck for a week and that the bank had stopped responding to her complaints. Humo offered her a new card if she traveled to Tajikistan, valid only for the duration of her legal stay and for no longer than a year.

With Visa and Mastercard gone from Russia since 2022, Russians have relied on cards issued in “friendly” countries to make payments abroad. When Kazakhstan limited non-resident cards to 12 months and required in-person issuance in January 2025, intermediaries moved their business to Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan, and Uzbekistan. Humo and the International Bank of Tajikistan began offering remotely issued five-year cards in U.S. dollars and euros, sold through intermediaries for roughly 15,000 to 70,000 rubles.

Humo is a newcomer to banking. Owned by the Japanese investment holding Gojo & Company, the former microcredit deposit organization received a full banking license from the National Bank of Tajikistan in July 2025. It was also among the few Tajik financial institutions with access to Visa Direct, a real-time payment service that became a conduit for Russian money headed to Europe. An investigation by The Bell found last year that Sberbank clients could send money to Revolut and N26 accounts through Central Asian intermediaries, with the funds appearing to originate from Dushanbe or Tashkent.

The Humo ultimatum follows a year of Western pressure on Tajik banks. In October 2025, the European Union included Dushanbe City Bank, Spitamen, and Commercebank of Tajikistan in its 19th sanctions package, targeting banks closely linked to Russia’s financial system or processing cross-border payments that support the Russian economy. The three banks held roughly a fifth of all deposits in Tajikistan, and other Tajik banks responded by restricting transfers to Russia. In December, Revolut stopped accepting top-ups from cards issued in Tajikistan, Kazakhstan, and Uzbekistan for EU residents, citing payment systems’ classification of those countries as high-risk. The EU removed the three Tajik banks from its sanctions list in April 2026, with the National Bank crediting improved compliance and anti-money laundering standards.

For Dushanbe, the stakes go well beyond fees collected from Russian cardholders. Remittances, mostly from Tajik migrants in Russia, reached $5.8 billion in 2024, or the equivalent of 45.3 percent of Tajikistan’s GDP, the highest share in the world. By the end of 2024, over 90 percent of payments in Tajik-Russian trade were settled in rubles, and the head of the National Bank said Tajik banks work only with Russian banks not under sanctions. Tajikistan needs its financial channels to Russia open and its banks connected to SWIFT and Visa at the same time.

Neither Humo nor the National Bank has said whether the decision came from regulators, payment systems, or the bank’s own risk assessment. But a young bank that watched three of its peers cut off from European counterparties has every reason to shed remotely onboarded Russian clients before Brussels or Visa forces its hand. Russians will likely take their business to Kyrgyz and Uzbek banks, as they did when Kazakhstan closed its doors, until those banks face the same pressure.
tag: reached; Humo Bank; Russia SWIFT; Russian invasion of Ukraine; Tajikistan banking sector; Tajikistan sanctions evasion

title: ‘A Tower of Jelly’
description: The United Nations, U Thant, and the 1967 Arab-Israeli War.
text:
“What is the use of a fire brigade which vanishes from the scene as soon as the first smoke and flames appear?” asked Abba Eban, addressing an emergency session of the United Nations General Assembly soon after the 1967 Arab-Israeli War had ended.

In a fiery speech, the foreign minister of Israel lashed out at the U.N. for pulling peacekeeping troops out of the Sinai Peninsula and the Gaza Strip. The “disastrously swift” withdrawal, Eban argued, had endangered the “national survival” of the Jewish state.

Israel’s Six-Day War was nevertheless a spectacular military success. The Israel Defense Forces neutralized three Arab armies (Egypt, Jordan, and Syria) within a week and occupied the Sinai Peninsula, the Gaza Strip, the West Bank, East Jerusalem, and the Golan Heights.

In his latest book, “Peacemaker,” historian Thant Myint-U offers new insights on the U.N.’s role in the events leading up to the six-day conflict.

The book’s title refers to U Thant, the author’s grandfather. As U.N. secretary-general, the Burmese diplomat was the chief “firefighter” charged with deploying peacekeeping troops to conflict zones. The “most successful peacekeeping operation” was UNEF (United Nations Emergency Force), which had maintained a fragile peace along the border between Egypt and Israel for more than a decade.

When the Egyptian military sent the U.N. an informal communication in mid-May requesting a withdrawal of peacekeeping troops, Thant faced a dilemma. Denying Cairo’s request would violate Egypt’s sovereignty, but removing the forces might jeopardize the U.N.’s conflict-prevention mission. The Secretary-General acquiesced after receiving an official letter from the foreign minister. However, as Thant was negotiating UNEF’s exit, Israeli jets strafed a convoy in the Egyptian-administered Gaza Strip, killing three soldiers.

Thant faced “a deluge of criticism” for the troop withdrawal and for his inability to counter “Egyptian bluster.” Former British Prime Minister Alec Douglas-Home called the Secretary-General’s visit to Egypt in late May a “dreadful mistake.” When Thant landed in Cairo, President Gamal Abdel Nasser was already in war mode, having closed the Straits of Tiran, a vital shipping route for Israel. A Western diplomat quoted in The Wall Street Journal called the U.N. chief “a tower of jelly.”

Gideon Rafael, the Israeli ambassador to the U.N., defended his friend in the Hebrew-language newspaper Maariv, saying, “U Thant is not responsible for the situation in the Middle East.”

In a chapter titled “Gaza and the Sinai,” the author highlights an intriguing detail on how misinformation played a role in the lead-up to the war. Nasser’s actions were influenced by false intelligence reports relayed by Moscow and Damascus about a buildup of Israeli forces along the Syrian border. Arab leaders did little to verify the claims, even as U.N. observers cast doubt on the report’s veracity.

“The Syrians could have looked from the Golan Heights (which they controlled) down into Israel and seen that there were no troop concentrations, as alleged, but they were happy to pass on to Cairo the misinformation as it confirmed their longstanding claim of an imminent threat,” commented the author.

In 1959, U Thant was the frontrunner for the top U.N. job as the only candidate acceptable to both Israel and the Arab states. Golda Meir, then Israel’s foreign minister, indicated that Thant was Tel Aviv’s sole choice for the position. However, the first Asian secretary-general of the U.N. did not have a “feel for the passions surrounding the conflict” once war broke out in the Middle East.

His low-key style worked when both parties were motivated to defuse a confrontation. During the Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962, the U.N. Secretary-General helped create “an opening for diplomacy.” U Thant “injected himself into the very heart of the simmering crisis,” the author wrote, giving the Soviet Union and the U.S. a face-saving option to back away from a nuclear showdown. In 1965, the veteran diplomat was nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize for his mediation efforts.

The goodwill earned during his first term had evaporated by the late 1960s. In certain circles, Thant was considered “Israel’s nemesis,” and his relationship with Washington deteriorated. The secretary-general was a critic of the Vietnam War and spoke out against the Johnson Administration’s bombing campaign in Southeast Asia.

“Thant retired, then virtually disappeared,” wrote his grandson, almost as if he was “airbrushed from history.”

The former Secretary-General spent his final years in a colonial-style house outside New York City with “a meditation room, a glass-enclosed annex with images of the Buddha and views of the Westchester countryside.”
tag: Arab-Israeli War; Israel-Palestine conflict; Myanmar diplomacy; Six-Day War; Thant Myint-U; U Thant; United Nations; United Nations General Assembly

title: A US Pivot Toward Commercial Espionage?
description: However justified or inevitable it might be, this represents a major shift in how the U.S. has thought about intellectual property for the last three decades.
text:
Washington has spent three decades lecturing the world about intellectual property protection. Now it looks as if the United States wants to start stealing economic secrets from China and elsewhere.

According to the Washington Post, the Pentagon is standing up an intelligence unit geared toward the acquisition of economic secrets from foreign companies to benefit American companies. Although details remain hazy, the unit is expected to use operatives disguised as private business persons in order to infiltrate foreign companies and appropriate their commercial secrets. This shift was presaged in a Foreign Affairs article by David Cohen, former deputy director of the CIA.

This represents a significant, if not necessarily unwarranted, change in U.S. commercial espionage policy. In its recent history the United States has refrained from direct theft of economic secrets. During the Obama administration the United States attempted to establish norms of commercial espionage that rejected thefts of intellectual property that would award private firms with stolen secrets. The theft of information in order to improve the strategic position of the U.S. was fine; handing stolen goods to an American firm was across the line. This was in accord with a broader U.S. diplomatic effort to improve intellectual property protection across the world.

That the Trump administration would reject such norm-building efforts is unsurprising. The administration has made it clear that it does not believe that anything approaching a “fair” system of global trade exists; the United States has leverage over its trading partners and should use that leverage in order to generate favorable trade arrangements. It is also clear that while Chinese trade policy and practice has become more complex, especially with respect to intellectual property protection, Beijing never accepted anti-espionage norms. China would of course be a primary target for such espionage, especially in fields such as artificial intelligence.

But the effort also suggests that the Pentagon has no confidence that U.S. firms will remain ahead of Chinese and other foreign firms on the innovation curve. The Obama administration’s policy reflected the convenient reality that U.S. companies were, by and large, well ahead of most of their international competitors. Playing “fair” thus benefitted the United States more than it benefitted anyone else. The Pentagon now believes (probably correctly) that America’s technological advantage is not as secure as it would like.

While aggressive industrial espionage is obviously in contrast with some of the norms of the liberal international order, it is not exactly unprecedented for liberal democratic states to play hardball on technology theft. France, for example, has long conducted espionage to benefit French firms, to the endless frustration of French partners. South Korea and Japan have long made light technology appropriation a key part of their industrial strategies. And at its inception, even the United States undertook aggressive steps to steal foreign intellectual property, a practice that paused only when the US achieved a dominant technological position.

In any eventuality, this change in U.S. espionage policy, however justified or inevitable it might be, represents a major shift in how the United States has thought about intellectual property for the last three decades. Moreover, given the technological challenge that China represents to the United States, it seems unlikely that a future administration will reverse this effort.
tag: China IP theft; China-US economic espionage; commercial espionage; economic espionage; Espionage; Intellectual Property; intellectual property protection

title: A Warm Welcome for US Secretary of State in Central Asia
description: Not only can Rubio avoid the most pressing international crises by jetting off to Central Asia, but he – and the Trump administration more broadly – were guaranteed to receive a warm welcome in the region.
text:
As U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio departed the U.S. capital on October 17, bound for Uzbekistan and India, a journalist asked, “With everything going on in the world and with crisis all over, why are you choosing now, at this time, to go to Uzbekistan?”

Rubio replied that it was the time that worked for the Central Asians. “This is an important relationship,” he added without expounding on that importance.

In response to questions from the Associated Press regarding Rubio’s schedule, the State Department said the secretary’s “responsibility is not to generate a public profile around every challenge; it is to help the president develop and execute a strategy that advances American interests. Some of the most consequential diplomatic work takes place outside the public spotlight.”

The AP’s October 18 article was titled “Rubio heads to Central Asia as some wonder if he’s keeping the most pressing matters at a distance.” Rubio is involved in discussions on a blooming array of international crises, from Iran to China, Gaza to Ukraine, both in his role as secretary of state but also as national security adviser. But he’s not the public face of any of those issues, as the AP argued.

“The Iran, Gaza, and the Russia-Ukraine conflicts each demand serious attention, but they cannot be approached in isolation from the president’s broader national security objectives,” the State Department told the AP, pushing back against the implication that Rubio was avoiding tackling politically risky issues publicly. “The right question is not whether the secretary is visible enough on a particular issue.”

Not only can Rubio avoid the most pressing international crises by jetting off to Central Asia, but he – and the Trump administration more broadly – were guaranteed to receive a warm welcome in the region. There is no free press in Samarkand lobbing difficult questions. There are no allies feeling sour about how much Washington has changed. Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, in particular, have been enthusiastic to endorse Trump administration initiatives, such as the Board of Peace, that traditional U.S. allies have avoided.

In Samarkand, Rubio commented to the media that “Central Asia has simply not received the level of attention from our policymakers over the last 20 years that it deserves. But that’s changing. That’s why we’re here now.” That’s a common refrain from the Trump administration, but it does not match reality.

U.S. foreign policy regarding Central Asia over the last decade has been fairly consistent, as epitomized by the 11-year-old C5+1 format that brought Rubio to Samarkand in the first place to meet with the foreign ministers of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan.

The format was launched in 2015 when then-U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry visited all five regional countries in one trip – a feat Rubio promised to repeat last year during celebrations marking the C5+1’s 10th anniversary. While Rubio did meet bilaterally with the Central Asian foreign ministers, his only regional stop was in Uzbekistan.

The overarching consistency of U.S. policy toward Central Asia does not mean nothing has changed. No longer do U.S. officials mention human rights or press freedom, areas which Central Asia’s autocratic governments score poorly on. And the Trump administration’s transactional style and its focus on business deals resonates with regional states, even as it narrows relations to the economic sphere.

When Rubio’s trip to Uzbekistan was first announced in a late September press release from the U.S. Embassy in India – the U.S. ambassador to India is Sergio Gor, who also wears the hat of special envoy for South and Central Asian Affairs – it remarked that the secretary would be traveling with “a historic business delegation of more than 100 American companies.”

When the trip’s dates were announced in an October 13 press release, the delegation had become “over 200 business leaders.”

In Samarkand, Rubio referred to the commercial delegation as “incredible,” with representatives of almost 300 American businesses joining.

On October 14, The Diplomat had asked the State Department if it had a list of the participating businesses. That question went unanswered.

RFE/RL reported that the delegation would include representatives from Boeing, Citibank, and Franklin Templeton, “as well as businesses operating in critical minerals and other strategic sectors.”

In comments to RFE/RL, Daniel Rosenblum, formerly deputy assistant secretary of state for Central Asia from 2014 to 2019 and then U.S. ambassador to Uzbekistan (2019-2022) and Kazakhstan (2022-2025), noted that the secretary of state’s large business delegation was unusual but “may lead to more successes in terms of deals being signed and new investments.”

He added, however, that “the realities of investing in Central Asia remain the same.” He pointed to “the realities of distance, logistics, financing, finding a good partner. All of those things remain the same, regardless of whether you have 100 companies, 200 companies, or 20 companies.”

The joint statement published on October 19 – titled “C5+1: Historic Partnership, Prosperous Future” – concluded with this: “We envision C5+1 cooperation that continues to deliver regional solutions to global challenges.”

Of course, per usual with the Trump administration, those challenges don’t include climate change, a major complicating issue for regional states bent on building their future economies on the back of AI and mining, both of which are water and energy-intensive industries. And they didn’t touch on human rights, either.

Instead, the statement highlighted trade and connectivity, specifically the Trans-Caspian Trade Route, as well as security. It references “untapped natural resources” and states, “we will combine our strengths to be a collective, powerful driver of regional energy sector development.”
tag: C5+1; Central Asia; Marco Rubio; U.S. Central Asia policy

title: A Woman Exposed China’s Cat-Abuse Networks – and Paid a Terrible Price
description: When the law lags behind, citizens end up doing investigative work themselves, and pay for it when the people they expose strike back.
text:
In April, a 29-year-old woman traveling in Hainan swallowed a bottle of pills in a hotel room. Two days earlier, a fellow volunteer had told her that her national ID number, her parents’ home address, and her grandparents’ phone numbers were circulating online. Her offense, in the eyes of the people who posted her and her family’s private information, was reporting cat abusers to the police.

The woman goes by the alias Zhima. She had spent early 2026 investigating networks devoted to torturing and killing cats on camera, working with other volunteers to gather evidence, identify participants, and repeatedly bring their findings to police. What happened to her afterward illustrates a recurring problem in Chinese online governance: when the law lags behind a form of harm, citizens end up doing the investigative work themselves, and pay for it when the people they expose strike back.

Zhima’s involvement began almost by accident. According to Southern Metropolis Daily (Nandu), on January 4, she was in a pet-owners’ chat group when strangers flooded in, posted graphic videos of cats being mutilated, and renamed the group to advertise cat abuse. She reported it to Shanghai police on January 8, and the case was opened as an administrative matter.

That report drew her deeper into the world she had stumbled onto. Volunteers who track these networks describe a tiered structure: joining the most restricted core groups reportedly requires a “pledge of allegiance” (投名状) in the form of an unedited video of the applicant abusing a cat, a practice Chinese media have documented for years.

Zhima and fellow volunteers spent the following months identifying suspects and pushing police in multiple cities to act. One man she reported, a Jiangxi university student surnamed Qiu, kept posting abuse videos even after police opened a case against him.

Instead, it was Zhima who faced consequences. On April 8, a volunteer told Zhima her ID information had been leaked. Within days, her employer, education history, and her family’s identity numbers and addresses were circulating online, according to Nandu. Strangers were seen photographing her family’s home. The next day, in that Hainan hotel room, Zhima attempted suicide; she was found and rescued, Taiwan’s World Journal reported.

The harassment continued. Chat screenshots her father shared with Cover News showed vulgar doctored images, made using her profile photo, circulating in group chats. Rumors falsely claimed she had shared explicit photos of herself. Her father said the leaks did not come only from the cat-abuse networks: some appeared to originate from within the volunteer community itself, from people who had gained trust as fellow investigators before leaking information.

On July 17, overwhelmed by the renewed harassment, Zhima attempted suicide again and was hospitalized.

Accountability came slowly and unevenly. Qiu was placed under 10 days of administrative detention and expelled from his university on May 14, Tencent News reported. Shanghai police separately opened a criminal case against him on April 17 over the leak of Zhima’s personal information. But as of her father’s interview in July, whoever first obtained and circulated her family’s identity documents remained unidentified and unpunished.

Despite public demand for such a law following high-profile cases of animal abuse, China has no standalone national law against animal cruelty. Qian Yefang, a law professor at Zhongnan University of Economics and Law, has told reporters that while existing statutes cover wildlife, livestock, and laboratory animals, companion animals like cats and dogs fall into a regulatory gap with no dedicated law of their own. Police are left relying on public order and cybersecurity statutes, an approach that works case by case but offers no consistent standard.

One local government tried to close that gap this year, then quickly backed away. In March, Sanming, in Fujian province, published a draft regulation that would have been China’s first local rule explicitly banning abuse and abandonment of “companion animals.” Less than a month later, before the public comment period ended, the draft was quietly taken down with no official explanation, Hong Kong’s The Standard reported.

Legal experts cited in that report noted a related weakness: even where rules exist, the absence of specific penalties in China’s Public Security Administration Punishments Law makes them hard to enforce.

The gap in animal-protection law that pushes accountability onto volunteer investigators, and another gap in the legal system offers little protection to those investigators once exposed. Some of the doxxing reportedly took place on Telegram, outside the platforms Chinese authorities can police directly, helping explain why the trail went cold.

China can punish individual animal abusers, case by case. Its personal-information protections offer little accountability for those who release others’ personal information out of spite. Until that changes, citizens like Zhima will keep shouldering investigative work the state has left undone, with far less protection than the people they investigate.
tag: China animal cruelty; China animal welfare; China civil society; China doxxing; China personal data protection

title: Afghanistan and the BLA’s Evolving Capabilities
description: Reported discussions in Kandahar point to a possible expansion of the BLA’s external support networks as the group comes under pressure in Pakistan.
text:
On October 1, Pakistan’s military said that representatives of several militant groups had met in Kandahar in August to discuss coordinating manpower and operations against Pakistani security forces. Military spokesperson Lt. Gen. Ahmad Sharif Chaudhry said the meeting was chaired by Mullah Shirleen, the Taliban-appointed governor of Kandahar, and involved representatives of the Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA) seeking additional fighters from networks associated with Hafiz Gul Bahadur, a Pakistani militant leader based in North Waziristan. A separate intelligence report identified figures linked to al-Qaida in the Indian Subcontinent (AQIS) among those present.

For the BLA, the significance of the meeting lies less in the presence of other militant groups than in what access to Afghanistan could provide the organization: additional manpower, relationships with established militant networks, and a deeper operating environment beyond Balochistan. The reported discussions therefore point to a possible expansion of the BLA’s external support networks at a time when the group has been developing more sophisticated operational capabilities.

Afghan officials denied that the meeting took place, and the allegations have not been independently established. Pakistan has long accused the Taliban government of sheltering militants, and relations between the two countries are openly hostile. Fighting in October 2025 killed dozens and nearly closed the border; cross-border strikes resumed in February 2026 and continued intermittently through September. Each side’s claims therefore deserve caution. But we can still consider the basic question: what role is Afghanistan playing in the BLA’s evolving military capabilities?

A United Nations Security Council monitoring report published in August found that BLA members had access to U.S.- and NATO-origin equipment left behind in Afghanistan, including M4 and M16 rifles, reconnaissance drones, night-vision devices, and thermal equipment. The report also cited information from a member state that BLA members had trained alongside Tehreek-e-Taliban (TTP) personnel at facilities in Afghanistan, including in drone and urban warfare.

The BLA’s January 2026 offensive illustrated these capabilities being put to use in its operations. On January 31, the group claimed simultaneous attacks across Balochistan, including Quetta, Gwadar, Noshki and Panjgur. Pakistan’s military said 18 civilians and 15 security personnel died and that its forces killed 92 militants, while the BLA said it killed 84 security personnel. Neither tally has been independently confirmed.

A February assessment reported that the group had used drones, satellite communications, and U.S.-made weapons, linking some of the weaponry to equipment left behind in Afghanistan. That does not mean every drone or rifle came from there, however, since commercial drones, communications equipment, and weapons can be obtained through multiple channels.

One such channel is Balochistan’s western border with Iran. BLA and Balochistan Liberation Front (BLF) members have reportedly maintained a presence in Iran’s Sistan-Baluchestan province, and in January 2024 Pakistan struck locations there that it identified as belonging to the two groups. The BLF denied having hideouts there, and there is no established evidence that Iran supplies the BLA with weapons. Afghanistan is different, because the U.N. report documents both equipment access and training.

The BLA’s outreach to Kandahar may also reflect pressure rather than strength. The Associated Press, which saw the intelligence report, paraphrased the document as saying that “BLA representatives told participants that Pakistani military operations had left the group short of fighters and resources.” According to the report, Afghan intelligence officials responded by assuring the BLA that militants with the TTP and AQIS could provide manpower, weapons, and logistical support for operations in Balochistan.

The same report alleged that Afghan and Indian intelligence officials helped arrange the meeting. India has consistently denied backing the BLA, so that claim also warrants scrutiny. Taken together, however, the reported discussions suggest that the BLA may be looking to Afghanistan not simply as a sanctuary, but as a source of personnel, equipment, and connections that could help offset pressure from Pakistani military operations.

Meanwhile, Pakistan has escalated its response to the Taliban’s support for militant groups. Hours before the army’s briefing, Pakistan said it had carried out airstrikes in Helmand and Kunar provinces, while on September 24 it reported strikes on 10 locations in Kandahar, Paktia, and Khost. Such airstrikes may disrupt specific sites, but they do not by themselves cut the flow of weapons, training and recruits.

Three indicators will help clarify the extent of Afghanistan’s support for the BLA: independent verification of the Kandahar meeting, further U.N. monitoring of equipment and training links, and whether the group’s use of drones and coordinated assaults expands beyond the scale documented in earlier operations. The evidence of BLA access to equipment and networks in Afghanistan is significant. What remains unproven is how much of the group’s growing operational sophistication can be attributed to that access.

For Pakistan, the way forward is to address the BLA threat without reducing the wider Balochistan issue to a security response alone. Preventing militant groups from using Afghanistan as a source of recruits, training, and equipment will require continued engagement with Afghan authorities, particularly over the TTP and other groups operating from Afghan territory.

At the same time, greater attention to the security, economic and political concerns of Baloch communities can help separate the grievances of local populations from the armed groups seeking to exploit them. A combination of diplomacy with Kabul, stronger border coordination, and targeted counterterrorism measures, alongside greater engagement with communities in Balochistan, would give Pakistan a more sustainable way to contain cross-border militant networks while reducing the risk of further regional escalation.
