title: Afghanistan’s Wakhan Transit Road Is a Long Shot to Connect with China
description: The road has been officially inaugurated, but China and the Taliban have very different views of its function.
text:
On October 4, Taliban officials inaugurated the 121-kilometer-long Wakhan Transit Road connecting Afghanistan to China via the Wakhan Corridor after approximately three years of construction work. The road stretches from Afghanistan’s Broghil border area, on the Afghanistan-Pakistan border, along Badakhshan province’s Wakhan district, finally reaching the border with China. According to Afghanistan’s de facto government under the Taliban, beyond China, the road will connect the country with third parties like Central Asian countries and global markets.

This corridor is expected to play a significant role for Afghanistan’s trade as well as its regional transit. Its opening marks an important milestone for the Taliban since the corridor was ignored for years due to security concerns.

A remote region in northeast Afghanistan, the Wakhan Corridor is 350 kilometers long and 13 to 65 km wide. The corridor, which shares borders with Pakistan (through the Durand Line, which the Taliban has started referring to as a “hypothetical” line), Tajikistan, and China, was created as a buffer zone between the Russian and British empires in 1895-96 when the Anglo-Russian Boundary Commission awarded the area to Afghanistan. Once a part of the famous Silk Road trade route, the Wakhan Corridor has been closed for regular transit for almost a century now.

Taliban Minister of Rural Rehabilitation and Development Abdul Latif Mansour, speaking at the inauguration ceremony, said that the road held “political, economic, and strategic significance” for Afghanistan. “The Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan has prioritized such public projects, especially in provinces that are most in need,” Mansour said, according to Tolo News. He further emphasized the homegrown nature of the project, saying, “There are no foreign engineers or advisers; all the engineers are Afghans.”

Governor of Badakhshan Rahmatullah Najib highlighted the road’s opening as a milestone. “After 45 years of war in the country, the Afghan people are witnessing the completion of such a major project in one of Afghanistan’s most remote areas,” Tolo News paraphrased Najib as saying.

This project is said to have cost 365 million Afghanis ($5.6 million) and was funded by the Taliban’s Ministry of Rural Rehabilitation and Development.

According to Afghanistan’s Deputy Prime Minister for Economic Affairs’ website, this trade route will benefit Afghanistan by providing direct access to imports from and exports to China. The minister highlighted that China is Afghanistan’s largest trading partner, with annual trade exceeding $1 billion between the two countries. The website claimed that the Wakhan Corridor is now the “closest, safest, and most reliable” route for China to export its goods not only to Afghanistan, but to the Central Asian countries, and beyond: to the Arab world, Turkiye, Iran, and the European countries.

That assumption is questionable; China has direct borders with three Central Asian countries – Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and Tajikistan – and has invested millions in upgrading its trade and transit infrastructure to the region. China already has well-developed rail links with Kazakhstan. The Khorgos Gateway, which opened for operations in 2012 on the China-Kazakhstan border, is the world’s largest dry port. And construction on the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan (CKU) railway is underway. It’s unclear why China would choose to route exports to Central Asia via Afghanistan.

The benefits for Afghanistan are more obvious. Due to the ongoing conflict between Afghanistan and Pakistan, trade across their border has come to a halt. That cuts off landlocked Afghanistan’s primary trade and transit route for reaching third countries. If the Wakhan Corridor route becomes fully operational, it will provide an alternative route for Afghanistan to trade with the regional countries, particularly with China. Afghanistan could then connect directly with China’s Belt and Road Initiative (BRI), rather than linking itself to the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) as previously discussed.

In 2016, Afghanistan – then under the Republic government – and China signed a memorandum of understanding to integrate Afghanistan into the BRI. The following year in December, foreign ministers from Afghanistan, China, and Pakistan agreed to discuss ways to extend the CPEC to Afghanistan. In 2023, Afghanistan – now ruled by the Taliban – again reiterated its intention to join CPEC. This was also discussed during last year’s trilateral foreign ministers’ dialogue in Kabul. However, there has been no further progress in this regard due to the ongoing conflict between Pakistan and Afghanistan.

The Taliban government views the new road via the Wakhan Corridor as an opportunity to lessen Pakistan’s leverage. Islamabad has a history of closing the border crossings between the countries, affecting trade and inflicting heavy losses on Afghanistan’s economy. Thus, the de facto regime is jubilant with the inauguration of the Wakhan transit road.

As per Afghanistan’s Deputy Minister for Economic Affairs’ website, “With the opening of the Wakhan Corridor, Afghanistan will be forever freed from the pressure of neighboring countries, which often exploit the Karachi route, Gwadar Port, and Chabahar for political purposes and cause heavy financial losses to our traders and compatriots every year.”

Even though the inauguration of the route is expected to alleviate the transportation challenges for the residents of Pamir and Wakhan, its role as a trans-regional route, or even just connecting Afghanistan to China, seems to be a distant dream.

Despite the Taliban regime’s completion of the road, China still has not opened its border with Afghanistan, arguably due to security concerns vis-à-vis the crossing. Moreover, China neither sent its representative to the inaugural ceremony on October 4, nor did it acknowledge the road’s completion diplomatically.

China built the road that the Taliban’s Wakhan transit road aimed to link up with over a decade ago. The goal wasn’t to increase trade, but to secure its militarized border with Afghanistan by advancing access for its armed patrols. The Taliban refer to the transit route as a trading link to gain access to Chinese markets; Chinese media refers to this approximately 76-kilometer-long border as a “major counterterrorism front line.” This media framing aligns with Chinese officials’ narrative that Uyghurs in the region have frequently visited the corridor in order to “return to Xinjiang for Jihad.”

China’s major security concern in Afghanistan is the potential threat from the members of the East Turkestan Islamic Movement (ETIM), a group that seeks self-determination for the Uyghurs and independence of Xinjiang province from the Chinese government.

According to some estimates, there are over 3,000 Uyghurs living in Afghanistan. China has asked the Taliban to ensure that Uyghur separatists would not be allowed to use Afghan soil as a base for their activities in Xinjiang. Besides this, China wants the Taliban to extradite Uyghurs affiliated with ETIM to China.

China’s lukewarm reaction to the Taliban’s completion of the Wakhan transit route emanates mainly from its security concerns. Until the Taliban completely secure the route and convince Beijing that it will not be used as a route by ETIM members to infiltrate Xinjiang, the use of the Wakhan Corridor as a trade route between the two countries will remain a distant dream.
tag: Afghanistan infrastructure; China-Afghanistan border; China-Afghanistan connectivity; China-Afghanistan trade; Wakhan Corridor

title: After 8 Months in Power, How Much Has the BNP Changed Bangladesh?
description: It remains to be seen how willing the new government is to change the institutions that it now controls.
text:
Tarique Rahman had been Bangladesh’s prime minister for just 11 days when war broke out in the Middle East. He took office on February 17; on February 28, the United States and Israel attacked Iran. By March, disrupted fuel supplies had forced Bangladesh to introduce rationing, putting further pressure on its economy.

Eight months into Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) rule, the results are mixed. Remittances have risen and inflation has eased. But living costs keep rising, businesses remain cautious, and law and order remains a concern. Mob violence continues.

The government inherited serious problems, but its decisions also need to be examined. Constitutional reforms endorsed in a referendum alongside February’s national election remain under negotiation. New rights laws have drawn criticism for weakening independent oversight.

How far is the BNP willing to change the institutions it now controls? And are its decisions making people’s lives better, safer, and freer than before?

Crime and Law and Order

Law and order remains a concern eight months into BNP rule. According to monthly data from Bangladesh Police, the force registered fewer murder, robbery, and kidnapping cases between March and September than during the same months in 2025. Burglary cases, however, increased, while mob killings continued.

Police recorded 2,122 murder cases during these eight months, down from 2,317 a year earlier. Robbery cases fell from 1,159 to 1,077, while kidnapping cases declined slightly, from 628 to 618. Burglary cases rose from 1,796 to 2,022, an increase of nearly 13 percent.

The total number of registered cases increased by 14 percent, from 110,296 to 125,763. Narcotics cases accounted for about 90 percent of that increase, rising from 31,111 to 45,091. The increase alone cannot establish whether drug offenses became more common or police became more active in registering them.

Mob violence remained a serious concern. A comparison of cumulative reports from Ain o Salish Kendra, a human rights organization in Dhaka, gives a toll of 131 people killed in mob beatings between March and August 2026.

On April 11, a mob killed a Sufi spiritual leader in Kushtia’s Daulatpur upazila following allegations that he had insulted religion. His shrine was vandalized and set on fire. Media reports said law enforcement personnel were present but failed to control the attack.

Similar incidents occurred in Dhaka in September. On September 25, more than 200 masked attackers looted and demolished the Radda MCH-FP Center, a maternal and child healthcare facility in Dhaka. A preliminary police investigation found that officers were present but failed to stop the looting.

A day later, hundreds of attackers stormed a property and vandalized content creator Salman Muqtadir’s studio. Police linked the attack to a land dispute involving the property owner.

Police officers themselves have also faced violence. In June, a mob assaulted two officers in Savar and freed a suspect. In July, three police officers were attacked in Kutubdia while taking a suspect into custody. On September 5, Special Branch Sub-Inspector Altaf Hossain was beaten to death in Savar. More recently, on October 10, a police inspector was seriously injured in an attack by muggers in Khulna.

The government says the police are recovering. On August 26, Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed claimed that suspects in almost all criminal cases filed during the government’s first six months had been arrested within a reasonable time. He said the administration had inherited a fragile security situation and was working to improve police morale.

Extortion also remained a concern. Court records cited in media reporting show that 723 extortion cases were filed across 49 police stations in Dhaka between January and August, a period that includes several weeks before the BNP took office.

Dr. Md Tawohidul Haque, an associate professor and crime analyst at the Institute of Social Welfare and Research, University of Dhaka, described the government’s law and order record as mixed. “We cannot say that there has been any significant improvement compared with the previous one and a half years. At the same time, we cannot say that the situation has deteriorated dramatically,” he told The Diplomat.

Haque attributed the lack of progress partly to uneven enforcement and the government’s failure to control its own personnel: “Unless a political party takes a firm position against wrongdoing within its own ranks, the situation will not improve.”

Haque also questioned whom drug enforcement was reaching. While drug users, small retailers, and couriers faced arrest, he said, influential figures continued to benefit from political protection. “The real patrons and powerful figures behind the drug trade remain beyond the reach of the law,” he argued

Addressing that protection would require deeper changes in policing. “The Bangladesh Police has still not been depoliticized,” Haque said. “Its internal structure also remains largely unchanged.”

The Economy

Inflation eased during the BNP’s first months in office, but the improvement was uneven. In March, consumer prices were 8.71 percent higher than a year earlier. Inflation climbed to 9.42 percent in May before falling to 8.34 percent in September, barely below the 8.36 percent recorded in September 2025. Prices were still rising, adding to costs households had already absorbed.

Earnings offered little protection. In August, the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics’ wage index rose by 8.05 percent, trailing inflation. The index covers selected lower-paid occupations, including agricultural laborers, construction workers, and transport workers. For these workers, the figures suggest that wages still bought less than a year earlier, despite the slowdown in price increases.

There was more encouraging news from Bangladeshis working abroad. Remittances reached $18.94 billion between March and August, up 13.1 percent from the same months in 2025, according to Bangladesh Bank. These inflows helped replenish foreign exchange reserves and supported families receiving money from overseas. The improvement continued a rise in remittances that had begun before the BNP took office.

Businesses remained cautious. Bankers interviewed by The Business Standard (TBS), a Bangladeshi daily, described weak demand, expensive borrowing and energy shortages. Sohail R. K. Hussain, managing director of Bank Asia, told TBS that factories had unused capacity, giving businesses little reason to invest in expansion. The return of an elected government has yet to produce a strong recovery in borrowing.

The government inherited much of this difficulty. Bangladesh Bank had maintained tight monetary policy, while loan defaults continued to constrain lending. Its July–December policy statement acknowledged that higher interest rates alone could not resolve inflation caused by problems in markets and supply chains. It also announced a 600 billion taka financing package for industry, agriculture, and smaller businesses.

Fuel costs brought another setback in September. The government raised diesel prices from 115 to 135 taka a liter as the Middle East conflict drove up international energy costs. The Energy Ministry said the increase was needed to reduce losses at the state petroleum corporation. For businesses and households, it threatened further increases in production and transport costs, making the recent easing of inflation harder to sustain.

The government is also struggling to fund its spending plans. Banik Barta, a Bangladeshi daily, reported that the record 9.38 trillion taka budget relies on collecting nearly 7 trillion taka in revenue. Yet collections are falling as economic activity slows.

Citing National Board of Revenue sources, the newspaper said revenue in July–August stood at 518.9 billion taka, down from 547.7 billion a year earlier and 291.6 billion below the target for those two months. Meanwhile, higher energy import costs, subsidies, increased public sector salaries, and major project commitments are adding to expenditure.

Dr. Khondaker Golam Moazzem, an industrial economist, policy analyst, and president of the Knowledge Hub Institute, said that high inflation, weak growth, and rising unemployment pointed to economic stagnation. He argued that the government had shown too little interest in the structural reforms needed for recovery. “The problem is that the government does not have the revenue support required to finance these activities,” he told The Diplomat, referring to its expanding spending commitments.

Moazzem questioned the timing of salary increases for government employees and large projects that he believed could be postponed. One such example is the large expansion of Biman Bangladesh Airlines’ fleet. Its orders for 25 Boeing aircraft from the United States and 10 Airbus jets from the European Union would total 35 new aircraft, compared with its current fleet of just 19. Moazzem warned that without reforms to the airline’s management and service quality, the massive purchases could leave Biman with a long-term debt burden that would be difficult to service.

New spending commitments are adding pressure at a time when businesses and households were already struggling, he added. High inflation, borrowing costs, and an uncertain business environment also discouraged private investment.

While acknowledging the problems inherited by the BNP, he argued that this could not indefinitely excuse its performance. “After all, this government assumed office with the promise of reversing the economic deterioration,” Moazeem pointed out.

Foreign Policy

Eight months into his premiership, Rahman has visited Malaysia, China and the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York but has yet to travel to India. The delay reflects the difficulty of repairing relations with New Delhi while Sheikh Hasina remains there. Her political activities from India, and Dhaka’s demand for her extradition, continue to complicate efforts to arrange a visit.

Speaking in Dhaka on October 3, Indian High Commissioner to Dhaka Dinesh Trivedi said that Hasina’s return was subject to a legal process and offered no timeline. His remarks provided no assurance of an early resolution to one of the main disputes between the two countries.

Rahman declined to attend the BRICS Summit’s outreach session, with Dhaka objecting that the invitation addressed Rahman as BIMSTEC chair rather than Bangladesh’s prime minister. India replied that it had issued two separate invitations, including one for a bilateral visit. Behind the dispute over protocol were more practical concerns: Bangladesh wants progress on visas, trade restrictions and water sharing. The Ganges water treaty’s expiry in December gives those discussions particular urgency.

China offered a more welcoming reception. During Rahman’s June visit, Beijing backed cooperation on Mongla Port, the Chinese Economic and Industrial Zone in Chittagong, and the Teesta river management project. The two governments also agreed to explore a dialogue involving their foreign and defense ministries, suggesting an interest in closer security coordination alongside investment.

The Teesta River project is of particular interest. The joint communiqué promised Chinese assistance and faster feasibility work; it did not announce a completed financing arrangement. In any event, managing the river within Bangladesh would not settle the separate dispute with India over sharing the Teesta’s water. Beijing’s support gave Dhaka another way to pursue a long-delayed project, but negotiations with New Delhi remain necessary.

The government pursued closer ties with the United States through purchases as well as diplomacy. On September 23, during Tarique’s visit for the UNGA, Biman ordered another 11 Boeing aircraft, taking its orders that year to 25. Biman described the purchase as part of its fleet renewal, but it had a wider diplomatic purpose: increasing U.S. imports to ease trade tensions and protect Bangladesh’s garment exports from further tariff pressure.

The main Bangladesh-U.S. tariff agreement, however, was inherited by the BNP as a fait accompli. Announced on February 9, two days before the election, the deal provided for a 19 percent U.S. tariff and a mechanism allowing a specified volume of garments preferential treatment linked to purchases of U.S. textile inputs. It also locked Bangladesh into substantial agricultural and energy purchase commitments.

The Rohingya crisis remains a focal point for Bangladesh’s foreign policy. At the UNGA in September, Rahman sought a credible plan for voluntary return, protection of refugees’ rights in Myanmar and dependable humanitarian funding. He also acknowledged that people were still fleeing violence into Bangladesh.

Rahman also sought international backing for his government’s domestic agenda. He outlined a strategy of “recovery, restoration and reconstruction” and asked development partners to support jobs and manufacturing. He called for continued market access and financing as Bangladesh prepares to graduate from least-developed country status. His speech presented economic recovery as a central foreign policy priority, alongside appeals for climate finance and a lasting solution to the Rohingya crisis.

In October and November, Rahman is scheduled to visit Japan and Saudi Arabia on bilateral visits,as well as traveling to Turkiye to attend the 31st U.N. Climate Change Conference (COP31).

Political Environment and Freedom of Expression

The BNP’s first months in office brought open arguments between the government and its former allies. Jamaat-e-Islami, now leading the parliamentary opposition, challenged the government’s claims of success. In August, its 11-party alliance questioned the handling of rising prices, energy shortages, and public safety. National Citizen Party leader Nahid Islam also accused the government of withholding opposition chairmanships of parliamentary committees, limiting its ability to scrutinize those in power. These disputes showed that political competition was continuing after the election.

That competition remained restricted, however. The Awami League’s activities were still banned under an order issued by the interim government in May 2025, pending trials of its leaders and activists at the International Crimes Tribunal. The restrictions extended beyond rallies and meetings to publications and online publicity. The BNP inherited the ban, but chose to uphold it. That left a major segment of Bangladeshi citizens without the ability to organize through their preferred party.

Journalists continued to face attacks, threats and legal pressure. Ain o Salish Kendra recorded 242 incidents of journalist harassment between March and September. The category includes several forms of abuse and does not mean that the government was responsible for every incident. It nevertheless documents the risks that persisted after the elected administration took office.

The treatment of detained political opponents also drew criticism. In August, Human Rights Watch said hundreds of people linked to the former Awami League government remained imprisoned without charge. It reported that at least 10 Awami League office holders had died in prison since the BNP took office, most without having been charged. Families and lawyers alleged that detainees were denied adequate medical care and that fresh cases were used to prevent their release after bail orders. While acknowledging that some former officials faced allegations of serious abuses, HRW called for individual reviews of detention and independent investigations into all prison deaths.

Proposed changes to the cyber law added to concerns over media freedom. In September, the Committee to Protect Journalists warned that draft amendments could expose journalists to prison terms of up to 10 years for circulating material authorities considered rumors or misinformation. It also warned that courts could suspend or cancel news outlets’ licenses when reporting challenged their accounts.

The government said the amendments were not intended to target journalists. Following objections from editors and media organizations, it agreed in late September to form two committees to recommend safeguards.

Asif M. Shahan, a professor of development studies at the University of Dhaka and a political analyst, saw these concerns as part of a wider problem. He warned that changes to cybersecurity legislation and the weakening of human rights oversight could strengthen the government’s hand against its critics. “We are seeing the beginnings of institutional mechanisms that could be used to weaken the opposition and dissenting voices,” he told The Diplomat.

Nur Khan Liton, a human rights activist, said eight months was too short for a definitive assessment, but he saw some improvement compared with the period of Awami League rule. “In some areas, we have seen substantial efforts by the government. Even so, it has no alternative but to take firmer action,” he told The Diplomat.

Liton pointed to alleged extrajudicial killings, deaths in police custody and prison, and attacks on Hindu communities. Mob violence was another persistent concern. “We are witnessing people being labeled in different ways and then subjected to violence by mobs,” he noted.

Political freedom also remained insecure, Liton said. He cited the September 26 incident at the Dhaka headquarters of the Jatiya Samajtantrik Dal (JASAD), or National Socialist Party. The party alleged that activists from the BNP and its youth wing, Jubo Dal, assaulted participants at a scheduled meeting before police detained a large number of people. Police said they were acting on information that Awami League members had gathered there; JASAD rejected that account. A Jubo Dal leader denied assaulting anyone. Liton described the incident as both undemocratic and unlawful, saying he had seen no legal action against the attackers.

Liton also questioned whether recent legal changes would leave people with fewer protections against state abuse. He criticized the replacement laws governing the National Human Rights Commission and enforced disappearances as weaker than the measures they replaced. In his assessment, they would limit the commission’s ability to respond to violations by law enforcement agencies.

He feared that proposed cyber legislation would further restrict expression, while attacks on media workers continued. “We cannot say unequivocally that journalists are safe under this government,” he said.

Reform Promises

By late September, the government was still consulting on constitutional changes that voters had endorsed in February’s referendum. These included limits on the prime minister’s tenure, a second chamber of parliament, and stronger safeguards for judicial independence.

On September 29, Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said the parliamentary committee aimed to finish discussions by December. A report and an amendment bill would follow at an unspecified date.

Disagreement over the reform package began almost immediately after the election. The July Charter implementation order envisaged elected MPs serving separately as a Constitutional Reform Council, with 180 working days from its first sitting to complete constitutional reforms. BNP lawmakers declined to take the council oath, arguing that changes should follow the existing constitution. Jamaat-e-Islami and NCP lawmakers took both oaths and insisted that the referendum required the council route. The timetable was thus tied to a process the parties could not agree to begin.

The government instead formed a parliamentary committee in July, leaving five places for opposition nominees. The opposition refused to join. This dispute also concerned who would determine the substance of reform. The BNP maintained that its objections recorded when signing the charter must be respected; its opponents argued that the referendum provided a mandate for implementation.

On September 29, Salahuddin offered room for compromise on those objections if opposition parties joined the talks. He reaffirmed support for a 10-year limit on any individual’s premiership, but said the caretaker government’s structure remained undecided.

Other institutions had seen action, although that did not always amount to the changes promised. New appointments in August restored the Anti-Corruption Commission’s leadership after a 168-day vacancy. That allowed it to resume work on accumulated complaints and investigations. But the appointments followed the existing law. The Center for Governance Studies’ Reform Watch noted that they did not establish the independent appointment mechanism envisaged in the charter. Restoring an institution’s functioning and reducing political influence over it are separate tasks.

September’s legislation raised a more serious question about the direction of reform. Parliament passed laws on the National Human Rights Commission and enforced disappearances on September 6. The disappearance law provided for prosecution, victim support, and compensation. Yet it placed investigations involving security forces with another force chosen by the government, rather than the independent commission.

Human Rights Watch argued that this reversed protections introduced under the interim government. It also criticized restrictions on the commission’s ability to investigate security agencies directly and the restoration of government influence over appointments.

The restructuring of the Rapid Action Battalion drew similar criticism. September’s legislation replaced the Rapid Action Battalion with the Special Response Battalion, transferring its personnel, powers and property. Human Rights Watch said the change lacked adequate provisions for independent oversight and accountability. For families seeking answers about disappearances and killings, the practical question remained whether investigators could examine security agencies without depending on those agencies’ cooperation.

Eight months into BNP rule, constitutional promises were still being negotiated, while some laws already passed were being challenged for preserving the powers reform was supposed to restrain.

Shahan, the University of Dhaka professor, said holding an election was only the first step toward rebuilding democracy. Institutions also needed the independence to check government power. “I do not see any clear direction regarding how the government actually intends to build democratic institutions,” he told The Diplomat. While Shahan cautioned that eight months is too early for a final judgment, he said moves to weaken independent oversight raised concerns.

Shahan feared that the BNP would choose which reforms to pursue according to its political interests, despite voters having endorsed changes in February’s referendum. He cited the proposed separate administrative office for the Supreme Court, intended to reduce its dependence on the government. The BNP had not formally opposed that proposal, yet it was not moving forward.

“I think the BNP will ultimately proceed according to its own preferences and priorities,” Shahan said.

title: After War of Words, China Says Relations With Philippines at ‘Critical Juncture’
channel_text: ASEAN Beat; Diplomacy; Politics; Southeast Asia
description: Growing political polarization has the potential to undermine Manila’s ability to handle its ongoing maritime disputes with Beijing.
text:
China on Friday expressed willingness to improve its relationship with the Philippines, but admitted that relations were at “an extremely sensitive and critical juncture” due to the actions of unnamed “outside forces.”

The two governments have been engaged in a war of words since Friday, when Jing Quan, China’s ambassador to Manila, declared that China could “easily win” a war with the Philippines. Jing was responding to a remark by Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro, who the day prior described China as the lone “troublemaker” in Southeast Asia, due to its aggressive actions in contested parts of the South China Sea.

Speaking to the press after a Diliman Dialogues organized by the Philippines-China Studies Center of Diliman College in Quezon City, Jing said that the remark was “nonsense.”

“We should feel fortunate enough that you have a neighbor like China in this region,” he said. “If we want to use force, we may easily win. But no, we will not choose force, and we love peace. In this region, we enjoy peace.”

Asked on Friday about Ambassador Jing’s remark, Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr ‌said that ⁠it “sounds very much like a threat” and that he would summon the ambassador to provide an explanation. Jing, who began his posting last December, was previously summoned by Marcos in July, after a Philippine marine was injured in a melee with the China Coast Guard at Second Thomas Shoal in the Spratly Islands and the subsequent publication of a video by the state-run China Daily depicting Filipinos as monkeys and U.S. puppets.

Yesterday, the Chinese embassy issued a statement in which it said it considered the Philippines a “close neighbor and friend with deep historical and cultural ties.” It also said the Philippines need not choose between China and the United States and that the two sides “should maintain dialogue, manage differences, and expand cooperation in trade, investment, people-to-people exchanges, and law enforcement.”

At the same time, it said that China-Philippines relations were “at an extremely sensitive and critical juncture and require prudent, careful handling” and lambasted “anti-China politicians” who it said, “deliberately ignore China’s clear and consistent position on China-Philippines relations, instead twisting its words out of context and maliciously distorting the facts for political gain.”

It concluded by saying that differences “should be managed through dialogue” and that “outside forces” – i.e., the United States and its allies – “should not be allowed to steer bilateral relations toward confrontation.”

“China is ready to work with all sectors of Philippine society to promote dialogue, deepen trust, and expand mutually beneficial cooperation,” it added.

Such exchanges have taken place periodically between the two governments over the past few years, often linked to events in the South China Sea, where the two nations have overlapping maritime claims. Besides, Chinese and Philippine coast guards have engaged in a string of confrontations, some involving the use of physical force, which have pushed relations to their worst point in years.

Jing’s comments were preceded by a chain of public comments and responses emanating from the Philippines’ fractious domestic politics, hinting at the apparent growing polarization of foreign relations along partisan lines.

This began on October 6 with the airing of allegations that Chinese entities had sent just over $5 million in remittances to a Philippine company linked to the husband of Vice President Sara Duterte, a major rival of Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. The claims, which came to light during Duterte’s ongoing impeachment trial in the Senate, prompted Marcos to state that the involvement of Chinese money made the issue “a national security issue.”

“If it is true, it is a threat – a threat at the highest level to the republic,” Marcos said on October 12.

Duterte responded the same day by stating that the Philippines was becoming the main “troublemaker of Southeast Asia” by treating business ties with China as a national security concern. Teodoro’s comment about China being the main “troublemaker” in the region was a direct response to Duterte. At this point, Jing made his incautious entry into the “debate,” turning the domestic war of words into a potential diplomatic incident.

The incident is notable for what it says about how bitter political rivalries in the Philippines have the potential to impact Manila’s delicate balancing of relations with China and the United States. In late 2016, the administration of President Rodrigo Duterte, Sara’s father, initiated a bold turn toward China, downplaying maritime disputes in order to gain Chinese financial support for major infrastructure projects. The needle swung back under Marcos, who, after coming to office in 2022, strengthened the Philippines’ relationship with the United States and became much more forceful in his condemnations of Chinese behavior in the South China Sea.

There is now some danger that as the country moves toward the next presidential election in 2028, the two rival camps will come to see benefits in depicting each other as agents of foreign forces (the U.S. and China, respectively). The impacts of this could stretch beyond the periodic diplomatic incident. Indeed, they could begin to impact Manila’s ability to maintain a stable and predictable approach toward the challenges posed by China’s aggressive actions in the South China Sea.

title: AI and the Risk to Democracy
description: Insights from Matthew Botvinick.
text:
The Diplomat author Mercy Kuo regularly engages subject-matter experts, policy practitioners, and strategic thinkers across the globe for their diverse insights into U.S. Asia policy. This conversation with Dr. Matthew Botvinick – author of “AI and Political Reform: The Risk to Democracy and How to Respond” (Princeton University Press 2026), world-renowned AI researcher and neuroscientist, senior fellow at Yale Law School and member of the technical staff at Anthropic, leading research on AI and the rule of law – is the 529th in “The Trans-Pacific View Insight Series.”

Explain how AI will pose fundamental challenges to constitutional democracy.

We are in a remarkable political moment right now, where two trends are converging. First, AI is generating feelings of insecurity and vulnerability across society. Second, in many democracies, trust in government institutions is low – in the U.S., trust is at historic lows. This is a combustible combination, because it provides ideal conditions for what has been called “the demagogue’s playbook,” where populist sentiment is exploited by political leaders to undermine democracy.

Democracy has always been vulnerable to this risk. The problem now, though, is that AI dramatically raises the stakes. As others have noted, if an authoritarian government can get a foothold, AI makes it much easier for such a government to entrench itself, through surveillance and control of the information citizens can access or share. So the problem is two-fold: AI is creating conditions that can be exploited by aspiring authoritarian leaders, and it is also making available tools that such leaders might use to achieve their goals.

It is important to add that all of this is about risks, not certainties. In fact, if democracies rise to meet the moment, AI might prove to be a benefit to democracy, rather than a detriment. The first order of business is to get our institutional houses in order, instituting government reforms – in emergency law, surveillance law, separation of powers, and free speech doctrines – that increase democratic resilience. If we can do that and make it past the immediate challenge, then we can start thinking about how AI might be used to empower and inform citizens, support democratic deliberation, and enhance government transparency and accountability. If we are careful and strategic, AI may be a boon rather than a curse.

Examine the dynamics between rising powerful AI systems and eroding democratic institutions and implications for political and economic freedom.

Democracy depends on a balance between the power of government and the power of society. What keeps that balance in place is a combination of two things. On the government side, to keep power in check, it must be subdivided. Things must be structured to prevent perfectly coordinated action, which would make abuse of power too easy. This is why we have separation of powers and traditional checks and balances. On the societal side, in contrast, adequate power depends on factors that support coordinated action – the news media, the activities of civil society, a free marketplace of ideas, free and fair elections, and so forth.

All of this means that democracies face danger when (1) the checks and balances within government erode, and (2) when the ability of society to engage in collective action is diminished.

If we are not careful, AI will threaten to do both of those things. My book unpacks this in a number of ways but let me give just two examples. On the government side, AI might over-empower the executive branch relative to legislative and judicial branches, if AI is used to automate perfect obedience to central executive authority. On the society side, the ability of citizens to act in concert could be undermined by AI-enhanced surveillance or propaganda. Society’s power decreases, government power increases, and the balance required for democracy is lost.

Again, these are risks, not inevitabilities. If we act wisely, AI could enhance society’s capacity for collective action, and keep government’s power in balance, through exactly the means I mentioned earlier. But that won’t happen without strategic and proactive interventions.

Analyze how the propagation of AI fuels authoritarianism in China and the United States.

The situation in China stands as a warning of what is possible. China’s use of AI to monitor and control its people has been detailed in excellent books like Josh Chin’s and Liza Lin’s “Surveillance State.” The importance of AI is this: Cheap and ubiquitous sensors, cameras for example, and online activity like that on social networks generate huge amounts of data. Finding the most important bits within that flood of information, and making sense of larger patterns, is a difficult problem. AI solves that problem, matching analytic capacity to the scale of the data. The result is that there is no place to hide from an authoritarian government’s gaze – that, of course, is the situation in China.

The current challenge in the U.S. and other democracies is to leverage AI for legitimate law enforcement and national security needs, without creating tools that are too easy to abuse. The U.S. has a long history of such abuse, running from FDR and J. Edgar Hoover to the activities revealed by Edward Snowden. This time, we must act to ensure civil liberties and the rule of law ahead of such problems, rather than only in reaction to them.

Explain why there can be no genuine AI safety without democracy and the rule of law.

I’m really pleased to see that people across society, people who have no direct involvement in the AI industry, are now talking about AI safety. It’s the right moment for that conversation, as AI systems become more capable and also increasingly permeate our activities, from commerce to education to science and beyond.

But there is one part of the AI safety conversation that is not getting enough public attention, and it’s the one you’ve brought up: the fact that constitutional democracy is absolutely mandatory for AI safety. To see this point clearly, imagine an AI system that is safe in every way: It cannot launch cyberattacks, cannot escape human control, cannot create bioweapons, and so forth. Now picture this AI system in two settings. The first is a democracy with free and fair elections, an open marketplace of ideas, protection of civil liberties, and robust rule of law. The second is an authoritarian state, with none of those features.

In that latter setting, our hypothetical “safe” AI is anything but safe. It will, quite reliably, be used to oppress dissent and enforce political compliance. Again, we needn’t read science fiction to understand what that looks like; it is playing out in many countries today, not only China but also Venezuela, Russia, some Gulf states and elsewhere. The take-home message is very simple: As we pursue AI safety, through technical and regulatory means, we must also work to assure that our democracies are robust and resilient as well. Real AI safety absolutely requires that.

Assess how U.S., Chinese, and other AI companies should be held accountable for the political and economic impact of their technologies on their societies and the global community.

Here I should start by stating clearly that I am speaking in a purely personal capacity, rather than on behalf of Anthropic. That said, I think the answer to the question follows directly from the points I just made about the connection between AI safety and democracy. Any company that purports to care about AI safety – and this includes all of the major AI labs – has a responsibility to use whatever power it has to protect and enhance the health of democracy, both where the company is based and worldwide.

It is important to acknowledge that this responsibility faces the AI industry with an extremely tricky task. Our tendency is to worry about the economic and political power of AI companies, and of course corporate power has been a recurrent problem in the U.S. and other democracies. However, at the same time, people underestimate how vulnerable corporate power – including the power of the AI labs – is to government power, especially when authoritarian tendencies seep into a democracy’s leadership.

Over recent decades, democratic backsliding around the globe has more often involved the subjugation of corporate power by government than the opposite. And when authoritarian-leaning governments bring companies to heel, they gain access to their assets, which here include AI. So we need to watch the relationship between government and industry power very carefully and support the labs when – as we hope – they stick their necks out to defend democratic institutions and the rule of law.
tag: AI and democracy; AI and disinformation; AI and human rights; China AI; U.S. AI

title: Amid Economic Challenges, China Turns to Vulnerable Workforce to Fix Its Social Security Problems
description: China is looking to “optimize and enhance” its social security program. People fear that will translate to pressure on gig economy workers and rural migrant workers.
text:
“It is critical that we utilize data to identify individuals who have not contributed to the social security program. Currently, some people have not participated in the program, but we will use different means to identify and find them to encourage them to join.” These are quotes from Li Zhong, deputy minister of the Chinese Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security (MOHRSS), on the government’s goal to increase the number of individuals in the Chinese social security program.

Li’s remarks at the ministry’s news conference on October 10 quickly gained the public’s attention. Using digital technology to identify individuals is one of multiple measures announced by the MOHRSS toward its goal to “optimize and enhance” the sustainability, fairness, security, convenience, and standardization of the Chinese social security program. The Chinese government will encourage gig economy workers, rural migrant workers, and individuals in new forms of employment to join state-managed pension plans. On the corporate side, the government will focus on small and mid-size businesses and social groups to increase its pool of social security funds.

With low birth rates and high retirement numbers in the coming years, the Chinese social security program is under increasing stress. Warning signs began emerging as early as 2014. According to predictions from the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences (CASS) in April 2019, the Chinese pension plan could see a funding deficit by 2028. The financial gap could jump to 11.28 trillion yuan by 2050 – or 16.73 trillion yuan in a scenario without government financial assistance.

At the rate CASS projected seven years ago, the Chinese state pension plan will see its funds depleted by 2035. Given that the Chinese economy is facing continuous challenges in its post-COVID recovery, the Chinese state pension plan is likely facing a worse scenario than researchers predicted back in 2019.

The Chinese government has already taken steps such as increasing the basic social security deduction to maintain contribution inflow. China has also implemented a gradual delay in the retirement age since January 2025. Starting in September 2025, the Chinese government announced plans to force businesses to contribute to social security funds. Now Li’s comments have raised speculation that MOHRSS will use data-tracking tools to force individuals to join the pension scheme as well.

However, in a deteriorating economy, both employers and employees show little faith in the state-managed social security program. Businesses view this as a substantial cost that could lead to shutdowns, and employees view the mandatory contribution as a significant reduction of their disposable income. Younger Chinese workers have doubts about the likelihood of them getting the contributions back in the form of payments when they reach retirement age.

In the first quarter of 2026, approximately 58 million individuals paused their social security contributions. In some regions, banks and local governments have started low-interest loan products to encourage individuals to contribute to the social security program amid financial difficulties.

For low-income individuals, pension plan deductions become an additional burden because of the continuously increasing minimum contribution base. For example, in Shanghai, a job with a monthly salary of 7,546 yuan or less would require the employer and the employee to contribute a combined minimum of 2,712 yuan each month. But, the monthly minimum salary in Shanghai is just 2,740 yuan. As a result, the social security contribution ratio could reach as high as 98.9 percent to hire a minimum-salary worker.

Facing pressure to maintain the employment rate and address youth unemployment, the Chinese government decided to target its “flexible employment” population, who rely on the gig economy to survive in China’s post-COVID economic downturn. Research from the Chinese Academy of Labor and Social Security indicates that 34.9 percent of China’s 200 million gig economy workers participated in the social security program, far lower than the 95 percent participation rate set by the MOHRSS. Media reports also predict that the flexible employment population could reach 320 million in 2026. That suggests the social security gap will grow even larger as the Chinese economy creates fewer high-paying, stable jobs.

With a struggling economy and a challenging employment market, the Chinese government needs solutions to maintain the financial contributions to its social security program. Yet targeting individuals already facing significant challenges in flexible employment is unlikely to lead to positive results.
tag: China demographics; China gig workers; China pension system; China social security

title: Anas Alhajji on the Three Seas Crisis and the Race for Energy Dominance
description: Dr. Anas Alhajji joins host Tushar Shetty to examine how the Hormuz crisis is reshaping global energy markets – and the overlooked impact of the loss of Russian and Kazakh supply.
text:
