title: Anwar is Bargaining Myanmar Lives For Political Gain – And He Will Lose
description: Min Aung Hlaing should not be trusted to resolve a refugee crisis that is a direct result of his own past policies.
text:
This week, Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim received Min Aung Hlaing, Myanmar’s junta chief, who led the 2017 genocide against the Rohingya, to arrange the transfer of 200,000 refugees, including Rohingya, back to Myanmar. The first deportations have already begun.

The plan is not just morally bankrupt. It makes no practical sense. It appears driven by months of coordinated online hate speech against Rohingya refugees in Malaysia and the targeting of community leaders by authorities, including the recent arrest of Zafar Ahmad Abdul Ghani.

In case anyone needs reminding, Min Aung Hlaing is the subject of an arrest warrant from the Argentine Federal Court for commissioning the atrocities against Rohingya as commander-in-chief. Prosecutors at the International Criminal Court have also requested an arrest warrant for him on similar grounds. He is yet to face justice, and the military remains as brutal as ever. He led the coup in 2021 and has razed half the country in the years since in his desperate bid for power. He still represents the Myanmar military, an institution whose sole purpose is to exploit the population through force, as it has for more than 50 years, and is the root cause of all Myanmar’s suffering.

Deporting refugees to Myanmar under an agreement with Min Aung Hlaing is a violation of international law and the fundamental principle of non-refoulement. And it will not ease the burden of the Myanmar crisis on Malaysia or the wider region; indeed, it will worsen it.

Time and time again, Min Aung Hlaing has proven that he can’t be trusted, not only by the people of Myanmar, but also by our neighbors. He has treated ASEAN with contempt since the coup, ignoring the basic requirements of the Five-Point Consensus, which called for an immediate cessation of violence, inclusive dialogue, and humanitarian access to the country. This is the precise reason why the refugee numbers continue to grow.

Min Aung Hlaing is also not the sole arbiter of power in Myanmar. He controls less than half of the country. He does not even control northern Rakhine State, the Rohingya homeland. That region, and most of Rakhine, is now largely held by the Arakan Army, which is committing its own grave abuses against Rohingya.

Just last week, the military bombed a market in Kyauktaw township in Rakhine State, killing nearly 50 civilians, including Rohingya. Where then will these refugees be returned to? To the killing field? Or will they be housed in internment camps outside Sittwe alongside 120,000 other Rohingya who have been confined there for 14 years? Or will they be left to face the exploitation of trafficking networks and armed groups, including the military, that will forcibly recruit them and send them to die on the front lines?

The plan will fail, while emboldening Min Aung Hlaing and fueling instability, making a lasting solution harder to reach.

Malaysia has offered safety to Myanmar refugees, and those refugees have in turn contributed to Malaysia’s economy. But this is not a permanent solution. Of course, Anwar has an obligation to address the issue, and he is right to pursue diplomatic efforts in that regard.

But if he genuinely wanted to improve the situation and resolve the crisis, rather than reacting to populist pressure, these are a number of diplomatic steps he would take. The first is to work through ASEAN and the U.N. to secure a nationwide ceasefire in Myanmar and uninhibited humanitarian access to all parts of the country, including by defining concrete benchmarks to measure Min Aung Hlaing’s implementation of the Five-Point Consensus.

Second, he should support efforts to hold Min Aung Hlaing and leaders of the military and other armed actors to account for the genocide and decades of grave violations against Rohingya and other civilians across Myanmar. The same principles that Anwar applies to Palestine apply in Myanmar: without an end to impunity, the devastating cycles of violence will not end.

Third, Anwar should develop a diplomatic strategy that responds to the reality of Myanmar’s multiple centers of authority, engages Myanmar’s legitimate authorities and stakeholders, and works toward inclusive dialogue for a genuine political solution.

Fourth, he should lead a coordinated international effort to dismantle the regional human trafficking networks that are flourishing in the conflict, exploiting the most vulnerable and fueling the refugee crisis.

Finally, he needs to consider how a mission of independent international monitors could be stationed in Rakhine State, with a mandate to monitor and report on the protection of civilians, as a means of building confidence towards the eventual sustainable, voluntary, and dignified return of Rohingya and other refugees from Myanmar.

Rohingya and other Myanmar refugees want nothing more than to return safely to our homes. We are not objecting to Anwar’s plans because we want to live the rest of our lives in insecurity and exile; we are objecting because we know it will only make things worse.

And deep down, I believe Anwar knows this too. These are not the actions of the wise and principled leader whose release many human rights activists and I supported. These actions are a dangerous betrayal that bargains away our lives, in the vain hope of short-term political gain.
tag: Anwar Ibrahim; Malaysia Rohingya refugees; Malaysia-Myanmar relations; Myanmar human rights; Myanmar refugees; Myanmar refugees in Malaysia; Rohingya refugees

title: As Indonesian Fires Continue, Singapore Records Highest Air Pollution Reading Since 2015
description: Jakarta is the focus of increasing criticism for its failure to contain – or prevent – the fires that continue to rage in Borneo and Sumatra.
text:
Air pollution readings in some parts of Singapore yesterday spiked to their highest levels in more than a decade, as Indonesia came under increased pressure for its failure to contain the wildfires that have caused a dramatic decline in air quality across the region.

Hourly PM2.5 readings rose across all regions of Singapore yesterday afternoon, with the reading in the west of the island climbing to 288 micrograms per cubic meter. The reading, which is in the National Environmental Agency (NEA)’s “very high” range, was the highest recorded since 2015, Channel News Asia reported.

PM2.5 readings were in the “high” range in the south, east, and central regions of the country, while the reading in the north was in the “elevated” range.

With readings entering the “very high” range, the government also began the phased distribution of N95 masks to vulnerable segments of the population, and temporarily closed all outdoor and non-air-conditioned sports facilities in western Singapore.

Indonesia is currently battling the most intense wildfire season in 11 years, which has been exacerbated by an unusually severe dry season linked to a global El Niño weather pattern. The fires, which are concentrated mostly on the islands of Borneo and Sumatra, have created a haze that has affected much of maritime Southeast Asia, forcing school closures and impacting the health of tens of millions of people.

The government of Timor-Leste, which borders Indonesia, said in a statement yesterday that it was suspending face-to-face learning activities for three days starting from ​October 15 “due to contamination by pollutant particles from wildfires in neighboring regions or countries.” This comes after the Malaysian government last week ordered the closure of schools across peninsular Malaysia, including in the capital Kuala Lumpur, due to the worsening haze.

In Indonesia, authorities said more than 280,000 respiratory problems have been recorded in affected regions since August 18. In the province of Central Kalimantan, the country’s ISPU air pollution index yesterday exceeded 1,200, four times higher than the “hazardous” level of 300.

While some fires naturally occur during the annual dry season, many are caused by agricultural burn-off on monoculture plantations, such as palm oil, maize, paper pulp, and sugar, that are controlled by powerful Indonesian conglomerates. The country’s Forestry Minister Raja Juli Antoni said last month that most of the fires in Kalimantan and Sumatra had been deliberately set by individuals or companies, and pledged to investigate and punish those responsible.

As I noted earlier this week, the crisis has highlighted the inadequacy of regional mechanisms for combating transboundary haze. Malaysia this week announced that it would raise the issue with Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) foreign ministers ahead of the bloc’s summit in the Philippines next month.

For now, however, the region is reliant on the actions of the Indonesian government, which has been subject to increasing criticism for its failure to contain – or prevent – the fires. In addition to a wave of complaints from Singaporean and Malaysian social media users, the frustration is now breaking into the political realm. Andrew Chen Kah Eng, the head of ​the Johor state branch of Malaysian Prime Minister ​Anwar Ibrahim’s Pakatan Harapan coalition, ⁠said on Monday that Indonesia “must be held accountable” for its failure to contain the wildfires.

“Indonesian spokespeople need to stop being indifferent and unapologetic to all ASEAN countries affected, including its own people, by human-induced haze pollution,” he said. “Allowing toxic haze containing PM2.5 fine particles ​to pollute the air of neighboring countries is unacceptable.”

The following day, Malaysian lawmaker Syed Saddiq Syed Abdul Rahman called on Southeast Asian governments to lodge formal diplomatic protests with their Indonesian counterparts, suggesting that Malaysian and Singaporean banks cut off financing to Indonesian companies linked to land burning. “You need to treat them like an outcast in the region,” he said.

On Tuesday, Indonesian President ‌Prabowo Subianto ordered the mobilization of additional resources to combat the wildfires, which are particularly difficult to control due to the fact that many are in geographically remote areas and are burning on areas of dried peatland, where fires can smolder for weeks underground.

“This is a top priority for us. We must ​resolve it immediately,” Prabowo told a meeting with the relevant Indonesian authorities, according to a government statement.

Even if it is successful, without continuing action to control the activities of powerful agri-business interests, the region will continue to be subject to the choking externalities of Indonesia’s dysfunctional political economy.
tag: ASEAN transboundary haze; Indonesia environment; Indonesia wildfires; Malaysia haze; Prabowo Subianto; Singapore haze; Transboundary haze

title: As Tide Turns Against Modi, More Parties Back INDIA Bloc Protests
description: Police detained scores of opposition lawmakers, who held a sit-in to press their demand for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
text:
Police detained scores of opposition lawmakers, including Leader of the Opposition Rahul Gandhi, his sister and Congress parliamentarian Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, and Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav, on the evening of October 6, in a bid to clear the INDIA bloc of opposition parties’ sit-in protest at Akashvani Bhavan in New Delhi.

Delhi Police subsequently registered complaints against the detained opposition parliamentarians for entering a government building without permission.

The detention of the leaders came at the end of a day of protests called by the INDIA bloc, which is demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. They accuse Kumar of vote chori (stealing votes) by overseeing an electoral process that has benefited Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

The call for Kumar’s resignation gathered momentum after an investigative report in The Indian Express revealed that Kumar made unilateral decisions and issued orders despite two other election commissioners raising objections “at least 14 times over the last 10 months” to issues relating to the ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of the electoral rolls.

At a meeting on September 30, leaders of the INDIA bloc decided on a schedule of protests to press their demand for Kumar’s resignation. The October 6 march was the first of several planned demonstrations in the coming weeks.

The plan was to march from parliament to the Election Commission building. However, legislators were blocked by police and barricades from reaching the planned destination. It did seem initially that the Modi government had scored an early victory against the opposition.

However, the Gandhi siblings quickly changed the plan and headed to Akashvani Bhavan, located adjacent to the Election Commission building, and continued their sit-in protest there.

The march saw the participation of most of the INDIA bloc’s constituents. However, the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) and the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) stayed away. While the DMK is miffed with Gandhi for aligning with its rival, the Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam, to form the government in Tamil Nadu, the AAP’s decision seems motivated by factors that are more complex and controversial.

The Congress party has long suspected the AAP of being the “BJP’s B-team” – that is, it believes the AAP’s electoral strategy of opposing the Congress strengthens the BJP.

Interestingly, the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), which led the Jantar Mantar protests in July, did not participate in the INDIA-led march on October 6, although it too has called for Kumar’s resignation. Indeed, its leaders were quiet on social media through much of the day’s dramatic events, posting mild support only later, as criticism of their silence mounted on social media.

The CJP is widely believed to be close to the AAP. Of the 12 members of its core team, six – including its leaders Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das, and Ashutosh Ranka – “were either directly associated with the AAP or supported it publicly,” The Print reported.

Indeed, apprehension over the CJP’s likely links with the AAP kept the Congress away from the July protests at Jantar Mantar. Although Gandhi did subsequently meet activists of the leftist organizations, he has maintained distance from the CJP.

The rift between the Congress and the AAP is over 15 years old. In 2011, India Against Corruption, a grouping of NGOs, civil society organizations, and right-wing activists, held massive protests against corruption in the then Congress-led coalition government. The IAC movement not only birthed the AAP but also severely weakened the Congress, paving the way for the BJP’s victory in the 2014 general elections.

For many Congress leaders and their supporters, the Jantar Mantar protests evoked memories of the 2011 IAC protests. They believe that the Jantar Mantar protests, although directed against the BJP government, would end up benefiting the AAP and the BJP rather than the opposition.

There are other important differences between the INDIA bloc and the CJP.

On October 5, Congress President Mallikarjun Kharge said the Congress and its INDIA bloc partners have three “non-negotiable demands” – the resignation of CEC Kumar, annulment of the ongoing Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls, and restoration of voting via ballot paper instead of electronic voting machines. It wants a level playing field in elections.

The CJP, meanwhile, is calling on opposition parties to boycott elections.

An opposition boycott of elections could deprive the election of legitimacy. However, a boycott could benefit the BJP. The BJP would get a few friendly parties to contest the election to lend the process legitimacy. At a time when mass support for the BJP is declining and support for the opposition parties is growing, staying away from elections would hurt the latter’s interests.

Such sharp differences among opposition forces can only weaken their efforts to defeat the BJP. The BJP can be expected to step up efforts to deepen these divisions in the coming months.

While last week, the INDIA bloc showed some signs of unity at its meeting, the October 6 demonstrations have upset some partners. What was supposed to be a joint INDIA event turned into a “Rahul Gandhi show” that showcased only the Gandhi siblings and the Congress party, they are complaining.

Meanwhile, the AAP, the DMK and the CJP appear to be rethinking their strategy of staying away from INDIA-led protests. In a sharp about-turn, the DMK today expressed solidarity with INDIA’s protests. “This government doesn’t want Rahul Gandhi to protest against Gyanesh Kumar,” it said today, after deriding him on October 6. And AAP participated in today’s protests.

The CJP and leftist organizations have called for protests in Delhi on October 10. Will the INDIA bloc back their effort? Importantly, can the Congress overcome its misgivings to extend them support? It seems unlikely at this point.

Building a mass movement is always challenging. Given its stellar role in leading India’s independence struggle, the Congress has immense experience in this regard and needs to draw on that experience. It will need to consult partners and pull together with them if it is serious about taking on the Modi government successfully.
tag: CEC; Chief Election Commissioner; CJP protests; CJP-Congress; Congress Party; Congress-AAP; Gyanesh Kumar; India protests; Rahul Gandhi

title: As University of Tokyo Gets Its First Female President, How Far Is Japan From Gender Equality?
description: Fujigaki Yuko’s selection sparked controversy – and shone a light on Japan’s stubborn gender gap.
text:
On September 28, 2026, Fujigaki Yuko was selected as the next president of the University of Tokyo. Following formal appointment by the minister of education, culture, sports, science, and technology, she will take office on April 1, 2027, for a six-year term.

As the university marks its 150th anniversary, Fujigaki will become the first woman to lead it. Yet at the institution she is about to head, only about one in five undergraduates is a woman.

Fujigaki is not Japan’s first female university president. In 1997, Niwa Masako became president of Nara Women’s University, the first woman to head a national university in Japan, and in 2001, Honda Masuko became the first female president of Ochanomizu University. Coeducational national universities also have earlier precedents: Ikehata Setsuho became the first female president of Tokyo University of Foreign Studies in 2001, and Kina Ikue became the first female president of the University of the Ryukyus in 2025.

Even so, the appointment of a woman to lead the University of Tokyo, often seen as Japan’s most prominent university and an institution with considerable social influence, carries particular symbolic weight.

The Selection Process

Fujigaki, 64, is a professor at the University of Tokyo’s Graduate School of Arts and Sciences, specializing in science and technology studies and scientometrics. She earned her bachelor’s, master’s, and doctoral degrees at the same university, completing her doctorate in 1990. Apart from nearly four years as a senior researcher at the government’s National Institute of Science and Technology Policy, she has spent her career at the university, becoming a professor in 2010. Starting in 2021, she served for five years as an executive vice president, overseeing areas including admissions, student support, and research ethics.

Her selection has nevertheless generated controversy both inside and outside the university. Most notably, Fujigaki did not receive the most votes in the university’s opinion vote. On September 28, eligible faculty and administrative staff took part in two rounds of voting, with the top three candidates in the first round advancing to the second. The vote was intended only as one source of information for the selection process and did not directly determine the final choice.

In the first round, Someya Takao, a professor at the Graduate School of Engineering, received 818 votes, or 38.0 percent of the 2,155 ballots cast, including blank ballots. Fujigaki received 400 votes, or 18.6 percent. In the second round, Someya received 1,107 votes, or 51.0 percent of the 2,169 ballots cast, while Fujigaki received 553, or 25.5 percent. Fujigaki therefore finished second in both rounds, with less than half as many votes as Someya. According to The Todai Shimbun, this appears to be the first time under the university’s established presidential selection system that a candidate who did not finish first in the opinion vote was ultimately chosen.

The final decision rested with the University President Screening & Inspection Committee. Half of its 16 members are chosen by the university’s Education and Research Council and include senior officials such as graduate school deans; the other half are external members of the university’s Administrative Council, with backgrounds in business, media, and other fields. Kuniya Hiroko, who chairs the committee, is a trustee of Tokyo University of the Arts and anchored NHK’s current affairs program “Close-up Gendai” for many years. The committee considers candidates’ policy statements, interviews, the opinion vote, and other materials before making its final decision.

Selecting the second-place candidate therefore did not violate the university’s procedures. But the committee’s authority to make the final decision does not eliminate the need to explain the gap between the vote and the eventual outcome. When one candidate receives majority support from participating faculty and staff but another is selected as president, members of the university can reasonably ask how much weight was given to the various criteria, what strengths outweighed the vote, and ultimately how much significance the university still attaches to its long-standing internal ballot.

In its statement, the committee said that through her experience as an executive vice president, Fujigaki had become keenly aware of the university’s role as a symbol of academia, and that she had the strong will and ability to restore trust in academia, drawing on her skill in communicating science and technology to the public. It also said that, drawing on her extensive international experience, Fujigaki had the ability to make the university more open by integrating the arts and sciences and strengthening communication within and beyond the university.

The committee’s reference to “restoring trust” has a clear context. In November 2025 and January 2026, an associate professor and a professor at the University of Tokyo Medical School Hospital were arrested on suspicion of bribery. The associate professor was accused of favoring a medical device company in procurement decisions and receiving roughly 700,000 yen (around $4,400) through a donation arrangement. The professor was accused of repeatedly accepting expensive entertainment, including at upscale clubs, from the head of an organization that had partnered with the university on a collaborative program. The university apologized, and the hospital director subsequently resigned.

At the same time, the University of Tokyo’s application to be designated a University for International Research Excellence, a status that would give it access to grants from the government’s University Fund, has remained under continued review since December 2025. The Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science, and Technology said the university still needed to clarify how it allocates resources and strengthen its institution-wide governance. Restoring trust and advancing governance reform are therefore important challenges for the next president.

The Controversy

Kuniya also said at the press conference that gender had not been a subject of discussion during the committee’s deliberations.

It is important to distinguish questions about the transparency of the process from arguments about Fujigaki’s gender. Questioning how the selection was made does not amount to opposition to female leadership. Nor, in the absence of evidence, should the outcome simply be attributed to a preference for appointing a woman. Supporting more women in leadership and asking a university to explain a major personnel decision are not contradictory positions.

At the same time, debates of this kind can reflect the unusually demanding standards sometimes applied to female leaders, making it important to remain alert to gender-based double standards.

Some critics have also compared Fujigaki’s academic record unfavorably with Someya’s. Japanese internet personality Nishimura Hiroyuki, for example, amplified claims on X that Someya’s papers had received roughly 70 times as many citations as Fujigaki’s.

Someya is an engineer specializing in flexible electronics. His best-known work includes ultrathin electronic devices that can be attached directly to the skin. He has received numerous academic honors, including the Japan Society for the Promotion of Science Prize in 2008, the Leo Esaki Prize in 2019, and the Fujiwara Prize in 2024, and has repeatedly appeared on Clarivate’s list of Highly Cited Researchers. Fujigaki, by contrast, mainly uses approaches from the humanities and social sciences to examine the relationship between science, technology, and society.

Publication practices, research team size, language of publication, and citation patterns differ greatly across disciplines. Simply comparing total citation counts or numbers of awards therefore offers only a limited basis for judging the academic achievements of two scholars in different fields.

More importantly, a university president is responsible not only for research but also for educational and research administration, organizational coordination, resource allocation, and public communication. Academic achievement is only one part of the selection criteria.

Japan’s Remaining Gender Gap

There is a broader context to the debate. Even as the University of Tokyo prepares to install its first female president, the gender imbalance among its students remains pronounced. As of May 1, 2026, the university had 14,098 undergraduate students, of whom 3,023 were women – just 21.4 percent.

Across Japan, more than half of women now go on to university, but the overall figure conceals substantial inequalities between fields of study and stages of education. In 2025, 56.5 percent of women and 60.7 percent of men advanced to undergraduate programs, a gap of 4.2 percentage points. The gap becomes much wider at the graduate level: only 6.9 percent of female university graduates went directly on to graduate school, compared with 16.0 percent of men.

Differences by field are equally striking. In 2025, women accounted for 29.4 percent of undergraduates in science and just 17.9 percent in engineering. At the master’s level, their shares fell further, to 24.0 percent and 15.9 percent, respectively. The fact that more women are entering higher education does not mean that they participate equally across academic disciplines.

Women remain underrepresented at senior levels after entering academia as well. In 2025, women accounted for 28.2 percent of full-time faculty at Japanese universities and graduate schools, but only 20.1 percent of presidents, vice presidents, and professors. In 2024, just four of the 86 presidents of Japan’s national universities were women, or 4.7 percent, compared with 14.9 percent at public universities and 15.1 percent at private universities.

The same pattern is evident in corporate management. In 2025, women made up 16.1 percent of section managers and 9.3 percent of department managers at companies with at least 100 regular employees. As of October 2025, women headed only 8.6 percent of Japanese companies. Although this was a record high, the figure remained below one in ten.

Politics shows a similar imbalance. Takaichi Sanae became Japan’s first female prime minister in October 2025. Yet after Takaichi’s September 2026 Cabinet reshuffle, only three of the 19 Cabinet members, including the prime minister herself, were women. As of February 2026, women accounted for 30.0 percent of members of the House of Councillors but only 14.6 percent of members of the House of Representatives. These gaps show that women’s expanding access to higher education has not yet translated fully into representation in leadership and decision-making positions.

The appointment of the University of Tokyo’s first female president is symbolically important, but substantive progress will depend on what universities do to support women at different stages of their education and careers. That means encouraging women to continue into graduate education, supporting their participation in science and engineering, and creating classrooms in which they feel comfortable expressing their views and taking part in discussion.

For researchers, it means reducing gender discrimination in the workplace, ensuring fair and transparent recruitment and promotion, and making it easier to combine research careers with caregiving responsibilities. Together, these measures can give women greater opportunities to develop their abilities and participate in decision-making, not only in academia but also in business and society more broadly.

title: At Least 8 Dead in Myanmar Air Strikes, Rakhine Rebel Group Claims
description: In a desperate bid to claw back territory from the Arakan Army, the Myanmar military has ramped up its use of air power.
text:
Myanmar’s military has launched airstrikes on camps for internally displaced people in Rakhine State, killing at least eight people and leaving more injured, according to a local ethnic rebel organization.

The Arakan Army (AA), a Rakhine nationalist group that controls much of the state in western Myanmar, said yesterday that a Y12 aircraft bombed a displacement shelter and a nearby village in AA-controlled Ponnagyun Township, The Irrawaddy reported. One civilian was killed and two injured in the attack, it added.

This came after six were killed in an air attack on a separate displacement camp in the township on Sunday night, the AA claimed. Several more were injured in the attack, which also destroyed buildings.

The two attacks were also confirmed by ​the Ponnagyun Youth Association, which told Reuters that everyone killed or injured was a “displaced civilian.”

“Attacking these civilian targets with aircraft was a deliberative move,” Wai Hun Aung, a prominent Rakhine writer and aid worker, told The Irrawaddy, adding that the camps were located far from the active combat zone in Rakhine State.

This week’s airstrikes are just the latest to take place in Rakhine, as the Myanmar armed forces attempt to claw back territory from the AA. Much of the state has fallen under the control of the AA since late 2023, when the group and its allies launched an offensive known as Operation 1027. The military has only a few precarious footholds in the state now, including the state capital Sittwe and several other coastal areas. As it has done in other parts of Myanmar, it has begun to lean heavily on its air power to punish civilian populations and stave off further losses.

The attacks came a week after a major aerial attack in neighboring Kyauktaw township on September 28, which killed 50 people and wounded at least ​58, according to the AA and other local sources. In December, an attack on a hospital in Mrauk U township killed at least 30 people.

The attacks indicate that despite the efforts of the new quasi-civilian government to project a sense of stability and normalcy, the situation in much of the country is unstable. Since taking office as president in April, coup leader-turned-President Min Aung Hlaing has launched a diplomatic offensive aimed at normalizing Myanmar’s relations with its neighbors. This includes the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), which has excluded Myanmar from its summits since late 2021 over its failure to implement the bloc’s Five-Point Consensus conflict resolution plan.

In a response to the September 28 attack, the Philippines, ASEAN’s current chair, said that it was “closely monitoring developments” and expressed “concern” over the attacks, ​Foreign Affairs Assistant Secretary for ASEAN Affairs Ana Marie ​Hernando told Reuters on Saturday. The air strike was also condemned by U.N. human rights chief Volker Türk.

While Myanmar’s military has recently succeeded in halting the loss of territory to ethnic armed groups and other resistance factions, nearly 3.8 million people remain displaced across the country, according to the United Nations, and the central state’s hold on much of the country remains either loose or non-existent.

With the failure of a recent military offensive aimed at seizing territory around Sittwe, the Myanmar armed forces will likely compensate by relying ever more heavily on the use of air power in Rakhine State.

title: Australia as an AI Middle Power
description: As a middle power, with a range of assets and resources, Australia is not powerless in the face of change.
text:
Australia’s role in the frontier world of artificial intelligence was the focus in Canberra last month, with two events bringing together hundreds of defense, diplomacy, development, and industry experts. The Australian Strategic Policy Institute (ASPI) gathered the national security and defense community for an AI Masterclass on September 14. The next day, the Development Intelligence Lab’s Situation 2026 explored how AI can solve Indo-Pacific development challenges.

The events revealed a country grappling with what it means to be a middle power in the age of AI. As ClearAI founder Jisoo Kim put it, at a time when AI is developing at breakneck speed and reordering economies and societies, “Where in this ecosystem, where in this global economy is Australia going to sit?”

Judging from opinion polling, many Australians would probably prefer that AI had never been invented. But now that the cat is out of the bag, Australia needs to think about what it means for its security and prosperity, and the risks and opportunities it brings.

As a middle power, with a range of assets and resources, Australia is not powerless in the face of these changes. It has some capacity to influence the new world that AI is making.

Assistant Minister for the Digital Economy Andrew Charlton addressed this openly. Asking how middle powers manage AI, he identified four plays: alignment with a superpower, leverage in the value chain, competition through different models and capabilities, and sovereign capability. Charlton stated that Australia is pursuing all four simultaneously.

Shadow Minister for Industry and Sovereign Capability Andrew Hastie broadly agreed, particularly emphasizing the U.S. relationship as Australia’s “line to sovereignty.” Hastie suggested using Australia’s relationships in Washington to encourage a hyperscaler to invest in Australia.

Without data centers, frontier labs, and talent, Australia remains dependent on what comes through submarine cables, and this may make Australia a “supplicant state” – with Hastie using the analogy of the nuclear race, where once the U.S. convinced Australia to withdraw, it has been reliant on Washington ever since. He gave a sense of the stakes for Australia: countries with AI will pull ahead and Australia will fall further behind.

According to Minister for Industry and Innovation Tim Ayres, the government’s “aim is not to do everything, but to make ourselves the indispensable country.” That is, to find what Australia can excel at in this new ecosystem and make it the country’s comparative advantage.

Australia brings assets in policy expertise, talent, and trust. Ayres also highlighted capabilities in chip packaging, quantum computing, and specialized datasets, alongside institutional advantages such as firms and unions working together in the national interest.

Throughout the discussions, there were multiple calls for Australia to work with other countries including the United Kingdom, Canada, Japan, South Korea, and India.

As the American Enterprise Institute’s Ryan Fedasiuk put it, middle powers have a path forward if they “conceive of AI as a global megaproject which everyone can contribute to.” Importantly, “Sovereignty doesn’t mean autarky. Sovereignty means being able to choose your own dependencies rather than having them foisted on you.”

Aditya Maheshwari of the Indian Institute of Management Indore outlined how middle powers could energize their own ecosystems through talent, research, joint projects, and shared computing facilities, rather than competing with the United States and China on frontier models.

Australia also has considerable opportunities to shape international standards. Australian Signals Directorate Director-General Abigail Bradshaw argued that having a place in the AI industry strengthens Australia’s sovereignty and gives it a voice in global standards.

Australian AI Safety Institute head Kate Conroy highlighted Australia’s ability to punch above its weight internationally, drawing on its experience in developing standards adopted globally.

Australia’s Ambassador for Cyber Affairs and Critical Technology, Jessica Hunter, argued that Australia has the assets, relationships, and agency to be a shaper of the AI world rather than merely a consumer.

It’s interesting that this proactivity is being actively encouraged by frontier labs, including OpenAI Vice President Ann O’Leary and Anthropic Special Envoy and former U.S Ambassador to Australia Jeff Bleich.

An important element of being an AI middle power is to think about how it contributes to development outcomes. As Minister for International Development Anne Aly put it, “The value of technologies lies in the way that people’s lives are improved.” The challenge is “to ensure the benefits of emerging technologies are shared widely rather than used to widen inequalities.”

Through this lens, Australia’s Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade sponsored a competition on what Indo-Pacific development challenge AI could solve in the next five years, gathering more than 100 proposals. From disaster warning systems to healthcare and protecting Pacific maritime zones, there are countless ways Australia can use AI to contribute as a development partner.

Times of change are generally good for middle powers, enabling them to play an entrepreneurial role. These discussions demonstrated the benefits of Australia inserting itself into the AI economy, shaping global safety standards and enabling positive diffusion of technology across the region.

title: Australia’s Billionaire Problem and the ‘Corruption of the Democratic Process’
description: Australia’s incoming political finance laws will cap donations and electioneering spending for the first time, but the limits are generous, the rules complex, and the two-year delay suspiciously convenient for the major parties.
text:
Mining magnate Gina Rinehart and close associates have reportedly gifted over AU$3 million to the One Nation Party in the last financial year, in cash and even an entire aircraft. “Reportedly,” as none of this has to be declared publicly until February 2027.

Clive Palmer splurged over AU$260 million on electioneering at the last three national polls, and then some. The land of the “fair go” has never been as egalitarian as it thinks. As long as billionaires dress down and speak rough, they can speak with a loud hailer and burn money to inflate their interests.

Yet even before the billionaires, Australia had a money-in-electoral-politics problem.

The two parties of government, Labor and Liberal, have been running business “forums” or “networks” and charging over AU$100,000 for membership, permitting access to front-benchers at regular gatherings. The electoral commission even held, bafflingly, that these sums were not disclosable “gifts,” because they bought something of value. That is the very form of privileged access that most citizens believe corrupts the democratic process.

Current national laws are laissez-faire, by world standards. Disclosure, as noted, is rooted in an untimely model from the paper-and-pen era of the 1980s. And it only applies to “gifts” over AU$17,300 per annum. Unlike the majority of states, there have been no caps on donations – aside from recent bans on “foreign source” donations, inspired by fears of Chinese influence. Nor have there been caps on national electioneering spending.

Hence the Rinehart, Palmer, and party network examples have all been lawful. And parties at the national level have long enjoyed public funding – “clean money,” but it has been extra cream rather than compensation for any limits.

That legal permissiveness is set to change, from sometime next year. For the first time, party and lobby group electioneering at national elections will be capped. So too will donations. Disclosure of donations will be at a lower level, and closer to “real time.” The change has been a long time coming.

The new laws – around 250 pages, including transitional rules – were the result of protracted negotiations across 2024. They passed in early 2025 with support from the Coalition. One upside of this is that buy-in, from both major parties, means the principles underlying caps and transparency are accepted for the foreseeable future.

This doesn’t mean the laws are ideal. The Greens support the principles, but (rightly) decry that the caps are too generous. The headline cap prevents donations of more than AU$50,000 to one political entity. But that obscures the ability to donate that amount to each division of a nationally organized party, several of its candidates and even a couple of sympathetic lobby groups. The effective cap is more like AU$1.6 million per annum.

The spending cap will be AU$90 million for a national party. That’s roughly at the Palmer level, which in his hands was both a record and a turnoff for voters. Within that total cap, there is a limit of AU$800,000 per targeted, marginal seat campaign. The “Teal” independents say that all the caps need redrafting, alleging unfairness to them. Party candidates benefit from the nationwide spending of their party, promoting its brand, policies, and leadership. Also, parties can fund that wider campaign with multiple donations from a single source, something independents cannot. There is a legitimate concern that rules shouldn’t artificially shield established parties, at a time when party politics is realigning.

Lobby groups will face an AU$11.25 million “electioneering” cap. So sugar daddies of the Teals will be able to do background electioneering supporting them. Interest groups will also still be able to mount unlimited single interest campaigns, providing they just promote their policy interests rather than boosting or attacking parties or candidates.

All-in-all, the new laws are better than nothing, if far from ideal. First, the limits are exceedingly generous. No one wants parties to be starved of resources. Party democracy beats billionaires directly campaigning – like Bloomberg and Musk in the U.S. party machines, however derided, have an ongoing interest in their long-term reputation. Channeling donations through parties, in the Australian way, insulates against corruption. It is far easier to buy a self-interested individual politician, as U.S. experience also shows.

The new laws will dampen the ability of incumbent and business friendly parties to rely on mega-donations, from corporations or unions, into their campaign budgets. In return, the regime will ramp up public funding to AU$5 per vote – or AU$10 per elector given we have House and Senate votes. In addition, mimicking state practice, parties (and independent MPs) will get a second flow of subsidies. In the form of “administrative” assistance, paid at a metric based on the number of Commonwealth MPs they have.

Second, the new laws are unduly complex. Admittedly, regulating the flow of money is hard. There are waterbed effects. So, to mix metaphors, regulation engages in a cat-and-mouse game. But these laws numb my brain, and I’ve spent 30 years studying the area. Parties, especially small or new ones, rely on volunteers at ground level. Not all can afford legal advice. The electoral commission will do well to focus not on missteps by small fry, but on lurks by the well-to-do and well-advised.

Finally, why is there a two-year delay for the new restraints and obligations to come into effect? The official explanation is that the commission needs time to gear up the new disclosure portal and educate itself and others as to the new complexities. One doesn’t have to be too cynical, though, to suspect another motive. Seeing Rinehart shower big money on One Nation – and its explosion in the polls – the major parties want time to catch up, to fill their election coffers ahead of a late 2027 or early 2028 poll. As St. Augustine quipped, “Lord make me chaste; just not yet.”

One thing to watch for is unintended effects. Will big money just reappear in other guises? Palmer, capped in what he can give to his own party, may just run more oblique campaigns directly through a corporate vehicle. Unions and business groups too may campaign more nakedly to help Labor and the Coalition. Astro-turfed groups may appear to strain the law.

Ultimately, there is no perfect regime of regulating money in electoral politics. Integrity values, the ideals of political equality and liberty, and the pragmatic need for fair party resourcing, have to be accommodated. Being part of a cat-and-mouse game, the new laws will inevitably be revisited by the end of the decade.

Originally published under Creative Commons by 360info™.

title: Bangladesh’s First Dollar Bond Can Wait
description: The BNP government plans to issue sovereign bonds in December amid slow economic growth, fiscal strain, rising dollar bills, and a global downturn in the bond market.
text:
Bangladesh is set to issue its first-ever sovereign bond denominated in dollars, most probably in December. The initiative aligns with the current Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP)-led government’s economic vision to strengthen the country’s bond and capital markets and reduce reliance on IMF and World Bank loans.

Initially, the government plans to issue bonds between $500 million and $1 billion, offering a regular yield, known as a “coupon,” of 7-8 percent to bondholders.

For months, Bangladesh has struggled to attract foreign direct investment and raise funds through the capital market, with zero initial public offerings since March 2024, while its banking sector has been distressed, with overwhelming non-performing loans. Amid the worsening economic situation, IMF loans came with stringent conditionalities to raise revenue collection and cut public spending, which at times means cutting social welfare expenses for the most underprivileged. Hence, the government’s decision to cancel the IMF loan and issue its debut sovereign bond in dollars promises autonomy in fiscal decision-making and an alternative channel to increase dollar reserves.

However, fiscal conditions, combined with the global bond market outlook and political instability, suggest that Bangladesh may not yet be ready to bear the cost of issuing the bond and making regular coupon payments in dollars.

Historically, Bangladesh has met its loan repayments while maintaining steady reserves, except during 2022-2024, when it faced a temporary balance-of-payments crisis due to the contraction in the global supply chain following the pandemic and the Russia-Ukraine war. The current external balance sheet signals a positive outlook, with remittances reaching a record ceiling of $35.6 billion in 2026. The public debt-to-GDP ratio is 41 percent, lower than in most of its neighboring South Asian countries, including India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, and Nepal.

For developing countries, sovereign bonds establish a clear benchmark for domestic and international lenders, reducing the cost of capital. A finance ministry, considering these factors separately, could plausibly move forward.

Yet, two questions require robust answers before issuance: whether Bangladesh can meet its obligations to foreign creditors and whether its fiscal condition can support the debt.

On the first question, the record favors Bangladesh, as it has never defaulted on its loans since independence. As of June 2026, its total outstanding external debt stands at $110.93 billion, with debt servicing at $4.49 billion, about 5 percent of total export and remittance receipts. According to the Economic Relations Division, less than three months’ worth of remittances would meet annual external obligations, even in the year with the highest repayment level. This raises the question of whether the reliance on remittance inflow as the source of funding coupon payments is prudent. A global slowdown might cause remittance flows to fluctuate. For example, in September 2026, Bangladesh saw one of its slowest remittance inflows in recent times. Interest on a $1 billion bond at 7.5 percent is roughly $75 million per year, a sum the balance of payments can absorb. However, the bond is not a one-year obligation.

Second, Bangladesh’s fiscal condition requires more nuanced consideration. According to the World Bank, GDP growth fell to 3.4 percent for FY26-27, only ahead of Afghanistan, amid rising inflation. Sluggish growth combined with price inflation can affect Bangladesh’s ability to service debt in two ways. It narrows the revenue base of the Bangladeshi taka used to buy dollars to pay bondholders’ coupons, effectively depleting foreign reserves and putting downward pressure on the taka’s value. A weaker taka raises the cost of coupons owed in dollars. The correlation between local currency value and borrowing power is significant, because when the local currency’s value drops, borrowing costs in dollars rise (known as “original sin” in economic terms) and the government, rather than creditors, bears the exchange risk.

For example, Zambia, Ghana, Ethiopia, and Sri Lanka previously launched their first sovereign bonds. All four later defaulted, as most borrowed again and spent the proceeds on projects that earned no foreign exchange. Depreciation then raised the local currency cost of every coupon.

That exchange rate exposure can be costly. Since the government must pay bondholders in dollars, every fall in taka’s value makes the debt more expensive at home. At 7-8 percent interest, the dollar bond looks cheaper than the roughly 8.5 percent the Treasury pays on ten-year taka bonds, but only if the taka loses less than 0.5-1.5 percent of its value each year. Over the past decade, it has fallen faster than that, so the cheaper-looking dollar bond could end up costing more.

Additionally, Bangladesh’s foreign loan commitments are gradually dropping, meaning fewer dollars will be on the country’s external account. In contrast, grace periods on loans used to finance Rooppur, the metro rail, and the Padma rail link are ending, and external debt servicing is expected to rise to about $5.5 billion by FY30. At home, interest has become the largest item of current spending, standing at 1,275 billion taka (approximately $10.4 billion) in the FY27 budget. In short, more dollars will go out while less comes in.

On the income side, tax revenue offers little help either, as the National Board of Revenue (NBR) fell 875 billion taka short of its FY26 target. For FY27, the revenue target requires growth of more than 45 percent in one year, a target Fitch says is unlikely to be reached. Therefore, spending is likely to exceed NBR’s revenue collection target.

Initiating more sovereign bond programs, such as Panda, Samurai, Sukuk, and diaspora bonds, and oversubscription could worsen Bangladesh’s debt situation. In Zambia, for example, the country’s initial outstanding Eurobond debt rose from $750 million to $3 billion within three years, leading to its subsequent default.

Beyond fiscal pressure, Bangladesh should also consider investor sentiment in the global bond market, which is experiencing a significant sell-off. Spiking energy prices, geopolitical tensions, and the boom in the equity market are pushing bond prices lower. As a result, central banks are being forced to offer higher yields to stabilize the market. As of October 9, the U.S. Federal Reserve – the largest bond issuer – raised interest rates to 5.34 percent on 10-year Treasury bonds, the highest since 2002, while the British 30-year bond offers 6 percent – the highest since 1998. With higher-yield bonds denominated in dollars, euros, or pounds available in comparatively stable markets, along with the boom in the artificial intelligence-led equity market, the question is: will Bangladesh’s sovereign dollar bond generate any enthusiasm among foreign investors?

Politics adds further risks. Although the February election gave the BNP a two-thirds majority, the Awami League’s non-participation and a ban on its political activities are a ticking time bomb that could increase political instability and drive away risk-averse investors. Further, Sheikh Hasina – the leader of the Awami League – has said she intends to return in December, when the bond is to be priced. Investors will factor that into their considerations.

Bangladesh’s standing as a good borrower stems from prudent debt management and timely repayment over the years. However, issuing a Eurobond could change that record, since payments would have to be made in a currency the central bank cannot produce. Slow economic growth, fiscal strain, low dollar inflows, political instability, and a downturn in the international bond market mean Bangladesh should proceed with caution. The country should not take on the risk if it is not ready to meet the long-term payment obligations to its foreign creditors.

title: Behind the Veil of Religious Harmony in Cambodia
description: Aggregate rankings mistake the absence of overt conflict and the fear of speaking up for genuine tolerance.
text:
On paper, Cambodia often appears as a site of religious tolerance, boasting favorable scores in global indices that measure selected elements of freedom of religion or belief (FoRB). Over the years, these “rankings” have manufactured a facade of harmony that masks realities on the ground. State influence over Buddhist institutions, structural inequalities, and the quiet marginalization of minority groups and the destruction of Indigenous sacred places are routinely obscured by aggregate rankings that mistake the absence of overt conflict and the fear of speaking up for genuine harmony.

This gap in analysis is the central focus of Asia Centre’s report, “Religious Freedom in Cambodia: Unpacking the Rankings,” published on September 28. At its core, the report interrogates what standard metrics capture and, more importantly, what they deliberately or inadvertently leave out.

Several existing reports provide valuable insights into Cambodia’s Freedom of Religion or Belief (FoRB) landscape. The Pew Research Center’s Government Restrictions Index and Social Hostilities Index both offer comparative global measurements of religious freedom and tolerance. In 2023, Cambodia scored 5 out of 10 on the Government Restrictions Index and 0.2 out of 10 on the Social Hostilities Index, indicating relatively favorable performance compared with its neighboring countries.

The U.S. Department of State’s International Religious Freedom Reports provide detailed annual documentation of government policies and religious-freedom conditions. Its 2023 report on Cambodia identified several areas of concern, including state influence over Buddhist institutions and monks’ political affiliations, Muslim representation in local government leadership, and Indigenous Peoples’ land rights.

The report “Diving Deep into Cambodia’s FoRB: An Exploration of Community Hopes and Collective Hurdles” (2024), produced by Women Peace Makers in collaboration with Danmission Cambodia, offers insights into the experiences of different ethno-religious communities in Cambodia, particularly regarding religious education, participation in religious leadership, and access to sacred sites.

Asia Centre’s report builds on this research by examining the institutional relationships. Our report draws attention to power structures that shape how religious freedom is exercised and protected in practice. It also considers developments since 2024, including the leadership transition and the Cambodia-Thailand border conflict. Drawing on the latest cases and consultations with experts and affected communities, the report goes beyond aggregate rankings to examine the political, institutional, and structural conditions underlying Cambodia’s FoRB landscape.

Four findings are particularly significant. First, Cambodia’s appearance of religious harmony obscures the structural inequalities. Existing research pays limited attention to tensions and hostilities between religious communities, particularly between majority and minority groups. This risks mistaking silence and the absence of overt conflict for “harmony.” Asia Centre’s findings instead suggest that “harmony” is a by-product of state influence, structural inequalities and fear that constrain religious expression. By examining these underlying conditions, the report brings greater visibility to grievances and experiences that may otherwise remain unspoken.

Second, state influence over religious institutions constrains religious autonomy and serves political objectives. Buddhism’s central role in Cambodian national identity makes this relationship particularly significant: political influence over Buddhist institutions can shape not only religious expression but also political expression. Institutional and material pressures discourage Buddhist monks from challenging state expectations, while political actors mobilize religious authority to legitimize government objectives, including during the 2025 Cambodia–Thailand border conflict. By examining these dynamics, the report highlights the often-overlooked links between religion and political power.

Third, the intersectionality of rights is obscured. Existing human rights reporting frequently treats religious discrimination, restrictions on fundamental freedoms, and Indigenous land dispossession as separate issues. Asia Centre connects these concerns through a FoRB lens, showing how development projects and land concessions that destroy Indigenous sacred sites can undermine communities’ ability to sustain their religious and cultural practices, while raising broader questions about equal access to institutional protection and accountability.

Fourth, limited FoRB literacy prevents government officials, civil society, independent media, and even some faith-based organizations from recognizing violations. Hence, unequal treatment in administrative procedures, inadequate protection against prejudices, or absences of effective remedies for affected communities are ignored. Asia Centre’s report highlights the need to strengthen FoRB literacy among these stakeholders to ensure that they have the capacity to correctly identify violations, report them, and make sure remedial actions are taken.

Building on these stakeholder capacities, ultimately Asia Centre’s report moves beyond aggregate global indices to expose the institutional and political mechanisms shaping Cambodia’s actual religious landscape.

By examining state influence over Buddhist institutions, the intersectionality of rights, and the systemic challenges faced by minorities and Indigenous communities, the report provides a comprehensive country-level analysis. Its recommendations translate these insights into concrete responsibilities for the Cambodian government, civil society, international organizations, independent media, and faith-based groups.

Rather than treating Freedom of Religion or Belief (FoRB) as an isolated concern, the report connects it to broader social and political dimensions, offering practical guidelines to bridge the gap between formal legal protections and lived realities in Cambodia.

This op-ed is based on Asia Centre’s new report, “Religious Freedom in Cambodia: Unpacking the Rankings.” Download the full report here. For more information about Asia Centre, visit asiacentre.org.

title: Beyond Deference: India’s Bangladesh Reckoning
description: A course correction is needed in New Delhi.
text:
On October 6, Indian High Commissioner to Bangladesh Dinesh Trivedi called on Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi in New Delhi. It isn’t unusual for heads of Indian missions assigned to critical or sensitive bilateral stations to provide direct update or receive specific strategic directives during visits or consultations in New Delhi. Modi’s office maintains an active and hands-on approach to foreign policy implementation, making direct communication and briefings with key diplomatic personnel a standard part of administrative routine. However, Trivedi’s case and the circumstances of the meeting are rather unique.

Trivedi was appointed as India’s high commissioner to Bangladesh in April 2026, a rare political appointment to a key neighboring diplomatic mission. A businessman and a politician of the ruling BJP from the eastern state of West Bengal, he has direct access to Modi and does not need to route his meetings through the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA). His appointment to Dhaka in April 2026, replacing a career diplomat, came at a time when bilateral relations between India and Bangladesh had hit a rough patch.

Bangladeshi demands for the deportation of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, who has found refuge in India since August 2024, has been a particular sore point. India has ignored repeated pleas by the new BNP government and its predecessor interim government to extradite Hasina, despite the existence of an extradition treaty between the two countries since 2013. The treaty’s terms (Article 6) allows either country to refuse extradition if the offense is of a political nature.

Three days before his meeting with Modi, Trivedi’s response to a direct question at the Bay of Bengal Conversation (BoBC) 2026 in Dhaka had hit the headlines. The BoBC is an annual international conference with participants from over a hundred countries comprising world leaders, policymakers, diplomats, researchers, academics, experts, and civil society representatives organized by the Centre for Governance Studies (CGS). I participated in the conference, held this year on October 3-4, as a panelist and a guest of the CGS.

A participating Bangladeshi student asked the Indian high commissioner: “When will India send back Hasina?” Trivedi appeared to diplomatically avert the direct query and instead passed the buck to the Bangladeshi military, who had sent her to India on a military aircraft before she even resigned from her post. Moreover, Hasina was meant to be transiting via Delhi to a third country, which never actually materialized. This put New Delhi in a quandary.

“At that point in time, she [Hasina] was still the prime minister of Bangladesh. We had hardly any choice on that. It was our duty as a neighbor to accept the reality of life,” Trivedi said. He added that New Delhi cannot set a deadline for her return, as her extradition request is under review as part of the legal process. “Nobody can give you a time frame [over Hasina’s return],” he concluded.

While no press statements were issued, the meeting between Modi and Trivedi may reflect an effort on New Delhi’s part to gauge Dhaka’s mood from its own representative. Dhaka has ignored the MEA’s invitations to new Prime Minister Tarique Rahman to visit Delhi. In fact, Bangladesh’s State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir, who attended the same conference, was categorical in saying, in a subsequent media interview on the sidelines of the BoBC, that the “principal challenge” in planning Rahman’s visit to India are the activities of Hasina, who he termed a “terrorist,” and her team, who are there. Trivedi could be suggesting a course correction in New Delhi’s policies toward Dhaka.

Since November 2025, India’s MEA has maintained that the formal request for Hasina’s extradition is being “examined as part of ongoing judicial and internal legal processes.” Yet, these “processes” remain inconclusive even after 11 months. While New Delhi is unwilling to sacrifice its former ally, it hasn’t closed the door to mending ties with its eastern neighbor, given their interdependencies and strategic compulsions.

New Delhi still envisages that a visit by the Bangladeshi prime minister to India could create opportunities for an exchange of views and break fresh ground in normalizing relations, but it has yet to embark upon a path that will create the enabling environment necessary for such movement. To the contrary, India’s actions have not inspired much confidence in Bangladesh.

First, from time to time India has allowed Sheikh Hasina to issue press statements denouncing the BNP government, despite Dhaka’s objections. Second, India continues to forcibly deport “illegal Bangladeshi migrants.” A large part of the process involves physically pushing these people under the cover of darkness into Bangladeshi territory while ignoring Dhaka’s objections to such a practice. Third, while Dhaka’s imports from India have risen, restrictive trade measures implemented by both countries have stifled Bangladeshi exports to India. Fourth, the number of visas issued by India’s missions in Bangladesh, mostly for medical patients to access India’s affordable private healthcare facilities, has fallen sharply. Fifth, even two months after Dhaka informed Delhi of its choice for its next ambassador to India, India hasn’t approved the posting. This can be seen as a pressure tactic at its very best.

The irony is that, to New Delhi’s discomfiture, Dhaka is carving out a new framework to deal with India. India is used to conformity and deference from its small neighbors while conducting its neighborhood policy. While that worked for New Delhi for almost 15 years, as long as Hasina was in power, the Rahman government has emphasized its desire to pursue its India policy based on two principal pillars: strategic autonomy and a principle of equality, as it sees itself as an emerging middle power and a major hub in the Bay of Bengal region.

In his opening address at the BoBC 2026, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman emphasized the importance of dialogue, partnership, and mutual respect in strengthening regional and global cooperation, while highlighting various national priorities for Bangladesh — including the protection of national interests, economic stability, institutional reforms, investment, and social safety nets. This translates to Dhaka revisiting its relations with a number of countries, including China and Pakistan, heightening New Delhi’s concerns of being surrounded by a hostile neighborhood – ironically, the same misguided calculation that led to poor relations with Sri Lanka during the Indira Gandhi period.

This new outlook on the part of Dhaka has led it to voice its preference to possibly join the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, which has caused much consternation in New Delhi’s policy circles. More importantly, this further implies that Bangladesh’s negotiations with India to share the water of rivers such as the Ganga and Teesta will start afresh rather than being rolled over as extensions of the lapsing agreements, which Dhaka now considers “flawed.”

Predicting the direction Bangladesh-India ties will take in the coming months is thus a challenge, but the Trivedi episode offers a useful marker of where things stand now. New Delhi appears caught between its reluctance to part with a longtime ally and its recognition that the costs of inaction are mounting. Dhaka, for its part, has made clear that it will no longer treat India’s comfort as the central principle of its own foreign policy. Unless India moves beyond symbolic gestures and ambiguous legal processes to address the substantive issues on the table, the relationship risks settling into a prolonged standoff rather than the hoped-for course correction hinted at by Trivedi’s remarks.

title: Beyond Ideological Blocs: The ICDPP’s New Intercontinental Political Dialogue
description: Insights from an Interview with Chung Eui-yong on the Origins, Principles, and Future of the ICDPP
text:
In September 2026, political leaders and party representatives from Asia, Africa, the Americas, and Europe gathered in Seoul to launch a new forum: the Inter-Continental Dialogue among Political Parties (ICDPP). Your correspondent attended the inaugural meeting as part of the CDP delegation and spoke with Chung Eui-yong about how the ICDPP emerged and the principle behind it.

The inaugural meeting brought together 23 political parties from 23 countries, including 19 governing and four opposition parties. Participants included Chung Eui-yong, chair of the Standing Committee of the International Conference of Asian Political Parties (ICAPP) and former South Korean foreign minister; Mushahid Hussain Sayed of the Pakistan Muslim League, a former information and broadcasting minister; Adem Farah Ibrahim, Ethiopia’s deputy prime minister and vice president of the ruling Prosperity Party; Milton Morrison of the Dominican Republic, vice president of the Permanent Conference of Political Parties of Latin America and the Caribbean (COPPPAL) and leader of the País Posible party; Zsolt Németh of Hungary, chair of the European Conservatives, Patriots and Affiliates group in the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe; and Maiko Tajima, director of the International Department of Japan’s Constitutional Democratic Party.

The variety of political traditions represented in Seoul is central to understanding the ICDPP. This is not a forum limited to ideologically like-minded parties. Its purpose is to provide a forum in which parties with different political orientations – including governing and opposition parties – can remain in dialogue.

That principle was formally incorporated into the Seoul Declaration, unanimously adopted on September 7.

The declaration describes the ICDPP as a voluntary platform for consultation, cooperation, and confidence-building among political parties, open “irrespective of ideological orientation, governing status, or level of development.” It also stresses that the ICDPP is intended to complement, rather than replace, existing regional and international organizations.

The declaration addresses a broad range of challenges, including geopolitical tensions, armed conflicts, climate change, economic uncertainty, technological transformation, and inequality. Participants reaffirmed their commitment to the purposes and principles of the United Nations Charter, international law, human rights, the rule of law, sustainable development, and multilateral cooperation. They also agreed to continue ICDPP meetings and develop institutional arrangements and future work programs.

Its concluding phrase summarized the aspiration behind the new forum: “dialogue over dispute, cooperation over confrontation, and partnership over polarization.”

From ICAPP to ICDPP

The ICDPP did not emerge suddenly. It builds on more than two decades of political party dialogue developed through the ICAPP and its regional partners. The ICAPP was founded in 2000 at the initiative of former Philippine House Speaker Jose de Venecia Jr. Chung, who became involved after entering South Korean politics in 2004, later played an important role in its institutional development, including drafting the ICAPP Charter and helping establish its Standing Committee and regular meetings.

In addition to this institutional development, the ICAPP gradually expanded its dialogue beyond Asia. It established regular exchanges with the Permanent Conference of Political Parties of Latin America and the Caribbean (COPPPAL), developed the Asia-Europe Political Forum with European political groups, and promoted contacts with African political parties. The establishment in Ghana in 2025 of the African Political Parties Initiative (APPI) added a new institutional partner in Africa.

With ties established across the Americas, Europe, and Africa, Chung explained: “I thought it’s about time” to hold a meeting involving the four regions. He proposed the name “Inter-Continental Dialogue among Political Parties,” and the idea received support from the regional partners.

The ICDPP can therefore be understood as the culmination of a gradual process: regional political party dialogue in Asia expanding into cross-regional dialogue and, eventually, an intercontinental framework.

Why Talk Across Ideological Divides?

The principle inherited from the ICAPP is as important as the network itself. The ICAPP developed as a forum open to political parties from different ideological traditions, rather than one organized around a single political family. Chung incorporated that principle into the ICAPP Charter when the organization was being institutionalized.

Asked why, Chung replied: “I tell you my conviction. Why should we be divided by ideological orientation? And why can’t we talk to each other?”

He explained that he had held the same view in domestic politics. When Chung entered politics in 2004, some in his own Democratic Party were skeptical of bipartisan diplomacy, while persuading the conservative opposition to cooperate was not easy. Today, however, South Korea’s major rival parties cooperate in ICAPP activities.

The same thinking is visible in the Seoul Declaration. It describes differences in political traditions and cultures not simply as obstacles, but as possible sources of “strength and mutual learning.” This does not mean that the ICDPP expects political disagreements to disappear. On the contrary, disagreement is built into the design of the forum.

At the welcome dinner on the eve of the inaugural meeting, Chung told delegates that they should not expect everyone around the table to think alike.

“Our political traditions, experiences, and perspectives are different,” he said. Those differences, he continued, should be acknowledged and respected. The aim was to create a space in which they could be discussed openly and constructively, while keeping channels of communication open – especially “when circumstances become difficult and dialogue is needed most.”

That may be the clearest expression of what distinguishes the ICDPP. Its purpose is not to create ideological unity, but to sustain political communication despite ideological difference.

From Dialogue to Action

The challenge now is whether that dialogue can produce results. A forum encompassing parties with widely different political traditions and geopolitical interests may find it relatively easy to meet, but much harder to reach common positions or act collectively.

Chung himself raised precisely this issue in his opening remarks. “The significance of this initiative,” he said, should not be measured simply by the number or diversity of participants around the table, but by the ability to “build sustained dialogue and turn our conversations into meaningful action.”

The Seoul Declaration provides the first steps: regular meetings, further discussions on rules and institutional arrangements, future work programs, and broader participation while retaining the voluntary and inclusive character of the forum.

Whether the ICDPP will develop into an effective mechanism for cooperation remains an open question. Its significance will ultimately depend not on the number of parties represented at future meetings, but on whether relationships built through repeated dialogue can survive periods of political tension – and whether those relationships can contribute to practical cooperation on common challenges.

At the welcome dinner in Seoul, Chung described what he hoped the gathering might eventually become: a community of political leaders who made a deliberate choice to continue talking, listening, and working together across continents, “even when our views are different.”
