title: Beyond the Pukpuk Treaty, Australia’s Strategic Footprint in PNG Grows
description: In the wake of the Pukpuk Treaty, Australia and PNG continued to deepen relations with a new rotation planned, defense infrastructure investment, and expanded ADF recruitment.
text:
Last week Australia’s foreign and defense ministers, Penny Wong and Richard Marles, travelled to Port Moresby in Papua New Guinea (PNG) to lead Australia’s delegation to the 32nd Australia-Papua New Guinea Ministerial Forum. The meeting was the first since the Pukpuk Treaty, which established PNG’s first formal defense alliance with another country, entered into force in July. The forum focused on turning the treaty’s commitments into practical initiatives for defense cooperation, infrastructure, recruitment, and new technologies.

The headline agreement was a new rotation of Australian defense personnel to PNG. A new combat group of 130 Australian Defense Force (ADF) personnel will be based in PNG on three month rotations. The deployment, known as the Magani Rotation, is intended to deepen military cooperation and increase familiarity between the two forces.

A rotation offers greater advantages over occasional military exercises. It allows personnel to develop more consistent working relationships, become familiar with how each defense force works, and be able to coordinate activities over longer periods. For PNG, it provides greater access to Australian military expertise, while for Australia, it strengthens its ability to operate alongside a neighbor whose geography makes it important to the defense of Australia’s northern approaches.

Alongside this, the two governments also announced a $77 million infrastructure investment fund for the PNG Defense Force. This funding is intended to upgrade PNG’s military facilities to be better able to house, train, and sustain additional personnel.

While the Magani Rotation may be a significant step in advancing the integration of the two defense forces, the more radical idea is the opening up of Australian military recruitment to eligible Papua New Guineans. Applications for the first intake will open on November 16, with an initial pilot program starting in 2027. The first two cohorts will comprise roughly 50 recruits each, with candidates initially sought from the University of Papua New Guinea, Pacific Adventist University, and the University of Technology in Lae. The program is intended to expand over time, although the initial recruitment numbers are modest.

In order to address recruitment shortages, Australia has already expanded ADF recruitment to Australian permanent residents from New Zealand, the United Kingdom, the United States, and Canada who are on the pathway to citizenship. However, the new PNG recruitment is different – it has been established under the Pukpuk Treaty and will allow eligible PNG citizens living in PNG to apply directly.

The initial rationale is similar – to overcome persistent personnel shortages – but it comes with a broader strategic goal. These recruits will train and serve alongside Australians, creating personal, cultural and institutional links as part of a longer-term alliance-building objective. Australia citizenship will be an eventual requirement, but this will come via the conventional permanent residency and citizenship application processes.

At the ministerial forum, Australia and PNG also formalized a partnership covering digital governance, network security, and emerging technologies. The agreement builds on a Telecommunications Blueprint designed to improve PNG’s connectivity and digital infrastructure. For Australia, the partnership has strategic as well as economic significance: secure telecommunications networks are essential to military coordination, government resilience, and the protection of critical infrastructure. It also gives Canberra a greater role in shaping the systems connecting PNG to the outside world, while helping the country strengthen its own digital capabilities.

Australia’s alliance with PNG builds on an existing security program. Since 2023, Canberra has committed AU$200 million under the bilateral security agreement to support PNG’s police and justice institutions, including upgraded training facilities, police helicopters, and a National Forensic Science Center. A second phase of support is planned after the current program ends in 2027. Though separate from the Pukpuk Treaty, this work strengthens PNG’s capacity to maintain internal security and exercise authority across its territory.

The challenge for both Australia and PNG is to turn these commitments into lasting capabilities. Australia is investing serious capital in PNG – including across issues like health and other social infrastructure – and hopes to gain a return for its investment. This return for Australia is PNG’s ability to develop its defense, economic, and social capabilities, and to be better equipped to contribute to its own security and regional stability. This also comes with the caveat that it keeps PNG within Australia’s orbit of influence. For Port Moresby, the objective will be whether its alliance with Australia actually increases PNG sovereign capabilities and improves its development objectives, rather than simply accommodating Australia’s strategic priorities.

title: Bhutan’s ‘Mindfulness City’ Hides a Dark Reality
description: As Bhutan sells its new Gelephu Mindfulness City mega-project to the world, exiled communities see a high-tech gloss over an unresolved past.
text:
On September 22, Prime Minister Tshering Tobgay of Bhutan stood at the podium at the United Nations General Assembly and made a direct sales pitch to foreign investors. “I stand before you today not as a prime minister, but as a salesman,” he told world leaders, openly seeking foreign investments to advance the concept of the Gelephu Mindfulness City (GMC).

For Chet Nath Timsina, Tobgay’s speech was deeply personal. Timsina was 20 when he and his family were evicted from southern Bhutan in the early 1990s after being coerced into signing a “voluntary migration form.” He resettled in New York in 2009 and has called the state home ever since.

Living just 250 miles from the United Nations headquarters, Timsina watched only half of Tobgay’s address. “I saw him just talk about GMC, which I feel is another way to disturb the living places of the Nepali-speaking population in Bhutan,” he said. The GMC is being developed across a vast tract of southern Bhutan, a region home to large Nepali-speaking communities, including thousands of families expelled in the early 1990s.

The Haunting Land Beneath the City

Tobgay told the U.N. that Bhutan wanted economic transformation without losing “what makes Bhutan, Bhutan.” But whose culture defines that identity?

In February 1989, under the “one nation, one people” policy, Bhutan removed Nepali from schools in the south. Human Rights Watch reported that ethnic Nepalis viewed such “Bhutanization” measures as attacks on their cultural identity, contributing to mass demonstrations.

Bhutan’s government then began to force the Nepali-speaking community out of the country entirely. In 1997, the United Nations’ refugee agency reported that about 92,000 Bhutanese refugees were living in seven camps in Nepal, plus another 15,000 living outside the camps. By 2015, more than 100,000 Bhutanese refugees were resettled in eight Western countries, the vast majority in the United States.

That history matters because the GMC is being presented not merely as an investment zone but also as a model for Bhutan’s future. The project’s promotional language combines ecological preservation, Buddhist values, technology, finance, and international investment, promising economic growth alongside environmental stewardship and human well-being.

Yet even today, Nepali remains absent from Bhutan’s southern schools. A project marketed as “mindful” development must also address the cultural rights and historical experience of the people whose homeland it is transforming.

The issue is not whether Bhutan wants to develop the south, nor whether foreign investors are interested in a new economic hub on the Bhutan-India border. Bhutan has every sovereign right to pursue economic development. The problem is that the language of a blank slate can obscure the history of the land on which the new city is being built.

The hard-sell to foreign investors also masks the reality of life in Bhutan today. The government continues to detain political prisoners, with international human rights organizations, alongside U.N. experts, documenting dozens of them being held for decades following unfair trials, arbitrary detention, and torture. The Global Campaign for the Release of Political Prisoners in Bhutan, a community-led advocacy organization, alongside other international watchdogs, has consistently raised deep concerns regarding the inhumane treatment of these prisoners.

Other international NGOs have also raised alarms as citizens and journalists continue to face criminal charges, fines, and jail terms under strict defamation and national security provisions for exercising freedom of expression online and offline. In recent months, The Diplomat exclusively reported how Bhutan has unjustly accepted dozens of former refugees deported from U.S. soil, only to leave them in limbo near the India-Nepal border, effectively rendering them stateless.

It was against this backdrop that Tobgay, during his recent speech, called for “judicial independence” for the GMC.

An AI-generated concept image of Gelephu Mindfulness City featured on the project’s official website.

Why Bhutan Needs the GMC

For decades, Bhutan’s economy has depended heavily on hydropower and tourism. That model generated significant revenue and helped preserve the country’s distinctive environmental and cultural policies, but it did not produce enough private-sector employment for a growing, educated population. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) reported that youth unemployment stood at 17.8 percent in the third quarter of 2025 and identified outward emigration as a continuing structural concern. It has also warned that Bhutan needs to expand beyond hydropower and low-productivity sectors to create private-sector jobs and retain young workers.

The strain is especially visible in the growing number of young Bhutanese leaving the country in search of better opportunities. King Jigme Khesar Namgyel Wangchuck even visited Australia, home to the largest Bhutanese community abroad, in October 2024. In Sydney, Canberra, and Perth, he addressed large crowds of expatriates, urging young professionals to acquire skills, save, and eventually return to help build the country’s future.

The GMC, in part, is designed to address that same challenge by creating new economic opportunities and attracting investment that could give young Bhutanese more reasons to stay or return.

The tiny Himalayan kingdom between India and China has deep economic and strategic ties to India, particularly in hydropower and trade. GMC allows Thimphu to widen its economic relationships while preserving those longstanding partnerships. At an Indian government foreign policy panel in June, participants highlighted the GMC’s ambitions to attract international investment while emphasizing the growing role of Indian private investment. In that sense, the GMC is part of Bhutan’s effort to expand the kingdom’s strategic autonomy in a volatile region.

The Forgotten Landowners

However, Bhutan is attempting to attract foreign investment to a contested, grief-soaked land – where dozens of Nepali-speaking citizens were tortured and killed in uprisings and countless others died in exile without reclaiming their homes. The GMC project thus risks turning unresolved history into someone else’s investment opportunity.

The over of Hari Adhikari’s book, which includes details of properties confiscated by the Bhutanese government and their assessed values. Photo by TP Mishra.

Currently based in Colorado, Hari Prashad Adhikari, a former National Assembly member from the GMC-affected area, was among thousands whose properties were seized by the regime before their eviction. In his book, “Ethnic Cleansing in Bhutan: A Stigma to 21st Century,” he recounted how his family lost their homes, farmland, and orchards. He valued his family’s lost property, business assets, and foregone income at 29.4 million Bhutanese ngultrum in 1990 prices, equivalent to roughly 204 million ngultrum (about $2.1 million at current exchange rates), using the IMF’s projected 2026 inflation rate.

While property claims from the past remain legally and politically complex, their existence poses a tangible risk for international investors. Capital cannot flow smoothly into a state developing lands once subject to mass displacement without transparent mechanisms to address the claims of those who were forced to leave. Now living in Adelaide, Australia, 76-year-old Bhanu Adhikari said he spent two years in prison after being accused of violence against the government following protests in the early 1990s. For a little over two decades, he called the very land now designated for GMC his home. While he was away, he says, corrupt officials forged documents to seize his family’s seven acres of fertile land and other properties for a fabricated price of just 51,000 ngultrum, roughly $500. His mother-in-law, Beni Maya Rai, who died in Adelaide in 2025 at the age of 91, had long wished to return to her ancestral land, carrying memories of the home she had lost.

Bhanu Adhikari plowing his farmland in the GMC-affected area in the mid-1980s. Photo courtesy of the Adhikari family.

For Adhikari, the GMC’s promise of a peaceful future cannot erase that history.

“If foreign investors are involved in the GMC project, we will try to seek legal counsel to hold them accountable and pursue compensation for the land the Bhutanese government looted from us,” he said.

From the Beldangi refugee camp in Jhapa, Nepal, where still close to 7,000 refugees continue to live awaiting a durable solution, Tilak Rai as the chairperson of the Bhutanese Refugee Representative Repatriation Committee (BRRRC), views the mega-project as a direct continuation of past injustices.

Calling the GMC an attempt to purify the regime’s atrocities against the Nepali-speaking population, Rai noted that even those currently living in the affected area are denied proper compensation and silenced by fear of retribution.

“The BRRRC appeals to the international community to prevent Bhutan from turning seized ancestral land into a high-tech façade designed to erase our history,” he said.

Tilak Rai, the chairperson of the BRRRC. Rai and others continue to demand repatriation from the refugee camp in Nepal. Photo from Rai’s FB page.

Rai’s concerns from across the border are now being echoed by people who still live on the affected land in Bhutan. The landscape there is already undergoing a rapid, state-directed overhaul. Recent months have brought intensive land leveling, corporate partnership pacts and construction progress across the special administrative zone, anchored by heavy development at the Gelephu International Airport site in Samtenling, Sarpang.

The airport will affect 552 landowners across roughly 1,400 acres, with authorities offering replacement land, tokenization, or monetary compensation. But affected residents have raised concerns over land fragmentation, the loss of land across generations, and whether they can remain in Sarpang. In an earlier expansion of the airport, 11 landowners appealed their replacement-land allocations, expressing dissatisfaction with the substitute plots.

Meanwhile, authorities have invited proposals for a 256-unit housing project intended primarily for relocated families. The concerns are therefore not confined to those who were driven from southern Bhutan decades ago; people who remain on the land today are also confronting questions of compensation, relocation and what development will mean for their homes and livelihoods. As the airport moves toward its 2029 target, those questions remain central to the project’s transformation. What Investors Need to Know

The GMC’s economic promise depends on international credibility, yet the IMF has already identified significant fiscal and financial risks associated with the project. Its independent tax regime could affect Bhutan’s national tax base, while the legal relationship between the GMC and the rest of the country still requires clarification in areas including labor, goods, and capital mobility.

Addressing the refugee question would not require Bhutan to halt economic development in the south. Economic modernization and historical reckoning can proceed together. Bhutan could establish an accessible historical record of the southern districts affected by the displacement of the 1990s, create a transparent process for documenting property claims and determining which claims have a legal basis, and incorporate the history of the region into the GMC’s own cultural and educational institutions rather than presenting the area as an untouched landscape awaiting transformation. The country’s leaders have invited investors to become co-founders of a new city. That invitation comes with a responsibility on both sides. Investors should ask not only what industries the GMC will create, what tax incentives it will offer, or what returns it might generate. They should also ask what kind of historical and institutional framework they are entering.

Beni Maya Rai poses in front of her home and property in the mid-1990s in the area now affected by the mindfulness city project. Photo courtesy of the Adhikari family.

Timsina and others in the diaspora see a cruel repetition unfolding in real time: “Watching Mr. Tobgay talk about building a future on the land I was evicted from felt like opening an old wound that never truly healed for me and my family.” Although neither of us originally came from the GMC-affected area, our families originally lived not that far from that region. We were children when our families were forced out of Bhutan, and we grew up in exile carrying memories of a home we barely knew. We are not arguing against development or investment in the south. But a city promoted to the world as “mindful” cannot claim a new beginning while leaving the people displaced from this land and the circumstances of their displacement outside the story.

A decade from now, the GMC may be fully operational, drawing thousands of visitors and investors, and most people may know little about the circumstances that preceded its construction.

Many of those forced from southern Bhutan have since rebuilt their lives elsewhere and become citizens of other countries, but they still cannot return, even as visitors. Our children will grow up with memories of Bhutan that come largely from the stories we tell them, and as they grow older, they will have the opportunity to look into that history for themselves.

Whatever the GMC becomes, the story of how this land was taken from those who once called it home will, at the very least, remain part of what we pass on to them. For investors in the project, that history may come with a cost, too.

title: Bougainville Needs a Credible Timetable for PNG’s Independence Vote. Australia Can Help.
description: Canberra should stay out of what Port Moresby decides on Bougainville, but it can push for a concrete timeline for the decision.
text:
In September, Kokoda constituency in Bougainville declared itself “independence ready.” At the ceremony, Ishmael Toroama, president of the Autonomous Bougainville Government, pledged funding for a hospital and a police station.

Similar ceremonies are being held across Bougainville, an autonomous region of Papua New Guinea (PNG). Each carries the same message: the long road from civil war to self-determination is nearing its end.

97.7 percent of Bougainvilleans voted in favor of independence in 2019, but that referendum was not binding. PNG’s parliament has the final say, and seven years later, the wait for a parliamentary decision continues.

This year, Prime Minister James Marape had proposed holding a vote on August 30. Parliament formally received the result on August 27, then adjourned without voting.

Now Peter Tsiamalili Jr, Bougainville’s regional MP and the leader of government business, has announced a two-day debate for October 20-21. That is progress. But it remains unclear whether the sitting will end in a vote, or what will follow if parliament adjourns without one.

Australia has been careful on the issue of Bougainville, with good reason. In 2022, Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles said Canberra’s job was to “support Papua New Guinea.” Bougainville’s leadership took that as a retreat from neutrality, and Canberra had to clarify that it would support whatever the two sides agreed.

Australia is right to keep its distance on what parliament decides, but it can – and should – help nudge PNG to make a decision.

The 2001 Bougainville peace agreement required a referendum within 10 to 15 years after the election of Bougainville’s first autonomous government. The agreement also gave PNG’s parliament authority to make the final decision on independence – but did not set a deadline for parliamentary action.

The 2022 Era Kone Covenant set 2027 as the outer limit for implementing independence or another settlement, but again it failed to fix a date for parliament to vote. The covenant’s one interim deadline – tabling the result in parliament by the end of 2023 – was missed by almost three years.

The lack of a deadline lets Port Moresby postpone a politically difficult decision; meanwhile Bougainville’s leaders must keep persuading supporters to accept the wait. Many who sustained the peace are former combatants who staked their credibility on the promise that politics would produce an answer. Toroama himself was once a rebel commander. He now warns that trust is under strain even as he urges Bougainvilleans to stay patient. Each postponement makes that appeal harder to sustain.

The approaching PNG election compounds the problem. Under the provisional timetable, voting will be held from June 26 to July 9 of next year. If PNG’s parliament does not vote before the election, the decision will pass to a new parliament, which may first need to decide how much of its predecessor’s groundwork it accepts. Bougainville’s leaders have set September 1, 2027, as the “firm timetable” for a further stage of self-government. At that point, the new PNG parliament would be barely a month old.

Without an agreed timetable, Bougainville and PNG are heading back toward potential conflict. “Trust is the foundation of every agreement. Where agreed processes have been departed from, concerns have naturally arisen,” Toroama said while announcing his timetable in June. He added that “recent events violating these existing understandings cannot be ignored or downplayed,” even as he urged the people of Bougainville to “remain patient.”

Australia has a stake in avoiding a new rift between PNG’s central government and Bougainville. Canberra witnessed the 2001 agreement and led the Peace Monitoring Group that helped hold the ceasefire. Under the Pukpuk Treaty that entered into force in July, Australia and the PNG are formal allies, with an obligation to consult on threats to either country’s sovereignty, peace, or stability.

If Bougainville moves on its own timetable in 2027 and Port Moresby treats that as a challenge to its sovereignty, Canberra might be asked to consult as an ally on the dispute. It’s better for Australia to press for a credible timetable now than be forced to take sides later.

Port Moresby may resent even that level of Australian involvement. Marape’s government frames the referendum as a matter for PNG’s constitutional process, and an ally’s question about parliamentary scheduling can easily be heard as pressure on parliament.

But in asking for a concrete deadline, Canberra would merely be aligning itself with voices from within the PNG. When the result was tabled in August, opposition leader James Nomane told parliament the government should “not kick the can down the road” and pressed it to say when MPs would vote. The PNG and Bougainville have already agreed that Marape and Toroama will jointly determine the date. Canberra would simply be holding them to their word.

A hurried vote under contested procedures could deepen mistrust. In June, parliament set the bar for ratification at a three-quarters majority: 89 of 118 members. Bougainville’s leaders dispute the threshold and how the rule was adopted. However, leaving the vote date open-ended risks pushing the issue past the election – and conflicting with Toroama’s timetable.

That is where Canberra can help. Its role is not to shape the outcome, but to help ensure the process does not drag on indefinitely. Through existing ministerial talks, it should seek a date for the vote and a timetable for addressing the disputed voting rules. A deadline alone is not enough; the covenant had one. What matters is what happens if the next deadline is missed. Both governments should then say publicly why it slipped, who must act next, and when parliament will return to the issue.

If a pre-election vote proves impossible, a joint record of what has been agreed, what remains contested, and when talks resume would at least protect the handover to the next parliament. Australia, already a backer of the transfer of powers, could help maintain that record with both sides’ consent.

Kokoda says it is ready for independence. If Bougainvilleans are asked to keep waiting for parliament to act, their governments owe them a clear account of what comes next.

title: Brewing in Japan: Price-Fixing Probes Test Consumer Confidence
description: The Japan Fair Trade Commission’s secretary general issued an unusual public warning against cartel-like activity amid rising prices.
text:
The Japan Fair Trade Commission (JFTC) is investigating suspected price-fixing in the beer and ice cream industries. While the jury is still out on the hops and frozen milk, Japanese consumer sentiment may already be at stake. How the agency handles these cases could shape consumer confidence in the economy during prolonged inflation.

On September 2, JFTC Secretary General Iwanari Hiroo began a regular press conference outlining the agency’s 2027 budget. What followed was not routine. Instead, Iwanari issued an unusual public warning against cartel-like activity amid rising prices. He said he could not recall a similar warning by the JFTC secretary general in his more than 30 years at the agency.

The statement came as prices for more than 8,000 consumer items were expected to rise during Japan’s autumn price hikes. Rising prices reflect a range of pressures on companies, from high energy prices to domestic logistics challenges. Iwanari acknowledged that price increases were a normal part of economic activity, even if they had a “severe impact” on daily life in Japan. The JFTC is concerned, however, that companies might use rising costs to justify coordinating price increases with competitors.

Five weeks later, the JFTC began investigating the country’s four largest beer companies over suspected coordination of price increases through an industry organization between 2022 and 2025. The move followed a similar investigation launched in June into six ice cream companies over suspected price-fixing.

Like the ice cream probe, the beer investigation has drawn extensive domestic and international media coverage. A Yomiuri Shimbun editorial described the alleged conduct as a “serious betrayal of consumers.”

The investigation could reinforce the broader perception that companies are seeking greater profits during an already difficult economic period. Japanese media have already drawn a parallel between the current investigation and the JFTC’s report on beer pricing in the 1990s, which resulted in no charges.

Japan’s experience of the 1990s also offers a useful reminder of how consumers react to economic uncertainty. In 1997, Japanese wages peaked at 4.67 million yen just as the Asian financial crisis began. These high wages did not necessarily translate into increased spending.

The financial crisis, combined with the domestic policy misstep of raising taxes, contributed to a more defensive consumer mentality. Low- and middle-income Japanese households began to save more as a precautionary move. Consumers increasingly bought only necessities and focused on cost. Retailers cut prices in response, helping bring about “price destruction” (価格破壊). The shift disrupted traditional pricing practices and promoted a more cost-conscious way of consuming.

Today’s economic conditions differ from those of the 1990s. Still, the lessons about consumer behavior remain relevant. In August, Japan had its eighth consecutive month of real wage growth (up 1.5 percent year over year). At the same time, household consumption fell 3.1 percent, marking the ninth consecutive month of declining spending. The divergence suggests that growing purchasing power has not translated into increased spending. The figures suggest consumers may be becoming more cautious throughout 2026.

The government of Japan recognizes the challenge of maintaining consumer confidence and strengthening household purchase power. Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae’s proposed reduction in the food consumption tax seeks to put more back in consumers’ pockets. Equally important is ensuring companies compete fairly and that prices are not shaped by unlawful coordination.

The JFTC’s investigation addresses this concern and aligns with the goals of the recent Food System Act. The act seeks to promote “reasonable food prices” by basing price formation on the necessary costs of sustainable production, enabling producers to keep operating while still ensuring “stable food security” for the public.

Beer and ice cream are not the same as vegetables, but they do offer daily enjoyment for many consumers. Both investigations will test the JFTC’s ability to prevent collusion and protect fair competition. The outcomes will matter beyond the industries involved and will likely shape public confidence in how prices are set.

The JFTC’s challenge, then, is to ensure companies compete fairly as Japan adjusts to prolonged inflation. If consumer confidence weakens, households may once again become even more defensive in their spending, as they did 30 years ago.

title: Cambodia’s NGO Sector Is Collapsing. Does It Matter?
description: Imported by international donors in the 1990s, NGOs have supplanted rather than strengthened local forms of political organizing.
text:
From the early 1990s through the early 2010s, Cambodia hosted one of the most vibrant, generously funded, and unchecked civil society ecosystems in Southeast Asia. Former Prime Minister Hun Sen once famously referred to the country as a “heaven for NGOs.” And indeed, up to 6,100 registered non-government organizations (NGOs) and associations have been able to flourish, including about 3,450 NGOs and 2,650 other civil society associations. This number of NGOs is very high by global standards, by one count making up the second highest number per capita in the world after Rwanda.

A confluence of disasters has changed all that. The heyday for NGOs effectively started closing following the 2013 national elections, when the ruling Cambodian People’s Party (CPP) faced a major electoral threat and began systematically dismantling the public sphere. Viewing NGOs as a vehicle for hostile foreign-backed “color revolutions,” the Cambodian government introduced a restrictive and controversial Law on Associations and Non-Governmental Organizations in 2015. It also began to use tax audits, lawsuits, and political pressure – such as monitoring or disturbing civil society meetings, refusing to give permission for activities, and other coercive tactics – to restrict the sector.

Not only are NGOs required to navigate a suspicious and unfriendly political environment, but they also face a critically strained financial environment. Recently, the international development landscape has endured its steepest funding decline on record. As global power relations go through a process of significant reconfiguration and Cambodia simultaneously moves toward graduating from Least Developed Country status in 2029, global official development aid has been dramatically curtailed. This is set to continue.

The dramatic reduction in funds has had a significant and increasing impact on Cambodia and its NGOs. Already 10 years have passed since funding for Cambodian NGOs reached its peak in 2016. A recent survey of civil society organizations in Cambodia revealed that 26 percent of NGOs say they are not financially viable beyond 2027. It is not unreasonable to suggest that only one in five NGOs may survive the next decade.

In response to this calamity, there have been calls to redesign the ecosystem of civil society in Cambodia. These are led by the Cooperation Committee of Cambodia (CCC), which serves as the professional association of NGOs. A roadmap prepared by the CCC points to how major transformation can be achieved. Options being considered include increased reliance on local philanthropy; the reinvention of NGOs as social enterprises or technical assistance offices; blended financing; increased sharing of resources and organizational infrastructure; and, if there is interest, mergers.

If undertaken, these initiatives would together mark a profound shift away from traditional NGO models toward leaner, more specialized structures grounded in local ownership.

But it won’t work. And here’s why.

First, local philanthropy is captured almost exclusively by the CPP and, for the purposes of making merit, by pagodas and other institutions associated with Buddhist practice. There is little appetite among everyday citizens for giving to NGOs, and it seems unreasonable to expect NGOs to try and compete with entrenched political parties and organized religion in their fundraising efforts. A notable exception to NGOs’ failure to inspire local giving is the Cambodian Red Cross, which is skilled at generating significant donations from wealthy individuals. While this is a large and prominent humanitarian organization in Cambodia specializing in disaster relief, it is also compromised by political entanglements – its president is Hun Sen’s wife Bun Rany – and is the recipient of questionable major donations.

In any event, international philanthropy sometimes funds the wrong things, as any effective altruist will tell you. Well-meaning donors tend to give to projects that look good or feel good, not necessarily those that do good. Just this week, Sunrise Cambodia, a Cambodian NGO that has traditionally been very successful at fundraising in Australia, was in the news again after a former chairman of the Australian Cambodian Foundation, the registered charity raising funds for Sunrise Cambodia, was found dead after being charged with possessing child abuse materials. Financial support for Sunrise Cambodia will reportedly continue.

Second, there is no demonstrable demand for technical assistance offices or social enterprises on a scale that may mop up excess NGO programs and human resources. To date, no evidence has emerged that presents a sensible business case for this model of transforming NGOs.

Third, blended finance models may be excellent for particular types of NGOs, such as larger organizations working in agriculture, water, sanitation and hygiene, and health. But it is not a suitable approach for smaller, grassroots NGOs and those that have adopted strong social welfare, human rights, and poverty alleviation mandates. Expectations of financial return sit awkwardly alongside such priorities.

Fourth, sharing of resources is laudable, but it will not magically make more funds appear. Local NGOs tend not to take the sort of decisive and strategic action that would support mergers, and there are simply no examples of local NGOs in Cambodia merging. Some, like the author, might wish to see the CCC and the NGO Forum on Cambodia merge and show other local NGOs how it can be done. However, this would require high levels of sustained support, including access to legal advice, and advice about governance and organizational structure, human resource management and change management, and program delivery, among other things.

It is unclear if international NGOs and other donors will have an interest in supporting local NGOs with such logistics when the prospect of a merger starts to become more real. Of course, international NGOs can and do rationalize themselves at scale – consider, for example, how Oxfam and ActionAid continue to consolidate administrative functions at regional levels, how Corus International formed, and how Save the Children absorbed Merlin – but this is not a pathway that is visible nor even conceivable to local actors. For the most part, merging is akin to death. Certainly, mergers are anathema to the idea that NGOs bring income and status to their founders and leaders.

A bigger and more important question is: are NGOs really worth saving? The answer to this is not straightforward. Let’s remember that NGOs are not the center of the civil society ecosystem in Cambodia. NGOs were imported by international donors and shaped in their own image. They have a short history and are not indigenous to Cambodia. The functional equivalent of Western-style civil society in Cambodia is the intersecting business and political networks and complex patron-client ties that dominate Cambodian society. NGOs have supplanted rather than augmented or strengthened local forms of organizing. Community members are unlikely to regard NGOs as capable of representing them. NGOs are attentive to what powerful actors such as international donors, the Cambodian government and, to a lesser degree, service users and community constituents expect of them, which means they are less adept at leading societal change on their own terms.

However, there are some NGOs that can be regarded as essential. NGOs that focus on human rights and advocacy such as Licadho, Equitable Cambodia, or COMFREL should be a priority for international donors, as it seems highly unlikely that they will secure sufficient income from local philanthropy or national government grants.

It is entirely possible that large numbers of NGOs have already collapsed. Informal advice is that many of the supposed 3,450 NGOs are no longer functioning but are either unable or unwilling to deregister themselves. The collapse of NGOs will thus remain largely invisible. The Cambodian government makes it difficult to deregister NGOs; there is no clear process for doing this. Moreover, it serves the government’s purposes to be able to point to a large number of NGOs as evidence of a supportive and enabling environment for civil society. This has the potential to deflect any criticism that may arise in response to further crackdowns on civil society.

What should we expect then? And what is to be done? It is true that the future is bleak and adaptation is required. The CPP has tried and tested strategies that have proven successful in exactly these types of situations. The trade union movement and media organizations have been undercut and diminished with the entry of government-supported institutions into their respective spaces. If the playbook is followed again, it seems likely that a rise in the number of government-organized NGOs (GONGOs) will also follow in Cambodia.

In this light, a more realistic roadmap for NGOs in Cambodia may involve calculated and conditional acceptance of the demise of NGOs. It may be appropriate to learn from the experiences of the trade union movement and media outlets. It could also be necessary to cede space to GONGOs and look for opportunities to collaborate with and strengthen them. In particular, this could involve working to transfer knowledge that has been accumulated by NGOs in recent decades – including the human resources that hold such knowledge – to the emerging GONGOs.

Finally, it may be necessary to return to older models of civil society that privilege hyper-local community-based care, perhaps linked to Buddhist pagodas or other community-based institutions. In particular, this could involve systematically transferring assets and other remaining resources held by NGOs to smaller community-based organizations in rural areas. Such organizations reportedly number about 25,000, or one per 724 Cambodians, which seems adequate for the task of providing a much-needed network of support for Cambodian families and community members.

title: Can Australia Create Lasting Climate Impacts For the Asia-Pacific?
description: Australia is set to preside over the negotiations at the upcoming COP31 climate conference in Türkiye, but its support for regional partners will need to be sustained.
text:
COP31 comes at a time when the world is facing the reality that it will soon exceed the 1.5°C global warming threshold enshrined in the Paris Agreement. Across the Asia-Pacific, extreme weather impacts are being felt more visibly and intensely, from the streets of Bangkok to towns across China and Nepal and the waters of the Pacific Ocean.

While these impacts are becoming more severe, global climate cooperation is facing tighter fiscal constraints and a more fragmented geopolitical environment. Elsewhere the need for strengthened cooperation is also being overshadowed by the discussion around energy security and the race for power availability for the technologies and infrastructure that will shape the future of industrial competitiveness.

In the coming days, with support from Australia and Pacific partners, up to 3,000 participants are expected to gather in Fiji alongside a leaders’ summit in Tuvalu for a Pre-COP31 preparatory meeting. This meeting will amplify voices from small state islands and explore what global solutions are needed and the speed required to protect countries whose exposure to climate impacts is rising despite their limited contribution to global emissions.

In November, Australia will then preside over the negotiations at COP31 hosted by Türkiye in Antalya. The global climate movement expects both countries to advance key outstanding agenda items, including mobilizing climate finance set out in the COP29 New Collective Quantified Goal on Climate Finance and advancing the phase-out of fossil fuels in the negotiation texts.

This will be a tough job. Last month, leaders of BRICS – a grouping of major emerging economies founded by Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa – met in New Delhi. The group has since expanded to 11 countries, accounting for 50 percent of the global population. The final endorsed text of the New Delhi Declaration has 34 mentions of climate, highlighting the importance of energy security but stating that “fossil fuels will still play an important role in the world’s energy mix, particularly for emerging markets and developing economies.”

Achieving an absolute consensus from 198 countries for phasing out fossil fuels, especially in the context of the U.S. withdrawal from the Paris Agreement, is not easy. But there are practical areas where Australia’s leadership can create lasting impacts for Asia Pacific: electrification and energy security; the rules and infrastructure for clean trade; and climate finance and resilience for the Pacific.

Across major Asian economies, including China, Japan, Korea and Southeast Asia, electrification is growing at a fast pace. Pairing this with renewable electricity will provide significant opportunities for lower import bills and better environmental outcomes.

The opportunity is particularly immediate in remote and island communities. For fishing communities in archipelagic states like the Philippines and Indonesia, solar-powered cold storage could reduce post-harvest agricultural losses for farmers and fishermen and avoid high electricity costs while improving food security and incomes. Across the Pacific, countries spend up to 13 per cent of their GDP on imported fuels. Replacing diesel generation with solar, batteries and other renewable systems has strong implications for energy security, but will require upfront investment.

With its strong electrification focus, COP31 can make this opportunity more visible and therefore connect investment, technology and development finance with policy support. For businesses, this means creating opportunities to invest in renewable-powered electrification in industrial export-led economies. For communities, it means combining solar and storage with concessional finance and development assistance to replace ageing, expensive equipment and enable long-term resilience for farmers and fishermen.

The Asia-Pacific is a center of industrial activities. Some clean commodity corridors and supply chains are emerging in the region, such as the Australia to Singapore’s green and digital shipping corridor, or the potential Australia to East Asia iron ore green corridors.

These go beyond high-level political endorsement. Lots of work has been done and will need to be done to develop a shared view of how emissions are measured, which standards are recognized, how products are certified and whether infrastructure exists to move them from producers to customers.

COP31 can strengthen a clean commodities economy through global coordination efforts on measuring, reporting, and verifying carbon reduction standards and action agendas related to green trade and certification. But beyond the negotiation room and climate action agenda, there are various collaborations taking place. An example is reaching consensus on a Net-Zero Framework for marine fuels under the International Maritime Organization. The framework, if advanced further in December, will be fundamental to drive global progress beyond the shipping sector.

Australia’s clear goal for COP31 is to support the best possible outcomes for the Pacific, including mobilizing finance through initiatives such as the Pacific Resilience Facility. This is very important, but Pacific countries should not be presented only as vulnerable countries in need of assistance.

Their economies, food systems, cultures, and identities are closely connected to global natural capital and security. Fisheries, tourism, coastal protection, and other ocean-based activities can form the foundation of future economic development if this natural capital is protected, including vast ocean territories, forests, coral reefs, mangroves and freshwater.

Earlier this year, Australia and Fiji signed the landmark Vuvale Union Treaty, recognizing the deep interconnectedness between climate, people, prosperity, and peace across the Pacific. The treaty has made its message clear: rising sea levels are not only an existential threat to Pacific nations; they also have profound implications for Oceania’s security and future prosperity.

At the end of the day, countries and communities are deeply connected by climate. One country’s security and prosperity depends on the livelihood and resilience of others.

title: Can Japan Counter China’s Dominance in AI?
description: Since 2025, Tokyo has acted boldly and decisively to ward off foreign AI-related threats by developing AI for Japan, in Japan.
text:
Japan, a nation historically known for innovations and new technologies, has not held that advantage in artificial intelligence (AI). The United States and China dominate AI’s development. According to one Japanese expert, Dr. Takahiro Tsuchiya of Kyoto University of Foreign Studies, Chinese companies even have a growing presence in Japan’s domestic market. A major factor is cost. Prices for Chinese-developed AI products are well below those charged by Japan’s home-grown AI enterprises.

This is a sea change in the global technology pecking order, but not one that the Japanese are willing to passively accept. While Japan has ceded market territory to Chinese firms in AI, Japan is nonetheless quickly establishing a leading position in “physical AI” – integrating AI into robotics and machinery – and sovereign AI deployment.

Critically, the Japanese government has woken up to the problem. Since 2025, Tokyo has acted boldly and decisively to ward off foreign AI-related threats by developing AI for Japan, in Japan.

The fact remains that Japan has not kept up with global leaders – the United States and China – in core AI, Tsuchiya confirmed. AI is globally considered to be both a revolutionary technology as well as a potential threat mechanism for those who dominate its use and development.

Speaking to reporters at the Japanese Embassy in Washington, D.C., and to his lecture attendees at the Japanese Consulate in Boston, Tsuchiya “strongly advocates for a robust U.S.-Japan alliance to counter regional threats” (read: China and North Korea). However, the readout highlighted “a growing school of thought in Tokyo regarding strategic autonomy.”

Tsuchiya emphasized that “while Japan must tighten technology export controls alongside the U.S. to counter China’s military-civil fusion, Tokyo’s defensive and economic calculations must remain grounded in its own reality.” Part of that reality, suggested Tsuchiya, is that Japan is not only geographically close to China, but is also deeply tied in trade with China, as well.

The Diplomat asked Tsuchiya to describe Japan’s priorities in handling the delicate balancing act of maintaining its strong and strategic relationship with the United States while maintaining at least a stable relationship with China.

Tsuchiya said that “Japan does not copy the U.S. Japan makes its own assessments” of the threats it may face, and how to handle them. Those assessments include risks related to AI development and rollout.

The Japanese government launched a $6.34 billion initiative beginning in fiscal year 2026 with the goal of wedding Japan’s unmatched industrial robotics industry with next-generation AI. Heavy industry, transport, and infrastructure are all planned to be AI-automated. As an example, autonomous AI pipelines are due to manage the heating and cooling infrastructure of Tokyo.

Japan’s population is aging. One of the most immediate impacts of that demographic dilemma is a labor shortage. As a result, some Japanese companies are heeding the call to modernize and develop new AI capabilities.

Nikkei reported on September 9 that trading house Sumitomo Corp. “has partnered with Sakana AI to bring the startup’s artificial-intelligence models to its 100,000 or so client companies, helping the Tokyo-based company sell its solutions even to small businesses and giving a huge push to Japan’s homegrown technology.” Nikkei added, “Sakana AI’s models are said to be comparable to cutting-edge overseas models.”

The new partnership reflects the AI-related security concerns facing Japan, particularly those related to and coming from China. “Japanese companies have fallen behind U.S. and Chinese rivals in leveraging AI for structural and operational reforms. Japan Inc. has been cautious, partially due to security concerns, as full-fledged adoption would mean exposing confidential data to a generative AI model,” Nikkei explained.

Critically, there are “high expectations for Sakana AI as a provider of AI models that do not rely on overseas companies’ services.” In other words, neither the U.S. nor China are involved, keeping the new Sumitomo-Sakana AI enterprise a Japanese homegrown venture, one intended to be safe from prying eyes.

Japan is now committing vast resources to its own AI development, Hello World Japan reported in May 2026. It started by putting an AI Act into force in June 2025. The government then “adopted a formal AI Basic Plan in December 2025, created a Prime Minister-led AI Strategic Headquarters, and committed more than 10 trillion yen in public support for AI and semiconductor infrastructure – all in under a year.”

The Japanese Cabinet then passed its Second Artificial Intelligence Basic Plan on July 14. The plan explicitly targets agentic AI and tech sovereignty. This is backed by a massive road map aiming to mobilize 370 trillion yen ($2.3 trillion) in public and private funding by 2040 for AI and semiconductors.

Hello World Japan noted that the official language in the initial plan is “unusually direct.” The plan explicitly noted “gaps between Japan and other growing countries in utilization rates and private investment” – gaps that “widened” up through 2025. As a result, Hello World Japan noted, “the strategy is framed as recovery, not regulation.”

Such stark and transparent language is indeed a rare phenomenon for the Japanese government.

“That is a different story from the ‘Japan is cautious on AI’ read that still circulates outside the country,” concluded Hello World Japan.

This proactive approach from the Japanese government is an antidote against Chinese dominance in Japan’s AI environment, and the risks that come with that presence.

title: Can Japan Optimize Its Record Defense Budget?
description: All nine priority areas require substantial spending, and the investment needs to be sustained over many years to come.
text:
Japan’s Ministry of Defense (MOD) released its fiscal year 2027 budget request in early August. At approximately 9.3 trillion yen – a 3.8 percent increase from FY2026 – it is the largest defense budget request in the country’s postwar history.

Predictably, all the attention has been paid to the size of the request, particularly the fact that the it is the highest in Japan’s postwar history. The topline number definitely matters, especially because it allowed Japan to hit the 2 percent of the Gross Domestic Product (GDP) target it set for its defense spending ahead schedule.

It is also noteworthy that the request has been followed by a couple of decisions that attracted little attention but are potentially consequential in Japan’s attempt to revitalize its defense industrial base. At the end of August, MOD announced a plan to acquire former Nippon Steel industrial sites in Kure, Hiroshima and turn them into mixed-use facilities that the government can lease to defense companies. In mid-September, Mitsubishi UFJ Bank, one of Japan’s megabanks, also announced new, more lender-friendly guidelines for financing defense firms.

This series of steps come as Japan finalizes the revision of its National Security Strategy (NSS), National Defense Strategy (NDS), and Defense Buildup Plan (DBP), which are slated to be released in December. Together, those documents will set the course for Japan’s national security policy over the next five years. As such, the FY2027 budget request offers a preliminary look at how these documents likely to take shape.

The request’s most notable feature is its emphasis on a “new way of fighting” (atarashii tatakai-kata), followed by operational sustainability and the industrial and personnel base. Across these categories, the MOD identifies nine priority areas for investment, including artificial intelligence, uncrewed systems, stand-off – or counterstrike – capabilities, space, cyber, sea-lane defense, the defense industrial base, and personnel. Investment in all of these areas is much overdue.

The request also appears to seek a better balance between what Japan calls shomen sobi (frontline equipment) and koho (the logistics and support systems that keep a force operating) in the budget allocation. Finally, it makes an explicit effort to harness emerging technologies such as AI and uncrewed systems.

In many ways, the FY2027 request could be a precursor to a genuinely transformational effort to strengthen Japan’s defense capabilities, if fully implemented.

At the same time, however, the request also reminds us of the challenges in executing such transformation. Nine priority areas is a lot. In other words, with this many so-called “priorities” running concurrently, Japan risks spreading its investment too broadly and too thinly. All nine areas require substantial spending, and not only in the initial stage – the investment needs to be sustained over many years to come. At a time when the government faces intense pressure to lower taxes, a basic question remains: does Japan have the fiscal capacity to fund all of them at the necessary scale?

A persistently weak yen makes the problem worse. Japan’s defense budget has risen steadily since FY2013 when Prime Minister Abe Shinzo returned to office. The increases accelerated after FY2023. But the impact of the increase is far less impressive when measured in dollars. The yen’s declining value, particularly since 2022, has eroded Japan’s purchasing power, especially for equipment and components that are imported. In other words, the label “largest defense budget in postwar history” obscures the extent to which currency depreciation can and has offset that budget increase’s real impact.

To be fair, the current government did not create this predicament. The reality is that Japan has been struggling to address the consequences of decades of underinvestment, including years when the yen was much stronger. For example, from FY2000 through FY2012, Japan’s defense spending remained largely flat even as China began to accelerate its military modernization. Put simply, Japan failed to invest when it could more easily afford to do so.

This forces Tokyo to try to recover those lost years while confronting mounting pressure from China, the impact of closer alignment among China, Russia and North Korea, and uncertainty about the long-term reliability of the United States’ defense commitments to its allies, including Washington’s capacity to uphold such commitments. As such, Japan must pursue two difficult goals at once: reverse the hollowing out of its defense force while racing to catch up with its China, its principal strategic threat.

In fact, Japan is not the only country which finds itself in this predicament. Other U.S. allies also spent years deepening economic ties with China in the hope that interdependence would discourage Beijing from using force to change the status quo, while making modest investment in their own national defense. They now face their own versions of the same reckoning underway in Japan.

Japan’s FY2027 request is therefore both encouraging and sobering. It shows that Tokyo finally seems to be grappling with the scale of the transformation required – from emerging technology and munitions to logistics, industry, and personnel – and has begun genuine efforts in tackling them. That said, in order for Japan to leverage this request to begin this strategic turn, it will also need to identify a roadmap to protect funding and ensure that every additional yen is set to be used most efficiently to contribute to these priorities.

The FY2027 budget can jump-start Japan’s real defense transformation. Whether it actually does, however, will depend on the choices that follow.
tag: Japan defense budget; Japan defense spending; Japan military modernization; Japan security policy

title: Can Kashmir Learn From India’s Gen Z Movement?
description: J&K has lost its statehood, local governance, and even the right to protest. But there is still a way to resist.
text:
On August 14, Jammu and Kashmir Chief Minister Omar Abdullah warned New Delhi of a potential Gen Z protest in the restive Himalayan region, while cataloguing the lieutenant governor’s endless attritions against his government – most recently the stalling on a reservation report that seeks to redress grievances over the open-merit category. On September 2, Abdullah’s Cabinet ministers descended onto Srinagar’s streets. Placards in hands, which named in bold, black letters the Narendra Modi regime’s repeated political incursions in Kashmir, they marched toward the headquarters of the Bharatiya Janata Party, the Hindu-nationalist party Modi heads.

The demonstration was scuppered within minutes, with the police, which reports to the lieutenant governor, dashing on them. After a scuffle, the ministers were shoved inside vans like common criminals.

Scores of television crews and YouTubers captured the excess, but no outrage followed on India’s primetime television that evening. Protest in Modi’s India rarely finds coverage on TV, except when it spirals out of control, like it did during the farmers’ march to Delhi in 2020-2021, or this summer’s Gen Z outburst over medical entrance test paper leaks. But that is less coverage and more of salvage job for the government. Media coverage often seems designed to provoke anger against the protesters, who are almost always depicted as foreign funded and scheming to weaken the country’s territorial integrity.

The dismantling of the idea of protest painfully and saliently stirs the question: how, then, does one keep a republic? This was a basic question asked by American Founding Father Benjamin Franklin. In 1789, when asked whether the Constitutional Convention had resulted in a republic or a monarchy, Franklin famously responded: “A republic, if you can keep it.”

But Franklin had reason for optimism. He had lived through, even helped shape, a colony’s epoch-making transition into the first modern democracy, after expelling the then most powerful nation of the world. He was likely persuaded that of all the formidable guarantees that this new system bestowed to its people, the right to stir – and throw the government on a retreat – in the face of repression would be non-negotiable.

Franklin was, of course, speaking without hindsight knowledge of multifarious assaults that eviscerated that right in several democracies. Steven Levitsky’s and Daniel Ziblatt’s 2018 book “How Democracies Die” provided a despairing elucidation how a band of demagogues succeeded in stymieing democratic push-backs, even as their regimes retained democracy’s outward trappings.

That paradox could not be more noticeable in contemporary Indian politics, especially in Kashmir, where Modi’s government has hubristically mounted campaigns to restrict federal rights. Since downgrading Jammu and Kashmir (J&K) to a union territory in the same decision that ended J&K’s partial autonomy in August 2019, the central government has dragged its feet on restoration of statehood. It has, at the same time, coercively erased dissent from Kashmir’s political lexicon.

A plurality of Indians approve of the government’s flagrant projection of force, and not merely because they have fallen for propaganda. Their rejection of dissent is, indeed, a measure of how deeply they are aligned with the BJP’s civilizational project which seeks not just to place Hindu interests on top in everyday political functioning, but to reclaim “Hindu pride” – which can mean anything from renaming roads, buildings, and cities, to erasing Mughal history from school textbooks, to creating conditions to dramatically erode Muslim representation in Parliament.

In Kashmir, where Muslims cannot be precluded from being elected, power has been concentrated in the hands of a Hindu lieutenant governor (LG), Manoj Sinha, handpicked by New Delhi, through a series of government decrees that threaten India’s foundational underpinnings. Omar Abdullah opined in a recent podcast: “Earlier officers would find ten different ways of doing a task I ordered, now they find ten different reasons why it ought not be done.”

National Conference spokesperson Imran Dar hinted that there could be a design to make the local government unpopular. “The LG’s office is procrastinating unnecessarily on a serious issue related to students’ future… which can do considerable damage [to the government’s reputation],” he told The Diplomat.

Sinha is an old brass of the BJP from Uttar Pradesh province, the theater of the Ram Janmabhoomi (birth place) movement. The culmination of the Ram Janmabhoomi agitations in a grand temple in January 2024 is Modi’s biggest selling point, besides Kashmir’s loss of autonomy.

Today, India’s secularist opposition coalition is palpably wary about entangling itself in Kashmir issues. That was not the case a few years ago, when opposition leader Rahul Gandhi signed off his Bharat Jodo Yatra in Srinagar, Kashmir’s capital, on an unexpectedly snowing, freezing January morning of 2023. Back then, Gandhi cited India’s syncretic traditions to re-etch the Muslim majority region more congenially in people’s minds. He talked of the parallels between shunyata, the concept of ego-less consciousness enshrined in Buddhism, and fanaa, the Sufi concept of annihilation of individual ego before God.

Gandhi’s exhortation failed. In the April-May 2024 national elections, the BJP won both parliamentary seats in adjoining, overwhelmingly Hindu Jammu, and thereafter swept the region in the provincial election. The message that Gandhi, his Congress party, and its allies inferred was that prioritizing Muslim minorities’ grievances would be an invitation to derision and defeat at the ballot box.

That explains their current silence – not just on Kashmir but on many other hot-button issues of concern to Muslims, such as the incarceration of activist Umar Khalid, or even Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath’s “bulldozer thuggery” that largely targets Muslims.

After Modi won his second term in 2019, he joked about the Congress’ inhibition. “In this election, not even a single political party could dare to mislead the country by wearing the mask of secularism,” he said.

Waheed Para, a senior leader of the Jammu and Kashmir Peoples Democratic Party (PDP), says there is no reason to be “too dependent on the national parties” to advance J&K’s cause. He cited Ladakh’s successful push for negotiations with New Delhi, which was predicated on regional solidarities. However, Para pointed out that “the mandate is with the chief minister and we do not want to undermine that by taking initiative, though Mehbooba Mufti unsuccessfully wrote to him.” Mufti, a former chief minister herself, is the PDP president.

In December 2023, Modi’s government told the Supreme Court that it would restore Jammu and Kashmir’s statehood after elections were held in the region. It reneged on that promise, but no censure has ever come from the judiciary.

That abandonment by the central institutions makes an urgent case for political unity to be fostered within Kashmir. When you cannot rely on institutions, when you cannot rely on the national mood to soften, when the country’s secular allies are looking the other way, you have to rely on each other. This local unity, as Para pointed out, is what got traction for Ladakh’s own demands.

To everyone’s bafflement, Kashmir is not doing that. Its political landscape is battered by daily one-upmanship – at public events, over carefully crafted podcasts, and more energetically on X, where some politicians choose to parade their superior moral fiber every day.

The common ground is the articulation of open scorn for the chief minister. Some of it is well deserved. Abdullah and his party promised 100,000 jobs to J&K’s unemployed youths besides restoration of Kashmir’s federal guarantees. On both counts its record is dismal, though that has to be judged in the context of his diminished authority. At any rate, reducing these fraught times into acerbic daily bulletins on a local government doesn’t help Kashmir. It helps individual ambitions.

When Omar Abdullah assumed office two years ago, he knew his path would be arduous. What he faced was not just a pugnacious lieutenant governor’s hindrances to his office but the ideology that enabled such obstructionism. Hindu supremacy operates from 57,000 separate cells across India, and has more than 1.5 million volunteers spreading the ideology throughout India’s educational, political, and cultural spaces, intensifying tacit pressure on minorities, especially Kashmiris, to get used to their marginality.

After taking office, Abdullah focused on repairing ties with New Delhi, hoping a calibrated navigation might be the key to negotiating federal concessions, or at least the flow of federal funds. Abdullah was right about the funds, but wrong about everything else. The BJP was prepared to cede nothing to him. It has gone too far promising an ideological pinnacle to its core constituency: the installation of a Hindu chief minister in Kashmir. The relegation of the Kashmiri Muslim leadership is necessary groundwork for that goal.

Abdullah’s failure to be alarmed in time allowed a range of politicians to provoke public backlash against him, while casting themselves as J&K’s true champions. That posturing brought them instant adulation from Kashmir’s overwrought population, which wanted to pin its hope somewhere. These politicians have been sharing their resentment on everything from the Modi government’s controversial waqf legislation, to burgeoning liquor shops in Srinagar, to the Israel-U.S. war on Iran, but even more so about Abdullah’s National Conference’s linguistic timidity on these very flashpoints.

That is undoubtedly the right thing to do, but there is a problem. Kashmir’s self-appointed champions almost always deploy their dissidence from the protected perch of X, or to camera crews, not once outside the BJP’s headquarters or outside the Raj Bhavan, which would involve subjecting themselves to the police’s rough handling. For all the mixed reactions about their politics, Abdullah and Mufti are the only prominent politicians who have shown that grit – Abdullah when he forced his entry into the martyrs’ memorial in July 2025, and Mufti when she took the fight against encroachment to New Delhi’s streets in February 2023.

There are no dearth of people who are enamored with the new “dissidents.” But there are also those – small businessmen, entrepreneurs, academics, rural voters disengaged from the internet’s firestorm of opinions – who point out that emphasizing the need for dissidence is not itself dissidence. Upbraiding a disempowered local government for its lack of dissidence is not empowering. No one has yet articulated a sustainable political roadmap to actually achieve J&K’s goals, starting with restored statehood.

That leaves Kashmir with motley emotions: fear, skepticism, despair, perhaps even a crestfallen urge in some to conform. Yet Sinha, the lieutenant government, depicts Kashmir as, in his own words, “at the threshold of a new future.” Roads, tunnels, and highways are being overhauled on a staggering budget. A digital economy and start-up culture are being imported from India’s metropolitan cities. Sinha sees a “cultural renaissance” unfolding, urging writers and thinkers to showcase “visionary craftsmanship.”

Others see lived experiences obliterated with a crackdown on collective memory – Sinha banned 25 books last year. Sinha’s bureaucrats hear foot-tapping by an influx of tourists and movie crews; others hear collective gasping underneath that ebullient surface.

Despite this profound temptation to mourn, that cannot be the way forward. No political power is insurmountable in the long term. That universal principle should goad people to organize against it, while preserving hope, human will, solidarity for each other, and incorporation of those who are already fighting, in order to more coherently tap undercurrents of public disillusionment.

The aptitude to take everyone on board despite deep disparities is what distinguished the recent students’ protest led by the “Cockroaches” – a moniker from India’s chief justice that the Gen Z adopted in a mimicking rebuttal to him – from the Congress party. Unlike the Congress’ insistence on ideological purity, the Cockroaches allied with whoever shared a sense of betrayal by the paper leak. Boys and girls from tier one cities’ middle class households who have unrepentantly rejoiced each time a Hindutva goal post was achieved were as much an ally as hardened ideologues clad in Marxist-styled khadi kurtas and screaming Faiz Ahmad Faiz’s “hum dekhenge,” a bugle against fascism.

This is not an ideal assembly, but it could be arguably a safeguard against electoral extinction. The Gen Z movement unleashed a tidal wave of uncertainty within the BJP’s stable by firing from its core supporters’ shoulders, creating a psychological advantage the Rahul Gandhi-led Congress’ ideological binary hadn’t achieved in 12 years.

There is a lesson embedded in that combat model for the Kashmiri leadership, especially the National Conference. With no dependable allies in India’s secular coalition or in the judiciary, the only plausible trajectory is to arouse restlessness over denial of statehood in Jammu, and put the BJP in the same predicament that it faced during the Gen Z protest.

A journalist close to to the J&K government told The Diplomat that “Omar has given up on Jammu.” But pessimism is not politics. Finding possibilities is. That is why a politician cannot give up on people even when they disappoint. The first step is to correctly evaluate the public mood.

The Congress’s decimation in Jammu is not a symbol of of its locals’ unwillingness for change, or their contentment with union territory status. Jammu hasn’t given up on those goals. It has given up on the Congress, which has been theme-hopping from caste census, to patriarchy, to a war against corporates, all of which are as abruptly abandoned as they are espoused. The party is also alienating as it seeks absolute ideological steadfastness from the voter without offering anything concrete.

The National Conference must make inroads in Jammu. And not just among the social and geographical peripheries that are usually left to it by the Congress, which contests almost all the seats in the region. Abdullah has a few advantages. Despite years of the BJP’s vilification, the average Hindu household doesn’t doubt that he or his family are moderates.

But the overture to the disaffected BJP voter should not rely on the Congress’ failed appeal to conscience. The NC should use the most enduring and powerful of all incentives to vote: selfish interests, and the capacity of politics of populism to turn it into allegiance. Despite the hollowing out of his office, Abdullah as the elected executive still has reasonable bargaining power to build social and economic solidarity networks.

A winning coalition would include business communities who feel threatened by an influx of outsiders, academic and cultural luminaries who thrive on patronage, disgruntled students, unemployed youths, dissenters within BJP’s over-filled organization, and everyone else who has the social and political capital to amplify the NC’s case as an alternative.

But for any return to normalcy to be accomplished, or even attempted, J&K must stand united. The other option is to fragment and get used to marginality as the country’s right-wing so obviously desires.
