title: Can Myanmar’s New Administration Revive the Stalled Dawei SEZ Project?
description: The flagship project struggled even during Myanmar’s decade of opening. Attempting to revive it amid conflict and sanctions will test its economic and strategic rationale.
text:
Myanmar’s military-backed administration is again trying to put the long-stalled Dawei Special Economic Zone (SEZ) project on the agenda. This time, Russia has emerged as a potential partner for some of its port and energy plans, but it remains unclear whether it can turn the area into a functioning economic zone.

The Dawei SEZ, with its proposed deep-sea port, sits on Myanmar’s Andaman coast. It faces the Indian Ocean and has an overland connection to Thailand and the wider Mekong region. The 138-kilometer-long Dawei-Htee Khee road, opened in 2013 but still requiring major upgrades, could connect the SEZ to the Southern Economic Corridor through Bangkok, Phnom Penh, and Ho Chi Minh City. For Thailand and the wider Mekong, Dawei could offer a westward route to the Indian Ocean that bypasses the Strait of Malacca. This position has long underpinned the project’s strategic and economic significance.

Dawei was an ambitious project from the beginning. Launched in 2008 under Myanmar’s military regime, it combined a deep-sea port, an industrial estate, power generation and utilities, and a road link across the border to Thailand. The early estimates for the entire project exceeded $50 billion. However, financial and development problems led to major restructuring in 2015–16, during Myanmar’s democratic transition. The challenge was raising enough capital and moving different parts of the project forward together.

The industrial zone needed power, water, transport, and access to a seaport. The port, in turn, relied on cargo and industrial activity. Investors also needed confidence that the wider infrastructure would be built. Much of Dawei’s regional potential also rested on having a reliable connection to Thailand. Yet the Dawei-Htee Khee road on the Myanmar side was poorly suited to serve as a major industrial corridor. Limited border facilities and cargo transfer capacity created additional bottlenecks.

Successive governments tried to address these constraints during Myanmar’s decade of political and economic opening. Myanmar and Thailand created a joint development vehicle in 2013, and Japan joined in 2015. Later, the government recast the Dawei project into initial and full phases. The first, smaller phase was estimated to cost about $1.7 billion. Financing remained difficult. In January 2020, under Myanmar’s elected civilian government, the Dawei SEZ Management Committee revised the concession terms to allow staged financing and reduce extra government risk.

By December 2020, it had terminated all nine initial-phase contracts with Italian-Thai Development after repeated delays and unmet financial obligations. The committee said the termination would allow it to rethink the project and seek new partners. The decision came just weeks before the February 2021 coup.

Dawei was hard to manage even when Myanmar had more access to international investors and development partners. Its problems with coordination and financing now exist in a much tougher economic, political, and security environment.

An ISP-Myanmar report based on official investment data shows recorded FDI falling from more than $28.7 billion in 2016-2020 to $7.4 billion in 2021-2025. Targeted post-coup sanctions remain in place, but the fall in investment reflects a wider deterioration that also includes armed conflict, policy uncertainty, difficult business conditions, and major corporate exits. Inflation and foreign-exchange pressure further complicate long-term investment.

The SEZ now effectively sits in a conflict zone. The fighting between military forces and local resistance groups has reportedly intensified around the project area, with reports of violence against civilians by military forces. The road toward Thailand crosses conflict-affected parts of Tanintharyi Region. The Htee Khee border trade area has also been controlled by the Karen National Union and its allied resistance forces since May 2025. For a cross-border SEZ, reliable access and security will remain central to long-term investment and development.

In this tougher setting, the Myanmar military-backed administration began making efforts to revive the project last year. Closer post-coup ties with Russia have brought Dawei back into active investment talks on power plants, oil refineries, and seaports. In June 2026, the Russian state-owned firm Inter RAO and the Myanmar military-controlled Launglon Economic Development Company signed an agreement for a 660-megawatt coal-fired power plant. Russia is seeking majority stakes during the project payback period to meet its banks’ lending conditions. The broader project plan is under discussion. Financing remains unsettled and undisclosed.

Beyond Russia, Dawei is reappearing in regional economic diplomacy. In August, Thailand also held bilateral talks on the Htee Khee-Dawei corridor under its policy of “calibrated re-engagement” with Myanmar. A month later, when coup leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing visited Vietnam, Myanmar’s military-backed administration promoted Dawei to Vietnamese investors at a business forum in Hanoi. Dawei appears to be part of the new administration’s regional re-engagement talks, despite unresolved issues around financing, security, and implementation.

Alongside these challenges, the project’s revival raises concerns about its impact on local communities. A 2014 survey of more than 1,500 households reported concerns about land loss, limited consultation, and incomplete compensation. These concerns are now compounded by questions about ownership, transparency, environmental safeguards, and local benefits.

Dawei’s viability depends on more than building individual assets, but even that will be difficult under current conditions. The seaport, power plant, and transport links must support industry while also creating economic opportunities and benefits for communities. Without that wider ecosystem, Dawei could remain a scattered collection of infrastructure rather than a functioning and sustainable economic zone.

title: Can the China-US Detente Last?
description: Competition can generate incentives for restraint, and restraint can create opportunities for further competition.
text:
The recent thaw in China-U.S. relations – highlighted by reciprocal visits by President Donald Trump and Xi Jinping – raised the prospect of a more stable relationship between the world’s two largest powers. After years of escalating tariffs, technology restrictions, and strategic mistrust, both governments appear willing to step back from the brink. The emerging language of “constructive strategic stability” suggests that Washington and Beijing may be converging on the need to manage their rivalry rather than allow it to define every aspect of their relationship.

But agreement on the need to manage competition is not the same as agreement on its terms. The two sides may have reached a shared conclusion that escalation is too costly without resolving the underlying disputes that drove them toward confrontation in the first place. If so, the current detente could prove less a turning point than a temporary adjustment in a much longer strategic contest.

The history of Soviet-U.S. detente offers a useful way to understand this possibility – not because the China-U.S. relationship is destined to follow the same trajectory, but because it highlights a central problem of great power relations: the conditions that encourage rivals to seek restraint may also make that restraint difficult to sustain.

Why Now?

The current thaw cannot be understood in isolation. It is the latest stage in more than a decade of intensifying strategic competition between China and the United States.

The Obama administration’s “Pivot to Asia” signaled a stronger U.S. commitment to the region as China’s power grew. Washington presented its policy as an effort to sustain regional order, while Beijing increasingly viewed U.S. initiatives through the lens of strategic containment. Yet competition remained partly bounded by the hope that economic interdependence and diplomatic engagement could prevent rivalry from overwhelming the relationship.

The first Trump administration marked a more decisive turn. The 2018 trade war transformed economic grievances into a central instrument of strategic competition. The Biden administration subsequently retained much of the competitive framework while expanding restrictions in areas such as advanced technology. Across successive administrations, Washington’s approach increasingly treated China not simply as a difficult partner but as a long-term strategic competitor.

The escalation of 2025-26 exposed the limits of this approach. Tariffs and countermeasures, particularly China’s leverage over rare earths and other critical supply chains, demonstrated that both countries possess vulnerabilities the other can exploit. But the ability to impose costs does not necessarily translate into a sustainable strategic advantage. Escalation can inflict damage on the opponent while simultaneously disrupting domestic industries, unsettling markets, and narrowing the room for diplomatic maneuver.

This gave both governments incentives to pursue a pause. Washington wants to stabilize trade, reduce supply chain exposure, and avoid a prolonged confrontation that complicates its broader economic and strategic priorities. Beijing has reasons to ease external pressure, preserve access to important markets and technologies, and secure a more predictable environment for economic development.

Their objectives for the detente, however, might not be identical. Washington may see a truce as an opportunity to rebuild leverage and reduce dependence on Chinese inputs. Beijing may see it as an opportunity to protect its economic position, limit U.S. pressure, and consolidate gains made during the confrontation. Each side can welcome stability while preparing for the possibility that competition will intensify again.

The significance of “constructive strategic stability” therefore lies less in whether it signals a fundamental reconciliation than in what the two governments understand it to mean. Does stability imply shared limits on competition, or merely a shared interest in preventing competition from becoming unmanageable? The distinction will determine whether the current thaw can endure.

What Detente Can – and Cannot – Do

The Soviet-U.S. experience is instructive in this regard. During the Cold War, detente emerged not because Washington and Moscow overcame their ideological rivalry, but because both recognized the dangers and costs of unconstrained confrontation. Arms control negotiations and diplomatic engagement could reduce the risks of escalation even while the two superpowers continued to compete for strategic advantage.

Yet detente never eliminated the underlying sources of rivalry. Disputes over regional conflicts, military competition, and divergent conceptions of international order repeatedly strained the Soviet-U.S. relationship. Changes in strategic calculations and domestic political environments also affected the willingness of leaders to sustain restraint. Detente could manage competition, but it could not make incompatible interests disappear.

The lesson for Washington and Beijing is not that their relationship will inevitably reproduce the Soviet-U.S. trajectory. Their economic interdependence, technological competition, and regional strategic dynamics differ substantially from those of the Cold War. Rather, the historical comparison directs attention to the conditions under which detente becomes self-reinforcing – or begins to unravel.

First, relative power matters. If either side believes that time is working decisively in its favor, it may view restraint as an unnecessary concession. Conversely, if leaders conclude that neither side can impose its will without incurring prohibitive costs, compromise may become more attractive. But a temporary balance of leverage can be unstable, especially when both governments are racing to reduce their dependence on the other.

Second, detente is vulnerable to miscalculation. Measures intended as defensive preparations may be interpreted as offensive moves, prompting countermeasures that gradually erode trust. Washington’s efforts to diversify critical supply chains and strengthen technological resilience may reduce its exposure to Chinese coercion. Beijing’s efforts to insulate itself from American economic pressure may serve a similar purpose. Such measures can make future crises less costly to withstand, but they can also weaken the mutual vulnerabilities that currently encourage restraint.

Third, domestic politics can narrow the space for compromise. Leaders must defend their policies against critics who regard accommodation as weakness or believe that strategic competition requires sustained pressure. Electoral cycles, economic pressures, and leadership changes can alter the political value of engagement. Even when leaders reach an informal understanding, they may struggle to preserve it if their domestic coalitions interpret restraint differently.

These dynamics suggest that detente is not simply a one-time choice between confrontation and cooperation. It is an ongoing contest over the boundaries of acceptable competition.

From a Pause to a Durable Arrangement?

The central question is therefore not whether the current China-U.S. detente will last, but what would make it more resilient.

One indicator is whether diplomatic engagement produces mechanisms that can survive political shocks. Regular communication, crisis-management procedures, and clear expectations about military interactions would matter more than the symbolism of leader-level meetings alone.

Another sign is whether both sides develop a more consistent understanding of the limits of competition. They need not agree on the ultimate distribution of power, but they must have some shared sense of which actions risk turning rivalry into a crisis.

A third indicator is how each government uses the breathing room created by detente. If restraint primarily enables both sides to prepare for a more intense confrontation, the thaw may postpone rather than resolve the next crisis. If it creates incentives to preserve communication, contain disputes, and cooperate where interests overlap, it may gradually acquire a more durable foundation.

Washington and Beijing may be learning that neither can easily defeat the other without paying an unacceptable price. But recognizing the costs of escalation is only the beginning of strategic stability. Competition can generate incentives for restraint, and restraint can create opportunities for further competition. The same reduction in tensions that makes diplomacy possible can also give both sides time to reduce their vulnerabilities and reassess their strategic positions. That is the paradox of the current moment.

The immediate thaw should therefore be welcomed without being mistaken for a permanent settlement. The ultimate significance will depend on whether the two powers use restraint to establish more predictable rules for managing rivalry – or simply to prepare for the next round of confrontation.

title: Censorship in Pakistan Goes From ‘Pleasant’ to ‘Unpleasant’
channel_text: Blog; Politics; South Asia; The Pulse
description: Authorities have directed satellite TV channels to refrain from broadcasting or providing live coverage of unpleasant incidents, meaning shootings, blasts and terrorist attacks.
text:
The famous Pakistani satirist and playwright, Anwar Maqsood, once said at the Karachi Literature Festival: “The biggest lie in Pakistan is PTV’s weather report. Outside it is scorching hot, but the news announces: ‘The weather across the country is pleasant.'”

The man, a master of puns and wordplay, used the weather analogy to highlight the censorship imposed on the state broadcaster to keep people away from the harsh realities of the country. He used “scorching hot” as a metaphor for unemployment, inflation, poverty and social unrest.

Now, things have gone from “pleasant” to “unpleasant.”

The Pakistan Electronic Media Regulatory Authority (PEMRA) on October 13 directed satellite television channels to refrain from broadcasting or providing live coverage of “unpleasant incidents,” meaning explosions, blasts, firing and terrorist attacks.

“All satellite TV channel licensees are once again hereby directed to refrain from broadcast, re-broadcast and live coverage of any unfortunate/unpleasant incident such as explosion, blast, firing, terrorist attack etc,” the notification said, adding, “Satellite TV channels must broadcast only such verified information, warranted by the concerned department/law enforcement agency.”

The notification also directed channels to “effectively use time delay mechanism” and ensure the constitution of an independent editorial board in accordance with PEMRA laws, a Supreme Court judgment in suo motu case No. 28 of 2018, and an Islamabad High Court order issued on September 5, 2022.

Before the PEMRA notification, Pakistani satellite TV channels had refrained from broadcasting the “most unpleasant” – the name of former Pakistan Prime Minister Imran Khan and his image. Following the May 9, 2023, protests triggered by Khan’s arrest, PEMRA asked television licensees to ensure that “hate mongers, rioters, their facilitators and perpetrators” were “completely screened out from media.” Although it did not name Khan, television channels got the message.

Now, TV anchors have devised a new nomenclature while referring to news regarding Khan’s court proceedings. The preferred terms are “chairman Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI)” or “PTI chief.” One TV anchor satirically uses “Kasim ke Abba” (father of Kasim), which is the name of Khan’s elder son.

Recently, Pakistani journalist and author Mohammed Hanif, in his satirical blog on BBC Urdu, said people of his age had seen posters saying, “Please avoid political discussions in Pakistani restaurants.” Hanif says that, though he has not seen any restaurant owner pushing guests out for indulging in political discussion, this rule will now be implemented by Pakistan’s cyber authorities.

Any comment or discussion can be construed as anti-national or as disturbing public peace because the cyber authorities have not specified what constitutes such content. So, even a harmless post can invite the government’s wrath if a comment below it is seen as an attack on a government department. In the end, Hanif suggests that the safest way to avoid the midnight knock on your door is to discuss cooking recipes.

title: Central Asia’s Diplomatic Balancing Act on Display from Bishkek to New York
user_author_name: Bimal Adhikari; Zhuldyz Gabdsattarova; Arailym Munaitpas
description: Central Asia aligns rhetorically with Beijing and Moscow in regional group settings, materially with Washington in bilateral deals, and with no one in particular at the United Nations.
text:
The general debate of the 81st U.N. General Assembly closed this week, and the Central Asian speeches put the region’s balancing act on full display. As the world moves toward multipolarity, the five Central Asian states find themselves in a tight spot. They must manage relations with the two leading global powers, the United States and China, while preserving their ties with Russia, with which they share deep historical, economic, and political bonds.

Three weeks before the debate opened, Kyrgyzstan hosted the Shanghai Cooperation Organization’s (SCO) 25th-anniversary summit on August 31 and September 1. Four of the five Central Asian states – Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan – are SCO members, while neutral Turkmenistan remains formally out, although it occasionally participates as a guest. The SCO is widely seen as a vehicle for Beijing and Moscow to limit Washington’s footprint in Eurasia, and the 2026 summit’s Bishkek Declaration gave the United States plenty to dislike, from a firm condemnation of military strikes on Iran to opposition to “unilateral coercive measures.”

Taken together, the two gatherings reveal a clear division of labor in Central Asian diplomacy. The region’s governments echo Beijing’s and Moscow’s grievances in regional group settings like the SCO, court Washington with concrete deals via bilateral channels, and use the U.N. General Assembly (UNGA) podium to say as little as possible that might offend any of the three.

The balancing starts with who showed up. Presidents Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, Emomali Rahmon, Shavkat Mirziyoyev, and Sadyr Japarov all attended the SCO summit in person, alongside China’s Xi Jinping, Russia’s Vladimir Putin, and India’s Narendra Modi. Three weeks later, only Japarov traveled to New York, after making a stop in the U.S. state of Utah. All five Central Asian countries had sent their heads of state last year for the U.N.’s 80th anniversary. Xi and Modi also skipped this year’s session, though Xi was in Washington on a state visit around the same time.

This does not mean, however, that Central Asia has abandoned Washington for its rivals. Kazakhstan, for one, backed Security Council Resolution 2803, the November 2025 measure endorsing Trump’s Gaza peace plan and his Board of Peace, even though Russia and China abstained. Tokayev sits on that board. Kazakhstan, which announced it would join the Abraham Accords last November, also took part in its first accords meeting in New York on September 24. Japarov, for his part, carried the SCO’s complaint about Western sanctions to the UNGA podium, yet he also thanked Trump for cutting U.S. funding to foreign NGOs.

These are low-cost gestures aimed at a transactional White House, and they come bundled with commerce. In mid-October, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio will lead a delegation of more than 100 American companies to Samarkand for a C5+1 ministerial meeting, his first trip to the region. With the United States and China racing to secure critical minerals, Central Asian capitals have something Washington wants.

Beijing, meanwhile, offers trade on a scale Washington cannot match. Xi paired the Bishkek summit with a state visit to Kyrgyzstan and pledged an SCO center for AI cooperation and 100 joint technology projects over three years. He arrived as the region’s largest trading partner, after China-Central Asia goods trade hit a record $106 billion last year. In Bishkek, all four Central Asian members also reaffirmed their support for China’s Belt and Road Initiative. Competition between the two powers lets Central Asian capitals bargain with both.

Central Asia is also building influence inside the U.N. system, and the great power scramble for its mineral wealth may give it more leverage to raise its global profile. Kyrgyzstan joins the Security Council in January, having been elected with 142 votes in June. Tajikistan used its UNGA address to announce its first-ever U.N. Security Council bid, for 2028-2029. Uzbekistan declared its candidacy for 2035-2036 and will chair the Non-Aligned Movement next year, while Turkmenistan will chair the group of landlocked developing countries.

Uzbekistan’s statement, delivered by the president’s daughter and head of the presidential administration Saida Mirziyoyeva, captured the balancing act neatly. Observing that countries are being asked which side they choose, Mirziyoyeva answered with “human dignity” rather than a camp, echoing the Bishkek Declaration’s own rejection of “bloc-based and confrontational” approaches. Uzbek President Mirziyoyev sat beside Xi and Putin in Bishkek; next month, Samarkand hosts Rubio.

Central Asia’s multivector strategy has not disappeared, but it has changed form. The region now aligns rhetorically with Beijing and Moscow in regional group settings, materially with Washington in bilateral deals, and with no one in particular at the United Nations. As great power rivalry intensifies, the open questions are how long Central Asian governments can hold this position and how much they can gain from it.
tag: 2026 SCO Summit; Central Asia; Central Asia geopolitics; Kyrgyzstan UNSC; multi-vector diplomacy

title: Central Asia’s Leaders Gather in Turkmenistan for 8th Consultative Meeting
description: Grand outcomes aren't necessary at every meeting to prove the value of a format. But at a certain point, the lowest hanging fruit has been picked.
text:
On October 8, Turkmenistan hosted a flurry of region meetings in Avaza, including the 8th Consultative Meeting of the Heads of State of Central Asia and Azerbaijan, and the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) Council of Heads of State, as well as related foreign minister-level meetings.

According to Turkmen state media, Turkmen President Serdar Berdimuhamedov laid out “five key objectives,” which included “building the potential of the six-party format,” ensuring lasting peace and stability in the region, joint efforts “to transform Central Asia and Azerbaijan into key transport, logistics, energy, and industrial hubs on the continent in the East-West and North-South directions,” creating the conditions for “accelerated technological growth and the active implementation of artificial intelligence,” and finally, expanding “cultural, humanitarian, educational, and civilizational ties.”

These were all vaguely, and inoffensively, stated, as per Turkmen diplomatic style.

Remarks from Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev were more ambitious and concrete – or at least more readily accessible. Mirziyoyev remarked on the atmospheric change in Central Asian regional diplomacy. He pointed to the completion of the Treaty on Friendship, Good-Neighborliness and Cooperation for the Development of Central Asia in the 21st Century. The treaty was signed during the fourth Consultative Meeting of Central Asian Leaders in 2022 by the presidents of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and Uzbekistan. It took until 2025 for Tajikistan to sign on, and Turkmenistan only did so earlier this year, in July during a visit by Kazakh Foreign Minister Yermek Kosherbayev to Ashgabat.

Mirziyoyev did not remark on the gap between 2022 and 2026 for all five countries to sign onto the treaty; he also didn’t address the fact that while Azerbaijan has joined the grouping – and is taking over as chair – it isn’t a party to the treaty.

This is, perhaps, by design. Mirziyoyev did remark that “we do not seek to create cumbersome structures.”

The friendship treaty codifies this position, baking in possibilities while committing to little beyond words and consultation. The treaty lays out commitments to cooperate across a wide range of areas and build relations “on the basis of mutual respect, equality, understanding and comprehensive consideration of each other’s interests.”

But it contains hints of possible future pathways. For example, its Article 5 states that the parties “shall provide each other with comprehensive support and mutual assistance in matters of preventing threats to their independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity.” It goes on to stipulate that should a situation arise that “poses a threat to the security, sovereignty and territorial integrity” of one of the parties, “appropriate consultations” may be held bilaterally or within the consultative format “in order to determine measures that will contribute to the effective prevention of the threat that has arisen.” That’s a long-winded diplomatic way of saying that should a crisis develop, the Central Asian states may act together to confront it.

Of course, history – and the track records of other regional groupings such as the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) or the Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO) – suggest that defaulting to inaction is the most likely outcome, even amid a crisis.

It’s hard to divorce the friendship treaty, which was signed by Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and Uzbekistan in July 2022, from the Russian invasion of Ukraine earlier that year. Similarly, Tajikistan only joined after its long-standing border disputes with Kyrgyzstan were settled. Turkmenistan, which maintains a foreign policy of “positive neutrality,” is the most surprising signatory by far – but that it did sign on may reflect less a change of heart in Ashgabat than the low commitments demanded by the treaty.

Grand outcomes aren’t necessary at every meeting to prove the value of a format. But at a certain point, the lowest hanging fruit – the ability to sit around a table together and discuss priorities amicably – has been picked. Mirziyoyev – and Kazakh president Kassym-Jomart Tokayev – have made clear that they have grander ambitions for what Central Asia can accomplish collectively. The economic sphere – particularly trade, transit, and investment – got special attention from both presidents and represents the next lowest hanging fruit. Who can argue with expanding trade?

In his remarks, Tokayev noted that intraregional trade amounted to approximately $13 billion, representing 8 percent of total trade turnover between the countries. He set the aim of reaching $20 billion. Tokayev suggested deepening regional trade cooperation, linking across borders the logistics centers most of the countries in the region are building. “In the near future,” he said, “we can link them together to build regional value chains. We have all the conditions for expanding cooperation in investment, energy, industry, and other strategic areas.” Tokayev referenced the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, or the Middle Corridor, while also noting that “North-South route, in cooperation with Russia, remains particularly important for Kazakhstan.”

Mirziyoyev argued that “economic cooperation must be elevated to a new level.” He noted the importance of continuing to address trade barriers, but looked to the future: “We have already reached a point where standard mutual trade is no longer sufficient; we need to create finished products together.”

Mirziyoyev closed with a focus on the youth and cooperation, saying that “it is important that students, young professionals, scientists, researchers and representatives of creative professions have more opportunities to communicate, learn from one another and work together.”

That’s a great sentiment, but delivered in light of virtual silence on the matter of Dr. Ikboljon Qoraboyev it rings hollow. Qoraboyev was a well-known Uzbek international relations professor at a top Kazakh university. He was was detained this summer in Kazakhstan, apparently on espionage charges, and there has been very little said officially about the case – either by Astana or Tashkent – since. It serves to highlight the distance between remarks delivered at a round table and the reality of what it takes to inspire and support cooperation and collaboration.

There is much hard work ahead for Central Asia.

title: China Capitalizes on America’s Scientific Brain Drain
description: For generations, the flow of global talent was almost entirely one directional. Now China is increasingly attracting top researchers from U.S. institutions.
text:
This summer, the departure of more than a dozen established scientists from American universities to China caused a stir in the international press. They were established figures across a variety of disciplines – mainly in the sciences – from quantum computing to biochemistry to artificial intelligence. In one high-profile example, Nobel Prize winner Omar Yaghi left the University of California, Berkeley to lead an AI research institute at Tsinghua University. Several National Academy members also left U.S. universities for positions in China. Many had spent more than a decade, and in some cases several decades, building long careers in the United States.

These departures had been long in the making. Fueled by frustration with the Trump administration’s stringent immigration and national security policies in both its first and second terms, an unprecedented number of researchers say they are considering leaving the U.S.

“Actually, I have been thinking about returning to China for the past few years, especially in the last year or two, due to some geopolitical issues and the state of Sino-U.S. relations,” Zhang Yitang told Phoenix TV in August 2025. Zhang, a renowned mathematician, joined Sun Yat-sen University in 2025 after more than a decade in the United States. “Many Chinese scholars and professors in the United States have already returned, and many others are currently considering it.”

Like Zhang, several of these departing scholars are ethnically Chinese academics who earned their initial degrees on the mainland before rising to build elite careers in the United States.

For generations, the flow of global talent was almost entirely one-directional: “China trained the foundational talent while the United States absorbed the top tier,” explained Dai Mingjie, a scholar at South China University of Technology’s Institute of Public Policy. American institutions, which have long led the world in research funding, facilities, and influence, were highly coveted destinations for foreign talent. Researchers also had ample pathways to enter the domestic workforce after graduation through the H-1B visa, while U.S. universities offered early career researchers levels of independence that were rarely found in the more hierarchical academic systems of Europe or East Asia.

This arrangement supplied the United States with a deep well of scientific talent for over half a century. In 2021, foreign-born scholars accounted for 43 percent of the U.S. science and engineering workforce holding doctoral degrees. Chinese-origin researchers in particular showed exceptionally high stay rates: among those who earned doctorates on temporary visas at American universities, 81 percent were still in the country a decade later.

But the current is now beginning to flow in reverse. The change began with the first Trump administration, when the Department of Justice launched the China Initiative in 2018. Though the program’s ostensible purpose was to investigate suspected spying and theft of trade secrets, it resulted in few successful espionage prosecutions – instead largely indicting academics for minor mistakes on administrative forms. Several prominent cases, including that of MIT professor Gang Chen – who was arrested in 2021 over non-disclosure of Chinese affiliations on federal grant applications before prosecutors dropped all charges a year later – drew widespread condemnation from Asian American organizations for racial profiling. “The community was concerned that the initiative was reinforcing the perpetual foreigner stereotype,” said Dr. Jeremy Wu of APA Justice.

Although the Biden administration nominally ended the China Initiative in 2022, the chilling effects on the academic community were clear to see. In a survey of U.S.-based scientists of Chinese descent, 72 percent reported feeling unsafe conducting academic research, and 61 percent indicated they had considered leaving the United States. By the advent of the second Trump administration, experienced Chinese-origin researchers were returning to China at an annual rate several times higher than they had two decades prior.

Under the second Trump administration, the federal government has pressed forward with an aggressive “America First” agenda. Against a backdrop of escalating China-U.S. tensions, the administration has restricted visas, increased scrutiny of foreign scholars, and limited federal research funding – all meant to curb foreign influence at U.S. universities. In May 2025, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced plans to “aggressively” revoke visas held by Chinese students with ties to Chinese Communist Party (CCP) institutions, or those enrolled in technology fields with sensitive national security applications.

One affected student was Xiaotian Liu, a computer science doctoral researcher at Dartmouth, whose status was terminated that spring. Although a federal judge restored his status after Li sued the Department of Homeland Security, the enforcement action caused widespread anxiety among international students. “Who knows if they’ll be hit by the iron fist tomorrow?” one student told Chinese media.

The anxiety has only been compounded by the uncertain state of federal research budgets. For the 2026 fiscal year, the administration proposed to cut several billion dollars across federal science agencies, including a nearly 57 percent cut to the National Science Foundation (NSF). Although Congress ultimately rejected the most severe funding reductions, the threat alone was enough to alter plans for early-career researchers. Han Fu, a biomedical doctoral applicant who spoke with Chinese media, said he started eyeing Singapore and Europe early last year. “I originally wanted to choose the United States because of its leading position in biomedical research,” said Han. “But if the broader environment is unfavorable, I have no choice but to look elsewhere.”

Meanwhile, Beijing has deliberately moved to capitalize on this mass exodus of talent. Speaking at a national science and technology conference over the summer, President Xi Jinping urged China to “seize the window of opportunity created by global talent flows and actively attract outstanding young talent and teams from overseas.” Ahead of China’s 15th Five-Year Plan – which launched this year with a heavy emphasis on technological self-reliance – the country’s annual spending on research and development reached 3.63 trillion yuan, or approximately 2.7 percent of GDP in 2024. Beijing also offers incoming researchers generous perks, including startup capital, housing subsidies, and up to 800,000 yuan directly in research grants for eligible scholars.

Such incentives have been frequently cited by returning academics as a decisive factor in their relocation. Jiaming Chen, a former Duke University professor who spent over three decades working in the United States, told China Science Daily: “In recent years, the overall research environment in China has changed enormously… investment in science and technology has increased substantially, and research conditions are comparable to those of world-leading institutions.”

Chinese universities are also trying to tackle their notorious reputation for neijuan – the hypercompetitive culture of “involution” that has long plagued mainland academia. In August 2023, the State Council and the Central Committee issued a joint directive seeking to alleviate burdens on early-career faculty by curbing administrative tasks and mitigating the pressure to “publish or perish.” The directive mandates that early-career scientists spend over 80 percent of their working time directly engaged in active research.

Several new research institutes are implementing these operational changes to a seemingly positive effect. Neuroscientist Dan Yang, who left UC Berkeley in 2025 to join the Shenzhen Medical Academy of Research and Translation, highlighted its “research-without-worries” model designed to minimize administrative overhead and grant application burdens. As Yang told China Science Daily: “I can now confidently devote all my energy to research.”

For others, the attraction of China lies less in government subsidies than in the chance to apply their work more quickly to its large and rapidly-expanding industrial base. “The rapid development of China’s biomedical industry allows me to translate my research results into clinical applications more quickly, benefiting more people,” said Ma Shixin, an immunologist who joined the Shenzhen Medical Academy of Research and Translation last year. “This was the most important reason that prompted me to choose to return to China.”

Whatever their individual motivations, the influx of returning scholars has made a significant impact on Chinese scientific output, as researchers bring back the expertise and connections they established during their time in the United States. In 2023, China surpassed the United States for the first time on the Nature Index, which tracks contributions to papers in a set of leading natural science journals.

A study analyzing scientific publications estimated that returnees contributed to 38 percent of China-addressed papers, while Chinese diaspora scholars accounted for 27 percent of U.S.-addressed papers. Papers involving either group also received more citations on average than other papers from their respective countries, a sign of the lasting value of those international networks.

All this jockeying for talent sits within a larger great power competition over who will control crucial technologies ahead. Washington seeks to preserve its edge in the race, while restricting Beijing’s access to advanced technologies such as high-end semiconductors crucial for training frontier AI models. Beijing, for its part, aims to achieve breakthroughs that bypass foreign chokepoints and close the gap in key industries. Both powers are also keeping an eye on the future, seeking to gain early ground in frontier fields like quantum computing.

China and the United States are fishing in the same pool of talent, particularly in fields both countries see as top priorities, like AI research. A report from the Carnegie Endowment found that 57 percent of elite AI researchers in its 2025 sample earned their undergraduate degrees in China. The United States is ultimately still a net importer of this talent, while China still suffers a net loss. But the U.S. edge depends heavily on its ability to keep drawing foreign-trained talent – a questionable assumption as more researchers decide to stay in their home countries or leave the U.S., driven in no small part by tighter immigration rules.

For the United States, the long-term cost of this slow attrition could prove much harder to reverse than the departure of any single star researcher. Lizzi Lee, a fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute’s Center for China Analysis, explained: “If fewer top Chinese students come to the U.S. for Ph.D.s, fewer stay for postdocs, and faculty become less funded… then the U.S. loses not just top talents today, but a large part of the mechanism through which it has historically replenished its scientific pipeline.” As key research hubs once concentrated in the United States are dispersed globally, foreign institutions gain greater influence over the trajectory of global science, threatening the dominant position U.S. universities have long held in shaping future research frontiers.

But for many, nativism will always be the enemy of scientific progress. In an interview with Chinese media, Director of Carnegie China Ma Yang warned against politicizing scientific research. “So far, humanity has not found a better way to continuously generate breakthrough innovation than bringing together large numbers of talented people from different backgrounds and allowing them to openly exchange different ideas,” Ma said.

He added: “If the movement of people were to stop completely, both countries would suffer enormous negative consequences.”
tag: China research and development; China sciences; U.S. brain drain; U.S.-China technology competition

title: China Coast Guard Says It Monitored Philippine Resupply Mission at Contested Shoal
description: Last month, Manila accused Beijing of obstructing a similar mission to resupply troops stationed aboard a grounded warship on the shoal.
text:
The China Coast Guard (CCG) said that it monitored a Philippine delivery of “living necessities” to troops stationed at Second Thomas ​Shoal yesterday, a month after the Philippines accused the CCG of obstructing a similar mission.

Manila undertakes periodic missions to resupply the small unit of marines stationed aboard the BRP Sierra Madre, a grounded World War II-era warship that functions as the Philippines’ foothold at the contested shoal.

In a statement yesterday that was paraphrased by Xinhua, CCG spokesperson Jiang Lue said that it had “inquired and verified the Philippine vessel conducting the delivery, and monitored the entire process.” He added that the CCG “will continue to conduct law-enforcement and rights-protection operations” in the Spratly Islands and at Second Thomas Shoal, which Beijing refers to as Ren’ai Jiao.

China claims the majority of the South China Sea, including the entire Spratly archipelago, where the Philippines currently occupies nine features. In recent years, these have become the subject of a Chinese pressure campaign that has led to confrontations between the two sides, some involving the use of ramming tactics and high-pressure water cannons by the CCG.

Second Thomas Shoal has been a particular focus of Beijing’s efforts. Yesterday’s resupply mission, which has not been confirmed by Manila, came just under a month after the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) accused the CCG of obstructing a resupply ​mission to the BRP Sierra Madre. The vessel was grounded on the shoal in 1999 in order to strengthen the Philippines’ claim over it, an act that China considers illegal.

According to PCG spokesperson Jay Tarriela, the mission on September 25 was “temporarily suspended after a CCG vessel carried out dangerous maneuvers” against the Philippine resupply vessel M/V Lapu-Lapu. The maneuvers “put Filipino personnel at risk” and prevented the mission from being completed, he said. In July, a Philippine marine was injured in a melee with Chinese sailors after a CCG boat carrying eight personnel approached within close range of the BRP Sierra Madre.

These incidents broke a period of relative calm at Second Thomas Shoal, following a string of increasingly dangerous confrontations between the two sides in 2023 and 2024. After a physical clash between the two sides in July 2024 that left eight Philippine naval personnel injured, including one who lost a thumb, Beijing and Manila agreed to de-escalate the situation at Second Thomas Shoal, reaching a “provisional understanding” that allowed the Philippines to resupply the Sierra Madre without hindrance.

While the agreement appeared for a time to have calmed the situation at Second Thomas Shoal and prevented it from spiraling into a broader conflict, the two sides have disputed the details of the arrangement.

China argues that the resupply operations must be reported in advance and subjected to its inspection. In its statement yesterday, for instance, the CCG stated that the Philippines had completed its resupply missions with China’s “approval,” in line with the earlier “provisional arrangement.” The Philippines does not acknowledge any obligation to comply with such conditions or inform China of resupply missions.

The recent incidents suggest that the tacit understanding to avoid further clashes at Second Thomas Shoal has now collapsed, and the feature has once again moved to the frontline of the maritime disputes between China and the Philippines.
tag: China Coast Guard; China-Philippines maritime disputes; China-Philippines relations; Philippine Coast Guard; Second Thomas Shoal; South China Sea; South China Sea disputes

title: China, Djibouti Express ‘Serious Concern’ Over Threats to Red Sea Shipping
channel_text: Blog; China Power; Diplomacy; East Asia
description: A joint communique ups the diplomatic rhetoric but offers no solutions.
text:
Djibouti’s Foreign Minister Abdoulkader Houssein Omar is visiting China from October 19 to 25. On October 21, he held a meeting with his counterpart and host, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi. According to a spokesperson from China’s Foreign Ministry, “They had an in-depth exchange of views on the Horn of Africa situation and the safety of shipping lanes across the Red Sea.”

The Red Sea is under siege – a major concern for Djibouti, which sits on the Horn of Africa, at the junction between the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden.

For most of 2026, the world has been focused on another crucial waterway: the Strait of Hormuz, a transit route for around one-fourth of all global crude oil shipments and one-fifth of the world’s LNG. Israel and the U.S. began strikes against Iran on February 28; Iran retaliated in part by shutting down shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. Traffic through the strait has been constrained ever since.

In response, Saudi Arabia began rerouting some its oil via pipeline to the Red Sea. Saudi oil shipments on this route jumped nearly fivefold, going from 1 million to 4.9 million barrels per day. But new attacks by the Houthis, Iran-backed militants that occupy much of Yemen, are now jeopardizing that shipping. Starting in September, the Houthis began a concerted effort to seize control of the Bab al Mandeb Strait, the body of water between Yemen and Djibouti and a crucial chokepoint for shipping via the Red Sea.

Red Sea map

While Yemeni government forces have taken back much of the territory, the threat to shipping remains high. A Washington Post article, citing “Iranian officials and diplomats in the region,” said that Iran saw the weeks before the U.S. midterm elections on November 3 as a “critical window” for weakening U.S. President Donald Trump. Iran is accordingly stepping up attack in the Strait of Hormuz – and may have the Houthis do the same in the Red Sea.

That leaves regional states like Djibouti to reckon with the fallout.

China, as the world’s largest exporter, has a direct stake in the outcome as well. Wang and Omar not only discussed the shipping threat during their talks but issued an entire joint communique on the subject.

Unfortunately, there’s not much new in the document. It serves more as a vehicle for both countries to express their concerns than an attempt to offer concrete solutions.

Djibouti and China agreed that “the recent escalation of tensions in the Red Sea poses a serious threat to the global economy, particularly to economic activities in the Horn of Africa region, including trade, investment, energy, and food security.” But they also made it clear that the onus is on other countries to solve the issue. “Both sides believe that easing tensions in the Middle East is key to resolving the security challenges in the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea,” the statement declared. In other words, this is ultimately a problem for Israel, Iran, and the United States to tackle.

The joint statement called on “all parties” involved to “take concrete actions through dialogue and diplomacy to address the serious challenges facing the Middle East, the Red Sea, and the Horn of Africa, preventing the escalation or further complication of regional tensions.” There’s no indication that either China or Djibouti will take new steps to facilitate that “dialogue and diplomacy.”

“The Horn of Africa must never be used as a geopolitical arena, and the flames of war in the Middle East must never be brought to the Horn of Africa,” the statement avowed. How China or Djibouti plan to prevent exactly that outcome is left unsaid, other than Djibouti’s enthusiastic backing for China’s vague and largely unactionable peace plans for both the Middle East and “African hotspots.”

The reason for China’s concern is obvious. The Red Sea is a vital shipping link for Chinese exports to Europe, especially with the Strait of Hormuz looking increasingly unstable. That was highlighted during President Xi Jinping’s visit to Egypt in early September. Egypt controls the Suez Canal, which links the Red Sea to the Mediterranean – and Europe. China has already plowed over $5 billion into the Suez Canal Economic Zone in Egypt.

On the southern end of the Red Sea, China also has a lot invested in Djibouti specifically. The state-owned firm China Merchants Group helped build Djibouti’s Doraleh Multipurpose Port project, to the tune of $590 million. Separately, CMG has a 23.5 percent stake in the Port of Djibouti.

China also funded and built the Addis Ababa-Djibouti railway, to give landlocked Ethiopia another trading route for its exports. And let’s not forget that Djibouti hosts China’s first overseas military facility, whose stated purpose is to provide logistics for Chinese anti-piracy patrols in the region.

During their talks, Wang told Omar that China will “support” Djibouti “in building itself into a regional hub for trade, logistics, and connectivity.” But Djibouti’s ambitions – and China’s billions in investments – have little hope if the Red Sea is closed to shipping by militant attacks.
tag: China and the Houthis; China Djibouti port; China-Djibouti relations; Chinese investment in Djibouti; Houthi attacks on shipping; Red Sea trade

title: China Spied on Taiwanese President’s Son – in the US
description: The incident shone a spotlight on China's growing repertoire for transnational repression targeting Taiwanese leaders.
text:
News broke earlier this month that the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) had arrested real estate agent Wanying “Heather” Zhang for spying on Lai Ting-yu, the eldest child of Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te. Zhang lived in Irvine, California, where she worked as a real estate agent. She was originally from Changsha, China, before emigrating to the United States and naturalizing.

Lai Ting-yu is not a political figure – members of the Lai family tend to keep a low profile. Lai Ching-te’s wife, First Lady Wu Mei-ju, does not often make public appearances with her husband. Arguably, the most famous members of the Lai family outside of Lai Ching-te himself are the family dogs, Murphy, Banban, and Luke, though Luke has since passed away. Banban in particular is best known as a dog that had lost a leg to a wild boar trap before being adopted by the Lai family.

Lai Ting-yu, who holds a doctorate in bioengineering from the University of Washington, works for electronics company Philips and lives in Seattle with his wife and son.

The FBI alleged that Lai was being surveilled by Zhang, along with other accomplices, in September 2025. It is unclear what Zhang was attempting to accomplish, given Lai Ting-yu’s lack of a political background.

There could be a domestic political angle. Lai Ching-te has long been criticized by members of the pan-Blue camp over allegations that his son lives in the United States. The suggestion is that Lai is hypocritical in calling for Taiwan to increase defense spending to ward off Chinese threats, even as his own children live abroad.

Alternatively, China may have sought to project its reach, or possibly to threaten Lai Ting-yu in order to have leverage over Taiwan’s president. Indeed, the idea that China might seek to kidnap the children of influential government officials in the course of an invasion, so as to blackmail political leaders during the turmoil of armed conflict, has occasionally been raised. This sort of political kidnapping is a plot thread that comes up in several episodes of “Zero Day Attack,” the hit 2025 television show dramatizing a Chinese invasion.

Whatever the motive, according to the FBI, Zhang was working in coordination with Chinese handlers and demonstrated signs of tradecraft to cover her tracks, such as renting vehicles for several hours then returning them, or booking short-range flights with little notice. It is unclear how evidence of her activities was detected, but Zhang was arrested in October 2026 while attempting to board a flight to Shanghai.

The FBI did not comment on when Zhang was recruited, or her motivations, seeing as she lived in a $6 million home and handled real estate transactions that were in the millions. Though there have been reports of China increasingly recruiting “disposable” agents that are used temporarily and then cast aside, tradecraft by Zhang may indicate professional training.

The Taiwanese government has criticized such actions as Chinese transnational repression. This is not the first case occurring in the United States. Individuals allegedly working for China’s government were arrested for surveilling Taiwan’s then-President Tsai Ing-wen’s travels in California in 2023. Reports indicate that Taiwanese government officials such as Joseph Wu were surveilled during past trips to Europe.

Most famously, news broke in June 2025 of an attempt by the Chinese military attaché in Prague to ram a vehicle into the motorcade of Taiwan’s then-vice president-elect Hsiao Bi-khim. Allegations of Chinese espionage against visiting Taiwanese government officials are fairly common; reports of China attempting direct kinetic action – what could be construed as either an attempt at intimidation or an assassination attempt – are rare. The timing of the car crash attempt raised some questions domestically in Taiwan, as this took place in a similar timeframe to the Kuomintang (KMT) introducing a bill that would require a new set of presidential elections to be held if the vice president-elect died.

China has repeatedly sanctioned senior government officials with the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP), preventing them or their family members from doing business in China. Such sanctions have disproportionately honed in on figures involved in civil defense efforts, such as UMC founder Robert Tsao, former Sunflower Movement student leader Lin Fei-fan, or DPP legislator Puma Shen.

Shen in particular has often been targeted, He is the founder of the disinformation research organization Doublethink Lab and the civil defense organization Kuma Academy. Sanctions have honed in on his father, a businessman who sells auto parts in China. Likewise, Shen has reported threats directed at his children, as well as cases of attempted impersonation while attending conferences abroad.

DPP senior political figures and their families likely know better than to travel to China at this point. That being said, according to the Mainland Affairs Council in June, the number of Taiwanese who have been detained in China is on the rise. While most have been detained due to fraud or criminal charges, 23 were detained for religious reasons, and one was detained on a national security charge. Past precedent shows that when Taiwanese are detained in China on national security charges, they are usually prevented from returning to Taiwan even after being released at the end of their sentences.

China’s surveillance of the relatives of Taiwanese government officials abroad also raises the possibility of surveillance or acts of repression within Taiwan. In particular, some analysts have raised the possibility of fifth-column groups becoming active in the event of an invasion. Such groups could be constituted out of pro-China organized crime groups, such as those linked to the Bamboo Union. A number of recent espionage arrests in Taiwan in the past two years have also alleged the existence of paramilitary cells that would become active in wartime.

That being said, it has been more common to see acts of vandalism rather than outright violence in Taiwan. An attack in late September on a comedy club in Taipei saw the club’s entrance smeared with a mixture of white paint and feces. The vandalism was carried out by a 35-year-old man surnamed Kuo, who was reportedly paid NT$50,000 by a 33-year-old man surnamed Liu for the attack. It is thought that the attack occurred because of past mockery of Chinese President Xi Jinping by one of the comedians performing at the club in a clip that went viral online.

Nevertheless, acts of violence do occur. In July, political commentator Akio Yaita was attacked at a hotel in Taichung, where Yaita was giving a speech. The accused was a Chinese man who traveled using a Hong Kong passport.

There have also been reports in the past month of individuals attempting to impersonate the distributors of the documentary “State Organs,” which details allegations of China conducting organ harvesting on members of the Falun Gong religious group. There have also been threats directed against screenings of “State Organs.”

The highly partisan political environment in Taiwan is likely to stymie efforts to strengthen legal measures against transnational repression or surveillance, especially ahead of November’s local elections. In the past, the opposition KMT accused the ruling DPP of attempting a power grab when the DPP proposed the reintroduction of military courts for espionage cases.
