title: China’s Advance in the Bahamas
description: Beijing's presence in the Bahamas and its military implications for the U.S. are often overshadowed by discussion of Chinese activities elsewhere in the region.
text:
The December 2025, the U.S. National Security Strategy (NSS) committed the U.S. to resisting influence by extrahemispheric actors, including control over strategic assets and shipping corridors in the Western Hemisphere. Today, China has accumulated a strategically problematic commercial presence and web of influence relationships in the Bahamas. The archipelago is just 80 kilometers from the United States at its closest point, nearer than Cuba. U.S. military maritime routes for deploying and sustaining forces go through the islands, which the State Department has called the U.S. “third border.”

Beijing’s presence in the Bahamas and its military implications for the U.S. are often overshadowed by discussion of Chinese activities in Cuba, the Panama Canal, the Port of Chancay, Peru, or the “Deep Space Radar” facility in Neuquen, Argentina. However, China’s influence in the Bahamas is just as problematic, both in peacetime and if the U.S. had to transit through the archipelago to deploy and sustain forces supporting action against the Chinese in the Indo-Pacific. While that presence appears more commercial and political than military, it includes a labyrinth of China-controlled businesses in the Bahamas and relationships with its political, military, and commercial figures that could give Beijing options to observe – and potentially threaten – U.S. forces.

A map of the Bahamas. Credit: Shutterstock.

Business Projects

Chinese commercial ventures in the Bahamas boost Beijing’s influence – and in the worst case could support and provide cover for People’s Liberation Army or Ministry of State Security operatives. Such ventures include port operations, hotels and resorts, other construction projects, and an array of telecommunication and electricity sector activities.

The Hong Kong-based firm Hutchison is the operator of the Bahamas’ principal port and container terminal at Freeport, as well as its cruise ship terminal. Hutchison is currently engaged in a $100 million modernization effort there, bringing cranes and other equipment that have been associated in the past with data security concerns.

China’s flagship commercial ventures in the Bahamas include the $4.2 billion Baha Mar resort, owned by Macau-based Chow Tai Fook Enterprises. The venture’s Chinese-owned builder, China Construction America (CCA), was found by U.S. courts to have caused $845 million in damages by defrauding and breaching its contract with the original developer Sarkis Ismirlian.

Other significant Chinese commercial operations involving CCA and its owner, the China State Construction and Engineering Company, include The Pointe, the associated Margaritaville Resort, and the nearby British Colonial Nassau hotel. The China-based owners have long defied Bahamian government control with the workers they maintain on the property. Examples include the government’s arrest of 65 Chinese nationals doing renovations on the British Colonial Hotel with improper work authorizations. The Pointe was also found to employ 229 Chinese nationals and 35 other foreign workers versus only 90 Bahamians, although the Chinese company’s agreement with the government required that 70 percent of the workers be locals.

Beyond hotels, Chinese companies have established a presence through a loan-financed hospital, renovation work on the national stadium, which they previously built, and a gifted “demonstration farm,” creating an opening for regular visits by Chinese personnel.

In the telecommunications sector, which presents risks for the compromise of sensitive government, commercial, and personal data, Huawei is a major supplier to the national telecom operator ALIV, as well as BTC. In 2013 Huawei Marine Systems was selected to upgrade BTC’s BDSNi fiber-optic network, including submarine cables.

In the equally sensitive digital surveillance sector, China’s Hikvision provided more than 2,000 cameras at the Chinese-operated Baha Mar casino, among other work in the country.

Chinese companies also have a significant presence in the Bahamas’ energy sector, particularly solar projects. Examples include Chinese-based Sungrow, which provided an energy storage system on Sampson Cay, and Chinese-based Kehua and GSL, which similarly supplied solar sector products and services. Huawei advertises itself as an integrator for solar solutions in the country.

People-to-People Ties

As a complement to its investments in the Bahamas, the Chinese has built an extensive web of relationships and influence with military, political, and other figures.

According to their own reporting, the Royal Bahamas Defense Force (RBDF) and Royal Bahamas Police Force (RBPF) regularly send personnel to China for courses. Six RBDF personnel participated in training at Chinese military, naval, and air force institutions in 2025. Specifically, RBDF personnel have attended training in China on maritime law enforcement and Chinese language.

On the police side, RBPF Deputy Commissioner Leamond Deleveaux reportedly attended a “Peaceful Resolution Course” in China.

For security forces, such personal relationships have been complemented by periodic gifts of material, including two Tiger armored vehicles in August 2017, equipment for the military band in November 2024, as well as donations of advanced workout equipment, jet skis, and harbor patrol equipment from the Chinese-affiliated Baha Mar Foundation.

The web woven by Beijing through its people-to-people diplomacy, however, extends far beyond the military. The Chinese government reportedly brought 100 Bahamians to China during the past year alone, including parliamentarians, senior security officials, doctors, nurses, students, and business representatives. In July 2026, China brought representatives from both of the country’s major political parties, the Progressive Liberal Party and Free National Movement, to Beijing for party-to-party consultations.

During the past year, the Chinese hosted significant Bahamian groups for the first “China-Bahamas Forum on Dialogue Among Civilizations,” and separately, the first “China-Bahamas Trade and Economic Cooperation Forum.” In October 2026, 23 Bahamian doctors and nurses are scheduled to travel to China for a medical event.

For a country with a population as small as the Bahamas, the Chinese government has been very active in courting its journalists, particularly those from The Tribune, Eyewitness News, and other organizations. Prominent recent examples include Leandra Rolle of The Tribune, who attended a July 2026 seminar in China called “on Media Co-operation on World Political Parties”; Genea Noel of Eyewitness News and Alicia Wallace, who attended a China-paid three-week Caribbean Media Exchange in June-July 2026; and Jade Russell from The Tribune, who spent three weeks in Shanghai in April 2025 for a training program for International Young Talents from “Belt and Road Countries.” Less recently, Ricardo Wells of The Tribune went on four-week visit to China in May 2018; Rashad Rolle, also of The Tribune, attended a three-week journalism seminar in September 2015; and Eric Rose, of the Bahamas Information Services, served as a panelist in a July 2015 film festival event.

Many of these trips resulted in enthusiastic op-eds on China and the “lessons” it offers the Bahamas.

Beyond media, as in other countries, the Chinese government-staffed Confucius Institute at the University of the Bahamas has played an important role in capturing young Bahamians interested in China, its language, and culture. What began as a Confucius Classroom in 2009 became a full Confucius Institute in October 2012. By 2019, the institute had trained over 1,000 students and had brought over 100 Bahamian teachers and students to China.

Conclusion

While the majority of Chinese engagement in the Bahamas is not military in character, the extent of the presence and influence it affords China in a country just 80 kilometers from U.S. shores – and along routes strategically important for the U.S. in a war in the Pacific – should draw Washington’s attention. Given the U.S. administration’s strong record in acting on the policies and priorities it has highlighted in the NSS, that possibility should make the Chinese presence in the Bahamas a matter of concern for the Bahamian government as well.
tag: Bahamas; China in the Caribbean; China-Bahamas relations; Trump National Security Strategy

title: China’s AI Governance Push and the Race to Shape Global AI Rules
description: In contrast to Washington's fragmented approach, Beijing is showing an impressive ability to enact and coordinate regulations, policies, technical standards, and enforcement.
text:
On September 12, China’s National Data Administration (NDA) announced that it would develop standards for embodied artificial intelligence (AI) data. The announcement followed a September 10 meeting chaired by NDA head Liu Liehong, where seven key digital companies called for shared public data infrastructure for smart physical machinery and robotics, along with unified data standards. The participants included the startups ModelBest, Infinigence AI, and X Square Robot.

While much remains to be seen regarding raw AI development and emerging technologies in general, this announcement is an indicator of a broader trend, with China increasingly building a centralized and coordinated framework for governing how AI is developed and deployed. This is critical because establishing usable rules around AI has significant implications, potentially becoming nearly as vital as the ability to develop the underlying AI models themselves. As a result, safety and governance are becoming strategic components of the global competition over AI.

The AI Arms Race

AI governance is a critical front in the broader arena of non-kinetic competition between China and the United States. Instead of direct armed conflict, some have described a new “Silent Cold War,” which focuses on topics like AI, semiconductor chips, and foreign investment. AI is especially important because of its dual-use nature, with its capabilities ranging from advising a fifth-grade child on her homework to providing a 99 percent facial verification match on a suspected human trafficker at a border crossing.

China’s history of increased AI model exportation, which could result in increased information influence, has been detailed as one of the implications originating from the AI arms race between the U.S. and China. This is particularly important for countries in the Global South, due to the influx of Chinese infrastructure designed to support AI, with many of these efforts being made as part of the Belt and Road and Digital Silk Road Initiatives.

If Chinese firms become major providers of AI models and their corresponding cloud services, data centers, and energy grids, then China may also gain influence over technical standards, data practices, content controls, and what defines responsible AI in the first place.

This makes AI governance a regulatory issue that must be tackled at an international level rather than at a regional or domestic level. For developing countries deciding which AI systems to adopt, governance frameworks can be a key driver for these nations, with a country selecting an AI provider simultaneously adopting the same standards for data management, content moderation, privacy, and system oversight.

AI Governance

Consequently, AI governance has become a key frontier topic that must be top-of-mind for policymakers worldwide. AI has and is already being leveraged for nefarious purposes, ranging from human-driven prompts promoting deepfakes and impersonation to AI-generated misinformation.

Most recently, U.S.-based Claude maker Anthropic and ChatGPT’s OpenAI faced significant backlash due to key AI safety concerns, with both AI makers disclosing that their own models went rogue in their own capacities. This was compounded by the resignation of a former Anthropic and OpenAI researcher around the same period, with this researcher openly citing these same elements as the reason for his resignation.

Therefore, the core regulatory dilemma has become how to regulate AI while still enabling innovation. The U.S. has often approached this challenge through things like voluntary commitments, state-level laws, and a smattering of sector-specific rules. This approach prioritizes flexibility, but at the cost of fragmentation.

For example, the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology released an AI Risk Management Framework in early 2023, with this currently being revised as part of the White House AI Action Plan released in early 2025. However, this framework remains entirely voluntary. Fragmentation in America’s governance space has remained significant, with some states like Colorado, New York, and California issuing AI-specific legislation, while the vast majority of other states have not.

China’s Efforts

In stark contrast to America’s fragmented approach, China’s top-down approach has resulted in the creation of a multi-layered regulatory system that covers different parts of the AI lifecycle. This model gives specific regulators concrete levers over AI deployments, even as AI development continues to advance at a blistering pace.

The National Data Administration’s approach is the most recent epitome of this approach. It is focusing on developing standards for the data used to train AI for physical machinery and robotics, while also establishing common standards. This is significant because embodied AI depends heavily on data collected in the physical world. Establishing common approaches to collecting, organizing, and evaluating this data could become an important part of building an AI-enabled domestic robotics ecosystem.

China has pursued similar governance measures in other efforts in AI. On July 15, the Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC), China’s top internet regulator, brought its Interim Measures for the Administration of Anthropomorphic AI Interaction Services into effect. This law specifically regulates AI systems that simulate human personality traits, with the CAC introducing prohibited content, rules for minors, and highlighting necessary safety assessments for compliance, among others.

Additionally, on May 8, the CAC, the National Development and Reform Commission, and the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology jointly released the Implementation Opinions on the Standardized Application and Innovative Development of Intelligent Agents. This marked China’s first comprehensive national policy framework specific to agentic AI, introducing tiered risk governance, priority scenarios, and “off-switches” for exigent circumstances.

The rapid and cohesive pace of this legislation highlights China’s desire to govern AI in a more stringent and systematic manner. Chinese regulators are already connecting policy, technical standards, data infrastructure, and implementation. These efforts could increase the amount of Chinese-built AI systems used on a worldwide scale, particularly as Beijing increasingly positions its systems as usable and trusted due to its leadership in AI governance.

For many, the AI race seems to be determined by who will create the fastest and most advanced AI system. However, China is demonstrating that this race is instead being decided by which country creates an environment in which AI can be trusted, deployed, and adopted at scale.

China’s growing advantage is increasingly visible in its ability to connect regulations, policies, technical standards, and enforcement. As Chinese AI systems and infrastructure become more prevalent internationally, establishing clear governance practices could enable China increased influence over how AI is regulated and deployed on an international level. If America continues to rely on its fragmented and voluntary approach, it risks enabling China to play a larger role in setting the rules that shape the future of the world’s AI economy.
tag: Artificial intelligence; China AI regulations; China artificial intelligence; U.S. AI regulations

title: China’s AI Industry Brings Both Gains and Challenges for Its Fragile Economy
description: China’s exports are surging, driven by AI-related technologies. National security-driven export bans could change that.
text:
China is attracting global interest and achieving record-breaking export growth as a trailblazer in the field of artificial intelligence (AI). However, the sector’s growing importance for China’s economy is a double-edged sword. The delicacy of the ongoing AI race, coupled with its national security implications, could lead to curbs on the sharing of certain technologies, casting new doubt on the frontier as an economic driver.

China’s exports are growing at a phenomenal rate, recording a 36.3 percent year-on-year boost in September to reach $447.18 billion. That’s the highest growth level for Chinese exports since 2021, and even then figures were somewhat unreliable due to the disruption caused by the COVID-19 pandemic.

September’s figures extended a positive run. China’s exports grew 25 percent year-on-year in August. In both months, high-tech trade was a critical contributor to the surging growth. China’s semiconductor exports grew more than 108 percent over the past month, and automatic data processing machine shipments, recorded a boost of 55 percent.

The AI industry has been providing economic tailwinds for China, bolstered by government initiatives to support the development of the technology domestically. In turn, China’s tech-focused exports have helped to support the national economy. However, it appears that China is mulling placing new bans on exports focusing on emerging technologies. That includes AI as well as biotechnology and solar power.

In recent days, China has unveiled a draft plan to establish a fresh series of export bans that will impact 14 different forms of technology. The notice, issued by China’s Ministry of Commerce and Ministry of Science and Technology, proposes bans or restrictions that cover 40 technologies in total. The Ministry of Commerce has claimed that the implementation of export bans is necessary to reinforce security while preventing misuse and abuse.

If implemented, those curbs could significantly impact the nation’s ongoing export boom. Critically, the restrictions would see domestic AI models with parameter counts of 2 trillion or more excluded from exports. Parameter counts are important measures of the learning capacity of models, and controlling higher-end models is likely to be China’s way of maintaining an edge in a highly competitive buildout. Both of China’s leading AI models – Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 and Alibaba’s Qwen 3.8-Max – exceed parameter counts of 2 trillion, meaning that their export could be banned entirely.

However, it’s worth noting that foreign businesses and users would still be able to use AI models via front-end software like APIs, websites, or cloud apps, just so long as the underlying core technology remains hosted securely inside China.

There’s also the potential for foreign-owned businesses to enter foreign-trade zones like Beijing to maintain their access to Chinese AI technology. However, the intricacies of market entry in China mean that higher degrees of access to domestic AI tools aren’t assured forever.

As China’s government considers tighter restrictions on technology-related exports, it will have to confront the economic implications. The nation has secured significant growth off the back of its strength in AI. Alongside the nation’s export strength, growing interest in Chinese AI from overseas is helping to transform both trade and the economy on a fundamental level. It’s also supporting China’s economic ties with other countries in a way that boosts global integration.

Chinese exports of integrated circuits surged 99.1 percent year-on-year in the first three quarters of 2026. Other sectors of technology, such as computer parts and accessories, have seen Chinese exports more than triple over the same period.

Even so, the latest figures show that China’s economy expanded 4.4 percent in the third quarter. That’s below the government target of between 4.5 percent and 5 percent GDP growth for the year – China’s lowest growth target in decades.

Although AI exports have helped to support the economy, Beijing is still struggling to address its sinking real estate sector in the post-pandemic landscape. Multiple geopolitical stresses and macroeconomic headwinds linked to both trade rows and global conflicts have stifled growth in a way that has absorbed China’s high-tech export success story. The prospect of tighter controls over AI exports could create fresh pressures for an economy that’s already facing severe challenges.

At this stage, it’s important to note that China’s AI export bans would largely be limited to the distribution of its high-end models, meaning that we can still expect a sustained upturn in high-tech exports throughout the final quarter 2026. But with AI helping to strengthen China’s international ties with other countries, stronger restrictions on its frontier technology could stunt its growth at a time when the economy appears set to miss its annual targets.

For a nation that’s still seeking to plot its recovery from a deep real estate crisis, AI has emerged as a major economic opportunity. However, China’s strong stance on protecting national security could create more economic disruption, making the road to 5 percent growth even more challenging.
tag: China AI governance; China AI industry; China export bans; China tech export controls; China tech industry

title: China’s Bid to Define the ‘Global South’
description: Beijing has adopted its own, quite different, definition of the term.
text:
In the leadup to the U.S.-China summit in September 2026, President Xi Jinping attended the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, and the BRICS summit in Delhi. He also visited the Middle East — all between August and September. What is notable is that in speeches delivered at both the SCO and BRICS summits, Xi made heavy use of the term “Global South.” This reflects China’s positioning of the SCO and BRICS as gatherings of the Global South, even though Russia and Turkey are among their members. How, precisely, does China understand and deploy this term “Global South” (全球南方, Quanqiu Nanfang)?

In academic usage, “Global South” originally carried the meaning that “South” issues exist within developed countries too, and that the North-South divide should not be understood in spatially separate terms; South issues are, rather, global in character. From around 2020, however, the term began to be used differently in international forums. In particular, following the war in Ukraine, a view spread — especially in Western countries — that sharply delineated the advanced democracies against China and Russia, drawing an axis of confrontation between the developed world and China, Russia (plus Iran and North Korea), and treating the remaining countries as the “Global South.” China responded to this by becoming very wary of the term, viewing “Global South” as a Western-originated concept designed to drive a wedge between China and the developing world. China’s self-identification has been as a developing country —indeed, as the representative of the developing world. For this reason, it was unwilling to accept a term that would separate China from developing countries.

Despite this, the term “Global South” became increasingly prevalent globally. In particular, when India hosted the “Voice of Global South Summit” online on January 12 and 13, 2023, and did not invite China, this appears to have come as a significant shock to Beijing. Yet even after the “Voice of Global South Summit,” Chinese criticism of the term continued. The shift came in the period following the enactment of the Foreign Relations Law on June 28, 2023. That law, in Article 4, calls for upholding the five principles [of peaceful coexistence], and also uses the term “developing country” (发展中国家) in two places, reaffirming China’s identity as a developing country.

From July 2023, Foreign Minister Wang Yi suddenly began using the term “Global South” at international conferences, albeit with quotation marks around it. At the Meeting of BRICS National Security Advisers and High Representatives on National Security held in Johannesburg on July 25, when Wang used “Global South” in quotation marks, Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Mao Ning then offered a definition of the term at a press conference: “The ‘Global South’ is the family of emerging markets and developing countries.” Wang Yi listed “independence,” “development,” and “justice” as the defining qualities of the Global South, and declared that “China is a natural member of the Global South and will always be part of the developing world.” This was a definition of the Global South that clearly differed from that used in developed countries.

China has offered no explanation for this shift in approach. The most plausible interpretation is that, as the term came to be widely used globally — particularly among leaders of developing countries — and as the term’s definition remained unsettled, China made a deliberate policy shift: to define the term itself, on its own terms, and thereby shape global discourse in its favor. This too can be counted as one instance of China’s pursuit of what it calls “discourse power.”

Subsequently, not only Wang but Xi himself began using the term with quotation marks. This signaled that the term had become domestically usable within China as well. By the end of 2024, quotation marks began to be dropped from “Global South” in Chinese documents, and in a piece by Wang published in Qiushi in 2025, the quotation marks were also absent. There remain, to be sure, some inconsistencies in usage (instances can still be found in 2025 where Chinese officials used “Global South” with quotation marks) but these have gradually become less common, and at the SCO and BRICS meetings in 2026 cited at the outset, Xi Jinping’s use of Global South carried no quotation marks.

Globally speaking, “Global South” remains a term without an agreed definition, with each actor investing it with its own meaning. China has positioned itself as a member of the Global South and has come to behave as its representative. China defines Global South as “the family of emerging markets and developing countries” — which amounts to the “non-West.” The contest over this term “Global South” throws into relief the differences in worldview between the developed world and China. The contest over this seemingly simple term, it turns out, is anything but.
tag: China and the Global South; Global South

title: China’s High-Tech Ambitions Have a Blue-Collar Status Problem
description: Most Chinese still view vocational schools and skilled labor as low status and undesirable.
text:
As China celebrated its dominance at the Asian Games that concluded days ago in Nagoya, Japan, its achievement at another global sporting festival in Shanghai has been largely overlooked. In the 2026 edition of WorldSkills, what the organizers call an Olympics for vocational skills, the Chinese team topped the medal table with 41 gold, 11 silver, and 4 bronze medals. In fact, the Chinese team has topped the medal table five straight times in the biennial competition, a phenomenon that has been attributed to the country’s unparalleled investments in providing systematic coaching and training for athletes in the same way it does for the regular Olympics.

Beyond simply winning medals, the Chinese authorities felt the need to drum up public interest in the competition. Local and national media, and even governments, covered WorldSkills extensively while it largely went unnoticed in other countries. Given that whatever prestige that China earns from WorldSkills is largely geared toward a domestic audience rather than an international one, it begs the question of why China would even bother with prompting something that leads to little gain in global stature.

The answer to the question may be found in a February 2026 announcement from the Chinese Ministry of Education (MoE) suggesting vocational school reforms. The document criticized the current system’s lack of connection between education and employers, producing few skilled industrial workers essential for driving China’s next generation of high-tech manufacturing.

China’s 2026-2030 Five-Year Plan emphasized that manufacturing remains central in ensuring the technological self-sufficiency underlying long-term economic growth and safeguarding national security. The MoE implied that the country’s vocational schools, without reforms, would be incapable of producing the human resources needed to achieve that goal.

But for vocational schools to urgently produce talent for high-tech manufacturing, they need more than just an appropriate curriculum. They also need the best raw talent that China has to offer. Here is where vocational schools fall short.

China’s university enrollment increased from 1 million in 1999 to 9.6 million in 2020. The country’s brightest increasingly aspire to join the ranks of what used to be a tiny segment of the intellectual elite signaled by a university diploma. The expanding path toward college education has cemented a social hierarchy in which a bachelor’s degree followed by white-collar work is seen as more desirable than a vocational one followed by a career in manual labor, no matter how technically sophisticated.

That norm of high-education aspirations is most clearly seen in study abroad. My primary job as a college admissions consultant leads me to interact with hundreds of Chinese families who are first and foremost attracted to higher-ranked institutions with well-recognized names. In choosing between the likes of the American Ivy Leagues and the British Oxbridge, they care less about what practical skills they can acquire, but whether the degrees indicate a highly competitive environment, and by proxy, the intelligence of successful applicants. Despite much cheaper costs and clear paths for employment, very few indicate interest in English-language higher-education programs in Germany and other European countries anchored by technical apprenticeships.

It is this cultural norm that the MoE must fight against as it seeks to overhaul the vocational school system in China. The proposed collaboration with major manufacturers will help. In a slowing economy, many applicants may be interested in blue-collar work with the likes of Huawei and Xiaomi, rather than a bachelor’s degree that comes with unemployment afterwards. But without changing the cultural norms of seeing technical education as “lower” than the university one, vocational schools in China, no matter how reformed, can still only attract those who are not afraid to be seen as desperate and obtuse enough to work on the factory floor.

Hence the glowing coverage of WorldSkills. The prestige of China’s medalists is about bringing pride not just to the country, but to their professions. And to further bestow status, China is turning hundreds of vocational schools into diploma-granting colleges, slapping bachelor’s degrees on vocational training. If better prospects for jobs do not bring brighter talent into technical education, the hope is that erasing the difference in visual appearance between universities and vocational schools can break down the hierarchical thinking.

It remains to be seen whether China’s dwindling ranks of youngsters will be sufficiently lured by the more attractive job prospects offered by manufacturing. As Chinese firms wow domestic and foreign audiences with fully automated dark factories, the image of grittiness associated with manufacturing is being chipped away. But will that overcome an ingrained educational culture that sees the work of the brain as higher in social status as that of the hand, even if the hand is increasingly replaced by robotics? It will depend on whether the Chinese mentality will evolve as fast as the country’s approach to industrial policies and technologies.
tag: China blue-collar workers; China higher education; China manufacturing; China vocational schools; China youth unemployment

title: China’s LinkedIn Espionage Is Only Getting More Advanced
description: The U.S. has benefited from hard-earned lessons in the fight against transnational online scams. It’s time to apply them to address China’s sophisticated and relentless cyber spying.
text:
On June 3, in a rare – and telling – indication of collective alarm, the member states of the “Five Eyes” intelligence-sharing alliance published an unprecedented joint bulletin highlighting China’s use of professional networking sites like LinkedIn to carry out an aggressive, industrial-scale online espionage campaign. Armed with the personal data of millions of U.S. security clearance holders and applicants, acquired during China’s 2014-15 hack of the Office of Personnel Management (OPM), spies from the Chinese Ministry of State Security (MSS) have approached tens of thousands of U.S. and NATO government staffers, military personnel, academics, and others with access to sensitive information through LinkedIn and other professional networking sites over recent years.

The massive scale of China’s spy campaign does not preclude precision: MSS agents use generative AI to craft messages tailored to each individual target’s resume and expertise. Posing as corporate recruiters or business consultants, agents promise their targets easy money in exchange for writing freelance “consulting” reports on seemingly innocuous topics related to their targets’ work. These fictitious identities are often bolstered with AI-generated profile pictures and fake corporate websites. Once the agent has established a relationship with their target, they’ll push the target to divulge more sensitive information or even pass classified documents directly to the agent.

The environment is target-rich. LinkedIn is widely used by current and former U.S. government employees. Spies on the prowl can easily browse lists of users with specific career experience to quickly build a list of viable targets. This makes online espionage recruitment especially appealing to China’s intelligence apparatus, and the extensive use of fake company webpages and AI-generated messages means that targets often don’t initially realize they’re being deftly cultivated by a foreign spy agency.

Although less bombastic than China’s efforts to hack American critical infrastructure or cultivate U.S. politicians as agents of influence, China’s networking site espionage has proven particularly long-running and pernicious. Reports of Chinese intelligence operations using LinkedIn to recruit informants go back to at least 2011. In 2018, then-head of the U.S. National Counterintelligence and Security Center William Evanina publicly called on LinkedIn to address the issue. LinkedIn responded by “restricting” a few dozen fake accounts, but the problem continued. Evanina told the New York Times a year later that China’s espionage activity on the platform had not decreased. Despite periodic media attention and U.S. counterintelligence efforts over the past 15 years, China’s intelligence apparatus has continued to run aggressive online spying campaigns on an industrial scale, obtaining technological, military, and economic secrets through these efforts.

China’s online espionage recruitment poses an urgent threat to the U.S. and allied governments, but solutions for detecting and preventing it have remained frustratingly elusive. Fortunately, there exists a wealth of research and real-world models for cooperation between governments and industry to address a similar threat: transnational online fraud and scam rings. Government and industry stakeholders should draw on this existing body of expertise and best practices and adopt a novel approach to combating China’s network espionage.

China’s online espionage shares some key characteristics with transnational online fraud. Both Chinese espionage recruitment and online romance scams, such as the “pig butchering” operations that earn billions of dollars each year for cybercriminals operating internet scam compounds in Southeast Asia, use deceptive, flattering initial approaches to their target. These initial messages are often written and translated with the aid of generative AI and tailored to fit the target’s profile. MSS spy handlers and online scammers also seek to cultivate a relationship and build trust with their targets before eventually pressuring them to disclose sensitive information, such as military secrets or personal financial details.

Finally, both transnational fraud schemes and China’s online espionage recruitment originate from overseas but use U.S. and partner nation platforms and internet infrastructure to contact their targets. This leaves scammers and spies similarly vulnerable to disruption efforts by law enforcement and counterintelligence authorities in the US and partner nations.

One recent example is “Disruption Week,” organized by the U.S. Department of Justice’s “Scam Center Strike Force.” From May 18 to 21, U.S. law enforcement bodies met and shared information with major private sector firms like Apple, Meta, and Microsoft to identify and shut down fraud activity on over 1.4 million scam-linked social media and email accounts, as well as decommissioning servers, hosting infrastructure, and platforms linked to scam networks operating from Southeast Asia. Law enforcement agencies also identified and opened new investigations into overseas scammers and arrested several suspected cybercriminals with the cooperation of partner nations.

On June 10, the FBI seized 13 web domains used by Chinese intelligence agents to lure targets on LinkedIn and other networking sites. The domains hosted webpages for fake consultancies – fronts for MSS spies posing as recruiters online. The deception paid off. FBI documents show that China’s spies used the fake consulting firms to recruit at least eight current and former U.S. government and military personnel with security clearances.

While U.S. counterintelligence officials’ work in disrupting part of China’s illicit digital intelligence infrastructure is praiseworthy, 13 domains represents a mere drop in the bucket of China’s extensive online espionage. Researchers at the Foundation for the Defense of Democracies (FDD) have already identified over 100 web domains and fake firms likely serving as fronts for Chinese espionage recruitment – none of which were seized during the FBI’s June operation.

One of these fake firms, “Nimbus Hub Consulting,” was also independently identified as a front for Chinese espionage by publicly-available industry and media reports. The U.S. government, think tanks, and industry should establish information-sharing channels to allow law enforcement agencies and professional networking sites like LinkedIn to cross-reference suspicious firms with a list of known front companies and flag or delete profiles linked to these fronts. Authorities should be catching these fraudulent sites as they are identified, not playing catch-up with siloed and incomplete data.

On the industry side, professional networking and job site operators can draw on recent advances in scam detection and prevention to combat Chinese espionage on their platforms. Online scammers often create and follow AI-generated scripts that function as templates for enticing and exploiting victims, even across language barriers. These scripts allow the scammers to automate and expand the scope of their operations, targeting victims en masse. China’s cyber spies use similar techniques to quickly generate personalized messages, allowing them to approach thousands of targets with minimal time and effort.

But AI cuts both ways for scammers: recent anti-scam research has demonstrated that AI models can effectively identify scam messages. Google has already developed tools to detect and flag likely scams in real time on its Android devices, and this technology could be easily adapted to detect likely Chinese espionage recruitment approaches, which make similar use of AI models to generate and customize approach messages for each target. LinkedIn and other professional networking platforms should implement a similar feature in their chat functions to detect likely espionage attempts and warn users in real time.

The U.S. government shouldn’t be shy about pressing LinkedIn to take this much-needed step to address rampant espionage recruiting on the platform. The Department of Defense’s Transition Assistance Program (TAP) explicitly encourages servicemembers to use LinkedIn to search for their next role, and the platform’s well-established ecosystem of professionals and employers has attracted a significant community of current and former U.S. government employees and clearance holders. All fo this makes it a particularly appealing target for Chinese intelligence. If the platform’s operators drag their feet on improving security and addressing rampant abuse by China’s spy agencies, authorities could strip it from federal programs like DOD’s TAP. Legislators could even move to treat the platform similarly to pre-divestiture TikTok or WhatsApp, banning its use on government-issued devices. It would also behoove the House Select Committee on the CCP to use its subpoena power to call recalcitrant platform operators to account. After all, MSS spies targeted the Committee itself in December 2025, using a fake consulting firm (complete with a falsified LinkedIn presence) in an attempt to solicit sensitive information from a Committee staffer.

A hardball approach would create predictable headaches for both parties, though, and a more cooperative arrangement based on establishing information-sharing channels, clear efforts towards identifying and banning spies from the platform, and improved safeguards against espionage recruitment in LinkedIn’s chat client would be preferable.

While detection and disruption are the most immediate concerns for authorities and platform operators, the ease with which Chinese intelligence agents can create new front companies and fake identities means that preparing platform users to protect themselves is also crucial. Preventative measures warning potential targets and equipping them to recognize the signs of espionage recruitment attempts are urgently needed.

Much like China’s AI-enabled online espionage recruitment, phishing and other traditional cybersecurity threats use social engineering techniques to manipulate targets into engaging with malicious messages. An extensive body of scholarship, including anti-fraud research sponsored by the Federal Trade Commission, has explored the effectiveness of anti-phishing cybersecurity education and has identified some best practices for helping internet users protect themselves from malicious actors.

One surprising and relevant finding from this research concerns the effectiveness of regular cybersecurity trainings. Multiple large-scale studies concluded that formal cybersecurity trainings are largely ineffective in preventing users from engaging with phishing messages, indicating that oft-repeated calls for more or intensified counterespionage training sessions for U.S. government and military personnel, while well-intentioned, are unlikely to be effective.

Researchers studying anti-phishing training found that simple reminders about cyber threats are likely to provide an equivalent benefit to detailed cybersecurity trainings, while being much less costly and time-consuming. With this in mind, LinkedIn and other professional networking sites should implement occasional short, attention-grabbing, and user-friendly reminders about espionage recruitment threats to warn users while avoiding desensitizing them through the overuse of warning messages.

Fortunately, more robust preventative measures are available to platform operators: anti-phishing research has identified prominent warnings that flag probable scam messages within email clients as an effective tool for alerting users to malicious activity. LinkedIn and other professional networking sites should implement highly-visible warnings embedded within their chat functions to warn users about likely espionage recruitment attempts. LinkedIn has already introduced an optional feature designed to detect and flag malware and harassment in chat messages; adding espionage recruitment to the list of threats is an obvious next step. TAP and programs like it should also highlight and explain this feature to DOD and other federal personnel when discussing LinkedIn use.

Research on phishing prevention also found that simple, user-friendly reporting functions to flag phishing attempts can help organizations rapidly identify and disrupt likely phishing campaigns without putting significant strain on the organization’s operational load. LinkedIn should implement a user-friendly reporting feature directly into the chat function to enable users to quickly and easily report likely espionage recruitment attempts. This feature could also support information-sharing and collaboration between LinkedIn and law enforcement agencies, allowing for faster and easier cross-referencing and identification of likely Chinese intelligence agents and front companies.

Chinese espionage recruitment may be occurring on an unprecedented scale, but the U.S. is far from powerless to stop it. Easy wins are readily available in the form of research-backed measures for dramatically reducing the effectiveness of Chinese intelligence activities online. LinkedIn announced in March that it had joined (alongside Meta, OpenAI, and other major tech firms) an industry accord dedicated to combating online scams and fraud. Signatories promised to increase their cooperation with law enforcement and government bodies, develop scam detection tools that utilize advanced AI, and create user-friendly reporting channels to flag likely scams. Meta has also publicly discussed its cooperation with OpenAI to crack down on online transnational scam and fraud activity operating across their respective platforms. Taking advantage of these tools, techniques, and channels to address China’s online espionage operations is a clear next step for policymakers, law enforcement authorities, and professional networking platforms.

title: China’s Military Open New Logistics and Training Facility in Laos
description: The center north of Vientiane, a counterpart to a similar naval facility in Cambodia, marks a further extension of Beijing's security presence in mainland Southeast Asia.
text:
This week, the Chinese military opened a new logistics and training facility at an airport in Laos, further expanding its regional security presence and establishing the first overseas presence of the Chinese air force.

In a statement, China’s Ministry of Defense said that the China-Laos Military Joint Support and Training Center was inaugurated on Tuesday, in a ceremony that was attended by Lao Defense Minister Khamlieng Outhakaysone and a delegation from the Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA).

The facility, which is based at Ban Keun Airport, which sits close to the Nam Ngum River around 50 kilometers north of the capital Vientiane, also includes a China-Laos Friendship Aviation Academy.

“The center, jointly maintained and operated by both sides, is aimed at helping Laos strengthen the training of its air force pilots,” the Ministry said, but offered no details about what personnel or equipment would be based at the airport.

“The construction and use of the center reflect mutual respect and equal consultation between China and Laos, comply with both countries’ domestic laws, relevant international law and common practice,” it said. “It is not directed against any third party and contributes to enhancing practical military cooperation as well as promoting regional peace and stability.”

Satellite imagery of the Ban Keun facility shows it also includes the construction of an extensive airfield. According to Reuters, work began on the new airfield in late 2025 and work was ongoing as of early September. “In place of green fields,” it reported, “a large paved runway and a parallel taxiway and apron were visible, along with a number of new buildings.”

The airport was built on the site of an airfield known as Lima Site 44, one of a network of airstrips that were used by the U.S. military and Central Intelligence Agency during the Vietnam War, when the U.S. secretly supported an insurgency by anti-communist Hmong rebels. However, satellite images show that the new airfield expands far beyond the narrow, red-earthed strip established during the Vietnam War.

The new center adds to the handful of overseas facilities now operated by the PLA, since the opening of its first official overseas military base in Djibouti in 2017. It also complements a similar training and logistics facility that has been established at Cambodia’s Ream Naval Base on the Gulf of Thailand. The Cambodian facility was officially inaugurated by Prime Minister Hun Manet in April 2025, after three years of Chinese-funded refurbishments that include a 300-meter-long deep-water pier, a 5,000-ton dry dock, and a 1,000-ton slipway.

China’s involvement at Ream has attracted the suspicion of Western, and particularly American, security officials, who fear that the base may evolve into a full-blown Chinese base. Cambodia has sought to allay these fears by inviting foreign navies, including those of Japan, Vietnam, and the U.S., to visit the base.

Collin Koh, a scholar at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies in Singapore, said in a post on X that unlike Ream, the base in Laos is “more ostensibly similar to the one in Djibouti.” He added, “It may not be wrong to conclude this is the first full-fledged PLA overseas base in Southeast Asia.”

The development at Ban Keun is perhaps unsurprising given the rapid expansion of China’s influence in Laos over the past 15 years. During that time, the north of the country has become economically fused to southern China, as new highways and an impressive China-built railway have improved overland connections. The Chinese investment presence is clearly visible in most parts of the country, and there is a large Chinese expatriate community in Vientiane and the provincial towns of northern Laos.

Defense relations have proceeded more slowly, perhaps due to the sensitivities of Vietnam, Laos’ traditional defense patron, which has had close ties with Laos dating back to the communist struggle of the 1960s and 1970s. In ⁠June, however, Lao President Thongloun Sisoulith visited Beijing for meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping, during which the two leaders agreed to enhance defense cooperation.

Xi also suggested that China and Laos should establish a “3+3” strategic dialogue mechanism involving their foreign, defense, and public security ministers, “as an opportunity to strengthen law enforcement and security cooperation and crack down on cross-border crimes.” (A similar mechanism was established with Cambodia earlier this year.) Last month, Beijing and Vientiane also concluded “Peace Train 2026,” a 16-day joint military exercise aimed at “humanitarian assistance and military medical services.”

One Chinese security analyst told the state-run Global Times that the base at Ban Keun was a means of providing the Lao People’s Liberation Army Air Force, which operates a small and obsolescent fleet of Chinese and Russian craft, with a “systematic training system for pilots, maintenance crew and flight personnel” that will reduce its reliance on overseas training. More broadly, the analyst said, the facility will deepen “practical exchanges” between the two militaries, “upgrading from simple equipment assistance to long-term integrated cooperation in talent training, joint exercises and equipment support.”

Perhaps most tellingly, the analyst drew an explicit parallel between Ban Keun and the facility at Ream Naval Base, noting that together they “cover inland airspace in the Indochina Peninsula and the maritime direction in the Gulf of Thailand.”

In both cases, the Chinese military has emphasized that the facilities have been established on the basis of “mutual respect” and are not directed at any

Nonetheless, the Ban Keun facility has the potential to alter the strategic map of mainland Southeast Asia, pulling Laos and Cambodia further out of the Vietnamese sphere of influence.

Nguyen Khac Giang, a visiting fellow at the ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore, told Bloomberg that in light of the recent expansion of China’s military presence in Cambodia and the South China Sea, Vietnam in particular could have “serious grounds for concern” if the Ban Keun facility becomes a foothold for a more permanent PLA presence in Laos.

“These developments could give Beijing greater leverage over strategic access routes around Vietnam, raising concerns about its ability to monitor, and potentially constrain, Vietnam’s room for maneuver in time of crisis,” Giang told the newspaper. “Much depends on how the facility is used.”

Vietnam has not yet officially commented on the opening of the new facilities in Laos.

title: China’s Rare Earth Strategy and the Future of the South China Sea
description: The rise of seabed mining will add new complexity to the South China Sea disputes.
text:
In August 2026, Japan and the United States worked together to explore extracting rare-earth-rich mud from the seabed near Minamitorishima. It offered a glimpse into the next phase of critical minerals competition. The race for rare earths is no longer confined to land mines and export control policies. As deep-sea minerals become part of national security planning, maritime spaces that were once mainly discussed in terms of sovereignty, shipping lanes, and fisheries may acquire a new layer of strategic value.

The South China Sea is not currently central to China’s rare earth advantage, but it may become increasingly relevant to how Beijing and its competitors think about the future geography of critical minerals security.

For now, China’s rare earth strategy and its South China Sea strategy remain largely distinct. China’s leverage in rare earths comes less from pure geology than from the country’s dominant position in refining, separation, and magnet production, combined with regulatory instruments that allow Beijing to manage outward flows of selected minerals. The April 2025 export control measures on several medium and heavy rare-earth-related items underscored how critical minerals have become part of China’s national security toolbox.

By contrast, the South China Sea has traditionally been discussed and understood through a different strategic vocabulary: sovereignty claims, maritime jurisdiction, military presence, fisheries, hydrocarbons, and sea lanes of communication. This kind of separation, however, may not hold indefinitely, because the critical minerals competition is acquiring an increasingly prominent maritime dimension.

As governments search for ways to reduce dependence on existing rare earth supply chains, attention is gradually shifting toward deep-sea muds, polymetallic nodules, cobalt-rich crusts, and other seabed resources. These resources are not immediate substitutes for today’s land-based mines and processing systems, but they are entering strategic planning and industrial policy. Once critical minerals are imagined not only as terrestrial commodities but also as seabed resources, the boundary between resource security and maritime security begins to blur.

The South China Sea disputes have always had a strategic dimension, in addition to the sovereignty disputes alone. Yet oil, gas, fisheries, and shipping are the dominant drivers of maritime competition; seabed resources have thus far remained a less developed part of the story. Studies of Fe-Mn crusts and polymetallic nodules in the South China Sea have identified the presence of cobalt, nickel, rare earth elements, yttrium, and other critical materials.

That does not mean that the South China Sea is about to become a commercially viable rare earth mining zone. But as deep-sea mineral technologies and governance frameworks mature, the South China Sea’s significance may be reinterpreted through the language of critical minerals security.

That shift, if it occurs, would not replace the existing logic of South China Sea competition but add another layer to it. Critical minerals could make seabed mapping, marine scientific research, environmental regulation, and deep-sea mining rules more politically sensitive. Activities that once appeared primarily scientific or commercial could come to be viewed through the lens of supply chain resilience and national security.

China is especially well placed to think across these domains because it already possesses capabilities on both sides of the equation. It is not only a central actor in the rare earth supply chain, but also an active participant in deep-sea exploration and seabed governance. China adopted a national law on deep seabed resource exploration and development in 2016. Chinese entities already hold exploration contracts with the International Seabed Authority for polymetallic nodules, polymetallic sulphides, and cobalt-rich Fe-Mn crusts. Its deep-sea technological capacity has also expanded, symbolized by the Fendouzhe manned submersible’s dive to more than 10,000 meters in the Mariana Trench.

Rare earths are not about to become the central driver of South China Sea disputes. The more important trend is that two strategic arenas for competition are beginning to converge. China’s rare earth strategy is about control over critical supply chains, while its South China Sea strategy is about control over maritime space, rights, and access. As critical minerals competition expands offshore, these two forms of strategic control may begin to interact. The South China Sea, in the longer term, may become part of a broader debate over who maps, governs, regulates, and eventually exploits the seabed resources that underpin future industrial and military power.

Rare earths may not define the South China Sea today, but they could help reshape how its strategic value is imagined tomorrow.

title: China’s Revised Defense Mobilization Law Touches Nearly Every Sector
description: The circumstances under which mobilization can be declared are wider than ever, and a large number of entities – including private firms – are legally obligated to the state during wartime.
text:
The revised version of China’s National Defense Mobilization Law came into effect on October 1. It’s the first major overhaul since the statute came into existence in 2010. On its face, the law governs how China can convert civilian economic capacity into military capability during wartime, facilitating a rapid transition for national defense. However, a closer reading of the law indicates that it involves many critical stakeholders and has bearing on many aspects of the economy.

The law, in its original conception in 2010, was construed as Taiwan-centric. It helped build an underlying legal and military architecture to respond if Taiwan were to declare independence. Thus, it had a very clear purpose: war preparation in relation to the longstanding mission of national unification.

However, the recent revision goes beyond the war preparation narrative and Taiwan contingency. Now, the circumstances under which mobilization can be declared are widened, and the law encompasses a large number of entities that are legally obligated to the state during wartime, including private organizations that are required to assist in mobilization. It also mandates that anything required for mobilization can be levied or expropriated by the state. These revisions make the law relevant for a wide variety of stakeholders, including foreign governments and firms, in scenarios beyond Taiwan – and even in peaceful conditions.

The revision defines defense mobilization as steps taken by the state in response to threats to national sovereignty, unity, territorial integrity, security, and, interestingly, “development interests.”

“Development interests” can’t be read in the same breath as the former categories. Sovereignty, unity, and territorial integrity, and security can be broadly defined with strict bounds, but the definition of “development interests” can be as loose as officials want it to be.

The Chinese Defense Ministry spokesperson mentioned that the law need not be overinterpreted and is line with similar legislation in place in other countries. In general, the mention of “development interests” in Chinese national discourse acts as a central legitimizing framework, linking the Chinese Communist Party’s (CCP) authority with continuous economic growth and modernization.

However, with the phrase’s invocation in the operative definition of the defense mobilization statute, “development interests” has acquired a new extension. A blockade on the Strait of Malacca would not be an attack on territory or sovereignty but might hamper China’s development interests. The long-standing maritime dispute in the South China Sea may also be counted as jeopardizing China’s development interests.

This raises the question of what would qualify as a development interest – and thus authorize the conversion of civilian resources into military resources. The law delineates no threshold test. The revision has an expansive breadth with abysmally low precision, and it has been designed this way. An elastic law allows authorities to potentially co-opt private resources across a variety of scenarios, not just armed conflicts.

The law, with loosely defined and vague triggers, keeps a wide variety of stakeholders in its range. There is an obvious Taiwan angle, of course. Taiwanese media outlets report that experts perceive the law as wielding a clear legal warfare dimension for Taiwan. Taiwan’s independence is antithetical to the law, just as it was with the first version from 2010.

But the new revision has implications far beyond Taiwan. Foreign and domestic firms, under the revised law, become another stakeholder. Military-civil fusion has been a high-priority national strategy of the CCP to systematically eliminate barriers between its commercial civilian research sector and its military-industrial complex. The revised law provides a framework to establish a “data service support system,” giving the state explicit legitimate authority to “collect and use data closely related to defense mobilization” (Article 7).

The law also envelops emerging technologies, including AI. Article 8 of the law states that the state “promotes the application of advanced technologies in national defense mobilization and develops national defense mobilization forces in emerging fields.” It should be read along with Article 7.

The law requires strategic materials stockpiling and formal security assessments of military product supply chains. It allows the requisition and expropriation of civilian facilities, equipment, vehicles, and premises once mobilization is declared. As a whole, these revisions pave the way for a self-contained system, where a state systematically maps its own dual-use industrial base, making a massive share of the Chinese economy a contingency-based defense asset, while insulating itself against external disruption.

The “development interests” trigger matters to New Delhi as well. India’s exposure to China is mostly economic, including pharmaceutical inputs, rare earths and magnets, electronics components, solar modules, and capital goods. The new defense mobilization law is elastic enough to cover economic disputes with India as well in its purview, which can act as a formal extension to export restrictions on India already in place since April 2025.

The law plays on an undefined threshold and an expansive perimeter. This makes the revision a significant move by Beijing, given the almost exhaustive list of contingency sectors including transport, telecom, network security, medical, food supply, construction, energy and chemicals, nuclear facilities, news media, and municipal infrastructure. For firms in the Chinese market, due diligence now includes not only asking whether a Chinese partner has identifiable military links, but whether the partner operates in any listed sector, which would be most likely given the vast breadth of the law.

The law doesn’t imply that an emergency is imminent. The revised law can be seen as a part of Beijing’s wider institutional project to restructure its mobilization architecture into an all-encompassing trigger that legitimizes economic coercion. That new reality should shape how the world rates risk in China.

title: China’s Stake in the Russian Duma Elections
description: The topic is a controversial one in China due to the obvious parallels between the Russian and Chinese political systems and the stake the Chinese leadership has in the stability of their neighbor.
text:
What did observers in China think about the Russian State Duma election on September 20? While retaining a veneer of democratic procedure, Vladimir Putin has steadily eliminated potential rivals and term limits, much like Xi Jinping has done. In past Russian election cycles, Chinese officials and experts by large have emphasized the importance of outcomes reinforcing political stability in Russia.

In terms of the latest election, most Western commentary criticized the unfair process preventing Putin’s primary opposing party, Yabloko, from running. Yabloko – which means apple in Russian but actually is an acronym for the last names of its three founders – is the only pro-democracy and anti-war party in Russia. By contrast, China’s Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun congratulated Russia for the “smooth conclusion” of the process and hailed the elections for representing “the will of the Russian people.”

Chinese media commentary did note that Yabloko was prohibited from participating in the election as a party, although some Yabloko candidates were still running in single-member districts (and all lost). Given the lack of real electoral competition, a Hong Kong media outlet, China Review News Agency, pointed out that the 59 percent turnout (7.6 percentage points higher than the previous Duma election in 2021) reflected “the state’s mobilization capabilities,” not increased political participation.

Putin’s televised address in the lead-up to the election framed it as an opportunity for Russians to express their support for the war in Ukraine and as “a collective response to those who seek to weaken Russia,” Chinese commentary reported. More than 200 Russian veterans of the war in Ukraine ran for the Duma and election commission chair Ella Pamfilova reported that 46 of them won seats – 41 of whom belonged to United Russia, the ruling party that has dominated the Russian political landscape throughout Putin’s leadership.

With the elections held against a background of Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian soil and rising prices, Ma Bin, deputy director of the Center for Russian and Central Asian Studies at Fudan University, called the Duma election a major test and demonstration of Russian political stability. Chinese military analyst Shi Hong agreed that United Russia’s overwhelming victory demonstrated that for Russia “stability was paramount” and would support continuity in Russia’s military strategy and appropriations. Zhang Yanjun, a research fellow at the Institute of International Studies in Shanghai, predicted that the results of the election (held for the first time on occupied Ukrainian territory) would make Putin more intent on demonstrating strategic resolve and less likely to make concessions on Ukraine.

Since the failed coup attempt by the (since deceased) Wagner Group chairman, Yevgeny Prigozhin, in 2023, Chinese officials have made some efforts to reach out to officials beyond Putin’s inner circle. Wu Dahui, deputy director of the Russian Research Institute at Tsinghua University, emphasized that the Sino-Russian partnership has become institutionalized in a dense network of 60,000 channels at all levels of society, which he likened to the “blood vessels” sustaining the partnership.

Nevertheless, recently Chinese and Russian officials have emphasized the importance of top leader ties for their partnership. Following their most recent summit in May 2026, a Chinese diplomat hailed the relationship between Xi and Putin as “the fundamental guarantee” of the partnership. Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov credited the “diplomacy of leaders” for codifying progress in the partnership in concrete agreements.

With the Russian ruling party, United Russia, capturing the majority of seats in the latest election (349 out of 450), Guo added that China would continue to work with Russia to implement “the important common understandings between the two presidents to make fresh progress and bring bilateral relations to new heights.”

A 2019 article by Professor Wang Zhihua in the Rule of Law Forum of the Shanghai University of Political Science and Law about the role of the Duma in the Russian political system noted that in the Russian system the president has “absolute power” and constitutionally outlined checks and balances are “merely nominal, resulting in a unique presidential system with Russian characteristics.” Wang concluded that “In short, in Russia’s political system, the president has too much power, the parliament has less power, and the judiciary is also weak.”

In Wang’s view, the configuration of the Russian political system based on a strong president with personal charisma may be expedient in the short term for the country’s revival and rise. However, he cautioned that the expansion of presidential power may ultimately lead to a crisis and undermine the long-term development of legally based governance.

Such conclusions could easily be applied to China and it is not surprising that this article, which I obtained on September 11, 2026, is no longer accessible on the CNKI database of academic articles and or on the Baidu search engine.

Chinese scholars’ assessments of Russian political developments also contribute to our understanding of Chinese views about the long-term viability of the Sino-Russian partnership. An analysis of the Duma election by a Chinese military blogger emphasized the importance of Putin’s continued hold on power and his ability to restrain hardline factions from even more escalatory actions in Ukraine. The blogger wrote: “For China, while the specific choice of Russian leader is important, Russia’s ability to maintain stability and policy continuity is even more crucial. This is why Sino-Russian relations have been continuously strengthening institutional ties in recent years.”

The results of the Russian Duma election startled no one in Beijing, but Chinese observers followed them closely. The topic is a controversial one in China due to the obvious parallels between the Russian and Chinese political systems and the stake the Chinese leadership has in the stability of their neighbor.
