title: Clean Energy Must Avoid the Mistake of Overdependence
description: The world must diversify its energy dependence, not simply relocate it from the Middle East to China.
text:
For decades, energy security has meant oil. Countries worried about their dependence on the Middle East and Russia, the security of shipping lanes, and the geopolitical consequences of relying on a small number of producers for the oil that powered global economies. The transition to renewable energy was supposed to rebalance that equation. Yet in doing so, we may be creating a potentially greater vulnerability, since the clean energy supply chain is dominated by China.

Take Europe as an example. The year before Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, Russia supplied 45 percent of the EU’s natural gas imports. The war has forced European countries to scramble for new energy sources.

The war in the Middle East showed again how quickly concentrated energy supplies can become an economic liability. Roughly one-fifth of global oil consumption passes through the Strait of Hormuz – or did, before the strait was effectively closed by the conflict.

Clean energy can reduce exposure to these specific chokepoints, but the world must diversify its energy dependence without simply relocating it.

China leads in the industries powering the next phase of the global economy. It is the world’s largest supplier and exporter of green technology. In July 2026, China’s green energy exports rose 51 percent year-on-year, with new energy vehicles rising an astonishing 90 percent.

China dominates the clean energy value chain. Today, the country provides roughly 85 percent of global solar production capacity and 80 percent of lithium-ion batteries. This is essentially a monopoly. In electric vehicles, China accounted for almost three-quarters of global production in 2025.

Its control also extends upstream. China holds critical positions in processing and refining the minerals essential to new energy technologies, from batteries to electric motors and wind turbines. It also possesses much of the manufacturing expertise – and increasingly the equipment – needed to turn those materials into finished products.

Therefore, clean energy dependence extends across an entire industrial ecosystem – from processing through technology, components and manufacturing equipment to the finished product. A disruption at any point in the supply chain could reverberate through the entire system.

The International Energy Agency (IEA) estimated that each month of a halt in Chinese battery supply chain exports could reduce output from EV factories elsewhere by some $17 billion, with more than half of those losses occurring in Europe.

The risk is not hypothetical. China’s use of export controls on rare earths and other critical materials has demonstrated how concentrated supply chains translate into strategic leverage. China mines roughly 60 percent of the world’s rare earths but produces about 90 percent of its rare earth permanent magnets, leaving downstream manufacturers with few immediate alternatives.

Oil reserves are fixed by geology, while China’s dominance in clean technology is the product of industrial policy, capital investment, and accumulated manufacturing expertise. That should, in theory, make clean energy dependence more reversible. In practice, however, diversification is difficult.

A critical part of China’s advantage is manufacturing efficiency. The IEA attributed more than 40 percent of China’s battery cost edge over Europe to automation and efficiency. In critical mineral mining and refining, China’s position also rests on decades of accumulated processing capacity and a willingness to bear environmental costs that many other countries have been reluctant to accept. None of this can be replicated quickly.

China’s enormous investment and innovation in clean technology has helped drive down costs and accelerate deployment. Attempting to exclude China entirely would make the energy transition slower and more expensive. Interdependence is not the problem, and energy security has never required producing everything at home. It requires enough diversity that no single supplier can disrupt the system.

As with trade, the answer is not decoupling but diversification.

Countries should identify where domestic capacity is strategically necessary, build alternative sources of supply with allies and emerging markets, and continue trading and investing with China where it makes economic sense.

It can be done, but it takes time, capital, and political will. Las Vegas-based MP Materials operates North America’s only rare earth mine of scale, producing more than 10 percent of global rare earth supply. The company is building heavy rare earth processing capacity and investing more than $1.25 billion in a magnet manufacturing campus. Importantly, its strategy is becoming international: in 2025, MP Materials, the U.S. government, and Saudi Arabia’s Maaden agreed to develop a Saudi rare earth refinery to supply rare earth oxides to U.S., Saudi, and allied manufacturers.

This one refinery is not, on its own, a solution, but it points to the kind of allied, government-supported investment in processing that rebalancing requires.

While the world will remain dependent upon fossil fuels for the foreseeable future, the diversification to clean energy will continue, and the stakes will rise as demand grows. The world should not spend decades reducing its dependence on Middle Eastern and Russian hydrocarbons only to discover that it has exchanged one form of strategic dependence for another – this time on China.
tag: China clean energy; China critical minerals; China electric cars; China new energy vehicles; China rare earths

title: Concerns About ‘WWII Allies’ at US-China Summit
description: How China is weaponizing WWII history
text:
At the U.S.-China summit in September 2026, both leaders spoke of the fact that the United States and China had been allies in World War II and had fought together. Of course, the United States and China (the Republic of China) were indeed Allied nations in WWII and fought together against Japan and others, and if the summit remarks were intended simply to reaffirm that historical fact and invoke shared memory, then they should give rise to no particular concern.

It is also worth recalling that in 2015, the 70th anniversary of the end of the war, U.S.-China relations were relatively stable, and China was emphasizing that it had fought alongside the United States and other major Western powers as key members of the Allied coalition, and had jointly created the postwar order. At that time, China was using the phrase “New Model of Major-Country Relations” in its relations with the United States. If the invocation of wartime partnership at the recent summit was intended to evoke memories of that 2015 period and signal an intention to restore the “New Model of Major-Country Relations,” that too would be comprehensible as a matter of Chinese policy.

However, more than ten years have now passed since 2015, and China’s narrative on history today is different from what it once was. So the fact that wartime partnership was raised by both sides at this summit is, in fact, a cause for concern. To explain, it is necessary to look at how China has recently been employing its historical narrative — with particular attention to its relationship with Russia.

The COVID-19 pandemic of 2020 and China’s response to it, together with Russia’s war in Ukraine beginning in 2022, generated widespread international criticism of both countries. That criticism brought China and Russia closer together, and the two countries more openly positioned themselves in opposition to Western nations. In 2024, the 75th anniversary of the establishment of Sino-Russian diplomatic relations and a year in which the pandemic was still fresh in mind and the war in Ukraine was very much ongoing, Russian President Vladimir Putin made an official visit to China in May and issued a joint statement. It included the following passage:

“China and Russia will continue to firmly defend the results of the victory of the Second World War and the postwar world order enshrined in the Charter of the United Nations, and oppose the negation, distortion, and falsification of the history of World War II. They plan to solemnly celebrate the 80th anniversary of the victory of the Chinese People’s War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression and the Soviet Union’s Patriotic War in 2025 and jointly promote a correct view of the history of World War II.”

This statement signaled that China and Russia intended to jointly insist on what they view as the “correct history” of WWII to the world, while refusing to accept any historical perspective that differs from their own.

In March 2025, at a press conference on the occasion of China’s National People’s Congress, State Councilor Wang Yi stated that, marking the 80th anniversary of victory in WWII, China and Russia were reaffirming that they had fought together in Asia and Europe at the cost of blood, and went on to say that, building on this past, the two countries would jointly promote a correct understanding of WWII history, defend the fruits of that victory, uphold the international system with the United Nations at its core, and advance the international order in a more just and reasonable direction. China and Russia have thus pledged not only to reaffirm their wartime partnership but to jointly seek to shape the present international order on that basis. For China and Russia, historical narrative is inseparable from the shaping of the current international order.

Then, on May 9, 2025, Russia’s Victory Day commemorating the defeat of Nazi Germany, Chinese President Xi Jinping visited Russia and issued a joint statement with the Russian president. This statement explicitly identified Japanese militarism and Nazi Germany as the adversaries China and Russia fought in WWII, and made clear that China and Russia would together resist any moves to revive the militarism or Nazism of the past. On Japan specifically, the statement declared that “the Japanese government should learn lessons from the brutal crimes it committed in history, exercise caution in its words and deeds on historical issues such as the Yasukuni Shrine, and completely cut ties with militarism that once brought deep disasters to the peoples of the world and Japan itself.”

In its discourse on WWII, China was not only seeking to spread what it calls the “correct historical perspective” together with Russia, but was also issuing strong warnings against “Japanese militarism.” And this was positioned not merely as a matter of the past but — particularly in the context of the Sino-Russian relationship — as something linked to joint efforts toward a “just” reshaping of the international order.

In 2025, China made a qualitative leap in its narrative on history, in both substance and in method. China generated narratives connected to the invalidity of the San Francisco Peace Treaty, the Taiwan issue, and the status of Okinawa — areas directly linked to China’s interests in the First Island Chain. Yet China’s actions were moving faster than its words; its military activity had already extended well beyond the First Island Chain, expanding into the Second Island Chain, the Western Pacific, and the South Pacific.

From around the time of Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae’s remarks in November 2025 and into 2026, China’s verbal attacks on Japan began to employ the term “neo-militarism,” and its criticism of Japan became more comprehensive. Japan’s security policy as a whole began to be characterized and challenged as “neo-militarism.”

In May 2026, when Putin made another official visit to China and a Sino-Russian joint statement was issued, language criticizing Japan’s “neo-militarism” and “remilitarization” was incorporated into the text, which represented an expansion of Sino-Russian historical cooperation on WWII. China also sought to extend its criticism of Japan to countries beyond Russia, inserting language critical of Japan — such as opposition to “militarism” — into joint statements issued in the context of bilateral relationships with various countries. At the UN General Assembly in September 2026 as well, the Chinese representative strongly criticized Japan using terms such as “remilitarization” and “neo-militarism,” and Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov joined in, expressing agreement with the Chinese position by similarly characterizing Japan as following a path of militarism.

Which brings us to the recent U.S.-China summit, where Xi and U.S. President Donald Trump raised the subject of the wartime relationship between the United States and China in WWII. The United States and China were Allied nations in WWII. But in light of the account above, China’s recent discourse on WWII is certainly not limited to pointing out historical facts or evoking memories of the past. And for Japan, that is cause for concern.
tag: China historical revisionism; China history; China-Japan Relations; China-Russia Relations; China-Russia summit; Chinese historical narrative; historical narratives; U.S.-China summit; World War II

title: Data Centers in the Asia-Pacific
description: Navigating a new era of resource regulation
text:
As artificial intelligence receives continued investment and media hype on promises that it will remake the global economy, investment is pouring into digital infrastructure, particularly data centers. The Asia-Pacific region is experiencing its own data center boom with resource consumption emerging as the defining flashpoint between digital infrastructure ambitions and the communities hosting them. Water is the most acute concern: hyperscale facilities draw millions of liters daily in regions already facing groundwater depletion, drought, or agricultural competition for supply, from South Asia’s water-stressed corridors to Central Asia’s shrinking basins. But energy demand runs a close second, as straining grids raise the threat of higher electricity prices and increased pollution from fossil fuels despite decarbonization targets adopted by countries and companies around the region. Other issues such as land acquisition and construction disruption — noise, dust, traffic, and questions over fair compensation — add a further layer of friction, particularly where regulatory oversight and environmental impact assessment requirements have not kept up with construction.

Underlying Asia’s data center buildout is a deeper grievance: that the benefits of digital infrastructure (tax revenue, jobs, grid investment) are diffuse and national, while the costs are concentrated and local. As protest activity spreads from established flashpoints like South Korea to newer markets including Japan, Malaysia, Indonesia, and India, politicians are taking notice and regulation aimed at controlling data center resource consumption is spreading across the region.

Australia has moved to become the first country to bring data center location, energy, and water requirements under a single national regulatory framework. On July 15, 2026, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced that the National Framework will require large-scale operators to become “net-generators” of power, meaning that they must fund their own generation capacity and grid connection costs rather than passing them to consumers. In addition, operators must meet mandatory energy efficiency and water conservation standards. A new Office of AI will coordinate design of the framework, which is intended to replace the current fragmented state-by-state approval system and streamline compliance. The proposal follows growing community concern over data centers straining local grids and drinking water supplies, and reflects lessons drawn from overseas markets where rapid buildouts have provoked local backlash. Legislation is expected early next year, pending agreement with state and territory governments at the National Cabinet.

title: Debunking Alarmist Narratives on the ‘China Air Base’ in Laos
description: The most widespread narratives regarding the Laos-China Support and Training Center lack evidence and demonstrate a limited understanding of air power.
text:
The opening of the Laos-China Joint Support and Training Center and the Friendship Aviation Academy in Ban Keun, Laos on September 29 has sparked an intense media storm. China hawks claim that the innocuous airfield represents Beijing’s third overseas military base, following the Djibouti facility in East Africa and the Ream Naval Support facility in Cambodia, and the first Chinese air base in Southeast Asia.

International media has framed the Ban Keun facility as a “base” or an “air base,” and the training aircraft spotted on satellite imagery as “attack aircraft” or “light attack aircraft.” Further, alarmists warn that China could extend the airfield’s runway and expand its infrastructure to enable power projection across mainland Southeast Asia and beyond, or to use the facility for intelligence collection. Still others have proposed that an enlarged base could facilitate bomber operations or to out-flank or surround Vietnam.

Critically, however, whether due to intentional framing or simple ignorance, many of the above claims lack evidence and realism. This article attempts to debunk some of the more persistent and glaring narratives repeated in the media and expert commentary regarding the new airfield and its purpose.

First, images of Ban Keun airfield taken by a commercial satellite provider Vantor and shared first by Reuters show eight Chinese-made JL-8/K-8 basic jet trainer aircraft on the facility’s apron. The aircraft are termed as “light attack aircraft” or “attack aircraft” by media. That is an inaccurate framing, making the aircraft appear more threatening by nature than they actually are.

The K-8 is a joint China-Pakistan training aircraft project, operated by many countries, including in the region by China, Laos, Myanmar, and Pakistan, among others. The K-8 is primarily a basic or intermediate training aircraft. The type typically feeds into phases two and three of a flight training syllabus, like introduction to jet flight and advanced jet training, and an introduction to tactical flight, before moving on to more advanced and higher performance trainers.

In the Lao People’s Liberation Army Air Force (LPLAAF), the phase one elementary training is carried out on Chinese-build SAIC LE-500, the K-8 is used in the phase two and three basic jet training, and the Russian YAK-130 is used for phase four tactical training.

Unlike Myanmar’s air force, which has reportedly employed the K-8 in a light attack role, there is no evidence of LPLAAF use of the type in that role. Tellingly, no visual evidence of the type participating in exercises or carrying air-to-ground munitions has surfaced in the aircraft’s almost a decade of service in Laos. Thus, framing the Laotian K-8 as a “light attack aircraft” is simply an inaccurate description, which causes confusion and alarm.

In contrast, the Russian advanced jet trainer is a substantially more capable platform than the K-8 and can be armed with various air-to-air and air-to-ground munitions for ground support.

Another persistent claim suggests that Ban Keun airfield is a Chinese “air base” with a long runway and a “large” apron for aircraft parking, supposedly capable of supporting Chinese military power projection across mainland Southeast Asia.

However, the airfield’s single runway is approximately 2,000 meters in length, which, in fact, is not very long for a military airfield. Other major LPLAAF operating locations like the Wattay International Airport in Vientiane and Xieng Khouang (Phonsavan) air base have runways extending to approximately 3,000 m and 2,500 m, respectively, measured in Google Earth.

By way of comparison, neighboring Thailand’s military airfields are generally built to 3,000 m length. Similarly, the People’s Liberation Army Air Force (PLAAF) fighter bases in the Southern Theater Command area have 2,500 m runways, while bomber bases at Shaodong and Leiyang have longer, 3,000 m runways.

The 2,000 m runway at Ban Keun was not built to support power projection but, instead, to handle training aircraft.

In addition, claims that the facility has a large apron for aircraft parking and potential for significant expansion to support power projection are also incorrect. Judged from the available satellite imagery, the airfield’s apron is in fact relatively small and can only support a dozen trainers with associated sun shelters, hangars, and maintenance infrastructure.

To support sustained power projection operations, the airfield should have truly vast aprons, numerous aircraft shelters, and large fuel and munitions “farms,” which can be seen in similar imagery from Chinese air bases across the border.

None of this is visible at Ban Keun. What can be parsed out is an airfield with modest infrastructure suitable for the stated intended training role.

Some experts have proposed that together with the Cambodia-China Support Center in Ream (often framed as a Chinese naval base), the Ban Keun “air base” will help China “encircle” Vietnam. Writing for the Interpreter, Hunter Marston suggested that “Beijing has effectively pulled off an end run around Hanoi’s air and maritime flanks.”

Such statements demonstrate limited understanding of air power’s key attributes and China’s existing military posture and options to project power in the South China Sea or mainland Southeast Asia. Air power allows maneuver in the third dimension (altitude). Its key attributes – speed, reach, and ability to overfly any terrain – provide military aircraft significant operational flexibility.

The PLAAF does not have to base its combat aircraft physically in Laos to attempt to “surround” or “encircle” Vietnam. It can do so from its current bases within the Southern Theater Command and the South China Sea.

Under the Southern Theater Command, the PLAAF has an extensive network of well-equipped air bases that stretch from Hunan and Guangdong provinces in China’s southeast to Guangxi and Yunnan provinces in the south, directly bordering Vietnam, Laos, and Myanmar. In addition, Hainan Island, Woody Island in the Paracels, and Fiery Cross Reef, Subi Reef, and Mischief Reef in the Spratlys provide the PLAAF with a chain of well-equipped operating locations for any regional contingency.

Importantly, from its current bases, such as Mengzi in Yunnan Province or Bose/Tianyang in Guangxi Province, PLAAF combat aircraft can comfortably reach anywhere in mainland Southeast Asia. Moreover, operating from China’s Spratly outposts, the PLAAF can reach nearly all corners of the subregion. The reach of China’s air power can be further expanded by the growing fleet of indigenous aerial refueling aircraft.

The PLAAF’s primary combat aircraft in the Southern Theater Command area of operations – such as the JH-7A, Su-30MKK, J-16, and J-20 – are designed for long combat radius, extending from 600 nautical miles to up to 1,000 nm. The smaller J-10C can also reach more than 600 nm with drop tanks. With such operational flexibility, PLAAF strike aircraft can execute multipronged attacks against targets up to central Vietnam from their existing bases. Dispatched from Woody Island or Fiery Cross Reef in the South China Sea, Chinese fighters can easily cover the entirety of Vietnam and more, offering options for multiple approaches.

As a result, there is no reason for Beijing to position its bombers forward to the Ban Keun airfield to project power across mainland Southeast Asia and the Gulf of Thailand and Gulf of Bengal in conflict. With an estimated combat radius of 1,350 nm combined with the use of long-range precision-guided weapons, China’s H-6K bombers can cover all the above areas while operating from their home bases at Shaodong and Leiyang in Hunan Province. Any forward deployment of Chinese bombers would occur within the Southern Theater Command area, Hainan Island, or the Spratlys, offering the PLAAF multiple options and operational flexibility.

Experts have suggested also that China could deploy spy aircraft, surveillance radars, and signals intelligence gathering systems to Ban Keun. Commenting on the matter for the South China Morning Post, Abdul Rahman Yaacob proposed that China could use the facility for “keeping an eye on Vietnam” and to “monitor air activities deep into Myanmar, Thailand, and Vietnam.” Others have noted that the facility offers improved reach for Chinese spy planes to monitor U.S. military activity up to the Singapore Strait.

However, it is unclear from such commentary what the purpose of increased monitoring of mainland Southeast Asia is.

Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, and Cambodia all hold very close relations with Beijing. When it comes to Vietnam, which has maritime disputes with China in the South China Sea, Hanoi’s military bases can be easily monitored from Southern Theater Command area of operations, with little additional benefit from dispatching such capabilities to Laos.

These assertions are among the most frequently disseminated narratives regarding the Laos-China Support and Training Center. Many are pure speculation that fuels unnecessary alarmism – particularly those that lack evidence and demonstrate a limited understanding of air power, its key attributes, and China’s regional air projection capabilities.

What the official statements and available evidence suggest is that the Ban Keun facility is a joint training facility to help the LPLAAF develop its capacity for the future and meet its own modernization goals.

China has assisted the Lao air force (and the broader civil aviation sector) not just through hardware sales (i.e., the LE-500 and JL-8 for the LPLAAF and the C-909 for the Lao Airlines) but also by developing the entire aviation ecosystem, including infrastructure, management, maintenance, and training. This is the context in which the Laos-China Joint Support and Training Center and the Friendship Aviation Academy should be viewed.
tag: Ban Keun airport; China overseas basing; China power projection; China-Laos Military Joint Support and Training Center; K-8 training aircraft; Lao People's Army; Laos-China relations; PLA Air Force

title: Deepavali vs Diwali Sparks New Political Row in Malaysia
description: Is the Malaysian Indian Congress using Hindu identity politics to regain its political relevance ahead of the next general election?
text:
In India, religious sentiment has become such a fragile commodity that it can be hurt by almost anything: a joke, a film song, a movie title, or even a slogan printed on a T-shirt.

Far from India, a slight change in spelling and pronunciation has sparked a political maelstrom. In Malaysia, the Hindu festival of lights is celebrated as a public holiday. This time a controversy erupted because the traditional terminology, “Deepavali,” was not used in public greetings.

After Kuala Lumpur City Hall erected festive arches wishing the public a “Happy Diwali,” M. Saravanan, deputy president of the Malaysian Indian Congress (MIC), accused the authorities of erasing the traditional terminology. For him, the change in spelling has become a question of cultural identity and religious sentiment.

Saravanan subsequently wrote to Hannah Yeoh, minister in the Prime Minister’s Department responsible for Federal Territories, asking her to restore the legally gazetted name. He said that the choice of name was not merely a matter of semantics but one of respect for the linguistic and cultural heritage of Malaysian Hindus.

Saravanan’s objection is linked to the fact that he, like the majority of Malaysian Hindus, traces his ancestry to southern India, particularly Tamil Nadu. He says the term “Diwali” is typically associated with North India, while most southern states in India continue to use “Deepavali.”

The controversy highlights the apprehension that minorities face in any country, where tinkering with religious or cultural symbols can be seen as an attempt to dilute their identity, particularly given Malaysia’s history of ethnic tensions.

However, there is a political dimension to this debate. Critics see Saravanan’s objection as an attempt to bring back MIC in political discourse, as the party, after being drubbed in the 2018 general election, lost the sobriquet of sole representative of the country’s 2 million Hindus. Even the party’s supreme leader Samy Vellu could not retain his parliamentary seat, which he had held since 1974.

The historic 2018 election completely reshaped the political landscape. For the first time, Indian voters moved away from the MIC, in favor of Pakatan Harapan and its two main parties, the Democratic Action Party and People’s Justice Party.

Critics and political commentators argue that the MIC’s focus on semantic issues is a calculated effort to regain its relevance amid its declining influence in Malaysian politics. The “Deepavali versus Diwali” debate may generate headlines, they say, adding that the party needs to address deeper socioeconomic challenges, such as the forced relocation of Hindu temples and the long-standing economic disparities facing Malaysian Indians.
tag: Deepavali; Diwali; Indian community in Malaysia; Indian Malaysians; M. Saravanan; Malaysian Indian Congress

title: Democracy Is Not Silence Between Elections
description: A vote gives a government the authority to rule. It does not give it the right to silence the people.
text:
In a democracy, an election’s credibility depends not only on the votes cast by citizens, but also on their confidence in the institution responsible for conducting it. India’s Election Commission (EC), a constitutional body entrusted with safeguarding the integrity of elections, is therefore expected to stand above partisan interests. Yet, allegations by opposition parties and activists that the EC has favored the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) in elections as well as processes determining who can vote, alongside questions about electoral transparency and institutional independence, have brought this constitutional responsibility into sharp public debate.

The concern extends beyond any single election or political party. When citizens begin to question whether institutions designed to act independently are functioning impartially, the issue becomes larger than electoral competition. There is something deeply political about being made to stand outside, whether outside parliament, outside a university auditorium, outside government offices, or outside the very institutions that claim to represent you. In a democracy, the distinction between being inside and outside is never merely geographical.

India is a constitutional republic founded on popular sovereignty. The opening words of its Constitution, “We, the People of India,” establish that political authority ultimately derives from the people. Yet, we often reduce democracy to a single moment, the casting of a vote. We elect our representatives, celebrate electoral victories and expect the machinery of governance to function. But what happens between elections? What happens when citizens believe their representatives have failed them? What happens when people must stand outside the corridors of power to make themselves heard? A vote determines who governs. But a voice determines whether those who govern remain accountable.

Disagreement is natural in a plural society. The problem arises when criticism is treated as disloyalty, opposition to government policy is confused with opposition to the nation, and peaceful protest is viewed as a threat simply because it challenges authority. A government may win an election, but it cannot claim ownership of the republic.

When the People Challenge Power

India’s democratic history cannot be told through elections and parliamentary proceedings alone. It must also be told through the people who marched, organized, protested, and challenged the established order. The freedom struggle transformed streets, villages, and public spaces into arenas of resistance against colonial rule. Ordinary people did not wait for permission from those in power to demand freedom. Their participation was central to the making of independent India.

One of the most consequential examples of public resistance in contemporary India was the anti-corruption movement led by Anna Hazare and his colleagues in 2011. During Prime Minister Manmohan Singh’s tenure, thousands gathered at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar and then at Ramlila Maidan demanding a strong Lokpal institution to investigate corruption. The movement emerged amid major corruption controversies and growing public dissatisfaction with the Congress-led United Progressive Alliance government.

The confrontation was not without controversy. Hazare was arrested in August 2011 during a hunger strike, provoking further demonstrations. Yet, the movement could not simply be dismissed. Public pressure brought institutional accountability to the center of national debate, and the UPA government enacted the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act in 2013. The movement also contributed to the wider anti-establishment sentiment preceding the 2014 change of government, although it was not the sole cause of that electoral outcome.

The Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan (MKSS) movement stands as another powerful reminder that democracy is not secured by elections alone, but by citizens’ ability to question power. Beginning in Rajasthan, rural workers and farmers peacefully demanded access to official records on wages and development spending, exposing corruption through jan sunwais (public hearings) and a historic 40-day dharna (sit-in) at Beawar in Rajasthan in 1996. Their discipline, courage and refusal to retreat showed that a protest can transform a local grievance into a national democratic demand.

The first UPA government responded by enacting the Right to Information Act in 2005, converting a citizen’s moral claim into a legal right. This landmark law empowered ordinary Indians to inspect government records and hold public authorities accountable, proving that protest remains essential to protecting transparency, justice, and democracy itself.

The lesson is significant. A government can disagree with a movement, but it cannot expect public anger to disappear merely by containing it. The MKSS movement demonstrated how resistance can compel political institutions to confront uncomfortable questions. Democracy is strengthened when public demands find meaningful institutional responses.

The same lesson emerges from the defense of civil liberties during the Emergency of 1975-77. The suspension of fundamental freedoms and restrictions on the media demonstrated how quickly democratic institutions can be weakened when political authority becomes concentrated.

The electoral defeat of Indira Gandhi’s government in 1977 subsequently showed that citizens could use the ballot to reject authoritarian excesses. Indian democracy has endured not because dissent disappeared, but because people continued to demand their constitutional rights.

Dissent Is Not Disloyalty

The Constitution guarantees freedom of speech and expression and the right to assemble peacefully and without arms under Article 19, subject to constitutionally permitted reasonable restrictions. These freedoms are not absolute, but restrictions cannot become a convenient instrument for silencing criticism. In Amit Sahni v. Commissioner of Police (2020), concerning the Shaheen Bagh protest in the national capital, New Delhi, the Supreme Court addressed the limits of indefinitely occupying public ways. The democratic challenge is to protect peaceful dissent while respecting the rights of other citizens.

Recent events in India’s neighborhood offer a sobering warning. In Bangladesh in 2024, student protests over government job quotas escalated into a wider uprising against Sheikh Hasina’s government. A violent crackdown and mounting public anger preceded her resignation and departure from the country. Likewise, Nepal’s Gen Z-led protests in 2025 exposed the dangers of political alienation and declining public confidence in established leadership.

These events are not templates for India, nor should violence be romanticized. India’s political and societal culture is different. They demonstrate, however, that suppressing grievances does not necessarily extinguish them. When peaceful channels of dissent are obstructed, institutions fail to respond, and citizens lose faith in the possibility of change, a political crisis can grow beyond the control of those governing. Governments that mistake silence for consent may discover too late that public anger has merely accumulated.

Democracy is not merely an administrative arrangement; it is an inheritance secured through struggle and sacrifice. A republic needs institutions where decisions are made, but it also needs doors that remain open, and institutions willing to listen when concerns go unanswered. A vote is an act of citizenship, but so is a question put to a minister, an investigation published by an independent journalist, a student assembly, a worker’s march, or a peaceful protest outside the gates of power.

The republic belongs as much to the critic as to the supporter, and as much to the citizen standing outside as to the representative seated inside. Its strength will be measured not only by how people vote, but by whether they remain free to speak afterwards, and whether those in power are willing to listen. A vote gives a government the authority to rule. It does not give it the right to silence the people.
tag: Election Commission of India; India's democracy; Indian constitution; Indian Elections; Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan; Right to protest

title: Digital Asset Regulations in the Asia-Pacific
description: The risks of fragmentation
text:
Over the past decade, the Asia-Pacific region has become a global leader in digital asset adoption. Broadly defined as the representation of resources and other instruments that are issued and transferred using blockchain technology, a number of Asia-Pacific financial institutions have made big investments on this new wave of financial technology. Surveys have indicated that 62 percent of Asia-Pacific institutions have already committed capital to digital asset infrastructure, compared to 27 percent in North America. The amount of resources deployed to build out digital asset offerings is significant, with nearly eight in 10 Asia-Pacific institutions allocating more than $1 million. The result is that the Asia-Pacific just recorded the world’s fastest regional growth in blockchain-based crypto-asset transactions, expanding by 69 percent between mid-2024 and mid-2025, according to the OECD’s 2026 Asia Capital Markets Report.

The types of digital assets offered by Asia-Pacific financial institutions extend far beyond cryptocurrency. In April 2026, Singaporean bank OCBC and its asset management arm, Lion Global Investors, partnered with the digital asset exchange DigiFT, to issue the OCBC-LionGlobal Physical Gold Fund Token (“GOLDX token”). This token claims to be Southeast Asia’s first tokenized physical gold fund available on a public blockchain and allows institutional and corporate investors to own physical gold with the liquidity and verification benefits of blockchain technology. In 2026, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) granted two stablecoin licenses to HSBC and a joint venture backed by Standard Chartered Hong Kong, facilitating easier trade in traditionally illiquid assets. Japan’s largest bank, Mitsubishi UFJ Trust and Banking (MUFG) recently launched Progmat, a digital asset infrastructure for issuing and managing security tokens, which represent traditional financial assets like bonds, real estate, or corporate shares. Progmat is now backed by other large Japanese financial institutions, such as Mizuho, the Tokyo Stock Exchange and SBI Group.

However, these sophisticated digital assets are the result of complex and constantly evolving regulatory regimes that differ significantly from each other. Hong Kong’s recently finalized regulations on Virtual Asset Trading Platforms (VATP) are particularly comprehensive, covering service providers under distinct licensing categories, mirroring traditional securities rules. Singapore regulates cryptocurrency through a tailored, activity-based approach rather than a single framework. The Payment Services Act covers e-money or digital payment tokens and the Securities and Futures Act governs digital assets resembling securities. The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) emphasizes consumer protection via mandatory customer asset segregation, statutory trusts, and licensing thresholds. Japan runs one of the world’s most sophisticated and onerous digital asset regimes, featuring granular legal categories (Crypto Assets, stablecoins, and security tokens) each under tailored oversight, paired with strict investor protections like mandatory cold-wallet segregation. Recent reforms in July 2026 signal a friendlier trajectory, reclassifying crypto as financial instruments under the Financial Instruments and Exchange Act, cutting taxes to a flat 20 percent, and aligning treatment with stocks to attract institutional investors.

Continue reading for free at The Diplomat’s new companion publication, The Investor.

title: Don’t Call It a Reset: The Modi-Xi Meeting Wasn’t a Turning Point
description: Both sides are trying to prevent another crisis while their core disagreements remain unresolved.
text:
Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to New Delhi last month for the BRICS summit prompted speculation that India and China are moving toward a reset. Some see an opening for rapprochement, while others attribute the renewed engagement to deteriorating India-U.S. relations. Both interpretations overstate the shift in bilateral ties. Xi’s visit was important, but it did not mark a turning point.

Xi came to New Delhi for the BRICS summit in September, which also gave him an opportunity to meet Prime Minister Narendra Modi. India and China’s participation in BRICS and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) should not be mistaken for an alignment of interests. India’s engagement within multilateral organizations is a longstanding feature of its foreign policy, and China has not been a decisive factor in that approach.

Since the 2020 Galwan clashes, India has sought to stabilize ties and manage differences with China. These efforts have gained momentum amid U.S President Donald Trump’s increasingly hostile policies toward India and much of Asia. Yet the reasons for renewed engagement with Beijing go beyond the state of India-U.S. relations.

The resumption of high-level dialogue, leadership meetings, and direct connectivity are important developments. Another Galwan-like border confrontation would carry heavy domestic costs and could be difficult to recover from. Preventing a recurrence of such violence is a priority. But this does not require India to reconsider its position on the underlying differences.

It is also important to note that India never abandoned dialogue with China after Galwan. Keeping communication channel open has remained part of its approach, even as tensions persisted along the border. The latest meetings continue that policy; they do not demonstrate that the relationship or India’s approach to it has fundamentally changed.

The border remains the principal obstacle. China’s recent statement that it does not recognize the Union Territory of Ladakh underlined the depth of the disagreement. There is little basis for expecting a reset while the two sides remain so far apart on territorial issues. Nor is the border the only source of friction. China’s relationship with Pakistan and the persistent trade imbalance remain contentious issues, too. There is little evidence of progress on any of these fundamental differences.

The separate readouts issued after the Modi-Xi meeting offered further evidence of the distance between them. There was no joint statement. The Chinese readout included a reference to Tibet and Taiwan that was absent from the Indian account. Beijing described India as a partner, but the Indian readout did not use the same language. The differences in wording hardly suggest a shared political understanding.

Deteriorating India-U.S. relations and uncertainty over Washington’s commitment to Indo-Pacific security have shaped the circumstances in which New Delhi engages Beijing. But it would be a mistake to explain India’s China policy primarily through its relationship with the United States. India has its own reasons to avoid another border crisis, and its willingness to maintain dialogue with China predates the current difficulties with Washington.

The suggestion that worsening ties with the U.S. have left India isolated, or made the Indo-Pacific less relevant, also overlooks the agency of regional countries. Their security concerns remain, regardless of changes in Washington’s priorities. The U.S. remains important to collective regional security, but uncertainty over its commitments does not remove the need for cooperation among countries in the region. The more immediate concern for Washington is the effect of its policies on its credibility among regional allies and partners. If confidence in the U.S. weakens, the consequences could extend across the Indo-Pacific.

India’s security interests do not begin and end with its relationship with the U.S. Even as ties with Washington come under strain, New Delhi must contend with its own regional challenges. This does not mean India and China will draw closer. New Delhi can manage relations with Beijing while reassessing its ties with Washington; neither relationship necessarily dictates the other. Efforts to manage differences with China are consistent with India’s longstanding approach of preserving options without compromising its security concerns.

China-India relations are still short of their pre-2020 status quo. Security cooperation is limited, and military exercises such as Hand-in-Hand remain suspended. The trust needed for closer cooperation has yet to be restored, and the prospects seem far-fetched for now.

For India, the unresolved border dispute remains a central security concern. The Galwan clashes changed India’s view of and threat perception from China and raised serious questions about the viability of the existing arrangements in ensuring peace along the Line of Actual Control (LAC). High-level meetings can help manage tensions for the time being, but they cannot substitute for progress on the ground. India is also unlikely to return to its previous position on the One China policy without some reference to, or assurance regarding, a corresponding One India policy from Beijing. Such an assurance appears unlikely in the foreseeable future.

Just a couple of years ago, a meeting between Xi and Modi on Indian soil seemed difficult to imagine. That is one of the reasons why their meeting drew so much attention. But it has not changed the scope or nature of the issues dividing the two countries. For now, both sides are trying to prevent another crisis while their core disagreements remain unresolved. Until those differences are addressed, dialogue may keep the relationship from deteriorating further, but it will not put China-India ties on the path to a reset.

title: Drones and Missiles Are Rewriting the Military Balance on the Korean Peninsula
description: North Korea’s ability to disperse, conceal, and employ its drones, missiles, and nuclear weapons is outpacing South Korea’s capacity to destroy them.
text:
The two Koreas have been close observers of the wars in Ukraine and Iran – not least because aspects of the conflicts mirror how both sides think they will win a potential war on the peninsula. The ongoing exchange of long-range drones and missiles, in particular, resembles the type of war both Koreas envision for themselves: a deep strike contest. To this end, both have recently begun developing low-cost, long-range attack drones, with some systems slated to be operational in the near term.

Long-range artillery, ballistic missiles, and nuclear weapons have, so far, shaped each side’s view of the military balance and whether deterrence holds on the peninsula. Armed drones will soon enter the picture.

These drones will exacerbate the South Korean military’s existing gaps in surveilling the North. Pyongyang’s growing missile and nuclear arsenal and diversified launch platforms have made the problem acute. With cheap attack drones, North Korea’s ability to disperse, conceal, and employ offensive firepower will further outpace South Korea’s capacity to destroy it.

This trend is at odds with the Lee administration’s ambitious timeline for gaining wartime operational control from the United States. South Korean forces will need additional capabilities to meet the qualitative conditions previously established by the two allies.

Drones on the Korean Peninsula

Long-range drones – unarmed aerial vehicles with operational range far beyond the forward edge of battle along the armistice line – have been a feature of the inter-Korean military competition for the past two decades. The first known operational use was in 2010 when a North Korean reconnaissance drone was spotted during the Yonpyeong Island shelling. Since then, periodic drone incursions have been a feature of the inter-Korean low-intensity skirmishes.

In 2014, South Korea recovered the wreckage of three North Korean drones less than 50 miles from the border. In December 2022, five North Korean drones overflew Seoul, including the presidential office, and returned North. In response, then-President Yoon Suk-yeol floated the idea of South Korean forces conducting reciprocal drone incursions into North Korea. North Korea claimed South Korean drones overflew Pyongyang in October 2024. While officially denied, public analysis of North Korean-released images visually matched developmental South Korean reconnaissance systems.

Rudimentary platforms – small, fixed-wing, turboprop, and unarmed – have featured in these largely symbolic aerial incursions so far, alongside unpowered balloons. There is no evidence that either side has employed armed drones in cross-border operations. Drones that had been operationally used on the peninsula, however, represent only a small subset of a broader inventory that includes systems with greater range and capability.

North Korea has been importing Chinese and Soviet drones and has been developing indigenous models for reconnaissance missions since the 1980s. In 2023, North Korea unveiled a high-altitude, long-endurance (HALE) reconnaissance drone and a medium-altitude, long-endurance (MALE) multi-role drone. Both are qualitatively different from its existing unmanned aircraft – the latter, for example, is capable of firing a missile – though limited numbers are in the inventory.

For South Korea, abortive development efforts in the late Cold War resumed in the 1990s with a focus on the tactical surveillance drones supporting the Army’s ground operations. Interest in long-range systems came in the late 2000s when the Agency for Defense Development (ADD) started developing a domestic MALE, KUS-FS, and the Republic of Korea Air Force procured Global Hawks from the United States. Four Global Hawks were delivered by 2020, and the KUS-FS is expected to enter service in 2027.

The wars in Ukraine and Iran have catalyzed the two Koreas’ interest in massed, cheap, and armed long-range drones while they continue to invest in large, sophisticated unmanned systems. In 2024, Kim Jong Un ordered officials to “establish a mass-production system and begin full-scale operation” of “suicide attack drones.” Thousands of North Korean laborers, and possibly engineers, have also reportedly been sent to the Yelabuga factory in Russia producing copies of Iran’s Shahed one-way attack (OWA) drone.

For South Korea, the ADD is developing the KUS-LM – dubbed the “K-LUCAS” with reported range and payload figures comparable to the American OWA drone called LUCAS – with plans to deploy it before 2030. The system has started trials on land and sea.

Theories of Victory

These investments by both Koreas in long-range unmanned systems, for both strike and surveillance, will alter the terms of the inter-Korean military competition. In the past few decades, the main domain of the inter-Korean military competition has become a deep strike-centric contest. The ability to wage a strategic air campaign – one not directly connected to the ground fight – is now central to how each side assesses the balance. Both sides appear to believe loitering munitions fit into this air power paradigm.

North Korea has pursued missile and nuclear weapons technology to hold at risk its neighbor and its ally, the United States, with long-range fires. South Korea’s Ministry of National Defense assessed that, in a contingency, North Korea plans a surprise massive firepower attack to create favorable conditions and force a rapid end to the war. Even absent an offensive intent, the threat of catastrophic damage from nuclear missiles and conventional munitions that bypass defenses creates a powerful deterrent intended to prevent attack and ensure regime survival.

Under Kim Jong Un’s rule, North Korea has expanded its missile force to deliver both conventional and nuclear warheads deep into South Korea and, increasingly, beyond the peninsula. The nuclear arsenal, too, has increased both numerically and in centrality to North Korea’s security policy. The KPA Ground Force also operates thousands of artillery pieces – with sufficient range to reach Seoul – out of hardened sites concentrated south of the Pyongyang-Wonsan line.

North Korea appears to see drones as a complementary element of its deep strike strategy, enabled by mass, concealment, and dispersal. Indeed, Kim Jong Un noted three attributes that make OWA drones a needed investment for the Korean People’s Army: low production cost, simple manufacturing process, and ease of integration into existing firepower. Drone salvos launched in conjunction with ballistic and cruise missiles could overwhelm South Korea’s air and missile defenses. Their relatively low cost also reduces the economic burden of procurement on North Korea’s constrained economy.

In response to a nuclear-armed adversary and fear of abandonment from its ally, South Korea has pursued a counterforce “Three Axis system” to serve as a non-nuclear deterrent. This idea has seen iterative conceptual updates over the past decade. Today, the approach rests on a three-pronged framework that combines preemptive strikes on North Korean nuclear and missile facilities (“Kill Chain”), multi-layered missile defense (Air Force-operated “Korea Air and Missile Defense” against ballistic missiles and the Army’s in-development “Low-Altitude Missile Defense” against artillery and short-range rockets), and overwhelming retaliatory firepower against military and leadership targets (“Korea Massive Punishment and Retaliation”).

Efforts in the past five years have sought to integrate drones into the strategy. The Yoon administration established the Drone Operations Command in September 2023 with an explicit mission to develop an offensive concept of operations – before that, South Korea’s military had only used drones for reconnaissance and surveillance. Despite initial criticism of the command as redundant, and its subsequent disestablishment for its implication in Yoon’s 2024 self-coup attempt, the South Korean defense community appears to acknowledge the need for this function. The mission continues in the Defense Drone headquarters, the recently formed successor body that focuses on force development, manning, and equipping – albeit shedding any operational role to the services.

South Korea’s Surveillance Problems

Deterrence on the peninsula holds today as both sides possess long-range strike assets that impose what, for now, are unacceptable risks and costs if the shooting starts. While ground forces remain important in both Koreas’ force structures, the main arena of the inter-Korean competition today lies in deep strike. The drone incursions in the past decade and a half introduced an additional low-intensity element to this competition. The development and eventual deployment of armed drones will create new requirements for South Korea to operationalize its Three Axis strategy and for the United States to defend its treaty ally.

South Korea’s limited intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) capacity stands out as a glaring vulnerability in anticipating this future. All three “axes” of its strategy depend on a near-perfect and near-persistent intelligence picture over North Korea, to monitor leadership movements, locate concealed facilities, track mobile missile launchers and submarines, identify incoming missiles – and now, detect drone launch sites and their launches. This is a tall order. South Korea’s ISR capabilities have long been identified as a weakness, as it historically has relied on U.S. capabilities.

ISR drones and additional ISR satellites are intended to supplement existing gaps to operationalize the Three Axis strategy, but even with systems expected to come online in the next five years, mobile targets will remain difficult to find, fix, and track. South Korea’s space-based ISR layer, in development since 2023, leaves roughly 2-hour windows between observation opportunities over potential launch sites. The South Korean Army’s Low Altitude Missile Defense, expected to come online in 2029, was designed to counter artillery threats and may be constrained by insufficient interceptors and sensor networks against drone salvos.

Thus, in the near to medium term, North Korea’s ability to disperse, conceal, and employ its drones, missiles, and nuclear weapons will outpace South Korea’s capacity to destroy them. In fact, North Korea’s rapid operationalization of OWA drones may require greater dedication of U.S. ISR assets to the peninsula.

The added challenge to South Korea’s defense strategy thus poses questions about the Lee administration’s ambitious push for wartime operational control transfer by the end of his term in 2030. The proposed change to the command structure of U.S. and South Korean forces has been tied to improvements in South Korea’s capabilities to lead the Combined Forces Command, including the capacity to operate its own ISR assets to meet operational requirements. The Lee administration has insisted on “no additional conditions” being placed on the transfer requirements. Yet, the deteriorating military balance in this domain will necessitate additional capability to meet the established qualitative conditions for making major changes to the Combined Force.

The author appreciates feedback from colleagues at the Center for Strategic and International Studies – Pat Bazylczyk, Mark Cancian, Emma Gargiulo, and Andy Lim – and the 2026 cohort of the National Committee on American Foreign Policy Korea fellowship.

title: Ecological Imbalance Is Driving Bear Encounters in Mongolia
description: As of early October, the Mongolian authorities have received 754 calls reporting bear sightings in various provinces and towns.
text:
In recent months, Mongolia has experienced rare bear sightings in its northern provinces. Local authorities have so far been successful in capturing the bears alive and placing the animals back into their natural habitat. The sudden movement of such a large number of bears indicates a deeper ecological imbalance not only in Mongolia but also Russia and Japan.

As of early October, the Mongolian authorities have received 754 calls reporting bear sightings in various provinces and towns. Solo bears, bears with cubs, and lost cubs have been sighted. More alarmingly, bears have encountered nomadic herders, killing one person and injuring several others. People from remote towns and herding communities have reported attacks on livestock. Most of these bears encounters have been reported in Khuvgsul, Bulgan, Darkhan-Uul, and Tuv provinces – all Mongolia’s northern provinces with robust habitat for bears, wolves, elk, deer, and wild boars.

The sudden surge and the possible migration of bears clearly demonstrate the changing environment in their natural habitat. Khuvsgul, Bulgan, and Darkhan Uul provinces are 51 percent forest and considered a perfect habitat for bears. Mongolia’s boreal forests, known as taiga, offer cedar and pine nuts, types of berries, and water access for bears. In the fall, particularly in the months of August, September, and October, bears forage throughout the taiga with their cubs in preparation for hibernation.

The increased movement of these bear populations points to several issues in Mongolia’s ecological system. One of the speculated causes is a shortage of food. Mongolia’s extreme weather fluctuations, including shorter summers with amplified heatwaves, can impact vegetation and dry out grasslands. Particularly in Khuvsgul and Bulgan, given the short summer, there is a risk of shortage of berries and nuts.

In addition, Khuvsgul and Selenge provinces hold one of Mongolia’s critical river basins, which is crucial to the forestry and its natural habitat. One of the remaining questions concerning bear movements is whether these river basins and other water sources are experiencing a fish shortage, caused by climate change and mining activities.

Given the pristine nature of Northern Mongolia, these provinces are subject to strict environmental scrutiny and protection. Still, mining does occur. Bulgan Province, in particular, is known for its extractive industries, including gold and polymetallic mining (although in comparison to other notable extractive sites, the scale of mining in Bulgan is relatively moderate).

According to the World Resources Institute, Mongolia’s gold rush has become one of the leading sources of water contamination. Gold extraction sites particularly are a major issue for the local environment. “Lead, arsenic and other toxic chemicals released during gold extraction processes have leached into Mongolia’s groundwater and flowed untreated into rivers,” the WRI found.

Thus Mongolia’s bear sightings may be related to the country’s mining activities, along with extreme weather aggravated by climate change-caused food shortages. In response, the government and conservation groups are taking a humane approach. Local authorities and the population continue to capture bears and place them back into the wild.

In comparison, Russia and Japan, both experiencing a similar bear issue, are handling it very differently.

In Russia’s Far East, in the Siberian forests, the bear population thrives. This October, local authorities in Siberia (Krasnoyarsk), Tuva, and Buryatia reported a surge of bears entering local towns and villages. In Buryatia, the local authority has deployed 24 specialized teams to kill bears. With Russian authorities allowing an “open season,” bear killings will likely increase.

In 2025, the Environmental Ministry of Japan reported a historic surge in bear sightings and attacks, during which more than 14,600 bears were killed. The ministry believed that “climate change and poor tree-nut harvests have reduced natural food supplies in the mountains.” The ministry also highlighted that around 12,000 brown bears in Hokkaido and Asiatic black bears elsewhere have expanded their roaming range.

While Northeast Asia faces a shared ecological challenge in conserving bear populations and managing their movements, Mongolia, Russia, and Japan have adopted vastly different approaches. Mongolia emphasizes strict legal protections and non-lethal management whereas Russia and Japan both have implemented aggressive population control methods.

According to Rebecca Watters, founder and director of the Mongolian Wolverine Project and a biologist, bears are attracted to any kind of predictable food source. Once they associate people with food – in the form of garbage, livestock, gardens, birdfeeders, etc. – they will continue to seek out human settlements.

In Mongolia’s case specifically, she added, “I wonder too whether some of the increase in sightings and conflict is due to population shifts, in both people and the bears. Paradoxically, some of these issues might also be related to conservation successes and more bears cubs surviving.”

title: Exercise Tarang Shakti: A Mirror to India’s Multipronged Engagements
description: The exercise reflects two trends: the Indian military’s deepening interoperability with key partner nations, and India’s multi-vector foreign policy.
text:
“The defense relationships of the future will be about technology and trust, not just about platforms,” India’s Defense Minister Rajnath Singh said at an event and demonstration in Jodhpur on October 10 as the multilateral Exercise Tarang Shakti neared its end. A fly-past after that featured an arrow-shaped formation that included the Indian Air Force Su-30MKI (Russian origin) at the center, flanked on one side by a U.S. F-35 and an Indian Light Combat Aircraft (LCA), and on the other side by a French Rafale and an F-16 of the United Arab Emirates Air Force. This was an impressive formation; the technology and firepower they represented cannot be easily beaten.

An American fifth-generation fighter flying alongside a Russian-origin jet bears testimony to India’s multi-pronged foreign policy and military engagements.

Beyond Tarang Shakti, some bilateral exercises have culminated while others are lined up, showcasing the busy calendar of India’s military diplomacy and military-to-military engagements. For instance, at Vladivostok in Russia, the Indian and Russian Navies are holding their annual Indra exercise from October 13 to 18.

Together, these reflect two trends: one is the Indian military’s deepening interoperability across land, sea and air with key partner nations and like-minded countries, and the other is India’s multi-vectored foreign policy in line with its much-espoused strategic autonomy.

Thunder in the Skies

A biennial exercise, Tarang Shakti is now in its second edition. It was themed “Power in Partnership” and was held at Jodhpur near India’s western borders. It commenced on September 26 and ended on October 12. It brought together the Indian Air Force (IAF) and seven other countries – Australia, Bangladesh, France, Germany, Sri Lanka, the UAE, and the U.S. – who deployed their aerial assets. Thirty-two other nations participated as observers.

The real metric of an exercise’s utility is not what the host nation deploys but what partner nations bring in, reflective of the value they see from it. The U.S. fifth-generation F-35 jets exercised over Indian skies for the first time, operating alongside the entire gamut of IAF fighters – the LCA, Rafale, SU-30MKI, Mirage 2000s, MiG-29s, Jaguars, French Rafales and the UAE’s F-16s. These were completed by A-400M and C-130/ C-130J transport aircraft, aerial refueling tankers, G-6000 and other support platforms. An IAF official, citing a post-exercise data brief, told The Diplomat that Tarang Shakti saw more than 800 sorties and 600 hours flown.

The U.S. Pacific Air Forces deployed six F-35A Lightning IIs and one KC-135R Stratotanker along with over 200 personnel. Speaking at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum, U.S. Ambassador in India Sergio Gor remarked that their F-35s do not go all over the world and termed their presence at Tarang Shakti as “another example of trust” between the two countries. France, a resident Indian Ocean power, fielded four Rafales, three A330 Phoenix aerial refuellers, two A400M transport aircraft and 300 personnel. This was part of its larger Pegase26 mission that set out on September 8, traveling across the Arctic, Indo-Pacific, Middle East and North Africa. Over 40 days across nine destinations and covering over 40,000 miles, the mission demonstrates its capacity for long-range deployment, sustenance and adaptability.

Exercises typically involve subject matter exchanges, and India, as the host nation, utilized this to brief visitors on the outcomes of Operation Sindoor of May 2025, which has generated significant operational lessons for military planners. Encapsulating this, Exercise Director Air Vice Marshal Raj Thakur noted that Operation Sindoor was one of the remarkable operations carried out by India, and there was a lot of interest in knowing about it. “And that’s why in one of the subject matter expert exchanges, we briefed them about what exactly has happened in Operation Sindoor and our part of the story, and that was very well received,” Thakur said.

Back-to-back Engagements

India has had a very busy diplo-military calendar in recent years. These were quite often simultaneous engagements with nations that are warring or adversaries. To appreciate the busy calendar and the diversity of engagements by the Indian military, it is worth looking at some of the notable engagements since July.

The India-U.S. bilateral Army exercise Yudh Abhyas was conducted from September 15 to 27. It saw 600 personnel from each side exercise at a high-altitude area at Auli in Uttarakhand, followed by long-range firepower drills, including U.S. HIMARS, Indian Pinaka rocket systems, and counter-drone systems in action, at Mahajan Field Firing Range in Rajasthan. Yudh Abhyas began in 2004 as a platoon-level exercise focused on peacekeeping operations and has since significantly expanded in scope and complexity. This is the case with all other India-U.S. military exercises: Cope India, the bilateral air exercise, or Exercise Malabar, which began as a bilateral naval exercise, have now become quadrilateral exercises featuring submarines and aircraft carriers practicing highly complex scenarios.

In addition to Yudh Abhyas, the Indian Army held bilateral wargames with Thailand (Maitree-XV), Mongolia (Nomadic Elephant), Kazakhstan (KAZIND) and UAE (Mountain Guardian), whether incoming or outgoing, with the last one set to conclude on October 18.

The Indian Navy has been the busiest with at least eight engagements. In addition to Indra, a trilateral exercise between India, Brazil and South Africa (Exercise IBSAMAR) is currently underway off South Africa. The Quad grouping, which includes India, Australia, Japan and the U.S., conducted a Tabletop Exercise on September 3 and 4 hosted by Japan to advance the Quad Indo-Pacific Logistics Network. In end-September, Quad Coast Guards carried out the second joint sail under the QUAD‑at‑Sea Ship Observer Mission. Indian Coast Guard Ship Shaunak sailed from Chennai on September 25 for Perth in Australia with six sea riders—two officers each from India and Japan, and one officer each from Australia and the U.S. embarked.

On October 8, the Indian Coast Guard conducted the 12th national Maritime Search and Rescue Exercise (SAREX-2026) off the coast of Odisha, which in addition to all Indian stakeholders, had 32 observers from 30 countries. It underscores the extent of deepening engagement, especially in the maritime domain, which has implications far and wide.

The IAF held two bilateral exercises with Japan (Veer Guardian) and Malaysia (Udara Shakti). More importantly, it joined the multilateral exercise Pitch Black hosted by the Royal Australian Air Force from July 7 to August 7.

Operationalizing Interoperability

The oft-repeated “interoperability” is more than just flying together in a fly past. It is extremely complex, necessitating understanding tactics, techniques, procedures, and cultural practices to seamlessly integrate the diverse range of equipment while also preserving one’s sensitive operational aspects. For instance, while the U.S. F-35s took part in war games, they were kept away from any prying eyes, even of the participating nations, highlighting the sensitivity of its most advanced technology. This prompted Air Chief Marshal Amar Preet Singh to take a friendly jibe at Gen. Kevin Schneider, the U.S. Pacific Air Forces Commander. At a press conference on October 10, the IAF chief pointed out: “Your people don’t even let us go near the aircraft, and you talk about selling it to us.”

While deepening engagements point to the evolving balancing and hedging in the Indo-Pacific, exercises are a way to prepare for evolving threats rather than be directed at anyone. This was underscored by Air Chief Singh at a press conference along with other chiefs and heads of participating forces. As far as the Indo-Pacific is concerned, the exercise was not meant to be projecting anything in any region, Singh stressed.

What do these exercises translate to in real time? As Gen. Schneider succinctly put it, “We don’t know what the security situation holds or what the future holds. Some of us may be called to do humanitarian assistance disaster relief, or there may be other challenges that we face. But when we come together, we don’t do it cold; we do it on a foundation of teamwork that is established at Tarang Shakti, Pitch Black, Red Flag Alaska, or the myriad of other exercises that take place throughout the Indo-Pacific region.”

Both Exercise Tarang Shakti and Exercise Yudh Abhyas were barometers of the extent of interoperability that has been achieved over the years by India with its key strategic partners.

The aim of Tarang Shakti was to enhance mutual understanding of tactical air power application, strengthen interoperability among participating Air Forces, and foster seamless multinational cooperation through integrated air operations, joint administration, logistics support, and maintenance coordination, a handout given at the event said. From the feedback and observations of participants, the exercise seems to have achieved what it set out to do.

It only reiterates India’s continuing expansion of military-to-military engagements in various formats and across geographies in line with its strategic objectives and in turn, the outcomes shaping the objectives.

title: Expanding the Military Footprint: China’s New Air Base in Laos
description: Establishment of the Laotian base follows a pattern in China’s growing external military presence and access.
text:
As China’s power and self-confidence grows, it’s becoming much more active in projecting that power by establishing military bases abroad. The latest is at Ban Keun Airport near Vientiane, where China has established a joint support and training facility with Laos, according to a September announcement by the Ministry of National Defense in Beijing.

It is the first overseas military facility that China has openly acknowledged, unlike the ones in Djibouti and Cambodia. This has several implications for the region.

But first, the base itself. Satellite imagery procured and analyzed by CNN shows a 2,000-meter-long runway, taxiway, and parking apron for 22 aircraft. CNN also reports rapid construction at the site. Other media reports mention that satellite photos show eight aircraft, likely Chinese-Pakistani Hongdu JL-8 training and light attack jets (also called K-8s), and more than two dozen support vehicles. Laos is known to own this type of aircraft, but fewer than the eight seen at the facility. Laos could have bought more, or the extras may be Chinese.

China has said that the facility is strictly for training Lao air force pilots, “enhancing practical military cooperation,” and “promoting regional peace and stability.” This sounds reasonable enough, but it conflicts with China’s own previous positions on foreign military facilities. It has been a vocal critic of the global U.S. military presence.

Establishment of the Laotian base follows a pattern in China’s growing external military presence and access. China established its first overseas military facility in Djibouti in 2017, maintaining then and now that it is merely a logistical facility. This is still its most distant foreign military base, sitting astride the crucial waters overlooking the Bab al-Mandab strait leading to the Red Sea.

Closer to home, a Washington Post story in 2022 revealed that China was upgrading the Cambodian Ream Naval Base, with the Chinese military being given “exclusive use” of parts of it. China and Cambodia initially denied the report, but last year they formally inaugurated the facility. Soon warships from both countries visited it, conducting joint military drills. Though the base is not very far from China’s own territory, it’s on the strategically crucial Gulf of Thailand and thereby strengthens China’s position in the Indo-Pacific and particularly in the South China Sea.

With the Ream Naval Base in Cambodia and Ban Keun Air Facility in Laos, China now has both naval and aviation logistics hubs in the area.

There are at least four implications from the establishment of the base in Laos, both for neighbors such as Vietnam and the whole region.

First, sitting to the west of Vietnam, it gives China one more pressure point on that country. Vietnam already has a complicated relationship with China, with close economic ties but also significant territorial disputes.

Second, it adds an air power dimension to China’s foreign base activity. The two foreign bases that China previously built were both naval ones. The latest base at Ban Keun provides China’s air force with an air power footing in a strategically sensitive region. China can be expected to later extend the runway to support Chinese surveillance aircraft or bombers. Though Laos is land-locked, its long and narrow geography could provide China with an excellent site for monitoring activity across Southeast Asia.

Third, this represents a new type of military basing activity. For China, what matters is assured access. By packaging access as joint training facilities or disaster relief and humanitarian support hubs, Beijing secures a more lasting presence while avoiding the diplomatic and political cost of building traditional military bases. As far as China is concerned, it has created pretty much the same strategic effect without investing in a dedicated Western-style base of its own. Also unlike Western bases, China’s decision to act on Ban Keun, as ASPI senior analyst Rachel Vandenbrink told Reuters, was “more about a target of opportunity than filling an obvious operational need.”

Finally, the ratcheting up of military pressure increasingly strains Southeast Asia’s traditional strategy of hedging, in which countries of the region integrate with China’s manufacturing strength while balancing it with U.S. military power. Regional powers will need to consider how long they can hedge when Chinese military power looms ever larger over them.

This article was originally published in ASPI’s The Strategist.
