title: Face-Offs at India-China Border Are Continuing at Multiple Points, ITBP Chief Confirms
description: Since June, civil society groups and local media warned of PLA encroachments into Arunachal Pradesh. Hitherto, Delhi’s response was to deny and dismiss their claims.
text:
Claims by civil society groups and media in India’s northeastern state of Arunachal Pradesh that Chinese troops have been crossing into Indian territory, which the Narendra Modi government has repeatedly denied, were confirmed by a top Indian official last week.

At an event in Alwar, Rajasthan, on October 22, Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) Director General Shatrujeet Kapur said that face-offs are happening between Indian and Chinese forces “at several locations in Arunachal and it still continues.”

Kapur’s remarks on Thursday about the face-offs are hardly a revelation. Civil society groups and media in the northeast Indian state of Arunachal Pradesh, which borders China, have been drawing attention to the fragile, even alarming situation along the frontier since June-July.

In a letter dated June 26, 2026, to the deputy commissioner of Upper Subansiri, the Nah Welfare Society (NWS) said that the Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA) had occupied Indian territory in and around Taksing, including Oying in the Asaphila area, Paniar in the Chujarta area, Marpan in Marnafe, Portrang Lake, and Tingdingtang. In addition to establishing a military camp in the area, the PLA has also built roads, bridges, and military camps in several locations traditionally used by local communities for grazing, hunting, and collecting forest produce. A Taksing-based tribal organization, the NWS expressed “deep grief” over the PLA’s gradual occupation of ancestral lands, which it said, has intensified since 2020.

Soon after the contents of the NWS’ memorandum became public, the Indian Army categorically dismissed the “reports” as “incorrect and without any basis.” Then came videos claiming the PLA had advanced 50-60 km into Indian territory. The Indian government’s Press Information Bureau Fact Check unit dismissed the reports as ” fake;” the videos did not pertain to the India-China border, it said. This was followed by reports and videos of “skirmishes” in the Taksing Circle on July 25-26. The “confrontation” reportedly “continued for nearly a week before the situation was brought under control following intervention by senior commanders from both sides.” However, Arunachal Pradesh’s Home Minister Mama Natung dismissed the reports of Chinese encroachment as “just rumors.”

Now, for the first time, there is official confirmation of confrontations at multiple locations along the India-China border in Arunachal Pradesh. And this confirmation has come from the head of the ITBP, the force that guards the India-China border.

The entire India-China border is disputed. The two countries not only have differing perceptions of where the Line of Actual Control, the de facto border, runs, but they also claim swathes of territory under the other’s control. China claims 90,000 sq km of territory that roughly coincides with Arunachal Pradesh. India claims 38,000 sq km of territory in Aksai Chin that China occupied during the 1962 border war, and another 5,300 sq km in the Shaksgam Valley of Jammu and Kashmir that Pakistan occupied in 1947-48 and gifted to China in 1963.

Besides the war in 1962, which China won, the two sides have engaged in skirmishes and standoffs several times over the decades, including at Samdurong Chu in Arunachal in 1986-87, at the Doklam trijunction of China, India and Bhutan in 2017, and at Galwan in Ladakh in June 2020, which resulted in the death of 20 Indian soldiers and four Chinese soldiers.

Interestingly, China’s interest in Arunachal Pradesh has waxed and waned over time. After occupying Arunachal, then known as the North East Frontier Agency, for several weeks during the 1962 war, the PLA pulled out. Indeed, it did not seem interested in pressing any claims here, and under a swap proposal, was willing to give up claims in the eastern sector, in return for India accepting its control over Aksai Chin in the western sector.

It was only from the mid-1980s that China began reasserting claims over what it calls “Zangnan” or “South Tibet,” at bilateral talks, through military intrusions, by pushing back Indian patrol teams, objecting to visits of Indian leaders to Arunachal Pradesh, refusing to issue visas to Indian passport holders from the state on the argument that they are not Indian, and announcing “standardized” or Chinese names for places and geographical features in the state. According to a 2025 Pentagon report, Arunachal Pradesh is among China’s “core interests.”

In recent months, India and China have engaged in a slew of talks. On August 6, the 36th meeting of the Working Mechanism for Consultation and Coordination on India-China Border Affairs was held in New Delhi. Then on August 26, National Security Adviser Ajit Doval met with China’s Foreign Minister Wang Yi at the 25th round of Special Representatives’ talks on the Boundary Question in Beijing. On September 6, the Indian Army and the PLA held their first Corps Commander-level meeting in the Eastern Sector at the Vacha-Damai Border Personnel Meeting Point in Arunachal Pradesh.

India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping shook hands and chatted at the SCO Summit at Bishkek on August 31, and held a meeting on the sidelines of the BRICS Summit in Delhi on September 12.

If the India-China face-offs are continuing, as the ITBP Director General Kapur said they are, it is clear the talks have had little impact in deterring the PLA.

One obvious reason is that Prime Minister Modi’s China strategy is guided more by his interest in beefing up his image among his supporters than taking a strong position against China. His government has repeatedly denied PLA encroachment into Indian controlled territory. “Neither is anyone inside our territory nor is any of our post captured,” Modi grandly declared at an all-party meeting days after the Galwan clashes. The recent spate of denials by the government over PLA’s encroachments in Arunachal is part of the same short-sighted vision. It has weakened India’s hand at talks.

Even more baffling is the Modi government’s withdrawal of ITBP companies from the border. Since June-July, massive anti-government protests in the capital have rattled the Modi government. In response, it has pulled out ITBP personnel from the India-China border and redeployed them in Delhi at a time when the border situation is volatile. Clearly, using the ITBP to crush unarmed civilian protestors in Delhi is more important to Modi than using the force to push back PLA advances at the Arunachal border.

Under the BJP government, almost every Indian state/union territory bordering China is roiled in unrest. Arunachal’s civil society has strongly opposed a mega dam being constructed in the state’s Upper Siang district. The state’s inept handling of public concerns raised over displacement, environmental impact, and loss of livelihoods, and its use of force to deal with protests have resulted in the escalation of the conflict. On October 23, Upper Siang witnessed unprecedented scenes of violence.

Already, Arunachalis are upset with the government for not acting on their apprehensions over PLA encroachment into their traditional lands and hunting grounds. Delhi’s use of the iron fist now to put down their protests will fuel further anger. This will only add to India’s troubles in a sensitive border region.

title: Farewell to Russia: The View From Kazakhstan
description: Karaganda and its environs are home to some of the largest-scale coal-mining on the planet. And once, the home to an immense gulag.
text:
In “Farewell to Russia: A Journey Through the Former USSR” journalist Joe Luc Barnes travels across the 15 states that once comprised the Soviet Union. In the excerpt below, Barnes stops off in Karaganda, the heart of Kazakh coal country and once the site of a notorious gulag.

***

The steppe stretches in all directions under the massive sky. There are no trees, no hills, no natural points of interest of any sort, save for a herd of horses grazing by the roadside. The openness of Central Asia makes itself felt immediately. Kazakhstan alone spans an area larger than Western Europe.

But these northern plains are not featureless. Factories dot the landscape, their chimneys raised like middle fingers in defiance of the mighty heavens. Thin trails of smoke seep from them and a vast network of pylons and railway tracks sprawl from their feet. Karaganda and its environs are home to some of the largest-scale coal-mining on the planet. At the time of my visit, much of this industrial landscape belonged to steel giant ArcelorMittal.

“We don’t like them here. They don’t care about employees; they pay us nothing, and don’t give a shit about our safety,” my taxi driver tells me.

“Do you work down the mines?”

“Used to. I’m an invalid now; was forced to retire. My lungs can’t take it any more.”

“Would you like to be back down there?”

“Of course!” he says, displaying that gritty courage you often get in mining communities, where a hard day’s graft is the highest form of honor.

As it happens, this former miner is taking me to one of the predecessors of ArcelorMittal – another institution that has a rather patchy record when it comes to worker rights.

Around a century ago, Karaganda didn’t really exist. Coal had been discovered here in the late 19th century, but the nascent mines were soon abandoned – for some reason it proved difficult to persuade people to leave their families behind and toil down the pit in the middle of the frigid steppe. Besides, there were too few houses and nowhere near enough food to supply a large-scale mining settlement. But all that changed in February 1927, when Article 58 of the Russian penal code was brought into force.

Article 58 justified the arrest of those suspected of counter-revolutionary activity. The law cast a wide net as the precise meaning of “counter-revolutionary activity” was left deliberately vague, leaving Alexander Solzhenitsyn to ask: “Who among us has not experienced its all-encompassing embrace? In all truth, there is no step, thought, action, or lack of action under the heavens which could not be punished by the heavy hand of Article 58.”

People may not have fancied moving to the steppe, but fortunately for economic planners the Soviet justice system had suddenly created a large pool of laborers who had little choice in the matter.

Between 1921 and 1953, an estimated 18 million people passed through the Soviet forced-labor camp system known as the Gulag. The number of those who died is disputed, but is thought to be around 1.5 to 1.6 million. These numbers suggest that while the Gulag experience was unimaginably brutal, it was not necessarily the death sentence it is often portrayed as.

The Karaganda Camp (or Karlag) was created in 1930 to solve the problem of supplying the coal mines. It grew so rapidly that, by 1940, the area of the camp covered 6,500 square miles and was home to 65,000 prisoners. The Kazakh SSR became a repository for all manner of “undesirables,” from the political dissidents convicted under Article 58 to the so-called rich peasants, or kulaks, who were seen to be standing in the way of the equal distribution of land. They were joined by whole groups of “disloyal” ethnicities such as Poles and Chechens, Koreans and Crimean Tatars. In the early 1940s, half a million ethnic Germans, who had been living along the banks of Russia’s Volga River for almost two centuries, were also forced to relocate here.

Between them they played a large part in the building of Karaganda, which went from a small settlement in the late 1920s to a city of over 200,000 twenty years later. The camp headquarters, and now the site of the Karlag Museum, was in a small town called Dolinka, about 30 miles from Karaganda proper. There are few other visitors, so the young woman at the ticket office is happy to give me a free tour.

She takes me to the dormitories first. It’s draughty even at the height of summer. Rough woolen sheets filled with straw are draped over bunk beds whose supporting planks are so thin I doubt they would have supported any but the scrawniest of inmates – though I suppose the diets here were unlikely to have left anyone particularly rotund.

“Local people used to ride here on horseback and throw kurt over the walls of the camp for the prisoners to eat,” my guide tells me.

Kurt is a hard, extremely salty ball of dried cheese. It’s not particularly appetizing but lasts a long time and has been used for centuries as a protein-rich snack for those spending days in the saddle. The traditional Kazakh diet is heavy on these milky staples. Another is kumis – fermented horse’s milk – which I was made to sample on my first evening here. It wasn’t the tastiest of concoctions, but I imagine that both kurt and kumis would hit the spot if you’ve been forced to build a coal mine on Oliver Twist’s rations.

I also imagine that this story isn’t true – the idea of noble, empathetic Kazakh horsemen coming to the aid of the desperate, oppressed prisoner is, well, a stretch. However, there is well-documented evidence of large-scale black-market trade in food and rations in the Karlag, whose walls were more porous than other camps due to its size and proximity to Karaganda.

We come to the commandant’s study, set up as it would have been in the early 1950s: portrait of Stalin on the wall behind the desk and some heavy bookshelves, well stocked with the works of Lenin, Marx, and Engels. The only touch of personality is betrayed by an old gramophone.

“Concerts were organized on Sundays and Mondays,” she tells me. “Those were the days when the prisoners were tortured; the music drowned out the screams.”

The other rooms are dedicated to the fate of the Kazakhs – that is, the people who had lived here for centuries before these lands became an integral part of the Gulag.

In 1897, under the tsars, the land we now call Kazakhstan was 82 percent Kazakh. The early years of the 20th century saw the authorities encourage Slavic people to settle in the areas that had traditionally been inhabited by Kazakh nomads.

“Kazakhs lived at one with the steppe,” Klara, an IT worker who lived in Kazakhstan’s capital, Astana, had told me before my trip. As soon as she found out about my post-Soviet odyssey, she made it her mission to make her country my next destination.

“They traveled to where food and water was before moving on. This way, the land was allowed to recover in the meantime. The European arrivals began to change that, and the Soviets put it on fast-forward. They were obsessed with collectivizing people. The idea of being a nomad didn’t fit into their concept of a worker-led revolution. Maybe Marx skipped our role in his grand theory of history,” she said, giving me a wan smile.

The result of this crash-collectivization was famine. The room has exhibits on the famines of 1919–22 and 1932–3. Kazakhs suffered disproportionately as they lived on fertile land that could produce a lot of wheat. They were forced to abandon their nomadic lifestyle and produce food first for the Red Army, and then for Stalin’s five-year plans. Those who resisted were shot. Many fled to China or Mongolia. Many more starved.

In the Soviet census of 1926 the Kazakh population was 3.6 million; by 1939 this had dropped by a third to 2.3 million. By 1959 Kazakhs numbered a mere 30 percent of the population of the Kazakh SSR.

Along with the demographic assault came the attempts to destroy Kazakh identity. The room next door has a small exhibition dedicated to the entire class of Kazakh intellectuals who were exterminated in the purges of the late 1930s. Just as their way of life was destroyed and their people forced onto farms, their thinkers, authors, and anyone who might be able to articulate the uniqueness of the Kazakh identity were wiped out by NKVD bullets.

Klara had told me about the legend of the Mankurt.

“When a warrior was captured in battle, his head would be shaved by his captors and a piece of damp camel skin would be wrapped tightly around it. He would then be left, tied up in the desert sun, which would dry the camel skin and cause it to contract. His hair would also have no room to grow, so it would grow inwards, into his skull. The resulting pressure on the head would break the prisoner’s mind, causing him to lose all memory, all sense of self, all knowledge of his past and his family. Once broken, he became the perfect slave: the Mankurt, loyal only to his master.”

The story sounds like an ancient steppe legend, but it actually comes from “The Day Lasts More Than a Hundred Years,” a novel by the celebrated Kyrgyz writer Chingiz Aitmatov. The Mankurt became a powerful metaphor across Central Asia for a people stripped of their history and identity. That was precisely how Klara saw the Soviet experience.

“This is what the Soviets did to the Kazakh people, to all the people of Central Asia. They tried to destroy us so completely that we would not even recognize who we were,” said Klara.

title: For Uyghurs in Central Asia, US Diplomacy Could Be a Lifeline
description: By pressing Central Asian governments to protect Uyghurs and resist Beijing’s coercion, Secretary Rubio can demonstrate that America’s moral leadership still matters.
text:
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio will be leading a delegation of more than 200 American business leaders to Uzbekistan this coming weekend. With this visit, Rubio has an opportunity to give hope to Uyghurs worldwide by publicly raising their plight in Central Asia.

In 2019, then-Secretary of State Mike Pompeo raised the Uyghur issue publicly at a meeting with Central Asian foreign ministers, urging them not to send Uyghurs back to China. Pompeo pressed the issue again with Kazakh leaders during a 2020 visit. His words resonated deeply, and Uyghurs in Central Asia felt like they finally had an advocate. Rubio now has an opportunity to reaffirm and strengthen that message.

Central Asia is both a critical refuge and a dangerous crossroads for Uyghurs fleeing China’s genocide. More than 400,000 Uyghurs live in Central Asia – making up the vast majority of the Uyghur diaspora outside of East Turkestan. China’s transnational repression extends deep into the region. Central Asian governments face mounting pressure from Beijing to silence Uyghur activists, suppress Uyghur civil society, and deport refugees to China.

Amid these conditions, Uyghurs in Central Asia face suffocating uncertainty. Some who escaped China’s abuses are in hiding. Many Central Asian-born Uyghurs self-censor out of fear. They are pressured not only by Beijing, but also by Central Asian governments that worry about Chinese retaliation. When we speak privately with Kazakhs, Kyrgyz, Uzbeks, and others, we hear sympathy and support for Uyghur communities, but also fear of repercussions should they raise Uyghur human rights issues publicly. They fear not just provoking China, but angering their own governments.

As a result, Uyghurs in these countries often have no one to speak for them. In Central Asia, nearly every sizable ethnic minority group has a neighboring state that may intervene when their rights are violated – except the Uyghurs. Uyghurs have no government defending their rights, no state advocating for their safety. When Uyghur refugees escaped into Kazakhstan in the past, local Uyghurs who quietly offered food or shelter were themselves detained or threatened. This is what happens in a region where China’s shadow looms large and where silence has become a survival strategy.

Rubio has long been one of the most prominent American voices defending the Uyghur people. As a senator, he co-authored the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act, groundbreaking legislation that barred goods made with forced labor from entering the U.S. market. During his secretary of state confirmation hearing, he pledged to press Thailand not to deport at-risk Uyghur refugees. However, the U.S. failed to stop Thailand from deporting 40 Uyghurs to China in February 2025. These individuals disappeared and their fates remain unknown.

This upcoming trip to Central Asia gives Rubio a chance to show that the United States won’t countenance a repeat of that tragedy. With the right messaging, the trip can fortify China’s neighbors to stand firm against Beijing’s pressure to return Uyghurs to China. International law is clear: no one should be returned to a country where they face torture, detention, or other grave abuses. The principle of non-refoulement is not optional. Uyghur refugees who are returned to China face near-certain detention and abuse.

The trip should also highlight U.S. policy to work with other governments to resist the expanding apparatus of Chinese influence. The same companies who helped build the surveillance state in the Uyghur region have exported their technology to Central Asia. Governments in Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan, and Kazakhstan have adopted “smart city” surveillance networks with facial recognition cameras and data-monitoring tools that enable the tracking of Uyghurs. Beijing-backed hackers have used telecommunications networks to spy on Uyghurs in Kazakhstan. Under pressure from the CCP, the Kazakhstan government sentenced 19 Kazakh activists to prison for peacefully protesting the Chinese government’s policies in East Turkistan.

With Uyghur life under assault in our homeland, especially after the implementation of China’s “ethnic unity” law, diaspora communities in Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, and Turkmenistan have become vital guardians of our people’s history. They deserve the freedom to promote their culture, language, and traditions without fear.

The Uyghur people have not forgotten Rubio’s past advocacy. By pressing Central Asian governments to protect Uyghurs from deportation, resist Beijing’s coercion, and safeguard the cultural and human rights of Uyghur communities, Rubio can demonstrate that America’s moral leadership still matters.

A key objective of this visit must be to show that commitment endures – and that the United States will take concrete action to counter China’s malign influence in the region.

title: Former Philippine President Duterte Fit to Stand Trial, ICC Says
description: An independent panel of experts said that the 81-year-old has the capacity to understand the charges and the purpose and consequences of the trial proceedings.
text:
Judges at the International Criminal Court (ICC) have ruled ‌that former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte is fit to stand trial on charges linked to his violent “war on drugs.”

The ruling by Trial Chamber III, which was made on September 28 but only made public yesterday, was “based on the findings of an independent Panel of Experts as well as on submissions made by the parties and participants on these issues,” the ICC said in a statement.

“The Expert Panel unanimously found that the Accused has the capacity to understand the charges, understand the purpose and consequences of the proceedings, follow the course of the proceedings, including the nature and implications of entering a plea, understand the evidence, and instruct counsel in the preparation and conduct of his defense,” it said.

Duterte, 81, is set to go on trial on November 30, and faces three charges of crimes against humanity for extrajudicial killings carried out during the anti-drug campaign, a flagship policy of his administration between 2016 and 2022.

Duterte’s attorneys claimed last year that he was in frail health and that his condition was deteriorating in the ICC’s detention unit. In one filing in June, they argued that the ex-president’s illness and “advanced age” created “compelling humanitarian grounds” for judges to grant his interim release. In January, judges rejected the defense claims, arguing that Duterte “is able effectively to exercise his procedural rights and is therefore fit to take part in the pre-trial proceedings.”

The September 28 ruling comes in response to a separate petition, submitted in September 2025, in which Duterte’s lawyers claimed that he was unfit to stand trial due to “cognitive impairment in multiple domains.”

The former leader has been in the court’s custody since his arrest in the Philippines in March 2025. In April, the ICC’s Pre-Trial Chamber I confirmed the charges against Duterte and ordered the case to go to trial. The chamber’s judges concluded that “there are substantial grounds to believe that Mr. Duterte is responsible for the crimes against humanity of murder and attempted murder.” These crimes “were committed as part of a widespread and systematic attack against a civilian population on the territory of the Republic of the Philippines.”

Specifically, Duterte is charged with the murders of at least ⁠76 people and the attempted murder of two ​others. Nineteen of the alleged murders were carried out between 2013 and 2016, when Duterte was mayor of Davao City. The remainder were committed during the “war on drugs” campaign, which Duterte launched upon becoming president in 2016. The campaign resulted in a death toll of at least 6,000 – the official estimate of the Philippine police – but independent estimates run as high as 30,000.

However, during an in-person appearance at the ICC last month, Duterte was thin and haggard, suggesting that questions about his health and advanced age will continue to hang over his trial. With this in mind, Presiding Judge Joanna Korner at a status conference last month expressed concerns about the volume of evidence in the case against Duterte and the length of the prosecution case. She said the chamber was “very anxious” that the prosecution case should conclude “as swiftly as possible in the circumstances,” so that Duterte lives to see a verdict.

title: From Data Localization to Digital Openness: Uzbekistan’s Regulatory Shift
description: Uzbekistan courts tech companies to boost its economy by easing its once infamous data localization law.
text:
During a visit to New York in late September, the head of Uzbekistan’s presidential administration, Saida Mirziyoyeva, met with Google Vice President Karan Bhatia to discuss the possibility of launching YouTube monetization in Uzbekistan. Uzbekistan has been actively seeking to expand its partnership with global digital companies in line with the country’s growing digital economy. Tashkent even re-wrote the laws that once made it difficult for international technology platforms to operate in the country.

The 2021 amendment to Uzbekistan’s Law on Personal Data imposed a restriction on the storage and processing of Uzbek citizens’ data abroad, raising the question of how domestic regulation could accommodate services operating across borders. PayPal, Stripe, Netflix, Spotify, and Amazon Web Services refused to enter the Uzbek market while Apple Pay, Google Pay, and Google Cloud limited their functionality.

However, it soon became clear that the regulations introduced to protect personal data got in the way of generating money. Last year, the Center for Economic Research and Reforms (CERR) calculated Uzbekistan’s annual losses without YouTube monetization alone as $50 million annually. Mirziyoyeva’s efforts reflect the country’s wider attempt to re-attract global tech-companies by revising local regulations.

The Economic Cost of Data Sovereignty

In May 2021, Uzkomnazorat, Uzbekistan’s digital and telecommunications regulator, announced that VKontakte (Mail.ru Group), Twitter (Twitter Inc.), and WeChat (Tencent Inc.) were processing Uzbek citizens’ data abroad in violation of the data protection law. On July 2 of that year, Uzkomnazorat blocked access to those social media sites over alleged non-compliance with data-localization requirements.

“If the internet companies are planning to work in Uzbekistan, they have to observe the legislation of Uzbekistan,” noted Temur Akhmedov, then with the Institute for Strategic and Interregional Studies under the President of the Republic of Uzbekistan. In August 2022, just over a year later, Uzkomnazorat walked its enforcement decision back, removing Twitter, VKontakte, and WeChat from its “register of violators of the rights of personal data subjects.” The platforms were unblocked with no explanation given for the change.

By 2024, the data protection law’s cost for Uzbekistan’s economy became more apparent. As the government sought to integrate international payment systems like PayPal, AliPay, UniPay, Apple Pay, and Google Pay into the country’s banking system to attract more tourists, requirements to store citizens’ personal data locally emerged as a major obstacle.

During the negotiations with Apple and Google, the Central Bank of Uzbekistan noted that “in order to connect Visa and Mastercard cards issued by Uzbek banks to the Apple Pay and Google Pay systems, it is necessary to review some requirements of the current legislative documents, in particular, the Law of Uzbekistan ‘On Personal Data.’”

TBC Bank Group PLC’s representative Oliver Hughes, during a December 2024 presidential meeting with entrepreneurs, suggested allowing banks to store their data in the cloud both in Uzbekistan and offshore jurisdictions.

“We are talking about the personal data of citizens,” President Shavkat Mirziyoyev said. “This is a very serious matter. We have no right to make mistakes.” He emphasized the need for a carefully considered solution.

By 2025, the debate on data localization increasingly focused on its economic costs. In July 2025, Kotib AI Research, an AI company, estimated the potential cost of the localization law to Uzbekistan’s economy at $3.2 to $4.5 billion a year. The absence of PayPal alone had cost the country at least $1.8 billion in revenue over the previous five years. Uzbekistan is the only country in Central Asia without access to the service. PayPal’s global payment system is built on a single data infrastructure, and it does not keep each country’s data separate. It is reportedly technically inconsistent to store only Uzbek users’ data on a separate local server, as a single server cannot isolate the national user traffic.

International payment systems have further been affected by the data protection law, increasing the cost of operating digital services and limiting access to the international payment infrastructure. Limited access to international payment systems costs Uzbekistan around $500-800 million annually.

Apart from affecting the e-commerce and fintech sectors, the data localization rules also impact AI development. Since AI technologies rely on cloud servers, APIs, and international platforms, strict localization can increase compliance costs and complicate the entry of international service providers into the Uzbek market. Requiring data to be stored locally conflicts with the objective of the country’s AI Strategy 2030. The strategy aims to strengthen cooperation with international organizations and leading foreign technology companies and encourage the exchange of knowledge through joint research projects.

Article 27 of the Data Protection Law also complicates YouTube monetization. The platform cannot run its ads in the country, which limits the creative economy’s ability to generate jobs and revenue. In 2024, the estimated value of the advertising market in the country reached 2.1 trillion Uzbek soms ($164.3 million), with 29 percent coming from digital ads. According to the CERR, the introduction of YouTube monetization might increase Uzbekistan’s gross domestic product by 0.05-0.1 percent.

What began as an effort to protect citizens’ data was increasingly being questioned on economic and legal grounds. In July 2025, government representatives, lawyers, technology companies, and financial services firms met to further highlight concerns about Article 27 of the Personal Data Law. During the meeting, the experts discussed the ambiguity of the law’s language and the problems with its drafting. To the business experts, the law seemed unclear, which raised the question of the absence of a dedicated body for obtaining authoritative guidance. While some experts suggested the full repeal of the data localization clause, others argued that only government agencies and companies with more than 20 percent state ownership should follow the law’s rules, while those with commercial operations should have more flexible rules, provided user consent is in place for cross-border data transfer.

From Regulatory Uncertainty to Legislative Reform

In January 2026, on the third reading, the Legislative Chamber of the Oliy Majlis passed an amendment allowing certain data to be stored and processed abroad, provided that certain security requirements are met. In March, the proposed amendment to the law on personal data was officially adopted. Biometric and genetic data of individuals, along with data associated with telecommunications operators, must be stored domestically. Other categories of personal data may now be stored and processed abroad if the foreign state provides adequate protection.

In July 2026, the Cabinet of Ministers published a list of 49 countries where the personal and anonymized data of Uzbekistan’s citizens can be transferred automatically without informing the authorized body, these included the United States, Austria, and the United Kingdom.

The amendments to Uzbekistan’s data protection legislation mark a bold step toward the development of the country’s digital economy and integration with global digital services. Central Bank official Jamshid Usmanov said that the regulators, together with the national card payment networks Humo and Uzcard and commercial banks, had begun negotiations on launching Apple Pay and Google Pay following the legislative amendments.

The reforms have not yet brought in the major international services Tashkent hopes to attract. The legal changes reflect the country’s vision to align national legislation with global standards to strengthen its digital economy. While the state might not have abandoned the principle of data sovereignty, this development reflects a shift from rigid, sovereignty-based control to a more pragmatic, economically oriented regulatory model. That said, the liberalization of data localization might bring changes, but the success of the reform will depend on whether international technology and payment services believe Uzbekistan’s regulatory environment is predictable enough to risk entering the market.

title: From Military Base to Pax Silica: Clark and Capas in Philippine History
description: The history of U.S. involvement in the region demonstrates how domestic political dynamics can get entangled with regional and global geopolitics.
text:
New Clark City in the Philippines is in the news for being the site of the planned industrial hub of the Luzon Economic Corridor under the United States-led Pax Silica coalition. It is part of the Clark special economic zone and also covers the municipalities of Capas and Bamban in the province of Tarlac. The history of this place can help us better understand the political narratives in favor of and opposed to Pax Silica.

As the colonial ruler of the Philippines in the first half of the 20th century, the U.S. established an air base in Angeles in the province of Pampanga in the central part of Luzon, the country’s biggest island. After the end of World War II, the Philippines became an independent republic but the U.S. maintained the Clark base in Pampanga. It soon became the largest overseas U.S. military camp and a crucial hub during the Cold War era. In 1991, Clark was turned over to the Philippine government after the Senate rejection of the U.S. bases treaty. It was converted into a commercial area and designated a special economic zone to attract investments.

Today, Clark is a strategic business center since it is only less than a two-hour drive from the capital region of Metro Manila. Its international airport is already one of the country’s busiest aviation terminals.

Meanwhile, Capas is outside of Clark but it used to host Camp O’Donnell, an American military reservation. Thousands of prisoners during World War II died in a “death march” from Mariveles in Bataan to Capas. The communist-led New People’s Army was also established in this rural municipality in 1969.

Parts of Capas were incorporated into the New Clark City, which was originally envisioned as a government center and alternative capital to decongest Metro Manila. Sports facilities were built here when the country hosted the Southeast Asian Games in 2019. The stadium cauldron was reported to be overpriced, which implicated key allies of former President Rodrigo Duterte.

The pandemic affected the development of New Clark City and there has been no substantial discussion about the earlier plan to build a new capital in the area.

It generated attention again when it was named as a possible location of the Luzon Economic Corridor, a trilateral initiative unveiled in 2024 between the Philippines, the U.S., and Japan. This was confirmed last April after the Philippines officially joined the Pax Silica coalition.

In several social media posts, U.S. Undersecretary of State Jacob Helberg stated that the hub will be a “forward deployed industrial base” aimed at securing vital supply-chain inputs for American companies and its allies.

“Four thousand acres. Roughly one-third the size of Manhattan – the equivalent of everything from Times Square south to the very tip of the island,” Helberg added, referring to the land “gifted” by the Philippine government for the Pax Silica project.

After this, concerns were raised about the project’s potential grave impact on energy and water resources in the provinces of Pampanga and Tarlac. Farmers and indigenous peoples said their communities have been threatened with eviction to give way for the rise of the industrial hub.

In response, authorities said data centers will not be a component of the Pax Silica site, although these facilities will still rise in other parts of Luzon. They also assured local communities that consultations will be conducted, even if they initially denied that there were residents in the project site.

The Philippine government also assured the public that the country’s laws will prevail and no immunity will be granted to foreign investors in the hub. Nevertheless, concerns persist about the role of Pax Silica in supporting the military operations of the U.S. in the country and in the Asia-Pacific. What is clear is that it is seen as a counterpart to the China-led World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization.

Negotiations are ongoing and expected to continue for the next two years. A framework deal could be signed next month during the summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, and it could be the highlight of U.S. President Donald Trump’s visit to Manila.

Pax Silica is more than just a real estate transaction since it is touted as the next big opportunity for the Philippines to promote industrial development through mineral processing and technology transfer. The history of Clark and Capas is a reminder that local political dynamics can get entangled with regional and global geopolitical issues. The Pax Silica hub will rise on a land that hosted foreign bases, military operations that led to war atrocities, and protests that represented the Filipino people’s assertion of sovereignty.

As the Philippines under the government of Ferdinand Marcos Jr rushes forward with this bold initiative, the challenge is to address the criticism that this is another unfair deal that favors the country’s former colonizers rather than a development blueprint that prioritizes the national interest.
tag: Clark Air Base; Jacob Helberg; Luzon Economic Corridor; New Clark City; Pax Silica; Philippines and Pax Silica; U.S.-Philippines alliance; U.S.-Philippines relations

title: Gen Z Women Take to the Streets Over Spate of Rapes in India’s Capital
description: Urban Indian women are refusing to be cowed down or slut shamed or policed for their attire or forced to stay indoors in the evenings to ensure their safety.
text:
India is globally perceived as an unsafe country for women, with its capital, New Delhi, often described as the “rape capital” of the country. Statistics from the National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB) affirm that Delhi is “the most unsafe metropolitan city for women” and children in the country.

The NCRB’s Crime in India 2024 report substantiates this with statistics. In 2024 Delhi recorded 13,396 cases of crimes against women – the highest among all metro cities. The capital also has the dubious distinction of having the highest number (1,058) of reported rape cases among all metro cities.

While these statistics reveal that crimes against women in Delhi continue unabated, the greater irony is that India’s capital is the most policed city in the country with the highest police to people ratio. Delhi has 410 police personnel per million population, three times the national average of 153 personnel per million population.

And yet, Delhi’s streets remain unsafe.

These crime statistics made the headlines once again recently, after a spate of rapes and sexual assaults in the capital in August and September.

On September 21, a 17-year-old girl was gang-raped by three men posing as policemen in Astha Kunj Park, in posh South Delhi, barely 2 kms from the prestigious Lady Sri Ram (LSR) College for Women. Police nabbed the suspects and shot one of them. The incident sparked nationwide outrage, and panic and anger among the student community.

Prior to that, in early September, another 17-year-old was gang-raped and murdered in northwest Delhi’s Swaroop Nagar. The accused allegedly raped and stabbed her to death, and then dumped her body in a field. What makes these rape cases particularly distressing is that the victims were minors. In August, an 11-year-old and a 6-year-old were reportedly raped in separate incidents. The gang-rape of a 16-year-old in a moving bus on the Delhi-Noida border the same month brought back memories of the gruesome gang-rape of “Nirbhaya” 14 years ago in the capital. That victim subsequently died of her injuries. The incident, which led to massive protests in Delhi and other cities, resulted in major changes in sexual assault laws, including the introduction of the death penalty for rape.

These recent shocking incidents occurred amid massive youth and student protests by India’s Gen Z in Delhi and other Indian cities since July this year. The wave of protests started over leaked question papers for medical entrance exams. Protests led by the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) and leftist student organizations at Jantar Mantar in June-July forced Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign.

The success of the Jantar Mantar protests triggered realization among students that if they stand united, peaceful protests could yield unprecedented results. It has given them confidence to raise other pertinent issues like women’s safety.

So when a series of rapes occurred in the capital in August-September, youth anger erupted into widespread protests. On September 23, LSR students, triggered by the Astha Kunj rape and the failure of the authorities to ensure women’s safety, held a women-only solidarity march in Delhi University’s South Campus.

What distinguishes the recent protests against rape from earlier ones is the bold and unfiltered approach of the youth protestors. While some girl students held placards declaring, “Our body is our own,” others demanded freedom to step out at night without fear. Student protestors questioned the methods the authorities used to ensure women’s safety. The LSR college shifted to online classes to ensure the safety of their students, and police authorities mulled closing access to parks in the evening.

Instead of questioning patriarchy, they are restricting the movement of women, imposing late-night curfews for women living in hostels, and shifting classes online, the student protestors pointed out. “Smash the Patriarchy” was the theme of their protest march and they used catchy tunes, memes, and humor, making their anti-patriarchy slogans go viral.

The young women protesting against patriarchy are not intimidated by authority. They are demanding accountability from Home Minister Amit Shah while also lampooning him. Student wings of the opposition Congress and leftist parties organized protests against the failure of the Delhi Police to enforce the law. These protests were held amid ongoing protests in Delhi calling for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over election process irregularities.

Youth anger about women’s safety forced the Supreme Court to address the issue. Describing the recent spate of rapes as a clear “systematic failure” on the part of law enforcement authorities, a two-judge bench said that “accountability needs to be fixed.”

The judges stressed the need for a focused approach to prevent rapes and not on penalty. Merely installing CCTV was not enough, it pointed out, calling for the Delhi Police to monitor it around the clock. Better policing and patrolling would “instill fear in criminals,” it said, adding that public spaces, including parks and buses, should not ​become “high-risk” zones because of poor lighting and poor surveillance. Having strict laws was not enough, the court said, calling for effective implementation of laws to discourage serious offences like rape. The court will be taking stock of the progress made on its directives again next month.

Young women have been turning up in large numbers at all student protests in Delhi, asserting their place and demanding equal rights. So, when Delhi Police cracked down on women students and journalists protesting at Jantar Mantar, even molesting some of them, they marched to the nearest police station demanding a case be filed against the police officials. On October 4, Neha Bora, president of the All India Students’ Association (AISA), led a Citizens’ March from India Gate to Jantar Mantar, calling attention to the fact that “from streets to protests, women are not safe.”

It is evident that women in India, at least in its cities, are refusing to be cowed down or slut shamed or policed for their attire, or forced to stay indoors in the evenings, to ensure their safety. Rather, they are now vocal in their demands for a safer city and, more importantly, a change in patriarchal mindset within homes and in society at large. As 17-year-old Subhani told The Guardian, “My generation is not afraid to stand up and protest. We know that society has to change.” As she summed it up, “The days of women being silent is over.”
tag: India's Gen-Z; Indian Gen Z women; Protests against patriarchy; Rape in India; Rapes in Delhi; Sexual assault in India

title: Hindutva Goons Unleash Violence on Anti-Modi Protesters
description: Activists of the Hindu Raksha Dal, an outfit that furthers the Sangh Parivar’s agenda, were caught on camera beating students and youth participating in the Delhi protests.
text:
In recent weeks, New Delhi and other Indian cities have witnessed massive anti-government demonstrations and flash protests demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, over allegations of manipulating voter rolls to benefit the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

To prevent students and youth from gathering, the BJP government has used intimidation and force. In addition to arresting protesters, it has heavily barricaded roads, shut down metro stations, and deployed tens of thousands of police and paramilitary personnel, including the Delhi Police, Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF), Border Security Force, Indo-Tibetan Border Police, and Sashastra Seema Bal.

Several of these forces are normally deployed along India’s borders or in insurgency-wracked regions. For example, the CRPF companies deployed in the Delhi protests were shifted from former Maoist strongholds in Chhattisgarh and parts of militancy-hit Jammu and Kashmir. In Delhi, these paramilitary forces are being used against unarmed youth activists of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), the All India Students’ Association, and other leftist organizations.

What makes the government’s crackdown particularly reprehensible is that un-uniformed men are being allowed to assault the protesters. These are not isolated incidents; several young women and men have come forward with horrifying accounts of the violence they faced at the hands of these thugs.

Importantly, these men are unleashing violence in full view of the police. They have the blessings of the ruling dispensation.

Photographs and videos circulating on social media show men sporting saffron scarves — saffron is the color of the Sangh Parivar, a family of Hindutva-espousing organizations, of which the BJP is a part — shouting slogans in support of the Narendra Modi government, chasing young men and women, dragging them and beating them up mercilessly with sticks. They are brazen about their violence, describing their victims as “anti-national elements” who “deserve to be thrashed.”

“Delhi Police tum lath bajao, hum tumhare saath hain” (Delhi Police, you wield the baton, we are with you), they chant, egging on the police to beat the protesters.

The police and paramilitary personnel in whose presence the vigilantes acted took no action to force them off the streets. None of them was packed into police vans the way unarmed students were dragged and pushed into buses.

A video filmed during the crackdown on October 10 in central Delhi showed goons beating up young men and women, even minors. When a woman intervened on a male victim’s behalf, the goons can be seen falling upon her, pushing her to the ground, and pulling at her clothes. All this was done in the presence of at least one policeman. The footage showed a policeman eventually intervening, but he did so not to stop the assault or restrain the assailant and detain him, but to lead him away rather gently.

The video triggered anger and outrage in India, forcing the police to eventually detain four men — Raman Saini, Vivekanand alias Vivek, Kapil Kumar, and Ravinder Singh alias Govind Hindu — of the Hindu Raksha Dal (HRD) or Hindu Protection Organization.

Admitting that the four were members of his organization, HRD chief Bhupendra Singh Tomar aka Pinky Bhaiyya described them as “warriors” who were “working for Sanatan Dharma” (literally, universal truth i.e., Hinduism). In an interview with Outlook magazine, Tomar justified the violence they unleashed at the October 10 protests. The CJP activists “tried to vitiate the atmosphere in the country” during the protests at Jantar Mantar in July. “We will deal with these people who are resorting to violence, and we will set them straight. We take pride in our actions, and we will continue to do so,” Tomar said.

Founded in 2013, the Hindu Raksha Dal is among dozens of vigilante groups that have mushroomed under Modi’s rule. They have thrived under the Sangh Parivar’s patronage. Their activists cannot be dismissed as mere street gangs. They are the Sangh Parivar’s foot soldiers and unleash violence to further its Hindutva agenda. Outfits like the HRD and the Bharatiya Gau Raksha Dal (Indian Cow Protection Organization) freely engage in violence as they enjoy state protection.

HRD activists are rarely convicted or punished. Saini, Vivek, Kumar, and Singh were caught on video and were arrested under public pressure, but they were freed on bail soon after. Delhi Police did not raise objections to their release by the courts. On their release, Tomar was there to welcome and garland the four men.

Tomar himself has over 30 cases against him for hate speech, distributing weapons, issuing death threats, damaging property, assault, extortion, and raising inflammatory slogans. The list of complaints and cases against him is long. He has been arrested in a few cases only to be let off on bail soon after. His supporters have an apt slogan to describe this: “Aaj jail, kal bail, aur phir wahi khel” (jail today, bail tomorrow and then again, the same game).

The HRD has carried out dozens of attacks on Muslims, secular Indians, and the BJP’s critics. In 2020, Tomar claimed credit for the attack on students at the Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU) in New Delhi. “JNU is a hotbed of anti-national activities and we cannot tolerate this,” he said, taking “full responsibility” for the violence that left at least 30 people, including teachers and students, injured.

In August 2024, HRD activists burnt down houses and property of Muslims in a slum in Ghaziabad, claiming that they were Bangladeshis living illegally in India. In December 2025, Tomar and his son were arrested for distributing swords in Ghaziabad for the “self-defense” of Hindus.

Outfits like the HRD enable the Sangh Parivar and the BJP government to not only freely unleash illegitimate violence but also deny their links to the perpetrators of such violence. The membership of Sangh Parivar outfits and their fellow travelers is nebulous. Consequently, it is hard to pin such violence on the Modi government.
tag: Bhupendra Singh Tomar; BJP government; Hindu Raksha Dal; Hindu vigilante violence; Hindutva militias; Narendra Modi government; Pinky Bhaiyya; Protests in Delhi; Sangh Parivar

title: Hong Kong’s Vanishing Rainbow Shows How China’s Social Control Travels
channel_text: Blog; China Power; East Asia; Society
description: From Hong Kong to Bangkok, Paris, Taiwan, and North America, LGBTQ communities are encountering censorship, surveillance, and coercive pressure linked to China.
text:
China’s growing pressure on LGBTQ communities is increasingly transnational. Chinese nationals who attend Pride events overseas can attract police attention after returning home; overseas Chinese LGBTQ groups remain vulnerable to censorship on Chinese platforms; cultural spaces in Europe can lose access to Chinese social media for promoting transgender films; and mainland writers publishing gay fiction on overseas platforms have faced prosecution at home. Hong Kong offers a particularly revealing entry point because similar pressures are visible there even though same-sex relationships are legal (though not legally recognized as marriages).

In October, the organizing committee of Hong Kong Pride canceled its annual Rainbow Market at Central Market after being told that an administrative error had resulted in double-booking. Organizers had already received confirmation, paid a deposit, and announced the venue.

The cancellation followed a wider pattern. Earlier in 2026, Pink Dot HK, the city’s largest annual LGBTQ carnival, canceled its event after the operator of Stanley Plaza and Murray House withdrew the venues, citing unresolved licensing issues. It was the second consecutive year in which Pink Dot failed to proceed. In 2025, negotiations to hold the event at West Kowloon Cultural District’s Art Park had also collapsed.

Hong Kong Pride itself lost a planned venue at Kwun Tong Promenade in 2025 after organizers had already paid rent and announced the event.

These cases illustrate how LGBTQ public life in Hong Kong is being narrowed through administrative and institutional means rather than formal criminal prohibition. Consensual same-sex conduct remains legal, and LGBTQ organizations continue to exist. But these groups find it harder and harder to organize publicly, retain venues, sustain institutions, and remain visible in civic life.

This is striking because Hong Kong once had one of the most visible LGBTQ communities in East Asia. The city decriminalized consensual homosexual conduct between adult men in 1991, while its courts later expanded legal protections for same-sex couples in areas including immigration, taxation, and public housing. Social acceptance also rose significantly. Survey research published in 2023 found that 69 percent of respondents were “moderately” or “very accepting” of gay men and lesbians, while 60 percent supported same-sex marriage and 71 percent supported anti-discrimination legislation based on sexual orientation.

Hong Kong Pride once drew thousands into the streets, but its last full Pride march took place in 2018. In 2019, police declined permission for a march amid the citywide protests and permitted only a static rally. Pandemic restrictions later pushed Pride activities online, after which organizers shifted toward indoor markets and smaller events. The large public march never returned.

Most LGBTQ organizations in Hong Kong were never primarily political in the conventional sense. Their work focused on discrimination, health, family acceptance, culture, community support, and legal equality. Their shrinking space therefore shows how Hong Kong’s post-2020 transformation has moved beyond suppressing explicit political opposition and into regulating autonomous social life.

The same pattern is visible in mainland China. China decriminalized homosexuality in 1997 and removed homosexuality from its official classification of mental disorders in 2001 (in practice, if not in actual fact). During the 2000s and early 2010s, LGBTQ organizations, university groups, online communities, and cultural events expanded in major cities. Under Xi Jinping, that space has contracted sharply. Shanghai Pride ceased operations in 2020, the Beijing LGBT Center closed in 2023, university LGBTQ groups have faced mounting restrictions, and social media accounts associated with sexual minority organizations have been deleted or suspended.

Foreign connections have become increasingly important to this repression. Chinese authorities often treat independent organizations with international ties as possible channels of foreign influence. LGBTQ groups are especially exposed because contemporary sexual minority advocacy is highly transnational, involving foreign NGOs, embassies, academic institutions, cultural organizations, and legal networks. This allows questions of private identity and social equality to be reframed as questions of sovereignty and political security.

The reach of this logic now extends beyond China’s borders. In 2026, France’s Le Monde reported that Chinese nationals who had participated in Bangkok Pride later received police attention after returning to China. How the authorities identified them remains unclear, but participation in a lawful LGBTQ event in Thailand had become a matter of interest to Chinese police.

This fits within the broader discussion of transnational repression, but LGBTQ communities also reveal a related form of cross-border control that operates through information systems. Chinese platforms and censorship practices increasingly project domestic restrictions into overseas Chinese-speaking communities.

The Chinese Rainbow Network illustrates this problem. The organization operates overseas, yet material on its WeChat public account became inaccessible. Citizen Lab had already shown the structural basis for such control when it found that content exchanged between non-China-registered WeChat accounts could still be subjected to analysis for politically sensitive material. Overseas users can therefore remain inside an information environment shaped by the political requirements of the Chinese party-state.

Recent cases involving the LGBTQ community show how this extends to cultural expression. The Paris-based Chinese-language cultural space 8lithèque reportedly had its Xiaohongshu (RedNote) account banned after promoting a screening of a transgender-themed film. The event was taking place in France, but the organizers remained vulnerable to the content rules of a Chinese platform.

The Haitang Literature City prosecutions show another dimension of this expanding reach. Haitang, a Taiwan-based platform, became popular among mainland Chinese writers of danmei and boys’ love fiction, including sexually explicit material. Chinese authorities later summoned, detained, and prosecuted mainland writers who had published on the platform, citing China’s obscenity laws. The platform was outside mainland China, but the writers were not beyond the reach of Chinese law enforcement.

Taken together, these cases show how China’s control increasingly travels through people, platforms, and language communities. Whether joining a cultural space in Paris, a platform in Taiwan, a Pride parade in Bangkok, or a community organization in North America, Chinese citizens and Chinese-language communities remain exposed to censorship, surveillance, or coercive pressure originating from inside China.

Why should LGBTQ communities matter so much to the party-state?

One reason is autonomous organization. Community centers, university societies, legal aid groups, online networks, cultural organizations, and Pride events create horizontal ties among citizens outside structures supervised by the Communist Party. Chinese authorities have become increasingly suspicious of such organization across many fields, including labor rights, feminism, religion, public health, and environmental activism.

Sexual minority rights also raise broader questions about pluralism. The principle that individuals should retain dignity and rights even when they depart from majority social norms places limits on the authority of the state, family, and society over private identity.

Family structure adds another dimension. Under Xi Jinping, official discourse has placed growing emphasis on marriage, reproduction, family responsibility, and demographic duty. These themes have become more prominent as China confronts low fertility, population decline, delayed marriage, and rapid aging. Women are increasingly encouraged to marry and have children, while official rhetoric emphasizes “good family traditions” and reproductive responsibility.

LGBTQ identities sit uneasily within this model because they challenge the assumption that adult life should culminate in heterosexual marriage and biological reproduction. They also complicate fixed gender roles within the family.

These tensions acquire greater political significance because Xi has tied social order to the broader project of the “great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation.” The Communist Party increasingly presents itself as a guardian of Chinese civilizational continuity and social morality.

This emphasis on tradition also represents a shift in the party’s own ideological history. The early People’s Republic was explicitly revolutionary in its approach to family hierarchy. The 1950 Marriage Law attacked arranged marriage, concubinage, male superiority, and other practices described as remnants of the feudal family system. Maoist discourse framed women’s emancipation as part of the destruction of inherited social hierarchy.

Mao-era China was never sexually liberal, but the contrast shows that the Communist Party’s current appeal to traditional family values is selective rather than timeless. During the revolutionary period, dismantling inherited hierarchies served the party’s claim to be creating a new society. Under Xi, family hierarchy, reproductive responsibility, and civilizational continuity serve a different political purpose by reinforcing social order and distinguishing Chinese values from supposedly foreign liberal influence.

LGBTQ communities therefore sit at the intersection of several Xi-era concerns: autonomous organization, minority rights, gender hierarchy, demographic policy, foreign influence, and individual autonomy.

Repression can be effective at weakening the organizational capacity of such groups. Authorities can close community centers, prevent events, delete accounts, restrict fundraising, discourage international partnerships, and make public participation more risky. But these measures cannot remove the identities and experiences that produced these communities.

That creates a long-term political problem. Concepts such as constitutionalism or representative government can remain abstract for citizens who encounter them mainly through rhetoric. Sexuality and gender are experienced through everyday life. Government policy reaches LGBTQ people through relationships, family formation, public expression, employment, access to community, and the ability to describe oneself openly. Feminists encounter a similar dynamic when state-defined expectations concerning marriage, reproduction, and gender roles collide with their own lives.

Repeated discrimination turns political authority into a personal experience. Not every LGBTQ person or feminist will become politically oppositional, but a state that continually restricts people at the level of identity, family, and bodily autonomy risks creating durable alienation that cannot easily be displaced by nationalism or civilizational rhetoric.

The contraction of LGBTQ space in Hong Kong therefore matters beyond sexual minority rights. It shows how the logic of political control can expand into social life and how Chinese digital platforms, information systems, and law enforcement practices can extend that control across borders.

For LGBTQ communities, the immediate result is the erosion of public and organizational space. For Beijing, the longer-term consequence may be a widening gap between its civilizational narrative and the everyday experience of those whose identities increasingly fall outside the social order it seeks to define.

title: How Australia’s Gambling Lobby has Successfully Avoided Any Reform
description: Political donations, lobbying, and community influence help gambling companies block major policy reforms and protect huge profits.
text:
Gambling businesses in Australia have a long history of effectively influencing and controlling government policy and regulation over a national pastime that makes Australians the world’s biggest gamblers per capita. The gambling industry can wield that level of control because it turns over AU$244.3 billion (2022–23) and generates more than AU$10 billion a year in gambling tax revenue to financially stretched state governments. This substantial financial contribution from gambling provides access to government decision-makers.

Meanwhile, gambling businesses have adopted parts of the tobacco industry’s “corporate playbook” to resist regulation. These tactics have allowed the gambling industry to effectively avoid regulation and instead allowed them to expand their highly profitable commercial activities.

Gambling businesses are well resourced because the products they sell are extremely profitable, and they have worked hard over many years to ensure gambling remains deeply embedded in Australian social life. A key development toward that came with the introduction of gambling machines, known as poker or “pokie” machines, into suburban social clubs from 1956 onward, and later into pubs and hotels. This helped make gambling seem like a normal part of community life. In most Australian states and territories (except Western Australia, which restricts poker machines to a single casino), poker machines are widespread and operate largely without question in venues that are also used for family meals and social and sporting activities.

The development of these social clubs in New South Wales was particularly important. They helped provide sporting and recreational facilities in new postwar suburbs at a time when governments were unable to provide enough financial support for community infrastructure. This gave the clubs a strong community image and helped make their gambling activities more acceptable.

This approach continues today. It is not unique to Australia. Gambling businesses around the world use similar strategies, sometimes described as the “alibi model.” Clubs NSW, the largest gambling network in Australia, has carefully maintained this tradition and uses it whenever possible to promote the image of these social clubs as organizations that give generously to their communities. The close connection between local community clubs, sporting organizations, and some of Australia’s largest commercial gambling operators makes it harder to challenge the normalization and influence of the gambling industry.

Gambling operators are also among Australia’s biggest political donors, according to research. Political donations can provide access to decision-makers, which can then give gambling businesses greater influence over policies that affect them. Australia has also developed a strong “revolving door” between politics and the gambling industry.

There are some restrictions on politicians taking jobs after leaving office, but the definition of a “lobbyist” is narrow. It generally excludes people working directly for companies or industry associations to influence government. As a result, many people involved in lobbying are not subject to the same rules. Former senators, premiers, ministers, political advisers, and senior public officials have taken jobs with some of Australia’s largest gambling companies, sometimes soon after leaving public office.

Hospitality is another form of influence. This can range from MPs given private boxes at major sporting events, or the sports minister attending football grand finals and tickets for MPs attending the Melbourne Cup racing carnival, to “policy briefing” lunches and dinners for the minister responsible for oversight of the gambling industry at expensive restaurants.

These benefits may have to be declared, but the conversations that take place are not made public. The access provided by hospitality can be significant. A politician may spend several hours with an industry representative at an event, giving the host much more time and access than they would normally have during a visit to a parliamentary office.

Some states have introduced new rules that limit political donations from certain businesses, including gambling operators. The federal government has weaker rules around political transparency and integrity, with limited enforcement and relatively weak penalties. In practice, this means that Australia has a political system in which powerful interests can influence governments while making that influence difficult for the public to see.

Recent experience suggests they can be extremely effective. In 2010-11, the minority Gillard government sought to introduce a system that would allow poker machine players to set limits on how much they could spend. ClubsNSW, representing clubs with poker machines across New South Wales, launched a highly effective campaign to block the change. It targeted Labor politicians in marginal seats in New South Wales and Queensland.

Although Clubs NSW remained the public face of the campaign, partly because of the positive community image created by the “alibi” of community benefits, it brought much of the gambling industry together behind the campaign and had access to almost unlimited financial resources. Nervous backbenchers became increasingly concerned, and Prime Minister Julia Gillard eventually found a way to abandon the commitment. No major reform followed.

More recently, a 2023 federal parliamentary inquiry into “online gambling and its impacts on those experiencing gambling harm,” chaired by MP Peta Murphy, concluded that “enough is enough.” It recommended major reforms to online gambling in order to reduce its harm to Australians. The recommendations included banning gambling advertising across all media, developing a national strategy for gambling regulation, and establishing a new national gambling regulator. Once again, the gambling industry responded quickly, with wagering companies taking the lead.

Sporting organizations and broadcasters, which now receive significant revenue from gambling, were among those most strongly opposed to the proposed reforms. They successfully stymied the changes. The reforms eventually announced by the government in 2026 fell well short of those recommended by the parliamentary committee.

In both cases, the gambling industry organizations successfully utilized their enormous lobbying powers to influence government. In both cases, those methods worked. And the Murphy inquiry’s important reform proposals were weakened or abandoned.

The gambling industry provides a clear example of how the corporate playbook can be used to prevent reforms that could significantly reduce gambling harm. The reason is simple: the all-powerful gambling industry knows only too well that effective regulation could reduce their revenues and profits.
