title: How Chinese Clean Tech Is Reshaping Ukraine’s Wartime Energy Security
description: Despite China’s close ties with Russia, Chinese solar energy technology is giving Ukraine badly needed energy resilience.
text:
Russia’s war against Ukraine has shown that energy security is no longer just about access to fuels, pipelines, and large power stations. It also depends on solar panels, batteries, and other distributed energy equipment that can keep homes, businesses, and critical services operating when the electricity grid is under attack.

Ironically, most of the equipment helping Ukraine keep the lights on comes from China.

Beijing has maintained close strategic ties with Russia. Yet through trade and global supply chains, Chinese-made clean energy technologies are helping Ukraine reduce the vulnerability created by Russian attacks on its energy system.

Russia’s attacks exposed the vulnerability of Ukraine’s highly centralized power system. The International Energy Agency (IEA) estimated that around half of Ukraine’s generation capacity was occupied, damaged or destroyed during 2022-23, while around half of its large network substations were damaged by missiles and drones. After another wave of attacks in spring 2024, Ukraine lost a further 9 GW of generation capacity, leaving it with only around one-third of its pre-war capacity. On January 20, 2026, another major Russian attack on energy infrastructure left almost half of Kyiv without heat and power.

Such attacks turned Ukraine’s large, fixed energy assets into major points of vulnerability, making energy decentralization an increasingly important source of resilience. Consequently, there has been a resurgence of solar power in Ukraine.

The country was already a significant solar market before Russia’s full-scale invasion, ranking ninth globally for new solar capacity addition in 2019. But deployment and trade collapsed after February 2022. Chinese module exports to Ukraine fell from 83.9 MW in February 2022 to just 7.5 MW in March, and totaled only 15.8 MW in 2023.

Since then, the market has recovered. The Solar Energy Association of Ukraine estimated that around 800 MW of solar was installed in 2024 and 1.5 GW in 2025. Businesses and households have been installing solar power to reduce their dependence on the grid. Distributed solar PV, often combined with battery storage, has therefore become an important part of Ukraine’s wartime energy security.

International organizations, such as the IEA and the Center for Strategic and International Studies, have recently examined Ukraine’s energy reconstruction, covering aspects such as decentralization, solar power, battery storage, financing, and electricity-market reform. However, these reports tell us remarkably little about the sources of the equipment needed for this transition.

In particular, the role of Chinese-made equipment in this shift has received much less attention. According to the IEA, China accounts for around 85 percent of global solar supply-chain production capacity and around 80 percent of lithium-ion battery production capacity. Its share in some specific segments is even higher – for example, China supplies around 95 percent of global PV wafer capacity.

Currently there is no authoritative estimate on the specific share of Chinese-made equipment in Ukraine’s solar and battery markets, not least because some products reach Ukraine through third countries, international procurement channels, and aid programs. Still, given China’s dominance of these supply chains, Chinese-made equipment is likely to have played an important role in Ukraine’s decentralized energy expansion and will probably continue to do so.

This raises an intriguing question. Does China’s position in these supply chains give Beijing significant leverage over Ukraine? Could China, particularly given its close relations with Russia, use access to clean energy equipment as a coercive geopolitical tool?

Supply chain concentration undoubtedly creates structural influence. But as I argued in an article in September 2025 in The Diplomat, it does not translate automatically into the kind of coercive power historically associated with oil and gas.

In Ukraine’s case, three factors are particularly relevant.

First, clean energy equipment moves through complex international commercial networks. A substantial volume of Chinese products can reach Ukraine indirectly through third countries, distributors, international procurement, and aid programs. This makes it difficult for Beijing to control the ultimate destination or end user. Blocking such flows would require much wider restrictions and would be commercially and politically difficult.

Second, weaponizing clean-energy supply would impose considerable costs on China’s own industries. It could expose Chinese companies to greater regulatory and compliance risks while strengthening Western arguments for supply chain diversification, domestic manufacturing, and “friend-shoring.” In the long run, that could accelerate precisely the reduction in dependence that Chinese manufacturers would prefer to avoid.

Third, such restrictions would contradict Beijing’s stated approach to the Russia-Ukraine war. China has repeatedly called for promoting peace talks while maintaining civilian trade. Deliberately restricting technologies important to civilian electricity supply would be difficult to reconcile with that position and could carry diplomatic and reputational costs.

When it comes to clean energy, China’s industrial dominance does not necessarily translate into the ability to exercise political control. Global commercial networks can significantly constrain a government’s ability to determine where clean technologies ultimately go and how they are used.

A further question is how the Chinese government and Chinese companies might participate constructively in Ukraine’s ongoing energy transformation and eventual reconstruction.

The potential market is substantial. The IEA estimates that Ukraine would need to add around 4 GW of distributed solar PV each year through 2030 to build a more decentralized and secure electricity system while meeting its national energy and climate objectives. It would also require an additional 5.6 GW of battery energy capacity by 2030.

For Chinese companies, the opportunities extend beyond exporting more solar modules and batteries. There is considerable scope for cooperation in system integration, energy management, technology transfer, joint project development, local assembly and production, and operations and maintenance.

But such involvement would not be straightforward. Chinese firms would have to navigate wartime risks, technical standards, financing constraints, supply chain security screening, and an increasingly complex geopolitical environment. Companies seeking to participate will therefore need to create value locally, build trusted partnerships, and adapt to an institutional and regulatory environment, particularly as Ukraine becomes more deeply integrated into European energy markets.

Ukraine’s experience offers a broader lesson about the geopolitics of clean energy. Countries still need secure fuel supplies and reliable power grids, but they also need access to the equipment used to produce and store electricity locally. China’s lead in manufacturing gives it considerable influence, though not complete control. Once solar panels and batteries enter global trading networks, they can contribute to energy security in ways that go beyond the intentions or expectations of their country of origin.

title: How Christian Networks in Asia Are Shaping Support for Israel
description: As Israel faces growing pressure in the West, Eagles’ Wings mission brings Christian leaders from across the globe to show support for the Jewish people and Israel
text:
With much of the international discourse, specifically in North America and Europe, focused on criticizing Israel, a large group of international Christian leaders congregated in Jerusalem to show support. One of the key participants was senior Filipino pastor Bishop Dr. David A. Sobrepeña who leads a large evangelical community across the Philippine islands. Bishop Sobrepeña is the founder of Word of Hope Christian Ministries which includes 43 satellite churches and hosts 70 services on any given Sunday across Manila. Partaking in this year’s event, Bishop Sobrepeña stated, “For Christians in the Philippines, the opportunity to come here and pray in Jerusalem is deeply meaningful. We also come to listen to the people of Israel and to carry their stories back to the churches and communities we serve.”

The Bishop was one of more than 550 prominent Christian leaders with vast followings who recently participated in a 10-day Eagles’ Wings delegation organized in conjunction with Bishop Sterns and Israel’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Attendees hailed from 51 different nations and congregated around the Jewish holiday of Sukkot (Feast of Tabernacles) in Jerusalem, commemorating the third anniversary of the October 7th attack. The gathering offers a window into a less frequently discussed dimension of the Israel debate: the continued mobilization of Christian communities in parts of Asia and the wider Global South around Israel.

Taking a closer look at Israel sentiment in Western countries, antisemitism interwoven with anti-Israel sentiment is on the rise. In 2025 the Anti Defamation League (ADL) recorded 6,274 antisemitic events in North America alone. The Hillel organization reported 2,334 incidents across U.S. campuses in the 2024-2025 academic year, stating that, “Antisemitic incidents on campus are at a record high in the past school year.”

In Western Europe the Community Security Trust (CST) recorded a staggering 3,700 antisemitic incidents across Britain over the course of 2025, the second highest annual total of such events ever recorded. French authorities cited 1,320 antisemitic acts in 2025, with France’s Interior Ministry calling it a “historically high” figure.

As sentiment over Israel grows increasingly polarized in the West, there are a number of well-educated Asian evangelical Christian communities who unequivocally support Israel, comprising the backbone of its support in the region. South Korea is home to nearly 9 million evangelical and Pentecostal Protestants who display the Israeli flag during rallies and prayers. Roughly 8 percent of Singapore’s population run a network of influential evangelical megachurches while boasting an active Christian Zionist movement that mobilizes fundraising initiatives, educational tours and pro-Israel forums.

The Philippines is a particularly heavy hitter on the East Asian evangelical pro-Zionist front with an estimated 13 million evangelical adherents within a predominantly Catholic milieu. A Pew study surveying Pentecostals across 10 nations highlighted that 67 percent of Filipino Pentecostals surveyed said they sympathized with Israel.

In this context, Eagles’ Wings has been working for the last three decades to bring tens of thousands of evangelical Christians from around the globe to Israel. The organization was founded by Bishop Robert Stearns who is a staunch supporter of Israel and an outspoken supporter of moving the United States Embassy to Jerusalem. In Stephen Spector’s 2008 book Evangelicals and Israel: The Story of American Christian Zionism, Bishop Stearns discusses Israel’s regional threat profile while declaring himself willing to “die defending Israel.” He has spoken on Israel’s behalf both at the House of Lords in London and the Israeli Knesset.

Stearns founded Eagles’ Wings with a clear mission in mind: Firsthand encounters with Israel can be utilized to strongly shape how large Christian networks around the world understand Israel and antisemitism. They have been working to achieve this goal by having brought 25,000+ Christians to the Holy Land, organizing Nexus Leadership Missions which offer intensive educational tours to global pastoral leaders, as well as spearheading the Christian answer to Birthright, dubbed the ‘Israel Experience’, bringing college-age Christian students to Israel.

One of the key events as part of this year’s Eagles’ Wings 10-day delegation was “Awake Jerusalem at the Tower of David.” The event took place on October 3 at Jerusalem’s iconic Tower of David with hundreds of Christian leaders from 51 different countries in attendance. The event showcased international Christian artists while also including communal worship being covered and broadcasted by Daystar Television Network, a media partner of Eagles’ Wings.

For Israel, the challenges that lie ahead are not merely diplomatic. As the international stage becomes increasingly harder to navigate the relationships that Israel fosters with Asia and the Global South may become of increasing strategic importance. This gathering of 550 Christian leaders from 51 nation-states demonstrates merely one aspect of this shifting climate. Prominent religious communities from the Philippines to Korea and Brazil to Kenya will be able to shape the conversation about Israel within their respective societies. The mobilization of these groups shows the potential benefits that Israel stands to reap from fostering non-traditional alliances and that vis-à-vis culture, religion and interpersonal connections a new path to diplomacy may emerge.

title: How Indonesians Are Being Recruited Into the Russian Army
description: So far, Jakarta is yet to come to grips with problem that has arisen alongside President Prabowo Subianto’s efforts to build a closer relationship with Russia.
text:
On September 18, Indonesia’s ambassador to Russia, Jose Tavares, told the state news agency Antara that his embassy had taken dozens of calls from families who believed their relatives had been recruited into Russia’s army by agents on social media promising large salaries. Jakarta has so far dealt with these cases one by one, in line with standard consular procedures. On September 19, the Indonesian embassy sent a note verbale, a formal diplomatic letter, asking the Russian Foreign Ministry to verify the names, and bring home those who failed Russia’s medical examination. Arrmanatha Nasir, the career diplomat who was sworn in as foreign minister on October 1, has inherited that approach.

However, the current approach is ill-equipped to handle a problem that has arisen alongside President Prabowo Subianto’s efforts to build a close relationship with Vladimir Putin’s Russia. Indonesian institutions have been promoting Russia as a labor destination, including in a special economic zone that assembles attack drones, even as they warn their citizens against the job offers that might lead to the frontlines in Ukraine. Meanwhile, Jakarta counts the personal closeness between Prabowo and Putin as an asset, yet it has made no public use of that closeness to aid the citizens caught in this recruitment trap.

Most of the public record on these cases comes either from one of the warring parties or from the recruits and their families. Ukraine’s foreign intelligence service said on August 27 that it had documents on at least eight Indonesians who were recruited into Russia’s army. However, Kompas noted that the documents are Russian e-visa notices, while Russia’s embassy in Jakarta called the release a disinformation campaign. Meanwhile, a man who told Republika that he was among those named said that an agent had promised him a security job and then pushed him into a military contract, although he had failed his medical examination in Moscow. He was in hospital when he spoke to the newspaper, after a Ukrainian drone had taken one of his fingers. In Natuna, the parents of a 30-year-old man said that a comrade had reported him killed by a Ukrainian drone on September 20, which the regent of Natuna still called uncertain and unclear 10 days later.

The cases point to three problems, the first of which is that recruitment follows the logic of labor migration long before it turns into military service. Hartyo Harkomoyo, Indonesia’s deputy ambassador in Moscow, told RRI that most recruits are promised civilian jobs, some of them as drivers, builders, cooks, or nurses under Russia’s Defense Ministry. Some are recruited from Indonesia through social media, and others from among Indonesians already in Russia, especially students. A content creator from Central Java told Republika that a Russian contact on social media had offered him a post in a government ministry or a large company and paid for his flight and his e-visa. The contract he was handed in Moscow was a military one, written in Russian, which he could not read. An Indonesian man filmed by Ukrainian soldiers after his capture in early September said he had been working as a cleaner when he was put into uniform and sent to the front.

The case of the man from Natuna shows the same path from a civilian job to the frontline. According to his family, the young man had worked as an electrician in the Philippines before going to Russia with seven other Indonesians. He believed he had been hired to deliver food to the troops. The head of his neighborhood said that he refused a transfer to a combat unit because it was not in his contract. He could not leave because his passport was being held. And yet, the migrant-worker protection office in his province found no record of him as a registered worker.

The second problem concerns the fact that Indonesian institutions themselves opened a formal labor channel to Russia this year. In January, the Ministry for the Protection of Migrant Workers (KP2MI) welcomed a plan by the aluminum producer RUSAL to take 50 vocational-school graduates, with departures scheduled for September. They presented it as part of Prabowo’s “SMK Go Global” program. A month later, KP2MI named Russia a new placement destination in manufacturing and shipbuilding. It also said it had received a draft Memorandum of Understanding from Russia’s Federal Service for Labor and Employment. In the same meeting, the deputy minister received a warning from the defense attaché in Moscow that Indonesians should beware of well-paid job advertisements for private military companies, suggesting that the Ministry knew of the risk from the start.

The West Java provincial labor office went further in June, when its one-stop service for migrant workers advertised jobs for women aged 18 to 24 in Russia’s Alabuga Special Economic Zone, with salary in dollars and a flight paid by the employer. The United States Treasury sanctioned the company that runs the zone in February 2024 for producing Iranian-designed Geran-2 attack drones under a contract with Russia’s military. An Associated Press investigation found that young African women recruited there, with offers of work in hospitality and catering, ended up assembling drones. The West Java advertisement, now marked closed, names no employer and gives no number of applicants or departures. No documented recruit is known to have left through these channels. Their effect is to present Russia, including the defense industry, as an ordinary destination for Indonesian workers.

In July, Indonesia’s embassy in Moscow warned Indonesians against taking job offers on tourist visas and signing contracts in a language they could not read. The warning did not mention military service, and a month later the embassy’s own job fair for Indonesians in Russia, held on August 17, listed Alabuga SEZ among the employers, beside RUSAL, En+ Group, and Rusagro. The ambassador presented the fair as a way to widen Indonesians’ chances to work and build careers in Russia. Indonesia’s national placement system still listed 76 places in Russia on October 1. Among them, 60 places are for fishery workers whose placement permits were issued on September 1.

The third problem is that Jakarta’s response to these recruitment traps has treated the issue as a series of separate cases. The Foreign Ministry’s spokesperson said on September 18 that the government would look into claims of fraud and exploitation, protect any Indonesians found to be victims, and prosecute recruiters. She added that any verified service in a foreign army would be seen as an individual act that does not represent the policy of the Indonesian government. Tavares described the embassy’s note verbale to the Russian Foreign Ministry as a request for verification and clarification. Meanwhile, KP2MI’s deputy minister, Christina Aryani, said the recruits had been lured by advertisements and declined to treat the cases as trafficking without proof of exploitation, thereby leaving any kind of repatriation for the Foreign Ministry to negotiate. Moreover, as of press time, the ministry’s online travel advisory for Russia still said nothing about recruitment.

I would suggest that the reason for this restraint lies in the relationship itself. Prabowo has met Putin five times since taking office, and in Vladivostok last month, he offered Indonesia to Russian businesses as a natural entry point to ASEAN. A government that has invested this much in the relationship at the presidential level is unlikely to seek a public quarrel with Moscow over a few dozen citizens. Therefore, it treats each case as a matter of individual choice and consular care. Friction between KP2MI and the Foreign Ministry, visible in Aryani’s remarks, explains why the cases pass between agencies, but not why no one has raised them with Moscow at the political level. The cost of that restraint falls on the men themselves, because Moscow has little reason to act on the cases of a partner that has not raised them at the political level publicly.

It is true that not every Indonesian in Russia’s army was deceived by a job offer. Among the eight named by Ukraine is a former activist and party cadre from Aceh whose friends told Generasi.co that he had spoken of going to Russia to fight if a business project failed, and Harkomoyo distinguishes recruits who were tricked from those who signed knowingly and were aware that they could lose their citizenship. Aryani made the same point when she compared the recruits to Indonesians who had knowingly taken jobs in scam compounds in Cambodia. However, the choices of individual recruits do not explain why Indonesians became a target in the first place, which is a question about Jakarta’s dealings with Moscow.

A West Java provincial labor office notice dated June 19, 2026, advertising placements for young women in Russia’s Alabuga Special Economic Zone. (Screenshot by Radityo Dharmaputra)

An investigation published by Germany’s public broadcaster in July suggests an answer. Tagesschau’s reporters followed an agency called WorkVia, which ran Instagram videos addressed to Indonesians and paid Facebook advertisements offering $3,200 a month and a $30,000 signing bonus for a contract with Russia’s army. Posing as an Indonesian applicant, one reporter was told by the agency’s recruiter that the job was risky but well paid. Since February 2026, according to the investigation, WorkVia has addressed mainly men from Cambodia and Indonesia, two countries from which Russia had hardly recruited before. Ukraine’s Defense Ministry told the reporters that Russia keeps 36 countries off its recruitment lists to avoid negative reactions from their leaders, and a version of that list obtained by the independent Russian outlet iStories includes India, Nepal, Sri Lanka, Vietnam, and Laos (although it does not mention Indonesia and the Philippines). iStories links the list to diplomatic pressure: Nepal, India, and Sri Lanka have appealed to Moscow since mid-2024, and Jordan was added after making similar demands in November 2025. Read together, the two findings suggest that recruiters moved toward countries whose governments had not objected, and that Indonesia was one of them.

Other governments have raised the issue with Moscow, and several have obtained concessions. Nepal suspended work permits for Russia and Ukraine in January 2024, after nine of its citizens were killed in the war. Prime Minister Narendra Modi raised the issue with Putin in July 2024, after which New Delhi said Russia had promised to discharge all Indians in its army. India reported 139 of its nationals released by the end of July this year, although New Delhi says its citizens are still being recruited despite its warnings. Sri Lanka’s foreign minister obtained an assurance from Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov in June 2024 that no further recruitment from the island would take place, and South Africa’s president secured Putin’s support for the return of 17 men in a telephone call in February. Colombia formally asked Russia and Ukraine in September to stop enlisting its citizens. None of these governments had to break with Moscow to do so.

Jakarta’s first step should be political, since its leverage lies in the relationship itself. Prabowo, or his new foreign minister, can ask Moscow to stop recruiting Indonesians and to release those already under contract. India and South Africa, fellow BRICS members, made such requests at the highest level. Putin, for his part, has called Indonesia one of Russia’s trusted friends in ASEAN. A partner that close should have no difficulty in asking for the same treatment as others. The recruiters’ stop-list suggests that Moscow adjusts when a government’s leaders object.

Jakarta should also bring its own labor channels into line with its warnings. Until Russian employers can be checked, KP2MI and the provincial labor offices should stop placing Indonesians with firms tied to Russia’s defense industry, beginning with the Alabuga SEZ. The embassy in Moscow should not invite such firms to its job fairs. The draft labor memorandum with Russia’s Federal Service for Labor and Employment is the place to write that exclusion down. The cost would be small, since the national placement system lists more than 2,200 places in Slovakia and more than 1,400 in Poland, against 76 in Russia.

Indonesia’s warnings also need to reach the people whom the recruiters already reach on social media. WorkVia found Indonesians through Instagram videos and paid Facebook advertisements, although Meta has barred advertising from Russia since 2022, while the embassy’s warning was posted on a ministry website. The Foreign Ministry and KP2MI could run Indonesian-language warnings on the same platforms where the advertisements appear. The Communications Ministry could also ask Meta to enforce its own ban. Colombia offers a working model, since its Foreign Ministry has added an awareness campaign to a screening protocol in its passport offices for applicants who say they intend to fight abroad.

Lastly, Indonesia need not act alone, since other states in the region face similar recruitment challenges. The Philippines, which is also missing from the recruiters’ stop-list, said in September that it was verifying reports of Filipinos recruited into foreign armed forces, in terms close to Jakarta’s own, and WorkVia has turned to Cambodia as well. Indonesia, the Philippines, and Cambodia could take the matter up together in ASEAN, which would raise the political cost to Moscow of recruiting in Southeast Asia.

As I have argued elsewhere, calling these men mercenaries narrows the protection Indonesia can still give them. Treating them as a series of individual cases narrows it in the same way, because it leaves the routes that brought them to Russia intact. A government that offers itself as Russia’s entry point to Southeast Asia is well placed to ask Moscow to keep its recruiters away from Indonesians. It should make that request at the level at which the relationship itself is conducted, which is the presidential one.

title: How the Fossil Fuel Industry ‘Captured’ Australia and Maintains Its Political Dominance
description: By framing coal and gas as essential to jobs, prosperity and national identity, the industry continues to resist the transition to renewable energy.
text:
Australia is one of the world’s largest exporters of coal and gas and has among the world’s highest per capita carbon emissions. As a leading “petrostate,” it is perhaps unsurprising that the fossil fuel sector has been central in shaping the nation’s energy and climate policies.

The political capture of Australia by the fossil fuel industries has stymied any meaningful attempt to move away from fossil energy. They have historically obstructed attempts to regulate and reduce carbon emissions through lobbying, networking, and financial donations to parties in the political arena. The end game is to promote fossil energy to the public as essential to the past, present, and future of Australian society; what can be termed a form of “carbon populism.”

Unpicking this complex web of political influence is essential if meaningful decarbonization is to be achieved.

Shaping the Political Arena

The outsized political influence of the fossil fuel industries in Australia has a long history. As former political staffer Guy Pearse noted in his book “High and Dry,” the so-called “greenhouse mafia” of corporate executives and lobbyists played a key role in the years of the Howard government (1996-2007) in shaping the rejection of climate and emissions regulation. That defensive political activity continued in the campaigns against carbon pricing under the Rudd and Gillard Labor governments (2007-2013) and the following nine years of conservative rule. Indeed, under the current Albanese Labor government (2022-present) fossil fuel interests in gas and coal continue to have significant influence over energy and climate policy.

This influence has been achieved through various practices, such as lobbying, networking, and industry association representation. This has involved direct representations by corporate executives and paid lobbyists to senior government ministers and bureaucrats or more informal interactions in the halls of parliament. Here, coal and gas representatives stress their role as creators of public value through employment, revenue for public coffers and broader economic growth. Financial donations have further amplified political influence, with fossil fuel corporations donating close to AU$4 million to Australia’s major political parties during 2024-25 which included the last Federal Election.

The blurring divide between politics and the fossil fuel industry is particularly evident in the social embeddedness of industry representatives and executives within the political sphere. This involves personal and professional relationships. A common theme here has been the concept of a “revolving door” between industry and government. For example, several reports have listed the career trajectories of retiring politicians and bureaucrats as they move into senior industry and consulting roles, as well as industry representatives taking up political advisory appointments. This inter-connectedness of industry and politics has included both major political parties, highlighting a strong capital-state nexus that is committed to the continued expansion of fossil energy resources.

This close “understanding” between different levels of government and the fossil fuel sector is often explicitly highlighted in the public statements of politicians expressing their loyalty to the resources sector. Here, politicians depict the industry as the backbone of the Australian success story and deserving of a seat at the table. Examples have included: advocating for the appointment of a former resources minister to chair a peak mining industry association; the federal treasurer displaying a lump of coal in the parliament and declaring its national benefits; and a former minister for resources posting a heartfelt note of farewell to the Australian mining sector on Facebook. As one interviewee in our research acknowledged: “Yes, there is a revolving door of consultants and management personnel between ministerial offices and industry groups, and companies. There always has been!”

Winning Hearts and Minds

More broadly, the fossil fuel industry has been central to the shaping of public attitudes and understandings of economic development and national identity. For instance, as the CEO of coal giant Peabody Energy declared in promoting the continued expansion of the Australian coal industry: “Coal has transformed society over hundreds of years by fueling industrial revolutions and digital economies. It’s the pride of Australia’s past, and the pride of its future.”

In its public relations, the industry has sought to bring together a range of discourses on how coal and gas underpins the collective welfare of Australia. This has included arguments about the role of coal-fired power in providing cheap and reliable electricity, the economic contribution of export earnings and mining royalties, and employment and job creation. For instance, many of the industry’s public statements have for years stressed the way in which fossil fuel extraction is one of the nation’s highest export earners and contributes to the collective good through mining royalties and tax revenue which contribute to the provision of essential government services.

Despite being highly capital intensive, coal mining has also been presented as a major source of employment, emphasizing its role in regional development and as a key part of many communities. This focus on local communities, job creation, and regional development has been reinforced through the industry’s advertising and community programs, showcasing local conservation and sustainability programs, profiles of mine workers and their family lives, sponsorship of local sporting teams and schools and hospitals, Indigenous employment programs, and “education” programs promoting the benefits of fossil fuel energy. As critics have noted, these practices act as a form of “inoculation PR” aimed at defusing more negative perceptions of the industry and winning over the hearts and minds of local communities and the general public to the worthiness of fossil fuel extraction.

The Magical Thinking of a Fossil-fueled Future

In a context of growing public concern over worsening climate change, the fossil fuel industry has sought to highlight its current benefits and also project an image of the future in which it continues to grow. Despite the rapidly declining cost of renewable energy and growing global moves towards decarbonization, the coal and gas industries and aligned politicians have sought to promote a “fossil fuels forever” imaginary.

This has involved asserting the central role of coal and gas in the economic response to the COVID-19 pandemic as well as technological innovation and the need for energy security. Examples have included the framing of Australia’s export gas industry as a “transition fuel” in contributing to global emissions reductions, as well as the coal industry’s on-going promotion of so-called “clean coal” via phantom technologies such as carbon capture and storage. In response, state and federal politicians have continued to talk up the future of fossil energy, and new coal and gas projects continue to be green-lit.

Despite decades of political debate over climate and energy policy, Australia’s role as a major fossil energy producer remains unchanged. As current and future generations watch a world unravelling under the weight of ever worsening climate disruption, the legacy of the fossil-fuel industry’s outsized influence on the failure to decarbonize weighs heavily.

title: How to Fix South Korea-Ukraine Relations
description: Clear ground rules could not only help resolve the North Korean POW standoff but prevent the next case.
text:
The transfer of two North Korean soldiers to South Korea was intended to be a quiet diplomatic success. Ukraine captured them in January 2025 while they were fighting for Russia in the Kursk region. After months of bilateral talks, they arrived in South Korea in mid-September. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced the transfer at the U.N. General Assembly on September 23. That started a spat that culminated in South Korea recalling its ambassador to Ukraine on October 8, its first protest recall since 2008.

Seoul is still demanding acknowledgment and an apology, while Kyiv considers the matter closed. On October 20, Seoul announced plans to withdraw roughly half its embassy personnel, citing what it described as Ukraine’s failure to take constructive steps to resolve the dispute.

Ukraine had a clear strategic interest in drawing the world’s attention to North Korea’s participation in Russia’s war. Instead, the episode exposed something else: a lack of sufficiently clear ground rules for managing the sensitive political consequences of South Korea-Ukraine cooperation.

Nearly a month after Zelenskyy’s revelation, the two governments still can’t agree on what they agreed on in terms of confidentiality. Seoul says confidentiality governed the talks from the start, even though no formal nondisclosure document was signed. It says internal records support that account and that it told Kyiv before Zelenskyy’s speech not to breach the understanding. Kyiv initially denied that a confidentiality agreement existed; Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha later said the dispute stemmed from differing interpretations of the confidentiality requirements at various stages of the transfer.

Sybiha’s explanation points to the more useful lesson. An informal diplomatic understanding is not inherently defective, but whatever understandings and consultation process existed were not enough to prevent the disclosure dispute. Seoul had substantial reasons for discretion, including possible risks to the soldiers and their relatives who remain in North Korea. Ukraine had strong motives for publicity: North Korean troops are participating in the ongoing Russia-Ukraine war, and more are expected to arrive on the frontlines.

South Korea’s intelligence service has also told lawmakers that Ukraine originally requested secrecy, partly because the transfer of North Korean POWs could invite criticism that Ukraine had forgone a possible prisoner-exchange opportunity. If that account is correct, the incentives for secrecy and publicity shifted over time. Agreements that must survive shifting incentives need to be written down.

Of course, given the lack of clarity around confidentiality, Kyiv should have consulted with Seoul rather than proceeding with a public announcement. South Korea was justified in demanding an explanation and safeguards to prevent a recurrence. Ukraine later sent language that South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun said contained an apology, but Seoul deemed it insufficient. Kyiv later declared the controversy closed.

For now, the two governments are stuck defending incompatible accounts of the past. What they should be doing is figuring out how to handle the next case.

The deeper problem is that the issues passing through their bilateral channels have evolved faster than the practices for handling them. To give an idea of the robustness – or lack thereof – of bilateral mechanisms before Russia’s invasion, the eighth round of foreign ministry political consultations in 2019 came after a seven-year gap and focused largely on conventional bilateral diplomacy.

As recently as September 16, a week before Zelenskyy’s speech, Ukrainian officials were discussing reviving those consultations. But the older platforms for discussion aren’t fit for purpose anymore. After North Korean troops entered Russia’s war, Zelenskyy and then-South Korean President Yoon Suk-yeol agreed in October 2024 to intensify intelligence and expertise exchanges. Their foreign ministers have discussed battlefield conditions, North Korean prisoners, and Russia-North Korea military cooperation. In 2019, they were talking about “trade, investment, science, technology, and agriculture” – far less sensitive topics.

That means the same questions are likely to recur in South Korea-Ukraine relations. Ukrainian forces encounter North Korean troops and weapons in combat; South Korea wants to know what those encounters reveal about tactics, missile performance, battlefield adaptation, and Russian assistance. Future cases could involve another prisoner, captured equipment, debriefing materials, sanctions intelligence, or evidence of Russian technology transfers. Each could raise the same basic questions: what information is jointly sensitive, who may disclose it, and what happens if the other government objects?

Ukraine’s foreign minister has called the two countries “natural allies,” but Seoul has not adopted Kyiv’s strategic position toward Russia and continues to withhold direct lethal assistance. Seoul has its own reasons to preserve diplomatic space with Moscow and Pyongyang. The two governments do not need identical interests, but they do need ground rules for handling the information they are already sharing.

First, South Korea and Ukraine should define confidentiality in writing. For jointly handled information or information shared under agreed restrictions, the two governments should document what is protected, how long the restriction applies, and who may authorize disclosure. In the POW spat, Kyiv’s first response was to deny that any agreement existed; a written text would have clearly established the existence and scope of any commitment.

Second, an objection should trigger a defined escalation process. Advance notice was insufficient in the POW case. Kyiv warned that Zelenskyy would speak at the U.N. and might raise the case, and Seoul responded by objecting to public disclosure. But the speech went ahead, even though the disagreement remained unresolved. Future cases should require another round of consultation when either government objects to disclosure – first among the officials handling the issue and, if necessary, between senior political offices. That would not guarantee compromise, nor should it give either government an indefinite veto over the other’s public statements. It would move the disagreement to a point where compromise remains possible.

Third, South Korea and Ukraine need to give Russia-North Korea security cooperation a standing, quiet place within the bilateral relationship. If Seoul and Kyiv do revive their political consultations, those talks should include a regular security track to compare assessments of North Korean battlefield performance, weapons, Russian assistance, North Korean personnel returning from the war, and other lessons relevant to the Korean Peninsula. Their existing intelligence and expertise exchanges should feed into this track.

The point is continuity: officials should not have to rebuild priorities, contacts, and disclosure boundaries every time a new incident forces the issue. The same track should host the written terms and escalation contacts, so officials who know one another can try to resolve an objection before it reaches the leaders.

These principles could help resolve the current standoff. Seoul wants Ukraine to acknowledge that confidentiality was part of the talks; Kyiv maintains that there was never a firm agreement. A possible compromise would acknowledge that confidentiality was discussed, that the two sides understood its scope differently, and that future sensitive cases will use written terms and a defined consultation process before any disclosure. The first two elements broadly align with Sybiha’s own formula, so the statement would ask Kyiv to concede less than it may seem.

Ukraine could also express regret for any added risk to soldiers’ relatives. That would differ from the regret Kyiv’s Foreign Ministry has expressed so far, which focused on the dispute’s escalation into public criticism, and would give Seoul something closer to the acknowledgment it has sought. Such a statement would not require Seoul to abandon its account of the negotiations or Kyiv to admit a deliberate breach. Three European governments have reportedly offered to help ease tensions, suggesting that outside assistance may be available.

Even as Seoul reduces its diplomatic presence in Kyiv, it says humanitarian and reconstruction support for Ukraine will continue. Still, the expanding confrontation shows how difficult it can be to keep one grievance from overshadowing broader cooperation. Ground rules will not eliminate the larger differences between the two governments – Seoul’s interest in preserving room for dialogue with Pyongyang and Kyiv’s in exposing North Korea’s role in the war – and leaders can always ignore procedures. But a written agreement and clear procedures for handling disclosure will help head off similar cases before they erupt into public view.

Russia and North Korea have built a partnership suited to the war they are now fighting together. Seoul and Kyiv don’t need a formal alliance, but they do need better channels to handle the sensitive information that’s now a part of their partnership: the next prisoner, the next captured weapon, the next intelligence finding, and the next disagreement over who gets to tell the world.

title: In a Diplomatic Shift, Malaysian PM Hosts Myanmar’s Min Aung Hlaing
description: While the talks focused on the repatriation of refugees, Anwar also appeared to endorse Myanmar's reintegration into ASEAN.
text:
Malaysia’s Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim met today with Myanmar’s military-appointed leader Min Aung Hlaing, pledging to work for Myanmar’s reintegration with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).

Min Aung Hlaing arrived in Myanmar yesterday evening for a two-day visit, part of a campaign of diplomatic outreach aimed at shoring up key diplomatic partnerships normalizing his country’s relationship with the Southeast Asian bloc.

After being granted an official welcome at the Perdana Putra Complex in Putrajaya this morning, Min Aung Hlaing held a one-on-one meeting with Anwar, the Malaysian state news agency Bernama reported. This was followed by a meeting involving senior ministers and officials from both countries. Min Aung Hlaing also spoke to Malaysian business leaders late yesterday, urging them to invest in his country.

In a post on X after the meeting, Anwar said that his half-hour discussion with Min Aung Hlaing “focused on the plight of Myanmar refugees in Malaysia and the prospects for their voluntary, safe and dignified return, regardless of ethnicity.” He added, “I believe direct dialogue and negotiations with President Aung Hlaing and Myanmar’s leadership are essential to securing a lasting resolution.”

Both Anwar and the Malaysian Ministry of Foreign Affairs had previously indicated that this would be a primary point of discussion. The two nations recently agreed to the repatriation of around 5,000 Myanmar nationals currently being held in Malaysian immigration detention centers. The first batch of 1,476 people departed Malaysia via ship on September 29.

Speaking to the press after the meeting, however, Anwar suggested that his engagement with Myanmar extended beyond the refugee issue. Indeed, according to Reuters, he said his government had ongoing concerns about the situation in Myanmar but was willing to respect outstanding differences. He also appeared to endorse the normalization of Myanmar’s relations with ASEAN, , which has excluded Myanmar from its summits since late 2021, for its lack of effort to implement its Five-Point Consensus conflict resolution plan.

“I would say that we and our part in Malaysia, will do whatever is possible to make sure that we enhance this collaboration and ultimately, take ​Myanmar as part of ​our community of ⁠nations, without prejudice, and particularly in the context of ASEAN,” Anwar said. According to Bernama, Anwar also “welcomed Myanmar’s efforts to pursue reforms and policy adjustments aimed at addressing the country’s complex challenges.”

Malaysia is the fifth member state of ASEAN to host Min Aung Hlaing since he took office as president in April, after trips to Laos, Thailand, Cambodia, and Vietnam. It is also the first nation from maritime Southeast Asia to take such a step.

The visit marks a significant diplomatic shift for Malaysia, which had previously been among the ASEAN member states most critical of the military coup of 2021. Speaking last month, Anwar justified the invitation to Min Aung Hlaing on the basis that Malaysia needed an authority to negotiate with on returning Myanmar nationals who he claimed were in Malaysia illegally.

This has become a pressing domestic political issue for Anwar this year, due to the growing public hostility toward Myanmar asylum seekers, particularly Rohingya Muslims. Large numbers of Rohingya have come to the country since 2017, when the Myanmar military launched an ethnic cleansing campaign that pushed more than 740,000 from their homes in Rakhine State into Bangladesh. Around 126,000 Rohingya asylum seekers are currently registered with the U.N. refugee agency in Kuala Lumpur, around half of the agency’s total. Both Anwar and his government have claimed that the refugees have become a financial burden, a security risk, and a source of social discord.

Needless to say, Anwar has drawn heavy criticism both for acquiescing to the repatriation of refugees to a country still wracked by civil war, and for hosting Min Aung Hlaing, whose policies prompted many refugees to flee the country in the first place.

In a statement, the Burmese Rohingya Organization U.K. noted that Min Aung Hlaing is the subject of an international arrest warrant by the Argentine Federal Court for genocide and crimes against humanity allegedly committed against the Rohingya between 2012 and 2017. It urged Anwar to order Myanmar’s arrest on the Argentine warrant, stating that “he belongs on trial, not on a red carpet.”

The Malaysian Foreign Ministry said in a statement yesterday that Anwar’s engagement with Min Aung Hlaing was consistent with the principles of the Five-Point Consensus, and that it followed a decision made by ASEAN at its last summit “to continue constructive and principled engagement with Myanmar.” During bilateral meetings between the Malaysian and Myanmar delegations today, Anwar also said that he emphasized “the importance of inclusive dialogue to realize peace and reconciliation efforts in Myanmar” and expressed Malaysia’s “readiness to facilitate this process towards sustainable peace.”

Interestingly, when Min Aung Hlaing spoke at the joint press conference in Putrajaya, he said that his administration would only take back refugees who were confirmed to have Myanmar citizenship. As Jonathan Head of the BBC noted on X, this effectively rules out most Rohingya, who have been denied citizenship by successive Myanmar governments.

While this is in some ways good news – civil society groups have expressed concern that any Rohingya returned to the country could be confined to ghettos in Rakhine State or conscripted into the military – it does raise the question of whether Anwar’s outreach to Min Aung Hlaing, and the reorientation of Malaysia’s policy toward Myanmar, will address its stated domestic political purpose.

In any event, the fact that Malaysia, previously the ASEAN state that was most outspoken about Myanmar, has accorded de facto recognition to Min Aung Hlaing’s quasi-civilian government suggests that full normalization with the bloc is likely just a matter of time.

title: In Confronting China, The West Needs Partners in Southeast Asia
description: A plan to confront Beijing without subsequent outreach toward Southeast Asian countries will sacrifice national imperatives for willing partners, and those are hard to come by.
text:
Leaders from across Southeast Asia will be meeting in Manila on November 10 for the upcoming ASEAN summit. This is the same date on which the China-U.S. trade truce was set to expire. While the September 24 summit between Presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump has widely been characterized as “heavy on pomp and light on substance,” it did deliver one tangible benefit: more time. The extension of the trade truce offers Washington a modicum of breathing room. With that extra time, engaging leaders at the ASEAN summit should be top of the U.S. priority list.

Meanwhile, Europe is signaling a greater willingness to confront China’s unsustainable trading practices. The limits of this relationship must be managed, so that Western countries can reindustrialize and regain market share. However, that effort should not come at the cost of compromising economic partnerships with countries in Asia.

Since 2020, ASEAN and China have been each other’s largest trading partner. Furthermore, Southeast Asian countries have come to rely heavily on China as a provider of intermediate goods. Economic partners in Asia are restrained in their options; for them, some form of relationship with Beijing remains unavoidable. Thus, as the West seeks to shift its relationship with Beijing, it must not do so at the cost of Southeast Asian countries who are willing to cooperate toward a fairer global trade picture.

The U.S. and European position is valid. China is fully integrated into the global economy, and continues to be a manufacturing powerhouse. Problematically, however, Beijing seems to have abandoned its attempts at fixing its domestic consumption issues, as it also looks ahead to an impending demographic crisis. While the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) may outwardly project that it can sustain a globally competitive manufacturing sector, analysis of its economic outlook reflects that Beijing is far more restrained in the kind of development it can pursue. Crucially, however, China’s massive trade imbalance is likely a symptom of internal factors, and not a concerted policy objective.

The CCP’s legitimacy continues to be derived, in large part, from its ability to guarantee domestic economic prosperity. As such, the regime’s targeted growth rates can be observed as a political goal, with overarching implications for the economy. In past years, to achieve a consistent 5 percent growth rate, Beijing has leveraged subsidies and targeted sectoral investments, while growing its exports. The net effect of these policies has resulted in a competition crisis marked by diminishing returns amongst different industries, which is further compounded by the problem of weak domestic consumption. A less ambitious growth target this year, coupled with Xi’s call for “high-quality growth,” signals that there is pressure to restructure aspects of the economy.

Further, in the context of both global and regional trade, Beijing itself has shown an unwillingness to keep trade relationships entirely separate from its political ambitions. A study of China’s relationship with trading partners, published in 2020, has revealed a trend of politicization over time. Researchers considered the case of China-U.S. trade, and their findings were intriguing: “A positive shock to America’s exports to China leads to persistently worse relations with China… It stands to reason that Chinese officials genuinely do feel that China’s relations with the U.S. worsen when the U.S. increases its exports to China.”

Trade activities themselves are not necessarily immune from political effect, and Chinese officials are sensitive to greater market penetration by foreign countries. In effect, this also demonstrates Beijing’s unwillingness to work toward a balanced trading relationship, and its preference for exporting more than it consumes, unless it is importing energy and commodities.

Southeast Asian countries have no choice but to confront this reality. Despite Beijing’s territorial claims in the South China Sea, China’s neighboring states continue to seek agreement on economic issues where it is possible. Interdependence runs deep, as evidenced by China’s $296 billion trade surplus with ASEAN in 2025. There is simply no other option for Southeast Asian countries seeking to move up the global value chain.

This does not mean that these countries are unaware of Beijing’s coercion, or that they are not responding. Yet, with few international options, they are exposed to Beijing’s attempts at intertwining foreign aid with its regional ambitions. To that end, while simultaneously increasing its trade surpluses, China has also created parallel institutions such as the Belt and Road Initiative, the Silk Road Fund, and the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, which have been used as leverage to reward countries that support its political objectives.

It is a fundamentally positive development that the West is looking to take a stronger stance against China’s global trading practices, in pursuit of a more balanced relationship. This position opens the door to Western reindustrialization and stimulates a push for innovation, while harboring high domestic political support within democracies. However, both Washington and Brussels must not lose sight of the constrained position of Southeast Asian countries, which rely on Chinese intermediate goods to develop and rise within the global value chain. A plan to confront Beijing without subsequent outreach toward these same countries will sacrifice national imperatives for willing partners; and those are hard to come by.

For Brussels, an alternative would be its accession to the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP), with the goal of stimulating market access between the West and its Southeast Asian partners. For Washington, the fact that it has become ASEAN’s largest export market is a positive step, but subsequent policies should seek to displace China as the supplier of intermediate goods without punishing Southeast Asian countries seeking to develop away from Beijing.
tag: China-EU trade talks; China-Southeast Asia trade; U.S. Southeast Asia policy; U.S.-China trade dispute

title: Inaccessible by Design: AIIB’s Complaint Mechanism
description: The Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank has yet to approve a single complaint involving its projects for dispute resolution or compliance review.
text:
On September 28, the first day of the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB)’s annual meeting in Doha, 108 Indigenous people from Lombok, Indonesia, filed a complaint with the bank’s grievance body, the Project-affected People’s Mechanism (PPM). They said the AIIB-financed Mandalika Urban and Tourism Infrastructure Project forced them from their homes, took their farming land, cost them their livelihoods, and ignored their right to be consulted. Many now struggle to make ends meet and fear future evictions.

Headquartered in Beijing, with China its largest shareholder, the AIIB began operations in 2016. In a decade, it has grown to 111 members and invested almost $70 billion in more than 350 projects across 40 economies. At the Doha meeting, AIIB President Zou Jiayi announced plans to double its annual financing to about $20 billion by 2030. A growing footprint in Asia and beyond demands an accountability and risk management system to match.

Like its peer multilateral development banks (MDBs), the AIIB has committed to “do no harm” and to offer people a route to seek redress when its projects cause harm. Independent accountability mechanisms, separate from bank management, exist at most MDBs and other development finance institutions. Complaints pass through an initial screening stage, known as admissibility, eligibility, or registration, to establish whether they fall within the mechanism’s mandate. The mechanism then offers dispute resolution or, if parties do not agree to it, examines whether the bank followed its environmental and social rules through a compliance review.

Complaints Hit an Admissibility Wall

Communities affected by AIIB-financed projects have never been able to test whether the PPM process works. Since the mechanism’s creation in 2019, none of the 45 complaints tracked on its website as of September 15 this year had passed the admissibility stage. By contrast, peer mechanisms at other development banks regularly take complaints into dispute resolution or compliance review. One of the largest handled more than 60 cases in each of the last two financial years.

The revised policy introduced in 2026 raised hopes that the PPM would become more effective and improve its track record. Since it took effect, however, the PPM has found 14 out of 16 complaints inadmissible. The remaining two, submitted in May, are still awaiting an admissibility decision. The Mandalika complaint would be the 17th complaint of 2026.

The PPM’s entry requirements are significantly more restrictive than those of its peers. These “roadblocks to accountability” include referring complaints about co-financed projects to the lead lender, imposing narrow time limits on complaints about loans to governments, and requiring prior “good-faith efforts” to resolve grievances with both the project-level grievance mechanism and bank management.

Complainants must also establish at the admissibility stage that their complaint concerns the AIIB’s failure to comply with its policies, while the complaint mechanism must conduct an assessment that other mechanisms carry out only in later steps.

A central obstacle to accessibility is the requirement that complainants make “good-faith efforts” with both the project-level grievance mechanism and AIIB management. Under the PPM policy, complainants must explain why they could not resolve their concerns through these channels, and the PPM decides whether their efforts were sufficient.

The rule has previously been used to reject complaints, including one regarding the Bhola gas power plant in Bangladesh, despite attempts to engage amid legitimate constraints and fears of retaliation. The two complaints filed in May 2026 remain pending while complainants have been asked to engage with the client and management.

Requiring prior engagement at both levels is unique among these mechanisms. Some peers require good-faith efforts with bank management, but not with the project-level grievance mechanism as well. Nor do they require complainants to explain why those efforts failed. The PPM’s approach places that burden on the people seeking redress.

There are legitimate reasons why such engagement may be impossible. A client’s grievance mechanism may be inaccessible or ineffective. The client or management may refuse to engage meaningfully. Restrictions on movement and the threat of retaliation can create further barriers. In many of the AIIB’s borrowing countries, restrictive civic space makes these risks particularly acute.

The PPM policy lists risks of retaliation against complainants as a factor allowing the PPM to accept a complaint despite the absence of engagement with client and management. That provision has yet to be tested. It will only work only if the PPM trusts complainants’ accounts of why they could go no further and considers all relevant circumstances, including the risks they face. The Mandalika complaint will be an important test, as communities report continuing and increasing attempts at retaliation.

For complaints seeking a compliance review, the threshold is higher still. In addition to meeting the general criteria, they must relate their claim to the AIIB’s noncompliance with its environmental and social policy. The policy excludes complaints relating to actions “that do not involve AIIB’s failure to comply.”

As we understand the rules, complainants must show the bank’s noncompliance at the outset and, on the strictest reading, that it caused their harm. The evidence for this sits in AIIB’s due diligence and supervision records, which communities cannot see. They cannot know whether the AIIB checked a resettlement plan or what its staff found on supervision visits. Establishing these facts is the purpose of an investigation. Unlike most of its peers, the PPM asks complainants to supply evidence that the mechanism itself should establish.

These restrictions raise doubts about whether any complaint could qualify for compliance review under a strict interpretation of the criteria. Without a compliance review there are no findings: nothing to establish what went wrong, to support remediation for affected communities, or to help the bank improve its procedures and practices.

An Opportunity to Change Course

These technical restrictions run counter to a simple principle: admissibility is a straightforward step to establish whether a complaint falls within the mechanism’s mandate. At peer mechanisms, apart from formal exclusions, the substantive screening focuses on the complaint’s connection to a bank-financed project and its environmental and social policies, and on indications of actual or potential harm. Detailed examination comes later.

In a compliance review for instance, the mechanism must investigate whether the bank failed to comply with its policies and whether those failures relate to the alleged harm. That work can involve reviewing hundreds of project preparation and supervision documents, conducting field visits, and consulting intensely with affected people and other stakeholders. The admissibility phase is not the place for such an investigation.

Yet the PPM Policy and Rules of Procedure complicate this initial step, impose unduly strict restrictions, and demand substantial work from both complainants and the mechanism before a case can proceed. It is little surprise that no complaint has cleared this hurdle.

At the AIIB’s annual meeting, Zou spoke of infrastructure “connecting people to opportunities” and of “people-centered development.” Carmen Nonay, the new managing director of AIIB’s Complaints-resolution, Evaluation, and Integrity Unit, which includes the PPM, can help turn that vision into practice by bringing the mechanism into line with its peers. There are 22 other mechanisms with established practices to learn from.

The managing director has the authority and responsibility to interpret the PPM’s Rules of Procedure. The pending complaints offer an immediate opportunity to do so. We urge her to apply the policy and rules in line with established accountability practice: treat admissibility as a quick, straightforward first step; trust complainants’ accounts of their efforts and the risks they face; and hear them impartially before making a decision. The PPM should use its unrestricted access to management information to identify indications of noncompliance, rather than place that burden on complainants. This approach follows the PPM peers’ shared principles, reiterated this year, which put accessibility first: “A recourse mechanism is not effective if affected people do not know it exists or are unable to access its services.”

Because the PPM sits within the institution it reviews, its managing director may not feel sufficiently independent to pursue this approach. The AIIB board should make it clear that it expects the mechanism to follow its peers’ good practice. If the PPM still struggles to deliver on its mandate, the board should review the obstacles and require changes to the policy, particularly its accessibility provisions.

Almost eight years after the PPM’s creation, workers and communities affected by AIIB-financed projects deserve the same care and accountability as those affected by other MDBs. That is a matter of fairness and credibility for the AIIB and its shareholders. An accessible, effective complaints mechanism would strengthen the bank’s reputation and its ability to finance development sustainably.

title: Indian Family Offices Eye Southeast Asia’s Startups
description: Patient capital, real risk.
text:
India’s family offices are becoming a significant force in the global economy. According to a report by The Economic Times and market intelligence firm 1Lattice, the country now hosts more than 300 family offices managing over $30 billion in assets. High-net-worth families with more than $30 million in assets are projected to nearly double, from 16,000 in 2025 to 26,000 by 2030, with intergenerational wealth transfer reaching $1.3-1.5 trillion over the next decade. A generational shift is underway as well, with over half of family offices now featuring millennials or Gen Z members in investment decisions.

The rise of younger generations has helped precipitate a change for Indian family office investment strategy: roughly 30% now favor startup allocations in healthtech, fintech, and AI, versus traditional investments such as real estate and gold. According to Tracxn data cited by CNA, family office-backed startup funding nearly doubled to $1.62 billion in 2024 from $876.7 million the year before. Analysts attribute this shift to family offices’ “patient capital” — funds without the eight-to-ten-year return pressure that constrains institutional VC — making them attractive to founders navigating longer development cycles. Cases like Sattva Group’s family office (which diversified from real estate into tech, backing firms like InCred) and Artha India Ventures (an early Oyo investor) illustrate the trend. Geopolitical volatility has reinforced the appeal of relationship-led capital, though PwC’s Falguni Shah notes governance and intrafamily alignment remain key challenges as these offices scale.

One notable growth trend among Indian family offices is the rise of impact investing, those made to achieve measurable social or environmental outcomes alongside financial returns, distinct from pure philanthropy and blended finance. Between 2021 and 2024, 923 unique HNW families made impact investments, with 86 investing through formal family office structures. Climate-tech has emerged as a leading sector, along with financial inclusion platforms and healthcare. While engagement is still early-stage and often exploratory, it signals a meaningful shift toward more value-based capital deployment among India’s wealthiest families.

Continue reading for free at The Diplomat’s new companion publication, The Investor.

title: Indian IT Companies Are in Trump’s Crosshairs
description: Top companies like Infosys, Wipro, and Cognizant will not be able to apply for green cards for H-1B visa workers.
text:
U.S. President Donald Trump is pressing home the advantage, as they say in sports. After showcasing the biggest advertisement for his stiff tariff policy against India — the Essar Group’s American subsidiary announcing an $18-billion investment in a U.S. steel project — Trump is going full throttle. This time, the target was Indian information technology (IT) companies.

On October 8, the U.S. suspended several companies from the Permanent Labor Certification Program, which allows firms to apply for green cards for H-1B visa workers, saying the practice takes jobs away from Americans. The most affected companies are Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, and HCL.

U.S. Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said the U.S. government would not accept or process any new or pending permanent labor certification applications involving these companies.

U.S. journalist Fareed Zakaria said that Trump, a real estate developer, assesses who holds more leverage and pushes as hard and publicly as possible to dominate and extract the maximum price. Trump knows very well that the U.S. market is India’s Achilles’ heel.

The United States is a major destination for Indian goods, a crucial market for its IT companies, and an important source of employment opportunities for Indian professionals. Trump is using this leverage. The U.S. president, like the chief minister of any Indian state, is claiming that his tariff policies are bringing investment and manufacturing jobs to the U.S. He is welcoming foreign capital, not foreign labor. Vice President J.D. Vance said that the action was a response to companies abusing the system to hire lower-paid foreign workers at the expense of U.S. workers. His ire was directed at Microsoft, whose CEO, Satya Nadella, is of Indian origin.

According to Microsoft’s diversity data, Asian employees make up approximately 34.9 percent of Microsoft’s overall workforce. Some say a major chunk of this comprises Indians. This is why Vance lashed out at Microsoft, saying the company had abused the H-1B visa system to replace laid-off American citizens with foreign workers. He asserted that “no company in the United States, unfortunately, has abused this system more than Microsoft.”

The pressure is coming from several directions. On September 18, Trump signed a bill that gives him the power to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on goods from countries that continue to buy Russian oil and natural gas. India is one of the world’s biggest importers of Russian oil.

One reason why India has avoided taking a confrontational position is that the United States is the only country with which India has a trade surplus, unlike China and Russia. India recorded a goods trade surplus of nearly $34 billion with the U.S., while the U.S. goods trade deficit with India reached $58.4 billion in 2025.

Trump has frequently criticized this imbalance, saying it has been “one-sided for years.” Trump argues that while India sells “massive amounts of goods” to the U.S., its largest client, high tariffs prevent reciprocal access for American companies. He has used the threat of tariffs to pressure India into opening its heavily protected domestic markets, such as its agricultural and automobile sectors, to American companies.

This is where Zakaria’s real estate analogy becomes particularly relevant. Trump has several points of leverage. But the question is: how far can India go in reducing the trade imbalance?

Indian Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman’s statement in this regard is very significant. She said that trade talks with the U.S. had reached a plateau “beyond which giving or taking might be very, very difficult.”

This is the first time India has admitted to the pressure being exerted by the Trump administration.

Sitharaman said the U.S. wants to “reduce” its trade imbalance with India and wants to make up “for all that they’ve lost over these years.”

“When you’re talking of trade and trade imbalance being the sole criteria to reduce the imbalance, to what extent beyond negotiation can you go?” Sitharaman said.

This plateau has become a sort of war of attrition between India and the United States. How long it will continue, only time can tell. But the longer the stalemate persists, the greater the economic costs for both countries.
