title: India’s Energy Transition Is Complicated, But Progressing
description: While coal continues to dominate India’s power supply, the country is also building clean energy at one of the fastest rates in the world.
text:
Across Western climate commentary, India is frequently portrayed as a coal-dependent laggard whose rising emissions threaten to offset progress elsewhere. This framing obscures a more complex reality: While coal continues to dominate India’s power supply, the country is also building clean energy at one of the fastest rates in the world. Understanding this contradiction requires reassessing how climate progress is conventionally measured.

The concerns behind India’s continued use of coal are real. India recorded the world’s largest absolute rise in emissions in 2024, and thermal power still generates around 70 percent of its electricity. Yet these figures describe where India stands today, not where it is heading.

At the 2015 Paris climate conference, India pledged that 40 percent of its installed power capacity would come from non-fossil fuel sources by 2030. It reached that goal in November 2021, almost a decade early. After raising its target to 50 percent, India crossed that threshold in June 2025, this time five years ahead of schedule.

As those figures suggest, India’s renewables expansion is significant. India’s non-fossil fuel energy capacity passed 300 gigawatts in July 2026, more than half of its total installed capacity. The country added a record 55 gigawatts of clean capacity in the 2025–26 financial year and now ranks third in the world for installed renewable energy. On July 29, 2025, renewables met more than half of India’s electricity demand, a record share and, in the Indian government’s words, “a remarkable sign of change.”

Many of today’s high-income economies industrialized on coal for over a century before shifting to cleaner energy. India is attempting to do both simultaneously, expanding electricity access and industrial growth for 1.4 billion people while building one of the largest clean-energy systems in the world.

Yet significant challenges remain. The largest is the gap between capacity and generation. Although more than half of India’s installed capacity is now non-fossil, these sources produce under a third of the electricity the country consumes. Solar output peaks in the afternoon while demand often peaks in the evening, and the storage and transmission networks needed to bridge this gap are still under construction. Until they are complete, coal will remain the backbone of reliable energy supply.

Rising demand compounds the difficulty. Rapid economic growth, urbanization and more frequent heatwaves are driving up electricity consumption, which is why India’s total emissions continue to climb even as its power mix becomes cleaner. Clean capacity is being added quickly, but demand is rising almost as fast.

Heavy industry presents a further hurdle. Steel and aluminum are among the hardest sectors to decarbonize. Indian exporters now face carbon border rules in key markets; the Global Trade Research Initiative estimated that Indian steel and aluminum exporters may need to cut prices by 15 to 22 percent to remain competitive in Europe. Smaller firms struggle the most with the cost of measuring and reporting emissions.

Finance is the final, perhaps most binding, constraint. A transition of this scale requires enormous investment, much of it in grids and storage with long payback periods. At COP29, India objected to the new climate finance goal of $300 billion a year, which was less than one-fourth of the $1.3 trillion that developing countries had demanded.

Still, India continues to push forward. Its national carbon market became operational in January 2025, providing industry with a price signal to reduce emissions. The growth of India’s fossil fuel emissions is projected to have slowed sharply in 2025.

Energy transitions are rarely linear, as recent Western experience shows. During the 2022 energy crisis, several European countries temporarily returned to coal to maintain supply before renewable growth resumed. This was a reasonable response to an emergency, and it illustrates that every country balances climate goals against energy security and affordability. India faces the same trade-offs at a lower income level and with more people still gaining reliable power.

International partners can also play a constructive role. Expanded financing for grid infrastructure and battery storage would directly address India’s generation gap. Mechanisms that recognize domestic carbon pricing, such as India’s carbon market, could ease the burden of border carbon rules on smaller exporters. The International Solar Alliance, which India co-founded, already offers a strong base for wider cooperation on clean technology and supply chains

Coal will remain part of India’s energy mix for some time, and the obstacles ahead are real. But measuring climate commitment through coal dependence alone risks misreading one of the world’s largest clean-energy transitions.

Assessments of India’s climate performance should therefore shift their focus. Rather than asking whether India still uses coal, the question should be whether it is moving decisively away from it. A fairer yardstick would weigh a country’s direction of travel, per capita emissions, and historical responsibility alongside its current energy mix. After all, the average Indian emits about 2.2 tonnes of carbon dioxide a year, less than half the global average, and India has contributed under 4 percent of cumulative carbon dioxide emissions since the industrial revolution.

Future analysis of India’s climate role should account for both its achievements and the constraints shaping its choices.
tag: India clean energy; India coal industry; India energy policy; India renewable energy

title: India’s Foreign Minister Jaishankar Openly Calls Out the US
description: Previously, India sorted out its differences with friendly nations quietly. Last week, it aired its grievance with Washington publicly.
text:
On September 28, India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi had a telephone conversation with U.S. President Donald Trump to review progress in bilateral cooperation. In a post on X, Modi described the conversation as “productive.” “We reviewed our bilateral cooperation in trade, defence, energy, critical technologies and other areas. We agreed to maintain close engagement to take our Comprehensive Global Strategic Partnership forward,” he said.

While Modi’s post about his conversation with Trump was not negative, it was far less effusive than in the past, even bland. As Yashraj Sharma observed in an article in Al Jazeera, it was a “cold and formal depiction far removed from his description of the US president as a ‘good friend’ in previous years.”

The Trump-Modi phone call came at a time when already fraying bilateral relations hit yet another difficult phase.

Ten days earlier, Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act (SRIA) of 2026, which gives the U.S. president the authority to impose up to 100 percent tariffs on countries that continue to purchase Russian oil and gas. India, which is among the largest buyers of Russian energy, could potentially be impacted.

India-U.S. cooperation has deepened and widened over the past two decades. Despite “complexities,” ties were expected to grow under Trump; the outlook was upbeat.

However, Trump 2.0 has not been good for the partnership. Within weeks of the inauguration of Trump’s second presidential term, ties began unravelling not only over tariffs and immigration but also Washington’s cozying up to Pakistan on a raft of issues, including terrorism, an issue that Delhi is highly sensitive about.

India was among the countries that were hit the hardest by Trump’s “reciprocal tariffs” announced last year. Adding insult to injury, India was then slapped with another 25 percent “punitive tariffs” for buying Russian oil.

Should the U.S. press ahead with imposing SRIA on India, it would hit India’s oil imports and, consequently, its energy security.

Over the past 19 months, although Indians took note of Trump’s abrasive remarks and insensitive tweets, they took it in their stride. The diplomatic establishment seemed to have adopted a patient wait-and-watch policy. India, after all, needed the U.S and benefited from economic and security cooperation with Washington. The current uncertainty was seen as temporary.

However, that mood in Delhi is changing. Its patience with Trump seems to be wearing thin. Officials and analysts are calling on the government to be more realistic in its assessment of the current India-U.S. relationship.

In an article in The Week, Navtej Sarna, a former Indian ambassador to the U.S., wrote: “We need to accept, without caveats, that the relationship has cratered significantly. In America’s eyes, India is not the strategic partner that we believed we were.”

A change is evident not just in Delhi’s mood but also, in its approach.

“India has reached the end of its tether with Trump,” a former official in India’s MEA told The Diplomat. “In the past we abhorred megaphone diplomacy, preferring to sort out nettlesome issues with friends quietly and only via diplomatic channels. That was India’s approach towards Russia’s intervention in Afghanistan in 1979, and its invasion in Ukraine in 2022, for example. But that is clearly changing,” he said. “India today is not averse to calling out, even friends, on difficult matters if core concerns are being undermined.”

This change was on full display last week during India’s Minister for External Affairs S. Jaishankar’s visit to the U.S.

At an event at the Asia Society in New York, Jaishankar did not hold back in drawing attention to Washington’s lack of “understanding or appreciation or empathy” for Delhi on issues of concern and sensitivity to the latter. He was referring to Washington’s courting of Pakistan despite the latter’s support for anti-India terrorism. “If one of my primary concerns is not fully appreciated by my partner, then clearly there is an impact of that on the relationship,” he said. Although he did not mention the U.S. by name, it was evident who he was referring to.

Strong India-U.S. relations have enjoyed bipartisan support in the U.S. over the past two decades. Whenever differences surfaced or ties frayed, Indian officials would avoid airing grievances to the media. They seemed willing to bide their time in the hope that this was a mere hiccup, a troubled phase that could be navigated. India being important to the U.S. in its strategy to contain a rising China, it was widely believed that the strategic partnership was solid.

But with the U.S.-China relationship seemingly moving to a phase of competitive coexistence rather than confrontation, India’s role in Washington’s containment strategy against China could decline. As Indian academic Atul Mishra pointed out, “If balancing China is no longer a priority, then India’s importance within America’s strategic calculus goes down.”

Especially after the recent meeting between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, cracks are visible in the once-solid belief that India is important to the U.S. Apprehensions have deepened further amid Trump’s courting of Pakistan.

There are other reasons why the current troubled phase in India-U.S. ties may not be as temporary as Delhi believed over the past year. There is a growing perception that the fraying partnership may survive the end of Trump’s term.

According to Sarna, the current downturn in India-U.S. relations cannot be attributed to Trump alone. “Economic nationalism, racial supremacism, moral poverty, naked aggression and wanton disregard for international law and norms are trends which will outlast Trump; on many issues the centre has moved in American politics,” he argues, pointing out that Trump’s successor, be it U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance or Secretary of State Marco Rubio or even a Democrat politician, “may not be much different [from Trump], though a tad predictable.”

Meanwhile, all eyes in India have turned to India’s Minister of Commerce and Industry Piyush Goyal’s ongoing visit to the U.S. Many rounds of talks have taken place so far, and while India and the U.S. reached a framework for an interim trade agreement in February 2026, a final Bilateral Trade Agreement remains elusive.

Ahead of his U.S. visit, Goyal said that the India-U.S. trade pact was “almost done and dusted.” Should the two sides firm up an agreement soon, that could lighten the gloomy mood in Delhi somewhat. Of course, much will depend on what the final agreement brings India.

An agreement that is heavily weighted against Indian interests can be expected to deepen the prevailing pessimism in Delhi over its ties with the U.S.
tag: Dr S. Jaishankar; India and Trump; India foreign policy; India-US and Pakistan; India-US and terrorism; India-US Relations; India-US trade; Trump 2.0; Trump's tariffs on India

title: Indonesia Needs to Do More to Tackle the Region’s Transboundary Haze Problem
description: Under Prabowo Subianto, leadership on the issue has been lacking – and tens of millions are suffering as a result.
text:
Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto is the key leader in ASEAN who can and should do better in haze management in the coming years. The current haze situation affecting Southeast Asia is, to a certain extent, a reflection of his leadership and management, given that most of it stems from fires happening in his country.

Forests and peatlands in Indonesia have been burning substantially this year and millions of people in Southeast Asia are suffering as a result. In early September, Kuching had the worst air quality of any large city on earth. Malaysian authorities declared a state of emergency in the Serian district of Sarawak, as the Air Pollutant Index exceeded 500. The Philippines closed schools throughout Metro Manila and more than 12 provinces. The regional haze monitor in ASEAN reached level three, the most severe on the scale.

Indonesia needs to improve its leadership on the haze management issue.

Fire has been used to clear land as it is cheaper than alternative methods. Plantations, companies, and farmers burn the vegetation before the planting season, instead of paying for mechanical clearing. The drained peatlands of Sumatra and Kalimantan also get burnt and this adds fuel to the fire. These fires continue for weeks and release even more toxic particles than an ordinary forest fire. Due to the current El Niño climate cycle, there are drier and longer dry seasons, worsening the situation, as experienced in 1997, 2015, and 2019.

The solutions are relatively straightforward. They are to rewet the drained peatland, enforce a moratorium on new plantation permits in forest and peat areas, punish the recalcitrant companies, and publicize their names so they can be held responsible.

Importantly, there needs to be close tracking of fires and smallholder burning, as well as enhanced local fire-response capacity so as to minimize, control, and extinguish fires before they get out of control. Satellite technology can be used to facilitate the tracking too. These pre-emptive and preventive measures, in addition to effective firefighting capabilities, need to be in place to address this haze situation effectively.

There is precedent for effective action. In 2015, during his first term in office, President Joko Widodo encountered the disastrous 2015 fires, during which 2.6 million hectares were burned and more than a hundred million lives were affected. He created the Peatland Restoration Agency that rewetted more than a million hectares of degraded peat. He also set up a standing haze task force. Furthermore, in 2019, he put a permanent moratorium on new peatlands and primary forest permits.

The results were positive. The fires decreased subsequently. For instance, significant fires in 2023 burned about 1.6 million hectares, a decrease of a million acres compared to 2015. Towards the end of Jokowi’s term in 2024, the Ministry of Environment and Forestry reported a 59.4 percent year-on-year drop in hotspots.

This year, President Prabowo visited fire-hit provinces in Sumatra and Kalimantan. He deployed police and military staff on the ground, and in addition to police investigations, he pledged to revoke the permits of guilty companies. However, these efforts may be inadequate. The cumulative hotspots in late July 2026 exceeded the dreadful 2019 numbers. More needs to be done to anticipate and prevent the wildfire problem.

Other than naming the responsible corporations and holding them accountable, there should be the public prosecution of the indicted corporate leaders, open publication of the concession-ownership data and increased resources for peatland wetting, along with enhanced fire-fighting capabilities.

The ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution, signed in 2002, will only work when the Prabowo administration intentionally and effectively implements the full range of effective, preventive, punitive and responsive measures. Prabowo and his government can implement a combination of measures for the well-being of their citizens and the neighboring countries.

Along with the hundreds of millions in Southeast Asia affected by the haze, we share the hope that the Indonesian administration can be more effective and efficient in managing and reducing the causes of the haze problem, which has plagued Southeast Asia over the past month, so that we can all benefit from cleaner, haze-free air again.

title: Indonesia Reduces Gas Supply to Singapore, Citing Domestic Energy Needs
channel_text: ASEAN Beat; Blog; Economy; Southeast Asia
description: Energy Minister Bahlil Lahadalia said last week that Jakarta would prioritize its own needs, and might cut off supplies to nations that did not respect Indonesia.
text:
Indonesia on Saturday began reducing natural gas exports to Singapore in order to divert more supplies to domestic electricity needs, the country’s upstream oil and gas regulator SKK Migas said.

According to reports by Reuters and Channel News Asia, SKK Migas chairman Djoko Siswanto said that the diversion involves 31 million standard cubic feet of gas per day, which would be redirected to meet electricity needs in Batam, Bintan, and Sumatra. This comprises 15 million standard cubic feet of gas per day from Natuna and 16 million from Sumatra, which makes up around 9 percent of Indonesia’s total exports of natural gas to Singapore.

“In order to safeguard the reliability of domestic gas supplies for electricity generation, effective today, gas supplies previously ​destined for Singapore ​are being redirected ⁠for domestic use,” Djoko said, as per Reuters.

The latest cut comes after a series of serious power outages in Indonesia, including a major blackout across at ​least six provinces in Sumatra in May and rolling ‌outages ⁠in Java and Kalimantan in June and July. More recently, the island of Batam in Riau Islands Province was last week hit with a 16-hour power outage.

Singapore is highly dependent on imported gas for electricity generation, generating more than 90 percent of its power from this source. Last year, around 43 percent of the country’s imported gas was shipped by pipeline from Indonesia and Malaysia, with the remaining 57 percent made up of liquefied natural gas shipped by sea.

Despite Singapore’s reliance on Indonesian gas, the reduction is unlikely to have much impact on the country’s electricity supply. Singapore’s Energy Market Authority said on Saturday that the reduction would amount to around 17 billion British thermal units per day over a period of 18 days. This, it said, equated to “less ​than 2 percent of our total daily gas demand.”

Tan See Leng, Singapore’s minister for energy, trade, and industry, said yesterday that Singapore has sufficient gas supply to meet its demand, and was seeking continuously to diversify its sources of gas to guard against any potential future shocks.

“In the short term, the prices would not really affect that much,” he said. “I would like to urge all of our fellow Singaporeans: keep calm and carry on. We have dealt seamlessly with such reductions in the past without any incident, and the government will continue to ensure the reliability and the resilience of Singapore’s energy supply.”

The gas supply cut is consistent with Indonesia’s long-standing policy of prioritizing the use of natural resources for its domestic needs. Under Jakarta’s regime of Domestic Market Obligations, producers of key natural resources and commodities are required to reserve a specific portion of their production for the local market at below-market prices, before being allowed to export the remainder. For instance, in January 2022, the Indonesian government banned coal exports for a month after supplies at domestic power plants ran low.

Indonesia has also banned the export of unprocessed nickel, bauxite and raw copper to encourage companies to refine minerals domestically and boost the local economy.

The gas cut was foreshadowed by Indonesian Energy Minister Bahlil Lahadalia, who told reporters on October 21 that Indonesia would not hesitate to prioritize natural resources for its own domestic needs and that President Prabowo Subianto had ordered Indonesia “to adopt a survival-oriented approach amid geopolitical tensions and global energy challenges,” in the words of the Jakarta Globe.

The following day, he said that the government might also cut off supplies to nations that did not respect Indonesia.

“Don’t come asking for help only when you’re in need, but when other issues that can actually be discussed arrive, act like you have no sense of propriety, like someone who doesn’t know how to conduct yourself properly,” Bahlil said, as per the South China Morning Post.

The minister’s remarks were cryptic, and he made no mention of Singapore, but they come at a time of growing friction between the two neighbors due to the toxic haze resulting from months of Indonesian wildfires, and the recent turbulence in the Indonesian stock market.

In recent weeks, Singaporean citizens have grown increasingly frustrated with the haze, a result of raging forest and peatland fires in Sumatra and Kalimantan, and the apparent inaction of the Indonesian authorities – a sentiment that has not been helped by the defensive statements of some Indonesian officials.

Singapore’s government, too, has begun to express its discontent with Jakarta over the haze, albeit in much more measured language. On October 15, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said that the government was looking into Indonesian companies that could be responsible for the fires in Indonesia, and potentially take action under its Transboundary Haze Pollution Act.

Senior Minister K Shanmugam said on October 19 that Singapore will “sustain pressure” on these companies even after the haze passes. “If companies refuse to cooperate, regardless of whether they have a presence in Singapore or do not have a presence in Singapore, we will use every legal and regulatory lever at our disposal to exert pressure where it matters,” he said.

There have also been tensions related to the recent threat of global index provider MSCI to downgrade Indonesia to “Standalone Market” status due to a lack of transparency in its stock market. The possible downgrade, which was announced on October 16, led to an immediate plunge in the Indonesian stock market, which shed 15 percent of its value over two days of trading.

In the aftermath, Indonesia’s former Trade Minister Muhammad Lutfi claimed on social media last week that the Singaporean state investment firms GIC and Temasek had pressured MSCI to downgrade Indonesia in order to suppress stock prices. The two firms have denied his claims. Prabowo himself responded to the downgrade threat with strident nationalism, claiming that MSCI “intended to intimidate us.”

Prabowo’s two years in office have been marked by increasingly strident nationalism and rhetoric about national self-sufficiency, which have resulted in ever-more overt state involvement in the economy. While this policy may serve to safeguard Indonesia’s domestic energy and food security in the short term, the longer-term impact will be to undermine business confidence and potentially to generate friction with Indonesia’s neighbors. In this particular instance, it is hard to see that Indonesia’s main regional economic partners will begin to look elsewhere for their energy supplies, as indeed, Singapore is already doing.

title: Indonesia Seizes More Than 2 Tons of Narcotics in Major Anti-drug Operations
channel_text: ASEAN Beat; Blog; Security; Southeast Asia
description: In recent years Indonesian waters have become an important route for the trafficking of Golden Triangle drugs to Asian and global markets.
text:
Indonesian authorities have made two major drug busts in Sumatra that led to the seizure of more than 2 tons of ketamine and methamphetamine, authorities said on Friday.

National Police Chief Gen. Suyudi Ario Seto told a press conference that police and customs officers intercepted a ship carrying 1.1 tons of ketamine in the waters off Sumatra on October 20, the AFP news agency reported.

The tanker MT Global 168 was intercepted after intelligence officers detected irregularities in its route through the Malacca Strait and the Andaman Sea. It was then taken to Belawan Port in North Sumatra for inspection.

“From this search operation, the joint team managed to seize illicit drugs in the form of ketamine HCL (hydrochloride). The evidence was found in 58 sacks with a total weight reaching 1.16 tonnes,” Suyudi said, adding that the shipment had an estimated value of 3.48 trillion rupiah ($210 million).

The police chief added that the MT Global 168 flew the Mongolian flag but is owned by a company based in Johor Bahru, Malaysia.

The following day, Suyudi added, in what the National Narcotics Board (BNN) described as a joint operation with the National Narcotics Control Commission of China, Indonesian authorities raided a clandestine drug laboratory in Aceh province’s Pidie regency. There, they seized around 1.2 tons of liquid and crystal methamphetamine, assorted equipment for converting liquid into crystal meth, and arrested 11 suspects, including two Chinese nationals. Authorities put the value of the drugs at around 2.16 trillion rupiah ($119 million).

“The back-to-back operations underscore how Indonesia remains a major target for international drug trafficking organizations,” Suyudi said, as per the Associated Press.

The AP added that Indonesian authorities are investigating possible connections between the meth lab and drug syndicates in China, Malaysia, and Indonesia, as well as criminal groups in the Golden Triangle – the tri-border region between Myanmar, Thailand, and Laos – a region long associated with large-scale narcotics production and trafficking.

The two drug operations, which come after the seizure in August of 1.3 tons of ketamine from a ship near the Riau Islands, reflect the booming state of the illicit drug trade in Southeast Asia.

In its most recent annual report on the Asian synthetic drug market, released in June, the U.N. Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) reported that methamphetamine seizures spiked to a record 349 tons in East and Southeast Asia in 2025, a 48 percent increase over last year’s record of 236 tons. Last year was also notable for a surge in ketamine seizures, which rose to 52.5 tons, a whopping 185 percent increase on 2024’s total.

The majority of last year’s methamphetamine seizures – around 94 percent – occurred in Southeast Asia. As The Diplomat explored in a video last week, most of these narcotics are produced in areas of Myanmar controlled by rebel groups and militias of various stripes. While drug production in Myanmar is nothing new, production and trafficking have spiked since the military coup of 2021.

The resulting conflict, chaos, and economic dysfunction have created lucrative opportunities for criminal syndicates. The civil war has weakened the state’s hold on outlying regions of the country, where most drug production has historically been concentrated, while disrupting law enforcement efforts and heightening the nation’s reliance on drug-related proceeds.

As a result, flows of narcotics from Myanmar have increased in all directions. In its June report, the UNODC noted the increasing trafficking of drugs via maritime routes, for the purposes of “both domestic distribution and transit trafficking to third countries.”

In addition to Indonesia, last year saw record seizures in Thailand, Malaysia, Myanmar, and the Philippines, including numerous multi-ton seizures.

title: Indonesian President Replaces Foreign Minister With Career Diplomat
description: The appointment of Arrmanatha Nasir is likely to result in a reassertion of the Foreign Ministry's role in Indonesian foreign policymaking.
text:
Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto has replaced his foreign minister with a career diplomat, in a cabinet reshuffle that saw more than a dozen other posts change hands.

In yesterday’s reshuffle, Prabowo appointed Arrmanatha Nasir, Indonesia’s former permanent representative to ‌the United Nations in New York, as the country’s new foreign minister. The outgoing foreign minister, Sugiono, was shifted to the post of coordinating minister for human development.

In this latest change to his “Red and White Cabinet,” Prabowo appointed three new coordinating ministers and a new minister of industry. He also reshuffled a handful of deputy ministerial posts and leadership positions at major government agencies, including the National Police and the office of the Ombudsman.

The changeover at the top of Kemlu, however, was the most significant position to change hands, and the second major cabinet change ​in the past few weeks.

In mid-September, Prabowo removed his finance minister, Purbaya Yudhi Sadewa and replaced him with ​his deputy, Suahasil Nazara, amid growing investor concern about Indonesia’s economic trajectory.

Arrmanatha Nasir comes to the post with years of experience, having joined Kemlu in 1997. Since then, he has risen through the ranks, serving as the Ministry’s spokesperson between 2014 and 2019, Indonesia’s ambassador to France (2019-2021) and Indonesia’s ambassador to the U.N. (2021-2024). He was then appointed vice foreign minister when Prabowo took office.

After taking his oath of office yesterday, Arrmanatha said that his priorities included “maintaining ​stability in the region and promoting multilateralism,” Reuters reported.

Arrmanatha’s advent is likely to mark a significant change in the process of Indonesian foreign policymaking. His predecessor Sugiono was a political novice who came to the post with little hands-on experience in foreign affairs. While he served as the deputy head of the parliamentary commission overseeing foreign policy, his main credential was that he had served as deputy chairperson of Prabowo’s Gerindra Party.

Indeed, the appointment of such a junior figure appeared to mark a sharp break from the tenure of outgoing Foreign Minister Retno Marsudi, a career diplomat who had nearly two decades of experience in the diplomatic corps before her appointment as foreign minister in 2014.

The result has been that, in effect, if not in intention, the Foreign Ministry under Sugiono became largely subordinate to the presidential palace. As in the realm of economic policy-making, this has injected a degree of unpredictability into Jakarta’s foreign policy. As Trystanto Sanjaya, visiting fellow at the Norwegian Institute of International Affairs, posted on X, “Under Sugiono’s tenure, Indonesia’s Foreign Policy has been criticized as inconsistent and there has been reports where views of Indonesian diplomats are not considered when making important foreign policy decisions.”

Perhaps the most notable of these instances was the joint statement issued during Prabowo’s visit to Beijing in late 2024, which mentioned that the two countries had “reached important common understanding on joint development in areas of overlapping claims.”

The release of the joint statement was interpreted by some South China Sea watchers as marking a (perhaps unwitting) break from a long-standing Indonesian policy, and was quickly walked back by the Foreign Ministry. At the time, I argued that the incident “may represent less a conscious shift in policy than a cautionary tale about the perils of turning a nation’s foreign relations into a political sinecure.”

Dewi Fortuna Anwar, a foreign policy analyst at Indonesia’s National Research and Innovation Agency, told Reuters that Nasir, who was an “even-keeled” professional, would likely be more assertive in its relationship with the presidential palace. “He can be a foil to Prabowo,” she said.

Trystanto concurred that Nasir’s appointment “can be interpreted as a return to the traditional way of doing business at MoFA where the minister is appointed from within its ranks. However, will there be a return to the usual way of doing business regarding Indonesia’s Foreign Policy?” Given Prabowo’s bull-headed and unilateral style of governance, he wrote, “I am not too optimistic.”

title: Indonesian President Replaces Head of Disaster Management Agency
description: The move comes amid growing scrutiny of Jakarta's response to the forest and peatland fires that have drastically reduced air quality across the region.
text:
Indonesia’s President ​Prabowo Subianto yesterday replaced the head of the country’s disaster management agency in a bid to restore confidence in the government’s ability to bring intensifying land and forest fires under control.

Lt.-Gen. Kristomei Sianturi, 50, was sworn in as the chief of the National Disaster Management Agency (BNPB) at the State Palace in Jakarta, replacing Lt.-Gen. Suharyanto. Speaking after the ceremony, the two-star army general said that Prabowo had given him orders to move as quickly as possible to bring the fires under control.

“The directive is clear: keep pushing forward and start your duties promptly,” he said, according to Kompas. “The target is as soon as possible, because the people are already affected.”

Kristomei said that he would review the BNPB’s response procedures to ensure faster action during disasters and prevent avoidable deaths.

“Responsiveness must be measured in minutes, not hours. That is what we will evaluate going forward, so there are no more unnecessary casualties,” he said.

No official reason was given for Suharyanto’s replacement, but the change came a day after the outgoing BNPB chief’s younger brother was arrested over alleged corruption involving emergency relief funds, the Straits Times reported. The Corruption Eradication Commission said that the investigation centers on BNPB’s ready-to-use emergency funds, which are used to meet urgent needs during disasters, but did not say whether money intended to fight the forest fires was misappropriated.

Kristomei’s appointment – the second major change to Prabowo’s cabinet since the appointment of a new foreign minister on October 1 – is also likely intended to reassure Indonesia’s neighbors that it remains committed to fighting the wildfires that are currently raging on the islands of Borneo and Sumatra. The forest and peatland fires have created a thick toxic haze that has darkened the skies above Indonesia, Singapore, Malaysia, Timor-Leste, Brunei, and parts of the Philippines, forcing school closures and impacting the health of tens of millions of people.

As the haze has persisted, Jakarta has become the focus of increasing criticism for its failure to contain – or prevent – the fires, many of which Indonesian officials admit were lit deliberately to clear agricultural land. As I noted yesterday, Social media users in Malaysia, Singapore, and Indonesia have become increasingly angry at Jakarta’s response to the fires, with some Indonesian netizens even urging Singapore and Malaysia to impose sanctions on their own government.

Meanwhile, politicians in Malaysia have called for Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s government to lodge formal diplomatic complaints with Jakarta, and the country’s foreign minister said that he plans to raise the issue at an upcoming meeting of his ASEAN counterparts.

Yesterday, after air quality readings in some parts of Singapore reached the worst levels in more than a decade, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said that the government was looking into which companies may be responsible for the fires in Indonesia.

“Where warranted, we will take action under Singapore’s Transboundary Haze Pollution Act, and explore joint action with other countries,” he said on social media.

Under the Transboundary Haze Pollution Act, passed in 2014, Singaporean authorities can take legal action against companies responsible for causing or contributing to haze pollution in Singapore, even if their activities take place overseas. History suggests that Singapore will refrain from confronting Indonesia directly over the haze issue, but the fact that Wong raised the prospect of investigations is a sign of the government’s growing frustration with its large neighbor.

Indonesia has announced a number of other measures designed to combat the fires. Prabowo yesterday approved foreign assistance for its fire-fighting efforts, Foreign Minister Arrmanatha Nasir said yesterday. “The president has also given his approval, and discussions are now underway at the technical level. In this case, the technical discussions are being handled by BNPB,” he said at a closed-door meeting.

“What we need to emphasize is that this is a matter of great seriousness and is receiving the President’s direct attention,” Arrmanatha said, although he did not specify which countries had offered assistance or what form the assistance would take.

Also yesterday, the BBC reported that aircraft were deployed to scatter pellets of dry ice (solid carbon dioxide) in the air above South Sumatra province, one of the regions most affected by the haze. Indonesian police have also named more than 200 people and nine companies as suspects in forest and land fire investigations across the country.

Wasisto Raharjo Jati, a political analyst at the National Research and Innovation Agency, told the Straits Times that the fires had “damaged the government’s image” within ASEAN, and that the reappointment of the BNPB head was “certainly part of efforts to restore the government’s image domestically and internationally.”

One way or another, the current fires will come to an end. Whether Indonesia succeeds in winning back the confidence of its neighbors will also depend on whether it puts in place policies and structures that can prevent a recurrence of a similar crisis in future.

title: Indonesian Stock Exchange Plunges After Fresh MSCI Downgrade Threat
description: Citing the lack of action on promised reforms, the global index provider has proposed demoting the country from emerging market to standalone market status.
text:
Indonesia’s stock market fell more than 11 percent on Friday, the steepest one-day drop since 1998, after the global index provider MSCI proposed the country’s removal ‌from its global stock indexes.

In a statement on Friday, MSCI said that it had launched “a consultation on a proposal to reclassify the MSCI Indonesia Indexes from Emerging Market to Standalone Market status.”

The proposal is more serious than MSCI’s earlier threat, announced in January, to downgrade Indonesia from “emerging market” to “frontier market” status due to a number of transparency concerns in its stock market. Chief among these were the high concentration of ownership in certain companies and the limited “free float” of shares – i.e., those openly available for public trading.

On Friday, MSCI again cited “significant concerns regarding the investability of the Indonesian equity market, including persistent opacity in shareholding structures and suspected coordinated trading behavior.”

MSCI said it would procure feedback from market participants until the end of April 2027, and then announce its decision by June 30.

MSCI’s role as the primary benchmark for institutional investors gives it considerable power over emerging economies. As Reuters explains, a downgrade to “standalone” status “would exclude Indonesian stocks from indexes tracked by global funds, potentially triggering billions of dollars in capital outflows.”

Markets responded to the news as one would expect, with the Jakarta Composite Index falling by 11.6 percent, losing $65 billion of value. It was the largest single-day drop since the Asian financial crisis.

After MSCI’s January announcement, which also caused a hemorrhage in Indonesian equity markets, Indonesia announced a long list of reforms to address MSCI’s concerns, including a doubling of the ​minimum free float for listed companies to 15 percent. Top executives of the exchange and regulatory body also ​stepped down.

However, in its statement on Friday, MSCI said that “sufficient progress has not been observed consistently across the Indonesian equity market.”

“Despite the announced reforms, significant concerns remain around market dysfunction, including continued suspected coordinated trading behavior and lack of evidence of meaningful enforcement,” it stated. “Feedback from market participants suggests that a reclassification to Frontier Markets would not properly recognize the depth of the market problems.”

MSCI said that it “expects to proceed with the proposed reclassification” barring clear evidence of “material improvements in market governance and functioning.”

If downgraded, Indonesia would join Argentina, Lebanon, Palestine, Ukraine, and Zimbabwe in the standalone category, becoming both the largest economy and the only Asia-Pacific market in the grouping. MSCI has said that reclassification to “standalone” status is typically done in cases of “severe deterioration in market accessibility or size and liquidity.”

The announcement, which came ahead of MSCI’s expected verdict on Indonesia’s reclassification to “frontier” status next month, came as a shock to many observers. Rully Arya Wisnubroto, head of research at Mirae Asset Sekuritas in Jakarta, told Reuters that the proposal “goes well beyond what we had considered our worst-case scenario.” Another analyst described it as “a wake-up call for Indonesia.”

Reza Priyambada, an analyst and director at Reliance Sekuritas, told the Jakarta Globe that given the reputational impact a downgrade to “standalone” status would have, the government had to act urgently to show it was serious about reform.

“Reforms should not focus solely on market development and the enforcement of sanctions,” he told the paper. “Authorities also need to ensure a level playing field in market mechanisms and address other issues that shape international investors’ assessments of the quality of Indonesia’s capital market.”

If the government fails to stave off a downgrade, it would severely impact Indonesia’s attractiveness as a destination for foreign investment and put significant pressure on President Prabowo Subianto, whose administration has marked a break with the conservative financial stewardship of its predecessors.

Coming to office in late 2024, the former general set an ambitious goal of 8 percent annual GDP growth for the rest of his term, and has introduced a number of high-spending populist policies, including a multibillion-dollar free meal program, that, along with the global spike in fuel prices, have widened the fiscal deficit. Prabowo has also increased the state’s involvement in the Indonesian economy in a bid to maximize the country’s returns from natural resources and international trade.

The president’s pugnacious and highly personalized style of governance, which has affected everything from fiscal policy to foreign relations, is at the root of much investor concern. In March, both Moody’s and Fitch announced ratings outlook downgrades for the country, with the latter citing the “increasing ⁠policy uncertainty and erosion of Indonesia’s policy mix consistency and credibility” and the “growing centralization of policymaking authority.”

Perceptions have also been shaped by the growing sense of volatility and unpredictability in how Indonesian institutions as a whole operate. A good example is the jailing in June of Gojek co-founder Nadiem Makarim, previously a leading member of Indonesia’s tech scene, on flimsy corruption charges related to the procurement of Google Chromebooks during his time as education minister.

As one observer noted at the time, the Nadiem case confirmed many investors’ perception of Indonesia as a country where “the line between a business decision, a policy misjudgment, and a prosecutable offense is drawn after the fact by whoever holds power at the time.”

As a reflection of the general economic malaise, the rupiah has fallen to record lows this year, passing the psychological threshold of 18,000 rupiah to the U.S. dollar in June.

In addition to the aforementioned reforms, the Prabowo administration has reshuffled its economic team in a bid to restore investor confidence. In July, the governor of the central bank stepped down, followed by Prabowo’s replacement of his finance minister in September. It will no doubt also announce a host of new reforms in the days and weeks to come.

Whether all of this has much effect on MSCI’s verdict remains to be seen. Judging by the wording of its latest announcement, some kind of downgrade for Indonesia is certain; it is now merely a question of how severe the shock will be.

title: Indonesia’s Energy Investment Potential
description: Too big to ignore
text:
The recent economic headlines in Indonesia have been pessimistic to say the least. There are serious concerns that President Prabowo Subianto’s signature social development initiatives – the free nutritious meals (Makanan Bergizi Gratis, “MBG) program and the Red-White Village Cooperatives (Kopdes Merah Putih) – are straining the national budget and will limit long-term growth. The president’s reluctance to abandon or significantly downsize these programs has helped inspire protests in June against an agenda which many fear is “bankrupting Indonesia.” Protestors and investors alike have additional complaints about Indonesia’s policy trajectory, including creeping militarization of the civil service, state control over key commodities sectors, and weaponization of the legal system against the government’s political opponents. Amidst the uncertainty, the rupiah and the Indonesian stock market have also experienced major slides, with the currency hitting an all-time low against the U.S. dollar on June 8 and the Jakarta Composite Index falling 36 percent from a record high in January.

Despite the serious economic headwinds, there are still opportunities for investors in the Indonesian economy, particularly in the energy sector. Indonesia ranks among global leaders in terms of energy potential and has recently improved its regulatory environment for international developers in upstream oil and gas as well as renewables. Major agreements are being signed and capital is being deployed by leading international energy companies. This momentum in domestic energy production and exploration is unfolding against the backdrop of renewed conflict in the Middle East, which has sharpened investor and policymaker focus on the risks of import dependence across the APAC region.

Recent studies have estimated that the country has technical renewable energy potential of 3,686 GW, with hundreds of suitable locations for solar, wind and hydropower facilities. To tap more of this potential, the Indonesian government has set a target energy mix of 35 percent from renewables, up from the current level of 18 percent, by 2035. However, Indonesia’s proven oil and gas reserves are also immense, totaling 2.33 billion barrels and 34.8 Tcf respectively. To utilize these reserves, Indonesia has opened 116 new oil and gas blocks to global investors.

Continue reading for free at The Diplomat’s new companion publication, The Investor.

title: Indonesia’s Stock Market Crisis Is Self-Inflicted
description: Jakarta has serious questions to answer about the credibility of its capital markets and the effectiveness of the institutions responsible for regulating them.
text:
On Friday, October 16, Indonesia’s stock market suffered its worst one-day decline since the 1998 Asian financial crisis. The Jakarta Composite Index plunged 11.6 percent following the global index provider MSCI’s announcement that it was considering removing Indonesia from its Emerging Market classification and placing it directly into its Standalone Market category. The selling continued when markets opened on Monday, with the index falling another 3.9 percent, bringing the combined decline over the two trading days to approximately 15 percent.

For Southeast Asia’s largest economy, this is a serious development. However, the most important issue is not the decline in share prices or even the possibility of losing Emerging Market status. It is what this crisis reveals about the credibility of Indonesia’s capital markets and the effectiveness of the institutions responsible for regulating them.

MSCI’s concerns about concentrated share ownership, questionable free-float calculations, coordinated trading, and the reliability of market prices are not new. In January, MSCI restricted certain increases in Indonesian securities’ index representation, and announced that it was considering downgrading Indonesia from Emerging Market to Frontier Market status. By June, it had acknowledged reforms introduced by the authorities but emphasized the need for sustained implementation. However, MSCI was still concerned enough this month to propose removing Indonesia from both its Emerging and Frontier Market classifications.

Market Manipulation and Inflated Valuations

One of the main concerns is coordinated trading, where groups of investors work together to influence share prices rather than allowing them to be determined by genuine buying and selling. Such activities can involve transactions through multiple brokerage accounts, including accounts held by related parties or nominees, creating the appearance of greater trading activity and investor demand than actually exists.

The problem is especially serious when a company’s shares are concentrated among a small number of shareholders. With only a limited number genuinely available for trading, relatively modest transactions can have a disproportionate impact on the market price. If prices are pushed higher through coordinated buying, the resulting increase in market capitalization can give investors a misleading impression of the company’s value. Investors, including foreign institutions and index funds, may subsequently purchase shares at prices that do not reflect genuine independent demand.

For example, on October 16, Indonesia’s Financial Services Authority (OJK) announced that its investigation into trading in Dian Swastatika Sentosa (DSSA), a company associated with the Sinar Mas Group, had uncovered planned and structured market manipulation involving individual and institutional investors operating through several brokerage firms.

According to OJK, the investigation examined transactions between 2024 and 2026 and identified coordinated activities that significantly increased DSSA’s share price. The regulator questioned brokerage directors, individuals, and foreign legal entities, suspended certain individual licenses and announced penalties totaling Rp1.5 trillion (around $83 million) in connection with the case.

The regulator has not publicly established that the company’s controlling shareholders directed these activities, and it would be wrong to assume their involvement without evidence. However, the case demonstrates that trading on a regulated stock exchange can produce prices that do not reflect genuine independent demand.

There is also a broader concern about how inflated valuations affect the financial system. Higher share prices increase the apparent wealth of major shareholders and, where shares are accepted as collateral, may influence the financing available against those holdings. They can also affect index weightings and investment decisions by institutions relying on reported market prices and liquidity.

The obvious question is how such activities could continue over several years without being stopped earlier. Modern stock exchanges have surveillance systems designed to identify unusual trading patterns, concentrated ownership, and potentially coordinated transactions. Were these warning signs missed, were investigations delayed, or did the authorities lack the resources or willingness to intervene?

The Indonesia Stock Exchange (IDX), OJK, and Central Securities Depository have taken steps to address these concerns. In response to MSCI’s first downgrade threat in January, the authorities have introduced measures to improve transparency, including reducing the shareholding disclosure threshold from 5 percent to 1 percent, expanding investor classifications from nine to 39 categories, and establishing a roadmap to increase the minimum free-float requirement from 7.5 percent to 15 percent. They have also introduced measures to identify companies with highly concentrated shareholdings, improve beneficial ownership disclosures, strengthen scrutiny of IPO allocations, and enhance market surveillance and enforcement.

These are all sensible reforms, but announcing new regulations and actually enforcing them are two different things. For instance, increasing the minimum free float means very little if shares supposedly held by independent investors are actually controlled through nominee arrangements, affiliated companies, or other parties connected with principal shareholders.

Indonesia’s listed companies have historically been dominated by family-controlled business groups, with various studies estimating that 60–70 percent of companies listed on the IDX are controlled by families. Many of these groups have played an important role in Indonesia’s economic development. While there is nothing inherently wrong with concentrated family ownership, the problem arises when complex ownership structures make it difficult to determine who actually controls publicly traded shares, whether transactions are conducted at arm’s length, and whether market prices reflect genuine trading between independent investors.

An example of this is Barito Renewables Energy. Following its 2023 IPO, the company’s market capitalization rose dramatically, at one point exceeding that of Bank Central Asia, one of Indonesia’s largest banks. The valuation attracted considerable attention, particularly given the company’s relatively limited earnings relative to its market capitalization.

In 2024, FTSE Russell excluded Barito Renewables from its global indices over concerns about concentrated share ownership. This should have been another warning that international investors were questioning whether the reported public shareholdings represented shares genuinely available for trading.

More recently, OJK announced penalties of Rp500 billion ($27.9 million) and Rp100 billion ($ 5.5 million), involving irregularities connected with the IPOs of Barito Renewables and Petrindo Jaya Kreasi, respectively, both associated with businessman Prajogo Pangestu. According to the regulator, shares intended for public investors had been allocated to parties associated with controlling shareholders, including through arrangements that obscured the identities of the ultimate beneficiaries. The penalties were directed at parties involved in the violations rather than the listed companies themselves.

Another example is the transaction involving Bayan Resources, in which founder Low Tuck Kwong and his daughter Elaine Low sold a combined 30.25 percent stake to PT Jhonlin Baratama, associated with businessman Haji Isam. According to regulatory filings, the shares were sold at Rp2,588 each, approximately 80 percent below the prevailing market price of Rp13,000–14,000.

There may be legitimate commercial reasons for selling such a large block of shares at a substantial discount. While this does not establish market manipulation, the difference between the negotiated price and the market price raises questions about whether the quoted share price accurately reflects its value.

Whither Regulatory Independence?

The involvement of some of Indonesia’s most influential business families raises questions about whether financial regulators are sufficiently independent and willing to take action against powerful business interests.

Indonesia’s large conglomerates often have longstanding relationships with political figures, government institutions, and other influential groups. Such relationships are hardly unique to Indonesia and do not, by themselves, imply wrongdoing. However, they create concerns about whether regulators can operate without political or commercial pressure, particularly when enforcement actions could affect prominent shareholders or companies with political connections.

OJK deserves credit for pursuing the recent investigations and announcing substantial penalties, particularly given the prominence of the corporate groups involved. Although OJK maintains that its investigations were underway before MSCI’s announcement, it should explain why these problems persisted for so long and what steps it has taken to prevent them from happening again.

Investors should also be entitled to know who was responsible for the violations, what penalties have actually been collected, whether further proceedings are being pursued and whether those involved remain permitted to operate in the market.

Restoring Investor Confidence

Indonesia has considerable economic advantages, including its large domestic market, natural resources, and opportunities in infrastructure, energy, and manufacturing. However, international investors also value the reliability of financial information, minority shareholder protection, regulatory independence, and the predictability of government policies.

When confidence in these areas weakens, investors may demand higher returns or simply invest elsewhere. For Indonesian companies, this can mean lower valuations, a higher cost of capital, and greater difficulty raising funds for expansion.

The proposed MSCI reclassification could compound these problems. Funds required to track Emerging Market benchmarks may have to reduce their Indonesian holdings if the downgrade proceeds, while other investors may reassess their exposure because of concerns about governance and market integrity.

The government’s response should therefore concentrate on restoring confidence rather than simply supporting share prices. Danantara’s reported plans to invest $5 billion in domestic businesses may provide support during a period of market weakness. However, using public investment funds to support the market cannot resolve concerns about ownership transparency, coordinated trading, or regulatory enforcement. Such investments should be based on commercial considerations, with transparent investment criteria and proper accountability.

The IDX and OJK should concentrate on enforcing existing regulations rather than continuing to announce additional reforms. Beneficial ownership must be reliably identified, free-float requirements must reflect shares genuinely available to independent investors, and suspicious trading must be investigated promptly. The authorities should also publish regular reports identifying companies that remain in breach of the regulations, the corrective measures required and the outcomes of enforcement proceedings. Investors should not have to rely on general assurances that improvements are being made.

Indonesia has until April 30, 2027, to respond to MSCI’s consultation, with a final decision expected by June 30. However, the government’s objective should be more than simply retaining its Emerging Market classification. The underlying problem is that Indonesia has allowed legitimate concerns about the integrity of its capital markets to remain unresolved for too long. IDX and OJK must demonstrate that they, not Indonesia’s powerful business groups or politically connected shareholders, are responsible for overseeing Indonesia’s capital markets. The rules must apply equally to everyone, regardless of their wealth, influence, or political connections. Unless the authorities are prepared to assert their independence and hold those responsible accountable, restoring international investor confidence will remain difficult, no matter how many new regulations are announced.

title: Investigation Finds That Former High-Ranking Uzbek Security Official Acquired UAE Citizenship
description: According to an OCCRP and Ozodlik investigation, Otabek Umarov, the Uzbek president’s son-in-law, obtained Emirati citizenship in 2023, while he was deputy head of the Presidential Security Service.
text:
In April 2023, when he was serving as deputy head of the Presidential Security Service, Otabek Umarov – Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev’s son-in-law – reportedly acquired citizenship in the United Arab Emirates. He’s also alleged to be the owner of around $7 million worth of Dubai real estate.

Those are the central allegations of a new investigation published by the Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project (OCCRP) and RFE/RL’s Uzbek Service, Ozodlik.

Under Uzbek military law, which governs the position Umarov held at the time, holding a second citizenship is prohibited. Since acquiring citizenship typically includes swearing an oath of allegiance, many countries bar security (and other) officials from doing so – a second passport represents possible divided loyalties and a counterintelligence risk.

As OCCRP and Ozodlik reported, “Under UAE law, foreigners can only obtain citizenship through a nomination by a royal court or senior official, and [the process] requires swearing an oath of allegiance to the Emirates.”

Umarov was shifted out of his security service role in November 2024, in the extended wake of the assassination attempt on Komil Allamjanov.

Allamjanov, at the time of the October 2024 attempt, had recently stepped down from his role as deputy head of the presidential administration. He has since returned to government service, as an adviser to the powerful head of the presidential administration, Saida Mirziyoyeva (the president’s eldest daughter). As of January 2026 he was also appointed to a seemingly bespoke role: advisor-ambassador and representative of the presidential administration in the United States.

Umarov, meanwhile, was named first deputy chairman of Uzbekistan’s National Olympic Committee – his father-in-law, the president, is the chairman.

According to OCCRP and Ozodlik, at some point in 2025, Umarov became the owner of 13 properties in Dubai, worth around $7 million. The properties previously belonged to his younger brother, Oybek Umarov, who purchased them in 2021 and 2022, according to leaked Dubai real estate data obtained by OCCRP.

It is not clear precisely how or when they came to be listed with Umarov’s name on the deeds, whether the properties were gifted or purchased.

While Umarov has notably expensive tastes – for example, he’s been pictured wearing a limited edition Richard Mille watch valued at up to $1.9 million – his government position doesn’t quite explain his apparent wealth. Uzbek officials do not have to disclose their income declarations publicly.

OCCRP and Ozodlik reported, “Public commercial registries show no record of [Otabek Umarov] owning private companies during his time as deputy presidential security chief.” His brother, however, does have extensive business holdings, including in banking, cement, and metalwork.

A high-ranking government source told The Diplomat in late 2024 that Umarov’s assets and businesses were held in the names of others, including Ulugbek Shadmanov who was implicated in an apparent attempt to manipulate the U.S. sanctions system to target Allamjonov and another Uzbek official in the months before the assassination attempt. Shadmanov was earlier named in the Pandora Papers as connected to an offshore company, though there are few details available. In December 2024 he was detained in Dubai and extradited rapidly – apparently without the proper legal process – to Uzbekistan, regardless of the fact that he held what’s known as a “Golden Visa” in the UAE. Despite high-powered legal representation and a campaign on his behalf, very little has been reported since about his case.

Ultimately, the OCCRP and Ozodlik investigation raises far more questions than it answers; that’s the nature of investigations into the opaque underbelly of Uzbek politics (and those of the UAE, to boot). As I told Ozodlik, we don’t know exactly how Umarov acquired UAE citizenship, who was involved, and who knew about it. As noted above, the process to acquired UAE citizenship necessitates a nomination by a royal court or senior official. It’s nearly impossible to believe that Umarov’s role and connections were unknown at the time to the UAE’s authorities.

Then there are questions of what comes next. Uzbekistan does not officially recognize dual citizenship. Holding a second citizenship isn’t illegal per se – though it does violate laws related to Umarov’s specific position at the time. Nevertheless, “voluntarily acquiring a passport of a foreign state” is listed as possible grounds for revocation of Uzbek citizenship.

title: Iran War Highlights 2 Challenges for Japan in a Taiwan Contingency
description: Japan can use the Iran war to reexamine its security framework, with particular attention to preparations for a contingency involving Taiwan.
text:
On February 28, the Iran-U.S. war began. Despite ongoing negotiations between the United States and Iran at the time, Israel and the U.S. launched a barrage of attacks, and Iran retaliated across a wide area, including Israel and the Gulf region. In the Strait of Hormuz, attacks on commercial vessels, heightened vigilance against mines and drones, traffic control measures, and a U.S. maritime blockade of Iran combined to impose severe constraints on shipping routes that are vital to global energy transportation. Even in late September, traffic through the strait had not returned to prewar levels, and the crisis had yet to be fully resolved.

Against this backdrop, Japan can use the Iran war to reexamine its security framework, with particular attention to preparations for a contingency involving Taiwan. The Iran war has raised many issues, but two are especially important for Japan. The first is how to evacuate Japanese nationals and travelers when a crisis begins sooner than expected and civilian transportation networks suddenly cease to function. The second is how Japan can help ensure the safety of maritime traffic while avoiding becoming a direct party to the conflict. Both expose gaps in the institutional arrangements Japan has developed with a Taiwan contingency in mind.

Evacuating People from a Sudden Crisis

The first lesson of the Iran war is that the traditional approach of waiting until a crisis escalates before evacuating people is no longer sufficient. Even before the outbreak of hostilities, the Japanese government had warned of the deteriorating situation in Iran and encouraged Japanese nationals to leave early. Once the fighting began, however, it became necessary to confirm the safety of Japanese nationals and assist with their departure not only in Iran but also across neighboring areas, including Israel, Qatar, Bahrain, and the United Arab Emirates.

In March, the Japanese government supported multiple overland evacuations from Tehran to Azerbaijan and also assisted Japanese nationals in Gulf countries with their return home. Importantly, these evacuations were not carried out solely by Self-Defense Forces aircraft or charter flights; they relied on a combination of overland routes, commercial aviation, and transit through third countries.

An even larger problem was the temporary degradation of airports and airspace across the Gulf, including major hubs such as Dubai, Abu Dhabi, and Doha. Dubai is not simply one airport in the Middle East; it is one of the world’s leading aviation hubs linking Asia with Europe and Africa. Disruption there complicated movement not only for people evacuating Iran and Israel but also for travelers and foreign residents throughout the Gulf. The experience demonstrated once again that a crisis may not remain confined within the borders of one country and can quickly engulf regional transportation hubs.

This lesson applies directly to a Taiwan contingency. In peacetime, large numbers of Japanese nationals are in Taiwan for tourism, business, study, and long-term assignments. Once hostilities begin, not only Taiwan’s airports and ports but also the surrounding airspace and waters could become dangerous. Transportation in Hong Kong, coastal China, Okinawa, and the Sakishima Islands could also be affected. In other words, a plan designed only to move Japanese nationals out of Taiwan would be insufficient. Japan must prepare for a scenario in which multiple transportation nodes across East Asia become unavailable at the same time.

Within Japan, civil protection plans to evacuate residents and tourists from the Sakishima Islands to Kyushu and Yamaguchi have become increasingly concrete, with field exercises scheduled for fiscal year 2026. This is an important development. Yet civil protection planning primarily concerns the evacuation of people inside Japan. By contrast, the evacuation of Japanese nationals from Taiwan, Hong Kong, coastal China, and other overseas locations spans several frameworks, including consular assistance by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, transportation under the Self-Defense Forces Act, and the securing of civilian transportation. If domestic evacuation and overseas evacuation occur simultaneously, Japan would still face the unresolved question of how to allocate aircraft, ships, airports, and ports between the two missions.

The lesson from the Iran War is not simply that Japan should increase the transport capacity of the Self-Defense Forces. Moving tens of thousands of people within a short period ultimately depends on cooperation with commercial airlines, shipping companies, airports and ports, and third countries. Japan therefore needs, in peacetime, to identify which civilian services could be maintained during a crisis, which third countries could serve as evacuation hubs, and which ports could be used if air routes were closed.

Plans must also address how to provide shelter, food, communications, and medical care for those who cannot be evacuated immediately. An evacuation plan cannot consist only of a plan for getting people out; it must also include a plan for keeping them safe until evacuation becomes possible.

Ensuring Safe Navigation Without Becoming a Party to the Conflict

The second challenge is how to ensure the safety of maritime traffic. During the Iran War, the Strait of Hormuz was not completely closed, but normal commercial navigation became extremely difficult because of the risk of attacks on and seizures of merchant vessels, heightened vigilance against mines and drones, Iranian traffic control measures, and the U.S. blockade of Iran.

In June, the United States and Iran reached a memorandum of understanding that included the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, and the Japanese government also called for the early restoration of free and safe navigation. Yet even in late September, traffic through the strait remained well below prewar levels.

On September 22, Iran indicated that it was prepared to reopen the strait quickly if the United States eased military pressure and lifted its blockade of Iranian ports. This, in turn, shows that as of late September, the restoration of safe navigation remained a matter of diplomatic and military negotiation.

This raised a further question: who should be responsible for ensuring safe navigation? If the United States, as a party to the conflict, leads convoy escorts or other maritime operations, participating states are more likely to be perceived as having been militarily incorporated into the U.S. side. Yet civilian shipping cannot simply be left exposed in dangerous waters.

European states have therefore sought arrangements that would protect freedom of navigation while maintaining a degree of distance from U.S.-led operations. In September, France was reported to be considering a United Nations Security Council resolution for an international mission to ensure safe navigation through the Strait of Hormuz. Such an approach can be understood as an attempt to distinguish, as far as possible, alliance military operations from the protection of maritime traffic as an international public good.

A similar dilemma would arise in a Taiwan contingency. If the Taiwan Strait and surrounding waters became dangerous, maintaining maritime traffic would be a major economic and security concern for Japan. Yet the threshold for participation would be extremely high if measures to protect shipping could immediately lead to armed conflict with China. What is needed is an institutional distinction, to the greatest extent possible, between joining combat operations and supporting the safe navigation of civilian vessels. Japan should therefore clarify in advance options that are not integrated into the use of force, including post-ceasefire mine clearance, information sharing, sea-lane monitoring, rescue of vessels in distress, and cooperation with escort frameworks led by third countries.

This issue is also related to the limits of Japan’s 2015 Legislation for Peace and Security. The legislation permits the minimum necessary use of force only when the so-called three new conditions are satisfied, including cases in which an armed attack on a foreign country that is in a close relationship with Japan poses a clear threat to Japan’s survival and to the fundamental rights of its people. It is important to note that, as a matter of law, U.S. participation in a conflict is not itself a requirement for recognizing a situation that threatens Japan’s survival. The Japanese government has also stated with regard to a Taiwan contingency that whether a particular situation constitutes such a threat must be determined comprehensively in light of the specific circumstances actually arising. It is therefore inaccurate to frame the issue as one in which Japan can do nothing unless the United States participates.

However, what is legally possible and what can actually be recognized in practice are different questions. A situation threatening Japan’s survival can be recognized only when there is a clear danger to Japan’s existence and to the rights of its people, and when no other appropriate means are available. Disruption to maritime traffic or higher resource prices alone would not automatically meet that threshold.

Moreover, when Japan seeks to secure safe navigation in a manner that is not directly connected to combat with the opposing state, the framework of a situation threatening Japan’s survival may in some cases be too weighty. In March 2026, views were expressed within the Japanese government that minesweeping in the Strait of Hormuz after a ceasefire could be considered as one option. This is one example of the importance of maritime security measures that are institutionally separated from direct participation in combat.

The same perspective should guide discussion of a Taiwan contingency. The debate should not be reduced to a binary question of whether Japan would exercise the right of collective self-defense. Japan instead needs to strengthen the legal and institutional arrangements that apply before that threshold is reached and in adjacent areas. Specifically, it should clarify the legal basis and timing for measures such as the evacuation of Japanese nationals, maritime security, mine clearance, information sharing, warnings to civilian vessels, coordination with third countries and international organizations, and the alternative use of ports and airports. A U.N. resolution or an international framework led by third countries could be one option. Yet because China is a permanent member of the Security Council and possesses a veto, it would be unrealistic to rely solely on a U.N. resolution. Japan therefore needs multiple legal and diplomatic pathways.

What Should Japan Learn From the Iran War?

The Iran-U.S. war became a major crisis that simultaneously challenged the protection of Japanese nationals and the security of maritime transportation. It demonstrated that preparing for contingencies cannot be reduced to the question of how far the Self-Defense Forces can be used. In the initial phase of a crisis, airport closures and airspace restrictions may halt civilian transportation, while the population requiring evacuation may rapidly expand from the belligerent state to neighboring countries. At sea, Japan may be called upon to help ensure safe navigation even without participating in hostilities, while still facing the risk that such activity could be interpreted as support for one of the parties to the conflict.

The same problems could arise in a Taiwan contingency. The central issue is not to reduce a Taiwan crisis immediately to the questions of a situation threatening Japan’s survival or the exercise of collective self-defense. Rather, Japan needs to institutionalize and operationalize the measures that would become necessary before such a determination: the evacuation of Japanese nationals, the evacuation of residents, the maintenance of air and maritime transportation, protection of sea lanes, and cooperation with third countries. The Iran war has revealed a new “intermediate domain” within the legal and institutional framework Japan has developed with a Taiwan contingency in mind.

Diplomatic efforts to prevent a Taiwan contingency must of course continue. Yet considering what should be done if deterrence fails is also part of security policy. The most important lesson Japan should draw from the Iran War is that the issue should not be framed as a binary choice between participation and non-participation in war. Instead, the many practical tasks that lie between those two poles must be institutionalized in advance.
