title: Iranian Ships Test Sri Lanka’s Sovereignty Again
description: The U.S. has threatened Sri Lanka with sanctions if it provides supplies to Iranian vessels stranded off its coasts.
text:
On Sept. 30, 2026, the Wall Street Journal (WSJ) reported that U.S. officials threatened Sri Lanka with sanctions if it continued supplying around 20 Iranian tankers stranded off its coast. According to WSJ, the tankers are running short of food, fuel, and fresh water.

Sources in Sri Lanka’s Foreign Ministry told The Diplomat that the U.S. embassy in Colombo and visiting American civilian and military officials have repeatedly warned Sri Lanka against providing the Iranian vessels with essential supplies, despite the potential humanitarian crisis. Sri Lanka’s national security establishment reportedly objected to these demands and called on the government to convey its displeasure to Washington, as they are opposed to leaving the Iranian crew stranded and suffering.

With the WSJ report, the matter has now become public, restricting the maneuvering space of the Sri Lankan government.

The incident reveals the limits of sovereignty of small states like Sri Lanka that depend on exports to the Global North. Washington has considerable means to punish any resistance from Sri Lanka, and the question before Colombo now is how it can protect its economic interests while retaining the freedom to provide basic humanitarian assistance to friendly nations.

Foreign Minister Vijitha Herath has tried to distance the government from any private suppliers who might be supplying the stranded Iranian ships. Speaking to the Sunday Times, Herath said that the authorities had identified 15 Iranian vessels among 47 foreign ships outside Sri Lanka’s territorial waters. He confirmed that Iran had requested essential supplies for the stranded ships but said that the government had provided nothing and did not intend to do so.

Herath described provisioning the ships as a private business. Companies could make their own decisions, he said, after considering the possibility of U.S. secondary sanctions. Foreign Ministry spokesman Thushara Rodrigo told local media that U.S. sanctions apply globally and that these are not threats targeted at one country.

Colombo’s caution has an obvious economic explanation. The Export Development Board’s report for the first six months of 2026 puts the United States’ share of Sri Lanka’s merchandise exports at approximately 22 percent. The European Union accounts for 25.5 percent, with Britain providing another substantial market. These figures explain why Sri Lankan policymakers worry about disputes with Western governments.

Yet accepting every U.S. demand also carries costs.

If Colombo does not provide drinking water to hundreds of stranded Iranians due to the fear of economic punishment, it invites further U.S. interference in decisions that should be its own. Officials urging a firmer response recognize that Sri Lanka must sometimes express disagreement to preserve any freedom of action.

In the past, Sri Lanka has indicated that it is willing to risk U.S. ire on humanitarian grounds.

After an American submarine sank an Iranian naval frigate, IRIS Dena, off the Sri Lankan coast in March, Sri Lanka rescued survivors. Colombo subsequently took custody of IRIS Bushehr, brought its sailors ashore and repatriated over 230 Iranians to safety.

India’s recent conduct complicates the decisions before Colombo. New Delhi presents itself as a regional security provider and has had a longstanding relationship with Tehran. Smaller neighbors expect India to take charge when external powers take military action in its backyard. However, when the U.S. sank IRIS Dena, India was nowhere to be found. Sri Lanka had to do the heavy lifting without any military support or diplomatic cover from India.

In recent years, India has grown closer to the United States and Israel. On the other hand, Sri Lanka has taken a strong pro-Palestinian stance and refused to sponsor a Bahrain-led United Nations Security Council resolution against Iran in March 2026.

However, these pressures must not let Sri Lanka diminish its sovereignty. Economic dependence on the West makes exercising its sovereignty difficult, but surrendering its foreign policy decision-making to Washington now would gradually reduce the matters over which Sri Lanka exercises meaningful control.

Sri Lanka cannot afford a reckless confrontation with the United States. Its government must consider the Sri Lankan livelihoods that depend on Western markets. But protecting those livelihoods also requires judging which risks the country can bear. Treating every American objection as a veto would leave Colombo with little foreign policy of its own. Fear of U.S. pressure has already constrained Sri Lanka’s willingness to pursue Russian oil and nuclear energy agreements or certain investments with China.

The government should convey its objections to American officials and allow willing private suppliers to deliver essential provisions to the stranded Iranian vessels. It should explain the risks to the public and defend its decision to prevent a humanitarian emergency.

Sri Lanka took a calculated risk when it rescued Iranian sailors in March. It must now show the same willingness to act before hunger and thirst endanger lives. Dependence on Western markets cannot become a justification for abandoning people at sea.

title: Is China Getting Involved in the Japan-Russia Territorial Dispute?
description: Amid deepening China-Russia ties, a Chinese delegation visited one of the disputed Southern Kuril Islands.
text:
According to information released by the government of Russia’s Sakhalin Oblast on October 13, a delegation from China’s Heilongjiang Province, including government officials and entrepreneurs, recently visited Iturup Island (Etorofu in Japanese). The island is part of the Southern Kuril Islands, known as the Northern Territories in Japan, which are currently under Russian de facto control, though Japan claims sovereignty over them.

The Chinese group’s visit led to an immediate expression of dissatisfaction from Tokyo, with Japanese Foreign Minister Motegi Toshimitsu declaring it “absolutely unacceptable.” In response, Beijing stated that it “consistently advocates for respecting and upholding the outcomes of the victory [of World War II].” A Japanese media outlet suggested that this reflects “a coordinated stance between China and Russia regarding the Northern Territories issue and a joint approach in dealing with Japan.”

The islands in question were under Japanese control until they were occupied by the Soviet Union at the end of World War II. The Japanese government has maintained its claim ever since. Tokyo has made repeated attempts to advance negotiations on the territorial issue with Russia by leveraging economic cooperation and investment. Ultimately, however, these efforts have not yielded satisfactory results.

Despite possessing abundant fishery and mineral resources, the economic potential of these islands remains largely untapped due to the lagging economic development of the Russian Far East, inadequate infrastructure, and high transportation costs. In 2022, Russia announced the establishment of a special economic zone on the islands to foster economic growth. If Chinese enterprises become more involved in the economic development of the Southern Kuril Islands in the future, it would not only exert political pressure on Japan but could also strengthen Russia’s de facto control over these islands.

Although maps currently published in China label these islands as Japanese territory under Russian occupation, Beijing generally avoids taking an explicit stance on their sovereignty. In August 2026, following Russian President Vladimir Putin’s visit to Iturup Island, the Chinese and Russian ambassadors to Japan co-authored an article stating: “The preservation of historical memory of World War II and its outcomes is particularly important for our countries.” This appeared to imply China’s acknowledgment of the status quo without an overt declaration. Some Japanese media outlets perceive Beijing as shifting away from the position it held during the later Mao era and moving toward the Russian side.

It remains unclear whether this delegation’s visit was intentionally orchestrated by Beijing. However, given that the delegation included officials from the Heilongjiang provincial government, the visit clearly had at least the tacit approval of the authorities.

Over the past few months, Japanese lawmakers from various political parties have visited Taiwan, and most notably, a group of 27 Japanese parliamentarians arrived in Taiwan around the same time as this delegation’s visit. Beijing typically views such actions as an infringement upon China’s territorial sovereignty. Consequently, this visit by the Chinese delegation may well be a countermeasure by Beijing against Japan.

One disadvantage for Japan is that it is involved in territorial or maritime disputes with nearly all of its neighbors. These disputes currently remain largely a matter of bilateral relations between Japan and the respective countries involved. However, the Chinese delegation’s visit to the Southern Kuril Islands against the backdrop of deteriorating China-Japan relations may signal that Beijing has deployed a diplomatic card against Japan that had previously received little attention.

The deepening of China-Russia relations has further complicated this issue. In recent years, the frequent joint patrols conducted by Chinese and Russian military aircraft and naval vessels in the vicinity of Japan have drawn concern from Tokyo.

Concurrently, China and Russia have aligned their historical narratives. In May 2025, the two nations issued a joint statement commemorating their respective victories in the War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression and the Great Patriotic War, while also pledging to strengthen bilateral cooperation and uphold the authority of international law. The statement characterized both China and Russia as “pivotal forces in the fight against militarism and fascism” and asserts their commitment to “defending the outcomes of the Second World War” and resisting any “resurgence of militarism.” This aligns with Beijing’s accusations that Japan is pursuing a “new-type militarism.”

Given these shared historical perceptions, China and Russia can be expected to coordinate more closely on historical and security-related issues in their diplomatic approaches toward Japan.

However, it remains highly likely that Beijing will continue to avoid formally recognizing Russian sovereignty over the islands. This is not only because China needs to maintain diplomatic maneuvering room vis-à-vis Japan, but also because it seeks to avoid becoming entirely tethered to Russia’s interests.

Japan’s response, meanwhile, is constrained by both its own policy toward Russia and the state of its relations with China. Japan’s continued imposition of sanctions against Russia makes any substantive improvement in its relations with Moscow in the near term highly unlikely. At the same time, there are no signs of any meaningful improvement in Tokyo’s relations with China. Against this backdrop, it is difficult for Japan to effectively counter the activities of China and Russia in the region.

More significantly, should China begin to actively engage in economic activities or even pursue military cooperation with Russia on the islands, the issue could gradually evolve from a bilateral dispute between Japan and Russia into a new variable affecting China-Japan relations and, by extension, the security landscape of Northeast Asia.

title: It’s Time For Thailand to Amend Its Controversial Lese-Majeste Law
description: Over the past decade, hundreds of political activists and ordinary people have been subjected to criminal prosecution under Article 112.
text:
On September 26, 2023, my fellow human rights lawyer Arnon Nampa was imprisoned in Thailand for calling for the reform of the Thai monarchy. He has been behind bars ever since.

I had the opportunity to talk to him early last month at the Bangkok Criminal Court, where he appeared for a hearing in one of the remaining three lese-majeste cases he is facing under Article 112 of Thailand’s Criminal Code. This draconian provision punishes with prison terms of three to 15 years whoever defames, insults, or threatens the Thai king, queen, heir apparent, or regent. Eleven additional lese-majeste cases filed against Arnon have already resulted in 11 convictions and a cumulative prison term of more than 31 years.

When I met Arnon in court, he was barefoot, wearing his prison uniform. I was shocked to see he was being kept ankle-shackled the entire time, a clear form of ill-treatment and a violation of his right to be treated humanely and with respect for his dignity. I briefly spoke with him about his trial and expressed my full solidarity. When he was eventually escorted out of the courtroom to return to prison, he turned to me, and knowing I am from beer-loving Belgium, he smiled and promised me the next time he would meet me in Brussels for a beer. This rendezvous will likely have to wait many years.

A day earlier, I was in the same court for another lese-majeste case. This time, the defendant was a young woman pro-democracy activist, Tantawan Tuatulanon, known as “Tawan.” Visibly stressed but putting on a brave face, she reminded me of my own daughter – same age, same studies, same demeanor. This was the day of the verdict, which, as it happens in most lese-majeste cases, turned out to be a conviction. Her crime? She livestreamed on Facebook the relocation of a farmer sit-in protest in Bangkok to make way for the passage of a royal motorcade. She was violently arrested on the spot and charged with violating Article 112. The Criminal Court sentenced her to two years in prison without suspension. Tawan spent the rest of the day in the holding cell in the court’s basement, while awaiting the outcome of her bail application, which was successful and resulted in her temporary release pending appeal. I managed to talk to her through a phone line across a series of partitions to convey my support and encouragement.

In a striking and surreal contrast, just before Tawan’s verdict, the same judge had delivered another verdict, in which a convicted child sex offender was sentenced to six years in prison. His sentence was suspended for two years so that he could be free and have a chance to demonstrate he is “a good person.”

Like Arnon and Tawan, in recent years, hundreds of Thais have faced criminal prosecution under Article 112. About 30 of them are currently behind bars, with 19 serving prison terms of up to 50 years. Those who are on trial have little or no hope of avoiding prison. In a discriminatory move, Article 112 has been excluded from offenses covered by recently adopted legislation designed to promote a “peaceful society” to clear records, dismiss pending cases, and release individuals detained in connection with the political turmoil that Thailand experienced for two decades (2005-2025). In addition, authorities have made no progress in the adoption of alternatives to detention (such as home detention) for prisoners convicted of certain crimes – which should include non-violent offenses such as lese-majeste.

Like Thailand, my own country, Belgium, is a constitutional monarchy with the King as the head of state. In October 2021, the Constitutional Court ruled that Belgium’s lese-majeste law – introduced in 1847 and rarely used – violated freedom of expression and that monarchs were not entitled to greater protection than ordinary people for defamation. As a result, in Belgium’s current Criminal Code, lese-majeste can only be punished by a fine, and no deprivation of liberty is possible for those who insult the monarch.

This sensible reform could provide a blueprint for Thailand and would bring Article 112 closer to compliance with international human rights law. Indeed, under international human rights law, imprisonment is never an appropriate penalty for insult or defamation, including when insults are directed towards public figures, such as heads of state.

The task of reforming Article 112 falls exclusively on the Thai people. Nonetheless, like-minded states, including Belgium, must play a positive role by supporting such domestic efforts and backing them with calls for the amendment of Article 112 and respect for international human rights law.

Freedom of expression is a fundamental and universal right that protects all opinions, including those that shock, offend, or hurt – let alone those that call for the reform of the monarchy or question the appropriateness of royal motorcades. As Thailand has learned in recent years, without freedom of expression there is no “peaceful society.” It is as simple as that.

title: Japan and Australia: Toward a More Autonomous and Resilient Partnership
description: As Washington’s reliability wavers, Tokyo and Canberra are learning to depend on each other.
text:
The security environment in the Indo-Pacific is undergoing a profound transformation. Cooperation among revisionist powers, including China, Russia, and North Korea, is deepening, while the strategic priorities of the United States — the country that has long underpinned the regional order — are also changing. At the same time, technological advances in areas such as artificial intelligence, autonomous systems, unmanned platforms, quantum technologies, and cyber capabilities are fundamentally changing the character of warfare and the sources of military advantage.

Against this backdrop, Japan and Australia have deepened their comprehensive security partnership across military and economic domains. What matters increasingly is their ability to build both strategic autonomy and strategic resilience.

Strategic autonomy does not mean “independence” from the United States. Rather, it means reducing excessive dependence on any single major power and preserving greater room for strategic choice and freedom of action. Strategic resilience, meanwhile, refers to the ability to withstand and recover from strategic shocks, whether they take the form of military conflict, economic coercion, supply-chain disruption, or energy crises. Together, these two concepts provide a useful framework for thinking about the current state and future direction of Japan–Australia cooperation.

For much of the post-Cold War period, both Japan and Australia benefited from what might be called “dual dependence.” In security terms, both relied heavily on the United States, while economically they developed increasingly deep interdependence with China. This arrangement allowed them to enjoy security at relatively low defense costs while benefiting substantially from China’s economic growth.

As U.S.–China rivalry and broader great-power competition intensify, however, this model is becoming increasingly difficult to sustain. Yet neither replacing dependence on the United States with dependence on China, nor pursuing economic decoupling from China, is a viable option for either country. Rather, the goal is to diversify dependence itself — to expand the range of partners and capabilities available so that neither country becomes excessively vulnerable to the decisions of any single major power.

This is the direction the Japan–Australia relationship has taken over the past few years. While maintaining their respective alliances with the United States, Japan and Australia have strengthened their own capabilities and built a more autonomous bilateral security relationship — one that goes beyond simply “supplementing” the U.S. military presence in the region.

The cooperation surrounding the Australian Navy’s acquisition of Japanese-designed Mogami-class frigates is a good example. Its significance extends well beyond the transfer of a particular platform. Developed into sustained cooperation across joint development, production, maintenance, and future technologies, it could strengthen the defense industrial bases of both countries — enhancing their ability not just to acquire military capabilities but to produce, maintain, and sustain them over time.

Australia’s strategic depth is equally important. Japan is geographically located on the front line of the First Island Chain, whereas Australia can provide vast training areas as well as logistics, maintenance, and rear-area support. By developing these arrangements during peacetime, the two countries can build the capacity to sustain military operations over a prolonged period in the event of a crisis or conflict. This will also become increasingly important as the operational horizon of the Japan Self-Defense Forces expands beyond the First Island Chain toward the wider Pacific.

The same logic applies to economic security. Building more diversified supply chains for energy, critical minerals, critical technologies, and other strategic goods can enhance the autonomy and resilience of both Japan and Australia. Importantly, however, such efforts are not limited to the bilateral relationship.

One example is a regional initiative such as “POWERR Asia.” Through mechanisms for energy stockpiling, sharing, and emergency supply arrangements, Japan and Australia could help strengthen energy resilience across the wider Indo-Pacific. The objective would be to create regional networks capable of absorbing shocks rather than leaving individual countries vulnerable to sudden disruptions or external pressure.

A similar logic should guide engagement with Pacific Island countries. Assistance to these countries should not be viewed solely through the prism of strategic competition with China; instead, Japan and Australia have focused on strengthening resilience in areas such as infrastructure, energy, communications, and economic security. The aim should be to create an environment in which smaller states are not forced to “choose” between the United States and China simply because they lack viable alternatives.

Ultimately, this strategy is neither about achieving “independence” from the United States nor about “containing” China. The U.S. military presence will remain indispensable to regional stability, while economic and diplomatic relations with China will continue to matter greatly. The challenge is therefore not to eliminate dependence, which is neither possible nor desirable, but to diversify it in ways that preserve greater freedom of action.

This logic should eventually be extended to the region as a whole. By building networks through which regional countries complement one another’s capabilities across defense, energy, technology, infrastructure, and economic security, the Indo-Pacific can become more resilient to strategic shocks and less vulnerable to sudden changes in the policies or preferences of major powers.

The ultimate purpose of Japan–Australia cooperation, therefore, extends beyond conventional alliance management or burden-sharing with the United States. It should contribute to building a region in which countries of the Indo-Pacific possess greater agency and a greater capacity to sustain stability and order.

In this sense, Japan–Australia cooperation should evolve from a partnership designed primarily to adapt to an order dominated by great powers into one that enables regional countries to play a greater role in shaping the regional order themselves.

title: Japan Has Been Here Before: The 1987 Persian Gulf Crisis
description: When the Gulf was last closed to tankers, Tokyo faced the same dilemma it faces today.
text:
The Strait of Hormuz was effectively closed following the U.S. and Israeli attacks on Iran in February, leaving oil tankers unable to transit the strait, which is both the entrance to the Persian Gulf and one of the world’s most critical trade arteries. Japan imports more than 90 percent of its crude oil from the Middle East. Gasoline prices have surged, and the effects on daily life have been wide-ranging. The current crisis has a precedent. During the Iran-Iraq War of the 1980s, the Japanese government actively debated whether to send Maritime Self-Defense Force (MSDF) minesweepers and Japan Coast Guard (JCG) patrol vessels to the Persian Gulf — and ultimately chose not to.

Iraq invaded Iran in September 1980, beginning the Iran–Iraq War. Around 1984 the conflict spread to the sea, and passage through the Persian Gulf became hazardous for tankers as missile attacks and mines proliferated. In July 1987, at Kuwait’s request, the U.S. government dispatched warships and began escorting tankers, but a tanker still struck a mine. Washington then asked Western countries, including Japan, to send minesweepers. The U.K., France, Italy, the Netherlands, and Belgium all subsequently contributed to the minesweeping effort.

The Japanese government began exploring how it could contribute to navigational safety in the Gulf. Prime Minister Nakasone Yasuhiro was personally in favor of deploying personnel via MSDF minesweepers. On August 27, 1987, speaking before a Lower House committee, he argued that while he did not intend to order the dispatch, the act of removing mines would not, in his view, constitute the use of force, and that sending vessels to the Persian Gulf would not constitute the overseas dispatch of troops.

Naval mines constitute weapons of naval warfare, and laying them is an established means of naval combat. Under international law, minesweeping operations conducted during an armed conflict are themselves considered a use of force. This posed a legal challenge to Nakasone’s position: his argument applied only to the removal of abandoned mines in peacetime, after a ceasefire had been reached — not to active operations in an ongoing conflict.

Within the Japanese government, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs led efforts to identify feasible forms of contribution. It became clear that any MSDF minesweeper dispatch would require a destroyer escort, and amid strong public opposition the government decided against sending minesweepers. Instead, it developed alternative proposals: providing economic cooperation in the Gulf region, sharing the costs of ensuring safe passage, increasing Japan’s host-nation support for U.S. forces, and dispatching JCG patrol vessels as a means of contributing personnel.

A senior Foreign Ministry official argued that dispatching JCG patrol vessels would circumvent constitutional constraints while signaling Japan’s proactive stance to the world. Under then Transport Minister Hashimoto Ryutaro, the Ministry of Transport and the JCG continued to explore this option. The JCG faced no statutory geographic limits on its activities, and operations in the Persian Gulf would have been legally permissible. The problem was operational: the Gulf was a war zone, and the safety of any JCG vessels deployed there could not be guaranteed.

Chief Cabinet Secretary Gotoda Masaharu would later describe Nakasone as one of the most outstanding postwar Japanese leaders, noting that they rarely differed in their political judgments — with one exception. That exception was the proposed dispatch of JCG patrol vessels to the Persian Gulf. Gotoda risked his position to oppose it, telling Nakasone that while the Cabinet would make the final decision, he personally would not sign off on it regardless.

Gotoda’s stand proved decisive. At U.S. urging, Japan instead agreed to fund the installation of high-precision radio navigation aids known as Decca chains. The resulting Decca Navigator stations allowed vessels to chart safe routes through the Gulf while avoiding the war zone, a practical and politically viable contribution that did not require deploying personnel into a combat area.

The 1987 episode established a precedent: Japan would not send vessels into an active conflict zone. That caution carried forward. Those 1987 deliberations directly shaped Japan’s approach to the subsequent Gulf War, and continue to shape its response to the current Strait of Hormuz crisis. During the Gulf War, Japan dispatched MSDF minesweepers to the Persian Gulf only after the ceasefire agreement took effect.

When Iraq invaded Kuwait in August 1990, the U.S. again asked Japan to dispatch minesweepers and supply vessels. Senior Foreign Ministry officials resisted, citing the 1987 precedent against sending vessels into areas of armed conflict. Japan instead provided $13 billion in financial support, a contribution that drew a cold response from the international community, as it was widely viewed as checkbook diplomacy without strategic commitment. After the Gulf War ceasefire took effect in April 1991, with the Persian Gulf no longer a combat zone, Japan dispatched MSDF minesweeper units that same month. The pattern established in 1987 held: deployment was permissible, but only once hostilities had ceased. As Japan weighs its options in the current Strait of Hormuz crisis, that calculus — and the political constraints behind it — remain fundamentally unchanged.

title: Japan Has Considered Nuclear-Powered Submarines Since 1958. Why Has It Never Built One?
description: From a 1958 design study to reported approaches to the U.S. Navy, Japan has repeatedly examined nuclear-powered submarines without making an acquisition decision.
text:
Japan is once again considering acquiring nuclear-powered submarines. As Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae’s government prepares to revise its three key national security documents by the end of 2026, proposals have emerged to include further research into their acquisition. On October 14, Takaichi told parliament that her government would deepen its “concrete and realistic consideration” of the issue. Defense Minister Koizumi Shinjiro has said no options should be ruled out.

Yet Japan has been here before. Parliamentary records and contemporary newspaper reports reveal that nuclear-powered submarines have repeatedly been considered for nearly 70 years, without Japan ever acquiring one.

The earliest evidence of Japan’s consideration dates to May 1958, less than four years after the USS Nautilus, the world’s first nuclear-powered submarine, entered service. A preliminary design document bearing the name Kawasaki Heavy Industries examined a nuclear propulsion system for a 2,500-ton submarine. The 1958 study concluded that the submarine concept was technically feasible but acknowledged that Japan could not independently manufacture its reactor and would need extensive U.S. technology.

The document’s existence was revealed in February 1974, when Japan Socialist Party lawmaker Narazaki Yanosuke questioned the government in parliament. The government and Kawasaki maintained that the document represented an individual engineer’s work rather than an official corporate development project. Narazaki challenged that explanation, but institutional involvement was never conclusively established.

In June 1964, a government-industry advisory group concluded that nuclear-powered submarines would provide the most effective means of countering foreign nuclear submarines’ superior underwater speed and endurance. However, legal obstacles remained.

In April 1965, then-Science and Technology Agency chief Aichi Kiichi stated that using nuclear propulsion aboard Self-Defense Forces vessels was impermissible under Japan’s Atomic Energy Basic Act because nuclear propulsion had not become generally established for civilian maritime use. At the same hearing, then-Defense Agency chief Koizumi Junya declared that Japan had no intention of building nuclear-powered submarines “at the present stage.”

On November 14, 2025, the Takaichi Cabinet reaffirmed that longstanding legal interpretation in a formal written response to a parliamentary question

The issue resurfaced in 1986. The Mainichi Shimbun reported that the Maritime Self-Defense Force had informally approached the U.S. Navy about acquiring nuclear-powered attack submarines. Japanese naval officers reportedly believed conventional submarines could no longer match U.S. nuclear submarines in speed and endurance.

According to a 2011 investigative report by the Sankei Shimbun, Defense Agency officials also secretly examined the possibility of developing nuclear-powered submarines domestically or acquiring them from the United States while preparing Japan’s 2004 defense guidelines. The idea was abandoned as premature.

Across these episodes, recurring obstacles included legal restrictions, technological challenges, substantial costs, and public opposition shaped partly by the 1974 radiation leak aboard Japan’s experimental nuclear-powered ship Mutsu.

Today’s strategic environment is markedly different.

China is expanding its naval presence across the western Pacific. The U.S. Department of Defense’s 2025 report on China’s military power assessed that Beijing aims to field nine aircraft carriers by 2035. China is already building a fourth carrier that is widely believed to be nuclear-powered.

North Korea has announced construction of a nuclear-powered submarine, while South Korea is pursuing its own acquisition plans.

Japan, meanwhile, is studying a next-generation submarine equipped with vertical launch systems (VLS) for long-range missiles. Incorporating VLS would require design modifications, potentially including a larger hull. Advanced sonar systems and unmanned underwater vehicles (UUVs) would further increase power demands. Conventional submarines, however, face limits on the electrical energy available while submerged, particularly because of their finite battery capacity.

Nevertheless, VLS does not necessarily require nuclear propulsion: South Korea already operates conventionally powered submarines equipped with such systems.

Nuclear propulsion could enable Japanese submarines to remain submerged for extended periods and maintain high underwater speeds, strengthening their ability to monitor Chinese naval movements and support deterrence.

But nuclear-powered submarines are no panacea. They entail major financial and technical burdens, while conventional submarines can offer acoustic advantages under certain conditions. Japan must also address the need for nuclear safeguards, specialized crew training, maintenance infrastructure, and public acceptance.

At a September government advisory meeting, one expert urged Tokyo to commit to acquisition, warning that reactor development and crew training would take a decade or more. Others argued that it was too early to decide.

In 1965, Koizumi Junya said Japan had no intention of building nuclear-powered submarines at that stage. Sixty-one years later, his grandson, Defense Minister Koizumi Shinjiro, says no options should be ruled out. But keeping an option open is not the same as making a decision. Another open-ended study risks repeating a familiar pattern: identifying the advantages, recognizing the obstacles, and postponing a decision.

Long development timelines justify timely decisions. They do not, however, establish which decision is correct. Japan needs a clear timetable, defined responsibilities, and a rigorous assessment of the legal, technological, financial, and operational questions. Deciding against acquisition after such an assessment would itself constitute a decision.

Nearly seven decades after the first documented study, Japan’s forthcoming security strategy revision will test whether Tokyo is finally prepared to move beyond perpetual consideration.

title: Japan Needs Higher Interest Rates
channel_text: Blog; East Asia; Economy; Tokyo Report
description: Japanese exporters enjoy high demand and strong profit margins, but importers are under severe pressure. The weak yen also hurts Japanese consumers.
text:
On a recent visit to Sapporo, the city on Japan’s northern island where my parents came from, my wife and I found gentle people, mild autumn days, and excellent food. As tourists who live and work in the United States, we also enjoyed very low prices: lunch at a high-quality restaurant cost only about $20 per person. While that was convenient for us, like so many other tourists who have headed to Japan to take advantage of favorable exchange rates, the cheap yen (yen yasu) has been hard on Japan’s economy.

To understand the pressure Japan is under, it is worth looking at the purchasing-power-parity equilibrium exchange rate – the rate at which a representative basket of goods and services would cost the same across two countries. This month, the OECD reports a PPP equilibrium exchange rate between Japan and the United States of around 93 yen per dollar. That is a far cry from the actual yen-dollar exchange rate, which has been hovering in the 150–160 range.

This means that goods produced in Japan cost much less than goods produced in the United States. As a result, Japanese exporters enjoy high demand and strong profit margins, but importers are under severe pressure. The weak yen also hurts Japanese consumers, as it creates strong incentives to raise prices: With imported goods more expensive, domestic producers know that their output will find buyers, and importers might pass their mounting costs on to buyers.

Japan used to have the opposite problem. In the early 1980s, it was a dominant economy experiencing strong growth. But the 1985 Plaza Accord, under which major economies agreed to take coordinated action to strengthen their currencies vis-à-vis the U.S. dollar, changed everything. After the accord was implemented, the PPP exchange rate was higher than the actual exchange rate, reaching almost double in 1995.

The strong yen (yen daka) persisted for decades, contributing to chronic deflation and stagnant growth. During this period, a visit to Tokyo strained tourists’ pocketbooks, Japanese goods found few customers abroad, and Japan’s once-formidable industries struggled. The situation deteriorated further around the 2008 global economic crisis, when the United States embraced monetary easing.

In the decades after the Plaza Accord, Bank of Japan (BOJ) governors (with the possible exception of Fukui Toshihiko) consistently failed to loosen monetary policy in line with changing economic conditions. Deflationary pressures intensified.

After returning to power in 2012, Prime Minister Abe Shinzo sought to turn things around with an economic-reform package, which came to be known as Abenomics. (I served as an adviser to Abe.) This package included a recommendation for monetary expansion, which then-BOJ Governor Kuroda Haruhiko embraced.

Now, conditions have changed. After the COVID-19 pandemic, the United States experienced a surge in inflation, which forced the U.S. Federal Reserve to abandon monetary expansion and raise interest rates. As the dollar strengthened, and the Japan-U.S. interest-rate differential widened, the yen depreciated in value, and deflationary forces gave way to inflationary pressures.

When circumstances change, so, too, must policy. For the BOJ today, this means pursuing monetary tightening in order to reduce the domestic money supply, and raising the interest rate.

To some extent, Japanese policymakers seem to recognize this. After keeping the short-term interest rate around 1 percent for some time, the BOJ raised its policy rate to 1.25 percent last month. This is high for Japan – the highest in 31 years, to be precise. But with the U.S. short-term money market pushing the interest rate close to 4 percent, and more U.S. rate hikes likely, it is not nearly enough. Speculators continue to exploit the interest-rate differential via the so-called carry trade (borrowing cheaply in yen to invest in higher-yielding assets abroad).

Under the gold standard or a fixed exchange rate, if a major country pursued monetary expansion, another, weaker country might need to reduce its money supply and raise its interest rate. Under a flexible exchange-rate regime, however, an expansion in one country should be met with a (moderate) expansion in another, just as tightening should be met with tightening.

We know that U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Japanese Finance Minister Katayama Satsuki are communicating about fiscal and monetary matters. Ultimately, however, monetary policy must be pursued autonomously, with BOJ Governor Ueda Kazuo doing what is best for Japan’s economy. Under the current circumstances, that means reducing the money supply and raising interest rates more aggressively.

title: Japan’s Nuclear Revival Has a Trust Problem
description: Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae has made it clear that the nuclear restart is part of the answer to Japan’s energy uncertainty, but questions remain about safety and accountability.
text:
When Tokyo Electric Power Company (TEPCO) brought Unit 6 at Kashiwazaki-Kariwa back online in January, it became the first TEPCO reactor to resume since the Fukushima Daiichi accident. An alarm halted the restart the next day; the unit resumed operation in February and entered commercial service in April. Unit 7 at Kashiwazaki-Kariwa, meanwhile, is not expected to restart before 2029–30, according to the EIA.

Clearly, the restart announcement in January was a bit of a false start. Still, the symbolism was unmistakable: The utility responsible for Fukushima is again operating a nuclear plant, the world’s largest by installed capacity.

The timing was also consequential. The Israeli-Japan strikes on Iran on February 28 and the resulting effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz exposed Japan’s reliance on imported energy. In 2025, the Middle East supplied 94 percent of Japan’s crude oil imports; 93 percent of the country’s crude imports passed through Hormuz, according to Reuters.

Japan’s exposure to Hormuz through LNG is much smaller: around 6 percent of total LNG imports, according to IEEFA. Yet Japan imports more than 97 percent of the LNG it consumes, and LNG generates about a third of Japan’s electricity, according to the government’s 2025 energy overview. The Hormuz shock therefore mattered both as a direct risk to Japan’s oil supply and as the cause of higher global gas and electricity prices.

The International Energy Agency reported that Japanese wholesale spot electricity prices in the second quarter of 2026 were more than 30 percent higher year on year. Futures in mid-July pointed to prices in the second half of 2026 nearly 40 percent above the same period a year earlier. These are wholesale-market figures, not household bills, but they show how a disruption to a relatively small share of Japan’s direct LNG supply can still transmit through global markets.

Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae has made it clear that the nuclear restart is part of the answer to Japan’s energy uncertainty. She said in March that the newly reopened Kashiwazaki-Kariwa Unit 6, combined with a temporary increase in coal-fired generation, could cut Japan’s LNG imports passing through Hormuz by about 40 percent.

That logic extends beyond the Gulf. A country dependent on LNG imports for a large share of its electricity is exposed to disruptions elsewhere in the Indo-Pacific, including scenarios involving shipping routes around Taiwan or in the East China Sea. For example, Japan’s continued reliance on Russian LNG has become a problem. The Sakhalin-II supply relationship has become a question of energy security, diplomacy, and policy autonomy.

The strategic case for nuclear power is therefore not just about decarbonization or energy bills. It is also about preserving Tokyo’s strategic autonomy by reducing its reliance on overseas energy providers.

Japan’s nuclear energy targets remain well ahead of the fleet it can count on today. The government’s Seventh Strategic Energy Plan set a target for nuclear power to supply about 20 percent of electricity generation in fiscal year 2040. The U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) estimated that meeting that target would require up to 30 reactors in operation. As of September 16, the latest date on the Nuclear Regulation Authority’s operating-status register, 11 reactors were classified as “Operation.”

On August 26, the Green Transformation Implementation Council adopted a package calling for the maximum use of nuclear power, with safety as a prerequisite, as NucNet reported. The plan set out plans to replace two to five reactors in the 2040s and a cumulative 11 to 14 by the 2050s, alongside investment in domestic supply chains for perovskite solar, next-generation geothermal, and offshore wind.

As Reuters reported, specific measures, including legislative steps, are expected by year’s end. The package is therefore more than a statement of intent, but key details – including the specific sites for nuclear plants – remain to be worked out.

Japan’s government may have a sense of political urgency, but its nuclear companies still lack institutional credibility. In September, an independent inquiry found that Chubu Electric Power, which operates the Hamaoka Nuclear Power Plant in Shizuoka Prefecture, had selectively used seismic-wave data to keep its estimates within internal parameters, despite earlier internal reports of irregularities. The inquiry also found that senior management had pressed staff to restart the reactors as soon as possible, according to Reuters. In response, Chubu said it would withdraw its applications to restart Units 3 and 4 at Hamaoka, and that its president and chairman would resign.

The episode shows what can happen when the commercial and political pressure for speedy restarts overtakes the discipline of safety review. It also gives opponents of restarts a concrete reason to doubt assurances from both utilities and government. Chubu says it may reapply after restructuring its organization and processes. Before it does, the company must show that its internal controls can withstand pressure to produce a favorable answer. Japan’s nuclear regulator, in turn, must be able to demonstrate that review standards are applied independently and transparently.

Public opposition, especially at the local level, is a related issue. Niigata’s governor approved the restart of Kashiwazaki-Kariwa, but a survey conducted before that decision found 50 percent of residents supported restarting Unit 6 and 47 percent opposed it. Nearly 70 percent said they were concerned about TEPCO operating the reactor.

The governor’s approval came with demands for clear safety explanations, evacuation planning, road improvements, and continued monitoring of TEPCO. In other words, local acceptance will require continued action on TEPCO’s part. A serious incident, a poor safety disclosure, or another data scandal at any plant can shape public opinion across the country.

Three tests will show whether Japan’s nuclear revival can provide a reliable source of energy – especially in large enough quantities to make a meaningful difference for Japan’s energy security. First, can the Nuclear Regulation Authority retain public credibility while the government presses for a faster energy transition? Second, can utilities with past governance failures repair their internal controls and earn the right to re-enter the review process? Third, will the August package’s promised legislation and funding arrive by year’s end, and will the longer-term replacement targets be matched by realistic project timetables and local consent?

Japan’s government can designate nuclear energy a security asset; it cannot legislate the public confidence required for the nuclear revival to proceed.
tag: Japan nuclear energy; Japan nuclear power; Japan Nuclear Regulatory Authority; Japan nuclear restart; TEPCO

title: Japan’s Potential as a ‘Third Option’ for ASEAN
description: ASEAN is looking for a third partner. Japan fits the bill — if it plays its cards right
text:
The countries of ASEAN have traditionally sought to maintain their autonomy under the banner of “centrality,” avoiding excessive dependence on any particular external power — the United States, China, or others — through what might be called an omnidirectional strategy. Expanding cooperation across as many extra-regional partners as possible in areas such as trade, investment, and infrastructure development has been a useful strategy for building the foundations that sustain that autonomy.

Among the challenges this entails, none is more important than determining how to engage with the United States and China, respectively, and how to keep a balance between them. The United States remains the world’s preeminent military power and occupies the central position in the global financial and monetary regime. It is also the largest source of investment in ASEAN and the largest export market for many ASEAN member states. As such, its influence in the region should not be underestimated. Yet the second Trump administration’s highly unpredictable foreign policy is eroding American soft power, while China is intensifying its outreach to the Global South, including ASEAN countries. China’s cooperative relationships with the ASEAN states are clearly deepening.

Beijing presents its relationship with ASEAN countries as an opportunity, one offering member states the potential for greater stability and development. Evidence for this can be found in China’s four major initiatives for engagement: the Global Development Initiative (GDI), the Global Security Initiative (GSI), the Global Civilization Initiative (GCI), and the Global Governance Initiative (GGI). The GDI, which calls for invigorating the global economy and advancing win-win cooperation toward stronger, greener, and more balanced development, and the GSI, which calls for a common, inclusive, cooperative, and sustainable approach to security, are the cornerstones of these initiatives.

In response to this Chinese outreach, ASEAN countries have uniformly endorsed the GDI. ASEAN’s principal documents welcome it, and all ASEAN countries have joined the Group of Friends of the GDI at the United Nations. For ASEAN countries, more active investment, financial support, and technical assistance from China channeled through the GDI aligns with their own development needs. The GSI is a different matter: while Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, and Timor-Leste have explicitly expressed support, ASEAN as a whole has not. Malaysia, however, has indicated a willingness to begin consultations on joining the GSI. In August 2026, Indonesia and China also agreed to strengthen joint military exercises, defense industrial cooperation, and technology cooperation.

ASEAN countries have not, however, abandoned their commitment to autonomy. In March 2025, for example, in response to the launch of the second Trump administration, ASEAN established the ASEAN Geoeconomic Task Force (AGTF); in response to the Middle East crisis, this was subsequently reorganized in March 2026 into the ASEAN Geoeconomic Group (AGG). The AGG is examining what measures ASEAN should adopt amid intensifying geoeconomic competition — measures of existential significance for the bloc. For ASEAN countries grappling with the “geoeconomic turn” as a new challenge, maintaining an omnidirectional strategy and expanding cooperative relationships with third partners beyond the United States and China is becoming ever more critical to securing their autonomy.

Japan should recognize these needs and play a role as that third partner, or option, for ASEAN countries. Potential areas for cooperation are wide-ranging: energy security, environment and green transformation (GX), digital infrastructure including AI and semiconductors, infrastructure development, and security cooperation through defense equipment transfers and capacity-building support. The Updated FOIP announced in May 2026 also signals Japan’s intention to reinforce a range of issues that ASEAN countries consider important. Japan should make full use of the key schemes it has available for deepening cooperation with ASEAN: the Asia Zero Emission Community (AZEC), the Partnership on Wide Energy and Resources Resilience Asia (POWERR Asia), Official Security Assistance (OSA), and an ODA framework that now makes it easier to leverage private-sector financing.

RCEP, the broad mega-FTA encompassing Japan, ASEAN, and other regional partners, is due for review in 2027. Japan and ASEAN should work together in maintaining a freer and more open rules-based regional economic order. Beyond that, supporting ASEAN countries in their efforts to expand their role in broader global forums, and working together to uphold a rules-based international order, will become increasingly important.

The annual survey “The State of Southeast Asia” conducted by the Singapore-based think tank ISEAS–Yusof Ishak Institute has shown consistently that Japan commands the highest level of trust among extra-regional countries from ASEAN nations. The reasons behind this deserve attention. According to the latest edition, published in 2026, the top response to the question of why Japan is trusted was: “Japan is a responsible stakeholder that respects and champions international law” (41.4 percent). This was followed by “Japan has vast economic resources and the political will to provide global leadership” (22.7 percent). In working with ASEAN countries to sustain a desirable regional order, Japan’s reputation as a supporter of the rules-based international order may be its most valuable asset.
tag: ASEAN autonomy; ASEAN-China relations; ASEAN-Japan relations; ASEAN-U.S. relations; Free and open Indo-Pacific; Global Development Initiative; Global Security Initiative; Updated FOIP

title: Karakoram 2026: Inside China-Pakistan Joint Military Training in Xinjiang
channel_text: Asia Defense; Blog; Security; South Asia
description: The deteriorating security environment in the region thus reinforces the importance of China-Pakistan military cooperation.
text:
On October 14, China and Pakistan began joint military training known as Karakoram 2026. According to official sources, the training’s opening ceremony was held in Korla city, Xinjiang, China. The main objective of this training is to focus on joint counterterrorism operations in high-altitude areas, according to China’s Ministry of National Defense.

The nine-day exercise encompassed a range of operational and tactical training activities that are significant not only for bilateral military cooperation but also in the context of a changing regional security environment.

Bilateral military exercises between Pakistan and China are a well-established and recurring feature of their defense cooperation. The two countries conducted the Sea Guardian IV naval exercise earlier this year to enhance interoperability and maritime cooperation. Joint counterterrorism drills are also a constant feature of their defense cooperation, with the previous example being Warrior IX held in December 2025.

Karakoram 2026 particularly focused on joint counterterrorism in high-altitude areas, with “skills training in UAV [unmanned aerial vehicle] operation, on-the-move target search and firing, and long-range sniping, and joint command and live-force exercises,” according to a Chinese Defense Ministry spokesperson.

China Central Television’s military channel said that China provided all the equipment, including Type 191 rifles, Type 201 squad machine guns, Type 11 armored assault vehicles, Type 08 infantry fighting vehicles, artillery, and both unmanned and anti-unmanned systems. The use of Chinese equipment and subsequent Pakistani familiarization with equipment could boost the likelihood of future Pakistani procurement.

However, the most notable feature of Karakoram 2026 is that this is the first time both countries are moving away from counterterrorism training by specialized units to regular army forces. This development will further strengthen defense cooperation and reinforce the broader all-weather strategic partnership between Pakistan and China. The main aim of this is to increase interoperability and joint cooperation on terrorism-related issues.

Karakoram 2026 is a reflection of broader convergence between China and Pakistan over shared security concerns in the region. Their respective threat perceptions may not be identical, but they have a shared interest in preventing terrorist organizations from exploiting territorial vulnerabilities. Beijing continues to have concerns about the potential for attacks in China, while Chinese nationals operating in Afghanistan and Pakistan have faced attacks on occasion. Joint counterterrorism training provides an institutional mechanism to translate these shared concerns into practical military cooperation.

One key component of these exercises was UAV operations. The motivation is obvious considering the emergence of drone warfare in the Afghanistan-Pakistan border region, especially the use of UAVs by terrorist outfits. Training in this domain will increase situational awareness while simultaneously supporting surveillance operations. At the same time, mobile target detection and engagement will strengthen coordination under dynamic battlefield conditions.

Long-range sniping and live-force exercises further test tactical proficiency, decision-making, and interoperability. For participating forces, this exercise would be helpful in coordinating response and improving communication during complex operations.

Looking at all the capabilities involved in Karakoram 2026, it is evident that the exercises were specially designed in relevance to the difficult terrain of northern Pakistan and the bordering Chinese region of Xinjiang. The China-Pakistan border region has difficult, mountainous terrain with extreme weather conditions complicating security operations. However, one should not perceive these exercises as evidence of China and Pakistan preparing for a specific operation in the region. Rather, Karakoram 2026 is significant mainly due to improved preparedness for shared counterterrorism contingencies and strengthening military-to-military familiarity.

Another major dimension setting the scene for these exercises is the fraught security environment between Afghanistan and Pakistan, which has complicated Pakistan’s counterterrorism efforts. Islamabad has repeatedly raised concerns about the presence of Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) militants on Afghan territory and their ability to conduct cross-border attacks. For Pakistan, the recent surge in drone attacks especially by the militants across the border raises another challenge that needs to be addressed.

A 2026 report by the U.N. Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team documented escalating cross-border attacks involving Pakistan and Afghanistan and reported continued support for the TTP by Afghanistan’s de facto Taliban government. In this context, joint training in drone operations may help Pakistan improve both surveillance and defense. The value of such experience will greatly depend on whether the units and police forces bearing the brunt of these attacks, received practical training in counterdrone defense.

The biggest implication of Karakoram 2026, however, is not the specific training received; it is the institutionalization of cooperation. With air, naval, and now army training exercises, China and Pakistan have developed a framework covering all three services. Pakistan used Chinese platforms during the May 2025 conflict with India, and army-level interoperability is a natural and logical next step in defense cooperation.

Karakoram 2026 is not merely a military training but a broader reflection of evolving security priorities of China and Pakistan. With the resurgence of terrorist attacks, counterterrorism cooperation sits at the forefront of Islamabad’s national security concerns. On the other hand, Beijing remains heavily invested in Pakistan under the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), and the security of Chinese nationals in Pakistan remains an important dimension of bilateral relations.

The deteriorating security environment in the region thus reinforces the importance of China-Pakistan military cooperation. The UAV-related training, coordination in command, and realistic field exercises at Karakoram 2026 can be understood against the broader need to improve situational awareness, tactical coordination, and responsiveness to emerging threats.

However, the effectiveness of military training cannot be measured solely by the completion of an exercise. Its lasting value will depend on the extent to which the participating forces incorporate lessons from joint training into their operational practices and adapt to emerging security challenges.
tag: China-Pakistan counterterrorism cooperation; China-Pakistan defense relations; China-Pakistan joint exercises; China-Pakistan military relations; Karakoram 2026; Pakistan counterterrorism

title: Korean Dramas: Ukraine, Russia, and Where South Korea Begins
description: A diplomatic spat and a comment that caused controversy.
text:
In this episode of The Diplomat’s Asia Geopolitics Podcast, hosts Katie Putz and Ankit Panda take stock of two tiffs: the recent diplomatic tensions between South Korea and Ukraine, sparked by the disclosure by the Ukrainian president that Kyiv had sent two North Korean POWs to Seoul; and the root of recent furor over comments made by the commander of U.S. Forces Korea regarding where South Korean territory begins.
