title: Laos Replaces Prime Minister in Major Leadership Reshuffle
description: Saleumxay Kommasith, a former foreign minister and permanent representative to the UN, has been appointed to the top job.
text:
Laos’ National Assembly yesterday approved a major leadership change that included the removal of Prime Minister Sonexay Siphandone.

In what the state-run Vientiane Times described as “a significant change in senior state leadership,” lawmakers yesterday voted unanimously to appoint Sonexay’s deputy Saleumxay Kommasith as the country’s new prime minister. Sonexay was appointed president of the National Assembly, succeeding the late Xaysomphone Phomvihane.

The position has been vacant since Xaysomphone, the son of revered communist leader Kaysone Phomvihane, died in August at the age of 70. The Central Committee of the ruling Lao People’s Revolutionary Party described his passing as “an immense loss for the Party, the State and the Lao people of all ethnic groups.”

According to the Laotian Times, 57-year-old Saleumxay has a background in diplomacy, having spent much of his career in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. He has previously served as Laos’ representative to the United Nations and as foreign minister between 2016 and 2024, and was also appointed as a deputy prime minister in 2022.

Beyond the need to fill the vacant National Assembly position, Lao media reports were reticent about the reasons for Sonexay’s removal, and in Laos it is often hard to separate performance-based from patronage-based appointments. Nonetheless, the fact that he was kept on as prime minister at the last national congress of the LPRP in January, presumably with the expectation that he would serve for a full five-year term, suggests that the reasons for his removal are probably more short-term.

Indeed, his successor’s address to the National Assembly after yesterday’s vote may offer some clues as to the change. In his remarks to lawmakers, Saleumxay praised the country’s current economic trajectory, stating that the economy grew by 4.8 percent in the first nine months of 2026, up from 4.6 percent over the same period last year. But according to the Vientiane Times, he also noted that agriculture “continues to face difficulties. Floods, pest outbreaks, and African swine fever have affected production, while fuel price volatility has increased production and transport costs.”

Laos’ economy has been under severe strain in recent years. After the COVID-19 pandemic, the country was hit by a debt-driven economic crisis that was marked by spiraling inflation, a rapid depreciation of the kip, and, for a period in mid-2022, fuel shortages that threatened the country’s food security. While Laos has since managed to stabilize its economy somewhat, the impact of the energy supply shock emanating from the U.S.-Iran war has threatened to disturb this progress, as the new prime minister’s remarks yesterday suggest.

Whatever the drivers, yesterday’s leadership shake-up is just the latest in a number of reshuffles that have broken the historically placid surface of Lao political life. The most recent of these was in late 2022, when Phankham Viphavanh was removed as prime minister, in a move that was widely recognized as a response to the economic crisis. On that occasion, the beneficiary was none other than Sonexay.

According to the Laotian Times, Laos also reshuffled nine senior government officials in June 2025, including the governor of the central bank and ministers responsible for finance, education, health, labor, agriculture, and industry and commerce.
tag: Laos National Assembly; Laos politics; Phankham Viphavanh; Saleumxay Kommasith; Sonexay Siphandone

title: Malaysia to Raise Transboundary Haze Crisis With ASEAN Foreign Ministers Ahead of Summit
description: This year’s particularly severe haze season has once again exposed the void in national and regional efforts to combat the problem.
text:
Malaysia’s government will raise the issue of transboundary haze at an Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) foreign ministers’ meeting ahead of the bloc’s 49th Summit in Manila next month.

Over the past four months, massive wildfires have raged across Indonesia, particularly on the islands of Borneo and Sumatra, causing a toxic haze that has seriously impacted Malaysia, Brunei, Singapore, and parts of the Philippines.

Foreign Minister Mohamad Hasan told reporters in Sepang yesterday that the haze issue required special attention as it was not covered by existing ASEAN mechanisms for natural disasters, the state media agency Bernama reported.

“We already have an ASEAN mechanism for natural disasters, but haze is not included or classified as a natural disaster,” he said. “So, this will be one of the issues that I will personally raise at the meeting with my counterparts.”

Air pollution from the fires, which have been prolonged and exacerbated by an unusually severe dry season, has forced the closure of schools across Malaysia in recent weeks. Last week, the government ordered schools to close in Melaka, Negri Sembilan, Selangor, Kuala Lumpur, and Putrajaya due to the worsening haze. The Malaysian capital rated among the world’s most polluted major cities globally. This came after hundreds of schools across the state of Sarawak on Borneo shut last month due to the hazardous air pollution in neighboring Kalimantan.

Malaysia has already been in touch with the Indonesian authorities about the fires. Last week, Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said that he had discussed the situation with Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto, who had “agreed to take the necessary steps.”

Mohamad Hasan said yesterday that Indonesia’s new foreign minister Arrmanatha Nasir had informed him that poor visibility in affected areas was hampering aerial firefighting operations. Many of the fires were also located deep inland, where water supplies were limited, and that some were in peatland areas, where fire-fighting is particularly challenging.

“Indonesia has between three to four aeroplanes and 34 helicopters, but they cannot take off because visibility is so poor that it is unsafe for any flights in the affected areas,” he said, as per Bernama.

Rizal Irawan, a senior official at Indonesia’s Environment Ministry, said last month that the country’s authorities were investigating 19 companies that it believes may be linked to the wildfires, and said it would investigate who might be responsible. Whether or not these investigations result in prosecutions and punishments remains to be seen.

“Transboundary haze” has become a seasonal crisis in large parts of Southeast Asia, much of it caused by agricultural burn-off on monoculture plantations, including palm oil, maize, paper pulp, and sugar. These are compounded by vehicle and industrial emissions and naturally occurring dry season forest fires.

This year’s particularly prolonged haze season has once again exposed the void in national and regional efforts to combat the problem. Some nations have introduced their own legislation to tackle the haze problem, but effective enforcement requires support from the nation where the fires are located, something which has not always been forthcoming.

In 2002, ASEAN member states signed the ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution (AATHP), a recognition of the need “to co-ordinate national action for preventing and monitoring transboundary haze pollution.” In April, the 11-nation bloc inaugurated the ASEAN Coordinating Center for Transboundary Haze Pollution Control in Jakarta, which reflects member states’ “shared determination to achieve a haze-free region through stronger cooperation and faster response,” as Environment Minister Hanif Faisol Nurofiq put it at the time.

Much like the bloc’s human rights instruments, however, the AATHP and other ASEAN mechanisms are weighted heavily toward consensus and national sovereignty. As Rizky Ihsan of Griffith University put it in a recent article, “rather than restricting the states that signed up to it, the AATHP was designed to be acceptable to them.” Under the agreement, Rizky argued, “national governments have considerable control over how problems are reported, how emergencies are defined, and when outside help is requested.” He noted that similar issues also apply to the new Coordinating Center, which “will assist only when the national authority declares an emergency and asks for help.”

ASEAN is clearly aware that more effective regional mechanisms are necessary to combat the problem. Further discussions at next month’s ASEAN Summit to this end could be a welcome, if belated, move in this direction.

The challenge is that it not only requires cooperation between nations that often jealously guard their own sovereign prerogatives; it also, in many cases, requires confrontations with entrenched business interests that are unpalatable for national governments, and likely very challenging for regional mechanisms. Without serious coordination and a willingness to cede a degree of sovereignty in the service of the regional interest, Southeast Asia’s annual haze problem is only likely to continue.
tag: ASEAN Agreement on Trans-boundary Haze Pollution; ASEAN Coordinating Center for Transboundary Haze Pollution Control; ASEAN transboundary haze; Indonesia wildfires; Mohamad Hasan; Transboundary haze

title: Malaysian PM Anwar Bans Civil Servants From Using Israel-developed Navigation App
channel_text: ASEAN Beat; Blog; Security; Southeast Asia
description: Anwar Ibrahim said that Waze, which was developed in Tel Aviv before being acquired by Google in 2013, could be exploited by the Israeli regime.
text:
Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim has prohibited civil servants from using Waze, a popular navigation app developed in Israel, warning that its use could compromise “national security and sovereignty.”

In a Facebook post on Wednesday, Anwar said that the ban was intended to “protect government information and users’ personal data from the threat of misuse by the Israeli regime.”

Anwar said his administration was looking into potential security risks arising from the use of Waze, which, despite now being a subsidiary of Google, remains subject to Israeli law. For the same reason, he urged Malaysians to stop using the app, and suggested that they switch to local alternatives including Tuju, an app developed by the Malaysian Highway Authority.

“The MADANI Government’s stance is firm and we will close any space that can be exploited by the Israeli regime to threaten the security of the country and the people,” Anwar stated.

Waze originated in 2006 as an open-source project called FreeMap Israel, created by Israeli software engineer Ehud Shabtai. It grew quickly and was subsequently acquired by Google for around $1 billion in 2013.

The prohibition on the app’s use was issued a day after Anwar chaired a meeting of the National Cyber Security Committee (JKSN), at which the potential risk of Waze being used to monitor Malaysian citizens’ data was discussed, Anwar said in a separate Facebook post on Tuesday.

The JKSN meeting also reviewed the development of cyber threats and efforts to strengthen Malaysia’s “digital preparedness and sovereignty.” It also discussed the security of MyDigital ID, Malaysia’s national digital identity verification platform, and efforts to implement the country’s Cyber Security Act 2024.

“This effort is crucial to ensure that the digitalization of public services continues to benefit the people, without neglecting the security, trust, and sovereignty of the nation,” he said.

Waze yesterday rejected Anwar’s allegations that it collects sensitive government information or allows users’ personal data to be exploited by third parties. In a statement to Reuters, a Waze spokesperson said that the company “operates under strict privacy policies that protect user data and comply with global legal data protection standards.”

The directive reflects the Malaysian government’s long-standing hostility toward Israel, with which it does not have diplomatic relations, and its support for the Palestinian national cause. Anwar has been particularly outspoken on this issue, condemning Israel’s assaults on Gaza in the wake of the militant group Hamas’ attacks on southern Israel on October 7, 2023.

Speaking at a large pro-Palestine rally in Kuala Lumpur several weeks after the Hamas incursion, Anwar described the Israel’s military response as “the height of barbarism in this world,” and called on Israel to end its occupation of Palestinian territories. Unlike other critical leaders, Anwar has also continued to engage publicly with Hamas, which Israel, the U.S., and many Western nations view as a terrorist organization.

Anwar also claimed that the U.S. government had brought diplomatic pressure to bear on his government to shift its position on Hamas, but that it would maintain “its independent position.”
tag: Anwar Ibrahim; Hamas; Israel-Palestine conflict; Malaysia Israel; Malaysia Palestine; National Cyber Security Committee (JKSN); Waze

title: Maldives Opposition Eyes Sweeping Constitutional Overhaul
description: The MDP’s constitutional reform program calls for splitting the executive into two separate offices: head of state and head of government.
text:
The Maldives’ main opposition party, the Maldivian Democratic Party (MDP), held its fifth National Congress from October 1 to 3.

The congress, which is the party’s highest decision-making body, adopted significant changes to the MDP’s internal structure. It abolished the posts of party president and vice president, consolidating leadership under the chairperson, a position currently held by former President Mohamed Nasheed. Yet its most consequential decision was the overwhelming endorsement, by 520 of the 563 delegates present, of a sweeping constitutional reform program titled Bodu Badhalu (meaning “Big Change” in Dhivehi).

Formally submitted by former Economic Development Minister Fayyaz Ismail, the program seeks to address perceived weaknesses in the constitution adopted during the country’s transition to multiparty democracy in 2008. It argues that, despite the formal separation of powers, the president can exercise excessive authority, particularly when backed by a parliamentary majority. It further contends that constitutional safeguards for fundamental rights, including freedoms of expression, assembly, and the press, offer inadequate protection against executive overreach.

To remedy this, its central proposal is to split the executive into two separate offices: head of state and head of government. The latter would be directly elected by voters in a national election but could be removed by parliament. The head of state would instead be appointed by a special assembly comprising parliamentarians and elected local councilors.

The program also proposes several changes to the legislature, including setting a fixed limit on parliamentary seats, whose number currently increases with population growth; introducing preferential voting; reserving seats for women; and exploring a bicameral system. Citizens would gain the power to recall elected officials, while the removal of Supreme Court judges would require approval through a public referendum. The program further proposes reforms to the appointment and oversight of independent constitutional bodies to reduce political interference.

Regardless of its merits or prospects for implementation, the program’s overwhelming endorsement marks a dramatic shift in the MDP’s internal politics. Most notably, it reflects Nasheed’s renewed grip on a party that, until recently, had treated him as a pariah. Although formally proposed by Fayyaz, the program also advances Nasheed’s longstanding ambition to change the Maldives’ system of government, an ambition he now pursues alongside Fayyaz, with whom he has forged an unlikely political alliance.

Nasheed has long championed a parliamentary system, having backed it unsuccessfully in a 2007 referendum before winning the presidency under the new constitution in 2008. Following his controversial ouster in 2012, he narrowly lost the disputed 2013 presidential election to Abdulla Yameen. A controversial terrorism conviction subsequently barred him from contesting the 2018 election, which was won instead by his erstwhile close ally Ibrahim Mohamed Solih. Nasheed went on to win a parliamentary seat in 2019 and became speaker, eyeing a return to executive power as prime minister under a parliamentary system.

However, Solih resisted Nasheed’s efforts to hold a referendum on replacing the presidential system with a parliamentary one. Nasheed sought to advance the proposal at the MDP’s fourth National Congress in August 2022 but faced opposition from Solih and Fayyaz, then party chairperson and economic development minister in Solih’s cabinet. Nasheed subsequently shelved the proposal.

Relations with the party deteriorated further after Nasheed challenged Solih during the MDP’s January 2023 presidential primary and lost. He subsequently vowed to “destroy” the MDP and left to join The Democrats, a new party formed by his loyalists. Ahead of the presidential runoff, The Democrats demanded a referendum on the system of government as a condition of their support. Although the MDP agreed to hold one after the election, The Democrats withheld their endorsement.

Following Solih’s defeat to current President Mohamed Muizzu, the MDP’s National Council voted overwhelmingly against a parliamentary system, reflecting widespread resentment toward Nasheed, whom many blamed for contributing to Solih’s electoral defeat.

Yet Nasheed has since made a remarkable political comeback, reclaiming leadership of the very party he once threatened to dismantle. After a two-year hiatus from Maldivian politics, during which he served as secretary general of the Climate Vulnerable Forum, he rejoined the MDP in 2025. Strikingly, his return to the party’s helm was aided by former Solih loyalists, most notably Fayyaz. It was Fayyaz’s resignation as chairperson that created the vacancy Nasheed subsequently contested.

For now, the partnership serves both men’s political ambitions, with Fayyaz having supported Nasheed’s return to the MDP leadership and Nasheed, in turn, backing Fayyaz’s presidential ambitions for 2028. Bodu Badhalu was unveiled in April 2026 as the centerpiece of Nasheed’s chairperson campaign. It culminated in his landslide victory over a Solih-backed candidate, reflecting a profound shift in the party’s internal balance of power. The congress’s subsequent endorsement of Bodu Badhalu demonstrates that Nasheed has, at least for now, brought the party behind his constitutional vision.

Although that vision differs significantly from the traditional Westminster-style parliamentary system Nasheed has long championed, it nevertheless offers him a potential path back to high office. While Nasheed has repeatedly pledged not to contest the presidency in 2028 and reaffirmed his support for Fayyaz, he has nonetheless expressed interest in serving as head of state under the proposed arrangement, with Fayyaz as head of government. The precise powers and titles of the two offices, however, remain unclear.

Whether their alliance will endure remains an open question. Nasheed’s previous partnership with Solih fractured once the latter secured the presidency and asserted his political independence from Nasheed. Although Fayyaz formally proposed Bodu Badhalu, he had previously opposed Nasheed’s efforts to amend the constitution, and his embrace of reform now serves the purpose of securing Nasheed’s support for his presidential bid. Should Fayyaz win the presidency, it is unclear why he would pursue reforms that could curtail his own powers and establish a rival center of authority.

Even if sincerely pursued, Bodu Badhalu faces several challenges. Fayyaz must first win a competitive MDP primary against contenders including former Foreign Minister Abdulla Shahid and former Vice President Faisal Naseem, who claims to have Solih’s backing (although earlier reports suggested Solih himself was considering a bid). Should another candidate secure the nomination, the congress’s endorsement offers no guarantee that the party would remain committed to the program.

Beyond the primary lies the 2028 presidential election. Even if the MDP returns to power, it would initially face a hostile parliament in which Muizzu’s People’s National Congress holds a two-thirds supermajority. The composition of the next parliament, to be elected in 2029, remains uncertain. Meanwhile, constitutional amendments require a three-quarters majority.

Public approval would present a further hurdle, as changes to the nature of presidential elections require a referendum. Indeed, despite commanding a parliamentary supermajority, President Mohamed Muizzu failed to secure public support for his own constitutional reform proposal in April 2026, when voters rejected his plan to merge presidential and parliamentary elections.

For now, Bodu Badhalu underscores Nasheed’s remarkable political comeback. Barely three years after vowing to dismantle the MDP, he has reclaimed its leadership and secured its backing for reforms that could return him to high office. The question remains whether he can translate that influence into electoral victory and bring the program to fruition.

title: Mine Blast Tests South Korean Engagement Policy as Pyongyang Rejects Any Contact
description: North Korea has denied planting the mines and refused talks on the boundary line.
text:
On September 21, two mines exploded inside the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) that divides North and South Korea. Three South Korean soldiers were injured in the blast, two of which suffered serious injuries.

Two weeks later, on October 5, the South Korean military concluded that the explosion was caused by a mine North Korea had buried south of the Military Demarcation Line (MDL) that serves as a de facto border.

“Based on the results of the joint investigation with the United Nations Command (UNC) and scientific evidence, we have made a final determination that our service members, who were carrying out normal DMZ operations south of the MDL, were seriously injured by a plastic antipersonnel mine that North Korea planted south of the MDL under the pretext of so-called border fortification work,” Kwon Dae-won, deputy chief of the South’s Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) said during the military’s press conference on Monday. Both the UNC and the South Korean military assessed that the mines had been buried for at least 12 months.

Along with Kwon’s briefing, the military also said that it had launched an operation to remove the North Korean mines buried around the explosion site by detonating them. It also urged North Korea to offer a sincere apology to the injured service members and to remove the mines it installed in violation of the Armistice Agreement.

However, Pyongyang already rejected these findings and then refused an offer of talks on the border when Seoul released its initial assessment on the cause of the land mine explosion days ago. The dispute now places the engagement policy of South Korean President Lee Jae-myung under direct strain.

To understand the issue, it helps to begin with the geography of the border. The MDL separates the two Koreas, and the DMZ extends for two kilometers on either side of it. The Armistice Agreement forbids hostile acts inside the DMZ and bars any crossing of the MDL without permission from the Military Armistice Commission. The U.S.-led UNC holds the authority to judge violations of the armistice.

The Demilitarization Zone (DMZ) and Military Demarcation Line (MDL) between North and South Korea. Map via Wikimedia Commons.

Nevertheless, the line has grown difficult to read on the ground. Only around 200 of the 1,292 signs placed along it in 1953 remain intact. Seoul’s Defense Ministry has acknowledged that the baselines of the UNC and the South Korean military differ across roughly 60 percent of the border coordinates.

The September 21 explosions occurred during an operation to clear a path for a joint inspection with the UNC. The inspection was meant to examine terrain changes near the MDL, which military officials suspected were signs of mine-laying by North Korea. The blast site lay about 10 meters south of the line.

On September 28, the South’s JCS assessed a very high possibility that North Korean mines caused the explosions. Forensic analysis detected traces of trinitrotoluene and a brown synthetic material consistent with North Korean plastic antipersonnel mines. Next, investigators found another unexploded North Korean mine near the site. As a result, the South Korean military believes the area held at least four mines.

In addition, South Korean Defense Minister Kang Shin-chul told lawmakers on September 29 that Pyongyang appeared to have planted mines at several locations south of the MDL.

On September 30, Lt. Gen. Kang Hyun-woo of the JCS demanded an apology and responsible measures from North Korea, and he urged Pyongyang to halt its border fortification. Meanwhile, the UNC reported that investigators had identified an active North Korean mine south of the line. The command added that it was addressing the violation through established armistice mechanisms. For now, the military has said that it will announce the final results of its joint investigation at a later date.

North Korea answered with a flat denial from Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of the North’s autocratic leader Kim Jong Un and the main voice on inter-Korean relations. The Korean Central News Agency (KCNA), one of the North’s key state-controlled media, carried her statement on September 30.

“The incident is a clear farce reminiscent of the ‘wooden-box mine incident’ which disturbed the world more than ten years ago, in consideration of the time and method of provocation,” Kim said in her statement. “Clearly speaking, our soldiers have never crossed the border.”

On October 2, South Korean Unification Minister Chung Dong-young proposed that the two Koreas should meet to confirm and survey the MDL again. In his view, the fading visibility of the line was a primary factor behind the blast. While Chung said that demanding an apology from North Korea is natural, he opposed resuming loudspeaker broadcasts toward the North as a dangerous step.

Pyongyang replied the same day. Kim Yo Jong rebuffed Chung’s proposal as a “wild dream and unilateral jargon.”

Her statement then turned to the border line itself. “It is the fixed stand of the DPRK government to define the borderline, our sovereign boundary line, through the full exercise of sovereignty, that is, by the use of force, not by means of negotiation,” Kim said. (DPRK is an acronym of North Korea’s official name: Democratic People’s Republic of Korea.)

Behind the rejection stands a fortification campaign that North Korea launched in 2024. In late 2023, Kim Jong Un declared that the two Koreas are hostile states. Since then, North Korean troops have installed barbed-wire fences and landmines along the MDL.

Kim Yo Jong has described the work as a matter of sovereignty with no military purpose. Moreover, her statement published on September 30 said that North Korea had decided to strengthen counterattack capability opposite the 21st Infantry Division of the South Korean army on the eastern front.

South Korean officials counted more than 20 crossings of the MDL by North Korean troops in August alone – more than the 17 cases recorded during all of 2025. A JCS official attributed the crossings to work in unfinished areas. Under the rules of engagement, South Korean forces fire warning shots when North Korean troops cross the line. Pyongyang has threatened swift retaliation should South Korean troops fire directly at North Korean soldiers at work on the border project rather than firing warning shots.

The episode recalls a crisis in 2015 – the same chain of events that Kim Yo Jong mentioned in her own statement. On August 4, 2015, wooden-box mines detonated near the MDL south of Paju and severely injured two South Korean noncommissioned officers. Of the two, one lost both legs and the other lost part of one leg. Six days later, Seoul determined that North Korean troops had deliberately laid the mines.

In response, Seoul resumed loudspeaker broadcasts along the border for the first time in 11 years, and the two sides exchanged artillery fire on August 20. Soon after, senior officials between the two Koreas opened marathon negotiations at Panmunjeom on August 22. Three days later, they reached a six-point agreement. According to the agreement, Pyongyang expressed regret over the explosions and Seoul agreed to halt the broadcasts. The agreement eventually led to further contacts and to reunions of families separated by the 1950-53 Korean War.

Still, the circumstances of 2026 differ from those of 2015. For one, Seoul no longer has loudspeakers along the border because the Lee administration removed them to reduce tensions. For another, Pyongyang has denied responsibility and refused talks. Accordingly, Kang has cautioned against repeating the measures of 2015.

The contrast matters because Lee has pursued de-escalation since taking office. In August 2025, he pledged to restore the 2018 inter-Korean military agreement. His government suspended loudspeaker broadcasts directed at the North in a unilateral concession.

A day before Chung made his proposal for inter-Korean talks, Lee discussed the mine blasts in a speech marking the 78th Armed Forces Day. Lee said he still felt pain over the soldiers wounded in the explosions. Moreover, he pledged that his government would keep pursuing practical measures to lower military tensions with Pyongyang. Lee’s tone contrasted with the warning of retaliation that the North’s state media had published a day earlier.

In this context, many critics in South Korea wondered why Seoul chose to keep to its dovish stance on Pyongyang even after North Korea caused injuries to three South Korean troops., Seoul has stated that it will “take necessary measures” after establishing the facts based on the investigations; however, the military has not yet specified what corresponding measures it would take.

Meanwhile, North Korea fired a ballistic missile toward the waters off its east coast from the Wonsan area on October 3. The launch came one day after Kim Yo Jong ruled out any contact with Seoul. The JCS said that the missile flew more than 700 kilometers. However, KCNA claimed on October 4 that the missile, which was reported as an intermediate-range strategic missile, hit a target 1,000 kilometers away.

“We must continue our responsible efforts nonstop to constantly and repeatedly make the enemy recognize the reliability and fatality of our strategic offensive means,” Kim Jong Un said.

A separate announcement by Kim Yo Jong on October 3 addressed the flight distances reported by South Korea and Japan. She said that those figures exposed the limits of the tracking capability of the two militaries. In her account, a wave-like flight path caused the enemy to lose the missile from its first skip points. She described the missile as able to change its orbit at low altitude and said it was equipped with artificial intelligence.

“The enemy always made such a lame excuse that there is a limit to the detection capability because of the curvature of the earth’s surface, but in fact this just serves as a proof of our perfect missile capability and the most scientific ‘evaluation index’ confirming the power and reliability of our weapon system,” Kim said. “In other words, this means that there is no way to avoid this attack.”
tag: Demilitarized Zone; inter-Korea relations; Military Demarcation Line; North Korea landmine

title: Missing the Forest for the Trees in Taiwan’s Defense Preparations
user_author_name: K. Tristan Tang; H. Rion Wu
description: Beyond exercises and equipment, strategic developments in Taiwan’s military preparedness are being overlooked.
text:
In recent years, Taiwan’s military issues have received considerable discussion, from changes in Taiwan’s annual large-scale Han Kuang exercises to recommendations on equipment procurement. These are all quite important areas of change, but the most core issue seems to have received much less discussion: how exactly the Taiwan military may fight. The aforementioned changes in exercises and equipment procurement, in the end, are all meant to serve the kind of war Taiwan is prepared to fight. Taiwan has had some developments in this area that have received limited attention and discussion, but their importance is definitely no less than the developments in exercises and equipment.

The key is to comprehensively understand Taiwan’s efforts and preparations from the strategic level, using what the Taiwan military most often says about what kind of war to fight, what equipment to have, what kind of force structure is needed, and what training to conduct. Taiwan has moved from its past concepts of defeating the enemy on the opposite shore or seeking a decisive battle in the littoral area to actually carrying out an erosion strategy and sustained operations in recent years. To that end, Taiwan has continued to strengthen the army’s active-duty combat power in the northern region to build a layered defensive network and regional force superiority. Meanwhile, the cumulative duration of large-scale exercises in 2026 has already accumulated to nearly one month. There is also something that many people might have noticed but not realized: the significant expansion of Taiwan’s navy in recent years.

At the same time, these developments also bring out the current difficulties Taiwan faces in joint operations across the services. This is one of the most critical areas to watch in Taiwan’s future defense development. In recent years, experts have paid considerable attention to the Taiwan military’s efforts toward decentralization, but in practice, joint command and control is the key to whether Taiwan’s combat capability can be improved.

Further Concentration of Forces in Northern Taiwan

The key to an erosion strategy and sustained operations is to delay and strike enemy forces through layered forces. Although Taiwan emphasizes decentralized command and control, this means emphasizing that a single operational unit can continue to carry out assigned actions based on higher-level operational objectives when command and control is disrupted. In terms of military operations, strategically concentrating forces to make it difficult for the enemy to break through and advance is quite important. And this is also what Taiwan is doing.

Northern Taiwan is where the political center is located, and it also concentrates important operational command organizations and transportation hubs. More than one-third of Taiwan’s population lives there. More than about half of the Taiwan active-duty brigade-level forces of the Republic of China (ROC) Army and Marine Corps are normally stationed in the northern region (north of Miaoli and Yilan), including the main combat forces, combined arms brigades, Army Aviation units, and Marine Corps forces.

In particular, in recent years Taiwan has continued during exercises to additionally move units from other regions into the northern region to conduct reinforcement missions. This makes the forces concentrated in the northern region possibly reach nearly two-thirds of Taiwan’s active-duty ground forces. During the 2025 Han Kuang Exercise, the main reinforcement was carried out by units from the Marine Corps 99th Brigade moving north from southern Taiwan to reinforce Taoyuan and the greater Taipei area. The 2026 Han Kuang Exercise further expanded the reinforcement forces, including forces under the Marine Corps 99th Brigade and Army 564th Combined Arms Brigade from southern Taiwan, and the Army 586th Combined Arms Brigade from central Taiwan, which moved and deployed to the northern region.

Map by K. Tristan Tang and H. Rion Wu based on information collected and compiled from Military News Agency and Liberty Times.

This kind of deployment and training concentrates forces in northern Taiwan and is, to a considerable degree, a focus of Taiwan’s current sustained defensive operations. In September 2026, during the ROC Army’s annual large-scale Lu Sheng exercise, Maj. Gen. Lin Shih-wei, deputy commander of the Army Education, Training, and Doctrine Development Command, clearly stated at a press conference that this exercise was centered on the concept of successive resistance and sustained operations under Chief of the General Staff Admiral Mei Chia-shu’s erosion strategy. Most importantly, the exercise area was changed to northern Taiwan in order to conform with the focus on defensive operations and allow troops to become familiar with key terrain in the area of operations and the deployment and employment of troops and firepower.

Nearly One Month of Large-Scale Military Exercises

Another development deserving more attention is that in recent years the Taiwan military has begun extending the training duration of various live-force exercises. In addition to extending existing exercises such as the nationwide Han Kuang exercise and the brigade-level Lu Sheng exercise, it has also added several large-scale exercises.

The accumulated time of these military exercises has led the Taiwan military this year to spend almost an entire month participating in various live-force exercises, far more than in the past few years. This includes the five-day Immediate Combat Readiness Exercise in June, the five-day Joint Defense Exercise in July, the 10-day Han Kuang Exercise in August, and the 10-day Lu Sheng Exercise expected in October.

Besides allowing units to have more time to complete continuous training events that could not be conducted in the past, this also allows participating units to become familiar with scenarios related to long-duration sustained operations during a future Taiwan conflict. The longer training and exercise duration allows units to validate operations under prolonged combat scenarios, as well as the maintenance of combat capability and coordination with civilian sectors in the use of civilian resources, including manpower and material mobilization.

Taiwanese Navy’s Expanded Mission

Another aspect worth attention in recent years is that the ROC Navy has been playing more and more roles in Taiwan’s current defensive operations. In the past, the Taiwan government mainly planned naval units in wartime as fleet task forces. In recent years, there have been three notable changes.

First, the Marine Corps under the Navy has undergone a major transformation in recent years, shifting from a force responsible for offensive amphibious operations and power projection in the past to a defensive force for urban areas. In recent years, Taiwan’s Marine Corps has gradually given up its tanks and self-propelled artillery in favor of drones and anti-tank equipment. As the strategic reserve directly under the General Staff Headquarters, the Marine Corps has been deployed to the Taipei area, with its mission shifting to become a defensive force for the capital garrison area.

Second, the ROC Navy this year established a new Coastal Operations Command within the service. Its commander holds the same vice admiral rank as the Fleet Command commander, and it integrates units related to shore-based anti-ship missiles, shore-based radar, intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR), and unmanned aerial systems, with the goal of establishing a coastal operations system across units and platforms.

Third, Taiwan’s Coast Guard this year added one new deputy director-general position, and in late September formally appointed a vice admiral from the Navy to the position. The purpose is to bring the Navy’s tactical thinking into the Coast Guard, inject key new momentum into the Coast Guard’s transition from peacetime to wartime, effectively connect communication channels between the military and Coast Guard, and deepen joint maritime-air defense and response mechanisms.

In addition, Taiwan’s Coast Guard has also begun, during the military’s annual exercises, to expand training events related to the transition from peacetime to wartime, allowing its Coast Guard vessels to undertake part of the sea-denial strike missions during wartime. Specifically, this year’s Han Kuang exercise had the Coast Guard conduct exercises under the control of the Navy’s Coastal Operations Command.

These changes all show that the ROC Navy is playing an increasingly important role in Taiwan’s current defensive operations. This includes sea denial and coastal operations, and also includes the capital garrison mission during the defense-in-depth phase.

Policy Implications

Taiwan’s current defense preparations are not only changes in concepts and efforts in equipment procurement, but have also seen quite significant developments in military training and deployment validation. More importantly, as the relatively weaker side in the cross-strait military balance, Taiwan must necessarily concentrate its resources to a greater degree and use them more efficiently. Therefore, we can also notice that there is now more Navy involvement in maritime and coastal denial operations, and even in the land-based attrition strategy and the defense-in-depth phase. The Coast Guard is also practicing the transition from peacetime to wartime,

But at the same time, these changes also point to a more critical area to observe in the future, which is whether Taiwan’s joint operations across the services, especially its command and control preparations, are in place. In the past, land operations were usually considered something for the Army to handle by itself. In a hypothetical scenario where the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) would be able to conduct an amphibious assault on Taiwan and then offload follow-on forces, it was typically assumed to mean that Taiwan’s air and naval combat power had already been largely paralyzed, while China had air and sea superiority. Now, this situation has changed to a considerable degree. Navy shore-based units and Air Force air defense units will also play important roles during the defense-in-depth phase, and therefore preparations for joint operations become quite important.

The first question mark is the joint command and control capability under the concentration of large numbers of forces, including Army and Navy forces concentrated in the northern region, as well as Air Force air defense assets. Efficient command and control of different units in conducting joint operations is quite critical.

Second, and even more critical, is whether Taiwan can increase the capacity of its joint operations training. The Taiwanese military’s only Joint Operations Training Base has limited training capacity. Because of geographic space limitations and the need to avoid disturbing nearby residents, it can usually only provide battalion-level training. The ROC Navy, Army Aviation, and Air Force also have difficulty participating together as formed units in exercises because of the limited airspace. Although annual large-scale exercises can validate and train service members’ ability to conduct joint operations, in practice they cannot fully replace basic joint operations training.

Taiwan has far fewer resources compared with China, so joint operations capability is key to allowing Taiwan’s combat power to be used more efficiently. This is also a key area of Taiwan-U.S. military cooperation. In January 2026, media reports stated that U.S. personnel had been stationed at Taiwan’s Ministry of National Defense Joint Firepower Coordination Center, which is responsible for cross-service fires deployment and coordination, and that joint staff work had reportedly already been conducted.

It is important to know that decentralization is a key capability when the command and control system is cut off, in order to maintain operational resilience. But for Taiwan, in the event of war, the best situation for resisting a Chinese invasion to the greatest extent should be to have a sound joint operations capability, so that resources can be converted into combat power to the greatest extent. Therefore, although experts in recent years have paid considerable attention to the Taiwan military’s efforts toward decentralization, joint operations capability is also critical.

title: Myanmar Coup Administration Releases Photos of Detained Leader Aung San Suu Kyi
description: The photos reportedly show the 81-year-old receiving two books and a sealed diplomatic package from Britain's King Charles III.
text:
Myanmar’s military-backed government yesterday released two photos of detained former leader Aung San Suu Kyi, as she received a package from Britain’s King Charles III.

Presidential spokesperson Khaing Khaing Soe announced on Facebook that Home Ministry officials met the 81-year-old and handed her two gardening books, as well as “one sealed envelope, and a sealed diplomatic communication” from the British monarch. The two books were “The Land Gardeners – Soil to Table” and “SOIL: The World at Our Feet,” the latter of which appears to be connected to an exhibition that was held at Somerset House in London earlier this year. The meeting was subsequently reported by state media, albeit with no further details about the meeting.

The announcement was accompanied by the release of two photos that show Nobel laureate sitting with two officials at a table in a wood-paneled room – the same where she was photographed meeting with an official from the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) in August.

The images of Aung San Suu Kyi that were released yesterday were among just a handful that have been made public by the military since her removal in a coup in February 2021. Since then, she has been in the military’s custody, and is currently serving an 18-year prison term for a range of far-fetched charges, including incitement, corruption, election fraud, and violation of Myanmar’s Official Secrets Act.

The announcement of the delivery of the package from King Charles III, which could easily have been kept secret, comes amid a push by the new military-backed government to normalize its relations with important international partners, in particular the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).

The 11-nation bloc has barred Myanmar from its summits since late 2021, over its failure to implement its Five-Point Consensus plan for resolving the country’s post-coup conflict, which involved pledges to cease violence, allow humanitarian access, and engage in political dialogue involving “all parties” to the country’s conflict.

In recent months, Min Aung Hlaing has visited five of ASEAN’s 11 member states – Laos, Thailand, Cambodia, Vietnam, and Malaysia – with Indonesia and Brunei possibly to come.

Given her iconic status, Aung San Suu Kyi is an important form of leverage. Shortly after coup leader Min Aung Hlaing took office as president in April, his administration announced Suu Kyi’s relocation from prison to house arrest, alongside a broader amnesty of political prisoners. It also reduced her sentence by one-sixth.

While refusing a request from Philippine Foreign Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro, ASEAN’s special envoy, for a meeting with Aung San Suu Kyi, the authorities in August allowed her to meet with Arnaud de Baecque, the ICRC’s resident representative in Myanmar, and released four photos of the meeting. The meeting, her first publicized meeting with a foreign official since the coup, also sought to address the concerns of critics, including Suu Kyi’s son Kim Aris, about her condition in custody.

Given Naypyidaw’s desire for normalization, and the symbolic role that Aung San Suu Kyi still plays in Myanmar’s politics, it is likely that Myanmar state media will continue to drip-feed news about its most famous detainee.
tag: Aung San Suu Kyi; Min Aung Hlaing; Myanmar diplomacy; Myanmar political prisoners; Myanmar politics

title: Myanmar Establishes New Committee to Advance Normalization With ASEAN
description: The creation of the body, which comes ahead of next month's ASEAN Summit in Manila, is intended to “regain the country’s original role and rights” in the bloc.
text:
Myanmar’s military-backed government has formed a new ASEAN Affairs Committee in order to support its efforts to reintegrate itself into the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.

The Southeast Asian bloc has excluded Myanmar from its summits and foreign ministers’ meetings since late 2021, due to its failure to implement ASEAN’s Five-Point Consensus plan. Promulgated in April 2021, two months after a military coup, the Consensus calls for an immediate cessation of violence, dialogue among “all parties” to the country’s conflict, and access for humanitarian aid.

The Irrawaddy reported yesterday that the new body, which met for the first time on Tuesday, ahead of the 49th ASEAN Summit next month, is intended to “regain the country’s original role and rights” in the 11-nation organization. Tuesday’s meeting was chaired by Foreign Minister Tin Maung Swe and attended by representatives from the President’s Office and ministries of Defense, Home Affairs, Information, and Social Welfare.

Tin Maung Swe told the meeting that Myanmar had suffered “discriminatory treatment” from ASEAN since 2021, The Irrawaddy reported. The meeting also discussed “Myanmar‑led approaches” for restoring the country’s position in the bloc.

Since taking office in April, Min Aung Hlaing’s quasi-civilian government has launched a diplomatic charm offensive, involving visits to India, China, Russia, Belarus, and Kazakhstan, aimed at consolidating key partnerships and seeking injections of much-needed foreign investment.

A priority has been the normalization of Myanmar’s relations with ASEAN. Many of the latter’s member states appear to be supportive of Naypyidaw’s goal, and five of them – Laos, Thailand, Cambodia, Vietnam, and Malaysia – have rolled out the red carpet for the coup leader in recent months, with Indonesia and Brunei possibly to come.

The Philippines also appears to be softening. In a recent interview, Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., who holds the rotating chairmanship of ASEAN for 2026, said that while the Five-Point Consensus was “absolutely correct,” the bloc needed to try a “new approach” on Myanmar.

At the same time as it has wooed individual ASEAN member states, the military-backed government has forcefully rejected the Five-Point Consensus. In July, Myanmar’s military proxy parliament adopted a motion rejecting the Consensus as an unwarranted interference in Myanmar’s internal affairs, which “does not align with the current political developments in Myanmar.” Min Aung Hlaing said in a speech the following month that some member states had “adopted positions and practices that it regarded as discriminatory towards Myanmar.”

While most member states are now leaning in the direction of reopening ASEAN’s door to Myanmar – Thailand and Malaysia have both explicitly stated that this is their goal, and Singapore and Timor-Leste appear to be the last hold-outs – full normalization, like all ASEAN decisions, will require a consensus among all 11 member states. As I noted earlier this week, however, there are “evidently still differences within ASEAN over how fast engagement should proceed, and to what end.”

Unless ASEAN agrees to abandon the Five-Point Consensus altogether, normalization would seem to require at least some effort to implement it, however nominal. With the Myanmar military ramping up its attacks on resistance groups and civilian populations accused of harboring them, this seems unlikely in the current circumstances.

title: Myanmar War Crimes Survivors Look to Denmark for Justice
description: The country's legal system may provide one of the few remaining means of bringing Myanmar's generals to justice.
text:
Forty homes. That is how many a woman, now living in Denmark, watched burn in her village in Chin State, western Myanmar. Family members and friends were killed or left permanently disabled by landmines planted by the junta. Like tens of thousands of others from Chin State, she was driven across the border into India.

On Monday, October 26, she asked the Danish authorities to investigate the men responsible.

She has filed a criminal complaint in Copenhagen against members of the Myanmar junta. For her safety, she cannot be named. The crimes in the complaint include deliberate killing, mass arson and the forced displacement of tens of thousands of people.

This is possible because of a change in Danish law. Legislation that came into force last year specifically criminalizes war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide. It gives Danish prosecutors a route that did not exist before.

Her lawyer, Copenhagen-based Eddie Omar Rosenberg Khawaja, puts it plainly. “Under the new Danish legislation, it no longer matters where the crimes took place, or the nationality of the perpetrators or the victims,” he says. “Victims living in Denmark can request that Danish authorities hold commanders under whose watch atrocities against them occurred responsible.”

That matters because there is nowhere else to go. Myanmar’s courts are controlled by the generals. The Security Council has failed to act. International courts in The Hague – the International Criminal Court and the International Court of Justice – have also been slow. For the people of Chin State, a Danish police station may be one of the few doors that open.

It also fits Denmark’s own history. Tracy Bawi Hlei, Chairperson of Myanmar Action Group Denmark (MAGD), which supports the case, says, “Denmark has a history of aligning itself with the pro-democracy movement in Myanmar since before the 1990s, through development aid, support of activists, bypassing the military government and standing in solidarity with human rights movements.”

She sees this case as the next step. “Now, Myanmar people and Danish activists who are part of communities and movements in Denmark are taking a stand for accountability and the international rule of law,” she says. Survivors and crucial evidence, she explains, were identified within Denmark through a collaboration of civil society groups, including MAGD and the Chin Community Denmark, which also supports the case.

I run the Myanmar Accountability Project, which supports cases against the junta in Southeast Asia and Europe. I believe the basis for a Danish case is strong.

The Danish government has said so itself. In a statement to the U.N. on September 30, 2025, Denmark said, as a matter of public record, that Myanmar suffers from a lack of accountability and continued impunity. This complaint invites Denmark to act on that.

The timing is pointed. The Danish Foreign Ministry is closing its embassy in Myanmar. This case allows the Danish government to send a signal that it remains engaged with issues of justice and accountability, and that the rightful aspirations of the people of Myanmar to a just, peaceful and dignified life must be respected.

Meanwhile, the junta is seeking legitimacy. Min Aung Hlaing, the general who led the coup, is now president after sham elections that offered the people of Myanmar no real choice. Those who lived through his campaigns of burning and killing are expected to accept this as normal. They do not.

The country’s condition leaves no room for complacency. According to the latest U.N. report, more than 16 million people need aid, and the junta is blocking humanitarian access to vast areas where the need is greatest. Nearly 3.8 million people are estimated to be displaced, many of them several times over. A U.N. Development Programme report published last month found that two-thirds of the population are living in poverty or at immediate risk of falling into it.

The violence is taking place on a scale that few outside the region grasp. More than 100,000 people have died in conflict-related violence since the coup. That makes Myanmar the fourth most deadly conflict in the world. Far from being a frozen conflict, this is a war on civilians, and state-wide repression compounds the inhuman levels of killing, which makes justice and accountability even more important.

What the complainant seeks is limited. She is not asking Denmark to end a war. She is asking its police to open an investigation and its prosecutors to take her evidence seriously. She is asking that the commanders responsible be held accountable.

Denmark has said impunity in Myanmar must end. Its new law now gives it a way to act on that. She has come forward, at a risk to herself that most of us will never face. It is now for Danish authorities to decide whether the law means what it says.
