title: Myanmar’s Aung San Suu Kyi Speaks With Son For First Time Since Military Coup
channel_text: ASEAN Beat; Blog; Diplomacy; Southeast Asia
description: Kim Aris called for the release of all political prisoners in Myanmar and said that his mother must never be held hostage or used as a bargaining chip.
text:
The son of Myanmar’s detained former leader Aung San Suu Kyi says that he has spoken to his mother for the first time since the military coup of 2021, reiterating calls for her release.

“Today, I was able to speak directly with my mother, Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, for the first time in more than five years,” Kim Aris said in a statement yesterday. “Hearing her voice again means more to me than words can express.”

The call came after the military-backed administration released two photos of Aung San Suu Kyi receiving two books and a sealed diplomatic pouch from Britain’s King Charles III.

Yesterday’s call was also publicized by Myanmar’s presidential spokesperson, who posted on Facebook that the “convicted prisoner” had spoken to her son with the assistance of the Myanmar embassy in London. It also released photos of the pair talking on the phone.

In this statement, Aris thanked all of those who had campaigned for his mother’s freedom, and those who facilitated the phone call, but said the conversation was no substitute for regular contact, let alone his mother’s freedom.

“This moment must not be mistaken for freedom,” Aris said, “My mother is 81. She remains unjustly detained, and a single conversation cannot restore the years taken from her or the rights she is still denied.”

As Aris detailed in an interview with my colleague Luke Hunt last month, he has waged an international campaign for his mother’s release since February 2021, when she was ousted in a coup and placed under tight military custody. She is currently serving an 18-year prison term for a host of criminal charges, including incitement, corruption, election fraud, and violation of Myanmar’s Official Secrets Act.

Despite spending most of the past five years in seclusion, with virtually no contact with the outside world, in recent months the authorities have loosened the terms of Aung San Suu Kyi’s detention and been more forthcoming about the activities of the Nobel laureate.

Shortly after coup leader Min Aung Hlaing took office as president in April, his pseudo-civilian administration announced Aung San Suu Kyi’s relocation from prison to house arrest at a “designated residence” in the capital Naypyidaw, alongside a broader amnesty of political prisoners. It also reduced her sentence by one-sixth. In August, the authorities also allowed her to meet with Arnaud de Baecque, the resident representative of the International Committee of the Red Cross in Myanmar, the first foreign official that she had met since the coup.

This recent “leniency” is clearly connected to Naypyidaw’s ongoing efforts to normalize its relations with important international partners, in particular the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).

The 11-nation bloc has barred Myanmar from its summits since late 2021, over its failure to implement its Five-Point Consensus plan for resolving the country’s post-coup conflict, which involved pledges to cease violence, allow humanitarian access, and engage in political dialogue involving “all parties” to the country’s conflict.

Recognizing that Aung San Suu Kyi’s international fame and status as a political symbol, the authorities in Naypyidaw have hoped that loosening the conditions of her detention will help pave the way to normalization with ASEAN member states and other governments. At the same time, it has ruled out (at least for now) any prospect of her release.

In his statement, Aris expressed an awareness of the role that his mother had long played in the Myanmar military’s diplomatic strategy.

“My mother must never be held hostage or used as a bargaining chip for diplomatic recognition, sanctions relief, or political advantage. Basic humanitarian rights cannot be exchanged for legitimacy,” he said.

“Regular, direct, and private family contact and independent medical access must be guaranteed. Above all, my mother and all political prisoners must be released immediately and unconditionally.”
tag: Aung San Suu Kyi; Kim Aris; Myanmar coup; Myanmar military; Myanmar political prisoners

title: Myanmar’s Leaders Tried to Erase My Rohingya Identity 11 Years Ago
description: The repression of Rohingya identity is connected to Myanmar’s broader failure to establish an inclusive political order. It's time for ASEAN to realize that.
text:
In July 2015, I was invited to the residence of U Aung Thaung, a senior and influential leader of Myanmar’s Union Solidarity and Development Party (USDP), in Naypyidaw. We discussed the approaching general elections and parliamentary nominations for the constituencies in northern Rakhine state.

What happened during that meeting has remained outside the public record for more than 11 years. I want to disclose it now because the political question at its center – the recognition of Rohingya identity and rights – remains unresolved. It is also relevant to how ASEAN engages with Myanmar’s military leadership today.

I was elected to Myanmar’s house of parliament, the Pyithu Hluttaw, from Buthitaung township of Rakhine state in November 2010 as a USDP candidate. In the summer of 2015 I was preparing to secure my office for another term. But, during our private conversation, U Aung Thaung proposed a condition that went far beyond ordinary electoral politics.

As I recall it, he told me that he, the USDP leadership, President U Thein Sein, and then Commander-in-Chief Min Aung Hlaing did not accept “Rohingya” as an ethnic identity. He urged me to stop advocating for that identity and to persuade my constituents to identify themselves as “Bengali” instead. He presented this change as a pathway toward obtaining citizenship documentation and restoring political participation. He also advised me to give a media interview stating that “there is no Rohingya but Bengali,” without mentioning our private meeting and his name.

My parliamentary nomination, he indicated, depended on my willingness to support that position.

I refused.

I could not ask my constituents to surrender their identity in exchange for the possibility of receiving documents, voting rights, or another parliamentary term. Political representation should protect the rights of a community, not become an instrument for bargaining those rights away.

U Aung Thaung encouraged me to consult my constituents and reconsider. I subsequently informed community leaders and constituents about the conversation. They supported my position and we were all on the same page. I did not disclose the meeting to the media at that time because of the political consequences of making such an account public while living in Myanmar.

During my visit, I saw large portraits of President Thein Sein, Min Aung Hlaing, and nationalist Buddhist monk U Wirathu in an office at the residence. An assistant told me that the office also served U Wirathu whenever he comes to Naypyidaw. These are my recollections of what I saw and I was told 11 years ago.

The statements about Thein Sein and Min Aung Hlaing were made to me by U Aung Thaung. I cannot claim that I heard either man personally authorize the proposal. But U Aung Thaung confirmed the proposal with Union Immigration Minister U Khin Yi, today’s USDP chairman and speaker of Pyithu Hluttaw, over the phone in front of me.

The central proposition was unmistakable: I was being asked to abandon public advocacy for the identity of the people I represented as a condition of continuing my political career.

On August 4, 2015, I resigned from the USDP. Two days later, I applied to contest the upcoming Pyithu Hluttaw election as an independent candidate for Buthitaung.

On August 22, the Maungdaw District Election Subcommission rejected my candidacy. Its decision concluded that my parents had not been Myanmar citizens at the time of my birth in 1965. I appealed, together with concrete documents, to the Rakhine State Election Subcommission, which upheld the rejection on September 1, 2015. The Union Election Commission subsequently affirmed the decision, communicating its ruling in a letter dated September 6, 2015.

This outcome presented a profound contradiction in my political life.

The same Union Election Commission had formally recognized me as an elected member of parliament following the November 7, 2010 election. Its recognition certificate, dated January 10, 2011, identified me as the elected representative of Buthitaung and recorded my citizenship card.

Five years later, election authorities found me ineligible to stand for the same parliamentary seat because they now considered the evidence of my parents’ citizenship insufficient.

The State Election Subcommission acknowledged that my father possessed a national registration card, which serves as a primary document for full citizenship, and that my maternal grandparents also held national registration cards. Nevertheless, it concluded that those records did not adequately establish the citizenship qualifications required under the election laws.

I maintained that I had submitted the same family citizenship documentation in both electoral processes. The surviving recognition certificate and 2105 rulings represent contrasting official outcomes, although a complete comparison of the underlying applications would require examination of the original 2010 candidate file.

I believe the circumstances of my exclusion cannot be separated from the political pressure I experienced over my Rohingya identity. But the official election decisions do not themselves establish that my refusal of U Aung Thaung Thaung’s proposal caused my disqualification.

In November 2015, I publicly described the disenfranchisement of Rohingya voters and candidates in an opinion article for the New York Times. What I did not reveal then was the private conversation that had proceeded my departure from the USDP. I am revealing it now not simply to revisit my personal experience, but because it illuminates a continuing political problem.

For decades, Rohingya identity has been contested by successive Myanmar authorities, often through the characterization of the community as “Bengali” migrants. Questions of citizenship, documentation, and political participation have been intertwined with that dispute. The consequences extended beyond elections.

The mass atrocities committed against Rohingya in 2017 drove hundreds of thousands of Rohingya people into Bangladesh and intensified international demands for accountability. The Myanmar military coup in February 2021 subsequently plunged the country into wider political and humanitarian crisis.

Today, the Rohingya question cannot be treated as an isolated refugee-management problem. It is connected to Myanmar’s broader failure to establish an inclusive political order in which citizenship and fundamental rights are protected without discrimination.

This why ASEAN’s diplomatic engagement with Min Aung Hlaing deserves close scrutiny.

Regional governments have legitimate reasons to maintain channels of communication concerning humanitarian access, armed conflicts, migration, and regional security. Diplomatic contact is not necessarily equivalent to recognition or endorsement. But engagement must be judged by what it achieves for people affected by Myanmar’s crisis.

For Rohingya, discussions of repatriation are incomplete unless they address the conditions that forced people to flee and the rights they must be able to exercise upon return. A refugee cannot be expected to regard return as durable when questions of identity, citizenship, personal security, and political belonging remain unresolved.

ASEAN should therefore make these issues substantive elements of its discussions with Myanmar’s authorities. They include equal citizenship rights, recognition of the right to self-identification, meaningful political participation, protection against further atrocities, accountability for grave violations, and conditions for voluntary, safe, dignified, and sustainable return. The wider realities of Myanmar’s conflict must be taken into account. The aspirations of people resisting military rule, the safety of civilians across the country, and political future of ethnic communities cannot be separated from efforts to resolve the Rohingya crisis.

My experience in 2015 taught me how readily the question of identity could become a condition imposed upon political participation. The documents from my parliamentary career show that official recognition in one election offered no assurance of eligibility in the next.

Eleven years later, I remain convinced that Rohingya rights cannot depend on whether individuals agree to relinquish the name by which they identify themselves.

ASEAN cannot settle Myanmar’s political future on its own. But it can insist that engagement address the rights and security of the people whose lives are at stake.

A sustainable future for Myanmar requires more than meetings among political leaders. It requires a political order in which no community must choose between its identity and its rights.
tag: ASEAN and the Rohingya Crisis; Min Aung Hlaing; Myanmar; Myanmar Rohingya policy; rohingya

title: Myanmar’s Min Aung Hlaing to Visit Indonesia and Brunei, Regime Spokesperson Says
description: Since taking office in April, the former general has visited five ASEAN member states as he seeks normalization with the Southeast Asian bloc.
text:
Myanmar’s military-appointed President Min Aung Hlaing could follow up his controversial state visit to Malaysia with trips to Indonesia and Brunei, according to a Myanmar government spokesperson.

Speaking at the conclusion of Min Aung Hlaing’s two-day visit to Malaysia on Thursday, spokesperson Khaing Khaing Soe told reporters that the two nations planned to invite the Myanmar leader to make an official visit on an unspecified date. She added that Malaysia’s Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim had shared the information with Min Aung Hlaing during their meeting in Putrajaya last week.

Malaysia was the fifth member state of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) to host Min Aung Hlaing since he took office as president in April, after trips to Laos, Thailand, Cambodia, and Vietnam. It was also the first nation from maritime Southeast Asia to host him.

The spokesperson’s comments, if confirmed, would represent just the latest diplomatic success for Min Aung Hlaing, who led the military coup of 2021. Since shedding his military fatigues and taking office as president in April, he has been on a regional charm offensive aimed at consolidating key partnerships and seeking injections of much-needed foreign investment.

In addition to visits to India, China, Russia, Belarus, and Kazakhstan, a particular priority has been the normalization of Myanmar’s relations with ASEAN. Since late 2021, the 11-nation bloc has excluded the country from its summits over its failure to implement its Five-Point Consensus conflict resolution plan, which called for a cessation of violence, access to humanitarian aid, and inclusive dialogue involving “all parties” to the country’s conflict.

Since the military coup of 2021, Myanmar’s mainland Southeast Asian neighbors have been less publicly critical of the military and shown more inclination to engage the military government. The six maritime ASEAN states – Malaysia, Indonesia, the Philippines, Singapore, Brunei, and Timor-Leste – have generally been more critical and advocated a tougher regional line on Myanmar. But with a new and more legitimized government now in office in Naypyidaw, and after five years of apparently scant progress on the Five-Point Consensus, it appears that ASEAN and its member states have coalesced around a new approach.

In an interview with Singapore’s Straits Times, Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., who holds the rotating chairmanship of ASEAN this year, said that while the Five-Point Consensus was “absolutely correct,” the bloc needed to try a fresh approach to Myanmar.

During the bloc’s last summit in May, Marcos said, “I proposed and said we need to have a new approach on Myanmar. Nothing’s happening, so we had to do something else. And I am happy to know, because today I saw the news that the leader of Myanmar has visited Malaysia, has visited Cambodia. And that is the beginning which has never happened before.”

Whether this push towards engagement results in the full normalization of Myanmar’s relationship with ASEAN remains unclear. As Marcos’ comments suggest, the bloc has not formally abandoned the Five-Point Consensus, and there are also evidently still differences within ASEAN over how fast engagement should proceed, and to what end. While some nations, including Thailand and Malaysia, have explicitly stated that their goal is Myanmar’s eventual reintegration into ASEAN, others place more emphasis on the implementation of the Consensus.

In February, Singapore’s Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan told Parliament that the Five-Point Consensus remained the primary ASEAN reference for the Myanmar conflict, and that as such it would continue to uphold “the decision to maintain Myanmar’s non-political representation at ASEAN Summits and ASEAN Foreign Ministers’ Meetings,” until there is “meaningful progress” in its implementation. More recently, Singapore, which holds ASEAN’s chairmanship next year, defined this as the “permanent cessation of violence,” the release of all political detainees, and access for the ASEAN Coordinating Center for Humanitarian Assistance.

Meanwhile, Timor-Leste, which has been outspoken in its criticism of the Myanmar junta, has even permitted its legal authorities to initiate a legal case against Min Aung Hlaing and other senior officials. Indeed, Dili’s position on Myanmar may offer the first real test of whether it has been successfully socialized into the “ASEAN way.”

This suggests that even with more member states willing to roll out the red carpet for Min Aung Hlaing, full normalization with ASEAN, which will require a consensus among its 11 member states, will necessitate at least some gestures of compliance with the Five-Point Consensus. Myanmar military’s continued violent attacks on civilian populations, as well as its increasingly explicit rejection of the Consensus and ASEAN demands such as for an audience with detained civilian leader Aung San Suu Kyi, suggest that this is unlikely anytime soon.

The main question going forward, therefore, is how little ASEAN’s member states will be willing to accept in order to approve full normalization – if they don’t choose to abandon the Five-Point Consensus altogether.
tag: ASEAN five-point consensus; ASEAN Myanmar; ASEAN Myanmar coup; Myanmar diplomacy; Myanmar foreign policy

title: Nepal Should Not Shoulder the Himalayan Climate Crisis Alone
description: “No matter how much we reform our internal engineering, a frontline nation simply cannot manage the shocks of a global systemic failure alone.”
text:
Have you wondered why the current global order expects frontline geographies to absorb the astronomical shocks of climate disasters entirely on their own, especially when those very states face the unprecedented brunt of a crisis born from a total failure of global collective action? Who funds the recovery when the baseline geography of a nation is structurally altered overnight, especially when the crisis is entirely outside of their own making?

Of course, Nepal’s civilizational history has been a long, adaptive iteration to deal with an unforgiving topography and the sheer gravity of terrains that constantly pull everything down. But the scale of what we saw on August 26, 2026 was entirely unprecedented. The staggering images of landscapes dissolving that looked like a terrifying sci-fi reel made rounds among global audiences,

The Unprecedented Shock

Seven weeks have passed since a massive rockslide detached from a high mountain face in northern Nepal’s Langtang Lirung massif, slamming into the glacial lake below and triggering a catastrophic debris torrent along the Rasuwa-Trishuli corridor. The mud remains heavy, unyielding, and thick with the wreckage of a singular, devastating event. Ever since that unimaginable disaster, Nepal has grappled with the heartbreaking loss of close to 1,500 lives. Thousands remain missing. And thousands more are desperately trying to rebuild their shattered lives from scratch.

The loss is vast. And that stretches far beyond human lives and the statistical tallies of washed-away bridges and infrastructural damages. Or of erased roads or buried houses.

Take the sudden megawatt loss of hydropower assets clustered along this single corridor, projects that were either already online delivering power or actively under construction. Cumulatively, this single cascading hazard knocked over 400 megawatts of clean energy offline in a single afternoon. This is a fundamental blow to a country that has courageously looked toward a future of 30,000 megawatts of clean energy capacity by the next decade. Crucially, much of that power was not meant for domestic consumption alone but was strategically destined to flow southward across the border to anchor the green transitions of our neighbors too. The disaster wiped out roughly 10 percent of Nepal’s total installed electrical capacity in a single afternoon; that does more than disrupt domestic energy equations.

The damage also includes the immediate destruction of the primary cross-border trade artery to our northern neighbor, China, the vital and the nearest entry point for the electric vehicles driving Nepal’s national green transition. Against all conventional global assumptions, Nepal has emerged as a global leader in green mobility, with new passenger EV adoption skyrocketing past 75 percent as the nation aggressively pursues the goal of becoming a fully electric economy. These efforts have now been paralyzed.

Even more devastating is what this corridor represents to the human spirit, and to our resilient high mountain communities. The tragedy impacted the sacred artery for international pilgrims journeying toward the ancient Kailash-Mansarovar sanctuary, a landscape deeply revered across Hindu and Buddhist civilizations, and a legendary frontier of adventure for global explorers. Tragically, many of those currently dead or missing under the mud include these very pilgrims and tourists.

By flattening connecting bridges, stranding cross-border travelers, and decimating localized ecotourism infrastructure, these disasters have dismantled the historic human and economic ties and spiritual sanctuary of the region that bind South Asian nations together, directly threatening the collective dream of an interconnected green grid.

Then came September. Then came October. And both months bought multi-front disasters that defied everything we thought we could predict.

In September, extreme late-monsoon saturation triggered massive landslides across multiple districts simultaneously, repeatedly snapping grid transmission lines and fracturing vital economic corridors just as fast as recovery teams could repair them.

October stripped away any remaining illusion of predictability. On October 11, a morning landslide and the subsequent breach of the natural dam along the steep Budhigandaki River corridor in central Nepal, west of Kathmandu, did more than wash away roads. The landslide slammed directly into the construction site of the 341 MW plant down the valley, specifically engineered to run off the river’s natural flow and step in during our hours of highest electricity demand. While the major structure was not entirely wiped away, the impact leaves us with fundamental questions about systemic safety, early warning capabilities, and the steep costs of re-engineering our infrastructure for a volatile future.

Ultimately, if these vulnerabilities are left unaddressed, the cascading risks will not stop at our borders; they will inevitably strip the entire region of the very clean energy opportunities needed to power our collective green transition.

Nepal, of course, has a lot of serious reflection to do regarding its own development thinking; we are by no means oblivious to that. But the broader crisis remains clear, because no matter how much we reform our internal engineering, a frontline nation simply cannot manage the shocks of a global systemic failure alone.

This gives immediate, painful validation to the warning delivered by Prime Minister Balendra Shah at the United Nations General Assembly in New York. Addressing the international community, the prime minister laid bare a grim economic reality, warning that physical recovery from these escalating disasters could consume up to 10 percent of Nepal’s national GDP. For a nation that contributes less than 0.1 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions, isn’t this far more than a localized setback? Is it not a crushing, completely unjust financial penalty imposed by an unequal global architecture?

Why should a frontline nation independently underwrite the immense physical and financial risks of cross-border infrastructure that the entire subcontinent’s survival depends on? Rather than pointing fingers among ourselves, isn’t this a definitive wake-up call for all of us in the region to come together, align our strategies, and act as a unified front? If our collective green future is at stake, is this massive burden truly for Nepal to shoulder alone, or is it the ultimate test of shared regional solidarity and global accountability?

As we prepare to gather next month at the U.N. Climate Change Conference in Antalya, Nepal will undoubtedly be discussed as a definitive case study. But what will the optics of that discussion be? Will we once again be treated as a passive, flat statistic on a ledger, or as a living warning of what happens when climate shocks freeze a real-world green transition?

The current global climate financing architecture remains stubbornly blind to the high-velocity crises of the Himalayas. If a nation that did everything right, pioneering citizen-funded hydro-infrastructure and skyrocketing its EV adoption, can have its clean energy core paralyzed in a single afternoon, who is it that truly needs to change? Is it Nepal that must reshape its ambitions, or is it a broken global financial system that must finally overhaul its slow-moving bureaucracy before the millions who revere and depend on these ecosystems downstream pay the ultimate price?
tag: 2026 Nepal floods; August 26 Nepal floods; climate change mitigation in Asia; Nepal climate change; Nepal natural disasters; South Asia climate change

title: New Governor, Old Problem: Koja Confronts US Base-Related Crimes in Okinawa
description: Whoever is governor, waves of Okinawan anti-base sentiment and protest will continue in the wake of every violent crime.
text:
Okinawa’s September 2026 election made headlines as incumbent Denny Tamaki was ousted by the Liberal Democratic Party’s (LDP) preferred candidate, Koja Genta. Koja became the first LDP-backed candidate to win the position since Hirokazu Nakaima in 2006.

Tamaki and his predecessor, the late Onaga Takeshi, vocally opposed the expansion of the U.S. Marine Corps’ Camp Schwab in Henoko and were generally critical of Okinawa’s excessive base burden, relative to other Japanese prefectures. Newly-elected Governor Koja was perceived by the LDP-led Japanese government to be more favorable to the U.S. bases in Okinawa, specifically the completion of the relocation of Marine Corps Air Station Futenma in Ginowan City to Camp Schwab.

Perhaps most emblematic of the shift in the Okinawan Prefectural Office was Koja’s abolition of the Henoko New Base Construction Issue Countermeasures Division, the office that had handled legal, environmental, and political issues surrounding the construction. Instead, Koja’s administration created the Early Return Countermeasures Office, which is less overtly critical of the Henoko project.

Only days after his inauguration, however, Koja has had to confront the same perennial problem that his predecessors faced: crimes (allegedly) committed by U.S. military personnel in Okinawa and their impacts on the Japan-U.S. alliance.

On October 3, Okinawan police arrested a U.S. Marine on suspicion of murdering Anna Yagi, an Okinawan woman. While it remains to be seen if the U.S. soldier is convicted of the crime, this incident represents an unfortunate continuity of crimes committed by U.S. soldiers in Okinawa, particularly against women. In recent years, for instance, a U.S. Marine was convicted of attempted rape, and a U.S. Air Force member was found guilty of the kidnapping and rape of a minor; in both cases the victims were female.

As the U.S. and Japanese governments increasingly worry about conflict with China in the Taiwan Strait, which borders Okinawa, they must work to prevent these crimes to ensure the stable operation of their alliance.

Crimes Committed by U.S. Servicemembers Contribute to Okinawa’s “Base Burden”

Several factors impact Okinawans’ perception of the prefecture’s “excessive base burden.” One is the fact that Okinawa hosts 70 percent of the U.S. soldiers stationed in Japan, but Okinawa’s landmass is just 1 percent of Japan’s total area. Okinawa also has a contentious and traumatic history with Tokyo, which increases suspicions that the central government doesn’t have the prefecture’s best interests in mind.

A major factor that contributes to the perception of the U.S. bases as burdens is the negative externalities that periodically come from U.S. bases and troops. That includes various forms of chemical pollution, such as Agent Orange (historically) and per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) (in recent years), and other environmental issues.

Crimes attributed to U.S. military personnel are another type of negative externality. Violent crimes such as sexual assault and murder may be especially likely to mobilize protests against the U.S. military presence, in part because of the strong emotions that they can invoke. These events serve as opportunities for anti-base activists to remind Okinawans and mainland Japanese citizens alike of the island prefecture’s traumatic history involving both mainland Japan and the U.S., such as the Battle of Okinawa during World War II. Through this lens, crimes committed by U.S. military personnel in Okinawa are interpreted as further examples of the ways that the U.S. and Japanese governments have and continue to marginalize Okinawa in the name of national and regional security.

Unsurprisingly, anti-base protests in Okinawa often occur after a crime such as the murder of Anna Yagi. For example, the 1995 kidnapping and rape of a 12-year-old girl by U.S. servicemen kicked off a massive wave of protests against the U.S. bases, and more recently, the 2016 murder of Rina Shimabukuro by a U.S. contractor was followed by protests with tens of thousands of participants.

Despite the election of Koja to the governorship, which some observers may interpret as a sign that Okinawans are deprioritizing base politics, protests are likely to follow Yagi’s murder. They have already started in Tokyo, as well as Naha, the capital of Okinawa Prefecture.

The Threat Perception of China Can’t Overshadow Crimes

For some observers, Koja’s election win signaled that Okinawans’ concerns about potential Chinese hostility in the nearby Taiwan Strait may trump their concerns about the “burdens” from the U.S. bases. Koja himself stated that “the fact that the security environment around Okinawa has become more severe is something we can’t help but acknowledge.” He said that “we have to have the ability to defend ourselves and deter aggression,” presumably referring to the U.S. and Japanese Self-Defense Force (SDF) bases in the prefecture.

However, it would be a mistake to assume that the perception of China as a threat to Japanese and Okinawan security will automatically counteract the negative impacts that crimes committed by U.S. soldiers have on public opinion toward the U.S. military, at least in the short term. Recent research has suggested that threat perception does not always increase support for a U.S. military presence.

Some of my own research found that crimes committed by U.S. personnel have a negative impact on public opinion toward the U.S. military. Furthermore, it is unclear if the presence of U.S. bases makes locals feel more or less secure, particularly in the event of a military conflict, especially given Iran’s recent attacks on U.S. military installations in the Middle East. In Okinawa, surveys suggest that a majority of residents worry that military bases (which could include SDF bases as well) in the prefecture could serve as military targets.

Therefore, although recent surveys suggest that Okinawans, like mainland Japanese citizens, are wary of Chinese military aggression, U.S. and Japanese officials should not assume that threat perceptions will automatically result in Okinawan public support for U.S. bases, particularly when a crime linked to U.S. personnel is in the headlines.

An Ounce of Prevention Is Worth a Pound of Cure

If the U.S. and Japanese governments believe, as they say, that the bases in Okinawa Prefecture are crucial to regional security, they need to take more proactive measures to prevent rather than react to crimes allegedly committed by U.S. military personnel. Even if Anna Yagi’s accused murderer is ultimately found innocent, the damage to civilian-military relations between U.S. soldiers and Okinawans is already done.

For his part, Koja has issued a formal protest with the U.S. military and expressed his “outrage” at the crime. Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae has lodged a “strong protest” with the U.S.; meanwhile, U.S. officials have temporarily prohibited U.S. soldiers from going off base in Okinawa. However, reactive actions by officials are not new, and Okinawans are wary of the crime, protest, and apology routine. As one Okinawan resident put it, “I am deeply disappointed by the same kinds of government comments we have been hearing for decades – that they will protest or that they take the matter seriously.”

One of the biggest elements in preventing such crimes against civilians is the training that U.S. soldiers receive when they deploy to a specific location. Such training may impact soldiers’ perceptions of the host communities in which they live and with which they interact, as well as how they interact with host community civilians. In the case of Okinawa, a recent study suggested that the orientation materials that U.S. Marines are exposed to depict Okinawans as obstacles to be overcome and the media as agitators of anti-base sentiment. In doing so, these materials delegitimize opposition to U.S. bases, instead of asking how U.S. troops can avoid stoking anti-base sentiment. This study drew on training materials from the 2010s. Since then, the materials have hopefully been updated in a way that seeks to better understand where Okinawan anti-base sentiment comes from and the role of individual U.S. soldiers in facilitating (or inhibiting) the Japan-U.S. relationship.

The U.S. military and its municipal and gubernatorial partners also have a role to play in shaping the narratives around the U.S. military presence in Okinawa, which may help ameliorate the negative impacts of crimes on civilians’ relationships with U.S. soldiers. Recent studies suggested that contact between U.S. soldiers and civilians in base-hosting countries can facilitate positive public opinions of the U.S. military. The same research found that contact combined with exposure to base-related crime – being the victim or having a friend or family member who is a victim of such crime – does not consistently lead to negative attitudes toward the U.S. military. Thus, creating and strengthening the relationships between U.S. troops and the community members that host them is essential to maintaining a positive Japan-U.S. alliance. This can include activities such as base festivals, English or Japanese language courses, or other exchanges.

Anna Yagi’s murder comes at a time of other high-profile cases of violence against women, and joins a history of crimes committed by U.S. military personnel against women in Okinawa. For the stability of the Japan-U.S. security alliance, it is imperative to facilitate more positive relationships between U.S. soldiers and Okinawan citizens; crimes attributed to U.S. soldiers have the opposite effect. While the United States has tried to address this issue in the past, it is clearly not enough, as Koja has said.

Until the U.S. military and its Japanese partners can solve this puzzle, waves of Okinawan anti-base sentiment and protest, which threaten the Japan-U.S. relationship, will continue in the wake of every violent crime.

title: New Zealand’s Climate Report Tests Its Pacific Leadership
description: Wellington’s latest environmental assessment highlights the growing economic risks of climate change, raising questions about whether government policy can keep pace.
text:
New Zealand’s latest climate assessment presents a challenge that extends beyond environmental protection, raising questions about whether the country can translate growing evidence of climate change into policies that protect its economy and strengthen its standing in the Pacific.

Published October 7, “Our Atmosphere and Climate 2026” documents rising temperatures, changing rainfall patterns and mounting pressure on infrastructure, ecosystems and communities. New Zealand’s annual average temperature has risen 1.36 degrees Celsius since records began in 1909, while seven of its 10 warmest years occurred between 2016 and 2025. Concentrations of carbon dioxide, methane, and nitrous oxide also reached record highs in 2025.

The report’s significance lies in what these trends mean for government policy. New Zealand must reduce emissions while preparing for climate impacts that are already occurring. How effectively it manages that balance will affect not only its economic resilience but also its credibility as a partner to Pacific island countries confronting similar challenges.

The government’s accompanying publication, “Our Atmosphere and Climate 2026: The Stories Behind the Numbers,” examines how communities and organizations are responding to climate-related risks. Read alongside the government’s “Second Emissions Reduction Plan for 2026–30,” the publications highlight the gap policymakers must bridge between documenting environmental change, reducing emissions, and preparing for its consequences.

Efforts to reduce emissions must be balanced against the economic importance of key industries and the livelihoods of those who depend on them. Agriculture accounted for 53 percent of New Zealand’s gross greenhouse gas emissions in 2024, according to the assessment, while remaining central to its export economy. Reducing agricultural emissions therefore presents difficult choices involving competitiveness, rural livelihoods, and the pace of economic transition.

Climate impacts add to those economic pressures. Drought and changing rainfall patterns threaten agricultural production, while flooding and landslides can damage roads, disrupt supply chains, and increase infrastructure costs. Coastal hazards create additional risks for homes and communities. The extent of the damage will depend partly on how effectively the government incorporates climate projections into land-use planning, infrastructure investment, and public spending.

The emissions reduction plan addresses the government’s approach to cutting emissions. But reducing emissions does not eliminate the need to adapt to further climate change. New Zealand must also decide which infrastructure to protect, where new development is appropriate, and how to distribute the costs of preparing for future hazards.

These decisions have consequences beyond its borders, as across the Pacific, rising seas, coastal erosion, and extreme weather threaten communities, infrastructure, and freshwater resources. Many island countries have limited financial capacity to respond, despite contributing relatively little to global greenhouse gas emissions.

New Zealand has a direct interest in the region’s resilience through its economic, social, and security relationships with Pacific countries. Supporting adaptation, disaster preparedness, and resilient infrastructure can strengthen those relationships. But effective cooperation requires more than emergency assistance after disasters; it depends on sustained investment and respect for the priorities of Pacific governments and communities.

New Zealand’s domestic response will also shape its regional credibility. Wellington cannot control global emissions or eliminate every climate risk, but it can demonstrate that environmental evidence informs its own infrastructure decisions, economic planning, and emissions policies. A disconnect between international commitments and domestic implementation would weaken the force of its regional advocacy.

The new publications provide a foundation for that work, not proof that it is already being done effectively. The companion report’s case studies may offer practical lessons, but their broader value depends on whether those lessons influence government decisions. Similarly, an emissions reduction plan must be judged by implementation and outcomes, not simply by the existence of published targets.

New Zealand’s latest climate assessment therefore presents a test of governance as much as an environmental warning. The government has consolidated evidence of a changing climate and published a plan for reducing emissions. The next step is to ensure that those efforts translate into practical adaptation, more resilient infrastructure and sustained cooperation across the Pacific.

For Wellington, the stakes are clear: its ability to manage climate risks at home will help determine the strength of its economy and the credibility of its leadership in a region where climate change is already a defining concern.

title: North Korea Wants Security Talks With the US, Not Nuclear Talks
description: For decades, Washington tried to change Pyongyang’s nuclear policy. Now North Korea is trying to do the reverse: use its nuclear weapons to change U.S. policy.
text:
Since the start of his second administration, U.S. President Donald Trump has repeatedly proposed renewed talks with North Korea. Pyongyang has said that relations could improve if Washington respected its nuclear status and abandoned what it calls its “hostile policy.” But what would North Korea be willing to talk about if discussions resumed?

Pyongyang increasingly seeks talks on its security concerns, particularly U.S. military policy and the regional security environment, while treating its own possession of nuclear weapons as non-negotiable. It may even demand a halt to U.S. military exercises with its allies as a precondition for talks.

What Pyongyang Learned From Hanoi

The failure of the 2019 North Korea-Trump summit in Hanoi may have prompted Pyongyang to reassess its negotiating strategy and strengthen its commitment to retaining nuclear weapons. At the summit, North Korea sought partial relief from United Nations sanctions in exchange for dismantling its Yongbyon nuclear facilities. Washington, however, sought denuclearization measures extending beyond Yongbyon in exchange for a broader package of economic benefits. The summit ended without an agreement.

Why did North Korea not accept Washington’s “big deal”? Shortly after the summit collapsed, North Korean Foreign Minister Ri Yong Ho explained that security guarantees mattered more to Pyongyang than sanctions relief. North Korea had nevertheless proposed partial sanctions relief in return for dismantling Yongbyon because it believed Washington would find it difficult to take military measures at the time.

North Korea may have recognized the limits of what the United States could offer in terms of security guarantees. U.S. military strategy in Northeast Asia is not solely a response to the North Korean threat. It also reflects Washington’s alliance commitments to South Korea and Japan and its broader strategic competition with China. Even if North Korea gave up all its nuclear weapons, Washington might not be able to offer the security guarantees Pyongyang wants, given its regional interests and alliance commitments. From this perspective, North Korea’s attempt in Hanoi to exchange partial denuclearization for partial sanctions relief may have been a realistic approach. The failure in Hanoi appears to have convinced Pyongyang that giving up its nuclear weapons would not secure the guarantees it sought. After Hanoi, North Korea reinforced its commitment to retaining nuclear weapons through legislation and constitutional changes. In September 2022, it adopted a new law on nuclear forces policy. Kim Jong Un declared that North Korea’s status as a nuclear weapon state was irreversible and ruled out further negotiations on giving up its nuclear weapons or on denuclearization.

North Korea did not begin identifying itself as a nuclear weapon state in 2022. It had already codified that status in a 2013 law “consolidating the position of nuclear weapons state for self-defense.” Article 9 of that law, however, expressed support for international nuclear disarmament efforts. The omission of that provision from the 2022 law was therefore significant.

The 2022 law not only entrenched nuclear possession as a permanent foundation of national strategy but also called for qualitative and quantitative improvements in nuclear forces in response to external threats and changes in the international nuclear balance. In this context, a freeze on nuclear weapons production or a reduction in its nuclear arsenal could conflict with this policy if North Korea’s security environment remained unchanged.

Setting the Terms for Renewed Talks

North Korea’s recent statements on relations with Washington indicate that it expects changes in U.S. policy before talks resume, while treating its nuclear possession as non-negotiable.

In October 2025, Trump publicly expressed his desire to meet Kim Jong Un again during his trip to Asia. That didn’t eventuate, but Trump is reportedly looking at the possibility of a meeting with Kim during his next trip to Asia in November 2026.

At the Ninth Workers’ Party Congress in February 2026, Kim Jong Un stated that relations with the United States could improve if Washington respected North Korea’s status as a nuclear weapon state and abandoned its hostile policy. He thus linked improved relations to a change in Washington’s attitude toward a nuclear-armed North Korea and its policy toward Pyongyang.

In August, Trump again expressed interest in meeting Kim and ordered a reduction in South Korea-U.S. military exercises. Kim Yo Jong, Kim Jong Un’s sister and an authoritative voice for the regime, dismissed the move as insufficient. She argued that holding the exercises at all demonstrated Washington’s hostility. Kim Yo Jong’s response suggested that Pyongyang wanted the exercises halted altogether, rather than merely scaled back, before agreeing to talks. In the same statement, she also criticized South Korea’s push to acquire nuclear-powered submarines.

In September, Foreign Minister Choe Son Hui reaffirmed that North Korea’s nuclear status was irreversible. She rejected the coexistence of confrontation and dialogue in relations with North Korea and argued that a geopolitical realignment centered on a nuclear-armed North Korea was inevitable. Her statement reinforced the message that Washington could not maintain policies Pyongyang regarded as hostile and expect dialogue to follow.

North Korea has long sought security guarantees and an end to Washington’s hostile policy. The difference now is that Pyongyang treats its nuclear possession as non-negotiable and expects changes in U.S. attitudes and military policy before talks resume. A reduction in South Korea-U.S. military exercises alone appears insufficient to meet its demands. Its criticism of South Korea’s nuclear-powered submarine plans also suggests concern about potential U.S. support for such capabilities.

This departs from the Singapore agreement, which paired a commitment to denuclearization with improved relations and the establishment of a peace regime. Pyongyang now seeks U.S. policy changes as the starting point for diplomacy, rather than as part of a bargain over giving up its nuclear weapons.

North Korea’s strategy notwithstanding, its ability to change U.S. policy is not guaranteed. Despite Trump’s efforts to engage Pyongyang, the United States, South Korea, and Japan continue to reaffirm the goal of North Korea’s denuclearization, while Washington maintains its defense commitments to its allies.

Pyongyang may see no need to rush into talks. It continues to build up its nuclear forces, citing security threats, while strengthening ties with its partners.

In September 2026, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) reported signs of a new uranium enrichment facility at Yongbyon and indications of expanded operations at Kangson. North Korea has also recently increased the frequency of its missile tests. Meanwhile, expanding military cooperation with Russia and improving relations with China are giving Pyongyang greater room to resist international pressure, including sanctions. Both countries oppose further sanctions on North Korea and have become quieter on its denuclearization.

North Korea may believe that time is on its side: As its nuclear capabilities grow and its diplomatic options expand, Washington may eventually have no choice but to enter talks on the basis that North Korea will retain its nuclear weapons.

How the United States Should Respond

Washington’s first task is to clarify the conditions under which North Korea is willing to negotiate and the agenda it is prepared to discuss. Some experts argue that a nuclear freeze or reductions should serve as interim goals if complete denuclearization cannot be achieved in the short term. This may be a realistic alternative for the United States, but Washington should not assume that Pyongyang will accept it as a topic for negotiation. North Korea may instead demand that negotiations focus on regional security issues or insist on changes in U.S. policy before agreeing to talks.

To clarify these issues, working-level meetings should precede any new North Korea-U.S. summit. Washington must coordinate closely with Seoul and Tokyo before negotiating measures that affect their security. If Pyongyang raises concerns about U.S. military activities on the Korean Peninsula, Washington should assess whether its demands can be addressed through reciprocal military measures.

Discussing regional security does not necessarily mean recognizing North Korea as a nuclear-weapon state or weakening allied military readiness. With South Korea’s agreement, for example, the United States could consider adjusting the scale or format of joint exercises in exchange for limits on North Korean exercises in specific areas, with arrangements for both sides to verify compliance. Once military crisis-management measures are in place and the security environment improves, Washington could argue that Pyongyang should move toward a nuclear freeze or reductions.

The United States must also challenge North Korea’s calculation that time is on its side. Maintaining existing sanctions and deterrence alone is unlikely to change Pyongyang’s strategic judgment. The United States should make clear that North Korea’s continued nuclear buildup could lead South Korea and Japan to strengthen their military capabilities and fuel calls in both countries for nuclear weapons of their own. An offer to discuss regional security should accompany that message. The aim should be to create incentives for diplomacy without triggering another arms race.

Washington should use security talks to pursue reciprocal military measures and build a path toward limits on North Korea’s nuclear capabilities. Knowing what each side is willing to offer before the next summit would improve the chances of reaching an agreement.
tag: North Korea nuclear freeze; North Korea nuclear weapons; Trump-Kim summit; U.S.-North Korea diplomacy; U.S.-North Korea talks

title: Officials Detained as Kazakhstan Mourns Soldiers Perished at Sea
description: Five military officials were arrested in connection to the deaths of 14 servicemen lost at sea during a combat exercise in southwestern Kazakhstan, as a day of national mourning is observed.
text:
Kazakhstan is mourning the deaths of 14 servicemen who were lost during a military drill. The tragedy took place on September 24 during the 2026 Caspian Defense exercise in southwestern Kazakhstan. The episode has led to the dismissal of the defense minister, while five officials are being investigated for negligence in relation to the case.

According to the Kazakh Ministry of Defense, a total of 17 servicemen were swept out to sea during one of the naval exercises due to a sudden deterioration in weather in the area, including strong winds. While rescue teams did manage to save three servicemen, the remainder were lost, their bodies recovered over the following days.

While President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev declared a day of mourning out of respect for the soldiers who passed away, criticism has hit the authorities hard, both regarding the accident and the subsequent approach by the authorities to the relatives of the deceased.

The accidental deaths prompted criticism at all levels of authority, not least in regards to how the tragedy was communicated to the relatives who were left behind. As news about the September 24 accident spread, relatives of servicemen involved in the exercise started to gather outside the Aktau morgue located close to the scene of the accident. There they sought answers regarding who was lost, demanding the names of those who had been identified.

Separated by a fence surrounding the morgue, military personnel later that day read out the names of the identified servicemen, most of whom were under the age of 25. The scene, which was captured on video and shared on social media, quickly gained attention for its impersonal and monotonous tone, with both activists and journalists calling out the authorities for handling the announcement in a way that was “Shocking [and] heartless.”

In the week following the accident, disciplinary actions were rolled out, with five officials from the Ministry of Defense being detained and put under investigation for their role in the accident. Among those detained were the chief of staff working with the naval forces, two military unit commanders, and a naval infantry company commander connected to the incident. The men are allegedly to blame for the accident due to negligence of service and violation of navigation rules, according to Kazakh police.

The incident did also force consequences at the highest levels of governance. Initially, Tokayev gave his condolences to the affected families and declared a day of mourning, to be observed on September 25. Days later, he sacked the minister of defense, Dauren Kosanov, who had been in the post just over 15 months. In his place, the now former commander of special operation forces, Aidos Myrzakhmetov, was appointed.

This is not the first accident of its kind. Four servicemen died as strong winds hit a military exercise in the same area of southwestern Kazakhstan in 2015. While this time the investigation and reshuffling of people connected to the Ministry of Defense might help prevent the recurrence of such accidents, military analyst Yermek Seitbattalov, whom the outlet Kaztag spoke to, still sees multiple shortcomings that the military has not fixed. The retired colonel, among other things, mentioned flaws in combat training and the preparation of officers, specifically in relation to the safety of servicemen during exercises. He said this issue was one of the most important matters of attention for the new defense minister.

The Kazakh authorities have shown themselves unequipped not only to properly communicate the passing of soldiers to their loved ones, but also to ensure the safety of those participating in military exercises. While Kazakhstan still mourns the tragedy, the test will be what the military learns from it.
tag: Kazakhstan; Kazakhstan military

title: ‘One Day at a Time’: Inside an IDP Camp in Myanmar, Survival Is a Daily Challenge
description: Some of those living in the Old Kran Khun camp were once well off. Now they forage in the fields and forests around the IDP camp for food and firewood.
text:
Sam Sam burst into tears when asked to narrate the circumstances that compelled her to become an internally displaced person (IDP). She pointed to clothes and utensils in her single-room thatched hut, the only things she could carry while fleeing her village. Then, she pulled out a tattered photograph from a bag.

“This was our home,” she said, pointing to the sprawling house in the photograph. “I never imagined that we would end up at a refugee camp someday.”

On February 6, 2024, the Myanmar military torched Kyar Ma Thout village in Sittwe township in Myanmar’s Rakhine State. It has burned down several other settlements in the area in order to deprive the Arakan Army (AA) of a base in the city’s suburbs.

Sittwe, the capital of Rakhine State and a military hub that houses the Regional Operations Command (ROC), is among three of 17 townships in the state that remain under the military’s control. By emptying its suburbs, the military is hoping to secure its control of the city and surrounding areas.

When Kyar Ma Thout was burnt by the military, most of its 650 residents, including Sam Sam, her husband, and two children, fled for safety in the areas under the control of the AA. About a third of the village’s residents, including a sizable number of elderly and disabled people, settled in monasteries in Sittwe city.

Sam Sam and ten other families from Kyar Ma Thout landed at the Old Kran Khun IDP Camp in Ponnagyun township about 80 kilometers to the north of Sittwe. The township was captured by the AA in mid-March of 2024 after weeks of fierce fighting with the military.

Their journey to the camp was perilous and involved travelling on the Kaladan River as well. With the arrival of IDPs from Sittwe, the camp’s population swelled to 1,643.

Old Kran Khun camp is one of 93 IDP camps scattered across AA-held areas. An estimated 100,000 people live in these camps, as per data compiled by the AA’s political wing, the United League of Arakan (ULA). Another 100,000 are sheltering in monasteries and in the homes of their relatives. Those numbers could not be confirmed independently.

On February 8 this year, I visited the Old Kran Khun camp located 150 meters north of the highway between Ponnagyun and Kyauktaw. The mood there was heavy with sorrow and quiet desperation. There were around 400 huts in the camp. These were cramped and identical shelters built of straw, bamboo, and tarpaulin. The IDPs staying here are struggling to cope with myriad problems, including the loss of their traditional livelihoods, neighborhood networks, and support systems.

Maung Tin Hla was a businessman in Sittwe who relocated with his family in March of 2024 to Old Kran Khun Camp IDP camp. Photo by Rajeev Bhattacharyya.

Riches to Rags

Maung Tin Hla is an affluent businessman from Ma Jay Mying (Ward No. 3) in Sittwe city. He owned five acres of land on the city’s outskirts, which was cultivated throughout the year and provided him with additional income.

Since the military’s offensives were directed at villages surrounding Sittwe, Ma Jay Mying had little reason to believe that the gun would be pointed at households like his own that were inside the city. But everything changed on March 16, 2024, when the military began targeting some localities and burning houses inside Sittwe.

Several people were arrested on suspicion of being AA functionaries. “We heard that the Arakan Liberation Party, which has joined hands with the military, had provided the military with information about some households. And I got the feeling that my name was also on the list,” Maung Tin Hla recalled.

On March 17, Maung Tin Hla began frenzied preparations to leave the village around midnight after a young man in his mid-20s was killed by the military near his residence. He hit the escape trail to the AA’s area of control with his wife and son and seven bags containing gold ornaments, money, clothes, and utensils.

After a grueling 90-km journey that lasted five days, the family reached the IDP camp in Ponnagyun township. Maung Tin Hla then purchased materials needed to build a thatched hut to shelter his family. He then arranged for food and water in the camp.

“I had around 1 million kyats (around U.S. $476), but this lasted just for a month. Then we began selling the gold ornaments. Almost half of the total amount I brought from home has been exhausted,” Maung Tin Hla said. “We can last for another year by selling whatever is left.”

Fishermen among the IDPs have been catching fish from the nearby Kaladan River and selling them for a livelihood. Others gather firewood, bamboo, and vegetables from the hills, which they consume themselves or sell in the camp and neighboring villages. But Maung Tin Hla is neither a fisherman nor is he adept at climbing the hills to gather food and firewood. His wife is busy all day with household chores and takes care of their 7-year-old son, who is enrolled in Grade 1 at a school about 2 km from the camp.

“So far, I have not been able to identify any source of income that will sustain my family,” Maung Tin Hla said. He is keeping his “fingers crossed and is hopeful of returning home soon.”

There are many like Maung Tin Hla in the Old Kran Khun camp, who have similar riches-to-rags stories to share. Their houses were either burnt by the military or destroyed by shelling. Forced to flee their villages, they are now sheltering in the IDP camp and are foraging forests and hills for food and firewood.

Inmates of the Old Kran Khun Camp IDP camp in Ponnagyun Township in Myanmar’s Rakhine State. Photo by Rajeev Bhattacharyya.

Hills Emerge as a Savior

The daily itinerary in the IDP camp is dictated by scarcity. Long before sunrise, residents begin preparations to search for food and livelihood. Many embark on an 8-km trek to the hills that lie to the west of the camp. They return by noon with whatever vegetables and firewood they could lay their hands on.

For Maung Aye Tun and his 14-year-old son, going to the hills has been a daily routine ever since they arrived at the camp from Mrit Nar village in Sittwe township two years ago, after it was burned by the military. “The hills are getting depleted owing to the unrestrained scavenging by camp inmates over the past three years,” he lamented.

“Now more effort is required to gather vegetables and firewood compared to the situation two years ago. We have to go deeper into the hills every day. And there is no certainty that the same quantity of food and firewood can be fetched daily,” Maung Aye Tun said. Alarmed over the rapid deforestation of the hills, the ULA imposed restrictions five months ago on logging.

The daily expenditure on food alone for Maung Aye Tun’s family of four, including his wife and two children, is around 60,000 kyats. But his daily income from selling vegetables and firewood sometimes does not exceed 10,000 kyats. Whatever is earned is mostly spent on buying foodgrains.

During the rainy season, which extends from April to September, the availability of food in the hills drops, and there is excess firewood in the camp but not enough buyers in the rest of the year. Almost every third hut in the camp has bundles of chopped logs placed at the entrance waiting to be sold.

Larger households are able to send some of their family members to markets in the neighboring villages, where the scope of selling commodities at a higher price is brighter. But there have been times when the markets remain shut for days on end after airstrikes or shelling in neighboring areas. This has eaten into the income and reduced food consumption for every household.

Oo Tin Nyunt, who relocated from Sittwe last year, at her hut in Old Kran Khun Camp IDP camp in Ponnagyun Township in Myanmar’s Rakhine State. Photo by Rajeev Bhattacharyya.

One Meal a Day

During my stay at the Old Kran Khun IDP camp, I came across three households for whom two square meals per day or being able to add vegetables to rice was a luxury.

Oo Tin Nyunt (75) is a widow without children, who was displaced from Kran Daw village in Sittwe township when it was bulldozed and then torched by the military in August 2025. She reached the IDP camp with the assistance of her neighbors who were also headed to the same camp. Except for 80,000 kyats, Oo Tin Nyunt had nothing else that could have helped sustain her in the camp. She survived on donations from two NGOs and the ULA till the end of last year.

She is currently dependent on assistance from other households in the camp. She is too frail to gather food from the hills. Neither can she work as a daily wager.

When I asked her about her plans, Oo Tin Nyunt stared for a few seconds and then, with a smile, said: “It’s one day at a time for me. I don’t know what will happen tomorrow.”

The uncertainty looming over the IDP camps is also due to the reduced supply of foodgrains by NGOs and the ULA.

“There are more than 50 NGOs that offered assistance to the IDP camps in the liberated zone. But support has never matched the requirements. Funding from global organizations has decreased drastically over the past year owing to many factors, including the crackdown on the networks that remitted funds,” said Hla Nwe, an official with the Humanitarian and Development Coordination Office (HDCO) under the ULA.

Wong Myint, who heads an NGO, confirmed that funding from global organizations has diminished substantially.

The difficult situation has prompted some camp inmates hailing from Ponnagyun township to return to their fields for cultivation.

Owing to continuous shelling by the military, Nyein Nyein Tun and her family of five were forced to leave Kyay Thoe village in late 2024. Her husband could not work as a daily wager or trek to the hills for firewood and vegetables as he was injured from the shelling.

For almost the whole of last year, the family subsisted on one meal a day and was entirely dependent on assistance from other organizations. Last year, after recovering from his injury, Nyein Nyein Tun’s husband decided to follow others from Ponnagyun township who had returned to cultivating foodgrains in their fields. This required him to live in the fields about 50 km north of the camp for two months, and to return again for the harvest five months later.

However, the harvest last year was not very encouraging for these farmers, Nyein Nyein Tun said. “We are hopeful of a better situation this year if the selling price of foodgrains does not drop sharply. And then we can afford two meals every day.”

A woman fetches water from a well at Old Kran Khun Camp IDP camp in Ponnagyun Township, Myanmar’s Rakhine State. Photo by Rajeev Bhattacharyya.

Struggle for Water

All the IDP camps in Ponnagyun township suffer from a shortage of water. The groundwater level in the township is lower than in the adjoining regions. Water levels in the wells dug in the camp and the two ponds nearby fall sharply during the winter months.

According to a ULA functionary, water in the area around the camp is available at a depth of 600 feet. To dig functional wells, mechanical equipment is needed, but this is not easily available.

Between December and April each year, every household in the camp has to fetch water from the Kaladan River, located 500 meters away. This is difficult for the elderly, especially those who do not have younger relatives to assist them. Therefore, they must manage with small amounts of water every day.

Last year, with the assistance of the ULA, an NGO installed five large-sized water storage tanks at the camp. Previously, trucks were used to ferry water from the river, but their services came to a halt early this year when funds from global organizations shrank.

In addition to the water shortage, IDP camps have to make do with water that has a tinge of turbidity, whether it is from the river or from wells and water bodies. NGO activists claimed that facilities for filtration of water have been provided in a few IDP camps, but the demand is far too high. More funds and equipment are needed to cover more camps.

Myo Aung, who recovered five months ago from skin ailments due to contaminated water, said that while some households boil the water for drinking, “many do not.” “Water is the source of most diseases in the camp,” he said. Besides skin diseases, inmates suffer from diarrhea and malaria during the rainy season. There were two deaths in the camp due to illnesses over the past three years.

A doctor at a health unit run by the ULA in a village about a kilometer from the IDP camp diagnoses patients and prescribes medicines. But medicines are not always readily available as they are imported from different sources, including India and Bangladesh.

Ma Mya Oo with the handloom at her thatched hut in Old Kran Khun Camp IDP camp in Ponnagyun Township in Myanmar’s Rakhine State. Photo by Rajeev Bhattacharyya.

An Exception With the Handloom

The battle for survival in the IDP camps has prompted some residents to devise ingenious means to earn a steady income. Ma Mya Oo journeyed from her home in Padetha village in Ponnagyun township with her family of six members sometime in the middle of last year. The village was evacuated after it was shelled, resulting in the death of one and injuries to four others.

Ma Mya Oo was an established weaver of traditional shawls and skirts, which she sold at shops in Ponnagyun and Kyauktaw. During the relocation from her village located 60 km east of the camp, the family could carry only necessities, like clothes and utensils. The raw materials for her handloom products were left behind in the village. Thankfully, these were not destroyed in the shelling.

“Three months after arriving in the camp, I decided to install the loom at our hut in the camp. This was necessary for additional income as my husband’s earnings as a daily wager were erratic,” Ma Mya Oo said. She then made two trips to her village and transported the materials for the handloom back to the camp. “Only the foot pedals for the loom had to be chiseled from wood in the camp,” she said.

The work soon began, and the first shawl woven in the IDP camp rolled out in November last year. Five more followed in the next couple of months. “This is much less than what was produced at home,” Ma Mya Oo said. Besides, the quality of the shawls fell, as did their price.

Subsequently, Ma Mya Oo helped another woman from Kyaukhyu, who was also a weaver, install a handloom in the camp. However, since not all the materials were easily available, production proved challenging.

Similar to Ma Mya Oo’s case was that of an artisan from Sittwe, who carves figurines out of materials like wood. Small pieces of chopped logs were stacked outside his thatched hut in the camp. He had finished carving three figurines depicting a boat and elephants.

A child slices a log in Old Kran Khun Camp IDP camp in Ponnagyun Township in Myanmar’s Rakhine State. Photo by Rajeev Bhattacharyya.

A Third of All Children Have Opted Out of School

Anxiety and sorrow are writ large among the inmates in the Kyar Ma Thout camp over an uncertain future. This is most discernible among the parents of children who do not go to school. They would like their children to study, but difficult circumstances force parents to send children to work. Around a fourth of all inmates in the camp are children, and one-third of them have opted out of school.

As I strolled around the camp, I met some teenagers engaged in fetching water, slicing logs, and selling vegetables and firewood. Many of these youngsters belong to smaller households with fewer members, where their contribution to family income is vital.

Instead of being in classrooms, their daily curriculum is shaped by the exigencies of survival in a hostile environment. As a middle-aged father of a 15-year-old hailing from Sittwe said, “We cannot afford to send our son to school. That could change only with better sources of livelihood.”

The ULA has slashed the fees in schools it runs to enable impoverished parents to educate their children. Last year, several NGOs worked on persuading parents to send their children, but the results were hardly encouraging. Only four families reportedly agreed to admit their children to a school; the rest remained unconvinced.

Besides financial reasons, at least 20 children have dropped out of school for fear of airstrikes. They are mostly from villages in Ponnagyun and Sittwe townships that were devastated by airstrikes and shelling. The trauma of being nearly killed and uprooted from their homes is deeply etched in their memories. It has impacted many facets of the lives of children.

A trench dug between two thatched huts in Old Kran Khun Camp IDP camp in Ponnagyun Township in Myanmar’s Rakhine State. Photo by Rajeev Bhattacharyya.

Sitting Ducks for Airstrikes

On October 4-5 this year, at least eight IDPs were killed and 13 others injured during airstrikes on two separate IDP camps in Ponnagyun Township. There have been several such military’s attacks on IDP camps in the region. The ULA has claimed that 16 IDPs were killed and more than 40 injured over the last couple of years across Rakhine in aerial attacks before the recent airstrikes in Ponnagyun. The figures could not be independently verified.

Many IDPs in the region, therefore, suffer from trauma and phobia about aerial attacks. Khin Maung, who was displaced from Che Lay Than village in Sittwe in the middle of last year, said that such fears among IDPs have been compounded by the lack of trenches in the camp. “The fear is so high that some IDPs rush out of their huts with their children whenever a rumble is heard,” he said. He recalled a “stampede-like situation” at the camp on the evening of January 19 when the sound of fighter jets was heard. Fearing that the IDP camp would be targeted, people rushed out of the camp and stayed outside for the whole night.

There is no space to dig trenches in the Old Kran Khun camp. I saw only three small trenches in the entire camp in the narrow spaces between the thatched huts. Usually, children are made to take cover in them whenever there is apprehension of aerial attacks. Two families had dug trenches inside their huts, and these were covered with wooden planks.

Many dwellings in the camp have long bamboo poles with hooks that are attached to the huts. I was told that in the event of an airstrike, these poles would be quickly used to pull down a burning chunk of thatch to prevent the whole hut from being incinerated.

Last year, the Old Kran Khun camp committee proposed to dig trenches in the vicinity of the settlement. However, accommodating 1,643 people required a large number of trenches. Digging them would involve a huge amount of time and labor. Consequently, the proposal has remained unimplemented so far.

As Sam Sam noted, “Survival in an IDP camp hinges on luck ultimately. Many things have to work out correctly all the time for the inmates to survive.”
