title: One Year On, China’s K Visa Remains an Opaque Promise
description: China’s flagship talent visa can be found in the official application system, but most of the specifics on who can apply, and how to do so, are still missing.
text:
In September 2026, a British physicist posted an update to a months-long Reddit thread, writing that he finally had a K visa and that the visa “does exist.” The process had taken roughly five months from application to passport collection, although he acknowledged that part of the delay was his own doing, since one of his degree certificates had to be reissued and an embassy email sat unnoticed in his spam folder.

The application itself, as he described it, was simple; there was no interview, no invitation letter, and no question about his plans in China, and he found the visa center staff patient and helpful. The visa he received is valid for ten years, permits multiple entries, and allows stays of 180 days.

What made his post notable was its rarity. His is one of the few first-person accounts I found of a successful K visa application online. That is why applicants from Pakistan to the United States had followed his thread for months, asking for updates on his application and comparing their own experiences in the absence of detailed official guidance.

China’s Foreign Ministry’s own online application guide shows why that guidance is needed. For São Paulo, the submission city I examined, the guide lists the K visa among the available categories and allows applicants to identify themselves as graduates of well-known universities or as employees of well-known research institutions. Although the category is therefore visible, the page neither explains how “well-known” is assessed nor displays a checklist of supporting documents specific to the K visa. As a result, applicants can find the category but cannot determine from the online guidance whether they meet its requirements or what evidence they should submit.

The K visa exists, and there are public accounts of successful applications. What applicants cannot obtain from the sources I reviewed is the information needed to assess their own prospects. There is also no public indication of scale, since China has not published how many K visas it has issued.

The K visa was announced in August 2025 through a State Council revision of China’s entry-exit regulations as a new category for young foreign professionals in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) who graduated from “well-known” universities. It requires neither employer sponsorship nor an invitation letter and there is no numerical cap on the total number of K visas. It took effect on October 1, 2025, shortly after the Trump administration announced a $100,000 fee on new H-1B petitions. International media promptly described the K visa as “China’s H-1B.”

The domestic reception was far less welcoming. In the days before the launch, hashtags about the K visa drew tens of millions of views on Weibo, where the policy arrived at a difficult moment. Urban youth unemployment stood near 19 percent, and recirculated clips of Indian media celebrating the visa persuaded many commenters that foreign competitors were about to enter China’s already strained job market. On September 30, the state-run People’s Daily responded with a commentary titled “Distorting the K visa will only mislead the public,” which rebutted the criticisms one by one and promised that the new visa would come with “supporting management systems.”

Those supporting systems have not been published in the year since. In December 2025, two months after the visa was launched, The Diplomat reported that the K visa was absent from the official list of China’s visa application service centers and unmentioned on embassy websites. In January, University World News reported that four government agencies were still jointly drafting implementation guidelines, which were expected to specify university rankings, subject lists, and age limits. Applications were expected to open by April 2026 at the earliest.

April passed without an announcement. In May immigration practitioners noted that the parameters for the K visa – including the age range defining “young,” the standard for “well-known” universities, document checklists, and fees – remained unpublished. As of early October, the public guidance I have reviewed still does not resolve these questions.

A comparison with China’s other openings is instructive. China has expanded visa-free access; such entries rose 49.5 percent in 2025. More directly related to the K visa, Shanghai’s Lingang new area published new measures designed to facilitate foreign talent residence in 2026. For both visa-free access and the Lingang new area measures, the guidance clearly states who qualifies and on what terms.

The K visa, by contrast, specifies the related fields and its minimum degree requirement, while the age boundary defining “young,” the standard for “well-known” universities, and the evidence required remain unstated. Applicants cannot determine whether they meet the requirement or how to demonstrate that they do.

In the vacuum, the standards that applicants encounter depend on the office they approach. An applicant in Pakistan reported that, after a month of waiting, the embassy told him the K visa “hasn’t been rolled out yet” in his region, and that the local document portal demanded a master’s degree although official explanatory guidance specifies a bachelor’s degree. Another applicant recounted being told in Beijing that the visa was reserved for fresh 2025 graduates, a criterion that doesn’t appear in any public document. The British physicist, by contrast, was approved in London as a Ph.D. holder who had graduated several years earlier, facing no such constraints.

These accounts are self-reported and should be read with caution. The difficulty is that, one year in, such self-reports are the only available accounts of how K visa applications are handled, because no official source settles these questions. When terms such as “well-known universities” remain undefined, applicants cannot assess their eligibility in advance, while the interpretation of these requirements remains with the officials reviewing their applications.

It’s not clear why the implementation guidelines have not appeared. Practitioners and scholars have offered technical explanations. Shi Hui, a senior partner at the law firm Dacheng, attributed the delay to the need for government departments to finalize supporting operational details, update the visa application and review system, and coordinate processes across agencies. Liu Guofu of the Beijing Institute of Technology, a leading scholar of Chinese immigration law, identified system upgrades and the establishment of procedures for an “employer-independent” visa, a category new to China’s immigration framework, as the primary technical challenge.

There is precedent for such a gradual path. The R visa for high-level foreign talent was created in 2013 and was supplemented in 2017 by implementation measures that further specified its conditions and procedures. These measures were extended nationwide in 2018 after trials in nine provinces and cities. That means the R visa took five years to go from the initial announcement to national application.

There may be a political explanation for the delay as well. The backlash to the K visa’s launch plausibly raised the political cost of visible implementation. The absence of published guidelines – and especially the lack of hard counts of the number of visas being issued – is consistent with that reading as well as theories about administrative difficulty.

Chinese officials justified the K visa by pointing to global talent competition; in its editorial, People’s Daily cited a projected shortfall of nearly 30 million workers in key manufacturing fields. However, critics evaluate the K visa against domestic youth unemployment, which reached 18.9 percent again in August 2026, its highest level in a year. These are two different standards for judging what openness is for.

The reaction among the visa’s supposed beneficiaries suggests a parallel misalignment. In one thread on an Indian diaspora forum – admittedly a single discussion rather than a representative survey – the top-voted response to a question about the K visa held that “Chinese government want K Visa folks but Chinese people won’t want K Visa folks.” Another commenter wrote, “I might consider a BYD car in India sooner than I’d consider a second innings as an NRI [Non-Resident Indian, an Indian citizen living abroad] in China.” The reasons offered – including language, “996” work culture, geopolitics, and China’s own youth unemployment – mirror the anxieties voiced on the Chinese side.

Such threads suggest that both the feared influx of foreign workers and the promised talent wave may be overstated. Each public is responding to domestic concerns at least as much as to the policy itself.

The K visa thus merits continued observation. Upon its launch, the visa was widely read as China’s entry into an intensifying global competition for scientific and technological talent. Its opaque beginning shows how much administrative work it takes to go from declaring an opening to building a channel that qualified foreigners can actually use. Whether the coming year brings published criteria, issuance figures, and consistent consular practice will indicate how far China intends to pursue that competition in practice as well as in announcement. This makes the K visa a case worth following for anyone watching how the global contest over STEM talent unfolds.

title: OPCON Transition: Now It Is Time for the Commanders-in-Chief
description: It’s time for the OPCON transition process to move beyond military assessments into the realm of political responsibility.
text:
The debate over wartime operational control (OPCON) transition once again stands at the threshold of decision. At the 57th Security Consultative Meeting (SCM) in 2025, South Korea and the United States agreed to pursue verification of the full operational capability (FOC) of the Future Combined Forces Command headquarters in 2026, and the 2026 U.S. National Defense Strategy (NDS) assessed that South Korea is capable of taking primary responsibility for deterring North Korea with “critical but more limited” U.S. support.

More than 20 years have passed since the allies formalized OPCON transition, and more than a decade of preparation and verification has accumulated since they adopted the conditions-based transition plan. Meanwhile, South Korea has grown into an ally with military and economic capabilities entirely different from those it had when this arrangement was created some 70 years ago.

With the next SCM approaching, the question must change. Until now, the debate has centered on asking: have the military conditions been met? The purpose of a conditions-based approach was not to avoid a decision, but to make a responsible decision possible. Military preparation always carries residual risk, and from the moment one judges what level of risk is acceptable, the question moves beyond military assessment into the realm of political responsibility.

Whose Decision Is It?

The wartime OPCON exercised by the commander of the ROK-U.S. Combined Forces Command derives from two sources. For U.S. forces, this authority is delegated through the chain of command from the U.S. president, through the secretary of defense, to the combatant commander. For South Korean forces, it is delegated under the South Korean president’s authority as commander-in-chief. OPCON transition, then, is neither a one-directional “return” of operational control nor simply a change in military structure. It is a political decision by the two commanders-in-chief to delegate their respective authorities to a new structure.

This distinction matters. If transition is seen as South Korea’s demand alone, the United States becomes the examiner and South Korea the examinee. If it is seen as a joint decision of the two commanders-in-chief, both sides have things they must do to make the decision possible. What OPCON transition needs, therefore, is not only the military authorities’ assessment of conditions, but a responsible decision by the supreme commanders, the presidents of South Korea and the United States.

The political tasks for transition can be sorted into four lines of effort. They are tasks the two countries’ political leaders must carry out, and at the same time political criteria for agreeing on transition at the summit level.

1: Understand and Address Military Concerns

The vulnerability of a transition period cannot be denied. Viewed from a purely military perspective, OPCON transition can only be postponed indefinitely, for a perfectly prepared military does not exist. Yet denying it only deepens distrust within the alliance. What is needed is for the two countries’ political leaders to jointly acknowledge this vulnerability, and to offset and manage it with alliance-level political-strategic means alongside military compensating measures.

The starting point is understanding that the two sides’ concerns differ. South Korea’s concerns converge on the credibility of extended deterrence, the deployment of reinforcements in a contingency, and a command gap during transition. On the U.S. side, the main concerns are possible degradation of the combined defense posture, the institutional and political problems of U.S. forces operating under a South Korean general, and the risk perceptions of the Combined Forces Command and parts of Congress.

The South Korean president must demonstrate, through exercises and verification, that South Korea has a working crisis decision-making structure to lead theater operations, running from the president to the Ministry of National Defense, the Joint Chiefs of Staff, and the Future Combined Forces Command. The U.S. president must reaffirm the defense commitment and extended deterrence at the summit level and continue institutionalization through the Nuclear Consultative Group. The scope and procedures of the bridging and enduring capabilities the United States will provide should be codified in the relevant agreements and strategic directives. The NDS’s reference to “critical but more limited support” needs to be fleshed out with specifics.

There are also things the two countries must do together. Whether to accept or limit escalation in a crisis, and under what conditions to begin and to end a war, are matters for the commanders-in-chief to judge. The two leaders must therefore identify and align, in peacetime, their perceptions of war aims, escalation thresholds, and war termination conditions. The allies should also adopt a “No Surprise” principle: changes in posture, command reorganization, and the movement of forces in and out must be consulted in advance.

2: Commit Resources and Assets Continuously

A decision not backed by the necessary resources is no more than a political declaration. The investment South Korea must bear is considerable, but what is needed is not money alone. It also includes the commitment of national capacity for the employment and posture of military forces. Both sides need multiyear, bipartisan commitments that can survive changes of government.

South Korea must link its roadmap for core military capabilities to the Mid-Term Defense Plan and secure its sustainability through the National Assembly. Recent defense spending increases should be explained not as burden-sharing, but as part of the national goal of transition and independent capability.

The United States must back the assets, posture, and budget needed to provide bridging and enduring capabilities, such as intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR), space, strategic asset deployment, and reinforcement plans. A responsible answer by the administration to the National Defense Authorization Act provision concerning transition-related funding and certification is also part of this effort.

South Korea’s commitment of resources becomes the basis for a capability-based voice within the alliance. The U.S. commitment of assets ensures that “limited support” is never read as “uncertain support.” OPCON transition is not a single event, but part of a process of completing a future-oriented combined command structure – one that the legislatures and executive branches of both countries must resource together.

3: Develop a Future-Oriented Alliance Architecture

Security and alliance issues must not be treated as transactions, like trade negotiations. If OPCON transition is transactionally linked to other issues, it becomes something obtained by paying a price. This can fuel political backlash against transition in both countries and damage trust in the alliance. Defense cost-sharing, reductions in U.S. Forces Korea, and the Northeast Asia Command concept could all become subjects of such transactional linkage. These issues are not entirely unrelated to OPCON transition, but they must be handled on separate tracks and must not become terms of exchange.

For the U.S. president, policy alignment within the administration is needed above all. Within Washington, OPCON transition can be viewed through the White House’s alliance policy and negotiations, the defense establishment’s burden-sharing, and the combatant command’s command relationships. Aligning these into a single strategic direction is a task only the commander-in-chief can perform.

The South Korean president, for his part, should not make out-of-area contributions a term of exchange for progress on transition. Leading the defense of the Korean Peninsula and making selective contributions in the Indo-Pacific are separate matters, each under its own principles. At home, OPCON should not be consumed merely as a symbol of sovereignty. The two countries can begin by describing these issues separately in official documents such as the SCM joint communiqué.

Of course, not every link can be cut. Command relationships among the Future Combined Forces Command, the United Nations Command, and U.S. Forces Korea, access to United Nations Command rear bases in a contingency, and the alliance’s regional role cannot be thought of apart from transition. Transactional linkage and structural linkage must therefore be clearly distinguished. Structural linkage should not be hidden or postponed, but discussed transparently and established together in designing the transition.

4: Take Responsibility for and Explain the Political Decision

If OPCON transition is not made by military judgment alone, responsibility for the decision should not rest on the military alone either. The military assessment that “the military is ready” and the political judgment that “the two governments have decided” must be kept distinct. Otherwise, when problems arise, responsibility shifts to commanders, and political leaders hide behind military outcomes.

The U.S. Congress is already involved through the National Defense Authorization Act, overseeing whether conditions are met, the Future Combined Forces Command’s national command reporting chain, the relationship with the United Nations Command, the impact on nuclear proliferation, and military risk. If the administration does not answer these questions systematically, caution in Congress and in the field will delay the decision at the working level.

The South Korean National Assembly, by contrast, has no equivalent procedure. As the body that must provide the budget and institutional arrangements, it should be involved through regular reporting and verification, and the executive branch must explain why transition needs to happen now, what changes and what does not, and what is required.

Political accountability also includes the management of trust. South Korea must not treat transition only as a political timetable and neglect military preparation, nor give that impression. The United States should refrain from messages suggesting that the Combined Forces Command could be dissolved if conditions are not met. That, too, is part of the responsibility for completing an agreement the two countries have pursued together for 20 years across administrations.

The Politics of Decision and Responsibility

In the end, the last gateway of OPCON transition is not military assessment alone but the responsible political judgment of the two commanders-in-chief. For 20 years, military assessments have often provided grounds for deferring political decisions. What is needed now is not to keep asking whether the conditions have been met, but for the commanders-in-chief to decide and to take responsibility for that decision.

That means four lines of effort: identifying and managing the military risks of transition; continuously providing the resources and assets to support it; designing the future alliance’ command structure together rather than treating transition as a transaction; and explaining the decision to the public and the legislature and taking responsibility for its results.

These are not South Korea’s homework alone. If only one side carries out these steps, transition remains one side’s demand or a one-sided transfer of burden. Only when carried out together do they work as political criteria and as a driving force. OPCON transition is not an event that settles the past, but a process of jointly designing the alliance’s future command structure – and completing that design is, in the end, the commanders-in-chief’s responsibility.

title: Pakistan Imposes Emergency and Governor’s Rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa
description: By invoking Articles 232 and 234, the federal government has essentially neutralized PTI’s institutional presence in the province.
text:
On October 11, Pakistan’s federal government imposed an emergency and governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) province, which was being governed by former Prime Minister Imran Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI).

The move, which was approved by President Asif Ali Zardari on the advice of Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif following a federal cabinet meeting, marks a decisive takeover by the federal government of a province that has long been a PTI stronghold. The federal government justified the decision by pointing to a sharp surge in terror attacks across KP, alleging that the provincial administration was obstructing counterterrorism efforts, failing to maintain public order and allowing militant groups space to operate.

The federal government invoked Articles 232 and 234 of the constitution, which grant extraordinary powers to the federal government over provincial affairs.

However, the two articles address different circumstances and operate within distinct mechanisms. For instance, Article 232 empowers the federal government to declare a state of emergency when security is threatened by war or internal disturbance beyond the provincial government’s control. Under this provision, the provincial assembly continues to function, but federal laws take precedence in cases of conflict.

On the other hand, Article 234 allows the president to impose governor’s rule when a provincial government is judged unable to function in accordance with the constitution. Once implemented, the article suspends the provincial cabinet, transfers executive authority to the federal government or the governor, and permits parliament to exercise the assembly’s powers.

By deploying the two articles together, the federal government has essentially neutralized PTI’s institutional presence in the province. Article 234 has removed the PTI provincial cabinet and chief minister, which has effectively cut the party off from the province’s administrative system, official resources, and day-to-day levers of governance.

Moreover, Article 232 has shifted key legislative and public order authority to the center and provided federal authorities with stronger legal tools to enforce order, restrict street mobilization and limit any form of organized political activity.

By invoking Articles 232 and 234, the federal government has made a comprehensive effort to deny PTI any realistic prospect of regaining political or institutional influence in KP province in the near term.

This institutional confrontation is the culmination of months of friction between the federal government and PTI. The current setup in Islamabad is governed by a multi-party coalition, which is led by Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif of the Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) and supported prominently by the Pakistan People’s Party (PPP) under President Asif Ali Zardari. It is pertinent to mention that after having assumed power following a highly contested election in 2024, the ruling coalition in Islamabad has remained engaged in an intense political feud with Imran Khan’s party.

The latest decision indicates that the relationship between the PTI-led provincial government and the federal government had become virtually unbridgeable.

From Islamabad’s perspective, the core dispute between the two sides centered on counterterrorism policy and the provincial government’s perceived defiance of federal priorities. It is important to note that security conditions in the province have deteriorated sharply in recent months with a marked rise in militant attacks.

Information Minister Attaullah Tarar on Sunday went as far as saying that the PTI-led government had developed a nexus with terrorist groups and that a “power-sharing formula was gradually taking shape between terrorists and the PTI’s KP government, which was starting from southern districts and was ingressing further into the entire KP.”

The PTI leadership has questioned these assertions, arguing that security concerns are being leveraged to justify political measures aimed at diminishing the party’s footprint in the province. Furthermore, PTI leaders maintain that the central government refused to adopt a consultative approach to address the militancy challenge and also consistently denied party leaders access to consult with Imran Khan, who is languishing in prison.

The timing of this development is significant for many reasons. The emergency measures were imposed as the PTI prepared a long march from KP to Islamabad, the national capital, to demand Khan’s release from prison. Moreover, the provincial leadership, particularly Chief Minister Sohail Afridi, have refused to come on board the federal government’s counterterrorism policy. This stance hardened in recent months.

For decision makers in Islamabad, the provincial government had become both a political irritant and a security liability that was obstructing coordinated action against the militancy emanating from KP, which has become a threat to national security.

Following the declaration of emergency, one of the central government’s first administrative steps has been to establish a direct administrative framework for KP’s border and former tribal districts. The federal government has approved the immediate establishment of an Area Development Secretariat, which will be supervised by an Area Representative and Development Council and covers Dera Ismail Khan, Tank, Lakki Marwat, Bannu, Bajaur, Mohmand, Khyber, Kurram, Orakzai, North Waziristan, and both Upper and South Waziristan. The ADS will be responsible for restoring law and order, protecting citizens, and ensuring governance and development.

Under this arrangement, civil administration, police and military coordination have been placed under a streamlined federal framework. It has created a more direct channel for Islamabad to manage high-risk districts. Moreover, this has also arguably reduced the scope for any future provincial government to impede security operations in these areas.

The move also carries clear external implications.

On Monday, KP Governor Faisal Karim Kundi stated that the days of lack of coordination between the center and the province on terrorism related issues are over, adding that “our policies will come from Islamabad … not Kabul, Jalalabad or Kandahar.” Arguably, Kundi’s statement was meant to emphasize that the state will not entertain dialogue or local deals with militant elements. By emphasizing that policy will originate from Islamabad rather than Afghanistan, he signaled that the federal government will no longer tolerate cross-border sanctuaries and will implement security policy unilaterally.

Kundi’s statement is important as it carries clear policy-level implications. If the new administrative framework is any indication, Pakistan is set to confront Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) threats and presence in its border regions more forcefully than before, and will likely pursue an uncompromising approach toward the Afghan Taliban on issues of militancy, border management, and cross-border sanctuaries.

One can argue that while the PTI government in Peshawar had become a political problem for the center, it had also evolved, in Islamabad’s assessment, into a security challenge. The party’s resistance to the measures now being imposed in the former tribal districts was viewed as untenable by both the federal government and the military leadership.

For now, the federal government has imposed its will in the province. Whether the new direct-rule arrangement can deliver improved security and reduced terrorist threats will determine whether it ultimately gains public acceptance. The immediate challenge for Islamabad is to ensure that the policy it is seeking to implement actually produces results on the ground.

title: Pakistan Is Treating Every Grievance as Terrorism, and It’s Failing
description: From KP to Balochistan and beyond, instead of addressing the underlying causes of unrest, the country's rulers are hell-bent on targeting the opposition.
text:
Pakistan faces mounting political, economic, and security crises. But instead of addressing the underlying causes, the country’s rulers are hell-bent on targeting the opposition and treating it as the problem.

I have seen this approach firsthand in Balochistan, Pakistan’s militancy-ridden southwestern province. For years, the state has responded to political dissent and social, economic, and political grievances primarily through a security lens, via arrests, enforced disappearances, and extrajudicial killings. The consequences have been severe: such policies have pushed thousands of youths toward a violent insurgency. But this approach is no longer confined to Balochistan.

Recent developments in the northwestern province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa suggest that the same logic is increasingly being applied elsewhere. On October 11, Pakistan’s President Asif Ali Zardari declared a state of emergency and suspended the provincial government led by Sohail Afridi, an ally of imprisoned former Prime Minister Imran Khan. Pakistani media reports said Afridi had been arrested and his whereabouts remain untraceable.

Enforced disappearances are a longstanding practice in Pakistan, particularly in its peripheries. But the disappearance of a politician who was the chief minister until Sunday morning raises disturbing questions about the rule of law and the fate of ordinary citizens with far less visibility or political influence.

The scenes from Peshawar, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s provincial capital, tell a similar story. Security forces have filled roads with brightly colored shipping containers to prevent Khan supporters from reaching Islamabad. On October 4, Khan’s party, Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), took to the streets to demand his release. The federal government has defended the barricades and its latest actions as necessary to prevent unrest.

Such restrictions on political dissent go beyond the PTI.

In Balochistan, the authorities have confronted the Baloch Yakjehti Committee, a large grassroots movement against enforced disappearances and extrajudicial killings. Its popular crowd-puller leader, Mahrang Baloch, was sentenced to life imprisonment on June 22 by an anti-terrorism court, alongside fellow activist Sibghatullah, over the alleged killing of a paramilitary soldier during a protest in Pakistan’s new emerging port city Gwadar in July 2024. The court found they had incited the crowd. Baloch’s lawyers boycotted the proceedings, held inside Hudda jail, and called it a faceless trial.

In Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, the Pashtun Tahafuz Movement, another civil rights movement demanding rights for ethnic Pashtuns, has faced an intensive crackdown. Its soft-spoken, 34-year-old charismatic leader, Manzoor Pashteen, has been among those targeted, as the government has attempted to ban the movement and its leadership.

Authorities have used similar tools in Pakistan-administered Kashmir, long described by Pakistani leaders as the country’s “jugular vein.” On June 5, the Azad Jammu and Kashmir government designated the Jammu Kashmir Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC), a grassroots coalition that has organized protests over economic and political demands, as a proscribed organization under the region’s anti-terrorism law.

These are different movements, with different demands. But the state responds in a common way: it treats every political grievance as a security threat.

Laws such as the Fourth Schedule, once intended for terrorism, are also being used against lawyers, journalists, and political opponents. In particular, the controversial cyber law, the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act (PECA), is frequently used against activists and journalists.

In January, an Islamabad court handed prominent human rights lawyers Imaan Zainab Mazari-Hazir and her husband, Hadi Ali Chattha, prison terms totaling 17 years over social media posts the state called anti-state. The sentences were to run concurrently, so they were to serve 10 years. In September, the Supreme Court suspended the sentences and ordered their release on bail. Within hours, authorities rearrested them in an earlier protest case.

Since the controversial 2024 elections, Pakistan’s Parliament, the judiciary, and the media have come under intense pressure. Citizens on the periphery, especially ethnic minorities such as Baloch, Pashtuns, and Kashmiris, have little reason left to take a political complaint to those institutions.

Meanwhile, the security crisis has worsened.

The Global Terrorism Index ranked Pakistan the country most affected by terrorism in 2025. It recorded 1,139 deaths and 1,045 terrorist incidents, with Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa bearing the brunt.

An Islamabad-based think tank, the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies (PICS), documented 606 deaths and 232 injuries from militant attacks and counter-militancy operations in July 2026 alone, the deadliest month of the year to date. Most of the dead were militants: 401, against 112 security personnel and 74 civilians. The raw numbers still argue against the idea that more force is closing the war.

Some years ago, Pakistan spent millions of dollars on fencing its roughly 1,600-mile border with Afghanistan to contain cross-border attacks from militants allegedly based in Afghanistan. But militancy continues. Islamabad has since taken the war across the border.

On March 16, a Pakistani airstrike hit the Omid Addiction Treatment Hospital in Kabul, a drug-rehabilitation center on the site of a former NATO base. Pakistan said it had struck a militant storage site. The U.N. mission in Afghanistan confirmed at least 269 civilian deaths and 122 injured. Amnesty International later said the strike should be investigated as a possible war crime.

Cross-border strikes have continued. On October 1, Pakistan launched airstrikes in Kunar and Helmand provinces in Afghanistan. The Taliban government said at least nine civilians, mostly children, were killed and 11 injured. The U.N. mission said at least 10 civilians, most of them children, were killed and nine were injured. Pakistan said the strikes targeted militant hideouts and claimed 22 militants were killed.

There is a clear contradiction here. Pakistan’s leaders want to be seen internationally as peacemakers and mediators. At home, they have refused to engage politically with Imran Khan, Mahrang Baloch, the Kashmir committee, and Manzoor Pashteen, and they have preferred force with Afghanistan as well. The economic cost of that instability is why Islamabad is asking Washington for a $10 billion exchange-stabilization facility to strengthen its foreign-exchange reserves.

Western governments should be careful not to confuse that request, or Pakistan’s field Marshal General Asim Munir’s usefulness in mediating with Iran, with a diplomatic settlement. Pakistan matters to the West because of its size, its nuclear weapons, its position between South and Central Asia, and its role in regional security. Engagement with the army should not mean ignoring a provincial capital closed off with containers, civil rights movement leaders tried under anti-terror laws, or a strike on a Kabul hospital. Nor should Pakistan’s leaders assume that economic assistance or geopolitical usefulness can substitute for public trust.

Militancy cannot be excused, and the state has a legitimate responsibility to protect its citizens. But military action alone, whether inside or outside Pakistan, is not resolving the political alienation underneath the violence. Pakistan’s leaders need to face the hard questions. Why are educated Baloch in Balochistan being drawn toward a deadly insurgency? Why has resentment among Pashtun youth against the state increased? Why have large crowds in Kashmir repeatedly taken to the streets?

The West has tried to build a relationship solely through military generals before. It did not produce a stable partner. It is unlikely to do so while the same generals answer political protest with emergencies, repress dissent with terror and cybersecurity laws, target Afghanistan with airstrikes, and then ask the West to finance the country for economic stability.

title: Pakistan’s Counterterrorism Campaign Is at an Inflection Point
description: If the new security framework fails to adopt a holistic approach to counterterrorism, it will once again end up treating the symptoms while ignoring the causes.
text:
For the last several years, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) has been the epicenter of terrorism in Pakistan. However, 2026 marks an exception to this rule, as Balochistan has emerged as the most volatile region in terms of both the number of attacks and casualties. As of October 19, according to the South Asia Terrorism Portal’s open-source data, Balochistan had suffered 1,147 terrorist attacks, and 2,394 deaths (424 civilians, 736 security personnel, and 1,233 insurgents or terrorists, plus one death that was not categorized). However, numbers provide only one aspect of a disturbing and complex security situation.

With 12 of KP’s 36 districts witnessing a worsening law-and-order situation and a receding writ of the state, Pakistan recently imposed emergency and governor’s rule in the province. Two militant networks, Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) and Ittehad-ul-Mujahideen Pakistan (IMP), have been carrying out large-scale attacks from their hideouts in Afghanistan and reconstituted networks in the Afghanistan-Pakistan border areas. Since the Taliban’s return to power, the organizational coherence, operational capacity, recruitment strategies, propaganda methods, and fundraising techniques of these terrorist networks have significantly evolved.

Against this backdrop, Pakistan’s counterterrorism approach must be grounded in an accurate assessment of a complex and fluid threat landscape. Taking an over-simplistic view of a complicated threat picture would result in temporary respite instead of permanent peace. Therefore, taking a holistic and nuanced view of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s security situation is the first step in restoring peace in the province.

Terrorism in KP predates the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf’s (PTI) three successive governments in the province. In fact, its contemporary roots can be traced to the May 1994 Malakand uprising of Sufi Muhammad’s Tehreek-e-Nifaz-e-Shariat-e-Muhammadi (TNSM). Since then, terrorism has persisted in KP in one form or another. Therefore, terrorism in the province is despite, and not because of, the PTI’s provincial regime. The PTI’s lack of cooperation is just one of the several factors that have contributed to a worsening law-and-order situation in the restive province. Nevertheless, it is quite unfortunate that the PTI politicized internal security.

Pakistan’s flawed pro-Taliban Afghan policy, kinetic-heavy counterterrorism approach, governance deficit, underdeveloped non-kinetic counterterrorism framework (or a Preventing and Countering Violent Extremism policy), and absence of structural reforms have cumulatively contributed to the current security situation in KP. If the new security framework fails to adopt a holistic approach to counterterrorism, it will once again end up treating the symptoms while ignoring the root causes.

Since the military is Pakistan’s most developed and capable security institution, the country has heavily leaned on it to suppress terrorism. By and large, military operations have proved successful in dismantling terrorist networks, their command-and-control nodes, organizational infrastructure, and logistical pipelines. However, the absence of political processes required to translate those tactical advantages into permanent strategic gains reversed improvements in security.

Going forward, transparent and timely strategic communication is crucial in fighting and discrediting terrorist networks. Pakistani security institutions must ensure transparent and timely communication grounded in the rule-of-law approach to reclaim the narrative domain from violent nonstate actors. They must provide a realistic assessment to the public that the military has no magic wand to bring an overnight improvement in the security situation. It will be a long struggle before peace can be restored. The first step would be to reduce the intensity of terrorist attacks and their impact. Then, large-scale kinetic operations will be required to blunt the sharp edge of terrorism.

Here, strategic communication is important. It will involve a two-pronged effort. First, the government must comprehensively address public concerns about why previous operations, despite their mixed results, were necessary. Faulting them alone for terrorism’s recurrence is unfair. The blame equally goes to the absence of political processes and good governance. There is a need for constitutional and administrative reforms too.

Second, the government must unambiguously convey to the masses how and why the new counterterrorism operations will be different from their previous iterations. Persistent and timely communication to the public will bridge the existing perception gaps about previous counterterrorism policies and their outcomes. Especially in the age of social media, terrorists are exploiting communication gaps and information blackouts. Malevolent actors jump into these situations to misguide public perception through misinformation and disinformation campaigns. Therefore, ensuring continuous and consistent communication about the progress of counter-terrorism operations and challenges confronting them will be critical.

Likewise, unlike in the past, the security institutions will do well to avoid premature victory declarations. Such pronouncements, especially without consolidating security gains through kinetic operations into permanent strategic advantages, can result in complacency and a false sense of security. This time around, the absence of violence must not be mistaken for peace. This happened during the 2015-2020 period when a decline in terrorist attacks and the displacement of terrorist networks was confused with their elimination. The premature victory trap is tempting but dangerous, as it erodes public trust, which is central to the success of counterterrorism initiatives.

Similarly, a clear distinction between eliminating terrorists and terrorism is important. Terrorists, despite their elimination, keep returning to the battlefield as long as the roots of terrorism are not adequately tackled. Terrorism keeps the recruitment pipeline alive by exploiting ideological, political, and socioeconomic grievances. Terrorism is effectively tackled when terrorists are ideologically and discursively discredited to a point where the masses reject their appeal despite having reservations about the state. For that, strengthening state-society relations, or renewing the social contract, is important. The glue that keeps states and societies together is governance. Making state policies and administrative apparatus receptive to people’s needs and demands will drain the swamp where terrorists germinate.

Finally, terrorism in Pakistan has its internal and external dimensions. Internal consolidation against terrorist networks constitutes a necessary but not sufficient condition to overcome the challenge of terrorism. Pakistan will have to evolve a two-pronged policy, involving proactive diplomacy and coercion.

Diplomatically, Pakistan must highlight the Taliban’s support for the TTP, IMP, and Baloch separatist groups. At the same time, Pakistan should impose punitive costs on Kabul for allowing Afghanistan’s soil to be used for cross-border terrorism against it. Pakistani air strikes in Afghanistan should aim to destroy terrorist hideouts as well as the Taliban’s military capabilities to a point where they revisit their strategic calculus of supporting the TTP and IMP.

The declaration of emergency in KP marks an inflection point in the evolution of Pakistan’s counterterrorism policy. A prudent, holistic, transparent, and proactive approach with a long-term vision will deliver peace dividends. A reactive, kinetic-heavy approach, lacking concomitant non-kinetic interventions and a transparent communication strategy, will deliver short-term respite at the cost of long-term peace.

title: Pakistan’s GSP+ Advantage Is Fading. Competitiveness Must Come Next
user_author_name: Ahmed Bilal Rathore; Muhammad Rauhan Rasheed
description: Preferential access has taken Pakistan about as far as it can without deeper reforms at home.
text:
The EU Generalized Scheme of Preferences Plus (GSP+) was launched to provide exemptions to vulnerable and developing countries. The scheme was special because it lifted tariffs on almost two-thirds of EU tariff lines. For an economy like Pakistan’s, it has been a lifeline in building exports and filling up its coffers. GSP+ is also designed to incentivise commitments on international human rights, labor laws, environmental safeguards, and governance improvements, so participation would benefit Pakistan in non-economic ways as well. Pakistan joined the scheme in 2014 and has been its biggest beneficiary.

GSP+ really boomed trade, especially Pakistani exports to the EU. In 2025 alone, bilateral trade totalled 12.2 billion euro, with Pakistan enjoying a 5.2 billion euro trade surplus. According to the latest figures published for 2024, a total of 7.5 billion euros’ worth of exports were eligible for the scheme, which generated an estimated 732 million euros in tariff exemptions for Pakistan, making Pakistani exports more competitive and attractive.

However, there is a caveat. Although Pakistan’s exports are high, they have yet to reach their 2022 peak – 9.50 billion euro in 2022 vs 8.68 billion euro in 2025 – signalling an underlying problem. Textiles and textile articles accounted for 77.7 percent of Pakistan’s exports to the EU in 2025, concentrating exports and posing a risk, according to the EU Commission’s own Trade and Economic Security profile on Pakistan.

India is close to a similar tariff-access agreement with the EU, and Pakistan has to adhere to a stricter set of international conventions to maintain its GSP+ status in the next cycle. The problem is no longer being part of the GSP+, but how Pakistan can use this benefit to become more diversified and competitive before this access loses its edge.

A Surplus That Hides a Plateau

Pakistan has come a long way since 2014, with exports rising from 4.29 billion euro in 2014 to 8.68 billion euro in 2025. But not everything is going smoothly on that ascent. In 2022, Pakistan achieved its highest export value to the EU, totaling 9.50 billion euro, which then dropped significantly to 7.97 billion euro in 2023 before rising to 8.68 billion euro by 2025. The decline in 2023 can be attributed to a number of factors, including the post-COVID shock, low demand for textiles in Europe, and Pakistan’s own economic problems, including record-high inflation, devaluation of the rupee, import restrictions, and floods that hit the country and disrupted industrial production and exports.

Figure 1. Pakistan–EU Goods Trade, 2014–2025. Source: European Commission, Directorate-General for Trade and Economic Security. Figures are presented from Pakistan’s perspective; the trade balance equals Pakistan’s exports to the EU minus its imports from the EU.

Even though, as previously mentioned, Pakistani exports haven’t returned to their 2022 peak, Pakistan’s trade surplus with the EU has risen from 4.12 billion euro in 2022 to 5.17 billion euro in 2025. This was due to Pakistan’s imports from the EU dropping from 5.39 billion euro in 2022 to 3.52 billion euro in 2025. Therefore, Pakistan’s record surplus should not necessarily be lauded or attributed to its competitiveness; it’s just the simple math of decreasing imports into Pakistan from the EU.

Nor is the issue whether or not the exporters are taking advantage of the preferences they have available to them. “GSP+-eligible” imports relate to goods falling within tariff lines eligible for the preferential treatment of the scheme. At the same time, the utilization rate refers to the share of eligible imports that enter the EU under the GSP+ scheme. In 2024, 90.4 percent of EU imports from Pakistan qualified for the GSP+ provisions, while Pakistani exporters benefited from 95.1 percent of the preferences. The mechanism is doing exactly what it was designed to do.

The problem is the use to which it is being put. Textiles and textile articles alone contributed 77.7 percent of EU imports from Pakistan in 2025. The next-biggest sectors were raw hides at 4 percent, vegetable products at 3.7 percent, foodstuffs and beverages at 3.1 percent, and miscellaneous manufactured goods at 2.6 percent. The preferential treatment for exports has thus been in place for over a decade or more and has increased exports without significantly altering their composition. A failure of this sort does not mean GSP+ was a failure. It is the successful use of preferential access by Pakistan, but not the use of that opportunity to diversify to an adequate extent.

India Changes the Competitive Equation

The second pressure comes from next door. In January 2026, India and the EU concluded negotiations on a long-awaited free trade agreement. As South Asian Voices has noted, the deal may affect the economic landscape of South Asia. In Pakistan, one immediate implication will be that the advantage its exporters have had in Europe will lose its distinctiveness.

According to the agreed deal, duty-free access will be granted to Indian apparel and textiles, which were previously subject to duties of up to 12 percent. The agreement must undergo legal processes before its provisions take effect, and it doesn’t necessarily mean that Indian companies will replace Pakistani exporters. Pakistan continues to have loyal European customers and commanding stakes in cotton garments and home textiles. However, the competitive balance changes once a large regional competitor no longer faces a tariff disadvantage.

Pakistan can’t match the magnitude of India by merely attempting to export more of the same low-value textile products. Competing differently means additional diversification into more specialized and more valuable products, faster delivery times, higher productivity and energy reliability, and more traceability and standards compliance, something that European buyers are increasingly demanding.

The opportunity also extends beyond textiles. Pakistan Business Council research identifies optical, medical, and surgical instruments as “rising stars,” while pharmaceuticals and machinery appear among the “lost opportunities” where EU demand has grown faster than Pakistan’s exports. The gap is also striking in medical and surgical instruments, where the EU imported approximately $24.9 billion globally in 2024, while Pakistan supplied only $128.7 million despite exporting $446.6 million in the same category worldwide. Other avenues of expanding the export base include processed foods, engineering and electrical products, and higher value finished goods. The message isn’t to give up on textiles; it’s to end the practice of trying to shoulder almost all of the burden for the European relationship with one industry.

The Next GSP+ Test Goes Beyond Renewal

Pakistan also has a near-term policy challenge. The EU will be rolling out new GSP regulations as of January 1, 2027. Current beneficiaries of GSP+ will be given their preferences over a two-year transition period until the end of 2028, but will need to re-apply for GSP+ following the new admission criteria. The framework increases the number of related international conventions from 27 to 32, and current beneficiaries will be required to ratify six new conventions and provide a plan to implement the full set of conventions going forward. It also enhances monitoring and enables the quicker withdrawal of preferences in cases of serious violations.

That is significant because the EU 2026 Pakistan report noted Pakistan’s progress in areas such as labor rights legislation and anti-torture laws, but also reported that it had “regressed in several areas, while positive change was limited” and that enforcement was a recurring weakness. Reapplication should not, therefore, be a diplomatic exercise out of the context of domestic implementation.

The commercial rules are changing too as the EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism has gone into effect, though textiles are not currently covered under this regime. The more immediate challenge for Pakistani exporters is the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation and the coming Digital Product Passport (DPP). The passport is effectively a digital record that contains product information on composition, origin, sustainability, traceability, and compliance. Textile apparel is a priority product group, with the European Commission planning textile-specific rules for late 2027. Following adoption, businesses will have a transition period of at least 18 months before the requirements become applicable.

For Pakistan, this is not an abstract environmental requirement, as even with tariffs at zero, firms lacking a reliable supply chain and product information might be less able to retain European buyers. Islamabad should therefore now engage with textile and apparel associations, chambers of commerce, exporters, certification bodies, and standardization experts to create a common system of traceability and reporting, rather than burdening individual companies, particularly small ones, with the task of interpreting new EU requirements.

From Access to Competitiveness

Going forward, Pakistan should focus on three priorities. Firstly, Islamabad should regard the re-application for GSP+ as a whole-of-government compliance program and rectify shortcomings in EU monitoring well before the stipulated deadline at the end of 2028. Secondly, export policy should focus on strengthening the sectors where Pakistan has production capacity but is limited in the European market, such as medical and surgical instruments, pharmaceuticals, processed foods, engineering and electrical goods, and high-value textile products. Thirdly, government and industry should prepare exporters for Europe’s new traceability and sustainability requirements before they become costly barriers to market access.

GSP+ has provided Pakistan with unparalleled access to one of the world’s largest markets for the past 12 years. That access remains valuable; however, the idea of preferential access was never meant to replace competitiveness. In a nutshell, Pakistan’s EU trade boom is not simply ending, nor is GSP+ the problem. The more difficult reality is that preferential access has taken Pakistan about as far as it can without deeper reforms at home. With the beginning of India’s access to the same market and the evolving regulatory model in Europe, that weakness is being revealed. Preserving GSP+ is important, but it is more important to convert preference into competitiveness.

title: Pakistan’s Solar Revolution is Reshaping its Power Sector
description: Solar power generation has expanded rapidly in recent years and has overtaken nuclear power generation for the first time.
text:
Pakistan’s solar power generation has surpassed 20 percent of the country’s total electricity production. While this transition toward clean energy is a positive development, it is the outcome of an unplanned shift in the country’s energy landscape.

According to the World Nuclear Industry Status Report (WNISR) 2026, solar generation in Pakistan reached an estimated 36.3 terawatt-hours (TWh) in 2025. This accounts for roughly 21.6 percent of Pakistan’s total electricity generation after growing about 85 percent in a single year.

The WNISR report offers important background on this transformation. In Pakistan, solar-led power generation has not only expanded rapidly in recent years but has also overtaken nuclear power generation for the first time. The report further notes that Pakistan installed roughly twice as much solar capacity in five years as France managed in a decade.

Moreover, Pakistan imported more than 58 gigawatts (GW) of solar panels from China between the beginning of 2017 and mid-2026. Of this, around 40 GW arrived in just two and a half years, from 2024 to mid-2026. These imports over such a short period illustrate how quickly Chinese solar manufacturing found a major market in Pakistan amid falling panel prices and surging domestic electricity costs.

The surge has made Pakistan the second-largest single-country import market for Chinese solar panels, just behind the Netherlands. This data underscores the scale and speed of the change underway in the country.

Besides, the solar generation figures coming out of Pakistan are likely underestimations for several reasons.

A substantial amount of privately installed solar capacity across the country remains unregistered and does not pass through the state-controlled grid. In many cases, much of this capacity is installed on rooftops and industrial sites, where households and businesses generate and store power for their own use without becoming part of the national grid. This trend has largely been driven by high electricity tariffs, frequent load-shedding and the falling cost of Chinese solar panels. All of this has created a strong incentive for consumers to bypass the national grid system altogether.

While this shift is likely reducing the demand for grid-supplied electricity, it is impacting Pakistan’s power sector challenges and the country’s mounting capacity-related debt significantly.

For instance, as high-usage households, businesses, and industrial consumers leave the national grid, power distribution companies and remaining customers are left to shoulder a heavier burden of fixed costs. This essentially means that capacity payments for underutilized power plants continue in Pakistan. At the same time, overall electricity consumption recorded by distribution companies has declined across the country.

This situation has put coal-based power agreements reached by Pakistan previously with local and international firms under intense scrutiny. While solar adoption is surging across the country, Pakistan remains committed to long-term contracts that require heavy fixed payments to coal plant operators even if their plants remain idle or operate well below capacity. As a result, long-standing power purchase commitments have become a major financial burden for Pakistanis, even as they grapple with pressures due to the current economic strains facing the country.

It is important to note that Pakistan’s 23 loss-making state-owned enterprises accumulated roughly $1.24 billion in losses in the first half of Financial Year 2026. This is roughly equivalent to around $10 million per working day. At the same time, total state-owned enterprises’ debt, excluding sovereign guarantees, rose 14 percent to approximately $36.5 billion.

In this context, the rapid growth of solar power generation is not only a story of clean energy access and cost savings for those who can afford panels, but it is also accelerating financial stress within the formal power sector and complicating efforts to manage circular debt and capacity obligations of the Pakistani state.

For example, for ordinary consumers who remain fully dependent on the national grid, costs will likely continue to rise as the customer base continues to shrink. Meanwhile, for the energy market as a whole, the transition raises fundamental questions about planning, tariff design and the future role of large-scale coal and nuclear power in a system increasingly shaped by solar power generation.

That said, Pakistan’s energy future will depend on better planning and reform by the state. Policymakers should reorganize and renegotiate power-sector contracts and grid management to fit the new reality shaped by widespread solar power generation.

Without proactive reforms, the gap between solar power consumers and the struggling national grid will only continue to widen and strain the economy.

title: Philippine Energy Security Could Determine the Outcome of a Taiwan Contingency
channel_text: Blog; Opinion; Southeast Asia; The Debate
description: Any Sino-American conflict would place enormous pressure on fuel supplies. U.S. fuel dependence turns Manila’s energy fragility into a strategic vulnerability.
text:
In March, a U.S. ally declared a “state of energy emergency” after experiencing disruptions to its crude deliveries. After gaining a waiver from Washington, Petron, the Philippines’ only refinery, bought Russian oil. The episode exposed a decades-old vulnerability in U.S. strategy: Philippine fuel insecurity.

Beginning in 2010, across three Pacific tours, I’ve watched China erode regional security through its increased power and aggression. For the United States to deter China from a Taiwan annexation attempt, it requires access to the Philippines and its oil. However, a conflict that draws in the U.S. will likely disrupt the Philippine oil imports that sustain American operations.

The Philippines sits at the Pacific’s crossroads, in the middle of the First Island Chain, connecting Taiwan and the South China Sea. The Philippines’ placement makes it vital to U.S. deterrence. Economically, this region carries 43 percent of global crude shipments and 21 percent of trade. Geographically, control of the Luzon Strait would allow China to isolate Taiwan.

For 20 years, Chinese coercion has revealed Beijing’s desire to control these crossroads, annex Taiwan, and dominate the Pacific. To deter China and sustain American operations 6,500 miles from California, the U.S. needs reliable access to the Philippines and its oil. Yet Manila’s small, nearly import-only oil industry leaves it and U.S. forces vulnerable.

During my last tour in the Pacific, then-Speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives Nancy Pelosi visited Taiwan. China’s response, and its subsequent isolation “rehearsals,” demonstrated its power and aggression. Several isolation zones extended across the Luzon Strait, and, based on recent events, Beijing intends to contest Philippine sovereignty in these areas.

Luzon is critical to deterring “a conflict over Taiwan” and safeguarding global shipping routes, because it’s within ground-based missile range of Taiwan. For China to annex Taiwan, it must control the Luzon Strait to blockade Taiwan, threaten Philippine sovereignty, and degrade U.S. intervention. However, if the United States can maintain reliable access, it can resupply Taiwan and deny a Chinese annexation operation.

But geography is only one part of the equation. Operations from Luzon depend on reliable Philippine oil. American fuel dependence turns Manila’s energy fragility into a strategic vulnerability.

In 2022, the U.S. Department of Defense required over 73 million barrels for operations, training, and exercises globally, with 48 percent purchased overseas. Unsurprisingly, air and maritime operations account for 91 percent of demand, roughly 66.5 million barrels. Any Sino-American conflict would place enormous pressure on fuel supplies thousands of miles from the U.S. homeland.

The Philippines alone consumes 474,000 barrels per day and maintains only a 40-45 day reserve. Since Caltex and Shell closed their refineries, Petron has capacity to support only a limited share of national demand. Manila relies on imports, with almost 97 percent of crude coming from the Middle East and nearly 95 percent of refined products coming from Asia.

In a crisis, U.S. demands on Philippine oil would rapidly deplete Manila’s reserves. At the same time, Chinese maritime interdiction operations in the South China Sea would disrupt Philippine import routes and constrain American operations. The result would be another “state of energy emergency.”

Proven Philippine oil reserves stand at 139 million barrels, with another 202 million more locked in Bangsamoro’s Liguasan Marsh, which is a historical insurgency hotspot. Developing these resources and expanding refining capacity strengthens Manila’s resiliency. It’s also a mutually beneficial opportunity for Philippine-U.S. commercial cooperation.

Currently, the Pentagon is building extra oil capacity in Davao to “enable U.S. naval vessels to receive fuel.” The new depot is a positive step forward, but its limited capacity and continuous resupply needs mean that storage alone cannot solve the underlying problem.

American security requires more than stockpiles; it requires stronger Philippine extraction and refining capacity. The U.S.-Venezuela framework offers one possible model. This year, several U.S.-based oil companies signed agreements to develop Venezuelan reserves in support of both countries’ interests. The Philippine context differs, but the underlying mechanism, a bilateral agreement to unlock private-sector investment in domestic production, could be adapted to Washington’s and Manila’s needs.

Many existing Philippine-U.S. energy programs cover renewables, nuclear power, energy costs, and critical minerals, but none specifically targets Manila’s weak fuel extraction, refining, and distribution system. The November ASEAN Summit in Manila, where U.S. President Donald Trump and Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. may meet, offers an opportunity.

Washington should create a targeted Philippine oil resilience program directly linked to U.S. strategy. An ideal model to emulate is the Philippines Energy Threshold Program. Both nations’ commercial investment sectors can strengthen Manila’s fuel security and expand its capacity. To be sure, one program cannot address every wartime need, but it will reduce U.S. vulnerabilities.

My proposal benefits both nations’ prosperity, commercial industries, and U.S. strategy. From my tours, I’ve seen how oil underpins strategy. In a Sino-American conflict, we cannot assume fuel will arrive. Both nations should create an oil resilience program now, before the crisis begins.

title: Philippine Lower House Passes Bill Restricting Social Media Access of Minors
description: If passed into law, the country will become the fourth in Southeast Asia to introduce youth social media restrictions of some kind.
text:
The Philippine House of Representatives yesterday approved a measure barring children under the age of 13 from social media. It has become the latest nation in Southeast Asia to tighten online safety provisions for minors.

The Safe and Friendly Environment for Kids in Digital Spaces Act was passed nearly unanimously, with 287 lawmakers voting in favor and three against, Inquirer.net reported.

The measures align the Philippines with a growing global effort to restrict minors’ access to social media platforms, in the interests of protecting them from cyberbullying, online fraud, and exposure to pornography, among other perceived threats.

In the Philippines, the legislative push has come after a string of incidents of school violence that the government believes were driven by online content. Last month, a 16-year-old shot dead two fellow students and injured eight others at a school in the southern Philippines, before taking his own life.

This followed a similar incident in the same region in August, in which a student at a Catholic school live-streamed himself shooting and killing ​a classmate before taking his own life. Also in June, two students shot and killed three and injured seven of their peers at a school in Tacloban, allegedly in response to bullying.

Under the proposed bill, children aged 13 and below would be prohibited from creating social media accounts. Meanwhile, a variety of restrictions would be put in place for those under 18 years of age. They will be barred from making online purchases and engaging with “gambling-like mechanisms” and other features that may pose “reasonably foreseeable and material risks” to their well-being. They would also be shielded from harmful ads and algorithmic short-video feeds that encourage limitless scrolling, according to Inquirer.net.

Filipinos are heavy users of social media. The country has the sixth-largest pool of Facebook users in the world, with more than 102 million accounts registered, and an estimated 78.1 million TikTok accounts, the seventh-largest of any country. According to research, Filipinos spend an average of nearly 34 hours per week on social media.

Yesterday’s vote came after ⁠the Senate’s recent endorsement of a similar but slightly stricter bill, which would ban a minor under 18 years of age from registering, accessing, using, or maintaining an account on any age-restricted social media platform. According to Inquirer.net, the two dueling bills are now set for a “legislative showdown,” and it remains to be seen exactly what the final version of the legislation will look like.

These moves follow Australia’s introduction of the world’s first social media ban for under 16s. The policy, which took effect in December of last year, forces social media firms to block users under 16 from having accounts on their platforms, rather than penalizing young people or their parents. Despite the lingering questions about the effectiveness of such restrictions, a long list of countries, including India, China, Türkiye, the United Kingdom, the European Union, and several in Europe, have since followed suit and announced the introduction of curbs of some kind.

Within Southeast Asia, Indonesia in March became the first nation to ban under-16s from having accounts on what it termed “high-risk” digital platforms, including YouTube, TikTok, Facebook, Instagram, Threads, X, Bigo Live, and Roblox. Malaysia started enforcing a similar ban on June 1, and ordered major social media platforms to conduct ​age verification against government-issued records. It has given them until January to ​implement the ⁠measure.

Vietnam also announced in July that it planned to introduce social media restrictions for minors. While Hanoi will not ban minors’ access to social media platforms, the new rules would bar under 16s from posting, commenting, sharing, or reacting to posts on social media.
