title: Philippine Senator Files Resolution Seeking Chinese Ambassador’s Expulsion
description: Jing Quan prompted controversy last week when he told reporters that China could easily win a war against the Philippines.
text:
A Philippine Senator has filed a resolution seeking the expulsion of the Chinese ambassador and declaring him persona non grata, as the Department of Foreign Affairs summoned him over his recent comment that China could “easily win” a conflict against the Philippines.

Senate Resolution No. 739, which was filed yesterday by Senator Erwin Tulfo, expressed the Senate’s “serious concern” over the envoy’s statement, which it said threatened “the potential use of force against the Philippines.” It then called on the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) to declare Ambassador Jing Quan as persona non grata “in view of the severity of his remarks and their implications for Philippine sovereignty, national dignity, and bilateral relations.”

Speaking to the press on October 16, after a dialogue organized by the Philippines-China Studies Center of Diliman College in Quezon City, Jing declared that the Philippines was “fortunate” to have a neighbor like China.

“If we want to use force, we may easily win. But no, we will not choose force, and we love peace,” he said. “In this region, we enjoy peace.”

Jing was responding to a remark by Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro, who the day prior had described China as the lone “troublemaker” in Southeast Asia, due to its aggressive actions inside Philippine-claimed portions of the South China Sea. As I noted yesterday, this remark was in turn related to Vice President Sara Duterte’s response to revelations about her husband’s alleged China-linked business dealings that arose during her ongoing impeachment trial in the Senate.

Asked on Friday about Ambassador Jing’s remark, Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. ‌said that ⁠it “sounds very much like a threat,” and the DFA yesterday summoned the Chinese envoy to express its “serious concern and strong ​objection” about his remarks.

Philippine Foreign ⁠Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro told Jing that “provocative and unacceptable” comments “aggravate an already sensitive bilateral atmosphere,” the DFA said in a statement. She added that the DFA would “keep open lines with China and work to stabilize bilateral relations, especially in non-sensitive areas, while firmly upholding the country’s consistent positions on important issues.”

Jing, who began his posting last December, was previously summoned by the Philippine government in July, after a Philippine marine was injured in a melee with the China Coast Guard at Second Thomas Shoal in the Spratly Islands. This was just one of a string of confrontations between the two sides over the past few years in contested parts of the South China Sea, some of them involving the use of ramming tactics and high-pressure water cannons, mostly on the part of the China Coast Guard.

Senators first raised the possibility of senators filing a resolution to declare Jing persona non grata over the weekend. The Chinese Embassy responded with a post on Facebook in which it dared the government to follow through on its threat.

“We are fed up with these old and low tricks. If they really want to do something, do it quickly and immediately, please,” the embassy stated, implying that any such move would be followed by the reciprocal expulsion of the Philippine ambassador to Beijing.

While the DFA is unlikely to declare Jing persona non grata, the Senate’s decision to pursue the issue, as well as the Chinese embassy’s undiplomatic response, reflects the depth of the trench to which China-Philippines relations have fallen.
tag: China-Philippines maritime disputes; China-Philippines relations; Erwin Tulfo; Jing Quan; South China Sea disputes

title: Philippines Rejects Chinese Claim to ‘Sovereign Rights’ Over Waters Around Batanes
description: The Chinese activities around the Philippines' northernmost province represent the opening of a new front in the maritime struggle between the two nations.
text:
The Philippine government today rejected China’s assertion that it has sovereign rights and jurisdiction over waters off Batanes, the country’s northernmost province, a day after the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) drove away a Chinese research vessel operating in the area.

The PCG said yesterday that it had deployed its largest vessel and an aircraft to challenge the Jia Ha Ke 7, a Chinese research ship, that had been “loitering” around 37 nautical miles northwest of Batanes for the past four days. During the confrontation, PCG spokesperson Jay Tarriela said that a China Coast Guard vessel also moved in and “repeatedly tried to shield the research vessel and block the PCG ship.”

The Philippine operation nonetheless “successfully disrupted the unauthorized marine scientific research” being conducted by the Jia He Ke 7 and “compelled it to leave the position it had held off Itbayat, Batanes, for four days.”

China’s embassy in Manila responded by claiming that the Chinese research vessel was “conducting normal operations in waters under China’s jurisdiction in accordance with international law.” It urged the Philippines to “genuinely respect China’s sovereign rights and jurisdiction in the relevant waters,” and to cease its “provocative interference with China’s normal scientific research activities.”

In a statement today, the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) said it “firmly and strongly rejects” the Chinese claims of sovereignty over the waters around Batanes, a group of islands lying midway between Taiwan and the Philippines’ Luzon island. It argued that the Chinese research vessel was operating well within the country’s 200-nautical-mile Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ), where, according to the U.N. Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), marine scientific research can only be conducted “with the consent of the coastal State.”

The Chinese activities around Batanes represent the opening of a new front in the maritime struggle between Beijing and Manila, which has manifested at different features in the South China Sea, particularly at Scarborough Shoal and at various parts of the Spratly Islands.

In late June, at a symposium at Jinan University in Guangzhou, Chinese scholars from several institutions argued that China enjoyed sovereignty over Batanes. According to a report by Jinan University, which was later published by the Guangdong-based news outlet Newsgd, participants described the Batanes Islands as a “natural geographical extension” of Taiwan, and said that they therefore belonged to China.

Philippine Defense Minister Gilberto Teodoro subsequently dismissed the claims, describing them as “baseless” and “ludicrous.” “So this is concerning, and it is something that must be challenged,” he added.

This week’s events seem to validate the warnings of observers who said at the time that the scholars’ remarks might open the way to official claims by Beijing. Collin Koh, a scholar at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies in Singapore, argued that the claims about Batanes were little more than the “territorial wet dreams” of Beijing-aligned scholars, but that such ideas “could potentially seep into official discourse if they fit ethno-nationalist agendas.”

While Manila does not view its South China Sea possessions any differently from its “home islands” – it considers all to be inalienable parts of the Philippines – it has reason to be concerned about this latest development. Batanes is both the smallest and least populated of the Philippines’ 82 provinces, and is home to 18,937 people, as per the 2024 Philippine census. This nonetheless compares to just 406 for the Kalayaan Island Group, as Manila refers to its nine occupied features in the Spratlys.

The extension of Chinese gray zone tactics to “core” Philippine islands over which Manila’s sovereignty has never seriously been challenged could mark a considerable escalation of the maritime dispute between the two nations.
tag: Batanes; China claim to Batanes; China-Philippines maritime disputes; China-Philippines relations; South China Sea; South China Sea disputes

title: Poland’s President in the Philippines: Black Hawks, ASEAN, and US Defense Interests
description: Could Nawrocki’s visit to Manila serve to promote further Black Hawk sales across ASEAN, potentially benefiting U.S. industrial interests?
text:
President of Poland Karol Nawrocki arrived in Manila on October 5 for a three-day official visit to the Philippines. It is the first visit by a Polish president to the Philippines since diplomatic relations were established in 1973.

According to Marcin Przydacz, secretary of state and head of the International Policy Bureau of the Chancellery of the President of the Republic of Poland, the visit is part of a broader Polish strategy to strengthen the country’s position among the countries of the Global South. Nawrocki described the visit as an opportunity to seek backing for Poland’s continued presence in the G20 by gaining informal support from the Philippines, which is chairing ASEAN this year. Nawrocki also described the trip in the context of a broader strategy of engaging with the Global South – a direction that has recently been highlighted in Polish foreign-policy discussions.

There is also a military cooperation angle, raising the question of possible broader American defense interests within the Polish administration and opposition.

In August, PZL Mielec, an aerospace manufacturer based in Poland, completed the delivery of 32 S-70i Black Hawk helicopters to the Philippine Air Force. The Philippines had previously ordered 16 helicopters from Mielec in 2019.

PZL Mielec presents itself as a Polish company: the helicopters are manufactured in Poland and the workforce is Polish. But since 2015, PZL Mielec has been owned by Lockheed Martin, one of the world’s largest U.S. defense contractors.

This makes Nawrocki’s visit to the Philippines particularly interesting.

Former Polish Defense Minister Mariusz Błaszczak, now a leading opposition figure and a strongly pro-American and Eurosceptic politician, has argued that Europe is effectively helpless against Russia and that Poland should rely on the United States rather than Europe for its security. He was also highly critical of the EU’s SAFE program, an EU initiative providing up to 150 billion euro in loans for defense investment. Błaszczak has argued that the program could push the United States out of Europe and questioned its compatibility with Poland’s reliance on U.S. defense technology.

In July 2026, Błaszczak, together with a group of MPs with the conservative party Prawo i Sprawiedliwość (PiS), submitted a parliamentary interpellation concerning the lack of new orders for S-70i Black Hawk helicopters from PZL Mielec. The MPs warned that the end of the Philippine contract could put the future of S-70i production in Poland at risk.

Supporting PZL Mielec can be presented as supporting Polish jobs and industrial capacity, but it also directly supports the commercial interests of Lockheed Martin.

Ironically, it may be easier for the Polish president to persuade the ASEAN countries to place an order than Poland’s own Ministry of Defense.

Given the tense relationship between Nawrocki and the Polish government led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk, as well as Nawrocki’s alleged close relationship with U.S. President Donald Trump, one possible aim of the Philippine visit could be to encourage the government in Manila to consider another contract, or to promote PZL Mielec and its capabilities through the Philippines at the ASEAN level.

Given the ownership structure of PZL Mielec, Błaszczak and Nawrocki’s political alignment, and support for stronger U.S. defense ties, the timing raises questions. Within the span of a few months, a parliamentary interpellation called for new orders for PZL Mielec, the factory completed its Philippine contract, and Poland’s president made his first-ever visit to the Philippines.

Could Nawrocki’s visit also serve to promote further Black Hawk sales across ASEAN, potentially benefiting U.S. industrial interests?
tag: Black Hawk helicopters; Karol Nawrocki; Philippines Black Hawk helicopters; Philippines-Poland relations; Poland foreign policy

title: Prabowo Accuses MSCI of Attempting to ‘Intimidate’ Indonesia After Downgrade Threat
description: We possess strength, we have courage, we are willing to make sacrifices, and we refuse to surrender, said the former general.
text:
Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto has accused MSCI of attempting to “intimidate” Indonesia, after the global index provider threatened to downgrade the country due to serious stock market transparency issues.

In a statement on October 16, MSCI announced that it had launched “a consultation on a proposal to reclassify the MSCI Indonesia Indexes from Emerging Market to Standalone Market status.” Among its concerns are coordinated trading practices, the high concentration of ownership in certain companies, and the limited “free float” of shares – i.e., those openly available for public trading.

Speaking to his cabinet yesterday, Prabowo said that MSCI “intended to intimidate us,” Reuters reported. “I simply say to the MSCI: the Indonesian nation fears no one and will not be cowed… We possess strength, we have courage, we are willing to make sacrifices, and we refuse to surrender.”

MSCI’s proposal was more serious than its threat in January to downgrade Indonesia to “frontier market” status due to the transparency concerns in its stock market. The “standalone market” category, which includes the likes of Argentina, Lebanon, Palestine, Ukraine, and Zimbabwe, is a rung below “frontier market.”

MSCI said last week that it decided on a more serious downgrade because the long list of reforms announced by Indonesian policymakers to address its concerns had not achieved “sufficient progress.”

“Despite the announced reforms, significant concerns remain around market dysfunction, including continued suspected coordinated trading behavior and lack of evidence of meaningful enforcement,” it stated. “Feedback from market participants suggests that a reclassification to Frontier Markets would not properly recognize the depth of the market problems.” MSCI said that it “expects to proceed with the proposed reclassification” barring clear evidence of “material improvements in market governance and functioning.”

The announcement prompted a bloodbath on the Jakarta Composite Index, which plunged by around 15 percent over two days of trading. The Indonesian stock market has been among the worst performing in the world in 2026, losing around 40 percent of its value, while the rupiah has fallen to levels not seen since the Asian financial crisis of 1997-1998.

The prospect of a further outflow of capital – a likely result of a downgrade to “standalone” status – has heaped pressure on Prabowo’s administration, which since coming to office in late 2024, has rattled markets with its centralized and free-spending approach to economic management. This has included both a multibillion-dollar free meal program and an increase in the state’s involvement in the Indonesian economy.

Perhaps less important than specific policies is Prabowo’s volatile, unpredictable and highly personalized style of economic governance, which represents a significant change from the conservative stewardship of the past few administrations. In March, both Moody’s and Fitch announced ratings outlook downgrades for Indonesia, with the latter citing the “increasing ⁠policy uncertainty and erosion of Indonesia’s policy mix consistency and credibility” and the “growing centralization of policymaking authority.” George Xu, a Director in Fitch Ratings’ Sovereigns team, said in a statement on Tuesday that MSCI’s announcement and the subsequent market sell-off only “reinforce the risks” identified by Fitch during its downgrade in March.

Prabowo’s defiant remarks about the MSCI threat, which have also been echoed by other Indonesian politicians in recent days, are characteristic of his political style and nationalist leanings. They are also unlikely to do much to address the growing concerns about Indonesia’s investability, making it likely that Indonesia will face more economic turbulence during the remainder of his term.
tag: Indonesia economy; Indonesia Stock Exchange; MSCI; MSCI emerging market indices; Prabowo Subianto

title: Professor S.I. Keethaponcalan on Two Years of the AKD Presidency in Sri Lanka
description: “The NPP government made a sensible decision to accept and continue most of the economic policies and programs Ranil Wickremesinghe introduced.”
text:
It is a little over two years since Anura Kumara Dissanayake, or AKD as he is popularly known, was elected Sri Lanka’s ninth executive president. His victory was an unambiguous vote for change. Unlike his predecessors, AKD did not belong to a political dynasty, nor did he hail from an elite background. Seven weeks after he took over the reins as president, AKD’s National People’s Power (NPP), a coalition of leftist parties, won an emphatic victory in general elections, not only securing a two-thirds majority in parliament but also performing well in the Tamil-dominated Northern Province. Understandably, expectations for AKD ran high.

So how has his government performed? In a discussion with Sudha Ramachandran, South Asia editor of The Diplomat, Professor Soosaipillai I. Keethaponcalan, former chair of the Conflict Analysis and Dispute Resolution Department at Salisbury University in Maryland, said that while AKD has done a “commendable job” on the economic front and has sought to prosecute corrupt politicians, he has done “very little, if anything” in finding a political solution to the ethnic conflict. “There have been no significant prosecutions of those responsible for wartime atrocities,” he said.

Besides, the AKD government has taken no steps towards revoking the executive presidency — a key election campaign pledge. “Like many of its predecessors, [the AKD government] may have come to appreciate the extensive powers of the executive presidency and may believe that these powers are necessary for political stability,” Keethaponcalan said.

Although Anura Kumara Dissanayake and the NPP were at the forefront of the criticism of Ranil Wickremesinghe’s debt restructuring strategy, as president he followed the same strategy to satisfy IMF norms. How different has his presidency been from that of his predecessors?

I used to believe that in Sri Lanka, two entities were firmly committed to their ideological positions and goals. One was the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE), and the other was the Janata Vimukti Peramuna (JVP). The LTTE perished partly because of its unwavering commitment to the cause of Tamil Eelam. However, I have been surprised by how adaptive and flexible the JVP has become in its ideological positions over the last two years. The party, which forms the core of the NPP government, has demonstrated remarkable flexibility in responding to current realities and political compulsions.

The JVP launched two unsuccessful armed rebellions to establish a socialist state in Sri Lanka. Given this history, I was surprised to see how readily the party moved away from its socialist ideology after coming to power. Its dramatic shift in its traditionally anti-Indian position is another example of this ideological flexibility.

Similarly, while in opposition, the JVP strongly resisted Ranil Wickremesinghe’s strategy of securing an IMF bailout and implementing the associated economic restructuring program. However, once in power, the party appears to have recognized the importance of the IMF program and has continued with essentially the same strategy. The current IMF program is scheduled to expire in March 2027, and I would not be surprised if the NPP government sought a new agreement with the IMF. Such a decision would further demonstrate the remarkable transformation of the JVP’s economic policy orientation.

However, I see some differences, particularly the government’s apparent determination to prosecute former political leaders accused of corruption and other malpractices. During his presidency, Wickremesinghe failed to adequately address corruption, one of the major grievances highlighted by the Aragalaya (“struggle” in Sinhala) — the mass protests in 2022 that toppled the Gotabaya Rajapaksa government and created the political circumstances that eventually brought him to power.

Nevertheless, in my view, the incumbent NPP government has largely continued the policies of its predecessors, particularly those pursued by Wickremesinghe. The most striking change, therefore, is not in the direction of government policy but in the JVP’s willingness to abandon or modify positions it had defended for decades.

AKD had promised to abolish the executive presidency. He has the numbers in parliament to push through constitutional change. So why hasn’t he acted?

Sri Lanka has had, and continues to have, a political movement advocating the abolition of the executive presidential system and the restoration of a parliamentary form of government. Traditionally, the JVP, including President Dissanayake as one of its leaders, played a pivotal role in this movement. That is precisely why the party promised to abolish the executive presidency in its 2024 election manifesto.

As you know, the NPP secured a comfortable majority of more than two-thirds in parliament. Yet it has taken no significant steps toward constitutional reform. Instead, in September 2026, it amended the constitution to increase the retirement age of Supreme Court judges — a relatively minor and, in my view, unnecessary change.

Consequently, two years after Dissanayake came to power, the constitution introduced by the JVP’s former arch-enemy, President J. R. Jayewardene, remains largely intact. I doubt that the NPP government will demonstrate much enthusiasm for constitutional reform in the near future.

I see two possible reasons for this reluctance. First, the NPP government, like many of its predecessors, may have come to appreciate the extensive powers of the executive presidency and may believe that these powers are necessary for political stability. Second, initiating a comprehensive constitutional reform process could force the government to confront several politically uncomfortable questions. One such question concerns the future of the provincial council system, which the JVP vehemently opposed in the past. Should the system be retained, reformed, or abolished? Any of these choices could create political difficulties for the government.

What steps has AKD taken with regard to finding a political solution to Tamil grievances?

Very little, if anything. Traditionally, the JVP, like many Sinhala nationalist organizations, did not recognize the existence of an ethnic conflict in Sri Lanka or acknowledge that Tamils faced grievances specific to their community. Instead, the party viewed Sri Lanka’s problem primarily as one of terrorism. Therefore, I am not surprised that the NPP government has shown little interest in pursuing a political solution to Tamil grievances. There has been no meaningful dialogue with Tamil political leaders specifically aimed at finding such a solution.

In his 2024 election manifesto, Dissanayake promised to hold the long-delayed provincial council elections. That promise remains unfulfilled. This is particularly significant because the NPP won parliamentary seats in the Jaffna district in 2024, with Tamil voters electing JVP-affiliated candidates in a remarkable departure from traditional voting patterns.

I do not necessarily believe that the government’s reluctance to hold provincial council elections is motivated by racism or ethnic discrimination. Rather, I suspect that the government is uncomfortable facing voters at this juncture because its political appeal appears to be eroding.

Interestingly, I do not see much public pressure from the Tamil community over the continued postponement of provincial council elections. The major Tamil political parties have also failed to make this issue a significant central political demand. Consequently, the government faces little sustained pressure to address the Tamil question through meaningful political negotiations or constitutional reform.

How would you rate this government’s performance in bringing to justice those who carried out horrific crimes, even atrocities, against the Tamils during the civil war?

Not encouraging. The government has yet to meet many of the demands made through the United Nations Human Rights Council processes in Geneva. Nor has it introduced significant new initiatives to address the grievances of the victims. Families of those who disappeared during the final phase of the war continue their protests and campaigns demanding justice. To my knowledge, there have been no significant prosecutions of those responsible for wartime atrocities.

For example, more human remains have recently been recovered from the Chemmani mass graves in Jaffna, where hundreds of individuals are believed to have been buried. Yet the government has not established a systematic, adequately empowered mechanism to investigate such crimes and ensure accountability.

In Sri Lanka, regardless of who is in power, investigating and prosecuting war-related crimes, particularly those allegedly committed by members of the armed forces, is politically extremely difficult. Such a move could amount to political suicide for any government. Therefore, I have little hope that the families of those who disappeared or were killed during the civil war will receive the justice they have been demanding for so long.

An infant’s feeding bottle is among the items found at the Chemmani mass grave site in Sri Lanka’s Jaffna peninsula.X/Tamil Genocide Education Project

How is the Sri Lankan economy doing under President Dissanayake?

I think the NPP government has done a commendable job on this front. However, the credit for pulling Sri Lanka out of the 2022 economic crisis and restoring some economic stability should go primarily to Wickremesinghe. The NPP government made a sensible decision to accept and continue most of the economic policies and programs Wickremesinghe introduced. That strategy has worked, and Sri Lanka’s economy remains relatively stable.

The NPP government has also made its own progress. For example, Sri Lanka’s foreign reserves increased from approximately US$4.5 billion in 2023 to around US$7 billion in August 2026. This is a significant achievement.

Nevertheless, I believe a more meaningful assessment of the government’s economic performance can be made after the current IMF bailout program expires in March 2027. How the government manages the economy beyond the current IMF arrangement will be a crucial test of its economic policies.

There are plans to replace the Prevention of Terrorism Act (PTA) of 1979 with new anti-terrorism legislation. Does Sri Lanka have a terrorism problem today?

After the civil war ended in 2009, human rights organizations, both domestic and international, began demanding the repeal of the Prevention of Terrorism Act, arguing that the defeat of the LTTE had removed its principal justification. The Rajapaksa government rejected these demands, while the Yahapalana government led by Maithripala Sirisena and Wickremesinghe failed to deliver the promised reforms.

Against this backdrop, the Easter Sunday bombings took place in 2019. This was a major terrorist attack carried out by Islamist extremists with links to ISIS. Therefore, we cannot argue that Sri Lanka faces no terrorist or security threats. The government needs effective mechanisms to address such threats. However, these mechanisms must not violate citizens’ fundamental rights or undermine democracy.

During the 2024 elections, the NPP appealed to liberal-minded voters, among others, and promised to repeal the PTA. Yet, nearly two years after assuming power, the government has failed to fulfill that promise. Instead, it has continued to use the PTA, including in connection with domestic issues such as drug-related offenses. There have also been allegations that the law has been used to restrict freedom of expression.

Now, the government proposes to replace the PTA with the Protection of the State from Terrorism Act (PSTA). However, the proposed legislation has already attracted serious criticism from human rights organizations, particularly over its broad definition of terrorism and the extensive powers it would confer on the executive and security forces. Therefore, from a human rights and democratic freedoms perspective, the proposed legislation does not look particularly promising.

Dissanayake has support in parliament and also among the public. Are Sri Lankans satisfied with his presidency?

In the 2024 presidential election, Dissanayake secured about 42 percent of the first-preference vote. His party, the NPP, then received a major boost, winning about 61 percent of the national vote and securing 159 seats in parliament in the November 2024 parliamentary election. However, the party could not sustain this momentum, as its share of the national vote declined to approximately 43 percent in the May 2025 local government elections. Some recent opinion polls also suggest that the government’s popularity has been declining.

I suspect that this declining popularity is one of the main reasons the government is reluctant to hold further elections, particularly the long-delayed provincial council elections. The high cost of living, heavy taxation, and the failure to adequately address pressing social problems, such as organized crime and drug-related activities, appear to have contributed to growing public dissatisfaction.

The emerging controversy involving Gnanasara Thera, a Buddhist monk who is the general secretary of the militant Bodhu Bala Sena, could also create political difficulties for the government. The decision to have police escort the monk to court in prison attire instead of his Buddhist monk’s robes, which carries considerable religious and cultural significance, could anger sections of the Sinhala Buddhist community, particularly nationalist voters. This controversy could further undermine the government’s popularity among these groups.

Nevertheless, it is important to distinguish between declining popularity and a complete loss of public support. The NPP still enjoys a substantial electoral base. In my view, the more important question is not simply whether the government retains public support, but how much of its original electoral momentum it has lost.
tag: AKD; AKD and ethnic reconciliation; AKD governance; AKD presidency; Anura Kumara Dissanayake; National People's Power; NPP and executive presidency; Sri Lanka constitutional reform; Sri Lanka ethnic conflict; Sri Lanka Executive Presidency; Sri Lankan economy

title: Protests Escalate in Delhi Despite Modi Government’s Heavy-handed Crackdown
description: Indiscriminate arrests, detentions, police brutality, and blockades have not been able to demoralize protesters seeking the removal of the chief election commissioner.
text:
On October 12, Congress leader Rahul Gandhi, India’s main opposition leader, led a march to the Supreme Court of India, seeking the judiciary’s intervention in what he called the election commission’s loss of integrity.

The Chief Justice of India, Surya Kant, had declined to meet the opposition delegation, arguing that it would violate the principle of separation of powers. Yet tens of thousands of people, including opposition lawmakers, activists, and ordinary citizens, marched towards the apex court premises.

Monday’s protest march drew unprecedented crowds, despite the Narendra Modi government’s brutal crackdown on protestors calling for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar.

Kumar, the first CEC to be appointed under a new law that allowed the government to pick an election commissioner of its choice, has been at the center of political controversies since the launch of a Special Intensive Revision of the electoral roll last year that has left millions outside the roll, leaving them at the risk of disenfranchisement. Opposition parties have alleged pro-government bias on a range of issues related to election conduct, including targeted voter roll manipulations.

Over the weekend, India stood witness to some unprecedented scenes. Police in the national capital of New Delhi raided hotels, hostels, the offices of political parties, and the residences of activists in search of suspected protesters. The goal was to foil the satirical youth network Cockroach Janta Party (CJP)’s October 10 protest in New Delhi. The CJP too is seeking Kumar’s resignation.

The CJP’s protest at Jantar Mantar in Delhi in June-July resulted in Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan’s resignation. This time the Modi government was determined to prevent the CJP protests on Saturday.

To this end, it turned Delhi into a fortress. The assembly of five or more persons was prohibited across large parts of the city, and an estimated 30,000 police and paramilitary personnel were deployed. Police reportedly asked hotel owners to refrain from accepting fresh room bookings from people coming to the capital. To prevent protesters from gathering in New Delhi, the government took the unprecedented step of suspending or diverting dozens of Delhi-bound trains. Metro rail station gates closed across the city from 9 pm on Friday. Metal barricades blocked most roads leading to the designated protest venue, Jantar Mantar, in central Delhi. Checkposts multiplied at the city’s borders and Internet access was restricted in central Delhi. Early on Saturday morning, the police boarded a flight as soon as it landed in New Delhi to detain three CJP leaders. On Oct 10, Delhi was a city under siege. Daily life in the capital was suspended to prevent one political gathering.

And yet, thousands of protesters hit the streets in different parts of Delhi on Saturday. Thousands were detained, including lawyers, journalists, legislators and four former chief ministers of different states from the opposition parties. The police clashed with protesters at different locations. Young people on the streets were indiscriminately detained. Many alleged police brutality. Leftist student organizations kept cops busy on the streets on Sunday.

Even a U.N. human rights spokesperson expressed concerns over the situation, prompting the Modi government to accuse the Office of the U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights of bias.

The Modi government may have been able to prevent youth and student protestors from gathering at one place on Saturday. But its problems are far from over, as the INDIA bloc and the CJP will be holding a wave of protests not only in the national capital but in other major cities as well. Besides, almost all opposition parties have thrown their weight behind the protests despite their internal rivalries – even if only for the time being. This has complicated matters for the Modi government.

“How long will you keep Delhi locked down? The minute you open the barricades & send police off, protestors will come in. Nobody, but nobody, can stop us,” said opposition parliamentarian Mahua Moitra on the night of October 10. The “government will never be able to ‘normalize’ life again.”

Meanwhile, a Supreme Court bench has directed the authorities to review their use of barricades, ensure normal metro and railway operations, and keep internet services running except where its suspension is legally justified.

By Monday, the government had adjusted its tactics. Instead of a citywide shutdown, it closed entry and exit at six central Metro stations from 6 a.m. to 4 p.m. Delhi’s borders, railway stations, and bus terminuses remained tightly guarded. Traffic was diverted from selected roads. The government also denotified Jantar Mantar as a protest venue and designated three other places for protest purposes.

The CJP top leadership, who were released on Sunday, vowed to continue their protests. “If Modi thinks taking away Jantar Mantar [as a protest venue] will put an end to protests, he is mistaken,” said CJP founder-convenor Abhijeet Dipke, adding that Jantar Mantar was no longer just another location “but a spirit of resistance that nobody can ever take away.”

There does not seem to be an easy way out for the Modi government. It will not be easy for it to let CEC Kumar go. After all, Kumar is the Modi government’s appointee. Conceding ground here could encourage the opposition to aim higher next time.

On the other hand, if the opposition manages to maintain pressure on the government through intense and continued street protests, the credibility of the election commission could be further undermined in the eyes of the public.

The ruling Bharatiya Janata Party has alleged that anti-national and foreign-funded forces have joined hands to destabilize the country. “We will deal firmly with all such forces active outside or inside the country,” said BJP president Nitin Nabin.

With the administration designating new locations away from central Delhi as protest venues and the opposition announcing continued protests, the coming few weeks look set for tense conflicts.

title: Pyongyang’s Ukraine Gamble: What Kim Jong Un Bought With North Korean Blood
description: For a military that has not fought a large-scale war since 1953, experience on the Ukrainian front is tremendously valuable to North Korea.
text:
Four years into Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and one of the war’s stranger subplots may be its most consequential: soldiers from an Asian country with no direct stake in the conflict, and no public declaration of belligerency, are dying by the thousands on European soil, thousands of kilometers from home.

Since October 2024, North Korea has sent an estimated 15,000 to 20,000 troops to Russia’s Kursk region, and absorbed roughly 6,000 casualties based on the intelligence estimates of South Korea and the United Kingdom. According to Ukrainian officials, North Korea may be asked to contribute tens of thousands more troops. What has Kim Jong Un bought with that blood?

North Korea’s calculus was never primarily about Ukraine, a country with which it has no border, no quarrel, and little history. It was about what Pyongyang could extract from a desperate Russia. By mid-2024, Moscow badly needed manpower and ammunition and had few partners left willing to supply either.

In June 2024, Kim and Russian President Vladimir Putin signed a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty in Pyongyang that included a mutual defense clause, the first of its kind for North Korea since the Cold War. Troop deployments followed within months. In return, analysts at institutions from the Council on Foreign Relations to Chatham House point to a fairly consistent list of North Korean gains: cash payments estimated in the billions of dollars, food and energy supplies for an economy that chronically struggles to feed and fuel itself, and, most significantly for Pyongyang’s long-term ambitions, technology transfers that would otherwise have been unthinkable. Russia has reportedly supplied North Korea with air defense systems, older but still capable Su-27 and MiG-29 fighters, and, more sensitively, technical assistance connected to satellite launches and naval reactor technology for submarines.

Money and hardware, however, may be less important than what North Korean soldiers are learning. South Korea’s National Intelligence Service has assessed that despite considerable losses, North Korea’s military has gained something it could not otherwise buy: live experience of drone warfare, electronic warfare, and modern combined-arms combat, together with direct exposure to Russian battlefield tactics and equipment. North Korean soldiers rotated home from the front have reportedly gone on to serve as instructors, seeding lessons from Kursk through the wider Korean People’s Army, a pattern documented in detail by 38 North. For a military that has not fought a large-scale war since 1953, that is an intelligence windfall no amount of cash could easily replicate.

There is also a domestic and dynastic logic. Framing the deployment as solidarity with Russia – Kim has publicly praised soldiers for fighting “for the fraternal Russian people” – lets Pyongyang dress a mercenary arrangement in the language of ideological alliance, useful for internal propaganda about North Korea’s rising international stature.

Before 2022, Russia and North Korea were not especially close. Moscow had, at various points, supported U.N. sanctions against Pyongyang’s nuclear and missile programs. The war has inverted that relationship entirely. North Korea has gone from a marginal, sanctioned pariah state to a battlefield-tested security partner that Russia now treats as an equal in a way China never has. The mutual defense treaty, the flow of advanced military technology, and Putin’s own visit to Pyongyang in 2024 all mark a qualitative shift from transactional arms sales to what Foreign Affairs described as a long-term strategic and ideological partnership.

That shift has complicated, rather than strengthened, the informal China-Russia-North Korea alignment that Western officials sometimes describe (misleadingly, most regional specialists argue) as a unified axis.

Beijing has watched Pyongyang’s deepening entanglement with Moscow with open unease, as detailed in a Foundation for Strategic Research assessment of the evolving triangle. China has no formal say over what Russia transfers to North Korea, and reports of sensitive technology moving from Moscow to Pyongyang without Beijing’s knowledge have reportedly fed distrust between the two communist neighbors.

Kim, for his part, has gained new leverage over Beijing: with Moscow now willing to treat him as a peer and to backfill North Korea’s economic and military needs, Kim is less dependent on Chinese patronage than at any point in decades, and better positioned to resist Chinese pressure to rein in his nuclear program, a dynamic the Council on Foreign Relations has flagged as a growing headache for Beijing.

China is wary of jeopardizing its own relationship with Europe, and visibly uncomfortable with a North Korea-Russia partnership it can neither control nor fully endorse. Still, Beijing has responded with something closer to silence than alarm, avoiding direct criticism of either Moscow or Pyongyang. The result, as Modern Diplomacy put it, is less a trilateral alliance than a triangle of powers with overlapping but not identical interests, in which Pyongyang has quietly gained room to maneuver at Beijing’s expense.

Militarily, the record of North Korean troops in Kursk is mixed. In their first months of deployment, North Korean units suffered catastrophic losses. By some estimates, 40 percent of the initial 11,000-strong contingent was killed or too badly wounded to fight within three months. U.S. officials described North Korean assaults on entrenched Ukrainian positions as “human wave tactics” that were, in Washington’s assessment, largely ineffective. Soldiers were used as bait to draw out Ukrainian drone operators, and troops sometimes took their own lives rather than risk capture, a reflection of the harsh consequences reportedly awaiting the families of anyone who surrenders.

Yet the “cannon fodder” framing, embraced early on by Ukrainian and American officials, has been challenged by military analysts who argue it understates what is actually happening. Researchers at RAND have cautioned that dismissing North Korean troops as unsophisticated fanatics risks recycling old stereotypes about Asian communist militaries. Many of the deployed units come from North Korea’s elite special operations Storm Corps – troops that, by multiple Ukrainian frontline accounts, proved highly motivated, resilient under fire, and increasingly adept at countering the first-person-view drones that have come to define this war. Ukrainian intelligence has also reported the arrival of dedicated North Korean drone units and reconnaissance specialists, a more technical role than the infantry-assault image that dominated early coverage.

Materially, the more significant North Korean contribution to Russia’s war effort may not be soldiers at all but ammunition: Ukraine’s military intelligence chief estimated that North Korean-supplied artillery shells and missiles have accounted for roughly half of what Russian forces fire at the front. Troop deployments helped Russia recover Kursk territory that Ukraine had seized in its August 2024 incursion, but North Korean units have so far been confined largely to Russian soil, with reports suggesting Moscow has been reluctant, at least officially, to send them into Ukraine proper. That distinction lets both governments continue denying direct North Korean involvement in the invasion itself, even as evidence of attacks on Ukrainian border communities accumulates.

Whether North Korean troops have changed the trajectory of the war is, in the end, a narrower question than whether the deployment has changed North Korea. On the battlefield, the contribution has been real but bounded: enough manpower and ammunition to matter at the margins in one contested region, not enough to shift the war’s fundamental stalemate. Off the battlefield, the returns for Pyongyang look considerably larger: modernized air defenses, combat-tested doctrine, hard currency, food, and fuel, and a Kremlin now invested in North Korea’s survival and expansion for reasons of its own.

Four years ago, North Korea was a country largely locked out of great power politics, dependent on China and periodically threatened with further isolation over its nuclear program. Today it has a mutual defense treaty with Russia and North Korean soldiers are gaining experience in modern warfare on European battlefields. For a regime that has always measured success in decades rather than news cycles, that may be the trade Kim intended to make all along.

title: Rubio Gets a Medal. Russia Gets Military Drills. Karakalpakstan Gets Silence.
description: Washington celebrates closer ties as Tashkent strengthens its Russian alliance—and offers no announced relief for Karakalpak political prisoners.
text:
On October 19, Uzbekistan’s President Shavkat Mirziyoyev awarded U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio the Order of Outstanding Merit. On October 20, UzDaily reported the arrival of Russian troops for joint military exercises in Uzbekistan. For Karakalpak families awaiting the release of political prisoners, neither announcement offered relief. Uzbekistan celebrated American investment and welcomed Russian soldiers while making no publicly announced commitment to people imprisoned for exercising and defending their rights.

Mirziyoyev’s office announced $12 billion in agreements, while Rubio participated in the C5+1 ministerial meeting and witnessed Uzbekistan’s signing of the Artemis Accords on peaceful space exploration. Sustained American engagement with Central Asia serves legitimate interests, and investment can create opportunities across the region. But announced agreements must still become functioning projects.

The more immediate political benefit went to Mirziyoyev, who received the public appreciation of America’s top diplomat. Rubio wrote that he was “deeply honored to be awarded the Order of Outstanding Merit by President Mirziyoyev” on X. The public results of the visit offered no hint of discussion on Karakalpak prisoners or accountability for the July 2022 massacre in Karakalpakstan.

The Russian exercises make it harder to mistake American access for a strategic shift in Tashkent. According to UzDaily, citing Russia’s Central Military District, servicemen from the 201st Guards Military Base – a Russian base in Tajikistan – arrived for Hamkorlik-2026, scheduled for October 20-27 in Uzbekistan. The report described the participation of assault units, reconnaissance and strike drones, robotic systems, and Mi-24 helicopters. These drills need not have been organized as a message to Washington to illustrate Tashkent’s position. Uzbekistan could welcome an American secretary of state and Russian military personnel in the same week without treating either relationship as a concession to the other.

Mirziyoyev had already explained that position in his own words. During an October 7 birthday call with Putin, he praised the Russian president’s “historic role” in modern Russia and his contribution to their countries’ “comprehensive strategic partnership and alliance.” That same day, he received a delegation led by Denis Manturov to advance cooperation in industry, energy, metallurgy, nuclear energy, and industrial zones. Earlier, Putin had authorized negotiations to amend military-technical agreements with Uzbekistan. RFE/RL reported in August that the proposed changes remained undisclosed.

Uzbekistan has been equally adept at cultivating other partners. Mirziyoyev signed the charter of President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace in January. His Interior Ministry has described cooperation with Huawei, including plans for “intelligent video surveillance.” In September, an institute under the Agriculture Ministry announced a memorandum with Iran’s Sirang UAV covering agricultural drone training and service centers. That agreement concerns agricultural applications and does not establish military cooperation or imply sanctions evasion, but it does illustrate a developing relationship. Washington should judge its own successes by the commitments it obtains, rather than assume that a warm reception will translate into influence.

The commercial relationship requires the same scrutiny. In April, the EU imposed sanctions on Uzbek companies over their Russia links, citing cotton-cellulose supplies to Russian gunpowder manufacturers. Those findings give U.S. officials concrete reasons to insist on rigorous screening of counterparties, beneficial ownership, and supply chains before promoting investment. Uzbekistan’s political system presents additional concerns: Freedom House rates it “Not Free,” with a score of 12 out of 100, while the Human Rights Foundation classifies it as a fully authoritarian regime. Freedom House reports that no opposition parties operate legally and that the legislature and judiciary effectively serve the executive.

American investors have encountered the consequences of weak institutional protections before. In 2006, Newmont disclosed approximately $48 million in tax claims against its Uzbek joint venture despite written confirmation from Uzbekistan’s Justice Ministry that a relevant tax decree applied for the venture’s lifetime. Access to the venture’s bank accounts was restricted, its assets placed under legal restraint, and bankruptcy proceedings initiated. A 2007 settlement provided for $80 million in payments and the transfer of Newmont’s interest to Uzbek parties, without an admission of liability. These events occurred when Shavkat Mirziyoyev was Uzbekistan’s prime minister.

The OECD’s 2025 investment review identifies continuing concerns about executive influence over courts, inconsistent decisions in technically complex cases, and overlapping rules that undermine predictability. Investors therefore have reason to ask whether commitments will survive a change of leadership, a reshuffle of influential officials, or a dispute involving politically connected interests. Official assurances offer limited protection unless institutions can enforce them.

The U.S. also has a strategic lesson to remember. After the May 2005 Andijan crackdown, the United States supported calls for an independent international investigation. That July, Uzbekistan ordered American forces out of the Karshi-Khanabad airbase, which supported operations in Afghanistan. Years of security cooperation failed to preserve American access once accountability became a source of bilateral tension. If Washington now avoids difficult questions to protect its agreements, Tashkent again holds considerable leverage over the relationship.

For Karakalpak people, those questions are urgent. Dauletmurat Tajimuratov, a Karakalpak lawyer and journalist, received a 16-year sentence after opposing proposed constitutional changes affecting the Sovereign Republic of Karakalpakstan’s status. The United Nations Working Group on Arbitrary Detention found his imprisonment arbitrary and called for his immediate release. Another two and a half years were added to his sentence this year. Before Rubio’s visit, Kaitie Holland and Sergei Korotkov, both international legal associates at the Human Rights Foundation, urged him in an article published by Just Security to demand freedom for Uzbekistan’s political prisoners, detailing Tajimuratov’s reported beatings, degrading prison conditions, and attempts to force him to renounce his Karakalpak identity.

In June, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer reaffirmed strong support for Uzbekistan’s World Trade Organization (WTO) accession. Further discretionary benefits should accompany published commitments on prisoner protection, accountability, and predictable legal treatment. Washington should press for Tajimuratov’s release, independent medical and monitoring access pending release, and an independent international investigation into the 2022 massacre. Independent courts and limits on executive interference would also protect the American businesses the administration is encouraging to invest.

Tashkent played its hand well. Mirziyoyev secured American recognition and commercial support while strengthening ties with Russia and maintaining an iron grip at home. Rubio must now explain what Washington obtained in return. Until commercial promises become enforceable commitments and American influence helps secure freedom for political prisoners, the medal around Rubio’s neck offers clearer evidence of Mirziyoyev’s diplomatic success than America’s.

title: Rubio’s India Visit Focuses on Energy
channel_text: Blog; Diplomacy; South Asia; The Pulse
description: He visited Jamnagar, home to the world’s largest oil refinery, which is run by Reliance Industries. The latter plans to build a refinery in Texas.
text:
During U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s visit to India on October 20-21, the two sides discussed stepping up energy cooperation and increasing procurement of American technologies and weapon systems as part of a stocktaking of their bilateral relationship.

Unlike his trip to India in May, Rubio did not visit the Indian capital, New Delhi. Instead, he visited India’s commercial capital, Mumbai, and Jamnagar, where the world’s largest oil refinery run by Reliance Industries Ltd. (RIL) is located.

An Indian readout of Rubio’s visit to Mumbai said that “the two sides reviewed the entire gamut of India-U.S. relations and discussed ways to further strengthen the Comprehensive Global Strategic Partnership.” They exchanged views on trade, defense, technology and energy security, and Rubio and Jaishankar welcomed “the progress made in negotiations on the India-U.S. Bilateral Trade Agreement (BTA) and reaffirmed their commitment to working towards its early conclusion.”

According to a U.S. statement on the talks between Rubio and his Indian counterpart S. Jaishankar, Rubio “reiterated that increased energy trade with the United States can play a transformative role in diversifying India’s supply chains while meeting its sizable consumer demand.” Commending recent progress in bilateral defense and civil nuclear cooperation, Rubio advocated the increased purchase of U.S. technologies and systems. No details were provided about which technologies the United States wants India to purchase.

In addition to Jaishankar, Rubio met representatives of three top Indian business houses – the Tatas, Adanis, and Reliance – in Mumbai. He also participated in a trilateral meeting with Jaishankar and the UAE’s Foreign Minister Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan that focused on energy security and regional issues.

Rubio’s visit to Jamnagar was linked to the RIL-run refinery’s capacity to refine heavy crude oils and its plans to construct a refinery near the U.S. border in Texas.

The Rubio visit’s focus on energy is not surprising, as India is one of the top importers of petroleum products. The U.S. has been pressuring India to stop fuel imports from Russia, which surged after the outbreak of the Ukraine conflict in 2022, and to buy Venezuelan crude oil instead, especially after the Donald Trump administration took over Venezuela’s oil industry following its abduction of President Nicolás Maduro.

As Indian strategic affairs analyst C. Raja Mohan wrote in a recent opinion piece in Indian Express, “Washington wants greater energy cooperation with India and more Indian investment in the U.S. Reliance offers a substantial private-sector partner. The question is how Delhi can turn the company’s growing importance in American calculations into an asset for India-U.S. relations.”

Rubio’s latest visit to India came at a time when India-U.S. relations have plunged to their worst in several decades. In addition to imposing unprecedented levels of tariffs on India, the Trump administration has tightened immigration and visa rules that are likely to hit Indian professionals hard. Besides, it has cozied up to Pakistan.

Last month, the U.S. Congress passed a bill authorizing Trump to punish countries buying energy from Russia, which has major implications for India. However, days ahead of Rubio’s visit to India, U.S. President Donald Trump announced a waiver on sanctions and tariffs related to ‌Russian exports for a 60-day period, after he reached a deal on purchasing Russian diesel. The suspension of sanctions will give India some respite, albeit temporarily.

At a time when India-U.S. ties are strained, “Rubio’s visit seeks to shift the focus to energy security, corporate partnerships and resolving trade standoffs,” Indian analyst Brahma Chellaney observed in a post on X. By visiting Mumbai and Jamnagar rather than New Delhi, “Rubio is emphasizing pragmatic cooperation over diplomatic friction. The approach could help sustain momentum in energy, private-sector investment and economic ties, thus keeping the broader bilateral partnership productive,” Chellaney pointed out.

During his visit to India, Rubio made several statements that sought to reassure Delhi.

At an event to mark the 250th anniversary of American Independence, Rubio acknowledged differences between India and the U.S. “No two nations on Earth will ever be perfectly aligned on every issue, and of course there will be times and points of disagreement.” But on core issues “that define the national interest of both India and the United States – the alignment between our countries is extraordinary,” he said.

On the stalled India-U.S. trade deal that has cast a shadow over bilateral ties, Rubio said both countries were “incredibly close” to an agreement. “The way I would say it is we are weeks, not months away from I think, finalizing it. I think 99 percent of the work is done… I feel very positive about the trajectory that it’s on.”

In an interview published in Indian Express, Rubio sought to assure India that improved ties with Pakistan would not be “at the expense of our relationship with India.” On the new immigration rules, he said that the regulations were “not unique to Indians or India; it is tied more broadly to the world… We are trying to fix 20 years of neglect of an immigration system that was simply not being enforced. And that’s not targeting India.”

Reassuring as Rubio’s statements may be, it will take a lot of work to bring the troubled India-U.S. relationship back to an even keel, especially since Trump is known for unpredictable policy changes. Therefore, Rubio’s visit may be the first step on a long and winding road to rebuilding trust.

title: Rubio’s Unusual Visit to India Marks a Paradigm Shift in India-US Ties
channel_text: Blog; Diplomacy; South Asia; Trans-Pacific View
description: The U.S. secretary of state’s itinerary skipped the corridors of power in Delhi for boardrooms and a refinery.
text:
Since the February 2025 inauguration of the second Trump administration, New Delhi has struggled to find a way to deal with the constantly swinging moods in Washington. Although the still-emerging strategic partnership between the two has, at times, seemed to take center stage, on most occasions, U.S. President Donald Trump appears to have expressed very little affinity for India, his vice president’s matrimonial ties to the country notwithstanding.

The tariffs imposed on India – at one time among the highest for targeted countries – and the failure to arrive at a trade deal despite prolonged negotiations are among the many irritants that have seeped into the relationship.

Beyond all else, there is the stark reality that in Washington’s calculations India appears to matter only to the extent it episodically can be played off against China. In this context, U.S. Secretary of State Mark Rubio’s two-day visit to India on October 20-21 may not have provided the positive breakthrough New Delhi was earnestly looking for, highlighting instead the contours of the changing strategic partnership and the increasingly erratic nature of U.S. foreign policy under Trump 2.0.

Rubio broke a protocol of sorts. His first stop was Mumbai, India’s financial capital. As a result, there was no meeting between him and Prime Minister Narendra Modi, which would have been a foregone conclusion had he included New Delhi in his itinerary. In Mumbai, he met the top two industrial chiefs of the country: Gautam Adani of the Adani Group and N. Chandrasekharan of the Tata Group. India’s External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar, who recently aired his grievances against the U.S., flew down to Mumbai to meet Rubio as well as visiting UAE Foreign Minister Abdullah bin Zayed.

That the U.S. secretary of state could decide the venue of his meeting with his Indian counterpart while in India has been criticized by the opposition parties. It also dovetails squarely with emerging assessment that U.S. strategy is divorced from any cogent calculations, responding rather to rapidly shifting whims and fancies of a transactional leader.

Following the meetings – bilaterally between Jaishankar and Rubio, another between Jaishankar and bin Zayed and finally, all three together – a readout of cooperation was issued. Curiously missing were two important initiatives involving all three countries: the I2U2 and the India-Middle East Economic Corridor (IMEC).

The I2U2 was formed by the three countries along with Israel in 2021, and the IMEC was announced in 2023. Both projects have stalled due to a variety of reasons including the war in Iran. Jaishankar’s summation of the trilateral meeting as a “useful exchange of perspectives on energy, connectivity and contemporary developments” was a clear indicator of the limited outcome of the confabulation and served only to raise questions concerning U.S. intentions.

Rubio and U.S. Ambassador to India Sergio Gor did try to sound optimistic while predicting the future of the India-U.S. trade deal. Rubio said that the deal, which is allegedly 99 percent complete, could be only “weeks away” from being signed. This kind of temporal signaling is de rigor in Trump administration communications, but generally has little connection to real time. Rubio, in fact, uttered those same words on June 4 while testifying before the U.S. Senate Foreign Relations Committee. “We can wrap up the negotiations on our trade agreement, which we think we’re a few weeks away from being able to conclude,” he said roughly 20 weeks ago.

The latest statement of reassurance comes amid pessimistic Indian assessments, including that of the country’s finance minister. Speaking at the Munich Leaders Meeting on October 5, Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said, “The negotiations are still ongoing but we would like to believe that both sides have reached a plateau beyond which giving or taking might be very difficult.” Trump’s October 20 prediction about a “much different” trade deal with India hasn’t cleared the air of the ambivalence surrounding the future of the deal.

Rubio’s second and final stop was Jamnagar in the western Indian state of Gujarat, to visit the refinery of Reliance Industries to discuss energy cooperation and push for Indian imports of heavy Venezuelan crude. The latter may point to the true heart of the visit: seeking a way to involve India in transactional U.S. foreign policy by offering select Indian players a chance to profit from the questionable finances of ventures such as those in Venezuela. Jamnagar, which possesses the specialized high-capacity infrastructure required to process thick and high-sulfur heavy Venezuelan crude, is also the world’s largest single-location refining complex. A further tradeoff from the trip thus could also be to provide Rubio with a reason to claim, just before the impending U.S. mid-terms, that there is impending relief from high domestic diesel and energy prices.

Reliance Industries, led by Mukesh Ambani, is also embracing the prospect of such closer cooperation. Rubio and his wife were welcomed by the entire Ambani family, consisting of Mukesh’s wife, his sons, daughters, and their spouses. Apart from touring the oil-refining complex and Reliance’s emerging clean-energy manufacturing hub, Rubio also visited the Vantara, a controversial wildlife rescue and conservation center curated and led by one of Mukesh Ambani’s sons.

Although Rubio explained his trip as a measure to strengthen bilateral trade ties, the thrust of the trip seems more focused on American domestic politics, a search for mid-term talking points by courting new buyers and markets for expanded Venezuelan oil production. The opaque finances of the entire Venezuelan escapade notwithstanding – it has been widely reported that there has been no public accounting of just where Venezuelan oil profits are going – Reliance Industries is also planning investment in a new refinery in Texas, which Gor tweeted is “an opportunity to expand U.S. energy production and create jobs.”

Indeed, during the visit, Rubio termed India the “refining superpower of the world.” This was music to select Indian media, owned by Reliance Industries, which doubled down on the point that India, which imports 89 percent of its energy requirements from different countries, is the fourth largest exporter of refined petroleum products.

What India stands to gain out of the possible deal between Reliance Industries and the United States isn’t clear. Who will bear the cost if U.S. policies shift again remains an unanswered question. Given the fact that the U.S. is now importing Russian diesel against the will of the U.S. Congress – with its composition up for grabs in a matter of weeks – that would seem to raise questions concerning the rationale behind putting New Delhi’s import of Russian crude under permanent scanner and possible sanctions.

For decades, India has treated strategic, defense, and technology cooperation as the core of its partnership with the United States. But under Trump 2.0, the relationship is being recast as a transaction built on trade and energy, with India now viewed as buyer, refiner, and market. Rubio’s itinerary, which skipped the corridors of power for boardrooms and a refinery, made the point amply clear. Whether dancing to the American tune is a prudent strategy for India remains to be seen as transactionalism is gradually eroding what could have been the defining strategic partnership of the 21st century.

title: Russia’s Arrest of a Japanese Journalist Deepens the Freeze in Japan-Russia Relations
description: The case of Hokkaido Shimbun correspondent Imai Yuki could chill reporting from Russia’s Far East and narrow the space for even limited diplomatic engagement.
text:
Russia’s detention of a Japanese journalist on espionage allegations has triggered a diplomatic protest from Tokyo and raised fresh concerns about press freedom, threatening to further strain relations between Japan and Russia amid the ongoing war in Ukraine and their longstanding territorial dispute.

On October 13, Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) announced that it had detained a correspondent for Japan’s Hokkaido Shimbun in the Far Eastern Sakhalin region. Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova identified the journalist as Imai Yuki. Russian authorities said he was apprehended a day before his planned departure from Russia and transferred to Moscow, where a court ordered his detention until December 12. Espionage convictions in Russia can carry prison terms of up to 20 years.

The FSB alleged that Imai collected information about Russia’s defense capabilities under instructions from Japanese intelligence. Russian state media said the information allegedly concerned residents of the Russia-controlled Kuril Islands, including islands claimed by Japan, who had been mobilized or volunteered to fight in Ukraine.

The allegations have not been independently substantiated. Imai held press accreditation issued by Russia’s Foreign Ministry, and reporting on military recruitment and the human consequences of war is a legitimate journalistic activity.

Russian state television broadcast footage of masked officers handcuffing a man and his subsequent appearance in a Moscow courtroom. The Hokkaido Shimbun said it was establishing the facts while prioritizing its correspondent’s safety.

Japan’s Foreign Minister Motegi Toshimitsu said on October 14 that Japanese diplomatic missions had requested information, humanitarian consideration, and fair and impartial treatment. Chief Cabinet Secretary Kihara Minoru acknowledged that Japanese officials had not yet been able to contact the detained journalist.

Japan’s Foreign Ministry summoned Russian Ambassador Nikolay Nozdrev to protest the detention and Moscow’s unilateral announcement without prior explanation to Tokyo. Japan again requested prompt information and swift access to the detained journalist.

Zakharova, the Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson, accused Japan of using accredited journalists for intelligence gathering and linked the case to Tokyo’s sanctions against Moscow and its defense buildup. She also claimed that this was not an isolated incident.

On October 5, just eight days before the FSB announced his detention, Imai published an article on the Hokkaido Shimbun’s website titled “A Glimpse of North Korea in Sakhalin.” He described an encounter with two North Korean men in Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk and observed that North Korean workers appeared more numerous than when he arrived two years earlier. Imai also cited an acquaintance who said North Koreans were helping support major construction projects in the city.

For the Hokkaido Shimbun, Sakhalin and the disputed islands are neighboring communities with longstanding historical and economic ties to Japan. The arrest could have a chilling effect on Japanese journalism in Russia’s Far East. If reporting on military recruitment or the human costs of war risks being characterized as espionage, Japanese news organizations may reconsider assignments, while local sources may become reluctant to speak. Reduced independent reporting would make an already opaque relationship harder to understand, increasing the risk of misperceptions.

This isn’t the first time Russia has accused a Japanese journalist of espionage. In 2019, a Kyodo News correspondent was detained in Vladivostok over suspected collection of military information. However, in that case the journalist was told to leave Russia within 72 hours and departed the following day. Imai instead faces a criminal investigation and potentially years in prison. The contrast underscores the seriousness of his situation: Imai’s arrest could raise the specter of hostage diplomacy, complicating Tokyo’s efforts to secure his release.

Russia’s 2023 arrest of Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich provides a troubling precedent. He received a 16-year prison sentence before being released in a multinational prisoner exchange in August 2024. Imai’s case could become entangled in broader diplomatic negotiations, although there is no evidence that Moscow detained him for that purpose.

The detention of a Japanese journalist will make any eventual diplomatic thaw between Japan and Russia more difficult. Japan imposed sanctions following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Moscow subsequently designated Japan an “unfriendly country” and suspended peace treaty negotiations. The two countries remain divided over four Russian-administered islands that Japan claims as its Northern Territories.

Tensions intensified when President Vladimir Putin visited one of those islands – known in Russia as Iturup and as Etorofu in Japan – in August 2026. A subsequent visit by a Chinese provincial delegation drew another Japanese protest, highlighting growing coordination between Moscow and Beijing.

Security tensions now dominate Japan-Russia relations, while meaningful strategic dialogue has largely disappeared. Imai’s continued detention could make even limited efforts to restore contacts, including humanitarian visits by former island residents, more difficult.

Yet geography makes complete disengagement unrealistic. Japan retains interests in regional security, fisheries, and Russian energy supplies, including liquefied natural gas from Sakhalin.

Tokyo must therefore protect its citizen and defend press freedom while preserving the diplomatic channels necessary to secure Imai’s release.

How Moscow handles Imai’s case will test whether the two governments can maintain the basic communication needed to protect citizens and manage disputes, even while their wider relationship remains frozen.
