title: Russia’s Navy Shows Its Reach Around Japan’s Southwestern Islands
description: Vladimir Putin’s first-ever visit to a northern territory claimed by Japan comes amid a steady uptick in Russian naval activity near Japan’s southernmost islands.
text:
President Vladimir Putin’s mid-August visit to the Kuril Islands, his first as Russia’s leader, inflamed a decades-old territorial dispute with Japan and drew worldwide attention to the two countries’ border in the northern Pacific. But over the past several years, Russian forces have been increasingly active far to the south, around Japan’s southwestern-most islands, in a demonstration of the Russian military’s reach and its willingness to challenge its rivals on its own and alongside China.

The dispute centers on the southernmost islands in the Kuril chain, which Japan calls its Northern Territories and says the Soviets seized illegally after Tokyo’s surrender at the end of World War II. Thousands of former Japanese residents of the islands are still alive, and resolving the dispute is a high priority for Japanese leaders. Russia’s activity on the islands, especially its military buildup, is therefore a sensitive issue for Tokyo.

Putin’s visit to the island Russia calls Iturup and Japan calls Etorofu on August 13 struck a chord with Tokyo not only for its location but also for its timing. Putin first traveled to Sakhalin Island – his first visit there in 13 years – to observe drills by Russia’s Pacific Fleet, part of a month-long series of exercises in the area that Japan protested. His visit also came days after the anniversary of the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki and days before the anniversary of Japan’s World War II surrender announcement.

Putin’s Kuril visit coincided with another Russian movement much farther south. The same day, Japan’s Defense Ministry reported that it had observed a Russian navy Improved Kilo-class submarine and a search-and-rescue vessel sailing north between the two Japanese islands closest to Taiwan, Yonaguni and Iriomote. That was one of at least 14 transits by Russian vessels around Yonaguni so far in 2026, a considerable increase over recent years.

A review of releases by the Japanese military’s Joint Staff from the past five years shows no such transits in 2021 and just two in 2022, both between Yonaguni and Iriomote. 2023 saw another two transits between Yonaguni and Iriomote, followed by a jump to six transits – five between Yonaguni and Iriomote and one between Yonaguni and Taiwan – in 2024. After a dip to four Yonaguni-Iriomote transits in 2025, there have been 11 transits between those islands and three between Yonaguni and Taiwan so far this year, the most recent on September 25.

Activity around Japan’s Southwest Islands is a growing concern for Tokyo. China has increased its military operations there since the early 2010s, training to sail and fly around and through that island chain. Chinese activity near Yonaguni and its neighboring islands, known as the Sakishima Islands, has also picked up in recent years, a sign of Beijing’s interest in familiarizing its forces with the area around Taiwan. In late 2024, a Chinese aircraft carrier sailed between Yonaguni and Iriomote for the first time, drawing a formal protest from Tokyo. In response, Japan has increased its military presence on the islands, opening bases for radars, electronic-warfare units, and surface-to-air and anti-ship missiles on Yonaguni and Ishigaki, which is just east of Iriomote.

Some Russian transits around Yonaguni appear to be part of routine voyages to and from the Pacific Fleet’s bases near Vladivostok. There may be a practical reason to use that route. “For ships coming south from Vladivostok through the East China Sea, the passage between Yonaguni and Iriomote provides a convenient way into the Philippine Sea without going farther northeast through the Miyako Strait,” Thomas Shugart, an adjunct senior fellow at the Center for a New American Security and a retired U.S. Navy officer, said in an email. Shugart said Russia’s navy may also have a political reason to avoid the more direct route to the South China Sea through the Taiwan Strait: “Given Beijing’s sensitivity to foreign naval transits of the Strait, routine Russian use could invite the observation that even the Russians treat it as an international waterway.”

But the behavior of other Russian vessels around Yonaguni appears more likely to be “deliberate signaling toward Japan,” Shugart said. In some cases, Russian vessels have loitered in the area, perhaps to monitor Japanese activity and response measures. In its annual “Defense of Japan” report, Japan’s Defense Ministry singled out an unusual operation in January this year, in which a Russian Vishnya-class intelligence-gathering ship was seen “navigating for an extended period” around the Sakishima Islands and Okinawa. Joint Staff releases showed that over the course of 12 days the vessel sailed south between Taiwan and Yonaguni and circled the Sakishima Islands before crossing the Miyako Strait and lingering southeast of Okinawa for three days. “Notably, this marked the first confirmed instance of such a vessel circumnavigating the Sakishima Islands,” the report said.

The ministry’s report linked recent activity around the Sakishima Islands with a years-long uptick in Russian operations around Japan, “including exercises and training likely intended to verify the results of military reforms” and operations farther afield that are likely meant to keep the U.S., Japan, and others “in check.”

Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, its navy “has been continuously involved in active deterrent operations against the United States and its Western allies,” Alexey Muraviev, a professor at Edith Cowan University in Australia who studies Russian military strategy, said in an interview late last year. Regular deployments to Southeast Asia, where Moscow has sought to bolster its military ties, are a part of those operations, Muraviev said, but they also reflect continued concerns about the US and its allies, especially Japan. “Russia clearly sees Japan as a military risk – partially because of its alignment with the United States through security and defense ties, partially because of [the] unresolved territorial dispute,” Muraviev said.

Russia’s activity around Japan also shows its deepening military ties with China, which has become a more important partner amid Moscow’s international isolation following its invasion of Ukraine. Over the past several years, Sino-Russian bomber and naval patrols have incorporated a wider range of ships and aircraft, including diesel-electric submarines and nuclear-capable bombers, and traveled farther, sometimes circling the Japanese archipelago. During their most recent naval patrol, in July, their ships transited east through the Miyako Strait, headed north along Japan’s east coast, and then sailed west through the Vries Strait, which separates the Kuril Islands that Japan claims from the rest of the chain. The route demonstrated the two navies’ increasing ability to operate through “strategic waterways,” Chinese experts told state media.

Russia has also echoed China’s criticism of what it calls Japan’s “militarism,” a line of attack that Beijing started pushing late last year, likely in an attempt to stoke backlash to Japan’s growing military investments and regional security role. Russian officials returned to that talking point in the weeks following Putin’s visit to the Kuril Islands, lashing out at Japan for hosting a military exercise with the U.S. around Hokkaido, the Japanese main island closest to the Kurils, and objecting to its proximity to Russian territory. “The Japanese side was firmly informed that provocative military activity near our country’s far eastern borders is categorically unacceptable,” Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said on September 1.

title: Russia’s Wildberries Finding Fertile Ground in Central Asia
description: The Russian e-commerce retailer has announced yet another new logistics facility, this time in Uzbekistan.
text:
During World War II, Soviet authorities moved industry and people – often forcibly – away from the frontier in Europe into the heartland of Eurasia. The strategic relocation of factories and critical production to the Urals, Siberia, and Central Asia fundamentally changed economies across the union.

Now, amid a different war on the European front, Russian industry is looking again to Central Asia for relative safety to continue conducting business.

Wildberries & Russ, the parent company of Russia’s largest e-commerce retailer, Wildberries, reportedly signed an investment agreement this week with the Uzbek Ministry of Investment, Industry, and Trade to expand its logistics capacity in Uzbekistan. The deal comes in the wake of an early August announcement from Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Trade and Integration that Wildberries would expand its warehouse capacity in that country.

Starting in July 2026, Ukraine began targeting major Wildberries warehousing facilities in Russia. Through mid-August, Ukrainian drones had struck at least 20 Wildberries hubs, many of them near Moscow. According to the Moscow-based e-commerce consultancy Data Insight, as reported by DW in mid-August, Wildberries had lost 480 billion rubles worth of goods ($5.7 billion) and a third of its warehouse space.

As The Diplomat’s Albert Otkjær pointed out in August, WIldberries’ effort to build out its warehousing capacity in Kazakhstan predates the current crisis – though not the February 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine. Wildberries’ expansion into Kazakhstan began in 2023, when the company opened its first logistics center in Astana, followed by a warehouse complex in Almaty. In September 2023, Wildberries opened a sorting center in Uralsk, the company’s fifth logistics center in the country.

Similarly, in May 2023 Wildberries opened its first logistics center in Uzbekistan, in the Tashkent region, followed by plans for a second in Fergana. In October 2023 Wildeberries announced that it would build another logistics center in the Tashkent region.

The recently announced deal pertains to a planned logistics hub in the Zangiata district of the Tashkent region, to be built on a a 67.3-hectare site. According to the company, the facility will generate at least 7,500 jobs.

As such, the wave of attacks this summer targeting Wildberries is not the sole motivation for its efforts to expand capacity in Central Asia. Those efforts began earlier. The region is, even absent the ongoing conflict, a large market for Russian companies and a bridge deeper into Asia. Factoring in the war in Ukraine only deepens the commercial logic for expansion into Central Asia.

It also deepens the risks. Ukrainian authorities have justified the strikes on an ostensibly civilian enterprise by arguing that Wildberries warehouse are “involved in supplying the Russian military with drone components, navigation equipment, and other gear,” as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in late July.

Similarly, Ukraine justified attacks on Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC) infrastructure near Novorossiysk – in November 2025 and July 2026 – given the critical importance of oil revenues to the Russian war machine. But collateral damage to Kazakhstan’s export of oil through the CPC led to pushback from both Astana and Washington. In February 2026, Ukraine’s ambassador to the United States said that Kyiv had received a formal demarche from Washington. The complaint, Ambassador Olga Stefanishyna said, cited the risks posed to “American investments which are being performed through Kazakhstan.”

In early August, Bloomberg reported, citing a U.S. official, that Ukraine had agreed to not strike CPC infrastructure critical to Kazakhstan’s oil exports in the Black Sea, as well as avoid striking non-Russian vessels – provided they’re not separately sanctioned or carrying Russian cargo.

Could Ukrainian drone strikes target Wildberries facilities in Kazakhstan or Uzbekistan? It’s highly unlikely, though not impossible as the war drags on. Such a strike would mark a significant expansion of the conflict and be ruinous to Kyiv’s relations with the Central Asian states, and likely the United States, too, given Washington’s intercession on Kazakhstan’s behalf in regard to the CPC.
tag: Kazakhstan-Russia relations; Russia-Ukraine war; Russian invasion of Ukraine; Ukraine-Central Asia relations; Uzbekistan-Russia relations; Wildberries

title: Saudi Arabia Executes Two Bangladeshi Nationals
description: Dhaka says it learned of their execution only after it happened. Its diplomacy is under scrutiny
text:
On October 13, Saudi Arabia’s Supreme Court set aside the death sentence of Sri Lankan migrant worker Anojan Sivarasa. Sivarasa had been sentenced to death over a Facebook post deemed insulting to Prophet Muhammad and blasphemous against Islam.

The following day, Saudi authorities executed two Bangladeshis, Nazrul Islam Abdul Basir and Suety Akhter (Sweety Akhtar, according to family), in the holy city of Makkah. According to their families, both had moved to Saudi Arabia for work nearly four years earlier. They had been convicted of what Saudi authorities described as an “immoral act” inside a mosque.

The two cases put Bangladesh’s protection of migrant workers in Saudi Arabia under scrutiny. Sri Lanka organized legal and diplomatic support for Sivarasa, winning a reprieve for its citizen. Bangladesh said it learned of the execution of its nationals only after it happened.

Sri Lanka’s success does not mean Bangladesh could have secured the same outcome; the allegations in the two cases were different. But the fact that Dhaka claimed not to know about the sentences until it was too late to intervene is concerning.

Saudi authorities described the death sentences of the Bangladeshis as ta’zir, a discretionary punishment, and said judicial review and a royal order preceded execution. The public statement did not explain the precise “immoral act,” identify the mosque, or disclose the arrest dates.

What evidence supported the conviction of the two Bangladeshis? Did the defendants have lawyers and interpreters? Could they understand the proceedings and challenge the charges?

Bangladesh’s claims are hard to accept without scrutiny. Media reports said the Bangladesh consulate general in Jeddah had sought prisoner information in September. Saudi authorities supplied a list containing the two names on September 30, but no details of their death sentences.

The Jeddah consulate sent a report to Bangladesh’s Ministry of Expatriates’ Welfare and Overseas Employment on October 18. The Daily Star, a Bangladeshi daily, which obtained the report, says that the two Bangladeshis had been detained since August 2023. The list recorded cybercrime allegations against Nazrul and adultery allegations against Akhter.

The report also listed 306 Bangladeshis held in prisons across Saudi Arabia’s western region. Of them, 147 had received sentences ranging from one month to 15 years of jail time.

A Bangladeshi official said the consulate received no requests for assistance from the pair or their family members. Another official said following every case was impossible.

What the government said after the executions has also drawn criticism. Speaking to reporters on October 17, Bangladesh’s State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam described the executions as a lesson for Bangladesh and urged citizens abroad to follow their host countries’ laws. “When a law is violated, there is not much I can do for a Bangladeshi citizen,” she said.

However, Bangladesh could still have sought lawyers’ help and engaged in diplomatic discussions to help the two citizens appeal their sentences.

Did Bangladeshi officials ask for details of the charges or copies of the court records? Were cases that involved potentially severe punishment referred for legal advice? Who was responsible for following the cases? Bangladesh needs to explain what its officials did and when. The claim that the two citizens did not ask for help does not resolve questions about its own consular response.

Sri Lanka’s response shows what Bangladesh could have done. Sivarasa was arrested on July 1. A court initially imposed five years in prison and a fine of 3 million riyals (about $800,000) on him. On September 17, an appeals court increased the punishment to death. Amnesty International said he lacked access to a lawyer before his initial sentencing.

On September 18, Sri Lanka’s Foreign Ministry publicly confirmed that it was pursuing his case through diplomatic channels. Ambassador O. L. Ameer Ajwad visited him in prison on October 8 and provided contact details. A specialist Sri Lankan legal delegation supported the Supreme Court appeal.

The court overturned Sivarasa’s death sentence. That did not guarantee that he would be acquitted or could return home. Media reports also give little detail about why the court ruled in his favor. It is unclear how much the outcome was due to the legal appeal or Sri Lanka’s diplomatic efforts.

Still, Sri Lanka provided legal support, pursued the case through diplomatic channels, and visited its citizen in prison. Bangladesh has yet to provide evidence of comparable efforts in these two cases.

Saudi Arabia also needs to explain what happened. Both countries are parties to the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations. Article 36 requires authorities to inform detained foreigners promptly of their consular rights. If a detainee requests it, the consulate must be notified without delay. Consular officers have the right to visit, communicate, and arrange legal representation.

The convention does not expressly mention a duty to warn an embassy before every execution. Therefore, the absence of an advance warning alone cannot establish that Article 36 was breached. Even so, Saudi authorities could have taken greater care to inform Bangladesh of the death sentences while there was still time to seek legal help. Saudi authorities need to explain what the prisoners were told about contacting the Bangladeshi consulate. They also need to clarify what happened to any requests for help, and if consular officials were allowed to visit.

Bangladesh has strong reasons to preserve relations with Riyadh. More than 3 million Bangladeshis live in the kingdom. Protecting such a large community requires a large consular staff and a system for following serious criminal cases. Officials need to know which prisoners face severe punishment and when legal help is needed. That work cannot depend entirely on prisoners or their families knowing whom to contact.

Sri Lanka’s efforts helped its citizen challenge his death sentence. In Bangladesh’s case, it is still unclear whether officials could have acted in time. The executions have left Bangladesh’s diplomats facing a difficult question about whether they could have done more before they were executed.
tag: Bangladeshi diplomats; Bangladeshi nationals in Saudi Arabia; Saudi executions; Saudi-Bangladesh relations

title: South China Sea Code of Conduct: A Deal Is Not Enough
description: A COC that lacks credible enforcement mechanisms would do little to address security challenges.
text:
As ASEAN and China work toward concluding a Code of Conduct (COC) for the South China Sea in 2026, the central question is not simply whether an agreement can be reached, but whether it will meaningfully reduce tensions. A deal is not enough if it does not address the underlying drivers of tension and shape actors’ behaviors.

The South China Sea is a contested maritime zone, involving China and ASEAN members Brunei, Malaysia, the Philippines, and Vietnam. To address the overlapping maritime claims and disputes, ASEAN and China have been negotiating a COC to establish a rules-based framework to manage maritime disputes, reduce miscalculations, and prevent armed conflict.

After nearly two decades of negotiations, Manila, as the current ASEAN chair, has recently signaled that agreement on the COC is at hand. A COC would represent an important diplomatic achievement.

Yet an agreement that lacks credible enforcement mechanisms, preserves ambiguity over compliance, or constrains Southeast Asian countries’ strategic autonomy could do little to address the region’s underlying security challenges.

The substance of the agreement matters more than announcing its completion. A COC that primarily reiterates commitments to dialogue, restraint, and peaceful dispute resolution – like those contained in the existing Declaration of Conduct – would have limited practical value. The COC needs clear procedures for managing incidents, resolving disagreements, and addressing violations.

The South China Sea has seen increased military activities. China has built a network of military facilities in the Spratly and Paracel Islands, some of which are now equipped to host bombers. In 2025, Vietnam commenced its own reclamation work on occupied features, building infrastructure to support a larger military presence.

Naval confrontations between China and the Philippines continue, highlighting the fragility of stability in the contested waters. Diplomatic commitments alone cannot guarantee responsible behavior

If the COC is to improve regional stability, it must include practical measures to prevent escalation and hold parties accountable for their conduct.

This raises a second challenge: ASEAN’s ability to ensure compliance. Even if the agreement includes specific obligations, its effectiveness will depend on whether parties are willing to implement them when doing so conflicts with their strategic interests. ASEAN’s consensus-based approach, while essential to maintaining regional unity, can complicate collective responses to violations, particularly when member states have different economic and security relationships with China.

A credible COC should therefore establish transparent procedures for reporting incidents, conducting consultations, and addressing alleged breaches. Regular reviews and clearly defined dispute-management channels could help prevent disagreements from escalating. Without a meaningful accountability mechanism, the COC risks just becoming a declaration of intent.

The agreement must also protect Southeast Asian states’ strategic autonomy. China may seek arrangements that limit activities it considers destabilizing, such as joint military exercises with the United States. Provisions governing military exercises, defense partnerships, or cooperation with external powers could create constraints that extend beyond managing disputes in the South China Sea. If drafted too broadly, the COC could inadvertently restrict ASEAN members’ ability to pursue their own security interests.

The challenge is to distinguish between measures designed to prevent maritime incidents and provisions that limit legitimate defense cooperation. Southeast Asian states should retain the freedom to conduct exercises, modernize their armed forces, and establish partnerships with countries outside the region, consistent with international law. A COC that undermines these freedoms would risk weakening the very strategic independence ASEAN seeks to preserve.

The Philippines’ expanding defense cooperation with non-Southeast Asian powers such as Australia and Japan illustrates this tension. Manila’s partnerships strengthen its deterrence capabilities and provide additional options for responding to maritime pressure. However, Beijing may view these arrangements as contributing to strategic competition, complicating efforts to reach a mutually acceptable agreement.

Nevertheless, external partnerships should not automatically be regarded as obstacles to a COC. They can strengthen Southeast Asian states’ negotiating position by showing that China and ASEAN alone cannot determine regional security, given the South China Sea’s significance as an international maritime trade route. Extra-regional powers’ participation in maritime security, however, should not obscure ASEAN’s central role in shaping regional norms.

Ultimately, the COC’s credibility will depend on whether it can reconcile three objectives: reducing tensions, ensuring compliance, and preserving the strategic autonomy of Southeast Asian countries. These objectives are not mutually exclusive, but achieving them will require precise language, practical implementation mechanisms, and a willingness to address violations consistently.

The measure of success, then, is not whether ASEAN and China can sign an agreement, but whether that agreement changes behavior at sea. Without credible commitments and meaningful accountability, the COC may secure a diplomatic milestone while failing to deliver the regional stability it promises.
tag: ASEAN China COC; ASEAN China code of conduct; ASEAN South China Sea approach; China South China Sea; Code of Conduct for the South China Sea

title: South Korea Recalls Ambassador, Demands Public Apology From Ukraine
description: A diplomatic rift is growing after a North Korean prisoner transfer that Kyiv revealed against Seoul’s wishes.
text:
South Korea decided on October 8 to recall Ambassador Park Ki-chang from Ukraine. It’s Seoul’s first ambassador recall since 2008, when South Korea withdrew its envoy from Japan over a territorial claim to the Dokdo islets.

The decision came 15 days after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy disclosed the transfer of two captured North Korean soldiers to South Korea in a speech to the United Nations General Assembly. Seoul says the two governments had agreed to keep the transfer confidential. However, Kyiv first denied any such agreement before its Foreign Ministry attributed the dispute to differing interpretations.

The two soldiers at the center of the dispute were captured in January 2025 in the Kursk region of Russia. North Korea had sent troops there to support the Russian invasion of Ukraine. The captured soldiers arrived in South Korea in mid-September after saying they wished to settle there.

Zelenskyy’s public announcement of their arrival drew a response from South Korean President Lee Jae-myung on September 24 in a post on the social platform X. He called the disclosure deeply regrettable. Lee also cited the problems that disclosure could cause.

Kyiv rejected that account the next day. Dmytro Lytvyn, a communications adviser to Zelenskyy, denied that any confidentiality agreement existed.

The South Korean presidential office voiced strong regret over the disclosure and Ukraine’s denial on September 27. It demanded an official explanation and apology. It also signaled that additional measures were under consideration. Seong Ghi-hong, senior presidential secretary for public relations, said that Ukraine’s had sought the secrecy itself. He added that Kyiv had cited possible criticism at home for giving up a chance to swap the soldiers for Ukrainian prisoners held by Russia.

The next day, First Vice Foreign Minister Park Yoon-joo summoned Andrii Vieshkin, who is Ukraine’s acting ambassador in Seoul. The vice minister repeated the demands to him.

Still, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha described the dispute on October 1 as a diplomatic misunderstanding. Sybiha did not offer the public apology that Seoul had demanded.

In a post on X the next day, Lee wrote that Ukraine had made the South Korean head of state a “liar” by denying the agreement. He also warned of further measures unless Kyiv publicly apologized.

Lee also broadened his criticism to remarks by Kyrylo Budanov, head of the Ukrainian presidential office. Budanov had warned in an interview on September 27 that tension along the inter-Korean border was rising by the day. Days earlier, suspected North Korean mines had exploded inside the Demilitarized Zone between the two Koreas and wounded three South Korean soldiers. So Lee accused Kyiv of speaking of an imminent clash between the two Koreas as if wishing for war.

On October 6, Foreign Minister Cho Hyun told lawmakers that a message from Ukraine had included words of apology. However, he said it fell somewhat short of the expectations of Seoul.

Kyiv characterized the message differently. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi said on October 7 that Ukraine had expressed regret over the public criticism between the two countries. The spokesperson also attributed the dispute to differing interpretations of the confidentiality arrangement.

A separate dispute surfaced in the same week. Vladyslav Vlasiuk, the presidential commissioner of Ukraine for sanctions policy, said on October 6 that fuel shipments from South Korean ports had helped Russia offset refinery losses caused by Ukrainian strikes. The South Korean presidential office rejected the claim on October 7.

In the announcement recalling Ambassador Park the next day, the South’s Foreign Ministry said it hoped to settle pending issues through continued consultations with Ukraine.

The Foreign Ministry of Ukraine responded that diplomacy should prevail over emotions. Tykhyi added that diplomatic efforts were underway through private channels.

Park returned home on October 10.

Seoul had good reasons to want the transfer kept quiet. According to Seoul, the families of the two men remain in North Korea, where they could face reprisals over their relatives’ decision to defect.

The National Intelligence Service also told lawmakers on September 30 that the disclosure appeared aimed at building public support in South Korea for arms supplies to Ukraine. Seoul has supported Ukraine with financial and humanitarian aid but not with lethal weapons, even after North Korea began sending tens of thousands of soldiers to fight for Russia.

If Ukraine’s government was hoping to bolster its image with South Koreans, it badly miscalculated. Instead, Kyiv has lost the trust of Seoul, and the harm cannot be repaired in private. Because the disclosure was public, a message passed between ministers cannot solve the problem.

Meanwhile another Ukrainian official opened a second dispute. Vlasiuk raised the fuel claim on October 6 while Seoul was still waiting for an apology. The South Korean government says petroleum products are not on its list of controlled exports. Whatever the merits, the claim muddied a dispute that Kyiv had started. The fuel question belongs in a separate channel on sanctions compliance.

With that question set aside, Seoul has demanded three things. Kyiv should acknowledge that a confidentiality agreement existed. The Ukrainian government should offer an official, public apology. And Kyiv should commit to steps that prevent a recurrence.

Park may return to Kyiv only after Ukraine does all three.
tag: North Korean defectors in South Korea; North Korean troops in Ukraine; South Korea Ukraine response; South Korea-Ukraine relations; Volodymyr Zelenskyy

title: South Korea, US Pull Apart as the Alliance Strains
description: Restricted intelligence sharing, an investment spat, and remarks by a U.S. commander point to a widening gap between the allies.
text:
South Korea and the United States are in a tug-of-war over the terms of their alliance. Since March the two governments have clashed over intelligence sharing, investment, and military command. The friction is now visible in small and concrete ways.

The dispute began on March 6 when the South’s Unification Minister Chung Dong-young named the North Korean city of Kusong as the site of a uranium enrichment facility. Washington treated the remark as a disclosure of classified information and has since partially restricted the imagery intelligence shared with Seoul on North Korea. Chung has said he learned of the facility from open sources. Washington did not accept the explanation. In April, National Security Adviser Wi Sung-lac acknowledged that the two governments held different views of the remark.

A second dispute has become entangled with the first. The U.S.-listed e-commerce company Coupang is under investigation in South Korea over a data breach. A July report by the U.S. House Judiciary Committee accused South Korea’s National Intelligence Service of pressuring officials to pursue the company; the NIS called the claim false. In the same April briefing, Wi said the Coupang case concerned a single company. He nonetheless acknowledged that it was affecting security talks and delaying negotiations.

The intelligence service has been affected directly. Washington barred the agency from a June meeting with Japan on North Korean cyber threats and notified Seoul in writing, according to local media reports. The agency called the exclusion a one-time measure. South Korean Ambassador to the U.S. Kang Kyung-hwa also confirmed that visas for two or three agency employees bound for the embassy in Washington had been delayed. The agency attributed the delays to stricter U.S. entry procedures and denied any link to the intelligence dispute.

Each incident can be explained on its own, but together the impact is mounting on the intelligence relationship.

Economic pressure has followed a similar course. Seoul hoped that progress on its $350 billion investment pledge under a trade deal with Washington would restart stalled security talks on nuclear-powered submarines and uranium enrichment. However, the specific terms of investment have become a cause of more tension.

U.S. President Donald Trump announced on September 30 that South Korea would invest $54 billion in the Alaska liquefied natural gas project. The trade ministry in Seoul said no decision had been made on whether to invest or how much. Trump pressed the point two days later. On October 2, he warned Seoul of higher costs for staying out of the project. He repeated the investment claim on October 14 in a post on Truth Social.

Before the November 3 midterm elections, Trump has been presenting investment pledges from allies as proof that his tariff policy works. Now Seoul is facing pressure to turn a campaign claim into a financial commitment. The link to security talks gives the dispute weight beyond money.

The strain is also jeopardizing a long-held South Korean military goal. The Lee administration aims to regain wartime operational control (OPCON) of South Korean forces by 2028. U.S. Forces Korea commander General Xavier Brunson – the officer who currently hold wartime OPCON over Korean forces – has cited the first quarter of 2029.

Then, on October 14, Brunson said at a policy forum in Washington that the conditions for the handover had changed. He pointed to recent North Korean missile launches as evidence. He voiced support for the OPCON transfer but opposed rushing it to meet a political deadline.

South Korean Defense Minister Kang Shin-chul said the next day that Seoul had already conveyed its concerns to Washington. The Defense Ministry maintained that the agreed conditions for the transfer remain unchanged.

On October 19, South Korean President Lee Jae-myung was asked about Brunson’s comments. Speaking at the presidential Blue House, Lee told reporters that Seoul must regain wartime OPCON quickly. He added that talks with Washington are basically moving toward its return. Lee also argued that the process should be called a recovery rather than a transfer.

A second remark from Brunson drew sharper criticism in Seoul. The Demilitarized Zone is a buffer strip between the two Koreas, and the Military Demarcation Line runs through its middle. At the same forum, Brunson said that South Korea begins at the southern fence of the DMZ from the perspective of the United Nations Command. He commands the U.S.-led United Nations Command, which manages the zone to uphold the armistice. A command official countered that there was no question about South Korean sovereignty.

Lawmakers of the ruling Democratic Party objected. Kim Byung-joo, a special presidential adviser on defense policy, demanded a retraction and an apology. The constitution defines the territory of South Korea as the Korean Peninsula and its adjacent islands. Even read narrowly, the remark did little to reassure a partner seeking more control over its own defense.

This isn’t the first time Brunson had sparked controversy. In May, he had likened South Korea to a “dagger in the heart of Asia,” implying that the U.S. would use military assets stationed on the peninsula to thwart China’s “ambitions beyond that.” Seoul has conveyed its concerns about Brunson through several channels and reportedly received a sympathetic reply from the U.S. side.

The latest frictions in South Korea-U.S. relations came as North Korea stepped up its weapons tests. On October 15, North Korean state media reported that the country had tested two types of submarine-launched strategic cruise missiles the day before. That followed a launch of tactical ballistic missiles on October 12.

A land mine explosion wounded three South Korean soldiers in the DMZ on September 21. The South Korean Joint Chiefs of Staff have determined that North Korea planted the mines.

On October 19, Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, said in a statement that South Korean troops had fired warning shots at North Korean personnel working on border fortifications. She accused South Korean forces of carrying out 2,870 loudspeaker warnings and 201 warning shots between August 1 and October 17.

Kim added that the North Korean military was considering deploying more tactical strike weapons along the southern border and resuming loudspeaker broadcasts against the South. She also accused the Lee administration of escalating confrontation faster than his conservative predecessor, Yoon Suk-yeol.

On one level, the alliance is still robust. Communication continues between South Korea and the U.S. as usual. But behind the facade of normal interactions, analysts worry that Seoul is increasingly facing steep costs for saying no to U.S. demands. Across intelligence, trade, and military command, Washington is interlinking issues so that Seoul faces restrictions and threats on all fronts. That looks more like a transactional relationship than the “ironclad” alliance the two foreign ministers reaffirmed on September 18.

A partner that can only follow is not an ally in the full sense of the word.
tag: Future of the U.S.-South Korea alliance; OPCON transfer; South Korean investment in the US; U.S.-South Korea alliance; U.S.-South Korea military intelligence sharing

title: South Korea’s $60 Billion Semiconductor Exports to Drive the KOSPI’s Resurgence
description: South Korea’s economy has become intrinsically linked to the ongoing artificial intelligence boom.
text:
With semiconductors amounting to around two-thirds of the Korea Composite Stock Price Index’s (KOSPI) market capitalization, South Korea’s economy has become intrinsically linked to the ongoing artificial intelligence boom. As exports reach record highs, optimism is growing among investors that the KOSPI can recapture momentum to close out 2026.

Monthly export value for semiconductors surpassed $60 billion in September, breaking the $120 billion total export threshold for the first time in South Korea. The trend was driven by accelerating demand for AI and memory chips and is paving the way to $1 trillion in annual exports domestically.

Critically, September’s export figures represented an 83.5 percent boost compared to the same period last year, while daily averages for the month reached a 105 percent year-over-year increase to $5.63 billion per day.

The KOSPI responded to the news with a 2 percent jump. Despite a clear heavy reliance on semiconductor stocks following years of exponential growth, signs of strength in South Korea’s export activity are likely to instill a newfound confidence in the long-term outlook for the nation’s markets.

South Korea’s strength in exports has helped to further deepen the growth of the KOSPI’s star players, Samsung and SK Hynix, which posted growth of 2.79 percent and 3.21 percent, respectively, after September’s figures were released by government sources. The two stocks now account for 66 percent of the entirety of the KOSPI index by market capitalization, underlining the nation’s reliance on the performance of the semiconductor giants.

“There’s a clear case for South Korea as the most impacted market by the rise of artificial intelligence,” explained Vsevolod Smirnov, CMO at Just2Trade. “Since the launch of ChatGPT by OpenAI in November 2022 and the beginning of the GenAI boom, the KOSPI gained more than 270 percent to reach its 2026 peak, but the fact that the index has since tumbled 22.5 percent over the past three months is a warning sign of overreliance.”

The KOSPI surpassed 9,000 in June, a historic high water mark for the index. But it didn’t remain there long. The KOSPI dropped back into the 8,000s just a week after hitting its all-time record, and spent most of July, August, and September in the 6,000-range.

However, Smirnov sees cause for optimism moving forward. “The good news is that export momentum means that these two semiconductor leaders aren’t selling magic beans. There’s a clear product and evident investor appetite,” he explained. “Both Samsung and SK Hynix have a relatively grounded trailing price-to-earnings ratio of around 10.9 and 7.4, respectively, indicating that both companies are well-positioned to fill their boots moving forward.”

Analysts expect a return to the positive momentum that helped to push the KOSPI to new highs. Mirae Asset Securities analyst Kim Young-gun noted that DRAM and NAND memory chips are likely to stay undersupplied through 2028, which is likely to drive prices higher in the mid-term future.

The climate surrounding Samsung, in particular, has remained more optimistic in recent weeks, with the company avoiding a workers’ strike by offering bonuses averaging $400,000. Given that the tech leader is single-handedly responsible for a quarter of South Korea’s exports, the resolution is set to support the national economic outlook.

The biggest threat to the long-term performance of the KOSPI is wider economic uncertainty, which has become increasingly pertinent as the conflict in Iran has brought higher global oil prices and U.S. Treasury yields. Although the index naturally correlates to the ongoing AI boom, the KOSPI tumbled into the 6,600 range earlier in September as a result of international oil prices climbing beyond $100 a barrel and 10-year U.S. Treasury yields exceeding 5 percent.

These factors could lead to shortfalls in net buying due to macroeconomic uncertainty. This, coupled with the traditional underperformance of the KOSDAQ following the Chuseok holiday season, could create a weaker conclusion to 2026 for South Korean markets.

However, the sheer strength of the AI boom appears to be offering some resilience. There is increasing U.S. demand for AI infrastructure, as Wall Street’s “Magnificent Seven” collective of hyperscalers and AI adopters have committed more than $750 billion in capex toward their own AI buildouts.

With competition over AI investment accelerating beyond GPUs and memory chips toward infrastructure and power, as well as servers and communications, Samsung and SK Hynix are well-positioned to continue achieving their collective potential on the KOSPI throughout the fourth quarter and beyond – in spite of ongoing macroeconomic concerns.

Although a return to 9,000 is unlikely at a time when U.S. Treasury yields are expected to rise further, South Korea’s positive export figures show a level of resilience that should encourage investors. The KOSPI has been one of the world’s best performers since 2022, following the emergence of the AI rally. While headwinds are continuing to mount, there’s no reason the optimism has to subside looking ahead.

The upcoming earnings season for South Korea’s semiconductor giants will be critical. Should the likes of Samsung and SK Hynix show that they can justify their momentum, there’s no reason why 9,000 can’t be a legitimate target for the first quarter of 2027.

title: South Korea’s Ruling Democratic Party Is Tumbling in the Polls
channel_text: Blog; East Asia; Politics; The Koreas
description: Its in-house gaffes and disputes are largely to blame for the DP's plummeting approval ratings.
text:
On October 19, Gyeonggi, South Korea’s most populous province, held a post-funeral ceremony ahead of a firefighter’s internment. More than 2,700 people filled the indoor stadium. Choo Mi-ae, the provincial governor, stood on the green sports surfacing, tears streaming down her face. File after file of uniformed firefighters weaved around her amid dirgeful tributes.

Of course, the firefighter’s burial signified the loss and sacrifice of a serviceman who braved a conflagration to save lives. Yet, it also rang the death knell for the ruling Democratic Party’s approval ratings.

The same day, Realmeter, an authoritative pollster, released a poll. The DP’s approval rating, at 36.2 percent, was lower than the opposition People Power Party’s 40.9 percent. It was the first time since the June local elections that the PPP had outpolled the DP.

The alienation of DP supporters happened fast. Less than five months ago, the June local elections handed the DP a resounding victory. Since then, the DP has registered a double-digit plunge in approval ratings.

The party’s fall was particularly steep in Seoul, with the DP polling at 26.7 percent as opposed to the PPP’s 45.7 percent. One-fifth of South Koreans live in Seoul; track records in the capital thus tend to reflect where the swing voters stand. Oh Se-hoon, its current mayor, may lose the post should the Supreme Court uphold the special counsel’s charge that Oh allegedly paid a pollster to rig polls in his favor. (On October 23, the appellate court overturned his guilty verdict. The Supreme Court will rule on the case early next year.) The DP hopes to retake Seoul in a potential by-election, but with these poll numbers success is far from assured.

The DP’s popularity may still crater further. Given the touchy nature of the reform agenda still ahead for the Lee Jae-myung administration, the rest of this year and next year may not really be a rosy picture for the party. And then it will already be time for the 2028 general elections.

The party’s poor polling performance is of its own making, though. Choo, the governor of Gyeonggi-do, dealt the most immediate damage in a controversy that preceded the firefighter’s funeral.

On October 13, during a parliamentary audit, Choo said that “firefighting is like a financial straw, causing the biggest headache.” She then elaborated on how much firefighters are setting back the province’s coffers. Firefighters’ unions went up in arms, wondering how the sacrifice of constantly putting their lives in jeopardy could be reduced to a budgetary complaint.

Choo ignored their calls for an apology. The province explained that her remark was in reference to the ballooning budgetary burden on the local government due to decreasing financial contributions from the central government – even though the firefighters are directly employed by the central government. Despite her true intention, Choo’s phrasing was no doubt inappropriate and hurtful. She was already facing steep criticism. Then October 16 changed everything.

A fire erupted in a metal printing factory in a town in Gyeonggi. Flames engulfed firefighter Kim Jin-seok, who passed away in the line of duty. The nation became even more infuriated with Choo’s callous analogy earlier.

The next day, Choo attended Kim’s funeral, where she finally apologized: “Since you want an apology, I wholeheartedly apologize.” You have to want to apologize for an apology to feel sincere. But she made it clear she was forced. Her apology duly backfired, to the point where she might have been better off not apologizing at all.

Making matters worse, when Kim Min-seok, the DP’s leader, arrived at the funeral his car parked in a spot reserved for emergency patients. It was a collective PR disaster for the party.

Choo has also been stirring the pot within the DP. She openly clashed with President Lee Jae-myung on the latter’s choice for head of the Serious Crime Investigation Agency (SCIA). It’s a new institution born out of abolishing the prosecutor’s office. The prosecutor’s office used to wield unchecked political powers through its dual authority to investigate and indict. Lee’s criminal justice reform and the DP’s legislation kiboshed this practice by distributing investigatory powers to the police and the SCIA, and indictment authority to the Prosecution Service, also a new body.

In September, when Lee picked Kim Ji-yong, a former prosecutor, to lead the SCIA, Choo maligned Lee by wondering out loud, “Why is he shivering before the insurrection forces?” Kim Yong-min, a popular hard-line DP legislator, joined forces with Choo. They believe Kim Ji-yong huddled around former President Yoon Suk-yeol when Yoon was chief prosecutor and that appointing Kim means giving in to the prosecutors and insurrection forces that aided and protected Yoon for his authoritarian practices and failed self-coup. For his part, Lee maintains that Kim was anti-Yoon.

Their public disagreement continued into this month. “Why appoint someone who can turn their back to the people and justice as the captain of our reform ship?” Choo wrote on October 2. On the same day, Kim Yong-min held a press conference publicly denouncing Kim Ji-yong for having always opposed prosecutorial reform. Meanwhile, Lee made repeated social media posts and a parliamentary submission arguing that the nominee had appropriate qualities needed to establish a trustworthy criminal justice system.

Voices in and out of the DP expressed concerns that such open defiance seemed to challenge Lee’s authority over personnel. The spat peaked in rhetoric on October 9, when Lee made a social media post maligning “those incompetents … who stage internal attacks purportedly for radical reform as a noble cause” when in fact they were complaining because “personnel and national policy didn’t go the way they wanted.”

Separately, the president’s online spat with Cho Kuk, a former justice minister who founded the Rebuilding Korea Party (RKP), further fractured the support for the DP. With 12 legislators in the National Assembly, Cho’s RKP is the third largest party after the DP and the PPP. Cho is also frequently mentioned as a strong contender for the next presidency. The RKP collaborated with the DP to boost liberal voters’ turnout during the 2024 April general elections.

The DP-RKP alliance became uncomfortable in June, however. When Cho ran for a parliamentary by-election, the DP fielded a candidate of its own – a choice many questioned. Liberal votes naturally split, and the PPP easily nabbed the seat.

Ever since, talk of merging the two parties has become fraught with grudges. Cho and Lee have also exchanged criticisms over each other’s stance on the extent of prosecutorial reform. Lee must have targeted Cho as well when he wrote on October 5 that his detractors “shouldn’t try to influence personnel choices and specific affairs of investigation and indictment in the name of prosecutorial reform and for selfish reasons.” (Cho and his wife served prison time after the prosecutors dug every dirt on them to stem former President Moon Jae-in’s and Cho’s effort to curtail the prosecutor’s office’s undue investigative and political powers.) Cho retorted that “the sense of crisis over the dissolution of our alliance has reached the boiling point.”

The past couple of months has seen Lee devoting a large portion of his time and energy to putting in place vociferous elements within the liberal camp. There are two reasons the president rolled up his sleeves to personally engage with critics.

First, Lee must be feeling isolated and betrayed. In September, he shared someone else’s post: “What hurts more are words from within than foes from without … In this chess game, we need to protect the queen that is Lee Jae-myung.” Second, Kim Min-seok, the DP leader who had Lee’s support in the August chair election, has failed to set the party’s house in order. He is kind and voluble but ineffective in quelling the internal unrest. His frequent warnings against those critical of Lee have fallen flat.

While the DP’s big shots are preoccupied with aggrandizing their own presence, the RPK’s support rating reached 9 percent, its highest since the onset of the Lee administration, according to the October 22 figures released by Media Tomato, another major pollster. On the one hand, it indicates the degree to which the DP let down even its core supporters. On the other hand, at least the overall support for the liberal bloc is still more robust than for the PPP. The most pressing thing would be learning how to coalesce at critical moments.
tag: Cho Kuk; Democratic Party (DP); DP infighting; Lee Jae-myung; Rebuilding Korea Party; South Korea politics; South Korea progressives; South Korea prosecution reform

title: Southeast Asia Has a Serious Drug Problem
description: Southeast Asia’s drug labs are pumping out unprecedented amounts of meth and other synthetic drugs.
text:
Southeast Asia is awash in meth.

In June 2025, anti-drug police in Thailand descended on a small tourist boat moored at a pier in Rayong, a seaside town south of Bangkok. Aboard the ship, inside plastic bags disguised as corn flour packages, they found an alarming cargo: 2.4 metric tons of crystal methamphetamine. This one shipment, bound for overseas markets, was bigger than the entire annual total of meth seizures that Thailand made in 2016. An official from the Department of Special Investigation later told the press that the shipment was worth an estimated $9.15 million – and would sell for ten times that once it hit foreign shores.

Thailand’s meth bust was just the tip of the iceberg. Just a few weeks before that, authorities in Indonesia seized a cargo ship near Batam Island, just south of Singapore. On board they found a similar haul: 2.1 tons of crystal meth. It was the largest drug confiscation in Indonesia’s history.

There were more mega-seizures in late 2025 and early 2026. In September 2025, authorities in Yangon confiscated 1.8 metric tons of crystal meth and 4 million methamphetamine tablets, which authorities said were set to be smuggled to Malaysia. In February 2026, Malaysia confiscated 76 sacks of crystal meth, totaling around 1.5 tons, from two vessels off the east coast of peninsular Malaysia. Two months after that, Thai authorities confiscated 2 metric tons hidden in a pickup truck en route to a port in eastern Thailand.

According to experts, all of these meth shipments originated in the Golden Triangle, the rugged region where Thailand’s borders converge with those of Myanmar and Laos. For decades the Golden Triangle has been associated with narcotics – initially heroin, synthesized from the poppies that grow well in the region’s cool upland climate.

But over the past decade, the Southeast Asian drug trade has shifted decisively toward synthetic drugs – particularly methamphetamine. These are cheaper to make, easier to transport, and not dependent on the weather for a good harvest.

Southeast Asia’s drug labs are now pumping out unprecedented amounts of meth. According to the U.N. Office on Drugs and Crime – or UNODC – regional seizures of methamphetamine hit a new record of 349 tons in 2025, up from 236 tons the year before. In 2015, regional seizures captured just 65 tons. And these drugs are being sold all around the world.

The UNODC says that last year, Southeast Asia accounted for around 94 percent of all the methamphetamine seizures in the entire world. The UN agency reported an “immense volume of methamphetamine trafficked through land-based and maritime routes.”

Everybody knows that drug seizures represent only a small fraction of the total amount of drugs being trafficked through the region. Southeast Asia is facing down the biggest drug crisis in its history.

title: Supporting Asia’s Energy Transition
description: The role of alternative financing
text:
The Asia-Pacific region faces a substantial financing gap to power its clean energy transition. The need amounts to $79-89 trillion in investment by 2050 to meet net-zero targets, requiring annual low-carbon investment to nearly triple from $840 billion in 2023 to roughly $2.3 trillion by 2030, according to Deloitte. Government sources and multilateral development banks are covering only a fraction of this financing need. The Global Energy Alliance for People & Planet noted that the ADB’s $10 billion and the World Bank’s $2.5 billion commitments together account for “about 1.5 percent of the total investment needed.” Private capital must therefore play a far larger role.

However, two separate forces are now working in favor of closing this gap. On the demand side, the Iran war has sharpened the urgency of energy independence for import-reliant economies. On the supply side, several financing mechanisms, largely independent of the conflict, are maturing at the same time and expanding the pool of capital available to developers.

When the Iran war closed the Strait of Hormuz and sent fuel prices spiraling, Asian countries dependent on imported energy were among the most severely affected by this geopolitical shock. Asia’s economies run on oil they do not produce. The region sources nearly 60 percent of its crude from the Middle East, some 14.74 million barrels a day, leaving countries like Japan and South Korea more than 70 percent dependent on the route through the Strait of Hormuz. When the Iran war threatened to close that chokepoint, it exposed just how fragile this arrangement is: most Asian refiners lock in over half their crude through long-term contracts, with little room to diversify on short notice.

The conflict exposed a particularly significant structural vulnerability in the Philippines, which had long lived with a near-total dependence on imported crude. With roughly 98 percent of its oil sourced from the Middle East, the country found itself acutely exposed to a conflict thousands of kilometers away: electricity bills spiked, cooking gas prices nearly doubled, and diesel climbed toward PHP 85 ($1.38) a liter. But rather than simply absorbing the shock, Filipino households and businesses appear to be accelerating a shift already underway toward rooftop solar and electric vehicles, reshaping payback calculations, purchasing decisions, and even long-standing consumer wariness toward Chinese-made technology.

These consumer-level shifts illustrate rising demand for clean energy at the household level, but closing Asia’s financing gap also requires capital at utility and grid scale, the kind that governments and multilateral banks cannot supply alone. Several financing channels are emerging to meet that need.

Continue reading for free at The Diplomat’s new companion publication, The Investor.

title: Taiwan Can’t Fight Beijing’s History War While Erasing Its Own ROC Legacy
description: The push to emphasize Taiwanese identity is at odds with the government’s attempt to center the Republic of China in World War II history.
text:
At last week’s summit between U.S. President Donald Trump and China’s President Xi Jinping, the White House described the United States and China as World War II allies who “fought side by side to win the war.” It was a small phrase with a large omission. The government that represented China during the war, and fought alongside the United States against Japan, was the Republic of China (ROC). The government Xi leads – the People’s Republic of China (PRC) – did not exist until 1949, four years after Japan’s surrender. By collapsing the two into a single, unbroken “China,” the summit’s language risked allowing the PRC to inherit the legacy of a war it did not fight.

Taiwan’s government noticed. Its Mainland Affairs Council pushed back, insisting that the ROC was the “true ally” that fought with the United States during the war, and emphasizing that the PRC did not even exist during World War II. Deputy Foreign Minister Wu Chih-chung went further, calling the framing an act of “de-ROC-ization” – in which the Republic of China’s very existence is being erased from history, and replaced by the Chinese Communist Party. “We should feel very distressed,” Wu added.

Taiwanese scholars echoed the concern, warning that if Washington adopts Beijing’s version of events, the result could be a further hollowing out of the ROC’s place in the historical record.

There is an obvious irony in Taipei’s complaint, however. Taiwan’s government has been taking steps to distance itself from the ROC moniker.

This year, Taiwan’s representative office in Los Angeles sent out National Day invitations branded “Taiwan National Day.” The previous year’s cards had read “Republic of China 114th National Day.” The same government whose deputy foreign minister accused Beijing of erasing the ROC internationally was removing references to the ROC from its own diplomatic correspondence.

This trend also impacts how Taiwan’s government speaks about World War II. In August 2025, marking the 80th anniversary of Japan’s surrender, President Lai Ching-te referred to the occasion as the “end of the war” (終戰), rather than using the more traditional ROC-centered formulation, “victory in the War of Resistance” (抗戰勝利). Lai’s message emphasized the broader lessons of aggression, unity, and victory. Opposition lawmakers criticized the omission of the ROC’s wartime role, interpreting the terminology as part of a broader shift toward a more Taiwan-centered historical narrative.

The term “end of the war” is not new to Taiwan’s official vocabulary, nor does its use prove an effort to erase the ROC. But the choice of terminology in a major 80th anniversary commemoration illustrates a broader evolution in how Taipei frames the war and Taiwan’s place in it. The “Republic of China (Taiwan)” formulation associated with the Tsai Ing-wen era, together with Lai’s subsequent emphasis that the ROC and the People’s Republic are “not subordinate to each other,” has produced a more Taiwan-centered conception of ROC sovereignty. Critics argue that this can weaken the salience of the ROC’s pre-1949 history, the period when it controlled mainland China, even as Taipei continues to invoke the ROC as a sovereign state distinct from the PRC.

Successive Taiwanese governments have had domestic and diplomatic reasons to soften the ROC’s historical claims: a citizenry that increasingly identifies as Taiwanese rather than Chinese, a desire to avoid unnecessarily entangling Taiwan’s future with the mainland’s history, and a preference for language that does not appear to revive a rival claim to “all of China.”

The argument here is not that Taiwan’s evolving democratic identity is morally equivalent to Beijing’s historical revisionism. One is the normal evolution of a pluralist society’s self-understanding; the other is a state-backed effort to shape historical memory in ways that support a broader political narrative. But the two are not unrelated, either.

Taiwan’s own retreat from ROC symbolism complicates its ability to contest Beijing’s framing of “China.” It can narrow the space in which Taiwan is willing to defend the ROC’s history and identity, leaving more room for Beijing to present its own account of China’s wartime and postwar history.

Taipei has repeatedly emphasized that the PRC has never ruled Taiwan, and it has invoked the ROC’s historical continuity, as well as postwar arrangements including the San Francisco Peace Treaty, in making its case against Beijing’s territorial claims. These arguments depend in part on Taiwan being understood internationally as a political entity with its own historical trajectory – including a wartime and postwar history distinct from that of the PRC.

That creates a strategic paradox. The more Taipei reduces the visibility of the ROC’s historical identity in its own diplomatic and commemorative practice, the less salient that historical continuity may become internationally. This does not automatically strengthen Beijing’s legal case or alter Taiwan’s sovereignty. But it can give Beijing greater narrative space to portray the wartime “China” as an uninterrupted predecessor of today’s PRC, while making the ROC’s alternative historical continuity harder to communicate.

I have argued elsewhere that Taiwan’s assertion of sovereignty in its own waters suffers from a similar underlying problem: not insufficient assertiveness, but the absence of a coherent doctrine explaining when and why Taipei invokes its own claims. The same logic applies here. Beijing is contesting the historical identity of “China” itself, using the Trump-Xi summit as one more venue in which to do so.

Taiwan is right to object to historical formulations that erase the ROC’s role in World War II. But an objection becomes harder to sustain when the government’s own recent practice – from diplomatic invitations to commemorative language to evolving formulations of national identity – makes the ROC’s historical identity less visible.

None of this means Taiwan must reverse its democratic evolution or resurrect a mainland-centric ROC identity that most Taiwanese people no longer want. It does mean that Taipei cannot simultaneously retire the ROC as an inconvenient historical label and rely on it as part of the foundation of its case against Beijing. If Taiwan wants the ROC’s history to remain a live argument against the Chinese Communist Party’s claims to sovereignty over Taiwan, someone has to keep making that argument – including, consistently, the government in Taipei itself.
