title: Taiwan-Vatican Ties: The Dynamic Interplay Under Pope Leo XIV
channel_text: Blog; China Power; Diplomacy; East Asia
description: Regardless of the Sino-Vatican agreement, the practical, multifaceted ties between Taiwan and the Holy See have deepened over the past year.
text:
Pope Leo XIV succeeded Pope Francis in May 2025, becoming the 267th Pontiff of the global Catholic Church. According to academic and media analyses, Pope Leo XIV’s diplomatic strategy continues Pope Francis’ approach of “engagement” and “openness,” placing a particular emphasis on “peace” and the “de-escalation of potential armed conflicts.”

For Taiwan, the most closely watched diplomatic development during Pope Francis’ tenure was the 2018 provisional agreement on appointing bishops, signed between the Holy See and the People’s Republic of China (PRC). This agreement led the Chinese government to formally recognize the Pope as the Catholic Church’s supreme religious leader, facilitating the joint appointment of multiple bishops by Beijing and the Vatican under its framework. Since taking office, Pope Leo XIV has not altered the Sino-Vatican agreement; instead, he has accelerated the bishop-appointment process, ushering in a “rejuvenated” roster of Chinese bishops.

The Holy See remains the Republic of China (Taiwan)’s sole diplomatic ally in Europe. Since 2000, public discourse has frequently debated whether the Holy See might sever formal diplomatic ties with Taipei in favor of establishing relations with Beijing. Pope Leo XIV’s continuation of his predecessor’s approach to China implies a further deepening of Sino-Vatican relations. However, from Taiwan’s perspective, society should not underestimate its own standing. In fact, since Pope Leo XIV assumed the papacy, the Pontiff has received numerous Taiwanese organizations and individuals.

Furthermore, Pope Leo XIV has not shied away from being photographed alongside the Taiwan national flag. These gestures show that the Chicago-born Pope is friendly toward Taiwan, understands Taiwan’s significance to the global community, and recognizes the distinct differences between Taiwan and the PRC.

When discussing Taiwan-Vatican relations, the analytical lens must not be restricted solely to the continuation of the Sino-Vatican agreement or ongoing negotiations. Instead, one must examine whether the practical, multifaceted ties between Taiwan and the Holy See have correspondingly deepened. From Taipei’s perspective, the answer is a resounding yes.

From September 23 to 26, 2026, Chen Chien-Jen, former vice president of Taiwan and current president of Academia Sinica, attended the Pontifical Academy of Sciences (PAS) meeting and its biennial plenary session at the Vatican. Chen presided over the seventh session, titled “Medicine, Neuroscience, and Human Well-being.” Following the meeting, Chen and the PAS issued a joint statement titled “The Future of Science in a Changing World,” serving as an action plan for the international scientific community. Through the Holy See’s global platform, Taiwan once again showcased its scientific prowess to the world.

Shortly after, from October 7 to 15, Bishop John Lee Keh-mien, president of the Chinese Regional Bishops’ Conference in Taiwan, along with Professor Chou Te-yu and Consultor Yeh Chia-yen – members of the Holy See’s Dicastery for the Laity, Family and Life – attended a major conference at the Vatican. Hosted by Pope Leo XIV, the event marked the 10th anniversary of Pope Francis’ apostolic exhortation, Amoris Laetitia. The grand-scale conference welcomed 187 invited guests, including 111 presidents of episcopal conferences from around the globe. Taiwan was not only present, but Taiwanese scholars attended in their official capacities as members of the Vatican’s Dicastery, underscoring Taiwan’s deep engagement with the Holy See.

Furthermore, on October 19, Pope Leo XIV appointed new members to the Holy See’s International Theological Commission. Sister Hu Shu-qin, an associate professor at the Fu Jen Faculty of Theology of St. Robert Bellarmine, was appointed as a new member of the Commission for the 2026-2031 term. Sister Hu is the first ethnic Chinese theologian to be appointed to the Commission since Archbishop Savio Hon Tai-Fai, S.D.B., who served from 2004 to 2014. Her long-standing dedication to theological education and academic research in Taiwan has deepened Taiwan’s participation in global Catholic theology, further demonstrating the Vatican’s high regard for theological development in Taiwan.

Immediately following, from October 22 to 24, the Vatican’s Dicastery for Evangelization hosted the “The Church of the Sheaves” international conference in Rome. Under the theme “A Church for All: Synodal in Method, Missionary in Spirit, Credible in Love,” the event gathered over a hundred scholars worldwide. Grounded in the spirit and method of synodality, the conference emphasized mutual listening and sharing, signaling a shift in the Catholic Church’s approach to evangelization from the traditional model of missionaries transmitting and teaching, to local churches sharing and receiving each other’s gifts to enrich one another.

Professor Tan Liang-chen, an assistant professor and well-known public Catholic theologian at the Fu Jen Faculty of Theology of St. Robert Bellarmine, was selected to attend the Rome conference. He brought Taiwan’s voice – and the voice of the Taiwanese Catholic Church – to the West and the Vatican, sharing it with the universal Church.

The relationship between Taiwan and the Holy See is concretely built upon these small yet monumental steps. Taiwan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs has been advancing an “Integrated Diplomacy” strategy, using “Values,” “Alliances,” and “Trade” to expand Taiwan’s friendships – a deeper diplomatic approach increasingly evident in Europe. The good that Taiwan can bring to the world extends beyond high-tech industries like semiconductors and AI; it also includes the vibrant space for religious faith nurtured within Taiwan’s free society.

The stable, deepening relationship between Taiwan and the Holy See is the fruitful result of joint efforts by Taiwanese civil society, the local Catholic Church, and the government. These rich fruits stem from the relentless educational and research dedication of the Fu Jen Faculty of Theology of St. Robert Bellarmine and Fu Jen Catholic University. More importantly, they rely on tireless diplomats on the front lines in Rome and on Ketagalan Boulevard in Taipei. Even when the road ahead is fraught with challenges, they keep working diligently, paving bridges for the present and the future, which is why Taiwan-Vatican ties remain so steadfast.

In the face of shifting Sino-Vatican dynamics, Taiwan has no reason to worry; in the eyes of the Holy See, Taiwan remains an undeniably “precious” presence.
tag: Catholic Church; Catholicism in Taiwan; Pope Leo XIV; Taiwan in Europe; Taiwan-Vatican relations

title: Taiwan’s Local Elections Are Not About China, President Lai, or the United States
description: Candidates across Taiwan are campaigning on local issues that vary by city – not topics like cross-strait relations. What can we learn from these elections?
text:
This November, Taiwanese voters go to the polls to elect mayors, city councilors, and village chiefs. Many foreign policy observers will read the results as a verdict on Taiwanese attitudes toward China, President Lai Ching-te, Trump, or a potential war. That would be an analytical mistake. The outcomes cannot be explained by how voters feel about independence, unification, China, the United States, or any other national issue. As the saying goes, local elections are about local issues.

Decades of data show that Taiwanese voters prioritize China, sovereignty, and Taiwan’s future in national elections, but we have little longitudinal data on how they decide in local ones. What we do know is that voters often cast ballots for mayor or city council differently than they do for president. For example, Taichung and New Taipei have elected a Kuomintang (KMT) mayor in each of the last two local elections, yet a majority of their voters still supported Lai and the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) in 2024. Electing a mayor from one party hardly means a city will back that party’s presidential candidate.

Candidates across Taiwan are campaigning on local issues that vary by city, such as housing, public transportation, and urban renewal. Some touch on national issues, but most mayoral and city council candidates avoid them, since talking about national issues or polarizing figures could cost them votes.

One telling example is the absence of both the DPP and KMT party leaders from most mayoral and city council election campaign advertisements. Lai, who is also the DPP chair, and KMT chair Cheng Li-wun are both deeply polarizing figures, specifically for their positions on national issues including China and Taiwan’s relationship with the United States. Featuring Lai or Cheng in a local campaign invites voters to see local candidates as extensions of their party’s divisive leadership rather than a local candidate. In Taichung, for example, former president Tsai Ing-wen can be found far more frequently in DPP campaign ads than Lai.

Regardless of which party does well, both will likely frame the results as a sign that Taiwanese civil society broadly supports their policies, including on cross-strait politics. It would again be a mistake to buy that message. Local election results are not a referendum on party support or on attitudes toward the party chairs. During Tsai’s presidency, for instance, the DPP performed dismally in both sets of local elections, yet won clear victories in the national elections that followed. In Taiwan, national and local elections are neither tied to nor predictive of each other.

So what can we learn from these elections? Most importantly, they will set the chess pieces for 2028. A few key races will show which parties gain confidence and may shift factional politics.

One key example is New Taipei City, traditionally a KMT stronghold, and arguably the most important race this cycle. Outgoing mayor Hou Yu-ih is leaving office with high approval ratings despite his failed 2024 presidential campaign. His replacement should have an easy race, but the KMT candidate, Lee Shu-chuan, is struggling. Although he has a history of being a strong bureaucrat, Lee has run a lackluster campaign and lacks charisma. So far, his campaign has been bland.

His DPP opponent, Su Chiao-hui, is performing strongly for a DPP candidate in New Taipei. As the daughter of DPP heavyweight and former New Taipei mayor Su Tseng-chang, she is both a family legacy and a demonstration of long commitment to the city. She has cleverly avoided national discourse, emphasizing instead her record of delivering for her community.

Su’s campaign is leaving a far stronger impression among New Taipei voters than many suspected she would. The race is very close, and a DPP victory would dent KMT confidence heading into 2028 because New Taipei was supposed to be an easy KMT victory.

Importantly, a Su victory would not necessarily be a victory for Lai. Su is not a member of Lai’s faction, and although her win would be a major boost for the party, it would not raise Lai’s standing within it. Her victory would, however, help the DPP campaign with strong leadership in 2028. It would also send a message to the KMT that their traditional voter strongholds need more from their candidates than just a strong bureaucratic record.

Another example is the increasingly contentious Taipei race between the DPP’s Puma Shen and the KMT’s Chiang Wan-an. Chiang, the incumbent mayor and a 2028 presidential hopeful, was expected to win re-election easily, but Shen is running a strong campaign. Though best known as the founder of the disinformation research organization Doublethink Lab and the civil defense organization Kuma Academy, Shen has focused not on national topics like civil defense, but on improving Taipei’s livability. Chiang, meanwhile, has faced more scandals this campaign than in the rest of his tenure, and has so far run a particularly lackluster campaign. He is still expected to win, but Shen’s showing is unexpectedly competitive.

To a degree, the Taipei race is less about who wins, and more about whether Chiang can build momentum for a 2028 presidential run. If Chiang wins by only a few percentage points, it would be a big victory for the DPP and would hurt Chiang’s momentum if he hopes to become the KMT’s 2028 nominee. Even if Shen loses, his performance has been strong enough that he likely has a political future in the DPP.

Though unlikely, if the DPP were unexpectedly successful in taking both Taipei and New Taipei, this would probably lead to a political narrative about the KMT losing its traditional territory in northern Taiwan – not dissimilar to the narrative that emerged in 2018 after Han Kuo-yu of the KMT unexpectedly captured the mayorship of Kaohsiung, a long-time DPP stronghold. It should not, however, be over-interpreted to infer a permanent change in Taiwan civil society or a reflection of national attitudes. If Taipei and New Taipei elect DPP mayors, it will be due to the KMT mismanaging their candidates and campaigns, combined with smart, effective campaigning from Su and Shen.

Even if Chiang wins, the KMT faces a difficult presidential primary season. The field is already crowded: outgoing Taichung mayor Lu Shiow-yen, Legislative Yuan president Han Kuo-yu, and KMT chair Cheng Li-wun are all contending for the nomination. Cheng herself faces a difficult future if the KMT does poorly. Though she is not on the ballot, her opponents within the party are likely to push her to resign, which would leave the KMT’s 2028 presidential leadership up in the air.

Finally, the elections have exposed a breakdown in cooperation between the KMT and TPP. While the “Blue-White Alliance” has been a steadfast partnership thus far during Lai’s first term, the outward show of friendship has buckled this cycle. TPP chair Huang Kuo-chang withdrew in favor of Li Shu-chuan in New Taipei, but in Zhubei, the administrative capital of Hsinchu County, neither party would withdraw for the other, and the two suspended election cooperation in the county. This suggests that the parties may split again over a joint ticket in 2028, as they did in 2024, dividing the pan-Blue camp among its many potential candidates.

The 2026 local elections matter because they set the stage for 2028, but they do not predict who will win it. Once the national cycle begins, discussion will shift from local issues back to the dominant topic in Taiwan’s national elections: cross-strait relations. The 2026 results are not about China, Lai Ching-te, or the United States, but those topics will soon become salient again. For now, they are on the back burner.

title: Taiwan’s Maritime Law Enforcement Operations Spark Anger in Chinese Society
description: The reaction to a Taiwan Coast Guard confrontation reflects the existence of a particularly hardline strand of opinion on Taiwan among mainland Chinese.
text:
On October 1, a Chinese mainland fishing vessel came into a confrontation with a Taiwan Coast Guard vessel near the Pratas (Dongsha) Islands. After the fishing boat refused to leave the waters, the Taiwan Coast Guard vessel used a water cannon against it, eventually forcing it to leave the area.

Just one day earlier, the Taiwan Coast Guard had detained another Chinese fishing vessel near Penghu and taken control of its seven crew members.

The incident quickly attracted widespread attention on Chinese social media. Videos showing a Taiwan Coast Guard vessel spraying the Chinese fishing boat with a water cannon were widely circulated, prompting widespread criticism of what many described as the Taiwanese vessel’s heavy-handed conduct. Some commentators interpreted the incident as a deliberate provocation by Taipei on the National Day of the People’s Republic of China.

However, much of the criticism was directed not only at Taiwan, but also at the Chinese government itself. Some argued that Beijing’s repeated “concessions” toward Taiwan had encouraged Taipei to become increasingly assertive. Others even questioned whether Beijing is capable of effectively protecting Chinese fishermen. The reaction reflects the existence of a particularly hardline strand of opinion on Taiwan in mainland Chinese society, which frequently criticizes the government for being “too weak” toward Taiwan.

This challenges a narrative in which Beijing is portrayed as the main driver of coercive pressure against Taiwan, while mainland Chinese society simply passively absorbs Chinese Communist Party (CCP) propaganda about national (re)unification. In fact, in recent confrontations between Taiwan’s government vessels and civilian vessels from the mainland, Beijing has often exercised restraint and refrained from using its superior military capabilities in response.

Following the October incident, for example, the Taiwan Affairs Office of the PRC State Council merely called on Taiwan not to “use dangerous methods to treat mainland vessels and crew members in a heavy-handed manner.” Beijing has so far refrained from escalating the situation through its maritime forces.

This resembles Beijing’s handling of the February 2024 fishing boat incident near Kinmen, in which two mainland fishermen died after their vessel capsized during a confrontation with Taiwan’s Coast Guard. At the time, visible anger emerged on mainland Chinese social media. Related Weibo posts received more than 50 million views, accompanied by calls for retaliation against Taiwan. However, Beijing ultimately responded in a relatively restrained manner.

This raises an important question. Beijing has conducted repeated military drills around Taiwan in recent years, and confrontations between Chinese fishermen and the Taiwan Coast Guard might appear to provide convenient opportunities to demonstrate Chinese military power. So why has Beijing refrained from doing so?

Beijing must strike a balance between military deterrence and the image of itself as a guarantor of peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait. A forceful response to Taiwan might satisfy public anger in the short term, but it could also reinforce Taiwanese society’s perception of the mainland as a security threat over the longer term.

Beijing frequently uses military exercises as a signal to Taipei and the international community of its determination to safeguard national unity. However, although Beijing continues to insist that such activities are directed only at the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) and “Taiwan independence separatist forces,” polling suggests that a substantial share of the Taiwanese public regards these activities as a threat to Taiwan. Against this backdrop, any retaliatory action by the China Coast Guard or the People’s Liberation Army Navy against Taiwan could be presented by Taipei as further evidence of a military threat from the mainland.

Therefore, it is necessary for Beijing to calibrate the use of force carefully, lest coercive measures produce the opposite of their intended effect and undermine the credibility of deterrence. This may help explain why incidents such as fishing boat confrontations are not necessarily regarded in Beijing as occasions warranting a military response.

However, growing public dissatisfaction with Taiwan in mainland China could push cross-strait relations into a more dangerous direction. It could transform tensions between the CCP and the DPP into a broader conflict between two societies across the Taiwan Strait. Although direct interaction between people on the two sides has declined substantially since 2016, the remaining interpersonal, economic, and cultural ties between the two societies continue to play an important role in preserving peace across the strait.

A recent poll found that mainland respondents still held broadly positive attitudes toward Taiwan. Their average feeling toward Taiwan rose from 57 points in 2025 to 61 points in 2026, on a 100-point scale. At the same time, 38 percent agreed that force should never be used to achieve (re)unification under any circumstances, while 47 percent disagreed. When asked what measures could be taken if Taiwan formally declared independence, 81 percent supported “limited military operations on offshore islands,” but only 32 percent supported “a full-scale military attack.”

When asked why (re)unification between the mainland and Taiwan was important, 71 percent pointed to the two sides’ shared cultural heritage. These findings reveal an important ambivalence in mainland Chinese attitudes toward Taiwan: Opposition to the independence of Taiwan coexists with a sense of cultural affinity toward Taiwanese society.

Maritime confrontations, however, could cause this attitude to deteriorate, and the Chinese government itself could become an early target of public anger. For years, alongside military deterrence, Beijing has sought to improve Taiwanese attitudes toward the mainland through economic incentives and other forms of preferential treatment. However, these policies are often interpreted within mainland Chinese society as evidence of the failure of Beijing’s Taiwan strategy. These sweeteners have not persuaded Taiwanese society to move toward support for (re)unification. When PRC citizens see Taiwan’s Coast Guard forcibly enforcing its regulations against mainland fishing vessels, Beijing’s preferential policies toward Taiwan may instead be interpreted as a betrayal of the interests of the Chinese people. Beijing is therefore caught in a difficult position: Its restraint toward Taiwan can frustrate nationalist sentiment at home, while a more forceful response could undermine its longer-term efforts to influence Taiwanese society.

If such public sentiments continue to intensify, they could place pressure on Beijing to adopt a harder line toward Taiwan. A historical example can be found in the 2012 China-Japan dispute over the Senkaku (Diaoyu) Islands. Although Beijing initially sought to balance a demonstration of resolve toward Japan with the need to preserve Sino-Japanese relations, growing domestic demands for a tougher response contributed to pressure for escalation. After Japan proceeded with the nationalization of the islands, Beijing significantly intensified its response.

Managing the expansion of radical voices within society will therefore be important to keeping cross-strait tensions under control. However, this is not solely Beijing’s responsibility. Taiwan’s firm maritime enforcement may appear to reinforce the DPP’s longstanding hardline position toward Beijing, but its immediate effect may be felt not only by the Chinese government but also by Chinese society. Therefore, Taiwan will also need to calibrate its actions carefully to avoid turning maritime confrontations into triggers for a much broader conflict.

title: Taiwan’s New F-16s: Why They Still Matter
description: The Republic of China Air Force waited 20 years for these aircraft. What are they for?
text:
The arrival of the first pair of the 66 F-16C/D Block 70 aircraft on order to the Republic of China Air Force (ROCAF) has been a long time coming – and not just because of production delays. First sought as 66 F-16C/Ds under U.S. President George W. Bush, the request was blocked by his administration and remained unapproved under President Barack Obama, before the sale was signed off in 2019 during the first term of President Donald Trump. Yet their arrival comes after years of debate over whether Taiwan’s vulnerable air bases could sustain fighter operations in wartime, raising questions over what role the aircraft can realistically play.

Taiwan’s F-16 story begins in the 1970s. During that decade, it was quickly becoming clear that the island’s fleet of F-100 and F-104 combat aircraft was heading toward obsolescence. While agreement had been reached between Washington and Taipei for the co-production of the upgraded F-5E/F for the ROCAF, many U.S. officials themselves regarded additional F-5Es as inadequate as a long-term solution. Complicating any follow-on agreements, however, was the steady reconciliation between the U.S. and mainland China.

In 1978, Taipei’s request for F-16s was dismissed out of hand, leaving the F-4 and additional F-5E/Fs as the main options. A decision that year settled on the latter. High-performance fighters again topped Taiwan’s arms requests the following year, but Washington maintained its refusal to supply the F-4, F-16, or F-18.

In December 1978, Washington announced that diplomatic recognition would shift to Beijing on January 1, 1979, and formally gave the one-year notice required to terminate the U.S.-ROC Mutual Defense Treaty, which became defunct on January 1, 1980. This appeared to close the door on a major new fighter sale, despite the 1979 Taiwan Relations Act specifying that it was U.S. policy “to provide Taiwan with arms of a defensive character,” although what sales that required would be determined by the President and Congress.

Washington repeatedly calibrated Taiwan’s fighter access to its assessment of China’s capabilities and to the wider U.S.-China relationship. Ronald Reagan’s 1980 election campaign featured positive rhetoric toward Taiwan. However, after considering Taiwan’s requests for the F-5G (which would become the F-20) and the F-16/79 (a deliberately lower-performance export version of the F-16), the decision was once again made to reject the request and focus on the F-5E/F, as well as giving authorization for the transfer of used F-104 fighters from West Germany. Washington judged the F-5E/F qualitatively adequate against China’s then-current fighters.

Reagan institutionalized the arms sales problem in 1982, when the Third Communiqué between Washington and Beijing featured a pledge that arms sales to Taiwan would not exceed recent levels, with Washington stating that it intended to gradually reduce them over time, conditional on Beijing’s continued peaceful approach to the Taiwan issue. At the same time, the Six Assurances issued to Taipei sought to confirm that the U.S. had not agreed to set a date for ending arms sales, but the communiqué nonetheless remained part of the U.S.-China policy framework. At this point, Taiwan began the journey down alternative aircraft procurement paths, including what eventually became the F-CK-1 Indigenous Defense Fighter, produced with extensive assistance from U.S. industry.

However, the end of the Cold War once again changed the dynamic, and in September 1992, during his re-election campaign, George H. W. Bush signed off on the purchase by Taiwan of 150 F-16A/B aircraft. The decision was in part justified by China’s purchase of Russian Su-27 aircraft. Domestic politics also favored the decision: General Dynamics built the F-16 in Fort Worth, and Bush announced the sale there during an election campaign in which Texas aerospace employment was politically salient.

Washington continued to approve substantial arms sales to Taiwan over the following decades. From 2006, however, Taipei’s campaign for 66 new F-16C/Ds repeatedly foundered amid changing U.S. concerns that included Taiwan’s own defense budgeting, cross-Strait stability and the broader U.S.-China relationship. The Obama administration instead approved a major upgrade of 145 of the ROCAF’s existing F-16A/Bs. Taiwan also continued to explore a more radical solution to its future fighter requirement: in March 2018, Defense Minister Yen Teh-fa said that future aircraft should ideally possess short-takeoff-and-landing capabilities, identifying the F-35B as one possible candidate. However, attention was increasingly shifting back toward new (and more obtainable) F-16s, and the Trump administration approved the sale of the aircraft the following year.

The backdrop to this was an increasing appreciation that the ROC would not be able to match the PRC on a system-for-system basis. This included combat aircraft, which were also thought particularly vulnerable as their reliance on large, fixed bases left them exposed to being destroyed or trapped on the ground – a concern that likely contributed to Taiwan’s interest in the less runway-dependent F-35B. While Taiwan possesses an extensive network of hardened and underground aircraft shelters, and has practiced operations from roadways, the volume of precision fire the PLA could be expected to deliver would mean the ROCAF would struggle to sustain operations.

Reflecting this, Taiwan’s wider defense strategy and procurement priorities have also evolved. The “Hard ROC” concept of the late 2000s emphasized hardening, survivability and denying China a quick victory, even as Taipei continued to seek major conventional systems such as new F-16s. Admiral Lee Hsi-ming’s Overall Defense Concept, launched in 2017, pushed related ideas substantially further by placing much greater emphasis on force preservation and asymmetry. Elements of both – particularly force preservation, resilience and asymmetric capability – are now visible in contemporary strategy. The procurement patterns of the 2020s have also reflected the asymmetry requirement, with truck-based anti-ship missiles, HIMARS rocket launchers, anti-tank missiles and mobile surface-to-air missiles receiving major funding.

During Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, Kyiv’s air force confounded expectations by not only surviving but continuing to operate through the dispersal of its assets away from major bases and wider efforts at concealment. However, while we cannot be sure of the maturity or effectiveness of China’s precision strike kill web in advance of a conflict, evidence indicates both a much larger precision-missile arsenal with a more persistent surveillance network than that available to Moscow in 2022. Taiwan’s limited size and proximity to the mainland leave restricted scope for defensive countermeasures. The 2026 conflict with Iran has provided another warning of the challenge the island faces, with repeated missile and drone attacks by Tehran demonstrating the vulnerability of bases sited in close proximity to an opponent with a precision strike capability.

So, the question becomes: if Taiwan already has modernized F-16s, and a substantial body of defense analysis argues that conventional fighters would play only a limited role during the opening phase of an all-out war, why buy new aircraft at all?

The biggest difference is also the simplest: the new aircraft will supplement an existing fleet that has seen decades of use. While possessing the same radar as the older upgraded aircraft, the F-16 Block 70 does have some real advantages over the upgraded fleet. More powerful engines and a greater range and endurance, thanks to conformal fuel tanks mounted on the fuselage (the ROCAF possesses no aerial-refueling tankers), make them more capable in the interception, patrol, reconnaissance (particularly when fitted with the new MS-110 multispectral pod), and strike roles. The aircraft should also be more survivable once airborne than their predecessors, as they are intended to be fitted with the AN/ALQ-254 Viper Shield enhanced electronic warfare suite – although reports indicate this capability has not yet been installed due to production delays. A structural service life of 12,000 hours is around 50 percent greater than that of previous-production F-16s.

How these aircraft can be utilized depends on the scenario. In the gray zone, fighters give Taipei a flexible means of visually identifying, shadowing, and escorting PLA aircraft, allowing it to demonstrate control and resolve without immediately escalating toward the use of surface-to-air weapons. The new Block 70s are also relevant because of the high tempo of Chinese military flights around Taiwan: Taipei believes Beijing is attempting to deplete the readiness of its air force with interception demands. New airframes help meet the operational tempo.

They could also be valuable during a limited blockade, quarantine or coercive operation. By patrolling threatened air corridors, escorting aircraft, investigating contacts and contesting Chinese attempts to establish de facto control of the airspace around the island, the F-16s could give Taipei options for resisting coercion short of opening a broader air campaign.

In the event of an all-out war, the ROCAF would serve as a complicating factor. Suppression of an opponent’s air operations is resource intensive: any surviving Taiwanese fighter force would require the PLA to continue allocating ISR, strike aircraft, missiles, and combat air patrols to finding, suppressing, and defending against it. Large-scale amphibious and airborne operations are particularly vulnerable to disruption and normally require the attacker to establish at least local and temporary control of the air and sea. Even a small surviving ROCAF fighter force would therefore be a threat the PLA could not safely ignore.

The new F-16s do not solve Taiwan’s wartime airpower problem, nor do they negate the need to invest in mobile and survivable asymmetric systems. Instead, they preserve Taiwanese airpower as a usable instrument across the spectrum from peacetime coercion to full-scale conflict. The strategic situation may have changed in the two decades since this purchase was first proposed, but they remain valuable assets.

title: Taiwan’s Tech Diplomacy Has a Labor Problem
description: Migrant worker recruitment debt threatens the island’s access to Western markets and its ties with Southeast Asia.
text:
In an investigation published this October, three migrant workers at a Garmin factory in Taiwan said recruiters had forced them to sign documents falsely denying the mandatory fees they had paid to get jobs. Two reported that the recruiters threatened to retaliate and deport them if they disclosed the charges. These workers were making products for a U.S.-based electronics company.

The nonprofit Transparentem interviewed 24 workers at seven manufacturers operating in Taiwan and documented recruitment fees totaling $6,400 each. Compal, the laptop maker, and Garmin claimed they had long prohibited worker-paid fees. But they only reimbursed current migrant workers after investigators contacted them, and excluded former workers from compensation. Despite corporate promises, these exploitative charges continued.

These findings expose a blind spot in Taiwan’s economic diplomacy. Taipei and Washington should stop treating their technology partnership and Taiwan’s Southeast Asian labor relationships separately. Recruitment abuse threatens Taiwan’s Western market access and regional goodwill. Fair recruitment is just as integral to supply chain security as factory investment.

A framework for reform already exists. The February 2026 Taiwan-U.S. trade agreement compels Taiwan to prohibit worker-paid recruitment fees and related costs in manufacturing and fishing within three years of entry into force. Yet on October 6, Premier Cho Jung-tai said unresolved U.S. trade measures were delaying ratification in Taiwan’s legislature. Tariff negotiations cannot excuse delaying recruitment reform.

Taiwan’s Labor Ministry counted more than 910,000 migrant workers at the end of August, including approximately 100,000 lacking valid work permits. Among permit holders, 515,000 worked in manufacturing, with 127,000 of those in the electronics industry. These numbers reveal just how critical migrant labor is to Taiwan’s technology sector.

Rather than stopping at a recruitment fee, the brokerage system often continually exploits workers. Agencies abroad initially charge workers to secure jobs in Taiwan, and Taiwanese brokers then skim recurring service fees off worker bank accounts that they control. Taiwan also restricts migrant workers from changing employment, requiring extensive paperwork and official authorization. Debt and restricted mobility thus reinforce each other.

My fieldwork has revealed what is at stake. In May 2024, I interviewed a Filipino worker at a Hsinchu semiconductor supplier. The worker described 12-hour night shifts, six days a week, and a broker who deducted fees from her wages. Only Catholic missionaries and more experienced migrants offered the worker reliable support.

While debt alone does not establish forced labor, the International Labor Organization (ILO) recognizes debt bondage as an indicator of it. For a worker still repaying heavy recruitment fee loans, the cost of reporting abuse could be exceptionally high. Losing their job could not only force them to default on the loan that secured it, but also threaten their family’s very livelihood. Such fear of whistleblowing also makes buyers and regulators less aware of actual factory conditions.

The commercial consequences are stark. In September 2025, U.S. Customs and Border Protection detained imported Giant bicycles and related products manufactured in Taiwan over forced labor concerns. Giant subsequently expanded recruitment fee reimbursements. By September 2026, companies comprising over 80 percent of Taiwan’s bicycle exports had joined an industry human rights initiative. Customer access restrictions accelerated reform.

Electronics manufacturers should take notice. The European Union will automatically block products made with forced labor by December 2027. Exporters will soon face significant overseas scrutiny and potential import bans. Continued broker charges could then lead to shipment delays and loss of customer trust. Taiwanese electronics firms cannot continue offloading their due diligence responsibilities.

The diplomatic stakes are just as important. Launched in 2016, Taiwan’s New Southbound Policy promised a “people-centered” partnership with its Southeast Asian neighbors through trade, education, and closer social ties. The Philippines, Vietnam, Indonesia, and Thailand are key partners in that initiative; they are also the home countries of virtually all migrant workers in Taiwan. With the world’s lowest birth rate, Taiwan’s reliance on Southeast Asian workers will only grow. Since Taiwan has no formal diplomatic relations with any of these countries, properly treating their migrant workers is especially important.

Taiwan’s electronics sector would particularly benefit from improved ASEAN-Taiwan relations. Filipinos account for nearly 83 percent of migrant permit holders across electronic components and computer, electronics, and optical manufacturing. Properly treating Taiwan’s Filipino workers is thus integral to sustaining the U.S.-Taiwan technology relationship.

Recruitment costs have already generated bilateral friction. In 2020, Taiwan’s Labor Ministry rejected Indonesia’s demand that employers cover recruitment expenses and said it would consider recruiting elsewhere. In February 2026, the Philippines’ envoy in Taipei suggested Taiwanese authorities crack down on exploitative brokers and encouraged direct hiring. These governments want Taiwan to treat their citizens better.

While worker exploitation may not determine an ASEAN government’s policy toward Taipei, it can definitely sabotage Taiwan’s New Southbound Policy. Taiwan cannot credibly offer a people-centered partnership with ASEAN countries while exploiting their citizens’ labor. Protecting these almost 1 million migrant workers would thus strengthen the New Southbound Policy much more than limited business delegations or university exchanges.

Labor reform stalls partly because its beneficiaries lack political influence. Migrant workers diffusely spread all over Taiwan cannot vote, while concentrated employers and brokers can organize to defend their interests. A petition against employer-paid recruitment drew 5,929 endorsements. The Labor Ministry rejected demands to halt the planned ban, but such opposition reveals why external pressure is so helpful for reforming Taiwan’s migrant labor system. When access to export markets requires reform, employers are more incentivized to remedy an exploitative recruitment model they previously embraced.

Not all hope for internal reform is lost. Just on October 2, Labor Minister Hung Sun-han described preparations to end certain overseas recruitment charges from the end of 2026 into 2027. The challenge is turning those promises into actually enforceable protections.

Opponents rightly point out that recruitment costs money. Someone must screen applicants, process visas, arrange travel, translate contracts, and resolve disputes. Small factories cannot operate their own overseas recruiting offices. So banning worker-paid fees alone would simply push them underground. Policymakers must more narrowly focus on freeing workers from broader recruitment burdens.

However, there are successful examples of alternative models. On September 14, Taiwan welcomed 35 Indonesian hotel workers into its first foreign skilled hospitality worker program. Indonesia’s representative to Taipei celebrated the program, stressing that employers paid all associated recruitment expenses. Fairer hiring thus directly contributes to more diplomatic goodwill toward Taiwan.

Taiwan should align with ILO principles in having employers cover all recruitment and related costs throughout the hiring chain, including payments abroad. Beyond simply promising reimbursement, Taiwan should ensure that these workers do not have to advance the money. Otherwise, workers may still have to borrow money and wait for a nebulous reimbursement.

Taiwan should also block brokers from leveraging wage deductions to evade recruitment fee bans. Workers who document prohibited payments should receive restitution from their employer, which should be obligated to sanction the responsible recruiter.

But Taiwan cannot wait for its ASEAN partners to crack down on local agency fees. Taiwan should provide temporary transition funding to smaller suppliers, along with separate financial aid for low-income families to hire migrant household caregivers. These measures would help relieve immediate employer cost concerns.

In addition, Taiwan should make direct hiring more compelling. Taiwan’s Direct Hiring Service Center already assists firms with worker selection, applications, and multilingual services. But for employers to actually use these services, direct hiring must be as fast and reliable as their brokerage competitors. Alongside improving direct hiring services, Taiwan’s Labor Ministry should more regularly audit private brokers.

Taipei should engage the Philippines, Vietnam, Indonesia, and Thailand on fee ban enforcement. Taiwan could strengthen these critical ASEAN relationships through shared fee disclosures, joint recruiter investigations, and more accessible reporting channels. Migrant workers and their advocates should help shape enforcement measures. Those running Taiwan’s industries should also have a stake in their governance.

Finally, workers in Taiwan must be able to leave. Workers should be allowed to change employers if faced with coercion, wage theft, or unsafe conditions. Labor Ministry investigators should confidentially interview these reporters outside their workplaces and in their own languages. Additionally, Taiwan should work toward making work permits transferable within certain sectors. Otherwise, migrant workers would be perpetually vulnerable to potential employer coercion.

Washington should backstop these changes. U.S. officials could monitor fees repaid and mandate anti-retaliation requirements into subsequent trade agreements. Furthermore, U.S. buyers should bake fair recruitment conditions into Taiwanese supplier contracts and help shoulder remediation costs.

Congress and the administration should also mandate that new semiconductor subsidy recipients and their suppliers fairly recruit. Juggernauts like TSMC could thus pressure their vendors to improve migrant labor conditions. After all, federal procurement contracts already include an anti-trafficking clause that prohibits contractors and subcontractors from charging recruitment fees. Incremental funding releases should reward worker repayment and compliance while punishing continued violations. Domestic grants, tax incentives, and purchases could thus further the Taiwan-U.S. trade agreement’s labor provisions.

Some may argue that protecting Taiwan from China is more important than strengthening Taiwan’s labor laws. But detaining Taiwanese exports and alienating Taiwan’s essential migrant workforce weaken the island’s industrial base. Taipei is better off preemptively strengthening its own labor laws than letting customs officials and overseas customers set them.

Still, U.S. customers should avoid broadly abandoning Taiwanese suppliers, which may leave more workers jobless and indebted. Instead, buyers should encourage worker repayment while selectively punishing companies that conceal abuse.

Taiwan should not have to choose between resisting coercion abroad or confronting it in its labor market. Washington should help it do both. Beyond simply protecting Taiwan’s chip factories, preserving Taiwan’s democracy requires defending the freedom of the people inside them.

title: Tajikistan Taps Iran as Russian Fuel Runs Dry
description: Dushanbe's emergency hedge against Russia's fuel crisis puts Tajikistan in the path of U.S. secondary sanctions.
text:
Tajikistan has started importing oil and petroleum products from Iran. Deliveries began in late August, the Ministry of Energy and Water Resources told Asia-Plus on September 24, without disclosing the volumes, prices, suppliers, or transit route.

The shipments followed August 15 talks in Tehran, where Energy Minister Daler Juma and Transport Minister Azim Ibrohim met Iranian Oil Minister Mohsen Paknejad and agreed to set up a working group to prepare a long-term supply agreement. Dushanbe asked for up to 2.55 million tons a year (2 million tons of crude, 300,000 tons of diesel, 150,000 tons of gasoline, and 100,000 tons of jet fuel) along with discounted prices, dedicated tank-car trains, and a “green corridor” across Iran’s rail network.

The scramble is a product of Russia’s fuel crisis. Russia supplied 91.1 percent of the 599,500 tons of petroleum products Tajikistan imported in the first half of 2026, free of export duty. Tajikistan is not a member of the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), and Carnegie Politika’s Galiya Ibragimova described the cheap Russian fuel as “payment” for Dushanbe’s “political loyalty” to Moscow. But loyalty bought less fuel once Ukrainian drones began disabling Russian refineries, including the Omsk plant, which was knocked offline in early July.

Moscow has extended its diesel export ban month by month, most recently through October 31. Deliveries under intergovernmental agreements are exempt, but the carve-out has not kept Tajikistan supplied: diesel shortages began in June. By July, some stations were capping sales at 20 liters per vehicle and diesel had climbed to $1.40-$1.66 per liter.

In Tajikistan, domestic refining covers about 0.5 percent of gasoline consumption. Alternatives are scarce and expensive. U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran began on February 28, and Iran’s subsequent restrictions on the Strait of Hormuz kept oil prices above $100 a barrel in September. Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan are competing with Tajikistan for the same limited supplies from Belarus, China, Kazakhstan, and Turkmenistan.

Iran is an unlikely lifeline. Relations collapsed after Tehran hosted exiled Islamic Renaissance Party leader Muhiddin Kabiri in December 2015, months after Dushanbe banned his party as an extremist organization. In 2017, Dushanbe accused Iran of involvement in political killings during the 1990s civil war. The thaw came with the 2022 opening of an Iranian drone factory in Dushanbe and accelerated with President Masoud Pezeshkian’s January 2025 state visit, when the two sides signed 23 agreements. Bilateral trade reached $438 million in 2025, up 28 percent from the year prior.

However, Tajikistan and Iran don’t share a border. Moving 2.55 million tons of petroleum products by rail through third countries would take about 51,000 tank cars a year, according to Tajikistan’s Transport Ministry – roughly 140 a day. Iran may have little to offer beyond crude oil and jet fuel: Hamid Hosseini of Iran’s Union of Oil, Gas and Petrochemical Products Exporters said gasoline and diesel exports were not under discussion because of shortages in Iran itself, and put likely shipments at around 5,000 tons a month. The requested crude also exceeds Tajikistan’s refining capacity. The TK-Oil plant in Danghara has a design capacity of 1.2 million tons a year but has long run below it for lack of feedstock; another Asia-Plus report put the country’s two refineries at about 500,000 tons combined.

Then there is Washington. On August 24, the U.S. Treasury launched Operation Economic Outcast, widening the range of Iran-related conduct exposed to secondary sanctions and promising every country a “defined timeline” to shut down Iran-related activity. A Treasury official told RFE/RL that anyone in Iran’s petroleum sector “incurs that risk themselves.” Edward Lemon of the Oxus Society noted that the modest scale of Tajik-Iranian trade may keep Dushanbe below Washington’s threshold of attention. The practical exposure likely lies with whichever Tajik banks settle payments for Iranian cargoes, particularly if they clear dollars or deal with designated Iranian entities.

Russia still supplies nine of every ten tons of Tajikistan’s fuel, and on available evidence the Iranian route is unlikely to change that this winter. But it gives Dushanbe a second supplier at a moment when Moscow cannot guarantee much, albeit at the cost of sanctions exposure that grows with every ton delivered.

title: Tajikistan, Turkmenistan to Import Indian Surface-to-Air Missile Systems
description: Indian Defense Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh confirmed that Tajikistan and Turkmenistan are newer customers for the indigenous Akash medium-range mobile surface-to-air missile system.
text:
India’s growing defense industry has set sights on Central Asia for new customers. In early October, Indian Defense Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh, speaking to Asian News International (ANI) held up the indigenously designed and produced Akash medium-range mobile surface-to-air missile (SAM) system as a “success story.” He highlighted exports of the system to Armenia, Tajikistan, and Turkmenistan.

“The first customer was Armenia, which has taken multiple batteries,” Singh said. “Thereafter, we’ve also exported it to Tajikistan and Turkmenistan. Production has stabilised. We have additional orders for our own services, and I’m sure there will be many more from various parts of the world…”

Singh’s comments confirmed a report from July, published in Indian business magazine BW Businessworld, which cited official data as listing Tajikistan and Turkmenistan as export destinations for the Akash system.

Although ANI reported that both India’s Defense Research and Development Organization (DRDO) and the Ministry of Defense had confirmed that “Tajikistan and Turkmenistan have joined the buyer list,” neither of the Central Asian countries has commented publicly on the reports.

Central Asia’s militaries have been diversifying suppliers, but the bulk of region forces remain Soviet and/or Russian in design and procurement, with newer additions of Chinese, Turkish, Indian, and Western equipment.

RFE/RL’s Zamira Eshanova recently explained the variety on display:

Recent military parades show just how much Central Asian armies are diversifying their equipment. At its Independence Day parade in Ashgabat on September 27, Turkmenistan displayed a newly acquired Chinese FK-2000 air-defense system, adding to its existing arsenal of Chinese-made missile systems. Also on parade were a Brazilian-made A-29 Super Tucano attack aircraft and Italian-made Leonardo M-346 training jets.

Tajikistan, meanwhile, has displayed China’s HQ-17AE air-defense system, along with Chinese-made armored vehicles used to transport and protect troops. During its 2026 Independence Day celebrations, Uzbekistan also showcased Chinese J-10CE fighter jets. And, in recent years, Kyrgyzstan has acquired several types of Turkish military drones.

Essentially nothing is known publicly about the Indian defense exports to Tajikistan and Turkmenistan: the number of systems, the delivery timelines, or the prices.

More is known about the Armenia exports, which may provide some insight for Central Asia watchers. Armenia signed a $720 million deal with Bharat Dynamics Limited in 2022 for an unknown number of Akash SAMs and 15 Ashwin ballistic missile interceptors. Although deliveries were pushed back, in November 2024 Yerevan took delivery of its first Akash battery, which included four launchers a Rajendra radar. A second delivery reportedly took place in July 2025.

As the Oxus Society noted in an October 2024 report on Tajikistan’s military, “India’s military involvement in Tajikistan dates back to the early 1990s and early 2000s, beginning with the refurbishment of Tajikistan’s Ayni Airbase.” But after the base was refurbished, Tajikistan pivoted back to Russia, walking back plans for India to station its own military assets at the site. Instead, Dushnabe signed and agreement with Moscow to allow Russian forces to use the base. India has had access to, though not a permanent presence, at the Farkhor Airbase near the Afghan border.

Prior to the apparent Akash deals, India hadn’t sold any defense equipment to Tajikistan or Turkmenistan.

The export of one type of system, if and when they arrive into Central Asian hands, won’t fundamentally alter the military supplier balance in the region. But it underscores that regional governments are looking for additional partners and pathways out of strict dependence on Russia for defense materials. Such a move introduces new problems, specially regarding interoperability – the ability of different systems to work together effectively.

title: TenPayGo and China’s Digital Opening to Foreigners
channel_text: Blog; East Asia; Economy; Pacific Money
description: Tencent’s new payment app shows how China’s tech companies can lower barriers for foreign users without fundamentally changing the systems behind them.
text:
Attracting foreign visitors to China takes more than easing visa rules or improving transport links; visitors also need to navigate the country once they arrive. In an economy where much of daily life runs through digital platforms, seemingly small tasks – from paying for a meal to accessing everyday services – can become obstacles that shape how accessible the country feels to outsiders.

China’s effort to make itself more welcoming to tourists has thus also extended into its digital ecosystem. Tencent’s TenPayGo offers a glimpse of how one of China’s largest technology companies is approaching that challenge.

TenPayGo is a standalone payment app built around Tencent’s existing Weixin Pay network. Tencent publicly launched the app on September 24, allowing foreign visitors to pay using supported international bank cards and overseas e-wallets, like Apple Pay. It also offers translation and travel-related features, with additional transport and lifestyle services being introduced gradually.

The ability to pay with international bank cards on China’s digital platforms is not entirely new: WeChat Pay and Alipay have supported such payments for years. TenPayGo’s main distinction is that it gives foreign visitors a dedicated entry point to Tencent’s existing payment services. This could lower the barriers to using Tencent’s services and make them more visible to foreign visitors.

China recorded more than 150 million inbound visits in 2025, with spending exceeding $130 billion. Spending through mobile payment platforms reached more than $11 billion. Tencent reported that, between January and August 2026, the value of transactions made through overseas wallets in China rose 80 percent, while the volume increased 81.8 percent. These figures point to rapid growth in cross-border payment activity.

Other Chinese fintech giants are already in this market. Ant Group, the parent company of Alipay, said in September 2024 that the number of international visitors using its mobile payment services in China had quadrupled over the previous six months. Both companies have already spent years adapting their payment services to foreigners. TenPayGo therefore looks less like the creation of a new payment service than a move to make Tencent’s existing network more accessible and competitive.

TenPayGo also arrives as Beijing seeks to address a problem its own officials have already acknowledged: Visitors still face barriers when navigating China’s digital services. On February 5, 2026, 11 government agencies issued a policy plan aimed at making these services more accessible. By 2027, China wants to significantly improve the convenience of digital services for visitors, largely removing barriers in areas including accommodation, healthcare, payments, tourism, and public services, while expanding the range of situations in which these services can be used.

By 2030, it seeks to establish a more interconnected digital ecosystem aligned more closely with international practices. The plan also calls for multilingual services, integrated digital service platforms, more convenient digital payments and stronger data security and personal information protection.

In July, authorities launched a year-long initiative in Beijing, Shanghai, Shenzhen, Hangzhou, Chengdu and Sanya to improve digital services for foreign visitors.

TenPayGo reflects this broader effort, but it also illustrates the difference between making China’s digital ecosystem easier to access and making it more open. TenPayGo uses Tencent’s existing merchant network while simplifying the way outsiders enter it. This is a first step. But whether China can achieve digital openness will depend on how far it goes beyond the individual apps.
tag: Alipay; China digital payments; China fintech; China tourism; TenPayGo; Weixin Pay

title: Thailand Tightens Its Belt With 2027 Budget
description: The country's budget planners have been wrestling with the same intractable challenge since the COVID-19 pandemic.
text:
Thailand’s budget for the 2027 fiscal year is out, and perhaps the most interesting feature is what it does not do: it barely increases spending at all. Approved expenditures came in at 3,788 billion baht, which is roughly $113 billion. This is a mere 0.2 percent increase compared to 2026, and marks the second year in which spending has been held just slightly above 2025 levels.

As a result of tighter spending, borrowing is expected to fall and the deficit is projected at 3.8 percent of GDP. This is tacit acknowledgement that the government is running out of policy space for prolonged deficits and more borrowing. A period of belt tightening, or at least an end to belt loosening, was not unexpected, and this budget seems to confirm that the time has arrived.

Budget planners in Thailand have been wrestling with the same intractable challenge for a few years now. The economy never fully recovered after the pandemic, remaining stuck in a low-growth equilibrium. With protectionist tendencies on the rise globally, and increasing competition from Vietnam, Thailand has struggled to export its way out of the economic malaise.

To make matters worse, Thailand has high household debt, which makes it difficult for consumers to drive an economic resurgence given constrained purchasing power. The digital wallet program was an ambitious attempt to jump-start the economy through an infusion of cash given directly to consumers, but it was not as effective as hoped for. It was also expensive and placed more pressure on Thailand’s capacity to run deficits and continue accumulating debt. As of March 31, 2026, total public debt was equal to 66.4 percent of GDP.

The 2027 budget suggests the government is now facing up to this reality by freezing spending. The ministries of transportation and agriculture are facing cuts, while police and military spending will hold steady. Capital expenditures are expected to fall. Health, education and social welfare will see small increases, but there are no major new and costly programs on the agenda. Revenue is expected to rise 3 percent. If all goes according to plan, and with spending held steady, this will provide an opportunity to start shoring up the fiscal situation which has been deteriorating since the pandemic.

In 2019, the Thai economy was doing well, which was reflected in its strong fiscal position. The economy was riding a years-long wave of current account surpluses thanks to booming exports. The budget that year forecast a fiscal deficit of 2.7 percent of GDP, but revenue came in higher than expected and actual borrowing ended up being just 2.1 percent.

The pandemic changed Thailand’s economic trajectory and its fiscal reality. In 2020 and 2021, Thailand ran large deficits as it borrowed money to fund stimulus programs and shore up healthcare and social protection systems. Every country in the region did the same. But Thailand tried to get back to business as usual sooner than most, slashing spending by 5.6 percent in 2022. When economic recovery remained weak, the government reversed course and ramped up spending again, including on the digital wallet program.

The fiscal deficit in 2025 shot back up to pandemic-era levels of nearly 5 percent of GDP, and in absolute terms the government borrowed more money in 2025 than it did at the height of the pandemic. Final numbers for the 2026 fiscal year, which ended in September, are not in yet, but preliminary figures indicate revenue has been lower than expected and borrowing higher, placing increased pressure on the deficit.

The 2026 budget was something of a holding pattern, and it seemed likely last year that if things continued as they were, the government would start making cuts. The 2027 budget avoids drastic cuts, but spending is essentially frozen. Among other things, this means less fiscal firepower for the kinds of targeted programs that could actually help get growth back on track.

As long as Thailand’s economy remains sluggish, the government will face fiscal constraints due to weak revenue collection. When it had some policy space following the pandemic, it fumbled over the stimulus and flip-flopped on whether to spend or cut. A lack of policy certainty, compounded by political instability and frequent changes of leadership, has not helped.

In the absence of a quick return to pre-pandemic levels of economic growth, Thailand will likely continue on its current course of fiscal consolidation as it pays down debt, all the while keeping a wary eye on interest rates and hoping they don’t rise. We don’t know what the long-term political and social impacts of this consolidation will be. But the 2027 budget makes it clear that Thailand’s era of belt-tightening has arrived.

title: The 2026 US Midterm Elections: Ramifications for Australia
description: From AUKUS to trade, for Australia, the implications of the midterms are particularly profound.
text:
The 2026 midterm elections in the United States represent a consequential juncture in the evolution of the U.S.-led international order and, by extension, Australia’s strategic environment. Their significance lies not merely in the redistribution of legislative power in Washington, but in what the electoral outcome may reveal about the durability of President Donald Trump’s political mandate, the institutional constraints on executive authority, and the future trajectory of U.S. engagement with its allies.

For Australia, the implications are particularly profound. Its post-war strategic posture has rested on the assumption that U.S. military predominance, institutional continuity, and alliance commitments will provide an enduring foundation for national security. However, as the last two years reveal, the contemporary United States presents a more complex proposition. It remains inextricably linked to Australian security, while its domestic political polarization, transactional approach to alliances, and increasingly protectionist economic orientation have introduced significant uncertainty into the strategic calculus of middle powers.

The consequences of the midterms must therefore be assessed through three interrelated dimensions: the domestic institutional constraints they may impose on the Trump administration, the implications for the credibility of U.S. strategic commitments in the Indo-Pacific, and the extent to which changes in U.S. trade and industrial policy may affect Australia’s economic sovereignty.

The Congressional Balance of Power and U.S. Policy Continuity

The U.S. midterm elections determine the composition of the House of Representatives and a portion of the Senate, thereby influencing the legislative environment within which a president exercises executive authority. Their effects, however, extend beyond the immediate capacity to enact legislation. They can alter congressional oversight, appropriations, appointments, policy implementation, and the political incentives governing presidential conduct. A strengthened Republican congressional majority would potentially consolidate Trump’s capacity to pursue an agenda centered on economic nationalism, immigration enforcement, industrial protection, and a more explicitly transactional conception of international relations.

For Australia, the implications would be ambiguous. Greater legislative alignment could facilitate the implementation of U.S. defense and industrial initiatives, but at the same time could equally reinforce policies that subordinate alliance management to narrowly defined domestic economic interests.

In particular, a congressional majority sympathetic to protectionism could legitimize further restrictions on international trade, including measures affecting allied economies. Canberra’s diplomatic relationship with Washington would not necessarily insulate it from such pressures. Indeed, the fundamental tension between strategic partnership and economic nationalism may become more pronounced precisely because Australia is both a close security ally and an independent trading nation.

On the other hand, a Democratic victory in either chamber would produce a different, although not necessarily more predictable, policy environment. Legislative resistance and intensified oversight could constrain the administration’s capacity to enact its domestic program. Nevertheless, congressional opposition would not automatically reverse executive trade measures, eliminate presidential discretion in foreign affairs, or restore the policy assumptions associated with earlier administrations. Here, a divided government may generate policy instability rather than moderation, particularly where disputes over appropriations, executive authority, and national security priorities impede coherent long-term planning.

For Canberra, the critical variable is therefore not simply which party controls Congress, but whether the electoral outcome increases or diminishes the predictability of U.S. statecraft. In this regard, Australia should not merely equate Republican control with strategic reliability or Democratic control with international engagement. Both parties operate within a political environment increasingly shaped by strategic competition with China, an overstretched U.S. foreign policy, concerns about domestic industrial capacity, and demands for a more equitable distribution of alliance costs. These structural pressures will only persist beyond the 2026 electoral cycle.

AUKUS and the Problem of Strategic Continuity

As has been well documented, the AUKUS partnership represents perhaps the clearest expression of Australia’s dependence on sustained American strategic commitment. Its submarine pathway and its Pillar II advanced technology initiatives are designed to strengthen deterrence, improve interoperability, and reinforce the capacity of the United States and its partners to respond to an increasingly contested Indo-Pacific.

At the same time, however, AUKUS also exposes an inherent asymmetry in Australia’s strategic position. The program requires decades of investment, complex industrial coordination, technological integration, and political continuity, whereas the U.S. political system operates through short electoral cycles and increasingly polarized partisan competition. The durability and cogency of the partnership therefore depends not simply on presidential support, but on sustained congressional appropriations, industrial capacity, and institutional commitment across successive administrations.

A change in congressional control could have vast material consequences even if formal support for AUKUS remains intact. Congressional scrutiny of submarine production schedules, shipyard capacity, workforce availability, technology transfers, and the allocation of U.S. defense resources could affect the program’s implementation. Such scrutiny would not necessarily constitute opposition to Australia; it might instead reflect legitimate concerns about whether the United States possesses the industrial capacity, not to mention political will, to fulfill its commitments while meeting its own naval requirements.

The broader implication is that Australia must distinguish between the durability of the alliance as a strategic concept and the reliability of particular programs as instruments of policy. Canberra should pursue bipartisan institutional engagement, demonstrating that AUKUS strengthens U.S. security, supports defense sector employment, and contributes to regional stability.

Equally important is the development of domestic defense-industrial capacity and capabilities that reduce Australia’s vulnerability to delays in U.S. production. The objective should not be strategic self-sufficiency, which is neither feasible nor necessarily desirable, but greater strategic resilience.

Trade Protectionism and Australia’s Economic Vulnerability

The economic reverberations of the midterms may also prove as consequential as their strategic implications. The defining tension in the Australia-U.S. relationship is the coexistence of deep security integration with an increasingly contested economic relationship. Whereas the alliance is premised on mutual strategic advantage, U.S. trade policy under Trump 2.0 has increasingly reflected the proposition that international economic relationships should be evaluated through their contribution to domestic production, employment, and national bargaining power.

For Australia, this creates a structural vulnerability. The United States is concurrently a security guarantor, a major source of investment and technology, and an economy whose trade policies can impose costs on close partners. Australian exporters may therefore find themselves exposed to policy decisions driven less by bilateral diplomatic considerations than by U.S. domestic political imperatives.

A Republican electoral victory could strengthen the political legitimacy of protectionist measures, although it would not necessarily produce a uniform escalation of tariffs. Conversely, Democratic gains could increase scrutiny of the administration’s economic policies without fundamentally displacing the bipartisan turn toward industrial protection and strategic supply chain security. The U.S. emphasis on domestic manufacturing, technological sovereignty, and reducing dependence on Chinese supply chains is not exclusively a Trump phenomenon; it reflects a broader reassessment of the relationship between economic interdependence and national security.

Australia must consequently resist the assumption that favorable diplomatic relations will reliably translate into preferential economic treatment. In this regard, critical minerals, energy, advanced materials, and defense-related technologies offer opportunities for cooperation, provided that agreements deliver commercially sustainable outcomes rather than merely political symbolism. Equally, diversification should not be understood as a retreat from the U.S. relationship. It is a means of reducing the economic costs associated with policy volatility and strengthening Australia’s bargaining position within the alliance.

China and the Strategic Balance in the Indo-Pacific

The regional outcomes of the midterms extend beyond the bilateral alliance. Australia’s strategic domain is defined by the interface between U.S. power, Chinese ambitions, and the calculations of regional states seeking to preserve autonomy amid intensifying great power competition.

A politically strengthened Trump administration might adopt a more assertive posture toward China, particularly in areas involving military deterrence, technological competition, and economic security. Such an approach could align with Australia’s concern about coercion and the deterioration of the regional balance of power.

Nonetheless, greater rhetorical or economic confrontation should not automatically be interpreted as a strengthening of regional security. As has already been evident across the last two years, a more transactional U.S. foreign policy has engendered uncertainty about the circumstances in which Washington is willing to support its partners, the conditions attached to that support, and the relative priority assigned to different theaters.

Alternatively, a Democratic-controlled Congress might seek greater oversight of the administration’s foreign policy, potentially reinforcing institutional scrutiny, and encouraging more deliberate consultation with allies. Still, partisan conflict could also undermine the coherence of U.S. external engagement, particularly if disputes over appropriations or executive authority hinder policy implementation.

For Australia, the central issue is credibility rather than electoral ideology. Deterrence depends not only on military capabilities but also on an adversary’s assessment of political resolve, alliance cohesion, and the likelihood that commitments will be honored under pressure. Canberra must therefore evaluate concrete indicators, including defense appropriations, force posture, operational coordination, diplomatic consultation, and the implementation of agreed commitments, rather than treating U.S. domestic politics as a reliable proxy for strategic behavior.

At the same time, Canberra must recognize that its interests are not identical to Washington’s. Its prosperity and security depend on maintaining a stable regional order, functioning economic relationships, and effective diplomatic channels. An escalation in China-U.S. confrontation could impose substantial costs on Australia even where the underlying U.S. objective is strategically defensible. The appropriate response is neither unconditional alignment nor strategic equidistance, but calibrated alliance management that combines credible defense cooperation with independent assessment of Australian interests and sustained regional diplomacy.

Strategic Autonomy and Australia’s Policy Response

The midterms raise a more fundamental question concerning Australian strategic autonomy. For decades, Australian governments have sought to reconcile dependence on U.S. military power with the economic importance of Asia, particularly China. This balancing act has become more difficult as strategic competition increasingly encompasses trade, technology, infrastructure, energy, and supply chain security.

A politically weakened Trump administration might become more unpredictable as it seeks to demonstrate presidential authority or mobilize domestic support. Alternatively, a congressional opposition could constrain certain initiatives and encourage greater scrutiny of executive decisions. Neither outcome necessarily implies a more conciliatory U.S. approach toward China. The danger for Australia is that domestic political conflict in the United States could produce abrupt policy changes, leaving regional partners to absorb the resulting uncertainty.

Here, Canberra should therefore invest in regional institutions, practical economic cooperation, and sustained diplomatic engagement with Southeast Asia and the Pacific. These relationships cannot substitute for the U.S. alliance, but they can strengthen Australia’s influence and reduce the extent to which its regional position depends on decisions made in Washington.

Strategic autonomy should not be confused with equidistance between the United States and China, nor does it require Australia to abandon its longstanding security commitments. Rather, it denotes the capacity to make independent judgments, maintain credible national capabilities, and preserve diplomatic options when allied preferences and Australian interests do not perfectly coincide. The objective is to transform dependence into managed interdependence: retaining the advantages of U.S. security cooperation while ensuring that Australia possesses sufficient economic, diplomatic, and military capacity to navigate periods of uncertainty.

Conclusion: “Sing Me Songs of No Denying”

The ramifications of the 2026 U.S. midterm elections for Australia will depend on the interaction between congressional control, presidential authority, and the deeper structural changes reshaping U.S. domestic and international policy. A Republican victory could consolidate Trump’s political agenda, while Democratic gains could constrain his legislative ambitions and intensify congressional oversight. Neither outcome, however, should be interpreted as a definitive resolution of the uncertainties and concerns confronting the Australia-U.S. relationship.

The more resultant development is the possibility that U.S. policy volatility has become a persistent feature of the strategic environment rather than a temporary consequence of one administration. For Australia, this will necessitate a recalibration of assumptions about alliance management, economic interdependence, and national security.

The appropriate response is neither to distance Australia from the United States nor to assume that historical ties guarantee future consistency. It is to pursue a mature alliance strategy grounded in institutional engagement, reciprocal contributions, and independent national capacity. Ultimately, Australia’s security will depend not simply on who controls Congress, but on its capacity to operate effectively in an international system where U.S. power still remains prevalent, but overstretched and increasingly difficult to predict. The midterms should therefore be understood as a test of Australia’s preparedness and capacity to adapt to a more volatile era of U.S. leadership.
