title: The Afghan Taliban’s Growing Drone War Against Pakistan
description: For Pakistan, the most worrying possibility is small, relatively cheap drone systems falling into the hands of terrorist groups.
text:
Pakistan’s air defense system shot down eight drones after they entered the country’s airspace from Afghanistan on September 23. Four drones were shot down near the border at Torkham and four were shot down near Kohat in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. In response, Pakistan struck 10 locations in Afghanistan that were being used to launch and store drones by the Afghan Taliban.

This growing use of drones has added a dangerous new dimension to an already fragile Afghanistan-Pakistan relationship. On its western border, Pakistan now faces a two-pronged security challenge: first, the direct use of drones by the Afghan Taliban against Pakistani security positions and other targets, and second, the transfer or facilitation of drone technology to affiliated militant groups such as the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), enabling them to conduct attacks against military check posts and other targets inside Pakistan. What was once primarily a tool of surveillance, propaganda, and battlefield observation has evolved into an instrument capable of extending the reach, precision, and lethality of militant violence.

The Afghan Taliban began using unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in 2016, initially for propaganda purposes. Over time, however, their use expanded into operational roles, including reconnaissance, surveillance, and the delivery of explosives. Between February 27 to March 15, 2026 the Afghan Taliban claimed responsibility for 15 drone attacks in Pakistan’s Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province and Islamabad.

The Afghan Taliban procures its drones from a mix of sources, including commercially available platforms, systems obtained through regional networks, and locally modified or assembled equipment. This has made drone technology more accessible and harder to control.

The Afghan Taliban’s 313th Battalion, associated with the Haqqani network, is using one-way attack drones, referred to as kamikaze drones. The Afghan Taliban drones are launched from Kandahar, Nangarhar, Paktia, and Paktika, reducing the distance to targets in Quetta, Peshawar, Islamabad, and Waziristan in Pakistan. Recently, the Afghan Taliban have reportedly acquired anti-drone systems and are preparing to deploy them at the 205th Corps in Kandahar and near Spin Boldak to counter Pakistani drones along the border.

The concern becomes more acute when this capability is viewed alongside the TTP and other militant groups operating from Afghanistan into Pakistan. These groups have shown considerable adaptability in adopting new technologies, especially drones. This low-cost technology gives militant groups capabilities once associated primarily with conventional military forces. For Pakistan, the challenge is therefore not simply the presence of drones, but the growing ease with which this technology can be acquired, adapted and deployed by multiple actors across the border.

Pakistan has so far effectively intercepted cross-border drone incursions from Afghanistan. However, it needs to take further concrete steps, as drone use is becoming a persistent feature of the Afghan Taliban’s military strategy against Pakistan.

The most worrying possibility is not necessarily that Afghanistan will develop a large drone fleet. It is the multiplication of small, relatively cheap systems. A conventional military platform represents a significant investment and is therefore used selectively. Small unmanned systems can be acquired in larger numbers and employed repeatedly. They can observe a security position, identify a target, test air defense responses, and also carry an explosive payload. Even when they cause limited physical damage, they can create disruption, fear, and uncertainty. Pakistan therefore needs to treat counter-drone capability as a central component of national security rather than as a specialized military requirement.

There has already been movement toward domestic drone production. Pakistan’s defense industry and armed forces have experience with UAVs for surveillance, reconnaissance, and combat roles. Indigenous production is important because reliance on foreign suppliers can become a vulnerability during a prolonged crisis. A country facing an evolving drone threat needs the ability not only to build systems but also to modify, repair, and upgrade them according to its own requirements.

Pakistan also requires a layered counter-UAV architecture. The first layer should be detection. Conventional radar does not always provide an adequate answer against small, low-flying drones, particularly in cluttered urban or mountainous regions like Pakistan’s western tribal borderlands. Pakistan therefore needs a combination of short-range radar, electro-optical and infrared sensors, radio-frequency detection, and other technologies capable of identifying unusual aerial activity.

The second layer is neutralization. Depending on the threat, this could involve electronic warfare, communications jamming, spoofing, and conventional interceptors. No single technology is likely to be effective against every type of drone. A layered approach is therefore essential for Pakistan to counter the layered threat.

Pakistan should also invest in artificial intelligence and data analysis. A modern counter-drone system should learn from repeated attacks: launch patterns, flight routes, frequencies, operating times, and target selection. The objective should be to move from reacting to drones after detection toward predicting likely attacks before they occur. Therefore, working in this direction should be a priority of Islamabad.

Airports, power stations, military facilities, government buildings, oil installations, and major communication centers all require appropriate protection. Border management must consequently become more technologically sophisticated. Pakistan’s long and difficult western border cannot be secured through conventional fencing and physical posts alone. Sensors, surveillance aircraft, drones, ground-based monitoring systems, and rapid-response units need to operate as one network. Intelligence sharing between civilian and military agencies is equally important.

At the same time, Islamabad must avoid allowing the drone issue to become part of a permanent cycle of escalation with Kabul. Retaliatory action may be presented as necessary when attacks occur, but military responses alone cannot produce a stable border. Each strike carries the possibility of further retaliation, civilian casualties, and a broader deterioration in relations.

The Afghan Taliban therefore needs to come to the negotiating table. Dialogue does not require Pakistan to abandon its security concerns or accept attacks against its territory. On the contrary, negotiations should be used to establish verifiable commitments by the Afghan Taliban: Afghan territory must not be used for attacks against Pakistan; militants should not receive access to military technology in Afghanistan; mechanisms for investigating cross-border incidents should be created; and both sides should maintain direct communication during crises.

title: The Africa Pivot: India and Japan’s Quest for Critical Mineral Security
description: India and Japan are betting on Africa’s critical minerals as the two Asian powers explore joint investment to secure supplies and expand mining capabilities across Africa.
text:
A new axis is emerging in the global race for resources, and the Indian Ocean serves as a bridge. It is emerging as a critical corridor linking Africa’s mineral wealth to Asia’s industrial ambitions. Africa sits at one end of a strategic corridor, and its minerals are becoming the new terrain of strategic competition.

The continent is home to critical minerals essential for the global energy transition, including 55 percent of the world’s cobalt, 47.65 percent of its manganese, 21.6 percent of its graphite, 5.9 percent of its copper, and 0.6 percent of its iron ore. Africa is already emerging as a priority in ongoing India-Japan discussions on economic security and supply chains and, as the India-Japan leaders’ recent summit and the subsequent India-Japan Joint Declaration on Economic Security Cooperation confirmed, it now sits squarely within the partnership’s formal architecture. Backed by the India-Japan Joint Economic Forum, a new JETRO strategic report, and renewed focus on the Asia-Africa Growth Corridor (AAGC), India and Japan are positioning themselves to deepen cooperation in critical minerals, digital infrastructure, healthcare, green energy, and resilient supply chains across the Global South, seeing it as an opportunity for the next phase of investment. At the heart of this push is Africa, where the race for critical minerals is reshaping economic partnerships into long-term strategic leverage.

Forging a Trilateral Partnership for Africa’s Critical Mineral Future

India and Japan recognize the world’s growing dependency on China for critical minerals. China controls roughly 90 percent of global rare-earth refining and has also achieved a monopolistic advantage in development aid programs in Africa. This realization comes at a time when the new Trump administration, through an executive order in January 2025, titled “Reevaluating and Realigning United States Foreign Aid” has suspended all U.S. foreign development aid, putting several welfare projects for African nations at risk. Given this situation, African nations are eager to diversify their partnerships.

In this context, India and Japan can step up to support Africa’s development in a sustainable manner. Institutional cooperation on Africa predates both the Free and Open Indo-Pacific (FOIP) and the AAGC. In October 2010, India and Japan held their first Dialogue on Africa in Tokyo, launched after the Japanese foreign minister’s visit to India earlier that year. The dialogue sought to coordinate the two countries’ approaches to Africa amid China’s expanding presence, highlighting Japan’s financial resources and India’s capacity-building model.

However, a significant triangular relationship is reflected in an MoU signed in June 2025 between Pensana Plc and Toyota Tsusho for rare earth offtake. Toyota Tsusho, the trading arm of Japan’s Toyota Group, committed to offtaking up to 20,000 tonnes per year of mixed rare-earth carbonate from London-listed Pensana’s Longonjo mine in Angola, with processing at Toyotsu Rare Earths India (TREI) in Visakhapatnam before final delivery to Japanese magnet manufacturers. This represents a significant step in developing a global rare earth supply chain and strengthening and diversifying the broader rare earth value chain.

Similarly, the Mozambique LNG project, worth roughly $20 billion and led by France’s TotalEnergies, includes two onshore trains capable of producing about 13 million tonnes per annum. Within the Mozambique LNG project, Indian companies, along with Japan’s Mitsui, are already working in tandem on a major energy project in Africa. Indian state-owned firms ONGC Videsh, Bharat Petroleum, and Oil India together hold a combined 30 percent of Mozambique LNG, while Japan’s Mitsui holds 20 percent. This model could also be replicated in mineral projects across East and Southern Africa. While Japan has financed the expansion of Kenya’s largest port in Mombasa, Indian companies have contributed to related logistics and trade facilitation. India and Japan are also working together to enhance road and rail connectivity in countries like Kenya, Tanzania, and Mozambique.

The principle underlining all of these engagements is that India provides ecosystem know-how, implementation capability, and processing capabilities, and Japan provides patient capital, technology, and industry standards. Above all, producers in Africa are the core of the resource base.

In February 2026, Japan hosted the Japan-India-Africa Business Forum in Tokyo, organized by the Ministry of Economy, Trade, and Industry (METI) along with Nikkei. It drew over 2,000 participants from 46 countries and regions. The forum was held to discuss collaborative efforts between the public and private sectors of Japan, India, and Africa. At the forum, Japan launched the Japan-India Cooperation Initiative for Sustainable Economic Development in Africa. The initiative aims to encourage Japanese companies to concentrate their industrial presence in India to boost trade with Africa. It also focuses on expanding private investment, job creation, technology transfer, and human resource development in Africa. Through the initiative, Japan and India aim to strengthen supply chains by integrating the growth markets of India and Africa into Japan’s economic activities, with a particular emphasis on value addition in key sectors such as critical minerals.

In July 2026, the 16th India-Japan Annual Summit was held in New Delhi during Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae’s visit to India. The Confederation of Indian Industry (CII) and the Japan External Trade Organization (JETRO) convened the India-Japan Joint Economic Forum, which brought together more than 150 Japanese and 80 Indian companies. The forum was notable for the explicit place it accorded to Africa within the India-Japan bilateral architecture, signaling an intent to move the relationship into effective third-country cooperation. Through these and other engagements – including the August 2025 Modi-Ishiba summit in Tokyo and the January 2026 18th India-Japan Strategic Dialogue in New Delhi – these two Indo-Pacific democracies have begun assembling a parallel, intersecting architecture for engaging Africa’s mineral economy.

India has been in talks with several African countries to acquire critical mineral blocks on a government-to-government basis. In August 2026, India resumed talks with Zambia to explore investment opportunities in copper and other critical minerals, as New Delhi looks increasingly overseas for raw materials to meet rising ​demand from its rapidly growing economy. In Africa, ​the Democratic Republic ⁠of Congo and Zambia in particular can play an important role in meeting India’s growing requirements for copper and cobalt.

Africa has become a crucial partner given India’s need to diversify energy supply sources to achieve its renewable energy and electric vehicle (EV) goals and the government’s “mines-to-magnets” industrial push. With demand expected to rise nearly fourfold by 2030, and near-total import dependency on lithium and high-purity rare earths, securing diversified offshore supply has become a national-security calculation. India’s mission to build a sustainable future depends heavily on critical minerals. New Delhi’s approach is not built on “extractive models” but rather on long-term capacity building, skill development, and technology transfer to ensure that African countries develop a self-sustaining growth ecosystem.

India’s historical ties, along with its experience in trade and project implementation in Africa, combined with Japan’s strengths in finance and quality infrastructure, can provide an alternative development model in Africa. Tokyo has also been working since the 2010 Chinese rare-earth embargo to engineer its way out of single-source dependency. Hence, this will be a model in which India serves as the industrial concentration and logistics hub for trade with Africa while Japan brings capital, standards, and processing technology.

From Architecture to Action: Making the India-Japan-Africa Partnership Work

The architecture of this partnership reflects solid progress, but design alone does not translate into delivery. While India wants to keep mineral processing at home, Africa, through the African Union’s Green Minerals Strategy and national plans, wants to keep it on the continent. Japan needs access to resources in both cases.

The ultimate test of an India-Japan-Africa trilateral partnership will be its capacity to turn agreements into tangible projects while accommodating the distinct and sometimes competing priorities of all three partners. A Joint Working Group could help bridge ambition and delivery. With no formal group yet established, however, its ability to do so remains untested.

Whether the existing efforts translate into concrete outcomes will depend on execution. This includes whether Japan’s commitment of 10 trillion yen ($68 billion) over a decade through the India-Japan Strategic Investment Pact of 2025, and the critical-mineral, green-ammonia, and pharmaceuticals priorities, convert into bankable third-country projects rather than another shared vision document. There is a deliberate attempt to re-anchor the India-Japan-Africa relationship in a more coherent institutional frame, routing this effort through FOIP rather than presenting Africa as a standalone strategy. In this framework, FOIP has become the umbrella vision under which Tokyo and New Delhi organize their joint external economic diplomacy, from Northeast India to the Indian Ocean to the African continent.

Japanese capital, India’s industrial and digital capabilities, and Africa’s demographic and market potential are increasingly complementary rather than separate strengths. The strategic question is whether these strengths can be integrated into durable investment and supply-chain partnerships. The real opportunity is to turn that complementarity into an economic architecture, one that moves India-Japan ties beyond diplomatic alignment and toward strategic co-investment. Africa is emerging as the arena where India-Japan diplomatic convergence could acquire real commercial weight.

title: The Bangsamoro’s New Government Faces a Test of Public Trust
description: The main challenge of the incoming administration will be to sustain the peace process with Manila while representing the interests of local residents.
text:
Last month’s parliamentary election in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) in the southern Philippines, the first ever, has settled one question but opened another.

The election results are now clear. The Bangsamoro Federalist Party (BFP) secured 31 seats across the party and district races, the United Bangsamoro Justice Party (UBJP) 30, and the BARMM Grand Coalition (BGC) 15, with the remaining seats going to other parties and sectoral representatives. No party has the 41 votes needed to elect the chief minister. The 80 elected members of the first regular Parliament are set to assume office on October 30, marking the formal transition from the interim government to the first elected Bangsamoro government.

Most attention has understandably been directed at the question of which parties might come together to form the “Government of the Day”. But whatever its composition, the coalition that eventually emerges will offer an early indication of what kind of political order is taking shape in the Bangsamoro.

The September 14 election marked a transitional milestone from a negotiated peace settlement to elected government. The election results bring together political forces with different origins. BFP is composed of former combatants of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF), including local political figures. The UBJP is associated with the MILF, while BGC brings together established political parties and clan-based political networks.

The poll also reflects the changing place of the Moro National Liberation Front, a Moro armed movement that signed a separate peace agreement with the Philippine government in 1996, in this political order. Its two political parties from its two major factions – the Mahardika and the Bangsamoro Party – did not secure seats as Sulu, where the MNLF has historically had a strong political presence, is no longer part of the BARMM electorate. But MNLF-linked voices have entered the new political order through other parties and individual representatives.

For the BFP, its coalition choice means defining what its break from the UBJP political camp means for the next phase of Bangsamoro politics. A BFP-UBJP alliance would bring together the two largest parties, potentially forming the “super majority”. The two share roots in the broader MILF political tradition but have since taken different political paths, particularly after President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. appointed Abdulraof Macacua, then chief of staff of the MILF’s armed wing, the Bangsamoro Islamic Armed Forces, as BARMM’s interim chief minister in 2025. Macacua later joined BFP and became its chair and president.

Such a coalition would test whether political differences within the former movement can be managed within the institutions created by the peace process. It could also allow BFP to broaden its political base through UBJP’s strong showing in the sectoral races, while bringing BFP’s relationship with Manila into a broader governing coalition.

For UBJP, a BFP coalition would likewise have significant implications. The party remains closely associated with the MILF and the peace agreement that produced the BARMM. An UBJP-BFP coalition could provide continuity with this political project within the new parliamentary system. BFP’s perceived close relationship with Malacañang could help move some of the remaining normalization commitments. At the same time, such a coalition would require UBJP to navigate the question of national government influence, which has contributed to political divisions within the MILF.

For a Bangsamoro public that has long been sensitive to Manila’s role in BARMM governance, the stakes would extend beyond securing a parliamentary majority. The two political strands that emerged from the MILF would have to work together without blurring the distinction between cooperation with the national government in implementing the peace process and preserving political autonomy for the Bangsamoro.

The BGC faces a different choice. With 15 seats, it has the numbers needed by either BFP or UBJP to form a majority. It has already indicated that it is open to working with either party, and its political forces bring established parties, local networks, and experience in governing into an arena increasingly shaped by MILF-linked politics. As such, it could bring familiarity with local government and the political relationships and practices that have shaped the region for decades. At the same time, its ranks include emerging political voices who may bring different priorities and forms of representation to the new Parliament. Depending on its choice, the BGC’s role in shaping the first elected government could either reinforce established ways of exercising political power or broaden what the new parliamentary system can represent.

BFP has since announced that it has secured enough support to form a majority, although coalition discussions among the parties are continuing. This makes the coalition combinations less hypothetical. A BFP-UBJP coalition signals an effort to reconcile competing strands of the MILF political project. A BFP-BGC or UBJP-BGC coalition would demonstrate how movement-linked politics and established political networks are negotiating power within the new parliamentary system. Much will depend on what the parties ask of one another in exchange for governing together and what they are prepared to commit to the Bangsamoro public. But the burden now falls more heavily on BFP to show what this majority is assembled around. Securing votes is one task; building a coalition with a shared governing agenda is another. A coalition can be politically viable without necessarily being ideologically coherent.

If the BGC and the established political networks aligned with it are central to the new government, that would not necessarily mean a reversal of the political transformation envisioned by the peace process. It could instead show that the new political order is becoming a negotiated space between movement-linked politics and longstanding sources of local political power.

However, the coalition question cannot be separated from the environment in which the new government will have to govern. As I noted before the polls, the challenge was not simply avoiding localized violence but ensuring that political disputes could still be contained through the institutions and relationships established by the peace process.

In Cotabato City, election-related violence before and on election day left several people dead and injured. Shortly after the election, localized fighting in BARMM’s Special Geographic Area prompted the deployment of joint Philippine government-MILF security mechanisms. These incidents exposed the complexity of the transition currently taking place in BARMM.

Another issue that may become more visible is the relationship between the new Bangsamoro government and Manila. With an elected government taking shape, the Bangsamoro public has stronger expectations that the BARMM should have greater political space to determine its leadership and governing arrangements. The issue will be how Manila’s involvement is perceived: as a support for Bangsamoro institutions or as an attempt to shape their political outcomes. If the latter perception takes hold, it could complicate the new government’s efforts to establish its own political authority.

For the incoming government, the mandate should extend beyond running the regional administration. It will also have to demonstrate a clear commitment to completing the remaining normalization commitments under the peace process, working closely with the MILF as a peace partner while maintaining a constructive relationship with the national government – while not becoming so closely identified with either that it loses the political space needed to govern in the interests of the Bangsamoro people.

The peace process in the southern Philippines sought to create institutions through which political authority could be acquired, exercised, and contested. The challenge for the new government will be to remain autonomous enough to govern in the interests of local people, but engaged enough to sustain the peace process.

title: The China-EU Trade Truce Buys Time
description: For the EU, the choice is increasingly difficult: secure real concessions from Beijing to address structural trade imbalances or deploy stronger unilateral measures to protect its industrial base.
text:
Like last month’s summit between the U.S. and Chinese presidents, the China-EU Trade and Investment Consultations in Beijing were primarily about stabilization rather than a breakthrough. EU Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic and Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao closed a handful of agreements and confirmed that neither side wants a trade war. However, the structural issues remain unresolved. What both sides gained is time.

For the European Union, the choice is increasingly difficult: secure real concessions from Beijing to address structural trade imbalances or deploy stronger unilateral measures to protect its industrial base. Compounding this dilemma is Europe’s risk of becoming an adjustment variable in the China-U.S. strategic competition, absorbing diverted Chinese exports when tensions escalate while losing market opportunities and negotiating leverage when Washington and Beijing strike bilateral deals. Washington holds the technology lever, while Beijing controls critical minerals and key nodes of global supply chains. Europe depends on both.

The most concrete outcome of the talks concerns the automotive sector. Under a preliminary deal, Chinese exports of hybrid and plug-in hybrid vehicles to the EU could be curbed more than half against projected levels over the next four years. The stakes are high. In 2025, the EU imported more than 1 million Chinese-made cars, worth $15.5 billion (13.7 billion euros) and up 30 percent in volume on 2024. Hybrids tell the story best: 659 Chinese hybrids sold in the EU in 2022, versus more than 160,000 in the first seven months of 2026, plus almost 218,000 plug-in hybrids.

Chinese brands now hold almost 12 percent of Europe’s new-car market, up from 1 percent five years ago, and roughly a third of plug-in hybrid sales. In the United States, Chinese cars are absent. Washington has effectively shut Chinese electric vehicles out of its market through 100 percent tariffs, while Europe remains far more exposed to Chinese automotive imports. The U.S., a market of 16.2 million new vehicles, bought fewer than 90,000 China-made vehicles in 2024, almost all of them Western brands built in China.

The rapid expansion of Chinese carmakers has intensified competitive pressures on European manufacturers, particularly in Germany and France, which had pushed for tougher trade measures. The proposed 50 percent reduction in Chinese hybrid exports is a step forward, but it is measured against projected growth, not current volumes.

China’s hybrid expansion accelerated after the EU imposed tariffs on Chinese battery-electric vehicles in 2024. Manufacturers shifted toward hybrids, which were exempt from those duties. While Washington imposed steep barriers to Chinese electric vehicles, Brussels left a significant loophole. The hybrid cars deal is therefore less a breakthrough than an attempt to correct a weakness in Europe’s trade policy.

As for whether the deal will work, much will depend on enforcement. Effective restrictions could give European automakers time to adjust. Weak implementation would allow Chinese exports to expand further, forcing Brussels to consider tougher measures and risking retaliation that could disrupt supply chains and investment on both sides. Meanwhile, Chinese automakers are increasingly moving from exports to manufacturing inside Europe. The strategic question is no longer simply how many Chinese cars are imported in the European market, but where industrial value is created, who controls the technology, and where the jobs are located.

The second result concerns market access and trade rebalancing. Brussels and Beijing agreed to cut tariffs on a range of EU products to the most-favored-nation (MFN) rates set under WTO rules. The goods covered, from car parts to olive oil and footwear, account for nearly $4.7 billion in exports. If implemented, the measure would save European exporters at least $260 million in duties.

Set against the trade figures, however, it is a small gain. In her State of the Union speech, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called the EU’s deficit with China “unsustainable.” It now runs at more than 1 billion euros a day. The goods deficit rose from 306 billion euros in 2024 to 360 billion euros in 2025 and could reach 400 billion euros ($470 billion) this year, according to Eurostat.

The United States, meanwhile, moved in the opposite direction. In 2025, its goods deficit with China fell by almost a third to $202 billion, the lowest in two decades, as imports from China dropped 30 percent. China’s share of U.S. imports fell to about 9 percent, the lowest since it joined the WTO in 2001. The EU’s goods deficit with China is now twice America’s. What Washington kept out with tariffs, Europe increasingly absorbs.

Sefcovic defended the new deal with China as the result of an intense negotiation, noting that Washington had needed far more rounds to get its own deal. But he warned against complacency.

The third result concerns critical raw materials, above all rare earths and permanent magnets. This is where Europe depends on China most – 98 percent of EU demand for rare earth magnets is met by Chinese imports. Beijing will ease export licensing for European companies through a green channel. That matters for carmakers, renewables, and defense. But Beijing keeps control of the licenses, and with it the power to turn supplies on and off.

Washington got more. At the Busan summit in October 2025, the United States secured a one-year suspension of China’s new export restrictions and general licenses for its companies. The White House summit in September 2026 extended that suspension until January 10, 2027. Brussels obtained faster procedures for licenses that remain individual and revocable. Washington negotiated with tariffs and semiconductor controls on the table. Europe only trade-defense tools it has yet to use.

The industrial strategies differ as well. The United States has stepped up directly, with the Pentagon taking a stake in MP Materials and Washington forging minerals deals with Australia and Japan. Europe is relying on the Critical Raw Materials Act and RESourceEU, a sound framework but slower and less funded. Faster licenses make Europe’s supplies more predictable, but they do not make it less dependent.

That’s not to say Europe has no leverage. Four days before the talks, France and Germany jointly called for stronger trade defense instruments against Chinese overcapacity, subsidies, and market distortions. Beijing got the message. In response, official Beijing urged Paris and Berlin not to push the EU toward protectionist tools. Germany’s position carried the most weight. The European Commission went to Beijing with more leverage than before.

EU leaders will discuss the deal at the European Council on October 15–16. They will find a difficult balance in it. The hybrid agreement limits Chinese exports that hurt European carmakers. The rare earth agreement eases Chinese exports that the same carmakers rely on. Europe wants fewer of some Chinese goods and a steady supply of others, and on both counts the decision rests with Beijing. The recent truce calms the relationship but leaves the imbalances in place.

What Europe does with the next few months will matter more than the deal itself. If it invests in competitiveness, innovation and economic security, it can negotiate from strength next time. If it doesn’t, it will remain the adjustment variable in a rivalry it does not control.

title: The China-Taiwan Diplomatic War Is More About Politics Than Economics
channel_text: Blog; China Power; Diplomacy; East Asia
description: Taiwan’s formal relationships in Africa and Latin America point to the real factors driving recognition decisions – and it’s not “dollar diplomacy.”
text:
Since the Chinese Civil War concluded in 1949, the People’s Republic of China (PRC) and the Republic of China (ROC) have battled endlessly for diplomatic recognition. Due to Beijing’s “One China” principle, states are forced to either pick one side or pick neither.

The ROC, now colloquially better known as Taiwan, initially enjoyed an advantage in international recognition due to U.S. anti-communist messaging and generous economic assistance programs. After U.N. Resolution 2758 admitted the PRC to the United Nations and expelled the ROC, the battle for international recognition has tilted increasingly in Beijing’s favor.

Nevertheless, Taiwan still holds formal diplomatic relations across the globe. Three Pacific island-nations – the Marshall Islands, Palau, and Tuvalu – recognize the ROC over the PRC, receiving major financial assistance in return. In Europe, Taiwan has one diplomatic ally, the Vatican. In Africa, Taiwan maintains formal relations with Eswatini (where President Lai Ching-te visited in May), and conducts high-level diplomatic exchanges with the partially-recognized East African state, Somaliland. The Americas, meanwhile, hold seven of Taiwan’s 12 remaining embassies. These states challenge Beijing’s extensive efforts to isolate Taiwan diplomatically, demonstrating that Taipei can maintain and strengthen relations with sovereign nations.

Analyzing Taiwan’s relations with Africa and Latin America comparatively, we can see how and under what circumstances Taipei’s Global South engagement has prevailed against Beijing’s diplomatic efforts. Although economic assistance programs have been critical, Taiwan’s formal relations ultimately depend on political leverage drawn from diplomatic recognition rather than purely economic considerations. The recognition of Taiwan will therefore continue to serve as a political tool for smaller countries, independence movements, and breakaway states that find greater gain from Taipei than Beijing.

Africa

Until UNGA Resolution 2758 passed in 1971, Taiwan maintained widespread recognition throughout Africa. During decolonization in the 1950s and 1960s, most newly-independent African states were wary of Beijing’s communist ideology and optimistic about their inclusion into the international community. Thus, incentivized by Taiwan’s foreign assistance, many African countries recognized the ROC over the PRC as the representative of China between 1960 and 1963.

By 1971, the year of Resolution 2758, the PRC and Taiwan had an almost equal number of African countries’ recognition (Taiwan’s 20 to the PRC’s 22). Only five African countries recognized the ROC by 1979, highlighting the UNGA Resolution’s devastating impact on Taiwan’s international legitimacy.

Since African decolonization, Taipei and Beijing have engaged in “dollar diplomacy,” leveraging favorable loans, technical knowledge-sharing, trade, and agricultural assistance to compete for support. Starting in 1960, Taipei began international development programs, trade incentives, and investments throughout Africa to preserve its influence despite being reliant on U.S. aid itself. Taiwan has become increasingly incapable of competing for African countries’ recognition as its economy has become dwarfed by the PRC in recent decades.

Burkina Faso was the latest African country to withdraw its recognition of Taiwan, doing so in 2018. Formerly known as Upper Volta, Burkina Faso first severed relations with Taiwan in 1973, along with much of the rest of the continent. In 1994, under coup-installed former president Blaise Compaoré, Burkina Faso reestablished relations with Taiwan in pursuit of a lucrative economic relationship.

Due to China’s expanding economy, the Belt and Road Initiative, and chaotic power transfers, Burkina Faso eventually switched its recognition back to the PRC in 2018 after Compaoré lost power.

Notably, Taiwan’s response solely blamed the PRC. Rather than condemning Burkina Faso’s decision to withdraw recognition of Taiwan, then-President Tsai Ing-wen attacked Beijing for its “serial acts of suppression against Taiwan in the diplomatic sphere” through economic coercion and political interference.

A series of coups over the past decade has placed Burkina Faso firmly within the PRC’s sphere of influence, with Western counterterrorism forces being expelled and China’s economic and military investment in the country increasing.

Facing dwindling formal relations, Taiwan has adopted a “pragmatic diplomacy” approach, which prioritizes de facto economic influence over political recognition. In Africa, Taiwan operates trade and political representative offices in Nigeria, South Africa, Côte d’Ivoire, and Somaliland. Several quasi-governmental and non-state organizations expand Taiwan’s economic influence on the continent, such as the Taiwan External Trade Development Council, the International Cooperation and Development Fund, and the Taiwan-Africa Business Association. While these organizations have failed to quell the rapidly expanding PRC influence across Africa, they highlight Taiwan’s capacity to maintain a diplomatic presence.

Eswatini’s continued support for Taiwan has resulted in both diplomatic condemnation and economic exclusion from Beijing. In 2026, the PRC prevented Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te from visiting Eswatini during celebrations of King Mswati III’s 40th year in power by pressuring Seychelles, Mauritius, and Madagascar to revoke flight permits for Taiwan’s delegation. Lai clandestinely visited Eswatini the following month despite Beijing’s efforts to prevent the trip. However the episode illustrated how the PRC can use its political and economic clout against Taiwanese diplomacy.

Additionally, Eswatini’s exclusion from PRC investment through institutions like the Forum on China-Africa Cooperation (FOCAC) introduces an opportunity cost that harms the country’s economic competitiveness. Eswatini’s status as a monarchy, however, reduces the salience of political grievances tied to broader social, political, or economic conditions derivative of its adversarial relationship with the PRC.

Somaliland, the breakaway region of northern Somalia, has developed a unique relationship with Taiwan. Most countries deny Somaliland’s political status. Since declaring independence in 1991, Somaliland has lobbied the international community to recognize it as a fully autonomous state, with Israel being the only U.N. member state to recognize its independence in 2025. In similar states of de facto independence, Taiwan and Somaliland enhanced their bilateral relationship in 2020 to increase shared economic investment in East Africa and cement their political willingness to explore new, Western-aligned friendships.

Taiwan has implemented many development programs there for public health, education, government modernization, democratization, and humanitarian assistance. Taiwan’s ICDF currently facilitates six development programs in Somaliland, while Taiwan benefits from increased political and economic access to East Africa. While Somaliland has not officially established diplomatic recognition of Taiwan, the relationship could prove to be consequential for China-U.S. competition and rising insecurity in the Horn of Africa.

In its pursuit of legitimacy, Taiwan will see more success in diplomatic initiatives targeting smaller, less established, or more politically unique states. Countries that have already carved their places in the international community are less likely to have political environments conducive to recognition of Taiwan over the PRC, as they will prioritize economic opportunity and stability over Taiwan’s aspirations.

The PRC’s rapid economic growth and its “One China” principle” create a geopolitical competition stacked against Taiwan. Moving forward, Taiwan will likely have to leverage future relationships with breakaway movements, global pariahs, and peculiar governments to rebuild its international influence.

Latin America

In Latin America, Taiwan’s diplomatic partnerships date back many decades. Unlike in Africa, where most countries were colonies until the 1960s, Latin American nations have been independent since the 19th century. Most established relations with the ROC before it relocated to Taiwan in 1949. Taipei then consolidated its diplomatic standing by establishing new relations with Haiti, Paraguay, and Uruguay in the mid-1950s. The ROC similarly established relations with newly-independent Grenada, Dominica, St. Kitts and Nevis, St. Vincent and the Grenadines, St. Lucia, and Belize in the 1980s.

The Cold War aided Taiwan, as Latin American governments could signal U.S. alignment by maintaining relations with the anticommunist ROC over the communist PRC. In fact, only Cuba and Chile cut ties with the ROC to establish relations with the PRC before 1971, both under leftist, Marxism-endorsing leaders. Although Mexico and most South American countries switched in the 1970s and 1980s, Taiwan continued commercial and cultural relations with these countries and still holds commercial offices in Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Ecuador, Mexico, and Peru.

As in Africa, Taiwan’s agricultural advisory missions significantly improved Latin American food production. One such mission more than doubled Dominican rice yields from 1972-82. Also like in Africa, Taiwan and China’s “dollar diplomacy” took off in the 1990s and 2000s, as Taiwan significantly increased economic donations to its allies, while China gave bountiful gifts in exchange for switching recognition, including stadiums in Dominica, Grenada, the Bahamas, and Costa Rica between 1997 and 2007.

Following the “diplomatic truce” with Beijing during Ma Ying-jeou’s 2008-16 administration, China resumed its diplomatic poaching after Tsai Ing-wen was elected in 2016. In 2017 and 2018, Panama, the Dominican Republic and El Salvador switched to China, reportedly securing hundreds of millions in Chinese funds in exchange.

Notably, the first Trump administration condemned El Salvador’s decision, and Trump signed the 2020 Taiwan Allies International Protection and Enhancement Initiative (TAIPEI) Act, which codifies U.S. support for Taiwan’s remaining diplomatic partnerships. The Biden administration rebuked Nicaragua’s dynastic dictatorship for ditching Taiwan and embracing China in 2021, and attempted to stop Honduras’ leftist government from doing the same two years later.

Despite Beijing’s best efforts, however, seven countries in the Americas continue opting for relations with Taiwan over China: Belize, Guatemala, Haiti, Paraguay, St. Kitts and Nevis, Saint Lucia, and St. Vincent and the Grenadines.

A country of 15 million, Guatemala has strengthened ties with both Taipei and Washington recently. Taiwan operates six developmental projects in Guatemala, spanning educational programs, medical technology, and agricultural assistance. These projects follow 26 completed ones, all through Taiwan’s ICDF. Taiwan has also signed commercial agreements, helping Guatemala become Taiwan’s fourth-largest coffee supplier. Taiwan boosts Guatemala’s human capital by giving several hundred scholarships to Guatemalan students studying in Taipei.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has commended Guatemala’s president for continuing to recognize Taiwan, and the U.S. and Taiwanese governments have jointly led development initiatives with Guatemala. With the United States being Guatemala’s largest export market and the source of 25 percent of its GDP via migrant remittances, Guatemala has pragmatic reasons to please Washington by recognizing Taipei.

Paraguay – Taiwan’s only remaining South American ally – has similarly maintained loyalty to Taipei. After its 35-year dictatorship fell in 1989, Paraguay maintained deep engagement with Taiwan. Economic engagements have solidified, with Taiwan becoming Paraguay’s second largest beef importer and largest pork importer. As agricultural exports generate 10 percent of Paraguay’s GDP and jobs, this commercial relationship is no trivial matter.

Paraguayan President Santiago Peña’s visit to Taipei in May cemented this relationship by expanding chicken exports to Taiwan and obtaining pledges for AI computing center investments in Paraguay. Notably, with the exception of the 2008–12 Fernando Lugo administration, Paraguay’s executive has always been a member of the Colorado Party, which holds a multidecade close relationship with Taiwanese officials.

These relations, however, are not set in stone. Paraguay’s last presidential runner-up pledged to switch recognition to the PRC if elected, and China’s government has gifted lavish all-expenses-paid trips to China to dozens of opposition lawmakers, who now lobby for Paraguay to switch. Similarly, in Guatemala, candidates in next year’s election could make the same pledge, especially considering how China canceled Guatemalan coffee and macadamia shipments after its president held a videoconference with Taiwan’s president in 2024.

But for the moment, Taiwan’s Latin American relations remain strong, boosted by the Trump administration’s stated priorities to counter China’s rising influence in the Americas. In fact, in Honduras’ presidential election last year, both opposition candidates pledged to restore relations with Taiwan if elected, citing low transparency and negative results from the 2023 switch under the previous government. One of those candidates, Nasry Asfura, won and became president.

Conclusion

Beijing claims that Taiwan’s diplomacy is merely a “scandal and a farce,” but 12 states continue supporting Taiwanese statehood. Countries have long recognized the ROC for legitimate reasons, most often political ones. Whether a ruling monarchy preserving multidecade relations (Eswatini), a strong U.S. ally aligning with Washington (Guatemala), or a ruling party continuing long-held ties with Taipei (Paraguay), political particularities have created diplomatic opportunities for Taiwan across continents. Somaliland’s contested status facilitating diplomacy with Taiwan proves this point further.

Due to China’s economic weight, Taipei cannot convince many countries to pick it over Beijing. Still, like David using a slingshot instead of a spear, Taiwan can exploit political circumstances for its diplomatic benefit.
tag: China Taiwan strategy; Taiwan diplomatic allies; Taiwan international space; Taiwan-Eswatini relations; Taiwan-Guatemala relations; Taiwan-Paraguay relations; Taiwan-Somaliland relations

title: The China-US Quantum Computing Contest
description: Insights from Matt Kinsella.
text:
The Diplomat author Mercy Kuo regularly engages subject-matter experts, policy practitioners, and strategic thinkers across the globe for their diverse insights into U.S. Asia policy. This conversation with Matt Kinsella – the CEO of Infleqtion, a leading U.S. quantum technology company – is the 531st in “The Trans-Pacific View Insight Series.”

Briefly describe U.S. advancements in quantum computing technology.

The United States is moving from experimental quantum systems toward logical, fault-tolerant computing. The key measure is no longer the number of physical qubits, but whether those qubits can be organized into reliable logical qubits and used for meaningful applications.

Infleqtion is at the forefront of that shift. Our neutral-atom platform has demonstrated 12 logical qubits with error detection and loss correction, a 99.73 percent two-qubit gate fidelity, and arrays of up to 1,600 neutral-atom sites. With Nvidia, we published a materials-science demonstration in which logical encoding reduced error approximately sixfold compared with physical-qubit execution.

Our roadmap achieves 30 logical qubits later this year, 100 by 2028, and 1,000 by 2030. We see approximately 100 high-quality logical qubits as the threshold for outperforming classical systems on selected valuable problems.

Hardware alone will not get us there. As our CTO, Pranav Gokhale, has emphasized, hardware-aware software can force-multiply quantum performance. Infleqtion is developing the complete stack – from atoms, photonics, and control systems to error correction, Superstaq compilation, resource estimation, and integration with GPU-accelerated computing. That full-system approach is how quantum computing becomes useful.

In what ways is the U.S. collaborating with partners in the Asia Pacific in developing quantum computing technology?

The United States is building a trusted quantum ecosystem with Asia-Pacific partners through joint research, technology development, workforce training, and access to advanced systems.

Japan provides a strong example. Japan’s Science and Technology Agency selected Infleqtion as the first foreign company – and the only foreign quantum-computing partner – to participate in its Quantum Moonshot program. In a consortium led by Professor Kenji Ohmori of the Institute for Molecular Science, we are contributing neutral-atom technology, photonics expertise, and systems engineering to the development of a large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computer based on atomic qubits.

This is more than a research exchange. It combines an American commercial platform with Japanese leadership in ultrafast atomic control and aligns both countries around a shared technical objective. To this end, Infleqtion has delivered neutral-atom systems, helping researchers build the practical experience required to operate and develop applications for advanced quantum machines.

In Australia, Infleqtion has established an Asia-Pacific presence at Swinburne University of Technology and worked with the Australian Army and Australian industry on trustworthy quantum computation. One collaboration with Australian quantum company Diraq explored quantum physically unclonable functions intended to help verify the identity and integrity of remotely accessed quantum computers.

We are also engaging Australian leaders on the future use of quantum computing in energy and infrastructure. This application-led approach is essential: allied programs should begin with consequential problems and jointly determine the hardware, software, and classical resources required to address them.

These partnerships expand the talent, facilities, test environments, and applications available to the United States. Our alliances are not simply diplomatic relationships; they are a practical technology advantage.

Analyze the scope and scale of the U.S.-China quantum computing competition.

The U.S.-China quantum competition is not a single race. It spans computing architecture, logical reliability, software, photonics, manufacturing, talent, supply chains, data-center integration, and applications.

China can concentrate substantial state resources behind selected national programs. The United States operates through a more distributed system of companies, universities, federal laboratories, private capital, and international partners. That diversity supports several technical pathways while creating strong pressure to demonstrate practical results.

Infleqtion represents the strength of the American model. We are advancing a vertically integrated neutral-atom platform while expanding from research milestones into deployed systems and application centers. Our technology is operational in national institutions, and our teams are working with government and industry on energy, materials, AI, and scientific discovery.

We have delivered a 100-physical-qubit system to the U.K. National Quantum Computing Centre, announced a fault-tolerant system for Illinois, opened a Chicago Quantum Innovation Center, and expanded our U.K. engineering and manufacturing presence. These are signs of an industry developing the infrastructure to scale – not merely producing individual experiments.

The competition will be decided by sustained execution: who can build dependable logical systems, reduce resource overhead, manufacture them, connect them to classical supercomputers, and solve consequential problems. The United States has a powerful innovation network, and Infleqtion is rapidly converting that advantage into operating capability.

Examine China’s quantum computing technology developments.

China has demonstrated credible progress in superconducting and photonic quantum computing, supported by centralized programs that coordinate across universities, national laboratories, and state-linked companies. In particular, the University of Science and Technology of China’s Zuchongzhi 3.0 superconducting processor and Jiuzhang 4.0 photonic system have now achieved world-leading results.

These are technically impressive demonstrations, but more consequential questions concern logical error rates, programmable circuit depth, application performance, system availability, and the resources required to outperform the best classical alternative. Of note, China’s leading results in neutral atom quantum computing have lagged developments here in the U.S., though there have been recent accelerations in China’s efforts over the past year.

China is also building domestic control electronics, cloud platforms, software, and industrial capacity. Its 2026-2030 planning framework treats quantum technology as a strategic emerging field, so the United States should expect continued progress.

The appropriate response is disciplined acceleration. We should measure China’s achievements accurately while investing in the capabilities that determine practical advantage: logical qubits, efficient error correction, hardware-aware software, advanced manufacturing, and application deployment. Those are the areas where Infleqtion is concentrating its computing roadmap.

Assess how quantum computing technology is integrated into U.S. national security and defense systems and its implications for the U.S.-China tech race.

Large-scale quantum computers are not yet embedded in operational defense systems. Current integration is occurring through research programs, independent technical validation, hybrid computing infrastructure, and development of mission-relevant applications.

An exemplar is DARPA’s HARQ program exploring heterogeneous systems that combine different quantum processors with classical resources. To meet that demand, Infleqtion is developing Multistaq, a software layer designed to compile and coordinate workloads across multiple qubit technologies.

Infleqtion is also supporting three Department of Energy Genesis Mission projects involving AI-optimized quantum circuits for nuclear applications, fusion research, and deployable atomic sensing. Our planned Illinois system will connect a neutral-atom QPU with Nvidia GPU infrastructure, providing a test environment for quantum-classical workflows and real-time error correction. The associated Chicago center is initially focused on energy-grid and nuclear optimization problems with direct implications for national resilience.

Quantum sensing and timing are closer to field deployment than fault-tolerant computing. Infleqtion’s work in GPS-independent navigation, spectrum awareness, precision timing, gravity sensing, and space systems gives the company operating experience with government missions while strengthening the shared photonics, controls, software, and manufacturing base behind our computers.

For the U.S.-China competition, the objective should be clear: move quantum computing from scientific potential to trusted national infrastructure. Infleqtion is helping the United States do that by combining technical progress, deployed systems, application development, and allied partnerships on one scalable neutral-atom platform.
