title: The Debate Over the Maldives’ Deal with Eagle Hills
channel_text: Blog; Politics; South Asia; The Pulse
description: Handing over prime land in a land-scarce country, on an island pitched as a lasting solution to an acute housing crisis, warrants deeper scrutiny.
text:
A proposed deal between the Maldivian government and Abu Dhabi-based developer Eagle Hills to build a waterfront and marina has dominated Maldives’ news cycle in recent weeks.

Founded in 2014 by Emirati businessman Mohamed Alabbar, who also founded Emaar Properties, the developer behind Dubai’s Burj Khalifa, the Eagle Hills project is planned for Ras Malé, an artificial island being reclaimed from the Fushi Dhiggaru lagoon, south of the capital, Malé. The project is being championed by President Mohamed Muizzu as one of his flagship initiatives.

Originally conceived as the Indian Ocean’s first “eco-city,” Ras Malé was meant to ease the housing crisis in the Maldives, a country where dry land makes up less than 1 percent of its territory.

Although the agreement signed in Abu Dhabi on September 21 is a letter of intent rather than a final contract, the project, if realized, would alter that original vision substantially. Under the reported terms, Eagle Hills would receive 500 of the 1,009 hectares earmarked for reclamation, on a 99-year lease, without paying an acquisition fee or rent, to develop resorts, commercial facilities, and residential properties marketed to foreign buyers.

That would leave only the remainder for other development, including housing for the Maldivians originally intended to be its primary beneficiaries.

In partial compensation, Eagle Hills has offered to finance 5,000 housing units in nearby Hulhumalé, though their cost would be recovered from the government’s share of project revenue.

Arguably, there is an economic case for the project. An investment of this scale could bring in much-needed dollars, create jobs, and generate revenue. Infrastructure and Housing Minister Abdulla Muththalib, who signed the agreement, also argues that the project could establish “a structured, world-class real estate sector,” helping diversify an economy heavily dependent on tourism.

Yet the opacity surrounding the deal makes assessing its economic merits challenging. The exact agreement itself has not been made public. Meanwhile, the numbers conflict. The government valued the project at $20 billion, while Eagle Hills reportedly envisaged a $12 billion development. Neither figure is a binding investment commitment. Nor did the developer repeat the government’s projection of more than 54,000 jobs. How these figures were calculated is unclear.

Critics have also questioned why the land is effectively being offered for free.

The government argues that its 10 percent share of the developer’s gross revenue, which it projects at around $3.1 billion over ten years, would earn it more than an upfront fee, and touts the added advantage of requiring no government loans or sovereign guarantees. Yet the project was never put out to competitive tender, and no independent valuation of the land has been made public. Without one, it is difficult to gauge whether the expected returns justify proceeding on the reported terms, especially given the hundreds of millions of dollars already spent on reclaiming Ras Malé.

Beyond price, the deal has also revived concerns over foreign land ownership. Article 251 of the constitution prohibits foreign ownership and limits leases to non-citizens to 99 years. An amendment allowing foreign ownership in return for large financial investments was introduced by President Abdulla Yameen in 2015, but repealed in 2019 by his successor, Ibrahim Solih.

Eagle Hills’ original announcement stated that a fresh 99-year lease would begin each time a property changed hands. Critics argue that this circumvents the constitutional limit, effectively allowing foreigners to retain control of the land indefinitely. The company has since revised the wording, and the government rejects this interpretation, insisting that the land would remain state-owned and that every transfer would require its approval. It also maintains that buying property would not automatically confer residency, even as Eagle Hills’ sales website advertises a renewable residency visa.

Much of the public opposition has played out on social media under the hashtag #EagleHillsOut, centering on the deal’s opacity and the prospect of foreign control of land. Alabbar has also drawn scrutiny over his past projects. In Serbia, his Belgrade Waterfront development, pushed through with little transparency under a special law favoring the developer, sparked mass protests.

Alabbar’s links with Israel have further fueled opposition in the Maldives, where support for Palestine runs deep, and entry on Israeli passports has been banned since April 2025 in response to the war in Gaza. In 2005, as Emaar’s chairman, Alabbar discussed purchasing homes Israeli settlers would vacate during Israel’s planned withdrawal from Gaza, as well as reconstruction with Palestinian leaders. In 2020, after the UAE normalized relations with Israel under the Abraham Accords, he publicly advocated closer Emirati-Israeli ties. Amid concerns that the development could enable Israelis to acquire property in the Maldives despite existing restrictions, Alabbar has insisted that Eagle Hills will comply with Maldivian law, including the passport ban.

Organized political opposition, however, has been divided, particularly within the main opposition Maldivian Democratic Party (MDP). In an official statement, the party demanded full disclosure of the agreement’s terms and a referendum on the project, while opposing any arrangement that would permit foreign ownership of land. Yet its chairperson, former President Mohamed Nasheed, supports the project in principle. After MDP lawmakers denounced Alabbar in parliament as a supporter of Zionism, Nasheed warned that such attacks could jeopardize investment from the UAE.

Nevertheless, nationalist opposition to foreign-backed megaprojects has been a recurring theme in Maldivian politics since the country transitioned to democracy in 2008. This time, the most strident criticism has come from Muizzu’s erstwhile mentor, Yameen, who has remained embittered against him since the 2023 presidential election. When a since-overturned corruption conviction barred Yameen from running, Muizzu, who had until then been campaigning for the former, stepped in at short notice as the opposition candidate and won. Yameen eventually endorsed him but has since publicly regretted it.

Yameen’s strategy appears to be to undermine the nationalist credentials central to Muizzu’s “pro-Maldives” platform, while challenging the government’s claim to champion the Palestinian cause. To this end, he has exploited public sympathy for Palestine to stir up opposition to Eagle Hills in openly antisemitic terms. In a characteristically bizarre post on X, he denounced the developer as a “depraved bunch” exploiting a “morally bankrupt regime” and claimed, without evidence, that the project would establish a Jewish settlement in the Maldives.

For all the public criticism, both genuine and opportunistic, Muizzu faces few legislative barriers to proceeding. No date has been set for a final agreement, but the president says a real estate bill underpinning the project will go to Parliament “very soon,” where his People’s National Congress has held a supermajority since 2024.

Yet the debate over Eagle Hills raises broader questions about how the Maldives balances its need for foreign investment with the public interest.

A small, import-dependent economy can ill afford to shun large investors whenever objections are raised on nationalist grounds, particularly when those objections are cynically motivated. For instance, scrapping Indian firm GMR’s airport contract in 2012 eventually cost the state $271 million. At the same time, handing over prime land in a land-scarce country, on an island pitched as a lasting solution to an acute housing crisis, warrants deeper scrutiny. That scrutiny cannot occur until the government publishes the full agreement.
tag: Abdulla Yameen; Eagle Hills; Maldives housing; Maldivian President Muizzu; Mohamed Alabbar; Ras Malé

title: The Impending Impeachment Conviction of Philippine Vice President Sara Duterte
description: Four months into her impeachment trial in the Senate, the political winds are starting to turn against Duterte.
text:
Recent political realignments in the Philippines suggest that a guilty verdict has already been secured in the ongoing impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.

The House of Representatives twice impeached Duterte, but it was only in July that a trial was convened by the Senate, which needs to deliver a verdict on the allegations that the vice president committed high crimes and betrayed public trust.

In several articles, I wrote about the slim prospect of a conviction given the dominance of Duterte supporters in the Senate. Even President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. publicly rejected a “divisive” trial, which eventually led to the archiving of the initial impeachment complaint in 2025.

The push to remove the vice president from office became clearer in the second half of the year when the Senate convened an impeachment court, and when the president allowed Duterte’s tax and bank records to be used as evidence. The prosecution panel’s first presentation was about the alleged grave threats made by Duterte against the First Family, which was intended to consolidate the ranks of the president’s supporters.

The start of the trial coincided with the filing of non-bailable plunder charges against two pro-Duterte senators, which prevented them from attending the impeachment sessions. Another pro-Duterte senator, who was a former police chief, went into hiding after an arrest warrant was issued against him by the International Criminal Court for his role in the bloody “war on drugs” during the previous administration of Rodrigo Duterte, the vice president’s father.

During the course of the trial, one member of the Senate Duterte bloc decided to join the majority. Another member went abroad to seek medical treatment, but it became an indefinite leave after a plunder complaint was filed against her. The absence of pro-Duterte senators has made it easier for the majority to lower the number of votes needed to convict the vice president. The Senate decision to lower the voting threshold was questioned by pro-Duterte lawyers at the Supreme Court, but the latter dismissed their petition on procedural grounds.

The prosecution’s presentation of evidence on the alleged unexplained wealth of Duterte and her husband provided the public with new information about the vice president’s undeclared assets and business dealings. Some of the suspicious financial transactions were traced to China, which prompted some Marcos officials to comment that it should be further investigated as a potential national security threat.

Duterte has denied ownership of the bank accounts and properties mentioned during her trial. She also insisted that doing business in China is legitimate. Nevertheless, she still needs to explain the mismatch and omissions in her statement of assets as a government official, and the large amount of earnings from her husband’s vague business operations in China.

The prosecution is confident that they can get a guilty verdict on the issue of Duterte’s unexplained wealth, and they made a bold move by dropping other charges in their presentation, including the grave threats against the First Family, misuse of confidential funds, and bribery.

This could also signal that there is now enough number of votes in the Senate to convict Duterte. The impeachment trial may last until the end of the year unless the defense panel decides to present additional witnesses to extend the sessions until early 2027.

The decision to limit the impeachment case to the issue of unexplained wealth has drawn mixed reactions. On one hand, it has been welcomed for expediting the trial and allowing the prosecution to focus on an issue with strong evidence. But it has also been criticized for its potential to undermine the public clamor for accountability, especially since the allegation about the anomalous spending of confidential funds was dropped from the charges. Critics said it could set a precedent by reducing the impeachment process to a transactional matter involving legislators and the presidential office, instead of upholding its role in exacting full accountability against erring officials.

Duterte’s political future will soon be decided by the Senate. Whatever happens, she can take comfort that she still leads in presidential election surveys. If she is convicted, her younger brother could run for president. So far, Marcos has no clear successor, which still makes the Dutertes the formidable team to beat at the 2028 presidential election.

In the meantime, the public awaits the counterarguments and evidence to be presented by Duterte’s legal team in the second half of the impeachment trial.
tag: Philippines politics; Philippines Senate; Sara Duterte; Sara Duterte impeachment

title: The Indian Government’s Job Statistics Are Misleading
description: Behind the surge in EPFO numbers lies an uncomfortable question: is Delhi measuring new jobs or merely recording existing workers differently?
text:
The Indian government claims that the formal job market in the country is booming. It cites as proof payroll data from the Employees’ Provident Fund Organization (EPFO).

The Employees’ Provident Fund is a mandatory government-backed retirement savings scheme in India for salaried workers. The question, however, is: does a rising EPFO count really amount to more good jobs?

The official story goes as follows. The Economic Survey 2023-24 reported that net EPFO payroll additions more than doubled, from 6.11 million in FY2018-19 to 13.15 million. The survey called it “healthy growth in formal employment.” The Union Labor Ministry hailed it as a “growing formal employment landscape.”

The Indian government has now gone further and linked formalization of employment directly to “quality jobs.” In August 2026, it promoted the Pradhan Mantri Viksit Bharat Rozgar Yojana as a scheme to expand formal employment, designed to encourage first-time employment and to reward employers for creating new formal jobs through EPFO.

Formalization is valuable. A worker brought under EPF coverage gains access to an institutional mechanism for retirement savings and social security. An enterprise complying with labor regulations represents progress over one that does not.

However, these claims ignore reality. An EPFO “net subscriber addition” is not a net new job. It can include a person moving from one EPFO-covered employer to another; an existing worker newly brought into EPFO coverage; a worker previously outside formal coverage becoming covered; workers rejoining after an employment break; changes resulting from EPFO administrative coverage; and, importantly, formalization of an already existing informal job.

September 2026 EPFO data showed contributors in 12 traditionally labor-intensive sectors (garments, textiles, leather, jute, beedi, tea, brick-making, cashew, coir, cotton ginning, diamond cutting, and others) fell 1.3 percent, from 5,536,000 in 2023-24 to 5,464,000 in 2025-26. These are precisely the sectors India must expand to absorb workers leaving agriculture.

There is a further fundamental statistical problem.

EPFO payroll statistics measure movements into and out of the EPF system. The monthly payroll series records first-time subscribers, members exiting coverage, and earlier members who rejoin. The government itself cautions that the numbers are provisional because employee records are continuously updated.

The Economic Survey 2025-26 carried the government’s claims further: organized manufacturing added 5.7 million jobs. This is potentially more interesting because it is not based on EPFO figures.

The National Sample Survey or NSS Survey uses Annual Survey of Industries (ASI) data and says organized manufacturing employment increased by more than 5.7 million between FY2015 and FY2024; grew at about 4 percent compounded annual growth rate (CAGR); and increased by more than 1 million in FY2024 alone, a 6 percent year-on-year increase.

This is probably the strongest official evidence currently being cited for actual employment expansion in the organized sector, rather than simply formalization. But there is a major definitional qualification: The ASI’s “persons engaged” category includes working proprietors, family members, and unpaid workers, as well as employees. So it is not synonymous with regular wage/salaried formal jobs.

The government is also pointing to the rise in regular salaried employment. Regular wage/salaried employment increased from 22.4 percent of workers in 2024 to 23.6 percent in 2025. That is a meaningful movement toward wage employment, although it is still very far from the claim that most new employment is formal.

In fact, what takes the wind out of the government’s claims is that the increase in organized manufacturing has been accompanied by growing contractualization. According to ASI, contract workers accounted for only about 13 percent of the formal manufacturing workforce in 1993-94. However, this share rose sharply to 20 percent by 1999-2000 and further to 37.8 percent in 2018-19. As per the latest ASI data (2022-23), it has reached 40.7 percent. So much for the claim of formalization – the ILO defines it as work with social security, and contract work does not offer that.

The percentage share of contract labor in capital-intensive industries has increased from 19.5 percent in 1999-2000 to 46 percent in 2018-2019, whereas it has increased from 22 percent in 1999-2000 to 33 percent in 2018-2019 in labor-intensive enterprises.

As though that is not enough, if EPFO was really creating so many new jobs, how is it that India’s Periodic Labor Force Survey (PLFS) continues to show that India’s share of informal workers without social insurance (i.e. pensions, death/disability insurance, maternity benefits, etc.) was 90 percent in 2004-5, 90 percent in 2017-18, and still 90 percent in 2024.

Job quality also matters: duration, earnings, working conditions, social protection, security of tenure, and prospects for advancement. India’s employment challenge has historically been not only unemployment but also underemployment, low productivity, and poor-quality work.

The latest PLFS data illustrate this complexity. Even after the increase in regular wage employment, 56.2 percent of workers in 2025 remained self-employed (mostly own-account and unpaid family labor) and another 20.20 percent were casual wage laborers. Agriculture still accounted for 43 percent of employment in 2025 (42 percent in 2019). The largest addition to the workforce since 2020 has been in agriculture (rising from 200 million to 280 million in 2024).

This matters most for the young. A graduate in a low-paid, insecure job is technically employed but not upwardly mobile. As we estimate in our new book, “India Out of Work,” real wages for casual and regular workers, and for the 53 percent of workers who are self-employed, have stagnated for 12 years. If non-farm jobs have grown at half the required rate (12 million a year) for a dozen years the Modi government has been in power, leaving youth unemployment double its 2012 level, from 6 percent to 12 percent in 2024, how can real wages rise, however loudly the government touts its low inflation?

The real test of India’s labor market is not how many names enter an EPFO database but whether the economy creates enough stable, productive, and decently paid jobs. If it did, the youth (those aged 15-29 years) not in education, employment, and training, would not have jumped from 50 million in 2012 to 100 million in 2024. Clearly, many became “discouraged workers” who stopped looking for work.

Originally published under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 by 360info™.
tag: India Economy; India employment; India unemployment; India working conditions

title: The Lessons the Taliban Have Learned
description: Afghanistan's leaders haven’t changed ideologically. But five years after returning to power, they have learnt from where the first emirate went wrong.
text:
In the female section of an upscale restaurant in Kabul’s Shar-e Naw, a waiter brings me a menu and a form. Only two lines are filled in: one bears an Italian name, the other a local one. The waiter explains that guests are required to fill it in at the request of the Ministry of Interior. It is for the guests’ own safety, he emphasizes, slightly uneasy. It is hard to tell if he believes it.

I look at the form. It asks for the guest’s name, date of birth, passport number, address in Kabul, as well as when they visited the restaurant.

“It is for your security,” the waiter repeats. I give him the blank form back. “I feel secure without it,” I say. He doesn’t insist. He takes my order and disappears.

Five years after the withdrawal of NATO troops from Afghanistan, and into the rule of the Taliban, the group’s control over the country is stable. While the Taliban might not have access to the newest surveillance technologies, their infiltration of local communities is high. They had learned their lesson from their first period of rule, the emirate that ended in 2001 with the U.S. invasion, a United Nations official tells me.

“You can say that fundamentally, ideologically, they haven’t really changed. But in terms of control, consolidation, management, messaging, they are far more sophisticated now,” he says. “The first emirate was a brand new experiment. The second emirate is still an experiment, but they have learned a lot of lessons. They are smart.”

Kabul still reminds me of its former self, as if time had stopped. The streets are bustling with life; street vendors cover the pavements, selling products ranging from food and cigarettes to clothes and electronics. The new regime is seen in the details: fewer women walk the streets, less rubbish lies scattered across the city center – a lasting feature of the corrupt rule back in the Republic days – and the streets seem less chaotic. But at first glance, the changes are small, sometimes imperceptible.

A Taliban checkpoint in Balkh province, Afghanistan. Photo by Agnieszka Pikulicka.

Everyone I speak with says that the country has become safer. Twenty years of war and decades of fighting have taken their toll on people. The Taliban, while brutal and devoted to anti-modern ideas, has nevertheless brought peace. The paradox is that the Taliban were the main perpetrators of violence during the Republic days. It was due to their attacks on cars that traveling between provinces used to be dangerous and caution was advised. Since they took power, traveling between different regions of Afghanistan has suddenly become possible.

Now, Taliban checkpoints cover the whole country. Some of them are stricter, with soldiers standing under the white flag bearing the Shahada, the Islamic declaration of faith, and the Taliban symbol, checking travel permits meticulously. Other checkpoints are more relaxed, and it is enough to slow down and let the Taliban gaze into the car.

There are few roads that the group does not control. To leave their place of residence, drivers need special permits, and so do tourists. A letter from “Afghan Tour,” a unit responsible for travelers, is required to travel and stay in another province. It is unclear what its purpose is, other than surveillance.

In Kabul, the “Afghan Tour” official says that getting a travel letter requires paying for an expensive tour. But it is possible to get it in Bamyan, another province, for a small fee. Most other regions also issue such letters in exchange for booking an inexpensive “tour” with an official guide. It is unclear if its price is official or simply a bribe paid for obtaining the letter. It is also hard to call it a tour.

As part of the “tour” I book to stay in Mazar-i-Sharif, the local guide shows me into the Blue Mosque, the shrine of Imam Ali, first built in the 12th century before Genghis Khan leveled the original building to the ground. But the tour included little in terms of a history lesson. The guide complained about his low earnings, suggesting I pay extra for his time. Then he demanded that I share my local contacts with him. For my own safety, of course.

Today the new Taliban administration is stable. Ministries work, and courts solve disputes without the need to pay bribes, I am told. 96 percent of the poppy fields have been eradicated and hundreds of addicts who formerly squatted on Kabul’s streets and under bridges have been forced into rehabs. This is the kind of “stability” I know all too well from Central Asia’s autocracies, Afghanistan’s neighbors: they are brutal and relentless, but the pavements are clean.

According to a recent report from Human Rights Watch, censorship of local media outlets and restrictions on freedom of expression have intensified, while journalists, activists, academics and other regime critics have faced repression, torture, and arbitrary arrests.

“The Taliban always accuse us of being spies, it’s hard to work these days,” one local photojournalist told me.

The Blue Mosque, the shrine of Imam Ali, in Mazar-i-Sharif. Photo by Agnieszka Pikulicka.

Women have been denied basic rights, such as the right to education beyond sixth grade. A woman visiting her parental home who does not return to her husband can be deemed a criminal. That includes survivors of domestic violence. A woman accused of touching, shaking hands with, or hugging a man who is not her mahram, a close male relative with whom marriage is prohibited, can spend a year in prison. Two months if a girl or a boy is seen dancing.

A new “Preachers’ law” defines Muslims as followers of the Hanafi school of Islam. Local Hazaras, or Ismaili minority groups, are now officially deemed heretics.

“Many Ismailis now hide their faith,” one man from the community tells me. He lost his job in a school in Badakhshan due to his faith.

All that in the name of the “peaceful and clear sky above us,” as Uzbekistan’s late President Islam Karimov used to say in justifying his own repressive rule.

Except that this is not the reality for most Afghans.

While the war might be over – except for skirmishes in Badakhshan province and regular attacks from Pakistan – Afghanistan is hardly facing a post-war recovery. The withdrawal of U.S. and NATO troops and the coming to power of the Taliban, a government recognized only by Russia, meant that the United Nations mandate became much more restricted in scope. Cooperation with the de facto Taliban authorities has focused mostly on securing people’s very basic needs.

Most international non-governmental and governmental organizations, and media, have left, and with them hundreds of local jobs disappeared. The biggest difference is noticeable in large cities: Kabul, Herat, or Mazar-i-Sharif, where previously educated, English-speaking men and women could find employment and develop careers. As another local journalist told me, during the Republic days he could support his family working as a photographer and videographer. Now, work is scarce. He has not had any projects for several months.

“The situation seems to get worse every day and every year. Unemployment has reached a very high level, especially for people like me who work in the arts and creative fields,” he says. “People of Afghanistan are facing many other serious problems, including unemployment, untreated illnesses, hunger, poverty, and lack of adequate shelter. I do not see a clear government plan to address unemployment at its roots.”

According to the United Nations, more than 17 million people, or 40 percent of Afghanistan’s population, are projected to face acute food insecurity. And the situation is worsening. While following the U.S. withdrawal, thousands of Afghans left the country in search of a better life, this trend is now reversing – though not voluntarily.

Over the last few years, Iran and Pakistan have forced millions of Afghans to return home. Even the European Union, including Germany, a country with the largest Afghan population in the region, began to deport people back despite fears of torture and imprisonment upon arrival. This has put a massive strain on the already impoverished nation with very limited resources. As the U.N. official told me, at the time of 9/11, in 2001, Afghanistan’s population was around 20 million. By the time of the return of the Taliban, twenty years later, it had doubled. Over the last five years of the second emirate, the population has grown by 5 million, and currently totals around 45 million.

“There has been almost triple pressure on resources, on communities, on infrastructure and humanitarian needs. And development hasn’t kept up. People are coming back to a country and to communities that are not equipped to sustain them,” the U.N. contact told me. “Even though we see economic growth, it’s not keeping up with population growth. And then on top of that a lot of people are coming back to urban areas, which is putting even more pressure on urban systems.”

In other words, over the past five years the population grew by 12.6 percent, while at the same time, the amount of skilled work opportunities fell amid the withdrawal of the West. Women have been banned from a number of professions, which pushed many families into even deeper poverty. While traditionally conservative and impoverished rural areas have not seen much change, cities, where women were more emancipated under the Republic, have experienced the greater shifts.

In Kabul, I meet with several young women, the friends and family members of my girlfriends who have long left the country. They are a lost generation. Unable to study beyond sixth grade, unable to follow their passions and have careers, they often live online. Some learn English, others open small businesses selling handmade accessories on Instagram, one of the few avenues left for Afghan women to make a living. But pressure is high.

A friend hosted a get-together for women in a female section of a Kabul restaurant. She was summoned by the Taliban. The meeting was deemed suspicious. She still hasn’t told her parents and brothers about the interrogation. That would mean she would not be allowed to leave the house on her own. For her own safety. My friend is a brave, educated woman with good English. She wants to work and develop new skills, something that the local government sees as sinful. Her very existence is a threat to the system.

Five years since the coming to power of the Taliban, tourism has appeared. Some travelers, hoping for an extreme experience, walk the streets of Kabul and other cities, talking to the Taliban and taking selfies. For someone like me, who had worked in Afghanistan for years under the Republic, this is an ominous view. People who only a few years back would want to kidnap a white traveler are now being depicted as dream hosts, embracing Western backpacking culture and adding an Oriental feel to flashy Instagram posts.

The spectators will continue watching the events taking place in Afghanistan like a sneak peek into the life of another planet. The Republic times were not perfect: corruption was rampant, violence omnipresent, and the Taliban, the Islamic State, al-Qaida, and other groups continued to operate. The U.S. occupation, which cost roughly $2.3 trillion, failed to build lasting institutions or even basic infrastructure. As one of my friends snarkily remarked: “We still use roads built by the Soviet Union. All the Americans did was bring the Taliban back.”

He is right. And following the American fiasco, no outside power is eager to get involved in Afghanistan again, no matter their horrific human rights record. Any militant challenge to the Taliban from within Afghan communities is limited and so far short-lived. The Taliban have learned their lessons and they know how to control their territory. This is something that China, Russia, and Central Asian states have already come to understand. They engage with the Taliban government in regional projects, China even makes investments. For the region, this is the new normal.

The Taliban are here to stay.

title: The Lingering Shadow of Rodrigo Duterte’s Drug War in the Philippines
description: The former Philippine president is on trial in The Hague, but the ghosts of his presidency and the system he put in place continue to haunt a deeply divided society.
text:
A few bags of chips and sweets line the modest storefront of Salvacion Ramos’ home in the Batasan neighborhood on the outskirts of Manila. At 68, she has turned the front of her house into a small convenience store to help pay for the education of her grandson, who has been in her care since her daughter’s death.

It was on that same doorstep one night in February 2017 that Cristeta Ramos was shot once in the back and three times in the head by four plainclothes police officers. “She died in my arms. I didn’t even get to say goodbye,” Salvacion recalls, tears in her eyes.

Beside her, her friend and neighbor Llore Pasco is also mourning her children. Her two sons, Cristanto and Juan Carlos, 34 and 31, were killed during a police operation as they were on their way to work in May 2017. “The police say they chased them because they thought they were thieves, but the bullet wounds were on the front of their bodies,” Llore says. She is now raising her five grandchildren.

“Cristeta was not a criminal” Salvacion says. “She did take drugs with the people she was with, but she wanted to get better. The barangay [neighborhood-level community] was offering a program for drug users to seek treatment, so I gave them her name.”

Llore’s sons had stopped using drugs well before Duterte’s election. After he took office, local officials insisted that former drug users register, presenting the process as a simple verification. Her sons initially refused. Llore eventually convinced them. They had been sober for more than a year. “Today I keep thinking that if they had not gone there, they might still be alive,” she says.

In neighborhoods across the country, barangays began compiling “watch lists” of current and former drug users. For some residents, getting off those lists came at a price. “At least five families I know paid 10,000 pesos (about $180) to the local government to get their names removed from the list, and their children are still alive,” Salvacion says.

Under Duterte, the war on drugs also became a source of income for some local actors. Along with the grief of losing their children and the guilt of having registered them with local authorities came the burden of paying to recover their bodies from the morgue. In Salvacion and Llore’s cases, authorities initially demanded 120,000 pesos and later 70,000 pesos, or about $1,350, after the intervention of the NGO Rise Up for Life and For Rights.

“Duterte destroyed these families, and now these mothers have to keep working to raise their orphaned grandchildren,” says Leah Valencia, a coordinator with the organization, which supports families in their search for justice.

Rise Up for Life and For Rights has also passed their testimonies to the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague, where Duterte has been held since his arrest in March 2025. The case accuses Duterte of crimes against humanity committed between 2011 and 2019, during his time as mayor of Davao City and later as president. Prosecutors have identified 78 victims in the incidents specifically detailed in the case: 76 alleged murders and two attempted murders. The figure does not represent the total number of deaths attributed to Duterte’s drug war, but a selection of incidents presented by prosecutors to establish the alleged crimes against humanity.

The historic trial is scheduled to begin on November 30.

If Duterte is found guilty of crimes against humanity, he would become the first former president convicted by the ICC.

“The ICC is a very small ray of hope, but we are asking the government to turn Bato over and open an investigation to prosecute all those responsible,” Salvacion Ramos and Llore Pasco say together.

Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte attends a status conference at Trial Chamber III at the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague, Netherlands, Sep. 16, 2026. (Photo credit: International Criminal Court)

Duterte could soon be joined by his ally Senator Ronald dela Rosa, known as “Bato,” whom Duterte appointed chief of the Philippine National Police after he took office in 2016. In this capacity, dela Rosa oversaw the launch of “Double Barrel,” a cornerstone of the drug war that would leave about 30,000 people dead, according to estimates by several NGOs. (The official death toll of the police is around 6,000.)

On May 11, an attempt to arrest dela Rosa on a warrant for the ICC ended with him taking refuge inside the Philippine Senate as shots were fired in the building. The former police chief was placed under a form of protective custody inside the chamber before leaving the building a few days later. He is currently at large and wanted by Philippine authorities.

The fact that such chaos is possible reflects how politically sensitive the drug war remains at the highest levels of the Philippine state. In 2022, Duterte completed his single six-year term and was succeeded by Ferdinand Marcos Jr., the son of the former dictator who ruled the country from 1965 to 1986, who was elected through an alliance with the Duterte camp. But the alliance did not last.

As relations between the two political clans deteriorated, Marcos gradually shifted his position on the International Criminal Court. In March 2024, he said the ICC had no authority to investigate the Philippines’ drug war and that his government would not cooperate with the court. Months later, as his alliance with the Dutertes unraveled, he adopted a softer stance, saying his government would not block an ICC investigation and would comply with its obligations to Interpol. By early 2025, his administration had also signaled that it was open to limited cooperation with the court.

Duterte was arrested by Philippine authorities, based on an Interpol Red Notice, at Manila’s airport on March 11, 2025.

While Marcos allowed police to enforce the ICC arrest warrant and accepted the presence of ICC investigators, he never openly opposed the drug war waged by his predecessor. He largely avoided the issue during the 2022 presidential campaign, particularly to preserve his alliance with the Duterte camp and its supporters.

He distanced himself from it only after taking office, when he promised a “bloodless” war on drugs. Joel Ariate, a social sciences researcher at the University of the Philippines and founder of the DAHAS project, which has tracked drug-war deaths since 2017, called the term “pure propaganda.”

“The Marcos government says there is no more blood being spilled. That is absurd. The drug war continues. The number of victims has dropped sharply, but there are still 200 to 300 deaths every year,” Ariate says. One-third of the victims are killed in police operations, he says, while the rest are mainly linked to private militias or hit men hired for less than $100 per killing.

Joel Ariate is one of the two academic researchers behind the “Dahas” project – the word means “violence” in Tagalog – which has documented drug-related deaths since 2017. (Photo credit: Aubin Eymard)

The decline in violence against drug users could be a sign of progress under the Marcos government, but Ariate remains pessimistic. “Those responsible for thousands of killings, particularly low-ranking police officers, are still in their jobs. The police know the details and who took part,” the researcher says.

So far, only five cases have resulted in the conviction of nine police officers for crimes linked to Duterte’s drug war, according to a report from Human Rights Watch published in June this year. Yet DAHAS has documented many other cases in which police officers themselves filmed killings and posted the footage online as trophies.

Sitting in the university library where he works, Ariate shares his main concern. “In reality, the institutions that failed during the drug war have not changed,” he says. “In two years, there will be another presidential election, and if a politician like Duterte wins, it could all start again because the mentality has not changed either.”

In May 2025, two months after his arrest and transfer to The Hague, 63 percent of registered voters surveyed by Pulse Asia said they still trusted Duterte.

“Populist leaders present themselves as defenders of order and the fight against crime,” says Christopher Magno, a criminologist specializing in political violence and co-founder of the Truth Commission. “To justify their policies, they identify a group as responsible for insecurity: immigrants in the United States under Trump, and poor people and those accused of using or trafficking drugs in the Philippines under Duterte. By identifying an ‘enemy,’ they can legitimize a repressive policy and strengthen their popularity. Duterte therefore left office with very high levels of public support.”

The Truth Commission, established in 2026, is an independent body that brings together civilian experts from different fields, including law, forensic medicine, journalism, trauma-informed care, and education. Its work centers on collecting testimonies from victims and their families, preserving their stories, and examining the institutions and practices behind the drug war.

“Our goal is to document the facts and establish a truthful account, but above all to humanize the victims and begin a process of healing through a change in mentality,” Magno says.

The commission’s work is expected to last two years and be completed before the next elections, with findings released every six months. It offers new hope to victims’ families, though they remain cautious.

“We are still observing what will happen with the Truth Commission,” Salvacion Ramos and Llore Pasco say, as if protecting themselves from another disappointment in their quest for justice in the Philippines.

Magno says that some police officers are “beginning to open up” during interviews conducted by the Truth Commission. He adds, “The national police have also supported us and say they will follow the conclusions of our commission.”

The criminologist knows the heavy responsibility facing his team: a process of truth and remembrance aimed at putting people and victims back at the center of this tragedy. There is also the challenge of having the commission’s findings recognized by everyone – from institutions to victims’ families, but above all by a divided society – so that the wound left by Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war can finally begin to heal.

title: The Mystery of Kyrgyzstan’s Newly Launched Satellite(s)
description: At first glance, the story of Kyrgyzstan’s satellite launch seemed like a genuine achievement. Then the story changed.
text:
On October 1, Kyrgyzstan reportedly joined Central Asia’s other spacefaring nations, successfully launching a domestically designed and produced nanosatellite aboard a SpaceX rocket from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California

According to Kyrgyzstan’s government, the unnamed, loaf-of-bread-sized spacecraft weighs 5 kilograms, cost around $130,0000, was equipped with high-resolution cameras, and was — nearly exclusively — the product of domestic innovation.

The satellite was assembled by two local companies, Kyrgyz Asman and Kyrgyz Electronics, Bishkek stated. The latter company’s director Ilya Cherny did admit that the technology behind the satellite was largely Russian, but pointed out that the team behind its production consisted of 10 homegrown engineers.

The government also said the satellite would help advance Kyrgyzstan’s top agricultural, environmental, and strategic priorities over its purported 15-year lifespan.

In a statement published on September 24, the country’s Ministry of Water Resources, Agriculture and Processing Industry stated the satellite’s data would track crop conditions, detect early signs of drought, and monitor glaciers.

Speaking from California on launch day, Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov said that the country had previously had to pay to obtain this kind of data from other countries, no matter whether it was “information on 100 hectares, 1,000 hectares, or the weather.”

Japarov suggested that the satellite would allow “every square meter” of Kyrgyzstan’s land to be studied to determine its potential arability, while touting the launch as an achievement in national self-sufficiency.

“We did not have our own satellite before… now we will no longer be dependent on [other countries],” Japarov added. “We will control it ourselves 100 percent from Bishkek.”

Imaged shared by the Kyrgyz Ministry of Water Resources, Agriculture and Processing Industry depicting the unnamed nanosatellite.

Cosmically Large Scandal

At first glance, the story of Kyrgyzstan’s satellite launch seemed like a genuine achievement. The country had joined Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, and – as of this August – Uzbekistan in the ranks of Central Asia’s spacefarers, largely thanks to its own ingenuity.

The success had been extensively covered in domestic, regional, and international media. And then came a confusing development.

On October 2, the day after launch, news reports began to include a previously unmentioned detail: the satellite was a joint effort between Kyrgyzstan and the United Arab Emirates.

Three days later, a Kyrgyz news site published a notice that Kyrgyzstan had established a new space monitoring center to receive, process, and utilize data transmitted from the newly launched Altair satellite.

This was striking for two reasons. First, the name “Altair” had been missing from earlier government press releases. Second – and more importantly – it said the monitoring center would be “provided” data coming from the “UAE-operated” satellite by a body called the Abu Dhabi Maritime Academy.

Suddenly, Japarov’s claims that Kyrgyzstan would be “no longer dependent” on other countries began to ring hollow.

Not only had Russian technology supposedly been used to design the satellite, but the UAE was apparently going to operate the craft, with Kyrgyzstan merely receiving “access” to its data.

It also didn’t help that Gulf-focused news sites were calling Altair the “first satellite developed and built by UAE engineers,” without even mentioning Bishkek’s involvement in the project.

What, then, had happened on October 1? Had Kyrgyzstan really launched a satellite of its own making? If so, in what ways were other countries involved? And if the craft launched from California was primarily an Emirati initiative, would Bishkek walk back its claims of national self-sufficiency?

A Second Satellite?

So far, none of the above questions have been definitively answered. And the matter, described by one prominent regional commentator as a “scandal of cosmic proportions,” has prompted a growing number of increasingly conspiratorial explanations.

Local news outlet Kaktus Media, for example, suggested that two satellites were likely launched on October 1, one developed by the UAE and one with Russian assistance. (It also noted that Kyrgyzstan’s first satellite initiative, launched in 2019 by a team of all-female engineers, seemed not to be involved, having been wound down previously with no details about the project’s completion.)

Tandyr Media, meanwhile, an independent media outlet known for its popular YouTube channel, drew attention in its video covering the launch to a series of Threads posts by an individual named Dima Balakirev, who claimed to have been personally involved in the satellite project’s development.

Threads / Dima Balakirev

In his post, Balakirev appeared to depict himself standing next to a different — much larger — satellite than had been shown in the government’s earlier press releases. Incidentally, the photo also clearly showed a line of text reading “Made in UAE” on one side of the satellite.

According to Balakirev, the spacecraft was a joint project with the UAE, entirely funded “by grants and the Abu Dhabi government,” and was an Earth Remote Sensing satellite – that is, likely the satellite that Japarov was referring to when he was talking about Kyrgyzstan’s newfound capacity to survey itself from above. (Subsequent reporting from government-affiliated sources mentioning the Altair satellite likewise suggested that its data would be used in agricultural planning, water resource management, and environmental monitoring.)

Notably, when questioned by Threads users citing the government’s original (smaller) size specifications, Balakirev insisted that national news outlets had confused two different projects:

“The first is a satellite for Kyrgyzstan, which was assembled in Abu Dhabi. This is a joint project with the UAE, and the Emirates are covering the entire cost. The second is a satellite being built by the team at Kyrgyz Electronics. This is a separate project with its own objectives. The figure of 5 kg and 10–12 million soms [$114,350 – $137,200] refers specifically to this one.”

Although Balakirev’s exact title and position are unknown, as Tandyr Media pointed out, the self-described “entrepreneur and techie” appeared to have been present in California alongside Japarov, and shared Instagram stories from the event.

Bishkek, Do We Have a Problem?

Given all that, as Tandyr host Dmitriy Lozhnikov himself concluded, what is left now is a substantially muddied picture.

According to one possible version of events, Kyrgyzstan did launch its smaller, unnamed bread-loaf-sized satellite, whose function is not entirely clear, on October 1. On the same day, meanwhile, the larger, UAE-designed Altair satellite also launched from California – data from which Bishkek has confirmed it is now paying to access.

In another plausible version, proposed by emigre political scientist Aidarbek Raev, the Kyrgyz-designed nanosatellite might not have been launched at all, which would mean that reports of Kyrgyzstan’s national technological achievements have been greatly exaggerated.

The government, meanwhile, has commented little on the affair since the satellite’s supposed launch day. But in any case, it appears the country’s leadership has further cosmic ambitions.

“If there is stability and peace in our country and Central Asia, in the next five to ten years, depending on our readiness, the day will come when we launch a [telecommunications] satellite as well,” Japarov said on October 1.
tag: Central Asia satellites; Central Asia space programs; Kyrgyzstan; Kyrgyzstan-Russia relations; Kyrgyzstan-UAE relations; Satellites

title: The New Development Bank Quietly Delivers During India’s BRICS Year
description: India is in a unique position as a founding member and one of its biggest borrowers.
text:
As India hosted the BRICS summit in New Delhi in September 2026, a familiar question returned: does the grouping produce anything beyond summit statements? The New Development Bank (NDB) offers the clearest evidence in the affirmative. India first proposed the bank at an earlier BRICS summit in New Delhi in 2012, and its 2026 chairship of BRICS brought that idea full circle.

Judging a development bank is not simple; big announcements matter less than the money that actually reaches projects. The NDB’s record can thus be evaluated on three broad counts. The first is how much it has lent and how much of that money has actually been paid out. The second is whom the bank lends to. The third is how it raises the money it lends. On all three, the picture is more encouraging than the NDB’s low public profile suggests.

By the end of June 2026, the NDB had approved loans worth about $44 billion for 141 projects in clean energy, transport, water systems and digital infrastructure. Of that amount, roughly $25 billion had already been paid out to borrowers. The second figure is especially important. Many development banks approve large loans but pay out much less, and much more slowly. A bank that has paid out more than half of what it approved is doing real work, not just signing agreements.

The NDB’s public figures show what this money is building: 2,400 megawatts of clean energy capacity under way, 1,400 kilometers of tunnels and canals, 43 schools built or upgraded and a large increase in sewage treatment capacity.

The bank’s reach has also grown. Its founding members were Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa. It has since added Algeria, Bangladesh, Egypt, the United Arab Emirates, and Uzbekistan. Its members now stretch from South and Central Asia to Africa, the Middle East, and Latin America.

India’s place in the NDB is unusual. It helped create the bank, it owns an equal share of it, and it is one of its biggest borrowers. Each founding member holds about 18.7 percent of the bank’s capital. This was designed so that no single country could control it. Even so, India has used the bank’s loans more than most members.

Since 2016 the bank has approved 32 initiatives for India, worth close to $9.5 billion, in transport, social development, and clean energy. Lending has continued into 2026 also. Recent approvals include a $300 million clean energy project involving REC Limited and an affordable housing project backed by the Housing and Urban Development Corporation (HUDCO). Earlier, the bank provided $500 million towards the 82-km long rapid transit line between Delhi and Meerut. This is not aid. It is an ordinary lending relationship.

Indian Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman has described the NDB’s value less in terms of money and more in terms of shared knowledge. In August 2026, she said development banks should help countries plan cities and infrastructure better, not just pay for them. NDB President Dilma Rousseff, a former president of Brazil, replied by pointing to India’s Viksit Bharat development plans as a model for other members. It is a small but telling detail: the bank India proposed is now led by a Brazilian who uses Indian policy as an example for everyone else.

The third count, how the bank funds itself, is where India’s chairship of BRICS this year has left its clearest mark. In August 2026, the bank and the Indian government held a joint meeting on bringing more private money into development projects. Rousseff called this a key priority, as members look for ways to fund large infrastructure beyond what governments alone can pay for. Sitharaman’s point was simple: development banks can make projects safer and more predictable for private investors, which brings in more private money.

Two more steps followed. On September 10, two days before the BRICS summit opened, the bank raised 7 billion Chinese yuan through a bond sale in China. This gave it a new source of funds, separate from its usual channels. On the same day, it launched a BRICS-NDB knowledge portal linked to India’s chairship.

These steps will not make headlines outside financial circles. But they matter. A bank that can raise money in different markets and attract private investors does not have to wait for its member governments to put in more capital. That makes it a more reliable lender for developing countries. At the same time, however, relying more on Chinese bond markets may raise questions about whether the bank’s funding is spread evenly across its members.

The NDB can be an important source of finance for the Global South, helping countries build power plants, transport links and water systems. But development lending is slow work. It needs steady funding, careful planning, and trust between members. India’s chairship year has pushed the bank toward a broader funding base. Whether that shift lasts will become clearer in 2027, when India will host the bank’s annual meeting and this year’s results can be measured against what follows.
tag: BRICS Bank; India and BRICS; India BRICS presidency; New Development Bank

title: The New Nixon Shock? Why Japan Fears a Trump-Xi Deal
description: Some history helps explain why the symbolism of the China-U.S. summit matters so much to Tokyo.
text:
The latest China-U.S. summit, held from September 23 to 25, raised concerns in Japan, not so much because of its substance as because of how it appeared. Japanese media have paid particular attention to Donald Trump and Xi Jinping’s references to their respective countries as former “allies” that fought against imperial Japan, as well as to Trump’s apparent intentions. Within the Japanese government, “confusion” has reportedly been expressed internally.

Before the summit, the Japanese government had been preparing for the worst-case scenario, a concern presumably heightened by the U.S. president’s suggestion, immediately after his previous summit with Xi, that arms shipments to Taiwan could be used as a possible “negotiation tool.”

Japan’s Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae was able to secure a meeting with Trump before his meeting with Xi. Following her brief meeting with Trump, Takaichi indicated that their conversation had “the U.S.-China summit in mind” and that they had exchanged views in a timely manner on various issues concerning China. She also noted that “it is important that U.S.-China relations contribute to stability in international relations, including between Japan and the United States,” implying that Japan would prefer the U.S. not to pursue a unilateral deal with China that could come at Japan’s expense.

After the Trump-Xi summit, Japan has seemingly sought to manage expectations and reassure the public. Immediately after the meeting, Takaichi posted on X in Japanese that Trump had provided her with a “detailed explanation of the recent U.S.-China summit.” She also highlighted the significance of holding “two meetings between our leaders within the span of a single week,” describing this as a “demonstration of the strength of the Japan-U.S. alliance.”

Reports reinforcing the narrative that the China-U.S. détente does not overshadow Japan-U.S. relations have also emerged from unofficial government sources. According to the Yomiuri Shimbun, several Japanese government officials told the newspaper that Trump reportedly praised Takaichi in his talks with Xi, describing her as a “strong leader,” and urged the leaders of Japan and China to hold talks with each other, among other remarks.

Despite Trump’s propensity for unconventional remarks, which understandably raise concerns about the future direction of U.S. policy toward Japan and the rest of the world, bureaucratic cooperation between the two countries has continued to deepen. Meanwhile, Piero Tozzi, a policy expert affiliated with the America First Policy Institute (AFPI), a conservative U.S. think tank close to Trump, has emphasized that the current administration continues to view China as a strategic competitor.

However, perceptions matter when it comes to maintaining a stable Japan-U.S. relationship, which helps explain the Japanese government’s considerable efforts to influence the outcome of the China-U.S. summit and shape the narrative surrounding it.

Following the Vietnam War, which a significant portion of the Japanese public regarded as an immoral and unnecessary war against the Vietnamese, and the two so-called “Nixon Shocks” – Washington’s abrupt shift toward China and its unilateral economic measures in 1971 – the Japanese public’s perception of the United States deteriorated sharply. Both developments were particularly jarring because they were undertaken with little or no prior consultation with Tokyo, reinforcing a sense in Japan that Washington could fundamentally alter the strategic and economic environment without taking Japanese interests into account.

Indeed, the U.S. government itself recognized that Nixon’s dual announcement, which came without prior consultation with Japan, had produced major shock waves in the country. Seeking to repair the damage to bilateral relations, Nixon subsequently made a point of meeting with the Japanese emperor and empress. While Nixon’s secrecy surrounding the opening to China, which rattled the Japanese public most deeply, was driven more by his desire to outmaneuver his “enemies” – ranging from State Department officials to the media – than by a commitment to unilateralism, what mattered to Japan was less the substance of the decision than the lack of diplomatic courtesy.

The deterioration in American popularity in Japan was striking. According to polling, the proportion of Japanese who said they liked the U.S. fell from 33 percent in 1970 to 18 percent in 1973 – a decline of nearly half. The dynamics seen in the 1970s attest to the importance of the “theater” of international relations and its impact on Japanese perceptions of the world. A similar concern – or perhaps the lessons learned from that period – seems to be shaping the present moment, as the notable shift in tone between the United States and China is generating speculation about how the structure of world affairs will continue to evolve.

However, there are important differences in the concerns of the Japanese public today. While U.S. distrust in the 1970s was partly driven by fears of being entrapped in the Vietnam War, as well as by a sense that the U.S. was attempting to contain Japan’s postwar economic miracle – a source of considerable national pride – these are not the same emotions that Japanese people are experiencing today. In one of the most tense security environments in recent decades, and amid the decline of U.S. relative strength, Japanese concerns are centered more on abandonment than entrapment. Moreover, Japan no longer sees the U.S. as an economic competitor, as it did during the 1970s, but rather as an opportunity for economic growth.

This is not to say that Japanese concerns are trivial. The highly personalized nature of U.S. foreign policy today will continue to fuel concerns that spheres of influence could emerge in the Indo-Pacific and that Taiwan could be “lost.” To avert such a situation, day-to-day diplomacy with the United States matters. In the immediate aftermath of the Trump-Xi summit, Japan’s approach appears to be working.
tag: China-Japan-U.S. triangle; Takaichi-Trump summit; Trump-Xi summit; Trump-Xi summit Japan; U.S.-Japan Alliance

title: The Next Chapter of Africa-China Climate Cooperation
channel_text: Blog; China Power; East Asia; Environment
description: China’s climate cooperation with Africa is becoming more investment-led, with a focus on industrialization.
text:
Nearly five years have passed since the adoption of the Declaration on China-Africa Cooperation on Combating Climate Change at the Eighth Forum on China-Africa Cooperation (FOCAC 8) in 2021. Since then, discussions have often centered on simple indicators to reflect on the progress made – for example, the number of projects announced, the size of new investments, and the scale of renewable energy commitments.

At first glance, Development Reimagined’s China-Africa Climate Action Tracker provides just this. The tracker captures 246 publicly announced climate actions across 50 African countries between 2022 and the first half of 2026, including nearly 49 GW of renewable energy in the development pipeline, clean technologies, clean transportation, and, more recently, critical minerals. However, while these results are important, they capture only part of a partnership that has evolved significantly over the past five years.

Beyond the numbers, the tracker reveals three structural shifts that have been taking place since FOCAC 8: that cooperation is becoming more investment-led; more closely linked to green industrialization; and increasingly focused on building long-term institutions. As FOCAC 10 approaches in 2027, these shifts have important implications for how future Africa-China climate cooperation should be designed and evaluated.

From Infrastructure Delivery to Long-term Investment

The first shift is a move from contractor-led cooperation toward longer-term investment partnerships.

For many years, Africa-China cooperation in the energy sector was largely associated with engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) projects. Often having bid and won procurement processes funded by African governments or banks, Chinese companies built power plants, transmission lines, and other infrastructure that supported African countries’ energy ambitions. That model remains important and continues to contribute to Africa’s energy transition.

However, the China-Africa Climate Action Tracker suggests that the partnership is evolving. Investment and equity-led projects, EPC-plus projects, and technology transfer are becoming increasingly prominent, while the share of traditional EPC-only projects is declining. And, although Chinese state-owned enterprises such as Power China and Energy China continue to play a dominant role in project delivery in Africa, a growing number of Chinese private firms are expanding their presence through investments in local manufacturing and production capacity.

For example, in Zambia, a Chinese firm announced a lithium battery manufacturing project in 2024 with an investment of approximately $30 million. The facility, located in the Zambia-China Jiangxi International Economic and Technical Cooperation Zone, is now operational. This illustrates how Africa-China climate cooperation can extend beyond infrastructure delivery to support local green manufacturing and industrial development.

Climate Cooperation Is Becoming a Green Industrial Agenda

The second shift is even more interesting. Africa-China climate cooperation is increasingly extending beyond individual renewable energy projects toward the development of integrated green industrial value chains

Hence, although new solar, wind, and hydropower energy infrastructure continue to dominate Africa-China climate cooperation, the tracker also highlights the rapid emergence of critical minerals as an essential component of climate cooperation.

Development Reimagined began systematically tracking Africa-China critical minerals projects in 2025 and has already identified close to 20 projects involving lithium, graphite, rare earth elements, and other strategic resources. More significantly, eight of the nine countries hosting these critical mineral projects also have renewable energy projects. This overlap points to opportunities that Chinese and African firms are taking up to extend cooperation beyond mineral extraction.

African countries are increasingly pursuing and implementing national industrial strategies that connect renewable energy, mineral processing, and manufacturing. The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is developing battery value chains. Nigeria is expanding clean technology manufacturing. Tanzania is positioning itself as a multi-mineral processing hub.

Looking at Africa’s green manufacturing progress, projects that involve Chinese stakeholders span electric vehicle assembly, battery manufacturing, energy storage, solar PV production, and related supply chains. These examples demonstrate growing interest among Chinese companies in localizing production in Africa markets rather than relying solely on exports of finished products.

That said, some of this manufacturing pipeline remains at the memorandum of understanding, feasibility, planning or pre-construction stage. Announced projects don’t always become operational manufacturing capacity. In addition, feasibility studies often miss the opportunity presented by the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), which could help make green manufacturing investments more commercially viable through access to the much larger continental market.

Cooperation Is Moving Beyond Individual Projects

The third trend is perhaps the least visible but could prove the most important. Climate cooperation is increasingly being built through and reinforcing African initiatives and institutions, not just project-by-project.

Since 2022, the tracker has recorded more than 40 climate “exchanges,” including strategic partnerships, technology cooperation, capacity-building initiatives, and industry collaborations. These initiatives receive less attention than utility-scale renewable energy projects, but they could prove fundamental in building the institutional foundations necessary for long-term economic transformation.

For example, pairing Chinese expertise in solar technology and energy storage with training for African engineers and technicians could do more than bring new clean-energy systems online. It could help build the local skills needed to operate and maintain these systems, support local businesses and expand access to reliable electricity over the long term.

Looking Ahead to FOCAC 10

So what do these three trends suggest for the next phase of Africa-China climate cooperation?

Our view at Development Reimagined is that while the number of megawatts installed will remain an important measure of progress – especially in the context of the 300 GW 2030 renewable energy goal announced by African leaders in the 2023 Nairobi declaration – the next stage of Africa-China climate cooperation presents an opportunity for FOCAC 10 to do more than announce the next generation of projects. It can help shape the conditions under which these projects deliver lasting value.

The first priority could be turning a growing pipeline into projects that are delivered. The real test for any announced project comes afterwards – including the need to securing affordable finance, reach construction, begin operations and ultimately deliver economic and climate benefits. FOCAC 10 could place greater emphasis on this implementation journey, including clearer mechanisms to track progress and identify where policy, financing, or technical support is needed. This would help shift the focus from the volume of commitments towards the results they generate.

The second priority could be to continue to connect individual projects to the bigger opportunity of green industrialization. Investments in renewable energy, critical minerals, EVs, batteries, and solar PV are beginning to form the building blocks of new green industrial value chains across African countries. More energy projects need to be directed to support local production, technology transfer, skills development, and value addition. Chinese companies are already exploring this shift, while African countries are developing policies to attract and anchor these investments. FOCAC 10 can help strengthen this convergence, with the AfCFTA providing an important platform for linking national manufacturing investments to a larger continental market.

The third is to invest even after a project is built. A solar farm, manufacturing facility, or battery plant can create important economic and climate benefits, but its longer-term contribution depends on the capabilities around it, including skilled workers, local suppliers, research institutions, effective regulators, and access to finance. These foundations are less visible than a new project, but they determine whether investments can be sustained, replicated and scaled.

Future Africa-China climate cooperation therefore has an opportunity to put greater emphasis on building these capabilities alongside physical infrastructure, while also responding more fully to African countries’ priorities on climate adaptation.

These three priorities, although they might be new, do not, in fact, require a departure from the progress made since FOCAC 8. Rather, they build on how the partnership is already evolving.

FOCAC 10, to be held in 2027, can help move Africa-China climate cooperation into its next active phase: one where success is measured not simply by what is announced or built, but by what actual power is delivered, what industrial goods are produced locally and what industrial capabilities are growing on the continent.
