title: The Proliferation of Illicit Drones in Southeast Asia
description: The past two years have seen the growing use of off-the-shelf commercial drones for criminal and militant activities.
text:
Drones have become synonymous with modern-day warfare. Recent conflict theaters in Russia-Ukraine, Myanmar, Sudan, parts of the Sahel, and the Middle East have witnessed the heavy use of drones, and the Russia-Ukraine war in particular has been a crucible of innovation in this regard. Southeast Asia has not been immune to the use of drones, which have been used widely in conflicts such as the 2017 Marawi siege, the Myanmar conflict since 2021, and the Thailand-Cambodia border conflict last year.

Beyond their use in conflict, the region has seen a steady increase in the illicit use of drones primarily involving commercial-off-the-shelf (COTS) consumer drones (Figure 1).

Figure 1: Illicit drone trends in Southeast Asia over time. (Chart by Rueben Dass)

Criminal and terrorist networks have begun adopting this tactic due in part to the media attention given to drones, the accessibility of these systems (particularly COTS drones), and the relatively low barriers to entry with regard to their usage. This article provides a brief overview of illicit drone use in Southeast Asia with the aim of highlighting current trends that may then be beneficial for developing targeted countermeasures in the region.

The analysis below is based on 22 illicit drone incidents as reported by the media up to August 2026, excluding the use of drones in conflict zones. Due to the open-source nature of the data, the analysis may be subject to reporting bias and could possibly be an under-representation of the actual phenomenon.

Criminal Use Cases

The major proportion of illicit drone use in the region – around 86 percent – has been linked to criminal activity. Of these, narcotics-related activity associated with prison incursions and cross-border smuggling has been the highest (Figure 2).

In August 2024, a commercial quadcopter drone was used to smuggle narcotics into the Tapah prison, the first recorded incident of illicit drone use in Malaysia. The Malaysian Home Ministry noted that there were 55 cases of drones being used to smuggle narcotics into prisons that year. Drones have also been used to smuggle other contraband into Malaysian prisons, with two individuals being apprehended for attempting to use a DJI Air 2S drone to smuggle tobacco into the Sungai Udang Prison in Malacca in July 2026. A similar case occurred in Machang prison in Kelantan in 2025.

In June 2025, a drone was used to smuggle drugs into a Class IIA Narcotics Prison in Bandung, West Java. Transactions were made between the buyer (an inmate) and the seller via social media. Similar incidents were recorded in Sragen Prison in 2023 and Nusa Kambangan in 2019, as well as at prisons in the Philippines.

Figure 2: Breakdown of recent illicit drone incidents in Southeast Asia by type of illicit activity. (Chart by Rueben Dass)

Aside from prison incursions, narcotics have also featured prominently alongside drones in cross-border smuggling and illicit sales. The United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime has reported that small commercial drones are increasingly being employed for cross-border smuggling of narcotics, particularly along the Malaysia-Thailand, Thailand-Myanmar and Thailand-Laos borders. In June 2020, Singapore and Malaysian authorities dismantled a drug-smuggling syndicate that was using a COTS drone to smuggle narcotics from Malaysia into Singapore.

Larger drones have also been linked to cross-border smuggling syndicates. In June 2025, two large hexacopter drones were found buried in Sadao district, Songkhla, Thailand. The drones were linked to three Chinese nationals who were allegedly involved in a narcotics syndicate. In Vietnam, a couple was apprehended for using a DJI quadcopter drone to deliver drugs and collect payments from buyers. Apart from delivery mechanisms, narcotics syndicates are also using drones to monitor the movements of law enforcement agents and evade detection.

Thailand has reported at least three major seizures of drones and drone-related parts over the last two years. A December 2025 raid on a warehouse in the 2nd Army Area led to the seizure of 2,500 drones that were believed to have been smuggled into the country, while a March 2026 raid on two warehouses in Lat Krabang outside Bangkok led to the seizure of 2,083 drones that were smuggled in and illicitly re-sold on social media platforms. In August 2025, Thai authorities raided another warehouse in Samut Prakan allegedly linked to a Singaporean company, where numerous drones, signal jamming devices, and a van with signal-disrupting equipment were found.

The possibility that some of these networks were linked to cross-border drone trafficking and smuggling syndicates cannot be ruled out. The December 2025 raid was followed by the arrest of four Myanmar nationals in a hotel near Suvarnabhumi airport in Bangkok. They were suspected of trafficking 10 Chinese drones into Myanmar to be resold to the country’s military junta. The drones were to be dismantled and transported across the border in parts on commercial passenger flights. The drones seized were large industrial multi-rotor drones.

In July 2026, another Myanmar national who was attempting to smuggle four first-person view (FPV) drones and other drone components across the border to Myanmar was arrested in Mae Sot, in Tak province, on Thailand’s border with Myanmar. The drones were “advanced systems” suitable for military applications and had originated in Chiang Mai. The end-user for the drones was not identified. A year earlier, a one-way attack drone with an explosive warhead believed to have belonged to the Myanmar military was found in the same province.

The use of drones by non-state armed groups (NSAGs) in Myanmar has been well-documented in several academic studies. The Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Centre documented more than 2,100 drone strikes by NSAGs across more than 600 distinct locations in Myanmar, noting it had “significantly reshaped battlefield strategy” by 2024. The junta has increased its reliance on airstrikes since late 2023, closing the gap in drone use with NSAGs. Illicit trafficking and smuggling networks through neighboring countries, as mentioned above, may be playing a role in helping both NSAGs and the military circumvent export controls on dual-use materials by China. U.K.-based Conflict Armament Research found that high-precision European satellite navigation systems that “harden” drones from jamming and spoofing were diverted through commercial resale to Myanmar for use by the junta, highlighting another possible entry pathway for these components into the region.

Commercial drones have also been used in several cases of suspected espionage. In August 2025, two Chinese nationals were arrested in Kuala Lumpur for trespassing into the Malaysian Ministry of Defense headquarters with a DJI Mavic 3 drone. They were accused of attempting to capture footage from the inside of the building. In the wake of the Thailand-Cambodia border conflict last year, numerous drone reconnaissance flights were detected over military installations and government agencies in Thailand, with the government hinting at possible espionage-related activity.

Terrorist Use Cases

The use of drones by terrorist groups in the region dates back to 2017 during the siege of Marawi in the Philippines by the Islamic State (IS)-linked Maute group. Inexpensive COTS drones were used during the siege primarily for intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance activities. The same tactic was also employed during the siege by the Armed Forces of the Philippines. No cases of weaponized drones were documented in the region, despite IS’ heavy use of them in Iraq and Syria during the same period.

Apart from the Philippines, there have been several cases of Malaysian and Indonesian terrorist cells that have been in possession of or attempted/planned to use drones in terrorist plots. In 2016, Malaysian authorities uncovered an IS-linked plot to attack the federal police headquarters in Kuala Lumpur with a drone. Apart from online discussions, there was no evidence of drone procurement or actual use. Recent arrests in the country apparently revealed the discovery of drone-related information, simulation games, and applications on electronic devices belonging to some of the terrorism suspects. These included instructions on drone operations. However, there was again no evidence of any operationalization of drones in plots or attacks.

In October 2020, a Jemaah Islamiyah cell in Bekasi, West Java, Indonesia was found to be in possession of a drone that they allegedly intended to use in an attack. In September 2024, counter-terrorism operations in Indonesia led to the arrest of seven individuals from West Sumatra and the Bangka Belitung Islands who were planning to attack then Pope Francis during his visit to the country. In their possession was a DJI mini drone that could potentially have been used for surveillance or an attack.

Apart from drones being used in attacks, Indonesian nationals have also been involved in attempting to smuggle drones to militants in the Middle East. Indonesian court documents viewed by this author revealed a syndicate involved in attempting to transport drones and drone components from Indonesia to militants linked to Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS) in Syria through Türkiye. The group had procured a Chinese-made Sonicmodell Sea Rescue fixed-wing drone, a Heewing RC F-01 delta-wing drone, an Indonesian-made Rajawali drone, a Diatone Manba MK4 F722 flight controller stack, and a pair of FPV goggles. Some of the items were procured through open websites, social media, and e-commerce sites such as AliExpress. The drone components were packed alongside foodstuff and transported via commercial post to Türkiye to be then sent to HTS militants in Syria. Indonesian authorities also uncovered the use of cryptocurrency in the financial trails.

Key Trends and Outlook

The cases of illicit drones in the region point to several trends. First, the use of cheap COTS drones for illicit activity remains a key issue of concern. These drones are easily available, have few purchasing restrictions, and are difficult to regulate given their dual-use nature. With drones becoming increasingly cheap and small, and more private companies/vendors engaging in the sale of these items, criminal and terrorist networks are not going to cease attempting to use these types of drones to enhance their illicit operations.

Second, within the crime sphere, narcotics have featured prominently with illicit drone use. Drones are not only being used to smuggle the actual drugs but also used for reconnaissance by these networks to evade detection. In the future, drones could also be used to traffic firearms across borders given the close relationship between illicit firearms and narcotics networks in the region. Drones have been used to traffic firearms across the India-Pakistan border in regions like Punjab. While there is no present need for illicit actors in the region to engage more sophisticated systems like fiber optic or FPV drones like the Latin American cartels, for example, this possibility cannot be discounted in the future.

Third, drone trafficking and smuggling networks possibly linked to conflict actors and NSAGs continue to exploit mainstream businesses through the use of front companies, commercial transport and logistical pipelines, and human mules to traffic drone parts through countries such as Thailand and Indonesia. The modular nature of some drones and the commercial availability of their associated components often facilitate the illicit smuggling and trafficking of these systems.

Given the above trends, counter-drone measures should focus on interdicting illicit supply chain networks, logistical and commercial pipelines, and the human nodes linking these networks together. Government agencies must invest sufficient resources in enhancing their individual counter-drone capabilities, both in terms of hardware and trained personnel, and hardening critical infrastructure such as administrative buildings and public infrastructure against attacks by drones.

Countries such as Thailand, the Philippines, Malaysia, Indonesia, and Singapore have already incorporated drones in their law enforcement operations and have set up specialized units within their services, which is a positive way forward. This should be complemented with robust legal frameworks that govern and regulate their use, alongside ensuring comprehensive drone forensics capabilities. To conclude, regional governments must be as innovative and effective in their approach to countering drones as their adversaries are in improvising and using them.

title: The Quiet, Careful Growth of Philippines-Taiwan Ties
description: Manila is exploiting the space between its One China policy and functional cooperation with Taipei.
text:
On October 2, the Philippine Coast Guard commissioned BRP Sarangani, a retired Taiwanese Coast Guard cutter formerly known as the Kinmen. The transfer is unusual because Taiwan only transfers decommissioned vessels to states that officially recognize Taiwan’s statehood, which the Philippines does not.

Furthermore, the vessel did not sail from Kaohsiung to Manila under the Taiwanese flag, government-to-government, the way Taipei’s other patrol-vessel donations have gone to Palau, the Marshall Islands and Tuvalu – states that recognize the Republic of China (Taiwan). Instead, the Philippine nongovernmental organization We Protect Our Seas (WPS) Foundation quietly acquired the Kinmen, renamed it, repainted it, and handed it to the Philippine Coast Guard in a ceremony that never mentioned where the ship had come from.

The reason for this indirect approach is obvious: the Philippines adheres to the One China policy and would not like to provoke China. Unofficial engagements with Taiwan, carried out by states like the United States, France, Singapore, the United Kingdom, and Germany that formally recognize China, are a global default. China explicitly tolerates their economic and cultural relations with Taiwan.

So what makes the Philippines’ engagement with Taiwan different, and why is Manila engaging with Taiwan so extensively now when its relationship with China is tenser than in the past two decades?

The Philippines as a Distinct Case

For most of the above-mentioned states, Taiwan policy is about standing up for democracy and alliance management, conducted at a safe distance – being geographically far away from the immediate threat of military conflict with China. However, the Philippines is in close proximity to Taiwan. The Philippine province of Batanes lies south of Taiwan, near the Bashi Channel, placing it closer to spillover from the Taiwan conflict.

Adding to this are 200,000 Filipino workers currently in Taiwan, whose evacuation during a Taiwan crisis would pose an emergency for the Philippine government. Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has publicly stated that Taiwan’s security is inseparable from the Philippines’ own, making clear that Taiwan is a national security question rather than an elective foreign policy stance.

Yet Manila must tread carefully. Anything it does with Taiwan that upsets China is directly visible in Chinese assertiveness in the South China Sea, affecting Filipino sovereignty and fisheries.

The Philippines’ increased engagement with Taiwan predates the Marcos administration. Taiwan is the Philippines’ ninth-largest trading partner, with established cooperation in education, agriculture, and healthcare and growing interest in semiconductors and start-ups. Under Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte (in office from 2016-2022), the Philippines and Taiwan signed a bilateral investment agreement in 2017 – the first major investment agreement in the last 25 years – under Taiwan’s New Southbound Policy, with cooperation extending across trade, investment, education, and labor mobility. But this engagement made sense given that the Philippines was in a state of rapprochement with China.

What has changed now is the strategic significance of Philippines-Taiwan engagement. Economic and cultural ties are increasingly accompanied by institutional and maritime cooperation. In April 2025, the Philippines eased restrictions on official exchanges with Taiwan, facilitating travel for economic and trade-related purposes. This was highlighted by Taiwanese Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung’s visit to Manila, the second such foreign minister visit to the Philippines since 1975. Taiwan’s subsequent proposal to open a second representative office in Cebu to deepen the “Taiwan-Philippine Corridor” further signaled an effort to deepen institutional engagement.

Maritime cooperation has become increasingly apparent. What began as crisis management following the 2013 killing of a Taiwanese fisherman by Philippine personnel has created a basis for maritime cooperation, despite the absence of diplomatic recognition.

The WPS Foundation confirmed that the recently transferred vessel, BRP Sarangani, will support maritime patrols, search and rescue, humanitarian assistance, disaster response, and training. The transfer of vessels between two coast guards without requiring an overt government-to-government transaction demonstrates how institutional informality can create political space for cooperation that formal diplomatic relations might otherwise constrain.

Last year, the Philippine and Taiwanese Coast Guard conducted patrols in the Bashi Channel. Taiwan’s Coast Guard is also planning to send vessels to visit the Philippines in 2027, the first visit since the Philippines switched its recognition from the ROC to the People’s Republic of China in 1975.

But why is the Philippines doing this now, when China has become more assertive? One plausible explanation is that the Philippines sees little benefit in restraining its engagement with Taiwan. Chinese pressure in the South China Sea continued despite Manila’s previously cautious approach to Taiwan, giving Philippine policymakers fewer reasons to believe that restraint will win China’s goodwill.

At the same time, the Philippines cannot match China militarily or economically. Deepening ties with Taiwan offer the Philippines a way to widen its strategic and economic options at a relatively low cost. Manila can strengthen cooperation with a partner that provides investment, technology, and security benefits, while also engaging with an issue that China considers highly sensitive. Whether this amounts to deliberate tit-for-tat is difficult to establish, but the effect is clear: the Philippines has less incentive than before to keep its Taiwan relationship within narrow limits simply to avoid displeasing China.

Keeping It Under the Threshold

While the Philippines has steadily expanded its engagement with Taiwan, it has stopped short of turning that engagement into overt alignment, as seen in the vessel transfer through a non-governmental organization and the Philippine government’s refusal to publicly recognize it as a formerly Taiwanese vessel. Manila has repeatedly affirmed that its One China policy remains “consistent, clear and unchanged” and that “economic, cultural, and functional cooperation with Taiwan” does not violate it. Military and security engagements such as tabletop exercises or patrols are consistently described as “unofficial and informal.” Even the April 2025 easing of visa restrictions excludes visits and exchanges over defense- and security-related issues. Furthermore, no agreements, Memoranda of Understanding (MoU), exchange of notes or similar documents can proceed without clearance from the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) and, where necessary, an authorization from the Office of the President.

This caution reflects Manila’s awareness that spillover from a Taiwan crisis would be unavoidable. Under the Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement, U.S. forces could rely on Philippine bases to support operations in a Taiwan crisis. Yet Filipino officials have been explicit that they do not want the Philippines drawn into such a conflict – a position echoed by the public, with roughly 86 percent of Filipinos saying that they want the country to remain neutral in a China-Taiwan conflict. Philippine Foreign Affairs Secretary Thersea Lazaro has said that Manila is open to discussions with China over evacuation plans for its citizens in the event of a Chinese invasion of Taiwan.

The throughline is consistent: Manila wants to preserve its One China policy so Beijing has less reason to treat Philippine security as fair game in any future crisis.

title: The Scam Industry Is Becoming a Big Problem in India
description: According to the FBI, American nationals lost around $50 million to one network of online scammers based in India.
text:
On September 15, investigators raided three call centers in Pune and Patiala, finding around 220 people at work. According to India’s Enforcement Directorate, the premises were being used to defraud Americans. Investigators said that they were establishing the workers’ identities and roles.

Officers also searched a Chandigarh property linked to a suspected organizer. They seized 66 mobile phones, 13 laptops, and unspecified records. Investigators said that they were examining calling scripts, internet telephony systems, and payment routes.

The published account did not provide an overall figure for victims’ losses.

Months earlier, another investigation exposed the damage one India-based network could inflict. An American woman’s $1.7 million loss helped investigators connect other victims to the operation. The FBI subsequently attributed more than $48.7 million in reported losses among over 600 American victims to the network. Indian authorities arrested six alleged leaders in December 2025.

These cases reveal an enduring threat to American households, while also hurting India’s image abroad. Organized networks operating from India can reach victims thousands of miles away. As has happened with Cambodia’s scam centers, a raid may shut down one office while the people who hire workers, move the money, and coordinate from outside remain untouched.

The Business of Scamming

The criminal organizations behind these calls can resemble a conventional business. A 2024 study published by Itad and commissioned by Britain’s Home Office described larger Indian scam centers with management structures, staff shifts, human resources departments, and quality control functions. It also documented recruitment agencies, prepared scripts, English and accent training, and performance incentives.

Roles can be divided between “openers,” who establish contact, and “closers,” who persuade victims to surrender money. Beyond the telephone operators sit facilitators who supply websites, deceptive pop-ups, recruitment services, and various forms of money laundering. The study also identified markets for phone numbers, calling scripts, and victim profiles. These arrangements allow different participants to specialize in separate parts of the fraud.

Reuters reported in 2016 that former workers at scam centers near Mumbai described memorizing scripts, learning from floor managers, and receiving commissions or incentives. The accounts describe a workplace where securing a payment from a victim could increase an employee’s earnings.

Technology helps conceal the operation. In a Noida case announced in July 2025, Britain’s National Crime Agency described spoofed telephone numbers and internet calls routed through servers in several countries. The scam center in Noida targeted both British and American victims. A familiar-looking number on a screen offered no reliable indication of where the caller actually worked.

An office can make a scam look like a real business. Reporting from Maharashtra has described scam centers posing as IT or outsourcing firms, while poor verification of businesses made such operations harder to detect.

How Scammers Extract Money

The details differ between networks, but documented cases show a recurring progression from an alarming first contact to demands for money.

Stage one is intended to trigger initial fear and gain attention from the intended victim. In technical support fraud, a person browsing the internet sees a warning claiming that their computer has been infected or compromised. The message supplies a telephone number. Calling it connects the victim to someone offering to resolve the supposed emergency. In the Noida case, investigators said callers falsely presented themselves as Microsoft employees and charged for unnecessary repairs.

Other schemes begin with unsolicited calls claiming unpaid taxes, compromised identities or criminal investigations. The goal is to create a false sense of urgency and then urge action before the victim has time to check it.

Scammers reinforce their claims through multiple impersonations. A supposed technical support worker may introduce a bank representative, followed by someone claiming government authority. Each apparent handover makes the preceding story seem independently confirmed.

The FBI’s warning about “Phantom Hacker” scams describes forged correspondence on government letterheads and instructions to keep transfers secret. The victim is encouraged to distrust the very people who could interrupt the fraud. The caller says the conversation must stay private to protect the victim. That stops the victim from asking someone else for advice.

Some operators persuade victims to install remote-access software. This can allow the scammer to inspect the computer and watch as the victim opens financial accounts. The supposed repair becomes an opportunity to identify available savings. A second impersonator then claims those funds face immediate danger and must be moved to a supposedly secure account.

In other schemes, threats of arrest or deportation supply the pressure. American prosecutions have documented India-based callers impersonating tax and immigration authorities to extract payments. The victim is made to believe that following instructions will protect a home, retirement account, or legal status. That belief is central to the deception.

Payment methods vary. Gift cards and prepaid cards allow scammers to demand value without asking victims to send money directly to an identifiable caller. Once card details are surrendered, criminals can use or transfer the value.

Cryptocurrency offers another route. Victims may be instructed to withdraw savings, buy digital assets and send them to wallets controlled by the fraud network. Wire transfers can similarly move money into accounts controlled by intermediaries. These methods feature in documented call-center investigations.

Cash and gold introduce a physical collection stage. The FBI has warned that scammers direct victims to buy precious metals or withdraw cash for supposed safekeeping, then dispatch couriers to collect them. The person arriving at an American doorstep can therefore be part of a fraud directed from abroad.

Money laundering adds further distance between the victim and the organizers. In one India-based operation that was prosecuted in the U.S. state of Virginia, American authorities documented couriers, bank accounts, and hawala transfers used to move proceeds. Such arrangements complicate efforts to trace the money and identify who ultimately received it.

After the transfer, the scammers may cease contact, leaving victims with unanswered calls and missing savings. But some schemes continue demanding transfers over days or months, so the first payment does not necessarily end the manipulation.

Either way, by the time a victim recognizes the fraud, the lost money may already have moved through several hands.

The same methods are used against victims in other countries. Canada’s Project OCTAVIA targeted callers impersonating tax officials; reported losses to that particular scam fell from C$6.4 million in 2018 to C$1.4 million in 2019.

In Australia, police alleged that Hyderabad-based Ridge IT Solutions had taken 80-100 million rupees from Australians over roughly two years. The allegations included payments passing through Australian accounts before moving toward India.

Why Scam Centers Survive

India is not unique in hosting these scam centers. The online scam industry is global, and the financial scale is substantial. The FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) received 1,008,597 complaints in 2025, with reported losses of $20.9 billion. People aged 60 and older reported approximately $7.7 billion in losses. Complaints involving technical or customer support fraud and government impersonation together exceeded 80,000, with losses above $2.9 billion.

Those totals cover perpetrators worldwide, and IC3 also receives complaints from outside the United States. These figures cannot be presented as American losses caused entirely by India-based centers; IC3 has not established the share of the 2025 losses originating from operations in India.

Nevertheless, India’s role is well documented: in a 2022 podcast, the FBI said most technical-support and telephone scams targeting Americans originated from India. And while scam operations based in Southeast Asia, especially Cambodia, have received more attention of late, scam centers operating out of India remain less discussed.

Recovering money presents a daunting challenge. Investigators must identify recipients, trace subsequent transfers, and seek the necessary legal cooperation. American agents cannot simply conduct arrests in India. Even successful prosecutions do not guarantee that every victim will receive full repayment. Often, the scammers are able to keep their ill-gotten gains, and use them to fund further crimes.

Scam centers can reopen after raids because the system around them often remains in place. In December 2025, The Indian Express reported concerns from Maharashtra police about weak business verification, scrutiny of network connections and coordination. Its reporting also described operations shifting toward smaller towns offering cheaper premises and access to English-speaking workers.

Those conditions lower the practical barriers to reopening. A group with access to staff, scripts, communications services, and payment intermediaries can establish another office even after one address is exposed.

Jurisdiction adds delay. Victims report crimes in the United States, relevant records may belong to banks or technology companies elsewhere, callers operate in India, and accomplices handling payments may be in another country. Investigators have to connect those dots before evidence can support arrests and prosecutions.

Within India, policing is primarily a state responsibility, while networks may operate across state boundaries. The Itad study identified limited collaboration between jurisdictions as an obstacle to connecting linked operations.

The Noida investigation revealed the work involved. It took 18 months of cooperation involving the Indian CBI, Britain’s National Crime Agency, the U.S. FBI, and Microsoft before the July 2025 raid.

In July 2025, the CBI arrested two people at a Noida call center that British investigators said had contacted more than 100 people in the UK. British victims were believed to have lost more than 390,000 pounds. Canada’s Royal Canadian Mounted Police Hyderabad(RCMP) said its Project OCTAVIA investigation had helped shut down 39 illegal call centers in the Noida and New Delhi areas.

In November 2025, Hyderabad police arrested nine people at an alleged fake call center targeting Australians.

These cases form part of a wider enforcement effort. According to the FBI, cooperation with Indian agencies since 2022 has involved more than 1,200 information exchanges and more than 475 arrests across 27 joint operations. That includes about 175 arrests in 13 joint operations in 2025 alone.

The harder task is finding the people who run these scams, move the money, and help new centers open. Raids can close an office, but another may take its place. Victims also need a chance to get their money back.

Until that changes, these networks can keep making money by frightening people in the United States and beyond. They also hurt India’s global image at a time when the country wants to be seen as a reliable technology and services hub.

title: The Strategic Implications of China’s Military Facility in Laos
description: Ban Keun poses only a limited direct threat to the South China Sea or Taiwan, but it will enhance China’s ability to place pressure on U.S. naval forces.
text:
China inaugurated an air force support and training center in Laos on September 29, marking China’s third overseas military facility. Analysts have noted that the arrangement could expand the People’s Liberation Army’s military presence in Southeast Asia and strengthen China’s regional interests, although there is currently no evidence that Beijing has deployed large-scale forces at the site.

According to China’s Ministry of National Defense, the China-Laos Joint Support and Training Center and the China-Laos Friendship Aviation Academy have formally begun operations at Ban Keun Airport. The two facilities are mainly intended to assist in the training of Lao Air Force pilots and will be jointly maintained and operated by China and Laos. Beijing has not disclosed details regarding the number of Chinese personnel or the equipment stationed there.

China has emphasized that the facilities comply with the laws of both countries and with international law, and that they are “not directed against any third party.”

Ban Keun Airport is significant because it is China’s first publicly acknowledged overseas military facility centered on airpower. This differs from China’s overseas facilities in Djibouti and Cambodia, which have largely been associated with naval operations.

China’s continued use of the “joint training center” model – also used in Cambodia – suggests that the PLA may be pursuing a gradual approach to expanding its overseas military presence. Ban Keun Airport may initially operate as a jointly used China-Laos facility, while allowing the Chinese presence to increase over time.

Geographically, Ban Keun Airport is located in Vientiane Province in northwestern Laos, around 45 kilometers from the capital, Vientiane. During the Vietnam War and the Laotian Civil War in the 1970s, the area had been part of the local airfield network used for tactical support operations, but it later ceased operations.

Satellite imagery suggests that construction work began around October last year, and by September this year the facility had already reached a considerable scale. Its longest runway is approximately 2,000 meters. From a geographic perspective, Ban Keun occupies an important location near the center of mainland Southeast Asia. It is also close to the China-Laos Railway, just north of Vientiane, giving the site convenient transportation access. This means that personnel and equipment sent from China would not necessarily have to rely solely on air transport. The China-Laos Railway could also be used to move personnel and certain equipment into Laos. For an overseas joint support base, this logistical advantage is highly significant.

A similar consideration may also apply to China’s other joint support facility in mainland Southeast Asia, at Ream in Cambodia. To a considerable extent, the future possibility of railway links extending directly into southern Cambodia may also enhance the logistical value of such a facility.

From the perspective of operational radius, however, Ban Keun Airport is unlikely to be primarily intended for operations in the South China Sea. China already has military facilities on Woody Island that can serve as forward bases for power projection in the area.

The greater significance of Ban Keun lies in its potential role as a transit base for the PLA Air Force. From this location, Chinese forces would have a certain level of operational reach toward Myanmar and farther south toward Singapore. For this reason, outside observers may view the airport’s most important function as providing the PLA Air Force with an additional staging and transit airfield for operations in Southeast Asia.

For the same reason, although Ban Keun currently poses only a limited direct threat to Taiwan Strait security, it still has significance for China’s broader ability to project military power abroad and to place pressure on U.S. naval forces operating around Singapore. For the United States, Singapore and Thailand are both important logistical and replenishment locations, particularly during periods when U.S. aircraft carriers are rotating or undergoing maintenance. These locations would potentially fall within the operational range of aircraft operating from Ban Keun.

From a broader strategic perspective, China’s decision to establish a military airfield near the center of mainland Southeast Asia is therefore noteworthy. In the future, the facility could also be used to complicate U.S. military operations in the Gulf of Thailand, the Andaman Sea, and even the Strait of Malacca. This is the broader geostrategic significance of Ban Keun Airport.

title: The Strategic Logic Behind Pakistan’s Defense Pacts
channel_text: Blog; Security; South Asia; The Pulse
description: Last week, Pakistan signed the Badr Pact with Türkiye, Qatar, and Indonesia, the latest in a string of defense-related agreements with key partners.
text:
On October 21, Pakistan, Türkiye, Qatar, and Indonesia signed the Badr Pact, a quadrilateral defense cooperation framework. As per the joint statement issued after the signing of the memorandum of understanding in Doha, the pact is aimed at deepening cooperation in defense manufacturing, joint research and development, technical training, and industrial capacity building among the signatory countries.

The pact is expected to pave the way for deeper technological integration and joint production by leveraging the complementary strengths of the defense sectors of the four countries.

This agreement is the latest addition to Pakistan’s expanding security partnerships. Over the past year, Islamabad has concluded multiple defense pacts with numerous countries in West Asia and neighboring regions.

In September 2025, Pakistan signed the Strategic Mutual Defense Agreement with Saudi Arabia, under which aggression against one will be treated as aggression against the other. In August 2026, Pakistan, Türkiye and Saudi Arabia concluded the Makkah Joint Defense Agreement, which contains an explicit collective defense commitment. The same month, Pakistan signed a Protocol Agreement with Kuwait, which has expanded military cooperation in training, capacity building and related areas between the two countries.

The Badr agreement has now added a multilateral industrial cooperation framework with Türkiye, Qatar, and Indonesia.

There are three interconnected reasons for Pakistan’s participation in these agreements, which highlight the strategic trajectory Islamabad is now pursuing in terms of its defense partnerships.

First, these agreements reflect Islamabad’s growing strategic engagement with key Muslim countries amid rapidly shifting regional security alignments in West Asia. It is important to note that Pakistan’s military performance during last year’s clashes with India demonstrated credible conventional capabilities and helped restore a measure of international strategic credibility. At the same time, Pakistan has played an important and visible mediating role between Iran and the United States, and has helped in keeping channels of communication open at a time when many other actors found themselves constrained by their own alignments.

Arguably, these developments have reinforced perceptions of Pakistan as a useful middle power, which is capable of engaging competing power blocs. In a tumultuous region like West Asia, traditional security umbrellas have shown their limits amid the U.S.-Iran war. Against this backdrop, countries are increasingly seeing value in deepening ties with a state like Pakistan that has maintained working relationships across multiple camps and has proven operational military capabilities in recent years.

Second, Pakistan has long pursued the idea of joint defense production and investment in its defense industry to elevate its security partnerships beyond transactional procurement of weapons. This vision has benefited Pakistan in many ways. For instance, cooperation with China has produced notable results, including the JF-17 fighter program and related industrial capacity. Similarly, ties with Türkiye have expanded into naval shipbuilding along with other technology and production initiatives.

A recent analysis published in Dawn newspaper observed that each of the recent defense agreements signed by Pakistan carried an explicit provision for joint defense production and investment in the defense industry. “This clause in every defense pact reveals Islamabad’s long-term strategic objective of moving from a buyer-seller relationship to a co-production partnership with reliable partners in the region,” it noted.

This essentially means that such opportunities can help Pakistan accelerate its defense modernization and help sustain credible conventional deterrence in a difficult neighborhood.

Third, Pakistan has been working to develop a more competitive defense industry, which is capable of supporting meaningful arms exports to a level where it could compete with major international players. In recent months, there has been a noticeable increase in reporting of export discussions and deals involving countries in Africa, West Asia and other regions, including substantial packages linked to platforms such as the JF-17 and related systems.

Moreover, Pakistan has long participated actively in international defense exhibitions, where it has showcased both domestically developed and jointly produced equipment with partners such as China. In this regard, the new agreements offer Pakistan a way to build on the idea of expanding arms exports, attract investment into the sector, and raise the competitiveness of Pakistani offerings. One can argue that over time these defense deals may also support the further development of Pakistan’s local production capacity, creating a direct link between increased industrial strength, export earnings, and operational self-reliance.

Taken together, the Badr agreement and Pakistan’s recent defense pacts reflect Islamabad’s growing role in shaping an emerging security architecture in West Asia. Arguably, through these frameworks, Pakistan is not only going to play a role in enhancing the security of its partners through military training, operational expertise, and joint manufacturing, but it will also likely benefit by securing foreign investment, technology transfer, and building defense industrial self-reliance.

It will be interesting to watch how Pakistan will navigate the opportunities these arrangements will bring, while also managing the constraints that will inevitably accompany a growing list of commitments.

title: The Surprising Drama in Taipei’s 2026 Mayor Race
description: Few gave the DPP's Puma Shen much of a chance in traditionally pan-Blue Taipei. But the race is proving more competitive than expected.
text:
Few would have expected the Taipei mayoral race to become one of the most hotly watched races of the 2026 local elections in Taiwan. With incumbent Mayor Chiang Wan-an of the Kuomintang (KMT) facing off against Puma Shen of the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP), polling shows Shen doing unusually well for a city that is traditionally seen as a KMT stronghold.

Another reason the campaign is attracting attention: the post is often a stepping stone to the presidency. Past presidents Chen Shui-bian and Ma Ying-jeou both previously served as Taipei mayor.

Taipei is generally understood to be a KMT bastion, given that many of those who came with the KMT to Taiwan in the wake of the Chinese Civil War settled in Taipei. To date, Chen Shui-bian is an outlier as the only DPP mayor of Taipei in history. While Ko Wen-je won the mayorship in 2014 as an independent who had the backing of the pan-Green camp, he was seen as having benefited from his independent political reputation, which did not necessarily link him with the DPP.

Shen running for Taipei mayor, then, was not initially seen as likely to be successful. If anything, Shen was originally seen as having agreed to be something of a political sacrifice for the DPP.

Shen is one of the DPP’s most visible legislators, and it would be a poor look for the DPP to field someone obscure to run in Taiwan’s capital. Taipei, after all, often sets the tone for other political races. Yet Shen was seen as unlikely to win and as having potentially signed up himself for a disastrous race.

In 2022, the DPP’s Taipei mayoral candidate lost by over 10 percentage points. The 2018 race was even more humiliating for the party, with DPP candidate Pasuya Yao finishing a distant third behind both Ko Wen-je and the KMT’s choice.

Shen is an unusual candidate for historically pan-Blue Taipei. Shen, originally an academic specializing in criminology, is best known as the founder of the Doublethink Lab and the Kuma Academy. The Doublethink Lab is Taiwan’s best-known disinformation research organization, while the Kuma Academy is one of the foremost civil defense groups that regularly conducts training in skills that might be useful in the event of a Chinese invasion or other catastrophes. Given this background, Shen is mostly publicly known for being tough on China-related issues.

Shen also played a prominent role in the eruption of the 2024 Bluebird Movement, which was partly sparked by anger over Shen being injured during a scuffle in the legislature.

Running for Taipei’s mayor seat, then, is mostly a test of whether Shen might have a political life beyond serving two terms as a party list legislator. Though Shen is still in his first term, if he did well or at least put a dent in Chiang Wan-an’s vote count, the DPP would likely keep him in rotation for future positions, as one of the party’s more visible younger politicians. Shen is currently 44.

Not many expected Shen to actually be competitive in the race. Survey polls in Taiwan that are not conducted by academic research institutions are largely partisan and are released in order to impact, not reflect, election results. With that caveat in mind, some polls show Shen within a few points of Chiang.

Shen’s campaign has focused on anti-incumbent sentiment by depicting Chiang Wan-an as a handsome but ineffectual figure who does not know about policy and largely relies on aides to provide him with information. Shen’s strong performance during interviews has also benefited him. One interview with a pan-Blue-leaning talk show host went viral due to Shen’s ability to casually answer the host’s questions about a range of policy issues with detailed proposals, without having to rely on notes or other information.

Likewise, analysts have noted that Shen only attacks the Chiang mayoral administration in areas where his own campaign has a detailed counterproposal for how to carry out city governance, thus avoiding a purely negative campaign.

Chiang was also recently hit by two political controversies. The first involved Chiang’s son winning a Taipei city-funded scholarship for a student exchange program with the United States, despite being the mayor’s son and a U.S. citizen. Subsequently, Chiang faced allegations of nepotism, leading Chiang to state that his family would not accept the scholarship.

The second controversy, which is decidedly more bizarre, involved Chiang being found to have discarded a ceremonial stalk of sugarcane he was gifted during a temple ceremony. Chiang threw the stalk by the side of the road after the event ended. Even if an aide was sent to retrieve the discarded stalk, the act was seen as reflecting arrogance and disregard for the common people.

Chiang’s struggle in the polls is surprising. He has sometimes been criticized for being a bit stiff during public speaking events, as well as for gaffes, such as being unable to remember a number of English terms during a speech at Harvard University in a clip that went viral online. Nevertheless, Chiang is usually seen as a leading politician of the KMT. As one of its most prominent younger politicians at age 47, he’s often considered a future presidential contender. Chiang has also differentiated himself from other KMT members by being more progressive on social issues such as gay marriage.

Chiang’s trips abroad during his administration – to Singapore, China, the U.S., France, and South Korea – were largely seen as signaling presidential ambitions, aiming to pad out his diplomatic credentials. Chiang is expected to throw his hat into the ring for the KMT’s 2028 presidential nomination.

With the unexpected rise of Shen in the polls, the DPP will be aiming to do as much damage to Chiang’s future electoral chances as possible.

It is also probable that backlash against Chiang reflects public dissatisfaction with political dynasties. Chiang is the son of former legislator John Chiang – not to be confused with the similarly named former KMT chair, Johnny Chiang, a politician of the same generation as Chiang Wan-an.

Chiang is also the supposed illegitimate grandson of Chiang Ching-kuo and great-grandson of Chiang Kai-shek. Both Chiang Wan-an and his father changed their last names from Chang to Chiang when they decided to seek higher office. Though some questions about the veracity of this claim have been raised – Chiang has refused DNA testing as an invasion of his privacy – the claim that he is descended from Chiang Kai-shek is generally accepted in Taiwanese politics. Notably, Chiang has more commonly referred to Chiang Ching-kuo in public messaging so as to steer clear of controversy about the authoritarian period under Chiang Kai-shek’s rule.

Because of his lineage, backlash against Chiang as the heir of a political dynasty has sometimes erupted into the open, even within the KMT. When passed over for political advancement within the KMT, for example, legislator Hsu Chiao-hsin – another youth politician in the KMT – lashed out at being passed over because her “last name is not Chiang.”

If Shen were, in fact, successful in taking Taipei, it would be a huge political upset. It is probable that talk of Shen as a future presidential contender would materialize immediately. In a similar case, when the KMT’s Han Kuo-yu was successful in winning the Kaohsiung mayorship in 2018 – in what is traditionally considered DPP heartland – this catapulted him to become the KMT’s presidential candidate in 2020

It also led to the political narrative that the DPP’s traditional grip over southern Taiwan was dramatically weakening. Even though Han was removed as mayor in a recall in 2020, the KMT has continued to place high hopes on winning away the DPP’s southern power base.

The DPP has clearly had its eye on making inroads into Taipei for some time. Indeed, the party has often fielded the younger, progressive politicians that emerged in the wake of the Sunflower Movement in downtown Taipei districts that are seen as having rising numbers of upwardly mobile, politically progressive young professionals.

If Shen were to win Taipei in an upset, this would probably be for the same reason that the DPP lost Kaohsiung to the KMT in 2018: city residents growing tired of what they perceived as complacency in governing a presumed electoral safe zone.
tag: Chiang Wan-an; Puma Shen; Taipei mayor election; Taiwan 2026 local elections; Taiwan politics

title: The Trump-Xi Summit Exposed the Problems in China-US Crisis Management
description: Military communication channels become bargaining chips precisely when a crisis makes them indispensable.
text:
Xi Jinping’s September visit to Washington ended without a major breakthrough on trade or artificial intelligence safety. Most media coverage focused on the ceremony and the limited results. The official accounts, however, raised important questions about crisis management, which has gone largely undiscussed.

China’s readout said the two militaries had “agreed to sign a memorandum of understanding as soon as possible on strengthening crisis communication and prevention.” The White House “fact sheet” did not mention that commitment. A later South China Morning Post report said a U.S. official denied that the discussion had taken place.

Before any MoU can improve crisis management, Washington and Beijing first need a consensus that they agreed to pursue such a mechanism.

China and the United States already have several ways to communicate during military tensions. These include the Defense Telephone Link, direct contact between their leaders, and regular meetings between defense officials. They have also agreed on rules for military encounters at sea and in the air.

Yet having these arrangements in place does not mean they will be used when a crisis occurs. Officials may delay answering a call, and political tensions might lead either government to suspend talks altogether. The proposed memorandum should therefore focus on keeping existing contacts available when they are most needed.

For more than a year after then-U.S. House Speaker Nancy Pelosi’s August 2022 visit to Taiwan, senior U.S. and Chinese military officers had few opportunities to speak directly. Beijing had canceled talks between theater commanders and suspended other defense meetings in protest against the visit. The military contacts themselves were not the source of the disagreement, but they became part of Beijing’s response.

Presidents Xi Jinping and Joe Biden eventually agreed to resume military talks when they met in California in November 2023, and the U.S. Department of Defense welcomed the move. But restoring contact after a leaders’ meeting is one thing; making sure those channels remain open when relations are strained is another.

The current Defense Telephone Link is not designed for situations that require an immediate response. According to the International Crisis Group, arranging a call normally involves giving 48 hours’ notice, and the other side has another 24 hours to respond to the request. Senior officials may be able to work with these rules when arranging meetings in advance. An emergency – say, an aircraft collision in the South China Sea – would leave little time for such procedures. By the time a call was arranged, commanders might already have made decisions without hearing from their counterparts.

The 2001 EP-3 collision offers another example of how difficult communication can be during a military crisis. The U.S. embassy tried to contact Chinese officials after the collision between U.S. and Chinese military aircraft, but received few answers during the first 12 hours. Washington had little information about how Beijing was handling the incident.

The Defense Telephone Link had not yet been established in 2001, making the circumstances different from today. But recent precedent is not encouraging either. In early 2023, after the U.S. military shot down a Chinese surveillance balloon that had overflown the U.S. mainland, the U.S. defense secretary tried to arrange a call with his Chinese counterpart. China reportedly rejected his request for contact.

That episode underscored the limited value of existing crisis management mechanisms. When urgent calls go unanswered, military officers have to make decisions with limited information about the other side’s intentions.

The proposed crisis management MoU needs to handle these two problems. Even if regular military talks break down, both sides should still be able to reach each other in an emergency. It should also require an acknowledgment within 30 minutes of an urgent message being sent. The officer receiving the message would simply confirm that it had arrived and that the information was being checked. Neither side would have to admit fault or agree with the other’s account at this stage. They could leave those disagreements for later, once the immediate risk had been dealt with.

For Beijing, accepting a message is different from deciding how to respond to it. Chinese officers may have to consult their superiors before commenting on an incident, particularly one involving sovereignty or military activity. That process can take time. A simple reply verifying receipt would allow those discussions to continue without leaving Washington unsure whether its warning had been heard. Beijing could still decide what to say after reviewing the incident, while keeping the military line open during the most urgent stage of a crisis.

The International Crisis Group has called for crisis simulations in which Chinese and American officials examine how each side might respond as tensions develop. A hypothetical aircraft collision over the South China Sea would be a useful scenario for a joint exercise before the November Trump-Xi meeting on the sidelines of the APEC summit. The U.S. military could make the initial test call and wait for a response from its Chinese counterpart, following the same procedures that would apply in a real incident. The exercise would give both sides a chance to see how long a message takes to reach the officer responsible for answering it. Any delay caused by the need to seek approval would become apparent.

An emergency channel should focus on what is happening at the time of a crisis. If an incident occurs, both sides need to know where it happened, whether anyone was injured, and whether their forces might come into contact again. They should not have to settle wider disagreements before sharing such information. Questions over Taiwan, technology restrictions, and U.S. military deployments can still be discussed through existing diplomatic and defense channels. Keeping these issues out of emergency communication would allow officers to deal with the immediate situation without waiting for progress in political negotiations.

Xi’s remarks in Washington called for the Chinese and U.S. militaries to “maintain regular dialogue, and improve mechanisms for crisis communication and prevention.” Leader-level diplomacy can authorize this work, but that doesn’t guarantee progress. By the next Trump-Xi summit at APEC, both governments should at least confirm the same commitment and complete a test of the contact route. The MoU itself may take longer if the two sides are still negotiating its terms.

The leader-level summits will matter more if the two governments can agree on how to handle calls during a military crisis. In the past, political disputes have led Beijing to suspend military exchanges with Washington. The same problem could arise again, leaving officers unable to contact their counterparts at a critical moment. One way to prevent this would be to keep emergency hotlines separate from regular defense talks. The first measure of progress is therefore simple: whether both militaries can agree that an urgent message must be acknowledged within 30 minutes.
tag: Trump-Xi summit; U.S.-China crisis management; U.S.-China military diplomacy; U.S.-China military hotline; U.S.-China military-military ties

title: The United States Has an Industrial Problem in the Indo-Pacific
description: A central part of the deterrence question
text:
The United States has spent years warning about China’s growing military power. Much of that discussion focuses on ships, missiles, aircraft, artificial intelligence, and other weapons, but considerably less attention is paid to the industrial capacity behind them. China has built an enormous manufacturing base capable of producing ships, electronics, machinery, batteries, components, and other goods at a scale the United States cannot easily match. In a prolonged conflict, that difference could become as important as the capabilities of the weapons themselves. The United States would need to replace damaged equipment, replenish munitions, repair ships and aircraft, and keep production running under wartime conditions. Its allies in the Indo-Pacific would face similar demands.

Washington is increasingly aware of the problem and is trying to bring new companies, private investment, and manufacturing methods into the defense sector. The Navy’s recently announced Arsenal-2 project with Anduril Industries is one example. Announced October 6, Arsenal-2 is a planned $6.6 billion manufacturing facility at Tradepoint Atlantic in Maryland. Anduril plans to invest $3.7 billion of private capital, while the Navy could provide up to $2.9 billion. The facility is intended to manufacture components and large assemblies for Virginia-class submarines, initially including torpedo tubes and potentially expanding to larger sections of the boats. The project addresses a genuine weakness in the American defense-industrial base: the Navy needs more production capacity, particularly as it tries to expand the submarine fleet.

The difficulty is that Arsenal-2 will not be operational tomorrow. Initial operations are not expected until 2030, and the manufacturing methods that will underpin the facility still have to be developed and validated. Anduril will have to establish the workforce, suppliers, quality systems, and production processes needed to meet the demanding requirements of the submarine industry. That raises a broader question for Washington as it tries to rebuild the defense-industrial base: how quickly can the United States create industrial capacity that can actually be relied upon in times of crisis?

The question is particularly important in the Indo-Pacific. A conflict with China would place enormous demands on American production while US forces were operating thousands of miles from the continental United States. Ships would require repairs, missiles and drones would need to be replaced, and munitions stocks would have to be replenished. The United States would also be relying on its allies. Japan, Australia, South Korea, the Philippines, and other partners are increasing their defense capabilities, but American credibility in the region depends partly on whether Washington can continue supplying and supporting those forces during a prolonged crisis. A military that can deploy advanced systems but cannot replace them at the required rate has a very different deterrent value from one that can sustain production.

China’s advantage is not limited to the size of its military. Its civilian manufacturing base supports military production in ways that are difficult for the United States to replicate quickly. China is already a major producer of ships, electronics, machinery, industrial components, and many of the materials and products that underpin modern manufacturing. The United States, by contrast, is trying to rebuild capacity that has contracted over decades. This is why the defense-industrial debate should be viewed as part of the broader strategic competition with Beijing rather than simply as a question of Pentagon procurement.

That effort will require private capital and new companies capable of challenging established defense contractors. It will also require the government to create sufficient and predictable demand for companies to invest in factories, equipment, workers, and supply chains. The traditional defense industry cannot simply be expected to expand on its own after years of consolidation. At the same time, Washington cannot assume that every new company or manufacturing concept will succeed merely because it offers a different approach.

The Pentagon has considerable experience with the consequences of moving production ahead of development and testing. The F-35 is the most prominent example, while the Littoral Combat Ship provides another. The issue is not that these programs were necessarily wrong to pursue, but that the government has repeatedly faced substantial costs when production proceeds before key technologies and capabilities have been sufficiently demonstrated. A 2013 GAO review found that the F-35’s concurrent acquisition strategy had led to substantial rework costs as deficiencies were discovered in testing. A later GAO review found continuing delivery delays and recommended that the program better align incentives with production outcomes. The LCS program likewise faced significant operational and testing problems, including delays in developing mission modules.

Arsenal-2 presents a related question at the industrial level. The United States is investing in a new production facility while the manufacturing processes behind it are still being developed and validated. That does not mean Arsenal-2 should be delayed or that Anduril should not receive the opportunity to build it. The more useful question is how Washington structures the relationship. What production targets will the Navy require? How quickly must the facility reach them? Who will independently verify performance? What happens if production falls short? And can procurement shift toward other suppliers if a new approach does not deliver? Those are basic questions for any major defense investment, particularly when the United States is trying to rebuild capacity under pressure from a much larger industrial competitor.

There is a strong argument for taking risks on new defense companies. The existing defense-industrial base has its own shortcomings, and established contractors have not always been able to deliver new capabilities quickly or at the required scale. Private investors should be able to back companies they believe can change that, and Washington should encourage competition rather than protecting incumbents. But government support should not become a substitute for performance. Companies should have the opportunity to demonstrate that they can deliver, and successful performance should lead to greater opportunities. If a project fails to meet its targets, the government needs to retain the ability to limit further exposure and turn to alternatives.

There are precedents for Washington taking early risks on companies that had not yet demonstrated their full capabilities. NASA supported SpaceX before Falcon 9 had flown, while the Department of Energy provided Tesla with a $465 million loan in 2010 that the company later repaid. Some early bets work and some do not. The lesson is not that the government should avoid risk. It is that government needs mechanisms that allow successful companies to grow while preventing unsuccessful projects from consuming resources indefinitely.

That approach is particularly important when the objective is to compete with China’s industrial capacity. The United States cannot deter China simply by developing more sophisticated technology or fielding a small number of advanced systems. It needs the ability to produce, repair, replace, and sustain military equipment over time. For the Indo-Pacific, that is a central part of the deterrence equation.
