title: The US and China Cannot Slow the AI Race, But They Can Make It Safer
description: The United States does not need to trust China, share frontier models with China, or slow its own AI development to have a national security interest in AI safety cooperation.
text:
The most important shift in artificial intelligence (AI) is not that models are becoming more intelligent, but that they are becoming more capable of acting.

Much of the first wave of AI safety governance focused on misinformation, bias, deepfakes, privacy violations and harmful content. Those risks remain. But increasingly capable AI agents can plan, write and execute code, use tools, obtain credentials, and interact with external systems. Recent incidents in which OpenAI’s autonomous systems slipped past their constraints show that as agents gain tools and autonomy, the boundary between a model and the outside world becomes harder to enforce.

That makes AI safety a collective-action problem. The AI superpowers face a prisoner’s dilemma. If one laboratory slows while competitors continue, it may lose its edge. Disclosure creates a similar tension: reporting failures can make the wider ecosystem safer, but the discloser bears the costs and may expose vulnerabilities to attackers. Governments face the same strategic impasse as the firms. Washington fears that slowing its AI development will allow China to catch up; Beijing fears that doing so will leave it further behind.

Yet cooperation can be narrow on AI safety. The United States does not need to trust China, share frontier models with China, or slow its own AI development to have a national security interest in such cooperation. It has an interest in ensuring that AI-enabled cyber incidents are contained before they cascade through third countries, shared software infrastructure and global supply chains. China has the same systemic interest.

This collective action has significant implications for middle-power countries. Helping others repair a vulnerability can be a form of systemic containment and a public good.

The Accelerating AI Race

The AI arms race is intensifying.

U.S. President Donald Trump has rejected calls to slow U.S. AI development, framing continued technological leadership as essential to winning the AI race. On September 29, he convened major technology companies at the White House, where six firms – OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, xAI and Nvidia – signed a voluntary accord built around four layers of oversight: internal capability assessments, internal audit teams, independent external auditors, and board-level review. His administration ordered federal agencies to replace the term “artificial intelligence” with “super intelligence,” presenting the technology as a source of economic and strategic leadership.

Taken together, these moves point to a U.S. approach combining continued AI power with developer responsibility, voluntary industry controls, external scrutiny, and ex-post legal accountability.

China approaches the problem through a more centrally coordinated system. In May 2026, guidelines on AI agents, issued jointly by the Cyberspace Administration of China, the National Development and Reform Commission, and the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, made “safety and controllability” a baseline requirement for agent development and deployment. Governance is tiered, with tighter filing, testing and recall requirements for agents used in sensitive sectors.

On September 14, China’s AI Safety Governance Framework 3.0 reiterated “safety and controllability” while updating its classification of AI risks and associated technical and governance measures.

Despite their institutional differences, the two approaches converge on one point: neither country wants safety policy to halt AI development, and both increasingly recognize that greater autonomy creates new problems of control.

Common Ground and Shared Risks

AI systems rest on overlapping technological foundations. Chinese AI development has relied heavily on U.S. chips and, in some cases, U.S. cloud infrastructure. Export controls may weaken those hardware links, but the stronger case for joint risk management lies in the software and services AI systems share.

Standards, certificates, identity infrastructure, model repositories, and open-source libraries support trust across networks. A compromised root certificate or a maintainer’s credentials can put the entire dependency tree at risk.

AI risks vary along two dimensions: severity of harm and whether responsible actors can recognize it in time. The biggest danger is severe and invisible harm, where nothing visibly breaks for days or weeks, yet time compounds the severity of the incident. An AI agent could quietly corrupt records, act on instructions planted in its memory or in documents it consults, or appear cooperative while accumulating access beyond operator intent. Infrastructure may operate normally while the means to disrupt it are already in place.

The dependencies and shared risks determine which code a system runs, which credentials it accepts, and which updates it trusts. Harm can cross borders quietly even when models and their owners remain separate.

That makes the speed of response critical. Delays in detecting a breach, assigning responsibility or authorizing a shutdown can allow damage to spread. Both China and the United States therefore need warnings to reach personnel with the authority and technical means to respond.

Make the Race Safer

There is no obvious diplomatic agreement that can resolve the paradox built into the AI race: it rewards speed and secrecy, while safety depends on collective restraint and disclosure.

China-U.S. cooperation should instead focus on measures that improve safety without requiring either side to slow unilaterally, transfer its most advanced models, or expose commercially and strategically sensitive capabilities. Four areas stand out:

1. Keeping humans in control

Before the Trump-Xi summit, American and Chinese security experts in a long-running bilateral dialogue proposed red lines around nuclear systems, human control over consequential cyber operations, and a dedicated mechanism for AI incidents.

When an AI agent can search, authenticate, write code, call external tools, and act within minutes or seconds, where should human intervention occur? Requiring approval for every step would undermine the autonomous value of AI agents; waiting until something goes wrong may make intervention too late.

The harder questions concern permissions, escalation thresholds, shutdown mechanisms and which actions should always require explicit human authorization. Researchers could cooperate on these engineering challenges without sharing model weights, training data, or proprietary frontier capabilities.

2. Test the guardrails, not each other’s secrets

Sandboxing, monitoring, permission controls, and model-level refusals are often treated as established safeguards.

The underlying technical risk is broad: with appropriate tools and access, advanced models could identify previously unknown vulnerabilities and develop exploits across well-protected systems without step-by-step human direction. The key question is not whether a developer has guardrails, but whether they still work as agents become capable enough to search for ways around them.

While frontier AI labs in the U.S. have voluntarily disclosed instances of their models escaping from sandboxed environments, public reporting from China on comparable containment failures remains limited. This lack of transparency shouldn’t stop the two sides from working together. Washington and Beijing could develop compatible methods for testing sandbox escape, scope violations, unauthorized tool use, shutdown resistance, and failures of human intervention. Independent auditors, potentially from trusted third countries, could help verify the results.

3. Contain first, attribute later with care

Cyber attribution has always been challenging. AI makes it harder.

A defender discovering unauthorized access may be looking at a state-directed operation, a criminal actor using AI, a human-directed autonomous agent, or an agent that has exceeded its instructions while pursuing a legitimate task.

Between strategic rivals, that ambiguity is especially dangerous when the trust deficit widens. An autonomous system interacting with critical infrastructure could be mistaken for reconnaissance or preparation for attack before either government understands what happened.

American and Chinese experts have already identified this risk: autonomous cyber exchanges could move faster than governments can determine whether an operation was deliberate, accidental, or unauthorized.

Washington and Beijing are unlikely to agree routinely on the attribution of contentious cyber incidents. They could instead develop common technical expectations about the evidence that should be examined before an AI-enabled incident is escalated politically, including agent logs, credential use, tool-invocation records, model provenance, human authorization, and network telemetry. In the first hours of a major cross-border incident, governments and trusted responders should be able to exchange technical indicators, containment measures, and patch information without first deciding who is responsible. Exchanging such information need not imply an admission of responsibility.

4. Close the AI remediation gap

Cybersecurity has struggled with remediation for decades. Critical infrastructure is fragmented across hospitals, utilities, telecommunications networks, ports, government agencies, and private vendors. A vulnerability may be understood and a patch may exist, yet deployment can still take days or weeks.

AI compresses the time between vulnerability discovery and exploitation. A capable model may identify a weakness, develop a working exploit, and begin using it faster than organizations can patch their systems.

This creates an emerging AI remediation gap: offensive capability increasingly operates at machine speed, while much of the world still responds at the slower pace of human decision-making and institutional coordination across multiple stakeholders.

Most countries will not train the world’s most capable AI models themselves. Their defensive capacity may therefore depend increasingly on capabilities developed in a small number of frontier ecosystems. If frontier defensive capability arrives only at another power’s discretion – or not at all – exposed systems have no reliable recourse in a crisis.

Closing this gap requires extending access to frontier defensive capability to these countries.

An affected operator or national CERT (Computer Emergency Response Team) could provide malware samples, vulnerable code, selected system logs, or configuration information through a trusted technical intermediary. A frontier defensive model could then help analyze the incident, validate vulnerabilities, generate and test patches, and return a remediation package, while the underlying model and its most sensitive capabilities remain with the provider.

The United States and China also have reasons to support such a system out of self-interest. An AI-enabled vulnerability left unpatched elsewhere can spread through open-source software, cloud infrastructure, model repositories, digital certificates, and global supply chains before reaching systems in either country.

Middle Powers as Security Intermediaries

Many middle powers sit outside the central China-U.S. frontier-model competition while remaining exposed to its consequences.

The upcoming APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting in Shenzhen offers a practical platform to move this agenda beyond bilateral China-U.S. cooperation. All 21 APEC economies, including the United States and China, share an interest in preventing AI-enabled cyber incidents from cascading through the region’s tightly connected digital infrastructure, software supply chains and trade networks. Their ability to detect and repair such incidents, however, varies widely.

The Shenzhen gathering of APEC leaders need not produce a common AI regulatory regime. It could instead task APEC’s technical bodies with developing several practical measures. They can build independent evaluation capacity, strengthen national and regional CERT networks, host trusted remediation infrastructure, and serve as intermediaries between frontier capability providers and countries that lack equivalent defensive capacity.

For the Asia-Pacific, this would turn the AI remediation gap from an abstract vulnerability into a regional capacity-building agenda. It is not simply about managing the rivalry between Washington and Beijing. It is about preventing that rivalry – or failures in the technologies produced by it – from becoming a regional systemic risk. The region has an interest in shaping the mechanisms for containment and remediation rather than waiting for the two AI superpowers to define them alone.

Competition Will Continue, But Cooperation Must Get Priority

AI competition will continue. Even the September Trump-Xi summit produced agreement on a bilateral communication channel for AI-related incidents, it also shows the differences: the U.S. readout called it the “U.S.-China Super Intelligence Dialogue” but Beijing’s readout called it the “China-U.S. AI Dialogue.” The naming difference shows how limited the shared vocabulary is.

At such a time, crisis communication becomes more important, not less. A hotline is not a safety regime; it is communication infrastructure. But both parties need minimum agreement to work together to make the AI race safer, for themselves and for everybody else. Disclosure itself can create security risks, so the appropriate principle should be calibrated reciprocity: enough information should move quickly enough to reduce common danger, while details that could create new vulnerabilities or expose sensitive capabilities remain protected.

The objective should be simple: to stop technical failures from becoming geopolitical crises, accelerate remediation, and extend defensive capability where it is most needed.

The U.S. and China do not need to agree on who should win the AI race. They need to agree on what red lines cannot be crossed in the competition, and how middle power countries can engage.

title: The US Army Looks to the Pacific – and Space – for Future Relevance
description: Army leadership has focused on developing tools to contribute to a potential fight against China, a fight in which space assets will be critical.
text:
The U.S. Army sees its future as preparing for a fight in the Pacific, and it’s taking lessons from both the current fight in the Middle East and Russia’s ongoing war with Ukraine. In addition to missiles, drones, and electronic warfare, that means an increasing presence for the land service in the space domain. The effort represents an attempt by the Army to maintain its relevance under geographical constraints that are less than ideal, and in an institutional context that increasingly favors long-range, high-end unmanned systems.

Both the U.S. Navy and the U.S. Air Force have experienced embarrassing setbacks in the present war against Iran, the former because of an overcommitment of its aircraft carrier fleet and the latter because of the loss of several key assets in combat. Nevertheless, both services have contributed immensely to ongoing operations. The contribution of the U.S. Army has been more limited and less visible, in large part because of the reluctance of the Trump administration to develop serious plans for an invasion of Iran.

Given the geography and the strategic issues at stake, a war in the Pacific is likely to resemble the Iran War much more than the Wars on Terror, which highlighted the Army’s strengths. Given this, Army leadership has focused on developing tools to contribute to a potential fight against China. The most recent and notable of these efforts is the stand up of a new Indo-Pacific task force, designed to conduct long-range missile combat and defeat area denial networks. The 4th Multi Domain Task Force is expected to integrate long-range strike with intelligence gathering and air defense capabilities in an effort to threaten and defeat efforts to impede the entry of the U.S. Navy and the U.S. Air Force into the Western Pacific. The 7th Infantry Division Multi-Domain Command has concentrated on developing plans for long-range drone and electronic warfare (EW) combat in the Western Pacific, assisted by AI tools that will manage data flow and the sequencing of targets.

These efforts build upon the Army’s work to establish itself in space and to institutionalize networked warfare. Space assets act as the connective tissue for all of the elements that the Army is attempting to integrate into a cohesive whole with a standard operational logic. The steadily increasing profile of the U.S. Space Force complicates the institutional landscape by creating overlapping claims of bureaucratic authority.

All of this is an artifact of the way that the U.S. military does business. Although the geography of the Western Pacific (like the Persian Gulf) favors air and sea power, the Army must be involved because its funding and future depend on its ability to contribute in critical sectors. That Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth has made reforming the Army’s senior leadership a focus of his tenure only makes the situation more urgent for the organization. In a sense, what the Army is preparing to fight in the Western Pacific in order to preserve its ability to fight in the halls of Congress and the Pentagon.

Arguably, the Army’s relatively low level of commitment in the Middle East may work to the Army’s advantage, as it can commit its focus and attention to fighting the next fight instead of an intractable slog against Iran. But new technological realities always require time, experience, and a careful negotiation with institutional reality. Whether Hegseth’s Army is capable of that negotiation remains open to question.

title: The US Is Losing to China in the Battle of Global Influence
channel_text: Blog; Diplomacy; East Asia; Trans-Pacific View
description: China is building a dense network of relationships across all pillars of influence while the United States continues to weaken the institutions it traditionally used to compete.
text:
Global influence is frequently a topic for conference panels, talk show pundits, and earnest think tank recommendations, but this nebulous measure of soft power has real-world impact for national security, economic strength and political power.

Today, this battle is unfolding rapidly, region by region, country by country, through security and commercial partnerships, emerging regional groupings, newly established diplomatic outposts, and academic partnerships.

As conflicts erupt and new trade and political alignments emerge, it’s clear: China is building a dense network of relationships across all pillars of influence while the United States continues to weaken the institutions it traditionally used to compete. The United States should do more than watch China’s intensive investment in building global influence – in diplomacy, in academic and cultural exchanges, in economic partnerships, and in national security pacts.

Influence is hard to gauge – and even harder to count on. Even the closest of diplomatic partners have sovereign interests and political differences. Historical relationships, either through war-hardened alliances or postcolonial reckonings, can shape perception and sway alignment. However, China’s transactional approach inherently reflects its genuine disregard for human rights, democratic aspirations, and welfare of citizens in other countries. This is China’s weak point, which the United States can leverage to regain lost ground.

Diplomacy: You Must Show up

The work of diplomacy is accomplished behind the scenes, by building connections, negotiating agreements, and advocating for businesses. The work of a diplomat is to know the government officials and trade contacts before you make an ask. This allows diplomats to build the trust required to get to agreement before a crisis happens or an ask is made.

China is succeeding at one of the first rules of diplomacy: showing up.

The Lowry Institute’s Global Diplomacy Index paints a clear picture. China has 274 diplomatic posts globally, compared with the United States’ 271. The strategic advantage is even clearer in Africa – where China has 60 to the United States’ 56 – and in East Asia, where China has 44 to the United States’ 27. While the numerical difference is small, the trend is concerning.

Beijing leverages its growing diplomatic presence as a strategic asset, populating its embassies with commercial, educational, and political professionals. It is gradually making inroads even with the United States’ longtime partners. Just this month, China’s President Xi Jinping traveled to Egypt, where Beijing and Cairo signed an array of agreements, from linking Egypt’s national development plan to China’s Belt and Road Initiative to a pledge to increase trade and investments in their own currencies, moving away from the U.S. dollar.

For the United States, the trend is going the other way, and that’s worrying. Despite a slate of recent nominations, 93 out of 196 ambassadorial slots remain vacant, according to the tracker maintained by the American Foreign Service Association. And while in many cases there are able professional diplomats serving as chargés d’affaires in these roles, a confirmed ambassador signals seriousness to host governments.

The State Department has also taken steps to close a number of smaller consulates and shrink operations at other embassies. While there is absolutely a strong case for prioritizing engagement, streamlining operations, and improving efficiencies, the narrative that the United States is retreating from the world continues to spread.

Academic opportunities and cultural exchanges are important forms of diplomacy and a path to increasing the United States’ global influence. Engaging with the next generations of global talent is a critical investment or opportunity, and China understands this.

At the 2024 Summit of the Forum on China-Africa Cooperation (FOCAC), Xi announced 60,000 government scholarships for African students. In addition to opportunities for students, FOCAC commitments will see some 20,000 African regional and city leaders receiving training in China every year, along with African journalists sent to China.

These programs are far from boondoggles: They enmesh these emerging officials, journalists, and business leaders into Chinese institutions and professional networks. And despite warnings from the United States, China has now established over 500 Confucius Institutes around the world. These institutes are purported to facilitate Chinese education and people-to-people exchanges, but effectively serve as propaganda arms of the Chinese government.

The United States has extraordinary assets of its own, including an open and free democracy, the best universities in the world, and an innovation economy. Traditionally, U.S. government-supported exchange programs showcase all three.

From the International Visitor Leadership Program (IVLP), which identifies rising stars in business, government, security, and media and brings them to the United States to showcase America’s story to world-class State Department programs, including the Fulbright, Gilman, Boren, and Critical Language Scholarships, these programs engage professionals at key junctures in their professional careers.

A scholarship or an exchange isn’t simply tuition assistance. These academic and cultural programs create alumni who may become government and business leaders in their countries. According to the State Department’s own accounting, over 500 IVLP alumni alone have become heads of state or government since the program’s founding in 1940. Another 12 have won Nobel Prizes, and thousands more have served as elected officials, government ministers, and community and business leaders.

The United States can benefit from having these leaders as counterparts; they leave these programs with firsthand knowledge and appreciation of America’s economic strength, tech savvy, entrepreneurship, pluralism, and values.

These programs continue, albeit after some stutters in funding in 2025. Yet there are deep proposed reductions in the 2027 fiscal year’s budget. And there is a long-term cost to making such programs unpredictable. China is rapidly expanding its networks, while the United States is offering uncertainty into its own powerful equivalents.

Economic Strength: Building Partnerships, Not Transactions

This isn’t a new trend. Pundits have warned for more than two decades that Beijing is approaching traditional U.S. partners with something tangible to offer.

Through its Belt and Road Initiative (BRI), as well as smaller bilateral and regional deals, China has smartly offered financing backed by its government for desperately needed infrastructure projects linked to access to African and Western Hemisphere markets.

At the most recent FOCAC summit in 2024, Xi announced approximately $51 billion in financial support to Africa over a three-year period. At the 2025 China-Community of Latin American and Caribbean States (CELAC) Forum, Xi pledged a credit line of more than $9 billion for Latin America, as well as additional bilateral infrastructure investment. According to China’s own accounting in its 2025 BRI Investment Report, agreements that are part of BRI reached over $213 billion in 2025, up 75 percent from the previous year, with about 150 countries participating.

The United States can compete. The Lobito Corridor, which links Zambia, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and Angola, provides U.S. support for a critical rail and infrastructure network spanning mineral production to port facilities. Through a $533 million loan from the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation (DFC), the United States both invested in these countries’ economic development and leveraged this financing with an eye to long-term regional security through employment, investment, and regional integration.

However, while the United States has (and uses) smart tools like the DFC and Millenium Challenge Corporation, it has stopped some other initiatives. Driven by the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), the 2025 reprioritization of foreign assistance sidelined early-stage economic development efforts, such as programs for emerging entrepreneurs, small business, and agriculture – including dedicated programs to encourage women in these fields. These and other opportunities were once administered through the now-shuttered USAID and State Department programs. The 2025 foreign assistance restructuring halted these incubator projects worldwide, ending a values-based and long-term approach to economic growth.

While reform of U.S. assistance was absolutely necessary, the geopolitical cost is clear. When the United States – with its commitment to human rights, democracy, rule of law, and anti-corruption measures – withdraws from a relationship, it is often China that surges to occupy the space.

Today, faced with the immediate challenge of global leadership in artificial intelligence (AI), the United States must be more than the leader in a technology footrace with China. The U.S. global role and responsibilities will require sustained investment in innovation, talent, infrastructure and trusted partnerships so the United States can continue in setting global standards that shape how AI is developed, governed and deployed. The United States can build on its standards of openness and accountability while ensuring that these emerging technologies reflect both U.S. interests and U.S. values.

Reclaiming the High Ground

China is intensifying its investment in its initiatives, building a worldwide network of infrastructure, finance, commercial, and political relationships. The United States absolutely has best-in-class competitive alternatives, but Washington must invest in and deepen those ties.

Many countries, especially across the Global South, see benefits to relationships with both China and the United States, but U.S. strength has traditionally meant that it is the first choice for security relationships, cultural and educational exchanges, and business partnerships. China’s approach has significant and public weaknesses, including debt controversies, debates over its political influence, and allegations of exploitation and human rights abuses in partner countries.

But Washington has its own work to do to right the soft power ship. The United States possesses enormous advantages in its world-class academic institutions, technology, alliances, and the sheer love of ordinary U.S. culture. We must remember, though: the United States didn’t become a superpower by looking backward.

The United States must maintain its influence – and its values of freedom, opportunity, accountability, and compassion – by continuing to show up.

title: The Uyghurs Who Fought in Syria’s Civil War
description: Insights from Emily Feng.
text:
The Diplomat author Mercy Kuo regularly engages subject-matter experts, policy practitioners, and strategic thinkers across the globe for their diverse insights into U.S. Asia policy. This conversation with Emily Feng – author of “Our Hearts Burned for Home: Uyghur Militants in Syria’s Civil War” (Columbia Global Reports 2026) and award-winning correspondent for NPR – is the 530th in “The Trans-Pacific View Insight Series.”

What was the impetus behind your reporting on Uyghur militants in Syria’s civil war?

For years, I had been reporting on the ground on the Xinjiang region and the sweeping detention campaign that began in early 2017. And one of the reasons cited in rare official comments from Beijing about why authorities were detaining and arresting hundreds of thousands Uyghur people mentioned the presence of Uyghur “terrorists” in Syria and Afghanistan, but offered no evidence and since these places were nearly impossible to access, no one had done interviews with any of these supposed Uyghur militants.

In late 2024, it suddenly became possible to go to Syria after the surprising collapse of the Assad regime there and the end of a terrible civil war. Coincidentally, I was in nearby Lebanon when the Assads fled to Russia, and I ended up spending much of the beginning of 2025 in Syria.

Imagine my surprise when I saw Uyghur fighters milling about Syria! Indeed, there were thousands of Uyghur fighters in Syria, and I was later to discover, their role in the civil war had been much more impactful than anyone expected.

But I sensed there was much more to the story about these Uyghur fighters than Beijing’s narrative – that these were masterminds behind fatal attacks on Chinese civilians who were now hellbent on destroying China. I wondered what had made them leave their families and livelihoods behind to live in an active war zone, and how they had transformed themselves from hairdressers and engineers and teachers into hardened militant fighters, working in alliance with Arabic-speaking, Syrian rebel groups.

I was also sensitive to the possible implications of reporting on Uyghurs. In no way is their existence in Syria justification for the detention and arrests, mostly without real due process, of so many Uyghur citizens of China. I resolved to find a way to contact the Syrian Uyghurs and interview them – a difficult task, as they had operated as a secretive and highly-disciplined force for more than a decade – and learn more about why they had come to the Middle East.

Analyze the factors propelling Uyghur militants to join the civil war and how they contributed to the overthrow of the Assad regime.

I don’t want to give too much away here! The details are in the book. But in short, many Uyghurs who ended up in Syria had initially hoped to put down roots in Turkey, where a sizeable Uyghur diaspora already exists. However, Turkey does not want these Uyghurs, and it has stymied their ability to get residence documents and even aided in their deportation back to China.

Turkey happens to share a long, mostly unfortified border with northern Syria, however, where a rebel-held swath of territory had been established in a growing civil war. And so that’s where a lot of Uyghurs headed, because Syria was not checking documents or asking for visas, frankly. All of them were also looking for a constructive way to help Uyghurs back in Xinjiang, or East Turkestan as the Uyghurs call it, and they hoped Syria would become a base to fight back politically or militarily against the Chinese Communist Party.

A good number of Uyghurs had also already heard of the possibility of Uyghur fighters in Syria, and they were eager to train militarily. An active war, one Uyghur commander later told me, was free practice.

The Uyghurs’ wholehearted embrace of violence for the sake of establishing an independent Uyghur state is controversial, I should mention, among the Uyghur diaspora globally. But of the five dozen or so interviews I did with Uyghur fighters and their families, all of them described experiences where they felt diplomacy or political activism had failed them, and they felt they had nothing left to lose anymore by taking up arms.

The deadly race riots that began July 5, 2009 in Urumqi, which left scores of both Han Chinese and Uyghur Chinese dead, was a real turning point for many Uyghurs I met. The mob violence they witnessed from all parties that week and the ensuing crackdown and racism Uyghurs experienced in the aftermath convinced the majority of the fighters I spoke to to seek their fortunes in Turkey and later Syria.

What surprised me the most after weeks on the ground in Syria with Uyghur fighters was discovering the reach and breadth of the Uyghurs’ role in the Syrian civil war. The participated in major battles, played a key role in helping rebels with Hayat Tahrir Al-Sham (HTS) take Aleppo, and eventually marched into Damascus to establish the new government. HTS’ Ahmed Al Sharaa, now Syria’s president, privately credits the Uyghurs with being a consistently loyal, effective fighting force, and for that reason, the Uyghurs now have an unusual political purchase in the new Syria.

Explain the difference between the Turkestan Islamic Party (TIP) and East Turkmenistan Islamic Movement (ETIM) and how China views their respective identities.

Both of these entities are part of a broader movement of Uyghurs who have taken up arms and seek to establish an independent Uyghur homeland in the Xinjiang region. I found evidence that members of both groups still maintain communication links, and some of the earliest TIP fighters in Syria initially tried to train with ETIM officials along the Afghanistan-Pakistan border.

But to call ETIM in particular an organization would be a stretch, based on what I was able to find. The ETIM-linked fighters I met said there were never many Uyghurs along the Af-Pak border, many were killed in American bombings, training was nearly impossible due to the difficult geography of the place, and there were ideological differences between the more relaxed Uyghurs and the more conservative al-Qaida-linked and Taliban fighters there.

TIP, the Syria branch of this nationalist Uyghur militant movement, was much more successful. They became highly disciplined and managed to remain organized, sharing scarce financial resources in self-sustaining communities in Idlib, in northern Syria, and setting up robust social services for a growing Uyghur population that has now reached 20,000 men, women, and children.

While TIP also maintained substantial links to al-Qaida affiliated groups, including with HTS, for years, these links later became problematic and internally divisive as TIP and HTS tried to brand themselves as politically more mainstream and welcoming to Syrians and Uyghurs of all castes. Yet TIP remains controversial within Syria, and also within much of the Uyghur diaspora community, who view their militant past with distaste.

Why are Uyghur militants controversial in Syria?

The Syria Uyghurs find themselves in an awkward position. At home, they were the oppressed. In Syria, they are widely viewed as oppressors, in the eyes of Syria’s many minority communities.

Foreign fighters, including the Uyghurs, are viewed with fear and suspicion, as the civil war quickly devolved into a proxy war for various nation states and Islamist groups. Many remain in Syria in peacetime, creating resentments among Syrians who wish for the foreigners to return to their home countries. All the time, Uyghurs are confused with Uzbek fighters, and so many Syrians also do not know why the Uyghurs came to Syria in the first place, and do not understand why they cannot simply return to China.

During the civil war, the Sunni Uyghurs were active in besieging Shiite Syrian villages. They were frequently attacked by Hezbollah proxy forces and retaliated against Shiite populations in response. And for many years, the Uyghurs occupied and lived in several Shiite and Christian villages whose residents had fled in advance of Sunni Islamist groups like TIP arriving, which sowed more distrust and fear among Syrian minority communities who are increasingly on edge under the Sunni HTS-dominated government in Damascus. The Uyghurs maintain they are friendly neighbors and open to Syrians of other faiths and have tried to moderate their religious beliefs somewhat, but there are often significant cultural and linguistic gaps between them and Syrians, which the Uyghurs themselves sometimes do not even fully grasp.

Finally, there were also reports that the Uyghurs were among the perpetrators, alongside Syrian government soldiers, of horrific massacres of mostly Alawi Syrians in 2025. I found no evidence to suggest Uyghurs were involved, and they have no interest in doing so, as involvement would certainly imperil their still uncertain and vulnerable status as stateless refugees in Syria.

Assess the role of Uyghur militants in China-Syria relations and the implications for China-U.S. relations.

In some ways, the Uyghurs are not very important to China-Syria, or broader China-Middle East, relations. Syria has made it clear that it will not let groups on its soil threaten China, even though they also have made it clear they will not send the Uyghurs to China, as Beijing has demanded.

For China however, the Uyghurs are the top issue for them in Syria, and successive diplomatic delegations to Damascus have always mentioned TIP and the Uyghurs as the dominant concern Beijing has for the new government.

The result is that Gulf states, notable Saudi Arabia, have become major investors in Syria’s post-war reconstruction. China was once one of Syria’s top economic partners before the civil war, and it does not look like it will regain that position.

It will be interesting to see how the Uyghurs navigate their future in Syria. Will they buy land and build houses — setting up a much more permanent community in Syria? Will their children born in Syria still maintain strong Uyghur identity links and a commitment to set up a Uyghur state, when they feel more and more wedded to their Syrian upbringing as the years go by?

title: The Woman Who Held Mahathir’s Hand For 70 Years
description: Siti Hasmah Mohamad Ali, who died this week aged 100, was a close companion of Mahathir throughout his long and tumultuous political career.
text:
Dr. Siti Hasmah Mohamad Ali had just one complaint about her husband, Dr. Mahathir Mohamad: that he was very shy about holding her hand in public. The man, who remained loyal and faithful to her for more than 70 years, felt a little embarrassed about showing his love for the Malay girl he met at King Edward VII College of Medicine in Singapore in 1947.

On Mahathir’s 93rd birthday, in an interview with Channel NewsAsia conducted by 10-year-old Kashika Selvam, Siti Hasmah narrated a funny incident about holding hands. She said that he was so shy that once, while driving through a highway toll booth, he pulled back his hand because he didn’t want the toll operator to see them holding hands.

Mahathir ruled Malaysia ruthlessly between 1981 and 2003, during which his critics and detractors were the subjects of sometimes furious political vendettas.

But when it comes to his fidelity and faithfulness to Siti Hasmah, even his critics cannot raise a finger against him.

At home, Mahathir was a loyal husband and an affectionate father, thanks in large part to Siti Hasmah. His daughter, Marina Mahathir, says her mother insisted that the siblings show their love and affection for each other openly by hugging and kissing.

Unlike many other politicians’ wives, Siti Hasmah’s conduct in public never gave a hint that she was the prime minister’s wife. Narrating a poignant incident in the 2019 documentary “M for Malaysia,” Siti Hasmah says: “I was taking my husband to the hospital, not the Prime Minister of Malaysia,” when Mahathir suffered a heart attack in 1989. Like any other devoted spouse, she was more concerned about her husband than the post he occupied.

Six years ago, on November 23, 2019, Malaysians saw a rare sight in Kuala Lumpur: the 94-year-old prime minister taking his 93-year-old wife out on a date. Driving Siti Hasmah in a Proton car, with no protocol or usual entourage, the couple went to a café on Jalan Bukit Bintang, where they had coffee and cake. It looked as if the two students who met at the medical college in Singapore were reliving those moments when they took a bus to Marine Parade to eat their favourite tauhu bakar, kangkong, and squid. The pictures touched such a chord with Malaysians that when Mahathir posted them on his official Instagram page, they received 55,000 likes and 2,000 comments.

Whenever the couple was asked about the secret of their marriage, both said in unison: tolerance. They married after a nine-year courtship. Both were in their thirties when they married. By that point, they were mature enough to understand each other’s goals in life. They never tried to portray themselves as the “perfect couple.” On many occasions, Siti Hasmah insisted that their marriage was like anybody else’s. There were happy moments and sad moments. They fought, made up and went on holidays together, she said.

Unlike others, there was nothing glamorous about this First Couple. They continued working towards their goals and made this marriage very endearing to Malaysians because they showed that accommodation and tolerance are a recipe for a lasting marriage.

On September 28, 2026, Siti Hasmah let go of Mahathir’s hand forever. On physical separation, Rumi once said: “Goodbyes are only for those who love with their eyes. Because for those who love with heart and soul there is no such thing as separation.” For 70 years, they were inseparable, and even death cannot separate them.

title: This Time, the Korean Loudspeaker Standoff Is Different
channel_text: Blog; East Asia; Security; The Koreas
description: Typically, South Korea has used loudspeakers to respond to North Korean provocations. Now Pyongyang has vowed to turn them on – and the prospects for de-escalation are dim.
text:
On October 21, after inspecting fortification work along North Korea’s southern border, Kim Yo Jong, the sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, announced that “within October, the loudspeakers for psychological warfare against the ROK will be in operation along the whole border.” (ROK refers to the Republic of Korea, South Korea’s formal name.)

Two days earlier, Kim Yo Jong had said Pyongyang was considering the step, along with deploying more “tactical strike means” near the border. As a rationale, she cited the behavior of South Korean troops near the border, claiming they had issued 2,870 warning broadcasts and fired warning shots on 201 occasions between August 1 and October 17.

South Korea has no large loudspeakers left on the border; it took them down in August 2025 as a sign of goodwill. The Ministry of National Defense said that the warnings Kim referred to were issued by smaller speakers at guard posts as a defensive measure against North Korean soldiers crossing the Military Demarcation Line (MDL).

If the North starts broadcasting, South Korea’s military said it would consider restarting its own loudspeakers on the principle of proportional response.

The loudspeaker broadcasts began in 1963, when North Korea began using the tool and South Korea responded in kind. The first bout lasted over nine years, with broadcasts only switched off in November 1972. North Korea resumed broadcasts in 1980; the loudspeaker contest lasted even longer this time, until 2004.

But since then, loudspeaker use has settled into a pattern: South Korea resumed loudspeaker broadcasts in response to North Korean actions in 2015, 2016, and 2024. The latest round ended in 2025, with the Lee administration’s unilateral decision to dismantle South Korean speakers. This time, North Korea is the one resuming broadcasts, citing a growing dispute over the MDL.

Since 2015, Seoul has used loudspeakers when it wants to respond to North Korean provocations without resorting to force. In August 2015, South Korea’s defense minister called the broadcasts legitimate retaliation after mines that Seoul said the North had planted in the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) seriously injured two South Korean soldiers. South Korea also used loudspeaker broadcasts to respond to North Korea’s nuclear test in 2016, and again in 2024 when North Korea sent balloons filled with trash and feces across the border.

There’s a reason South Korean governments turned to loudspeakers. A broadcast is non-lethal and can be switched off at will, yet it targets something Pyongyang guards closely: its control over information. South Korean broadcasts have carried news, weather forecasts, and pop music to North Korea’s front-line soldiers, and officials said in 2015 that the sound could carry 24 kilometers at night. In June 2017, a North Korean soldier who crossed to a South Korean guard post on the central front said the broadcasts had made him decide to defect.

While South Korea considered the broadcasts to be a proportional response, North Korea sees them differently. Pyongyang called the 2015 resumption “a direct provocation of war.” The North turned its own speakers on just days after Seoul did, though South Korean officials said they were so old that their messages were nearly impossible to understand. “It just sounds like a drone,” one official said.

On August 20, 2015, South Korea’s military said North Korean forces had fired toward a loudspeaker site in Yeoncheon, north of Seoul, and South Korean artillery answered with dozens of 155 mm rounds. Pyongyang denied firing, issued an ultimatum to stop the broadcasts and declared a “quasi-state of war.” The standoff closed on August 25, 2015 with a joint statement in which the North expressed regret over the mine blasts and the South agreed to stop broadcasting “unless an abnormal situation occurs.”

That “abnormal situation” came in January 2016, when North Korea conducted an underground nuclear test. Days later, South Korea restarted its loudspeaker broadcasts. This time, the broadcasts went on for over two years. Seoul only switched them off on April 23, 2018, four days before an inter-Korean summit. The resulting Panmunjom Declaration committed both sides to stop all hostile acts along the MDL, including loudspeaker broadcasts, from May 1.

When Seoul turned the speakers back on in June 2024, after suspending the September 2018 inter-Korean military agreement. South Korea held that North Korea had already voided the agreement through its trash balloons and over provocations. South Korea’s broadcasts in 2024 included BTS songs, regional weather, and market prices, along with a message urging North Korean soldiers laying mines to escape what it called a life of slavery.

North Korea answered not with propaganda but with sheer noise: gunshots, screams, eerie laughter, and sounds like howling wolves. Noise levels on Ganghwa Island, about two kilometers from the North, reached 80 decibels late at night. To many, North Korea’s purpose was simply to torment South Koreans.

South Korean law acknowledged the harm being done. A December 2024 amendment to the Framework Act on Civil Defense allows the state to compensate people harmed by enemy actions that fall short of a civil defense emergency. A decree issued in May 2025 included “noise broadcasting” among the “hazardous acts” it covers, alongside balloons, shooting or shelling, and drones. In July 2026, border counties began taking claims, with payments determined by the number of days residents lived with the noise.

Previously, North Korea and South Korea stopped their loudspeaker broadcasts through bilateral agreement, after discussions. But South Korea ended its last round unilaterally. New President Lee Jae-myung ordered the broadcasts stopped on June 11, 2025; the North’s broadcasts ended the next day. In August 2025, the military began dismantling its fixed loudspeakers in what the defense ministry called “a practical measure aimed at helping ease tensions with the North.” Seoul said it had not consulted Pyongyang.

Pyongyang rejected any suggestion of reciprocity. After South Korea’s military reported that the North was removing some of its own speakers, Kim Yo Jong said: “We have never removed loudspeakers installed on the border area and are not willing to remove them.” About a week later, in fact, two new North Korean speakers went up opposite the South Korean border counties of Cheorwon and Hwacheon.

Now North Korea has declared that it will resume broadcasts. If so, the new round of loudspeaker use will be different from recent history. In 2015, 2016, and 2024, Seoul began broadcasting first; this time Pyongyang has declared its intention to do so, in response to alleged South Korean provocations. This is despite repeated efforts on the part of the Lee administration in Seoul to show its goodwill toward the North.

Since Kim Jong Un declared the two Koreas hostile states in December 2023, North Korean troops have fortified the DMZ, laying mines and building roads, fences, and what appear to be anti-tank barriers. In September 2026, two mine explosions along the DMZ injured three South Korean soldiers. Seoul said the mines had been laid during the “so-called border fortification works” since 2023 – and that they were planted south of MDL that separates the two Koreas.

North Korean soldiers working near the line occasionally cross it, as evidenced by the recent mine incident. South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff counted about 50 crossings in August and September 2026; South Korean troops responded with warning broadcasts and warning shots.

Kim Yo Jong, however, insisted that “our soldiers have never crossed the border.” There may be disagreement over where, exactly, the MDL is situated. If so, it will be difficult to resolve; Pyongyang ignored Seoul’s November 2025 offer of military talks to set “a clear reference line for the MDL.”

Kim’s statements framed the loudspeaker broadcasts as about the border rather than propaganda. She also issued a threat, saying that North Korean troops would show “no mercy” if South Korean warning shots ever harmed a North Korean solider. Kim also reiterated her brother’s vision that the MDL is now “a permanent line never to be crossed.”

As long as North Korean troops keep working along – and crossing – the MDL, South Korean warnings are likely to continue. That means North Korea’s responses, including the broadcasts, will as well. Seoul has also reserved the right to carry out a “proportional response” to North Korean broadcasts, although no specific action has been selected yet.

Over the longer term inter-Korean relations are likely to be shaped by interactions along the MDL, which Pyongyang now calls a permanent border and Seoul still treats as a temporary demarcation line set by the armistice. Preventing an accidental clash is now an urgent task.

With inter-Korean hotlines silent since April 2023, South Korea’s Unification Ministry has called for reconciling the two sides’ understandings of the MDL and setting up a communication system to manage it. Thus far, however, Pyongyang has refused to engage. That leaves South Korea with few options for responding to North Korean escalations without raising the risk of conflict.
tag: inter-Korea relations; Korean DMZ; MDL; Military Demarcation Line; North Korean loudspeakers; South Korea propaganda broadcasts

title: Time for ASEAN to Revive its Customs Union Vision
description: An idea rejected in 1986 deserves a second look.
text:
As tariffs once again become bargaining tools for major powers, one of ASEAN’s key weaknesses is the fragmentation of its market across national tariff regimes. The revival of the Common External Tariff (CET) proposal, rejected four decades ago, raises a fundamental question: can ASEAN move beyond a mere “collection of assembly hubs” to become a higher-value-added economic region and a negotiating actor in its own right?

A Customs Union Proposal Rejected 40 Years Ago

ASEAN’s economic integration has been built on the ASEAN Free Trade Area (AFTA), agreed in 1992 and implemented through the Common Effective Preferential Tariff (CEPT) scheme from 1993. The CEPT lowered intra-ASEAN tariffs on goods originating in the region. A CET, by contrast, would require member states to apply a common external tariff schedule to imports from outside ASEAN. Its adoption would take ASEAN beyond a free trade area and towards a customs union.

The CET is not a new idea. In August 1986, exactly 40 years ago, the Philippines, then ASEAN chair, proposed a customs union at the ASEAN Economic Ministers’ Meeting. The proposal called for intra-regional tariffs to be reduced gradually within a fixed time frame and for a common tariff to be imposed on imports from outside ASEAN. No consensus emerged: Indonesia opposed the deadline, while Singapore objected that the proposal could result in higher external tariffs. Intra-ASEAN trade then accounted for only about 20 percent of member states’ total trade, and their heavy dependence on external markets made a CET difficult to accept.

AFTA’s Success—and the Borders That Remain

ASEAN instead chose AFTA. This flexible form of integration eliminated most intra-regional tariffs while preserving each member state’s discretion over external tariffs. It supported ASEAN’s model of open regionalism – welcoming foreign investment and imported intermediate inputs while producing for global markets – and helped expand regional production networks. Yet many member states remained concentrated in assembly operations and dependent on external suppliers for key components, advanced materials and research and development. As a result, the value added retained within ASEAN did not rise commensurately with the value of its exports.

Under a fully functioning customs union, goods imported from outside the region could, after paying the common external tariff upon entering ASEAN, circulate freely within the bloc in principle. Certificates of origin and customs clearance procedures currently required for preferential intra-ASEAN trade would, in principle, no longer be necessary. With national tariff borders and rules of origin removed, companies could source the most suitable mix of parts and materials from across ASEAN and allocate production stages accordingly. Lower border costs would encourage intra-regional sourcing, the consolidation of production, and investment in higher-value activities.

Yet the flexibility that was once ASEAN’s strength is becoming a weakness amid intensifying geoeconomic competition. As tariffs, export controls, subsidies, and scrutiny of circumvention become increasingly intertwined with economic security, individual ASEAN members risk accepting different terms in separate negotiations with major powers. If this continues, companies may find it increasingly difficult to treat ASEAN as a single production base. More importantly, if member states continue to bargain separately on critical trade issues, not only regional supply chains but ASEAN centrality itself could be hollowed out.

A CET as a Platform for an Industrial Upgrade

In response to these concerns, the ASEAN Geoeconomics Report 2025 recommended that ASEAN pursue a CET alongside a compatible regional industrial policy. A common tariff alone, however, will not deliver an industrial upgrade; it must be combined with policies that connect the complementary strengths of member states and promote technology adoption, skills development, R&D and intra-regional sourcing. Only then can ASEAN retain more value added and create more high-quality jobs within the region. A CET alone is not sufficient, but it can provide the market foundation for such upgrading.

Realizing this vision will not be easy. ASEAN would have to agree on the treatment of customs revenue, trade-remedy measures and negotiating authority vis-à-vis third countries. It would also have to reconcile the FTAs concluded separately by individual member states. Existing agreements would need either to be consolidated into ASEAN-wide trade agreements or to have their preferential tariff rates and rules of origin harmonized across trading partners and product categories. If national tariff differentials remained, ASEAN would still need origin checks and the collection of tariff differences at internal borders to prevent imports from being diverted through lower-tariff members. The result would fall short of a full customs union.

Even so, ASEAN should not bury the idea once again. As a first step, member states should harmonize tariffs at low levels on critical inputs that cannot be adequately sourced within the region, including semiconductor manufacturing equipment and critical minerals. This would not constitute a customs union, but would provide a practical test of whether a transition towards a CET is workable. In parallel, ASEAN should more closely integrate customs procedures, standards and conformity assessment, investment policy, skills development and R&D support. The objective should be to build a regional industrial base linking components and materials with more advanced stages of production.

ASEAN should aim for a customs union that preserves openness to critical inputs, reduces fragmentation within its regional market and encourages companies to invest on an ASEAN-wide basis. It should not become a “tariff fortress” that erects high barriers against the rest of the world. Rather, it should provide the institutional foundation for transforming ASEAN from a “collection of assembly hubs” dependent on cheap labor into an integrated economic region that builds deeper capabilities in technology, components and R&D—and retains more value added at home.

At a time when major powers are once again weaponizing tariffs, a common external tariff and unified negotiating authority would give ASEAN greater collective bargaining power as a single economic bloc. A customs union would be more than a foundation for industrial upgrading; it could also become a powerful shield for ASEAN against tariff coercion.
tag: ASEAN customs union; ASEAN fragmentation; ASEAN Free Trade Area; ASEAN market; ASEAN tariffs; Common External Tariff

title: To Import or Build? Southeast Asia’s Rolling Stock Dilemma
channel_text: Blog; Economy; Pacific Money; Southeast Asia
description: Some of the region's governments are moving toward manufacturing their own rolling stock – but this comes with trade-offs.
text:
Urban rail systems are growing fast across Southeast Asia. This is fueling demand for rolling stock – the train cars that actually carry millions of riders around town every day. The most common option is to import trainsets from established industry leaders in China, Japan, South Korea, or Europe. But some countries in Southeast are turning to domestic firms to meet their orders. This raises an obvious question: is this wise?

The trade-offs are clear enough. Importing trains from an established global brand like China’s CRRC means you are buying a proven product, with after-sales service and support that makes it easier to maintain the trains. Sometimes foreign firms also provide electronic systems like signalling, which makes system integration easier. For many rail providers, this is a fine deal. Metro and commuter rail systems in Bangkok and Manila rely mainly on imported rolling stock.

But some countries want more. They want to manufacture the rolling stock domestically because they believe it will generate local jobs, create long-term value, and develop important skills and technical expertise. If done well, it will allow domestic firms to grow and export their products. Indonesia is a prominent example of this strategy, with state-owned INKA producing rolling stock for the local market and for export.

INKA’s main customer is the state-owned railway company, KAI, with which it is currently in the process of merging. If you have ever traveled on an intercity train in Java it most likely was made by INKA. More recently, INKA supplied the rolling stock for the Greater Jakarta LRT and has been delivering new trainsets for Jakarta’s large, aging and very busy commuter rail system, the KRL.

INKA is a classic case of industrial policy. Rather than relying on foreign firms, the government requires KAI to procure some of its rolling stock from INKA and places restrictions on imports. This guarantees INKA a minimum level of orders while also protecting it from foreign competition, providing the train-maker some breathing room to develop industrial capabilities it might not otherwise be able to.

But here’s the catch. For such industrial policy to be effective, INKA needs to deliver the goods. It must deliver rolling stock on time and that meets basic quality standards. It must show evidence that it is making progress toward mastery of more complex technologies, skills and production capabilities. The government can bend the market to give a state-owned firm a leg up, but the firm needs to prove this intervention is worth it. Industrial policy fails when firms don’t make good use of the strategic advantage they have been given.

At the moment, INKA is struggling to deliver the goods. The train cars built for the LRT in 2023 were plagued with problems, including electrical and mechanical issues. Almost as soon as they went into service, many had to be pulled out and modified. The LRT project was run mainly by Indonesian SOEs, so the fact that it experienced growing pains was not necessarily evidence of policy failure. The key was that domestic firms, including INKA, learned from these mistakes and used them to improve.

In recent weeks, rolling stock made by INKA for Jakarta’s commuter rail system has been malfunctioning, throwing commutes into chaos. Doors are getting stuck open, forcing trains out of service. Seven cars were recalled after KAI raised concerns about structural weakness in the undercarriage. KAI is seeking special permission from the government to import used rolling stock from Japan to meet immediate operational needs while these issues are worked out. Public anger and scrutiny are rising.

Similar attempts by other home-grown firms in the region also have spotty records. In 2011, Malaysia’s Scomi won a nearly 500 million ringgit contract to supply trainsets for the Kuala Lumpur monorail. The rolling stock was delivered late, and faced performance and safety issues. The procurement became embroiled in legal disputes, and Scomi was eventually dissolved. So INKA is not alone in facing hurdles as it tries to expand its footprint. But if the government is to continue aiding such efforts, INKA needs to start delivering the goods.

This is especially true now that intra-ASEAN competition is intensifying. Vietnamese conglomerate Vingroup just announced it was launching a joint venture with France’s Alstom to co-produce 200 trainsets for the Hanoi metro under a technology licensing agreement. This is a very large and ambitious project, which would represent a major step-up in capabilities for Vingroup and Vietnam’s domestic railway industry. Of course, Vingroup has a history of taking huge swings that don’t always pan out. So we will have to see.

Most urban rail systems in Southeast Asia simply import their trains, working with established manufacturers who can deliver a proven product and after-sales service and support. For some countries, domestic manufacturing is a more important goal and the state will intervene to give local firms a head-start. Ultimately, no amount of state support or industrial policy can cover up for production failings that leave commuters stranded with unreliable products. The trains must run, and local firms like INKA must deliver the goods. Otherwise, the whole logic of industrial policy comes flying off the rails.
tag: Indonesia infrastructure; Indonesia railway sector; Southeast Asia infrastructure; Southeast Asia railways; Vingroup

title: To Rebuild the Nepali Congress, Gagan Thapa Must First Reform It
description: Recently re-elected president of the Nepali Congress, Thapa vowed to end the culture of nepotism and groupism in the party and to open it to a new generation of leaders.
text:
Among the most charismatic political leaders of his generation, Gagan Thapa was long talked of as a prime minister-in-waiting. As he rose up the ranks of the Nepali Congress — the social democratic party that has been the country’s dominant political force for most of the post-1990 period — this advocate of value-based politics with unmatched oratory skills seemed destined to lead his party and country.

Then came the Gen Z movement. In just two days of protests in September 2025, the movement upended the old political order. K.P. Oli, the communist prime minister at the time, had to run for his life. The top Congress leader, Sher Bahadur Deuba, was beaten black and blue. Along with the homes of hundreds of other political leaders, Thapa’s Kathmandu home was torched and he too had to go into hiding.

The Gen Z movement would also act as a catalyst for change in the Congress. In its aftermath, a set of second-generation leaders under Thapa finally dared to revolt and wrest party leadership away from Deuba, then age 79. Yet most Nepalis saw this as too little, too late, and the Congress under Thapa performed dismally in the first post-uprising national polls held in March 2026.

Today, the Congress is a diminished force, occupying just 38 seats in the 275-member lower House. Meanwhile, with 182 seats, the new Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP), which took ownership of the Gen Z movement, garnered a near two-thirds majority.

When the Congress was trounced in the March 2026 polls, old party leaders put the blame for the defeat on Thapa and his “mistimed” revolt that was orchestrated on the eve of the March elections. But the RSP was riding a wave of discontent with the established political parties, and Congress under its old leadership would arguably have fared even worse in the elections.

Now Thapa, 50, has been re-elected party president by its just-concluded general convention. While asking for votes, he vowed to end the culture of nepotism and groupism in the party and to open the outfit to a new generation of leaders.

His other proposals include a system of primaries to pick the party’s electoral candidates and amending the constitution charter to limit any individual to two terms as prime minister. Thapa’s proposed reforms, if implemented, could open up new democratic space, both in the party and in the national polity.

This is in sharp contrast to the centralizing and power-hoarding tendencies of Sher Bahadur Deuba, the erstwhile party president, who did much to discredit the image of a party that was long associated with principled leaders like B.P. Koirala and Ganesh Man Singh.

But Thapa has a monumental challenge on his hands. The RSP has captured much of the political space once occupied by the Congress. Under party chair Rabi Lamichhane and senior leader Balendra Shah, who is also Nepal’s prime minister, the RSP remains very popular. It is thus expected to replicate its federal poll success in the local and provincial elections scheduled for 2027.

The old rivalry between Congress, the old champion of liberal democratic values, and the communists appears increasingly irrelevant to Nepali voters today. Now it is upon Thapa’s party to show the skeptical electorate what liberal democratic values mean in practice, and why a reformed Congress can uphold them.

The other big challenge for Thapa would be to bring back into the party’s fold the disgruntled leaders who still back former party president Deuba. If a big chunk of old Congress stalwarts continue to side with Deuba, Thapa will have a tough time rebuilding the party organization. His efforts to reinvigorate the Congress will be dealt a further blow if the Supreme Court, which is currently considering a case on the legality of the Thapa-led Congress, chooses to identify the Deuba faction as the authentic Congress party.

Gagan Thapa has many strengths. He has worked his way up the ranks of the Congress. However, Thapa’s rise came even as the party’s top leaders were openly engaging in self-centered politics and corruption. In the eyes of many young Nepalis, he preferred to play it safe and bided his time. But Nepali youths were less patient — and revolted. Many thus reckon Thapa’s time has passed.

Whether or not that is true, it is important for the Congress under Thapa to continue to be electorally competitive in Nepali politics. Besides its role as the champion of liberal democratic values, a strong Congress will also make the RSP accountable.

With the discrediting of the Congress under the old leadership, the RSP has come to occupy the liberal democratic space without doing much to demonstrate its commitment to liberal values. In just six months in office, the new RSP government has taken a number of questionable decisions — from removing squatters without due process to jailing political leaders on flimsy legal grounds — that make people suspect the party’s democratic credentials.

Thapa has proven his credentials as a fighter for democratic rights, as a competent administrator during his tenure as health minister, and as a voice of reason in the cacophonous Nepali political landscape. Now, for the first time, he will be tasked with rebuilding a party organization. But to do so, he will first have to dismantle the old, ossified structures and ways of thinking that have held the party back in recent times.
tag: 2026 Nepal elections; Gagan Thapa; Nepali Congress; Nepali Congress convention; Nepali Congress reform; Sher Bahadur Deuba

title: Trade Agreement With US Close to Completion, Thai Prime Minister Says
description: Anutin Charnvirakul said that he expected to sign the Agreement on ⁠Reciprocal Trade during President Donald Trump's next visit to Asia.
text:
Trade negotiations between Thailand and the United States are in the final stages and an agreement is expected to be signed as soon as next month, Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul said yesterday.

Speaking at a forum ​in Singapore, Anutin said negotiations on the Agreement on ⁠Reciprocal Trade (ART) are now on “the last ​paragraph” and that he ​expected to sign the final agreement during U.S. President Donald Trump’s next visit to Asia, Reuters reported. This could take place during the ASEAN Summit in the Philippines on November 16–18, which Trump has confirmed he is attending, or the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meetings in Shenzhen on November 18–19. Trump’s attendance at the latter summit has not yet been confirmed.

Anutin said that he received a ​letter from the U.S. president last week ​confirming the deal is at its final stage. “He ‌told ⁠me that I was to make sure that my people and the United States Trade Representative would write ​up the ​final clause,” the Thai leader said.

The U.S. is Thailand’s largest export market, and the country’s imports of Thai goods totaled $91.3 billion in 2025, according to U.S. government figures.

Bangkok and Washington have been negotiating a “reciprocal” trade deal with the U.S. since Trump’s initial “liberation day” tariff day announcement in April 2025, which hit Thailand with a 36 percent tariff.

In October 2025, the U.S. and Thailand announced a “framework” for an agreement on reciprocal trade, which reduced the tariff to 19 percent in exchange for a Thai pledge to “eliminate tariff barriers on approximately 99 percent of goods, covering a full range of U.S. industrial and food and agricultural products.” Under the framework, Thailand also promised to purchase more American energy, agricultural products and aircraft in order to close its $71.7 billion goods trade surplus with the U.S.

However, the negotiation of a final agreement has been complicated and delayed by recent shifts in U.S. tariff policy. In February, the U.S. Supreme Court struck down the “liberation day” tariff regime.

As a workaround, Trump imposed a temporary 10 percent global tariff under Section 122 of the Trade Act, which expired in July. The Office of the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR) also used Section 301 of the U.S. Trade Act of 1974, which allows Washington to investigate and impose tariffs on foreign countries for unfair trade practices. In March, it initiated two separate investigations, one examining 60 nations’ alleged failures to take action on forced labor, and another examining excess industrial capacity on the part of 16 major trading ​partners.

Thailand was a target of both investigations, and in June, it was hit with a 12.5 percent tariff in the forced labor probe. The USTR has also accused Thailand of maintaining a “structural overcapacity” in three sectors – automotive and parts, machinery, and rubber products – although this investigation has not yet been concluded.

The Commerce Ministry says Thailand and the U.S. have already agreed on the main substance and principles of the ART, leaving technical teams to settle remaining details and legal wording. Thailand’s aim, according to The Nation, “is to keep the eventual overall tariff burden around the previous 19 percent benchmark, or at least no higher than that faced by regional competitors.”

The finalization of the ART would undoubtedly be a positive development for the U.S.-Thailand relationship, which has not been helped by the drawn-out negotiations. In August, Bloomberg reported that Thailand was going so far as to consider using military cooperation as leverage in the trade talks. According to its report, which quoted an unnamed Thai official, Bangkok was preparing to warn the Trump administration that steep U.S. tariffs might force it to scale back military cooperation, including the Cobra Gold exercises that have been a cornerstone of the U.S.-Thailand alliance since the 1980s.

Thailand’s government denied the reports.
tag: Anutin Charnvirakul; Donald Trump; Trump administration trade policy; Trump tariffs; U.S.-Thailand relations; U.S.-Thailand trade

title: Trial by Fire: The 2025 Thai-Cambodian Border Clashes and the Royal Thai Air Force
channel_text: Asia Defense; Blog; Security; Southeast Asia
description: In two outbreaks of war last year, the RTAF underlined its status as one of the region’s most effective and professional air forces.
text:
The long-simmering border conflict between Thailand and Cambodia erupted into a higher intensity military clash in July and December 2025, which saw the participation of the Royal Thai Air Force (RTAF) in a high-intensity conflict for the first time since World War II. During the conflict, the RTAF proved its status as a highly professional air force – one that belongs to the front ranks of Southeast Asia’s air forces.

This article uses available open-source information to assesses the RTAF’s air operations against the Royal Cambodian Army (RCA) during the July and December border clashes. It also discusses what the fighting revealed about the RTAF’s current capability today.

July 2025 – Operation Yuttha Bodin

Multiple clashes between Thai and Cambodian forces since the spring of 2025 led to a major escalation of hostilities on July 24, when Cambodia fired BM-21 rockets across the border, killing at least 11 Thai civilians and one soldier.

In response, the Thai military launched Operation Yuttha Bodin, a coordinated air and land assault, to defend Thai sovereignty, retaliate against Cambodian military actions along the border, and to reduce Cambodian military capability in order to preserve Thai state security and public safety.

On the first day of the operation, on July 24, the RTAF dispatched two missions totaling 10 strike sorties against RCA military command posts and army positions in the Ta Moan Thom temple area in Oddar Meanchey province.

During the five-day operation, the RTAF operated under a joint tactical plan, with Army Commander Gen. Pana Klaewplodthuk acting as the overall joint force commander. The RTAF provided direct support to a ground offensive by the Royal Thai Army (RTA).

The primary geographic focus of Operation Yuttha Bodin was on the disputed border area adjacent to Thailand’s Surin province and Cambodia’s Oddar Meanchey province (see Table 1). The RTAF provided support to the RTA, specifically in areas of active fighting, conducting air strikes to neutralize Cambodian C2 posts, troop strongholds and artillery positions, and weapons and ammunition supply depots.

Besides the Wing 1 F-16s in Korat, a major RTAF air force base located northeast of Bangkok, the 7 Wing, deployed its key assets from their home base in Surin to the base, including JAS39 Gripen fighters and Saab 340 Erieye AEW&C and Saab 340 ELINT aircraft to support the operation.

Together with the base’s 103 Squadron, 1 Wing, and 403 Squadron, 4 Wing F-16s, which had also dispatched aircraft to Korat from its base in Takhli, northwest of Bangkok, and the Gripen detachment, the three units represented the brunt of the RTAF’s offensive force.

The F-5TH and F-16s from the 21 Wing in Ubon Ratchathani, near the Thai-Cambodian border and the 4 Wing at Takhli executed all-important defensive counter air missions to protect critical military and civilian infrastructure.

The 702 Squadron’s Erieye aircraft flew day and night, providing a unified aerial picture, airspace management, and deconfliction between the different offensive and defensive assets in close coordination with the air force’s Air Command and Control System (ACCS) at Wing 6 Don Mueang base in Bangkok.

Critically, while the RTA led the overall joint force, the RTAF (through the ACCS) held control of all air assets and responded to requests from RTA for air support.

Other critical assets included the Sa Kaeo-based 3 Wing – the RTAF’s dedicated uncrewed aerial systems unit – which operated the Aerostar BP and Dominator XP UAS, and 7 Wing’s Saab 340 electronic intelligence platform, which provided critical intelligence, reconnaissance, surveillance, and targeting (ISTAR) and battle-damage assessment (BDA) support to the joint force during the operation.

In addition, the RTAF and the Thai Army deployed their ground-based air defense systems to provide additional cover for ground forces and forward bases against air-based threats.
