During the operation, the RTA employed multiple types of uncrewed systems that ranged from bomb-dropping quadcopters dropping munitions on RCA trenches to larger DP-20 MALE UAS, which provided additional battlefield surveillance and reconnaissance support.

Table 1. July 2025 – Operation Yuttha Bodin. Source: Author’s compilation from various sources.

December 2025 – Resumption of Air Campaign

In December, in response to what Thailand described as the RCA’s continued provocations and movement of heavy equipment and combat forces into disputed border areas, the Thai military launched Operation Sattawat, which aimed to “penetrate and destroy the opposing side’s combat support structures and strategic supply routes.”

To support the RTA’s operation on the ground, the RTAF targeted Cambodian C2, drone control facilities, weapons and ammunition depots, logistics, and equipment that could pose a threat to “national security and civilian safety.”

In a major departure from the more geographically constrained operations against RCA forces and supplies adjacent to Surin province during Operation Yuttha Bodin, the December air campaign saw the RTAF expand its target list to encompass the entire length of the shared border (see Table 2).

In addition to the frequent close air support missions along the border, the RTAF carried out some deep strike operations to destroy selected bridges and weapons depots deep inside Cambodia. For example, on December 24, Thai fighters penetrated as deep as 100 kilometers into Cambodian territory in Battambang Province to hit a weapons depot there.

Table 2. December 2025 – Resumption of Thai air campaign. Source: Author’s compilation from various sources.

Although not publicly disclosed like the 1 Wing and 4 Wing F-16s and 7 Wing Gripens use in strike missions, visual evidence of bomb mission marking on other units and combat aircraft like the F-5TH “Super Tigris” and T-50TH from the 21 Wing and 4 Wing verify their active participation in strike missions as well.

Tempo and Targeting

During the July operation, the RTAF flew two to three combat missions daily, involving two to four combat aircraft per mission. On the first day of heavy fighting, larger formations (up to 10 combat aircraft in total) were involved in strikes in anticipation of a greater level of resistance (see Table 1). The lower-than-expected opposition allowed required sorties to be reduced to an average of four sorties or two two-ship missions per day. In total, RTAF conducted 28 strike sorties during Operation Yuttha Bodin.

Compared to July, it appears that the RTAF operated at a higher operational tempo in December, based on the known targets struck and the geographic spread of combat operations (see Table 2). For example, during the more active phase of ground fighting on December 18-19, the RTAF flew a larger number of sorties against RCA forces along the length of the shared border, including in Siem Reap, Oddar Meanchey, and Banteay Meanchey provinces.

Critically, the publicly released sorties only consider actual strike sorties. Several supporting sorties, including defensive counter air, airspace surveillance and strike coordination, reconnaissance and target acquisition, electromagnetic domain monitoring, and airlift sorties were carried out simultaneously, even if not publicly acknowledged.

The bombing effort was preceded and supplemented by an attempt to locate any ground-based air defense threats and eliminate them. To achieve this, RTAF deployed crewed and uncrewed ISTAR assets, including the 7 Wing’s Saab 340 ELINT was used to establish the Cambodian forces’ electronic order of battle along the key operational axes opposite Ubon Ratchathani, Buri Ram, Surin, Si Sa Ket, Sa Kaeo, and Chanthaburi Provinces.

The RTAF and RTA uncrewed ISTAR aircraft deployed the Aerostar BP and Dominator XP UAS and Defense Technology Institute (DTI) DP-20 MALE UAS to reconnoiter the border area, locate RCA force disposition, and provide post-strike battle damage assessment.

To reconnoiter targets and provide precision-guidance for PGMs, RTAF combat aircraft employed Litening-III targeting pod (Gripen and F-5TH) and the Sniper ATP pod (F-16 and TA-50TH)—to find, fix, identify, engage, and BDA (battle damage assessment) targets.

Weapons Deployment

The RTAF dropped more than 30 tons of munitions on Cambodian positions during Operation Yuttha Bodin. Munitions employed included unguided general-purpose bombs (GPBs) and precision-guided munitions (PGMs), and direct attack and standoff weapons.

The most commonly employed munitions included the Mk. 82 high-explosive GPB and laser-guided 500-lb Lizard-III and/or GBU-12-kitted PGMs. Some 2,000-lb Mk. 84 high-explosive GPB and AGM-65 Maverick air-to-ground missiles were also employed against larger hardened targets and RCA armor.

In addition, the 500-lb Korean GPS-guided glide-bomb (KGGB) was used in combat for the first time. The KGGB was reportedly employed especially during the opening phase of the conflict to provide standoff range in the face of potential Cambodian deployment of its Chinese-made medium-range KC-1 surface-to-air missile system along the border.

Importantly, the RTAF sources many of these weapons from the United States and Israel, as well as South Korea. In addition, the Thai defense industry is thought to manufacture variants of the Mk. 82 bombs, which can be mated with the Israeli (Elta Lizard-III and GBU-12) and Korean (LIG Nex1 KGGB) precision-guidance kits. The diversified and largely non-U.S. supply of key munitions and their guidance kits make the RTAF more resilient against a potential U.S. arms embargo.

Pictures of RTAF fighters that have surfaced since the border clash show large numbers of sorties on individual aircraft. For example, an F-16B has been spotted with 63 bombing mission markings; T-50THs with 32 and 34 Mk. 82 bomb mission markings; an F-5TH with 20 Mk. 82 bomb mission markings; and a Gripen with seven GBU-12 mission markings. These indicate that the real sortie numbers may be higher than publicly reported. They also highlight the employment of all of RTAF’s primary combat aircraft in bombing sorties – something which has not been disclosed publicly.

In addition to aircraft delivered munitions, Thailand has also drawn lessons from recent conflicts by employing indigenous KB-5E and KB-10G long-range loitering munitions and one-way attack drones (OWADs) in combat for the first time. Thai forces deployed the capability alongside scouting drones, artillery and air support in a multilayered reconnaissance-strike complex.

Opposition and Losses

The RTAF’s losses during the July and December operations were very low. The Thai military is known to have lost at least two aircraft during December fighting. On December 17, a DP-20 UAV of the RTA was lost for an unknown reason. The second aircraft, an RTAF Aerostar BP UAV, was reportedly shot down over Cambodia’s Banteay Meanchey Province on December 21.

Importantly, enabling RTAF impunity of operations was the fact that Cambodia has no fast jet air power of its own. Despite having acquired Chinese-made KC-1 medium-range surface-to-air missile system and the very short-range QW-3 MANPAD, they posed little opposition to RTAF operations.

The Verdict

The July and December 2025 border clashes between Thailand and Cambodia were the first major conflict that saw a large-scale deployment of Thai air power in support of its ground forces. It was also the largest deployment of air power in Southeast Asia since the Vietnam War.

It employed and tested nearly all of the combat assets and enablers in the RTAF’s inventory, including both crewed and uncrewed tactical aviation.

Critically, the conflict successfully showcased results of the RTAF’s more than decade-long effort to create a truly network-centric force. It employed all key enablers in a demonstration of modern air power, using domestic datalink (the Link-T) to coordinate and communicate between C2 nodes, ISR assets, and strike aircraft.

The air force’s Erieye AEW&C platform provided effective airspace control, coordinating and deconflicting defensive counterair aircraft and ground-based air defenses from strike aircraft ingressing or egressing from target areas, while various crewed and uncrewed platforms provided effective tactical and strategic level ISR and targeting for the joint force.

The brief air campaign included many firsts. This was the first time the Swedish Gripen had dropped bombs in anger. It was also the first real-world test for the Korean KGGB glide bomb and the indigenous KB-series OWADs. The RTAF demonstrated that it has taken great strides in the integration of uncrewed platforms into the force.

Although Cambodia could not challenge RTAF in the air, the threat of “pop-up” air defense threats posed by the RCA’s VSHORAD and SHORAD systems and explosive-armed small drones remained real throughout the conflict.

Underlining its status as one of the region’s most professional air forces, the RTAF sustained only very limited losses, while meeting many of its stated objectives. These included reducing the threat posed by RCA heavy weaponry to the state and civilian population, and reasserting deterrence.
tag: Royal Cambodian Army; Royal Thai Air Force; Royal Thai Army; Thailand air force; Thailand military; Thailand security; Thailand-Cambodia border conflict; Thailand-Cambodia relations

title: Trial by Social Media? The Boundaries of Feminist Teaching in China
description: A law school professor was dismissed after online controversy over her course on women’s rights.
text:
On September 29, Beijing Institute of Technology (BIT) announced the dismissal of a teacher surnamed Pei, widely identified in reporting as law school assistant professor Pei Yi. The university canceled her eligibility to supervise graduate students, revoked her eligibility to hold a teaching position at BIT, and terminated her employment.

The university said a special working group had investigated allegations against Pei and found serious violations of teachers’ professional ethics and codes of conduct. Its public statement did not specify the conduct or disclose the supporting evidence.

The announcement followed an online controversy surrounding Pei’s elective course, “Protecting Women’s Rights in the Digital Age.” A message in a course group chat attracted accusations that she was insulting male students. Screenshots attributed to her subsequently circulated, broadening the backlash into accusations of “radical feminism.”

The case raises questions that BIT’s statement leaves unanswered: What conduct justified dismissal? How were the allegations assessed? And how should universities distinguish complaints about discriminatory teaching from opposition to feminist discussion itself?

The subject of Pei’s course is a legitimate field of legal inquiry. Women in digital spaces can face harassment, invasion of privacy, and discrimination; it’s important to know both their rights and their access to remedies. Teaching these subjects, however, requires examining unequal distributions of power, including inequalities that students may find uncomfortable or contest.

A video circulating online, purportedly from Pei’s classroom, featured her discussing the online harassment of law professor Lao Dongyan over her public positions on legal issues, including sexual consent. Pei mentioned that such harassment is difficult to counter because attacks come from dispersed individuals rather than a unified group with an identifiable leader. The discussion addressed a substantive question for a course on “women’s rights in the digital age”: how online hostility develops and what makes accountability difficult.

The initial dispute centered on Pei’s description of her course as having a “chocolate attribute” that might make some students uncomfortable. Critics interpreted this as a reference to an internet joke about chocolate being harmless to humans but dangerous to dogs, and therefore an insult to male students. Pei reportedly offered a different explanation, invoking the “Forrest Gump” metaphor of life as a box of chocolates.

The backlash was not simply a demand for clarification. Some commenters celebrated Pei’s dismissal, calling her a “女拳师” (“female boxer”), a derogatory pun on the Chinese word for feminism. Such responses suggest that, for at least some participants, the controversy became an opportunity to celebrate the removal of someone identified with feminism.

Other allegations concerned screenshots attributed to Pei expressing support for men being treated as inferior. Their authenticity and context, however, need to be established rather than inferred from their widespread circulation. Public approval of a dismissal cannot establish the truth of the allegations behind it. That distinction is especially important when hostility toward a teacher’s perceived feminist identity becomes entangled with complaints about her professional conduct.

The controversy surrounding Pei underscores the importance of distinguishing online hostility from substantiated complaints about professional conduct. BIT’s public statement leaves outsiders unable to assess how that distinction was made. For those teaching about women’s rights, that uncertainty may be enough to discourage difficult but necessary conversations.

A controversy in Hong Kong around the same time offers an imperfect contrast. According to students quoted in media reports, Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) academic Chong Tai-leung said that high grades were of little use to women, who would ultimately seek wealthy husbands. He reportedly also advised women against pursuing Ph.Ds, saying their youth was too precious. His presentation slides also discussed the “cost-benefit” of women marrying rich.

Chong later publicly apologized for his remarks. His college said it had reminded him to be mindful of his language and others’ feelings.
tag: China feminism; China gender inequality; China online harassment; China women's rights

title: Trouble in Shangri-La? Why Bruneians Are Going to Australia for Illegal Migrant Work
description: Unemployed Bruneians are using Australian tourist visas to work as fruit pickers.
text:
To the outside world, Brunei, the tiny Southeast Asian monarchy, looks like a Shangri-La. The country, with a population of less than half a million, has one of the highest levels of GDP per capita in the world. Its benevolent Sultan has ensured free healthcare and education and highly subsidized food and housing for his subjects.

There is no income tax. Brunei has the highest per capita car ownership in ASEAN – an average of two cars per household – and a high prevalence of foreign domestic workers, locally called “amah,” predominantly hailing from Indonesia and the Philippines.

Given this background, the news of educated Bruneians going to Australia to work illegally on agricultural farms as fruit-pickers was shocking for someone who has worked in Brunei for 10 years.

But a Reddit discussion on Brunei unemployment revealed that something is amiss in the Sultanate. Many unemployed people blamed foreign workers for taking their jobs in the private sector.

For some, the easiest way out was Australia. The Bruneian passport, ranked 19th in the world, opens visa-free or visa-on-arrival access to 163 countries.

The Electronic Travel Authority (ETA) gives a three-month tourist visa for just A$20. Although it is illegal for ETA holders to work, and if caught, the visa can be cancelled, for some desperate Bruneians the risk is worth taking, as A$30-A$50 per hour looks pretty good even after taking travel, board, and lodging into consideration.

Although Australia has a program called the Working Holiday Maker (WHM) scheme, also called backpacker visa, which allows travelers to work during their stay to help finance their holiday, it comes with several caveats. There is generally a six-month limit on working for the same employer. More importantly, the scheme is available only to citizens of more than 40 partner countries and Brunei is not among them. This may explain why some Bruneians are using the ETA as a backdoor route to Australia in search of farm work.

How has the situation come to this pass? One cannot find obvious signs of poverty in Brunei, unlike in many Southeast Asian countries. I have never seen a Bruneian begging on the streets.

The problem is that educated youth are not finding employment in one of the richest countries in the world. It sounds paradoxical. Even more ironic is the fact that the hydrocarbon sector, which brought so much wealth to the country, is also contributing to unemployment. The Dutch Disease is at work in Brunei. When 90 percent of export revenues come from oil and gas, it can stunt the growth of other sectors such as agriculture, tourism, and industry.

A communications consultant, who asked not to be named, said: “The economy is just broken and is too skewed in one direction. Too much emphasis on the hydrocarbon sector has not only shrunk the job market but also made different clusters of the economy stagnant.” She added: “Outside of oil and gas, what do we have? What job opportunities are there?”

Brunei’s 2025 Labor Force Survey, published in July using the International Labor Organization reference population aged 15 and above, showed unemployment rising to 11,800 people, or 5.1 percent, from 4.8 percent in 2024. Brunei’s national headline measure, covering those aged 18 and above, was 5.0 percent.

Youth unemployment among those aged 15 to 24 stood at 18.4 percent. The gap by sex was stark: 15.3 percent for young men and 23.7 percent for young women. This means nearly one in four young women in the labor force who were seeking work did not find it.

Time-related underemployment rose from 15,600 to 19,500 people. These were workers who wanted additional hours, worked fewer than 40 hours, and were available for more work.

The important highlight of the survey is that median monthly income from employment fell from BN$1,000 in 2024 to BN$950 in 2025.

Siti Fatimahwati Pehin Dato Musa and Pg Dr Siti Rozaidah Pg Hj Idris of Universiti Brunei Darussalam, in their seminal 2022 work, “Addressing Issues of Unemployment in Brunei: The Mismatch Between Employers’ Expectations and Employees’ Aspirations,” wrote that the majority of young people seek prestigious jobs and that there seems to be a risk-averse attitude among them. Most young people aspire to jobs that are in the professional, managerial, or technical sectors.

This preference for secure jobs is also reflected in Brunei’s employment structure. The government is the biggest employer in Brunei, and it is the most sought-after avenue for any young Bruneian because of lifelong financial security.

The 2022 study found that the mindset of relying on government jobs was responsible for a lower preference for jobs in the private sector and other sectors. Another factor highlighted by the study was that most Bruneians are averse to manual work.

A social media consultant said that in the good old days, when oil was hitting more than $140 per barrel, everything was humming along. He said the only way out of the current economic trap is diversification. Brunei should learn from Gulf countries, which have reduced their dependence on the oil and gas sector. Even a country like Saudi Arabia has started diversifying its economy, he pointed out.

“The notion that Brunei is a utopia that is shielded from turbulent economic and natural forces no longer exists today,” he added.

Discussion of agricultural work in Australia has been doing the rounds on Brunei’s social media. Australia is entering its harvest season, when farmers face a perennial shortage of seasonal labor. WHM travelers are an important source of this workforce and can legally take jobs such as fruit picking. But Bruneians are not eligible for the WHM scheme, and working on an ETA remains illegal.

The Australian High Commission in Bandar Seri Begawan has a dedicated page on its website warning Bruneians against visa scams and making clear that an ETA does not permit them to work in Australia.

Although the Bruneian dollar is stronger than the Australian dollar because of Brunei’s currency interchangeability agreement with the Singapore dollar, for an unemployed young Bruneian A$30-A$50 an hour is worth taking risk. According to wage.is, the minimum wage in Brunei is BN$2.62/hr (A$2.88) as of 2026. The average gross monthly salary is BN$2,500 (A$2,752); the same amount could be earned in just about two weeks of fruit picking in Australia.

This is the reason why some of Brunei’s educated young people are now leaving home to do agricultural labor in Australia.

A teacher at Universiti Brunei Darussalam pointed out the paradox: “The reason why we have so many foreign workers doing manual jobs, even in the agriculture sector, is that many times we are told that Bruneians are averse to manual work. Here, a young Bruneian, leaving the comforts of home, is ready to go to Australia to do manual work on farms. I am not sure about the monetary benefit if you take into account air tickets, board, and lodging.”

Is it a case of the grass looking greener on the other side of the fence? Or are young Bruneians simply trying to make a quick buck while waiting for their chance in the long queue of the unemployed? It might be both.
tag: Australia agricuture; Australia migration policy; Brunei economy; Brunei unemployment; Brunei youth

title: Trump’s Targeting of Indian IT Firms Hits India-US Ties Again
description: Washington announced last week that it would not accept or process applications from top Indian IT companies for H-1B visas.
text:
Ties between India and the United States hit another bump last week with the Trump administration freezing green card requests from eight technology firms, including those from India.

U.S. Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling announced on October 8 that Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL Technologies, Capgemini, Microsoft, and Adobe have been suspended from participating in the Permanent Labor Certification (PERM), a program that is largely used by technology companies and outsourcing firms to sponsor a foreign worker’s permanent residency in the U.S. “We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labor certification applications involving these companies,” Sonderling said.

The announcement came weeks before U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s visit to New Delhi.

Indian IT companies appear largely unperturbed by the U.S. policy change. Infosys, India’s second-largest IT firm, said it did ‌not anticipate a material impact from the PERM application suspension. The National Association of Software and Service Companies (NASSCOM), India’s IT industry body, said that Indian companies had significantly reduced their dependence on H-1B visas in recent years and had expanded their local ‌hiring ⁠in the U.S. Relatively few workers move from H-1B visas to permanent residency through PERM, it said.

Ajay Srivastava, who heads the Global Trade Research Initiative, a New Delhi-based trade and commerce think tank, said the U.S. move was a “warning for India’s IT industry.” “It covers four leading Indian IT firms and disrupts the permanent-residency plans of their employees, making long-term staffing in the U.S. more uncertain,” Srivastava told The Diplomat.

“The larger concern is India’s dependence on a market that accounts for 54.1 percent of its software and IT-enabled services exports. The measure signals a more protectionist U.S. approach to foreign technology workers. India should prepare for possible restrictions extending beyond green card sponsorship,” he said, adding that Indian firms should widen their export markets to reduce their vulnerability to sudden U.S. policy changes.

India’s software services exports to the U.S. fetched $221.4 billion in revenues in 2025-26, an 8.2 percent year-on-year increase.

Adding salt to injury was a comment by Vice President J.D. Vance. Speaking to reporters after Sonderling’s announcement, Vance said: “Our message to Microsoft is you’re a great American company, but you’ve got to hire great American workers. You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants.”

In a sharply worded statement, India’s Ministry of External Affairs said that “talent mobility adds value to both economies.” The measures announced by the United States “do not advance the shared ambitions of both countries.” Recalling that the U.S. was a country built by immigrants, the statement said that “resorting to terminology that carries painful historical and colonial legacy connotations is deeply offensive.” The allusion was to India’s British colonial rulers transporting more than a million Indians to work as contract labor in British colonies abroad after the abolition of slavery by the British in 1833.

There is speculation in India that the U.S. policy change on green card requests is aimed at showing President Donald Trump’s domestic audience that his administration is tough on immigration. The U.S. will vote in mid-term elections in November. Voters are reportedly unhappy with the Trump administration’s performance, especially on the handling of the economy, with job numbers falling short of expectations.

Last week’s restrictions on Indian IT companies, together with Vance’s comments, have added to the chill in India-U.S. relations, especially since Trump returned to the White House in January 2025.

A trade pact negotiated between the two sides remains unsigned despite many rounds of talks. Washington’s courting of Pakistan, which India sees as instigating terrorism against it, has not gone down well in Delhi.

Speaking at the Asia Society in New York in September, India’s Minister for External Affairs S. Jaishankar highlighted the U.S. anti-immigration push affecting the movement of Indian workers to the U.S. as among the main causes for the current strain in bilateral ties.

Since returning to the White House last year, Trump has implemented several measures to rework American immigration policy. These include bestowing more powers on officials to enforce domestic immigration laws as well as increasing anti-immigration raids and deportations. Last year, India accepted the return of almost 400 of its nationals deported by the Trump administration. Their arrival in India in military aircraft and in shackles caused a domestic outcry.

The Trump administration has also been squeezing the H-1B visa program that allows foreign nationals to temporarily work in the U.S. in specialty occupations for a maximum of six years. In August, Washington proposed a regulation to raise the fee on new H-1B visas to over $100,000. The ​H-1B program offers 65,000 visas annually, allowing American employers to hire highly skilled workers with specialty training. The program permits another 20,000 visas for workers with advanced degrees for a three-to-six-year period. Fees for the two categories of visas were between $2,000 and $5,000 earlier.

Trump’s proposed regulation was struck down by a California court in September, blocking the $100,000 fee tag. India has been the largest beneficiary of the H-1B visas program for many years.

With the U.S. narrowing the options for skilled Indian workers, the Indian government could look at asking American companies to follow the examples of Microsoft and Adobe and set up Global Capability Centers in India. These centers are offshore units set up by companies to deliver services for their parent organizations.

India presently has more than 2,100 centers employing 2.36 ​million people and generating nearly $100 billion in revenue. The Indian government is also looking to attract Indian workers currently employed in the U.S. to return home.

The denial of green cards under PERM is likely to figure in talks when Rubio, the U.S. secretary of state and national security adviser, arrives in India later this month. Also likely to figure in the agenda is the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026,” which authorizes Trump to sanction countries that buy oil from Russia and Iran. India is among the largest purchasers of Russian oil. Given that the U.S. itself is looking to import diesel from Russia, India is likely to seek clarification on the provisions of the Lindsay Graham Act should it import fuel from Russia.

People-to-people relations have always been the strongest anchor of India-U.S. bilateral ties. Washington’s latest move hits this anchor. Rubio and Jaishankar have a challenging agenda before them.
tag: H1-B visa; India-US Relations; Indian IT companies; Trump administration immigration policy; Trump-India relations

title: UN Refugee Agency Expresses Concerns About Malaysia’s Deportation of Asylum Seekers to Myanmar
description: The statement came as Kuala Lumpur confirmed plans to deport a further 3,500 people as part of its voluntary repatriation program with Myanmar.
text:
The United Nations refugee agency yesterday expressed its concerns over Malaysia’s return this week of nearly 1,500 asylum seekers to Myanmar, in spite of the ongoing conflict and dire humanitarian situation inside the country.

The 1,476 people were returned to Myanmar via ship on Tuesday, the first phase in the agreed “voluntary” repatriation of some 5,000 asylum seekers currently held in Malaysian immigration detention centers.

While Malaysia insists that the returns are strictly voluntary, the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) said yesterday that it was concerned about the fate of the 1,476 people, given the country’s continuing conflict and dire human rights and humanitarian situation.

Since those returned had been held in detention centers, it had “serious questions about whether decisions to return were genuinely free and informed,” UNHCR Assistant High Commissioner for Protection Edem Wosornu said in a statement. The U.N. agency has been blocked from accessing Malaysian immigration detention centers since 2019.

“We are concerned by these returns at a time when people sent back to Myanmar may face serious risks, and some within the group may be in need of international protection,” Wosornu said.

While recognizing Malaysia’s “sovereign responsibility” to manage asylum and migration issues, UNHCR urged the government “to ensure that all returns are subject to robust safeguards, including individual assessments and access to protection procedures.”

UNHCR’s statement came as Malaysia’s government confirmed that 3,524 refugees had been approved for the second phase of the “voluntary repatriation program.” Communications Minister Fahmi Fadzil said yesterday that the individuals had been identified by the Myanmar authorities, and that their names were submitted to Malaysia in a diplomatic note dated August 13. He added that Kuala Lumpur was awaiting notification from Myanmar on the date for the repatriation.

The ethnic make-up of the two groups is unclear, but Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim has justified the repatriations with reference to the recent wave of public hostility towards the large population of Rohingya Muslims in Malaysia.

Thousands of Rohingya have arrived in Malaysia since 2017, when the Myanmar military launched an ethnic cleansing campaign that pushed more than 740,000 from their homes in Rakhine State into Bangladesh. As of February, Rohingya made up 126,000 of the 193,800 asylum seekers from Myanmar registered with UNHCR in Kuala Lumpur.

A coalition of civil society groups last week raised grave concerns about the possible deportation of Rohingya Muslims to Myanmar, given the continuing conflict in Rakhine State and the likelihood that they would be subjected to mistreatment and abuse.

Among ASEAN governments, Malaysia has been among the most critical of the Myanmar military’s seizure of power in 2021, and its ruthless attempts to put down the armed uprising that followed. But the growing domestic pressure over refugees has forced Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim to adopt a more accommodating position toward Naypyidaw.

In a bid to expedite the return of refugees, Anwar is set to welcome coup leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing to Malaysia for an official visit later this month. Confirming the Myanmar leader’s visit yesterday, Communications Minister Fahmi said that Anwar would “hold discussions with Myanmar in the near future to facilitate the return of more Myanmar refugees to their country,” Bernama reported.

Given Malaysia’s previously principled position on Myanmar – to say nothing of its vocal advocacy for the Palestinian cause – rights groups have accused it of double standards.

“Malaysia has spoken forcefully about accountability, finding durable solutions, and the need to address the root causes of displacement in Myanmar,” Amnesty International Malaysia and Asylum Access Malaysia said in a statement yesterday. At the same time, it “is prepared to roll out the red carpet and host Min Aung Hlaing in Malaysia to facilitate the accelerated return of refugees.”

In response to these criticisms, Anwar has cited the need to prioritize the security and interests of Malaysia. “The issue of Myanmar refugees is not a new problem, but rather a legacy spanning decades that has placed pressure on the country in terms of security, social affairs and management,” he wrote in a Facebook post earlier this week.
tag: Anwar Ibrahim; Malaysia Rohingya refugees; Myanmar refugees in Malaysia; Rohingya refugees; UN High Commissioner for Refugees; UNHCR

title: UNDP Asia-Pacific Director Kanni Wignaraja on the Necessity of Redefining Security
channel_text: Central Asia; East Asia; Interviews; Oceania; Security; South Asia; Southeast Asia
description: “If governments are serious about security in the fullest sense, investment in development is non-negotiable.”
text:
In an age of intersectional crises, of threats that bleed across borders and between sectors, the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) believes what’s needed is a redefinition of security. In a new report, the UNDP argues that development ought to have a larger role in addressing insecurity – not as it is traditionally understood, but as it actually affects people across Asia and the Pacific.

It’s not about making a binary choice between defense and development, Kanni Wignaraja, UNDP regional director for Asia and the Pacific, told The Diplomat’s Managing Editor Catherine Putz. Instead, what’s critical is getting the balance right, investing in development and prevention, and leveraging development to enhance security.

In pursuit of this, the UNDP proposes in its report a framework of “development circuit breakers” addressing economic insecurity, weak institutions, digital disruption and climate-health pressures that interact and reinforce each other.

“Trust is the one switch that allows all four circuit breakers to work. Each switch depends on trust: between people and institutions, and among the institutions responsible for different parts of the system,” Wignaraja said.

In the following interview, Wignaraja expands on the structural vulnerabilities that define the modern security landscape, puts defense spending trends in context, and urges regional governments to shift their mindset from managing individual crises to managing shared risks.

Kanni Wignaraja, UNDP regional director for Asia and the Pacific.

What structural vulnerabilities define the modern security landscape across Asia and the Pacific? How is the current reality different from previous periods, what’s changed?

A lot has changed in the way we see and feel vulnerability and insecurity today across the region and the world.

Previously, maybe there were more episodic periods of intense pain, wars, for example, but more contained. Now I feel it’s almost like having chronic pain. It’s all of the time and in so many more places. And that is a very different scenario of insecurity and feeling unsafe.

Countries face overlapping shocks, often before they have recovered from the last. The old crisis-recovery-rebuilding cycle is breaking down, putting hard-won development gains repeatedly at risk.

The nature of the threats has changed too: many are not contained within borders. Climate shocks, pandemics, cybercrime, disinformation, supply-chain disruptions and water insecurity move across countries and systems. The scale is enormous. Online criminal economies are estimated at $1.03 trillion annually, with $114.1 billion in losses to cybercrime victims in 2025.

There is also an exponential factor, as these risks now travel faster, connect more quickly and spread like wildfires. Economic insecurity can erode trust; climate shocks destroy livelihoods and strain public finances; weak institutions create space for illicit economies. Sri Lanka illustrates the connections, amid its economic crisis, poverty rose from 11 percent in 2019 to more than 25 percent in 2023, alongside wider social and political unrest. Myanmar shows what can happen when several pressures converge and collide. Conflict, economic decline, poverty, weak governance and criminal economies increasingly reinforce one another. These cannot be neatly separated into security problems on the one hand and development problems on the other.

Our response systems were built for episodic emergencies. They now have to manage chronic, connected insecurity.

Defense spending is soaring across the world, including in Asia, while development budgets have been trimmed down, in some cases dramatically. Do these trends reflect – or do they ignore – the actual threats communities across Asia and the Pacific face?

Today recorded military budgets are close to US$3 trillion. At the same time official development assistance (ODA) has fallen to $175 billion. This is just 6 cents to the dollar if we compare the ratio between the two.

We are not arguing to choose between defense and development but getting the balance of investment right. And to optimize security spending that aligns with development outcomes. The questions is how to use both military and development budgets to invest in common outcomes. That’s the win-win. And how do you leverage one to get more of the other?

Military, police and intelligence institutions remain essential. And their budgets can also be a frontline to ensure dual outcomes that ensure national and people’s safety and well-being.

Investments in technology that enhances wellbeing with protection, early warning and preparedness systems, vaccine production and access, AI integrity and strong rule of law and justice institutions prevent risks from becoming crises.

Wherever the money comes from, we need to invest much more deliberately in prevention, and for the longer term. Each dollar invested in prevention can mean up to $103 in avoided conflict and crisis costs. For example, in the Philippines anticipatory systems can reach 125,000 vulnerable people three days before a Category 4 or 5 typhoon, before assets and savings are lost.

Some of the new risks also require us to work differently. Cyber scams are a good example: they combine cybercrime, human trafficking, illicit finance and organized crime, and in many case promote cross border conflict. No single institution can make a dent in this.

Ultimately, it is about getting a better security return from the investments we make. And where together, one-plus-one can be way beyond two. The opportunity is to find these investments that strengthen both.

What is meant by “the securitization of development” and why is it important to avoid securitizing development as you encourage governments to rethink the connections between development and security?

The risk is that development could come to be seen primarily through a security lens. Development through the lens of human wellbeing must remain an objective in its own right. That is reducing poverty, eliminating major diseases, a full education and decent jobs, affordable energy, water and food for all, protecting rights and enabling people to live with dignity.

The report argues that sustaining security – which is about a safer present and future for all not just a few – cannot be achieved without development defined as improved human wellbeing for all. Investing in people, institutions and resilience is not separate from security but is one of the most effective ways to achieve it. That is different from turning development into a security instrument. Development and security are mutually reinforcing.

Incentives matter. Development should be about enabling people to live free from fear, free from want and in dignity, expanding people’s capabilities, strengthening rights, improving access to services and creating opportunities.

This is why the report places such emphasis on people-centered security. Individuals and communities should be at the heart of both development policy and security decisions. These are not alternative or conflicting choices. Security seen through this lens is about whether people can feel safe in their homes, protect their livelihoods, access justice and basic services, and live without fear. That is very much the human security tradition that UNDP has championed since the early 1990s.

The central message is that if governments are serious about security in the fullest sense, investment in development is non-negotiable. Effective governance, economic opportunity, social protection, digital resilience, climate adaptation and access to justice are not substitutes for security; they are among its most important foundations.

One section of the report states that “Current responses generate the crises they were meant to prevent,” in reference to what’s termed “the response and reactive trap.” Why is it so difficult for regional governments to invest in prevention? How can governments break out of this particular trap?

The fundamental problem with prevention is that when it works, it is often invisible. Political and budget cycles reward visible results, while the return on prevention is often a crisis that did not occur. This makes it easier to finance response and reconstruction than investments that could have reduced the losses in the first place.

We have to make prevention politically meaningful, economically visible and financially viable. That means translating risks into investments with clearer costs, returns and avoided losses. We need to move from paying for disasters to investing in resilience before they happen.

The shift is from managing each emergency to managing compounding risks over time. Countries need the capacity to anticipate and absorb shocks, protect development gains and recover faster, rather than rebuilding over the same vulnerabilities after every crisis.

The public budget leads the way. Finance ministries, local governments and financing institutions increasingly shape resilience through decisions on public finance, regulation and development planning. Prevention needs to become a criterion for allocating public resources, as we are already beginning to see across the region.

A better integrated financing architecture is central to breaking the reactive cycle. UNDP’s Integrated National Financing Frameworks (INFFs) which are being implemented in over 90 countries show how countries can align public and private finance around interconnected risks, making prevention economically visible and investable. Mongolia’s green energy transition where UNDP is supporting implementation of the INFF, illustrates this: a single integrated financing pathway strengthened climate resilience, energy security and economic stability at once.

We need to change the economics and politics of prevention. Making risks, avoided losses and returns more visible makes prevention easier to justify politically and more investable financially. Security is not only about our capacity to respond when something goes wrong, but our capacity to stop disruption from becoming an explosive crisis. Bangladesh and Nepal are recent examples of doing so.

One of the report’s key messages frames governance and institutional legitimacy, digital system integrity, economic security, and climate-health resilience as integrated “circuit breakers.” Can you briefly describe how these are intertwined and why they can’t necessarily be separated?

For too long, I think we’ve run responses, even analytically, looking at some of the big issues, the big disruptors of our times as separate systems. Think of it as a building. If an electrical fire starts in one place, you need to stop it from spreading and burning down the whole house. That is the purpose of the circuit breakers.

The four circuit breakers presented in the report are distinct, but the risks they address do not operate separately. The Big Four address economic insecurity, weak institutions, digital disruption and climate-health pressures that increasingly interact and reinforce each other. The most volatile risks that can set the place on fire often lie in the connections between them.

A shock in one area can quickly travel through the whole system. Climate shocks can undermine economic security; economic insecurity can erode trust; weak governance can enable criminal networks and disinformation; digital harms can deepen social divisions. That is how one vulnerability can become a much wider crisis.

Trust is the one switch that allows all four circuit breakers to work. Each switch depends on trust: between people and institutions, and among the institutions responsible for different parts of the system.

Trusted institutions can avoid or reduce the tensions through which risks escalate. In Pakistan, virtual courts and community access points have improved perceptions of police and justice institutions, while in Bangladesh, village courts help resolve everyday disputes before they grow. These examples show how strengthening trust at the community level reinforces all four circuit breakers.

The same on the digital and this AI spurt. How do we make sure that something like AI does not undermine trust that has been built over time, but it is used as an extender or accelerator on the positive side.

It is about managing these four circuit breakers, but in one system.

The report’s central message is that new approaches to “anticipating, preventing and managing both internal and transboundary challenges” are needed. Can you summarize some of those new approaches?

We need to move from managing individual crises to managing shared risks. Cybercrime does not recognize borders. Neither do climate risks, human trafficking, illicit financial flows or many of the other pressures we face today. No country or institution can address these challenges alone.

It requires a level of multi-country, regional and global cooperation that we have not seen before. And that, I think, is where institutions like the United Nations are so key.

That means cooperation itself becomes a form of prevention. But cooperation works when countries see it in their own interest. Shared interest and self-interest are not contradictory. They can be mutually reinforcing. That requires trust, particularly when countries are being asked to share information, coordinate responses or make decisions whose benefits extend across borders. Subregional cooperation mechanisms, such as ASEAN and the Mekong River Commission, show how countries can move beyond purely national responses and ask: how can we collectively address shared risks?

Institutions of development and security need to work differently together, starting with where outcomes align. The goal is not to expand everyone’s mandate, but to build a shared understanding of risk and clearer responsibilities for managing it in the collective interest.

Ultimately, we need to move to strengthen these connected systems. Success is not only how well we will respond to the next crisis, but how well we prevent a shock from becoming one.

title: Unpacking Indonesia With Marcus Tantau
description: The country is currently beset by wildfires, political ructions, and intensifying economic troubles.
text:
Marcus Tantau is a senior associate at Templeton Research with a focus on Indonesia, which is beset by El Nino-fueled wildfires, political ructions amid a cabinet reshuffle, and confusing signals over the economy.

This month’s reshuffle was the biggest since President Prabowo Subianto took power two years ago and Tantau says the Indonesian leader is clearly focused on shoring-up support ahead the next election, which is not due until 2029.

The reshuffle also sidelined supporters of former president Joko Widodo, who helped Prabowo win the vote in 2024. It came amid intense speculation regarding the state of the country’s finances and its efforts to combat the wildfires, which politicians are attempting to justify.

But arguments that food security and rice production justify the burning-off and clearing of land remain out of step with the region, where climate change and this year’s El Nino weather phenomena are taking a heavy toll.

“The mood towards Prabowo isn’t that great,” Tantau said. “It’s all these issues, around job security. The rupiah has declined significantly since Prabowo came to power. It’s all of these issues that are linked to one another.

“But I think Prabowo is mostly focused on improving or consolidating his political hold on Indonesia. And we saw that recently with the cabinet shuffle where he was, for all intents and purposes, sidelining Joko appointees.”

Tantau also publishes the Substack newsletter “Five Things You Should Know About Indonesia.”

title: Urban Rail in Southeast Asia Is Booming
description: Due to rapid economic growth and Chinese knowhow, public transit in the region's cities is entering something of a golden age.
text:
The last few years have seen a rapid expansion of urban rail systems throughout Southeast Asia, with major new lines going into operation in Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, Vietnam, and the Philippines, and more on the way. From 2015 to 2026, well over 400 kilometers of new track and extensions were completed across Bangkok, Kuala Lumpur, Jakarta, Manila, Hanoi, and Ho Chi Minh City. Between now and 2032, at least 200 kilometers are in an advanced stage of planning or already well into construction.

In addition to that, Chinese-backed high-speed rail lines are already operating in Indonesia and Laos, with construction on additional lines in Thailand and Malaysia well underway. For rail enthusiasts and fans of public transit generally, the region is going through something of a golden era. And that’s not even counting Singapore, which has an extremely comprehensive transit system spanning the entire island.

In 2015, Bangkok was operating its famous Skytrain, a single subway line and a rail link. The Philippines had an MRT that was over a decade old and two light rail lines, one of which was built in the 1980s. Kuala Lumpur had an airport link and commuter system, along with three rapid rail lines. In the decade since, tens of billions of dollars have poured into new and expanded lines all across the region, boosting capacity by hundreds of millions of passengers.

Between 2016 and 2023, Bangkok opened the Purple, Yellow, and Pink lines at a combined cost of around $5 billion. The Orange line, with a price tag in excess of $4 billion, is expected to become operational in phases between 2028 and 2030. The Skytrain was extended, a commuter line was added, and extensions to the Purple line are underway. Ridership across the system increased from 359 million in 2017 to 520 million last year.

Malaysia inaugurated its Shah Alam Line earlier this year, a project that cost approximately $5 billion, including five new stations still under construction. The Putrajaya line, which fully opened in 2023, cost around $7 billion and added over 50 kilometers of track. Kuala Lumpur and the surrounding area now have six rapid rail lines, not including commuter rail or bus, with total ridership of 330 million in 2025. Malaysia is also one of the few countries in the region that is starting to build urban rail in cities outside of the capital.

Manila has been operating at least one light rail service since 1984. The MRT was fully opened in 2000 and a second LRT in 2003. Then very little progress was made, despite the fact that the system carried over 411 million passengers in 2014. That will change soon, as a new MRT line is nearing completion and should open next year. A $7 billion subway project is also underway, which is expected to be operational in the next few years, along with the 147-kilometer North-South Commuter Rail valued at around $14 billion.

Indonesia and Vietnam are the newest entrants to the region’s modern urban rail club. Until recently, commuters in Jakarta had to make do with an aging commuter rail system that traces its roots to the colonial era. In 2019, the Jakarta MRT was opened, followed by a pair of light rail systems. The total cost was around $4 billion, and the system carried over 81 million passengers in 2025. Expansion plans, particularly for the MRT, are in various stages of development and construction.

Vietnam opened its first metro line in Hanoi in 2021, and in Ho Chi Minh City in 2024. A second Hanoi metro line is partially operational, with full operations expected in 2027. More lines are planned. Progress on Vietnam’s metro lines has been very slow, however, in large part because of cumbersome land acquisition. If that bottleneck can be solved, we should expect the pace and scale of urban transit in Vietnam’s major cities to pick up in the years ahead.

It’s clear that urban rail in the region is experiencing a huge resurgence. But what is driving this trend? One obvious factor is economic growth. Manila, Bangkok, and Kuala Lumpur invested in their metro systems in the late 1990s, but momentum slowed with the onset of the Asian Financial Crisis. It took over a decade to reach a point where they were comfortable investing in urban rail again and as their economic resources increase, more of those resources are being directed to building out urban infrastructure.

We should also consider the role of China. It would be wrong to say that China is driving all of this. We see a range of financing and development arrangements across these projects, including a major role for Japanese development finance, multilateral lenders like the Asian Development Bank, European firms and even some domestic players.

But Chinese capital and technology are certainly an important part of the story. It gives rapidly growing economies in the region more options as they look to upgrade and expand their urban transit systems, and it may encourage competitors to more aggressively pursue projects for fear of losing market share. We can debate the mechanism, but the result is clear: urban transit in Southeast Asia is absolutely booming, and looks set to keep growing in the years ahead.

title: US Allied Shipbuilding Gains Momentum, But Ambitions May Collide
description: Japan, South Korea, and the U.S. appear to have given little thought to which country should build what, or who controls the key technologies that every shipyard depends on.
text:
Allied efforts to revive shipbuilding are picking up steam, but they are moving along separate tracks. On October 2, Nikkei Asia reported that Japan’s government fund for revitalizing the industry has begun to spur a wave of private investment. Among the projects, Hakodate Dock, which repairs vessels for the Maritime Self-Defense Force, plans to bring back a dock that has sat out of commission since an earthquake in 1993. The fund, launched in fiscal year 2025, has already approved eight projects and will provide up to 311 billion yen ($1.97 billion) through 2034, with total spending expected to reach around 900 billion yen ($5.69 billion) once private investment is included. South Korea, meanwhile, has taken a more direct route, with its companies pouring money into U.S. shipyards.

Both efforts come as the U.S. leans on its allies to counter China’s dominance in commercial shipbuilding and to ease the delays and backlogs plaguing the U.S. Navy. Yet for all this momentum, Japan, South Korea, and the U.S. appear to have given little thought to which country should build what, or who controls the key technologies that every shipyard depends on.

Japan’s ambitions to revive its shipbuilding industry come amid a long-running erosion of its share of the global market. Japan was once the largest shipbuilder in the world, but was overtaken by South Korea around 2000 and by China soon after, and now ranks third. This is largely due to expansive Chinese investments and policies, alongside South Korea’s specialization in key vessel classes such as LNG carriers. In response, Tokyo has renewed its attention and investment in the sector, designating it one of 17 strategic industries and partnering with industry on roughly 1 trillion yen ($6.33 billion) in public and private investment.

However, chronic issues plague the industry and any efforts on Tokyo’s part to alleviate them. Labor remains a major constraint, shipyards are booked three to four years in advance, and Japan won just 5 percent of new orders in 2025. Yet despite these constraints, Japan offers many benefits for the U.S. In 2025, Mitsubishi Heavy Industries completed a major overhaul of a U.S. Navy vessel in Yokohama, and last October the two countries signed a memorandum of cooperation to expand shipbuilding ties.

South Korea occupies a stronger position as the world’s second-largest shipbuilder, but its position largely rests on specialization in LNG carriers, an expensive and technologically advanced vessel class. South Korean shipbuilders now hold roughly 70 percent of the global LNG carrier market. Additionally, South Korean shipyards have mastered production methods that allow them to compete on quality, while Chinese yards leverage mass and dominance in less complex classes, like dry bulk carriers.

South Korean companies, backed by government financing, have also made active efforts to invest in American shipyards, such as Hanwha’s purchase of Philly Shipyard and its pledge to invest $5 billion there. All of this is part of a $150 billion package that South Korea has touted as “Make American Shipbuilding Great Again.” Although it occupies a stronger position in the global market, South Korea faces similar labor constraints to Japan, as well as the domineering presence of Chinese shipyards, which are increasingly competing for LNG orders as well.

The motivations behind these investments and cooperation agreements are sound. The reliance on Chinese shipbuilding prowess poses significant risks, particularly in light of the woeful state of U.S. commercial shipbuilding, which accounts for only 0.1 percent of the global market. However, these various policies and schemes are siloed off. Even the U.S. Maritime Action Plan largely treats allies as investors in American shipyards rather than as partners with their own strengths. Without a broader coordinating scheme, however rough, there will be major overlap and competition between allies and partners, causing major inefficiencies.

This cooperation need not be perfectly specialized. It is highly unrealistic that South Korean shipyards would be willing to concede their advanced production methods to Japanese yards and risk losing market share. Yet, at the same time, Japan is looking to rejoin the LNG carrier market, a class it hasn’t built since 2019. Imabari Shipbuilding, Kawasaki Heavy Industries, and Namura Shipbuilding aim to resume construction around 2035, possibly with South Korean technology. Some level of redundancy and overlap will occur and may even be necessary, but pouring significant funds into a capability that depends on what another partner already has may prove foolhardy.

Instead, some of these investments could be partially diverted toward the key technologies of the future. Japan has paid the price for failing to do so before, when its specialization in Moss-type LNG carriers allowed South Korea to eclipse it once the market shifted to newer membrane-type designs. Additionally, many subcomponents can serve as dangerous chokepoints. For example, the French firm GTT dominates the membrane containment technology used in most LNG carriers. While the risks are reduced because it is a French company, if a firm like it were held by an adversary like China, the potential for weaponization would be profound. China’s willingness to weaponize chokepoints has been felt most acutely with rare earths. And in at least one case, a key maritime technology is already under Chinese control. WinGD, one of the largest designers of marine engines, is a nominally Swiss company wholly owned by China State Shipbuilding Corporation, and its engines are the most popular choice for LNG carriers currently on order.

The single biggest constraint to any such development will be the massive political capital required to create a framework and get all participants to agree. Yet this need not be perfect, as a framework that eliminates even some redundancies can redirect funds that would otherwise go to waste. It is important to caveat that Japan and South Korea remain commercial competitors, and no framework will change that.

Some production of the same vessel classes in both countries will still be useful, since no ally should rely on a single partner for critical ships. But the best value in industrial policy, especially among allies and partners, lies in recognizing their differences and the areas each should focus on. This is especially true for future technologies, such as ammonia-fueled ships, where South Korean and Chinese yards are already competing for early orders. If allies do not coordinate now, the same overlap seen in LNG carriers is likely to repeat itself in the next generation of ships.

title: US Drops Sanctions on Daughter of Prominent Myanmar Businessman Thein Win Zaw
description: Is Theint Win Htet's removal from the Treasury Department's blacklist a sign of a looming rapprochement between Washington and Naypyidaw?
text:
The U.S. government has lifted sanctions on the daughter of a Myanmar businessman accused of supporting the country’s military, after she filed two lawsuits seeking her removal from the Treasury Department’s Specially Designated Nationals List (SDN List).

According to a Reuters report, Theint Win Htet’s name was removed from the website of the Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) on Friday. OFAC confirmed the deletion of her name from the SDN List in a statement the following day.

Theint Win Htet was added to the SDN List in January 2024 alongside her father Thein Win Zaw and his Shwe Byain Phyu Group of Companies. The Treasury Department said at the time that the company “has developed a historic relationship with Burma’s military to import and distribute petroleum,” including on behalf of Myanma Economic Holdings Public Company Limited (MEHL), a sanctioned military-linked conglomerate with tentacles in numerous sectors of Myanmar’s economy.

The listing announcement also stated that Thein Win Zaw has “provided fuel to Burma’s navy while using his companies to import petroleum and share profits with MEHL” and that he and his family members “own at least 20 companies in various sectors of the Burmese economy and are also closely associated with the regime.”

The following May, Theint Win Htet filed a lawsuit seeking her removal from the SDN List, claiming that President Joe Biden exceeded his authority under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act by listing the adult children of a designated individual. She also said that it had breached due process by not permitting her to contest her inclusion on the SDN List. Her case was dismissed in February 2025.

Theint Win Htet then filed a new complaint in July of this year, arguing that she has no active role in her father’s business affairs and that the sanctions had interrupted her studies in the United States. In the complaint, Reuters reported, Thein Win Htet stated that her “U.S. credit cards have been blocked, her foreign bank accounts have been restricted, closed, or refused, and she has been ​unable to complete her university studies.”

Her removal from the SDN List comes after the news agency reported that the U.S. had engaged in direct talks with the military-backed government for the first time since the February 2021 coup. According to the report, U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for Intelligence and Research Michael Vance “joined talks” with coup leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing in Naypyidaw on September 15-16. Numerous sources told Reuters that the talks were aimed at securing the release of detained American businessman Adam Castillo, but “also provided an opening for further engagement.”

Whether the removal of Theint Win Htet’s name is related to a possible broader diplomatic thaw remains unclear. A State Department spokesperson contacted by Reuters did not offer much explanation for the move, simply saying that the decision “reflects the administration’s determination that this designation no longer effectively supports U.S. policy objectives related to Burma.”

This is also not the first time since the coup that the name of a Myanmar individual or entity has been scrubbed from the SDN List. In July 2025, the U.S. government lifted sanctions on three Myanmar companies and a number of individuals linked to them, including KT Services & Logistics and its founder, Jonathan Myo Kyaw Thaung, who were sanctioned in 2022 for leasing Yangon’s port from MEHL. Also included on the list was Thein Win Htet’s mother Tin Latt Min.

As with last week’s announcement, OFAC did not offer a reason for the deletions, although The Irrawaddy noted that the move came after Min Aung Hlaing praised President Donald Trump in a letter responding to his threat of tariffs, in which he also commended him for shutting down U.S.-funded media outlets covering the country’s conflict. Trump administration officials said that there was “no connection between these decisions and the letter.”

Getting one’s name off the SDN List is hard even at the best of times, usually requiring the enlistment of one of a handful of specialist white shoe law firms. (Theint Win Htet was represented by Erich Ferrari, a prominent Washington-based lawyer who specializes in “economic sanctions, export controls, regulatory licensing, federal investigations, and prosecutions.”)

While the addition or removal of names from the SDN List is guided in part by legal criteria, OFAC’s decisions are often influenced by the broader policymaking climate. It is therefore plausible that a turn toward engagement with Myanmar would be accompanied by a loosening of U.S. sanctions on the country.

Whether or not this is the case here, any further shortening of the SDN List would suggest that the first steps toward engagement are evolving into a more substantial rapprochement.
