title: US Economic Diplomacy With Allies Becomes an Election Showcase for Trump
description: Investment pledges by Japan and South Korea make tempting achievements for Trump to hold up ahead of the voting.
text:
On September 28, Trump invited Iowa Representative Ashley Hinson, the Republican running for an open Senate seat, to the Oval Office to announce a new $15 billion steel plant in her home state, which is being built by the local subsidiary of an Indian conglomerate. Two days later, with Alaska Senator Dan Sullivan standing beside him, Trump announced roughly $54 billion in prospective South Korean investment in the Alaska LNG pipeline.

Notably, both announcements came a little over a month before the midterm elections. The Associated Press noted that it was “the second time in three days” Trump had paired a major investment announcement with a Republican Senate candidate in a race that had become unexpectedly competitive.

Seoul described the Alaska announcement quite differently. South Korean Industry Minister Kim Jung-kwan said it went “far beyond what was agreed,” while his ministry said it had not decided whether to invest or how much. The U.S. Commerce Department’s fact sheet was more conditional: the two sides had agreed to begin work on Alaska LNG, subject to commercial reasonableness and domestic legal requirements.

Similarly, Washington also presented a roughly $22 billion Texas project and a nuclear framework valued at up to $120 billion. Again, Seoul has indicated a more cautious approach to those investments, with individual reactor projects still under review. In other words, the headline figures may not all materialize.

The election wasn’t the driving force behind these projects or negotiations, which have been in the works for nearly a year. But the announcements have clear electoral value. On September 30, Trump said he had done “a very bad job of explaining how good the country is doing.” The Iowa and Alaska events show how investment announcements involving U.S. partners are being caught up in Trump’s pre-election economic messaging.

The approaching elections – and polling suggesting that a number of Republican seats in Congress are at risk – increases the political value of presenting long-term allied investment plans as immediate economic wins. Both South Korea and Japan had agreed to invest hundreds of billions of dollars in the United States as part of overall economic deals reached in 2025 with the Trump administration. The upcoming election may be impacting the announcement of specific projects under those investment pledges – although it’s hard to establish the connection definitively. It’s also possible that Japan and South Korea could use Trump’s sense of urgency over specific projects to leverage better terms.

The structure of the deals is responsible for some of the confusion. The Korean and Japanese “agreements” are actually administrative arrangements that create no legally binding obligations. Under the standard timetable, actual funding is not required until at least 45 business days after an ally is notified that the president has selected a project. South Korea’s domestic law adds another layer: investments are, in principle, reviewed for commercial reasonableness and other considerations, examined by a government committee, and reported to relevant National Assembly committees before Seoul consults Washington. In other words, there’s a month-plus gap between any political announcement and the point at which money actually changes hands.

Before the Alaska announcement, Washington was pressing for faster progress, while Seoul emphasized commercial rationality. The planned announcement had already been postponed while such differences remained unresolved. The election may have given Seoul temporary bargaining room, even as Washington remained the much stronger party. When one side values speed more than the other, delay itself can become bargaining leverage.

Japan offers an important comparison because its investments have been moving more quickly. On February 17, Trump announced the first $36 billion of Japan’s $550 billion investment pledge. Tokyo’s first financing agreement came about 10 weeks later, on May 1, and provided roughly $2.2 billion for that initial batch of projects. By September, Japan had announced two project rounds totaling about $109 billion.

The gap between announcement and financing is relatively baked in. In that sense, the midterms may be amplifying an existing practice rather than creating a new one.

When evaluating major investment announcements, it’s important to look beyond the topline figure to other data points: what the partner government has actually approved, when funding will actually arrive, and which political or diplomatic events might be impacting the timing.

A new Japanese investment package before November 3 would strengthen the case that the U.S. election calendar is influencing announcement timing. If the next investment announcement isn’t made until the November 18-19 APEC leaders’ meeting in Shenzhen, however, it would mean the diplomatic calendar is more influential. These explanations are not mutually exclusive: an announcement can advance negotiations abroad while producing political value at home.

The same logic applies to allied behavior. Resistance, delay, or demands for safeguards by Japan and South Korea may suggest the allies have greater bargaining room, but would not by themselves prove that electoral pressure caused a concession from the Trump administration. Remember, these investment pledges are around a year old; the process has been moving slowly from the start.

The midterms are not overhauling U.S. economic policy toward Seoul and Tokyo, but they could make the Trump administration keen to announce progress early – even before funding actually comes through.
tag: Japanese investment in the U.S.; South Korean investment in the US; U.S. 2026 elections; U.S.-Japan trade talks; U.S.-South Korea trade negotiations

title: US Has Opened Direct Talks With Myanmar Government, Report Claims
description: The outreach, which marks a significant shift in U.S. policy, is aimed at curbing online scamming operations and gaining access to the country's rare earth deposits.
text:
Yesterday, Reuters published a report stating that the Trump administration has begun direct talks with Myanmar’s military-installed government for the first time since the 2021 coup, marking a significant change in U.S. policy toward the country.

According to the report, which was authored by Reuters’ Simon Lewis and cited seven current and former U.S. officials and others familiar with the ‌policy shift, this engagement has so far focused on discreet issues, such as efforts to shut down the online scam centers, but “could lead to broader engagement, including on Myanmar’s rare-earth mineral deposits.”

The report claimed that U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for Intelligence and Research Michael Vance “joined talks” with coup leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing in Naypyidaw on September 15-16. The meeting was nominally aimed at securing the release of detained American businessman Adam Castillo, but also provided an opening for further engagement, four of the sources told Reuters.

Whether or not it is sustained, the engagement marks an important shift in U.S. policy towards Myanmar. When Min Aung Hlaing seized power in a coup in 2021, terminating a decade of political and economic reforms, the U.S. government quickly reimposed economic sanctions on senior generals and businesses linked to the military. The following year, it downgraded its diplomatic representation in the country, reverting to the policy that pertained between 1987 and 2012, when the U.S. was represented by a chief of mission rather than a fully credentialed ambassador.

The Reuters report also identified how Myanmar’s new military government used the detention of Castillo, a former head of the American Chamber of Commerce in Myanmar who was arrested at Yangon airport in June on opaque charges, in order to advance diplomatic re-engagement with Washington.

The September meeting between Vance and Min Aung Hlaing was preceded by back-channel negotiations between U.S. and Myanmar officials aimed at securing Castillo’s release. During these talks, Reuters reported, Myanmar “only asked for an official engagement at the right level with the U.S. government” in return.

The report makes clear that these were not the first engagements between U.S. and Myanmar officials. In June, the two sides held meetings in Tokyo; one source cited by the news agency said that in addition to Vance, “officials from the Treasury Department, which oversees sanctions, the Department of Homeland Security, and the Pentagon took part.” Josh Kurlantzick of the Council on Foreign Relations (CFR) wrote yesterday that several sources had also told him that prior to Vance’s visit to Naypyidaw, “U.S. officials had been secretly meeting with officials from Myanmar in Japan.”

The purpose of this engagement, the Reuters report states, was to combat the online scamming operations that have become deeply rooted in Myanmar since the coup, and which have defrauded Americans of billions of dollars. It added that “U.S. officials also discussed access to Myanmar’s massive ​deposits of heavy rare earths,” most of which are located in areas of northern Myanmar currently under the control of rebel forces including the Kachin Independence Army (KIA).

Myanmar’s rare earth deposits have gradually become something of an idée fixe for certain elements of the Trump administration, as it seeks to reduce its heavy reliance on China, which controls a large part of the world’s supply of these critical minerals.

In July 2025, Reuters reported that administration officials had “heard competing proposals” for changes to U.S. policy aimed at gaining access to the rare earth deposits in Kachin State. “Among the proposals,” it reported, “are one advocating talks with Myanmar’s ruling junta to get a peace deal with the Kachin Independence Army rebels and another calling for the U.S. to instead work directly with the KIA without engaging the junta.”

Among those advancing these proposals was none other than Adam Castillo, who was present during a July 17 meeting at Vice President J.D. Vance’s office in Washington.

It is hard to know how far things will proceed from here. The Reuters report makes clear that Vance “has also met in person and virtually with the democratic opposition and ethnic armed groups fighting the military,” and the State Department told the news agency that its engagement with the Min Aung Hlaing administration “does not diminish its relationships with other groups.”

Any step toward further re-engagement with Naypyidaw, let alone a dropping of U.S. sanctions against Min Aung Hlaing and other senior officials, is likely to prompt strong criticism. While the new quasi-civilian government has attempted to project an image of control and normalcy, the political situation in the country remains febrile. The post-coup civil war, which continues despite the inauguration of the new government, has now killed more than 100,000 people and displaced 3.8 million more. In a report released yesterday, the U.N. Development Programme stated that more than two in three people in Myanmar are now in “multidimensional poverty” or are at risk of falling into it, due to the “simultaneous collapse” of the healthcare and education systems, and the atrophying of the economy.

Since taking office as president in April, Min Aung Hlaing has embarked on a diplomatic charm offensive aimed at consolidating key partnerships and normalizing Naypyidaw’s relationship with key partners, including the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN). Indeed, the former general has just departed from Malaysia, where, in another notable policy reversal, he was accorded full state honors by Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim. He has also visited Vietnam, Cambodia, Laos, and Thailand in recent months, in pursuit of Myanmar’s full reintegration into the 11-nation bloc.

Re-engagement with the U.S., even to a limited degree, would be another diplomatic victory for Min Aung Hlaing. Whether this would end up yielding benefits for the U.S., however, remains unclear. In his article for CFR, Kurlantzick argued that the U.S. succesfully gaining access to Myanmar’s rare earths “is hard to imagine,” given their proximity to the Chinese border and their location in regions “where Beijing wields dominant influence.”

Beyond this, Kurlantzick argued, “Engaging with the regime now will simply show powerful autocrats that their collaboration works, and democracies accede. And it will cause more misery for the citizens of one of the most benighted places in the world.”

title: US Marine’s Arrest for Murder Tests Okinawa’s New Governor
description: An alleged killing days after Koja Genta took office threatens Tokyo’s hopes for closer cooperation with Okinawa on its expanding southwestern defense posture.
text:
Okinawa’s new governor had barely begun his effort to improve relations with Tokyo when an alleged killing involving a U.S. Marine confronted him with the prefecture’s most persistent political dilemma: how to support national defense while protecting residents who bear a disproportionate share of its costs.

Okinawa Prefectural Police arrested Lance Corporal Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, stationed at Marine Corps Air Station Futenma, early on October 4. He is suspected of killing Yagi Anna, a 39-year-old Naha resident, at a hotel and stealing her belongings. Ballard denies the allegations. The Marine Corps has pledged cooperation with Japanese investigators.

The case immediately drew protests from both national and prefectural authorities. Foreign Minister Motegi Toshimitsu summoned U.S. Ambassador George Glass, while Defense Minister Koizumi Shinjiro summoned U.S. Forces Japan commander Lieutenant General Stephen Jost.

On October 5, before delivering her policy speech to the Diet, Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae condemned the incident and demanded full investigative cooperation, tighter discipline, and effective measures to prevent further crimes.

For Governor Koja Genta, who took office on September 30, the timing was especially difficult.

His September 13 election ended 12 years of prefectural leadership opposed to relocating Futenma to Henoko in northern Okinawa. Koja has sought a more cooperative relationship with Tokyo. Effective October 1, he replaced the prefectural division handling opposition to the Henoko project with an office focused on accelerating the return of U.S. military land.

But his cooperation was never unconditional. Koja has acknowledged the need for defense capabilities while demanding advance explanations and local understanding.

In a protest letter read aloud to Lieutenant General Benjamin Watson, commander of III Marine Expeditionary Force, and U.S. Consul General Andrew Ou on October 5, Koja said that the recurrence of such a serious crime “leads us to conclude that U.S. military efforts regarding discipline and human rights education are completely ineffective.” He demanded stronger preventive measures and a review of the Japan-U.S. Status of Forces Agreement, or SOFA.

Watson expressed condolences and pledged continued cooperation with the investigation, saying the U.S. military was committed to being “good neighbors” and earning the trust of the Okinawan people.

That exchange reflects a longstanding problem.

Okinawa hosts approximately 70 percent of Japan’s nationwide area of facilities reserved exclusively for U.S. military use. Residents thus experience the alliance through noise, accidents, environmental concerns, and criminal cases, alongside its promised protection against external threats.

In 2025, police cleared 101 cases involving Penal Code offenses by U.S. military personnel, civilian employees, and their families, up from 73 in 2024. These figures count cases, not convictions or individual offenders, and do not establish a comparative crime rate. Nevertheless, there is good reason for scrutinizing measures introduced after earlier incidents, including restrictions on nighttime drinking and joint patrols.

Japan generally has primary jurisdiction over off-duty offenses against Japanese nationals. When American authorities already hold a suspect, however, the SOFA provides for U.S. custody until indictment. Following the 1995 rape of a schoolgirl by three U.S. servicemen, Washington agreed to give “sympathetic consideration” to Japanese requests for pre-indictment transfers in murder and rape cases.

Ballard was arrested by Japanese police and remains in Japanese custody. This is therefore not a case of Washington withholding a suspect. The broader question is whether existing arrangements under the SOFA provide sufficient accountability, information sharing, and preventive oversight.

The controversy comes as Japan’s defense buildup in its southwestern islands enters a more operational phase. Tokyo is connecting missile deployments, surveillance, transport, and logistics across Kyushu and the southwestern islands, while U.S. forces develop more dispersed operations.

Plans to store the U.S. Army’s Typhon and HIMARS systems at Kadena and deploy Marine NMESIS anti-ship missiles and MADIS air defense systems to Ishigaki during October’s Keen Sword exercise make cooperation with local authorities particularly consequential. Koja has so far withheld judgment on the storage plan, saying Tokyo has not adequately explained the reasons or its duration.

Koja’s election gave Tokyo reason to expect smoother negotiations. It did not give the Japanese government or the U.S. military a blank check. Anger over this case could make individual decisions on facilities, exercises, and base restructuring politically harder, even without reversing Japan’s overall defense policy.

For Koja, the test is whether cooperation with Tokyo and Washington can produce tangible protection for Okinawans. For the alliance, the stakes are broader: deterrence in Japan’s southwest depends not only on missiles, bases, and military units, but also on the trust of the communities expected to host them.
tag: Futenma Air Station; Futenma relocation plan; Koja Genta; U.S. military in Okinawa; U.S. soldiers crime; U.S.-Japan Alliance

title: Uzbekistan Wants Out of the Iran-US Social Media War
channel_text: Blog; Central Asia; Crossroads Asia; Diplomacy
description: Tashkent summoned the Iranian ambassador to lodge a protest regarding social media posts by Iranian diplomatic missions.
text:
On October 23, Uzbekistan’s Foreign Ministry summoned the Iranian ambassador in Tashkent in order to hand over a note of protest related to a recent slate of social media postings made by several Iranian diplomatic missions. The posts sniped at U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, using his recent visit to Samarkand as a touchstone.

“It’s great that you’re learning history! The place where you are standing is part of the Persian civilization and architecture. The same civilization you were babbling nonsense about last week at the Acropolis!” read a since-removed post on X from the Iranian embassy in Armenia.

In early October, Rubio delivered remarks during a visit to Greece that set off a history-based social media war that has now spilled over to Uzbekistan. With the ancient Acropolis as his backdrop, he mused on the meaning of Western civilization. Early in the speech he recounted the destruction of the Acropolis in 480 BCE by a Persian army.

“The Persians plundered the temples, burned the shrines, and razed the Acropolis to the ground but when the Athenians returned, they gathered the broken remains of the old Acropolis and buried them in the hill where it had stood. And decades later, under Pericles, they raised the Parthenon,” Rubio said before jumping ahead a 25 centuries to the modern era and the American obsession with antiquity.

Later in the speech, Rubio got the point: a rhetorical attack to match the physical war ongoing between the U.S. and Iran.

“It is from the Greeks that the West inherited its sense of duty – an unbreakable loyalty to one’s code, one’s cause, one’s country… This is wholly different from what we see, even now, for example from fanatics like the radical mullahs of Iran, whose cult of death hails child suicide bombers as national heroes, and portrays martyrdom as an end to itself.”

When Rubio landed in Uzbekistan two weeks later, Iran’s keyboard warriors were ready.

“At the Acropolis, you invoked civilizations. Samarkand invites you to a deeper conversation with history, in a city whose heritage is deeply interwoven with Iranian civilization,” the Iranian Permanent Mission to the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) stated in its post, which remains available as of publication.

On October 24, the Uzbek Foreign Ministry reported that it had summoned the Iranian ambassador, Mohammad Ali Eskandari, to complain about the posts, which it said in its own social media post, “interpret the historical and cultural heritage of the city of Samarkand for unilateral political purposes.”

“During the meeting,” the ministry said, “it was noted that the heritage of Samarkand, Bukhara, Khiva, and other historical cities of Uzbekistan is an integral part of the rich and multifaceted historical and cultural development formed over many centuries.” The ministry demanded that the offending posts be taken down, and those posted the Iranian embassies in Armenia, China, and Zimbabwe have been.

“Uzbekistan values ​​relations with Iran based on mutual respect and trust,” the Foreign Ministry stated. “At the same time, it maintains its principled position against one-sided interpretation of the historical and cultural heritage of our country.”

Of note: While a post regarding Tashkent’s summoning of the Iranian ambassador remains available on Instagram as of publication, there’s no trace of an earlier post on the Foreign Ministry’s website regarding the meeting – although a relic remains on Facebook.

Screenshot, Facebook.

Without recounting the entire history of Samarkand, it’s fair to say that the city’s history and culture is multilayered, with many empires having risen and fallen across (and from within) its territory. It has existed, in some form, since the 8th century BCE. In 329 BCE, Marakanda – as it was then known – was captured by Alexander the Great. It had been one of the most important cities for the Sogdian civilization; by the time of Alexander, Sogdiana was part of the greater Achaemenid Persian Empire.

The importance of Persian civilization to Central Asia is indisputable. What Tashkent took umbrage over, however, is the operationalization of the past into a weapon (albeit an online one) in a very modern, and very difficult, conflict.

To put it bluntly: Uzbekistan does not want to be invoked in the Iran-U.S. conflict, certainly not while it has tried to deepen relations with Washington while also maintaining ties with Iran.
tag: 2026 Iran war; U.S.-Iran war; U.S.-Uzbekistan relations; Uzbekistan-Iran relations

title: Vietnam Set to Sign Free Trade Pact With European Bloc This Week
description: Hanoi also says that a reciprocal trade deal with the United States is nearing completion and should be signed soon.
text:
Vietnam is set to sign a European ‌Free Trade Association (EFTA) this week, as Hanoi closes in on a final trade agreement with the United States.

Reuters reported yesterday that the agreement with the EFTA bloc, which consists of Switzerland, Norway, Iceland, and Liechtenstein, will be signed in Hanoi on Sunday in the presence of Swiss Economy Minister Guy Parmelin, who is currently on a trip to Asia.

The talks between Vietnam and the ETFA began in 2012 and have proceeded at a steady pace since. The two sides officially concluded the negotiations in July, following a ministerial meeting in Reykjavik that involved “intensive technical talks.”

At the time, the ETFA stated that the agreement covered “trade in goods, trade in services, rules of origin, sanitary and phytosanitary measures, technical barriers to trade, investment, intellectual property rights, trade remedies, government procurement, trade and sustainable development, small and medium-sized enterprises, and cooperation and capacity building.” Bilateral trade between EFTA and Vietnam amounted to $5.4 billion in 2025, up from around $561 million a decade earlier, according to the bloc.

Hovering over the planned signing ceremony is Vietnam’s recent arrest of a Norwegian national of Vietnamese descent on terrorism-related charges. Nguyen Duc Thuan, 52, was among three activists from the pro-democracy group Viet Tan whom the Vietnamese authorities said were arrested for entering the country illegally. Rights groups, as well as Viet Tan itself, say that the three men were abducted in Cambodia, although Phnom Penh said that it had no record of the men leaving the country.

According to Reuters, Norway’s Foreign Ministry said that ‌State Secretary ⁠Astrid Bergmal, who will attend the signing ceremony, “will raise the case of the detained Norwegian citizen with the Vietnamese authorities during her visit.” The Ministry added that it was treating Thuan’s case “as a high priority” and expressed hope that it “may be resolved without unnecessary delay.”

The imminent signing of the EFTA deal comes as Vietnam and the U.S. move toward the signing of their Agreement on Reciprocal, Fair, and Balanced Trade.

Vietnam has sent its “final wording” for a trade agreement to the U.S. with hopes the deal can be quickly signed, Deputy Prime Minister Pham Gia Tuc told a business summit yesterday, according to Nikkei Asia.

Hanoi and Washington began negotiations on the trade deal in April 2025, shortly after President Donald Trump’s “liberation day” tariff announcement, when Vietnam was hit with an eye-popping 46 percent tariff. The two nations signed a framework for a trade agreement in October that lowered the tariff rate by 20 percent, but despite months of negotiations, they have yet to reach a final agreement.

The negotiations have been held up by the turbidity in U.S. trade policy. Vietnam is currently the subject of a number of Section 301 investigations that the Trump administration has been using to get around the Supreme Court ruling in February that struck down the sweeping “liberation day” tariffs.

Vietnam was among 60 nations that the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative threatened in June with tariffs of 10-12.5 percent due to their alleged failures to take action on forced labor. It is also the subject of separate Section 301 probes into alleged excess manufacturing capacity and intellectual property rights.

After meeting with Vietnamese President To Lam in New York last month, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said that the two sides had made “substantial progress” and were “very close to reaching the final outcome.”

Vietnam signed a free trade agreement with the European Union in 2020.
tag: European ‌Free Trade Association (EFTA); U.S.-Vietnam relations; U.S.-Vietnam trade

title: ‘We Have Stitched Our Hearts to Hope’: The Unseen Resistance of Afghan Women Under Taliban Rule
description: Afghan women say that they respond to Taliban oppression in vastly different ways depending on their social, cultural, and personal contexts.
text:
“Life in Afghanistan has become… exactly like a dark grave.”

These words, spoken by a woman in Sar-e Pol province of Afghanistan, are not hyperbole. They are an accurate description of daily existence in the country ranked worst in the world for women.

Since August 2021, when the Taliban regime retook power, Afghan women have been subjected to unprecedented levels of gender-based oppression that they describe as akin to imprisonment. Many recall the pride of attending school or contributing to their communities through work. That pride has been replaced by feelings of isolation and frustration as doors remain closed.

“Families are now afraid to have daughters because they see them only as a burden in the home,” said Zulaikha from Parwan, one of 165 testimonies of Afghan women recently collected by the Organization for Policy Research and Development Studies (DROPS).

In rural areas, women are completely excluded from employment and education and must rely on male relatives for any public activity. They face extreme barriers to accessing health care with a severe shortage of female health workers. In urban areas, women face morality police in all spaces, bans on makeup and mobile phones, and constant surveillance and harassment for their clothing or any “unapproved” behavior such as speaking loudly or laughing.

These are not just policy setbacks, but personal blows to women’s dignity and future. As Zulaikha explained, “If you need even the smallest thing, you must ask a man for money and then face many questions: Why do you want it? What do you need?”

Unsurprisingly, this has led to a widespread mental health and fatigue crisis. Trapped inside homes with compounding trauma and fear, several testimonials detailed severe depression, exhaustion, anxiety, and rising suicide rates, often following incidents of sexual violence.

These accounts offer a glimpse into the unprecedented horror and heartbreak Afghan women navigate. However, while the world may only see them as victims, their reality is far more complex. Despite deep frustration, fear, and grief, many Afghan women have doubled down on their efforts to lead a better life.

As Behnaz from Herat put it: “What I see from [women in Afghanistan] every day is effort, creativity, and resistance in order to carry on living.”

In urban areas, many Afghan women report focusing on home-based economic activities such as tailoring, handicrafts, and food production in order to generate income. They also use online platforms for education and work, including teaching, translation, design, social media management, and networks that provide information, resources, and emotional support.

Women in rural areas have turned to agriculture, livestock, and cooperative solutions for skill development, and also rely on family and community support.

Afghan women emphasized that they respond to Taliban oppression in vastly different ways depending on their social, cultural, and personal contexts. While many practice active defiance such as teaching secretly, for others, survival strategies may mean more pragmatic adaptations, such as economic marriage or acceptance of restrictions. Women emphasized that recognizing this spectrum of responses is essential, as it highlights individual agency and varied realities without diminishing the systemic harm Taliban policies inflict on all women and girls.

“…Everyone finds a way according to the resources available to them,” Farida from Jawzjan said.

Resistance is not successful only when there is policy change. As many women articulated, any resistance in the face of such insurmountable odds is a success.

“It is women’s resistance that has at least prevented all schools from being closed and kept some fields of work open to women, though under severe restrictions,” Zohal from Baghlan explained.

This dual reality of an unprecedented human rights catastrophe alongside an indefatigable spirit of defiance was reinforced by a survey of 500 Afghan women peacebuilders conducted by DROPS and the Georgetown Institute for Women, Peace and Security (GIWPS). Afghan women who work across multiple sectors reported greater negative consequences (including from aid cuts) and fewer personal benefits from their efforts compared to women globally. And yet, the majority of Afghan women said they will continue their efforts.

These reports from Afghan women underscore why their perspectives are essential in charting the international community’s response to Afghanistan. Only they can accurately describe the impact of restrictions. Without their input, policies risk perpetuating harm and failing to address half the population’s needs. Afghan women insist on meaningful inclusion in peacebuilding, humanitarian response, and political decision-making processes.

The GIWPS-DROPS report includes a more comprehensive list of key demands of Afghan women, including pressuring Taliban authorities to urgently restore education and employment opportunities, as well as directing flexible funding to local organizations and setting up mentorship networks.

Afghan women have demonstrated unrivalled courage in unimaginably difficult circumstances and at great costs; the world must honor their persistence and begin by ensuring they have a seat at the table.

“Nevertheless, Afghan women still try to remain strong and build their lives and futures. We live in hope of a bright future. As the poet says, ‘We have stitched our hearts to hope,’” said Samana from Sar-e Pol.

title: Weapons to Russia, Wigs to China: How North Korea Balances Its Allies
description: A clear division of labor ensures North Korea’s alliances with Russia and China are complementary, not competitive with each other.
text:
North Korea’s balancing act is back in the spotlight. In September, it opened its first road bridge with Russia. Just last week, North Korea opened a similar one with China. Pyongyang’s land bridge with Russia will strengthen the bilateral arms trade while the one with China will provide it with energy products, raw materials, and heavy equipment for domestic consumption.

The two bridges are a microcosm of how North Korea seeks to benefit from improved relations with Moscow and Beijing. North Korea is looking for military assistance from Russia and economic help from China. The clear division of labor ensures North Korea’s alliances with Russia and China are complementary, not competitive with each other.

North Korea has decades of experience when it comes to managing relations with Moscow and Beijing for its own benefits. In July 1961, the country signed two separate alliance treaties with the Soviet Union and China by exploiting the Sino-Soviet Split. The more bitter Moscow and Beijing were toward each other, the more willing they were to meet Pyongyang’s demands.

The combined Soviet and Chinese economic aid meant North Korea enjoyed a relatively higher living standard compared to its communist peers China and North Vietnam in the 1960s and 1970s. Its military was also on par with that of South Korea thanks to generous Soviet and Chinese transfers of weapons and technologies.

However, North Korea’s balancing act failed when the Soviet Union encountered economic trouble and began to amend ties with China in 1986. Moscow was no longer interested in competing with China for influence over North Korea and began to cut back economic and military aid. China in turn reduced the amount of military and economic support due to Soviet retrenchment.

Without a split to leverage, Pyongyang could not demand that Moscow and Beijing maintain a generous level of aid. North Korea went bankrupt in the 1990s, and its military slipped behind South Korea’s.

North Korea has now crafted a new playbook on how to get Russia and China to support Pyongyang’s goals – even in the absence of a split. In the past, North Korea handled Moscow and Beijing by having them compete over both military and economic aid. Now, North Korea balances between its two patrons by assigning them a separate domain of cooperation suitable to their specific needs.

North Korea’s outreach to Russia revolves around military exchanges to get Moscow to assist in the development of its weapons of mass destruction program. North Korea leverages Russia’s need for weapons, troops, and ammunition for the war against Ukraine in exchange for Russia’s military technology. In return, Russia has been vocal about its support for North Korea’s nuclear program and even pledged to defend Pyongyang under the 2024 Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty.

North Korea-Russia arms trade nearly doubled from 2023 to 2025, growing from $7.7 billion to $14.4 billion. This amount overshadows the food and fuel trade, which reached a record high of $34 million in 2024. North Korean laborers in Russia work in drone factories or in warzones along the Russia-Ukraine border. Pyongyang is also stressing its blood sacrifice for Russia’s war to remind Moscow of its military debt.

North Korea’s outreach to China takes on a completely different tone. Pyongyang emphasizes economic cooperation with China because it understands Beijing desires political and economic stability on the Korean Peninsula. In 2026, bilateral trade increased to $1.5 billion, up 19.6 percent compared to the first half of 2025. This marks a record high since China imposed sanctions on North Korea for its nuclear test in 2017. Noticeably, weapons made up little of the trade rebound. Unlike their peers in Russia, North Korean laborers in China mostly work in the food service and textile industry.

When Chinese President Xi Jinping visited North Korea in June, he and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un agreed to bolster ties in politics, economy, and culture. The military aspect of the Kim-Xi summit was largely absent from public view although the visit corresponded with the 65th anniversary of the signing of the 1961 Treaty of Friendship, Cooperation and Mutual Assistance. Unlike Russia and North Korea, China and North Korea didn’t publicly praise the mutual defense clause in the treaty. However, Pyongyang got Beijing to quietly drop “denuclearization” in its North Korea policy and to stop enforcing international sanctions.

Russia and China have been comfortable with North Korea’s division of labor. Neither Moscow nor Beijing sees each other’s expanding cooperation with North Korea as a threat. China accepts Pyongyang sending troops to Russia’s war in Ukraine so long as North Korea’s participation doesn’t undermine China’s desire for stability in Northeast Asia. China even harbored a Russian ship involved in the North Korea-Russia arms trade, which had to be conducted by air and sea routes before the new land bridge was opened.

For its part, although Russia’s 2024 alliance treaty with North Korea mirrors the 1961 treaty, Moscow doesn’t treat it as a rival to China’s 1961 alliance treaty. Russia even supports trilateral dialogue with China and North Korea over Chinese vessels’ use of the Tumen River for access to the Sea of Japan. Russia’s support for North Korea’s nuclear and conventional forces modernization doesn’t come at China’s expense as North Korea doesn’t plan on invading South Korea anytime soon.

From North Korea’s perspective, selling weapons to Russia and wigs to China means its alliances with both are complimentary instead of competitive. Pyongyang can secure long-term support from Russia and China not through their spite toward each other but through their genuine interest in fostering a stable ally in the Asia-Pacific.

Thanks to Russian and Chinese backing, North Korea’s economy is booming and its military is undergoing the most comprehensive modernization program since 1991. Russia’s and China’s support also gives North Korea stronger diplomatic leverage in case it decides to restart dialogue with the United States. Importantly, North Korea doesn’t base its foreign policy on the state of Beijing-Moscow relations like it did during the Cold War. If either Russia or China loses interest in bolstering North Korea’s economy and military at some point in the future, the other patron will not reduce aid just because it has “won” the competition.

title: What ‘Beyond Advocacy’ Means for India’s Role in the Russia-Ukraine Conflict
description: India’s possible role as a facilitator will be driven by its own economic interests, rather than any need to increase its political heft on the global stage.
text:
Speaking at the Munich Leaders Meeting earlier this week, India’s Minister for External Affairs S. Jaishankar said that India’s consistent position that the Russia-Ukraine conflict should end through “dialogue and diplomacy” between the concerned parties remains unchanged. In the same breath, he acknowledged that New Delhi in “recent months” has been a “little more involved beyond advocacy” in negotiating an end to the conflict.

Without providing details, the Indian foreign minister said India was engaged in discussions with both sides on specific arrangements involving Black Sea shipping, grain and energy exports, and possible “non-attack” understandings. During the latest press briefing, the Indian Ministry of External Affairs confirmed that New Delhi was having “ongoing conversations with both Russia and Ukraine” on these matters.

Earlier, in his address at the United Nations General Assembly, Jaishankar said that New Delhi was “prepared to do everything possible” to ameliorate the conflict in Ukraine, “especially with regard to food and energy security.”

As part of this activism to broker peace and operational agreements, New Delhi, along with the United States, Egypt, and Turkiye, reportedly submitted a proposal for a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine, which Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha described as the “most extensive.” That proposal followed Jaishankar’s visit to Kyiv on September 3, the first-ever standalone bilateral visit by an Indian foreign minister to Ukraine.

According to a press release from the Embassy of Ukraine in India, the discussions between Jaishankar and Sybiha focused on the situation in the Black Sea and freedom of navigation, global food security, nuclear threats posed by Russia, and the development of India-Ukraine relations.

Indian media reports cited unnamed government sources to confirm that a truce plan was discussed during Jaishankar’s visit to Kyiv.

Despite moving beyond rhetorical calls for dialogue toward concrete proposal-based diplomacy, New Delhi has not formally described its role as a mediator. Its reticence probably stems from its own antipathy toward mediation when it comes to its disputes with Pakistan on the Kashmir issue. Referring to Pakistan’s mediation efforts in the ongoing war in West Asia, Jaishankar commented that India would not be a “dalal (broker)” nation like Islamabad.

New Delhi has strong relations with Russia. It would, therefore, not want to jeopardize ties with its trusted partner by taking any position that could go against President Vladimir Putin’s domestic interests, especially. This is why, despite repeated criticism from the West for its perceived “pro-Russia” position, New Delhi has refrained from publicly censuring Russian actions in Ukraine and voted against or abstained on most Ukraine-related resolutions at the United Nations.

So far, Moscow has responded positively to New Delhi’s peace efforts, with Putin publicly praising Prime Minister Narendra Modi for his “ideas and persistent efforts” for peace in the ongoing war in Ukraine. During his talks with Putin on the sidelines of the SCO summit in Bishkek earlier this year, Modi urged the Russian leader to move from “endless war” to the “end of war” for the sake of humanity.

Nevertheless, the shift in New Delhi’s tone, small as it is at present, is an important development. It reflects domestic concerns over the war’s economic costs on India.

Both Russia and Ukraine are major suppliers of several essential commodities to India, including agricultural products. Supply chain disruptions caused by the conflict have already had a major impact on the Indian economy. A notable example is the extraordinary surge in the price of sunflower oil, which Russia and Ukraine supply to India. Due to supply chain disruptions caused by attacks on cargo ships in the Black Sea, New Delhi’s sunflower oil imports fell to their lowest level in more than four years in September. Consequently, between October 2025 and October 2026, retail prices increased by 18.7 percent.

Beyond economic motives, humanitarian concerns also drive New Delhi’s position. Targeted strikes on commercial shipping in the Black Sea continue to claim the lives of Indian seafarers, who account for the second largest share of the global maritime workforce.

Additionally, Indian businesses have faced severe financial losses due to the recent escalation in the conflict. In August, a Russian airstrike targeted a site at ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih, owned by Indian businessman Lakshmi Mittal, forcing a partial shutdown of the plant. More recently, on October 4, Russian attacks heavily damaged the Indian-owned Kusum Healthcare pharmaceutical plant, resulting in estimated losses of $50 million.

New Delhi’s more robust approach toward negotiating an end to the Russia-Ukraine conflict is also being appreciated by its European partners. Previously, India’s “cautious” position on the Ukraine crisis has caused some friction in the EU-India relationship. As New Delhi’s traditional partnership with Washington encounters friction, strengthening alignments with partners in Europe is increasingly becoming a strategic necessity.

Going forward, New Delhi is unlikely to mediate directly between Russia and Ukraine, given the complexity and historical baggage of the conflict. More likely, it will play a more important, visible political and diplomatic role, acting as a facilitator of dialogue. This role will be determined by India’s own economic interests, likely to focus on issue-based negotiations, rather than to increase its political heft on the global stage by acting as direct mediator.

title: What Does Durga Puja Tell Us About Minorities in Bangladesh?
channel_text: Blog; Society; South Asia; The Pulse
description: The largest Hindu religious festival went off smoothly – a credit to the new BNP government.
text:
Durga Puja, the largest religious festival of Bengali Hindus, ended on October 21, and Hindus celebrated the festival peacefully in the Muslim-majority country without any major incidents. The Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) government passed its first major test of communal harmony since taking office in early 2026. Prime Minister Tarique Rahman also drew attention by visiting puja pandals in several divisional cities outside Dhaka, becoming the first Bangladeshi prime minister to do so.

Beyond the celebrations, this year’s Durga Puja highlighted a significant shift in Bangladesh’s political landscape. The long-held perception that religious minorities are safer under the Awami League now appears to be on the verge of breaking down.

A Test for the BNP

Durga Puja is celebrated on a large scale in both Bangladesh and the neighboring Indian state of West Bengal. West Bengal has around 70 million Hindus among its population of roughly 100 million, and nearly 58,000 puja pandals were set up across the state this year. Bangladesh, meanwhile, has about 13.1 million Hindus but hosted 33,851 puja pandals, around 1,500 more than last year. This means Bangladesh had more puja pandals relative to its Hindu population than West Bengal.

This was the first Durga Puja celebrated under the BNP government, which came to power in February this year. As a result, the festival carried significance beyond that of a religious celebration. In particular, it represented a test of the new government’s ability, political will, and commitment to ensure the security of religious minorities.

Some untoward incidents have occurred during the festival over the years. This year was no exception in the period leading up to the formal commencement of the festivities, with several incidents reported in different parts of the country. Given the precarious law and order situation, there were concerns that such incidents might escalate.

Nevertheless, the BNP government successfully met the challenge of ensuring that Durga Puja was celebrated peacefully.

Representatives of the Hindu community had long demanded three days of public holidays for Durga Puja. During the Awami League’s rule, there was one public holiday on Bijaya Dashami. Following the political transition in 2024, the interim government led by Muhammad Yunus increased the holiday to two days.

This year, the BNP government extended it to three days. With public holidays from October 20 to 22 followed by the weekly holidays on October 23 and 24, people enjoyed a continuous five-day break.

The government also allocated more financial assistance than requested to encourage a festive atmosphere during the celebrations. While the Hindu Religious Welfare Trust sought 40 million Bangladesh taka for Durga Puja, the government allocated 50 million. Similarly, for the Buddhist community’s Kathina Civara Dana, the government allocated 30 million taka against a request for 20 million. The significance lay not in the amount of money but in the message conveyed by the government.

Netizens described this year’s Durga Puja as having been celebrated with unprecedented security arrangements and a festive atmosphere.

The End of the Hindu Vote Bank?

On October 20, during Durga Puja, Rahman visited puja pandals in the capital, Dhaka, and three other divisional cities: Rangpur, Rajshahi, and Chittagong. Rahman exchanged greetings with members of the Hindu community and listened to their concerns.

Earlier, in his Durga Puja greetings message on October 16, Rahman urged Hindus to celebrate the festival with joy and confidence, free from fear. He emphasized religious harmony, mutual respect, and equal rights for all citizens, regardless of their faith. “Religion belongs to individuals, while the state belongs to all,” Rahman said, stressing that ensuring everyone’s security is a responsibility of the state. He also spoke of building a safe and inclusive Bangladesh where people of all religions and communities can live with dignity.

These comments were significant in Bangladesh’s political context. Many have historically viewed a large section of the Hindu community as supporters of the Awami League. In contrast, there have long been attempts to portray the BNP as a relatively conservative political party, which has previously formed alliances with Jamaat-e-Islami, though the BNP, as a party, believes in liberal democracy.

On October 16, while visiting a puja pandal in Dhaka’s Banani area, Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed told members of the Hindu community, “You do not need to be anyone’s vote bank.” He urged them to make political decisions based on their civil rights, religious freedom, and constitutional entitlements. Ahmed also remarked that various political parties had exploited the Hindu community for political gain in the past.

His statement carries considerable significance in Bangladesh’s political landscape. Although the Awami League has been perceived as a relatively safe political refuge for minorities, numerous instances of attacks and discrimination against minority communities occurred during the party’s long tenure in power. These include the attacks on the Buddhist community in Ramu, Cox’s Bazar, in 2012; the attacks on Hindu homes and temples in Nasirnagar, Brahmanbaria, in 2016; and the communal violence that spread from Cumilla during Durga Puja in 2021. According to the U.S. State Department’s human rights report, six people were killed in the 2021 violence. These incidents demonstrated that the Awami League was not necessarily effective in protecting religious minorities.

According to the 2022 Population and Housing Census, Hindus accounted for 7.96 percent of Bangladesh’s total population, down from 8.54 percent in the 2011 census. The Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS) identified migration, alongside a lower fertility rate, as a factor behind the declining proportion of Hindus in the population.

Following the fall of the Awami League government in August 2024, allegations emerged of attacks on minorities, vandalism of homes and businesses, and assaults on places of worship in different parts of the country. Although the fact-finding team of the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) found political rather than communal motives behind most of these incidents, neighboring India has continued to express concern over the situation.

According to the OHCHR’s 2025 fact-finding report, the violence was driven by several factors, including religious and ethnic discrimination, political revenge against people seen as Awami League supporters, land disputes and personal conflicts. The report also found that some local BNP and Jamaat-e-Islami leaders and activists were involved in the attacks. However, it found no evidence that either party had organized the attacks as part of party decision.

The Bigger Picture

The Awami League was banned from taking part in the national election held on February 12 this year. Of the 300 elected parliamentary seats, the BNP won 209, while Jamaat-e-Islami secured 68. The results showed that the BNP gained strong support in many Hindu-majority areas that were traditionally considered Awami League strongholds.

Netra News analyzed results and voter records from more than 40,000 polling stations. Of these, 1,088 were in areas where more than half of the voters were inferred to be Hindu, based on their names in the electoral rolls. The BNP led in 984 of these polling stations, securing 69.1 percent of the valid votes cast, compared with 14.9 percent for Jamaat-e-Islami. These figures suggest that minority voters migrated to the BNP after the Awami League was banned.

In this year’s election, only four candidates from religious and ethnic minority communities – two Hindus and two Buddhists – were elected to parliament, all nominated by the BNP. Four more women from minority communities were later nominated to parliament through reserved seats, also representing the BNP. This brings the total number of minority lawmakers to eight. Their representation remains low compared with the share of religious and ethnic minorities in Bangladesh’s population. It shows that more needs to be done to ensure meaningful political representation for minority communities, beyond symbolic inclusion.

The peaceful conclusion of Durga Puja should not overshadow concerns about incidents reported before the festival. On October 15, the Bangladesh Puja Udjapan Parishad and the Mahanagar Sarbajanin Puja Committee reported 34 alleged incidents across the country, including damage to idols, attacks on temples and other violence. The organizations said arrests had been made in 11 of these cases.

Bangladesh Police later said that investigations into some of the incidents found no evidence of plots to disrupt communal harmony. Instead, they pointed to local leadership disputes, theft, and other causes. Even so, transparent and credible investigations into all the allegations remain important, and those responsible must be brought to justice.

According to the Bangladesh Hindu Buddhist Christian Unity Council, 257 incidents of communal violence were reported across Bangladesh between January and June 2026 (a period covering both the interim government and the BNP government). The organization said 44 people were killed in 40 of these incidents.

The India Dimension

The changing political situation of religious minorities in Bangladesh also has implications for relations with India. Minority security has long been a sensitive issue between the two countries.

During Sheikh Hasina’s rule, close ties between Dhaka and New Delhi were shaped not only by security and strategic cooperation but also by the Awami League’s self-claimed secular political image.

However, Bangladesh-India relations became strained after Hasina fled to India and took refuge there in 2024. Even under Bangladesh’s current elected government, disagreements over Hasina, border issues, trade and water sharing remain unresolved.

Still, this year’s Durga Puja celebrations have drawn approval even from some Indian critics who have long raised concerns about minority security in Bangladesh. Among them is Kolkata-based journalist Mayukh Ranjan Ghosh, who praised the scale and grandeur of the celebrations. Such reactions suggest that perceptions of Bangladesh may be beginning to change across the border.

Whether this will lead New Delhi to reconsider its longstanding political suspicion of the BNP. Much will depend on whether the BNP government can sustain the same sense of security and confidence among religious minorities beyond the festival.

title: What Happened to Gwadar’s Rights Movement?
channel_text: Blog; Politics; South Asia; The Pulse
description: Haq Do Tehreek, the movement that once brought the world’s attention to Gwadar’s longstanding grievances, is a pale shadow of its former self.
text:
In November 2021, thousands of people rallied and participated in sit-ins along Gwadar’s Harbor Road, demanding rights for the local Baloch people. What came to be known as the “Haq Do Tehreek” (Give Us Our Rights Movement) began mainly as a movement of the fishing community to address their grievances. But soon, women, children, men, and people from different walks of life joined the protests, making it the largest mass mobilization in the history of Gwadar.

Gwadar is not just another town or port. Located on Pakistan’s Makran coast, it sits near the mouth of the Strait of Hormuz. Its proximity to this strategic waterway through which a significant amount of the world’s oil and gas passes, and China’s investment and foothold at its port, have cemented Gwadar’s role not only in regional trade but also in global maritime geopolitics.

Gwadar port and Balochistan’s mineral wealth have, however, long been points of contention and have contributed to the turbulent political situation in the province.

As the gateway of the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), Gwadar port triggered great expectations in the early days of the port’s construction. Many believed that the fishing town would be transformed into a modern city, bringing prosperity to Gwadar’s residents. But two decades later, most of the expectations are unfulfilled.

In 2021, the Haq Do Tehreek emerged. The movement drew attention to the wide gap between the development and prosperity that Gwadar port promised and the everyday realities that the majority of its residents encountered. It brought people together to demand basic services like water, electricity, economic security, a ban on illegal fishing and trawling, freedom of movement, and relief from excessive security checkpoints, along with a list of other longstanding grievances.

Thus, in 2021, the Haq Do Tehreek became a symbol of resistance, and an example of how collective action and local mass mobilization of people, mainly the fishing community, could bring their long-neglected grievances to the forefront.

One of the reasons for the Haq Do Tehreek’s rapid rise and mass participation was its leadership. Maulana Hidayat-ur-Rehman, the leader of Haq Do Tehreek, was already politically active as a member of the Jamaat-e-Islami (JI). He also belonged to the fishing community, rather than to elite or established political families. This helped him connect with the masses. Consequently, JI activists and fishing communities participated in large numbers in the movement. In December 2022, they participated in large numbers to protest and blockade the entrance to Gwadar port and the East Bay Expressway.

The Haq Do Tehreek began as a peaceful movement. However, it soon escalated and violence erupted. A police constable died from injuries in the unrest; more than 100 people were arrested and restrictions were imposed on public gatherings and telecommunications.

With the government cracking down on the movement, Rehman came under scrutiny, forcing him to go into hiding in December 2022. When he re-emerged weeks later in January 2023 and presented himself before the courts to surrender and seek bail, he was arrested. He denied allegations linking him to the constable’s death and was then granted bail by the Supreme Court in May 2023. Mass support for the Maulana increased after his arrest. In February 2024, Rehman contested provincial elections and won a seat in the Balochistan assembly.

His participation in elections was controversial; while some considered his contesting the election as a route for pursuing the movement’s demands through formal politics, others opposed it, seeing it as a step that would weaken the Haq Do Tehreek. There were doubts whether Rehman, who had built his reputation by challenging the authorities, could deliver results from within the same political system.

Many conspiracy theories circulated at that time. Some believed that Rehman’s political rise and participation in elections were engineered by the state. After all, his entry into the provincial assembly served the government’s interest, as the unrelenting rallies and mass protests that he led were putting pressure on the local police and undermining the law and order situation in an already restive province.

So, has Rehman, as a legislator in the Balochistan assembly, been successful in getting the grievances of Gwardar’s residents addressed? The results are mixed. Illegal fishing and trawling, which were major concerns during the protests, continue unabated, as do the presence of innumerable security checkpoints and shortages of water and electricity.

Although such issues cannot be resolved overnight, the people of Gwadar cannot help but wonder what the movement achieved through its leaders joining formal politics.

The Haq Do Tehreek has transformed over the last couple of years. From a grassroots movement, it has evolved into a political party. Since the 2024 provincial elections, Haq Do Tehreek is listed as a political party with Pakistan’s Election Commission. Maulana’s political party is listed as Haq Do Tehreek on the Balochistan Assembly’s website.

Haq Do Tehreek no longer conducts mass mobilizations, aside from a long march from Quetta to Islamabad in July 2025 that Rehman led to pressure the federal government to address longstanding Baloch grievances, including enforced disappearances, restrictions on border trade, and illegal trawling. Even then, some claimed the march was organized by JI, others described it as the “Haq Do Balochistan Long March.”

The movement also suffered a setback with the death of its secretary-general, Hafeez Kiazai, in a road accident in March 2026.

Rehman is reportedly taking up issues pertaining to the fisherfolk in the provincial assembly. In October 2026, he chaired a meeting of the Balochistan Assembly’s Standing Committee on Fisheries in Gwadar to review the proposed Balochistan Fisheries and Aquaculture Bill 2026. The meeting brought together fishermen and other stakeholders to discuss reforms to protect their livelihoods and marine resources.

However, Gwadar’s Haq Do Tehreek has clearly lost the momentum and energy it once displayed. The massive rallies that were seen in 2021-2023 are no longer visible.

The movement may have handed over its struggle to formal politics, but formal politics also comes with its own constraints. After all, blaming and criticizing the very system one has become a part of is a contradiction in itself.

title: What I Learned From a Year of Interviewing a Thai Sex Worker
description: Decades of research have identified economic privation as a leading cause of entry into the country's illegal sex trade.
text:
When I started interviewing a Thai sex worker named Ying for my recent book, I was initially looking for something far different from what I eventually wrote. I wanted sleaze: something raw and stimulating. I had wanted to write about a harlot, someone immoral, for whom money took precedence over all. I had expected to write about their greed, their lack of morals and the hypocrisy that arose from an industry surrounding a deeply religious society.

My assumptions were both critical and ignorant. In every way, I had already decided on the book I was going to write without attempting to understand the mechanics or psychology behind them. What I have since learned is about choices, and how few meaningful ones there were for someone caught between family obligation, economic status, and religion. What I learned was about the life of a tortured soul, fighting to make the best of what she had.

Ying had spent most of her adult life selling sex for a living, starting when she was 19 years of age. Like many girls around her, she had dreamed of a better life – one that seemed impossible for someone born into poverty with little education. Ying grew up in Thailand’s mostly agrarian northeast. She arrived in Bangkok at the age of 17, and began work in a restaurant, where she faced long hours and poor earnings with no hope of advancement. Alongside this, she became involved in sex work, present in every nook and cranny of Bangkok. As Ying told me, “There was no choice. It was the only way to earn enough for myself and my family.”

Of course, Ying knew what she was doing. She wasn’t coerced or forced. But still the question remains: what else was available to her? The economics of her situation were inescapable. Ying was earning 6,000 baht per month at a restaurant in the early 2000s. At her peak in the sex industry, she was making close to 80,000 baht each month. Her mother back home in Isan sold food by the road, making less than 200 baht per day. Her father was an odd-job laborer earning even less. For a family like hers, the difference was colossal.

Decades of research into Thailand’s illegal sex industry have long identified economic privation as a leading cause of entry into the trade, which offers substantially superior earnings than the agricultural, domestic, or other poorly paid forms of work available to women who come from rural provinces. Those findings do not apply to every woman in the sex industry, but they help us understand how seemingly voluntary decisions may be constrained in practice.

Another thing became clearer through the interviews. Customers were not buying sex; they were buying a performance. Ying had to convince customers she was interested in them. To make each man feel desirable. To fulfill their every desire, no matter how detestable. Each customer was its own enterprise, and she had to remember their every eccentricity in order to encourage their return. As the industry moved online through the years, women had to improve their skill sets, to understand how to digitally market themselves. To master the psychology of attraction, and the manner in which to exercise it. Ying explained, “You have to make every man like you, or he won’t come back.”

What further surprised me was the power the customer held, even after he had paid and left. The digital world brought private encounters into the public sphere: a displeased customer could affect a woman’s future earnings by becoming an online critic, capable of influencing the market value of her services. The strength of a single review could make or break the personal enterprise she had set up for herself.

Beyond performance, Ying’s experience of sex work also revealed many personal boundaries were up for sale. Many men refused to use condoms; others demanded violent or depraved acts. Blowjob bars in particular distinguish themselves by the absence of condoms. This is an easy boundary to maintain when a sex worker is first starting out, fresh and attractive. But that balance shifts rapidly when they remain in the industry for too long, presenting them with a hard economic decision: refuse the money, or accept a greater health risk. For Ying, ageing and increasing competition intensified those decisions; she described how quickly such considerations become typical when rooted in the industry. The same market that had rewarded her youth gradually made it more costly for her to protect herself.

Her account also revealed the darker experiences of rape and abuse. In one disturbing revelation, she recounted how she was heavily intoxicated, unable to defend herself, while men around her used her sexually. Yet, when pressed on her emotions during that encounter, she seemed more bothered by her boyfriend’s inability or refusal to protect her, rather than the assault itself, a reaction I found difficult to grasp. What affected me was how nonchalant she was in recalling these experiences. It made me question if her career in sex work had created an unavoidable overlap, where consent and violation had become intertwined with her professional need to please every man she came across.

The money Ying earned was not always spent on herself. One of the recurring themes in our interviews was the importance of family responsibility and karma – and how both of these contributed to her decision to enter the sex industry. According to her strict religious upbringing, filial piety is a source of merit that can help to expunge past transgressions and ensure a positive reincarnation. Parents give their children a life, food, and protection. Children repay this debt by sending money home – something that is a moral and religious responsibility.

The same Buddhist moral universe that rejects any immoral behavior now expects a diametrically opposed sacrifice in the name of filial piety, a devastating contradiction I had struggled to understand.

Years later, that contradiction became painfully obvious when even cervical cancer could not keep Ying from returning to sex work. Her family had already structured their lives around her regular financial sacrifices and were reliant on her. She said, “There was no other job at my age that could pay so much.” Nobody forced her back after her hysterectomy. There was no trafficker waiting at her door, no one imposing their will upon her. She did it because she had no other option.

I started out with a plan to write a book about the colorful life of a sex worker. In the end, I was writing about a human being – one of us – trying her best, imperfectly and relentlessly, to survive. I now understand how morality can appear from a distance and how simple any choice can be when proper alternatives exist. And really, given those circumstances, would we have done anything so very different?

title: What Is Behind Bangladesh’s Continuing Law and Order Crisis?
description: The government must rebuild public trust in the police force and insulate law enforcement from political influence.
text:
On October 12, Human Rights Support Society (HRSS), a Bangladeshi rights organization, reported that between July and September this year, 17 people were killed and 1,227 injured in 183 incidents of political violence in Bangladesh. This was a 12 percent increase in the number of incidents in the same period last year. Mob violence also rose sharply from 98 to 137.

These figures indicate that the Bangladeshi state is struggling to stabilize and normalize the law and order situation in the country since the revolutionary mobilization in 2024. So, the transition from the previous authoritarian ecosystem under Sheikh Hasina and the Awami League to the new democratic ecosystem has faced several challenges.

According to data from the human rights organization, Ain o Salish Kendra, deaths from mob violence increased from 51 in 2023 to 128 in 2024 and 197 in 2025. Police say that registered murder cases increased from 3,023 in 2023 to 3,786 in 2025. Besides that, reports of incidents of extortion, political clashes, and armed violence have raised concerns about the deteriorating law and order situation in Bangladesh.

After the fall of Hasina’s authoritarian regime in August 2024, public ire was directed against law and enforcement authorities; 450 of Bangladesh’s 639 police stations became nonfunctional following attacks, while approximately 30 percent of police positions were left temporarily vacant.

Building trust in the police forces was a daunting task. There was little trust in the police force to begin with, thanks to the colonial policing culture that East Pakistan and then Bangladesh inherited, and even embraced. Successive regimes initially used the police as a tool not so much to enforce law and order as to stifle dissent. Political connections and corruption determined professional advancement within the police force. As a result, the Bangladesh police were hardly a professional force.

Ahead of the 2024 national election, nearly 10,000 opposition activists were arrested, while politically motivated cases, enforced disappearances, and extrajudicial killings became recurring instruments of repression. Police authorities were reportedly involved in almost 708 enforced disappearance cases. Some also threatened women with rape if they didn’t fall in line.

The Hasina regime used the police to weaken its opponents, and as many officers became tools of the regime, the ladder to climb the ranks was less about hard work than about loyalty to the government and serving its agenda. For example, 349 police officers received awards, including one who received recognition for arresting photographer Shahidul Alam over his criticism of the government.

This broken and untrustworthy ecosystem could not be fixed in a few days, weeks or even months. When the anti-Hasina protests ended, people guarded the streets as the whole police and law-and-order maintenance system broke apart.

Even routine policing has become a challenge in Bangladesh. Officers who previously operated with strong political backing now face considerable risks when intervening in confrontations. Although the interim regime intervened to restore the law and order mechanism and revive the working of police stations, it has been difficult for people to trust the police.

The color of police uniforms and the logo of the police force were changed twice, but these superficial adjustments had little impact on how the public perceived the police.

Then came initiatives to rebuild the police force. However, a member of the Police Reform Commission that was set up post-2024 told The Diplomat that the recommendations for reforming the police have not been taken seriously by the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) government. It has not taken a single step towards reforming the police force, he said. As a result, public perception of the police force has not improved much. According to a survey by the International Republican Institute, 52 percent of respondents disapproved of the police’s performance, while 45 percent approved. Of all of Bangladesh’s public institutions surveyed, the police force secured the lowest public approval

Another reason for the poor law and order situation in Bangladesh is the changing structure of political authority at the grassroots level. During the Awami League’s 15 years in power, local political and economic influence was largely concentrated within very systematized networks connected to the ruling party. Control over transport terminals, markets, construction contracts, land, and other economic resources was often exercised through internally negotiated and mutually established political patronage networks. So the division and the hierarchy were clear.

The fall of the Awami League disrupted this hierarchy. Individuals and groups previously excluded from local power structures began competing for positions and resources formerly controlled by these networks. The clash for the new owner of the throne was on the table, and local political competition became intertwined with disputes over extortion, property, markets, and territorial influence. In May alone, Dhaka Metropolitan Police identified 1,280 active extortionists in the capital, including 148 armed criminals. Throughout the country, 600 incidents of political violence were documented between August 2024 and December 2025, resulting in 158 deaths and more than 7,000 injuries, where many confrontations involved struggles over local dominance and economic resources.

These rivalries have continued after the BNP formed the government in February this year. Of the 183 political-violence incidents documented by HRSS between July and September this year, 69 involved internal BNP conflicts, while another 92 involved confrontations between BNP members and other political groups. Rival factions seeking influence within the same political organization have become an important source of conflict and violence at the grassroots level.

So, post-2024, Bangladesh has entered an endless loop of conflicts as rival political groups compete for local authority. The government seems unable to control the police, even as the latter are weak and lack the moral authority to solve the problem. And most significantly, in this process, conflicts are reinforcing each other.

It is time that the BNP government wakes up to the grave law and order situation in the country. Its immediate task should be to rebuild police authority without restoring political control over policing.

The Police Commission Ordinance adopted in December 2025, which was intended to strengthen oversight and accountability, has since ceased to have effect. This means that the legal framework designed to regulate police conduct is no longer operative, leaving oversight mechanisms unenforced. Without institutional independence, the police risk becoming dependent on political patronage again, while competition over local resources continues to encourage violence.

Establishing law and order in Bangladesh will need more than increasing police deployment or arresting individual criminals. It will require rebuilding public trust, insulating law enforcement from political influence, and preventing local groups from converting political connections into coercive economic power. Otherwise, the country risks replacing one system of politically controlled order with another, without establishing the rule of law that the July uprising promised.
