title: What Pakistan Will and Won’t Do in Yemen
description: Operationally, it would make little sense for Pakistan to send in large conventional ground forces to Yemen simply to put the brakes on Houthi advances.
text:
On October 5, Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, and Pakistan moved ahead to activate their defense commitments and provide military capabilities agreed under the Mecca Defense Alliance. The decision came after weeks of Houthi drone and missile strikes against Saudi Arabia, even as the Houthis were ramping up their ground operations along the Red Sea coast.

Regardless of how the crisis plays out, the Houthi conflict has turned out to be the first major test of the Mecca Pact. The alliance must strike a balance. It has to demonstrate that its commitments have real military value without crossing the line into becoming an interventionist force or getting bogged down in a prolonged war of attrition.

For Pakistan, the Houthi crisis is a particularly difficult strategic problem.

There is broad agreement within Pakistan’s strategic community that the Mecca Pact is defensive rather than offensive. However, Pakistan cannot simply sit on the sidelines as the regional security environment goes downhill and its own defensive commitments come under strain. If the alliance cannot show up when one of its members faces a serious security challenge, its deterrent value could quickly erode.

At the same time, Pakistan is alive to the costs of direct intervention. Deploying large numbers of troops into Yemen would pile on additional pressure on an already stretched military, which is grappling with counterterrorism challenges at home and the threat from India. It could also put a strain on its relations with Iran and, perhaps most importantly, lock Islamabad into a commitment from which it would find it difficult to pull out without paying a heavy strategic price.

Diplomatically, Islamabad is trying to persuade Iran into restraining the Houthis. Nonetheless, there are limits to what Tehran can or is willing to do. Iranian influence over Houthi decision-making is significant but is not unlimited. The Houthis have an axe to grind when it comes to Saudi Arabia. Moreover, Tehran has little obvious incentive to do away with a source of pressure on Saudi Arabia while it is itself preparing for another round with the United States. Therefore, diplomacy is unlikely to resolve the crisis on its own.

Pakistan must demonstrate that the Mecca Pact has real teeth and practical military value. To understand what that support might look like, it is necessary to understand the alliance’s objectives and the means available to achieve them.

Pakistan understands that wiping out the Houthis altogether is neither realistic nor desirable. Even if such an objective were militarily achievable, the costs would be high. Sustained Houthi attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure, combined with the consequences of further stoking Yemen’s civil war, could make the price of total military victory prohibitively high.

The more realistic objective, therefore, is to constrain the Houthis’ ability to dominate the Bab al-Mandeb and tip the military balance sufficiently to open up space for a political settlement.

Any military support that Pakistan or Türkiye provides to Saudi Arabia or Saudi-backed forces in Yemen should be understood in this light.

Operationally, it would make little sense for Pakistan to send in large conventional ground forces to Yemen simply to put the brakes on Houthi advances. The decisive fighting is taking place in southwestern Yemen, particularly around Taiz and Mocha. These areas are far from the Saudi border. Operating a large Pakistani expeditionary force there would be logistically difficult and risky.

What is needed instead is a capable and better-organized anti-Houthi force in southwestern Yemen. This is where Pakistan and Türkiye can add value. Both countries can supply weapons and other military assistance to Saudi-backed forces, beefing up their ability to conduct counteroffensives. They can also help with command-and-control structures, where weaknesses have contributed to the inability of anti-Houthi forces to push back against recent Houthi advances.

Pakistan also has extensive experience with special operations and counterterrorism, particularly from its campaigns in Afghanistan. Türkiye, meanwhile, has built up considerable experience operating specialized forces in Syria and Iraq. Therefore, both could provide specialized personnel and advisers potentially inside Yemen without committing to large conventional formations. In this sense, Pakistan and Türkiye could contribute through force augmentation rather than direct intervention.

Another potential priority would be breaking up Houthi command structures. The Houthis have become more organized and militarily sophisticated, but they still retain many characteristics of a networked armed movement. Weakening their command and communications could pay off more than attempting to wear down the organization through conventional territorial warfare alone. Pakistan and Türkiye’s intelligence-gathering experience could offer useful lessons for Saudi Arabia and its local partners in this regard.

The alliance must also brace for further attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure. Saudi Arabia’s air-defense network could come under increasing pressure if Houthi missile and drone attacks intensify. Already, Saudi air-defense stockpiles are thinned due to Iranian attacks and continued Houthi onslaughts. Therefore, Pakistan and Türkiye would provide additional air-defense capabilities and personnel to shield critical infrastructure and strategic facilities.

Saudi Arabia already has a substantial air force and does not necessarily require Pakistani fighter aircraft or pilots. What it needs more urgently is support in battlefield operational planning, target identification and air-combat support functions. Such assistance could improve both the effectiveness and intensity of Saudi air operations.

This broader role explains why deployment of as many as 40,000 Pakistani troops should not be read as preparation for a conventional Pakistani ground war in Yemen.

Nonetheless, there are limits to what Pakistan can pull off. The operationalization of the Mecca Pact’s joint command remains in its infancy. Moreover, it is unclear how effectively Pakistan’s military capabilities can be integrated into a conflict with a very different geography and political environment. Pakistan also has considerably less experience in indirectly shaping a battlefield by strengthening another state’s forces.

There is another uncertainty. The strategic objectives of Pakistan and Saudi Arabia may not stay in lockstep as the conflict evolves. Riyadh may ultimately seek to tip the balance of power in Yemen decisively in its favor. Islamabad, by contrast, is likely to remain committed to its defense obligations while seeking to steer clear of a prolonged military commitment. The two countries’ objectives may overlap during the initial phase of the crisis, but they could diverge as the conflict drags on.

A far more serious crisis could flare up if Iran or its allies in Iraq move to support the Houthis. Iraqi militias have already attacked Saudi Arabia several times, including strikes on the East-West Crude Oil Pipeline. While Iran’s direct intervention remains off the table for the moment, the situation would change if the US resumes massive strikes on Iran, including on energy infrastructure. Iran will surely hit back at Gulf energy infrastructure, Saudi Arabia’s included. The conflict would then spill over beyond Yemen.

How the Mecca Defense Alliance manages the Houthi crisis will shape not only the integrity of the Mecca Pact but also its credibility as a foundation for the emerging regional security order.
tag: Pakistan and Mecca Pact; Pakistan-Houthis; Pakistan-Iran; Pakistan-Saudis

title: What States Make of Military Exercises: Ulchi and Beyond
channel_text: Asia Defense; Blog; East Asia; Security
user_author_name: Adrian Ang U-Jin; Jun Yan Chang
description: Repeated military cooperation can help build predictability, trust, interoperability, and institutionalized relationships among participants.
text:
Just before the South Korea-U.S. Ulchi Freedom Shield exercise began in mid-August, U.S. President Donald Trump ordered a substantial reduction in its scale. Describing the drills as “costly” and an “inappropriate and hostile” signal to North Korea – a state he termed “unthreatening and respectful” – Trump also criticized what he described as Seoul’s lack of support for U.S. operations against Iran.

Trump’s sudden decision raised concerns about South Korea-U.S. defense readiness, alliance reliability, and Washington’s wider commitment to Asia. Several analysts warned that reducing exercises could weaken deterrence and alliance coordination, while others questioned whether the move would secure reciprocal restraint from Pyongyang. Such concerns are understandable: joint military exercises are a visible manifestation of the South Korea-U.S. defense commitment, while North Korea routinely denounces them as rehearsals for war.

The reduction alone, however, does not carry a single, self-evident political meaning. U.S. commanders have since emphasized that other combined training continues and proposed changes to its frequency and geographic distribution. How audiences interpret these changes depends on the wider pattern of cooperation, established relationships, and political context.

Scale, Scope, and Strategic Meaning

Joint military exercises can serve two different but complementary strategic functions. They demonstrate capability and resolve to deter adversaries, but exercises also facilitate defense diplomacy. Repeated military cooperation can help build predictability, trust, interoperability, and institutionalized relationships among participants.

Our research suggests that an exercise’s scale and scope alone cannot reliably distinguish between these functions. Deterrence and defense diplomacy often generate the same observable characteristics, making it difficult to determine where one ends and the other begins simply by examining an exercise’s material features.

Larger and more complex exercises – featuring tens of thousands of troops, sophisticated command-and-control systems, live-fire maneuvers, and complex scenarios – can demonstrate greater warfighting capability and resolve to deter. At the same time, however, those same characteristics may instead reflect years of accumulated defense cooperation and deeper levels of trust and institutional integration between the participating militaries. Their material features reveal what militaries practice and provide evidence of their capabilities but cannot by themselves establish the political messages governments intend or how different audiences will interpret them. Rather, as a political signal, joint military exercises ultimately depend on what participating states and other audiences make of them.

Different audiences will not necessarily derive the same meaning from the same exercise. Washington might intend a reduction in Ulchi as restraint toward Pyongyang, while North Korea might interpret it as a concession, Seoul as uncertainty over U.S. commitment to the bilateral alliance, and Beijing as evidence of Washington’s transactional approach to alliance management. Established relationships and political contexts are therefore essential to interpreting an exercise’s strategic meaning.

Instead, established relationships and political contexts are more important in determining the strategic meaning of exercises than scale and scope alone. The history of Ulchi itself illustrates this.

Ulchi’s scale and scope have seldom increased in tandem with the danger from North Korea. This divergence is significant. If Ulchi’s scale simply tracked the North Korean military threat, as one would expect for greater deterrence, participation should have risen relatively consistently alongside Pyongyang’s expanding nuclear and missile capabilities. Instead, exercise participation has repeatedly risen and fallen according to changes in the diplomatic environment. Participation declined during periods associated with the Six-Party Talks and suspended altogether to facilitate diplomacy with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in Trump’s first term.

The scale of South Korean participation also reflects domestic politics. According to publicly available data, South Korean troop numbers were generally lower under the progressive administrations of Kim Dae-jung and Roh Moo-hyun, increased substantially under conservative presidents Lee Myung-bak and Park Geun-hye, and were again affected by diplomatic engagement under Moon Jae-in. These patterns are consistent with progressive administrations’ greater emphasis on creating diplomatic space for negotiations with the North and conservative administrations’ stronger emphasis on deterrence and alliance cohesion.

Trump’s decision should therefore be understood within this broader political context. Indeed, his own explanations identified several purposes for the same reduction: reducing costs, signaling restraint toward North Korea, and expressing dissatisfaction with Seoul over Iran. The reduction’s material features cannot establish which purpose predominates or how different audiences will interpret it.

Interpreting the Wider Exercise Program

Recent developments illustrate why Ulchi’s reduction should also be understood within the wider pattern of South Korea-U.S. military cooperation. In an interview with the Financial Times, U.S. Army Pacific commander General Ronald Clark emphasized both displaying military capabilities to influence adversaries’ calculations and strengthening military partnerships. His account illustrates how the two functions can reinforce one another: military partnerships help sustain the access and cooperation through which forces demonstrate capability and resolve.

South Korea-U.S. cooperation has continued despite the reduction in Ulchi. Eighth Army commander Lieutenant General Joe Hilbert clarified that other combined training continued, although some activities affected by Trump’s order were conducted by South Korean forces alone. Continued trilateral training through Freedom Edge and South Korea’s observer participation in Keen Sword also demonstrate different forms of military engagement. Observation offers opportunities for familiarity and relationship building without active participation in training. These activities do not cancel out Ulchi’s reduction, but they complicate its interpretation as a broader withdrawal from military cooperation.

Exercise design can also change in response to operational requirements. U.S. Forces Korea commander General Xavier Brunson has proposed more frequent training and geographically dispersed operations, drawing lessons from Ukraine about the vulnerability of concentrated command posts. He suggested the possibility of expanding the scope of exercises from Jeju Island to Gyeonggi Province, while also adjusting the training schedule to include additional smaller-scale drills between the two large annual exercises, Freedom Shield and Ulchi Freedom Shield. Frequency, geographic reach, and the concentration of forces need not change together. Thus, the size of a single exercise therefore provides an incomplete picture of the training program. Whether audiences interpret such changes as reinforcing alliance commitments or altering priorities depends on their political context.

Reducing Ulchi or cancelling a single amphibious exercise does not erase South Korea-U.S. warfighting capability. The institutional defense relationship between the two militaries established over decades – combined command structures, joint planning, interoperability, established procedures, and accumulated experience and “muscle memory” – remains in place. None of this is to suggest that exercises are irrelevant to preparedness; repeated reductions or cancellations over an extended period could eventually erode South Korea-U.S. interoperability and combined warfighting effectiveness. The effects, however, would be cumulative rather than instantaneous. A reduction or cancellation of a single iteration should not be conflated with the disappearance of capabilities built through decades of combined training.

Exercise scale and scope matter, but their strategic meaning is neither fixed nor self-evident. Rather than asking simply whether the United States is exercising more or less and with whom, the more pertinent questions are what particular exercises are intended to accomplish and how Seoul, Tokyo, Washington, Pyongyang, Beijing and other regional audiences interpret them. The deterrent or diplomatic value of an exercise ultimately lies not simply in how many troops participate, but in the political meaning that states attach to their participation – or absence.
tag: Military Exercises; U.S.-ROK alliance; U.S.-South Korea alliance; U.S.-South Korea military exercises; Ulchi Freedom Shield

title: What the Greens Misunderstand About the Ukraine Conflict
description: As a policy, the Greens decision to not support military assistance to Ukraine is a deeply flawed one. As a political position it is self-defeating, too.
text:
At the end of September, the Australian Greens elected David Shoebridge their new leader. Shoebridge had previously been the party’s spokesperson for foreign affairs and defense, and he retained those responsibilities. While he has always been a combative politician, he immediately created controversy by stating it would be the Greens’ policy to oppose providing further military assistance to Ukraine. Extraordinarily, in a meeting with a number of Ukrainian-Australian community groups last week he left a further sour taste by informing them to not “burn any bridges” by criticizing the Greens.

Shoebridge has said that the party is one of “peace and non-violence,” but within this perspective comes a number of often naïve assumptions about international relations and how states manage conflict. It leads to an odd scenario whereby in proclaiming to be advocates of peace and nonviolence the Greens end up supporting belligerents over victims.

There are some common traits that “pacifist” parties exhibit that are worth analyzing to understand the Greens’ position.

The first is that they see violence as a self-perpetuating system. War creates a cycle of fear, militarization, and retaliation. The participants become trapped in an escalating security dilemma – each interpreting the other’s actions as a threat. Therefore peace requires breaking this cycle through restraint, negotiation, and disarmament. This may seem rational on the surface, but it doesn’t account for bad faith actors who believe solely in domination and cannot be trusted to honor any negotiated deal. This is the type of state Ukraine is facing with Russia.

Alongside this, there is a distrust of the distinction between offensive and defensive power. There is a belief that all military power is essentially used for offensive purposes to varying degrees. Based on that assumption, states which arm themselves in defense – or become a part of an alliance system – are creating the conditions for aggressive actions to occur. Yet this assumes that larger states will naturally respect the sovereignty of their smaller neighbors if they are not armed. This, again, is a misunderstanding of Russia, which views weakness, not strength, as an incentive to escalate.

What pacifists often believe is that nonviolent resistance is an underutilized alternative to military resistance. There have, of course, been instances where nonviolent resistance has proved incredibly effective, in India during British rule, for example. But nonviolent resistance relies on two factors – when an occupying force requires the assistance of the invaded population, and when this force has enough of a moral compass to be able form some empathy for those it has invaded. Russia simply does not believe that Ukraine is a legitimate nation-state. A disarmed Ukraine is a nonexistent Ukraine.

For some pacifists the priority is to stop conflict, even if the resulting settlement leaves the aggressor state with territorial or political gains. A ceasefire can be argued as saving lives. Yet any settlement that rewards aggression may be an encouragement for further aggression. Russia not only sees Ukraine as an illegitimate state, but also Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Georgia, and Moldova. Rewarding Russia for its invasion of Ukraine sends a signal that it can make military gains in these states too.

The concept of deterrence is built on the assumption that there will always be belligerence in the world and that peace requires demonstrating and communicating clearly through credible military power that this belligerence will not succeed. For parties like the Greens this is a difficult assumption to swallow. Their belief is that peace can be secured through diplomacy and “good vibes” alone.

The danger within this pacifism is that it becomes an inflexible political doctrine that treats a refusal to use force as a self-perceived moral victory, and overlooks the actual victims of violence. It confuses the insisted innocence of their own actions with the justice of a real world outcome.

As a policy, the Greens decision to not support military assistance to Ukraine is a deeply flawed one, but as a political position it is self-defeating. Support for military assistance to Ukraine is a popular position in Australia, and many people believe that Australia should be doing more to help.

Support for the Greens themselves has plateaued at around 12 percent of the Australian public. The party’s approach is mostly to cultivate its status within this 12 percent and they seem disinclined to try to speak to anyone else. Therefore, the party’s position on military assistance to Ukraine probably has less to do with Ukraine itself, and was simply devised as a form of internal moral posturing with little comprehension how peace and security are actually achieved.
tag: Australia Ukraine response; Australian Greens; Greens; Pacifism; Russia-Ukraine war; Ukraine conflict

title: What the New China-North Korea Bridge Really Means
description: 12 years after construction finished, the New Yalu River Bridge is finally open. Will North Korea's economy open too?
text:
The New Yalu River Bridge, which links Dandong in China’s Liaoning province with Sinuiju in North Pyongan province, has finally opened, a full 12 years after construction finished in 2014. The two countries held an opening ceremony on October 15 and began running cargo trucks across the bridge, which is known as the Amnok River bridge in North Korea.

For years the bridge symbolized China-North Korea economic cooperation and also the practical limits on how far that cooperation could actually go. Now it is finally doing the job it was built for.

The two countries agreed to build the bridge in 2009, and construction began the following year. It was a major project meant to get past the logistical limits of the existing Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge. A four-lane bridge more than 3 kilometers (1.9 miles) long could greatly expand the flow of goods between Dandong and Sinuiju. China was willing to pay for construction to open a new channel for economic cooperation with the North.

Fifteen years ago, I was reporting for Daily NK in China. Back then, Dandong was full of anticipation about the bridge. People everywhere said a new crossing would bring a surge in China-North Korea trade, and that a new economic zone would grow up around Sinuiju and Dandong. Chinese businesspeople expected trade with the North to expand, and property prices near the planned development areas began to climb.

In August 2011, Daily NK reported that work on a pontoon bridge for the construction was 70 percent complete and that nearby real estate prices were rising. Some in Dandong even speculated that the bridge might lead North Korea to open its economy more widely. I still remember that mood clearly from my time on the ground.

Reality fell short of those hopes. The bridge was finished in 2014, but the North Korean side never properly built the connecting roads or customs facilities. Ups and downs in bilateral relations, international sanctions, and the COVID-19 border closure followed, and the bridge stayed shut for years. It was a long wait for the Chinese businesspeople who had hoped for new opportunities, and for everyone who had expected trade with the North to grow.

North Korea’s insularity alone doesn’t explain the delay. The two countries’ economic interests, the political climate, sanctions, and other factors all played a part. What is clear, though, is that North Korean authorities took a long and cautious approach to how much economic contact with the outside world they would allow, and how they would manage it.

In the end, the hard part was not building the bridge. It was getting past the North Korean authorities’ extremely narrow threshold. Pyongyang wanted the economic benefits, but it never let down its guard against the changes outside contact might bring. The 12 years the bridge sat effectively unused lay bare this contradiction at the heart of the North Korean economy.

More Trade Means New Opportunities and New Tests

So now that the bridge is open, will North Korea’s economy change? In the short term, we can expect more trade and more efficient transport between the two countries. Freight that used to pile onto the Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge can now be spread out, and there is finally a route that can reliably carry larger volumes of goods.

Still, it would be a mistake to assume the opening will quickly produce a jump in trade or better lives for ordinary North Koreans. How much actually moves will depend on customs procedures, transport costs, trade permits, and how goods are distributed inside North Korea. A wider bridge does not necessarily mean North Korea’s economy has opened any wider.

The bigger story may be how distribution inside North Korea changes. Markets are still central to how ordinary North Koreans make a living. Lately, however, the authorities have not simply been suppressing the general markets. They have been using state-run stores, state grain shops, and other retail outlets to expand state control over distribution and sales.

Under these conditions, if more imports flow across the bridge, state-approved trading companies and distribution agencies are likely to benefit first. In the past, private merchants brought in imported goods through various channels and supplied them to markets. That model may give way further to one where the state manages the import and allocation of goods, with markets and retail outlets operating beneath it.

Private merchants could still find new openings. More stable logistics and a larger supply of Chinese consumer goods and raw materials could mean more choice for shoppers and steadier prices for some items. If factories and enterprises can source raw materials more easily, production could benefit too.

But if the state tightens its grip on imports and distribution, the gains could concentrate in the agencies that hold trade permits and the power to allocate goods. Private merchants would become more dependent on state-designated distribution channels, and the various costs and informal payments they face could well rise.

How the bridge ties into North Korea’s “20×10” regional development policy is also worth watching. The North is racing to build local industrial factories, but putting up a building is one thing and running a factory is another. What matters is not how many factories have been built. It is how many days a month they actually run, where their raw materials come from, and what prices residents pay for what they produce. Without a steady supply of raw materials, electricity, and production equipment, these factories will struggle to operate.

Here, more Chinese raw materials and supplies could improve operating conditions at some local factories. Yet the more these factories rely on Chinese inputs, the further they drift from the self-reliant local economy the authorities keep promoting.

Development around Sinuiju also deserves attention. According to a recent Daily NK investigation, North Korea has reportedly pitched Chinese businesspeople on a plan to develop the area behind the bridge and some 40 square kilometers (15 square miles) of southern Sinuiju into an economic hub for logistics, processing, trade, and commerce. This suggests Pyongyang wants to use the bridge’s opening to make more economic use of the border region.

We should still separate development plans from actual investment and production. Current United Nations sanctions sharply restrict imports of industrial equipment, exports of North Korean processed goods, and joint ventures. Early on, the benefits will likely be limited to better customs and logistics, with any large-scale industrial cooperation moving slowly.

Above all, North Korea’s economy could become even more dependent on China. Deeper reliance on Chinese raw materials, consumer goods, capital, and logistics networks might give the economy a short-term lift. It could also leave the economy more exposed to shifts in Chinese policy and trade conditions. The gap between the self-reliance the regime preaches and its real dependence on China could grow wider.

Ultimately, the bridge’s opening is both an opportunity and a major test for North Korea’s economy. The question is what the authorities do with the extra goods and economic openings. Will they let ordinary people expand their economic activity, or will the state tighten its hold on profits and distribution channels? The answer looks set to shape the structure of North Korea’s economy in the years ahead.

The Real Measure Is How People Live

The number of trucks crossing the bridge is not the only thing to watch. Actual freight volumes, the goods being traded, customs procedures, and shipping costs all matter. But to really judge how North Korea’s economy is changing, we need to follow where those goods go, who controls the trade, and how it ultimately affects people’s daily lives.

That means tracking specific economic indicators over time. How many trucks cross the bridge each month? How much does the share of Chinese goods in markets change? How are people’s purchases split between state-run outlets and the general markets, and how is that changing?

We also need to look at how many days local factories with more Chinese inputs actually run and how much they produce, and how more imports affect consumer prices and people’s purchasing power.

With these questions in mind, the Daily NK sees a need to keep tracking changes in North Korea’s economic structure and in people’s living conditions. Comparing trends at three months, six months, and one year after the opening should give a clearer picture of how the economy is really changing.

What matters here is the direction of change, not whether a single number rises or falls. If imports go up but purchasing power doesn’t improve, we need to find out why. If state stores see more customers, we need to know whether private market trade is shrinking or whether both are growing. More goods coming in and people finding it easier to buy things are two very different matters.

In particular, comparing economic conditions in major cities such as Sinuiju (North Pyongan province), Pyongsong (South Pyongan province), and Hyesan (Ryanggang province) can show whether more border trade is reaching people inland and in the provinces. Even if imports grow at the border, distribution costs and local supply conditions mean residents in different areas may feel the change very differently.

We also need to see whether development in Sinuiju actually creates jobs and raises incomes. New facilities, roads, and housing are hard to count as a success if residents are hit with demands for money or forced labor mobilizations along the way. Beyond how the development looks, we need to see who bears the costs and who reaps the benefits.

Sanctions enforcement also remains an important issue. Expanded trade in legitimate goods for ordinary people must be clearly distinguished from transfers of sanctioned items. We need to check whether wider economic cooperation becomes a channel for evading sanctions. At the same time, we need to look closely at how much legitimate trade and economic activity, the kind needed to improve people’s lives, is actually happening.

The people I met in Dandong 15 years ago expected North Korea to change once the new bridge was built. Instead, the finished bridge stayed closed for 12 years. Things are clearly different now. North Korea needs more trade and practical economic gains, and China wants to expand its influence through economic cooperation with the North.

Even so, we shouldn’t simply repeat the hopes of that time. Expanded China-North Korea economic ties will not automatically mean freer markets or more freedom for people to make a living. North Korea has a history of chasing economic gains while tightening control over markets and ordinary people’s economic activity.

The New Yalu River Bridge is finally open. But the true test of change in North Korea’s economy won’t be the trucks crossing it. It will be what North Korean society does with the goods they carry.

We now need to look more closely at what is happening on the North Korean side of the bridge: how state control is shifting, how the markets are adapting, and whether people’s lives are getting even a little better. What matters more than the bridge opening is how far the changes it brings actually reach ordinary North Koreans. That is where our view of the New Yalu River Bridge, open after 12 years, should begin.

title: What the Ukrainian Strikes on Yandex Tell Us About Central Asia’s Digital Infrastructure
description: Drone strikes on Yandex data centers near Moscow triggered service outages in Central Asia, too.
text:
Over the last weekend, three Yandex facilities in Russia have been struck by Ukrainian drones, with Russian users subsequently reporting outages across Yandex’s services. After the third strike, on a data center east of Moscow in Vladimir, Central Asian users of Yandex’s superapp Yandex Go began reporting outages too.

Yandex is one of Russia’s largest technology companies, with a portfolio that resembles a hybrid of Google and Uber, but for the русский мир, the Russian world. Yandex Search holds an estimated 72 percent of market share in Russia while maintaining an estimated search engine market share in Kazakhstan of just under 30 percent. It is with its superapp, Yandex Go – which combines ride-sharing with food delivery and other services – that Yandex dominates in Central Asia.

In 2017 Uber effectively ceded Central Asia to Yandex, agreeing to merge operations in Azerbaijan, Armenia, Belarus and Kazakhstan, where the two companies had previously competed. Yandex Go expanded to Kyrgyzstan in 2017 and to Uzbekistan in 2018. A 2023 effort to enter the Tajik market was defeated by Dushanbe. In 2023, Yandex bought Uber out of the joint venture, becoming the undisputed ride-sharing and food delivery leader in the Central Asian region.

On October 11, following the strike on Yandex’s Vladimir facility, Yandex customers in Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan began reporting trouble booking rides, ordering food and accessing their accounts. The press services of Yandex Qazaqstan, Yandex Kyrgyzstan, and Yandex Uzbekistan all acknowledged technical issues to local media outlets and said they had teams working to restore services.

Although services have reportedly resumed, at least in Kazakhstan, Russian media reports stated that it could take months to restore operations at the affected data centers. And that doesn’t factor in possible future strikes.

Kazakhstan’s Agency for the Protection and Development of Competition reportedly issued a warning to inDrive, an alternative ride-sharing app which operates in the country, after its prices spiked during the Yandex outage. As users shifted from the inoperable Yandex Go app to inDrive, prices went up dramatically. The agency claimed that in some cases the cost of rides tripled.

According to RFE/RL’s Kazakh Service, InDrive founder Arsen Tomsky “attributed the price hike to a sharp increase in demand and a shortage of available vehicles.”

This is just another way in which the Russian war in Ukraine has had knock-on effects in Central Asia. While complicating deliveries of KFC, plov or lagman late at night may not rank as the most critical of issues, this incident does underscore that Central Asia’s digital infrastructure remains closely linked with Russia’s. Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development stressed that the personal data of Kazakh users of Yandex is safe because it is stored on servers in Kazakhstan. But the overarching architecture – the technical bits that connect a person to a driver – is not, and therefore risks posed to Russia’s digital infrastructure will continue to spill over into Central Asia.

Ukraine, for its part, positioned its attacks on Russian data centers as retaliation for Russia’s strikes against Ukrainian data centers. Kyiv also claimed that its attacks targeted centers that provide revenue streams to Moscow. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said at the Warsaw Security Forum on October 12 that “everyone noticed” a drop in Russian bot activity on social media after the strikes. The reality of that claim is, as these things tend to be, far more complicated.
tag: Central Asia Ukraine response; ride-sharing apps; Russia-Ukraine war; Russian invasion of Ukraine; Yandex

title: What the US and China Should Discuss at APEC
description: Both sides are feeding an AI investment bubble – and Shenzhen is the place to talk about it.
text:
On September 24, the presidents of the United States and China met in Washington and agreed to build what their joint language calls a “constructive relationship of strategic stability.” On November 18-19, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping are expected to meet again, on the sidelines of the APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting in Shenzhen. Two summits in three months is a rare occurrence in China-U.S. relations.

In the September summit, already their second of 2026, one key area stood out as the focus: artificial intelligence. The risks of AI now have a dedicated channel for discussion. There’s not yet a corresponding China-U.S. platform for talking about the economics of the AI race.

During Trump’s state visit to Beijing in May, the two leaders agreed to restart government-to-government AI dialogue. In September, at the eighth round of economic consultations in New York and Washington, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng held the first AI dialogue within that framework. They agreed to establish a channel for communications on AI incidents, and scheduled a second round of talks before the end of November.

Shortly thereafter, at the presidential summit, Xi described China and the United States as two AI powers that should “draw on each other’s strengths, not guard against each other.” He added, “The two sides can continue their dialogue on AI, exchange views on its risks and benefits, and jointly prevent the misuse and abuse of AI.” Trump noted that discussions on “pressing issues” related to (among other topics) AI, which he calls “superintelligence,” could “promote peace and prosperity for decades and decades to come.” Both leaders thus offered the new dialogue platform political cover.

That is genuine progress, with a revealing limit. All the steps thus far – the exchanges on risks and benefits, the incident channel, the push for lab self-regulation – concern the dangers AI might create. Nothing yet addresses the looming economic problem of the AI sector.

The Growing AI Bubble

In the United States, recent developments are rather worrying. The business model for U.S. frontier AI businesses assumes that compute demand will keep growing exponentially, model capability will convert reliably into revenue, and capital will stay patient. All three assumptions are looking increasingly risky.

The capex needed to remain at the frontier is heavier, relative to the industry’s age, than anything technology has carried before. Utilities are signing power contracts for gigawatts of capacity that do not exist.

Meanwhile, Wall Street has started asking a question it ignored a year ago: where, exactly, is the return? In July, efficient Chinese open-weight models showed that frontier-level performance could be reached with a fraction of the compute. AI-linked U.S. equities sold off hard; analysts stepped back from price targets built on the assumption of permanent scarcity.

China has the mirror-image problem. Chinese companies are trying to close the frontier gap under foreign constraints while having to produce returns large enough to justify the spending at home. In a September study, the Rhodium Group calculated that the combined free cash flow of Chinese tech giants Alibaba, Tencent, and Baidu swung from positive 170 billion yuan in 2025 to negative 16 billion yuan in the first half of 2026.

The five American hyperscalers saw their own fall from $191 billion to $14 billion and raised $163 billion in long-term debt in six months to keep building.

Clearly, neither the U.S. nor the Chinese AI sector can fund this race from operations anymore. Both countries’ capital markets are tired of narratives without actual returns. Patience on both sides is wearing thin.

The China-U.S. competition exacerbates these economic dynamics. Each new round of U.S. export controls accelerates the Chinese substitution process, which shrinks the market available for American firms. At the same time, deeper substitution raises the investment China must absorb, which worsens China’s return-on-capital problem.

In other words, further escalation in the AI race might drain away the capital both systems depends on. This is not a moral argument, but a real financial dilemma.

Washington and Beijing have already conceded, in their September dialogue, that they face some common risks from AI risks. What’s not clear is whether the economic problem is included on that agenda.

The Chance at Shenzhen

The November APEC summit offers an unusually practical setting for addressing this issue. The APEC CEO Summit will bring about 1,000 business leaders to Shenzhen with AI on the formal agenda and a Shenzhen Initiative to be released. The host city itself, long nicknamed the Silicon Valley of the East, holds China’s densest cluster of AI and robotics firms.

Unofficial channels are also in place. Tsinghua’s Center for International Security and Strategy and the Brookings Institution have hosted 14 rounds of China-U.S. AI dialogue since 2019, with Microsoft’s former chief research and strategy officer Craig Mundie serving as a co-chair.

Three deliverables should be on the agenda for the APEC meeting.

First, China and the United States should add the missing piece of the puzzle in Shenzhen. The official AI dialogue will be held in November; at the APEC summit, both sides can start a standing China-U.S. AI economics dialogue mechanism supported by think tanks and industry associations, the “track two” format long used in China-U.S. exchanges.

Every official AI conversation so far lacks the people who control the money: finance officials, stock market regulators, and executives. The first such dialogue could take place on the margins of the APEC meeting, convened by think tanks and industry associations rather than ministries.

In Shenzhen, the Guangdong Artificial Intelligence Industry Association – which operates the Guangdong AI & Robotics Overseas Service Center, the province’s platform for firms going global – could co-convene, alongside established think tanks, a working session between U.S. investors, analysts, and executives and their Guangdong counterparts, on the industry’s own ground.

Why start with the “track two” format? Because the U.S. and Chinese governments would find it hard to host this conversation. No U.S. administration can openly entertain the thought that its AI boom may be overextended; no Chinese ministry can candidly compare burn rates with a foreign power. Finance officials can talk to economists, and economists can talk to each other. An unofficial venue is the only why this particular talk can happen.

Second, China and the United States should set a floor under export controls and market access in Shenzhen. Neither side can afford to be seen conducting negotiations over such fundamental issues, but they can quietly exchange red lines in a private setting. Misjudgment, not malice, triggers most crises. The cheapest deterrent is a sentence spoken early.

Third, it’s time to increase collaborations on the periphery. Standards for AI deployment in third countries – things like data governance, safety evaluation, labor displacement – don’t always pit U.S. and Chinese interests against each other. In fact, that happens far less often than either side assumes. Shenzhen has already hosted APEC-track discussions on responsible AI under the Policy Partnership on Science, Technology and Innovation framework. A joint signal from Washington and Beijing supporting shared regional norms would cost little, match the CEO Summit’s own agenda, and keep third parties from profiting from dueling standards.

Time Is Short

By greenlighting discussions on the economic side of AI, Washington would be shifting a burden, not making a concession. Industry leaders and academic would be the interlocutors, meaning the administration does not need to make more promises even while the Treasury gains more insight into AI’s financial stability.

For its part, Beijing would reinforce its longstanding claim that Chinese AI is an economic project rather than a military one. The talks would also give China’s capital-hungry sector a forum to argue against escalation using commercial – not diplomatic – logic.

The dialogue wouldn’t release a communiqué or joint statement. This would be a recurring conversation that, over time, builds a shared vocabulary for what sustainable AI competition could look like.

The capital markets are not waiting; they are repricing both countries’ AI sectors now. There’s still a chance for China and the U.S. to get ahead of the bubble, but the window is closing. After the U.S. midterms, coalition politics in Washington will harden, and every unmanaged month afterwards would strengthen the case for constraint in Beijing.

title: What the US PERM Freeze Really Costs India’s IT Industry
description: The immediate impact of Washington’s decision on green card certification for eight IT employers may be limited, but the freeze adds uncertainty to an immigration system already strained by decades-long queues.
text:
On October 8, 2026, the U.S. Department of Labor decided to stop processing PERM labor-certification requests from eight technology firms, including Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL Technologies, and Capgemini. The Department of Labor said it would neither accept new applications nor process pending applications involving the named companies.

PERM, or Program Electronic Review Management, is the initial step in the employment-based green card process for most immigrants applying under the EB-2 and EB-3 categories. In order to proceed to the next stage, employers are required to prove that they have tried to hire Americans for the jobs in question.

The processing of the applications has been suspended in accordance with 20 CFR § 656.31(b), which allows for the temporary interruption of services if there are grounds to believe that fraud or willful misrepresentation is involved.

Vice President J.D. Vance accused companies that employ people on H-1B visas of creating a caste of foreign indentured servants. Notwithstanding the administration’s justification, allegations must not be confused with provided proof of fraudulent activity.

On the heels of the H-1B controversy came reports of investigations into the J-1 visa program, involving dozens of American universities. In the context of Vance’s comments on H-1B visas and intensified scrutiny of J-1, the latest development suggest that the debate over the United States’ immigration policy and the prospects of its labor market will continue to gain momentum. This would, in the meantime, systematically erode India’s IT service sector’s integrative loop with American companies and vice versa.

The H-1B-to-green-card process has three basic stages: entering the United States, living there as a worker, and eventually receiving permanent residency. Each of these possesses its own restrictions.

Indian nationals comprise a significant part of successful H-1B applicants. A U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services’ FY2024 H-1B characteristics report said that Indians comprised 71 percent of successful applicants in 2024.

The H-1B has become an IT program. Infotech workers made up 32 percent of H-1B holders in fiscal year 2003 and averaged over 65 percent across the last five fiscal years. H-1B status permits temporary employment, subject to immigration rules and the conditions of the petition. Workers may continue working lawfully while their green card applications are delayed, provided their existing authorization remains valid.

PERM falls under the third step, which concerns the transition from being a temporary resident to receiving permanent residency. The suspension interrupts a stage of the process for affected applications, potentially delaying workers’ transition to permanent residency. Its consequences depend on the status of each application.

Given a massive backlog, the PERM suspension impacts individual workers. But its immediate relevance for corporate profits is limited.

The Cato Institute estimated the U.S. employment-based waiting list to contain approximately 1.8 million people in 2023, around 1.1 million of whom are Indians. This puts the portion of Indians in the queue at around 68 percent. The report estimated the time necessary to clear the backlog for Indian applicants to be up to 134 years, with approximately 424,000 Indians expected to die before obtaining a visa.

This might have more of an impact than it seems. Permanent residency is a significant factor in the worker’s life, affecting their decision-making and planning. Another obstacle in their employment-based residency application might disrupt their lives severely.

Even before the PERM suspension, the U.S. immigration system was becoming more expensive and unpredictable. The Trump administration announced a $100,000 H-1B fine announced in September 2025. That was later clarified by USCIS to be applicable only to petitions made after September 21, 2025, as a one-time payment rather than an annual renewal.

Employers are adjusting their strategies accordingly. An RBI survey tracked an erosion in on-site revenues, from $19 billion to $18.4 billion. These are wages paid to staff members who work at client facilities overseas. The reduction implies that the traditional approach of sending numerous Indian professionals to work overseas is being de-emphasized relative to other approaches to technology services delivery.

Nasscom data revealed that Indian IT revenue totaled $315 billion in FY2025-26, up 6.1 percent, with exports of $246 billion, up 5.6 percent. The industry employed some 5.95 million workers and created about 135,000 net jobs in the past fiscal year. An American client can continue to buy software development, consulting, maintenance, and other tech services from an Indian team without requiring those professionals to be based inside the United States.

A restriction on permanent residency might well impose genuine costs on workers while having limited impact on the revenue-generating capabilities of their employers. The impact will vary from company to company, project to project, and staffing model to staffing model, but the market’s response to the policy change need not reflect the impact on individual workers’ circumstances.

For Indian IT companies, the PERM freeze may prove a small financial blow rather than a major threat to their business model. Most of their American revenue streams do not rely on having every employee on their payroll based in the U.S., and the fall in on-site earnings suggests an industry growing more capable of providing services beyond borders.

For Indian professionals, the implications are more personal. A green card process that already takes years to complete has just become even more unpredictable for those considering applying, and for whose employers are affected. Even if their American jobs are unaffected, their plans for permanent residency may be set back.

For India, the long-term impact is harder to assess. Restrictions on immigration may motivate multinational companies to invest more in local infrastructure, creating jobs and cementing India’s role as a center for tech production. But it would also shift work away from Indian outsourcing firms and toward the captive centers of their American clients.

The short-term financial pain may be minimal. The anxiety for those affected, however, is far greater. And the longer-term challenge will be whether the U.S. can prevent a rush to move work to where it will have value, by closing access to where it currently does.

This moment also marks a troubling low-threshold point in India-U.S. relations, almost causing an irreparable harm to the long diplomatic relationship between the two countries. First, tariffs on Indian imports, and now restrictions on skilled human capital mobility from India to U.S. companies could erode and dismantle core areas of economic integration between the two countries, which were cementing a strong political bond as well.

Where this leaves India and its economic integration strategy viz-a-viz the U.S. (amidst a more conflicted relationship with China) should trouble policymakers more than it seems to do in the current scenario.

title: What Would Europe Do in a Taiwan Crisis?
description: Washington should not take European assistance for granted, especially if states can't agree on how to label Beijing's actions.
text:
Imagine that, one morning, Chinese coast guard vessels begin stopping commercial ships approaching Taiwan. Beijing offers the official explanation that the operation is necessary to enforce customs regulations and maritime safety and makes clear that it does not consider this a blockade, let alone an act of war. Taipei clearly sees things differently and calls it an attempt to blockade the island. Washington agrees with Taipei.

Europe, however, is less certain, with some governments demanding that China stop its actions while others start calling for restraint and dialogue. Officials begin debating whether the operation constitutes an armed attack, what international law permits, and whether sanctions against China would be justified. Meanwhile the effects on global trade start to be felt as insurers raise premiums, shipping companies start to reroute vessels, and financial markets react nervously.

At that point, Washington steps up and asks its European allies to impose economic costs on Beijing. The answer from Europe could very likely be an attempt to win more time to determine what is happening. That delay could incidentally be precisely what Beijing is aiming to achieve: deliberate ambiguity, namely the systematic creation of legal and political uncertainty designed to make an adversary hesitate over how to respond.

We have already seen elements of this approach tested on Taiwan. In June 2026, Chinese coast guard vessels conducted patrols east of Taiwan, described by Beijing as lawful maritime enforcement, while Taiwan accused China of asserting jurisdiction over commercial shipping. The United States, Britain, France, and Germany subsequently expressed concern about the operations but their protest remained at the level of rhetoric. Barely a week later, in July, Taiwan observed a sharp increase in Chinese coast guard and research vessel activities and publicly warned that such operations could be connected to preparations to disrupt maritime supply routes.

Even though such actions can be seen as acts of rehearsal, they cannot be interpreted as definitive proof that Beijing has undeniably decided to blockade Taiwan. They definitely show one thing, though: namely, how easily a future crisis could be presented in opposite ways by different sides, and how this difference could complicate a unified response between Washington and its allies.

This is one fallacy Washington should avoid: assuming that because Europe is an ally and it has enormous collective economic power, that power will automatically be available as a coherent instrument in a crisis, side by side with Washington. It may not be. The United States should therefore be encouraging and, where necessary, nudging, European governments to develop contingency plans before a crisis begins, precisely so that their institutional structure does not become an advantage for Beijing.

There is a structural reason why Europe could struggle to use its leverage quickly. The European project was built above all through economic integration – a common market, common rules and, for much of the European Union, a common currency. Foreign and security policy evolved differently and remains largely in the hands of national governments. The EU’s Common Foreign and Security Policy generally requires unanimity, as do the sanctions decisions that would be among the most important instruments available in a Taiwan crisis.

This division matters because a blockade would sit precisely at the intersection of economic and foreign policy: European governments could agree that Taiwan’s security matters while disagreeing over whether Chinese actions constitute a sufficient trigger for collective economic measures. The European Parliament has already recognized the need for contingency planning, explicitly calling for preparations for scenarios including an economic blockade of Taiwan. But planning for a contingency is not the same thing as having a common response ready to deploy.

A blockade could therefore confront Washington with two crises at once: a crisis around Taiwan and a crisis within the coalition supporting Taiwan.

Beijing could exploit precisely those divisions by threatening restrictions against particular European countries or companies, using its monopoly on critical materials and rare earths as leverage, or offering selective economic incentives. The objective would be to make European governments reluctant to support measures that might trigger further retaliation.

And to this point, there is another complication that Washington should not overlook in its strategic planning. European governments are already reassessing their dependence on the United States as they assume a greater share of the burden for Ukraine and confront uncertainty over the future of the transatlantic relationship under President Donal Trump. At NATO’s 2026 summit, European allies and Canada acknowledged that they now finance the vast majority of security assistance to Ukraine, while Reuters has reported growing European efforts to diversify away from U.S. defense technology amid doubts about the reliability of American commitments.

European governments are not abandoning the alliance – many continue to emphasize its importance – but they are increasingly preparing for a world in which U.S. priorities may shift more abruptly than in the past. In such an environment, a Taiwan crisis could arrive at precisely the wrong moment: when Washington expects Europe to follow its lead, some European governments may opt instead for asking how far they should go in assuming the economic and political costs of confronting China and of following the United States, in spite of the obvious fact that a Taiwan crisis would have direct consequences for Europe’s own security, economy, and strategic interests.

Europe and the world should prepare for such contingencies. In less than two years Taiwan is scheduled to hold another presidential election on its regular four-year cycle, following the January 2024 election. This makes 2028 a useful planning horizon, since a new government in Taipei could produce renewed tensions with Beijing, depending on its policies and Beijing’s reaction. The point is not to predict that a crisis will occur in 2028, but to ensure that Washington and its European allies do not discover the limits of their respective contingency plans only after a new political configuration in Taiwan has already raised tensions.

Therefore, the United States and its European allies should privately work through concrete scenarios – prolonged inspections of commercial vessels, selective denial of port access, Chinese coast guard “escorts,” restrictions on shipping insurance, interference with critical infrastructure, and economic retaliation against individual European states. The objective would not be to predetermine every possible scenario or response, but to prevent the first days of a crisis from being consumed by arguments over terminology and definition.

More concretely than that, such preparation also needs to extend beyond the level of governments by including shipping companies, insurers, ports, banks, technology firms, and semiconductor manufacturers – actors who would would make decisions before diplomats reached an agreement. This would also have a plus side: European governments will be more willing to support collective measures if they know that the costs of Chinese retaliation will not fall disproportionately on one or two vulnerable countries.

None of this would require Europe to adopt Washington’s China policy or promise military intervention in a Taiwan conflict. The goal, instead, is agreement in advance about which forms of coercion would cross a line, what economic measures could be considered, and how their costs could be shared.

The United States has spent years strengthening military deterrence around Taiwan, yet the next Taiwan crisis may not begin with an invasion but with a disagreement over what to call what is happening. Washington’s task, therefore, is not to lament Europe’s fragmentation or demand that it simply follow the American lead, but to work with European governments now to overcome the structural obstacles that could turn hesitation into paralysis when a Taiwan crisis comes.

title: Whither Japan’s Three Non-Nuclear Principles?
description: A highly contentious debate is in the offing.
text:
Debate over the three non-nuclear principles has resurfaced in Japan as the government of Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae prepares a new National Security Strategy, due at the end of 2026. Even the status of the principles is contested. Some regard them as the country’s foundational principle (kokuze), while others describe them as a policy guideline, suggesting that the government is free to change it. Prime Minister Sato Eisaku first announced the principles in 1967, and the Diet has reaffirmed them on multiple occasions since then.

The principles state that Japan will neither possess nor produce nuclear weapons, nor permit their introduction into its territory. As long as Japan remains a party to the Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT), the only practical debate concerns the third principle: non-introduction. The commitments not to possess or produce nuclear weapons nevertheless sent an important message to the world when the principles were first articulated, before Japan ratified the NPT.

In March 2010, Foreign Minister Okada Katsuya revealed that a secret agreement (mitsuyaku), broadly defined, had existed between Washington and Tokyo over the introduction of nuclear weapons. Under the U.S. interpretation, “introduction” referred only to the permanent deployment of nuclear warheads in storage facilities ashore. The Japanese government, by contrast, regarded transit through Japan’s territorial waters or port calls by nuclear-armed vessels as introduction as well. Successive Japanese leaders maintained that, in the absence of a U.S. request for “prior consultation” under the arrangements associated with the U.S.-Japan Security Treaty of 1960, Tokyo assumed that visiting U.S. vessels were not carrying nuclear weapons. Yet such vessels could not simply leave their nuclear weapons elsewhere before entering Japan. It is now an open secret that, under the Japanese definition, the United States “introduced” nuclear weapons into Japan during the Cold War.

Since the revelation in March 2010, Tokyo has maintained that there is no need to be concerned about introduction because the United States does not deploy nuclear weapons on surface vessels and has no nuclear weapon system for the vessels that regularly visit Japan. At the same time, successive Japanese governments have upheld the position Okada first articulated in the Diet that month: in extreme circumstances in which Japan’s survival cannot be secured without allowing the introduction of nuclear weapons, the government of the day “shall make a decision by taking full responsibility.” This effectively leaves open the possibility of permitting introduction in a contingency. Some therefore argue there is no need to revise the three non-nuclear principles, since they have already become “two and a half” principles.

Okada’s formula, however, does not resolve all the problems surrounding the principles. First, it only addresses contingencies, leaving unanswered how Tokyo could handle the issue in peacetime. Second, the United States is developing a nuclear-armed sea-launched cruise missile (SLCM-N), with the aim of making it operational in the mid-2030s. While not officially confirmed yet, the missile is expected to be carried by attack submarines of the kind that regularly visit Japan. Third, Okada’s formula addresses introduction in the Japanese sense – transit and visiting – without addressing introduction in the U.S. sense: storage ashore.

Once U.S. attack submarines begin carrying SLCM-N – or, more precisely, once they become capable of carrying it – Tokyo will find it difficult to avoid allegations that the United States is introducing nuclear weapons into Japan, regardless of whether a particular visiting submarine actually carries them. Under its longstanding “neither confirm nor deny” (NCND) policy, Washington will not disclose whether visiting submarines carry nuclear weapons. Moreover, under the U.S. definition, neither transit nor port visits constitute introduction.

This will therefore be primarily a problem for Japan. Some, particularly critics of the U.S.-Japan alliance, will argue that Tokyo should ban visits by submarines that might be carrying nuclear weapons. Doing so, however, could undermine the alliance’s deterrence and damage relations with Washington.

If Tokyo rules out denying access to U.S. submarines, it has three options. First, it could drop or amend the non-introduction principle. Second, in the most far-reaching version of such a revision, it could explicitly permit the introduction of nuclear weapons, including storage ashore as well as transit and port visits, opening the way to possible future nuclear-sharing arrangements. Third, it could adopt a narrower, more technical change: revise its definition of introduction so that transit and port visits no longer fall within it, bringing Japan’s interpretation into line with that of the United States.

Whichever option Tokyo chooses, it will be highly contentious in political terms at home. Only strong political leadership could address this problem. Many politicians appear unprepared to tackle this issue now, believing that they still have time. But it is not too early to begin laying the groundwork for a decision.

title: Who Is Russia’s New Ambassador to North Korea?
description: What can Andrei Podelyshev’s appointment tell us about North Korea-Russia relations?
text:
Russia has finally filled the ambassadorial post in Pyongyang, which had sat vacant for nearly eight months. Under a decree signed by President Vladimir Putin on July 28, career diplomat Andrei Podelyshev – at the time, Russia’s ambassador to Nigeria, a post he had held since December 2024 – was named the new ambassador extraordinary and plenipotentiary to the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea. A companion decree released him from his Nigerian posting the same day.

Podelyshev arrived in Pyongyang nearly two months later, on September 26, together with his wife, aboard a direct Nordwind flight from Moscow. According to the Russian Embassy and TASS, he headed straight from the airport to the Soviet-era Liberation Monument to pay tribute to fallen Red Army soldiers, before visiting Pyongyang’s newly built memorial complex for North Korean troops killed fighting alongside Russian forces in Kursk.

Podelyshev is, on paper, one of the more genuinely “Korea-literate” diplomats Moscow could have sent. He graduated from MGIMO (the Moscow State Institute of International Relations) in 1984 and joined the Soviet Foreign Ministry that same year. He speaks both English and Korean, and over his career he has served at the Soviet embassy in Pyongyang itself, as well as at Russian missions in South Korea and the United States.

What stands out, though, is the decade he spent away from Asia desks entirely. From 2005 to 2015, Podelyshev was deputy director of the Consular Department of the Russian Foreign Ministry, the branch of the ministry responsible for visas, citizenship matters, and the movement of foreign nationals in and out of Russia.

That background is not a minor biographical footnote. Consular policy has become one of the most sensitive, and most scrutinized, levers of the entire North Korea-Russia relationship. Since 2022, Russian consular services have issued tens of thousands of visas to North Korean citizens, the overwhelming majority formally classified as “educational” visas.

According to Russia’s own data, the number of visas issued to North Koreans jumped from 9,239 in 2024 to 36,413 in 2025, with 35,849 of them, over 98 percent, nominally for education. Investigations by NK Pro and others have shown that these “student” visas are routinely used by Russian firms to bring in North Korean laborers while sidestepping United Nations Security Council Resolution 2375, which bars U.N. member states from issuing work permits to North Korean nationals.

The Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team, an 11-country group tracking sanctions evasion, went further in a report released September 16, 2026, stating, “The Russian government has created a student visa scheme to camouflage North Korean laborers in Russia as students,” including workers employed in drone manufacturing at Russian defense-industrial sites such as the Alabuga special economic zone in Tatarstan The report estimates that 15,000 to 30,000 North Korean laborers were working in Russia by the end of 2025, each generating roughly $7,500 a year in wages – up to five times what similar labor earns in China.

Sending an ambassador with nearly a decade of consular-management experience to preside over an embassy now processing this volume of visa traffic is unlikely to be a coincidence. Whether or not Podelyshev personally shaped this scheme during his 2005-2015 tenure at the Consular Department, he has strong professional grounding in the visa categories, documentation, and institutional workarounds that have made the “student visa” loophole possible in the first place.

The post of Russia’s envoy to North Korea had been empty since the death of Aleksandr Matsegora, who served as ambassador from December 2014 until December 6, 2025, when he died in Pyongyang at age 70. Matsegora, also an MGIMO graduate, held the job for just over a decade, the longest tenure of any foreign ambassador to North Korea, and was present for the relationship’s most consequential turning points, including hosting the reception marking the entry into force of the June 2024 Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty.

Matsegora’s profile was that of an Asia-desk veteran who rose through the ministry’s regional bureaucracy. His successor, Podelyshev, combines an earlier Korea specialization with a mid-career detour into consular administration and, most recently, a comparatively low-profile ambassadorship in Nigeria. He is not one of the Russian Foreign Ministry’s marquee Asia strategists; he is more of a technocrat suited to managing an embassy whose day-to-day workload – handling visas, labor migration, and logistics – has expanded dramatically alongside the military relationship.

Unlike the politically weighted appointments Russia sometimes makes to signal priority, Podelyshev is not a front-rank figure in shaping strategy toward Pyongyang. His nomination reads as a bet on administrative competence, someone who can run the visa pipeline and consular relationship, at a moment when the institution-building phase may be giving way to a more routine, logistics-heavy phase of the alliance.

Podelyshev will oversee the continued evolution of the deepest North Korea-Russia alignment since the Cold War. Since the 2024 security treaty was signed, North Korea has sent more than 10,000 troops to help Russia retake Kursk, along with supplying Russia’s military with munitions and ballistic missiles. South Korean intelligence estimates that North Korea has deployed over 16,000 troops to Russia since October 2024, alongside more than 15 million artillery rounds supplied. The United States estimates that Pyongyang earned somewhere from $7.7 billion to $14.4 billion through 2025 for its military assistance to Russia. Cooperation continues, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy saying that North Korea is preparing to deploy another 10,000 troops to Russia.

Podelyshev’s first public act, honoring both Soviet World War II dead and North Korean Kursk casualties on the same day, signaled Moscow’s intent to frame today’s military alignment as the natural extension of a Soviet-era blood bond, rather than as a wartime marriage of convenience.

But before Podelyshev arrived, Moscow left the Pyongyang post unfilled for nearly eight months, even during the most intense period of military cooperation in the relationship’s history. The extended vacancy suggests that the strategic decisions binding the two countries are being made elsewhere — through the direct leaders’ channel and military-intelligence links, rather than through the embassy itself.
