title: Why Afghanistan’s Neighbors Have Not Backed Pakistan’s Strikes on the Taliban
description: China, Uzbekistan, and Tajikistan are less exposed to the impact of cross-border terrorism – and less willing to risk smooth relations with Kabul over the issue.
text:
On October 5, Moscow hosted the eighth meeting of the special representatives and senior officials from regional countries for the Moscow Format to discuss political and economic relations with Afghanistan and counterterrorism and counter-narcotics cooperation. The Moscow Format includes Afghanistan, China, India, Iran, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Pakistan, Russia, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan.

But the meeting failed to adopt a joint statement because the Pakistani and Afghan delegates disagreed over the language on terrorism. The Taliban objected to the frequent mention of terrorism in reference to Afghanistan.

Russia’s special envoy for Afghanistan, Zamir Kabulov, said the Afghan delegates accepted similar language last year. He believed that the changed relations between Pakistan and Afghanistan might have caused Kabul’s objection this time.

The meeting was held only a week after the most recent confrontation between Islamabad and Kabul. On September 18 and 26, Pakistan suffered deadly terrorist attacks in its northwestern province, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, that together killed about 44 people and injured about 138. Pakistan responded with airstrikes on different targets in Afghanistan that it believes were the training camps and hideouts of the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) and its associated factions responsible for the cross-border attacks.

At the Moscow summit, Pakistan’s delegation said the Taliban were complicit in those attacks in Pakistan because the terrorist groups were operating on Afghan soil with impunity. The Taliban said Pakistan was using military aggression in violation of international law for an issue that could be resolved through political negotiations.

The Moscow Format meeting failed to bridge these differences enough to allow for a joint communique. What’s noteworthy is that other countries that share borders with Afghanistan – such as China, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan – did not use their diplomatic capital to reach an understanding on language that included everyone’s concerns.

Afghanistan’s neighbors have different levels of concern about militancy there. Their strategies, especially on counterterrorism, are a function of the nature of their border with Afghanistan, the extent of the threat from militant groups on Afghan soil, and the Taliban’s scale of cooperation regarding those groups. From their perspective, military force is not the most effective solution to address the issue.

China shares a border of only about 92 kilometers with Afghanistan, high in the Wakhan Corridor, marked by rough terrain and the nearly 5,000-meter high Wakhjir Pass. In terms of a terrorist presence in Afghanistan, Beijing considers the East Turkestan Islamic Movement (ETIM) its main concern and has pressed the Taliban to act against the group. The Taliban have reportedly relocated ETIM fighters away from the border, and they now have a dispersed presence. Therefore, the immediate cross-border threat to China is smaller, and any movement across the pass is easy to detect.

Uzbekistan similarly shares a short border of 144 kilometers with Afghanistan, almost entirely along the Amu Darya. Regular cross-border movement is concentrated at the closely guarded Termez-Hairatan road and rail crossing. But the militant groups in Afghanistan that concern Tashkent have shown only a limited capacity for cross-border attacks. There was one incident in 2022 of rockets being fired toward Termez, which didn’t cause any casualties. Therefore, the immediate cross-border threat is relatively small and easier to contain.

Tajikistan’s case is closer to Pakistan’s in terms of the long border and threat. Dushanbe shares about 1,374 kilometers of border with Afghanistan, much of which runs along the Panj River and passes through remote and mountainous territory and is difficult to monitor consistently. The cross-border threat therefore needs more immediate attention. In November 2025, two cross-border attacks from Afghanistan’s Badakhshan province killed five Chinese workers in Tajikistan.

As for Taliban cooperation, Kabul has offered these countries help in investigations and has arrested suspects after cross-border attacks.

Pakistan’s case is of a different magnitude on all these counts.

Pakistan shares 2,640 kilometers of border with Afghanistan, where Pashtun and Baloch communities live on both sides. Afghanistan has never recognized the border since Pakistan’s founding. Islamabad has been fencing it since 2017, but militants continue to cross it. A disputed frontier with kinship networks on both sides gives militants far more routes and tricks to enter Pakistan than Afghanistan’s northern borders offer.

Pakistan also faces a much larger threat. Its key concerns are the TTP, the Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA), and the Islamic State Khorasan Province (ISKP). Islamabad charges that all three groups have a presence in Afghanistan, especially the TTP. U.N. monitors estimate the TTP, which has carried out the most frequent and lethal attacks in Pakistan, has about 6,000 fighters in Afghanistan.

By September 2026, Pakistan’s terrorism situation had worsened sharply, with 1,232 militant attacks in nine months, already 169 attacks above those recorded in all of 2025. Consistent attacks on this scale raise domestic pressure to take firm action.

Moreover, the Taliban have shown limited willingness to cooperate with Pakistan on the issue of militant groups. The Taliban leadership describes TTP members as Pakistani refugees and refuses to classify them as militants. U.N. monitors report that the group enjoys greater liberty and support from Taliban authorities. Kabul has offered to relocate the TTP fighters away from the Pakistani border, but that step cannot stop the militant movement through the long and porous border with Pakistan.

Pakistan has, therefore, asked for written guarantees that the militants would not use Afghan soil as a base for attacks in Pakistan. The Taliban have rejected this demand, which was why the Istanbul talks failed in November 2025.

Pakistan has said its operations will continue until the Taliban take verifiable action against militant groups on Afghan soil. Yet none of Afghanistan’s neighbors has publicly supported Pakistan’s airstrikes. China, Russia, and Iran have called for restraint and offered to mediate, and Uzbekistan urged a diplomatic resolution. China hosted informal talks in Urumqi in April but those ended without agreement.

Whether in Urumqi or more recently in Moscow, repeated efforts at finding common ground have fallen flat. While none of Afghanistan’s neighbors is comfortable with the idea of cross-border terrorism, none of them has sanctioned Pakistan’s military retaliation, either.

title: Why Are Modi Government Critics Now Targeting India’s Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar?
description: A recent investigative report strengthens opposition charges that the Modi government is using Kumar to manipulate elections in favor of the BJP.
text:
“You must have heard of Dharmendra Pradhan,” student leader Neha Bora said in a video message on September 30, two days before a series of agitations is scheduled to start in major Indian cities like Delhi, Mumbai, and Kolkata, demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation.

“Gyanesh Kumar, it’s your turn now. We are coming,” Bora said with a cheeky smile. A leftist student leader, Bora was part of the youth agitation in July that forced the Narendra Modi government’s education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, out of office.

Now, students and youth are rallying around the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) and opposition parties against a new target: Gyanesh Kumar, who has been at the center of political controversies since his appointment as chief election commissioner about a year and a half ago.

Kumar has been accused of speaking political language and giving undue advantage to India’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). He is being compared with Adolf Eichmann, the central operational manager of the Holocaust.

The latest trigger for the nationwide protests that will begin on October 2 was an investigation by The Indian Express, which reported that two members of the Election Commission, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, had raised concerns with Kumar at least 14 times in 10 months, only to be overlooked. Some decisions were reportedly taken without their knowledge. The objections concerned electoral roll decisions and orders.

Notably, Kumar is the first chief election commissioner appointed under a new law that the Modi government brought, overturning a mechanism recommended by India’s Supreme Court. This new law gives the government the authority to pick election commissioners of its choice. The law also gives immunity to the election commissioner for any action they take with regard to conducting elections.

The opposition’s challenge to the law has not made much progress in the Supreme Court yet, with a five-judge constitutional bench expected to start hearing it.

The Indian Express report dropped like a political bombshell. Opposition parties jumped in to claim that the report vindicates what they have been alleging for a long time: that the BJP government is using Chief Election Commissioner Kumar to manipulate elections in favor of the BJP, starting with the voter roll.

Trying to downplay the internal rift, the commission’s reply was measured: differences are normal in any institution. Despite the concerns raised at different stages, the final decisions were unanimous, the commission said.

Its defense has not calmed the room. The Indian Express disclosures landed amid the highly contested overhaul of the voter roll, the Special Intensive Revision, which has removed millions of names from the electoral rolls. Several opposition leaders and civil society personalities, including Rahul Gandhi of the Congress, India’s main opposition party, have alleged that the electoral roll revision process is being used to steal votes.

A dispute inside a constitutional body has thus become evidence, for opponents, not only of a wider institutional failure, but also of “sabotage” of an institution that is most critical for the smooth functioning of an electoral democracy.

The CJP, a youth movement that spearheaded the July agitation, moved quickly. “Gyanesh, it’s done bro,” CJP leader Abhijit Dipke wrote on social media the day the Indian Express report was published. The CJP gave Kumar 48 hours to quit. In the national capital of New Delhi, the Jantar Mantar premises, the site of the June-July protests, were heavily barricaded on September 25 as organizations and activists, mostly leftists, marched. Several protesters were detained.

Opposition parties echoed the demand for Kumar’s resignation, accusing him of sidelining his fellow commissioners. Kumar, as expected, did not oblige.

Therefore, protests are expected in different parts of the country over the coming days, some led by the CJP, some by opposition parties. Over the past few days, Congress workers demonstrated in different states, with a rally outside the Election Commission’s office in the national capital.

The tension can perhaps be sensed from the fact that after some Congress workers defaced the gates and walls of Kumar’s residence in the BJP-ruled north Indian state of Uttar Pradesh, police booked them under charges of attempt to murder.

While Kumar is the visible immediate target, the movement’s demands go further than one man’s exit. The CJP and opposition parties also want the entire SIR exercise to be scrapped. Gandhi asked people not to forget that it was Modi who appointed Kumar, which means the prime minister cannot escape responsibility for Kumar’s deeds and misdeeds.

BJP supporters argue that cleaning the rolls is a legitimate duty of the government. Some BJP leaders have even demanded that Kumar be awarded some of India’s highest civilian awards for his service in electoral reforms.

As a target, Kumar is much tougher to unseat than Pradhan. A minister serves at the government’s pleasure, and a prime minister can sacrifice one minister to defuse a larger crisis. A chief election commissioner’s position is designed to be harder to dislodge, because the office’s independence depends on that insulation. Article 324(5) gives the CEC the same removal protection as a Supreme Court judge.

That means a parliamentary motion on the grounds of proven misbehavior or incapacity must be passed by special majorities in both houses of parliament. No such move has ever succeeded. Earlier this year, the chairpersons of both the upper and lower houses of Parliament rejected the opposition’s notice for Kumar’s removal.

Understandably, the Modi government would likely wait for the proceedings at the apex court, even as the ruling party is expected to garner public sympathy for Kumar and his “bold actions.”

The CJP and different student organizations and youth forces, on the other hand, seem to believe in the power of the street protests. To what extent the CJP, the student organizations, and opposition political parties manage to build sustained pressure through street protests remains to be seen. October being a month when festivals will be celebrated in most parts of the country, it would not be easy for them to maintain the momentum.

title: Why China Can’t Fix Its Broken Economy
description: China's economy has a huge problem: Chinese people aren’t spending enough money. And this is not just a problem for China.
text:
China has a huge problem: Chinese people aren’t spending enough money. China today has the lowest consumption rate of any major economy in the world – in fact, its consumption rate is lower than any major economy in the past 100 years.

Consumption makes up just about 56 percent of China’s GDP. In most economies, it’s 70 percent or more. To put this in perspective, China’s consumption as a share of GDP is about 10 percentage points lower that Japan’s was in the 1990s, at the worst point in its economic stagnation.

Why does low consumption matter? Because it’s a flashing warning sign that China’s economic model is fundamentally broken. That’s why GDP growth is coming to a screeching halt, dropping from highs of 10 percent or more in the early 2000s to under 5 percent today. It’s also why China’s debt is growing to alarming levels.

And this is not just a problem for China. Low consumption in China means its people aren’t buying all that much – but China can’t scale back production without mass layoffs. So what does China do with all the extra stuff? It exports more and more abroad, at lower and lower prices.

The technical term for that is “dumping” – and countries from Europe to Asia are starting to complain about it. China’s huge excess production is killing manufacturing industries around the world.

And all of these problems have the same root cause.

title: Why China’s Training Center in Laos Will Not Change Vietnam’s Non-Aligned Foreign Policy
description: Hanoi's best option to keep its western neighbors neutral is to resist further Chinese encroachment by political means.
text:
China’s recent announcement of the opening of a new Joint Logistics and Training Center to train air force pilots in Ban Keun, Laos, has caused much concern about China’s intentions and capabilities. The new center, together with the China-Cambodia Joint Support and Training Center at Ream Naval Base in Cambodia, gives China’s military the ability to cover inland airspace over Indochina and out toward the Gulf of Thailand.

Vietnam has not commented on the new base at Ban Keun, but Prime Minister Le Minh Hung just concluded a visit to Laos and Cambodia. Laos was Hung’s first official visit since assuming the prime ministerial post in April. Hung and Thongloun Sisoulith, the president of Laos and general secretary of the Lao People’s Revolutionary Party, affirmed the “great friendship, special solidarity, comprehensive cooperation, and strategic cohesion” between the two nations. Both countries will celebrate the 50th anniversary of the signing of the 1977 Vietnam-Laos Treaty of Friendship and Cooperation next year.

China’s new base in Laos signals one of the major developments in Indochinese affairs since 1991. The 1991 Paris Peace Agreements ended the Third Indochina War and laid the basis for how China and Vietnam would handle Indochinese affairs to avoid a repetition of the polarization and arms race that contributed to Vietnam’s invasion of Cambodia in December 1978 and China’s retaliatory invasion of Vietnam in February 1979.

The Agreements demanded the withdrawal of foreign forces and their equipment from Cambodia, thereby ending the direct Vietnamese and Chinese interference in Cambodian affairs. This agreement came two years after China and Laos had normalized ties and three years after Vietnam began to withdraw its troops from Laos. China and Vietnam normalized ties in November 1991, the month after the Paris Peace Agreements. One of the key conditions of normalization is that neither country would seek hegemony in Indochina, which was the main reason China and Vietnam fought in 1979. After 1991, neither Vietnam nor China has had a permanent military base in Laos or Cambodia.

The post-1991 status quo is now enduring a stress test with the opening of China’s joint training centers in Ream and Ban Keun. From Vietnam’s perspective, what matters is not just the current capability but China’s future intentions. Although these centers are of limited military utility, China’s military presence could polarize Indochina if Laos and Cambodia come under pressure to host more Chinese military personnel or equipment, grant China exclusive access to these centers, or give China the right to use them during wartime. If Laos and Cambodia sided with China, it would completely expose Vietnam’s western flank to a hostile foreign power.

However, Vietnam will stick to its non-aligned foreign policy (no military alliances, no siding with one country against another, no foreign military bases, and no use of force or threats to use force in international relations) to maintain its goal of keeping Laos and Cambodia neutral.

If the Third Indochina War taught Vietnam any lessons, it is that allying with a great power to keep Laos and Cambodia in its orbit is not a viable policy option. In 1977, after the Khmer Rouge attacked Vietnam with tacit Chinese support, Vietnam began to side with the Soviet Union to counter Chinese influence in Cambodia.

However, Hanoi’s decision elevated what was a local issue between China and Vietnam into a great-power rivalry between China and the Soviet Union. China could not accommodate Vietnam’s interest in Cambodia and Laos and mediate the Khmer Rouge’s conflict with Vietnam when it perceived that Vietnam was ushering a great power into China’s backyard. Such an involvement made China determined to rid Indochina of any interference by linking Vietnam’s Indochinese ambitions with Soviet “socialist imperialism.”

Beijing accused Hanoi of colonizing its western neighbors and rallied world opinion against Vietnam. Vietnam’s alliance with the Soviet Union could not help it maintain its grip on Laos and Cambodia despite Moscow bankrolling the endeavor because Chinese military and economic punishments were too severe. After the Soviet retrenchment from Indochina in 1991, the neutralization of Laos and Cambodia was inevitable.

If Vietnam hosted a foreign military base on its soil to counter China’s bases in Laos and Cambodia, this would only make China double down on its presence. The Soviet presence at Cam Ranh Bay did not end China’s support for anti-Vietnam insurgents in Laos and Cambodia. There are simply no countries that can help Vietnam compete with China over Laos and Cambodia to the degree the Soviet Union could. The United States is not a continental power in mainland Asia. As such, Hanoi cannot abandon its stance of non-alignment.

It would also not be viable for Vietnam to threaten to attack China’s bases in Laos and Cambodia. This is not the first time China set up a joint training center in either Laos or Cambodia. In 1977, China helped the Khmer Rouge construct the 2,400-meter-long Krang Leav airfield in Kampong Chhnang, which at the time would allow China to station short-range bombers to carry out raids in southern Vietnam. China trained Khmer Rouge pilots and pledged to donate fifty-six aircraft to Cambodia. China also stationed engineering troops to construct roads in northern Laos beginning in 1962.

When Vietnam invaded Cambodia in December 1978, it quickly captured the unfinished Krang Leav airfield, thereby ending the Chinese threat from the southwestern front. Hanoi also captured Kampong Som (Sihanoukville), Cambodia’s only major seaport, through which it received Chinese war material. Although China did not send troops to Cambodia, Vietnam’s use of force against Cambodia gave Beijing the pretext to launch a retaliatory attack in February 1979. Laos subsequently ceased all cooperation with China, ending China’s military presence in Laos, but it did not restrain Beijing’s military punishment of Vietnam along the China-Vietnam land border and in the South China Sea.

It is not hard to imagine that Vietnam’s decision to use force against Ban Keun and Ream in the future would result in another Chinese attack. Vietnam can use long-range missiles to attack Chinese bases in Laos and Cambodia, which can spare the country of an invasion and limit escalation. However, there is no guarantee that China would not launch missiles against Vietnam’s bases or maritime outposts.

Because Vietnam can neither arms race nor side with a great power against China, Vietnam’s best option to keep Laos and Cambodia neutral is to resist further Chinese presence by political means. Vietnam’s friendship treaty with Laos should provide some degree of consultation between the two countries, as the treaty commits both countries to come to the defense of the other. Laos being transparent with Vietnam over the extent of Chinese presence and any future expansion plans would allay Hanoi’s fear to some degree. Vietnam’s affirmation of the 1991 Paris Peace Agreements and Cambodia’s constitutional clauses barring foreign bases from Cambodian soil remain vital. Like Laos’ case, Vietnam should press for more transparency over China’s presence at Ream. Vietnam should also highlight the continued trilateral cooperation framework among the three Indochinese countries to lock in the economic and political benefits of them cooperating with rather than siding against Vietnam.

Besides direct approaches toward its western neighbors, Vietnam can dilute the significance of Chinese centers by supporting more foreign presences there. The Ream Naval Base is a case in point. Although China funded the renovation and expansion of the base, Cambodia has invited foreign warships from Vietnam, Japan, the United States, Australia, India, and others to visit the base. If China’s center in Ban Keun is not directed against any third party, foreign countries should seek regular access to the center to refuel aircraft or exchange technical expertise with the Lao People’s Liberation Army Air Force. Vietnam’s diversified foreign policy means that it doesn’t matter which country visits the center, just that no countries are excluded from stopping at Ban Keun. This is how Vietnam’s foreign partners can help it achieve its objectives in western Indochina without alarming China.

Finally, Vietnam keeping its relationship with China amicable is the best method of keeping Laos and Cambodia neutral. Some observers have argued that the new bases in Laos and Cambodia signal a failure of Hanoi’s China policy. Despite Vietnam joining China’s “Community of Common Destiny” in 2023, these analysts claim, China is continuing the “encirclement” of Vietnam. However, this assessment downplays China’s largely non-confrontational stance toward Vietnam’s land reclamation campaign at sea. It is also worth noting that China calls the two facilities joint centers and not exclusive military bases, which signals a desire on Beijing’s part not to provoke Hanoi. Importantly, it is China’s air force and the navy that are at those bases and not the army, which would be more threatening to Vietnam. China has an interest in keeping its undisputed southern border with Vietnam stable while it focuses on Taiwan. In exchange, Vietnam must continue assuring China that it has no intention of siding with another great power against it. Such an assurance deprives China of any rationale to turn Laos and Cambodia against Vietnam.

The post-1991 Indochina order is now being tested, but many facets of that order are worth preserving. Vietnam’s and China’s reciprocal commitment not to establish permanent foreign bases in Laos and Cambodia and not to seek hegemony over Indochina will prevent the peninsula from being plunged into another China-Vietnam conflict or a conflict between China and Vietnam’s great power ally. So long as China’s presence in Laos and Cambodia does not result in them turning against Vietnam, Vietnam will continue honoring the post-1991 order.

title: Why Did the Industrial Revolution Not Start in India?
description: Due to abundant labor, its social structure, and the inertia of an economic system, there was little incentive to initiate mechanization and the Industrial Revolution in India.
text:
Historians often ask why the Industrial Revolution began in Europe and not elsewhere.

The classical framing of this question is the Needham Problem. Writing in 1969, the British historian of science, Joseph Needham, asked: “Why did modern science, the mathematization of hypotheses about Nature, with all its implications for advanced technology, take its meteoric rise only in the West…[and] had not developed in Chinese civilization?” After all, Needham noted, “between the first century BC and the fifteenth century AD, Chinese civilization was much more efficient than occidental in applying human natural knowledge to practical human needs.”

The Industrial Revolution refers to the transformation from agrarian, handicraft economies to machine- and factory-based industrial economies. It began in the 18th century and was the harbinger of the modern world, enabling Western dominance over most of the rest of the world, either through outright colonization, as in much of India and Africa, or by means of indirect control, as in China and Iran. The Industrial Revolution built on the preceding Scientific Revolution in Europe, which emphasized the acquisition of knowledge through reason and empirical research.

Needham sought to answer the question of why the Industrial Revolution did not begin outside Europe by examining the evolution of science in China.

But the issue ought not to be seen as merely a dichotomy between Western and Chinese civilization. In fact, India and the Islamic world would arguably have been better candidates than China for the emergence of industrial civilization. As in Europe, large swathes of India and the Islamic world engaged in long-distance trade, patronized universities, and were divided into competing kingdoms fighting against each other and against pastoralist peoples from the neighboring steppes and deserts. The Islamic world and Europe, especially, had to compensate for a lack of abundant labor. Incessant warfare led to the adaptation of gunpowder, while trade spread innovations such as the compass and paper beyond the region.

In India, there are two periods that stand out as optimal times for an industrial revolution to occur there. The first is in the 6th century CE, when the Gupta Empire had disintegrated into a plethora of kingdoms and a shared elite culture across polities emerged. India thus experienced both political competition and was home to a pan-India culture. An exchange of ideas happened at a number of universities, such as Nalanda. These conditions were similar to those in early modern Europe. Some of India’s greatest advances in the arts, philosophy, and mathematics occurred in the centuries following the end of the Gupta Empire, with figures like mathematician Brahmagupta and philosopher Shankara living during this period.

A second period would have been in the Deccan peninsula during the early modern era. The topography and location of this region favored the persistence of several rival kingdoms seeking to gain an advantage over each other. They all had access to ocean-going trade and had a history of trade guilds, which allowed the easy flow of goods and ideas. In the early 16th century, the Deccan sultanates were some of the earliest innovators in cannon technology and military architecture. In the 18th century, the Kingdom of Mysore invented sophisticated rockets and other weaponry, whilst the Marathas established ordnance factories where skilled metalworkers created cannon and firearms adapted to local Indian conditions.

While it should be noted that the engine behind 18th-century Deccani manufacturing were skilled craftsmen rather than mechanization, the region had many of the right ingredients to commence industrialization around the same time as in Europe. The British conquest halted these initial local moves in that direction.

However, there were many other reasons the Industrial Revolution began in northwest Europe — and not elsewhere, such as in India — in the 18th century.

Industrialization is not inevitable. It is not the default outcome of human civilization. It takes certain institutions and worldviews as prerequisites and particular economic and geopolitical conditions — many of which came together by chance — to spark the process.

A great many factors must align, not least intense international rivalry in the state’s vicinity. For example, a polity ought to have enough labor to man its factories, but not too much labor — as China did — so as to make investment in industry more expensive than utilizing manual labor. A polity would ideally be sedentary rather than nomadic, stable enough internally to guarantee the continuity of institutions such as universities, companies, and land ownership, and home to a flexible labor market: the masses of peasants in many states were not permitted to move freely and offer their services anywhere. The polity must be strong enough to guarantee the rule of law, but not so bureaucratic so as to stifle private enterprise and innovation.

The historian Kyle Harper, speaking about the Roman Empire, noted that: “there [were] tinkerers and engineers, but they [were not] talking to the mathematicians and the physicists. If you were from on high to design self-sustaining innovation, I think you would want to bring those elements into proximity.” Harper argues that industrialization took off in early modern Europe because states funded scientific research and married the findings to the work of engineers and builders. Both groups seeded each other’s minds with ideas.

This process requires a state — or well-endowed institutions, such as corporations and universities — to facilitate scientific discoveries and its practical applications. This is a time- and capital-intensive process that was undertaken — more often than not — to improve the finances and security of the state through gains in efficiency and production. The benefits had to have been more than the costs.

On top of that, the state must overcome tradition and inertia: not an easy task. For example, after the victory of the Vijayanagara Empire against the Sultanate of Bijapur in 1520 at the Battle of Raichur, the two sides drew different conclusions on the efficiency of gunpowder.

Writing about the emperor of Vijayanagara, Krishadevaraya, historian Richard Eaton notes:

Though impressed with the matchlocks used by his Portuguese mercenaries, [Krishnadevaraya] failed to see firearms as the way of the future…there is no evidence that he followed up his victories by establishing an arsenal or a matchlock foundry in Vijayanagara. Nor did he or his successors ever mount cannon on the walls of their capital or provincial forts, or in other ways adapt their defensive systems to accommodate gunpowder technology…Bijapur, by contrast, responded quite differently to the battle’s outcome…[and] therefore launched an accelerated drive to pioneer new gunpowder technologies…from the small swivel guns that the Portuguese had placed on the gunwales of their ships, they took the idea of mounting a much larger cannon on a cubic block of granite set on an iron pin, enabling the gun to move horizontally.

Inertia is difficult to overcome. Research has found that in many parts of India, even when women are offered high-paying jobs in factories or offices, they decline due to family pressure and tradition that looks down on women working outside of the home. And for cultural reasons related to status, many Indians dream of becoming government bureaucrats or white-collar workers in the information technology industry, rather than seeking to work in factories or engaging in commerce or sales. These factors inhibit industrialization, development, and the spread of rational socioeconomic organization deriving from individualism.

For these reasons, for much of human history, it has been more efficient for most states — and most elites — to simply exploit land and people harder and harder. The Romans had a copious number of slaves and empires as diverse as the Ottomans and Mughals engaged in tax farming: the practice of a government contracting tax collection to private individuals, individuals who would often take a cut for themselves after fleecing peasants and merchants.

Many scholars have speculated that in India, mathematicians, artisans, scientists and builders were not often in the business of exchanging ideas, belonging to different endogamous jatis, or castes. According to economic historian Tirthankar Roy, “technology existed as tacit knowledge of artisan communities, and the evidence of partnership between diverse skills was rare. Scientific knowledge was often documented, but remained restricted within scholastic circles.”

Contrary to a widespread but incorrect belief, literacy was widespread amongst a number of castes, and was not restricted to just Brahmins. But different communities still interacted with and circulated texts mostly within their social milieu, and sometimes different jatis even used different writing systems. For example, in parts of North India, merchants used the Mahajani alphabet, scribes (Kayasthas) used the Kaithi alphabet, and Brahmins used Devanagari.

Another factor that may have inhibited industrialization in pre-modern India was its abundant quantity of specialized and cheap labor, which dampens the need for mechanization and labor-saving devices. China, too, had abundant labor, and thus, less incentive to mechanize in pre-modern times. The first Mughal Emperor Babur famously observed this phenomenon in his diary, the Baburnameh:

Another good thing in Hindustan is that it has unnumbered and endless workmen of every kind. There is a fixed caste (jam’i) for every sort of work and for every thing, which has done that work or that thing from father to son till now…680 men worked daily on my buildings in Agra and of Agra stone-cutters only; while 1491 stone-cutters worked daily on my buildings in Agra, Sikri, Biana, Dulpur, Gwalior, and Kuil. In the same way there are numberless artisans and workmen of every sort in Hindustan.

In fact, it was arguably not in the interests of a state to create a large number of unemployed people by introducing industry. Even today, if one were to observe construction in much of India, one would see a large number of individuals carrying and laying bricks with their bare hands instead of using machines or complex tools.

The historian Ada Palmer has noted that industrialization was less likely to begin in richer regions with more developed artisanal industries and vibrant trade, such as Italy. In fact, as per Palmer, even though Italians during the Renaissance had the technology for industrial looms, they did not want to pivot away from producing artisanal fabrics, which brought them wealth.

The parallels with India are striking. Due to its abundant labor, its social structure, and the inertia of an economic system that worked well enough, there was little incentive to initiate mechanization and the Industrial Revolution in India. The parts of India that came closest to industrialization — such as states in the early modern Deccan — did so when geopolitical conditions highly incentivized such an outcome. Survival trumped inaction in those cases. But more often than not, it was too late, or unnecessary, as the Industrial Revolution arrived fully formed from Europe in India.

title: Why Durga Puja’s Celebration in West Bengal This Year Was Different
channel_text: Blog; Society; South Asia; The Pulse
description: The BJP government in the state stripped the festival of its secular-cultural uniqueness to impose religious and ritualistic practices that are anathema to Bengalis.
text:
Amid the festive fervor that engulfs India in autumn, the eastern Indian state of West Bengal is immersed in the 10-day celebration of Durga Puja.

Durga Puja, or the worship of the ten-armed goddess Durga, who slayed a demon king, symbolizes the victory of good over evil. It is the biggest festival for Bengalis and for the Bengali diaspora. It is much more than a religious festival and has metamorphosed into the largest public art festival in the world as well.

Given the significance of Durga Puja in the lives of Bengalis, ruling parties in the state have always leveraged the festival for political purposes. This was the first Durga Puja held under the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), which came to power in Bengal just five months ago, after defeating the regional Trinamool Congress (TMC).

This year, however, the festival was in the news for all the wrong reasons. For the first time in Bengal, a stampede in a puja pandal (venue for worship) in north Kolkata left 19 dead and over 25 injured on October 17. The dead included 11 women and five children; the youngest was aged seven. A pall of gloom descended upon Bengal’s largest socio-cultural celebration. Kolkata has never witnessed such a tragedy during Durga Puja.

On the evening of the stampede disaster, there was another shock in store for Kolkata. Images of bulldozers demolishing bookstalls adjoining puja pandals in south Kolkata emerged.

For decades, leftist parties had set up bookstalls selling Marxist literature during the puja days. This time, Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari declared that his government would not allow communist culture to flourish. His government used bulldozers to flatten the stalls. In north Kolkata’s Dum Dum area, Hindutva goons vandalized a leftist-run book stall and even tore great classics of Bengali literature. Kolkata is famous for its love for intellectual banter and books.

Although Durga Puja revolves around the worship of a Hindu goddess, in Bengal it is a cultural phenomenon rather than a ritualistic-religious one. Unlike North India, where Navaratri (nine days) is observed through strict fasting, prayers, consumption of only vegetarian fare, and worship of the Mata Rani (Mother Goddess), in Bengal the connection with Durga is more personal. She is perceived as a loving daughter coming to her parental home and is therefore pampered with the best food and sweet offerings, including sacrificial meat.

What makes the Durga Puja of Bengal unique is the pantheon of gods it includes — Saraswati and Lakshmi, the goddesses of learning and wealth, respectively – regarded as Durga’s children along with the male gods, Ganesh and Kartik. Her annual arrival on earth, accompanied by her children, is the rationale behind the celebration. This celebration is marked by cultural dance, music, theatrical performances, publication of literary magazines, new clothes, revelry, and feasting. It is an inclusive, secular approach to an ostensibly religious festival, which the Hindutva-dominated North Indian psyche cannot comprehend.

Under former Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee of the TMC (2011-2026), the festival expanded both in scale and budget. Banerjee inaugurated thousands of community pujas every year in Kolkata, patronizing neighborhood clubs that organized the festival. Organizers would unleash their creativity and artistry through the pandal decorations and portrayal of Durga. Known as “theme pujas,” pandals depicted topical issues ranging from social problems to contemporary subjects like climate change, and even abstract concepts.

The dizzying creativity in the art installations attracted domestic and foreign tourists to Bengal during the puja season. As per a British Council study in 2021, the Durga Puja creative economy was worth around $4.53 billion, contributing 2.5 percent of the state’s GDP.

Bengal’s Durga Puja even earned the prestigious UNESCO tag for being an “Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity” in 2021. In its citation, UNESCO stated: “Durga Puja is seen as the best instance of the public performance of religion and art, and as a thriving ground for collaborative artists and designers.” Banerjee considered the UNESCO recognition a major achievement of her government and even started a Durga Puja Carnival to showcase the festivities.

Several ministers of Banerjee’s TMC became synonymous with their neighborhood pujas, which acquired political clout and prominence. Even prominent TMC leaders like former mayor Farhid (Bobby) Hakim, a Muslim, were famous for their patronage of the Durga Puja. In fact, this secular celebration of Durga Puja, where Muslims also participate, is what rankled the Hindutva organizations. The TMC under Banerjee was known for its secular credentials and its patronage of festivals of all major religions, be it Durga Puja, Christmas or Eid.

In contrast, the BJP has always harped on retaining the purity of the “sanatan dharma” (literally, universal truth, i.e., Hinduism). It has always encouraged sectarian and communal politics with scant regard for minorities. Even before it came to power in Bengal, the BJP and its ideological mentor, the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), had stoked the vegetarian versus non-vegetarian debate, projecting the Bengali tradition of offering meat to Durga as an aberration.

Not surprisingly, much before the festival, Adhikari issued a stern warning to puja organizers with a list of dos and don’ts, including strict adherence to religious rituals. Organizers were also given diktats not to take creative liberties with the idol and the pandal in any way that can defile the sanctity of the worship. Earlier Durga Puja pandal themes like taboos surrounding menstruation were anathema to the BJP government.

It was obvious that the BJP government in Bengal is intent on stripping Durga Puja of its cultural, secular, and artistic character and imposing a rigid ritualistic norm of worship in its stead. The state administration was more focused on such extraneous issues rather than basics like ensuring crowd management; this critical lapse led to the stampede on October 17. The Telegraph newspaper observed that the Adhikari government had replaced police personnel, who in the past were lauded for their efficient crowd control measures, with a new team of inexperienced officers.

Even the Left Front government, which ruled Bengal for 34 years (1977 to 2011) and was avowedly atheist, never interfered or restricted the festive celebrations of Durga Puja. Rather, it termed the puja as a “sharad utsav” (autumnal festival) and participated in it by setting up bookstalls at the venues.

The BJP’s victory in pluralistic Bengal surprised many. Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Home Minister Amit Shah had been desperate to oust the proud Banerjee, who had publicly challenged the prime minister several times. Therefore, Durga Puja 2026 was, to many Bengalis, an attempt by the BJP to erase the TMC’s contributions to the Durga Puja spectacle.

Soon after forming the Bengal government, BJP leaders replaced TMC politicians heading prominent puja committees across Kolkata. Banerjee’s government used to give around $1,000 to puja committees. This year, the BJP government provided a grant of $1,000 as well as free electricity to each puja committee across Bengal.

The BJP, which valorizes the deity Ram, celebrates the Dussehra festival as Ram’s conquest of the demon, Ravana. In Bengal, the party had to make an uncomfortable compromise; it had to worship goddess Durga, and in the way Bengalis celebrate the festival.

In keeping with its communally divisive agenda, Chief Minister Adhikari announced on Wednesday that only those who believe in “sanatan dharma” will be allowed to touch the Durga idols during immersion in the river. The opposition has accused him of advocating untouchability. But Adhikari is unperturbed.

title: Why Is China Proposing Reciprocal Nuclear Laboratory Visits?
description: While China and the U.S. still disagree on the size of nuclear forces and the path of arms control, can they exchange meaningful information on certain technical issues?
text:
On October 6, CNN reported that the United States and China are engaged in informal, preliminary discussion on reciprocal visits to nuclear facilities. According to the report, the idea was first raised by the Chinese side in meetings with U.S. officials this year, during which the two sides discussed U.S. Department of Energy national laboratories and their Chinese counterparts. The same source also indicated that the U.S. side is willing to discuss visits to nuclear test sites.

At the China-U.S. leaders’ summit held in September, the two sides agreed to build “a constructive relationship of strategic stability on the basis of respect, fairness, and reciprocity.” According to CNN, however, they didn’t discuss reciprocal nuclear facility visits at the summit.

Reciprocal laboratory visits could serve to test the feasibility of limited nuclear transparency and give the broad political goal of “strategical stability” something concrete to work on. The question is whether the two sides can learn about each other’s nuclear institutions, their roles, and some of their activities, without harming their own national security.

In the mid-1990s, the United States and China set up the “U.S.-China Lab-to-Lab Technical Exchange Program” (CLL). Nuclear weapons laboratories under the U.S. Department of Energy and Chinese institutions including the China Academy of Engineering Physics participated in the project. The exchanges were conducted by scientists from both countries responsible for the technical management of nuclear forces, under the supervision of both governments, and were initially limited to nuclear arms control and nonproliferation. The program listed a shared goal: the exchange of information about the operation and management of nuclear facilities, while safeguarding the national security interests of both countries.

China hosted American scientists at its nuclear weapon laboratory and the Lop Nur test site, and showed them a variety of facilities. According to a U.S. participant, the United States authorized only small scale, restricted exchange on nuclear material protection and nuclear arms control verification technologies. Although the U.S. side had initially expressed a willingness to host Chinese scientists at the Nevada Test Site on a reciprocal basis, it withdrew that commitment later.

The two sides also ran into other obstacles. In 1996, for example, regarding a joint analysis plan for seismic data from mining activities on both sides, the China Academy of Engineering Physics declined to participate because the work was outside its scope. The Northwest Institute of Nuclear Technology also declined, out of concern that the data might be used to estimate the yields of China’s past nuclear tests.

In the late 1990s, the program was halted as China-U.S. relations worsened. In particular, a 1999 U.S. Congressional report accused China of stealing nuclear technology, which Beijing allegedly used “to fabricate and successfully test its next generation of nuclear weapons designs.” Scientists from both sides tried to revive the program during the administrations of Presidents George W. Bush and Barack Obama, without success.

This history shows that laboratory exchanges were a form of contact China and the United States have tried before, where information sharing and confidentiality requirements coexisted. While the experience of the 1990s cannot directly explain China’s current motivation for reviving the idea of reciprocal visits to nuclear facilities, it left a precedent. Whether the concept of reciprocal visits described in the CNN report aligns with the experience of such limited exchanges needs to be considered together with China’s current position on nuclear transparency.

China’s official position stresses transparency of intentions, but it also insists on protecting national security. The 2025 White Paper on Arms Control stated: “Given the current international security situation, transparency in intentions and policies is the most practical significance.” The 2026 NPT Compliance Report noted, however, that “inappropriate transparency may also undermine strategic stability” and advocated that nuclear weapon states should raise transparency step by step, in accordance with their own security environments and actual circumstances.

The report also noted that in March 2026, China organized a visit by permanent representatives to the United Nations, disarmament ambassadors, and high-level representatives from nearly 20 countries to the decommissioned 816 nuclear facility in Chongqing. Beijing included this in the section on “transparency and confidence-building measures.” A visit to a decommissioned facility does not prove that China would open an active nuclear weapon laboratory in the same way. But it shows that China already uses facility visits as a way to explain its nuclear policy to other countries.

Visits to active laboratories, however, may sit in a middle ground between policy transparency and transparency about nuclear forces. Nuclear weapons research institutions also undertake specialized work in areas such as arms control and nonproliferation. The earlier CLL program set out to explore ways of sharing selected information about nuclear materials and facilities while protecting sensitive national security information. The exchanges at that time covered how a nuclear weapons research institution can organize its arms control work, staff its operations, and carry out management. These issues go beyond a nuclear policy statement, but there is no need to discuss the number of warheads, deployment locations, or readiness status.

In addition, professional exchanges among nuclear agencies can foster a better understanding of each other’s working methods. Following the 1997 CLL program export control workshop, a Chinese representative stated that the workshop had given him a clearer understanding of the functional relationships among the U.S. government, laboratories, and technical experts. If the new reciprocal visits include such substantive dialogue, the laboratories could serve as a starting point for limited transparency: providing access to institutions and personnel in the nuclear field without immediately delving into discussions regarding the numbers, deployment and use of nuclear forces.

Such professional engagement could also become part of China-U.S. strategic nuclear dialogue. Chinese expert Li Bin has suggested that strategic nuclear dialogue could take place at various levels and involve different partners, and that Track 1.5 dialogue could include diplomatic departments, the military, and nuclear weapons laboratories. He also stressed that transparency should be a tool for achieving strategic stability.

Finding a form of openness that both sides can accept is only the first step. Laboratory visits could also allow each side to ask direct questions about specific work and hear the other side explain the purposes of its activities and technical judgments. If these discussions can correct misunderstandings and are carried forward by participants into their respective policy debates, they may reduce overreactions stemming from misreading. This is also where limited transparency can contribute to strategic stability.

Laboratory visits will not automatically resolve the conflict between nuclear strategy and the security interests of China and the United States. But they could serve as a limited test for the China-U.S. nuclear relationship in a new period. While the two sides still disagree on the size of nuclear forces, deployment, and the path of arms control, can they first exchange meaningful information on certain technical issues and keep talking afterward? If so, this limited transparency could provide a concrete example of the “strategic stability” called for by the leaders of both countries.
tag: China nuclear build-up; Confidence Building Measures; nuclear arms control; U.S.-China arms control; U.S.-China Relations; U.S.-China science cooperation

title: Why Kim Jong Un Should Want a 4th Summit With Donald Trump
description: Here’s what Pyongyang’s Foreign Ministry might be telling Kim about a possible summit.
text:
U.S. President Donald Trump’s push for a fourth summit with Kim Jong Un has so far been rejected by the North Korean leader, who may be playing hard to get. However, based on our decades analyzing North Korea, participation in countless face-to-face meetings with North Koreans – official and unofficial – and numerous visits to North Korea, we think that some in Pyongyang may believe their country could benefit greatly from a fourth summit, though not in terms of what Washington may think.

In view of North Korea and Kim’s experience, especially his three summits during Trump’s first term in office, and Pyongyang’s analysis of the president’s current foreign policy, the North Korean Foreign Ministry would emphasize the following points that lay out a strong case with Kim Jong Un for a fourth summit.

First, it would point out that because of Kim’s policies in the military and economic fields, taking advantage of shifts in international geopolitics, especially Pyongyang’s close relationship with Russia and China, North Korea is in a position of strength for a summit, should the chairman choose to proceed.

The United States and Trump, on the other hand, are in a much weaker position than before. The president’s overconfidence and erratic personality will almost certainly result in missteps that further weaken the U.S. position. And he doesn’t grasp that another summit will greatly benefit North Korea, which is now working in opposition to Washington.

The ministry would add that, as Kim has said many times, the past – the previous summits in Singapore, Hanoi, and at the Demilitarized Zone – is gone. Back then, the chairman focused on improving relations with Washington in return for putting his nuclear program on the table and creating space for North Korea to modernize its economy.

But today, another summit would improve North Korea’s global position by supporting its friends – China and especially Russia – undermining Washington’s influence abroad, and, hopefully, nudging Trump to accept Pyongyang’s growing nuclear arsenal. The ministry would also observe that, more than ever, Trump’s missteps have made the situation ripe for creating tensions in the already fraying South Korea-U.S. alliance.

Time Is on Pyongyang’s Side

Just as in the past, should Kim decide to proceed, the timing and venue of a new summit will be the subject of considerable back and forth with the Americans. In this instance, the North Koreans may believe the result of a summit could be more consequential because of Trump’s personality and his growing domestic political weakness.

The ministry would applaud Kim Jong Un’s policy of delaying a summit decision to take advantage of Trump’s eagerness to meet and extract unilateral concessions has already resulted in victories. The president has shortened one South Korea-U.S. exercise and left a cloud hanging over the rest.

Trump has also inched away from Washington’s long-standing pursuit of denuclearization and toward accepting North Korea as a nuclear power. That appears to have had the added benefit of setting off an internal debate. The State Department continues to back denuclearization, contradicting Trump’s position and sending confusing signals to U.S. allies.

Looking ahead, the North Korean Foreign Ministry would predict that if the Republicans lose the upcoming November congressional elections, as expected, nothing will save Trump from a greatly weakened situation. As a result, he may be anxious to make even more concessions to paint any outcome – even simply holding a meeting with Kim – as a personal victory.

North Korea’s Real Assessment of President Trump

While North Korea’s media have avoided direct criticism of Trump and continued to note Kim’s personal relationship with him, in private, foreign ministry analysts probably believe that his worst personality traits, evident in 2018 and 2019, have only become worse. These, in turn, will provide openings to reach agreements that further support Pyongyang’s strategy.

They would emphasize seven traits that will affect Trump’s performance at a North Korea-U.S. summit. First, at 80, he is seven years older than when the last summit was held and has declined physically and mentally. As the aged typically do, he has good days and bad days. Second, he reacts well to flattery, more so than ever. Third, Trump has a higher opinion of himself and his negotiating ability than in the past, even in the face of repeated failures. Fourth since he is more likely to rely on his gut feelings rather than expert advice, Trump will act impulsively. Fifth, he is losing his grip on reality. American media often laugh at many of his claims. Sixth, Trump has rolled out the red carpet at summits with presidents Vladimir Putin of Russia and Xi Jinping of China, despite their opposition to Washington’s global interests. He mistakenly believes that flattery can overcome policy differences.

Perhaps even more important, Kim’s advisors will point out that Trump does not understand strategic thinking. Past summits with North Korea have demonstrated that he has no grasp of the wider picture; the U.S. war with Iran again underlined his short sightedness. It is doubtful he will understand that the North’s new objectives are different from the past and inimical to U.S. interests.

The American Negotiating Position

Given this analysis of Trump, North Korea’s Foreign Ministry would conclude that he will either repeat standard U.S. positions or come up with his own on the spur of the moment without expert advice from his staff.

Trump knows denuclearization is not in the cards. Instead, he may float the idea of a nuclear freeze. If he does bring it up, the chairman could simply repeat his insistence that Pyongyang needs a strong deterrent. From his perspective, that deterrent is not just to maintain North Korea’s security but an absolute requirement for regional balance, especially given the growing danger of Japanese militarism.

The president may also repeat his proposal made at the 2019 Hanoi summit for a moratorium on further testing of intercontinental-range ballistic missiles (ICBMs) that can reach the United States. South Korean President Lee Jae-myung advanced the same idea at the recent United Nations General Assembly session. The proposal wouldn’t include the shorter-range missiles that target Seoul and Tokyo. As a result, it will prove controversial in South Korea and could create new tensions in U.S. relations with Japan.

The ministry would suggest that Kim could easily parry such a proposal by insisting that any moratorium on ICBM launches must include other countries with those missiles. That would be consistent his position that North Korea is now a global power and cannot be expected to make concessions other nuclear powers will not. And, of course, neither the United States nor the others will be open to that idea,

Trump is likely to dangle sanctions relief for North Korea – a centerpiece of past summits – in return for concessions. The ministry would note, however, Pyongyang’s success in avoiding those restrictions with assistance from Moscow and Beijing, as well as the billions of dollars North Korea earns from illicit cyber activities. As a result, Kim should not see sanctions as the card that Washington once imagined them to be. Still, lifting them could have some secondary political value for North Korea, enhancing its international standing and further normalizing its status.

Moreover, a proposal to lift sanctions could backfire and cause problems for the United States. It could stir up trouble in the Western bloc in the United Nations Security Council since lifting restrictions would face stiff resistance from Britain and France. On the domestic front, fiddling with sanctions would spark criticism from both Trump’s own party and political opponents. While he will not care, such policy turmoil further weakens the United States.

Just as in the past, the president will probably showcase grandiose, even far-fetched, and unachievable schemes to modernize North Korea’s economy. He has done that more recently with a proposal to turn Gaza into a modern coastal metropolis. Pyongyang’s position is quite clear – foreign aid is poisoned candy and should be rejected out of hand unless the chairman decides otherwise.

Finally, Trump can be expected to try to interfere with North Korea’s strong support for Russia in its war with Ukraine. However, the ministry’s America watchers would note that Washington has consistently underestimated the chairman’s commitment to the new relationship with Moscow. Presumably, few if any in the White House read Kim’s last letter to Putin expressing continued full support for Russian operations in Ukraine. Just how hard Trump will push is an open question given his zigzagging approach to the war and his hopes for a better relationship with Putin.

A Potential North Korean Strategy

The Foreign Ministry will argue that a Trump-Kim meeting represents a golden opportunity to secure important objectives while only taking tactical steps that appear to be concessions. It will also open doors to significant strategic gains. It would recommend the following steps.

Kim’s overall summit approach should showcase his statements over the past year that North Korea is seeking “peaceful coexistence.” That theme has mesmerized the Americans. However, meaningless formulations used before by nuclear weapons states, such as “a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought,” would cloak the North’s real objectives. So would any pledge to “work for peaceful resolution of outstanding differences.”

All of this will appeal to Trump who is determined to declare peace in his time and secure the Nobel Prize. In reality, highlighting “peaceful coexistence” would put North Korea in a position to protest virtually any steps the United States takes in the region as contradicting Washington’s assertions of a desire for peace.

While Trump’s aides are sure to warn him ahead of time, the ministry would recommend that Kim press the president to go beyond his random public statements on the North’s nuclear capabilities to put it in writing, perhaps in a summit declaration. Any acknowledgment of North Korea’s nuclear arsenal coming out of the meeting, even only verbal, will create turmoil in Seoul and Tokyo.

The chairman should certainly encourage Trump to reduce the U.S. military commitment to South Korea. He will be pushing on an open door. Trump has made it clear in the past that he is willing to further limit U.S. military activity in and around the Korean Peninsula. One possibility is ending joint South Korea-U.S. military exercises. The ministry would caution that it is unclear how far the president will go. But its experts would point out that he has also been consistently looking to draw down U.S. forces in the South for years.

Finally, North Korea’s diplomats would recommend that Kim seriously consider accepting any offer Trump makes to recognize the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea as a sovereign state. Embassies in each capital could serve as a formal line of communication after decades of hostility. In theory, they can be framed as a step to reduce tensions and avoid accidental war. In practice, they will do neither.

If diplomatic recognition occurs, Trump will claim credit for taking another step to build peace. However, this measure will reinforce North Korea’s goal of demonstrating that it is a global player to be reckoned with and further its objective of gaining international acceptance as a nuclear power.

The Bottom Line

The Foreign Ministry is likely to conclude that a fourth summit will advance Kim Jong Un’s goals, especially in view of Trump’s poor foreign policy performance and personality flaws.

Even if there is no concrete outcome, the ministry would argue that the optics will be important in positioning North Korea for the future. Just having a summit will strengthen Kim’s standing abroad. Should an impatient Trump walk out again as he did in Hanoi, rather than an embarrassment to the chairman, it will emphasize Washington’s negative image and cause problems with Seoul and Tokyo.

No matter the outcome, it will also be possible to exploit Trump’s post-summit behavior to advance Pyongyang’s objectives. He will continue to insist he has a good personal relationship with Kim. That will be useful as a shield providing time for North Korea to continue to build up militarily for the remainder of the president’s term in office.

Finally, if the past is any guide, the Foreign Ministry will conclude that the chances are an erratic Trump will never stick to what he says. As a result, any agreement may not survive more than a few months. Then North Korea will be able to take tougher steps. For example, after the 2019 Panmunjom summit, Trump went back on his promise to cancel an upcoming joint South Korea-U.S. military exercise. As a result, Pyongyang stonewalled the U.S. in subsequent negotiations and ended its missile test moratorium.
tag: North Korea foreign ministry; North Korea foreign policy; Trump-Kim summit; U.S.-North Korea diplomacy

title: Why Pakistan Tested an Extended Range Version of the Fatah-IV
description: Pakistan is likely looking to counter the Indian Air Force’s future strategy of launching air-launched missiles from standoff ranges.
text:
On October 6, Pakistan tested an extended range (ER) version of the Fatah-IV ground-launched cruise missile. This was the third launch of the Fatah-IV missile system, the last having been conducted in May 2026. The latest test is unique compared to the first two, because this time the missile had a reported range of more than 750 kilometers.

The Fatah-IV is a byproduct of the 2025 India-Pakistan clashes. The missile was first unveiled publicly during Pakistan’s Independence Day event on August 14, 2025. It features terrain-hugging flight capability intended to reduce radar detection, has a maximum speed of Mach 0.7, and carries a 330 kilogram blast-fragmentation explosive warhead.

The ER version appears to have wings positioned on the underbelly, not in the center of the missile body, as was the case in its earlier version. The ER missile also appears slightly larger to store more fuel, allowing it to cover a longer distance than its reported 750 km range. Based on available imagery, the Fatah-IV ER could have a range of around 1,000 km.

What are the key rationales behind Pakistan testing the ER version of Fatah-IV? There seem to be quite a number of possibilities. First, Pakistan is likely looking to counter the Indian Air Force’s (IAF) future strategy of launching air-launched missiles from standoff ranges. It remains a strong possibility that the IAF will move its assets to rear bases in the next encounter with the Pakistan Air Force (PAF) because the IAF does not want to repeat what happened on the night of May 6-7, 2025, when it lost multiple jets in air-to-air engagement with the PAF. Therefore, the IAF will likely launch payloads from a distance beyond the range of both PAF air-to-air missiles and Pakistan’s long-range land-based missile defenses.

The IAF will be able to conduct such strikes in the future because the Indian government has already sanctioned an increase in range of the BrahMos supersonic cruise missile, with reports estimating the new range to be around 800 km. This posed a serious challenge to Pakistan because the Taimoor air-launched cruise missile and other conventional systems available in the country’s arsenal remained inadequate to threaten IAF installations located deep inside mainland India. The ER Fatah-IV will fill this gap by enabling Pakistan to strike radars and the fighter jet fleet of the IAF deployed at bases far away from Pakistan’s border.

Second, India’s key metropolitan cities and commercial hubs are located in southern and central India, far away from Pakistan’s border. By contrast, Pakistan’s major urban hubs are all located relatively close to India. This previously provided New Delhi an advantage over Islamabad, as India could target Pakistan’s commercial hubs with conventional munitions. However, with the introduction of the Fatah-IV, India’s main business metropolis, Mumbai, from now on will come within range of Pakistan’s conventional strike force, thus posing a credible threat to the Indian business capital.

The ER Fatah-IV will allow Islamabad to dissuade India from launching conventional counter-value strikes against Pakistan’s key cities because New Delhi’s own central commercial hub can be targeted in a similar manner. India is likely to remain dissuaded from approaching such a path in a limited confrontation with Pakistan because missiles striking Mumbai will not only create negative international headlines but also damage the morale of the people and investors in India.

Third, in the post-Operation Sindoor era, the Indian military ordered more air defense systems including the S-400, tested new ones like the Kusha long-range interceptor, and announced the integration of all of them under the aegis of Mission Sudarshan Chakra to formulate an impenetrable missile defense shield. To penetrate such a shield and strike targets at longer range, Pakistan will need systems to avoid radar detection. The Fatah-IV fulfills this requirement, thus posing a credible threat to Indian military installations and dissuading New Delhi from ordering pre-emptive military strikes against Pakistan.

Pakistan’s official policy eschews any arms race. The ultimate objective behind the development of the ER Fatah-IV is to strengthen Pakistan’s conventional deterrence vis-à-vis India. The development of the Fatah-IV did not occur in a vacuum; it became a compulsion after India launched “unprovoked” attacks against multiple locations inside Pakistan in May last year. The episode was the turning point for Pakistan. It led to the introduction of the conventionally armed Fatah-IV cruise missile because Islamabad wants to further reinforce its conventional counterforce strike capabilities.

The development of one system does not guarantee deterrence; however, the intent and posturing matter. By introducing the Fatah-IV and continuously developing it, Islamabad is signaling to New Delhi that the old days are gone now. Indian military installations located deep inside the country are no longer safe from Pakistan’s conventional missile force.

The ER Fatah-IV exists to protect Pakistan’s national security at a time when India believes that territorial victory remains the ultimate goal in modern conflict, as evident from the recent statement of India’s army chief General Dhiraj Seth. In the presence of such a belligerent mindset of the adversary, it becomes a compulsion for the other side to take appropriate defensive measures. The Fatah-IV is one such measure taken by Pakistan to boost the country’s defense and to protect its territorial sovereignty.
