title: Why the China-US Naval Encounter at Sabina Shoal Is Different
description: It’s a new kind of close encounter. Will it become a new normal?
text:
On October 20, China accused a U.S. naval vessel of “undermining regional stability” by entering waters near Sabina Shoal in the Spratly Islands. According to a spokesperson for the People’s Liberation Army’s Southern Theater Command Navy, the U.S. Littoral Combat Ship USS Charleston (LCS-18) “illegally ​intruded” into waters adjacent to Sabina Shoal “without approval from the Chinese government.” By contrast, a U.S.​ Navy 7th Fleet spokesperson maintained that the Charleston conducted “routine operations in international waters” consistent with international law.

This latest naval encounter reflects the long-standing legal dispute between China and the U.S. over the freedom of navigation of warships in the South China Sea. What makes it distinct is the location of the incident: unlike all previous U.S. Freedom of Navigation Operations (FONOPs) targeted at China in the South China Sea, the encounter occurred near Sabina Shoal, a maritime feature not occupied by China. Thus, this is also the first time that the PLA Navy (PLAN) officially admitted that it “dispatched forces to track and monitor the U.S. vessel” near a feature China doesn’t occupy.

This new kind of close encounter may reveal that the Chinese government is upgrading its strategy to respond to perceived U.S. naval intrusions in the South China Sea. At the same time, the incident may also serve as a warning to the Philippines, which considers Sabina Shoal to be a part of its Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ). These interpretations remain tentative, and non-exclusive, but they make the encounter worth examining beyond the immediate exchange of official statements.

Disputes Between China and the U.S. over “Freedom of Navigation” of Warships

The United States holds that the right to sail and operate its military vessels “wherever customary international law allows” is “a long-standing national interest.” The U.S. military uses FONOPs to challenge maritime claims and restrictions that it considers excessive.

China, by contrast, argues that freedom of navigation cannot be invoked to justify activities that it views as threatening its territorial integrity or security, including foreign warships’ operations near maritime features over which China asserts sovereignty. Beijing considers the intentional “intrusion” of warships into its claimed territorial sea to be “hegemonic freedom of navigation.” China argues U.S. FONOPs have no place in contemporary international law.

A semi-official research report published by the China Institute for Marine Affairs under the Ministry of Natural Resources in August 2025 highlighted this issue. The report concluded that the “U.S. Freedom of Navigation lacks a basis in international law and seriously distorts the interpretation and development of international law.” These competing positions have underpinned repeated Chinese protests against U.S. naval operations in the South China Sea.

Notably, news reports of the Charleston’s October 20 operation did not officially describe it as a FONOP. The U.S. spokesperson’s statement instead emphasized that “all nations enjoy freedom of navigation and other lawful uses of the sea in this area.” That language is consistent with Washington’s broader position on maritime access, but it does not establish that the operation was a formally designated FONOP or identify the specific legal claim, if any, that the vessel intended to challenge.

The distinction matters: a naval transit, a routine operation, and a FONOP may overlap in practice, but they are not necessarily interchangeable descriptions of an operation’s purpose.

Why Sabina Shoal Is Distinct

U.S. FONOPs generally identify a particular maritime claim or restriction they seek to challenge. For instance, the United States explicitly labeled a previous operation that took place on August 13, 2025, near Scarborough Shoal as a FONOP intended to challenge Chinese domestic legislation requiring prior authorization for foreign warships to enter China’s territorial sea. In such cases, the stated legal objective provides a relatively clear basis for interpreting the operation and anticipating a Chinese response. In the August 2025 case, the PLA said it had “organized forces to lawfully track, monitor, issue warnings, and expel the U.S. warship.”

Sabina Shoal presents a different situation for a number of reasons. First of all, unlike Scarborough Shoal, Sabina Shoal was not among the contested maritime features in the 2016 South China Sea Arbitration Award.

At the same time, there is no mutual understanding between China and the Philippines on the legal status of the shoal and its surrounding waters. The United States and the Philippines regard Sabina Shoal as a low-tide elevation that cannot, in its own right, generate a territorial sea. They thus regard the surrounding waters as part of the Philippines’ EEZ.

By contrast, the Chinese government disputes that Sabina Shoal (known in Chinese as Xianbin Jiao) is a low-tide elevation. In fact, a “Survey Report on the Coral Reef Ecosystem of Xianbin Jiao” published by the Ministry of Natural Resources of China in August 2024, said that there are at least three naturally formed cays above water at high tide. Accordingly, China considers Sabina Shoal to be a rock that can claim a territorial sea. This may explain why China accused the Charleston of an “illegal intrusion” into the “adjacent waters” of Sabina Shoal.

Nevertheless, the most peculiar scenario at Sabina Shoal is that this maritime feature has never been formally occupied by China, thanks to the 2002 Declaration on the Conduct of Parties in the South China Sea (DOC), which prohibits “inhabitation” on previously unoccupied maritime features.

Yet in Beijing’s view, Sabina Shoal is part of the “Nansha Qundao” (Spratly Islands), which as a whole belongs to China. That might be the reason that China never formally claimed any territorial sea around its occupied maritime features such as Johnson Reef (Chigua Jiao), Fiery Cross Reef (Yongshu Jiao), or Cuarteron Reef (Huayang Jiao). Instead, Beijing claims “indisputable territorial sovereignty, sovereign rights and interests” within the whole of the Spratly Islands group.

The ambiguity surrounding the nature of the Charleston’s operation makes it difficult to interpret. It’s unclear if the United States intended to challenge a Chinese claim to maritime entitlements around Sabina Shoal or a requirement for prior authorization of transiting its territorial sea. If, however, the operation was instead intended to demonstrate support for the Philippines, the significance would lie less in a specific legal challenge than in the strategic signal conveyed by a U.S. naval presence near a flashpoint in the China-Philippines dispute.

A Possible Warning to the Philippines

The encounter occurred amid heightened tensions between China and the Philippines. On October 14, Chinese Ambassador to the Philippines Jing Quan reportedly remarked that China could “easily win a conflict” against the Philippines if it chose to use force. The remark followed a serious confrontation between a Chinese Coast Guard vessel and a Philippine government vessel at Sabina Shoal on September 18.

In fact, since the beginning of October, at least eight close encounters between China and the Philippines have occurred across the South China Sea and Luzon Strait, according to Reuters. This wider context helps explain why the Philippines might view the Charleston’s presence at Sabina Shoal as a sign of U.S. support, even if the operation was not formally identified as a FONOP against Chinese maritime claims.

China’s response, on the other hand, could be interpreted as a fresh warning to the Philippines. By dispatching naval forces to track and monitor the U.S. warship at an unoccupied maritime feature for the first time, China showcased its determination to protect its claimed rights and interests at Sabina Shoal.

This upgraded response also sends a straightforward warning to the Philippines that any further provocation at Sabina Shoal, with or without support from the U.S., will predictably receive an escalated Chinese response.

The Outlook of China-U.S. Naval Encounters in the South China Sea

While international law provides a common framework for maritime conduct, its interpretation and application remain deeply contested by major powers. The United States advocates its naval operations as a defense of freedom of navigation, whereas China views U.S. naval operations near South China Sea maritime features as challenges to its territorial sovereignty and security. Without a shared understanding of the legal and strategic implications of such operations, similar encounters are likely to recur.

The outlook is therefore one of persistent competition accompanied by risks of unintended escalation. As both navies maintain a significant presence in the South China Sea, close encounters – including, as in this case – China-U.S. naval encounters at maritime features not occupied by China, may become increasingly frequent, particularly amid intensifying Philippine-U.S. security cooperation. Even when neither side seeks confrontation, miscalculation, communication failures, or domestic political pressure could turn a “routine operation” into a serious crisis.

Yet confrontation is not inevitable. Both China and the United States have strong incentives to prevent tactical incidents from escalating into broader military conflict. Maintaining effective military communication channels, strengthening incident-management mechanisms, and clarifying operational protocols should therefore remain priorities. Equally important is a willingness to address maritime disagreements through diplomacy and international law rather than relying exclusively on military assertions such as the FONOPs.

Ultimately, the significance of the Sabina Shoal naval encounter lies not simply in the actions of the two navies, but in what it reveals about the future of maritime order in the South China Sea. Whether such encounters become catalysts for escalation or opportunities for improved crisis management will depend on the strategic choices made in Beijing and Washington.

title: Why the Mecca Agreement Might Fail
description: If each member preserves its own partnerships while expecting the others to absorb its security risks, what does the promise that an attack against one is an attack against all mean when a crisis arrives?
text:
On August 7, 2026, Turkiye’s Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, Saudi Arabia’s Mohammed bin Salman, and Pakistan’s Shehbaz Sharif jointly signed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, which commits their countries to collective defense and expands defense cooperation. It builds on the Saudi-Pakistani Strategic Mutual Defense Agreement of September 2025. On August 31, their foreign ministers, defense ministers, and military chiefs met in Istanbul, announcing a secretariat in Saudi Arabia, initially headed by a Pakistani secretary general, alongside cooperation in military technology and production.

The most important question about the Mecca agreement is whose war they are prepared to fight. Although the text of the agreement is not publicly available yet, according to a Pakistan Foreign Ministry statement, Saudi Arabia, Turkiye, and Pakistan have agreed that an armed attack against any one of the three states shall be regarded as an attack against them all. However, with a look at their conflicting interests, one can easily predict that they will struggle to agree on what should happen next.

What makes one doubt whether such an accord could realistically function is the agreement’s central weakness: its publicly announced terms do not specify which forces would fight, under whose command, or on what timetable. All parties to the accord want greater security while retaining the freedom to decide which regional conflicts concern them. But when countries commit to collective defense, they must also agree on when and how they will defend one another, what strategic purpose the accord serves, and which threats they consider common. They must also be clear about who decides when military action is necessary, how they will share the costs, and how far each country is prepared to go if the conflict escalates; what economic interests they are willing to sacrifice, whether greater financial contributions give one country greater authority, and how they will reconcile their competing ambitions.

The first problem is that all three countries aspire to lead the Muslim world, but each has a different idea of what that leadership means. For instance, Erdoğan’s Turkiye invokes its Ottoman heritage to project authority beyond its borders. Turkiye’s reconversion of the Hagia Sophia into a mosque in 2020 to restore symbols of its Ottoman past was part of that ambition. In a 2018 speech to provincial muftis in Ankara, Erdoğan presented Turkiye as a country entitled to shape the Muslim world’s future because of the authority its Ottoman predecessors once exercised. Since Erdoğan’s rise to power, nostalgia for an imperial and caliphal past has helped shape Turkiye’s claim to leadership in the Muslim world today.

Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, bases its claim to leadership on its custodianship of Mecca and Medina and its established position in Islamic diplomacy. In the meantime, while Mohammed bin Salman wants to preserve that position and keep religion as a source of legitimacy, he is also making the kingdom a center for investment, technology, and regional diplomacy to serve the country’s economic and political ambitions. Saudi Arabia therefore wants a form of Islamic leadership that reinforces its own position, which raises the question of how far it would support an alliance that also strengthens Turkiye’s competing claim to that leadership.

For its part, Pakistan has long sought to turn its military strength into a claim to leadership of the Muslim world. This ambition is visible in how its leaders have explained the purpose of its nuclear program. Prime Minister Zulfikar Ali Bhutto famously said that other civilizations already possessed nuclear capability, writing: “Only the Islamic civilization was without it, but that position was about to change.” He was presenting Pakistan’s nuclear ambitions as an achievement that would alter the position of the entire Islamic civilization. Almost half a century later, addressing religious scholars in December 2025, Field Marshall Asim Munir, Pakistan’s first chief of defense forces and the country’s top military official, declared: “Among all Muslim countries, Allah has given Pakistan the honor of helping safeguard the Haramain,” referring to Islam’s holy sites in Mecca and Medina. Munir was thereby presenting Pakistan’s military role as a religious responsibility extending beyond its borders, giving Islamabad another basis for claiming a special position in the Muslim world.

Further, in 2020, Foreign Minister Shah Mahmood Qureshi threatened to organize Muslim countries outside the Saudi-led OIC over Kashmir. Pakistan has therefore shown a willingness to challenge the existing framework of Muslim diplomacy led by Saudi Arabia or Turkiye when it fails to serve Pakistani priorities, and this is where these ambitions could become difficult to reconcile with Saudi Arabia and Turkiye’s.

These three countries have also had differences in their foreign policies, and those differences have sometimes led them to work against one another’s regional objectives. For instance, during the 2017 blockade of Qatar by Saudi Arabia, it was Turkiye that sent troops and food supplies to Doha, helping Qatar to resist pressure from Saudi Arabia and its partners. Pakistan has also resisted Saudi expectations of military support. In 2015, after Riyadh requested Pakistani troops, aircraft, and warships for its intervention in Yemen, Pakistan’s parliament voted to remain neutral; this refusal showed that close relations did not mean Islamabad accepted Riyadh’s judgment about when military action was necessary.

Pakistan has also not shown up to defend Saudi Arabia against the current attacks by Iran, despite the so-called “NATO-like” agreement that both countries signed last September. Most recently, on September 11, Saudi Arabia announced a precautionary shutdown of its East-West pipeline following drone attacks that Riyadh said originated in Iraq. The pipeline provided a vital alternative for oil exports disrupted by Iran’s restrictions at Hormuz. Separately, the Houthis captured Mokha and Perim, also known as Mayun, strengthening their position at Bab el-Mandeb, the southern gateway to the Red Sea and the trade route through Suez. Again, despite both the Strategic Mutual Defense Agreement and the Mecca accord, Pakistan and Turkiye have not shown up to defend Saudi Arabia, concerned with themselves being drawn into the crisis, after being threatened by Houthis that they both would pay a “high price” if they intervened.

The military picture extends the problem. Turkiye brings decades of NATO experience and a substantial domestic defense industry, while Pakistan increasingly relies on Chinese equipment, and Saudi Arabia remains heavily dependent on foreign suppliers. According to SIPRI’s 2026 data, China supplied 80 percent of Pakistan’s major arms imports in 2021–2025, while the United States supplied 77 percent of Saudi Arabia’s. If Pakistani and Saudi forces were fighting together, they would need to exchange relevant operational intelligence and coordinate forces using different military systems. However, integrating those systems could require sensitive technical information and assistance from their suppliers. Washington could object to arrangements that exposed information about American equipment to Chinese technicians, while Beijing could have similar concerns about Western access to its technology. Both would want to prevent a rival from learning how their weapons operate, identifying their vulnerabilities, or developing ways to defeat them. Suppliers could therefore have more power to limit how closely Mecca accord parties could operate together, even if those governments agreed on the need for joint military action.

Turkiye has seen how serious these restrictions can become. In July 2019, the United States excluded Ankara from the F-35 fighter program following its purchase of Russia’s S-400 air defense system, arguing that the Russian system could collect sensitive information about the aircraft’s capabilities. Turkiye’s longstanding NATO membership did not overcome Washington’s security concerns. The implication for the Mecca accord is that political agreement among its members may be insufficient to secure the military integration they need. If competing suppliers’ security concerns could obstruct cooperation inside NATO, there is little reason to assume that American and Chinese equipment can be easily integrated for the Mecca accord parties.

Turkiye’s NATO membership creates another complication. Even though the NATO Treaty places limits on collective defense obligations through Articles 5 and 6, which define the attacks and geographical areas they cover, Turkiye cannot extend NATO’s protection to Pakistan or Saudi Arabia simply by signing another agreement. However, an armed attack on Turkish territory resulting from Turkiye’s intervention in defense of either country would raise a separate Article 5 question which limits Turkiye’s freedom of action under the Mecca accord, as Ankara would have to consider how far it could go in defending its new partners and what consequences its involvement could have for its NATO allies.

Moreover, from an economic perspective, the economic imbalance among the three members makes the Mecca agreement hard to sustain. Saudi Arabia brings substantial oil wealth, Turkiye brings industrial capacity but continues to struggle with inflation, and Pakistan remains an IMF borrower. These differences raise questions about how they would divide the costs of preparing for, fighting, and recovering from a common war. NATO members finance their own forces while contributing to common budgets through an agreed formula based on national income. The Mecca accord’s statement announces a secretariat and industrial cooperation without explaining an equivalent financial arrangement.

If Saudi Arabia is expected to provide most of the money, would it demand greater influence over deployments and procurement? Would Turkiye and Pakistan accept that influence while supplying forces and bearing casualties? Conversely, would Riyadh finance military commitments over which its partners retained a veto? Paying for weapons is also different from funding years of operations, replacing losses and compensating for disrupted trade. A further difficulty is that attacks on Saudi oil infrastructure could weaken the revenue supporting any Saudi financial commitment. According to current reports, oil loadings at Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea port of Yanbu have stopped following drone attacks by the Iran-backed Houthi militia. The port has served as a major outlet for Saudi oil exports following the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz, and, according to experts, this pause in loadings could cause further severe disruption to global energy markets.

The difficulty goes further: the three countries do not share the same enemies. Pakistan shares a border with Iran, and both Islamabad and Ankara maintain relations with Tehran, while Saudi Arabia faces attacks from Iranian rockets in its territory as well as from its Houthi allies. More importantly, Turkiye has said the accord is not directed against Iran, which puts Saudi Arabia’s situation in limbo, as it’s not clear what is in this accord for Saudi Arabia and what protection Riyadh can expect if its partners prioritize preserving relations with Tehran.

Moreover, the Mecca accord countries have different approaches to Israel, the other major player in the region. Turkiye’s relations with Israel are confrontational, and Pakistan does not recognize Israel as a state, while Saudi Arabia remains the subject of efforts to expand the Abraham Accords, although Riyadh conditions normalization on Palestinian statehood.

On the other hand, with India, Pakistan’s principal strategic rival, the complications are amplified Saudi Arabia maintains a close partnership with India, with bilateral trade reaching $41.88 billion in fiscal 2024-2025. Would Riyadh jeopardize that relationship to fight New Delhi on Islamabad’s behalf? Would Pakistan confront Iran for Saudi Arabia? If each member preserves its own partnerships while expecting the others to absorb its security risks, what does the promise that an attack against one is an attack against all mean when a crisis arrives?

title: Why the TTP Remains the Central Fault Line Between Pakistan and Afghanistan
description: The costs of confrontation are not confined to the security domain; it’s impacting every facet of the bilateral relationship.
text:
On October 11, Pakistan’s military reported that security forces had killed 12 militants and Afghan Taliban personnel during an attempted crossing from Afghanistan into Pakistan’s Kurram district. A Pakistani soldier was also killed in the exchange of fire. The Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), the military’s media wing, said Afghan Taliban border posts had opened fire in support of the attempted crossing.

The incident came 10 days after Pakistani airstrikes in Afghanistan, which Islamabad said targeted militant camps and hideouts. Pakistan reported that the strikes killed 22 militants. At the same time, the United Nations Assistance Mission in Afghanistan (UNAMA) confirmed that at least 10 civilians, most of them children, were killed and nine injured in Kunar and Helmand provinces. The U.N. mission called for de-escalation and greater protection of civilians, underscoring the humanitarian risks of continued cross-border hostilities.

These incidents reflect a wider deterioration in Afghanistan-Pakistan relations, driven in part by Islamabad’s concerns about militant groups operating from Afghan territory.

On September 18, a suicide car bombing at a mosque inside the Kohat Police Lines complex in Pakistan’s Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, followed by an armed assault, killed at least 31 people, including 16 police personnel, and injured more than 100, according to local police officials. Ittehadul Mujahideen Pakistan (IMP), a militant alliance linked to the Hafiz Gul Bahadur faction, claimed responsibility for the attack. The IMP operates within the broader network of militant groups active along the Afghanistan-Pakistan border and has had links with the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), a militant umbrella organization waging an insurgency against the Pakistani state.

The scale of the threat is reflected in the 2026 Global Terrorism Index, which ranked the TTP as the world’s third-deadliest terrorist organization in 2025. The index identified rising violence by both the TTP and the Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA) as contributing to Pakistan’s worsening security environment. Islamabad has maintained that the Afghan Taliban authorities are allowing the militant outfits, including the TTP and the BLA, to maintain sanctuaries in Afghanistan, an allegation Kabul denies.

The Kohat attack was just one manifestation of a broader security dispute that has strained Afghanistan-Pakistan relations for years. In 2022, shortly after the Taliban returned to power in Afghanistan, Pakistan negotiated with the TTP through mediation by Afghanistan’s Taliban authorities. They reached a ceasefire in June 2022, but the agreement collapsed in November, when the TTP announced a resumption of attacks across Pakistan.

A February 2023 U.N. Security Council monitoring report cited assessments by several member states that the Taliban’s return to power in Afghanistan had emboldened the TTP and contributed to an escalation in its attacks against Pakistan. The report also examined links between the TTP and other armed groups. Subsequent U.N. Security Council monitoring reports have provided further support for Pakistan’s security concerns. A July 2024 report noted that the TTP continued to operate from Afghanistan and conduct attacks inside Pakistan, citing member states’ assessments of Taliban tolerance and support for the group. The December 2025 report went further, describing the continued harboring of TTP leaders in Afghanistan and the facilitation of the group’s operations by the Taliban authorities.

As concerns about cross-border militancy persisted, Islamabad pursued a parallel response at home. In June 2024, the government approved Azm-e-Istehkam, a national framework intended to strengthen intelligence-based operations and law enforcement. However, domestic counterterrorism measures have not resolved the cross-border dimension of the threat.

Regional diplomacy has struggled to bridge the divide between Islamabad and Kabul. The eighth Moscow Format Consultations on Afghanistan, held on October 5, offered a recent example of this impasse. The meeting brought together Afghanistan and regional powers, including Pakistan, China, India, Iran and Russia, to discuss security and regional cooperation. It ended without a joint statement after the Pakistani and Afghan delegations struggled to agree on the language concerning terrorism. Pakistan’s Special Representative for Afghanistan, Mohammad Sadiq, emphasized the threat posed by militant groups operating from Afghan territory, while the Afghan Taliban delegation resisted the proposed wording. The disagreement illustrated a fundamental obstacle: the two sides have yet to agree on how to define and address the security problem itself.

The Moscow impasse followed earlier attempts to ease tensions through direct negotiations. After the October 2025 fighting, Qatar and Turkiye hosted talks that produced a ceasefire, followed by further rounds of negotiations in Istanbul, Doha, and Riyadh. These efforts did not resolve the central dispute. Pakistan seeks verifiable action against the TTP, while the Afghan Taliban authorities deny that the group operates from their territory in the manner Islamabad alleges. Without agreement on the underlying security concerns, diplomatic engagement has struggled to produce a durable settlement.

Economic ties have suffered as a result. In January 2026, Pakistani and Afghan traders agreed to establish a joint committee to discuss reopening border crossings. However, commercial negotiations could not overcome the wider security impasse. Since the October 2025 clashes, Pakistan has kept its border crossings with Afghanistan closed to trade – by far the longest closure in recent decades, disrupting a key transit route into Central Asia. The economic burden has fallen on traders and transporters on both sides, while Afghanistan has sought to diversify its trade through Iran, India, and other regional partners.

The costs of confrontation are therefore not confined to the security domain. Prolonged border closures disrupt livelihoods and commercial networks, while airstrikes and armed clashes expose civilians to further harm. The biggest challenge is to prevent the security dispute from becoming a self-reinforcing cycle in which militant violence prompts punitive measures, those measures deepen bilateral hostility, and deteriorating relations make cooperation against militancy even more difficult.

Breaking this cycle requires practical measures rather than competing declarations. First, Pakistan and the Afghan Taliban authorities could establish a verification mechanism, facilitated by a mutually acceptable third party such as Qatar, Turkiye, or China, to investigate specific allegations of militant activity and assess compliance with security commitments. Second, trade routes could be reopened gradually against measurable security benchmarks, linking economic recovery to demonstrable progress. Third, regional powers could support a sustained counterterrorism dialogue focused on information-sharing, specific incidents, and border management. Such targeted cooperation may offer a more realistic starting point than broader diplomatic forums where disagreements over the nature of the threat continue to prevent consensus.

title: Will Indonesia’s New Foreign Minister Be Allowed to Do His Job?
description: Arrmanatha Nasir is highly qualified, but his success may hinge on whether or not he has access to President Prabowo Subianto.
text:
On October 1, Indonesia’s President Prabowo Subianto finally replaced Sugiono, who had served as foreign minister for the past two years, with the veteran diplomat Arrmanatha Nasir. While one may welcome the appointment of a seasoned diplomat as foreign minister, it is unclear whether he will have enough power and presidential access to steer Indonesia’s foreign policy back to a steadier, more familiar course, as under previous administrations.

As the first foreign minister in decades without substantial foreign policy experience, Sugiono’s tenure was marked by consequential decisions that broke foreign policy precedent. During his time at the helm of the Foreign Ministry, Indonesia endorsed a joint statement with China that appeared to depart from its long-standing refusal to recognize its overlapping claim with China near the Natuna Islands, potentially lending credence to China’s illegal nine-dash line claim. Additionally, it joined both BRICS and U.S. President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace, and signed the unequal Agreement on Reciprocal Trade with Washington, despite this having dubious benefits to Indonesia. Internally, Indonesian diplomats made anonymous complaints to Indonesian media regarding the chaotic Foreign Ministry workflow and being left in the dark about vital foreign policy decisions that were deliberated within Prabowo’s inner circle.

In this context, Nasir’s appointment comes as a breath of fresh air. In contrast to the inexperienced Sugiono, Nasir has 29 years of experience as a Foreign Ministry insider who has filled two ambassadorial-level postings and served a five-year stint as the Ministry’s spokesperson, among other roles. Therefore, the Foreign Ministry has returned to its decades-long tradition of having career diplomats at its helm. More importantly, during his tenure as Sugiono’s vice foreign minister, Nasir was responsible for the Ministry’s internal dynamics, suggesting he should have had direct knowledge of discontent among the Ministry’s diplomats and staff. Thus, under his tenure, diplomats’ involvement in technocratic deliberations on important foreign policy matters could be improved.

While there is no doubt about Nasir’s ability to steer Indonesia’s foreign policy in the coming years, it is less clear whether he will be given the necessary opportunities and access to do so. Reports in the Indonesian news magazine Tempo indicate that access to President Prabowo, even for ministers, is very limited and heavily curated by members of his inner circle at the presidential palace, thus handicapping close coordination between the president and his cabinet members across a wide range of governmental affairs.

Foreign policy is not immune to this, and at least three major foreign policy decisions under Sugiono’s tenure were made without properly following the Foreign Ministry’s recommendations. In the lead-up to the 2024 Sino-Indonesian joint statement, Indonesian diplomats were ordered to reject any stipulation regarding joint development in overlapping areas of the South China Sea, only for the president to sign it anyway. Some reports suggest that Prabowo followed the advice of his closest confidants, who view the dispute purely in economic terms.

Additionally, high-ranking Foreign Ministry officials expressed grave concern about the one-sidedness of the U.S.-Indonesia Agreement on Reciprocal Trade signed earlier this year, yet the president signed it regardless. Lastly, Indonesia joined the Board of Peace without proper deliberation with relevant Indonesian ambassadors in the Middle East, and several Indonesian diplomats anonymously complained that Indonesia’s decision to join the organization was problematic in terms of Jakarta’s policy of support for the Palestinian cause. Even Sugiono himself admitted publicly that the decision to join was made “quite fast.”

These phenomena suggest a gap in foreign policy formulation between career diplomats at the Foreign Ministry and politicians at the Presidential Palace. Ideally, the two should work in concert: Foreign Ministry staff should work out the technocratic and strategic foreign policy details, while the palace uses that advice to shape and consider broader implications beyond foreign policy, and vice versa. Additionally, bureaucrats typically spend years or decades in the Ministry, accumulating knowledge and experience that help ensure Indonesia’s foreign policy does not wildly deviate and remains consistent. If the Palace isolates itself, the views and analyses of seasoned, capable Foreign Ministry diplomats that help maintain policy stability and consistency may not be reflected in the final strategic decision, making it vulnerable to decisions of dubious benefit for Jakarta.

Nasir’s appointment, therefore, must be seen in that context. One may justifiably have little doubt about his ability to steer Indonesia’s foreign policy and muster the Ministry’s diplomats to that end. Yet, the President will have to allow the Minister quick and easy access to the Palace and ensure close coordination between it and the Ministry, such as inviting the Foreign Minister into policy deliberations with foreign policy implications and implementing his recommendations, as well as accepting the Minister’s request for an audience whenever necessary. Without proper access and consultation, no matter how brilliant or qualified the foreign minister may be, the Palace could make more major foreign policy decisions with dubious benefits and high risks.

While Prabowo wants to be more hands-on in foreign policymaking, if given access and proper consultation, an able foreign minister and diplomats can ensure that Prabowo leaves a better foreign policy legacy, since they will be able to make refined analyses and policies to achieve his goals more strategically. The question is, will the President finally muster his able foreign service to that end?

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own.

title: Will There Be a Putin-Trump-Xi Summit?
description: If so, to what end? Panda and Putz discuss on the latest episode of the Asia Geopolitics podcast.
text:
In this episode of The Diplomat’s Asia Geopolitics Podcast, hosts Katie Putz and Ankit Panda discuss U.S. President Donald Trump’s upcoming travel itinerary to Asia, to include the ASEAN Summit in Manila, the Philippines, and the APEC Summit in Shenzhen, China. What’s grabbed headlines, however, is the possibility of a trilateral summit with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Putin and Trump have commented on the potential summit, highlighting very different agendas, and China has stayed mostly quiet about it.

title: Will US President Donald Trump Visit Central Asia?
description: No U.S. president has ever traveled to Central Asia while in office. Could Donald Trump be the first? Sure. But will he be? That’s a different question.
text:
As U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s planned trip to Uzbekistan – at the head of a large delegation of American businesses – approaches, once again Central Asian governments and people are angling for a presidential visit. Both Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan have repeatedly invited Trump to make the trek; he’d be very welcome in the region and they’re hoping the novelty of being the “first” will get them on the presidential calendar.

In an interview with an Uzbek TV station, U.S. Special Representative for Global Partnerships Paolo Zampolli, said, “I know [Trump] wants to come to Uzbekistan. The president has an extremely busy schedule. But he told me about his intention to visit Uzbekistan. I myself am constantly promoting this issue. So, he will definitely visit Uzbekistan one day. We hope this visit will take place as soon as possible.”

That’s not exactly a firm commitment from a notoriously fickle administration, no matter the rabid headlines about the comments.

There has been no shortage of U.S. officials traveling to Central Asia since the dawn of the second Trump presidency. These include an October 2025 trip to Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan by Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau and Sergio Gor, concurrently the U.S. ambassador to India and also special envoy for South and Central Asian affairs. In February 2026, Gor returned to Central Asia, visiting Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan. In July 2026, Senator Steve Daines, a Republican from Montana – who co-founded the bipartisan Senate Central Asia Caucus in 2024 – traveled to Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan (and also Azerbaijan).

U.S. engagement with Central Asia has shifted from Afghanistan – an all-encompassing subject that dominated relations from 2001 to 2021 – to critical minerals, an especially hot topic for governments keen on dealmaking.

In November 2025, amid the fanfare of the C5+1 summit in Washington, in which all five Central Asian presidents were welcomed to the White House for the first time (although it was not the first presidential level C5+1 summit, as some have erroneously reported) – Rubio declared his intention to visit all five Central Asian states in the coming year.

“I personally intend to visit in the coming year,” he said during a reception after meeting with his Central Asian counterparts, as reported by Reuters. “All five,” Rubio added. “So I know it would probably be a week-long trip. So we’ve got to work on that and make that happen together.”

To date, the highest-ranking U.S. official to complete what I dubbed the “grand Stan slam” was then-Secretary of State John Kerry in 2015. It was during that trip that the C5+1, at the foreign ministers level, was launched in Samarkand, a month after a preview event on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly.

Rubio’s own envisioned “grand Stan slam” has been apparently whittled down to a trip to Samarkand, with a heavy business focus. According to a September 24 press release published by the U.S. embassy in India, and attributed to Gor, Rubio “will lead a historic business delegation of more than 100 American companies to Samarkand, Uzbekistan in mid-October to advance the U.S.-Central Asia strategic partnership and strengthen bilateral diplomatic and commercial cooperation.”

The Diplomat has heard rumored dates for the trip, but they have yet to be confirmed publicly. And that’s of little surprise. Not only is Rubio serving as secretary of state, but he’s also national security adviser – a role he took over on an interim basis in May 2025 after Michael Waltz flamed out by inviting a journalist into a high-level Signal chat. That role was made permanent on September 22. Rubio’s the second person to wear both hats simultaneously – the first was Henry Kissinger under Presidents Richard Nixon and Gerald Ford. All that to say: Rubio is a busy guy. The planned trip to Samarkand could, frankly speaking, be spoiled by any number of sudden crises.

Aside from Zampolli’s recent comment that Trump “wants” to come to Uzbekistan, there’s been no official word on that front. Trump is often discussed as disliking international travel. Of the three most recent presidents – Barack Obama (2009-2016) Trump 1.0 (2017-2020), and Joe Biden (2021-2024) he’s made the fewest international trips and visited the fewest foreign countries. Obama made a total of 25 foreign trips during his first term, Trump made 19, and Biden 21.

The statistics alone don’t tell the full story. Trump’s presidency ended with the COVID-19 outbreak, and Biden’s began with its lingering impact. So far in his second term, Trump has made 14 foreign trips – six in 2025 and eight so far in 2026. Trump is scheduled, officially, for one more international trip this year: from November 16 to 19, to attend the ASEAN Summit and the East Asia Summit in the Philippines and then to attend the APEC Summit in Shenzhen, China.

The year is drawing to a close, rapidly. The looming mid-term elections, scheduled for November 3 – and not looking good, per most polls, for the president’s party – might jerk Trump’s attention back to the domestic arena, making a late-year junket to Tashkent nearly impossible and potentially ruining future plans, too.

Trump does have two years left in his term, so a Central Asia visit may eventuate – he could also visit any of the more than 75 other countries a U.S. president has never traveled to while in office. Spoilers abound both internationally and domestically that could dash the highest of hopes for a U.S. president to finally step foot in Central Asia. But hope springs eternal.

title: With Strict Agendas and Silent Corridors Kazakhstan’s Kurultai Is Muzzling the Press
description: Journalists covering the country’s parliament are pushing back against new rules that constrict their ability to question officials.
text:
When Kazakhstan’s Kurultai convened in late August for the first time, there were new rules for the media. Journalists in the Kazakh capital’s parliament building were no longer able to question deputies in the corridors. The new rules set firm boundaries not only on where, but what, they could ask members of the country’s new unicameral parliament.

At the opening of the Kurultai’s first session on August 28, Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev proclaimed the body would “radically modernize the system of government and provide a powerful impetus to the work of the entire state apparatus.” Later in his speech he urged the Kutultai to become “a platform for national dialogue to develop solutions to key issues in society.”

The boundaries of that dialogue, however, are to be set by the Kurultai itself.

As explained by the Kurultai’s Deputy Chief of Staff Bolat Kalyanbekov in a September 2 Facebook post, “All interactions between journalists and deputies – as well as invited members of the Government – will now take place exclusively within the press center and strictly in relation to the Kurultai’s agenda.”

Kalyanbekov stated that briefings would be held on a regular basis and laid out the rationale behind the decision to bar off-topic questions.

“Our goal is to communicate the substance of the draft laws under consideration by the Kurultai to the public as clearly and comprehensively as possible – explaining the significance of each new legal provision and how the decisions being made may impact the lives of citizens,” he wrote.

Kalyanbekov also argued that the new rules were consistent both with Kazakh law and “established global practices.”

That’s not quite how Fiona O’Brien, the Europe and Central Asia regional director for the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), sees it. “Allowing journalists to informally approach and question deputies in the halls of parliament, and to ask questions not strictly related to the agenda of press conferences, are standard practices of established democracies,” O’Brien told The Diplomat.

Although Kazakhstan deems itself a democratic state, human rights organizations such as Freedom House, classify the country as “Not Free.”

“The kinds of restrictions on movement and questions implemented in Kazakhstan are more common in authoritarian or hybrid environments, where the authorities try to maintain an appearance of democracy while retaining strict control of the information sphere,” O’Brien explained.

***

On October 20, Otkir Kurek – an independent media outlet headed by Nazymgul Kumyspayeva, who also runs a YouTube channel – reported that a group of around 40 journalists accredited to the Kurultai had sent an appeal to Aibek Dadebay, chair of the body, demanding revision of the new media rules.

Otkir Kurek means “sharp shovel” in Kazakh.

Dadebay is also leader of the Adilet party, into which the former ruling party Amanat (née Nur-Otan) merged earlier this year in the runup to the Kurultai elections on August 23. Until May 5, Dadebay headed Tokayev’s presidential administration.

In the recent appeal, as reported by KazTAG, the Kazakh journalists took particular issue with the restriction of questions to agenda-items only.

Under the present rules, “For a question that the moderator deems off-topic, the journalist receives a warning. Two violations mean the loss of accreditation for six months… For a journalist who covers parliament, this is effectively a six-month ban from the profession.”

The appeal noted that the purpose of accreditation is to enable journalists “to inform the public broadly and promptly.”

“Kazakhstan’s parliament and other state organs have long tried to stop journalists asking ‘off-topic’ questions during press conferences,” CPJ’s O’Brien explained. “Introducing sanctions for doing so and preventing journalists from mixing freely with deputies in the halls of parliament essentially closes down the last avenues for journalists to freely question parliamentarians on issues not decided in advance by the authorities themselves.”

“A briefing that repeats what has already been said at the meeting provides no new information,” the journalists argued in their appeal, seeking a revision to the existing regulations to allow journalists to ask questions outside the strict agenda but within the purview of the featured speakers.

“A minister or deputy can always refuse to answer a question, respond later, or respond in writing,” the appeal noted. The journalists characterized the existing policy as unjustified. Journalists, they argued, need to be free to question ministers, deputies, and other officials – who, the appeal pointed out, “rarely appear in public and for whom the public has many questions.”

Kazakh journalists have already run afoul of these rules.

In early October, in the wake of a tragic accident on the Caspian Sea in which 14 servicemembers drowned during a military drill, journalist Asem Gumarova of Ulysmedia.kz asked questions related to the incident during a briefing with a member of parliament, Unzila Shapak, and Deputy Minister of Internal Affairs Sanjar Adilov. The brief was to cover a draft cybercrime law.

Gumarova asked Shapak when the 146 million tenge that had been reportedly collected by Kurultai members would be transferred to the families of the fallen servicemen. She also asked Adilov about reports of pressure being exerted by mysterious callers masquerading as police demanding that the authors of critical posts related to the Caspian accident take their posts down.

Ulysmedia said it received a warning letter threatening to strip Gumarova of her accreditation. The publication cited the “extraordinary nature of the incident and public demand” as justifying Gumarova’s questions.

The recent appeal to Dadebay cited the incident directly, noting that “[t]he question concerned police work online or crimes carried out under the guise of police – that is, the very topic of the briefing.”

***

Accreditation procedures vary country to country. But broadly speaking accreditation confers a degree of legitimacy on a journalist and their outlet and, importantly, provides access to official spaces and proceedings. In Kazakhstan, the Foreign Ministry handles foreign media and individual state bodies, like the Kurultai, as well as the Ministry of Culture and Information, deal with the domestic media.

Kumyspayeva, the editor-in-chief and founder of Otkir Kurek, was earlier this month denied accreditation by the Kurultai. Kalyanbekov provided an official response, which The Diplomat has reviewed, stating that the reason was a mismatch in email addresses on her application materials.

“The official reason given for the denial was that I had provided my professional email address in the accreditation application rather than the email address listed on our media outlet’s website,” Kumyspaeva told The Diplomat. “In my view, this was merely a technicality used as a pretext to deny me accreditation. I suspect the real reason lies in my independent journalism.”

Kumyspayeva takes no government funding, and told The Diplomat that the outlet does not participate in government-funded media contracts.

“As a result, government institutions have no leverage to dictate our editorial policy, determine what subjects we cover, or tell us which questions we are allowed to ask,” she said.

Kumyspayeva has lodged a formal complaint with the Kurultai’s leadership and she intends to pursue the matter in court, if needed. “I believe my professional rights as a journalist have been violated,” she said.

Kumyspayeva also signed the appeal sent to Dadebay regarding the media rules. She told The Diplomat her concerns stretch far beyond her own case.

“In my opinion, these restrictions constitute a form of censorship and contradict Kazakhstan’s constitutional guarantees of freedom of expression and the prohibition of censorship,” she said. “For me, this is not simply a dispute over accreditation for my media outlet. It is about something much more fundamental: the public’s right to information, the freedom of independent journalism, and the accountability of those in power.”

***

The tension here – between the Kutultai leadership and the journalists who cover the Kazakhstan’s legislature – is rooted in diametrically opposed perspectives on the purpose and role of the media.

In the Kazakh government’s view, as implied by Kalyanbekov and the new rules, the media’s role is to disseminate information provided by the government. Based on that, anything not on the agenda just shouldn’t be on the agenda. The government believes that it has the authority to decide what is newsworthy, and pestering officials with questions they’d rather not answer is rank insubordination.

“What concerns me most is that the leadership of the legislative body is effectively assuming the power to decide which journalists and media outlets are allowed to cover its activities and which are not,” Kumyspayeva explained. “In practice, this means access to elected representatives may depend not on a journalist’s professional status, but on how acceptable their reporting and questions are to the authorities.”

The Kutultai’s media rules merely add to a host of challenges faced by independent journalists in Kazakhstan.

“These restrictions are part of a severe constriction of the media sphere in Kazakhstan since the start of this year,” O’Brien argued, noting the cases of Gulnara Bazhkenova and the heads of KazTAG Aset Matayev and Amir Kasenov. Bazhkenova, former editor-in-chief of Orda, was sentenced to eight years in prison in August. Matayev and Kasenov were each given 15-months of “restricted freedom” and banned from journalistic activity for five years in July. The CPJ and other media watchdogs have characterized these cases as politically motivated.

Kazakh courts have increasingly banned convicted journalists from engaging in journalism or engaging in other forms of public activity. The real goal, O’Brien told The Diplomat, “is to ensure that prominent journalists are silenced for years ahead.”

The larger political context is unmistakable.

“This repression appears designed to instill a chilling effect and strengthen control over the press as President Tokayev navigates the final years of his constitutionally mandated single term,” O’Brien told The Diplomat.

Tokayev was first elected in a snap presidential poll in the summer of 2019, following Nursultan Nazarbayev’s surprise resignation that spring. At the time, Kazakhstan’s presidency was limited to two five-year terms. Not even three years into his first term, however, in the wake of Qandy Qantar – Bloody January – Tokayev saw through a wide-ranging constitutional referendum. Later that year, and 18 months early, Tokayev announced another snap presidential election. He paired that announcement with a proposal to limit the presidency to a single seven-year term. In November 2022, Tokayev was elected to his second term, confirming his grip on power until 2029.

The tinkering did not end there. Six months after commenting that haste in changing the constitution again was “completely inappropriate,” Tokayev saw through another constitutional referendum that touched almost every aspect of the document.

As the new constitution went into effect on July 1, Tokayev asked the Constitutional Court to clarify what it meant for re-election, or re-appointment, of term-limited officials, as well as the implications for the timeline on elections. The court replied that the president is eligible to run for another single seven-year term – which would technically be his third. But who’s counting?

Tokayev “is widely thought to be either preparing to run again or attempting to maintain strict control of the succession process,” O’Brien told The Diplomat. “The passing of a new constitution earlier this year and Kurultai elections, which coincided with major waves of pressure on the press, appear to be part of this process. With key journalists in jail or banned from working, the people of Kazakhstan will be less informed as this political process plays out.”

Dadebay has not yet responded officially to the Kazakh Kurultai press corps’ appeal.

“Freedom of the press is not a privilege granted by the authorities,” Kumyspayeva stressed to The Diplomat. “It is a fundamental right, and it is the public – not the government – that ultimately pays the price when that right is restricted.”

title: Wolf Warriors in Sheep’s Clothing: China’s New Subnational Diplomacy in Australia
description: Beijing’s diplomatic officials are adopting the language of the Albanese government to press their demands upon local governments and communities.
text:
For the government of China, diplomacy is more than simply a means of cultivating international relationships and advancing national interests. It is also an instrument of regime maintenance. In this capacity it can take the form of coercive interventions in the domestic affairs of other states with the aim of suppressing conduct or critique considered hostile to the ruling Chinese Communist Party (CCP). Deploying diplomatic agents to secure compliance with CCP objectives is in fact a significant feature of China’s subnational relations with local governments and communities in Australia.

During Xi Jinping’s first decade as CCP general secretary and chairman of state, Beijing’s approach to Australia grew increasingly blunt and confrontational, a style known as “wolf warrior diplomacy.” More recently, Chinese diplomats have shifted to a quieter, more self-assured form of subnational diplomacy. In contrast to the bluster of the wolf warrior era, this approach is largely conducted behind closed doors and has become more evident since Prime Minister Anthony Albanese’s July 2025 visit to China.

The election of the Albanese government in 2022 early signaled a thaw in what had been an icy bilateral relationship between Australia and China under the preceding Coalition governments of Malcolm Turnbull (2015-18) and Scott Morrison (2018-22). On his second visit to China as prime minister, Albanese spent a week “stabilizing” relations through renewed business, trade, educational, cultural, and inter-governmental initiatives.

Among the knock-on effects in Australia was a flurry of Chinese diplomatic initiatives at the local level. Consular staff in Brisbane, Sydney, Melbourne, Adelaide, and Perth now plainly assumed they were licensed by Albanese and his business entourage to press for local Australian compliance with their own demands on a range of issues. In meetings with local governments and peak community bodies, they carried a message: tolerating comments or events that displeased or offended the Chinese state or CCP would embarrass not just China or its ruling party, but the government of Australia.

This was new. Rather than howling into the void, China’s diplomats were framing their demands in the Australian government’s own idiom. Wolf warrior diplomacy was giving way to “wolf warrior in sheep’s clothing diplomacy.” China’s officials were adopting the language of their hosts to press their demands upon local governments and communities. On evidence, to date the new approach is relatively effective but it carries risks for all parties.

The Evidence

A consular initiative in Melbourne undertaken shortly after the conclusion of Albanese’s trip to China shows the strategy in action. In August 2025, China’s consul general in Melbourne requested a meeting with an independent non-profit organization that will remain unnamed. Its board welcomed the approach. This was not a low-key visit. The cluster of consular colleagues accompanying the consul general almost outnumbered the hosts around the table.

During the formal presentation, the consul general reviewed Australia-China ties since 1972 and Melbourne’s consular opening in 1986. Past difficulties were behind us, he said. The Albanese government had corrected the errors of its Coalition predecessor. Canberra was restoring stability through trade, regional development, and people-to-people partnerships while recognizing China’s core interests – code for CCP rule and China’s claims over Taiwan, Tibet, Xinjiang, and the South China Sea, among other claims.

The consul general then urged the board to read a recent article by iron-ore tycoon Andrew (Twiggy) Forrest, who predicted a bright future if everyone came on board the China boat. But, Forrest also warned: “Treat a friend like an enemy, and one day they may well become one.”

A few locals around the table recalled hearing a similar warning five years earlier, when a Chinese diplomat presented a Canberra journalist with a list of 14 grievances, accompanied by the statement: “If you make China the enemy, China will be the enemy.” Most of those grievances presented in November 2020 concerned Canberra’s efforts to limit Chinese government engagement with subnational entities, on the one hand, and its failure to restrict independent Australian institutions critical of China and the CCP on the other. China’s representatives in Australia appeared to be agitated not so much by the Coalition government’s external relations as by its domestic political arrangements governing the states and its failure to suppress commentary on China and its ruling party in Australia’s media, think tanks, and civil society.

The public backlash to the “14 grievances” prompted China’s local representatives to park their threat for the time being. Events proved that they could afford to wait because the same warning would be reiterated by Forrest, one of Australia’s leading businessmen, in wake of Albanese’s visit.

Having invoked Forrest, consular officials came up with a pointed request for the Melbourne board to cancel an event it was hosting with Australian journalist Cheng Lei. Cheng had been recently repatriated following three years in a Chinese jail for alleged spying activities. Giving her a platform to discuss her imprisonment, the Chinese diplomats implied, would undo all the good work of Albanese and his business team.

Despite the consul general’s request, Cheng’s talk went ahead. Nonetheless, China’s coercive interventions around her activities continued. Six months later, her play “1154 Days,” which recounted her solitary confinement and imprisonment in China, was dropped from Melbourne’s premier arts festival. “I feel like I’m back in China,” Cheng Lei told The Age.

Her concern was justified. The play had received a provisional place on the arts festival program, normally a routine step toward inclusion, but the board – not the festival’s creative staff – ruled against it. The RISING arts festival is funded through Creative Victoria and managed through the City of Melbourne’s Arts House, placing the festival program in a classic pincer movement between state and city governments known for their habit of surrender under consular pressure.

Chinese government meddling in Victoria’s school textbooks, community organizations, Chinese-language media, and local government deliberations had been thought things of the past following the introduction of new federal laws around foreign interference in 2018 and legislation limiting state government overreach in foreign relations in 2020. Not so.

Interviewed for this article, Cheng said that City of Melbourne officials received several consular calls and a personal visit urging them to avoid her play. Some did resist the pressure and attended. Arts House, for its part, was supportive of the work and kept the dates even though it wasn’t part of the RISING festival. The problem was not costs but the risks to the city and state governments’ relations with the local consulate

Cheng’s play was performed off-festival with support from a venue outside the City of Melbourne’s jurisdiction. There is a curious historical parallel here. In 1936 an anti-Nazi play was banned from city theaters in Sydney and Melbourne following representations from the German consulate, then under the direction of the Nazi Party. To their credit, the players found a way around the ban by performing on the back of a truck.

For the fleet of Chinese consuls sailing in the wake of Albanese’s China visit, Melbourne was just one port of call. The Victorian consular team sought meetings with civic institutions and officials in Bendigo, Ballarat, Frankston, Geelong, and also Hobart in Tasmania, as well as with university executives and cultural institutions, including Melbourne’s Museum of Chinese Australian History. Consular officials based in Western Australia met up with local government officers in Perth, Joondalup, Cockburn, Gosnells, Geraldton, and Swan; Queensland-based ones visited Brisbane, Rockhampton, Mackay, Toowoomba, the Sunshine Coast, Gold Coast, and Southern Downs. The South Australian consulate paid visits to the local governments of Adelaide, Murray Bridge, and Clare Valley. In each state, consular officials also met with civic and community bodies.

In contrast to earlier consular tours, the nationwide consular outreach following Albanese’s visit drew little public attention. Not long beforehand, the Sydney consular team suffered public embarrassment when local newspapers reported on the consul general’s meeting with the mayor of Newcastle. At that meeting, the consul warned the mayor against the possibility of an AUKUS nuclear-submarine squadron possibly being based nearby, saying that this would harm China’s strategic interests. The mayor was reportedly taken aback to have been challenged on Taiwan, Tibet, and nuclear submarines – topics well outside the scope of Australian local government diplomacy – during a routine meet-and-greet with Chinese consular officials.

On Albanese’s return, consular teams adopted a quieter subnational style aligned with Canberra’s own “calm and measured” international diplomacy, which was explicitly contrasted with the former Coalition’s “bellicose megaphone diplomacy.” Albanese’s approach, while helping to restore bilateral commercial, ministerial, and people-to-people ties at the national level, raised expectations on the part of China’s representatives in Australia that their demands for local discretion on sensitive matters would yield willing compliance. Canberra’s restraint was being repurposed to serve Beijing’s coercive subnational diplomacy.

Backfire?

It is doubtless clear to China’s diplomats in Australia that the Albanese government’s measured diplomacy has not altered Australia’s broader strategy in the region. This geopolitical strategy was inherited intact from the Coalition government and is aligned with regional partners’ understanding of the challenges and threats China presents.

That does not inhibit consular officials from cajoling local governments and community organizations to silence talk of those threats in the interests of stabilizing bilateral relations. In May 2026, Melbourne’s consul general told a local city newspaper that claims of “so-called” threats would “backfire” and rebound “just like a boomerang” on any making them.

Backfire on whom? Most consular interventions have remained below Canberra’s threshold of awareness, but this is changing. In July 2026, Melbourne’s Museum of Chinese Australian History appeared to breach a federal funding agreement by hosting a consular speaker at its annual high-achievers program without notifying the government funding body. The rotating host for the 2026 Chinese Australian Achievers Awards was Lord Mayor Nicholas Reece of the City of Melbourne, which customarily invites China’s consular officials to speak at community events. By withdrawing funding, Canberra signaled its concern about consular officials piggybacking at federal expense on local events.

A more serious threshold was crossed later that month when the Museum first invited then disinvited Foreign Minister Penny Wong to launch journalist Emilia Tagaza’s book “Behind a Million Faces,” described by the Museum as “a seminal book on the history of Chinese Australians.” Wong accepted the invitation. Her office nominated September 1, 2026 for the launch, and it requested an advance copy of the book to be forwarded ahead of that date.

In July, however, according to emails reviewed by the author, members of the Museum board reviewed their own advance copies and objected to its contents on several grounds. These included the author allegedly underplaying the U.S. factor in Australia’s deteriorating relations with China and overemphasizing communism, exaggerating China’s “assertiveness,” and incorrectly suggesting that Chinese migrants to Australia sought to escape CCP control. It directed the CEO to forward the author 17 pages of corrections, none of a factual nature, most entailing reframing the agreed facts to minimize offense to the government of China. When Tagaza rejected the board’s amendments, the CEO was directed to cancel the launch and withdraw the invitation to the foreign minister.

That was not the end of it. The CEO reinstated the launch and Wong’s invitation after receiving advice that the board decision may have infringed the author’s free speech. Just weeks before the event, however, the board again reversed course and canceled the event and the invitation. September passed without the Museum book launch, and with the foreign minister wondering what on earth was happening in Melbourne.

She had more than one reason to wonder. In 2024 a former Museum board member had become the first Australian to be jailed for planning foreign interference on behalf of the CCP – although not in his role on the board. But in fact nothing out of the ordinary was happening in Melbourne. Conspicuous displays of anticipatory obedience toward the local consulate are the default position among state and city governments, elite cultural institutions, and peak organizations in the city. Given sufficient haranguing and inducement, institutions adapt their behavior to what they imagine local consuls want, in many cases without receiving specific requests. Self-censorship is commonplace.

The Museum too has a record of silencing voices and histories that could annoy China’s local officials. A small everyday instance of anticipatory obedience can be found in the Museum’s display on the recent history of immigration from China. A Museum volunteer told me that a draft text linked the 1989 Beijing/Tiananmen Massacre to Prime Minister Bob Hawke’s memorable offer of permanent residence after the massacre to tens of thousands of resident Chinese students. Were it not for the Chinese military’s slaughter of students and workers in Beijing, the 40,000 students would not have been invited to stay. The text on display elides this “offensive” context: “40,000 students arrived and studied whilst many stayed in Australia.”

More seriously, the Museum promotes certain histories while silencing others. The board raised no concerns before or after the launch in August 2026 of a book on the history of the Victorian branch of the Australia-China Friendship Society (ACFS), held at the Museum in association with events marking the 75th anniversary of that Society’s founding. The ACFS’s relationship with China is mediated by the Chinese People’s Association for Friendship with Foreign Countries under the direction of the CCP’s United Front Work Department. The consul general spoke at the historical commemoration along with Lord Mayor Nicholas Reece.

What was novel in the case of Tagaza’s aborted book launch was not the selective censorship but censorship undertaken in full gaze of the Australian foreign minister. The board’s customary deference to China’s official perspectives on Australian history, immigration, and bilateral relations is not normally acted out in front of federal ministers. And this time the coercive influence over local government and community affairs wielded by China’s consulate in Melbourne embarrassed a senior member of Albanese’s Cabinet.

Three considerations appear to have shaped the Museum’s decision to cancel the launch and the foreign minister’s invitation – not once but twice. First, as noted, there were concerns that parts of the text may prove problematic for sections of the “Chinese community.” Second, the Museum faced growing community opposition on unrelated matters. Third – and, in my view, most importantly – the Museum anticipated the local consul general’s likely response to a high-profile ministerial launch of a book that did not reflect the Chinese Communist Party’s perspectives on Australian history, immigration, and bilateral relations.

If invited to speak, the consul general would have been obliged to challenge the book’s shortcomings in the minister’s presence; if the Museum failed to invite him, it risked damaging its relations with the consulate. Faced with a choice between embarrassing Australia’s foreign minister and disappointing the local consulate, the Museum board chose to embarrass the minister.

Being Stabilized

Beijing’s diplomacy is directed at advancing China’s national interests and first among those national interests is securing the ruling party in power. The conventional separation of domestic and foreign policy collapses under this obligation because the top national security priority applies equally in both domains: preserving the status and power of the CCP is just as important outside China as it is within it.

The same goes for managing security risks. Domestically in China, a nationwide “stability maintenance” (weiwen) system anticipates and suppresses perceived threats to CCP rule before they arise. Outside China, this task falls to locally stationed consular officials. Those silenced by the weiwen system in China say that they have been “stabilized.” The same could be said of Australia.

Under the banner of stabilizing bilateral relations, Chinese consular staff apply their stability maintenance techniques to undermine initiatives and silence dissent across Australia’s local governments and communities. As they interpret it, Canberra’s softly-softly diplomacy gives China’s consulates the license and leverage to pressure cultural, arts, community, and government bodies to comply with their wishes by framing them as consistent with Australia’s policy of stabilization. As Cheng Lei told the Melbourne Age, Australia is starting to feel like China.

For now, the domestic risks of being stabilized bear on freedoms of expression, association, and religion that underpin the Australian way of life. International risks entail states such as Victoria missing out on Taiwan’s extraordinary growth spurt for fear of offending a local PRC consul. The broader geopolitical risk for Australia is that China’s diplomats could apply their new wolf-in-sheep’s-clothing strategy to Pacific Island communities at Australia’s expense. After all, if Australia can be shown to be compliant with China, how would it advantage smaller Pacific nations to do otherwise? There is a danger that Australia’s massive Pacific investment, made to counter the China threat, could serve CCP interests via the canny invocation of Australian words and actions on the part of Beijing’s representatives in the region.

Beyond the Pacific region, the wider lesson is that all countries seeking “strategic stability” in relations with China will, if they let down their guard, find China’s diplomats practicing stability maintenance in their own backyards – using the host country’s commitment to stability to keep the CCP secure and in command, everywhere.
